title: 20.1.1 Various approaches to artificial intelligence
text:
First, deep learning isn’t synonymous with artificial intelligence (AI), or even with machine learning:

Artificial intelligence (AI) is an ancient, broad field that can generally be understood as “all attempts to automate human cognitive processes.” This can range from the very basic, such as an Excel spreadsheet, to the very advanced, like a humanoid robot that can walk and talk.

Machine learning is a specific subfield of AI that aims at automatically developing programs (called models) purely from exposure to training data. This process of turning data into a program is called learning. Although machine learning has been around for a long time, it only started to take off in the 1990s, before becoming the dominant form of AI in the 2000s.

Deep learning is one of many branches of machine learning, where the models are long chains of geometric transformations, applied one after the other. These operations are structured into modules called layers: deep learning models are typically stacks of layers—or, more generally, graphs of layers. These layers are parameterized by weights, which are the parameters learned during training. The knowledge of a model is stored in its weights, and the process of learning consists of finding “good values” for these weights—values that minimize a loss function. Because the chain of geometric transformations considered is differentiable, updating the weights to minimize the loss function is done efficiently via gradient

Generative AI is a specific subset of deep learning, where models are capable of generating text, images, videos, or sound. These models tend to be very large— billions of parameters. They’re trained in a self-supervised manner; that is, they’re trained to reconstruct artificially missing or corrupted parts of an input— for instance, denoising images, predicting the next word in a sentence, and so on. This learning process enables the models to learn sophisticated “maps” (embedding manifolds) of their input space, which can be used for sampling new inputs. These models have launched AI into its “consumer” era with the rise of products like ChatGPT or Midjourney.

Even though deep learning is just one among many approaches to machine learning, it isn’t on an equal footing with the others. Deep learning is a breakout success. Here’s why.

Given sufficient training data (in particular, training data appropriately labeled by humans), deep learning makes it possible

to extract from perceptual data almost anything a human could. Hence, it’s sometimes said that deep learning has “solved perception”—although that’s true only for a fairly narrow definition of perception.

Due to its unprecedented technical successes, deep learning has singlehandedly brought about the third and by far the largest AI summer: a period of intense interest, investment, and hype in the field of AI. As this book is being written, we’re in the middle of it. Whether this period will end in the near future and what happens after it ends are topics of debate. One thing is certain: in stark contrast with previous AI summers, deep learning has provided enormous business value to both large and small technology companies and has become a huge consumer success, enabling human-level speech recognition, chatbot assistants, photorealistic image generation, human-level machine translation, and more. The hype may (and likely will) recede, but the sustained economic and technological impact of deep learning will remain. In that sense, deep learning could be analogous to the internet: it may be overly hyped up for a few years, but in the longer term, it will still be a major revolution that will transform our economy and our lives. One reason I’m particularly optimistic about deep learning is that even if we were to make no further technological progress in the next decade, deploying existing algorithms to every applicable problem would be a game changer for most industries. Deep learning is nothing short of a revolution, and progress is currently happening at an incredibly fast rate due to an exponential investment in resources and headcount. From where we stand, the future looks bright, although short-term expectations are somewhat overoptimistic; deploying deep learning to the full extent of its potential will likely take multiple decades.

title: 20.1.3 How to think about deep learning
text:
The most surprising thing about deep learning is how simple it is. Fifteen years ago, no one expected that we would achieve such amazing results on machine-perception and natural language processing problems by using simple parametric models trained with gradient descent. Now it turns out that all you need is sufficiently large parametric models trained with gradient descent on sufficiently many examples. As Feynman once said about the universe, “It’s not complicated, it’s just a lot of it.”1

In deep learning, everything is a vector; that is, everything is a point in a geometric space. Model inputs (text, images, and so on) and targets are first vectorized—turned into an initial input vector space and target vector space. Each layer in a deep learning model operates one simple geometric transformation on the data that goes through it. Together, the chain of layers in the model forms one complex geometric transformation, broken down into a series of simple ones. This complex transformation attempts to map the input space to the target space, one point at a time. This transformation is parameterized by the weights of the layers, which are iteratively updated based on how well the model is currently performing. A key characteristic of this geometric

snippet: The most surprising thing about deep learning is how simple it is. Fifteen years ago, no one expected that we would achieve such amazing results on machine-perception and natural…

title: 20.1 Key concepts in review
text:
transformation is that it must be differentiable, which is required for us to be able to learn its parameters via gradient descent. Intuitively, this means the geometric morphing from inputs to outputs must be smooth and continuous—a significant constraint.

The entire process of applying this complex geometric transformation to the input data can be visualized in 3D by imagining a person trying to uncrumple a paper ball: the crumpled paper ball is the manifold of the input data that the model starts with. Each movement operated by the person on the paper ball is similar to a simple geometric transformation operated by one layer. The full uncrumpling gesture sequence is the complex transformation of the entire model. Deep learning models are mathematical machines for uncrumpling complicated manifolds of high-dimensional data. That’s the magic of deep learning—turning meaning into vectors, into geometric spaces, and then incrementally learning complex geometric transformations that map one space to another. All you need are spaces of sufficiently high dimensionality to capture the full scope of the relationships found in the original data. The whole thing hinges on two core ideas: that meaning is derived from the pairwise relationship between things (between words in a language, between pixels in an image, and so on) and that these relationships can be captured by a distance function. But note that whether the brain implements meaning via geometric spaces is an entirely separate question. Vector spaces are efficient to work with from a computational standpoint, but different data structures for intelligence can easily be envisioned—in particular, graphs. Neural networks initially emerged from the idea of using graphs as a way to encode meaning, which is why they’re named neural networks; the surrounding field of research used to be called connectionism. Nowadays, the name neural network exists purely for historical reasons—it’s an extremely misleading name because they’re neither neural nor networks. In particular, neural networks have hardly anything to do with the brain. A more appropriate name would have been layered representations learning or hierarchical representations learning, or maybe even deep differentiable models or chained geometric transforms, to emphasize the fact that continuous geometric space manipulation is at their core.

title: 20.1.4 Key enabling technologies
text:
The technological revolution that’s currently unfolding didn’t start with any single breakthrough invention. Rather, like any other revolution, it’s the product of a vast accumulation of enabling factors—slowly at first, and then suddenly. In the case of deep learning, we can point out the following key factors:

Incremental algorithmic innovations, first spread over two decades (starting with backpropagation) and then happening increasingly faster as more research effort was poured into deep learning after 2012. One major such breakthrough was the Transformer architecture in 2017.

The availability of large amounts of image, video, and text data, which is a requirement to realize that sufficiently large models trained on sufficiently large data are all we need. This is, in turn, a by-product of the rise of the consumer internet and

The availability of fast, highly parallel computation hardware at a low price, especially the GPUs produced by NVIDIA—first gaming GPUs and then chips designed from the ground up for deep learning. Early on, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang took note of the deep learning boom and decided to bet the company’s future on it, which paid off in a big way.

A complex stack of software layers that makes this computational power available to humans: the CUDA language, frameworks like TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch that do automatic differentiation, and Keras, which makes deep learning accessible to most people.

In the future, deep learning will not be used only by specialists such as researchers, graduate students, and engineers with an academic profile; it will be a tool in the toolbox of every developer, much like web technology today. Everyone needs to build intelligent apps: just as every business today needs a website, every product will need to intelligently make sense of user-generated data. Bringing about this future will require us to build tools that make deep learning radically easy to use and accessible to anyone with basic coding abilities. Keras has been the first major step in that direction.

title: 20.1.5 The universal machine learning workflow
text:
Having access to an extremely powerful tool for creating models that map any input space to any target space is great, but the difficult part of the machine learning workflow is often everything that comes before designing and training such models (and, for production models, what comes after, as well). Understanding the problem domain to be able to determine what to attempt to predict, given what data, and how to measure success is a prerequisite for any successful application of machine learning, and it isn’t something that advanced tools like Keras and TensorFlow can help you with. As a reminder, here’s a quick summary of the typical machine learning workflow as described in chapter 6:

Define the problem. What data is available, and what are you trying to predict? Will you need to collect more data or hire people to manually label a dataset?

Identify a way to reliably measure success on your goal. For simple tasks, this may be prediction accuracy, but in many cases, it will require sophisticated, domain-specific metrics.

Prepare the validation process that you’ll use to evaluate your models. In particular, you should define a training set, a validation set, and a test set. The validationset and test-set labels shouldn’t leak into the training data: for instance, with temporal prediction, the validation and test data should be posterior to the training data.

Gradually refine your model architecture by tuning hyperparameters and adding regularization. Make changes based on performance on the validation data only, not the test data or the training data. title: 20.1.6 Key network architectures
text:
The families of network architectures that you should be familiar with after reading this book are densely connected networks, convolutional networks, recurrent networks, Diffusion Models, and Transformers. Each type of model is meant for specific data modalities: a network architecture encodes assumptions about the structure of the data—a hypothesis space within which the search for a good model will proceed. Whether a given architecture will work on a given problem depends entirely on the match between the structure of the data and the assumptions of the network architecture.

These different network types can easily be combined to achieve larger multimodal models, much as you combine LEGO bricks. In a way, deep learning layers are LEGO bricks for information processing. title: ConvNets
text:
Convolution layers look at spatially local patterns by applying the same geometric transformation to different spatial locations (patches) in an input tensor. This results in representations that are translation invariant, making convolution layers highly data efficient and modular. This idea is applicable to spaces of any dimensionality: 1D (continuous sequences), 2D (images), 3D (volumes), and so on. You can use the `Conv1D` layer to process sequences, the `Conv2D` layer to process images, and the `Conv3D` layer to process volumes. As a leaner, more efficient alternative to convolution layers, you can also use depthwise separable convolution layers, such as `SeparableConv2D`.

ConvNets, or convolutional networks, consist of stacks of convolution and max-pooling layers. The pooling layers let you spatially downsample the data, which is required to keep feature maps to a reasonable size as the number of features grows and to allow subsequent convolution layers to “see” a greater spatial extent of the inputs. ConvNets are often ended with either a `Flatten` operation or a global pooling layer, turning spatial feature maps into vectors, followed by `Dense` layers to achieve classification or regression. title: Transformers
text:
A Transformer looks at a set of vectors (such as word vectors) and uses neural attention to transform each vector into a representation that is aware of the context provided by the other vectors in the set. When the set in question is an ordered sequence, you can also use positional encoding to create Transformers that can take into account both global context and word order, capable of processing long text paragraphs much more effectively than RNNs or 1D ConvNets.

Transformers can be used for any set-processing or sequence-processing task, including text classification, but they excel especially at sequence-to-sequence learning, such as translating paragraphs in a source language into a target language. A sequence-to-sequence Transformer is made of two parts:

A `TransformerEncoder` that turns an input vector sequence into a context-aware, order-aware output vector sequence

A `TransformerDecoder` that takes the output of the `TransformerEncoder`, as well as a target sequence, and predicts what should come next in the target sequence

If you’re only processing a single sequence (or set) of vectors, you’d only use the `TransformerEncoder`.

title: Recurrent neural networks
text:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) work by processing sequences of inputs one timestep at a time and maintaining a state throughout (a state is typically a vector or set of vectors). They should be used preferentially over 1D ConvNets in the case of sequences where patterns of interest aren’t invariant by temporal translation (for instance, timeseries data where the recent past is more important than the distant past).

Three RNN layers are available in Keras: `SimpleRNN`, `GRU`, and `LSTM`. For most practical purposes, you should use either `GRU` or `LSTM`. `LSTM` is the more powerful of the two but is also more expensive; you can think of `GRU` as a simpler, cheaper alternative to it. To stack multiple RNN layers on top of each other, each layer prior to the last layer in the stack should return the full sequence of its outputs (each input timestep will correspond to an output timestep); if you aren’t stacking any further RNN layers, then it’s common to return only the last output, which contains information about the entire sequence. title: 20.2 Limitations of deep learning
text:
Building deep learning models is like playing with LEGO bricks: layers can be plugged together to map essentially anything to anything, given that you have appropriate training data available and that the mapping is achievable via a continuous geometric transformation of reasonable complexity.

Here’s the catch, though—this mapping is often not learnable in a way that will generalize. Deep learning models operate like vast, interpolative databases of patterns. Their pattern-matching strength is also their core weakness:

They fundamentally struggle to adapt to novelty. Because their parameters are fixed after training, they can only retrieve or replicate patterns similar to their training data. Faced with inputs significantly outside this familiar distribution—no matter how simple the underlying task—their performance degrades drastically, as they lack mechanisms for fluid generalization beyond their memorized experience. This explains why even large models fail on novel tasks or simple variations of familiar problems—like ARC-AGI tasks.

They’re very sensitive to phrasing and other distractors. Deep learning models exhibit high sensitivity to superficial variations in input presentation, such as minor phrasing changes (consider prompt sensitivity in LLMs) or imperceptible perturbations (consider adversarial examples in vision), indicating a lack of robust, human-like understanding.

They often can’t learn generalizable algorithms. The continuous, geometric nature of deep learning models makes them fundamentally ill-suited for learning exact, discrete, step-by-step algorithms, such as those that are the bread and butter of classical computer science. Models approximate such processes through interpolation rather than implementing robust, generalizable procedures.

text:

Five years of exponential scaling of base LLMs haven’t overcome these constraints because the underlying approach remains unchanged.

By 2024, this realization spurred a transition toward test-time adaptation (TTA), where models perform search or fine-tuning during the inference phase to adapt to novel problems. While TTA methods have yielded major breakthroughs, such as OpenAI’s o3 surpassing human baseline on ARC-AGI-1 in late 2024, this performance has come at an extreme computational cost. Efficient, human-like adaptation is still a completely open problem, and the slightly harder ARC-AGI-2 benchmark remains completely unsolved as of today. We still need further conceptual advances beyond mere scaling or brute-force search.

title: 20.3 What might lie ahead
text:
Solving human-like fluid intelligence (and ARC-AGI-2) requires moving beyond the limitations inherent in current approaches. While deep learning excels at value-centric abstraction, which enables pattern recognition and intuition, it fundamentally lacks capabilities for program-centric abstraction, which underpins discrete reasoning, planning, and causal understanding. Human intelligence seamlessly integrates both— future AI must do the same.

Future key developments may include

Hybrid models—Future models will likely integrate learned algorithmic modules (providing reasoning and symbolic manipulation) with deep learning modules (providing perception and intuition). These systems might learn to use programming primitives like control flow, variables, recursion, and complex data structures dynamically.

Deep-learning guided program search—Program synthesis—automatically discovering executable code that meets specifications—offers a route to program-centric abstraction. However, its reliance on inefficient discrete search is a major bottleneck. A crucial advance will be using deep learning to guide this search, utilizing learned intuition about program structure to navigate vast, combinatorial spaces of programs efficiently, much like human developers use experience and intuition to narrow down their choices.

Modular recombination and lifelong learning—We’ll move away from monolithic, end-to-end models trained from scratch. Instead, future AI systems will use massive libraries of reusable, modular components that can be repurposed across many problems, acquired from experience. These libraries will feature both “geometric” (deep learning based) and “algorithmic” modules. When faced with a new problem, such AI systems will fetch relevant modules and dynamically recombine them into a new model adapted to the situation at hand. title: 20.4 Staying up to date in a fast-moving field
text:
As final parting words, I want to give you some pointers about how to keep learning and updating your knowledge and skills after you’ve turned the last page of this book. The field of modern deep learning, as we know it today, is only a few years old, despite a long, slow prehistory stretching back decades. With an exponential increase in financial resources and research headcount since 2013, the field as a whole is now moving at a frenetic pace. What you’ve learned in this book won’t stay relevant forever, and it isn’t all you’ll need for the rest of your career.

Fortunately, there are plenty of free online resources that you can use to stay up to date and expand your horizons. Here are a few.

title: 20.4.1 Practice on real-world problems using Kaggle
text:
An effective way to acquire real-world experience is to try your hand at machine learning competitions on Kaggle (https://kaggle.com). The only real way to learn is through practice and actual coding—that’s the philosophy of this book, and Kaggle competitions are the natural continuation of this. On Kaggle, you’ll find an array of constantly renewed data science competitions, many of which involve deep learning, prepared by companies interested in obtaining novel solutions to some of their most challenging machine learning problems. Fairly large monetary prizes are offered to top entrants.

By participating in a few competitions, maybe as part of a team, you’ll become more familiar with the practical side of some of the advanced best practices described in this book, especially hyperparameter tuning, avoiding validation-set overfitting, and model ensembling.

title: 20.4.2 Read about the latest developments on arXiv
text: Deep learning research, in contrast with some other scientific fields, takes place completely in the open. Papers are made publicly and freely accessible as soon as they’re finalized, and a lot of related software is open source. arXiv (https://arxiv.org)—pronounced “archive” (the X stands for the Greek chi)—is an open access preprint server for physics, mathematics, and computer science research papers. It has become the de facto way to stay up to date on the cutting edge of machine learning and deep learning. The large majority of deep learning researchers upload any paper they write to arXiv shortly after completion. This allows them to plant a flag and claim a specific finding without waiting for a conference acceptance (which takes months), which is necessary given the fast pace of research and the intense competition in the field. text:

An important downside is that the sheer quantity of new papers posted every day on arXiv makes it impossible to even skim them all, and the fact that they aren’t peer-reviewed makes it difficult to identify those that are both important and high quality. It’s challenging, and becoming increasingly more so, to find the signal in the noise. But some tools can help: in particular, you can use Google Scholar (https://scholar.google .com) to keep track of publications by your favorite authors.

title: Inside cover: two key ideas
text:
Two summary diagrams: machine learning vs. classical programming (ch. 1) and going from a random model to an overfit model (ch. 5) The inside cover previews two central ideas of the book: machine learning inverts classical programming (data + answers in, rules out), and training moves a model from random to well-fit to overfit, which hurts performance on new data. This page (the inside front cover) has **no extracted text**, but the page image shows two diagrams that preview key ideas of the book.

**1. Machine learning vs. classical programming (chapter 1).**
- *Classical programming:* **rules** and **data** go in, **answers** come out. A human writes the rules.
- *Machine learning:* **data** and **answers** go in, **rules** come out. The system discovers the rules from examples.

This inversion is introduced in section 1.3, "Machine learning" (printed p.3, PDF p.27).

**2. Going from a random model to an overfit model (chapter 5).** Two classes of points (light and dark circles) and a dashed decision boundary are shown at four stages of training:
1. *Before training:* the model starts with a random initial state — the boundary is meaningless.
2. *Beginning of training:* the model gradually moves toward a better fit.
3. *Further training:* "a robust fit is achieved, transitively, in the process of morphing the model from its initial state to its final state" — a smooth boundary that separates the classes broadly.
4. *Final state:* the model **overfits** the training data, reaching perfect training loss — the boundary twists around individual points.

Two "test time" panels then show the same models on **new data points**: the robustly fit model's smooth boundary still separates the new points well, whereas the overfit model's contorted boundary misclassifies several of them.

The lesson, developed in chapter 5 ("Fundamentals of machine learning", starting p.160), is that the goal is **generalization**, not minimal training loss; the best model is found somewhere *during* training, before overfitting sets in.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a visual cheat sheet. Return to it after chapter 1 and chapter 5. Machine learning takes data and answers as input and produces rules; classical programming does the reverse. Training passes from a random model through a robust fit to an overfit; the robust fit generalizes better to new data. Perfect training loss is a warning sign, not a goal.

title: Praise for the Second Edition
text:
Endorsement quotes for the previous (second) edition Eight short endorsements from practitioners and academics praise the second edition for clear, code-first teaching, real-world examples and accessibility. This page collects **praise for the second edition** (2021) of the book — the predecessor of the third edition you are reading. Eight reviewers are quoted:

- **Martin Görner (Google):** Chollet is "a master of pedagogy", explains complex concepts "with minimal fuss, cutting through the math with practical Python code", and offers insights on architectures and training tips.
- **Sayak Paul (Carted):** an exciting introduction "with lots of real-world examples", a must-read for practitioners.
- **Edmon Begoli (Oak Ridge National Laboratory):** "The modern classic just got better."
- **Yiannis Paraskevopoulos (University of West Attica):** "Truly the bible of deep learning."
- **Raushan Jha (Microsoft):** one of the best books on deep learning with Python.
- **Viton Vitanis (Viseca Payment Services):** useful "both for the novice and the more experienced" professional.
- **Todd Cook (Appen):** "Deep learning well explained, from A to Z."
- **Kjell Jansson (GubboIT):** the book implements "the democratization of AI: 'AI to the people.'"

**What this tells the reader.** The recurring themes are (1) a **code-first** style that replaces heavy math with runnable Python, (2) **practical, real-world** examples and training advice, (3) **accessibility** for beginners alongside depth for experts, and (4) **democratization** of AI. These themes match the authors' own stated goals in the preface (p.18: "there are no difficult ideas in deep learning") and in "about this book" (p.20-21: reasonable Python proficiency and high-school math suffice).

Note: these quotes are about the *second* edition; the third edition is a complete rewrite (p.18), so specific content they refer to may have changed. The praise is for the second edition; the third edition is a complete rewrite. Reviewers stress a code-first, practical, accessible style that serves both novices and experts. title: Preface (part 1): why deep learning, and why democratize it
text:
The opening of the preface: the rapid progress of deep learning, the authors' belief that AI is still in its early days, and the mission of democratizing access to it, which is where Keras comes from. Deep learning went from barely usable to deployed everywhere in a few years, and the authors believe the coming AI transformation can only be beneficial if understanding of the technology is spread as widely as possible. Keras, written in March 2015 as a personal research tool, became a vehicle for that accessibility. This is the first page of the **preface**. It opens by noting the "extraordinary progress" deep learning has brought to AI: within a handful of years, computer vision and natural language processing went from *near-unusable* to *highly performant systems deployed at scale* in everyday products. The authors list how broad the impact is — medical imaging, agriculture, autonomous driving, education, disaster prevention, manufacturing — and note that digital assistants are now on nearly every consumer device.

The second paragraph pivots: despite this progress, the authors believe deep learning is **still in its early days**. AI will be "a much greater wave of disruption than anything that came before it", spreading to every problem where it is useful over *decades*, with profound global social consequences. Their response is a values statement: the only way to make this transformation beneficial for everyone is to **radically democratize access** — to put understanding of deep learning (*how it works, where it fails, and how to apply it*) in the hands of as many people as possible, including non-researchers.

The third paragraph, written in the first person by François Chollet, tells the origin of **Keras**: he wrote it in March 2015 for his own machine-learning experiments, not with democratization in mind. As newcomers entered the field and adopted Keras, accessibility became an explicit design goal. The sentence continues on PDF p.18, where the preface explains how this book continues the same mission.

**How to use this page:** read it as the book's mission statement. It explains why the book favors code and intuition over heavy notation (see PDF p.20) and why Keras is the main tool throughout (introduced technically on PDF p.114). Deep learning went from near-unusable to deployed at scale in vision and language within a few years. The authors believe AI is still in its early days and its societal impact will unfold over decades. Their mission is to democratize understanding of deep learning: how it works, where it fails, and how to apply it. Keras was written in March 2015 for personal research and later adopted accessibility as an explicit goal.

title: Preface (part 2): the Keras community and the aims of the third edition
text:
The end of the preface: what the Keras community achieved, what this book aims to do, and what is new in the free, fully rewritten third edition. The book continues Keras's accessibility mission: it explains deep learning without watering it down ('there are no difficult ideas in deep learning'), builds from the basics up to today's generative AI, and is a complete rewrite available free online. This page finishes the **preface**. It first completes the sentence from PDF p.17: accessibility became an explicit goal of Keras, and over the last decade the Keras developer community has made "remarkable progress" here — putting deep learning into the hands of **millions of people**, who use it to solve problems recently considered unsolvable.

The authors then present the book as **another step toward broadening access**. Their aim is to make both the *concepts* behind deep learning and their *implementation* as approachable as possible. Crucially, they say this does not require "watering anything down", because they believe **there are no difficult ideas in deep learning**. The book starts from the very basics and builds, "layer by layer" (our reading: a nod to neural network layers), up to the cutting-edge **generative AI** models deployed today.

Next come practical facts about this edition:

- It is the **third edition** of *Deep Learning with Python*.
- It is available **free online** at https://deeplearningwithpython.io/; the authors ask readers to consider buying a physical copy to support the project, and consider print the best presentation of the content.
- It is a **complete rewrite**, with a broader introduction to today's popular deep learning frameworks (JAX, PyTorch, TensorFlow; see chapter 3, PDF p.85) and greatly expanded content on large generative AI models (chapters 16–17).

The preface ends with the wish that the book helps you "solve the problems that matter to you". Most of the page is blank below the text. The Keras community has put deep learning in the hands of millions of people. The authors aim for approachability without watering down: 'there are no difficult ideas in deep learning'. The book progresses from basics to cutting-edge generative AI. The third edition is a complete rewrite, free online at deeplearningwithpython.io, with broader framework coverage and much more generative AI.

title: About this book: approach, outcomes, and intended readers
text:
What the book is for, how it teaches (intuition + theory + hands-on code, avoiding mathematical notation), what you will be able to do afterwards, and the first part of the list of intended readers. The book teaches deep learning from scratch through working code paired with explanations of the underlying principles, aiming to leave you with a solid understanding of what deep learning is, when it applies, what its limits are, and a standard workflow for solving ML problems. This page opens **about this book**.

**Audience in one line.** The book is for anyone who wants to explore deep learning *from scratch* or broaden their understanding — practicing ML engineers, software developers and college students alike.

**Teaching approach.** You start simply and work up to **state-of-the-art techniques**. The authors aim for a balance of **intuition, theory and hands-on practice**. The book **avoids mathematical notation**: core ideas are explained through **functioning code paired with explanations of the underlying principles**. You will train models from scratch in several problem domains and learn practical recommendations for writing deep learning programs and **deploying them in the real world**.

**Promised outcomes.** After the book you should:

1. understand *what deep learning is*, *when it is applicable*, and *what its limitations are*;
2. know the **standard workflow** for approaching and solving machine learning problems (chapter 6, "the universal workflow of machine learning");
3. know how to address commonly encountered issues.

**Who should read this book.** The primary reader has *some Python programming experience* and wants to get started with machine learning and deep learning. The list of other readers begins here: a **data scientist** familiar with machine learning will get a solid, practical introduction to deep learning, which the authors call "the fastest-growing and most significant subfield of machine learning". The list continues on PDF p.21 (Keras newcomers, graduate students, non-coders) along with the prerequisites (reasonable Python, high-school math).

**How to use this page:** keep the three outcomes as a checklist; at the end of the book (chapter 20's review, PDF p.621) check whether you can explain each. The book teaches from scratch to state of the art, balancing intuition, theory and practice. It replaces mathematical notation with working code plus explanations of principles. Promised outcomes: what deep learning is, when it applies, its limitations, the standard ML workflow, and handling common issues. The main expected background is some Python programming experience.

title: About this book: readers, prerequisites, and the road map
text:
The remaining reader profiles (Keras newcomers, graduate students, non-coders), the prerequisites (reasonable Python, no ML background, high-school math), and the road map of the book's 20 chapters in six groups. The book needs only reasonable Python and high-school math, and it is organized as foundations (1–7), computer vision (8–12), timeseries (13), NLP (14–15), generative modeling (16–17) and conclusions (18–20). **Remaining reader profiles.** Continuing the list from PDF p.20:

- **Deep learning researchers or practitioners** who want to get started with Keras will find the book an ideal *Keras crash course*.
- **Graduate students** studying deep learning formally will find it a practical complement, building intuition about how deep networks behave and teaching key best practices.
- **Technically minded people who don't code regularly** can still use it as an introduction to basic and advanced concepts.

**Prerequisites.** You need *reasonable Python proficiency* to follow the code. You do **not** need previous machine learning or deep learning experience — the book covers the basics from scratch — and you do **not** need advanced mathematics: *high-school-level mathematics should suffice*.

**Road map: 20 chapters in six groups.**

| Chapters | Theme | What the road map says |
|---|---|---|
| 1–7 | Foundations | History of the field; coding with JAX, PyTorch and TensorFlow; a practical guide to applying ML to real problems; a close look at Keras |
| 8–12 | Computer vision | Classifying whole images; recognizing and separating out individual objects; ConvNets, "the first big success of the deep learning era" |
| 13 | Timeseries forecasting | Data measured over time (weather, sales); using past patterns to predict future trends |
| 14–15 | Natural language processing | Sentiment classifiers; an English-to-Spanish translation model; special attention to the Transformer |
| 16–17 | Generative modeling | Models producing new images and text; chatbots like ChatGPT and image generators; training from scratch and using large pretrained models |
| 18–20 | Conclusions | Practical engineering concerns; a chapter on possible futures of the field (continues on PDF p.22) |

**How to use this page:** chapters 1–7 are the prerequisite for everything else; after them, the application groups can be read fairly independently, though the NLP chapters (Transformer) are the natural preparation for text generation in chapter 16 (an inference from the road map's ordering). Prerequisites: reasonable Python; no prior ML; high-school math. The book has 20 chapters: foundations (1–7), vision (8–12), timeseries (13), NLP (14–15), generative modeling (16–17), conclusions (18–20). ConvNets are the key vision architecture; the Transformer is the key text architecture. Generative chapters cover both training from scratch and using large pretrained models.

How the book's code is organized (literate programming, Jupyter notebooks from chapter 2), what it runs on (Python + Keras on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX; locally or in Google Colab), where to get it, and the liveBook discussion forum. The book is simultaneously prose and a runnable Python program; every chapter's code can be run as a notebook, locally or for free in Colab, and the authors strongly encourage running and modifying it as you read. From **chapter 2** on, each chapter contains code listings that can be run as a **Jupyter notebook** (an interactive environment for running Python and visualizing data). The authors *strongly suggest* running, modifying and playing with the examples as you read, to build your own intuition.

All code is in **Python** with the **Keras** library. Keras can run on top of **TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX**, "the most popular low-level deep learning frameworks as of 2025". You can run everything on a local machine or in the browser with **Google Colab**, a hosted Jupyter environment.

**liveBook discussion forum.** Purchase includes access to liveBook, Manning's online reader, where you can attach comments to the book or to specific sections/paragraphs, make notes, ask and answer technical questions, and get help from the authors and other readers. Manning provides the venue but does **not** commit the authors to any amount of participation, which is voluntary and unpaid; the forum stays accessible while the book is in print.

title: About the authors
text:
Short biographies of François Chollet (creator of Keras, co-founder of the Ndea research lab, creator of the ARC-AGI challenge) and Matthew Watson (Google ML engineer, core Keras maintainer focused on NLP tools). Both authors are core Keras developers: Chollet wrote Keras and works on measuring and building general intelligence; Watson maintains Keras's NLP tooling and has worked on Gemini at Google. This page gives two short author biographies, each next to a portrait photo.

**François Chollet** has worked with deep learning since it began gaining traction in academia in **2012**. He is the author of **Keras**, one of the most popular deep learning libraries, used in university classrooms, at companies such as Google, Netflix and Spotify, and in scientific organizations such as CERN and NASA. He co-founded the **Ndea** research lab for frontier AI systems and created the **ARC-AGI** challenge for measuring machine intelligence.

**Matthew Watson** has worked on machine learning at Google since **2018**, including on the **Gemini** model and Google's open-source deep learning ecosystem. He is a **core maintainer of Keras**, focusing on its **natural language processing** tools. He holds a master's in computer science from **Stanford**, where he researched procedural modeling techniques at the Stanford Graphics Lab.

**How to use this page:** the bios hint at where each author's expertise shows in the book. Chollet's work on Keras underpins chapters 3 and 7, and his ARC-AGI work is the basis for the discussion of intelligence, the ARC Prize and test-time adaptation in chapter 19 (PDF p.600–607 per the contents). Watson's NLP focus aligns with the text and generative chapters (14–16). François Chollet created Keras, co-founded the Ndea lab and created the ARC-AGI challenge. Matthew Watson works on ML at Google (including Gemini) and is a core Keras maintainer focused on NLP tools. Both authors build the main library the book teaches.

title: Chapter 1 opener: What is deep learning?
text:
Introduction to the chapter that defines AI, machine learning and deep learning, and frames the hype around them Chapter 1 sets out to give high-level definitions of AI, machine learning and deep learning, a gentle introduction to how machine learning works, and a sober assessment of deep learning's popularity and future. The opening paragraph motivates all of this: a practitioner must be able to separate real, world-changing developments from overhyped press releases. This is the opening page of **Chapter 1, "What is deep learning?"**. It is a chapter opener: a large chapter number, the title, a "This chapter covers" box, and the first paragraph of the chapter.

The box lists three things the chapter will do:

- give **high-level definitions of fundamental concepts** (AI, machine learning, deep learning — developed in sections 1.1–1.6, p.26–34),
- offer **a soft introduction to the principles behind machine learning** (how a model learns rules and representations from data, p.28–34),
- discuss **deep learning's rising popularity and future potential** (sections 1.7–1.12, p.34–39).

The opening paragraph starts from the media hype of the past decade. AI, machine learning and deep learning appear in countless articles, often in non-technical outlets, promising intelligent chatbots, self-driving cars and virtual assistants — a future painted sometimes as grim, sometimes as utopian, with scarce human jobs and most economic activity handled by robots or AI agents. The authors' point is practical: a machine learning practitioner must be able to **recognize the signal amid the noise**, telling world-changing developments from overhyped press releases. They add a motivating note — "our future is at stake" and you have an active role, because after reading the book you will be among those who can actually build these systems. The sentence breaks off with "So let's" and continues on p.26 with the questions the chapter will tackle: what deep learning has achieved so far, how significant it is, where we are headed, and whether to believe the hype.

How to use this page: read the bullet box as a map of the chapter, then keep the "signal amid the noise" theme in mind — it returns explicitly in section 1.10, *Beware of the short-term hype* (p.36), and section 1.11, *Summer can turn to winter* (p.38), and again in the book's closing reflections (p.621). Chapter 1 covers three things: fundamental definitions, a soft introduction to the principles of machine learning, and deep learning's popularity and future potential. AI has been the subject of intense media hype, with both grim and utopian visions; a practitioner must be able to recognize the signal amid the noise. The book positions you as a future builder of AI systems, not merely an observer of the hype.

title: AI hype vs. real progress
text: The gap between media and marketing claims about AI and what the technology can demonstrably do; the authors ask practitioners to be able to tell the two apart. Headlines promise either utopia or doom; a practitioner looks instead at what a given system actually learned from what data, and how well it generalizes. The chapter later gives the tools for this judgement: precise definitions of AI, ML and DL (p.26–31), a mechanistic picture of how deep learning works (p.32–34), a list of concrete achievements (p.35), and a historical account of previous AI summers and winters (p.36–38). A press release announcing 'human-level' performance on one benchmark is not the same as a system that handles arbitrary real-world situations (see the discussion of local vs. broad generalization on p.600).

title: Defining AI: the Dartmouth workshop and 'automating intellectual tasks'
text:
The relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning (figure 1.1), and a definition and brief history of artificial intelligence AI, machine learning and deep learning are nested fields (figure 1.1). AI, born in the 1950s and crystallized at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, is 'the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans' — a broad field that includes machine learning but also approaches that involve no learning at all, such as hardcoded rule systems. The page finishes the chapter's opening sentence with the four questions Chapter 1 will tackle: *What has deep learning achieved so far? How significant is it? Where are we headed next? Should you believe the hype?*

**Section 1.1** states that the first task is to define terms: what are artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning, and how do they relate? **Figure 1.1** answers the second question visually with three nested ellipses — *Artificial intelligence* contains *Machine learning*, which contains *Deep learning*.

**Section 1.2** gives a definition and a history of AI. The field was born in the 1950s when computer-science pioneers asked whether computers could be made to "think". The idea crystallized in **1956**, when **John McCarthy**, then a young assistant professor of mathematics at Dartmouth College, organized a summer workshop. Its proposal (quoted in full) rests on the conjecture that *every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it*, and it aims at machines that use language, form abstractions and concepts, solve problems reserved for humans, and improve themselves — all in one summer. The workshop did not solve the riddle, but many attendees became pioneers of the field and it started an intellectual revolution that is still ongoing.

The page then gives the concise definition used throughout the book: **AI is the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans.** Because this is so broad, AI contains machine learning and deep learning but also many approaches that involve *no learning at all*. Until the 1980s most AI textbooks did not mention learning; early chess programs consisted only of rules hardcoded by programmers and therefore do not count as machine learning. For a long time most experts believed human-level AI could be reached by handcrafting a large enough set of explicit rules for manipulating knowledge — the sentence continues on p.27, where this approach is named *symbolic AI*. AI, machine learning and deep learning are nested: deep learning ⊂ machine learning ⊂ AI (figure 1.1). AI is the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans — a definition about the goal, not the method. AI was born in the 1950s and crystallized at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop organized by John McCarthy, whose proposal conjectured that every feature of intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. For decades AI did not involve learning at all: early chess programs used hardcoded rules, and most experts expected human-level AI from a large enough set of handcrafted rules (symbolic AI, p.27).

title: Artificial intelligence (AI)
text: The effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans (book's definition on this page). If a computer does something that would require thinking if a person did it — playing chess, translating, recognizing faces — that is AI, regardless of how the program was produced. AI is defined by its goal, not its technique. It includes rule-based (symbolic) systems with no learning, classical machine learning, and deep learning. Figure 1.1 shows it as the outermost of three nested ellipses. An early chess program whose moves are chosen by rules written entirely by programmers is AI but not machine learning.
snippet: The effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans book's definition on this page.

title: Machine learning (as a subfield of AI)
text: The subfield of AI in which the rules for a task are learned from data rather than handcrafted; shown in figure 1.1 as a subset of AI that itself contains deep learning. Instead of a programmer writing the rules, the computer is shown examples and works out the rules itself. This page only positions machine learning inside AI; its definition and the contrast with classical programming are developed in sections 1.3–1.4 (p.27–30). A spam filter that learns which words indicate spam from thousands of labelled emails, rather than from a programmer's list.
snippet: The subfield of AI in which the rules for a task are learned from data rather than handcrafted; shown in figure 1.1 as a subset of AI that itself contains deep learning.

title: Deep learning (as a subfield of machine learning)
text: The innermost ellipse of figure 1.1: a branch of machine learning. Its defining feature — successive layers of learned representations — is explained in section 1.5 (p.31). Deep learning is a specific way of doing machine learning, which is itself a specific way of doing AI. On this page deep learning appears only in the figure; the book later characterizes it as models built from chains of geometric transformations organized in layers (p.31, p.620). An image classifier made of stacked convolutional layers trained end-to-end on labelled photos.
snippet: The innermost ellipse of figure 1.1: a branch of machine learning. Its defining feature — successive layers of learned representations — is explained in section 1.5 p.31.

title: Symbolic AI (handcrafted rules)
text: The approach of achieving intelligence by having programmers handcraft a sufficiently large set of explicit rules for manipulating knowledge; named 'symbolic AI' on p.27. Write down everything an expert knows as if-then rules and let the computer apply them. Rules and knowledge are explicit symbols manipulated by logic; no parameters are fitted to data. Early chess programs are the book's example. A chess program that evaluates positions with programmer-written heuristics and searches moves by fixed rules.

title: Symbolic AI's limits; Lovelace, Babbage and Turing on whether machines can originate
text:
Why symbolic AI gave way to machine learning, and the historical question — from Ada Lovelace to Alan Turing — of whether a computer can learn or originate anything Symbolic AI (explicit rules and knowledge bases) dominated from the 1950s to the late 1980s and handled well-defined logical problems like chess, but it was intractable for fuzzy problems such as image classification, speech recognition and translation; machine learning replaced it. The deeper question behind machine learning was posed by Ada Lovelace in 1843 — can a machine originate anything? — and answered provocatively by Turing in 1950: computers could in principle emulate all aspects of human intelligence. The page completes the sentence from p.26: handcrafting a large enough set of explicit rules for manipulating knowledge stored in explicit databases is **symbolic AI**, the dominant paradigm from the 1950s to the late 1980s, peaking in the **expert systems** boom of the 1980s. Symbolic AI worked for well-defined, logical problems such as chess, but writing explicit rules for complex, *fuzzy* problems — image classification, speech recognition, natural language translation — turned out to be intractable. A new approach took its place: **machine learning**.

**Section 1.3 Machine learning** opens with history. In Victorian England, Ada Lovelace collaborated with Charles Babbage, inventor of the **Analytical Engine**, the first-known general-purpose mechanical computer. Designed in the 1830s–1840s, it was not conceived as general-purpose (the concept did not exist yet) but as a way to automate computations from mathematical analysis — hence its name. It descended from earlier gear-based calculators: the **Pascaline** (Blaise Pascal, 1642, at age 19 — the first mechanical calculator, able to add, subtract, multiply and divide digits) and Leibniz's step reckoner.

In 1843 Lovelace wrote that the Analytical Engine *"has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform… Its province is to assist us in making available what we're already acquainted with."* The authors find this remark still arresting after 182 years and unpack it into questions: could a general-purpose computer originate anything, or only execute processes humans fully understand? Could it have original thought, learn from experience, show creativity?

Alan Turing quoted the remark as **"Lady Lovelace's objection"** in his 1950 paper *Computing Machinery and Intelligence* (footnote 1: *Mind* 59, no. 236, pp. 433–460), which introduced the **Turing test** (footnote 2: meant as a conceptual device in a philosophical discussion, not a literal goal for the field) and other ideas that shaped AI. Turing's then-provocative view: computers could, in principle, emulate all aspects of human intelligence.

The page ends by stating the usual way to make a computer do useful work: a human programmer writes down rules — a program — that turn input data into appropriate answers, just as Lovelace wrote step-by-step instructions for the Analytical Engine. The next page (p.28) shows how machine learning turns this around. Symbolic AI — handcrafted explicit rules over explicit knowledge — dominated from the 1950s to the late 1980s and peaked with 1980s expert systems. It handled well-defined logical problems like chess but was intractable for fuzzy problems (image classification, speech recognition, translation), so machine learning took its place. Ada Lovelace (1843) argued the Analytical Engine could not originate anything, only execute what we know how to order; Turing (1950) named this 'Lady Lovelace's objection' and argued computers could in principle emulate all aspects of human intelligence. The Turing test was a conceptual device in a philosophical argument, not a literal goal for AI (footnote 2). Classical programming: a human writes rules that turn input data into answers; the next page shows machine learning turning this around.

title: Machine learning as a new programming paradigm; the three ingredients of ML
text:
Figure 1.2's contrast between classical programming (rules + data → answers) and machine learning (data + answers → rules); machine learning as an empirical engineering discipline; and the three things needed to do machine learning Machine learning inverts classical programming: instead of a programmer writing rules that turn data into answers, the system is shown data and the corresponding answers and finds the rules itself. A machine learning system is therefore *trained* rather than programmed — it discovers statistical structure in examples. To do this one needs input data points, examples of the expected output, and a way to measure how far the algorithm's output is from what is expected. The page completes the sentence from p.27 and states the central reversal: in classical programming a human writes rules and the computer applies them to data to produce answers; **machine learning turns this around** — the machine looks at the input data and the corresponding answers and *figures out what the rules should be*. **Figure 1.2** draws this as two boxes: *Classical programming* takes **Rules** and **Data** and outputs **Answers**; *Machine learning* takes **Data** and **Answers** and outputs **Rules**.

A machine learning system is **trained rather than explicitly programmed**: shown many examples relevant to a task, it finds *statistical structure* in them, which eventually lets it come up with rules for automating the task. Example: to tag vacation pictures, present many human-tagged pictures and the system learns statistical rules associating pictures with tags like "landscape" or "food".

Machine learning only began to flourish in the **1990s** but quickly became the most popular and successful subfield of AI, driven by **faster hardware and larger datasets**. It is related to mathematical statistics but differs in important ways — as medicine relates to chemistry without reducing to it. Machine learning deals with large, complex datasets (millions of images with tens of thousands of pixels each) for which classical statistical analysis such as Bayesian analysis would be impractical. Consequently machine learning, and especially deep learning, has comparatively little mathematical theory — "maybe too little" — and is fundamentally an **engineering discipline**: hands-on, driven by empirical findings, and deeply reliant on advances in software and hardware.

**Section 1.4** begins: to define deep learning and distinguish it from other machine learning approaches, we first need to know what machine learning algorithms do. Since machine learning discovers rules for a data-processing task from examples of what is expected, doing it requires **three things**:

1. **Input data points** — e.g. sound files for speech recognition, pictures for image tagging.
2. **Examples of the expected output** — e.g. human transcripts of the sound files; tags such as "dog" and "cat".
3. **A way to measure whether the algorithm is doing a good job** — needed to determine the distance between the algorithm's current output and its expected output (the bullet continues on p.29, where this measurement becomes the feedback signal that drives learning). Classical programming: rules + data → answers. Machine learning turns this around: data + answers → rules (figure 1.2). A machine learning system is trained rather than explicitly programmed; it finds statistical structure in many examples and derives rules from it. Machine learning flourished from the 1990s, driven by faster hardware and larger datasets; it is related to statistics but is fundamentally an empirical engineering discipline with comparatively little theory. Doing machine learning needs three things: input data points, examples of the expected output, and a way to measure the distance between current and expected output.

section: 1.4 Learning rules and representations from data

title: Learning as feedback-driven adjustment; representations and the coordinate-change example
text:
The definition of learning as adjustment from a feedback signal, the notion of a representation (RGB vs. HSV), and the black/white points example in which a coordinate change produces a representation that makes classification easy (figures 1.3 and 1.4) Learning is the adjustment of an algorithm using the measured distance between its outputs and the expected outputs as a feedback signal. The central problem of machine learning and deep learning is to transform data meaningfully — to learn useful *representations* of the input that bring us closer to the expected output. A representation is a different way of encoding the same data, and a task hard in one representation can be easy in another; a rotation of the axes in figure 1.4 turns a tangled two-colour point cloud into one separable by a single rule. The page finishes the third ingredient from p.28: the measurement of how far the algorithm's output is from the expected output is used as a **feedback signal** to adjust how the algorithm works, and *this adjustment step is what we call learning*.

A machine learning model transforms its input data into meaningful outputs, a process learned from exposure to known examples of inputs and outputs. So the **central problem** of machine learning and deep learning is to *meaningfully transform data* — to learn useful **representations** of the input that get us closer to the expected output.

A representation is a different way to look at, represent or encode data. Example: a colour image can be encoded as **RGB** (red-green-blue) or **HSV** (hue-saturation-value) — two representations of the same data. Some tasks are hard in one and easy in the other: "select all red pixels" is simpler in RGB; "make the image less saturated" is simpler in HSV. Machine learning models are all about finding representations that make the data more amenable to the task.

The concrete example (**figure 1.3**): points in an $(x, y)$ plane, some white and some black, and the goal of an algorithm that takes a point's coordinates and outputs whether it is likely black or white. In the language of p.28:

- the **inputs** are the coordinates of the points;
- the **expected outputs** are the colours of the points;
- a **measure of success** could be the percentage of points correctly classified.

What is needed is a new representation that cleanly separates white from black points. One transformation among many is a **coordinate change**, shown in **figure 1.4** in three panels: (1) raw data, where the two colours form two tilted bands that no axis-aligned rule separates; (2) a new pair of rotated axes drawn over the data; (3) the better representation, where in the new coordinates the black points lie on one side of the vertical axis and the white points on the other. The next page (p.30) states the resulting rule — black points have $x > 0$ — and asks whether such a transformation could be found automatically rather than by hand. Learning is the adjustment step in which the measured distance between output and expected output is used as a feedback signal to change how the algorithm works. The central problem of machine learning and deep learning is to meaningfully transform data — to learn useful representations that bring the input closer to the expected output. A representation is a different way to encode the same data (RGB vs. HSV); a task hard in one representation can be easy in another. In the black/white points problem, a coordinate change (figure 1.4) is a transformation that produces a representation in which the two classes are cleanly separated — one of many possible transformations.

title: Learning as an automatic search for representations in a hypothesis space
text:
The concise definition of machine learning: searching for useful representations and rules within a predefined hypothesis space, guided by a feedback signal — motivated by the brittleness of hand-designed representations for handwritten digits The rotated coordinates of figure 1.4 are a good representation because they reduce classification to the rule 'black points have x > 0'. But that representation was designed by hand, and for handwritten digits hand-designed transformations (loop counting, pixel histograms) are brittle and unmaintainable. Machine learning automates the design: *learning* is an automatic search over a predefined set of data transformations — the hypothesis space — for representations that make the task solvable by simple rules, guided by a feedback signal such as the percentage of correctly classified digits. In the new coordinate system of figure 1.4 the points' coordinates are a new representation of the data — *and it's a good one*: the black/white classification problem becomes the simple rule **"Black points are such that $x > 0$"** (equivalently, white points have $x < 0$). Representation plus rule neatly solves the problem.

But the coordinate change was defined **by hand**, using human intelligence. That is fine for such a simple problem; could you do the same to classify **handwritten digits** — write explicit, computer-executable image transformations that separate a 6 from an 8, or a 1 from a 7, across all handwritings? To an extent, yes: rules based on representations such as *counting closed loops* or *vertical and horizontal pixel histograms* do a decent job. But finding such representations by hand is hard work, and the resulting rule-based system is **brittle and a nightmare to maintain**: every new handwriting example that breaks the rules forces you to add new transformations and rules while accounting for their interactions with all previous ones.

Could the process be automated? Suppose we *systematically searched* different sets of automatically generated representations and rules, judging them by the percentage of digits correctly classified on some development dataset. We would then be doing machine learning. **Learning**, in this context, is an *automatic search process for data transformations that produce useful representations of some data, guided by some feedback signal* — representations amenable to simpler rules.

The transformations can be coordinate changes (the 2-D example), pixel histograms and loop counting (the digits example), or linear projections, translations, nonlinear operations ("select all points such that $x > 0$"), and so on. Machine learning algorithms are not usually creative: they *search through a predefined set of operations* called a **hypothesis space** — for the 2-D example, the space of all possible coordinate changes.

The concise definition: **machine learning is searching for useful representations and rules over some input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal.** This simple idea solves a remarkably broad range of intellectual tasks, from autonomous driving to natural-language question answering. The page closes by turning to what makes *deep* learning special (section 1.5, p.31). In the rotated coordinates of figure 1.4 the problem reduces to the rule 'black points are such that x > 0' — a good representation is one that makes the rule simple. Hand-designed representations (closed loops, pixel histograms) can do a decent job on handwritten digits but are hard to find, brittle, and a nightmare to maintain. Learning is an automatic search for data transformations that produce useful representations, guided by a feedback signal such as the percentage of correctly classified digits on a development dataset. Algorithms are not creative: they search a predefined set of operations called the hypothesis space (e.g. all coordinate changes). Concise definition: machine learning is searching for useful representations and rules over input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal.

title: What “deep” means: successive layers of representations
text:
Definition of deep learning as learning successive layers of increasingly meaningful representations; depth of a model; shallow vs. deep learning; neural networks are not models of the brain Deep learning is the branch of machine learning that learns many successive layers of representations from data; “deep” refers to the number of these layers (the depth), not to any deeper understanding, and the neural networks that implement it are a mathematical framework, not a model of the brain. Section 1.5 defines **deep learning** as a specific subfield of machine learning: a new take on learning representations from data that emphasizes learning *successive layers* of increasingly meaningful representations. The word “deep” has nothing to do with deeper understanding; it refers to how many such layers are stacked. That number is the **depth** of the model. The authors suggest that *layered representations learning* or *hierarchical representations learning* would have been equally appropriate names. Modern deep learning models often have tens or hundreds of layers, and all of them are learned automatically from training data. By contrast, other machine learning approaches typically learn only one or two layers of representations — for example, computing a pixel histogram and then applying a classification rule — and are therefore sometimes called **shallow learning**.

The second paragraph introduces the models that implement these layered representations: **neural networks**, structured as literal layers stacked on top of each other. The authors then take pains to separate deep learning from neurobiology. The term *neural network* is a reference to the brain, and some core concepts were partly inspired by our understanding of the visual cortex, but deep learning models are **not** models of the brain. There is no evidence that the brain implements anything like the learning mechanisms of modern deep learning models. Pop-science claims that deep learning “works like the brain” are wrong, and the authors tell newcomers to forget any hypothetical links between the two: for the purposes of this book, deep learning is simply **a mathematical framework for learning representations from data**.

The page ends by asking what the learned representations actually look like, and points to **Figure 1.5**, a block diagram of a four-layer network that takes an image of a handwritten digit (a “4”) as *original input*, passes it through Layer 1 to Layer 4, and produces a *final output* over the ten digit classes 0–9, with the slot for “4” highlighted. The next page (p.32, Figure 1.6) opens these layers up to show the intermediate representations. Deep learning = learning successive layers of increasingly meaningful representations from data; 'deep' counts those layers (the model's depth), nothing more. Other machine learning approaches learn one or two layers of representations (shallow learning); modern deep models learn tens or hundreds, all automatically from training data. The models are neural networks: literal stacks of layers. Despite the name, they are not models of the brain, and the authors advise forgetting any supposed link to neurobiology. For this book, deep learning is a mathematical framework for learning representations; Figure 1.5 shows the template — digit image in, four layers, ten class scores out.

title: Deep representations as information distillation; layers parameterized by weights
text:
Figure 1.6 (what the layers of a digit classifier learn), deep learning as multistage information distillation, and the start of section 1.6: a layer's transformation is parameterized by its weights, and learning means finding the right weight values A deep network transforms its input into representations that are increasingly different from the input and increasingly informative about the answer — a multistage information-distillation process; the transformation each layer applies is stored in its weights, and learning means finding values for all the weights so that inputs map to their targets. The page completes section 1.5 and opens section 1.6.

**Figure 1.6 and information distillation.** Figure 1.6 opens up the four-layer digit classifier of Figure 1.5 and shows, for a handwritten '4', the *representations* produced by each layer: Layer 1 yields several image-like maps with scattered bright dots; Layer 2 yields maps containing stroke-like fragments of the digit; Layer 3 yields coarse grey grids that no longer look like the digit at all; Layer 4 is the final output, ten cells for the digits 0–9 with the '4' cell highlighted. The authors' reading: the network transforms the image into representations that are *increasingly different from the original image* and *increasingly informative about the final result*. They propose a mental model: a deep network is a **multistage information-distillation process**, where information passes through successive filters and comes out increasingly *purified* — that is, useful with regard to some task.

**One-line definition.** 'So that's what deep learning is, technically: a multistage way to learn data representations.' The authors add that the idea is simple, but very simple mechanisms, sufficiently scaled, can end up looking like magic — a refrain that returns on p.34.

**Section 1.6, part one: weights.** After recalling what the reader already knows (machine learning maps inputs such as images to targets such as 'cat' by observing many examples; deep networks do this with a deep sequence of simple data transformations, learned from examples), the section asks how the learning actually happens. The specification of what a layer does to its input is stored in the layer's **weights** — 'a bunch of numbers'. In technical language, the layer's transformation is *parameterized* by its weights (Figure 1.7, on p.33); weights are also called the *parameters* of the layer. **Learning** therefore means finding a set of values for the weights of *all* layers such that the network correctly maps example inputs to their associated targets. The difficulty, stated as the page ends and continued on p.33, is that a deep network can contain tens of millions of parameters, and changing one affects the behavior of all the others. Figure 1.6 shows that a deep network's representations become increasingly different from the input image and increasingly informative about the answer: a multistage information-distillation process. Technically, deep learning is 'a multistage way to learn data representations' — a simple idea that, scaled up, looks like magic. What a layer does is stored in its weights (a bunch of numbers); the layer's transformation is parameterized by them. Learning means finding values for the weights of all layers so that inputs map to their targets — hard because there can be tens of millions of interacting parameters.

section: 1.6 Understanding how deep learning works, in three figures

title: Information distillation
text: The authors' mental model of a deep network: a multistage process in which information passes through successive filters and comes out increasingly purified, i.e. useful for the task. Each layer throws away a little more of what does not matter (exact stroke shape, position) and keeps what does (which digit it is). title: Weights, the loss function, and the optimizer: how a network learns
text:
Figures 1.7 and 1.8: a network is parameterized by its weights; the loss function measures the distance between predictions and true targets; the optimizer uses the loss score as a feedback signal to adjust the weights (backpropagation); the training loop starts from random weights To learn, a network needs a way to observe how wrong it is — the loss function, which turns predictions and true targets into a distance score — and a way to act on that observation — the optimizer, which uses the score as a feedback signal to nudge the weights in a direction that lowers the loss. Starting from random weights, repeating this adjustment over many examples drives the loss down. The page continues section 1.6 with two of its three figures.

**Finishing the thought from p.32.** Finding the right value for tens of millions of parameters 'may seem like a daunting task, especially given that modifying the value of one parameter will affect the behavior of all the others!' **Figure 1.7** draws the situation: Input X enters a Layer (data transformation), whose Weights sit beside it; a second Layer with its own Weights follows; out come Predictions Y'. A callout marks the goal: *finding the right values for these weights*.

**The loss function (Figure 1.8).** 'To control something, first you need to be able to observe it.' To control a network's output you must measure how far it is from what you expected. That is the job of the **loss function**, also called the *objective function* or *cost function*: it takes the network's predictions and the *true target* (what you wanted it to output) and computes a **distance score** capturing how well the network did on this specific example. Figure 1.8 adds two nodes to Figure 1.7: *True targets Y* and a *Loss function* that receives both Predictions Y' and True targets Y and emits a *Loss score*.

**The fundamental trick: the optimizer and backpropagation.** The score is used as a **feedback signal** to adjust the weights *a little*, in a direction that will *lower the loss score for the current example* (Figure 1.9, on p.34). This adjustment is the job of the **optimizer**, which implements the **Backpropagation algorithm** — 'the central algorithm in deep learning'. The next chapter explains how backpropagation works.

**The training loop begins.** Initially the weights are random, so the network implements a series of random transformations; its output is far from ideal and the loss score is very high. But with every example processed, the weights are adjusted a little in the correct direction and the loss decreases. This is the **training loop**, which — as p.34 continues — repeated enough times yields weights that minimize the loss. Figure 1.7: a network is a fixed sequence of layers whose transformations are set by their weights; the goal of training is to find the right values for those weights. The loss function (objective/cost function) takes predictions and true targets and returns a distance score — the only way to 'observe' how wrong the network is (Figure 1.8). The fundamental trick: use the loss score as a feedback signal to adjust the weights a little in a direction that lowers the loss; the optimizer does this by implementing backpropagation, the central algorithm of deep learning. Training starts from random weights and a high loss; each example nudges the weights in the correct direction and the loss falls — the training loop.
