title: Closing the training loop (Figure 1.9) and why deep learning is different: simplicity and scalability
text:
Figure 1.9 and the end of the training loop (a trained network minimizes the loss); section 1.7's claim that deep learning is here to stay, and the first two of its three distinguishing properties: simplicity (automated feature engineering) and scalability (GPU parallelism) The optimizer feeds the loss score back into the weights; repeated tens of passes over thousands of examples, this loop yields weights that minimize the loss — a trained network. Deep learning's lasting importance comes from properties such as simplicity (it learns all features itself, replacing hand-engineered multistage pipelines with one end-to-end model) and scalability (it parallelizes on GPUs and trains on batches, so dataset size is no limit). **Figure 1.9 and the end of section 1.6.** The third figure completes the picture: Input X passes through two layers, each with its Weights, to Predictions Y'; the Loss function compares Y' with True targets Y and emits a Loss score; new on this figure, an **Optimizer** takes the loss score and sends a **Weight update** back to each Weights box. The text finishes the sentence from p.33: the training loop, 'repeated a sufficient number of times (typically tens of passes over thousands of examples), yields weight values that minimize the loss function'. A network with minimal loss — outputs as close as they can be to the targets — is a **trained network**. 'Once again, it's a simple mechanism that, once scaled, ends up looking like magic.'

**Section 1.7: What makes deep learning different.** The authors ask whether deep neural networks are the 'right' approach for companies and researchers to invest in, and whether we will still use them in 20 years. Their answer: deep learning has properties that justify calling it an AI revolution, and it is here to stay — even if the models of several decades hence are not neural networks, they will inherit directly from deep learning's core concepts. The properties fall into three categories, of which two begin on this page:

- **Simplicity.** Deep learning automates what used to be the most crucial step in a machine learning workflow: **feature engineering**. Shallow techniques transform the input into only one or two representation spaces, which is not expressive enough for most problems, so humans had to manually engineer good representations to make the data amenable to those methods. Deep learning learns *all* features in one pass. This has simplified workflows, often replacing sophisticated multistage pipelines with a single, simple, end-to-end model.
- **Scalability.** Deep learning is highly amenable to parallelization on GPUs or more specialized machine learning hardware, so it can take full advantage of Moore's law (the bullet continues on p.35 with the point that training on small batches allows datasets of arbitrary size).

The third category, *versatility and reusability*, follows on p.35. Figure 1.9 closes the loop: Loss score → Optimizer → Weight update to every layer; repeated tens of passes over thousands of examples, this yields weights that minimize the loss — a trained network. Deep learning is here to stay: even future non-neural models will inherit its core concepts. Simplicity: deep learning automates feature engineering, learning all features in one pass and replacing multistage pipelines with a single end-to-end model; shallow methods needed hand-made representations because one or two representation spaces are not expressive enough. Scalability: deep learning parallelizes on GPUs and specialized hardware, taking full advantage of Moore's law (continued on p.35).

title: Versatility and reusability; the age of generative AI and self-supervised foundation models
text:
End of section 1.7 (scalability via batch training; versatility and reusability, foundation models); section 1.8 on generative AI: foundation models trained by self-supervised reconstruction, their scale, the 'fuzzy database' view and prompting, and the long history of generative AI; opening of section 1.9 Deep learning models can keep learning from new data and be repurposed for new tasks — the idea behind foundation models. Generative AI is powered by very large foundation models trained by self-supervised learning, where the targets are taken from the input itself (reconstruct a noisy image, predict the next word), which removes the labeling bottleneck and unlocks unprecedented scale; such models act as a fuzzy database of human knowledge that can be queried by prompting. **Scalability, concluded.** Deep learning models are trained by iterating over small batches of data, so they can be trained on datasets of arbitrary size; the only bottleneck is the amount of parallel computational power, which, thanks to Moore's law, is 'a fast-moving barrier'.

**Versatility and reusability.** Unlike many prior approaches, deep learning models can be trained on *additional* data without restarting from scratch, which makes continuous online learning viable — important for very large production models. Trained models are also *repurposable* and thus reusable: this is the big idea behind **foundation models**, large models trained on humongous amounts of data that can be used across many new tasks with little or no retraining.

**1.8 The age of generative AI.** The best-known deep learning systems today are generative AI applications — chatbot assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) and image generators (Midjourney) — which produce informative or creative content from simple prompts, blurring the line between human and machine creativity. They are powered by very large foundation models that learn to *reconstruct* the text and image content fed to them: reconstruct a sharp image from a noisy version, predict the next word in a sentence. In terms of Figure 1.8, the **targets are taken from the input itself**: this is **self-supervised learning**, and it lets models use vast amounts of *unlabeled* data. Dropping the manual annotation that bottlenecked earlier machine learning unlocked unprecedented scale: some foundation models have hundreds of billions of parameters, are trained on over 1 petabyte of data, and cost tens of millions of dollars. These models act as a kind of **fuzzy database of human knowledge**, usable for a very wide range of applications without special-purpose programming or retraining: having memorized so much, they solve new problems via **prompting** — querying their learned knowledge representations and returning the output most likely to be associated with the prompt. Generative AI reached mainstream awareness in 2022 but has a long history: text generation experiments date to the 1990s, and the first edition of this book (2017) already had a hefty 'Generative AI' chapter predicting that much cultural content would 'soon' be created with AI's help.

**1.9 What deep learning has achieved so far** opens: over the past decade deep learning has produced a technological revolution, starting with remarkable results on perceptual tasks from 2013 to 2017 (continued on p.36). Batch-wise training means datasets of any size can be used; the only bottleneck is parallel compute. Deep learning models can keep learning from new data without restarting and can be repurposed — the big idea behind foundation models. Generative AI is powered by very large foundation models trained by self-supervised learning: the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself (next word, clean image), so unlabeled data at petabyte scale can be used. Foundation models act as a fuzzy database of human knowledge, queried by prompting, with no special-purpose programming or retraining. Generative AI went mainstream in 2022 but its roots go back to the 1990s and it was already in this book's 2017 first edition; the deep learning revolution began with perceptual tasks in 2013–2017.

title: Self-supervised learning
text: Learning in which the targets of Figure 1.8 are taken from the input itself — the model learns to reconstruct its input (a sharp image from a noisy one, the next word in a sentence). The data labels itself: hide part of it and ask the model to fill it in. A reconstruction loss between the model's output and the withheld or clean part of the input; no human annotation is needed, so vast amounts of unlabeled data can be used. Next-word prediction on text; denoising on images.

section: 1.9 What deep learning has achieved so far

title: Prompting
text: Solving a new problem by querying the knowledge representations a foundation model has learned and returning the output most likely to be associated with the prompt. Asking a fuzzy database a question in natural language. Because the model has memorized so much during reconstruction training, a prompt elicits the most probable continuation or completion, with no special-purpose programming or retraining. title: What deep learning has achieved, and the beginning of a warning about hype
text:
The three waves of the deep learning revolution (perception 2013–2017, NLP 2017–2022, generative AI 2022–now); a list of major breakthroughs; emerging applications across science, medicine and industry; and the start of section 1.10 on separating real impact from exaggerated predictions Deep learning has produced a genuine technological revolution — chatbots, coding assistants, image generation, human-level perception, autonomous driving, superhuman game play — and is spreading into every field of human endeavor; but the hype that followed (mass unemployment within a year, 10×–100× productivity) has not materialized, even though generative AI's real impact is considerable and growing fast. **The three waves (end of the sentence from p.35).** The revolution started with perceptual tasks (2013–2017), made fast progress on natural language processing (2017–2022), and culminated in a wave of transformative generative AI applications (2022 to now).

**Breakthroughs.** Deep learning has enabled major breakthroughs 'in extremely challenging problems that had long eluded machines': fluent, versatile chatbots (ChatGPT, Gemini); programming assistants (GitHub Copilot); photorealistic image generation; human-level image classification; human-level speech transcription; human-level handwriting and printed-text transcription; dramatically improved machine translation; dramatically improved text-to-speech; human-level autonomous driving, deployed to the public in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Austin as of 2025; improved recommender systems (YouTube, Netflix, Spotify); and superhuman Go, Chess and Poker playing.

**Still exploring.** Deep learning is being applied successfully to problems thought impossible a few years ago: transcribing tens of thousands of ancient manuscripts in the Vatican Secret Archive, detecting and classifying plant diseases in fields with a smartphone, assisting oncologists and radiologists with medical imaging, and predicting natural disasters such as floods, hurricanes and even earthquakes. Each milestone brings closer an age in which deep learning assists every field of human endeavor — science, medicine, manufacturing, energy, transportation, software development, agriculture, even artistic creation.

**1.10 Beware of the short-term hype.** These successes produced intense hype, 'some of which is somewhat grounded, but most of which is just fancy fairy tales'. In early 2023, after GPT-4's release, pundits claimed no one would need to work anymore, that mass unemployment would arrive within a year, or that productivity would jump 10× to 100×. Two years later none of this has happened: US unemployment remains low and productivity metrics are far from the promised explosion. The authors are careful not to overcorrect: AI's impact, especially generative AI's, is already considerable and growing remarkably fast — as of mid-2025 generative AI was generating tens of billions of dollars of revenue per year, impressive for an industry that did not exist three years earlier. But (continued on p.37) it does not yet make much of a dent in the overall economy and pales beside the promises made at its onset. The deep learning revolution came in three waves: perceptual tasks (2013–2017), NLP (2017–2022), generative AI (2022–now). Its breakthroughs span chatbots, coding assistants, image generation, human-level image/speech/text recognition, improved translation and text-to-speech, public autonomous driving in four US cities, better recommenders and superhuman game play. New applications reach into scholarship, agriculture, medicine and disaster prediction; the authors expect deep learning to assist every field of human endeavor. The successes spawned hype, mostly 'fancy fairy tales': the early-2023 predictions of mass unemployment and 10×–100× productivity did not materialize within two years. Real impact is nonetheless large and fast-growing — tens of billions of dollars of generative AI revenue per year by mid-2025 — though not yet a major dent in the overall economy.

title: AGI hype, cognitive automation vs. intelligence
text:
Why claims of imminent AGI deserve skepticism, and the distinction between cognitive automation (what today's AI is) and intelligence (cognitive autonomy) Today's 'artificial intelligence' is better described as cognitive automation — the encoding and operationalization of human skills — and it is adaptability to the genuinely unknown, not realism of output, that separates automation from intelligence. Historically, belief in near-term AGI preceded and helped fuel generative AI, not the other way round. This page continues section 1.10, *Beware of the short-term hype*. After finishing the thought from p.36 — that the realistic economic impact of AI pales next to the "unbridled promises" made at its onset — the authors turn to the most sensational part of the hype: claims that human-level **artificial general intelligence (AGI)** or even "superintelligence" is imminent, and that humanity might be replaced by its digital creations.

The authors then make a historical point that newcomers usually get backwards. It is tempting to think the practical successes of generative AI *caused* the belief in near-term AGI. In fact the belief came **first**: as early as 2013 some tech elites feared that DeepMind (a London startup acquired by Google) was on track to AGI within a few years; that fear was the impetus for founding **OpenAI in 2015** as an open-source counterweight; OpenAI then played a critical role in kick-starting generative AI. In 2016 OpenAI's recruiting pitch was that it would achieve AGI by 2020. Only a minority believed such timelines then, but by early 2023 a significant fraction of Bay Area engineers expected AGI within a couple of years.

The authors urge skepticism. Despite its name, today's "artificial intelligence" is more accurately **cognitive automation**: the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge. It excels at problems with narrowly defined requirements or with ample precise examples; it enhances computers rather than replicating minds. Cognitive automation is extremely useful, but **intelligence — cognitive autonomy — is a different creature**. The analogy: AI is a cartoon character that can only act out the scenes it was drawn for; intelligence is a living being that can adapt to the unexpected.

Anticipating the objection "if the cartoon covers enough scenes, what's the difference?" (or: if an LLM sounds human enough, does cognitive autonomy matter?), the authors answer: **adaptability**. Intelligence is the ability to face the unknown, adapt to it and learn from it; automation can only handle situations it was trained or programmed for — which is exactly why robust automation is so hard, since every scenario must be accounted for. Hence there is no reason to fear AI suddenly becoming self-aware: the technology is simply not headed that way. The sentence continues on p.38 with the clock-vs-time-travel comparison. The belief in imminent AGI predates generative AI: 2013 fears about DeepMind led to OpenAI's founding in 2015, and OpenAI then kick-started generative AI. Confident AGI timelines have a track record of failing — e.g. OpenAI's 2016 pitch of AGI by 2020 — so claims heard in 2023 deserve skepticism. Today's AI is best described as cognitive automation: the encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge, excelling at narrow problems or those with ample precise examples. Intelligence is cognitive autonomy — the ability to face the unknown, adapt and learn — whereas automation only handles situations it was trained or programmed for. Realism of output is not the test: a cartoon can be arbitrarily realistic yet only act out drawn scenes; the test is adaptability. Robust automation is hard precisely because every possible scenario has to be accounted for in advance. Current technology is not headed toward self-awareness; improvements make a better tool, not a sentient being.

title: Cognitive automation
text: The encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge in a computer system — the authors' more accurate name for what today's 'artificial intelligence' does. A deep learning model is like a very flexible recording of human know-how: it replays, on new inputs, skills that were present in its training examples. Deep learning automates tasks from exposure to data: given ample precise examples (or narrowly defined requirements), a model learns a mapping from inputs to outputs that reproduces the demonstrated skill. It works best precisely where the task can be fully specified by examples. Image classification, speech transcription, machine translation and chatbot answers — all items of the p.35–36 list — are human skills encoded from large example sets.
snippet: The encoding and operationalization of human skills and knowledge in a computer system — the authors' more accurate name for what today's 'artificial intelligence' does.

title: Intelligence as adaptability (cognitive autonomy)
text: The ability to face the unknown, adapt to it, and learn from it; contrasted with automation, which can only handle situations it was trained on or programmed for. A living being can cope with a scene nobody drew in advance; a cartoon cannot. Operationally, the criterion is behaviour on situations outside the training/programming coverage. Automation requires every scenario to be accounted for beforehand; intelligence generates appropriate behaviour for new scenarios on the fly. An LLM that answers familiar questions fluently may still fail on a genuinely novel puzzle; the fluency measures coverage, not autonomy.
snippet: The ability to face the unknown, adapt to it, and learn from it; contrasted with automation, which can only handle situations it was trained on or programmed for.

title: AI winters and the current AI bubble
text:
The two historical AI winters (symbolic AI in the 1960s–70s, expert systems in the 1980s–90s), the authors' assessment of the 2023–2025 AI bubble, and the opening of section 1.12 on AI's long-term promise Inflated short-term expectations have twice led to AI winters when the technology fell short and funding dried up; we are in the optimistic phase of a third cycle, and while a full retreat is unlikely because AI has proven its value, some air must come out of a bubble in which ~$200B of annual investment faces only ~$30B of revenue. The page opens by completing p.37's sentence: even with significant advancements, AI will remain a sophisticated tool, not a sentient being — like expecting a better clock to lead to time travel.

**1.11 Summer can turn to winter.** The danger of inflated short-term expectations is that when technology falls short, research investment dries up and progress slows for a long time. This has happened twice. The first cycle began with **symbolic AI in the 1960s**: Marvin Minsky claimed in 1967 that the AI problem would be 'substantially solved' within a generation and in 1970 that 'in from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being.' In 2025 that still appears far off — we have no way to predict how long it will take — but experts then (like many people today) thought it was around the corner. When expectations failed, researchers and government funding left the field: the **first AI winter** (named after nuclear winter, shortly after the height of the Cold War). The second cycle came with **expert systems in the 1980s**: early successes triggered corporate in-house AI departments; around 1985 companies spent over $1 billion a year; by the early 1990s the systems proved expensive to maintain, hard to scale and limited in scope, and interest died — the **second AI winter**. We may now be in the **third cycle**, still in the phase of intense optimism.

The author's current view: a full-scale retreat like the 1990s is unlikely; any winter should be very mild, because AI has already demonstrated world-changing value. Still, some air must come out of the **2023–2025 AI bubble**: AI investment, mainly in data centers and GPUs, exceeds **$200 billion per year**, while revenue is closer to **$30 billion**. AI is being judged not on what it has accomplished but on what it is said it might soon do — much of which will 'durably stay out of reach of existing technologies.' Something will have to give; exactly how the bubble deflates is still open.

**1.12 The promise of AI.** Despite unrealistic short-term expectations, the long-term picture is bright: we are only getting started applying deep learning to important problems, from medical diagnoses to digital assistants (continued on p.39). Improving AI makes a better tool, not a sentient being — like a better clock not leading to time travel. Inflated expectations are dangerous because disappointment dries up research funding and can slow progress for a long time. First AI winter: symbolic AI's 1960s optimism (Minsky 1967: solved 'within a generation'; 1970: human-level general intelligence in 3–8 years) collapsed in the 1970s. Second AI winter: 1980s expert systems (>$1B/yr corporate spending by ~1985) proved expensive to maintain, hard to scale and limited in scope; interest died by the early 1990s. We may be in a third cycle and are still in the phase of intense optimism; the author expects at most a mild winter because AI has already shown world-changing value. The 2023–2025 AI bubble: >$200B/yr investment (data centers, GPUs) against ~$30B/yr revenue; AI is judged on promised future abilities, many of which will stay out of reach of existing technology. Short-term expectations may be unrealistic, but the long-term picture is bright — from medical diagnoses to digital assistants, we are only getting started.

title: AI winter
text: A period of disappointment, skepticism and scarce funding that follows a phase of intense optimism about AI when the technology falls short of inflated expectations. A boom-and-bust cycle for research funding, named by analogy with nuclear winter. Two instances are documented on the page: (1) after the symbolic-AI optimism of the 1960s and Minsky's 1967/1970 predictions, researchers and government funds left the field; (2) after the 1980s expert-systems boom (>$1B/yr corporate spending c. 1985), systems proved expensive to maintain, hard to scale and limited in scope, and interest died by the early 1990s. The first AI winter began a few years after Minsky's 1970 claim that a machine with average human general intelligence was three to eight years away.

title: AI hype cycle

title: The promise of AI: 2017 predictions revisited in 2025
text:
The authors' 2017 forecast of AI's impact, checked against 2025 reality, the internet-bubble analogy for coming setbacks, and the chapter's closing motto: don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision AI's long-term trajectory resembles the internet's: a 2017 prediction that AI would become assistant, friend, interface to information and scientific collaborator has largely come true by 2025, and although a dot-com-style crash may interrupt the ride, AI will eventually be applied to nearly every process in society. The last page of chapter 1 continues section 1.12, *The promise of AI*. The author quotes what he wrote in the 2017 first edition: it may be hard to believe AI could have a large impact because it is not yet widely deployed — just as in 1995 few people could see how the internet would change their lives — but 'make no mistake: AI is coming.' The 2017 text predicted that AI would be your **assistant, even your friend**; answer questions, help educate your kids, watch over your health; deliver groceries and drive you from A to B; be your **interface to an increasingly complex, information-intensive world**; and, most importantly, help humanity move forward by **assisting scientists** in breakthroughs from genomics to mathematics.

Fast-forwarding to 2025, the authors say most of this has come true or is on the verge, and give four pieces of evidence:

- Tens of millions of people use chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude daily; question-answering and homework help ('educating your kids') turned out to be their top applications, and for many, AI is already the go-to interface to the world's information.
- Hundreds of thousands interact with AI 'friends' in applications such as Character.ai.
- Fully autonomous driving is deployed at scale in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Austin.
- AI is accelerating science: DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts protein structures with unprecedented accuracy, and Terence Tao expects that by around 2026 AI could be a reliable co-author in mathematical research when used appropriately.

The AI revolution is 'rapidly unfolding before our eyes.' There may be setbacks, as when the internet industry was overhyped in 1998–1999 and crashed, drying up investment through the early 2000s — but we will get there: AI will be applied to nearly every process in society and daily life, as the internet is today.

The chapter ends with its motto: **Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.** It may take a while for AI to reach its true potential — the full extent of which no one has yet dared to dream — but AI is coming and will transform the world in a fantastic way. In 2017 the first edition predicted AI would become your assistant and friend, answer questions, educate your kids, watch your health, deliver groceries, drive you, be your interface to information, and assist scientists from genomics to mathematics. By 2025 most of this has come true or is close: tens of millions use ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude daily (top uses: Q&A and homework help); hundreds of thousands use AI friends; autonomous driving runs at scale in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Austin; AlphaFold predicts protein structures, and Tao expects AI mathematical co-authors by around 2026. The internet is the authors' model: hard to believe in 1995, overhyped in 1998–1999, crashed in the early 2000s, ubiquitous today. Setbacks are possible — a crash that dries up investment — but AI will eventually be applied to nearly every process in society and daily life. Chapter 1's closing rule: don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision. The authors decline to bound AI's potential ('no one has yet dared to dream') just as they declined to give a timeline for human-level intelligence on p.38.

title: Chapter 2 opener: The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
text:
Introduction to chapter 2: the chapter's three topics (a first neural network, tensors and tensor operations, learning via backpropagation and gradient descent) and the authors' pedagogical approach of intuition and code over mathematical notation Deep learning rests on a handful of simple mathematical ideas — tensors, tensor operations, differentiation, gradient descent — and this chapter builds intuition for them through a concrete neural-network example and executable code rather than formal notation. This is the opening page of **chapter 2, *The mathematical building blocks of neural networks*** (PDF p.40–83). The 'This chapter covers' box lists three topics: a first example of a neural network; tensors and tensor operations; and how neural networks learn via backpropagation and gradient descent.

The two introductory paragraphs set out the approach. Understanding deep learning requires familiarity with many *simple* mathematical concepts — tensors, tensor operations, differentiation, gradient descent and so on — and the chapter's goal is to build intuition for them without getting overly technical. The authors deliberately steer away from mathematical notation, which can be an unnecessary barrier for readers without a mathematics background and is not needed to explain things well; in their words, 'the most precise, unambiguous description of a mathematical operation is its executable code.'

The plan: to give context for tensors and gradient descent, the chapter begins with a practical neural-network example (section 2.1, p.41 — classifying handwritten digits with Keras), then goes over every new concept point by point: data representations / tensors (2.2, p.45), tensor operations (2.3, p.52), gradient-based optimization including derivatives, SGD and backpropagation (2.4, p.63), and finally a from-scratch reimplementation of the first example (2.5, p.75). The authors stress that these concepts are essential for understanding the practical examples in the following chapters. The next page (p.41) adds a note on running the book's code in Jupyter notebooks and Google Colab.

How to use this page: treat it as a map. The bullets correspond to sections 2.1, 2.2–2.3, and 2.4–2.5 respectively; the concept list in the first paragraph (tensors, tensor operations, differentiation, gradient descent) is the vocabulary you should be able to explain by the chapter's end. Chapter 2 covers a first neural-network example, tensors and tensor operations, and learning via backpropagation and gradient descent. The required mathematics is simple — tensors, tensor operations, differentiation, gradient descent — and is taught through intuition and executable code, not notation. The chapter proceeds example-first (section 2.1), then explains each concept point by point (2.2–2.4), then reimplements the example from scratch (2.5). These concepts are prerequisites for every practical example later in the book.

title: Running the code, and a first look at MNIST digit classification
text:
How to run the book's code (Jupyter notebooks, Google Colab, local GPU) and the setup of the first neural-network example: classifying 28 × 28 grayscale MNIST digits into 10 classes with Keras The book is meant to be run, not just read — each chapter is a Jupyter notebook, easiest to execute on Colab's free GPU — and the first concrete example is the 'Hello World' of deep learning: a Keras network that learns to classify the 60,000 training / 10,000 test handwritten digits of MNIST. The page first closes the chapter introduction: after this chapter you will have an intuitive understanding of the mathematical theory behind deep learning and be ready for the modern frameworks introduced in chapter 3 (p.84).

The sidebar **Running the code in this book** explains the book's practical setup. Every chapter is paired with a **Jupyter notebook** containing all of its code — a 'live Python scratch pad' where you can run code interactively, graph data and view images. The authors urge you to run and experiment with the code as you read. The easiest environment is **Google Colaboratory (Colab)**, a hosted notebook service that has become the industry standard for ML practitioners; it runs in the browser on cloud runtimes with configurable hardware, and by default the book's notebooks use **Colab's free GPU runtime**. You can also run locally; a **GPU is recommended**, especially for the larger, more compute-intensive models later in the book. Code and instructions are at `https://github.com/fchollet/deep-learning-with-python-notebooks`.

**Section 2.1, A first look at a neural network**, begins the concrete example: a network built with **Keras** — a simple, high-level library used throughout the book — that learns to classify handwritten digits. The authors warn that unless you already know Keras you won't understand everything immediately; that's fine, since the next sections review each element in detail, so some steps may look like magic for now.

The problem: classify **grayscale images of handwritten digits, 28 × 28 pixels, into 10 categories (0–9)**. The dataset is **MNIST**, a classic almost as old as the field itself: **60,000 training images plus 10,000 test images**, assembled by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (the NIST in MNIST) in the 1980s. 'Solving' MNIST is the **'Hello World' of deep learning** — what you do to verify that your algorithms work — and you will see it over and over in papers and blog posts. Sample digits are shown in figure 2.1 on the next page. Each chapter is paired with a Jupyter notebook; run and experiment with the code as you read. Google Colab is the easiest environment and the book's default, using its free GPU runtime; local execution works too, with a GPU recommended for later, heavier models. Code and setup instructions live at github.com/fchollet/deep-learning-with-python-notebooks. The first example uses Keras, a simple high-level library used throughout the book, and is shown before its parts are explained — some steps will look like magic for now. The task is to classify 28 × 28 grayscale handwritten digits into 10 classes (0–9). MNIST: 60,000 training + 10,000 test images, assembled by NIST in the 1980s; 'solving' it is the Hello World of deep learning, a check that your algorithms work.

title: Loading MNIST in Keras: classes, samples, labels and the data arrays
text:
Machine-learning vocabulary (class, sample, label), loading MNIST as four NumPy arrays with `mnist.load_data()`, inspecting the shapes and labels of the training and test data, and the train-then-test workflow MNIST arrives as four NumPy arrays — training images of shape (60000, 28, 28) with 60,000 integer labels, and test images of shape (10000, 28, 28) with 10,000 labels — and the workflow is to learn the image→label association on the training set, then check predictions on the test set. The page opens with a **NOTE on vocabulary**: in machine learning a category in a classification problem is a **class**, data points are **samples**, and the class associated with a specific sample is its **label**. Beside it, **Figure 2.1** shows four MNIST sample digits.

MNIST comes **preloaded in Keras** as a set of four NumPy arrays. **Listing 2.1** loads it:

```python
from keras.datasets import mnist
(train_images, train_labels), (test_images, test_labels) = mnist.load_data()
```

`train_images` and `train_labels` form the **training set**, the data the model will learn from; the model is then tested on the **test set**, `test_images` and `test_labels`. Images are encoded as NumPy arrays; labels are an array of digits from 0 to 9; images and labels correspond one-to-one.

A second **NOTE** introduces **NumPy**: a highly popular Python library for numerical computation that you will meet constantly. It is rarely used to *implement* modern ML algorithms because it lacks GPU and autodifferentiation support, but NumPy arrays are the common **numerical data exchange format** — as here, for MNIST digits and labels.

Inspecting the training data in an interactive session: `train_images.shape` is `(60000, 28, 28)`, `len(train_labels)` is `60000`, and `train_labels` prints as `array([5, 0, 4, ..., 5, 6, 8], dtype=uint8)`. The test data: `test_images.shape` is `(10000, 28, 28)`, `len(test_labels)` is `10000`, and `test_labels` is `array([7, 2, 1, ..., 4, 5, 6], dtype=uint8)`.

The page ends by starting to describe the **workflow**: first, feed the network the training data, `train_images` and `train_labels`; the network will learn to associate images and labels; then (continuing on p.43) ask it to predict on `test_images` and verify those predictions against `test_labels`. Vocabulary: a class is a category, a sample is a data point, a label is the class of a specific sample. MNIST is preloaded in Keras; `mnist.load_data()` returns `((train_images, train_labels), (test_images, test_labels))` as NumPy arrays. `train_images.shape` is (60000, 28, 28) with 60,000 labels; `test_images.shape` is (10000, 28, 28) with 10,000 labels; labels are uint8 digits 0–9, one per image. NumPy is the numerical data exchange format of the ML world, but it lacks GPU and autodifferentiation support, so it is rarely used to implement modern ML algorithms. The workflow: train on the training images and labels, then predict on the test images and verify against the test labels.

title: Class, sample, label
text: In a classification problem, a class is a category, a sample is a data point, and a label is the class associated with a specific sample. Samples are the questions, labels are the answer key, classes are the set of possible answers. For MNIST, classes are the integers 0–9, samples are 28 × 28 `uint8` images, and labels form a `uint8` array aligned one-to-one with the images along the samples axis. `train_labels[0]` is 5, so the first training sample `train_images[0]` depicts the digit 5.

title: NumPy as a data exchange format
text: NumPy is the standard Python library for numerical computation; its arrays are the common format for exchanging numerical data between libraries, though it lacks GPU and autodifferentiation support and so is rarely used to implement modern ML algorithms. NumPy is the container everyone agrees on; the heavy lifting happens in frameworks built for GPUs and gradients. Keras accepts NumPy arrays as inputs and labels (as in Listing 2.1) and converts them internally to the backend framework's tensors. MNIST digits and labels are handed to the model as NumPy arrays.

title: Building the MNIST network: layers and the compilation step
text:
Defining a two-layer Dense network for MNIST with `keras.Sequential`, the idea of a layer as a data filter, and the three ingredients chosen at compilation: loss function, optimizer and metrics. A neural network is a chain of layers that progressively distill data into more useful representations; before it can learn, it must be compiled with a loss function (how to measure error), an optimizer (how to update the weights) and metrics (what to monitor). This page finishes stating the workflow of the first example (train on `train_images`/`train_labels`, then predict on `test_images` and compare against `test_labels`) and then builds the network in **Listing 2.2**: a `keras.Sequential` model holding two `layers.Dense` layers, the first with 512 units and a `relu` activation, the second with 10 units and a `softmax` activation.

The authors then introduce the central abstraction of the chapter: the **layer**. A layer is described as a *filter for data*: data goes in and comes out in a more useful form. Layers *extract representations* from their inputs, ideally representations that are more meaningful for the task. Deep learning mostly consists of chaining simple layers so that the chain performs *progressive data distillation*; the model is compared to a **sieve** made of a succession of increasingly refined filters.

Applied to Listing 2.2: the model is a sequence of two `Dense` (densely connected, a.k.a. fully connected) layers. The last one is a *10-way softmax classification layer*: it returns an array of 10 probability scores that sum to 1, each being the probability that the current image belongs to one of the 10 digit classes.

To make the model trainable, three more choices are made in the **compilation step**:

- a **loss function**, which lets the model measure its performance on the training data and so steer itself in the right direction;
- an **optimizer**, the mechanism by which the model updates itself from the training data it sees;
- **metrics** to monitor during training and testing; here only **accuracy**, the fraction of correctly classified images.

The authors postpone the exact meaning of loss and optimizer to the next two chapters (this one and chapter 3). **Listing 2.3** (the compilation step) starts at the bottom of the page with `model.compile(optimizer="adam", ...` and continues on p.44. A layer is a data filter that extracts a more useful representation; a deep model is a chain of such filters performing progressive data distillation. Listing 2.2 builds a `Sequential` model of two `Dense` layers: 512 units with relu, then 10 units with softmax. A 10-way softmax output layer returns 10 probabilities summing to 1, one per digit class. Compilation fixes three things: the loss function (how performance is measured), the optimizer (how weights are updated) and the metrics (what is monitored, here accuracy). The compile step in Listing 2.3 starts with `optimizer="adam"` and continues on the next page.

chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
section: 2.1 A first look at a neural network

title: Layer
text: The core building block of a neural network: a data-processing module that takes data in and returns it transformed into a (hopefully) more useful representation. A filter or sieve stage: raw data goes in, something more refined for the task comes out. Stack several and the chain progressively distills the information that matters. A layer is a function from input tensors to output tensors, typically parameterized by weight tensors learned during training. A `Dense` layer computes `activation(dot(input, W) + b)`. `layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` maps each 784-value image vector to a 512-value feature vector.
snippet: The core building block of a neural network: a data-processing module that takes data in and returns it transformed into a hopefully more useful representation.
chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
section: 2.1 A first look at a neural network

title: Dense (fully connected) layer
text: A layer in which every output unit is connected to every input value by a learned weight, plus a bias, followed by an activation function. Each of the layer's units looks at the entire input and computes one weighted 'opinion' about it; 512 units give 512 opinions. `output = activation(dot(input, W) + b)`, with `W` of shape `(input_dim, units)` and `b` of shape `(units,)`. Parameter count: `input_dim * units + units`. With a 784-dimensional input, `Dense(512)` has 784*512 + 512 = 401,920 parameters; `Dense(10)` after it has 512*10 + 10 = 5,130.
snippet: A layer in which every output unit is connected to every input value by a learned weight, plus a bias, followed by an activation function.
chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
section: 2.1 A first look at a neural network

title: Sequential model
text: A Keras model that is a plain stack of layers, each feeding the next, mapping a single input to a single output. A pipeline: the output of layer 1 is the input of layer 2, and so on. `keras.Sequential([layer1, layer2, ...])`. Input shapes are inferred the first time data flows through, so Listing 2.2 does not state the 784-dimensional input shape. Listing 2.2: `keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(512, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])`.
snippet: A Keras model that is a plain stack of layers, each feeding the next, mapping a single input to a single output.
chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
section: 2.1 A first look at a neural network

title: Softmax classification layer
text: A final layer with as many units as classes and a softmax activation, so its output is a probability distribution over the classes. Turn 10 raw scores into 10 shares of a single unit of confidence that add up to 1. `softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j)`. Every output is in (0, 1) and the outputs sum to exactly 1; the largest score corresponds to the largest logit. On p.44 the first test digit gets probability 0.99999106 at index 7, so the model predicts a 7.
snippet: A final layer with as many units as classes and a softmax activation, so its output is a probability distribution over the classes.

title: Loss function
text: How the model measures its performance on the training data, and therefore how it can steer itself in the right direction. A score of 'how wrong was I?' that training tries to drive down. A differentiable scalar function of predictions and targets; its gradient with respect to the weights is what the optimizer uses. For MNIST, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` (p.44) between the softmax output and the integer label.

title: Optimizer
text: The mechanism through which the model updates itself based on the training data it sees, to improve its performance. The part that turns 'I was wrong by this much' into 'nudge these weights this way'. An update rule applied to the weights using the loss gradient, e.g. SGD, RMSprop or Adam (used here as `optimizer="adam"`). `model.compile(optimizer="adam", ...)` in Listing 2.3.

title: Compile, preprocess, fit and predict on MNIST
text:
Finishing the compile call (loss and metrics), reshaping and rescaling the MNIST images, training with `fit()` for 5 epochs in batches of 128, and reading the probability vector returned by `predict()`. Training a Keras model is a short pipeline: compile with loss/metrics, turn the raw `uint8` images into flat `float32` vectors in [0, 1], call `fit()`, then call `predict()` and interpret the 10 softmax probabilities per image. The page opens with the tail of **Listing 2.3**: `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` and `metrics=["accuracy"]`, completing the compile call started on p.43 (the optimizer was `"adam"`).

Next comes **preprocessing**. The training images were stored as a `uint8` array of shape `(60000, 28, 28)` with values in `[0, 255]`. **Listing 2.4** reshapes them to `(60000, 28 * 28)`, i.e. one flat 784-vector per image, converts to `float32`, and divides by 255 so all values lie in `[0, 1]`. The same is done for the 10,000 test images. This gives the model the shape it expects and a well-scaled input range.

**Listing 2.5** trains the model with a single call: `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128)`. The authors describe this as *fitting* the model to its training data. During training two quantities are displayed: the loss over the training data and the accuracy over the training data; the model quickly reaches 0.989 (98.9 %) training accuracy.

With a trained model, **Listing 2.6** predicts class probabilities for *new* digits: `test_digits = test_images[0:10]`, `predictions = model.predict(test_digits)`. `predictions[0]` is a 10-element `float32` array; entry `i` is the probability that `test_digits[0]` belongs to class `i`. The largest entry, 9.9999106e-01 (almost 1), is at index 7, so the model says the first test digit is a 7. The page ends mid-sentence; p.45 checks this against the test label and evaluates on the full test set. `compile()` is completed with `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` (for integer labels and softmax outputs) and `metrics=["accuracy"]`. Images are reshaped from (60000, 28, 28) uint8 to (60000, 784) float32 and divided by 255 so values lie in [0, 1]; the test set gets the identical treatment. `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128)` trains the model; it prints training loss and accuracy and reaches 98.9 % training accuracy. `model.predict()` returns a 10-probability vector per image; the index of the largest value (7 for the first test digit, with probability 0.99999106) is the predicted class. Predictions are made on test images, i.e. data the model never saw during training.

text: Transforming raw input data into the shape, dtype and value range the model expects before training. Flatten each picture into one long list of numbers and shrink the numbers from 0-255 to 0-1 so the network starts from well-behaved inputs. `reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` turns each 28x28 grid into a 784-vector; `astype("float32") / 255` converts to floating point and scales into [0, 1]. Listing 2.4 applies the same operations to the 60,000 training and 10,000 test images.

section: 2.1 A first look at a neural network

title: Sparse categorical cross-entropy loss
text: The loss used for multiclass classification with integer labels; it measures how far the predicted probability distribution is from the true class. Penalize the model by how little probability it gave to the correct digit. For a sample with true class `y` and predicted probabilities `p`, the loss is `-log p[y]`. 'Sparse' means the labels are integers (0-9) rather than one-hot vectors. If the model assigns probability 0.99999106 to the true class 7, the loss is -log(0.99999106) ≈ 8.9e-6, nearly zero.
snippet: The loss used for multiclass classification with integer labels; it measures how far the predicted probability distribution is from the true class.

title: Epoch and batch size
text: An epoch is one full pass over the training data; the batch size is the number of samples processed per weight update. Read the whole textbook five times (epochs), studying 128 pages at a time (batches) and adjusting your understanding after each chunk. With 60,000 samples and `batch_size=128`, each epoch has ceil(60000 / 128) = 469 updates, so 5 epochs perform 2,345 gradient updates (p.76). `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128)`.
snippet: An epoch is one full pass over the training data; the batch size is the number of samples processed per weight update.

Press 'learn': the model iterates over the data, measuring the loss and updating its weights, printing loss and metrics as it goes. Iterates `epochs` times over the data in mini-batches of `batch_size`; for each batch computes the loss gradient with backpropagation and moves the weights (p.76). title: predict() and reading softmax outputs
text: The Keras method that returns the model's outputs for a batch of new inputs; for this model, a (n, 10) array of class probabilities. Ask the trained model 'what is this?' and get ten probabilities, one per digit, that add up to one. `model.predict(test_digits)` with `test_digits` of shape (10, 784) returns shape (10, 10). The predicted class is the index of the maximum entry. `predictions[0]` has 9.9999106e-01 at index 7, so the first test digit is predicted to be a 7.

title: Evaluating on the test set, overfitting, and what a tensor is
text:
Closing the first MNIST example (argmax of a prediction, checking the label, `model.evaluate()` giving 97.8 % test accuracy, the training/test gap named overfitting), then opening section 2.2 with the definition of a tensor as a container for numbers generalizing matrices to any number of axes. A model's real quality is its accuracy on data it never saw; the gap between 98.9 % training and 97.8 % test accuracy is overfitting. All the data flowing through such a model is stored in tensors, multidimensional arrays that generalize matrices. The page completes the first example. `predictions[0].argmax()` returns 7 and `predictions[0][7]` is 0.99999106; `test_labels[0]` is also 7, so the prediction for the first test digit is correct.

To measure how good the model is on average over *never-before-seen* digits, **Listing 2.7** calls `model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)`, which returns the test loss and test accuracy; the accuracy prints as `0.9785`. The authors point out that 97.8 % on the test set is *almost double the error rate* of the training set (98.9 % accuracy, i.e. 1.1 % error vs 2.2 %). This gap is an example of **overfitting**: machine learning models tend to perform worse on new data than on their training data. Overfitting is a central topic of chapter 5.

This concludes the first example: a neural network that classifies handwritten digits in fewer than 15 lines of Python. The rest of this chapter and the next will explain every moving piece: **tensors** (the data-storing objects that go into the model), **tensor operations** (what layers are made of), and **gradient descent** (how the model learns from training examples).

Section **2.2, Data representations for neural networks**, begins. The MNIST example started from multidimensional NumPy arrays, also called *tensors*; all current machine learning systems use tensors as their basic data structure, so fundamental that TensorFlow is named after them. A tensor is, at its core, a container for data, usually numerical data: a container for numbers. Matrices are rank-2 tensors; tensors generalize matrices to an arbitrary number of dimensions, where in tensor language a dimension is usually called an *axis*. The details may look abstract, but manipulating tensors will be the bread and butter of any machine learning code the reader writes. `predictions[0].argmax()` is 7 and `test_labels[0]` is 7: the first test digit is classified correctly. `model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)` returns the test loss and accuracy; test accuracy is 0.9785. 97.8 % test accuracy vs 98.9 % training accuracy is almost double the error rate: this gap is overfitting, a central topic of chapter 5. The whole example took fewer than 15 lines; the rest of the chapter explains tensors, tensor operations and gradient descent. A tensor is a container for numbers that generalizes matrices (rank-2 tensors) to any number of axes; manipulating tensors is the bread and butter of machine learning code.

chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks

title: Scalars, vectors and matrices: tensors of rank 0, 1 and 2
text:
The lowest-rank tensors, shown as NumPy arrays: a scalar (0 axes), a vector (1 axis), a matrix (2 axes), the `ndim` attribute as the rank, and the warning not to confuse a 5-dimensional vector with a 5D (rank-5) tensor. Rank is the number of axes of a tensor. A scalar has rank 0, a vector rank 1 and a matrix rank 2; 'dimension' is ambiguous (entries along an axis vs number of axes), so the book prefers 'rank' for the number of axes. The page walks up the first three ranks of tensors with NumPy examples.

**2.2.1 Scalars (rank-0 tensors).** A tensor holding a single number is a *scalar* (also scalar tensor, rank-0 tensor, 0D tensor). In NumPy a `float32` or `float64` number is a scalar tensor. The `ndim` attribute gives the number of axes; a scalar has `ndim == 0`. The number of axes is also called the *rank*. Example: `x = np.array(12)` prints as `array(12)` and `x.ndim` is `0`.

**2.2.2 Vectors (rank-1 tensors).** An array of numbers is a *vector* (rank-1 tensor, 1D tensor); it has exactly one axis. Example: `x = np.array([12, 3, 6, 14, 7])`, `x.ndim` is `1`. This vector has five entries, so it is a *5-dimensional vector*. The authors warn: do not confuse a 5D vector with a 5D tensor. A 5D vector has one axis with five dimensions along it; a 5D tensor has five axes, each of any length. *Dimensionality* can mean either the number of entries along an axis or the number of axes, which is confusing; for the latter it is more correct to say *tensor of rank 5*, although '5D tensor' remains common.

**2.2.3 Matrices (rank-2 tensors).** An array of vectors is a *matrix* (rank-2 tensor, 2D tensor) with two axes, usually called rows and columns; visually a rectangular grid of numbers. The page ends with the NumPy matrix `x = np.array([[5, 78, 2, 34, 0], [6, 79, 3, 35, 1], [7, 80, 4, 36, 2]])`, a 3 x 5 grid; p.47 continues by naming its rows and columns and showing `ndim == 2`. A scalar is a rank-0 tensor (one number, `ndim == 0`); a vector is rank 1 (one axis); a matrix is rank 2 (rows and columns). Rank means number of axes and is read from NumPy's `ndim` attribute. '5-dimensional vector' means five entries along one axis; '5D tensor' means five axes; say 'tensor of rank 5' to be unambiguous. A matrix is an array of vectors: a list of equal-length lists in NumPy, such as the 3 x 5 example on the page. Each tensor rank is built by packing tensors of the previous rank into a new array.

title: Rank, indices and the three lowest-rank tensors
text: x = np.array(12) / x.ndim -> 0;  x = np.array([12, 3, 6, 14, 7]) / x.ndim -> 1;  x = np.array([[5, 78, 2, 34, 0], [6, 79, 3, 35, 1], [7, 80, 4, 36, 2]]) (rank 2) \begin{aligned} &\text{scalar: } x \in \mathbb{R}, && \text{rank } 0, && \text{no index} \\ &\text{vector: } x_i,\; i = 0,\dots,4, && \text{rank } 1, && \text{one index} \\ &\text{matrix: } x_{ij},\; i = 0,1,2;\; j = 0,\dots,4, && \text{rank } 2, && \text{two indices} \end{aligned} Make precise what 'rank' counts: the number of independent indices, not the number of entries. title: Rank-3 and higher tensors; the three key attributes: rank, shape, dtype
text:
Rows and columns of a matrix; building a rank-3 tensor by packing matrices (and rank 4, 5 by packing further); the three attributes that define any tensor: number of axes (rank/`ndim`), shape (tuple of sizes per axis) and data type (`dtype`). Any tensor is completely described by its rank, its shape and its dtype. Higher-rank tensors are built by packing lower-rank ones, and deep learning mostly uses ranks 0 to 4 (5 for video). The page completes the matrix example of p.46: `x.ndim` is `2`. The entries along the first axis are the **rows** and along the second axis the **columns**: `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]` is the first row and `[5, 6, 7]` the first column.

**2.2.4 Rank-3 tensors and higher-rank tensors.** Packing such matrices into a new array gives a **rank-3 tensor** (3D tensor), which can be pictured as a *cube of numbers*. The example packs three copies of the 3 x 5 matrix, giving `x.ndim == 3`. Packing rank-3 tensors yields a rank-4 tensor, and so on. In deep learning you generally manipulate tensors of rank 0 to 4, up to 5 for video data.

**2.2.5 Key attributes.** A tensor is defined by three key attributes:

- **Number of axes (rank)**: a rank-3 tensor has three axes, a matrix two. Called `ndim` in NumPy, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch.
- **Shape**: a tuple of integers giving how many dimensions the tensor has along each axis. The matrix example has shape `(3, 5)`, the rank-3 example `(3, 3, 5)`; a vector has a one-element shape such as `(5,)`; a scalar has the empty shape `()`.
- **Data type** (`dtype`): the type of the data in the tensor, e.g. `float16`, `float32`, `float64`, `uint8`, `bool`; in TensorFlow also `string` tensors.

To make this concrete the authors turn back to the MNIST data: the page ends by announcing the reload of the dataset, whose `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` are inspected on p.48. In a matrix, the first axis holds the rows and the second the columns: `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]` is the first row, `[5, 6, 7]` the first column. Packing matrices gives a rank-3 tensor (a cube of numbers); packing again gives rank 4, and so on. Deep learning uses ranks 0 to 4, 5 for video. A tensor is defined by three attributes: rank (`ndim`), shape (a tuple with one size per axis) and dtype. Shapes: scalar `()`, vector `(5,)`, matrix `(3, 5)`, the page's rank-3 example `(3, 3, 5)`. Common dtypes are float16, float32, float64, uint8 and bool; TensorFlow also has string tensors.

title: The MNIST tensor: rank 3, shape (60000, 28, 28), dtype uint8
text:
Reading the three key attributes off the real MNIST training tensor (`ndim` 3, `shape` (60000, 28, 28), `dtype` uint8), interpreting it as 60,000 grayscale 28 x 28 matrices with values 0-255, and displaying one digit with Matplotlib (Listing 2.8, Figure 2.2) alongside its label. The abstract attributes rank, shape and dtype become concrete on the MNIST data: a rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers is an array of 60,000 image matrices, and selecting `train_images[4]` yields one 28 x 28 matrix that renders as the digit 9, whose label `train_labels[4]` is 9. The page applies the three key attributes of p.47 to the MNIST data. First the dataset is loaded again with `from keras.datasets import mnist` and `(train_images, train_labels), (test_images, test_labels) = mnist.load_data()`.

Then the attributes of `train_images` are read one by one: `train_images.ndim` is `3`; `train_images.shape` is `(60000, 28, 28)`; `train_images.dtype` is `uint8`. The authors interpret this: a **rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers**, more precisely an array of **60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers**, each matrix being a **grayscale image** with coefficients between 0 and 255.

**Listing 2.8** displays the fourth digit of this tensor with Matplotlib (part of the standard scientific Python suite): `digit = train_images[4]`, then `plt.imshow(digit, cmap=plt.cm.binary)` and `plt.show()`. **Figure 2.2** shows the result: a handwritten 9 on a 28 x 28 pixel grid, with pixel coordinates 0-25 marked on the axes.

Naturally, the corresponding label is just the integer 9: `train_labels[4]` returns `9`. The image and label arrays are aligned by index, which is the one-to-one correspondence stated on p.42. The next page (p.49) generalizes `train_images[i]` to tensor slicing and introduces the samples axis and data batches. `train_images` has `ndim` 3, `shape` (60000, 28, 28) and `dtype` uint8: a rank-3 tensor of 8-bit integers. Read together, the attributes mean 60,000 grayscale images, each a 28 x 28 matrix of integers between 0 and 255. `train_images[4]` selects one sample along the first axis, giving a (28, 28) matrix that `plt.imshow(digit, cmap=plt.cm.binary)` renders as the digit 9 (Figure 2.2). `train_labels[4]` is 9: images and labels are aligned by index. Inspecting `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` is the first step in understanding any data tensor.

title: Tensor slicing in NumPy and the samples axis
text:
Selecting sub-tensors with NumPy slicing syntax (start:stop per axis, `:` for a whole axis, negative indices), and the convention that axis 0 of any data tensor is the samples axis along which data is cut into batches. A slice like `train_images[10:100, 7:-7, 7:-7]` picks a contiguous range along every axis independently; the first axis of every data tensor indexes samples, and deep learning models consume those samples in fixed-size batches rather than all at once. This page closes section 2.2's tour of tensor attributes with two short subsections.

**2.2.6 Manipulating tensors in NumPy.** Selecting elements of a tensor is called *tensor slicing*. The authors start from the familiar `train_images[i]` (one digit along the first axis) and generalize. `train_images[10:100]` selects digits #10 through #99 (the stop index 100 is excluded) and returns a tensor of shape `(90, 28, 28)`. This is shown to be exactly equivalent to the more explicit `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and to `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]`: each axis gets its own `start:stop` range, and a bare `:` means "the whole axis". From there, any rectangular sub-tensor can be chosen. Selecting the bottom-right 14 × 14 pixels of *all* images is `train_images[:, 14:, 14:]`. Negative indices count from the end of an axis, as in Python lists, so a centered 14 × 14 patch is `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` (rows and columns 7 through 20).

**2.2.7 The notion of data batches.** Two conventions are stated. First, in every data tensor you will meet in deep learning, axis 0 is the *samples axis* (for MNIST, a sample is one digit image). Second, deep learning models do not process the whole dataset at once; they break it into small *batches* of samples of a fixed size. The page ends by starting a concrete example with a batch size of 128, which continues on p.50 (`train_images[:128]`, then `[128:256]`, then the *n*th batch, and the term *batch axis*).

There are no formulas or figures on this page; the content is the slicing syntax itself and the samples-axis / batch convention that the rest of the book relies on (for example, `fit()` iterating over mini-batches of 128 in the first example on p.44, and stochastic gradient descent on p.67). Tensor slicing selects a contiguous `start:stop` range on each axis independently; `:` means the whole axis and trailing axes default to `:`. `train_images[10:100]`, `train_images[10:100, :, :]` and `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]` are identical and yield shape `(90, 28, 28)`; the stop index is excluded. Negative indices count from the end: `7:-7` on a 28-long axis is `7:21`, so `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` is a centered 14 × 14 crop; `[:, 14:, 14:]` is the bottom-right 14 × 14. Axis 0 of every data tensor is the samples axis. Models process data in fixed-size batches (128 in the MNIST example), each of which is a slice along the samples axis.

chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks

title: Tensor slicing
text: Selecting a sub-tensor by specifying an index or an index range (`start:stop`) along each axis of a tensor. Think of the tensor as a stack of images; slicing lets you take a contiguous run of images from the stack, and optionally a rectangular window out of each image, in one expression. A NumPy index has one entry per axis. An integer fixes that axis (removing it); `a:b` keeps indices a ≤ i < b; `:` keeps the whole axis; omitted trailing axes default to `:`; a negative bound `-k` means `n − k` for axis length n. Output size on a sliced axis is `b − a`. `train_images[10:100, 0:28, 0:28]` → shape `(90, 28, 28)`; `train_images[:, 7:-7, 7:-7]` → shape `(60000, 14, 14)`.
snippet: Selecting a sub-tensor by specifying an index or an index range start:stop along each axis of a tensor.

title: Samples axis (axis 0)
text: The first axis of every data tensor in deep learning, along which individual examples (samples) are indexed. The shape tuple reads "how many examples, then what each example looks like": `(60000, 28, 28)` is 60,000 examples of 28 × 28. Indexing starts at 0, so the samples axis is axis 0. Slices along it select examples; the remaining axes describe one example. When the tensor is one batch, the same axis is called the batch axis (p.50). For MNIST, `train_images[i]` is sample i, a `(28, 28)` image; for the actuarial dataset on p.50, `(100000, 3)` is 100,000 people each described by 3 features.

title: Data batch
text: A group of samples of fixed size (the batch size) that a model processes together in one step, obtained by slicing the samples axis. With batch size 128, batch n is `train_images[128 * n:128 * (n + 1)]`, of shape `(128, 28, 28)` (p.50). Each training step computes the loss and its gradient on one batch and updates the weights (p.67). `train_images[:128]` is the first batch; `train_images[128:256]` is the second.

title: Batches, the batch axis, and the four shapes of real-world data tensors
text:
Building the n-th batch by slicing the samples axis, the term *batch axis*, and the standard tensor shapes for vector, timeseries, image and video data, starting with vector data. Batch n of size 128 is `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]`, and axis 0 of such a batch is the batch axis; almost all data you will meet is a rank-2 `(samples, features)`, rank-3 `(samples, timesteps, features)`, rank-4 `(samples, height, width, channels)` or rank-5 `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)` tensor. The page finishes subsection 2.2.7 and opens 2.2.8.

**Batches (end of 2.2.7).** Continuing the MNIST example with batch size 128, the first batch is `train_images[:128]`, the next is `train_images[128:256]`, and the *n*-th batch is `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]` (shown with `n = 3`, i.e. images 384..511). When you look at such a batch tensor, its first axis (axis 0) is called the *batch axis* or *batch dimension*, a term you will meet constantly in Keras and other libraries.

**2.2.8 Real-world examples of data tensors.** The authors give the four shape templates that cover almost all data you will manipulate:

- *Vector data* — rank-2, `(samples, features)`: each sample is a vector of numerical attributes.
- *Timeseries or sequence data* — rank-3, `(samples, timesteps, features)`: each sample is a sequence of `timesteps` feature vectors.
- *Images* — rank-4, `(samples, height, width, channels)`: each sample is a 2D grid of pixels, each pixel a vector of channel values.
- *Video* — rank-5, `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)`: each sample is a sequence of `frames` images.

Every template begins with `samples`, the axis from p.49. The pattern is that each extra level of structure in one sample adds one axis.

**Vector data.** The most common case: each data point is a vector, so a batch is a rank-2 tensor (an array of vectors) whose first axis is the samples axis and second axis the *features axis*. First example: an actuarial dataset of people with age, gender and income; each person is a vector of three values, and 100,000 people form a tensor of shape `(100000, 3)`. The second example (documents as word-count vectors, `(500, 20000)`) is on p.51, followed by the timeseries, image and video examples on p.51-52. Batch n of size 128 is `train_images[128 * n : 128 * (n + 1)]`; consecutive batches tile the samples axis without overlap because slices are half-open. In a batch tensor, axis 0 is called the batch axis (batch dimension); it is the samples axis seen one batch at a time. Four templates cover almost all data: vector `(samples, features)` rank 2, timeseries `(samples, timesteps, features)` rank 3, images `(samples, height, width, channels)` rank 4, video `(samples, frames, height, width, channels)` rank 5. Vector data is a rank-2 tensor whose axis 0 is samples and axis 1 is features; 100,000 people × (age, gender, income) is `(100000, 3)`.

title: Timeseries and image data tensors
text:
Concrete shapes for vector data (documents as word counts), timeseries/sequence data (stock prices, tweets) with the time axis at index 1, and image data with a channels axis, in channels-last vs. channels-first layout. A sequence sample is a matrix `(timesteps, features)`, so sequence datasets are rank-3 `(samples, timesteps, features)` with time always on axis 1; images always carry a channels axis (even grayscale, size 1), placed last in JAX/TensorFlow (`(samples, height, width, color_depth)`) or right after the batch axis in PyTorch. This page continues the real-world data-tensor examples of 2.2.8.

**Vector data, second example.** A dataset of text documents, each represented by how many times each of 20,000 common dictionary words appears in it. Every document is a vector of 20,000 counts, so 500 documents form a tensor of shape `(500, 20000)`.

**Timeseries or sequence data.** Whenever time (or sequence order) matters, store the data in a rank-3 tensor with an explicit time axis: a sample is a sequence of vectors (a rank-2 tensor), so a batch is rank 3. Figure 2.3 draws this as a stack of matrices with axes Features, Timesteps and Samples. By convention the time axis is always axis 1. Two examples:

- *Stock prices.* Each minute records the current price, the past minute's high and the past minute's low: a 3D vector. A trading day has 390 minutes, so one day is a `(390, 3)` matrix, and 250 days form `(250, 390, 3)`; each sample is one day.
- *Tweets.* A tweet is a sequence of 280 characters from an alphabet of 128. Each character becomes a binary vector of size 128 (all zeros except a single 1 at the character's index), so a tweet is `(280, 128)` and one million tweets form `(1000000, 280, 128)`.

**Image data.** Images have height, width and color depth. Grayscale images such as MNIST have one channel and could be stored as rank-2 tensors, but by convention image tensors are always rank 3 with a one-dimensional color channel for grayscale. A batch of 128 grayscale 256 × 256 images is `(128, 256, 256, 1)`; a batch of 128 color images is `(128, 256, 256, 3)` (figure 2.4 on p.52).

Two layout conventions exist. *Channels-last*, standard in JAX, TensorFlow and most other tools, puts the color-depth axis at the end: `(samples, height, width, color_depth)`. *Channels-first*, standard in PyTorch, puts it right after the batch axis: `(samples, color_depth, height, width)`. The next page gives the channels-first versions of the two examples and notes that Keras supports both. A bag-of-words document dataset is vector data: 500 documents × 20,000 word counts → `(500, 20000)`. Sequence data is rank 3, `(samples, timesteps, features)`, and the time axis is always axis 1. Stock prices: 3 values per minute, 390 minutes per day, 250 days → `(250, 390, 3)`; each sample is a day. One-hot characters over a 128-symbol alphabet make a tweet `(280, 128)` and a million tweets `(1000000, 280, 128)`. Image tensors always keep a channels axis (size 1 for grayscale): `(128, 256, 256, 1)` grayscale, `(128, 256, 256, 3)` color. Channels-last `(samples, height, width, color_depth)` is standard in JAX/TensorFlow; channels-first `(samples, color_depth, height, width)` is standard in PyTorch.

title: Timeseries / sequence data tensor
text: A rank-3 tensor `(samples, timesteps, features)` in which each sample is a sequence of feature vectors; the time axis is axis 1 by convention. A deck of spreadsheets, one per sample; in each spreadsheet, rows are moments in time and columns are the measurements taken at that moment. One sample is `(timesteps, features)`; stacking samples along axis 0 gives rank 3. `x[i, t]` is the feature vector of sample i at step t. Used whenever order matters, including non-temporal sequences such as characters. Stock prices: `(250, 390, 3)` (250 days × 390 minutes × 3 prices). title: One-hot (binary) encoding
text: Representing a categorical symbol from an alphabet of size K as a length-K vector that is all zeros except for a 1 at the symbol's index. A row of K light switches, exactly one of which is on, telling you which symbol it is without ranking the symbols. For symbol index k, the vector e_k has e_k[k] = 1 and e_k[j] = 0 for j ≠ k. A sequence of L symbols becomes an `(L, K)` matrix; a dataset of N sequences becomes `(N, L, K)`. Very sparse: N·L ones among N·L·K entries. 128-symbol alphabet, 280-character tweets: each character is a `(128,)` one-hot vector, a tweet is `(280, 128)`, a million tweets `(1000000, 280, 128)`.

A color image is three stacked grayscale pictures (red, green, blue); the channels axis is which of the three you are looking at. Grayscale keeps the axis with just one picture in it. Grayscale batch of 128 images of 256 × 256: `(128, 256, 256, 1)` channels-last or `(128, 1, 256, 256)` channels-first; color: `(128, 256, 256, 3)` / `(128, 3, 256, 256)`. JAX/TensorFlow default to channels-last, PyTorch to channels-first; Keras supports both (p.52). MNIST `(60000, 28, 28)` must become `(60000, 28, 28, 1)` to be a channels-last image tensor.

chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks

title: Video tensors and the Dense layer as a tensor function
text:
Finishing the data-tensor catalogue (channels-first image shapes, rank-5 video tensors and their memory cost) and opening section 2.3: every transformation a network learns is a composition of a few tensor operations, exemplified by `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` for a Dense layer. Data can be as large as a rank-5 video tensor, yet what a network does to it reduces to a handful of tensor operations; a `Dense(512, activation="relu")` layer is just the function `relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` with its own matrix `W` and vector `b`. **Channels-first examples.** In the channels-first convention, the two image batches of p.51 become `(128, 1, 256, 256)` and `(128, 3, 256, 256)`. Keras supports both formats.

**Video data.** Video is one of the few real-world data types that needs rank-5 tensors. A video is a sequence of frames and each frame is a color image. A frame is a rank-3 tensor `(height, width, color_depth)`, a sequence of frames is rank 4 `(frames, height, width, color_depth)`, and a batch of videos is rank 5 `(samples, frames, height, width, color_depth)`. Figure 2.4, placed alongside, draws the rank-4 image tensor with axes Color channels, Height, Width and Samples. Worked example: a 60-second 144 × 256 YouTube clip sampled at 4 frames per second has 240 frames; a batch of four such clips is `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`, a total of 106,168,320 values. In `float32` (32 bits per value) that is 425 MB. Real videos are far lighter because they are not stored as `float32` and are heavily compressed (e.g. MPEG).

**2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations.** Just as any computer program reduces to a small set of binary operations on binary inputs (`AND`, `OR`, `NOR`, …), every transformation learned by a deep neural network reduces to a handful of *tensor operations* (or *tensor functions*) on numeric tensors, such as adding or multiplying tensors. The first example stacked `Dense` layers; a Keras layer instance looks like `keras.layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")`. Such a layer is a function from a matrix to a new matrix, a new representation of the input. Specifically, with `W` a matrix and `b` a vector that are both attributes of the layer:

```
output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)
```

The next page unpacks this into three tensor operations (a tensor product `matmul`, an addition, and `relu(x) = max(x, 0)`) and notes that the book will express linear algebra as NumPy snippets rather than mathematical notation. Channels-first versions of the image batches are `(128, 1, 256, 256)` and `(128, 3, 256, 256)`; Keras supports both layouts. Video is rank 5: frame `(height, width, color_depth)` → clip `(frames, …)` → batch `(samples, frames, height, width, color_depth)`. Four 60-second 144 × 256 clips at 4 fps form `(4, 240, 144, 256, 3)`: 106,168,320 values, 425 MB in float32; real videos are smaller because of dtype and compression. All transformations learned by deep networks reduce to a handful of tensor operations, as programs reduce to logic gates. A `Dense(512, activation="relu")` layer computes `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`, with `W` (matrix) and `b` (vector) stored as attributes of the layer.
snippet: Channels-first examples. In the channels-first convention, the two image batches of p.51 become 128, 1, 256, 256 and 128, 3, 256, 256. Keras supports both formats. Video data.…

title: Dense layer as a function
text: A Keras `Dense` layer computes `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` (with relu as the chosen activation), where `W` is a weight matrix and `b` a bias vector stored as attributes of the layer. Each of the 512 output units takes a weighted sum of all input features, adds its own offset, and reports it only if positive. Input `(samples, n_in)`, `W` `(n_in, units)`, `b` `(units,)`, output `(samples, units)`. The matmul mixes features linearly, the bias shifts, relu introduces nonlinearity. For the first MNIST layer n_in = 784, units = 512, so W has 401,408 entries and b 512 (my count; the book gives the formula, not the numbers). `keras.layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")` on a `(128, 784)` batch returns a `(128, 512)` matrix.
snippet: A Keras Dense layer computes output = relumatmulinput, W + b with relu as the chosen activation, where W is a weight matrix and b a bias vector stored as attributes of the layer.
