title: Unpacking the Dense layer: relu, addition, and element-wise operations
text:
The three tensor operations inside `relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`, the book's policy of using NumPy code instead of mathematical notation, and element-wise operations (relu, addition) with naive double-loop implementations versus optimized BLAS-backed NumPy. relu and addition act independently on every entry of a tensor; that independence is what makes them trivially parallel (vectorized), so in practice they are never written as Python loops but delegated to optimized NumPy/BLAS routines. **Unpacking the Dense formula.** `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` (p.52) contains three tensor operations: a tensor product (`matmul`) between the input tensor and the tensor `W`; an addition (`+`) between the resulting matrix and the vector `b`; and a `relu` operation, where `relu(x)` is `max(x, 0)` and "relu" stands for *REctified Linear Unit*.

**NOTE on notation.** Although the section is entirely linear algebra, the book contains no mathematical notation. The author has found that programmers without a mathematical background grasp these concepts more readily as short Python snippets than as equations, so NumPy code is used throughout.

**2.3.1 Element-wise operations.** relu and addition are *element-wise* operations: they are applied independently to each entry of the tensors involved. This makes them highly amenable to massively parallel, *vectorized* implementations (a term from the vector-processor supercomputers of 1970-1990). A naive Python implementation uses `for` loops:

- `naive_relu(x)` asserts `x` is rank 2, copies it (so the input is not overwritten), and sets `x[i, j] = max(x[i, j], 0)` for every `i`, `j`.
- `naive_add(x, y)` asserts both are rank 2 with identical shapes, copies `x`, and does `x[i, j] += y[i, j]` for every entry.

Element-wise multiplication, subtraction and so on follow the same principle.

**In practice.** With NumPy arrays these operations are available as well-optimized built-in functions that delegate the heavy lifting to a *Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms* (BLAS) implementation. The sentence continues on p.54: BLAS are low-level, highly parallel, efficient routines usually written in Fortran or C, and the next page times `z = x + y` / `np.maximum(z, 0.)` against the naive loops (0.02 s versus 2.45 s). The Dense layer formula contains exactly three tensor operations: a tensor product `matmul(input, W)`, an addition `+ b`, and `relu(x) = max(x, 0)` (REctified Linear Unit). The book uses NumPy snippets instead of mathematical notation: the code is the definition. relu and addition are element-wise: applied independently to each entry, which makes them ideal for massively parallel (vectorized) implementations. `naive_relu` and `naive_add` show the semantics with double `for` loops; they assert rank 2 (and equal shapes for addition) and copy the input to avoid overwriting it. In practice, NumPy's optimized built-ins, backed by BLAS routines in Fortran or C, do the work; the naive loops are for understanding only.
snippet: Unpacking the Dense formula. output = relumatmulinput, W + b p.52 contains three tensor operations: a tensor product matmul between the input tensor and the tensor W; an addition…

title: relu (REctified Linear Unit)
text: The element-wise function relu(x) = max(x, 0): positive entries pass through, negative entries become 0. A one-way valve: lets positive signal through, blocks negative signal. Applied independently to every tensor entry. Piecewise linear with a kink at 0; cheap to compute; used as the activation of hidden Dense layers in the book's first model. relu([[-1.5, 2.0], [0.0, -0.3]]) = [[0, 2.0], [0, 0]]; `naive_relu` computes this with a double loop.
snippet: The element-wise function relux = maxx, 0: positive entries pass through, negative entries become 0.

title: Element-wise operation
text: An operation applied independently to each entry of the tensor(s) involved, such as relu, addition, subtraction or multiplication of same-shaped tensors. Like applying the same stamp to every cell of a grid; what happens in one cell never depends on its neighbours. output[i, j] = f(x[i, j]) for unary ops, or f(x[i, j], y[i, j]) for binary ops on identical shapes. Because entries are independent, the work parallelizes perfectly (vectorization, SIMD, GPU kernels). `naive_add` and `naive_relu` on this page; `x + y` and `np.maximum(x, 0.)` in NumPy.
snippet: An operation applied independently to each entry of the tensors involved, such as relu, addition, subtraction or multiplication of same-shaped tensors.

title: Vectorized implementation
text: An implementation that processes many tensor entries in parallel (or in one compiled loop) instead of one entry per interpreted step; the term comes from the vector-processor supercomputers of 1970-1990. Instead of a clerk adding numbers one pair at a time, a machine adds all pairs in one stroke. NumPy's built-in functions delegate to optimized, parallel routines (BLAS, written in Fortran/C); on GPUs, JAX/TensorFlow/PyTorch use CUDA kernels (p.54). Element-wise operations vectorize perfectly because entries are independent. `z = x + y; z = np.maximum(z, 0.)` takes 0.02 s where the naive loops take 2.45 s (p.54).

title: Vectorized element-wise ops and the start of broadcasting
text:
Why built-in NumPy element-wise operations are dramatically faster than naive Python loops, and how tensors of different shapes can still be added via broadcasting. Element-wise operations delegated to optimized BLAS (on CPU) or CUDA (on GPU) routines run around a hundred times faster than Python loops; and when two tensors have different shapes, the smaller one is broadcast — first by adding broadcast axes so its ndim matches the larger one. This page closes section 2.3.1 on **element-wise operations** and opens **2.3.2 Broadcasting**.

The opening line finishes a sentence from p.53: NumPy's built-in element-wise functions delegate the heavy lifting to **BLAS** (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms), which are *highly parallel, efficient tensor-manipulation routines typically implemented in Fortran or C*. As a result, the two lines

```python
z = x + y
z = np.maximum(z, 0.0)
```

perform element-wise addition and element-wise relu on whole arrays at once — and they are "blazing fast."

The authors then time it. With two random `(20, 100)` arrays, 1,000 repetitions of vectorized add-and-relu take **0.02 seconds**, while the same work done with the loop-based `naive_add` and `naive_relu` from p.53 takes **2.45 seconds** — over 100× slower. The same logic carries over to GPUs: when JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch code runs on a GPU, element-wise operations are executed by **fully vectorized CUDA implementations** that exploit the GPU's massively parallel architecture.

Section 2.3.2 then raises a problem: `naive_add` only handles two rank-2 tensors of *identical* shape, yet the `Dense` layer adds a rank-2 tensor (the output of `matmul`) to a vector `b`. What happens when shapes differ? Answer: *when possible, and if there's no ambiguity*, the smaller tensor is **broadcast** to match the larger one. Broadcasting has two steps; this page gives only the first — **broadcast axes** are added to the smaller tensor so its `ndim` matches the larger tensor's. The second step (repeating the smaller tensor along those new axes) and the concrete `(32, 10)` + `(10,)` example follow on p.55. `z = x + y` and `z = np.maximum(z, 0.0)` are the vectorized forms of element-wise addition and relu. Vectorized NumPy ran 1,000 add+relu iterations in 0.02 s versus 2.45 s for the naive loops — over 100× faster. The speed comes from delegating to compiled, parallel routines (BLAS/C/Fortran on CPU, CUDA on GPU). The Dense layer adds a vector to a matrix, which requires broadcasting. Broadcasting step 1: add broadcast axes to the smaller tensor until its ndim matches the larger tensor; step 2 follows on p.55.

title: Vectorized implementation
text: Implementing an operation so it applies to an entire tensor in one call to optimized low-level code, rather than with a Python loop over elements. title: Broadcasting: a worked example and a naive implementation
text:
How a smaller tensor is virtually expanded (broadcast) to match a larger one so that element-wise operations can be applied, illustrated with a (32, 10) matrix and a (10,) vector. Broadcasting adds axes to the smaller tensor and then (virtually) repeats it along those axes until both tensors have the same shape; NumPy performs this repetition at the algorithmic level without allocating a new tensor. This page completes the explanation of **broadcasting** begun on p.54. The second step of broadcasting is stated first: after new (broadcast) axes have been added to the smaller tensor, that tensor is *repeated* along the new axes until its shape matches the larger tensor.

The authors then walk through a concrete example. `X` is a random matrix of shape `(32, 10)` and `y` a random vector of shape `(10,)`. Step one: `y = np.expand_dims(y, axis=0)` inserts an empty first axis so that `y` has shape `(1, 10)`. Step two: `Y = np.tile(y, (32, 1))` repeats `y` 32 times along axis 0, producing `Y` with shape `(32, 10)` and the property that every row `Y[i, :]` equals the original `y`. Now `X` and `Y` have identical shapes, so the element-wise addition from p.53 applies directly.

A crucial implementation remark follows: no new rank-2 tensor is ever materialised when NumPy broadcasts, because that would be "terribly inefficient". The repetition is **entirely virtual** — it happens at the algorithmic level, not at the memory level. The mental model of a vector copied 32 times is nonetheless useful. To make the algorithm explicit the page shows `naive_add_matrix_and_vector(x, y)`: it asserts that `x` is rank 2, `y` is rank 1, and that `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]`; it copies `x` to avoid overwriting the input; then two nested loops add `y[j]` to every element `x[i, j]`. The vector index depends only on the column `j`, which is exactly what "repeat along axis 0" means.

Finally the page states the general rule: an element-wise operation between a tensor of shape `(a, b, … n, n + 1, … m)` and one of shape `(n, n + 1, … m)` is permitted, with broadcasting happening automatically over axes `a` through `n − 1` — i.e. the smaller tensor's shape must match the *trailing* axes of the larger one. Broadcasting = (1) add size-1 axes to the smaller tensor so ranks match, (2) repeat it along those axes to match the larger shape. Explicitly: np.expand_dims(y, axis=0) takes (10,) to (1, 10); np.tile(y, (32, 1)) takes (1, 10) to (32, 10). In a real implementation the repetition is virtual — no (32, 10) copy of y is ever stored. The naive loop x[i, j] += y[j] shows the algorithm: the vector index depends only on the column, so every row gets the same vector. Rule: shapes (a, b, … n, n + 1, … m) and (n, n + 1, … m) are compatible; broadcasting happens over axes a through n − 1.

title: Broadcast maximum, and the tensor (dot) product of two vectors
text:
A final broadcasting example with np.maximum on a rank-4 and a rank-2 tensor, then the introduction of the tensor product (matmul / dot product), starting with the product of two vectors. The tensor product (`np.matmul`, `keras.ops.matmul`, or `@`) is the most useful tensor operation; for two vectors of equal length it is the sum of element-wise products and returns a scalar. The page opens by closing the broadcasting subsection with one more example: `np.maximum(x, y)` where `x` has shape `(64, 3, 32, 10)` and `y` has shape `(32, 10)`. Because `y`'s shape matches the two trailing axes of `x`, the rule from p.55 applies — `y` is virtually repeated over the leading axes `(64, 3)` — and the output `z` has the same shape as `x`, `(64, 3, 32, 10)`. This shows that broadcasting is not limited to addition: any element-wise two-tensor operation, such as `maximum`, benefits from it.

Subsection **2.3.3 Tensor product** then begins. The tensor product — also called the *dot product* or *matmul* (short for matrix multiplication) — is described as one of the most common and most useful tensor operations. In NumPy it is `np.matmul`, in Keras `keras.ops.matmul`, and in Python the shorthand is the `@` operator: for two random vectors of shape `(32,)`, `z = np.matmul(x, y)` and `z = x @ y` are equivalent. In mathematical notation the operation is written with a dot, `z = x • y`, which is where the name "dot product" comes from.

To explain what `matmul` actually computes, the authors start with the simplest case — two vectors — and give `naive_vector_product(x, y)`. It asserts that both inputs are rank 1 and have the same length, initialises `z = 0.0`, then loops over `i`, accumulating `x[i] * y[i]`. The closing paragraph draws the two lessons from the code: the product of two vectors is a **scalar**, and only vectors with the **same number of elements** are compatible. The next page (p.57) builds matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products on top of this vector product. np.maximum(x, y) with shapes (64, 3, 32, 10) and (32, 10) broadcasts y over the two leading axes; z has x's shape. Tensor product = dot product = matmul; written np.matmul, keras.ops.matmul, or x @ y; mathematically z = x • y. For two vectors, the product is sum_i x[i]*y[i] — a scalar. Only vectors with the same number of elements are compatible. The vector product is the building block for matrix products on the next page and for every Dense layer.

title: Tensor product (dot product, matmul)
text: The operation that multiplies two tensors by summing products along a shared axis. For two vectors of the same length it is the sum of element-wise products, a scalar. Lay the two vectors side by side, multiply matching entries, and add everything up — a single number that measures how much the two vectors 'agree'. In code: `np.matmul(x, y)`, `keras.ops.matmul(x, y)` or `x @ y`. For vectors: $z = \sum_i x_i y_i$. Requires `x.shape[0] == y.shape[0]`. Generalises to matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products (p.57). `x = [1, 2, 3]`, `y = [4, 5, 6]` → `x @ y = 1·4 + 2·5 + 3·6 = 32`.

title: naive_vector_product — the dot product of two vectors from scratch
text:
def naive_vector_product(x, y):
    assert len(x.shape) == 1
    assert len(y.shape) == 1
    assert x.shape[0] == y.shape[0]
    z = 0.0
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        z += x[i] * y[i]
    return z Computes the dot product of two equal-length vectors by accumulating the products of corresponding entries into a running scalar sum. O(n) multiply-accumulate loop.

title: Matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products
text:
Extending the vector product to a matrix times a vector and a matrix times a matrix, with naive loop implementations, the shape-compatibility rule x.shape[1] == y.shape[0], and the fact that matmul is not symmetric. A matrix–vector product is a stack of vector products (one per row of x); a matrix–matrix product is a grid of vector products (rows of x against columns of y) and is defined only when x.shape[1] == y.shape[0], giving a result of shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]). The page builds up the tensor product from the vector product of p.56 in two steps.

**Matrix–vector product.** The product of a matrix `x` and a vector `y` returns a vector whose coefficients are the products between `y` and the rows of `x`. The first implementation, `naive_matrix_vector_product`, asserts `x` is rank 2, `y` is rank 1, and `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]` ("the 1st dimension of x must equal the 0th dimension of y!"). It allocates `z = np.zeros(x.shape[0])` — a vector of zeros with as many entries as `x` has rows — then for every row `i` and column `j` accumulates `x[i, j] * y[j]` into `z[i]`. A second version makes the structure explicit by reusing `naive_vector_product`: `z[i] = naive_vector_product(x[i, :], y)` for each row `i`. This "highlights the relationship between a matrix-vector product and a vector product": the former is just the latter applied once per row.

**Asymmetry.** The authors note that as soon as one operand has `ndim` greater than 1, `matmul` is no longer *symmetric*: `matmul(x, y)` is not the same as `matmul(y, x)`.

**Matrix–matrix product.** The tensor product generalises to tensors with any number of axes, but the most common application is the product of two matrices. `matmul(x, y)` is defined if and only if `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]`; the result has shape `(x.shape[0], y.shape[1])` and its coefficients are the vector products between the rows of `x` and the columns of `y`. The naive implementation begins on this page: three asserts, `z = np.zeros((x.shape[0], y.shape[1]))`, then a double loop over rows `i` of `x` and columns `j` of `y`, extracting `row_x = x[i, :]` and `column_y = y[:, j]`. The listing is cut off by the page break; the remaining lines (computing `z[i, j]` from `row_x` and `column_y` and returning `z`) are on p.58, where figure 2.5 also visualises the shape rule as a box diagram. Matrix–vector product: z[i] = row i of x dotted with y; output length = number of rows of x; requires x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]. It can be written as z[i] = naive_vector_product(x[i, :], y) — a stack of vector products. matmul is not symmetric once an operand has ndim > 1: matmul(x, y) ≠ matmul(y, x). Matrix–matrix product exists iff x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]; result shape is (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]). Each coefficient z[i, j] is the vector product of row_x = x[i, :] and column_y = y[:, j].

Lay every row of x against every column of y; each pairing gives one number; arrange the numbers in a grid with one row per row of x and one column per column of y. $z_{ij} = \sum_{k} x_{ik} y_{kj}$. Cost O(m·n·p). Non-commutative. The naive implementation loops over i and j and dots `x[i, :]` with `y[:, j]`. (2, 3) @ (3, 2) → (2, 2); (32, 784) @ (784, 512) → (32, 512).

title: Matrix product box diagram, higher-rank products, and the start of reshaping
text:
Finishing naive_matrix_product, visualising shape compatibility with the box diagram of figure 2.5, extending the product rule to higher-rank tensors, and introducing tensor reshaping via the MNIST reshape call. In a product x • y = z, the width of x must equal the height of y, and z inherits x's height and y's width; the same trailing-axis/leading-axis rule extends to tensors of any rank. Reshaping is a third essential tensor operation, already used to flatten MNIST images. The page begins with the last two lines of `naive_matrix_product` from p.57: inside the double loop, `z[i, j] = naive_vector_product(row_x, column_y)` and finally `return z`. Every coefficient of the product is thus a vector product between row `i` of `x` and column `j` of `y`.

To make shape compatibility intuitive, the authors present **figure 2.5**, a *box diagram*: `x`, `y` and `z` are drawn as rectangles — literal boxes of coefficients. `x` has shape `(a, b)` (height `a`, width `b`), `y` has shape `(b, c)` (height `b`, width `c`), and `z = x • y` has shape `(a, c)`. Because the rows of `x` and the columns of `y` must have the same size, the *width of x must match the height of y*; in the figure a highlighted row of `x` and column of `y` meet at the small cell `z[i, j]`. The authors remark that if you go on to design new machine learning algorithms you will be drawing such diagrams often.

The product then generalises to higher-dimensional tensors with the same compatibility rule: `(a, b, c, d) • (d,) -> (a, b, c)` and `(a, b, c, d) • (d, e) -> (a, b, c, e)`, "and so on". The last axis of the first operand is matched against the first axis of the second and contracted away; the remaining axes are concatenated.

Subsection **2.3.4 Tensor reshaping** opens: reshaping is a third essential tensor operation. It was not used inside the `Dense` layers of the first example, but it was used in preprocessing: `train_images = train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` turned the `(60000, 28, 28)` image tensor into a `(60000, 784)` matrix before it was fed to the model. The definition (same coefficients, rearranged to a target shape) and examples follow on p.59. naive_matrix_product ends with z[i, j] = naive_vector_product(row_x, column_y); return z — every cell is a dot product. Figure 2.5: x (a, b), y (b, c), z (a, c); the width of x must match the height of y; a row of x and a column of y meet at z[i, j]. Higher-rank rule: (a, b, c, d) • (d,) → (a, b, c) and (a, b, c, d) • (d, e) → (a, b, c, e) — contract the shared last/first axis, keep the rest. Tensor reshaping is the third essential tensor operation; MNIST used train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28)) before the model, not inside Dense layers.

title: Reshaping and transposition; vectors as points and arrows
text:
The definition of tensor reshaping with a (3, 2) → (6, 1) → (2, 3) example, transposition as a special case, and the start of the geometric interpretation: a 2-D vector is a point (or an arrow from the origin) and vector addition chains arrows. Reshaping rearranges a tensor's coefficients into a new shape without changing their number; transposition swaps rows and columns. Because tensor contents are coordinates of points, every tensor operation has a geometric meaning — addition, for instance, moves a point by a vector. **Reshaping defined.** Reshaping a tensor means rearranging its rows and columns to match a target shape; naturally the reshaped tensor has the same total number of coefficients as the original. The example starts with `x = np.array([[0., 1.], [2., 3.], [4., 5.]])` of shape `(3, 2)`. `x.reshape((6, 1))` produces a single column `[[0.], [1.], [2.], [3.], [4.], [5.]]` — the six values read off row by row. `x.reshape((2, 3))` then gives `[[0., 1., 2.], [3., 4., 5.]]`: the same six values, refilled three per row. In every case the count is 6.

**Transposition.** A commonly encountered special case of reshaping is *transposition*: exchanging the rows and columns of a matrix, so that `x[i, :]` becomes `x[:, i]`. With `x = np.zeros((300, 20))`, `np.transpose(x)` has shape `(20, 300)`.

**2.3.5 Geometric interpretation of tensor operations.** Because the contents of tensors can be interpreted as coordinates of points in some geometric space, *all* tensor operations have a geometric interpretation. Addition is the first example. The vector `A = [0.5, 1]` is a point in 2-D space (figure 2.6), commonly pictured as an arrow from the origin to the point (figure 2.7). Adding a second point `B = [1, 0.25]` is done geometrically by chaining the arrows: the resulting location is the vector representing the sum (figure 2.8). Adding `B` to `A` thus represents copying point A to a new location — the sentence continues on p.60, where the displacement is described by `B` and the idea is extended to translating whole objects. Reshaping rearranges rows and columns to a target shape; the total number of coefficients never changes (3·2 = 6·1 = 2·3). Transposition swaps rows and columns (x[i, :] → x[:, i]); (300, 20) becomes (20, 300). Because tensor contents are coordinates, every tensor operation has a geometric interpretation. A 2-D vector such as A = [0.5, 1] is a point, or an arrow from the origin. Adding B = [1, 0.25] chains the arrows: A + B = [1.5, 1.25], i.e. point A copied to a new location.

title: Vector addition as translation; geometric operations as tensor operations
text:
Figures 2.6–2.9 illustrate a vector as a point and an arrow, the sum of two vectors, and translation of a whole object; the text states that elementary geometric operations (translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, …) are expressible as tensor operations, starting with translation = vector addition. Adding a vector B to a point A copies A to a new location at a distance and direction given by B; applied to every point of an object, this is a translation — moving without distortion. All elementary geometric operations can be written as tensor operations. The top of the page holds **figure 2.6** (the point A = [0.5, 1] marked in a 2-D coordinate system) and **figure 2.7** (the same A drawn as an arrow from the origin). To the right of the text, **figure 2.8** shows A, B and A + B: B is drawn both from the origin and chained from the head of A, and A is also chained from the head of B, so the two routes form a parallelogram whose far corner is A + B.

The body text completes the sentence begun on p.59: adding B to A copies point A to a new location whose *distance and direction* from A are determined by B. If the same vector addition is applied to a group of points in the plane — an "object" — you create a copy of the entire object in a new location (**figure 2.9**). Tensor addition therefore represents *translating an object*: moving it without distorting it, by a certain amount in a certain direction.

The authors then generalise: elementary geometric operations such as translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, and so on, can all be expressed as tensor operations. A list of examples begins with **Translation** — adding a vector to a point moves it by a fixed amount in a fixed direction; applied to a set of points (a 2-D object) this is called a translation. Figure 2.9 shows a red square containing the letter K shifted right and up, annotated with `[horizontal_factor, vertical_factor] + [x, y]`: every point `[x, y]` of the K receives the same displacement vector. The list continues on p.61 with rotation, scaling, linear transforms and affine transforms, ending with the observation that `y = W @ x + b` — the Dense layer — is an affine transform. Adding B to A copies A to a new location whose distance and direction from A are given by B (figure 2.8). Applying the same addition to every point of an object copies the object elsewhere: tensor addition is translation, moving without distortion (figure 2.9). Elementary geometric operations — translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, and so on — can be expressed as tensor operations. Translation = vector addition: [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor] + [x, y] for every point.

section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations

title: Rotation, scaling, linear and affine transforms as matrix products
text:
Geometric meaning of the matrix product: rotation, scaling, general linear transforms, and the affine transform computed by a Dense layer Multiplying a 2-D point by a 2 × 2 matrix rotates, scales or otherwise linearly transforms it; adding a translation vector on top gives an affine transform — which is exactly the `y = W @ x + b` computation of a `Dense` layer without activation. This page continues the list of elementary geometric operations that can be written as tensor operations, begun on p.60 with translation. Four items are covered, each as a bullet.

**Rotation.** A counterclockwise rotation of a 2-D vector by an angle θ is obtained by multiplying the vector by the 2 × 2 matrix `R = [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]`. Figure 2.10 shows a red square with the letter K being rotated by θ, with the matrix–vector product written above it.

**Scaling.** Vertical and horizontal scaling of an image is obtained by multiplying by a 2 × 2 *diagonal* matrix — a matrix whose only non-zero coefficients lie on the diagonal running from top left to bottom right. (The printed text says `S =` but the matrix itself is missing from the body; the matrix in Figure 2.11 is `[[1, 0], [0, -0.5]]`, which leaves x unchanged and multiplies y by −0.5, so the K is squashed to half height *and* flipped below the x-axis.)

**Linear transform.** A product with an *arbitrary* matrix implements a linear transform; rotation and scaling are, by definition, special cases of linear transforms.

**Affine transform.** An affine transform (Figure 2.12, on the next page) combines a linear transform (a matrix product) with a translation (a vector addition). The authors point out that this is exactly the `y = W @ x + b` computation implemented by a `Dense` layer: a `Dense` layer *without* an activation function is an affine layer.

The practical payoff is that every ingredient of the Dense layer now has a geometric reading — `W @ x` rotates/scales/shears the input space, `+ b` shifts it — which the next page (p.62) uses to show that stacking affine layers without activations collapses into a single affine layer, motivating nonlinear activations such as `relu`. A counterclockwise rotation by θ is the matrix product with R = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]. Scaling along the axes is the product with a diagonal matrix (non-zero entries only on the top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal); Figure 2.11 uses [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]], which also flips the shape. A product with any matrix is a linear transform; rotation and scaling are special cases. Linear transform + translation = affine transform, and that is exactly y = W @ x + b — a Dense layer without activation is an affine layer. Matmul and addition, the two tensor operations of a Dense layer, therefore have clean geometric meanings: deform about the origin, then shift.

title: Rotation matrix
text: The 2 × 2 matrix `[[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]` whose product with a 2-D vector rotates it counterclockwise by θ about the origin. Its columns are where the two axis unit vectors end up after turning by θ; any point is a mix of those two unit vectors, so it turns the same way. Orthogonal (R.T @ R = I) with determinant 1, so lengths and angles are preserved. Rotations compose by adding angles: R(α) @ R(β) = R(α + β). θ = 90°: R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]], so [1, 0] ↦ [0, 1] and [2, 1] ↦ [−1, 2].
snippet: The 2 × 2 matrix cos θ, −sin θ, sin θ, cos θ whose product with a 2-D vector rotates it counterclockwise by θ about the origin.

title: Scaling (diagonal) matrix
text: A diagonal 2 × 2 matrix `[[s_x, 0], [0, s_y]]`; multiplying by it scales the x coordinate by s_x and the y coordinate by s_y. No mixing between axes — each coordinate is simply multiplied by its own factor, like stretching an image with independent width and height handles. A matrix is 'diagonal' when its only non-zero coefficients lie on the top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal. Negative factors reflect; factors with |s| < 1 shrink. Figure 2.11 uses [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]]. [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] @ [2, 4] = [2, −2]: width kept, height halved and flipped.
snippet: A diagonal 2 × 2 matrix sx, 0, 0, sy; multiplying by it scales the x coordinate by sx and the y coordinate by sy.

title: Linear transform
text: A map implemented by a product with an arbitrary matrix: x ↦ W @ x. Grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin never moves; rotation, scaling and shearing are all of this kind. Beyond the book: f is linear iff f(u + v) = f(u) + f(v) and f(c·u) = c·f(u); on finite-dimensional vectors every linear map is a matrix product and vice versa. [[1, 1], [0, 1]] is a shear: it slides points sideways in proportion to their height.
snippet: A map implemented by a product with an arbitrary matrix: x ↦ W @ x.

title: Affine transform
text: A linear transform (matrix product) combined with a translation (vector addition): y = W @ x + b. Turn/stretch the shape around the origin, then slide it somewhere else. Exactly the computation of a Dense layer without activation. The affine image of a straight line is a straight line and parallelism is preserved, but the origin generally moves. With W = [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] and b = [1, 0.25], the point [2, 4] goes to [2, −2] + [1, 0.25] = [3, −1.75].
snippet: A linear transform matrix product combined with a translation vector addition: y = W @ x + b.

title: Dense layer (as an affine layer)
text: A layer computing output = activation(W @ input + b); without activation it is an affine layer. A Dense layer is a geometric transform of the input space — a linear part learned in W, a shift learned in b, and (when present) a nonlinear 'bend' from the activation. W has shape (input_dim, output_dim) in Keras' convention (`dot(input, W)` on p.52) while the geometric presentation here writes it as `W @ x`; either way the computation is the same affine map. The 512-unit Dense layer of the MNIST model maps a 784-dimensional point to a 512-dimensional one via an affine transform followed by relu.

title: Counterclockwise rotation by θ as a matrix product
text: R = [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]  (and in Figure 2.10 the matrix is shown multiplied by the column vector [x, y]) R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad R \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta \\ x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta \end{bmatrix} Shows that a rigid rotation — a purely geometric operation — is a tensor operation of the kind a Dense layer performs. The columns of R, (cos θ, sin θ) and (−sin θ, cos θ), are the images of the unit vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1). Any point is x times the first unit vector plus y times the second, so it is carried to x times the first column plus y times the second column. chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations

title: Why activations are needed; deep learning as geometric transformation
text:
Composition of affine transforms collapses to one affine transform, so Dense layers need nonlinear activations; a neural network as a chain of simple geometric transformations in a high-dimensional space Two affine transforms composed are still one affine transform (`(W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)`), so a stack of `Dense` layers without activations is just a linear model in disguise; activation functions like `relu` break this and let chains of layers implement complex nonlinear transforms. A whole network is therefore a complex geometric transformation built from simple steps. The page opens with Figure 2.12, which shows an affine transform `W • x + b` in the plane turning the square K into a sheared, shifted parallelogram.

The main bullet, *Dense layer with relu activation*, makes an important observation: applying many affine transforms in a row still yields an affine transform. With two of them, `affine2(affine1(x)) = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)` — an affine transform whose linear part is the matrix `W2 @ W1` and whose translation part is the vector `W2 @ b1 + b2`. Consequently a multilayer network made entirely of `Dense` layers *without activations* would be equivalent to a single `Dense` layer: a 'deep' network that is just a linear model in disguise. This is why activation functions such as `relu` are needed. Figure 2.13 shows `relu(W • x + b)`: the same parallelogram, but with the part below the x-axis clipped off, a non-affine result. Thanks to activations, a chain of `Dense` layers can implement very complex, nonlinear geometric transformations, giving deep networks very rich hypothesis spaces (developed further in the next chapter).

Section 2.3.6, *A geometric interpretation of deep learning*, then draws the conclusion of the whole section: neural networks consist entirely of chains of tensor operations, each a simple geometric transformation of the input data, so a neural network can be read as one very complex geometric transformation in a high-dimensional space, implemented as a series of simple steps.

The final paragraph begins a 3-D mental image: take a red sheet and a blue sheet of paper, lay one on the other, and crumple them together into a ball. The ball is the input data; each sheet is one class of a classification problem. What the network has to do (continued on p.63) is figure out a transformation that uncrumples the ball so the classes become cleanly separable again. Two affine transforms compose into one: W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2) — linear part W2 @ W1, translation W2 @ b1 + b2. Therefore a network of Dense layers without activations is equivalent to a single Dense layer: a linear model in disguise. Activation functions such as relu break this collapse (Figure 2.13 shows relu flattening part of the transformed shape) and give chains of Dense layers rich, nonlinear hypothesis spaces. A neural network is a very complex geometric transformation of the input data in a high-dimensional space, built from simple tensor-operation steps. Mental image: two sheets of paper (classes) crumpled into a ball (the data); the network must uncrumple them so the classes become separable.

title: Composition of affine transforms
text: Applying one affine transform after another yields a single affine transform: W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2). Turn-stretch-shift followed by turn-stretch-shift is just one bigger turn-stretch-shift; you could have done it in one go. Uses associativity of matmul and distributivity over addition. The combined linear part is the product of the matrices (in order W2 @ W1), the combined translation is W2 @ b1 + b2. Extends by induction to any number of affine maps. W1 = [[2, 0], [0, 1]], b1 = [1, 0]; W2 = [[0, −1], [1, 0]], b2 = [0, 1]. Then W2 @ W1 = [[0, −1], [2, 0]] and W2 @ b1 + b2 = [0, 1] + [0, 1] = [0, 2]. For x = [1, 1]: step by step gives [3, 1] then [−1, 3] + [0, 1] = [−1, 4]; the collapsed map gives [[0, −1], [2, 0]] @ [1, 1] + [0, 2] = [−1, 2] + [0, 2] = [−1, 4].
snippet: Applying one affine transform after another yields a single affine transform: W2 @ W1 @ x + b1 + b2 = W2 @ W1 @ x + W2 @ b1 + b2.

title: Activation function (why it is necessary)
text: A nonlinear function, applied element-wise after a layer's affine computation, that prevents stacked Dense layers from collapsing into a single affine map. Affine maps can turn, stretch and shift a sheet but never bend it. The activation is what folds the sheet, so that a chain of layers can make shapes a single layer cannot. relu(x) = max(x, 0) is piecewise linear but not affine: it has no representation as W @ x + b. Interleaving it with affine layers makes the composition a nonlinear function whose complexity grows with depth. In Figure 2.13, relu(W • x + b) keeps the parallelogram above the x-axis but flattens everything below it onto the axis — a result no affine map could produce from the square K.
snippet: A nonlinear function, applied element-wise after a layer's affine computation, that prevents stacked Dense layers from collapsing into a single affine map.

title: relu
text: relu(x) = max(x, 0), applied element-wise (p.53); geometrically it clips every negative coordinate to zero. A one-way gate: positive values pass unchanged, negative values become 0. Piecewise linear with slope 1 for x > 0 and 0 for x < 0. Applied to a vector it projects any point outside the non-negative orthant onto its boundary, which is what makes the lower part of the shape in Figure 2.13 disappear. relu([2.5, −1.0, 0.0, 3.1]) = [2.5, 0, 0, 3.1].

title: Deep learning as geometric transformation
text: A neural network is a chain of simple geometric transformations (tensor operations) that together implement a very complex geometric transformation of the input data in a high-dimensional space. Each layer nudges the cloud of data points a little; many nudges in sequence can reshape it drastically. f = f_L ∘ … ∘ f_1 where each f_i is an affine map followed by an element-wise nonlinearity; the data lives in R^n with n equal to the number of input features. The MNIST model maps 784-dimensional pixel vectors through a 512-dimensional space to a 10-dimensional output, one affine-plus-relu step at a time.

Classes are tangled in input space; learning means untangling them with a sequence of simple moves. Each sheet is a low-dimensional manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space; a good representation flattens and separates these manifolds (continued on p.63). Images of 3s and 8s are mixed together in pixel space; after the hidden layer's transformation they should occupy distinct, easily separated regions.

The composed map has exactly the form W @ x + b with W = W2 @ W1 and b = W2 @ b1 + b2. Nothing about it is 'deeper' than a single layer; the extra parameters are redundant. x Input vector. title: The page says a neural network can be interpreted as 'a very complex geometric…
text: The page says a neural network can be interpreted as 'a very complex geometric transformation in a high-dimensional space, implemented via a series of simple steps'. What are the simple steps, and what is the high-dimensional space for the MNIST model of p.52? The simple steps are the tensor operations of each layer — matmul (rotation/scaling/shear), vector addition (translation), and the activation (relu, a fold). For MNIST the input space is 784-dimensional (one coordinate per pixel); the first Dense layer maps it to a 512-dimensional space and the second to 10 dimensions.

title: Uncrumpling manifolds; weights, random initialization and the training loop
text:
Deep learning as incremental uncrumpling of data manifolds; the layer's weights W and b, their random initialization, and the idea of training as gradual, feedback-driven adjustment in a loop Machine learning is about finding neat representations of highly folded data manifolds, and deep learning does it by decomposing one complicated geometric transformation into a long chain of simple ones, layer by layer. Section 2.4 then asks how the weights W and b of `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` get their values: they start random and are gradually adjusted, based on a feedback signal, inside a training loop. The page finishes the crumpled-paper image begun on p.62. What a neural network must do is find a transformation of the paper ball that uncrumples it so the two classes (the red and blue sheets) become cleanly separable again (Figure 2.14, a photo of a crumpled ball turning into a flat sheet). In deep learning this is implemented as a series of simple transformations of the 3-D space — like the movements you would make with your fingers, one at a time.

The authors then generalize: *uncrumpling paper balls is what machine learning is about* — finding neat representations for complex, highly folded data **manifolds** in high-dimensional spaces, where a manifold is a continuous surface like the crumpled sheet. Deep learning excels at this because it incrementally decomposes a complicated geometric transformation into a long chain of elementary ones, which is also how a human would uncrumple a ball. Each layer disentangles the data a little, and a deep stack of layers makes an extremely complicated disentanglement tractable.

Section 2.4, *The engine of neural networks: Gradient-based optimization*, then opens by recalling what each layer of the first model computes: `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)`. Here `W` and `b` are tensors that are attributes of the layer, called its **weights** or **trainable parameters** (the `kernel` and `bias` attributes); they hold the information the model has learned from training data.

Initially the weight matrices are filled with small random values — **random initialization**. With random `W` and `b` the expression yields no useful representations; they are meaningless, but they are a starting point. What follows is gradual adjustment of the weights based on a feedback signal: this adjustment, called **training**, is the learning that machine learning is all about. It takes place inside a **training loop**, whose steps (listed on p.64) are repeated until the loss seems sufficiently low. A network's job is to find a transformation that uncrumples the data manifold so classes become cleanly separable; deep learning does it as a long chain of simple transformations, one 'finger movement' per layer. A manifold is a continuous surface like the crumpled sheet; machine learning is about finding neat representations for highly folded data manifolds in high-dimensional spaces. Each layer computes output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b); W (kernel) and b (bias) are its weights / trainable parameters and hold everything it has learned. Weights start as small random values (random initialization); the resulting representations are meaningless but are a valid starting point. Training is the gradual adjustment of weights based on a feedback signal, done in a training loop repeated until the loss seems sufficiently low.

title: Manifold (data manifold)
text: A continuous surface, like the crumpled sheet of paper, on which the data of a class lies inside a high-dimensional space. Real data is not a random spray of points; each class is a folded sheet, and different classes are sheets crumpled together. A lower-dimensional continuous surface embedded in the input space (a 2-D sheet in 3-D in the analogy; in practice a low-dimensional surface in a space of hundreds or thousands of dimensions). All 28 × 28 images of handwritten 7s form a continuous family (thicker, thinner, tilted ...) — a manifold — inside the 784-dimensional pixel space.
snippet: A continuous surface, like the crumpled sheet of paper, on which the data of a class lies inside a high-dimensional space.

title: Representation (neat vs. folded)
text: A transformed version of the data produced by a layer; a 'neat' representation is one in which the class manifolds are unfolded and separable. The same data seen in a better coordinate system, where the answer is easy to read off. The output tensor of each layer is a representation; the chain of layers produces increasingly disentangled representations until the last one is linearly separable by the output layer. After the 512-unit relu layer of the MNIST model, images of different digits should occupy distinct regions that a single softmax layer can separate.
snippet: A transformed version of the data produced by a layer; a 'neat' representation is one in which the class manifolds are unfolded and separable.

title: Weights / trainable parameters (kernel and bias)
text: The tensors W and b that are attributes of a layer and are modified by training; in Keras the `kernel` and `bias` attributes. The dials of the machine. Everything the model has learned is the current setting of these dials. For a Dense layer W has shape (input_dim, units) and b shape (units,). They appear in output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b) and are updated in step 4 of the training loop. MNIST hidden layer: W is 784 × 512, b has 512 entries — 401,920 trainable parameters.
snippet: The tensors W and b that are attributes of a layer and are modified by training; in Keras the kernel and bias attributes.

title: Random initialization
text: Filling the weight matrices with small random values before training. You have to start somewhere; a random start is as good as any because training will move you from it. With random W and b the layer's output is a meaningless but well-defined representation; training then adjusts the weights from this starting point. (Beyond the book: 'small' avoids saturating or exploding activations, and random — rather than all-equal — values are needed so that different units can learn different things.) Keras initializes a Dense kernel with a Glorot-uniform distribution and the bias with zeros (not stated on this page).
snippet: Filling the weight matrices with small random values before training.

title: Training loop
text: The loop in which the weights are gradually adjusted based on a feedback signal, repeated until the loss seems sufficiently low. Guess, measure how wrong you are, nudge the dials to be a little less wrong, repeat. Its four steps (p.64) are: draw a batch (x, y_true); forward pass to get y_pred; compute the loss between y_pred and y_true; update the weights to slightly reduce that loss. Section 2.4 is about how to do the last step. The first example trained with model.fit for 5 epochs over batches of 128 images — thousands of iterations of this loop.
snippet: The loop in which the weights are gradually adjusted based on a feedback signal, repeated until the loss seems sufficiently low.

title: The training loop and the naive way to update a weight
text:
The four-step training loop, why updating the weights (step 4) is the hard part, the inefficiency of per-coefficient trial-and-error, and the motivation for gradient descent via differentiability Training is a loop of draw batch, forward pass, compute loss, update weights; the update step cannot be done by trying values for each weight one at a time, but because every operation in the model is differentiable, the gradient tells you how to move all weights at once in a loss-decreasing direction. The page completes the description of the training loop begun on p.63. Training repeats four steps: (1) draw a batch of training samples `x` and targets `y_true`; (2) run the model on `x` (the **forward pass**) to get predictions `y_pred`; (3) compute the loss, a measure of the mismatch between `y_pred` and `y_true`; (4) update all weights so the loss on this batch decreases slightly. Repeating this drives the training loss down: the model has "learned" the mapping from inputs to targets.

The authors then rank the steps by difficulty. Step 1 is I/O code; steps 2 and 3 are a handful of tensor operations already covered in section 2.3. Step 4 is the difficult one: for a single weight coefficient, how do you know whether it should go up or down, and by how much?

A **naive solution** is described: freeze every weight except one, and try different values for it. Worked numbers: with the coefficient at 0.3 the batch loss is 0.5; at 0.35 the loss rises to 0.6; at 0.25 it falls to 0.4. So moving the coefficient by -0.05 helps. But this must be repeated for every coefficient, costing two expensive forward passes per weight, and models have thousands to billions of weights. Hence the approach is "horribly inefficient".

The better approach is **gradient descent**, "the optimization technique that powers modern neural networks". Its gist: every function used in a model (`matmul`, `+`, ...) transforms its input smoothly and continuously. For `z = x + y`, a small change in `y` gives a small change in `z`, and the direction of the change is predictable. Such functions are **differentiable**, and chaining differentiable functions yields a differentiable function. In particular, the function mapping the model's coefficients to the batch loss is differentiable, so a mathematical operator called the **gradient** describes how the loss varies as the coefficients move in different directions. With the gradient you can move all coefficients at once, in a single update, in a direction that decreases the loss.

The page closes by telling readers who already know derivatives and gradients that they may skip the next two subsections (2.4.1 and 2.4.2). Training is a loop: draw a batch, forward pass to get y_pred, compute the loss against y_true, update all weights to lower the loss a little. Steps 1-3 are I/O plus a few tensor operations; step 4, deciding how each weight should change, is the hard part. Probing each coefficient separately (0.3 -> loss 0.5, 0.35 -> 0.6, 0.25 -> 0.4, so move by -0.05) works but costs two forward passes per weight, which is hopeless for thousands to billions of weights. All model operations (matmul, +, ...) are differentiable: small input changes give small, direction-predictable output changes, and chains of such functions stay differentiable. Therefore the coefficients-to-loss function has a gradient, which describes how the loss varies in every coefficient direction and lets gradient descent update all weights at once.

title: Training loop
text: The repeated four-step procedure: draw a batch (x, y_true), run the forward pass to get y_pred, compute the loss between y_pred and y_true, update all weights to slightly reduce that loss. Rather than solving for the best weights in one shot, the model is nudged a tiny bit toward lower loss on one batch at a time; thousands of nudges add up to a trained model. Each iteration processes one mini-batch. Steps 2 and 3 are compositions of tensor operations (section 2.3); step 4 requires knowing, for each weight, the direction and magnitude of change that lowers the loss. On p.68 step 4 is refined into a backward pass (gradient computation) and an update W -= learning_rate * gradient. On MNIST (p.76), 5 epochs with batches of 128 samples means 469 iterations per epoch and 2,345 iterations in total, each one running the four steps.

title: Forward pass
text: Running the model on a batch of inputs x to obtain predictions y_pred. Data flows forward through the layers, each applying its transformation, until the output layer produces predictions. For the two-layer MNIST model this is relu(matmul(x, W1) + b1) followed by softmax(matmul(h, W2) + b2) (p.63 gives the general layer formula). It is 'merely the application of a handful of tensor operations'. Probing a weight at 0.3, 0.35 and 0.25 required three forward passes on the same batch, producing losses 0.5, 0.6 and 0.4.
snippet: Running the model on a batch of inputs x to obtain predictions ypred.

title: Gradient descent
text: The optimization technique that uses the gradient of the loss with respect to the model's coefficients to move all coefficients at once in a direction that decreases the loss. Instead of asking each weight separately 'up or down?', you compute one object, the gradient, that answers the question for all weights simultaneously, then take a small step against it. Requires the coefficients-to-loss function to be differentiable, which holds because every model operation (matmul, +, relu, ...) is differentiable and compositions of differentiable functions are differentiable. The exact update rule, W -= learning_rate * gradient, and the variants (mini-batch SGD, true SGD, batch GD) are on p.68. In the probing example the loss rises with the weight (slope about +2 per unit), so gradient descent would decrease that weight, matching the -0.05 move the authors found by trial and error.
snippet: The optimization technique that uses the gradient of the loss with respect to the model's coefficients to move all coefficients at once in a direction that decreases the loss.

title: Differentiability
text: The property of a function that transforms its input in a smooth and continuous way, so that a small change of the input produces a small change of the output whose direction can be inferred. For z = x + y, nudging y up a little nudges z up a little by the same amount; there are no jumps or kinks that would make the response unpredictable. A function is differentiable if it admits a local linear approximation (a derivative) at every point; p.65 formalizes this as epsilon_y ≈ a * epsilon_x. The composition of differentiable functions is differentiable (this is the content of the chain rule, p.70). matmul and + are differentiable; relu is differentiable everywhere except at exactly 0, which in practice does not stop gradient descent (note: this detail is beyond the book's text on this page).

title: Gradient
text: A mathematical operator describing how the loss varies as you move the model's coefficients in different directions. It is the multi-dimensional version of a slope: one number per coefficient saying how fast the loss would change if only that coefficient moved. For a scalar loss L of weight tensor W, the gradient grad(L)(W) is a tensor with the same shape as W whose entries are the partial derivatives of L with respect to each coefficient (p.66). The naive probing estimates one such entry per weight by finite differences. For the probed coefficient, a finite-difference estimate of the gradient component is (0.6 - 0.4) / 0.10 = 2, positive, so the loss decreases when the weight decreases.
snippet: A mathematical operator describing how the loss varies as you move the model's coefficients in different directions.

title: What's a derivative?
text:
The derivative of a scalar function as the slope of its local linear approximation: continuity, smoothness, the formula f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x, the meaning of the sign and magnitude of the slope, and the derivative function f'(x) A continuous, smooth function can be approximated near any point p by a straight line; the slope a of that line is the derivative of f at p, its sign tells whether f goes up or down when x increases, and its magnitude tells how fast. Subsection 2.4.1 gives a from-scratch definition of the derivative for a function `f(x) = y` that maps a number to a number (figure 2.15 shows such a curve). Two properties are used in turn.

**Continuity**: a small change in `x` can only produce a small change in `y`. Increasing `x` by a small amount `epsilon_x` produces a small change `epsilon_y` in `y` (figure 2.16, which marks both quantities on the curve).

**Smoothness**: the curve has no abrupt angles. Consequently, when `epsilon_x` is small enough, around a point `p` the function can be approximated by a straight line of slope `a`, so that `epsilon_y` becomes `a * epsilon_x`. The page displays this as

`f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x`

and immediately adds the caveat that the approximation is valid only when `x` is close enough to `p`.

The slope `a` is called the **derivative** of `f` in `p`. Its **sign** says what a small increase of `x` does: if `a` is negative, `f(x)` decreases (figure 2.17 shows this case, with the tangent line labelled "local linear approximation of f, with slope a"); if `a` is positive, `f(x)` increases. Its **absolute value** (the magnitude of the derivative) says how quickly that increase or decrease happens.

Finally, for every **differentiable** function `f(x)` ("differentiable means 'can be derived'": smooth, continuous functions can be derived) there is a **derivative function** `f'(x)` that maps each value of `x` to the slope of the local linear approximation of `f` at that point. Two examples are given: the derivative of `cos(x)` is `-sin(x)`, and the derivative of `f(x) = a * x` is `f'(x) = a`.

The next page (p.66) draws the conclusion that matters for training: to reduce `f(x)`, move `x` a little in the opposite direction from the derivative. Continuity: a small change epsilon_x in x produces only a small change epsilon_y in y (figure 2.16). Smoothness: no abrupt angles, so near a point p the function is approximately a line: f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x, valid only close to p. The slope a is the derivative of f in p: its sign says whether f rises or falls when x increases, its absolute value says how fast (figure 2.17 shows a < 0). Every differentiable function has a derivative function f'(x) giving the local slope at every x; (cos x)' = -sin x and (a x)' = a. Next page: to reduce f(x), move x a little against the derivative; this is the seed of gradient descent.

title: Derivative
text: The slope a of the local linear approximation of a smooth, continuous function f at a point p; equivalently, the ratio epsilon_y / epsilon_x for small changes epsilon_x of the input. Zoom in on the curve at p until it looks straight; the derivative is how steep that straight line is, and in which direction it tilts. f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x for x close to p. The derivative function f'(x) maps each x to the slope there; e.g. (cos x)' = -sin x, (a x)' = a. For f(x) = 3x, the derivative is 3 everywhere: increasing x by 0.1 raises y by 0.3. For cos(x) at x = pi/2 the derivative is -sin(pi/2) = -1: increasing x slightly lowers cos(x) by about the same amount.

title: Smoothness
text: The property that the curve of f has no abrupt angles, so that near any point it can be approximated by a straight line. Rounded hills rather than sharp peaks; however far you zoom in, the curve flattens toward a line. Ensures the existence of the local linear approximation f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x with a well-defined slope a. cos(x) is smooth everywhere; |x| is continuous but not smooth at 0 (note: this example is not in the book).

title: Local linear approximation
text: The straight line of slope a that matches f around a point p: f(x + epsilon_x) = y + a * epsilon_x, valid only when x is close enough to p. The tangent line in figure 2.17: it hugs the curve near p and departs from it farther away. First-order Taylor approximation; the approximation error shrinks faster than epsilon_x as the step gets smaller. If f(p) = 0.5 and a = 2, then f(p - 0.05) ≈ 0.5 + 2 * (-0.05) = 0.4, matching the probing numbers on p.64.

title: From derivative to gradient
text:
Using the derivative for optimization (move x against the derivative to reduce f(x)), then generalizing the derivative to functions of tensors: the gradient, introduced through the machine-learning example y_pred = matmul(x, W), loss_value = loss(y_pred, y_true) If you know the derivative, minimizing f(x) is a matter of stepping x a little in the opposite direction; the same works for functions of tensors, whose derivative is called the gradient, and the loss of a model is exactly such a function of the weight tensor W. The page first closes subsection 2.4.1 with the payoff of derivatives for **optimization**, the task of finding values of `x` that minimize `f(x)`. If you want to update `x` by a small amount `epsilon_x` to minimize `f(x)` and you know the derivative of `f`, 'your job is done': the derivative completely describes how `f(x)` evolves as `x` changes, so to reduce `f(x)` you just move `x` a little in the opposite direction from the derivative.

Subsection 2.4.2 then generalizes. The function on p.65 mapped a scalar `x` to a scalar `y`, a curve in a 2D plane. A function mapping a tuple `(x, y)` to a scalar `z` is a **vector operation** and plots as a 2D surface in 3D space with coordinates `x, y, z`; likewise there are functions whose inputs are matrices, rank-3 tensors, and so on. Derivation applies to all of them as long as the surfaces they describe are continuous and smooth. The derivative of a tensor operation (or tensor function) is called a **gradient**: the generalization of derivatives to functions that take tensors as inputs. Where the scalar derivative is the *local slope* of a curve, the gradient represents the *curvature* of the multidimensional surface, characterizing how the output varies when the input parameters vary.

The authors then ground this in machine learning with four ingredients: an input vector `x` (a sample), a matrix `W` (the model's weights), a target `y_true` (what the model should associate to `x`), and a loss function `loss` measuring the gap between the model's current predictions and `y_true`. Using `W` you compute a candidate prediction and its loss:

```
y_pred = matmul(x, W)
loss_value = loss(y_pred, y_true)
```

with callouts: 'We use the model weights W to make a prediction for x' and 'We estimate how far off the prediction was.'

The question becomes: how to use gradients to update `W` so that `loss_value` gets smaller? The page ends by reframing the two operations: given fixed inputs `x` and `y_true`, they define a function mapping values of `W` (the weights) to loss values, a formula that continues on p.67 as `loss_value = f(W)`. Knowing the derivative solves 1-D optimization: to reduce f(x), move x a little in the opposite direction from the derivative. A function of a tuple (x, y) is a surface in 3D; functions of matrices and higher-rank tensors follow the same pattern, and derivation applies to all of them if they are continuous and smooth. The derivative of a tensor function is called the gradient; it describes how the output varies when the input parameters vary (the book says it represents the 'curvature' of the surface). ML example: y_pred = matmul(x, W), loss_value = loss(y_pred, y_true): use W to predict, then measure how far off the prediction was. With x and y_true fixed, those two lines define a function from W to loss values, f(W); its gradient (p.67) is what tells you how to update W.

title: Gradient
text: The derivative of a tensor operation (tensor function): the generalization of the derivative to functions whose input is a tensor. For a curve the derivative is the local slope; for a surface over many input coordinates the gradient records how the output tilts along every coordinate direction at once. For loss_value = f(W), the gradient at W0 is a tensor grad(loss_value, W0) with the same shape as W whose entry [i, j] is the partial derivative of the loss with respect to W[i, j] (p.67). f(W0 + dW) ≈ f(W0) + sum of grad[i, j] * dW[i, j]. If x is a 784-vector and W is 784 x 10, the gradient of the loss with respect to W is also 784 x 10: one slope per weight.
snippet: The derivative of a tensor operation tensor function: the generalization of the derivative to functions whose input is a tensor.

title: Gradient descent (one-dimensional principle)
text: To reduce f(x), move x a little in the opposite direction from the derivative. If the ground slopes up to your right, step left; take small steps because the slope you measured is only valid nearby. x_new = x - eta * f'(x) with small eta > 0. By the local linear approximation, f(x_new) ≈ f(x) - eta * f'(x)^2 ≤ f(x). For tensors: W1 = W0 - step * grad(f(W0), W0) (p.67). f(x) = x^2, f'(x) = 2x. At x = 2.5 the derivative is +5, so move left: with eta = 0.1, x_new = 2.5 - 0.5 = 2.0 and f drops from 6.25 to 4.0 (added example).
snippet: To reduce fx, move x a little in the opposite direction from the derivative.

title: Optimization
text: The task of finding values of x that minimize the value of f(x). Searching for the lowest point of a landscape. In deep learning the landscape is the loss f(W) over the space of all weight values, and the search is done iteratively with gradients because solving grad f(W) = 0 analytically is intractable (p.67). Minimizing loss(matmul(x, W), y_true) over W for a fixed batch (x, y_true).

title: Loss as a function of the weights, f(W)
text: With the inputs x and targets y_true held fixed, the chain y_pred = matmul(x, W); loss_value = loss(y_pred, y_true) is a function mapping weight values W to a scalar loss. Freeze the data and ask: if I turned the weight knobs, how would the loss respond? That response is the function f(W). f(W) = loss(matmul(x, W), y_true), a scalar-valued function of a matrix; it is differentiable because matmul and loss are, and its gradient is defined on p.67. For a single weight, this is the probing curve on p.64: coefficient 0.25 -> loss 0.4, 0.3 -> 0.5, 0.35 -> 0.6.

title: The gradient of the loss and the update rule
text:
Defining grad(loss_value, W0) as a tensor with the shape of W whose entries are partial derivatives, the update W1 = W0 - step * grad(f(W0), W0), and why the minimum cannot be found analytically by solving grad(f(W), W) = 0 The gradient of the loss with respect to the weights is a tensor shaped like W, each entry telling how the loss responds to that one coefficient; subtracting a small multiple of it from W lowers the loss, and this iterative approach is necessary because solving for zero gradient directly is intractable for thousands to billions of parameters. The page opens with the formula `loss_value = f(W)`, annotated: 'f describes the curve (or high-dimensional surface) formed by loss values when W varies.'

Let the current weights be `W0`. The derivative of `f` at `W0` is a tensor `grad(loss_value, W0)` **with the same shape as W**; each coefficient `grad(loss_value, W0)[i, j]` indicates the direction and magnitude of the change in `loss_value` observed when modifying `W0[i, j]`. This tensor is the **gradient** of `f(W) = loss_value` in `W0`, also called the 'gradient of loss_value with respect to W around W0'.

A NOTE explains that the tensor operation `grad(f(W), W)` can be expressed as a combination of scalar functions `grad_ij(f(W), w_ij)`, each returning the derivative of `loss_value = f(W)` with respect to the single coefficient `W[i, j]` with all other coefficients held constant; `grad_ij` is the **partial derivative** of `f` with respect to `W[i, j]`.

What does the gradient represent? Just as the derivative of a single-coefficient function `f(x)` is the slope of its curve, `grad(loss_value, W0)` is the tensor describing the curvature of `loss_value = f(W)` around `W0`; each partial derivative describes the curvature of `f` in one specific direction.

The update rule follows by analogy with p.66: to reduce `loss_value = f(W)`, move `W` in the opposite direction from the gradient, for example

`W1 = W0 - step * grad(f(W0), W0)`

where `step` is a small scaling factor. This means going against the curvature, which intuitively puts you lower on the curve. The scaling factor is needed because the gradient only approximates the curvature close to `W0`, so you must not move too far from `W0`.

Subsection 2.4.3, **Stochastic gradient descent**, begins by noting that a differentiable function's minimum could in theory be found analytically: a minimum is a point where the derivative is 0, so find all such points and keep the one with the lowest value. For a neural network this means solving `grad(f(W), W) = 0` for `W`, a polynomial equation in `N` variables, `N` being the number of coefficients. Solvable for `N = 2` or `3`, this is intractable for real networks, whose parameter counts are never below a few thousand and can reach billions. The page ends there; p.68 presents the iterative alternative. grad(loss_value, W0) is a tensor with the same shape as W; entry [i, j] gives the direction and magnitude of the change in the loss when W0[i, j] is modified. Each entry is a partial derivative grad_ij: the derivative of f with respect to W[i, j] with all other coefficients held constant. The gradient describes the curvature (local tilt) of the loss surface around W0, direction by direction. Update rule: W1 = W0 - step * grad(f(W0), W0); step is small because the gradient only approximates the surface close to W0. A minimum is where the derivative is 0, but solving grad(f(W), W) = 0 for N coefficients (thousands to billions) is intractable, so training must be iterative.

title: Gradient descent update rule
text: W1 = W0 - step * grad(f(W0), W0), with step a small scaling factor: move W in the opposite direction from the gradient to reduce loss_value = f(W). Go against the curvature, which should put you lower on the curve; take small steps because the tilt you measured is only reliable nearby. Element-wise: W1[i, j] = W0[i, j] - step * grad[i, j]. To first order the loss decreases by step * sum grad[i, j]^2. The step is renamed learning_rate on p.68. title: Analytic minimization (and why it is intractable)
text: Finding a minimum by solving derivative = 0 (grad(f(W), W) = 0 for a network) and comparing the candidate points. Instead of walking downhill, solve for all the flat spots on the map and pick the lowest; this is fine for 2 or 3 unknowns but hopeless for millions. grad(f(W), W) = 0 is a system of N polynomial equations in N unknowns, N being the number of coefficients (thousands to billions). title: Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent
text:
The five-step mini-batch SGD algorithm with the backward pass and the update W -= learning_rate * gradient; the role and sizing of the learning rate (figure 2.18); true SGD versus mini-batch versus batch gradient descent; loss surfaces in high dimensions Instead of solving for the minimum, training repeatedly draws a random batch, runs the forward pass, computes the loss and its gradient (the backward pass), and moves the parameters a little against the gradient; the learning rate sets how far, and the batch size trades update accuracy against cost. Having ruled out solving for the minimum analytically (p.67), the authors return to the four-step algorithm from p.64: modify the parameters little by little based on the current loss on a random batch. Because the loss is differentiable, its gradient gives an efficient way to implement step 4; updating the weights opposite to the gradient lowers the loss a little every time. The algorithm is restated in five steps: (1) draw a batch of training samples `x` and targets `y_true`; (2) run the model on `x` to obtain `y_pred` (the **forward pass**); (3) compute the loss on the batch; (4) compute the gradient of the loss with regard to the model's parameters (the **backward pass**); (5) move the parameters a little in the opposite direction from the gradient, for example `W -= learning_rate * gradient`. The **learning rate** is a scalar factor modulating the 'speed' of gradient descent.

This procedure is **mini-batch stochastic gradient descent** (mini-batch SGD); *stochastic* refers to each batch being drawn at random (a scientific synonym of random). **Figure 2.18** shows the 1-D case: one parameter, one training sample, a loss curve, a starting point at t=0 and successive points t=1, t=2, t=3 moving down the curve, with a bracket showing the learning rate as the step size.

Choosing the learning rate matters: too small and the descent takes many iterations and may get stuck in a local minimum; too large and the updates may land at completely random locations on the curve.

Variants: drawing a single sample per iteration is **true SGD**; using all data for every step is **batch gradient descent**, more accurate per update but far more expensive. Mini-batches of reasonable size are the efficient compromise.

Finally, figure 2.18 is 1-D, but in practice gradient descent runs in very high-dimensional spaces: every weight coefficient is a free dimension, and there may be tens of thousands or millions of them. A 2-D loss surface (figure 2.19, next page) helps intuition, but, as p.69 continues, you cannot visualize the real process. Mini-batch SGD: draw a random batch, forward pass, compute the loss, backward pass (gradient with regard to the parameters), then W -= learning_rate * gradient. The learning rate is a scalar modulating the speed of descent; too small is slow and can get stuck in a local minimum, too large sends updates to random locations. 'Stochastic' refers to the random draw of each batch; figure 2.18 shows the descent for one parameter and one sample. True SGD uses one sample per step, batch gradient descent uses all data (more accurate, far more expensive); mini-batches of reasonable size are the efficient compromise. Real parameter spaces have tens of thousands to millions of dimensions; 1-D and 2-D figures are intuition aids only.

title: Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (mini-batch SGD)
text: The iterative training algorithm: draw a random batch, forward pass, compute the loss, compute the gradient of the loss with regard to the parameters (backward pass), move the parameters a little in the opposite direction from the gradient (W -= learning_rate * gradient). Walk downhill on the loss landscape one small step at a time, measuring the slope on a fresh random handful of examples each time. Each iteration uses the gradient of the batch loss as a noisy estimate of the gradient of the full training loss; 'stochastic' refers to the random draw of the batch. Variants: true SGD (one sample), batch GD (all data), mini-batch (the compromise). MNIST with batches of 128: 469 iterations per epoch, 2,345 updates over 5 epochs (p.76).

title: Learning rate
text: A scalar factor in the update W -= learning_rate * gradient that modulates the 'speed' of the gradient descent process. Stride length: how far you move for a given slope. The displacement of each parameter is learning_rate times its partial derivative, so steep directions move more. Too small: many iterations, risk of getting stuck in a local minimum. Too large: updates land at essentially random locations on the curve. learning_rate = 1e-3 in the from-scratch MNIST loop (p.80); 0.1 for the batch-trained 2-D classifier (p.96).

title: Backward pass
text: Computing the gradient of the loss with regard to the model's parameters (step 4 of the algorithm). After the data has flowed forward to the loss, the slope information flows backward from the loss to every weight. Implemented by backpropagation (p.70): the chain rule applied to the chain of tensor operations, yielding one gradient tensor per weight tensor, each with the shape of its weight (p.67). In PyTorch loss.backward() populates .grad on every tensor involved (p.103); in TensorFlow tape.gradient(loss, weights) (p.80).

title: Batch size: true SGD, mini-batch, batch gradient descent
text: The number of samples used per gradient update: one (true SGD), a mini-batch of reasonable size (mini-batch SGD), or all available data (batch gradient descent). How many examples you consult before deciding on a step: one is quick but erratic, all is careful but slow. Batch GD gives the exact gradient of the training loss but each update costs a full pass over the data; true SGD gives the cheapest, noisiest updates; mini-batches are the efficient compromise. 128 samples per batch in the MNIST example (p.44, p.76); 2,000 samples (all data) in the chapter 3 toy classifier (p.96).

title: Local minimum
text: A point on the loss curve where gradient descent with a small learning rate can get stuck because every small move increases the loss, even though lower points exist elsewhere. A dip on a hillside: a slow walker who only ever steps downhill ends up at the bottom of the dip, not at the valley floor. A stationary point (gradient zero, p.67) that is not the global minimum; figure 2.18's hump to the right of the first dip, and figure 2.20 on p.69, illustrate it. In figure 2.18, from t=3 the slope points back into the dip; the curve descends again beyond the hump.
