title: High-dimensional loss surfaces, optimizers and momentum
text:
The limits of low-dimensional pictures of gradient descent, the existence of SGD variants (optimizers), and the motivation for momentum via local versus global minima. Real networks optimize in spaces with millions of dimensions, so 1-D and 2-D pictures of gradient descent are only rough guides. SGD variants such as momentum, Adagrad and RMSprop use past updates as well as the current gradient; momentum in particular speeds up convergence and helps escape local minima, as a rolling ball does. The page continues 2.4.3 on **stochastic gradient descent**.

It opens with a caution: you can draw gradient descent over one parameter (Figure 2.18, p.68) or two parameters (**Figure 2.19**, a colored loss surface with a winding path from a *Starting point* down to a *Final point*), but you **cannot visualize** what training a real neural network looks like — there is no way to represent a 1,000,000-dimensional space in a way humans can grasp. Intuitions built from low-dimensional pictures therefore *may not always be accurate in practice*, and the authors note this has historically caused problems in deep learning research.

Next the page introduces **optimizers**. Several variants of SGD compute the next weight update by taking into account **previous weight updates**, not only the current gradient: **SGD with momentum**, **Adagrad**, **RMSprop** and others. These are called *optimization methods* or *optimizers*. The concept of **momentum** deserves special attention because many of these variants use it. It addresses two issues with plain SGD: **convergence speed** and **local minima**.

**Figure 2.20** plots loss against a single parameter value. It has a **local minimum** (moving left or right increases the loss) and a lower **global minimum**. With SGD and a small learning rate, optimization could get stuck in the local minimum and never reach the global one.

Momentum, inspired by physics, avoids this. The mental image is a **small ball rolling down the loss curve**: with enough momentum, it rolls through the shallow dip and carries on. The sentence continues on p.70, which explains that momentum moves the ball according to its current velocity as well as the current slope, and gives a naive implementation. Low-dimensional pictures of gradient descent (Figures 2.18, 2.19) are only rough guides; real training happens in spaces of a million or more dimensions. Optimizers are SGD variants that use previous weight updates, not just the current gradient: SGD with momentum, Adagrad, RMSprop, and others. Momentum addresses two problems with SGD: slow convergence and getting stuck in local minima. At a local minimum the loss rises in both directions, so small-step SGD can get stuck there instead of reaching the global minimum (Figure 2.20). Momentum works like a ball rolling down the loss curve: its velocity can carry it through shallow dips.

title: Momentum
text: Updating parameters based on the current gradient and on the previous update (velocity), by analogy with a ball rolling down the loss curve. title: Momentum in code, and the chain rule behind backpropagation
text:
How momentum modifies the SGD update, and why computing gradients of a whole network reduces to chaining the derivatives of simple operations Momentum lets the parameter update depend on the previous update as well as the current gradient, so the optimizer can roll through local minima. Then the page opens subsection 2.4.4: a neural network is a chain of simple, differentiable tensor operations, and the chain rule of calculus lets us compute the gradient of the whole chain from the derivatives of its parts. The page finishes the discussion of **momentum** that began on p.69. In the ball-rolling-down-a-hill picture, a ball with enough momentum will not get trapped in a ravine (a local minimum) and will reach the global minimum. Momentum is implemented by moving the ball according to both the current slope (interpreted as acceleration) and the current velocity (the accumulated effect of past slopes). For a parameter `w` this means the update uses not only the current gradient but also the previous parameter update. The authors give a *naive implementation*: a loop that, while the loss exceeds 0.01, reads the current `w`, `loss` and `gradient`, computes `velocity = past_velocity * momentum - learning_rate * gradient`, updates `w = w + momentum * velocity - learning_rate * gradient`, stores the velocity, and writes the parameter back. The margin callouts label `momentum = 0.1` as a constant momentum factor and the `while` loop as the optimization loop.

Subsection **2.4.4 Chaining derivatives: The Backpropagation algorithm** then opens with a confession: the earlier description "casually assumed" that a differentiable function's gradient is easy to compute. The question becomes concrete for the two-layer network: how do we get the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights? The answer is the Backpropagation algorithm.

Under the heading **The chain rule**, the authors explain that backpropagation uses the derivatives of simple operations (addition, `relu`, tensor product) to compute the gradient of arbitrarily complex combinations of them. A neural network is exactly such a combination: many tensor operations chained together, each with a simple known derivative. The first example model is rewritten as one nested expression parameterized by `W1`, `b1`, `W2`, `b2`: `loss_value = loss(y_true, softmax(matmul(relu(matmul(inputs, W1) + b1), W2) + b2))`, built only from `matmul`, `relu`, `softmax`, `+` and `loss`, all easily differentiable. The page ends by introducing the calculus identity that differentiates such chains: the **chain rule**, set up with two functions `f` and `g` and their composition `y = fg(x) == f(g(x))`. The statement of the rule itself is on p.71. Momentum updates a parameter using the current gradient and the previous update (velocity), which speeds convergence and lets the optimizer roll through local minima. In the naive code, velocity = past_velocity * momentum - learning_rate * gradient and w moves by momentum * velocity - learning_rate * gradient; momentum = 0 recovers plain SGD. Differentiability alone does not tell you how to compute a gradient; backpropagation is the algorithm that does. A neural network is a chain of atomic tensor operations (matmul, +, relu, softmax, loss), each with a simple known derivative. The whole first-example model can be written as one nested function of W1, b1, W2, b2. The chain rule, set up here for y = f(g(x)), is the calculus identity that turns the derivatives of the pieces into the derivative of the chain.

title: Momentum (in gradient descent)
text: A modification of SGD in which each parameter update depends on the previous update (a decaying accumulation called velocity) as well as on the current gradient. A ball rolling down the loss curve: the slope is its acceleration, and the velocity it has built up can carry it through small dips (local minima) and speed it along long gentle slopes. On this page: `velocity = past_velocity * momentum - learning_rate * gradient`, then `w = w + momentum * velocity - learning_rate * gradient`. The scalar `momentum` (0.1 in the snippet) controls how much past velocity is retained; 0 recovers plain SGD. If the gradient has pointed in the same direction for several steps, velocity grows and steps get larger; if the gradient suddenly flips sign at the wall of a small dip, velocity only decreases a little and the parameter keeps moving in the old direction for a few more steps.
snippet: A modification of SGD in which each parameter update depends on the previous update a decaying accumulation called velocity as well as on the current gradient.

title: Backpropagation
text: The algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter of a network by applying the chain rule to the chain of tensor operations that make up the model. Instead of differentiating the whole network as one giant formula, differentiate each simple piece and chain the results together. Requires only that every atomic operation (matmul, +, relu, softmax, loss) has a known derivative; the gradient of their composition follows from the chain rule, applied from the loss backward to the parameters. For the MNIST model, backpropagation yields grad(loss_value, W1), grad(loss_value, b1), grad(loss_value, W2) and grad(loss_value, b2) from one backward sweep.

title: Chain rule
text: The calculus identity for differentiating a composition of functions: if y = f(g(x)), the derivative of y with respect to x is the derivative of f (at g(x)) times the derivative of g (at x). A small nudge to x causes a nudge to g(x) scaled by g's slope; that nudge in turn moves f's output scaled by f's slope. Scalings multiply. On this page only the setup is given: functions f and g and the composed function fg with y = fg(x) == f(g(x)). The rule itself, grad(y, x) == grad(y, x1) * grad(x1, x), is stated on p.71. With g(x) = 2x and f(u) = u + 1, y = f(g(x)) = 2x + 1 and dy/dx = f'(g(x)) * g'(x) = 1 * 2 = 2 (this is exactly the toy graph of p.72-73).
snippet: The calculus identity for differentiating a composition of functions: if y = fgx, the derivative of y with respect to x is the derivative of f at gx times the derivative of g at x.

title: Explain the physical analogy the authors use for momentum: what plays the role of…
text: Explain the physical analogy the authors use for momentum: what plays the role of acceleration and what plays the role of velocity? The optimization process is a ball rolling down the loss curve. The current slope (gradient) is the current acceleration; the accumulated effect of past accelerations is the current velocity. Each step moves the ball according to both, so a ball with enough velocity can roll through a local minimum (ravine) to the global minimum.

title: The chain rule and computation graphs
text:
Stating the chain rule for composed functions, naming its systematic application backpropagation, and introducing computation graphs as the data structure on which automatic differentiation operates If y = f(g(x)) with intermediate x1 = g(x), then grad(y, x) == grad(y, x1) * grad(x1, x); longer chains multiply more factors. Applying this to a network's operations is backpropagation, and the natural representation for doing so is a computation graph: a directed acyclic graph of tensor operations that treats computation as data. The page opens with the code for the composed function `fg`: `x1 = g(x)`, `y = f(x1)`, `return y`. Then it states the **chain rule** in the book's notation: `grad(y, x) == grad(y, x1) * grad(x1, x)`. Knowing the derivatives of `f` and `g` separately is enough to differentiate `fg`. The name comes from what happens with more intermediate functions: for `fghj` (with `x1 = j(x)`, `x2 = h(x1)`, `x3 = g(x2)`, `y = f(x3)`) the rule reads `grad(y, x) == grad(y, x3) * grad(x3, x2) * grad(x2, x1) * grad(x1, x)`, a chain of factors, one per link. Applying this rule to compute the gradient values of a neural network is the algorithm called **backpropagation**.

Under **Automatic differentiation with computation graphs**, the authors propose the computation graph as the right mental model for backpropagation. A computation graph is a directed acyclic graph of operations, here tensor operations; figure 2.21 (p.72) is the graph of the first model. The authors call it "the data structure at the heart of the deep learning revolution" and explain why: it lets us *treat computation as data*. Once a computable expression is a machine-readable structure, other programs can take it as input or produce it as output. Two examples: a program that rewrites a graph into a large-scale distributed version of the same computation (so you never write distribution logic yourself), and a program that takes a graph and automatically generates the derivative of the expression it represents. Both are far easier on an explicit graph than on "lines of ASCII characters in a `.py` file".

To explain backpropagation concretely, the page sets up a simplified version of figure 2.21 with a single linear layer and scalar variables (figure 2.22, p.72): two scalar parameters `w` and `b`, a scalar input `x`, operations combining them into an output `y`, and an absolute-value error loss `loss_val = abs(y_true - y)`. Since we want to update `w` and `b` to minimize `loss_val`, the targets of the computation are `grad(loss_val, b)` and `grad(loss_val, w)`. Chain rule: for y = f(g(x)) with x1 = g(x), grad(y, x) == grad(y, x1) * grad(x1, x); knowing the parts' derivatives suffices. Longer chains multiply more factors, one per intermediate function, which is where the name comes from. Backpropagation is the chain rule applied to the computation of a neural network's gradients. A computation graph is a directed acyclic graph of tensor operations; it treats computation as data so programs can distribute or differentiate it automatically. The worked example uses scalars w, b, x, an output y and loss_val = abs(y_true - y); the targets are grad(loss_val, w) and grad(loss_val, b).

title: Backpropagation
text: The algorithm obtained by applying the chain rule to the computation of the gradient values of a neural network. Start from the loss and multiply local derivatives backward along the chain of operations until you reach each parameter. Equivalent to reverse-mode automatic differentiation on the model's computation graph; one backward sweep yields the gradient with respect to every parameter. On the scalar toy graph: grad(loss_val, w) = grad(loss_val, x2) * grad(x2, x1) * grad(x1, w).

title: Chain rule for two composed functions
text: grad(y, x) == grad(y, x1) * grad(x1, x) y = f(g(x)),\quad x_1 = g(x) \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{dx_1}\cdot\frac{dx_1}{dx} = f'(x_1)\, g'(x) To differentiate a composed function knowing only the derivatives of its parts. A change epsilon in x becomes a change of about grad(x1, x) * epsilon in x1, which becomes a change of about grad(y, x1) * grad(x1, x) * epsilon in y. x The input to the composed function. x_1 = g(x) The intermediate value produced by the inner function g. y = f(x_1) The output of the outer function f. \frac{dy}{dx_1} grad(y, x1): the derivative of f evaluated at the intermediate value x1. \frac{dx_1}{dx} grad(x1, x): the derivative of g evaluated at x.

title: Chain rule for four chained functions (fghj)
text: grad(y, x) == grad(y, x3) * grad(x3, x2) * grad(x2, x1) * grad(x1, x) \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{dx_3}\cdot\frac{dx_3}{dx_2}\cdot\frac{dx_2}{dx_1}\cdot\frac{dx_1}{dx}, \qquad x_1 = j(x),\; x_2 = h(x_1),\; x_3 = g(x_2),\; y = f(x_3) To show why the rule is called a chain and how it scales to arbitrarily long compositions such as a deep network. Backpropagation computes these factors from right to left in the forward order, i.e. starting at y: first grad(y, x3), then multiply by grad(x3, x2), and so on, reusing each partial product. x_1, x_2, x_3 The intermediate values after j, h and g respectively. \frac{dx_{k}}{dx_{k-1}} The local derivative of one link of the chain, evaluated at the forward-pass values. y The final output, f(x3).

title: Computation graphs of the model and of a toy example; the forward pass
text:
Drawing the two-layer model and a one-layer scalar toy model as computation graphs, running the forward pass with concrete numbers, and preparing to reverse the graph for the backward pass A model is a graph of operations fed by input nodes (data and parameters). Running the forward pass means propagating concrete values from the input nodes down to loss_val; with x = 2, w = 3, b = 1 and y_true = 4 the toy graph gives x1 = 6, x2 = 7, loss_val = 3. The backward pass will reverse every edge and ask how much each node's output varies with its input. This page is almost entirely figures. **Figure 2.21** draws the first MNIST model as a computation graph: the input `x` flows down through `dot` (with `W1`), `+` (with `b1`), `relu`, `dot` (with `W2`), `+` (with `b2`), `softmax`, and finally `loss` (with `y_true`), producing `loss_val`. Parameters (`W1`, `b1`, `W2`, `b2`) are drawn as green input circles on the left, data (`x`, `y_true`) as blue circles, and operations as grey boxes. This is the expression of p.70 drawn as a directed acyclic graph.

**Figure 2.22** is the simplified scalar graph announced on p.71: `x` and `w` feed a `*` node producing `x1`; `x1` and `b` feed a `+` node producing `x2`; `x2` and `y_true` feed `loss`, producing `loss_val`. The text then sets concrete values for the four input nodes (**figure 2.23**): `x = 2`, `w = 3`, `b = 1`, `y_true = 4`. Propagating these values through the graph from top to bottom gives `x1 = 6`, `x2 = 7` and `loss_val = 3`. This is the **forward pass**.

The last paragraph begins the next step: "reverse" the graph. For every edge from `A` to `B`, create an opposite edge from `B` to `A` and ask "How much does `B` vary when `A` varies?", that is, what is `grad(B, A)`. The sentence continues on p.73, where each reversed edge is annotated with its gradient (figure 2.24) and the chain rule is applied along paths to obtain `grad(loss_val, w) = 2` and `grad(loss_val, b) = 1`. Figure 2.21 draws the two-layer model as a computation graph: dot, +, relu, dot, +, softmax, loss, with the parameters W1, b1, W2, b2 and data x, y_true as input nodes. Figure 2.22 is the one-layer scalar toy graph: x and w -> *, then + b, then loss against y_true. The forward pass propagates input values top to bottom: with x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4 we get x1 = 6, x2 = 7, loss_val = 3. Reversing the graph creates an edge B -> A for every edge A -> B, labelled with grad(B, A): how much B varies when A varies. This is the backward pass, continued on p.73.

title: Running the backward pass: local gradients and the chain rule on the graph
text:
Annotating every reversed edge of the toy computation graph with its local gradient and multiplying along paths to get grad(loss_val, w) = 2 and grad(loss_val, b) = 1 In the backward graph each edge carries one local derivative (grad(loss_val, x2) = 1, grad(x2, x1) = 1, grad(x2, b) = 1, grad(x1, w) = 2), each justified by asking how the edge's output moves when its input moves by epsilon. The chain rule says the derivative of one node with respect to another is the product of the edge derivatives along the path linking them, which yields grad(loss_val, w) = 1 * 1 * 2 = 2 and grad(loss_val, b) = 1 * 1 = 1. The page completes the sentence from p.72: each reversed edge is annotated with `grad(B, A)` (figure 2.24), and this **backward graph** represents the **backward pass**. Figure 2.24 shows the toy graph with arrows reversed: `loss_val` points up into `loss`, `loss` into `+` via `x2` with the label `grad(loss_val, x2) = 1`, `+` into `*` via `x1` with `grad(x2, x1) = 1` and sideways into `b` with `grad(x2, b) = 1`, and `*` into `w` with `grad(x1, w) = 2`. The forward values (x = 2, w = 3, b = 1, y_true = 4) remain attached to the input nodes.

The four local gradients are each justified by a one-line sensitivity argument:

- `grad(loss_val, x2) = 1`: as `x2` varies by epsilon, `loss_val = abs(4 - x2)` varies by the same amount (since x2 = 7 is above 4).
- `grad(x2, x1) = 1`: as `x1` varies by epsilon, `x2 = x1 + b = x1 + 1` varies by the same amount.
- `grad(x2, b) = 1`: as `b` varies by epsilon, `x2 = x1 + b = 6 + b` varies by the same amount.
- `grad(x1, w) = 2`: as `w` varies by epsilon, `x1 = x * w = 2 * w` varies by `2 * epsilon`.

The chain rule, applied to the backward graph, says that the derivative of a node with respect to another node is obtained by **multiplying the derivatives for each edge along the path linking the two nodes**. For instance `grad(loss_val, w) = grad(loss_val, x2) * grad(x2, x1) * grad(x1, w)` (figure 2.25, p.74). Plugging in the edge values gives the answers sought since p.71: `grad(loss_val, w) = 1 * 1 * 2 = 2` and `grad(loss_val, b) = 1 * 1 = 1`. The backward graph reverses every edge and labels it with grad(B, A), the local derivative evaluated at the forward values. Local derivatives here: grad(loss_val, x2) = 1 (prediction above target), grad(x2, x1) = 1 and grad(x2, b) = 1 (addition), grad(x1, w) = 2 (multiplication by the input x = 2). The chain rule on a graph: multiply the edge derivatives along the path linking two nodes. Result: grad(loss_val, w) = 1 * 1 * 2 = 2 and grad(loss_val, b) = 1 * 1 = 1, the quantities gradient descent uses to update w and b. Only grad(loss_val, x2) and grad(x1, w) depend on forward values, which is why the forward pass must precede the backward pass.

title: Backpropagation as the chain rule on a graph; automatic differentiation
text:
Finishing the toy backward-pass example: the path from loss_val to w (Figure 2.25), summing over multiple paths, the definition of backpropagation, and the role of automatic differentiation in modern frameworks. Backpropagation is simply the chain rule applied to a computation graph. You multiply edge derivatives along each path from the loss to a parameter and sum over paths, working backward from the loss. Modern frameworks automate this, so you only write the forward pass. This page completes the worked example of 2.4.4.

**Figure 2.25** redraws the backward graph from p.73, highlighting in red the **path from `loss_val` to `w`**. The nodes hold the values used in the example: input `x = 2`, weight `w = 3`, bias `b = 1`, target `y_true = 4`. The operations are `*` (giving `x1`), `+` (giving `x2`) and `abs_diff` (giving `loss_val`). The edges carry the local derivatives computed on p.73:

- `grad(loss_val, x2) = 1`
- `grad(x2, x1) = 1`
- `grad(x2, b) = 1`
- `grad(x1, w) = 2`

By the chain rule, multiplying along the red path gives `grad(loss_val, w) = 1 * 1 * 2 = 2` (stated on p.73).

A **NOTE** adds the general rule: if **several paths** link two nodes `a` and `b`, you get `grad(b, a)` by **summing the contributions of all the paths**.

The authors then conclude: *that* was backpropagation. **Backpropagation is simply the application of the chain rule to a computation graph — there's nothing more to it.** It starts from the final loss value and works backward from the top layers to the bottom layers, computing how much each parameter contributed to the loss. The name comes from this: we "back propagate" the loss contributions of the nodes in the graph.

Finally, the page introduces **automatic differentiation**. Modern frameworks such as **JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch** implement it using exactly this kind of computation graph. It retrieves the gradients of arbitrary compositions of differentiable tensor operations, with **no extra work besides writing the forward pass**. The author recalls writing his first neural networks in C in the 2000s and deriving gradients by hand. With modern tools, you will never have to implement backpropagation yourself. To get grad(loss_val, w), multiply the edge gradients along the path: 1 · 1 · 2 = 2 (Figure 2.25). With multiple paths between two nodes, sum the contributions of every path. Backpropagation is just the chain rule on a computation graph, starting from the loss and moving backward from top layers to bottom layers. JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch implement automatic differentiation with computation graphs, so you only write the forward pass. You will never need to implement backpropagation by hand in this book.

title: Backpropagation
text: The application of the chain rule to a computation graph, starting from the final loss value and working backward to compute each parameter's contribution to the loss. Pass the blame backward: each node gets its share of the error from the nodes it fed into, scaled by how sensitive they were to it. For a parameter $p$: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial p} = \sum_{\text{paths } p \to L} \prod_{\text{edges } (A \to B)} \frac{\partial B}{\partial A}$, computed efficiently by visiting nodes in reverse topological order. In Figure 2.25: grad(loss_val, w) = grad(loss_val, x2) · grad(x2, x1) · grad(x1, w) = 1 · 1 · 2 = 2.

title: Looking back: network, loss, optimizer, and the MNIST input data
text:
A recap of the training loop (Figure 2.26) and a re-reading of the MNIST data-preparation code in light of what the chapter taught about tensors. A model is a chain of layers that maps inputs to predictions. A loss function compares predictions with targets to produce a loss score, and an optimizer uses that score to update the layers' weights. The MNIST images enter this loop as float32 tensors of shape (60000, 784) and (10000, 784). Section **2.5 Looking back at our first example** begins here. The authors say that what was a "magical black box" at the start of the chapter should now be a clearer picture, summarized in **Figure 2.26**:

- The **model** is made of **layers chained together** (each a *data transformation* with its own **weights**). It maps the **input X** to **predictions Y'**.
- The **loss function** compares the predictions with the **true targets Y** and produces a **loss score**, which measures how well the predictions match what was expected.
- The **optimizer** uses this loss score to perform a **weight update** on the layers' weights. The arrows run from the optimizer back to both Weights boxes, closing the training loop.

The authors then go back over the first example piece by piece. First comes the **input data** code:

```python
(train_images, train_labels), (test_images, test_labels) = mnist.load_data()
train_images = train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))
train_images = train_images.astype("float32") / 255
...
```

With chapter 2 behind you, you can read it as tensor manipulation. The images are stored as **NumPy tensors**, here formatted as **`float32` tensors of shape `(60000, 784)`** for training and **`(10000, 784)`** for testing. Each 28 × 28 image has been flattened into a 784-dimensional vector, and pixel values have been scaled from the integer range 0–255 into [0, 1].

The page ends with "This was our model:", and the model code and its review continue on p.76. title: Re-reading the MNIST model, compile step and fit loop
text:
Revisiting the three code blocks of the first MNIST example (model definition, compile, fit) and reinterpreting each with the vocabulary of chapter 2: Dense layers, weight tensors, loss, optimizer, mini-batch SGD, epochs and backpropagation Every line of the first example now has a precise meaning: the Sequential model is a chain of two Dense layers whose weight tensors hold the model's knowledge; compile picks the loss to minimize (sparse categorical crossentropy) and the gradient-descent rule (adam); fit runs mini-batch gradient descent with batches of 128 for 5 epochs, i.e. 469 updates per epoch and 2,345 updates in total. Continuing the review begun on p.75, this page reprints the three remaining code blocks of the chapter's first MNIST example and annotates each with what the reader now knows.

**The model.** `keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(512, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])` is a *chain of two `Dense` layers*. Each layer applies a few simple tensor operations (a dot product, an addition, an element-wise activation) to its input, and these operations involve **weight tensors**, which are attributes of the layers. The authors stress that the weights are where the *knowledge* of the model persists.

**The compilation step.** `model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])` names the **loss function**, which is the feedback signal used to learn the weights and which training tries to minimize, and the **optimizer**. The loss is reduced through mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, and the exact rules of that particular use of gradient descent are set by the `"adam"` optimizer.

**The training loop.** `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=128)` iterates over the training data in mini-batches of 128 samples, 5 times over; one full pass over the training data is an **epoch**. For each batch the model computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights using **backpropagation** (which derives from the chain rule) and moves the weights in the direction that reduces the loss on that batch.

**The arithmetic.** After 5 epochs the model has made **2,345 gradient updates (469 per epoch)**: 60,000 / 128 = 468.75, rounded up to 469 batches because the last, partial batch also produces an update. By then the loss is low enough for the model to classify handwritten digits with high accuracy.

The next page (p.77) announces that you now know most of what there is to know about neural networks and sets out to prove it by reimplementing this example with low-level operations. The model is a chain of two Dense layers; its knowledge lives in the weight tensors W1, b1, W2, b2. compile chooses what to minimize (sparse categorical crossentropy) and how to use gradients to do it (adam, a mini-batch SGD variant). fit runs the training loop: batches of 128, 5 epochs, backpropagation for gradients, one update per batch. An epoch is one full pass over the training data; with 60,000 samples and batch size 128 it contains 469 updates, so 5 epochs = 2,345 updates. Every piece of the first example is now explained by chapter 2's concepts, setting up the from-scratch reimplementation on p.77.

text: A Keras model built from an ordered list of layers, each applied to the output of the previous one. Here: Sequential([Dense(512, relu), Dense(10, softmax)]) implements f(x) = softmax(relu(x W1 + b1) W2 + b2). Input batch (128, 784) -> Dense 512 -> (128, 512) -> Dense 10 -> (128, 10) probabilities.

text: A fully connected layer applying activation(dot(input, W) + b), with W and b as trainable weight tensors. Each output unit is a weighted vote over all inputs plus an offset, passed through a nonlinearity. Dense(512, activation="relu") on 784-dimensional inputs has a kernel of shape (784, 512) and a bias of shape (512,). Parameters: 784*512 + 512 = 401,920 (first layer), 512*10 + 10 = 5,130 (second).

title: Weight tensors (trainable parameters)
text: Tensors that are attributes of layers and whose values are adjusted by training; the page calls them the place where the model's knowledge persists. The architecture is the shape of the container; the weights are what is written into it by learning. For this model: W1 (784, 512), b1 (512,), W2 (512, 10), b2 (10,). Two models with identical code but different weights compute completely different functions.

title: Loss function
text: The scalar feedback signal used to learn the weight tensors, which training attempts to minimize. A score of how wrong the model is on a batch; lower is better. sparse_categorical_crossentropy: mean over the batch of -log p_y, where p_y is the predicted probability of the true integer label. If the model gives the true class probability 0.9, the per-sample loss is -ln 0.9 ≈ 0.105; at 0.1 it is ≈ 2.303.

title: Optimizer (adam)
text: The object defining the exact rules governing a specific use of gradient descent, i.e. how the gradient is turned into weight updates. The loss says where 'downhill' is; the optimizer decides how big and in what precise direction each step goes. Adam keeps exponential moving averages of gradients and squared gradients to set an adaptive per-parameter step size (beyond the book). Swapping optimizer="adam" for "rmsprop" or "sgd" changes training dynamics without touching the model or loss.

title: Backpropagation
text: The algorithm used by fit to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights; it derives from the chain rule. title: From scratch: the NaiveDense layer
text:
Starting a low-level reimplementation of the MNIST example: the scope of 'from scratch' and a NaiveDense class with Keras variables W and b and a __call__ method computing activation(matmul(input, W) + b) A Dense layer is nothing more than two tensors (a weight matrix W of shape (input_size, output_size) initialized randomly, and a bias vector b of shape (output_size,) initialized to zeros) plus a forward pass that applies output = activation(matmul(input, W) + b). Writing it as a plain Python class makes every computation step explicit. Having decoded the Keras version of the first example on p.75-p.76, the authors claim that **you already know most of what there is to know about neural networks** and propose to prove it by reimplementing a simplified version of the example step by step with only low-level operations.

**Section 2.5.1** clarifies what "from scratch" means here: basic tensor operations will *not* be reimplemented, and neither will **backpropagation**; but each computation step will be made explicit. The reader is told not to worry about every detail (chapter 3 covers the Keras API) and to follow the gist: the goal is to crystallize the mathematics through a concrete implementation.

**A simple Dense class.** Recalling p.63, the Dense layer implements

`output = activation(matmul(input, W) + b)`

where `W` and `b` are model parameters and `activation` is an element-wise function, usually `relu`. The page then gives `NaiveDense`, a Python class that:

- imports `keras` and `keras.ops` (callout: *keras.ops is where you will find all the tensor operations you need*);
- in `__init__(self, input_size, output_size, activation=None)`, stores the activation, creates `self.W = keras.Variable(shape=(input_size, output_size), initializer="uniform")` (a matrix of random values drawn from a uniform distribution) and `self.b = keras.Variable(shape=(output_size,), initializer="zeros")` (a zero vector);
- in `__call__(self, inputs)`, applies the **forward pass**: `ops.matmul(inputs, self.W)`, adds `self.b`, applies the activation if one was given, and returns the result.

The next page (p.78) chains such layers with `NaiveSequential` and builds a mock Keras model with 784 -> 512 (relu) -> 10 (softmax). 'From scratch' here means no high-level layers or fit, but still library tensor ops and automatic backpropagation. A Dense layer computes output = activation(matmul(input, W) + b), with W of shape (input_size, output_size) and b of shape (output_size,). NaiveDense creates W with random uniform values and b with zeros as keras.Variable objects in its constructor. __call__ is the forward pass: matmul, add bias, optional activation. keras.ops provides all the tensor operations needed, independent of backend.

title: Weight initialization
text: Choosing the starting values of parameters before training: here random uniform values for W and zeros for b. Training needs a starting point; random weights give each unit a different starting point. Beyond the book: Keras's "uniform" initializer is RandomUniform, by default in [-0.05, 0.05]. If W were all zeros, every unit in a layer would compute the same output and receive the same gradient, so they would never differentiate (the symmetry problem). Biases do not have this problem because W already breaks the symmetry. W for 784->512 holds 401,408 random numbers; b holds 512 zeros.

title: NaiveSequential: chaining layers into a mock Keras model
text:
The weights property of NaiveDense, the NaiveSequential class that chains layers and collects their weights, the mock MNIST model 784 -> 512 (relu) -> 10 (softmax), and the start of a batch generator A sequential model is just a list of layers applied in order, plus a way to gather all their parameters. With NaiveDense and NaiveSequential, the Keras model from p.76 becomes a plain Python object whose four weight tensors (W and b of each layer) are explicitly listed, ready to be updated by a hand-written training step. The page opens with the last three lines of `NaiveDense` (begun on p.77): a `weights` property returning `[self.W, self.b]`, which the callout calls *the convenience method for retrieving the layer's weights*.

**A simple Sequential class.** `NaiveSequential` chains layers. Its constructor stores a list of layers; its `__call__()` starts from `x = inputs` and replaces `x` by `layer(x)` for each layer in order, returning the final `x`. A `weights` property loops over the layers and concatenates their `weights` lists, so the model's parameters can be tracked easily.

**The mock Keras model.** With the two classes, the authors rebuild the first example's architecture:

- `NaiveDense(input_size=28 * 28, output_size=512, activation=ops.relu)`
- `NaiveDense(input_size=512, output_size=10, activation=ops.softmax)`

and check `assert len(model.weights) == 4`: two layers times (W, b). The shapes are (784, 512), (512,), (512, 10) and (10,), i.e. 407,050 scalars in total (count computed for these notes).

**A batch generator.** Next comes a way to iterate over MNIST in mini-batches, described as easy. The page shows only the start, `import math` and `class BatchGenerator:` with `def __init__(self, images, labels, batch_size=128):`; the body continues on p.79, where it stores the data, an index and `num_batches = math.ceil(len(images) / batch_size)`, and a `next()` method slices out the next batch.

Compared with Keras, the mock model must be told input sizes explicitly and keeps its weights in a hand-assembled list, but conceptually it is the same object as `keras.Sequential([...])` on p.76. NaiveDense exposes [W, b] through a weights property. NaiveSequential applies its layers in order and concatenates their weights into one list. The mock model 784 -> 512 (relu) -> 10 (softmax) reproduces the first example and has exactly 4 weight tensors. A batch generator is needed to feed the model mini-batches of 128 samples; it is completed on p.79.

title: Listing 2.9 A single step of training
text:
def one_training_step(model, images_batch, labels_batch):
    predictions = model(images_batch)
    loss = ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(labels_batch, predictions)
    average_loss = ops.mean(loss)
    gradients = get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights(loss, model.weights)
    update_weights(gradients, model.weights)
    return loss Performs one training step on a batch: forward pass, loss computation, gradient computation with respect to all model weights, and weight update. Forward pass, loss, backward pass, gradient-descent update.

title: Weight updates by hand and with an optimizer; gradients via GradientTape
text:
Implementing update_weights as w.assign(w - g * learning_rate) and with keras.optimizers.SGD, then explaining why gradients are obtained with automatic differentiation (tf.GradientTape) rather than hand-written backpropagation The two missing pieces of listing 2.9 are filled in. The update is plain gradient descent, subtracting gradient * learning_rate (1e-3) from each weight in place, which in practice is delegated to a Keras Optimizer's apply_gradients. Gradients come from the backend's automatic differentiation: TensorFlow's GradientTape records the operations run in its scope as a computation graph (a tape) and can then return the gradient of any scalar with respect to any inputs. The page completes the sentence from p.79: the magnitude of the weight move is set by the **learning rate**, typically a small quantity.

**Hand-written update.** The simplest `update_weights()` subtracts `gradient * learning_rate` from each weight:

```
learning_rate = 1e-3
for g, w in zip(gradients, weights):
    w.assign(w - g * learning_rate)
```

The callout notes that `assign` gives the variable a new value **in place**. Pairing by `zip` relies on the gradients list being aligned with `model.weights`.

**With an optimizer.** In practice you almost never write this by hand; you use a Keras `Optimizer`: `optimizer = optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=1e-3)` and `update_weights` becomes `optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(gradients, weights))`.

**Gradient computation.** The last missing piece is `get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights()`. The chain rule (backpropagation, previous section) could be reimplemented here, but it would be cumbersome, especially because a `softmax` and a crossentropy loss have fairly verbose derivatives. Instead the authors rely on the **automatic differentiation** built into one of the frameworks Keras supports (TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch), choosing TensorFlow for the example; chapter 3 covers all three.

TensorFlow's API for this is **`tf.GradientTape`**, a Python scope that records the tensor operations run inside it as a computation graph (a *tape*). The graph can then be used to retrieve the gradient of any scalar value with respect to any set of input values. The page starts a minimal example: `import tensorflow as tf` and `x = tf.zeros(shape=())`, a scalar tensor with value 0 (continued on p.81 with `y = 2 * x + 3` and `tape.gradient(y, x)`). update_weights subtracts gradient * learning_rate (1e-3) from each weight, in place via assign. In practice a Keras Optimizer does this: optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=1e-3).apply_gradients(zip(gradients, weights)). Backpropagation is not reimplemented because softmax and crossentropy have verbose derivatives; automatic differentiation is used instead. tf.GradientTape records operations in its scope as a graph (tape) and can return the gradient of any scalar with respect to any inputs.

title: GradientTape in the training step, and the full training loop
text:
A minimal GradientTape example (gradient of y = 2x + 3), one_training_step rewritten with GradientTape, the from-scratch fit() function looping over epochs and batches, and the start of a test drive on MNIST With GradientTape recording the forward pass, the training step becomes complete: predictions, per-sample loss and average loss are computed inside the tape scope, tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights) returns one gradient per weight, and update_weights applies them. An epoch is the training step repeated for every batch, and fit() is the epoch repeated epochs times. The page finishes the GradientTape demonstration begun on p.80. Inside `with tf.GradientTape() as tape:` (callout: *opens a GradientTape scope*) the code computes `y = 2 * x + 3` (*applies some tensor operations to our variable*), then `grad_of_y_wrt_x = tape.gradient(y, x)` *uses the tape to retrieve the gradient of the output y with respect to our variable x*. For this affine function the gradient is 2 everywhere, in particular at x = 0.

**Rewritten training step.** `one_training_step()` is rewritten with the tape, which removes the need for a separate `get_gradients_of_loss_wrt_weights()`. The forward pass (`predictions = model(images_batch)`), the per-sample `ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy` and `average_loss = ops.mean(loss)` run inside the tape scope; then `gradients = tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights)` gives one gradient per weight, `update_weights(gradients, model.weights)` applies them, and the function returns `average_loss`. Unlike listing 2.9 on p.79, the gradient is taken of the scalar average loss.

**Section 2.5.3, The full training loop.** An epoch is the repetition of the training step for each batch in the training data, and the full loop is the repetition of the epoch. The from-scratch `fit(model, images, labels, epochs, batch_size=128)` prints the epoch number, creates a new `BatchGenerator(images, labels)`, loops `num_batches` times calling `batch_generator.next()` and `one_training_step`, and prints the loss every 100 batches (`f"loss at batch {batch_counter}: {loss:.2f}"`).

**Test drive.** The page begins running it: load MNIST with `mnist.load_data()` and reshape the training images to `(60000, 28 * 28)`; the rest (type conversion, the call to `fit`, evaluation) continues on p.82. GradientTape records operations in its scope; tape.gradient(y, x) returns dy/dx (2 for y = 2x + 3). The complete training step records forward pass and loss on the tape, differentiates the scalar average loss with respect to model.weights, then updates the weights. An epoch is the training step repeated over all batches; fit repeats the epoch epochs times, here with a fresh BatchGenerator each epoch. With 5 epochs, the from-scratch fit performs the same 2,345 updates as Keras's fit. Inputs must be reshaped to (60000, 784) before training.

title: one_training_step rewritten with GradientTape
text:
def one_training_step(model, images_batch, labels_batch):
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        predictions = model(images_batch)
        loss = ops.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(labels_batch, predictions)
        average_loss = ops.mean(loss)
    gradients = tape.gradient(average_loss, model.weights)
    update_weights(gradients, model.weights)
    return average_loss A complete training step: forward pass and loss recorded on a tape, gradients of the average loss with respect to all weights, weight update, and return of the batch's average loss. Forward, loss, backward (autodiff), update.

title: Evaluating the from-scratch model, and the chapter 2 summary
text:
Finishing the hand-written MNIST training run, measuring test accuracy with argmax + equality + mean, and the start of the chapter summary Once the from-scratch model has been trained with the hand-written fit(), its test accuracy is computed by turning each 10-way probability vector into a predicted digit with ops.argmax(axis=1), comparing to the true labels and averaging the boolean matches (0.83 here). The chapter summary then compresses chapter 2 into a few claims: tensors are the data structure, tensor operations are geometric transformations, weights store the model's knowledge, and learning means minimizing a loss by moving weights against the gradient computed on random batches. The top of the page finishes the "test-drive" listing begun on p.81. After loading MNIST and reshaping the training images to `(60000, 28 * 28)`, the code converts them to `float32` and divides by 255, does the same reshape (`(10000, 28 * 28)`) and rescaling for the test images, and then calls the hand-written `fit(model, train_images, train_labels, epochs=10, batch_size=128)`, which runs ten epochs of mini-batch training with the `one_training_step()` function built on pp.79-81.

**Section 2.5.4, Evaluating the model.** The model is evaluated by:

1. running it on all 10,000 test images at once (`predictions = model(test_images)`, a `(10000, 10)` tensor of softmax probabilities);
2. taking `ops.argmax(predictions, axis=1)`, the index of the most probable class for each row, which is the predicted digit;
3. comparing those to `test_labels` with `==`, giving a boolean vector `matches`;
4. averaging it with `ops.mean(matches)`, which is the fraction of correct predictions.

The printed result is `accuracy: 0.83`. The authors call it "quite a bit of work" compared with a few lines of Keras, but argue that having done it you now have a "crystal-clear understanding" of what happens inside `fit()`, and that this low-level mental model will help you use Keras's high-level features well.

**Section 2.6, Summary** (first five bullets; the list continues on p.83):

- *Tensors* are the foundation of modern ML systems and are described by `dtype`, `rank` and `shape`.
- *Tensor operations* (addition, tensor product, element-wise multiplication) can be read as geometric transformations, and "everything in deep learning is amenable to a geometric interpretation."
- Models are chains of simple tensor operations parameterized by *weights*, which are tensors and are where the model's "knowledge" lives.
- *Learning* means finding weight values that minimize a *loss function* over the training samples and targets.
- Learning proceeds by drawing random batches, computing the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters on each batch, and moving the parameters a bit (by an amount set by the learning rate, p.83) against the gradient. Test images get exactly the same preprocessing as training images: reshape to (N, 784), cast to float32, divide by 255. Accuracy = mean(argmax(predictions, axis=1) == labels); the from-scratch model reaches 0.83. Everything fit() does (forward pass, loss, gradient, update, loops over batches and epochs) has now been written by hand, except the gradient computation itself, which uses autodiff. Tensors (dtype, rank, shape) are the data structure; tensor operations are geometric transformations. A model's knowledge lives in its weights; learning means minimizing a loss over the training data by mini-batch gradient descent.

title: End of the chapter 2 summary: mini-batch gradient descent, backpropagation, loss and optimizer
text:
The last bullets of the chapter 2 summary: naming mini-batch gradient descent and backpropagation, and introducing loss and optimizer as the two things you must define before training Moving parameters a small step, scaled by the learning rate, against the gradient computed on a random batch is mini-batch gradient descent. It works because every tensor operation in a network is differentiable, so the chain rule gives the gradient (backpropagation). Before you train, you must choose a loss (the measure of success to minimize) and an optimizer (the exact rule that turns gradients into parameter updates, e.g. RMSProp or SGD with momentum). This short page finishes the chapter 2 summary begun on p.82.

The first line completes the fifth bullet: after computing the gradient of the loss on a random batch, the model parameters are moved a bit, by an amount set by the **learning rate**, *in the opposite direction from the gradient*. The book names this **mini-batch gradient descent**.

The next bullet explains why the process is possible at all: **all tensor operations in neural networks are differentiable**, so the **chain rule** can be applied to obtain a gradient function that maps the current parameters and the current batch of data to a gradient value. This is **backpropagation**, the algorithm worked through by hand on pp.70-74 and delegated to `tf.GradientTape` in the from-scratch example (pp.80-81).

The final bullet introduces two concepts that will come up constantly in later chapters, **loss** and **optimizer**, described as the two things you must define before feeding data into a model:

- The **loss** is the quantity minimized during training, so it should represent a measure of success for the task you are trying to solve.
- The **optimizer** specifies exactly how the gradient of the loss is used to update parameters, for instance the RMSProp optimizer, SGD with momentum, and so on.

The rest of the page is blank; chapter 3 (Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras) starts on p.84. Mini-batch gradient descent: compute the loss gradient on a random batch, step against it by an amount set by the learning rate. Backpropagation is possible because every tensor operation is differentiable, so the chain rule yields the gradient. Before training you must define a loss (what success means) and an optimizer (how gradients update parameters). RMSProp and SGD with momentum are examples of optimizers.

title: Chapter 3 opener: Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
text:
What chapter 3 covers: the major deep learning frameworks usable with Keras, and how core neural-network concepts translate into code Chapter 3 moves from the from-scratch mathematics of chapter 2 to practical tooling. It introduces TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX, the three frameworks Keras can run on, and then reviews the core components of neural networks as Keras APIs, preparing you for the applications that begin in chapter 4. This is the opening page of **chapter 3, "Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras"** (PDF pp.84-127).

The *This chapter covers* box lists two goals:

- a closer look at all major deep learning frameworks and their relationships;
- an overview of how core deep learning concepts translate to code across all frameworks.

The introduction says the chapter is meant to give you everything you need to start doing deep learning in practice. First you get familiar with three popular frameworks that can be used with Keras: **TensorFlow** (tensorflow.org), **PyTorch** (pytorch.org) and **JAX** (jax.readthedocs.io). Then, building on the first contact with Keras in chapter 2, the chapter reviews the core components of neural networks and how they translate to Keras APIs. By the end you should be ready for practical, real-world applications, which start in chapter 4.

According to the chapter outline, the sections are: 3.1 a brief history of deep learning frameworks (p.85); 3.2 how these frameworks relate to each other (p.87); 3.3 TensorFlow, 3.4 PyTorch and 3.5 JAX, each with first steps, an end-to-end linear classifier written in that framework alone, and what makes its approach unique (pp.87-114); and 3.6 Keras (p.114), covering layers, models, the compile step, loss functions, fit(), validation monitoring and inference.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a map. If you already know one framework, the parallel structure of sections 3.3-3.5 (the same linear classifier in each) makes them easy to compare side by side. Chapter 3 introduces TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX, all usable with Keras, and then the core Keras APIs. Each framework section builds the same end-to-end linear classifier, which makes comparison easy. Practical applications begin in chapter 4.

title: A brief history of deep learning frameworks: the three key features and the road to Theano
text:
Why practitioners use frameworks, the three capabilities every deep learning framework combines, and the early history from the 1964 autodiff paper through CUDA to Theano All deep learning frameworks (Keras, JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch) combine three features: automatic differentiation, tensor computation on CPUs/GPUs/specialized hardware, and distribution across devices and machines. These ideas are old (automatic differentiation dates to 1964), but robust reusable packages came only after Python's rise, NVIDIA's CUDA (2006) and Theano (circa 2009), the conceptual ancestor of all modern tools. Section 3.1 opens by noting that in the real world you will not write low-level code from scratch as at the end of chapter 2; you will use a **framework**. Besides Keras, the main ones today are **JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch**, and the book teaches all four.

These frameworks are recent, with **Keras the oldest (launched March 2015)**, but the ideas behind them are old: the first paper on **automatic differentiation** was published in 1964 (Wengert, *Communications of the ACM*, footnote 1). All frameworks combine **three key features**:

1. computing gradients of arbitrary differentiable functions (**automatic differentiation**);
2. running tensor computations on **CPUs and GPUs** (and possibly other specialized hardware);
3. **distributing** computation across multiple devices or computers (several GPUs in one machine, or GPUs across separate machines).

"Together, these three simple features unlock all modern deep learning."

The history: from the 1960s until the 2000s, autodiff had **no practical application in machine learning**; people working on neural networks wrote their own gradient logic by hand, usually in C++, and GPU programming was "all but impossible." In the late 2000s things changed: **Python** and its ecosystem gained ground over MATLAB and C++ in science, and **NVIDIA released CUDA in 2006**, enabling neural networks on consumer GPUs. CUDA initially targeted physics simulation, but from **2009** ML researchers built CUDA-based networks, typically one-off, single-GPU, without autodiff.

The first framework combining autodiff and GPU computation for training deep models was **Theano, circa 2009**, "the conceptual ancestor of all modern deep learning tools." It gained traction in research in **2013-2014**, after the **ImageNet 2012** results ignited interest in deep learning. Around then, other GPU-enabled libraries were becoming popular in computer vision (the sentence continues on p.86 with Torch 7 and Caffe). In practice you use a framework; the book covers Keras, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch. Keras (March 2015) is the oldest of the four; automatic differentiation dates to a 1964 paper. Every framework combines automatic differentiation, CPU/GPU (and specialized hardware) tensor computation, and distributed computation. Before frameworks, gradients were hand-coded (usually in C++) and GPU programming was nearly impossible; CUDA arrived in 2006. Theano (circa 2009) was the first framework with autodiff and GPU training, the ancestor of modern tools, popularized after ImageNet 2012.

title: From Keras on Theano to TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX, and three certainties about the future
text:
The history of deep learning frameworks from 2015 onward and the authors' predictions: Python has won, the world is multiframework (which favors Keras), and new hardware will have to fit existing frameworks Keras launched in early 2015 on Theano; TensorFlow (late 2015) added large-scale distribution and brought deep learning to the mainstream, with Keras supporting it immediately; PyTorch (about a year later) drew on Chainer and NumPy-Autograd; Google's TPUs and the XLA compiler led to JAX. Today the four frameworks coexist, and the authors argue that Python is here to stay, that Keras's backend-agnostic design protects you in a multiframework world, and that new chips will adapt to existing frameworks. The page continues the history from p.85.

- Around 2013-2014, other GPU-enabled libraries were gaining popularity in computer vision: **Torch 7** (Lua-based) and **Caffe** (C++-based).
- **Keras** launched in **early 2015** as a higher-level, easier-to-use library **powered by Theano**, and quickly gained traction among the few thousand people doing deep learning then.
- In **late 2015** Google launched **TensorFlow**, which took many key ideas from Theano and added **large-scale distributed computation**. Its release was a "watershed moment" that brought deep learning into the mainstream developer zeitgeist. Keras added TensorFlow support immediately; by **mid-2016, over half of TensorFlow users** used it through Keras.
- About a year later, **Meta** (then Facebook) launched **PyTorch** in response, borrowing from **Chainer** (a niche, innovative framework from mid-2015, now dead) and **NumPy-Autograd** (a CPU-only autodiff library for NumPy, Maclaurin et al., 2014).
- Google released **TPUs** as an alternative to GPUs, with **XLA**, a high-performance compiler that lets TensorFlow run on TPUs. A few years later **Matthew Johnson**, one of the NumPy-Autograd developers, released **JAX** at Google as another way to use autodiff with XLA. It gained traction with researchers thanks to its minimalistic API and high scalability.
- Today Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are the top frameworks.

Asking what comes next (a new framework, language or hardware?), the authors give **three things they consider certain**:

1. **Python has won.** Its ML and data-science ecosystem has too much momentum; no new language will replace it, at least in the next 15 years.
2. **We're in a multiframework world.** All four frameworks are well established, and learning a bit of each is worthwhile, but new ones may still become popular (Apple's **MLX** is one possibility). Keras is an advantage here: existing Keras models should run on a new framework via a new Keras **backend**, providing future-proof stability as it has since 2015.
3. **New chips may arise** (AMD's GPU line likely has bright days ahead), but they will have to work with existing frameworks to gain traction, so new hardware is unlikely to disrupt your workflows. Keras (early 2015) started on Theano; TensorFlow (late 2015) added large-scale distribution and went mainstream, and Keras supported it at once. PyTorch (Meta, about a year later) drew on Chainer and NumPy-Autograd; JAX (Google) combined autodiff with the XLA compiler built for TPUs. Today's top four: Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX. Authors' predictions: Python has won; the world is multiframework, which makes backend-agnostic Keras valuable; new chips will adapt to existing frameworks.

title: TensorFlow as a platform; first steps and constant tensors
text:
The TensorFlow ecosystem, the roadmap of section 3.3.1, and creating constant tensors with tf.ones, tf.zeros and tf.constant TensorFlow is a platform with many deployment and tooling components, but learning it starts with the same low-level primitives as everywhere else: tensors. Constant tensors are created with an initial value via tf.ones, tf.zeros or tf.constant, which mirror np.ones, np.zeros and np.array. The page finishes the introduction to section 3.3 and begins section 3.3.1.

**TensorFlow is a platform, not just a library.** The authors list ecosystem components: **TFX** for industry-strength ML workflow management, **TF-Serving** for production deployment, the **TF Optimization Toolkit** for model quantization and pruning, and **TFLite** and **MediaPipe** for mobile deployment. Together they span "cutting-edge research to large-scale production applications."

**Roadmap of 3.3.1.** The section will cover four concepts:

1. tensors and variables,
2. numerical operations in TensorFlow,
3. computing gradients with a `GradientTape`,
4. making TensorFlow functions fast with just-in-time compilation,

and then conclude with an end-to-end, pure-TensorFlow linear regression (the chapter outline shows it under 3.3.2, p.93, framed as a linear classifier).

**Constant tensors.** Tensors need an initial value. The common constructors are `tf.ones` (like `np.ones`), `tf.zeros` (like `np.zeros`) and `tf.constant`, which builds a tensor from Python or NumPy values. Listing 3.1 shows that `tf.ones(shape=(2, 1))` prints `tf.Tensor([[1.], [1.]], shape=(2, 1), dtype=float32)`, `tf.zeros(shape=(2, 1))` gives the zero analog, and `tf.constant([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32")` produces a rank-1 tensor of shape `(3,)`. The callouts make the NumPy correspondence explicit.

**Random tensors.** The page ends by introducing the `tf.random` submodule, the analog of `np.random`, whose examples appear on the next page (Listing 3.2, p.89). TensorFlow is a platform: TFX, TF-Serving, TF Optimization Toolkit, TFLite and MediaPipe extend the core library to production and mobile. Section 3.3.1 covers tensors and variables, numerical ops, GradientTape, and JIT compilation, then an end-to-end linear model. tf.ones, tf.zeros and tf.constant mirror np.ones, np.zeros and np.array. Printed tensors show values, shape and dtype; Listing 3.1 produces shapes (2, 1), (2, 1) and (3,), all float32. Random tensors come from tf.random, the analog of np.random.

title: Random tensors, non-assignable tensors and tf.Variable
text:
Creating random tensors with tf.random.normal and tf.random.uniform; why TensorFlow tensors cannot be assigned to; tf.Variable as the container for modifiable state TensorFlow tensors are constant: unlike NumPy arrays, you cannot write x[0, 0] = 0.0. Because training must update model state, TensorFlow provides tf.Variable, a class for modifiable state that is created from an initial value such as a random tensor. **Random tensors (Listing 3.2).** `tf.random.normal(shape=(3, 1), mean=0., stddev=1.)` draws a (3, 1) float32 tensor from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1; the callout says this is equivalent to `np.random.normal(size=(3, 1), loc=0., scale=1.)`. `tf.random.uniform(shape=(3, 1), minval=0., maxval=1.)` draws from a uniform distribution between 0 and 1, equivalent to `np.random.uniform(size=(3, 1), low=0., high=1.)`. Note the naming differences: TensorFlow uses `shape`, `mean`, `stddev`, `minval`, `maxval`, while NumPy uses `size`, `loc`, `scale`, `low`, `high`. The printed values (e.g. -0.142, -0.953, 1.110 for the normal draw) will differ on every run.

**Tensors are not assignable.** "A significant difference between NumPy arrays and TensorFlow tensors is that TensorFlow tensors aren't assignable: they're constant." Listing 3.3 shows that NumPy allows `x[0, 0] = 0.0` on `np.ones(shape=(2, 2))`; Listing 3.4 does the same on `tf.ones(shape=(2, 2))` and fails with `EagerTensor object does not support item assignment`.

**Variables.** Training needs to update the model's state, which is a set of tensors. If tensors are constant, the state needs another container: `tf.Variable`, "the class meant to manage modifiable state in TensorFlow." A variable is created from an initial value, for instance a random tensor: Listing 3.5 builds `tf.Variable(initial_value=tf.random.normal(shape=(3, 1)))` and prints it (the output appears at the top of p.90). The next page shows how to modify a variable with `assign`, `assign_add` and `assign_sub`. tf.random.normal and tf.random.uniform create random tensors; argument names differ from NumPy's. TensorFlow tensors are constant: item assignment raises an EagerTensor error. Training needs mutable state, so TensorFlow provides tf.Variable. A variable is created from an initial value, typically a random tensor.

text: tf.random.uniform(shape=(3, 1), minval=0., maxval=1.) x_{ij} \sim \mathcal{U}(a, b), \quad a = 0,\ b = 1,\quad p(x) = \frac{1}{b-a} \text{ for } a \le x < b Formalizes the callout 'random values drawn from a uniform distribution between 0 and 1'. Every value in [0, 1) is equally likely; the mean is (a+b)/2 = 0.5. a Lower bound (minval=0.) b Upper bound (maxval=1.); for floats it is excluded p(x) Probability density, constant over the interval

text: Can you explain, in one sentence each, the role of a tf.Tensor and of a tf.Variable in a training step? Tensors carry intermediate values (inputs, activations, gradients) that are computed fresh each step; variables hold the weights that persist and are updated across steps.

title: Modifying variables and basic tensor math in TensorFlow
text:
Updating a tf.Variable with assign, sliced assign and assign_add/assign_sub; a first set of TensorFlow math operations (square, sqrt, +, matmul, concat) A tf.Variable's state is changed through methods: assign replaces its value, v[i, j].assign updates a subset of coefficients, and assign_add/assign_sub are efficient in-place += and -=. Plain tensor math in TensorFlow mirrors NumPy: tf.square, tf.sqrt, element-wise +, tf.matmul and tf.concat. The page opens with the printed value of the variable `v` created in Listing 3.5 (p.89): a (3, 1) float32 array of random normal values (-0.751, -0.487, 1.663 in the book's run).

**Modifying a variable.**
- `v.assign(tf.ones((3, 1)))` replaces the whole value: `v` becomes `[[1.], [1.], [1.]]` (Listing 3.6).
- "Assignment also works for a subset of the coefficients": `v[0, 0].assign(3.)` changes only the top entry, giving `[[3.], [1.], [1.]]` (Listing 3.7).
- `assign_add` and `assign_sub` are "efficient equivalents of `+=` and `-=`." Listing 3.8 runs `v.assign_add(tf.ones((3, 1)))` and prints `[[2.], [2.], [2.]]`.

(Notice that Listing 3.8's output is consistent with `v` being all ones before the call, i.e. the state after Listing 3.6 rather than 3.7; the listings are best read as independent illustrations. This observation is ours, not the book's.)

**Tensor operations: doing math in TensorFlow.** "Just like NumPy, TensorFlow offers a large collection of tensor operations to express mathematical formulas." Listing 3.9 starts from `a = tf.ones((2, 2))` and computes `tf.square(a)` (same as `np.square`), `tf.sqrt(a)` (same as `np.sqrt`), `b + c` (element-wise addition), `tf.matmul(a, b)` (the tensor product of chapter 2, same as `np.matmul`) and `tf.concat((a, b), axis=0)` (same as `np.concatenate`). With all-ones inputs, `b` and `c` are all ones, `d` is all twos, `e = [[2, 2], [2, 2]]`, and `f` is a (4, 2) tensor of ones.

The next page combines these ops into a TensorFlow equivalent of chapter 2's `Dense` layer and then revisits `GradientTape` (p.91). v.assign(x) replaces a variable's value; v[i, j].assign(x) updates part of it. assign_add and assign_sub are efficient in-place += and -=, the tools for weight updates. TensorFlow math mirrors NumPy: tf.square, tf.sqrt, +, tf.matmul, tf.concat. In Listing 3.9, d and e are both [[2, 2], [2, 2]], and f has shape (4, 2).

title: A Dense layer in TensorFlow and the GradientTape API
text:
Writing chapter 2's Dense layer with TensorFlow ops; computing gradients with tf.GradientTape; why only trainable variables are watched by default and how tape.watch() handles constants What distinguishes TensorFlow from NumPy is automatic differentiation: inside a GradientTape scope, operations are recorded so tape.gradient(result, inputs) returns the gradient of the result with respect to the inputs. Trainable variables are tracked automatically; constant tensors must be marked with tape.watch(), because recording everything would be too expensive. **A Dense layer in TensorFlow.** Using the ops from p.90, the chapter 2 `Dense` layer becomes a two-line function: `dense(inputs, W, b)` returns `tf.nn.relu(tf.matmul(inputs, W) + b)`, i.e. an affine transform followed by a relu.

**Gradients: a second look at GradientTape.** "So far, TensorFlow seems to look a lot like NumPy. But here's something NumPy can't do: retrieve the gradient of any differentiable expression with respect to any of its inputs." You open a `GradientTape` scope, apply computation to one or several input tensors, and ask the tape for the gradient of the result with respect to the inputs. Listing 3.10 creates `input_var = tf.Variable(initial_value=3.0)`, computes `result = tf.square(input_var)` inside the scope, and calls `tape.gradient(result, input_var)`; since $\frac{d}{dx}x^2 = 2x$, the gradient is 6.0. The common use is `gradients = tape.gradient(loss, weights)`.

**What the tape watches.** Chapter 2 showed that the tape accepts a single input or a list, scalars or high-dimensional tensors. So far the inputs were variables, but they can be any tensor. However, only **trainable variables** are tracked by default; for a constant tensor you call `tape.watch()` on it (Listing 3.11, `tf.constant(3.0)`, same gradient). The reason: "it would be too expensive to preemptively store the information required to compute the gradient of anything with respect to anything", so the tape must know what to watch, and trainable variables are watched by default because the gradient of a loss with respect to them is the most common use.

**Second-order gradients.** The page ends by noting the tape can compute the gradient of a gradient; the example (position, speed, acceleration of a falling apple) continues on p.92. A Dense layer is relu(matmul(inputs, W) + b) in TensorFlow ops. GradientTape gives TensorFlow what NumPy lacks: gradients of any differentiable expression. The common pattern is gradients = tape.gradient(loss, weights). Only trainable variables are watched by default; use tape.watch() for constants. Default watching is a cost trade-off: recording everything would be too expensive. Tapes can compute second-order gradients (continued on p.92).

title: Second-order gradients and compiling with tf.function
text:
Nested GradientTapes for second-order derivatives (falling apple: acceleration 9.8); eager execution versus compilation; the tf.function decorator Nesting two gradient tapes lets you differentiate a gradient: for position = 4.9·time², the inner tape gives speed = 9.8·time and the outer tape gives acceleration = 9.8. Separately, eager execution is easy to debug but slow; wrapping a function in @tf.function compiles it into an optimized program (with possible operation fusion), at the cost of a slower first call and harder debugging. **Second-order gradients.** Completing the sentence from p.91: the gradient of an object's position with regard to time is its speed, and the second-order gradient is its acceleration. If a falling apple's position satisfies `position(time) = 4.9 * time ** 2`, what is its acceleration? Listing 3.12 answers with two nested tapes: `time = tf.Variable(0.0)`; inside the inner tape, `position = 4.9 * time**2`; `speed = inner_tape.gradient(position, time)` is computed **inside** the outer tape's scope, so it is itself recorded; then `acceleration = outer_tape.gradient(speed, time)`. As the callout says, "Naturally, the answer is 4.9 * 2 = 9.8" (close to Earth's gravitational acceleration, 9.8 m/s²; that observation is ours).

**Making TensorFlow functions fast using compilation.** All code so far ran **eagerly**: operations execute one after another in the Python runtime, like NumPy. That is great for debugging but typically slow. Speedups come from parallelizing computation or **fusing** operations, for example replacing `matmul` followed by `relu` with a single, more efficient operation that never materializes the intermediate output.

This is achieved via **compilation**: take Python functions, lift them out of Python, automatically rewrite them into a faster compiled program, and call that program from Python. Benefit: performance. Drawback: "the code you write is no longer the code that gets executed," which can make debugging painful, so only compile once your code is debugged in the Python runtime.

In TensorFlow you wrap a function with the `@tf.function` decorator, as shown for `dense`. Every call then runs a compiled, optimized program; the first call takes longer because TensorFlow compiles the code, but this happens only once. The page closes with "TensorFlow has two compilation modes:", which p.93 describes (graph mode and XLA). Nested GradientTapes compute second-order gradients; the inner gradient must be computed inside the outer tape's scope. For position = 4.9·t², speed = 9.8·t and acceleration = 9.8. Eager execution is good for debugging but typically slow. Compilation improves speed through optimizations such as fusing matmul + relu. Compile only after debugging: the executed code is no longer your code. @tf.function compiles on the first call; later calls are fast.

title: Listing 3.12 Using nested gradient tapes to compute second-order gradients
text:
time = tf.Variable(0.0)
with tf.GradientTape() as outer_tape:
    with tf.GradientTape() as inner_tape:
        position = 4.9 * time**2
    speed = inner_tape.gradient(position, time)
acceleration = outer_tape.gradient(speed, time) Computes the first derivative (speed) of position = 4.9·time² with the inner tape, while the outer tape records that computation, then differentiates speed again to get acceleration = 9.8. Reverse-mode autodiff applied twice.

title: Graph mode vs XLA; starting a linear classifier in pure TensorFlow
text:
TensorFlow's two compilation modes (graph mode via @tf.function, XLA via jit_compile=True); the start of the end-to-end linear classifier: generating two linearly separable classes of 2D points with np.random.multivariate_normal @tf.function runs a function in graph mode by default; adding jit_compile=True compiles it with XLA, which is often faster but costs more on the first call. With tensors, variables, operations and gradients in hand, you can build any gradient-descent model, starting here with synthetic data: 1,000 points per class drawn from 2D Gaussians with means [0, 3] and [3, 0] and a shared covariance [[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]. **Two compilation modes** (completing p.92's sentence):

- **Graph mode**, the default: any function decorated with `@tf.function` runs in graph mode.
- **XLA** (Accelerated Linear Algebra), "a high-performance compiler for ML", enabled with `@tf.function(jit_compile=True)`, shown on the same `dense` function.

XLA often makes a function run faster than graph mode, but the first execution takes longer because the compiler has more work to do.

**3.3.2 An end-to-end example: a linear classifier in pure TensorFlow.** You now know tensors, variables, tensor operations and gradient computation, which is "enough to build any TensorFlow-based machine learning model based on gradient descent." The authors motivate the example as a classic interview task: implementing a linear classifier from scratch, which separates candidates with minimal ML background from those without.

**Synthetic data (Listing 3.13).** Two classes of "nicely linearly separable" points in the 2D plane, each with `num_samples_per_class = 1000` samples from `np.random.multivariate_normal`:

- negative samples: `mean=[0, 3]`,
- positive samples: `mean=[3, 0]`,
- both with `cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]`.

The callouts explain that the covariance matrix describes the **shape** of the point cloud and the mean its **position**; this covariance gives "an oval-like point cloud oriented from bottom left to top right." The two classes have different positions and the same shape. The next page stacks them into a `(2000, 2)` array and builds `(2000, 1)` targets (p.94). TensorFlow has two compilation modes: graph mode (@tf.function) and XLA (@tf.function(jit_compile=True)). XLA is often faster than graph mode but slower on the first call. Tensors, variables, ops and gradients suffice for any gradient-descent model. The end-to-end example is a linear classifier on two Gaussian clouds of 1,000 points each. Mean sets a cloud's position, covariance its shape; both classes share cov=[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]].
