title: Stacking the samples, building targets, plotting the data
text:
Turning two NumPy point clouds into a single training set (inputs + binary targets) and visualizing it before any model is built. The two classes generated on p.93 are stacked into one `(2000, 2)` float32 input array, a matching `(2000, 1)` array of 0/1 targets is built in the same order, and a scatter plot (figure 3.1) confirms that the two classes form two separate, roughly linearly separable blobs. This page finishes preparing the data for the pure-TensorFlow linear classifier started in section 3.3.2 (p.93).

- **Inputs (listing 3.14).** Listing 3.13 on p.93 produced two NumPy arrays, `negative_samples` and `positive_samples`, each of shape `(1000, 2)`: 1,000 points in the 2D plane per class. `np.vstack` concatenates them along the first axis (rows) to give one array `inputs` of shape `(2000, 2)`. The first 1,000 rows are class 0, the last 1,000 rows are class 1. The result is cast with `.astype(np.float32)` because NumPy's random generators produce `float64`, while TensorFlow variables and operations in this example work in `float32`.
- **Targets (listing 3.15).** The labels are another `vstack`: 1,000 rows of zeros (`np.zeros((num_samples_per_class, 1))`) on top of 1,000 rows of ones, both `float32`, giving `targets` with shape `(2000, 1)`. Because both arrays were stacked in the same order (negatives first), `targets[i, 0]` is 0 exactly when `inputs[i]` belongs to class 0, and 1 otherwise. The trailing axis of size 1 means each target is a length-1 vector, which matches the `(2000, 1)` output that the model `matmul(inputs, W) + b` will produce (p.95).
- **Plot (listing 3.16, figure 3.1).** With Matplotlib (preinstalled in Colab), `plt.scatter(inputs[:, 0], inputs[:, 1], c=targets[:, 0])` draws every point at its (x, y) coordinates and colors it by its label. Figure 3.1 shows two elongated, tilted clouds: one (dark purple) centered near (0, 3) and one (yellow) centered near (3, 0). The clouds touch slightly in the middle but are mostly separated by a diagonal line, which is what makes this a good toy problem for a *linear* classifier.

Nothing on this page involves TensorFlow yet; it is plain NumPy and Matplotlib. The model variables, forward pass, loss and training step follow on pp.95-96. Inputs from all classes are stacked into one array whose axis 0 is the sample axis: two (1000, 2) arrays become one (2000, 2) array. Targets must be built in exactly the same row order as the inputs; here 1,000 zeros followed by 1,000 ones, shape (2000, 1). Cast NumPy data to float32 before handing it to TensorFlow; NumPy's random generators produce float64. The (2000, 1) target shape is chosen to match the model's (2000, 1) predictions, avoiding accidental broadcasting in the loss. Plotting the data first (figure 3.1) shows two tilted Gaussian blobs that a straight line can mostly separate, which is why a linear classifier is appropriate.

title: The linear classifier: variables, forward pass, MSE loss
text:
Defining the model of a linear classifier in raw TensorFlow: its two variables W and b, the forward pass `tf.matmul(inputs, W) + b`, and the mean squared error loss. A linear classifier is just an affine transformation, `prediction = matmul(input, W) + b`, trained to minimize the squared difference between predictions and the 0/1 targets. For 2D inputs it reduces to three numbers, `w1`, `w2` and `b`, with `prediction = w1 * x + w2 * y + b`. Having prepared two blobs of 2D points with 0/1 labels (p.94), the authors now define the model.

**What a linear classifier is.** It is an affine transformation, `prediction = matmul(input, W) + b`, trained to minimize the square of the difference between predictions and targets. The authors note this is simpler than the toy two-layer network at the end of chapter 2, and that this time the reader should understand every line.

**Variables (listing 3.17).** With `input_dim = 2` (2D points) and `output_dim = 1` (one score per sample, close to 0 for class 0 and close to 1 for class 1), `W` is a `tf.Variable` of shape `(2, 1)` initialized with `tf.random.uniform` (values in [0, 1)), and `b` is a `tf.Variable` of shape `(1,)` initialized with `tf.zeros`. Variables are used because these are the values gradient descent will modify in place.

**Forward pass (listing 3.18).** `model(inputs, W, b)` returns `tf.matmul(inputs, W) + b`. Because the inputs are 2D, `W` is just two scalar coefficients `[[w1], [w2]]` and `b` is one scalar, so for a point `[x, y]` the prediction is $w_1 x + w_2 y + b$. Applied to the full `(2000, 2)` input matrix, the result is a `(2000, 1)` column of scores, with `b` broadcast to every row.

**Loss (listing 3.19).** `mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)` computes `tf.square(targets - predictions)`, a per-sample loss tensor with the same shape as targets and predictions, and then averages it with `tf.reduce_mean` into a single scalar, since gradient descent needs one number to minimize.

The training step that computes gradients of this loss with respect to `W` and `b` and updates them comes next (p.96). A linear classifier is an affine transformation, prediction = matmul(input, W) + b, trained to minimize squared error against 0/1 targets. W has shape (input_dim, output_dim) = (2, 1) and is randomly initialized; b has shape (output_dim,) = (1,) and starts at zero; both are tf.Variable objects so they can be updated. For a 2D point the prediction is simply w1 * x + w2 * y + b: the model has only three parameters. The forward pass maps (2000, 2) inputs to (2000, 1) predictions in one tf.matmul, with b broadcast across rows. The loss squares the per-sample differences and averages them with tf.reduce_mean into one scalar, which is what gradients are computed from.

title: Linear classifier
text: A model that computes an affine function of its input and assigns a class by thresholding (or comparing) the result; its decision boundary is a hyperplane. It draws one straight line across the plane and calls everything on one side class 0 and on the other side class 1. Here $\hat{y} = xW + b$ with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 1}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}$, trained with mean squared error against $y \in \{0, 1\}$; the predicted class is $[\hat{y} > 0.5]$ (p.96). With $w_1 = 0.15$, $w_2 = -0.15$, $b = 0.5$ (illustrative values), the point $(3, 0)$ scores $0.95$ (class 1) and $(0, 3)$ scores $0.05$ (class 0); the boundary is the line $y = x$.
snippet: A model that computes an affine function of its input and assigns a class by thresholding or comparing the result; its decision boundary is a hyperplane.

title: Affine transformation
text: A linear transformation followed by a translation: $f(x) = xW + b$. Rotate/scale/project the input with W, then shift with b. Applied to a batch, `tf.matmul(inputs, W)` has shape (2000, 1) and `+ b` broadcasts the (1,) bias across all rows. A Keras `Dense` layer without activation computes exactly this. `tf.matmul(inputs, W) + b` in listing 3.18.

title: Mean squared error
text: The average over samples of the squared difference between target and prediction. Penalizes errors quadratically: being off by 0.2 costs 0.04, being off by 1 costs 1. $\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$; implemented as `tf.reduce_mean(tf.square(targets - predictions))`. Its gradient with respect to a prediction is $-\frac{2}{N}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)$, linear in the error. Targets [0, 1], predictions [0.2, 0.7]: squared errors 0.04 and 0.09, MSE = 0.065.
snippet: The average over samples of the squared difference between target and prediction.

title: TensorFlow variable
text: A mutable container for a tensor value whose contents can be updated in place, used for model parameters. title: The training step and the batch training loop
text:
Writing one gradient-descent training step with tf.GradientTape and assign_sub, compiling it with tf.function(jit_compile=True), running it 40 times on the full dataset, and classifying points with a 0.5 threshold. A training step is: forward pass and loss inside a GradientTape, gradients of the loss with respect to W and b, and an in-place update `W -= learning_rate * grad`. Because each step uses all 2,000 samples (batch training), a relatively large learning rate of 0.1 and only 40 steps suffice to bring the loss to about 0.025. This page trains the linear classifier defined on p.95.

**Training step (listing 3.20).** `learning_rate` is set to 0.1. The function `training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)` is decorated with `@tf.function(jit_compile=True)`, which wraps it in a `tf.function` to speed it up (compiled with XLA, p.93). Inside a `tf.GradientTape()` scope it runs the forward pass, `predictions = model(inputs, W, b)`, and computes the loss. `tape.gradient(loss, [W, b])` returns the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight, and `W.assign_sub(grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate)` and the same for `b` move each variable a small step against its gradient. The function returns the loss.

**Batch vs mini-batch training.** For simplicity, each step uses the *entire* dataset rather than small batches. Each step is therefore more expensive (forward pass and gradients for 2,000 samples), but each update is more effective at reducing the training loss because it uses information from all samples instead of, say, 128 random ones. As a result, fewer steps are needed and a larger learning rate than usual for mini-batch training is appropriate: 0.1.

**Training loop (listing 3.21).** A plain Python `for` loop calls `training_step` 40 times and prints the loss with four decimals. After 40 steps the loss stabilizes around 0.025.

**Classifying.** Since targets are 0 and 1, a point is classified as "0" if its prediction is below 0.5 and "1" if above. The final snippet recomputes predictions on the training inputs and colors the scatter plot by `predictions[:, 0] > 0.5`, producing figure 3.2 on the next page (p.97). A training step = forward pass and loss inside tf.GradientTape, then tape.gradient(loss, [W, b]), then W.assign_sub(grad * learning_rate) for each variable. @tf.function(jit_compile=True) compiles the step with XLA to speed it up. Batch (full-dataset) training makes each step slower but each update more effective, so fewer steps and a larger learning rate (0.1) are used; mini-batch training is the norm for large datasets. 40 steps bring the loss to about 0.025. Predictions are turned into classes by thresholding at 0.5, the midpoint between the 0 and 1 targets.

text: TensorFlow's context manager that records operations executed inside its scope so that gradients of a result with respect to variables can be computed afterwards. A tape recorder for the forward pass; `tape.gradient` plays it backward. Trainable variables are watched automatically. `tape.gradient(loss, [W, b])` runs reverse-mode autodiff and returns a list of tensors with the same shapes as W (2, 1) and b (1,). `grad_loss_wrt_W, grad_loss_wrt_b = tape.gradient(loss, [W, b])`

title: Gradient descent update
text: Iteratively moving parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient of the loss, scaled by a learning rate. Take a small step downhill on the loss surface each iteration. $W \leftarrow W - \eta \nabla_W L$, $b \leftarrow b - \eta \nabla_b L$ with $\eta = 0.1$, implemented with `assign_sub`. If $\partial L / \partial b = 0.4$, then `b.assign_sub(0.4 * 0.1)` decreases b by 0.04.
snippet: Iteratively moving parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient of the loss, scaled by a learning rate.

title: Batch vs mini-batch training
text: Batch training computes each update on all training data; mini-batch training computes each update on a small random subset. Asking all 2,000 voters before every decision versus polling 128 of them: the full poll is accurate but slow; the small poll is quick but noisy. Full-batch gradients are exact and deterministic; mini-batch gradients are unbiased but noisy estimates. Per the book, batch training means slower steps, more effective updates, fewer steps and a larger learning rate. 40 full-batch steps over 2,000 samples, versus roughly 16 steps per epoch with batches of 128.
snippet: Batch training computes each update on all training data; mini-batch training computes each update on a small random subset.

title: Listing 3.20 The training-step function
text:
learning_rate = 0.1

@tf.function(jit_compile=True)
def training_step(inputs, targets, W, b):
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        predictions = model(inputs, W, b)
        loss = mean_squared_error(predictions, targets)
    grad_loss_wrt_W, grad_loss_wrt_b = tape.gradient(loss, [W, b])
    W.assign_sub(grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate)
    b.assign_sub(grad_loss_wrt_b * learning_rate)
    return loss Performs one full-batch gradient-descent update of W and b and returns the loss computed before the update. Full-batch gradient descent, one iteration.
snippet: Performs one full-batch gradient-descent update of W and b and returns the loss computed before the update.

title: The model as a line: decision boundary of the linear classifier
text:
Visualizing the trained linear classifier: its predictions on the training points (figure 3.2) and its decision boundary, the line w1 * x + w2 * y + b = 0.5 (figure 3.3). Thresholding the affine score at 0.5 splits the plane with the straight line $w_1 x + w_2 y + b = 0.5$, which can be rewritten as $y = -\frac{w_1}{w_2}x + \frac{0.5 - b}{w_2}$ and plotted directly from the trained W and b. This page shows what the trained linear classifier from pp.95-96 has learned.

**Figure 3.2** colors the 2,000 training points by the model's predicted class (prediction > 0.5). It looks very much like figure 3.1 (p.94), which used the true labels: the classifier gets almost every training point right.

**The decision boundary.** For a point `[x, y]`, the prediction is $w_1 x + w_2 y + b$. Class "0" means $w_1 x + w_2 y + b < 0.5$ and class "1" means $w_1 x + w_2 y + b > 0.5$. The boundary between them, $w_1 x + w_2 y + b = 0.5$, is the equation of a line in the 2D plane. Solving for $y$ puts it in the familiar form $y = a x + b$: $y = -\frac{w_1}{w_2} x + \frac{0.5 - b}{w_2}$. The book says class 1 is above the line and class 0 below; note that in figure 3.3 the yellow class-1 points are actually below/right of the line, which is what happens when $w_2$ is negative (dividing by a negative $w_2$ flips the inequality).

**Plotting the line.** The snippet generates 100 regularly spaced x values between -1 and 4 with `np.linspace`, computes `y = -W[0] / W[1] * x + (0.5 - b) / W[1]` (the line's equation), plots it as a red line (`"-r"`), and overlays the model's predicted classes on the same plot. **Figure 3.3** shows the result: a red line running diagonally from lower left to upper right between the two blobs.

The next page (p.98) sums up: a linear classifier is about finding the parameters of a line, or in higher dimensions a hyperplane, that neatly separates two classes of data. The trained model's predicted classes (figure 3.2) closely match the true classes (figure 3.1). The decision boundary is the line w1 * x + w2 * y + b = 0.5; in slope-intercept form y = -w1/w2 * x + (0.5 - b)/w2. Which side is class 1 depends on the sign of w2; here w2 is negative, so class 1 lies below the line in figure 3.3. The line is plotted by evaluating its equation on np.linspace(-1, 4, 100) and drawing it in red over the scatter plot. A linear classifier is entirely described by the line (hyperplane) it draws between classes.

title: What makes TensorFlow unique; introducing PyTorch
text:
The authors' assessment of TensorFlow's strengths and weaknesses, followed by a short history and positioning of PyTorch. TensorFlow is fast (graph mode plus XLA), extremely feature complete (string and ragged tensors, tf.data) and the most mature for production deployment. But its API sprawls, it is sometimes inconsistent with NumPy, and Hugging Face supports it less. PyTorch, developed mainly by Meta since 2016 in the Chainer and NumPy-Autograd tradition, dominates research and has a large ecosystem. **Finishing the linear classifier (3.3.2).** The first line concludes the end-to-end TensorFlow example. A linear classifier is about *finding the parameters of a line (or, in higher-dimensional spaces, a hyperplane) neatly separating two classes of data*. On p.97 that line was $w_1 x + w_2 y + b = 0.5$.

**3.3.3 What makes the TensorFlow approach unique.** Having covered TensorFlow's basic APIs, the authors ask what distinguishes it and when to use it. Their view of its **benefits**:

1. **Speed.** Thanks to *graph mode* and *XLA compilation*, it is usually significantly faster than PyTorch and NumPy, though JAX is often even faster.
2. **Feature completeness.** Uniquely among frameworks, it supports **string tensors** and **ragged tensors** (entries may have different dimensions, which is useful for sequences without padding). Its **`tf.data`** preprocessing API is so good that even JAX recommends it.
3. **Deployment.** It has the most mature production-deployment ecosystem, especially for **mobile and the browser**.

Its **flaws**:

1. A **sprawling API** with thousands of operations, the flip side of feature completeness.
2. A numerical API that is **occasionally inconsistent with NumPy**.
3. **Less support on Hugging Face**, so the latest generative AI models may not be available in TensorFlow.

**3.4 Introduction to PyTorch.** PyTorch is a Python-based, open source framework developed primarily by **Meta** (formerly Facebook). It was released in **September 2016**, as a response to TensorFlow, reached **1.0 in 2018** and **2.0 in 2023**. Its programming style comes from the now-defunct **Chainer** framework, itself inspired by **NumPy-Autograd**. It is used extensively in the **research community**, and it sits at the center of a large ecosystem: **torchvision**, **torchaudio** and **Hugging Face**. The page after this one adds that PyTorch's API is higher level, with layers and optimizers like Keras. A linear classifier learns the parameters of a line or hyperplane separating two classes. TensorFlow's strengths: speed (graph mode + XLA), feature completeness (string and ragged tensors, tf.data), mature deployment (mobile, browser). TensorFlow's weaknesses: sprawling API, occasional NumPy inconsistency, weaker Hugging Face support. PyTorch: Meta, September 2016 (response to TensorFlow), 1.0 in 2018, 2.0 in 2023; style inherited from Chainer and NumPy-Autograd; widely used in research. PyTorch's ecosystem includes torchvision, torchaudio and Hugging Face.

title: First steps with PyTorch: package name, constant tensors
text:
PyTorch's higher-level API, the roadmap of 3.4.1, the torch package name, creating constant tensors (Listing 3.22) and how random tensor creation differs. PyTorch includes layers and optimizers like Keras, and they are compatible with Keras on the PyTorch backend. Its core object is the tensor, created with NumPy-like functions that differ in details: the shape argument is called size, dtype must be a torch dtype object rather than a string, and torch.normal takes tensors for mean and std instead of a shape. The page completes the introduction to PyTorch and begins **3.4.1 First steps with PyTorch**.

**API level.** PyTorch's API is *higher level* than TensorFlow's and JAX's because it includes **layers and optimizers, like Keras**. When Keras runs on the **PyTorch backend**, these layers and optimizers are compatible with Keras workflows.

**Roadmap.** 3.4.1 covers five concepts:

1. tensors and parameters
2. numerical operations
3. computing gradients with **`backward()`**
4. packaging computation with the **`Module`** class
5. speeding up PyTorch with **compilation**

The section then concludes by reimplementing the end-to-end example in pure PyTorch.

**Tensors and parameters.** The first gotcha is that the package is named **`torch`**, not `pytorch`: you install it with `pip install torch` and import it with `import torch`. As in NumPy and TensorFlow, the **tensor** is at the heart of the framework.

**Constant tensors (Listing 3.22).** `torch.ones(size=(2, 1))` and `torch.zeros(size=(2, 1))` create a 2×1 tensor of ones or zeros. `torch.tensor([1, 2, 3], dtype=torch.float32)` builds a tensor from a list. The callouts point out two differences from other frameworks: the shape argument is named **`size`** rather than `shape`, and you **cannot pass `dtype="float32"` as a string**; you must pass a torch dtype instance such as `torch.float32`.

**Random tensors.** Random creation is similar to NumPy and TensorFlow but with divergent syntax. **`torch.normal` takes no shape argument**; instead, the mean and standard deviation are passed as tensors with the expected output shape. Listing 3.23 with the actual code is on p.100. PyTorch's API is higher level than TensorFlow's and JAX's: it includes layers and optimizers, compatible with Keras on the PyTorch backend. 3.4.1 covers tensors and parameters, numerical ops, backward(), Module and compilation, followed by an end-to-end example. The package is named torch: pip install torch, import torch. torch.ones and torch.zeros use size= instead of shape=, and dtype must be a torch dtype such as torch.float32, not a string. torch.normal has no shape argument; the output shape comes from the mean and std tensors.

title: Random tensors, assignment and torch.nn.Parameter
text:
Creating random tensors in PyTorch, in-place tensor assignment, and the Parameter class for trainable state PyTorch creates random tensors with its own idiosyncratic signatures (`torch.normal` takes tensors of mean/std, `torch.rand` takes the shape as separate integers). Unlike TensorFlow tensors, PyTorch tensors can be modified in place, and PyTorch offers `torch.nn.parameter.Parameter`, a tensor subclass that marks a tensor as trainable state so models can track it automatically. This page continues the tour of PyTorch basics in section 3.4.1.

**Random tensors.** Listing 3.23 shows `torch.normal`, which does *not* take a shape argument: you pass `mean` and `std` as tensors that already have the desired output shape — here `torch.zeros(size=(3, 1))` and `torch.ones(size=(3, 1))` — giving a (3, 1) tensor of standard-normal samples. The callout says it is equivalent to `tf.random.normal(shape=(3, 1), mean=0., stddev=1.)`. For uniform random values you use `torch.rand`, which, unlike `np.random.uniform` or `tf.random.uniform`, takes each output dimension as a separate positional argument: `torch.rand(3, 1)`, equivalent to `tf.random.uniform(shape=(3, 1), minval=0., maxval=1.)`.

**Tensor assignment.** Like NumPy arrays but unlike TensorFlow tensors (p.89), PyTorch tensors are mutable: after `x = torch.zeros(size=(2, 1))`, the statement `x[0, 0] = 1.` changes the tensor in place, yielding `tensor([[1.], [0.]])`.

**The Parameter class.** You *could* store a model's trainable state in plain tensors, but PyTorch provides a dedicated subclass, `torch.nn.parameter.Parameter`. The benefit is semantic clarity — a `Parameter` is always trainable state, whereas a `Tensor` could be anything — and, as a consequence, PyTorch can automatically track and retrieve the Parameters assigned to models, much as Keras does with its `Variable` instances. Listing 3.24 wraps a zeros tensor into a Parameter with `torch.nn.parameter.Parameter(data=x)`; the callout warns that a Parameter can only be created from a `torch.Tensor` value — NumPy arrays are not allowed.

The next page moves on to math operations and gradients with `.backward()` (p.101), and the Parameter class becomes essential when the book packages state in a `torch.nn.Module` (p.103). `torch.normal` takes mean and std tensors of the target shape; `torch.rand(3, 1)` takes dimensions as separate arguments. PyTorch tensors are assignable like NumPy arrays (`x[0, 0] = 1.`), unlike TensorFlow tensors. `torch.nn.parameter.Parameter` is a Tensor subclass that marks trainable state. Parameters let PyTorch automatically track and retrieve a model's weights, similar to Keras Variables. A Parameter must be created from a torch.Tensor, not a NumPy array.

text: Tensors filled with pseudo-random values drawn from a distribution, created in PyTorch with `torch.normal` (Gaussian) and `torch.rand` (uniform on [0, 1)). title: Math in PyTorch and gradients with .backward()
text:
Basic PyTorch tensor operations, a dense layer written with them, and PyTorch's hidden-tape autograd via tensor.backward() and .grad PyTorch math mirrors NumPy with subtle API differences (e.g. `dim=` instead of `axis=`). Gradients are computed without an explicit tape: PyTorch silently records a one-time computation graph, and calling `.backward()` on a result backpropagates through it, filling the `.grad` attribute of every tensor created with `requires_grad=True`; repeated calls accumulate. The page covers two topics in PyTorch's first-steps tour.

**Tensor operations.** Math in PyTorch works as in NumPy or TensorFlow, but — as with TensorFlow — the API often diverges subtly from NumPy. Listing 3.25 builds `a = torch.ones((2, 2))` and then computes `torch.square(a)` (same as `np.square`), `torch.sqrt(a)` (same as `np.sqrt`), an elementwise sum `b + c`, a tensor product `torch.matmul(a, b)` (same as `np.matmul`, see chapter 2), and `torch.cat((a, b), dim=0)`, which concatenates along axis 0 like `np.concatenate` — note the keyword is `dim`, not `axis`. A dense layer is then just `torch.nn.relu(torch.matmul(inputs, W) + b)`.

**Computing gradients.** PyTorch has no explicit "gradient tape" object. Instead, whenever you run a computation, PyTorch creates a one-time computation graph — a hidden tape — recording what happened. The public interface is on tensors themselves: `tensor.backward()` runs backpropagation through all previously executed operations that led to that tensor and populates the `.grad` attribute of every tensor that is tracking gradients. Listing 3.26 creates `input_var = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)` (the callout stresses that `requires_grad=True` is required to get gradients with respect to a tensor), computes `result = torch.square(input_var)`, calls `result.backward()`, and reads `input_var.grad`, which is `tensor(6.)` — the derivative $2x$ at $x=3$.

The page ends by warning that calling `backward()` several times in a row *accumulates* gradients: each call adds the new gradient to the existing `.grad`. The example and the reset (setting `.grad` to `None`) are on p.102. PyTorch math mirrors NumPy but with subtle differences, e.g. torch.cat(..., dim=0) instead of axis=0. A dense layer is relu(matmul(inputs, W) + b) built from basic ops. PyTorch has no explicit tape: a hidden one-time graph records operations as they run. tensor.backward() backpropagates and fills .grad on tensors created with requires_grad=True. Repeated backward() calls accumulate gradients into .grad.
snippet: The page covers two topics in PyTorch's first-steps tour. Tensor operations. Math in PyTorch works as in NumPy or TensorFlow, but — as with TensorFlow — the API often diverges…

title: Automatic differentiation in PyTorch (.backward)
text: PyTorch records a one-time computation graph during execution; `tensor.backward()` backpropagates through it and stores gradients in `.grad` of tensors with `requires_grad=True`. The tape is always running in the background; you press 'rewind' from the output you care about. Gradients are accumulated (summed) into `.grad` across repeated calls; they must be reset (e.g. `.grad = None`) between steps. x = 3 with requires_grad=True, y = x² → y.backward() → x.grad = 6.

title: Gradient accumulation, resetting .grad, and the PyTorch linear classifier's variables, model and loss
text:
How PyTorch's .grad accumulates across backward() calls, how to reset it, and the first three pieces (variables, forward pass, MSE loss) of the pure-PyTorch linear classifier In PyTorch, each call to backward() adds the newly computed gradient into a tensor's .grad attribute rather than overwriting it, so gradients must be reset (by setting .grad to None). With that in hand, the linear classifier from the TensorFlow section can be rewritten almost line for line: W and b become tensors created with requires_grad=True, and tf.matmul, tf.square and tf.reduce_mean become torch.matmul, torch.square and torch.mean. The page opens by finishing the gradient-accumulation example begun on p.101. There, `input_var = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)` was squared and `result.backward()` put the derivative $2x = 6$ into `input_var.grad`. Running the same two lines again does **not** overwrite that value: `.grad` is now the *sum* of the new gradient and the previously computed one, so it reads `tensor(12.)` — the value has doubled. The callout states the rule: `.grad` will sum all gradient values from each time `backward()` is called. To reset gradients you simply set `input_var.grad = None`.

Section **3.4.2** then rewrites the linear classifier from section 3.3.2 (pp.93-97) in pure PyTorch. The authors stress that it stays very similar to the TensorFlow version — the only major difference is how the gradients are computed.

1. **Model variables.** `input_dim = 2`, `output_dim = 1`; `W = torch.rand(input_dim, output_dim, requires_grad=True)` (random values, shape `(2, 1)`) and `b = torch.zeros(output_dim, requires_grad=True)` (zeros, shape `(1,)`). The reader is told not to forget `requires_grad=True`, because without it PyTorch would not track the operations needed to compute gradients with respect to `W` and `b`. Compare p.95, where TensorFlow wrapped the same initial values in `tf.Variable`.
2. **Model.** `model(inputs, W, b)` returns `torch.matmul(inputs, W) + b` — an affine transformation; the only change is `tf.matmul` → `torch.matmul`.
3. **Loss.** `mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)` squares the per-sample differences with `torch.square` and averages them with `torch.mean` (instead of `tf.square` and `tf.reduce_mean`).

The page ends with "Now for the training step. Here's how it works:" — the training-step listing and its numbered explanation (including the use of `.grad`, `torch.no_grad()` and resetting `.grad` to `None`) are on p.103. Each backward() call adds into .grad; a second identical call doubles the stored gradient (6 → 12). Reset gradients with tensor.grad = None before computing new ones. Trainable PyTorch tensors need requires_grad=True; W = torch.rand(2, 1, ...) and b = torch.zeros(1, ...). The PyTorch model and loss are direct translations of the TensorFlow ones: torch.matmul, torch.square, torch.mean. The only major difference between the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions is how gradients are computed (p.103).

title: Gradient accumulation in .grad
text: In PyTorch, each call to backward() adds the computed gradient to the existing value of a tensor's .grad attribute instead of replacing it. .grad is a running total. Ask for the gradient twice without clearing it and you get twice the answer. For input_var = 3.0 and result = input_var², one backward() gives .grad = 6; a second forward+backward gives 6 + 6 = 12. Resetting with `.grad = None` restores a clean slate. On this page: `input_var.grad` goes from tensor(6.) (p.101) to tensor(12.).
snippet: In PyTorch, each call to backward adds the computed gradient to the existing value of a tensor's .grad attribute instead of replacing it.

title: The pure-PyTorch training step, and introducing torch.nn.Module
text:
How one gradient-descent step is written in pure PyTorch (backward, .grad, no_grad update, gradient reset), and the start of the object-oriented Module + optimizer API A PyTorch training step runs the forward pass, calls loss.backward() to populate W.grad and b.grad, updates W and b inside a torch.no_grad() scope so the update is not itself tracked, and resets the gradients to None so they do not accumulate. The same thing can be expressed more compactly by subclassing torch.nn.Module (parameters in __init__(), computation in forward()) and using an optimizer from torch.optim. The page explains and then shows the training step of the pure-PyTorch linear classifier. The numbered explanation (printed before the code) has four points:

1. `loss.backward()` runs backpropagation starting from the `loss` output node and populates `tensor.grad` on all tensors involved in computing `loss`; `tensor.grad` is the gradient of the loss with regard to that tensor.
2. The `.grad` attribute is used to recover the gradients of the loss with regard to `W` and `b`.
3. `W` and `b` are updated with those gradients. Because the updates are not meant to be part of the backward pass, they are done inside a `torch.no_grad()` scope, which skips gradient computation for everything inside it.
4. The `.grad` of `W` and `b` is reset to `None`; otherwise gradients would accumulate across multiple calls to `training_step()`, giving invalid values.

The code sets `learning_rate = 0.1` and defines `training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)`: forward pass, `mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)`, `loss.backward()`, `grad_loss_wrt_W, grad_loss_wrt_b = W.grad, b.grad`, the in-place updates `W -= grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate` (and the same for `b`) inside `with torch.no_grad():`, then `W.grad = None`, `b.grad = None`, and `return loss`. (As printed, the forward line is `model(inputs)`, although the `model` function on p.102 takes `W` and `b` as well.)

"This could be made even simpler." The subsection **Packaging state and computation with the Module class** introduces PyTorch's higher-level, object-oriented API, which relies on two new classes: `torch.nn.Module` and an optimizer from `torch.optim`, such as `torch.optim.SGD` (the equivalent of `keras.optimizers.SGD`). You subclass `torch.nn.Module`, which holds some `Parameters` (state variables, defined in `__init__()`) and implements the forward pass in `forward()`. **Listing 3.27** begins: `class LinearModel(torch.nn.Module):` with an `__init__` that calls `super().__init__()`; the rest of the listing is on p.104. loss.backward() fills .grad on every tensor with requires_grad=True that contributed to the loss. Parameter updates go inside torch.no_grad() because they are not part of the backward pass. W.grad and b.grad must be reset to None after each step, or gradients accumulate across calls. Apart from how gradients are obtained, the PyTorch step mirrors the TensorFlow one (same learning rate 0.1, same update). The higher-level API packages parameters (in __init__()) and computation (in forward()) in a torch.nn.Module subclass and delegates updates to a torch.optim optimizer such as SGD.

text: loss.backward(); grad_loss_wrt_W, grad_loss_wrt_b = W.grad, b.grad \begin{aligned}\mathcal{L} &= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i - x_i W - b)^2\\ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W} &= -\frac{2}{N}X^{\top}(Y - XW - b)\\ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial b} &= -\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i - x_i W - b)\end{aligned} Shows the actual values PyTorch writes into W.grad and b.grad. title: The pure-PyTorch training step
text:
learning_rate = 0.1

def training_step(inputs, targets, W, b):
    predictions = model(inputs)
    loss = mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)
    loss.backward()
    grad_loss_wrt_W, grad_loss_wrt_b = W.grad, b.grad
    with torch.no_grad():
        W -= grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate
        b -= grad_loss_wrt_b * learning_rate
    W.grad = None
    b.grad = None
    return loss Performs one gradient-descent step on W and b for the linear classifier and returns the loss. Batch gradient descent with reverse-mode autodiff.
snippet: Performs one gradient-descent step on W and b for the linear classifier and returns the loss.

title: LinearModel as a torch.nn.Module, the SGD optimizer, and a simplified training step
text:
Completing the LinearModel Module (Parameters W and b, forward()), calling it via __call__(), creating torch.optim.SGD from model.parameters(), and the three-call training step backward() / optimizer.step() / model.zero_grad() Once W and b are torch.nn.Parameter attributes of a Module, the model can be called directly on inputs, its parameters can be handed to an optimizer with model.parameters(), and the manual no_grad update is replaced by optimizer.step() — so the training step shrinks to forward pass, loss, loss.backward(), optimizer.step(), model.zero_grad(). The page finishes **Listing 3.27**. Inside `__init__()` (after `super().__init__()` on p.103) the model stores `self.W = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.rand(input_dim, output_dim))` and `self.b = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(output_dim))` — the same initial values as on p.102, but now wrapped as Parameters and held by the Module. `forward(self, inputs)` returns `torch.matmul(inputs, self.W) + self.b`.

The model is instantiated with `model = LinearModel()`. When using a `torch.nn.Module` instance you don't call `forward()` directly; you use `__call__()` — i.e., call the model object on the inputs — which redirects to `forward()` but adds a few framework hooks. The example converts the NumPy data first: `torch_inputs = torch.tensor(inputs)`, then `output = model(torch_inputs)`.

Next comes an optimizer. To instantiate one you must give it the list of parameters it should update, which a Module exposes through `.parameters()`: `optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)`.

With the Module and the SGD optimizer, the training step becomes `training_step(inputs, targets)`: `predictions = model(inputs)`, `loss = mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)`, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`, `model.zero_grad()`, `return loss`. W and b are no longer passed as arguments, because the model owns them.

The page then contrasts the old update — `with torch.no_grad(): W -= grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate; b -= grad_loss_wrt_b * learning_rate` — with the new one: "Now we can just do `optimizer.step()`." The matching explanation of `model.zero_grad()` (replacing the manual `.grad = None` resets) and the warning not to forget it are on p.105. A Module stores Parameters in __init__() (self.W, self.b) and computes in forward(). Call the module itself, model(x); __call__() runs hooks and then forward(). An optimizer is built from model.parameters() and a learning rate: torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate). The training step reduces to loss.backward(), optimizer.step(), model.zero_grad(). optimizer.step() replaces the manual no_grad update; loss.backward() is unchanged.

title: model.zero_grad(), torch.compile(), and the start of what makes PyTorch unique
text:
Replacing manual gradient resets with model.zero_grad(), the backward–step–zero_grad 'incantation', compiling Modules and functions with torch.compile() (Dynamo), and PyTorch's first key strength: eager execution With a Module and an optimizer, gradients are cleared with model.zero_grad(), and the sequence loss.backward() → optimizer.step() → model.zero_grad() can be treated as a fixed recipe — forgetting zero_grad() is a major, common bug. PyTorch can compile Modules or functions with torch.compile() (its Dynamo compiler), but most PyTorch code runs eagerly, which is one of PyTorch's key strengths because it makes debugging easy. The page finishes the discussion of the simplified training step from p.104. Previously gradients had to be reset by hand with `tensor.grad = None` on each tensor; now `model.zero_grad()` does it for all the model's parameters. The authors admit this can feel confusing: the loss tensor, the optimizer and the `Module` instance all seem aware of each other through a hidden background mechanism — "spooky action at a distance". Their advice: treat `loss.backward()` - `optimizer.step()` - `model.zero_grad()` as a magic incantation to recite whenever you write a training step, and never forget `model.zero_grad()` — that would be a major bug, and an unfortunately common one.

**Making PyTorch modules fast using compilation.** Like TensorFlow, PyTorch can compile functions — and even `Module` instances — with `torch.compile()`, which uses PyTorch's own compiler, **Dynamo**. Applied to the linear-regression Module: `compiled_model = torch.compile(model)`. The resulting object should behave identically to the original, except that the forward and backward passes should run faster. `torch.compile` can also be used as a decorator, shown on a `dense(inputs, W, b)` function returning `relu(matmul(inputs, W) + b)`. In practice, however, most PyTorch code does not use compilation and simply runs eagerly: the compiler may not work with all models and may not give a speedup when it does. Unlike TensorFlow and JAX, where compilation was built in from the start, PyTorch's compiler is a relatively recent addition.

**3.4.3 What makes the PyTorch approach unique.** Compared with TensorFlow and JAX (covered next), why use PyTorch or not? The first of two key strengths: PyTorch executes eagerly by default, which makes it easy to debug. TensorFlow and JAX also run eagerly by default, but PyTorch is intended to run eagerly *at all times*, whereas any serious TensorFlow or JAX project will eventually need compilation, which can significantly hurt the debugging experience. The second strength and PyTorch's downsides are on p.106. model.zero_grad() replaces per-tensor `.grad = None` resets. Treat loss.backward() - optimizer.step() - model.zero_grad() as a fixed recipe; never forget zero_grad(). torch.compile() (Dynamo) compiles a Module or function; the result should behave identically but run faster. Most PyTorch code runs eagerly because the compiler doesn't always work or help, and it is a recent addition. PyTorch's first key strength: it is meant to run eagerly at all times, which keeps debugging easy.

title: PyTorch's strengths and downsides; introducing JAX and its stateless approach
text:
Finishing the assessment of PyTorch (Hugging Face support; API inconsistency, slowness, an immature compiler) and introducing JAX: its origin, adoption, and stateless model of computation PyTorch's ecosystem — especially Hugging Face's first-class support — is the main driver of its adoption, but its API is inconsistent, it is the slowest major framework, and its Dynamo compiler is (in 2025) ineffective. JAX, developed mainly by Google and released in 2018, takes a stateless approach to computation: functions hold no persistent state, which enables automatic parallelization and distributed computation at very large scale. The page opens with PyTorch's **second key strength** (the first, eager execution, is on p.105): the popular pretrained-model sharing platform **Hugging Face** has first-class support for PyTorch, so any model you'd like to use is likely available in PyTorch — the authors call this the primary drive behind PyTorch adoption today.

Then the **downsides**:

- **API inconsistency.** As with TensorFlow, the PyTorch API is inconsistent with NumPy, and it is also internally inconsistent: the common keyword `axis` is sometimes named `dim` depending on the function, and some pseudo-random number generation operations take a `seed` argument while others don't. This can make PyTorch frustrating to learn, especially coming from NumPy.
- **Speed.** Because of its focus on eager execution, PyTorch is quite slow — the slowest major framework by a large margin. For most models you may see a 20% or 30% speedup with JAX; for some, especially large ones, a 3× or 5× speedup, even after using `torch.compile()`.
- **Compilation.** `torch.compile()` can make PyTorch faster, but the Dynamo compiler remains, as of 2025, quite ineffective and full of trapdoors, so only a very small percentage of PyTorch users compile. Perhaps future versions will improve this.

**Section 3.5, Introduction to JAX.** JAX is an open source library for differentiable computation, primarily developed by Google. Released in 2018, it gained traction in research, particularly for its ability to use Google's **TPUs** at scale; today most of the top players in generative AI use it — DeepMind, Apple, Midjourney, Anthropic, Cohere and others.

JAX embraces a **stateless** approach: functions do not maintain any persistent state, in contrast to traditional imperative programming where variables hold values between calls. Statelessness enables effective **automatic parallelization and distributed computation**, since functions can run independently without synchronization; this extreme scalability is essential for the very large ML problems faced by companies like Google and DeepMind.

**3.5.1 First steps with JAX** lists the key concepts to be covered: the `array` class, random operations, numerical operations (and, on p.107, gradients via `jax.grad`/`jax.value_and_grad` and just-in-time compilation). Hugging Face's first-class PyTorch support is the primary driver of PyTorch adoption today. PyTorch's downsides: API inconsistent with NumPy and with itself (axis vs dim, seed arguments), slowest major framework, ineffective Dynamo compiler (2025). JAX can be 20–30% faster for most models and 3–5× for some large ones, even against compiled PyTorch. JAX: open source, primarily by Google, released 2018, strong on TPUs, widely used in generative AI. JAX is stateless — functions keep no persistent state — which enables automatic parallelization and distributed computation.

title: JAX arrays via jax.numpy, and why stateless JAX can't use NumPy-style global random state
text:
jax.numpy as a faithful implementation of the NumPy API, its two differences from NumPy (random number generation and array assignment), and how NumPy's hidden global RNG state conflicts with JAX's statelessness JAX does not invent a NumPy-like API — it implements the NumPy API as is, in jax.numpy (imported as jnp). The only two differences are random number generation and array assignment. NumPy's random functions return different values on each call because of hidden global state; a stateless framework cannot have such state, so the same call must always return the same value and different random values require passing different seeds. The page completes the list of concepts for **3.5.1 First steps with JAX** begun on p.106: besides the `array` class, random operations and numerical operations, the section covers computing gradients via `jax.grad` and `jax.value_and_grad`, and making JAX functions fast with just-in-time compilation. "Let's get started."

**3.5.2 Tensors in JAX.** One of JAX's best features is that it doesn't implement its own "similar-to-NumPy-but-slightly-divergent" numerical API (a dig at TensorFlow and PyTorch, pp.90 and 106): it implements the NumPy API as is, in the `jax.numpy` namespace, usually imported as `jnp`. **Listing 3.28** shows `jnp.ones(shape=(2, 1))` and `jnp.zeros(shape=(2, 1))`, each printed as an `Array` of shape (2, 1) with `dtype=float32`, and `jnp.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32")` → `Array([1., 2., 3.], dtype=float32)`. There are, however, two minor differences from NumPy: **random number generation** and **array assignment**.

**3.5.3 Random number generation in JAX.** The first difference concerns PRNG (pseudo-random number generation) operations. Because JAX is stateless (p.106), JAX code cannot rely on hidden global state. **Listing 3.29** shows the NumPy behaviour: two identical calls to `np.random.normal(size=(3,))` return two different arrays. How did the second call know to differ? A hidden piece of global state, which you can retrieve with `np.random.get_state()` and set with `np.random.seed(seed)`. In a stateless framework there can be no such global state: the same API call must always return the same value, so in a stateless version of NumPy you would have to pass different seed arguments to your `np.random` calls to get different values. How this is managed — and JAX's seed keys — continues on p.108. Section 3.5.1 also covers gradients (jax.grad, jax.value_and_grad) and just-in-time compilation. jax.numpy (jnp) implements the NumPy API as is; arrays print as Array(..., dtype=float32). The only two differences from NumPy: random number generation and array assignment. NumPy's random functions return new values each call because of hidden global state (np.random.get_state / np.random.seed). In stateless JAX, the same random call must return the same value, so different values require different seeds.

title: Seed keys: stateless random numbers in JAX
text:
How JAX replaces NumPy's hidden global random state with explicit, immutable PRNG keys that every random function takes as its first argument. Because JAX is stateless, random functions cannot remember where they are in a random stream. You pass the randomness in explicitly as a key: the same key always produces the same numbers, and you get fresh randomness by deriving new keys with `jax.random.split()`. This page continues section 3.5.3 on random number generation in JAX. The previous page (p.107) showed that NumPy's `np.random.normal()` returns different values on each call because it silently advances a **hidden global state**, and noted that a stateless framework cannot have such state: the same call must always return the same value.

The page first shows what this means in plain NumPy if you refuse to rely on global state across calls: a function such as `apply_noise(x, seed)` receives its seed as an argument, and the *caller* is responsible for changing the seed (`seed += 1`) between calls so that each call gets different noise. The seed state lives outside the function.

JAX works "basically the same", with one change: instead of integer seeds it uses special array structures called **keys**, created from an integer with `jax.random.key(1337)`. To make it impossible to forget the seed, **every** JAX random function takes the key as its **first positional argument**, e.g. `jax.random.normal(seed_key, shape=(3,))`, which with `key(0)` prints `Array([ 1.8160863 , -0.48262316,  0.33988908], dtype=float32)`.

Listing 3.30 demonstrates the consequence: calling `jax.random.normal` twice with the same `key(123)` returns exactly the same array, `[-0.1470326, 0.5524756, 1.648498]`, both times. Randomness in JAX is a pure function of the key.

The page ends by introducing `jax.random.split()`, which creates new keys from an existing one. It is deterministic, so the same sequence of splits always yields the same final key; the example code for this is on the next page (p.109), along with the authors' justification that statelessness makes code vectorizable and reproducible. JAX has no hidden global random state; randomness is an explicit input called a key. Create a key from an integer with `jax.random.key(seed)`. Every JAX random function takes the key as its first positional argument, e.g. `jax.random.normal(key, shape=(3,))`. The same key always produces the same values (Listing 3.30); reuse means repetition. Get fresh randomness by deriving new keys with the deterministic `jax.random.split()`. The NumPy `apply_noise(x, seed)` pattern, where the caller manages the seed, is the same idea in familiar syntax.

title: PRNG key (JAX)
text: A special JAX array that holds the state of the pseudo-random generator and is passed explicitly as the first argument of every JAX random function. Think of the key as a ticket: the same ticket always wins the same prize. To get a different prize you need a new ticket, which you derive from an existing one. Created with `jax.random.key(seed_int)`. Random functions compute their output purely from the key plus shape/dtype arguments; they never modify the key. New keys come from `jax.random.split()`. `jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(123), shape=(3,))` always returns `[-0.1470326, 0.5524756, 1.648498]` (Listing 3.30).

title: Stateless computation
text: A style in which functions keep no persistent hidden state: their outputs depend only on their inputs. A calculator rather than a notebook: press the same keys, get the same answer, and nothing is written down between presses. In JAX this applies to randomness (keys instead of a global generator) and to arrays (no in-place assignment, p.109). Any state the computation needs must be passed in and, if updated, returned. `apply_noise(x, seed)` receives the seed as an argument instead of relying on `np.random`'s hidden state between calls.

title: Pseudo-random number generation (PRNG)
text: Producing random-looking numbers with a deterministic algorithm driven by a seed. A very long, scrambled list of numbers; the seed tells you where to start reading. NumPy keeps the generator state globally (`np.random.get_state()` / `np.random.seed()`, p.107); JAX makes the state an explicit value (the key). `np.random.seed(1337)` followed by `np.random.normal(...)` is reproducible; calling `np.random.normal(...)` again without reseeding gives different numbers.

title: Key splitting
text: Deriving new PRNG keys from an existing key with `jax.random.split()`. Like a family tree: each key can have children, and the whole tree is fixed by the root seed. Deterministic: the same sequence of splits always yields the same final key (book). Beyond the book: it returns an array of new keys (two by default) that are statistically independent streams. `key, subkey = jax.random.split(key)` then `jax.random.normal(subkey, shape=(3,))` (idiom, not from this page).

title: Managing the seed outside the function (NumPy)
text:
def apply_noise(x, seed):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    x = x * np.random.normal((3,))
    return x
seed = 1337
y = apply_noise(x, seed)
seed += 1
z = apply_noise(x, seed) Defines a function that multiplies its input by random noise generated from an explicitly provided seed, then calls it twice with two different seeds so that `y` and `z` receive different noise. State-passing: the caller owns and advances the seed; the function is deterministic given `(x, seed)`.

title: Key splitting, immutable arrays and NumPy-style math in JAX
text:
Finishing JAX's PRNG story with `jax.random.split()`, explaining why statelessness pays off, then covering the second NumPy difference (no in-place assignment, use `.at[].set()`) and showing that ordinary math is identical to NumPy. Explicit keys are more work than `np.random`, but they make JAX code vectorizable and deterministic. The same stateless principle forbids in-place array updates: you build a new array with `x.at[i].set(v)`. Everything else, the math, is just NumPy. The page opens with the code that completes p.108's description of `jax.random.split()`. Starting from `jax.random.key(123)`, which gives `[-0.1470326, 0.5524756, 1.648498]` (as in Listing 3.30), the code derives `new_seed_key = jax.random.split(seed_key, num=1)[0]`; sampling with the new key gives different values, `[0.5362355, -1.1920372, 2.450225]`. A callout notes that you could split a key into multiple new keys at once.

The authors admit this is "definitely more work than `np.random`", but argue that the benefits of statelessness far outweigh the costs: it makes code **vectorizable** (the JAX compiler can automatically turn it into highly parallel code) while keeping it **deterministic** (the same code run twice gives the same results). Both together are impossible with a global PRNG state.

**Tensor assignment** is the second difference from NumPy. As in TensorFlow, JAX arrays are not assignable in place, because in-place modification would go against JAX's stateless design. To "update" a tensor you create a new one, using the `at()`/`set()` API. Listing 3.31 creates `x = jnp.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32")` and then `new_x = x.at[0].set(10)`, a new array whose first element is 10. `x` itself is unchanged.

**Tensor operations** look exactly as in NumPy. Listing 3.32 builds `a = jnp.ones((2, 2))`, then takes the element-wise square (`jnp.square`) and square root (`jnp.sqrt`), adds tensors element-wise, computes a matrix product with `jnp.matmul` (see chapter 2), and multiplies element-wise with `e *= d`. `jax.random.split(key, num=1)[0]` derives a new key that gives different but reproducible random values. Statelessness costs some convenience but gives vectorization and determinism together. JAX arrays cannot be modified in place; use `new_x = x.at[i].set(v)` to get an updated copy. JAX math is identical to NumPy math: `jnp.square`, `jnp.sqrt`, `+`, `jnp.matmul`, `*`. Randomness and assignment are the only two differences between `jax.numpy` and NumPy that the book highlights.

From `key(123)`, the split key gives `[0.5362355, -1.1920372, 2.450225]` instead of `[-0.1470326, 0.5524756, 1.648498]`.

In Listing 3.32 `b`, `c`, `d` and `e *= d` are element-wise; `e = jnp.matmul(a, b)` is the tensor product from chapter 2. title: The computation in Listing 3.32
text: a = jnp.ones((2, 2)); b = jnp.square(a); c = jnp.sqrt(a); d = b + c; e = jnp.matmul(a, b); e *= d \begin{aligned} a &= \mathbf{1}_{2\times 2}, \quad b = a \odot a, \quad c = \sqrt{a} \\ d &= b + c, \quad e = (a\,b) \odot d \end{aligned} Shows that JAX math is written exactly like NumPy math. title: A dense layer in JAX and gradients via jax.grad
text:
Writing a dense layer with `jnp` and introducing JAX's metaprogramming approach to gradients: `jax.grad` turns a loss function into a gradient function. Instead of recording operations on a tape (TensorFlow) or calling `.backward()` (PyTorch), JAX transforms a function: `jax.grad(compute_loss)` returns a new function that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the loss function's first argument. The page first closes the "Tensor operations" discussion with a **dense layer** written in JAX: `def dense(inputs, W, b): return jax.nn.relu(jnp.matmul(inputs, W) + b)`. It is the same affine-transform-plus-ReLU you saw in chapter 2, expressed with `jnp.matmul` and `jax.nn.relu`, and, notably, it is a pure function: the weights `W` and `b` are passed in as arguments rather than stored on an object.

The new subsection **Computing gradients with JAX** explains that, unlike TensorFlow and PyTorch, JAX takes a **metaprogramming** approach: it has *functions that return functions* ("meta-functions"). JAX lets you *turn a loss-computation function into a gradient-computation function*. The process has three steps:

1. Define a loss function, `compute_loss()`.
2. Call `grad_fn = jax.grad(compute_loss)` to retrieve a gradient-computation function.
3. Call `grad_fn` to get the gradient values.

The loss function must (a) return a **scalar** loss value, and (b) take as its **first argument** the state arrays you need gradients for, conventionally named `state`; that argument can be a single array, a list of arrays or a dict of arrays.

The simple example is `compute_loss(input_var)`, which returns `jnp.square(input_var)`. Calling `jax.grad(compute_loss)` returns `grad_fn`, a function that accepts the same arguments as `compute_loss` and returns the gradient of the loss with respect to `input_var`. Because the first argument is a single array here, `grad_fn()` directly returns one gradient array; the actual call and output are on the next page (p.111). A JAX dense layer is a pure function: `jax.nn.relu(jnp.matmul(inputs, W) + b)`. JAX computes gradients by metaprogramming: `jax.grad` turns a loss function into a gradient function. Three steps: define `compute_loss`, build `grad_fn = jax.grad(compute_loss)`, call `grad_fn`. The loss must return a scalar and take the state to differentiate as its first argument. `state` can be an array, a list of arrays or a dict of arrays; gradients come back in the same structure. `grad_fn` takes the same arguments as `compute_loss`.

title: jax.grad in practice: value_and_grad, state trees and auxiliary outputs
text:
Practical patterns for JAX gradients: calling the gradient function, getting the loss and gradient together with `jax.value_and_grad`, differentiating a whole state tuple/tree while passing extra inputs, and the setup for returning auxiliary outputs with `has_aux`. Real loss functions take a `state` of many arrays plus data inputs, and you usually want both the loss and its gradients. `jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss)` returns `(loss, grads)`, where `grads` mirrors the structure of `state`, the first argument. Extra by-products are handled with `has_aux`. The page opens with the call that finishes p.110's example: `input_var = jnp.array(3.0)` and `grad_of_loss_wrt_input_var = grad_fn(input_var)`. Since the loss is $x^2$, this gradient is $2 \cdot 3 = 6$ (the value is not printed in the book).

Under **JAX gradient-computation best practices**, the authors note that metaprogramming "is a big word, but it turns out to be quite simple", and present three real-world refinements.

**Returning the loss value.** You usually need the loss as well as the gradient, and recomputing it separately would be inefficient. `jax.value_and_grad()` works identically to `jax.grad()` but returns a tuple: first the loss value, then the gradient(s): `output, grad_of_loss_wrt_input_var = grad_fn(input_var)`.

**Getting gradients for a complex function.** If the state contains three variables `a`, `b`, `c` and the loss also takes two inputs `x`, `y`, you write `compute_loss(state, x, y)`, with `state` as the first argument (callout: "state contains a, b, and c. It must be the first argument"). Then `state = (a, b, c)` and `loss, grads_of_loss_wrt_state = grad_fn(state, x, y)`. A second callout notes that `grads_of_loss_wrt_state` has the same structure as `state`. Gradients are taken only with respect to `state`; `x` and `y` are treated as plain inputs. The state need not be a tuple: any nested structure of tuples, dicts and lists works, which JAX calls a **tree**.

**Returning auxiliary outputs.** If `compute_loss()` must also return a by-product, such as the model `output` computed along the way, you use the `has_aux` argument. The two-step recipe and code are on the next page (p.112). Call `grad_fn` with the same arguments as `compute_loss` to get gradients. `jax.value_and_grad` returns `(loss, gradients)` and avoids recomputing the loss. Pack all variables that need gradients into one `state` and make it the first argument; data inputs go after. The gradients have the same structure as `state`. `state` can be any tree: nested tuples, dicts and lists. title: has_aux, @jax.jit, and the start of the pure-JAX classifier
text:
Returning auxiliary outputs from a loss with `has_aux=True`, compiling stateless functions with `@jax.jit`, and the two differences between the JAX linear classifier and its TensorFlow/PyTorch counterparts. The JAX gradient toolkit is completed by `has_aux` (return by-products alongside the loss) and `@jax.jit` (XLA-compile any stateless function for speed). With these, the linear classifier can be rewritten as purely stateless functions that receive `W` and `b` as arguments, return new values, and get gradients from `value_and_grad()`. The page finishes the **Returning auxiliary outputs** recipe from p.111. To return an extra by-product from `compute_loss()`:

1. Edit the loss function to return a tuple whose first entry is the loss and second entry is the extra output.
2. Pass `has_aux=True` to `value_and_grad()`, so it returns not just the gradient but also the "auxiliary" output(s).

The code shows `return loss, output` (callout: "Returns a tuple"), `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss, has_aux=True)`, and the call `loss, (grads_of_loss_wrt_state, output) = grad_fn(state, x, y)` (callout: "Gets back a nested tuple"). *Note (not in the book):* in the JAX API the nesting is the other way round, `((loss, output), grads)`; see the code pitfalls.

The authors concede things are getting convoluted but reassure readers this is "about as hard as JAX gets".

**Making JAX functions fast with `@jax.jit`.** The `@jax.jit` decorator behaves identically to TensorFlow's `@tf.function(jit_compile=True)`: it turns any **stateless** JAX function into XLA-compiled code, typically with a considerable speedup. The example decorates the `dense` function from p.110. You can only decorate stateless functions; any tensors the function updates must be part of its return values.

**3.5.4 An end-to-end example: A linear classifier in pure JAX.** The JAX version of the linear classifier from the TensorFlow (p.93) and PyTorch (p.102) sections differs in two ways: (1) all functions are stateless, so `W` and `b` are passed as arguments and new values are returned; (2) gradients come from `value_and_grad()`. The model and MSE functions follow on p.113. To return extra outputs from a loss: return `(loss, output)` and pass `has_aux=True` to `value_and_grad()`. Only the loss is differentiated; the auxiliary output is passed through. (Check the tuple nesting against the JAX API: `((loss, aux), grads)`.) `@jax.jit` XLA-compiles stateless JAX functions, like `@tf.function(jit_compile=True)`, typically giving a big speedup. Jitted functions must be stateless: return any tensors they update. The JAX linear classifier passes `W` and `b` as arguments, returns new values, and uses `value_and_grad()` for gradients.

title: The pure-JAX linear classifier: model, loss and a stateless training step
text:
Implementing the linear classifier in JAX: a linear model function, an MSE loss, a `compute_loss(state, inputs, targets)` wrapper, `jax.value_and_grad`, and a jitted, stateless `training_step` that returns the updated `W` and `b`. Everything from p.110-112 comes together: package the loss so that the parameters `(W, b)` form the first argument, build `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss)`, and write a `@jax.jit` training step that computes loss and gradients in one go and *returns* new `W` and `b` instead of mutating them. The page builds the JAX version of the chapter's linear classifier.

**Model and loss.** `model(inputs, W, b)` returns `jnp.matmul(inputs, W) + b`, an affine transform with no activation. `mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)` squares the per-sample differences and averages them with `jnp.mean`. As the authors say at the bottom of p.112, these "should look familiar" from the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions.

**Packaging the loss.** To compute gradients, the loss is wrapped in a single `compute_loss(state, inputs, targets)` that returns the total loss as a **scalar** and takes `state` as its **first argument**, here a tuple `(W, b)` of all tensors needing gradients. It unpacks `W, b = state`, runs the model and computes the MSE.

**Gradient function.** `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss)` gives a function with the same arguments that returns both the loss and the gradients with respect to the elements of `state`.

**Training step.** With `learning_rate = 0.1`, `training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)` is decorated with `@jax.jit` to use XLA compilation. It calls `grad_fn((W, b), inputs, targets)`, which "computes the forward pass and backward pass in one go", unpacks `grad_wrt_W, grad_wrt_b`, applies the gradient-descent updates `W = W - grad_wrt_W * learning_rate` and `b = b - grad_wrt_b * learning_rate`, and **returns `loss, W, b`**. Unlike the TensorFlow and PyTorch equivalents, it must be stateless, so it must return the new values (callout: "Make sure to return the new values of W and b in addition to the loss!").

Because the learning rate is fixed in this example, it is treated as part of the function rather than as model state; if you wanted to change it during training you would have to pass it in as well. The page ends by announcing the training loop, which initializes `W` and `b` and repeatedly updates them via stateless calls to `training_step()` (code on p.114). The JAX classifier's model is `jnp.matmul(inputs, W) + b` and its loss is the mean of squared errors. `compute_loss(state, inputs, targets)` takes `(W, b)` first and returns a scalar. `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss)` returns the loss and gradients for W and b in one go. The `@jax.jit` training step must be stateless: it returns `loss, W, b`. A constant learning rate can live inside the function; anything that changes during training must be passed in. The training loop owns the state and rebinds W and b after each step.

title: A jitted, stateless training step
text:
learning_rate = 0.1
@jax.jit
def training_step(inputs, targets, W, b):
    loss, grads = grad_fn((W, b), inputs, targets)
    grad_wrt_W, grad_wrt_b = grads
    W = W - grad_wrt_W * learning_rate
    b = b - grad_wrt_b * learning_rate
    return loss, W, b Computes loss and gradients, performs one gradient-descent update, and returns the loss with the new W and b. One step of full-batch gradient descent.

title: Stateless (functional) computation
text: A programming style where functions keep no persistent state: all inputs come in as arguments and all changed values go out as return values. Like a vending machine that has no memory. You give it the current weights and data, it hands back a loss and new weights, and you have to keep hold of them yourself. In JAX, `training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)` returns `(loss, W_new, b_new)`. The caller rebinds `W, b` each iteration. Because the function is pure, `jax.jit` can trace it once and compile it with XLA. `loss, W, b = training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)` in the loop on this page.
snippet: A programming style where functions keep no persistent state: all inputs come in as arguments and all changed values go out as return values.
chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras

title: XLA compilation via jax.jit
text: Compiling a Python function into optimized device code through the XLA compiler. Instead of interpreting each operation one at a time, the whole step is translated once into a single fast program. `@jax.jit` (p.113) traces the function with abstract values on the first call and compiles the trace. Later calls with the same shapes and dtypes reuse the compiled code. The tracing is what makes debugging harder. The 40 loop iterations here all run the same compiled `training_step`.
snippet: Compiling a Python function into optimized device code through the XLA compiler.

title: Initializing W and b and running the JAX training loop
text:
input_dim = 2
output_dim = 1

W = jax.numpy.array(np.random.uniform(size=(input_dim, output_dim)))
b = jax.numpy.array(np.zeros(shape=(output_dim,)))
state = (W, b)
for step in range(40):
    loss, W, b = training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)
    print(f"Loss at step {step}: {loss:.4f}") Creates the initial parameters of a linear model with 2 inputs and 1 output, then runs 40 gradient descent steps. Each step replaces W and b with the updated values returned by the stateless training_step, and the loss is printed. Full-batch gradient descent with learning rate 0.1 (fixed inside training_step). Each step computes MSE loss and gradients with value_and_grad and applies W ← W − 0.1·∇W, b ← b − 0.1·∇b.

title: Keras workflows and picking a backend framework
text:
Keras' spectrum of workflows, its pluggable backends (JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch), the layered stack of Figure 3.4, and how to choose a backend Keras is a high-level API sitting on a pluggable low-level backend (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX), which in turn runs on CPU, GPU or TPU. Because backends can be swapped after the code is written, you can debug, train and deploy the same model with different frameworks. TensorFlow is the default; you change it, for example, with the KERAS_BACKEND environment variable. The page finishes the list of Keras users (Waymo uses Keras models to process sensor data, and Keras is popular on **Kaggle**). It then draws a design consequence. Because the user base is diverse, Keras **doesn't force a single "true" way** of building and training models. It offers a **spectrum of workflows from very high-level to very low-level**, with several ways to build models and several ways to train them, each a trade-off between **usability and flexibility**. Chapter 7 covers much of this spectrum.

Section **3.6.1, First steps with Keras**, starts with configuration that must be done *before* Keras is imported.

**Picking a backend framework.** Keras runs on **JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch**, its "backend frameworks". Through them it can run on GPU, TPU or CPU, scale to thousands of machines, and deploy to many platforms. **Figure 3.4** shows the stack:

- **Keras** on top, for deep learning development: layers, models, optimizers, losses, metrics, training loops;
- the **backend framework** in the middle, the tensor manipulation infrastructure: tensors, variables, automatic differentiation, distribution;
- **hardware** (CPU, GPU, TPU) at the bottom, which does the execution.

Backends are **pluggable**. You can switch backend *after* writing Keras code, so you aren't locked into one ecosystem. The authors' example is to debug a model with PyTorch, train it on TPU with JAX for maximum efficiency, then run inference with TensorFlow's tooling.

The **default backend is TensorFlow**: a plain `import keras` in a fresh environment runs on TensorFlow. There are two ways to change it. The first, begun on this page, is the environment variable **`KERAS_BACKEND`**, e.g. `export KERAS_BACKEND=jax` before starting Python. Setting it from inside a script, and the `~/.keras/keras.json` config file, are covered on p.116. Keras offers a spectrum of workflows trading usability for flexibility; chapter 7 explores it. Keras runs on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch, which handle tensors, variables, autodiff and distribution on CPU, GPU or TPU. Backends are pluggable: the same Keras code can be debugged, trained and deployed with different frameworks. TensorFlow is the default backend; change it with KERAS_BACKEND (e.g. export KERAS_BACKEND=jax) before importing Keras.

title: Calling a layer; automatic shape inference
text:
Using SimpleDense as a function, why call() and build() are separate from __call__(), layer compatibility, and the start of automatic shape inference with a two-layer Sequential model A Keras layer is used by calling it on a tensor: SimpleDense(32) maps (2, 784) to (2, 32). call() and build() are separate methods so that state can be created just in time. Layers only connect when shapes are compatible, but Keras layers build themselves to match the first input they receive, so a Sequential stack of Dense(32) layers needs no input sizes. The page continues 3.6.2 directly after Listing 3.33. The authors say the purpose of `build()` and `call()` will be explained shortly, so don't worry if it isn't fully clear yet.

**Using the layer.** Once instantiated, a layer is used like a function:

```
my_dense = SimpleDense(units=32, activation=keras.ops.relu)
input_tensor = keras.ops.ones(shape=(2, 784))
output_tensor = my_dense(input_tensor)   # shape (2, 32)
```

The batch of 2 vectors with 784 features becomes 2 vectors with 32 features.

**Why `call()` and `build()`?** We just called the layer through its `__call__()` method, so why implement two other methods? Because we want to **create the state just in time**, when the input shape is first known.

**Automatic shape inference: building layers on the fly.** As with LEGO bricks, only **compatible** layers can be clipped together. *Layer compatibility* means each layer accepts inputs of a certain shape and returns outputs of a certain shape. For example, `layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")` returns tensors whose non-batch dimension is 32, so it can only feed a downstream layer that expects 32-dimensional vectors.

In practice you rarely have to manage this, because Keras layers are **dynamically built to match the shape of their incoming inputs**. The page ends with a `models.Sequential` of `Dense(32, activation="relu")` followed by `Dense(32)`, with no input sizes given. p.119 explains that each layer infers its input shape from the first inputs it sees, and contrasts this with chapter 2's NaiveDense, which needed the input size in its constructor. Layers are callable: SimpleDense(32)(ones((2, 784))) returns shape (2, 32). build() and call() are separate so state can be created just in time, on first call. Layer compatibility means output shapes must match the next layer's expected input shapes. Dense(32) outputs tensors with non-batch dimension 32. Keras layers build themselves to match incoming inputs, so a Sequential model needs no input sizes for its layers.

title: Automatic shape inference
text: Keras layers create their weights on first use, sized according to the shape of the first input they receive. It is like a tailor who waits until the customer arrives before cutting the cloth. The base Layer.__call__ checks whether the layer is built. If not, it calls build(input.shape), then call(inputs) (p.119). Weight shapes such as W's (input_dim, units) are therefore resolved lazily. Sequential([Dense(32, relu), Dense(32)]): the second layer builds a (32, 32) kernel because it receives 32-d inputs.

title: Why build(): automatic shape inference vs NaiveDense
text:
How Keras layers infer input shapes, the burden of explicit input sizes in chapter 2's NaiveDense, and the base Layer.__call__() that builds on first call Keras layers infer their input shape from the first inputs they see. Chapter 2's NaiveDense needed input_size in its constructor, which forces every layer to know the previous layer's output size. Keras moves weight creation into build(input_shape), which the base __call__ runs automatically once before delegating to call(). The four-layer model then needs only output sizes. Following the Sequential example on p.118, the page notes that **the layers received no information about their input shapes**. They **inferred their input shape as the shape of the first inputs they see**.

**The alternative is worse.** Chapter 2's toy `NaiveDense` needed the input size passed to its constructor so it could create its weights. A model then looks like

`NaiveSequential([NaiveDense(input_size=784, output_size=32, "relu"), NaiveDense(32→64, "relu"), NaiveDense(64→32, "relu"), NaiveDense(32→10, "softmax")])`,

where every layer must be told the previous layer's output size. It gets worse when a layer's output shape follows a complex rule, such as `(batch, input_size * 2 if input_size % 2 == 0 else input_size * 3)`. Then you would have to work that rule out by hand for the next layer.

**The Keras solution.** Reimplementing NaiveDense with automatic shape inference gives exactly `SimpleDense` with its `build()` and `call()` methods. Weights are no longer created in the constructor but in a dedicated state-creation method, `build()`, which receives **the first input shape seen by the layer**. `build()` runs automatically the first time the layer is called through `__call__()`. That is why the computation lives in a separate `call()` instead of in `__call__()` directly. Schematically, the base layer's `__call__` is:

```
if not self.built:
    self.build(inputs.shape)
    self.built = True
return self.call(inputs)
```

With automatic shape inference, the earlier model becomes `keras.Sequential([SimpleDense(32, activation="relu"), SimpleDense(64, activation="relu"), SimpleDense(32, activation="relu"), …])`, giving only output sizes. The listing continues on p.120. Keras layers infer their input shape from the first input they see. Explicit input sizes (NaiveDense) duplicate information and break when widths change or output-shape rules are complex. build(input_shape) creates weights; the base __call__ runs it once, sets built = True, then calls call(). Put the forward pass in call(), not __call__(). With inference, models specify only output widths: Sequential([SimpleDense(32), SimpleDense(64), …]).
