title: From layers to models: topology as hypothesis space
text:
What the base Layer.__call__() does besides shape inference, the Keras Model class as a graph of layers, common network topologies, and why architecture choice defines the hypothesis space. A model is a graph of layers, and choosing its topology restricts learning to a specific family of tensor operations; training then only searches for good weight values inside that family. The architecture therefore encodes your prior assumptions about the problem. The page begins by finishing the `keras.Sequential` example from p.119, whose final layer is `SimpleDense(10, activation="softmax")`. Thanks to automatic shape inference, none of the `SimpleDense` layers needs to be told its input size.

The authors then point out that shape inference is **not the only job** of the base `Layer.__call__()` method. It also routes between **eager** and **graph** execution and handles **input masking** (covered in chapter 14). The practical rule: when you write your own layer, put the forward pass in `call()`, never in `__call__()`.

Section **3.6.3 From layers to models** says that a deep learning model is a **graph of layers**, represented in Keras by the `Model` class. So far you have only seen `Sequential` models, a subclass of `Model` that is a simple stack mapping one input to one output. Many other topologies exist: **two-branch networks**, **multihead networks** and **residual connections**. Figure 3.5 (on p.121) shows how complex the graph of a Transformer is. Keras offers two ways to build such models: **subclassing `Model`** or the **Functional API**. Both are covered in chapter 7.

The key conceptual point is that **the topology of a model defines a hypothesis space**. Recalling chapter 1's definition of machine learning as "searching for useful representations of some input data, within a predefined space of possibilities, using guidance from a feedback signal", the authors explain that picking a topology restricts the space of possibilities to a specific series of tensor operations. Training then only searches for good values of the weight tensors in those operations. To learn from data you must make assumptions about it, so **the architecture encodes your prior knowledge**. For example, a two-class classifier made of a single `Dense` layer with no activation (a pure affine transformation) assumes the two classes are **linearly separable**.

The page ends by saying that choosing an architecture is more art than science. There are best practices, but only practice makes you a good "neural network architect". The next chapters will teach both explicit principles and intuition (the sentence continues on p.121). Layer.__call__() handles shape inference, eager/graph routing and masking; your forward pass belongs in call(). A Keras Model is a graph of layers; Sequential is the special case of a linear stack with one input and one output. Two-branch, multihead and residual topologies need the Functional API or Model subclassing (chapter 7). The topology defines the hypothesis space; training only searches for weight values inside it. Architecture encodes prior assumptions. A single linear Dense layer assumes linearly separable classes. Architecture design is more art than science and is learned through practice.

title: Figure 3.5 (Transformer) and the start of the compile step
text:
A visual example of a complex graph of layers (the Transformer), the end of the discussion of architecture, and the first two of the three training choices made at compile time: loss function and optimizer. Real architectures such as the Transformer are intricate graphs of layers. Once an architecture is fixed, you still have to pick a loss function (what to minimize) and an optimizer (how to update weights using that loss), plus metrics (p.122). Most of this page is **figure 3.5, the Transformer architecture**, which p.120 used as an example of how complex network topologies can get. The diagram has two large blocks. The left **encoder** block stacks `MultiHeadAttention` → `+` (residual addition) → `LayerNormalization` → two `Dense` layers → `+` → `LayerNormalization`. The right **decoder** block has a `MultiHeadAttention` over its own input, then `+` and `LayerNormalization`, then a second `MultiHeadAttention` that also receives the encoder's output (the line crossing from the left block), then `+`, `LayerNormalization`, two `Dense` layers, `+` and a final `LayerNormalization`. Arrows that bypass blocks and enter a `+` node are **residual connections**. The caption admits "there's a lot going on here" and promises you will work up to understanding it in **chapter 15**.

The body text finishes the sentence from p.120. Over the coming chapters you will build intuition about which architectures suit which problems, how to build them in practice, how to pick the right **learning configuration**, and how to tweak a model until it gives the results you want.

Section **3.6.4, the "compile" step**, then begins. Once the architecture is defined, three more things must be chosen. Two are on this page:

- **Loss function (objective function)**: the quantity minimized during training, representing a measure of success for the task.
- **Optimizer**: determines how the network is updated based on the loss; it implements a specific variant of **stochastic gradient descent (SGD)**.

The third item, **metrics**, appears on p.122, together with the `compile()` call that receives all three. Figure 3.5's Transformer is a graph of MultiHeadAttention, Dense, residual + and LayerNormalization in an encoder and a decoder block; it is explained in chapter 15. title: Metrics and the compile() method
text:
The third training choice (metrics), how compile() takes optimizer, loss and metrics, and the difference between string shortcuts and object instances. Metrics are monitored but not optimized, so they need not be differentiable. compile() receives the optimizer, loss and a list of metrics, either as string shortcuts (converted to objects) or as configured object instances or custom callables. The page finishes the list of three training choices begun on p.121 with **metrics**: "the measures of success you want to monitor during training and validation, such as classification accuracy." Unlike the loss, training does **not optimize metrics directly**, so they **don't need to be differentiable**.

With loss, optimizer and metrics chosen, you can train with the built-in **`compile()`** and **`fit()`** methods. The alternative is to write a **custom training loop** (chapter 7), which the authors warn is "a lot more work!"

`compile()` configures the training process and was already used in chapter 2's first example. It takes `optimizer`, `loss` and `metrics` (a list). The first listing builds `keras.Sequential([keras.layers.Dense(1)])`, which the callout calls a linear classifier, and compiles it with `optimizer="rmsprop"` (names are case-insensitive), `loss="mean_squared_error"` and `metrics=["accuracy"]`.

The strings are **shortcuts that get converted to Python objects**. For example, `"rmsprop"` becomes `keras.optimizers.RMSprop()`. You can pass the objects yourself: `keras.optimizers.RMSprop()`, `keras.losses.MeanSquaredError()`, `[keras.metrics.BinaryAccuracy()]`. This is useful in two cases: to pass **custom** losses or metrics, or to **configure** the objects, for example `keras.optimizers.RMSprop(learning_rate=1e-4)`. The last listing shows a compile call with a configured optimizer, `loss=my_custom_loss` and `metrics=[my_custom_metric_1, my_custom_metric_2]`. These names are placeholders for functions you would write yourself; chapter 7 covers how (p.123). Metrics are monitored, not optimized, so they need not be differentiable; accuracy is the typical example. Train with built-in compile()+fit(), or with a custom loop (chapter 7) when you need more control. compile(optimizer=..., loss=..., metrics=[...]) configures training; metrics is a list. Strings like "rmsprop" are shortcuts converted to objects like keras.optimizers.RMSprop(). Pass object instances to set hyperparameters (learning_rate=1e-4) or to supply custom losses and metrics.

title: Built-in optimizers, losses, metrics; picking a loss
text:
The catalog of built-in Keras optimizers, losses and metrics, and why choosing a loss that truly matches the task is critical. Keras already provides most optimizers, losses and metrics you need. The loss deserves the most care, because a network will exploit any shortcut that lowers it. A loss that doesn't fully correlate with task success produces unintended behaviour. The page first finishes section 3.6.4. Custom losses and metrics are covered in chapter 7, but you will rarely need to build losses, metrics or optimizers from scratch, because Keras offers a wide range of built-in options:

- **Optimizers**: `SGD()` (with or without momentum), `RMSprop()`, `Adam()`, etc.
- **Losses**: `CategoricalCrossentropy()`, `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()`, `BinaryCrossentropy()`, `MeanSquaredError()`, `KLDivergence()`, `CosineSimilarity()`, etc.
- **Metrics**: `CategoricalAccuracy()`, `SparseCategoricalAccuracy()`, `BinaryAccuracy()`, `AUC()`, `Precision()`, `Recall()`, etc.

Concrete uses of many of these appear throughout the book.

Section **3.6.5, Picking a loss function**, stresses that choosing the right loss is **extremely important**, because "your network will take any shortcut it can to minimize the loss." If the objective doesn't fully correlate with success, the network will do things you didn't intend. The authors' thought experiment is a "stupid, omnipotent AI trained via SGD" told to "maximize the average well-being of all humans alive." It might kill all but a few humans and focus on them, since the *average* doesn't depend on how many people remain. Every network you build is "just as ruthless in lowering their loss function," so choose the objective wisely.

The page ends on a reassuring note that continues on p.124. For common problems (classification, regression, sequence prediction) there are simple guidelines for choosing the correct loss, such as binary crossentropy for two-class classification and categorical crossentropy for many-class classification. Keras ships most optimizers (SGD, RMSprop, Adam), losses (crossentropies, MSE, KL divergence, cosine similarity) and metrics (accuracies, AUC, precision, recall) you need. Custom losses and metrics are covered in chapter 7 but are rarely necessary. A network will take any shortcut that lowers its loss. If the loss doesn't fully correlate with success, expect unintended side effects, as in the 'average well-being' AI. Standard problems have standard losses (details on p.124).

title: Objective misspecification (shortcut exploitation)
text: When the stated objective does not fully correlate with success, the optimizer exploits shortcuts that lower the objective without achieving the goal. A student optimizing for test scores rather than understanding learns to game the test. Beyond the book: known in the literature as specification gaming or reward hacking; a form of Goodhart's law. The book's omnipotent AI; in ordinary ML, a skin-lesion classifier that learns to detect rulers in photos because malignant cases were photographed with rulers (illustrative, not from the book).

title: Crossentropy losses
text: The family of losses listed as BinaryCrossentropy, CategoricalCrossentropy and SparseCategoricalCrossentropy, used for classification. Measures how surprised the model is by the true label; confident wrong answers are punished heavily. Binary: −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]. Categorical: −Σ_k y_k log p_k. The sparse variant takes integer labels instead of one-hot vectors. True class probability 0.9 gives loss −log 0.9 ≈ 0.105; probability 0.1 gives ≈ 2.303.

title: Precision, recall and AUC
text: Built-in metrics listed on the page for evaluating classifiers beyond accuracy. Precision: when the model says yes, how often is it right? Recall: of all real yeses, how many did it catch? AUC: how well does it rank positives above negatives? Precision = TP/(TP+FP), Recall = TP/(TP+FN), AUC = area under the true-positive-rate vs false-positive-rate curve across thresholds. Out of 100 predicted positives, 80 are correct (precision 0.8); out of 200 actual positives, 80 are found (recall 0.4).

title: Loss guidelines and the fit() method
text:
Standard loss choices for common tasks, then fit(): its key arguments (data, epochs, batch size), listing 3.34, and the History object it returns. fit() implements the training loop. You pass data, a number of epochs and a batch size. It returns a History object whose history dict records the loss and each metric per epoch. The first paragraph finishes section 3.6.5's guidelines. Use **binary crossentropy** for two-class classification, **categorical crossentropy** for many-class classification, and so on. Only truly new research problems call for designing your own loss, and the next chapters will say explicitly which loss to use for many common tasks.

Section **3.6.6** introduces `fit()`, which comes after `compile()` and **implements the training loop itself**. Its key arguments are:

- the **data** (inputs and targets), typically NumPy arrays or a TensorFlow `Dataset` (covered in later chapters);
- the number of **epochs**: how many times the loop iterates over the data passed;
- the **batch size**: the number of training examples used to compute the gradients for one weight-update step of mini-batch gradient descent.

**Listing 3.34** calls `model.fit(inputs, targets, epochs=5, batch_size=128)`. The callouts identify `inputs` and `targets` as NumPy arrays and say the loop will iterate over the data 5 times, in batches of 128 examples.

`fit` returns a **`History`** object. Its `history` field is a dict mapping `"loss"` and each metric name to a list of per-epoch values. The printed example shows `binary_accuracy` rising from 0.855 to about 0.95 and `loss` dropping from about 0.657 after epoch 1 to about 0.074, then hovering around 0.074-0.077 for the remaining epochs. The metric is named `binary_accuracy`, consistent with the `compile()` call on p.122 that used `keras.metrics.BinaryAccuracy()` and MSE loss. Binary crossentropy for two-class, categorical crossentropy for many-class; custom losses are rarely needed. fit() implements the training loop; key arguments are the data, epochs and batch_size. An epoch is one pass over the data; the batch size is the number of samples per gradient update. fit() returns a History object whose history dict maps 'loss' and metric names to per-epoch lists. In the printed run, the loss falls from 0.657 to about 0.075 after one epoch and accuracy plateaus near 95%.

title: Monitoring loss and metrics on validation data
text:
Why training performance is not the goal, how to hold out validation data, and how to pass it to fit() via validation_data (listing 3.35). The goal is good performance on data the model has never seen, not on training data. To monitor this you hold out a shuffled subset of the data (here 30%) that is never trained on, pass it as validation_data to fit(), and watch the validation loss and metrics. Section **3.6.7** opens with a principle: the goal of machine learning is **not** good performance on the training data. That is easy, since "all you have to do is follow the gradient." The goal is models that **perform well in general**, especially on data points never encountered before. A model might simply **memorize** a mapping from training samples to targets, which is useless for predicting new targets. Chapter 5 treats this in detail.

To track performance on new data, it is standard to **reserve a subset of the training data as validation data**. You don't train on it, but you compute loss and metrics on it. In Keras you pass it through the **`validation_data`** argument of `fit()`, as NumPy arrays or a TensorFlow `Dataset`.

**Listing 3.35** rebuilds the `Dense(1)` linear classifier and compiles it with `RMSprop(learning_rate=0.1)`, `MeanSquaredError()` and `BinaryAccuracy()`. It then:

1. **shuffles** inputs and targets with the same random permutation (`np.random.permutation(len(inputs))`). The callout explains this avoids a validation set containing samples from only one class;
2. **reserves 30%** of the samples (`int(0.3 * len(inputs))`) as `val_inputs`/`val_targets` and keeps the remaining 70% as training data;
3. calls `fit(training_inputs, training_targets, epochs=5, batch_size=16, validation_data=(val_inputs, val_targets))`. The training data updates the weights, while the validation data is used only to monitor the "validation loss" and metrics.

The page ends by naming the loss on validation data the **validation loss**, as opposed to the **training loss**. It then begins to stress (continuing on p.126) that training and validation data must be kept strictly separate. The goal is performance on never-seen data; fitting the training data is the easy part. A model can memorize its training set and still be useless. Reserve a subset (30% in listing 3.35) as validation data, never trained on, and pass it via fit(validation_data=...). Shuffle inputs and targets with one shared permutation before splitting, so the validation set is not single-class. Validation loss is the loss on held-out data, distinct from training loss; the two sets must be kept strictly separate.
snippet: Section 3.6.7 opens with a principle: the goal of machine learning is not good performance on the training data. That is easy, since "all you have to do is follow the gradient."…

A student who memorized last year's answers aces that exam but fails a new one. A large network can reach near-zero training loss on randomly labelled data, which is pure memorization (a classic result, not from this page).

title: evaluate(), inference, and predict()
text:
Finishing the validation discussion with model.evaluate(), then introducing inference: calling the model directly versus using model.predict(). Validation data must stay strictly unseen during training; after training, evaluate() computes batched loss and metrics on it, and predict() is the batched, memory-safe way to run inference, whereas calling the model directly processes everything at once. This page closes subsection 3.6.7 on validation and opens 3.6.8, the last subsection of the Keras introduction.

**Keep validation data separate.** The sentence carried over from p.125 insists that training and validation data be *strictly* separate. The whole point of validation is to measure whether what the model learns is useful on **new** data; if the model has seen any validation sample during training, the validation loss and metrics are flawed (optimistically biased).

**`evaluate()`.** To compute validation loss and metrics after training, call
`model.evaluate(val_inputs, val_targets, batch_size=128)`. It iterates over the data in batches of `batch_size` and returns a list of scalars: the first entry is the loss, the following entries are the metrics configured in `compile()`. If the model has no metrics, a single scalar (the loss) is returned rather than a list.

**Inference.** Using a trained model to make predictions on new data is called *inference*. The naive way is to call the model like a function, `model(new_inputs)`, which (per the callout) takes a NumPy array or a backend tensor and returns a tensor of the current backend. The drawback: it processes all of `new_inputs` at once, which may need more memory than your GPU has.

**`predict()`.** The better way is `model.predict(new_inputs, batch_size=128)`: it iterates in small batches, returns a **NumPy array**, and, unlike `__call__()`, also accepts TensorFlow `Dataset` objects. As an example, the authors run `predict()` on the validation inputs of the linear model trained earlier (Listing 3.35, p.125) and print the first 10 predictions, which are scalar scores, one per input sample. The printed output appears on the next page (p.127). Training and validation data must be strictly disjoint; otherwise validation loss and metrics are flawed. model.evaluate(x, y, batch_size=...) returns [loss, metrics...] (or only the loss if there are no metrics). Inference means using a trained model to predict on new data. model(x) processes everything at once and returns a backend tensor; it can run out of GPU memory on large inputs. model.predict(x, batch_size=...) runs batched inference, accepts NumPy arrays or Datasets, and returns a NumPy array. The linear model's predictions are one scalar score per sample.

title: Prediction output and chapter 3 summary
text:
The output of model.predict() on the linear model, followed by the end-of-chapter summary for chapter 3. The trained linear model produces one scalar score per sample; with that, the Keras workflow (layers -> model -> compile -> fit -> predict) is complete, sitting on top of interchangeable low-level backends (TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX). The page opens with the output of `print(predictions[:10])` from p.126: a NumPy array of shape (10, 1) holding ten scalar scores, from `0.025846` to `0.82706255`. These are the raw outputs of the linear `Dense(1)` model of Listing 3.35, which was trained with mean squared error toward targets 0 and 1, so scores close to 1 point to one class and scores close to 0 to the other.

The authors then say that this is all you need to know about Keras models for now, and that chapter 4 moves on to real-world problems with Keras.

The chapter **Summary** has six bullets:

1. **TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX** are three popular low-level frameworks for numerical computation and autodifferentiation, each with its own way of doing things and its own strengths and weaknesses (sections 3.3-3.5).
2. **Keras** is a high-level API for building and training neural networks and runs on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX: pick the backend you like (section 3.6, p.115).
3. The central Keras class is **`Layer`**: a layer encapsulates weights and computation, and layers are assembled into models (sections 3.6.2-3.6.3).
4. Before training you choose an **optimizer, a loss and metrics** with `model.compile()` (sections 3.6.4-3.6.5).
5. **`fit()`** runs mini-batch gradient descent for you and can monitor loss and metrics on **validation data** the model does not train on (sections 3.6.6-3.6.7).
6. After training, **`model.predict()`** generates predictions on new inputs (section 3.6.8).

The summary leaves out `evaluate()`, which p.126 also covered. predict() on the linear model returns a (N, 1) NumPy array of scalar scores; thresholding at 0.5 turns them into class labels. TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are low-level frameworks for tensor computation and autodiff. Keras is a high-level API that runs on any of the three backends. Layers (weights + computation) are assembled into models. compile() sets optimizer, loss and metrics; fit() trains with mini-batch gradient descent and monitors validation data; predict() does inference. You now have the tools needed for the real-world problems of chapter 4.

title: Chapter 4 opener: Classification and regression
text:
Opening page of chapter 4: what the chapter covers and its three worked examples. Chapter 4 turns the tools of chapters 2-3 into three end-to-end workflows covering the most common uses of neural networks: binary classification (IMDb reviews), categorical classification (Reuters newswires) and scalar regression (house prices). This is the opening page of **chapter 4, "Classification and regression"** (PDF pages 128-159).

**This chapter covers:** your first examples of real-world machine learning workflows; handling binary and categorical classification problems; handling continuous regression problems.

The introduction says the chapter will consolidate what you learned in chapters 2 and 3 by applying it to three tasks that span the **three most common use cases** of neural networks:

- **Binary classification:** classifying movie reviews as positive or negative (section 4.1, IMDb, p.130).
- **Categorical (multiclass) classification:** classifying newswires by topic (section 4.2, Reuters, p.140).
- **Scalar regression:** estimating the price of a house from real-estate data (section 4.3, California Housing Price dataset, p.150).

These examples are your first contact with **end-to-end workflows**: data preprocessing, basic model architecture principles and model evaluation. Use this page as a roadmap: each section follows the same pattern (dataset, preparing the data, building the model, validating the approach, generating predictions, wrapping up), so you can compare how each choice changes with the problem type. Chapter 4 covers binary classification, categorical classification and scalar regression. The datasets are IMDb reviews, Reuters newswires and California house prices. The chapter introduces end-to-end workflows: preprocessing, architecture, evaluation.

title: Classification and regression glossary
text:
End of the chapter 4 introduction and a sidebar glossary of precise machine-learning terms for classification and regression. Before the worked examples, the authors fix a shared vocabulary: what samples, predictions, targets, losses, classes, labels and ground truth are, how the main task types (binary, multiclass, multilabel classification; scalar and vector regression) differ, and what a mini-batch is. The page finishes the chapter 4 introduction: by the end of the chapter you will be able to use neural networks for **simple classification and regression tasks over vector data**, and you will then be ready for the more principled, theory-driven treatment of machine learning in **chapter 5**.

Most of the page is a sidebar, the **Classification and regression glossary**. The authors stress that these terms have precise, ML-specific definitions:

- **Sample / input:** one data point that goes into the model.
- **Prediction / output:** what comes out of the model.
- **Target:** the truth, what the model should ideally have predicted according to an external source of data.
- **Prediction error / loss value:** a measure of the distance between prediction and target.
- **Classes:** the set of possible labels in a classification problem ("dog" and "cat").
- **Label:** a specific instance of a class annotation (picture #1234 is labeled "dog").
- **Ground truth / annotations:** all targets for a dataset, typically collected by humans.
- **Binary classification:** each sample goes into one of two exclusive categories.
- **Categorical / multiclass classification:** more than two categories, e.g. handwritten digits.
- **Multilabel classification:** each sample can receive several labels (an image with both a cat and a dog); the number of labels per sample is usually variable.
- **Scalar regression:** the target is one continuous value (house prices).
- **Vector regression:** the target is a set of continuous values (bounding-box coordinates).
- **Mini-batch / batch:** a small set of samples (typically 8-128, often a power of 2 for GPU memory allocation) processed simultaneously; in training, one mini-batch yields one gradient-descent update.

The three examples of the chapter map onto three of these categories: binary classification (IMDb), multiclass classification (Reuters), scalar regression (house prices). Sample = input data point; prediction = model output; target = what the dataset says it should be. Loss value measures the distance between prediction and target. Classes are the possible categories; a label is a sample's class annotation; ground truth is all targets of a dataset. Binary: 2 exclusive classes; multiclass: more than 2 exclusive classes; multilabel: possibly several labels per sample. Scalar regression predicts one continuous value; vector regression predicts several. A mini-batch (typically 8-128 samples) is processed together and gives one gradient-descent update.

title: The IMDb dataset
text:
Introducing the binary sentiment-classification example and loading the prepackaged IMDb dataset with a 10,000-word vocabulary limit. IMDb provides 50,000 polarized reviews (25k train / 25k test, each 50/50 positive/negative), already converted to lists of word indices; load_data(num_words=10000) keeps only the 10,000 most frequent training words so that the data can later become manageable fixed-size vectors. Section **4.1** begins the first worked example: **binary classification** of movie reviews as positive or negative from their text, which the authors call one of the most common kinds of ML problem.

**The dataset (4.1.1).** IMDb contains **50,000 highly polarized reviews** from the Internet Movie Database, split into **25,000 for training** and **25,000 for testing**; each split is **50% negative and 50% positive**. Like MNIST, it ships with Keras and is **already preprocessed**: each review (a sequence of words) has been turned into a **sequence of integers**, each standing for a word in a dictionary. This lets the chapter focus on model building, training and evaluation; processing raw text from scratch comes in **chapter 14** (p.420). The first load downloads about **80 MB**.

**Listing 4.1** loads the data:
`(train_data, train_labels), (test_data, test_labels) = imdb.load_data(num_words=10000)`.

**`num_words=10000`** keeps only the **10,000 most frequent words** of the training data; rarer words are discarded. Without it you would face **88,585 unique words**, unnecessarily many, and many of them occur in a single sample and are useless for classification. The limit gives **vector data of manageable size** (it fixes the dimension of the multi-hot vectors built on p.131).

`train_data` and `test_data` are NumPy arrays of reviews, each review a **list of word indices**; `train_labels` and `test_labels` are arrays of **0s (negative) and 1s (positive)**. The REPL shows `train_data[0]` starting `[1, 14, 22, 16, ...` and ending `178, 32]`, with label `1`. The page ends by noting that, because of the vocabulary limit, **no word index will exceed 10,000**; the check is on the next page. IMDb: 50,000 highly polarized reviews, 25k train and 25k test, each 50/50 positive/negative. It comes preprocessed: each review is a list of word indices into a frequency-ordered dictionary. num_words=10000 keeps the 10,000 most frequent words instead of all 88,585. Labels are 0 (negative) and 1 (positive); the first training review is positive. Reviews have different lengths, so they must be turned into tensors before training.

title: Decoding reviews and choosing a vectorization
text:
Verifying the 10,000-word limit, decoding an IMDb review back to text, and the two ways to turn variable-length integer lists into tensors (padding + Embedding vs multi-hot encoding). Word-index lists cannot be fed directly to a network because they have different lengths; you must vectorize them, either by padding to a common length (integer tensor for an Embedding layer) or by multi-hot encoding into fixed 10,000-dimensional 0/1 vectors. The chapter chooses multi-hot. The page opens with the check promised on p.130: `max([max(sequence) for sequence in train_data])` returns **9999**, so with `num_words=10000` every word index lies in 0-9999.

**Listing 4.2: decoding a review.** "For kicks", the authors turn `train_data[0]` back into English. `imdb.get_word_index()` returns a dictionary mapping **words to integer indices**; a dict comprehension **reverses** it into index -> word; then each index `i` of the review is looked up as `reverse_word_index.get(i - 3, "?")` and the words are joined with spaces. The callout explains the **offset of 3**: indices 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for **"padding", "start of sequence" and "unknown"**. The first 100 characters read `? this film was just brilliant casting location scenery story direction everyone`; the leading `?` is the **start token** prefixed to every review (index 1 has no dictionary entry after the shift, so `.get` returns the default `"?"`).

**4.1.2 Preparing the data.** You can't feed lists of integers directly to a network: they have **different lengths**, and a network expects **contiguous batches**, i.e. tensors. Two options:

1. **Pad** the lists to a common length, giving an integer tensor of shape `(samples, max_length)`, and start the model with a layer that handles integer tensors, the **`Embedding` layer** (covered later in the book).
2. **Multi-hot encode** the lists into vectors of 0s and 1s marking the **presence or absence** of every possible word; e.g. `[8, 5]` becomes a **10,000-dimensional** vector of 0s except 1s at **indices 5 and 8**.

The authors choose **multi-hot encoding** and announce a manual implementation, shown on the next page (Listing 4.3, p.132). With num_words=10000, the maximum word index is 9999. To decode, invert get_word_index() and subtract 3; indices 0, 1, 2 are padding, start of sequence and unknown. The leading '?' in a decoded review is the start token. Variable-length integer lists must be turned into tensors because networks process contiguous batches. Option 1: pad to (samples, max_length) and use an Embedding layer; option 2: multi-hot encode into 10,000-dimensional 0/1 vectors. The chapter uses multi-hot encoding, which captures word presence but not order or counts.

title: Multi-hot encoding the IMDb reviews and choosing a Dense architecture
text:
Turning integer word-index sequences into fixed-size multi-hot vectors, casting labels to float32, and the architecture decision for a stack of Dense layers Variable-length lists of word indices are converted into 10,000-dimensional 0/1 vectors with a small NumPy function, labels become float32, and the resulting vector-in/scalar-out problem is handled by a plain stack of Dense+relu layers: two hidden layers of 16 units plus a scalar output layer. The page opens with **Listing 4.3**, the manual implementation of the second option described on p.131: *multi-hot encoding*. The function `multi_hot_encode(sequences, num_classes)` allocates an all-zero matrix of shape `(len(sequences), num_classes)` and, for each review `i`, sets `results[i][sequence] = 1.0`. Because `sequence` is a Python list of integer word indices, NumPy's integer-array indexing sets every listed position to 1 at once. Applied with `num_classes=10000` to `train_data` and `test_data`, it yields `x_train` and `x_test`, each a 2-D float matrix with one 10,000-dimensional row per review. Printing `x_train[0]` shows a vector like `[0., 1., 1., ..., 0., 0., 0.]`.

The labels are vectorized too, which is trivial: they are already NumPy integer arrays, so `astype("float32")` converts them to floats (`y_train`, `y_test`). At that point "the data is ready to be fed into a neural network."

Section **4.1.3 Building your model** then characterizes the problem: inputs are vectors, labels are scalars (1s and 0s) — "one of the simplest problem setups you'll ever encounter." A plain stack of `Dense` layers with `relu` activations works well here. Designing such a stack means making two decisions: **how many layers** and **how many units per layer**. The authors defer the principled answer to chapter 5 and ask the reader to trust them for now: **two intermediate layers with 16 units each**, followed by **a third layer that outputs the scalar sentiment prediction**. The Keras code for this model (listing 4.4) and figure 4.1 come on the next page (p.133). Listing 4.3 turns each review into a 10,000-dim 0/1 vector using an all-zero matrix and fancy indexing. x_train and x_test have shape (25000, 10000); x_train[0] looks like [0., 1., 1., ..., 0.]. Labels only need a dtype change: astype("float32"). Vector input plus scalar 0/1 label is among the simplest setups; a stack of Dense+relu layers fits it. Architecture decisions for a Dense stack: number of layers and units per layer. The book's choice: two hidden layers of 16 units and one output layer producing a scalar.

title: Listing 4.4: the three-layer IMDb model, units, relu and sigmoid
text:
The Keras Sequential definition of the 16-16-1 sentiment model, the meaning of the number of units, and the roles of relu and sigmoid The IMDb classifier is a keras.Sequential stack of Dense(16, relu), Dense(16, relu) and Dense(1, sigmoid). Each Dense layer computes relu(dot(input, W) + b); its unit count is the dimensionality of the representation space it projects into, a knob trading expressiveness against cost and overfitting. The sigmoid output squashes a score into [0, 1] so it can be read as the probability that a review is positive. **Figure 4.1** draws the model as three stacked boxes: input (vectorized text) -> `Dense (units=16)` -> `Dense (units=16)` -> `Dense (units=1)` -> output (probability). **Listing 4.4** is its Keras implementation, written exactly like the earlier MNIST example: `keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"), layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")])`. No input shape is given; Keras infers it (10,000) the first time the model sees data.

The first argument of each `Dense` layer is its number of **units**, which the authors define as *the dimensionality of the representation space of the layer*. Recalling chapters 2 and 3, each such layer implements `output = relu(dot(input, W) + b)`. With 16 units, `W` has shape `(input_dimension, 16)`, so the dot product projects the input onto a 16-dimensional space before the bias `b` is added and `relu` is applied.

The dimensionality of the representation space can be understood as "how much freedom you're allowing the model to have when learning internal representations." More units allow more complex representations but cost more computation and can lead to learning *unwanted patterns* that help on training data but not on test data (an early hint of overfitting).

The hidden layers use `relu`, which zeroes out negative values (figure 4.2, next page); the final layer uses `sigmoid`, which squashes arbitrary values into `[0, 1]` (figure 4.3), so the output can be interpreted as the probability that the review is positive. A sidebar, **"What are activation functions, and why are they necessary?"**, begins: without a non-linearity, a `Dense` layer is just two linear operations, a dot product and an addition. The argument concludes on p.134. Listing 4.4: Sequential of Dense(16, relu), Dense(16, relu), Dense(1, sigmoid). The first Dense argument is the number of units = dimensionality of the layer's representation space. Each hidden layer computes relu(dot(input, W) + b) with W of shape (input_dimension, 16). More units = more freedom, but higher cost and risk of learning non-generalizing patterns. relu zeroes negatives; sigmoid squashes to [0, 1] so the output reads as a probability. Activation functions are needed because a Dense layer without one is only a dot product plus an addition.

title: Why activations are necessary; relu and sigmoid plots; choosing the loss and optimizer
text:
The hypothesis-space argument for non-linear activations, figures of relu and sigmoid, and the choice of binary_crossentropy loss and adam optimizer for the IMDb model Without an activation, a Dense layer is an affine map and a stack of them is still affine, so depth adds nothing; a non-linearity such as relu unlocks a richer hypothesis space. For a single sigmoid probability output, binary crossentropy is the best default loss (MSE is possible but worse), and adam is a good default optimizer; accuracy is monitored as a metric. The page finishes the sidebar **"What are activation functions, and why are they necessary?"** begun on p.133. Without an activation, a `Dense` layer computes only `output = dot(input, W) + b`: a dot product and an addition. Such a layer can only learn *linear (affine) transformations* of its input, so its **hypothesis space** is the set of all affine maps from the input into a 16-dimensional space. That space is too restricted, and it would not benefit from stacking: a deep stack of linear layers is still a linear operation, so extra layers would not extend the hypothesis space (as seen in chapter 2). To get a richer hypothesis space that benefits from deep representations you need a **non-linearity** (activation function). `relu` is the most popular, but there are many others with "similarly strange names", such as `prelu` and `elu`.

**Figure 4.2** plots relu: flat at 0 for negative inputs, then the identity line for positive inputs. **Figure 4.3** plots the sigmoid: an S-shaped curve rising from near 0 at -4 to near 1 at 4, crossing 0.5 at 0.

The last step of model building is choosing a **loss** and an **optimizer**. Since this is binary classification and the model outputs a probability (single-unit sigmoid layer), the best choice is the `binary_crossentropy` loss. `mean_squared_error` would also work, but crossentropy is usually best for models that output probabilities. Crossentropy comes from information theory and measures the distance between probability distributions, here between the ground-truth distribution and the predictions. For the optimizer the authors pick `adam`, "usually a good default choice for virtually any problem." The page ends by announcing the `compile` step (listing 4.5 on p.135), which will also monitor **accuracy** during training. Without an activation, a Dense layer is output = dot(input, W) + b, an affine map. Stacked linear layers remain linear, so depth would not enlarge the hypothesis space. Non-linearities like relu (or prelu, elu) unlock richer hypothesis spaces that benefit from depth. Figure 4.2: relu is 0 for negatives and the identity for positives; figure 4.3: sigmoid maps to (0, 1), 0.5 at 0. Sigmoid probability output -> binary_crossentropy loss; MSE is possible but usually worse. adam is the default optimizer; accuracy is monitored as a metric.

title: Compiling the IMDb model and holding out a validation set
text:
compile() with adam / binary_crossentropy / accuracy, why a validation set separate from the test set is needed, slicing off 10,000 validation samples, and training for 20 epochs with batch size 512 The model is compiled with the choices argued on p.134. Because validation results will be used to make design decisions (model size, number of epochs), they become biased; a separate, untouched test set is kept for the final unbiased evaluation. 10,000 of the 25,000 training reviews are set aside as validation data and the model is trained on the remaining 15,000 for 20 epochs in mini-batches of 512, monitoring validation loss and accuracy. **Listing 4.5** compiles the model: `model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])`, exactly the choices justified on p.134.

Section **4.1.4 Validating your approach** starts from a rule learned in chapter 3: a model should never be evaluated on its training data. The standard practice is to hold out a **validation set** to monitor accuracy during training; here, 10,000 samples are set apart from the 25,000 training reviews.

The authors anticipate the question *why not just use the test data?* Because validation results will be used to guide decisions such as model size or number of epochs. Once you do that, the validation score no longer reflects performance on brand-new data: the model has been deliberately modified to do better on it. A set of never-before-seen samples is needed for a final, completely unbiased evaluation, and that is the role of the **test set**. The next chapter develops this further.

**Listing 4.6** performs the split with NumPy slicing: the first 10,000 samples become `x_val`/`y_val`, the remaining 15,000 become `partial_x_train`/`partial_y_train`.

The model is then trained for **20 epochs** (20 passes over all training samples) in **mini-batches of 512**, while loss and accuracy are monitored on the 10,000 held-out samples by passing them as `validation_data` to `model.fit()`. **Listing 4.7** stores the result in `history`, which the next page inspects and plots. Listing 4.5: compile with adam, binary_crossentropy and accuracy. Never evaluate on training data; monitor a validation set. Do not use the test set to guide choices: tuning on validation data makes it biased, so the test set is kept for a final unbiased evaluation. Listing 4.6 slices 10,000 validation samples off the 25,000 training samples. Listing 4.7 trains 20 epochs with batch size 512, passing validation_data to fit().

title: validation_split, the History dictionary, and plotting the loss
text:
The validation_split alternative to manual splitting, training time, the keys of history.history, and the start of listing 4.8 plotting training vs validation loss Validation data can also be carved out automatically with fit(validation_split=0.2). The fit call returns a History object whose history dict holds per-epoch accuracy, loss, val_accuracy and val_loss; listing 4.8 begins plotting training loss (dashed red) against validation loss (solid blue) with Matplotlib. A sidebar, **"The validation_split argument"**, offers a shortcut: instead of slicing validation data by hand and passing `validation_data`, you can pass `validation_split` to `fit()`, a fraction of the training data to hold out. With `model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=20, batch_size=512, validation_split=0.2)`, 20% of `x_train`/`y_train` is held out from training and used for validation.

Back in the main text: on CPU, training with listing 4.7 takes less than 2 seconds per epoch, so it is done in about 20 seconds; each epoch ends with a short pause while loss and accuracy are computed on the 10,000 validation samples.

`model.fit()` returns a **`History`** object (seen in chapter 3) whose member `history` is a dictionary of everything that happened during training. Its keys are `"accuracy"`, `"loss"`, `"val_accuracy"` and `"val_loss"`: one entry per metric monitored during training and during validation (loss and accuracy, each for both sets).

The next two listings plot these with Matplotlib: training vs validation loss (figure 4.4) and training vs validation accuracy (figure 4.5). The authors warn your own numbers may differ slightly because of random weight initialization. **Listing 4.8** starts on this page: it extracts `loss_values` and `val_loss_values`, builds `epochs = range(1, len(loss_values) + 1)`, plots training loss as `"r--"` (dashed red line) and validation loss as `"b"` (solid blue line), sets the title `"[IMDB] Training and validation loss"` and the x-label `"Epochs"`. The listing continues on p.137, where figure 4.4 is shown. validation_split=0.2 holds out 20% of the training arrays automatically. Training runs under 2 s/epoch on CPU; each epoch ends with a validation pass. fit() returns a History object; history.history has accuracy, loss, val_accuracy, val_loss. Listing 4.8 plots training loss as a dashed red line and validation loss as a solid blue line. Results vary slightly between runs because of random initialization.

title: Figure 4.4 (training vs validation loss) and listing 4.9 (accuracy plot)
text:
The end of the loss-plotting listing, the resulting learning curves, and the analogous code for accuracy Figure 4.4 shows the training loss falling steadily to near zero over 20 epochs, while the validation loss bottoms out around epoch 3-4 (about 0.28) and then climbs to about 0.58: the visual signature of overfitting. Listing 4.9 clears the figure and plots training vs validation accuracy the same way. This page contains only code and a figure.

The last four lines of **listing 4.8** (started on p.136) set an x-tick at every epoch (`plt.xticks(epochs)`), label the y-axis `"Loss"`, add a legend and display the plot with `plt.show()`.

**Figure 4.4, "Training and validation loss"**, is the result. The dashed red training-loss curve starts around 0.56 at epoch 1 and falls monotonically, below 0.1 by epoch 7 and to almost 0 by epoch 20. The solid blue validation-loss curve starts lower (about 0.43), reaches its minimum of roughly 0.28 at epochs 3-4, and then rises steadily to about 0.58 by epoch 20. The two curves cross near epoch 2. (Values read from the plot; approximate.) The authors' interpretation follows on p.138: the validation metrics peak at the fourth epoch, after which the model is **overfitting**, learning representations specific to the training data.

**Listing 4.9** plots accuracy the same way: `plt.clf()` clears the figure (per the callout), then `history_dict["accuracy"]` and `history_dict["val_accuracy"]` are plotted as dashed red (`"Training acc"`) and solid blue (`"Validation acc"`) lines with the title `"[IMDB] Training and validation accuracy"`, epoch ticks, the y-label `"Accuracy"`, a legend and `plt.show()`. The resulting figure 4.5 appears on p.138. Listing 4.8 ends with xticks, ylabel, legend and show, producing figure 4.4. In figure 4.4 training loss decreases monotonically to near 0. Validation loss is lowest around epochs 3-4 (~0.28) and rises to ~0.58 by epoch 20: overfitting. Listing 4.9 clears the figure and plots accuracy with the same conventions (red dashed training, blue solid validation).

title: Reading the accuracy curves: overfitting after a few epochs
text:
Interpreting training vs. validation curves on IMDb, recognising overfitting, and retraining for the right number of epochs Training loss and accuracy keep improving with every epoch because that is what gradient descent optimises, but validation metrics peak after a few epochs and then degrade: the model has started overfitting. The simple fix used here is to retrain from scratch for only four epochs and evaluate on the test set. The page opens with **figure 4.5**, *Training and validation accuracy* on IMDb over 20 epochs, made with listing 4.9 on the previous page. The dashed red **training accuracy** rises steeply from about 0.76 after epoch 1 to about 0.99 by epoch 9 and stays close to 1.00 from epoch 12 on. The solid blue **validation accuracy** reaches its highest value, about 0.89, very early and then drifts slowly down to about 0.865 by epoch 20.

The text interprets this together with the loss plot (figure 4.4, p.137). Training loss falls and training accuracy rises with **every** epoch, which is what you expect from gradient descent, since the training loss is exactly the quantity being minimised. Validation loss and accuracy behave differently: the authors say they "seem to peak at the fourth epoch". (In the printed accuracy plot the highest validation point is actually at epoch 2. Exact peaks differ from run to run, but the shape of the curves is the same.) This illustrates the earlier warning that doing better on training data does not mean doing better on unseen data. The precise name is **overfitting**: after the peak, the model is *overoptimising* on the training set and learning representations specific to it that do not generalise.

The remedy here is the bluntest one: **stop training after four epochs**. The authors note that chapter 5 covers a range of better techniques for mitigating overfitting. They then begin **listing 4.10**, which trains a *new model from scratch* for four epochs and evaluates it on the test data. Only the first lines (`keras.Sequential([` and the first `layers.Dense(16, activation="relu")`) appear on this page. The rest of the listing, with the second hidden layer, the sigmoid output, `compile`, `fit(..., epochs=4, batch_size=512)` and `evaluate`, continues on p.139. Training loss and accuracy improve every epoch because gradient descent directly optimises them; this says nothing about new data. In figure 4.5, validation accuracy peaks early (about 0.89) and then declines while training accuracy approaches 1.00. This is overfitting. Overfitting means learning representations specific to the training data that do not generalise outside it. The simplest remedy is to stop at the best epoch: retrain a fresh model for that many epochs (four here). Chapter 5 covers more techniques. After using validation data to choose the number of epochs, judge the final model on the untouched test set. Listing 4.10 starts here with the same architecture; it continues on p.139.

title: Overfitting
text: The regime in which further optimisation on the training data makes the model worse on data it has not seen. The book's words: 'you're overoptimizing on the training data, and you end up learning representations that are specific to the training data and don't generalize'. A student who memorises the answers to past exam papers does better and better on those papers but no better on a new exam. The extra effort goes into memorising specifics, not understanding. Gradient descent minimises the empirical risk on the training sample. Validation loss estimates the expected risk on the data distribution. While these two decrease together, the model is learning transferable structure. Once validation loss turns upward while training loss keeps falling, the parameters are fitting sample-specific noise. In figure 4.5 this shows up as training accuracy approaching 1.00 while validation accuracy slides from about 0.89 to about 0.865. title: Training and validation curves
text: Plots of the loss and metrics on the training data and on the validation data, recorded at the end of each epoch (from History.history), as in figures 4.4 and 4.5. Two thermometers. One measures how well the model fits what it has studied, the other how well it does on new material. The point where they part ways is what you look for. History.history holds keys 'loss', 'accuracy', 'val_loss' and 'val_accuracy', each a list with one value per epoch. Training metrics are averaged over the batches during the epoch, while the weights are still changing. Validation metrics are computed once at the end of the epoch with the final weights. That is why at epoch 1 the training accuracy (about 0.76) can be below the validation accuracy (about 0.86). Figure 4.5: the dashed red training accuracy goes up steadily; the solid blue validation accuracy is flat or declining after epoch 2.

title: Final IMDb results, predictions on new data, and further experiments
text:
Completing listing 4.10 (retrain for 4 epochs, evaluate on test), interpreting the test results, using predict() for probabilities, and suggested architecture experiments Retraining the same two-layer network for only four epochs gives a test loss of about 0.29 and a test accuracy of about 88%. The trained model's predict() method returns a probability per review, and it is confident for some reviews but unsure about others. The section then invites you to vary the architecture, starting with the number of representation layers. The page finishes **listing 4.10**, which began on p.138. The model is the same as before: `Dense(16, relu)`, `Dense(16, relu)`, `Dense(1, sigmoid)`. It is compiled with `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="binary_crossentropy"` and `metrics=["accuracy"]`, trained with `model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=4, batch_size=512)`, and then `results = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)` is run. Note that this time `fit` uses the full training set and no validation data, because the number of epochs has already been chosen.

The printed result is `[0.2929924130630493, 0.88327999999999995]`. The callout explains that the first number (**0.29**) is the **test loss** and the second (**0.88**) is the **test accuracy**. The authors call this a *fairly naive approach* that reaches **88%**, and say that state-of-the-art approaches should get close to **95%**.

**Section 4.1.5** shows inference. After training you want to use the model in a practical setting: `model.predict(x_test)` returns a `float32` array of shape `(25000, 1)`, with one probability per review that the review is positive (e.g. 0.980, 0.998, 0.9998, ..., 0.822, 0.029, 0.654). The model is **confident** for some samples (0.99 or more, or 0.01 or less) and **less confident** for others (0.6, 0.4).

**Section 4.1.6** starts a list of experiments meant to convince you that the architecture choices were reasonable while leaving room for improvement. The first: you used **two representation layers** before the classification layer, so try **one or three** and see how validation and test accuracy change. The list continues on p.140. Listing 4.10 retrains the same 16-16-1 network for 4 epochs on the full training set and evaluates it once on the test set. evaluate returns [loss, accuracy]: test loss is about 0.29 and test accuracy about 0.88. 88% is a naive baseline; state-of-the-art approaches get close to 95%. model.predict returns one sigmoid probability per review; values near 0 or 1 are confident, values near 0.5 are uncertain. Architecture choices should be tested experimentally. Start by trying one or three representation layers instead of two.

title: IMDb experiments and wrap-up; introducing multiclass classification on Reuters
text:
Remaining experiments for the IMDb model, the six lessons of the binary-classification example, and the setup of single-label multiclass classification with the Reuters dataset The binary example ends with practical rules: preprocess raw data into tensors, use stacks of Dense+relu, end with Dense(1, sigmoid), use binary_crossentropy and adam, and always monitor out-of-sample performance. Section 4.2 then moves from 2 classes to 46 mutually exclusive topics, which is a single-label, multiclass classification problem, as opposed to a multilabel one. The page finishes the **further experiments** list for the IMDb model that began on p.139. Besides changing the number of representation layers, try **wider or narrower layers** (32 units, 64 units, ...), the **`mean_squared_error`** loss instead of `binary_crossentropy`, and the **`tanh`** activation, "popular in the early days of neural networks", instead of `relu`.

**4.1.7 Wrapping up** lists six lessons:
1. Raw data usually needs **quite a bit of preprocessing** before it can be fed to a network as tensors. Word sequences can be encoded as binary vectors, and other encodings exist too.
2. **Stacks of `Dense` layers with `relu`** solve a wide range of problems, including sentiment classification.
3. For **binary classification**, end with a `Dense` layer of **one unit and `sigmoid`**, which outputs a scalar between 0 and 1 encoding a probability.
4. With such a scalar sigmoid output, use **`binary_crossentropy`**.
5. **`adam`** is generally a good enough optimizer for any problem.
6. As networks improve on training data they eventually **overfit** and get worse on unseen data, so always monitor performance on data outside the training set.

**Section 4.2** asks what happens with **more than two classes**. You will classify Reuters newswires into **46 mutually exclusive topics**. With many classes this is **multiclass classification**. Because each data point belongs to exactly one category, it is more precisely **single-label, multiclass classification**. If a point could have several topics, it would be **multilabel, multiclass classification**.

**4.2.1** introduces the **Reuters dataset**: short newswires and their topics, published by Reuters in 1986. It is a simple, widely used toy dataset for text classification. The 46 topics are imbalanced, but each has **at least 10 training examples**. Probe the IMDb architecture yourself: layer width (32, 64 units), mse vs. binary_crossentropy, tanh vs. relu. Binary classification recipe: preprocess to tensors, Dense+relu stack, Dense(1, sigmoid), binary_crossentropy, adam. Always monitor performance on data outside the training set; networks eventually overfit. Reuters is single-label, multiclass classification: 46 mutually exclusive topics. Multilabel means a sample can have several classes, a different problem type with a different output layer. The Reuters topics are imbalanced, but each has at least 10 training examples.

section: 4.2 Classifying newswires: A multiclass classification example

title: Single-label vs. multilabel multiclass classification
text: Multiclass: more than two classes. Single-label: each sample belongs to exactly one class (Reuters: 46 mutually exclusive topics). Multilabel: a sample can belong to several classes. Single-label is like filing each article in one folder; multilabel is like attaching any number of tags. Single-label uses Dense(N) + softmax, giving outputs that sum to 1, with categorical (or sparse categorical) crossentropy. Multilabel uses Dense(N) + sigmoid, giving independent per-class probabilities, with binary crossentropy on k-hot targets (p.625). Reuters topics (one topic per wire) is single-label; tagging photos with 'beach', 'dog' and 'sunset' together would be multilabel.

title: tanh activation
text: The hyperbolic tangent, an S-shaped activation with outputs in (-1, 1), popular in the early days of neural networks and suggested here as an alternative to relu. A smooth, centred version of the sigmoid that flattens out at -1 and +1. tanh(x) = 2·sigmoid(2x) - 1, with derivative 1 - tanh²(x), which is at most 1 and approaches 0 for large |x|, so it saturates. relu's derivative is exactly 1 for x > 0, which helps deep networks train. tanh(0.5) is about 0.46; tanh(3) is about 0.995, with derivative about 0.01.

title: Loading and inspecting the Reuters dataset
text:
Loading Reuters with keras.datasets, its size, the integer-sequence representation of each newswire, decoding back to text, and integer topic labels 0-45 Reuters is packaged in Keras exactly like IMDb. With num_words=10000 each of the 8,982 training and 2,246 test newswires is a list of word indices, which can be decoded using the word index with an offset of 3. Each label is an integer topic index between 0 and 45. Like IMDb and MNIST, **Reuters comes packaged with Keras**. **Listing 4.11** imports `reuters` from `keras.datasets` and calls `reuters.load_data(num_words=10000)`, which returns `(train_data, train_labels), (test_data, test_labels)`. As with IMDb, `num_words=10000` **keeps only the 10,000 most frequent words** in the data; rarer words are dropped.

The dataset is small: **8,982 training examples** and **2,246 test examples**, as the `len()` calls show. As with IMDb, **each example is a list of integers (word indices)**. The page prints `train_data[10]`, a 31-integer sequence starting `[1, 245, 273, 207, ...]` and ending `..., 4329, 17, 12]`. The leading `1` is the start-of-sequence marker.

If you are curious, **listing 4.12** decodes a newswire back to words. It fetches `word_index = reuters.get_word_index()` (a word-to-index dictionary), inverts it into `reverse_word_index` (index to word), and joins `reverse_word_index.get(i - 3, "?")` for every index in `train_data[10]`. The callout explains the **offset of 3**: indices 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for "padding", "start of sequence" and "unknown", so a stored index *i* corresponds to word-index rank *i - 3*. Indices without a match, including those reserved ones, become `"?"`.

Finally, **each label is an integer between 0 and 45**, a topic index; `train_labels[10]` is `3`. With 46 classes, these labels will need either one-hot encoding with categorical crossentropy or sparse categorical crossentropy on the integers (the next pages and p.148). reuters.load_data(num_words=10000) loads Reuters just like IMDb, keeping the 10,000 most frequent words. There are 8,982 training and 2,246 test newswires, a small dataset for 46 classes. Each newswire is a variable-length list of word indices; index 1 marks the start of the sequence. Decoding needs an offset of 3 because indices 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for padding, start of sequence and unknown. Labels are integer topic indices from 0 to 45, which will need categorical handling.

title: Preparing Reuters inputs and one-hot labels; why 46 classes change the model
text:
Multi-hot encoding of inputs, one-hot (categorical) encoding of the 46-class labels by hand and with to_categorical, and the information-bottleneck argument for larger intermediate layers Inputs are vectorised exactly as for IMDb. Labels can stay integers or be one-hot encoded: an all-zero vector of length 46 with a 1 at the label index. Because the output space now has 46 dimensions instead of 2, small intermediate Dense layers risk discarding information that later layers can never recover. **4.2.2 Preparing the data.** The inputs are vectorised "with the exact same code as in the previous example". **Listing 4.13** calls `multi_hot_encode(train_data, num_classes=10000)` and the same for `test_data`, giving `x_train` with shape (8982, 10000) and `x_test` with shape (2246, 10000) of 0/1 values.

For the **labels** there are two options: leave them **as integers**, or use **one-hot encoding**, also called **categorical encoding**, a widely used format for categorical data. Here it means embedding each label as **an all-zero vector with a 1 at the label index**. **Listing 4.14** defines `one_hot_encode(labels, num_classes=46)`. It allocates `np.zeros((len(labels), num_classes))`, sets `results[i, label] = 1.0` for each sample, and returns the matrix. It is applied to `train_labels` and `test_labels` to get `y_train` (8982, 46) and `y_test` (2246, 46). Keras has a built-in way to do the same: `keras.utils.to_categorical`.

**4.2.3 Building your model.** The problem looks like the movie-review problem, since both classify short snippets of text, but there is a new constraint: the number of output classes has gone **from 2 to 46**, so the output space has many more dimensions. In a stack of `Dense` layers, **each layer can only access information present in the output of the previous layer**. If one layer drops information relevant to the classification, later layers cannot recover it (the sentence finishes on p.143, which goes on to call each layer a potential **information bottleneck** and to choose 64-unit layers instead of 16). Reuters inputs are vectorised with the IMDb code: multi_hot_encode(..., num_classes=10000). Labels can stay integers or be one-hot (categorical) encoded: an all-zero vector of length 46 with a 1 at the label index. keras.utils.to_categorical does the same thing as the hand-written one_hot_encode. Going from 2 to 46 output classes makes the output space much larger, and the hidden layers must carry enough information. In a Dense stack, information dropped by one layer cannot be recovered by later layers.

title: The Reuters model: 64-unit layers, a 46-way softmax, categorical crossentropy and top-3 accuracy
text:
Avoiding information bottlenecks with wider layers, the Dense(46, softmax) output, categorical crossentropy as the loss, and top-k accuracy as a finer metric Sixteen-dimensional layers may be too narrow to separate 46 classes, so the model uses two Dense(64, relu) layers. It ends with Dense(46, softmax), which outputs a probability distribution over the topics, and is trained with categorical_crossentropy, which measures the distance between the predicted and true distributions. Because plain accuracy ignores near-misses, top-3 accuracy is added as a metric. The page finishes the argument started on p.142: information dropped by one Dense layer cannot be **recovered by later layers**, so **each layer can become an information bottleneck**. The IMDb model used 16-dimensional intermediate layers, but **a 16-dimensional space may be too limited to separate 46 classes**, and such small layers may permanently drop relevant information. So the model uses **larger intermediate layers of 64 units**.

**Listing 4.15** defines `keras.Sequential([Dense(64, relu), Dense(64, relu), Dense(46, softmax)])`. Two things to note:
- The model ends with a **`Dense` layer of size 46**, so each sample gets a 46-dimensional output vector, one entry per class.
- The last layer uses **`softmax`**, as in the MNIST example. The output is a **probability distribution** over the 46 classes: `output[i]` is the probability that the sample belongs to class `i`, and **the 46 scores sum to 1**.

The best loss here is **`categorical_crossentropy`**. It measures the **distance between two probability distributions**: the one the model outputs and the true distribution of the labels. Minimising it trains the model to output something as close as possible to the true labels.

Accuracy is monitored again, but it is **a bit crude** here. If the correct class is the model's second choice, that sample still scores zero accuracy, even though such a model is much better than a random guess. A more nuanced metric is **top-k accuracy** (e.g. top-3 or top-5), which checks whether the correct class is among the model's *k* highest-scoring predictions. **Listing 4.16** starts by creating `keras.metrics.TopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=3, name="top_3_accuracy")`; the rest of the compile listing continues on p.144. Each Dense layer can be an information bottleneck; 16 units may be too few for 46 classes, so the Reuters model uses 64. Listing 4.15: Dense(64, relu), Dense(64, relu), Dense(46, softmax). A Dense layer of size 46 gives one output per class; softmax makes these a probability distribution that sums to 1. categorical_crossentropy measures the distance between the predicted and true distributions; minimising it brings predictions close to the labels. Accuracy is crude for 46 classes; top-k accuracy (top-3 here) credits the correct class being among the top predictions. Listing 4.16 creates TopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=3) and continues on p.144.
snippet: The page finishes the argument started on p.142: information dropped by one Dense layer cannot be recovered by later layers, so each layer can become an information bottleneck.…

title: Softmax output layer
text: An activation that turns the 46 output scores into a probability distribution: output[i] is the probability of class i, and the 46 values sum to 1. 46 candidates sharing one vote: more for one means less for the others. p_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j). It is invariant to adding a constant to all logits; the largest logit gives the largest probability. Logits [2, 1, 0.1] become probabilities of about [0.66, 0.24, 0.10].
snippet: An activation that turns the 46 output scores into a probability distribution: outputi is the probability of class i, and the 46 values sum to 1.
section: 4.2 Classifying newswires: A multiclass classification example

title: Categorical crossentropy
text: The loss that measures the distance between the model's predicted distribution and the true label distribution. The book calls it the best loss for this case. It measures how surprised the model is by the true answer: very surprised (high loss) if it gave the right topic a tiny probability. L = -sum_i y_i log p_i. With one-hot y, L = -log p_label. Combined with softmax, the gradient with respect to logit z_i is p_i - y_i. p_label = 0.9 gives L of about 0.105; p_label = 0.01 gives L of about 4.6.
snippet: The loss that measures the distance between the model's predicted distribution and the true label distribution. The book calls it the best loss for this case.
section: 4.2 Classifying newswires: A multiclass classification example

title: Top-k accuracy
text: Whether the correct class is among the model's k highest-probability predictions, averaged over samples. The page uses top-3. Being allowed three guesses in a quiz. Sort the 46 probabilities; the sample is correct if the true class is in the top k. Accuracy is top-1. Top-k accuracy never decreases as k grows; for random guessing it is k/46. If the true topic is ranked 2nd, top-1 = 0 and top-3 = 1 for that sample.
snippet: Whether the correct class is among the model's k highest-probability predictions, averaged over samples. The page uses top-3.

title: Information bottleneck
text: A layer too narrow to carry the information needed downstream; anything it drops cannot be recovered by later layers. A narrow pipe in a plumbing system limits the flow through everything after it. 16 hidden dimensions feeding 46 logits constrain the logits to a 16-dimensional subspace, which may prevent separating all 46 classes. Using 64 units removes the constraint. p.149: 4-unit intermediate layers cap validation accuracy at about 71%.
snippet: A layer too narrow to carry the information needed downstream; anything it drops cannot be recovered by later layers.

title: Softmax over 46 classes
text: output[i] is the probability that the sample belongs to class i. The 46 scores will sum to 1. \text{output}[i] = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=0}^{45} e^{z_j}}, \qquad \sum_{i=0}^{45} \text{output}[i] = 1 Turns arbitrary real scores into a valid probability distribution over mutually exclusive classes. Higher logits give higher probabilities, and the probabilities compete because they must sum to 1. z_i Raw score (logit) for class i computed by Dense(46): z = W h + b, with h the 64-dimensional hidden vector. \text{output}[i] Predicted probability that the sample belongs to topic i.

title: Categorical crossentropy

L(y, p) = -\sum_{i=0}^{45} y_i \log p_i \;=\; -\log p_{\text{label}} \quad (y \text{ one-hot}) The loss minimised during training. It is zero only when the model gives the true class probability 1. title: Validating the Reuters model: split, fit, plot loss
text:
Finishing the compile step with top-3 accuracy, holding out 1,000 validation samples, training for 20 epochs, and plotting training vs. validation loss The Reuters workflow repeats the IMDb validation recipe: set aside part of the training data as a validation set, train while monitoring it with `validation_data`, then plot the `History` curves to find where overfitting begins. The page opens with the **closing lines of listing 4.16** (begun on p.143). The model is compiled with the `"adam"` optimizer, the `"categorical_crossentropy"` loss (appropriate because the labels were one-hot encoded on p.142 and the last layer is a 46-way softmax), and two metrics: the built-in string `"accuracy"` and the metric object `top_3_accuracy`, a `keras.metrics.TopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=3, name="top_3_accuracy")` instance created at the bottom of p.143. Top-3 accuracy counts a prediction as correct when the true topic is among the model's three highest-probability topics, a gentler measure than plain accuracy for a 46-class problem.

**Section 4.2.4, Validating your approach**, then mirrors what was done for IMDb in section 4.1.4 (p.135):

1. **Listing 4.17** slices the first 1,000 of the 8,982 training samples off as a validation set (`x_val`, `y_val`), leaving 7,982 samples (`partial_x_train`, `partial_y_train`) for actual training. The same slice boundary is used for inputs and labels, so pairs stay aligned.
2. **Listing 4.18** trains for 20 epochs with mini-batches of 512 and passes `validation_data=(x_val, y_val)`, so Keras evaluates loss and both metrics on the held-out 1,000 samples at the end of every epoch. The returned `History` object is stored in `history`.
3. **Listing 4.19** pulls `history.history["loss"]` and `history.history["val_loss"]`, builds an x-axis `range(1, len(loss) + 1)` (epochs 1-20), and plots training loss as a red dashed line (`"r--"`) and validation loss as a solid blue line (`"b"`), with title, axis labels, a tick at every epoch (`plt.xticks(epochs)`) and a legend.

The text points ahead to figures 4.6 and 4.7 (p.145), which show the resulting loss and accuracy curves; the accuracy plotting code (listing 4.20) and the top-3 accuracy plot follow on p.146. Compared with the IMDb version (10,000 validation samples, p.135), the validation set here is much smaller because the whole Reuters training set has fewer than 9,000 examples. The model is compiled with Adam, categorical crossentropy and two metrics: accuracy and top-3 accuracy. 1,000 of the 8,982 training samples are held out for validation; 7,982 are used for training. `validation_data` makes Keras report `val_` versions of the loss and every metric at the end of each epoch. Twenty epochs is chosen on purpose to overshoot, so the curves can show where overfitting starts. Listing 4.19 plots `loss` vs. `val_loss` from `history.history`; the result is figure 4.6 on p.145.

title: Top-k accuracy
text: The fraction of samples whose true class is among the model's k highest-scoring predicted classes. A model that ranks the right topic second is better than one that ranks it 40th, but plain accuracy scores both as wrong; top-3 accuracy gives credit to the first. Implemented by `keras.metrics.TopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=3, name="top_3_accuracy")` (p.143), which expects one-hot targets. title: Categorical crossentropy
text: The loss used here: it measures the distance between the model's predicted probability distribution and the true (one-hot) label distribution. It punishes the model according to how little probability it put on the correct class. For one-hot $y$ and softmax output $\hat y$, the loss per sample reduces to $-\log \hat y_{c}$ where $c$ is the true class. The string `"categorical_crossentropy"` requires one-hot labels like those produced on p.142. If the model assigns 0.5 to the true class, loss = 0.69; if 0.05, loss = 3.0.
snippet: The loss used here: it measures the distance between the model's predicted probability distribution and the true one-hot label distribution.

Keys follow the metric names: `loss`, `accuracy`, `top_3_accuracy`, and the same names prefixed with `val_` when validation data is supplied. Each list has length `epochs` (20 here). `len(history.history["val_loss"]) == 20`.

title: Figures 4.6-4.7: Reuters loss and accuracy curves
text:
Training vs. validation loss and accuracy over 20 epochs for the 64-64-46 Reuters model Training loss keeps falling and training accuracy keeps rising, but validation loss bottoms out around epoch 9 and validation accuracy plateaus near 82%: the model starts to overfit after about nine epochs. This page contains only two figures, the output of the training run in listing 4.18 (p.144).

**Figure 4.6, Training and validation loss** (produced by listing 4.19): the red dashed training loss starts near 3.3 at epoch 1 and decreases monotonically to about 0.1 by epoch 20. The solid blue validation loss starts lower (about 2.6), drops quickly to about 1.0 by epoch 5, reaches its minimum of roughly 0.88 around **epoch 9**, and then creeps back up to about 1.0 by epoch 20. The curves cross around epoch 3-4; after that the training loss is lower.

**Figure 4.7, Training and validation accuracy** (produced by listing 4.20 on p.146): training accuracy rises from about 0.40 to about 0.96 and flattens out. Validation accuracy rises from about 0.49 to a plateau of roughly **0.81-0.83** from epoch 8 onward, peaking slightly around epoch 12 before drifting down a little.

How to use the page: the widening gap between the curves after about epoch 9 is the signature of overfitting described for IMDb on p.138. The book states the conclusion on p.147: "The model begins to overfit after nine epochs", and retrains a fresh model for nine epochs. Note (not in the book): the validation loss turns upward earlier and more clearly than validation accuracy, which stays nearly flat; loss is sensitive to over-confident wrong predictions even when the argmax does not change. Training loss falls steadily from about 3.3 to about 0.1 over 20 epochs. Validation loss is lowest near epoch 9 (about 0.88) and then rises. Validation accuracy plateaus around 0.82 while training accuracy reaches about 0.96. These curves justify retraining for nine epochs (p.147).
