**Listing 4.20** plots training and validation accuracy, the figure shown as figure 4.7 on p.145. It starts with `plt.clf()` to clear the current figure (the loss plot from listing 4.19), reads `history.history["accuracy"]` and `history.history["val_accuracy"]`, and reuses the `epochs` range defined in listing 4.19. As before, training is a red dashed line (`"r--"`) and validation a solid blue line (`"b"`), with title, axis labels, a tick at every epoch, and a legend.

**Figure 4.8, Training and validation top-3 accuracy**, is the output of **listing 4.21**, which follows the figure on the page. The listing is identical in structure but reads the keys `"top_3_accuracy"` and `"val_top_3_accuracy"`. Those names exist because the metric object was created on p.143 with `name="top_3_accuracy"`, and Keras prefixes validation versions with `val_`.

In the figure, training top-3 accuracy climbs from about 0.55 at epoch 1 to essentially 1.0 by epoch 12. Validation top-3 accuracy climbs from about 0.68 to around 0.92 by epoch 8 and stays roughly flat (about 0.92-0.93) up to epoch 20. Compared with figure 4.7, where validation accuracy plateaus near 0.82, this means that for roughly 10% of validation newswires the model's first guess is wrong but the right topic is its second or third choice. That is exactly the kind of near-miss that the book said plain accuracy ignores (p.143). As in figures 4.6-4.7, validation performance stops improving long before training performance does; the book's conclusion, that the model overfits after nine epochs, comes on p.147. title: Retraining for nine epochs and the random baseline
text:
Retraining the Reuters model from scratch for nine epochs, evaluating it on the test set (≈80% accuracy), and comparing with a shuffled-label random baseline (≈19%) Using the epoch count chosen from the validation curves, a fresh model trained on all training data reaches about 80% test accuracy, far above the roughly 19% a random classifier would get on this imbalanced 46-class problem. From the curves on p.145-146 the authors conclude: **"The model begins to overfit after nine epochs."** They therefore build a **new model from scratch** (listing 4.22) with the same architecture as listing 4.15 (Dense 64 relu → Dense 64 relu → Dense 46 softmax), compile it with Adam and categorical crossentropy, and this time monitor only `"accuracy"` (top-3 is dropped). It is trained on the **full** training set (`x_train`, `y_train`, all 8,982 samples, no validation split) for `epochs=9` with `batch_size=512`, and then scored with `model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)`.

The result is `[0.9565213431445807, 0.79697239536954589]`: a test loss of about 0.96 and a **test accuracy of about 80%**.

Is 80% good? The authors point out that for a balanced binary problem a random classifier would get 50%, but with 46 classes that "may not be equally represented" the right reference point is less obvious. They estimate it empirically: copy the test labels, shuffle the copy with `np.random.shuffle`, compare element-wise with the original labels, and average the resulting booleans. The result, **0.1866**, means a random classifier that respects the label frequencies would be right about **19%** of the time. Against that baseline, 80% is clearly meaningful.

Note (not in the book): 19% is far above $1/46\approx2.2\%$ because Reuters topics are heavily imbalanced; a shuffled-label baseline has expected accuracy $\sum_k p_k^2$, which is dominated by the few largest topics. The book develops the idea of common-sense baselines more generally on p.176. Overfitting starts after about nine epochs, so a fresh model is trained for nine epochs. The final model is trained on all 8,982 training samples, without a validation split. Test results: loss ≈ 0.96, accuracy ≈ 0.80. A shuffled-label random classifier gets ≈ 0.19, not 1/46, because the classes are imbalanced. Always interpret a metric against a trivial baseline.

title: Predictions on new data; integer labels and sparse loss
text:
Interpreting `predict()` output as a 46-way probability distribution, and switching from one-hot labels to integer labels with `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` For each newswire the model returns 46 probabilities summing to 1, and the predicted topic is their argmax. If you keep the labels as integers instead of one-hot vectors, the only change needed is the loss: `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`. **4.2.5 Generating predictions on new data.** Calling `model.predict(x_test)` on the trained model returns, for every test newswire, "a class probability distribution over all 46 topics." The authors check three properties on the first test sample:

- `predictions[0].shape` is `(46,)`: one score per topic (so `predictions` as a whole has shape `(2246, 46)`).
- `np.sum(predictions[0])` is `1.0`: the entries form a probability distribution, a consequence of the softmax last layer.
- `np.argmax(predictions[0])` is `4`: the predicted class is the one with the highest probability, here topic 4.

**4.2.6 A different way to handle the labels and the loss.** On p.142 the authors noted two ways to vectorize the labels. Instead of one-hot encoding, you can leave them as integer tensors: `y_train = train_labels`, `y_test = test_labels`. The text says the only thing this changes is the loss function. `categorical_crossentropy`, used in listing 4.22, expects labels in categorical (one-hot) encoding; with integer labels you should use **`sparse_categorical_crossentropy`**, shown in a `compile()` call with Adam and `metrics=["accuracy"]`. The continuation on p.149 adds that the sparse loss is mathematically the same as categorical crossentropy and only has a different interface.

Beyond the book: integer labels are also lighter in memory, a length-2,246 vector instead of a 2,246 × 46 matrix, which matters for problems with many classes (such as the vocabulary-sized outputs of language models later in the book). `model.predict(x_test)` returns a (2246, 46) array of probabilities. Each row sums to 1 because of the softmax output layer. The predicted topic is `np.argmax` of the row. Integer labels can be used directly if the loss is `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`. One-hot labels go with `categorical_crossentropy`; mixing them up causes errors.

title: Softmax output
text: An activation that turns a vector of real scores into a probability distribution: positive entries that sum to 1. Exaggerates differences between scores, then normalizes them into shares of 100%. $\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i = e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$; for Reuters, $z \in \mathbb{R}^{46}$. `np.sum(predictions[0])` → 1.0.

title: Information bottlenecks and further experiments
text:
Equivalence of the sparse loss; the effect of a 4-unit intermediate layer on a 46-class problem; suggested experiments with layer sizes and depth Squeezing the representation through a 4-dimensional layer before a 46-way classifier loses information: validation accuracy peaks around 71%, about 8 points lower than the 64-unit model. Intermediate layers should not be much smaller than the number of output classes. The page first finishes section 4.2.6: **`sparse_categorical_crossentropy` is mathematically the same as `categorical_crossentropy`**; it just has a different interface (integer targets instead of one-hot).

**4.2.7 The importance of having sufficiently large intermediate layers.** The authors recall their earlier warning (p.142-143): because the outputs are 46-dimensional, intermediate layers with much fewer than 46 units should be avoided. To show why, **listing 4.23** builds a model with an **information bottleneck**: `Dense(64, relu)` → `Dense(4, relu)` → `Dense(46, softmax)`. It is compiled as before (Adam, categorical crossentropy, accuracy) and trained on `partial_x_train` for 20 epochs with `batch_size=128`, monitoring `(x_val, y_val)`.

Result: validation accuracy now **peaks at about 71%, an 8% absolute drop**. The authors attribute this mostly to trying to compress "enough information to recover the separation hyperplanes of 46 classes" into a space that is too low-dimensional. The model manages to cram *most* (italicized in the book) of the necessary information into the 4-dimensional representations, but not all of it.

**4.2.8 Further experiments.** As with IMDb, the authors suggest experiments to build intuition about configuration choices:

- try larger or smaller layers: 32 units, 128 units, and so on;
- try a single intermediate layer, or three, instead of the two used before the softmax layer.

Note (not in the book): listing 4.23 also changes `batch_size` from 512 to 128, so it is not a perfectly controlled comparison, but the size of the drop and the reasoning about dimensionality make the bottleneck the main cause, as the book says ("mostly due to"). `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` and `categorical_crossentropy` are mathematically the same; only the label format differs. Hidden layers much narrower than the number of classes create information bottlenecks. A 4-unit hidden layer drops peak validation accuracy to about 71%, an 8-point absolute loss. The model can fit most, but not all, of the needed information into 4 dimensions. Experiment with widths (32, 128, …) and depths (1 or 3 hidden layers) to build intuition.

title: Listing 4.23 A model with an information bottleneck
text:
model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(4, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(46, activation="softmax"),
    ]
)
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
model.fit(
    partial_x_train,
    partial_y_train,
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=128,
    validation_data=(x_val, y_val),
) Trains a 64-4-46 model on the 7,982-sample training split for 20 epochs, monitoring validation accuracy, to show the effect of a too-narrow hidden layer. Mini-batch Adam; with batch size 128, each epoch has $\lceil 7982/128\rceil = 63$ updates.

title: Multiclass wrap-up and the start of regression
text:
Lessons from the Reuters multiclass example, then the definition of regression and the introduction of the California Housing dataset Single-label multiclass classification uses an N-unit softmax output with (sparse) categorical crossentropy and needs intermediate layers that are not too narrow; regression, by contrast, predicts a continuous value, and the next example predicts median house prices in California districts. The page opens with **4.2.9 Wrapping up**, the takeaways from the Reuters newswire classifier (46 topics):

- To classify among **N classes**, end the model with a `Dense` layer of size **N**.
- For **single-label multiclass** problems, use a `softmax` activation on that layer so the model outputs a probability distribution over the N classes.
- **Categorical crossentropy** is almost always the right loss: it minimizes the distance between the model's predicted distribution and the true distribution of the targets.
- Labels can be handled two ways: **one-hot (categorical) encoding** with `categorical_crossentropy`, or **integer encoding** with `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` (mathematically the same loss, different interface, as p.149 noted).
- With many categories, avoid **information bottlenecks**: intermediate layers that are too small (p.149 showed a 4-unit layer dropping validation accuracy by about 8 points).

Section **4.3** then turns to the third common task. The two previous examples predicted a single *discrete* label; **regression** predicts a *continuous value*, e.g. tomorrow's temperature from meteorological data, or how long a software project will take from its specifications. A NOTE warns that **logistic regression is not a regression algorithm** but a classification algorithm.

**4.3.1** introduces the **California Housing Price dataset**: the goal is to predict the **median price of homes** in areas of California using **1990 census** data. Each data point is a **block group**, a set of homes in the same area (think of it as a district). There is a *small* version with **600 districts** and a *large* version with **20,640**; the book deliberately uses the small one because real-world datasets are often tiny and you need to know how to handle that. The page ends mid-sentence ("For each district, we know"), and the list of the eight features continues on p.151. N classes means a final Dense layer with N units. Single-label multiclass: softmax output plus categorical crossentropy. One-hot labels go with categorical_crossentropy; integer labels with sparse_categorical_crossentropy; the math is identical. Avoid intermediate layers much smaller than the number of classes (information bottleneck). Regression predicts a continuous value; logistic regression is actually a classifier. The California Housing example uses the small 600-district version to teach small-data techniques.

title: Softmax output for single-label multiclass
text: An activation that converts N scores into N non-negative probabilities summing to 1. The classes compete for a fixed budget of probability mass. softmax(z)_i = e^{z_i} / sum_j e^{z_j}; placed on a Dense(N) output layer. Reuters: Dense(46, activation='softmax').

section: 4.3 Predicting house prices: A regression example

title: Categorical crossentropy
text: The loss for single-label multiclass classification, measuring the distance between predicted and true distributions. It heavily penalizes assigning low probability to the correct class. Beyond the book: L = -sum_i y_i log p_i; with one-hot y, L = -log p_correct. If the model assigns 0.7 to the true class, the loss is -ln 0.7 ≈ 0.357.

title: Normalizing features, scaling targets, and a small model
text:
Feature-wise normalization using training statistics, dividing the targets by 100,000, and choosing a small two-layer model because data is scarce Heterogeneous input ranges and large target values make learning hard, so each feature is standardized with the training mean and standard deviation, targets are rescaled to 0.6-5, and a small model (two 64-unit layers) is used to limit overfitting on 480 samples. **4.3.2 Preparing the data.** Feeding a network values in wildly different ranges is problematic: the model *might* adapt, but learning would definitely be harder. The widespread best practice is **feature-wise normalization**: for each feature (a column of the input matrix), subtract its mean and divide by its standard deviation, so it is centered on 0 with unit standard deviation. **Listing 4.25** does this in four NumPy lines, computing `mean` and `std` along `axis=0` of `train_data` and applying them to both `train_data` and `test_data`.

The book stresses that the **normalization quantities for the test data come from the training data**: you should never use any quantity computed on the test data in your workflow, not even for something as simple as normalization.

The **targets must be scaled too**. Normalized inputs are near 0 and weights start as small random values, so initial predictions are small. Targets of 60,000-500,000 would require very large weights, and with a small learning rate it would take a very long time to get there. The simplest fix is to **divide all targets by 100,000** (range becomes 0.6 to 5) and multiply predictions by 100,000 to get dollars back (**listing 4.26**).

**4.3.3 Building your model.** Because so few samples are available, the book uses a **very small model with two intermediate layers of 64 units**. The less training data you have, the worse overfitting will be, and a small model is one way to mitigate it. **Listing 4.27** begins with `def get_model():` and `keras.Sequential(`; the callout explains that a function is used because the same model must be instantiated **multiple times** (for K-fold validation). The rest of the listing (the layers and `compile` call) is on p.153. Standardize each feature with the training mean and std (listing 4.25). Never compute anything on the test data, not even normalization statistics. Divide targets by 100,000 so they range from 0.6 to 5, and multiply predictions back. Less data means more overfitting; use a small model (two 64-unit layers). get_model() is a factory because K-fold validation needs several fresh copies of the model.

title: Regression output, MSE/MAE, and why K-fold validation
text:
Completion of the regression model (linear Dense(1) output, adam, MSE loss, MAE metric) and the motivation and definition of K-fold cross-validation Scalar regression ends with a single linear unit so outputs are unconstrained, is trained with mean squared error and monitored with mean absolute error; with only a few hundred samples a single validation split is too noisy, so K-fold cross-validation averages scores over K train/validate partitions. The top of the page completes **listing 4.27** (started on p.152): the `Sequential` model contains `layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")` twice and a final `layers.Dense(1)`, and is compiled with `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="mean_squared_error"` and `metrics=["mean_absolute_error"]` before being returned.

The model **ends with a single unit and no activation**, i.e. a **linear layer**, the typical setup for **scalar regression**. Any activation would constrain the output range; a `sigmoid` would limit predictions to 0-1. A purely linear last layer lets the model predict values in any range.

The loss is **mean squared error (MSE)**, the square of the difference between predictions and targets, widely used for regression. A new metric, **mean absolute error (MAE)**, is monitored: the absolute difference between predictions and targets. Because targets were divided by 100,000, an **MAE of 0.5 means predictions are off by $50,000 on average**.

**4.3.4 Validating your approach using K-fold validation.** To tune parameters such as the number of epochs you could hold out a validation set as before, but with so few data points it would be very small (about 100 examples). Validation scores would then depend heavily on which points land in the validation set: they would have **high variance with respect to the validation split**, making evaluation unreliable.

The best practice is **K-fold cross-validation** (figure 4.9, next page): split the data into **K partitions** (typically K = 4 or 5), instantiate **K identical models**, train each on **K - 1 partitions** and evaluate on the remaining one. The model's validation score is the **average of the K validation scores**. The code (listing 4.28) follows on p.154. Scalar regression: final Dense(1) with no activation, so predictions are unconstrained. Train with mean_squared_error; monitor mean_absolute_error. MAE is in target units: 0.5 scaled = $50,000. Small validation sets give high-variance scores, making evaluation unreliable. K-fold: K partitions, K fresh models, train on K-1, validate on 1, average the K scores (K typically 4 or 5).

title: Three-fold diagram and the K-fold validation loop
text:
Figure 4.9 (three-fold cross-validation) and listing 4.28, a from-scratch NumPy implementation of K-fold validation with K = 4 on the house-price data K-fold validation rotates which contiguous slice of the training data is held out: for each fold, the code slices out a validation partition, concatenates the remaining partitions for training, builds a fresh compiled model with get_model(), trains it, evaluates its MAE on the held-out partition and collects the scores for averaging. **Figure 4.9** shows **three-fold cross-validation**: the data is split into 3 partitions. In fold 1 the first partition is used for validation and the other two for training; in fold 2 the middle partition validates; in fold 3 the last one does. Each fold yields a validation score (#1, #2, #3), and the **final score is their average**.

**Listing 4.28** implements this with **k = 4** on the normalized training data:

- `num_val_samples = len(x_train) // k` (480 // 4 = 120), `num_epochs = 50`, and an empty `all_scores` list.
- For each fold `i`, the **validation data** is the slice `[i * num_val_samples : (i + 1) * num_val_samples]` of `x_train` and `y_train` (callout: data from partition #k).
- The **training data** is all other partitions, joined with `np.concatenate([... [: i * num_val_samples], ...[(i + 1) * num_val_samples :]], axis=0)`.
- `model = get_model()` builds a **fresh, already compiled** model for every fold.
- `model.fit(...)` trains it for `num_epochs` epochs with `batch_size=16` and `verbose=0` (silent).
- `model.evaluate(fold_x_val, fold_y_val, verbose=0)` returns the loss and the metric; they are unpacked as `val_loss, val_mae`, and **`val_mae` is appended** to `all_scores`.

The page ends with "Running this with `num_epochs = 50` yields the following results:"; the per-fold MAEs (0.232 to 0.349) and their mean (0.296, about $29,600) are printed on p.155.

Note that all of this runs on the 480 training samples only; the 120 test samples are untouched, consistent with the rule on p.152 never to use test data in the workflow. Figure 4.9: each partition serves as validation once; final score = average of fold scores. Listing 4.28 uses k = 4, 120 validation and 360 training samples per fold, 50 epochs, batch size 16. Validation and training partitions are built by slicing and np.concatenate along axis 0. A fresh compiled model is created each fold via get_model(). model.evaluate returns [loss, MAE]; the MAE is collected in all_scores.

title: Listing 4.28 K-fold validation
text:
k = 4
num_val_samples = len(x_train) // k
num_epochs = 50
all_scores = []
for i in range(k):
    print(f"Processing fold #{i + 1}")
    fold_x_val = x_train[i * num_val_samples : (i + 1) * num_val_samples]
    fold_y_val = y_train[i * num_val_samples : (i + 1) * num_val_samples]
    fold_x_train = np.concatenate(
        [x_train[: i * num_val_samples], x_train[(i + 1) * num_val_samples :]],
        axis=0,
    )
    fold_y_train = np.concatenate(
        [y_train[: i * num_val_samples], y_train[(i + 1) * num_val_samples :]],
        axis=0,
    )
    model = get_model()
    model.fit(
        fold_x_train,
        fold_y_train,
        epochs=num_epochs,
        batch_size=16,
        verbose=0,
    )
    scores = model.evaluate(fold_x_val, fold_y_val, verbose=0)
    val_loss, val_mae = scores
    all_scores.append(val_mae) Runs 4-fold cross-validation of the get_model() regressor on the normalized training data, training 50 epochs per fold and collecting each fold's validation MAE. Standard K-fold cross-validation with contiguous partitions.

title: K-fold results and logging per-epoch validation MAE
text:
The four fold scores and their mean from listing 4.28, interpreting the mean in dollars, and listing 4.29, which trains for 200 epochs and records each fold's per-epoch validation MAE history The four fold MAEs differ substantially (0.232 to 0.349), so their average (0.296, about $29,600) is far more reliable than any single split; to choose the number of epochs, the loop is modified to pass validation_data to fit and keep the per-epoch val_mean_absolute_error histories for averaging across folds. The page opens with the output of the 50-epoch K-fold run from listing 4.28: the rounded fold MAEs are **[0.298, 0.349, 0.232, 0.305]** and their mean is **0.296**.

The runs show **meaningfully different validation scores, from 0.232 to 0.349**. The **average (0.296) is a much more reliable metric** than any single score, which the book calls *the entire point of K-fold cross-validation*. Undoing the target scaling, the model is **off by $29,600 on average**, which is significant given that prices range from $60,000 to $500,000.

Next the book tries **training longer: 200 epochs**. To see how the model does at **each epoch**, the training loop is modified to save the per-epoch validation score log. **Listing 4.29** is the same loop as listing 4.28 (k = 4, slicing and concatenating the partitions, a fresh `get_model()` per fold) with three changes:

- `num_epochs = 200`, and a list `all_mae_histories` replaces `all_scores`;
- `model.fit(...)` receives `validation_data=(fold_x_val, fold_y_val)`, so Keras evaluates the held-out fold at the end of every epoch, and its return value is kept as `history`;
- `history.history["val_mean_absolute_error"]`, a list of 200 per-epoch validation MAEs, is appended to `all_mae_histories` (instead of a separate `evaluate` call).

The page ends by noting that you can then **average the per-epoch MAE scores across all folds**; listing 4.30 and the plot (figure 4.10) follow on p.156. Fold MAEs were 0.298, 0.349, 0.232, 0.305; mean 0.296. Such spread shows why a single small validation split is unreliable; the average is the point of K-fold. 0.296 scaled MAE = about $29,600 average error, significant for $60k-$500k prices. Listing 4.29 trains 200 epochs and stores history.history['val_mean_absolute_error'] for each fold. Averaging per-epoch MAE across folds gives a reliable validation curve for choosing the epoch count.

k = 4
num_val_samples = len(x_train) // k

for i in range(k):

title: Averaging per-epoch K-fold scores and plotting validation MAE
text:
Turning the four per-fold validation-MAE histories into one averaged curve, plotting it (figure 4.10), and trimming the first 10 epochs to make the plot readable The four 200-epoch validation-MAE logs from listing 4.29 are averaged epoch by epoch into one curve. Plotted, the curve falls steeply at first and then flattens around 0.3. The first epochs are so much larger than the rest that they squash the interesting part of the plot, so the book drops the first 10 points. This page finishes the data-processing half of the K-fold experiment that starts on p.155. In listing 4.29 each of the $K = 4$ folds trained a fresh model for 200 epochs and stored its per-epoch validation MAE. The result, `all_mae_histories`, is a list of four lists, each 200 values long.

**Listing 4.30** collapses those four curves into one. For each epoch index `i` it takes the `i`-th value from every fold's history and averages them with `np.mean`. The result, `average_mae_history`, has 200 entries. Entry `i` is the cross-validated estimate of how good the model is after `i + 1` epochs of training. Averaging epoch by epoch is the K-fold idea from p.153 applied to a whole training curve instead of a single final score.

**Listing 4.31** plots this curve against `epochs = range(1, len(average_mae_history) + 1)`, so the x-axis reads 1...200 rather than Python's 0-based indices. The y-axis is labeled "Validation MAE". The result is **figure 4.10**. The MAE starts just above 1.0 (about \$100,000 of error, since targets were divided by 100,000 on p.152). It drops steeply over the first ~20 epochs, passes 0.4 around epoch 15 and settles into a noisy plateau just under 0.3 from roughly epoch 40 to 200.

The book then points out a **scaling problem**. The first few values are so much larger than the rest that matplotlib's automatic y-range is dominated by them. The plateau, which is where the decision about epochs is made, gets squeezed into a thin band where small trends are invisible. The fix is to drop the first 10 points.

**Listing 4.32** starts at the bottom of this page. `truncated_mae_history = average_mae_history[10:]` keeps entries 10...199 (190 values), and `epochs = range(10, len(truncated_mae_history) + 10)` builds a matching x-axis that runs 10...199. The x-labels therefore still show the original epoch numbering. The plotting calls that finish listing 4.32, and the resulting figure 4.11, are on p.157, where the book reads the best epoch count (120-140) off the zoomed curve. all_mae_histories is a 4 x 200 table. Listing 4.30 averages over the fold axis to produce a 200-point cross-validated learning curve. Plot epochs as range(1, n + 1) so the x-axis shows the epoch number after which each score was measured. Figure 4.10 drops from about 1.03 to a plateau just under 0.3 (about \$29,000 average error) by roughly epoch 40. Large early values compress the y-axis. Dropping the first 10 points (listing 4.32) makes the plateau, where the decision is made, readable. This curve is used to choose the number of epochs for the final model trained on all the data (p.157).

title: K-fold cross-validation (per-epoch averaging)
text: Split the training data into K partitions, train K identical models each on K-1 partitions and validate on the remaining one, then average the validation scores. On this page the averaging is done separately for every epoch, which yields a cross-validated learning curve. Each fold gives a noisy view of how the model generalizes after a given amount of training. Averaging four views cancels much of the noise caused by which 120 samples happened to land in the validation fold. With per-fold histories $h_k(e)$ for $k = 1..K$, $e = 1..E$, the averaged curve is $\bar h(e) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_k h_k(e)$. Here K = 4 and E = 200. Each fold trains on 360 and validates on 120 of the 480 training samples. If at epoch 50 the four folds report MAE 0.31, 0.34, 0.24, 0.30, the averaged point is 0.2975. (Illustrative numbers; the page does not print per-fold values at epoch 50.)

title: Choosing the epoch count and training the final model
text:
Reading the zoomed validation-MAE curve (figure 4.11) to pick ~130 epochs, then retraining a fresh model on all 480 training samples and evaluating it once on the test set With the first 10 epochs removed, the averaged K-fold curve shows validation MAE no longer improving meaningfully after 120-140 epochs. The book treats training beyond that as overfitting. Once hyperparameters are settled, a new model is trained on the full training set with the chosen settings (130 epochs) and evaluated on the untouched test data. The page opens with the last four lines of **listing 4.32** (begun on p.156). `plt.plot(epochs, truncated_mae_history)` draws the averaged validation MAE without its first 10 points, labeled "Epochs" / "Validation MAE". The result is **figure 4.11**. Now that the y-axis only has to span about 0.28-0.41, the curve shows real structure. It falls from about 0.41 at epoch 10 to about 0.30 by roughly epoch 40-50, then wanders in a noisy band between about 0.285 and 0.315 up to epoch 200.

The authors read this plot as: **validation MAE stops improving significantly after 120-140 epochs**. They add that this count *includes* the 10 omitted epochs, because the x-axis of listing 4.32 was offset to keep original epoch numbering. Beyond that point, *you start overfitting*: further training fits the training folds better without helping the held-out fold.

The second paragraph describes the end of the workflow. Once you have finished tuning the number of epochs and any other parameters (the book suggests the size of the intermediate layers), you **train a final production model on all of the training data** with the best parameters, and only then look at its **test** performance. The K-fold models were each trained on only 360 samples and are discarded. The final model gets all 480.

**Listing 4.33** does exactly this. `get_model()` returns a fresh, compiled model (callout). `model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=130, batch_size=16, verbose=0)` trains it on the entirety of the data (callout), using 130 epochs, the middle of the 120-140 range, and the same batch size as the K-fold runs. `model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)` returns the loss (MSE) and the metric (MAE), which are unpacked into `test_mean_squared_error` and `test_mean_absolute_error`. The result, an MAE of about \$31,000, is printed on p.158. Figure 4.11 is the averaged K-fold validation MAE from epoch 10 to 200, with a y-range of about 0.28-0.41. The book reads it as: no significant improvement after 120-140 epochs (x-values are true epoch counts), and overfitting beyond that. Other hyperparameters, such as hidden-layer size, can be tuned the same way before the final fit. The final model is a fresh get_model() trained on all 480 training samples for 130 epochs with batch size 16. evaluate(x_test, y_test) returns [MSE, MAE] on scaled targets. Test data is used once, at the end.

title: Test result, predictions, and the regression wrap-up
text:
The final test MAE (0.31, about $31,000), what predict() returns for a scalar regression model, and the five lessons of the California housing example The final model is off by about $31,000 on the test set. For scalar regression, predict() returns one unbounded number per sample, in the target's scaled units (hundreds of thousands of dollars). The section's lessons: use MSE loss and MAE metric for regression, scale features independently, use K-fold validation on small data, and keep the model small to avoid overfitting. The page starts with the **final result** of listing 4.33. `round(test_mean_absolute_error, 3)` prints `0.31`. Because targets were divided by 100,000 (p.152), the authors translate it: *we're still off by about \$31,000 on average*. That is slightly worse than the K-fold estimate of 0.296 (p.155), which is normal run-to-run variation on a 120-sample test set. Measured against prices of \$60,000-\$500,000, it is a sizable error. The word "still" signals that this small model on 480 samples has clear limits.

**4.3.5 Generating predictions on new data** compares the three tasks of the chapter. The binary IMDb model's `predict()` gave a scalar between 0 and 1 per sample (a sigmoid probability). The Reuters model gave a probability distribution over 46 classes (softmax). The scalar regression model has a linear final `Dense(1)`, so `predict()` returns the model's raw guess of the price **in hundreds of thousands of dollars**. `predictions[0]` is `array([2.834494], dtype=float32)`: one value per sample, wrapped in a length-1 array because the output layer has one unit. Multiplying by 100,000 gives about **\$283,000** for the first test district.

**4.3.6 Wrapping up** lists five takeaways:
- Regression uses a different loss than classification. **MSE** is the common choice.
- Metrics also differ. Accuracy makes no sense for continuous targets, and **MAE** is a common regression metric.
- Features with different ranges should each be **scaled independently** during preprocessing.
- With little data, **K-fold validation** gives a reliable evaluation.
- With little training data, prefer a **small model** with one or two intermediate layers to avoid severe overfitting.

The chapter summary follows on p.159. The final test MAE is 0.31, about $31,000 average error on the 120 test districts. For scalar regression, predict() returns one unbounded value per sample in the target's scaled units. 2.834494 means about $283,000. Use MSE as the loss and MAE as the metric for regression. Accuracy does not apply. Scale each feature independently, using training statistics. With little data: use K-fold validation and a small model with one or two hidden layers.

title: Chapter 4 summary
text:
The seven lessons of chapter 4: task types and their losses, preprocessing, feature scaling, overfitting, model size for small data, information bottlenecks, and K-fold validation The chapter's three examples (IMDb, Reuters, California housing) cover the three most common tasks on vector data, each paired with its own loss. They also share a set of practical rules: preprocess and scale the data, expect overfitting, size intermediate layers neither too large (with little data) nor too small (with many classes), and use K-fold validation when data is scarce. This is the end-of-chapter **Summary** of chapter 4. It condenses the three worked examples into seven bullets:

1. The three most common tasks on vector data are **binary classification** (IMDb), **multiclass classification** (Reuters) and **scalar regression** (California housing). Each uses its own loss: `binary_crossentropy`, `categorical_crossentropy` and `mean_squared_error`. Implicitly, each also needs its own output layer: `Dense(1, sigmoid)`, `Dense(N, softmax)` and a linear `Dense(1)`.
2. Raw data usually has to be **preprocessed** into tensors first, for example multi-hot encoding word indices (p.132) or one-hot labels (p.142).
3. Features with different ranges should each be **scaled independently** (feature-wise normalization, p.152).
4. Training long enough always leads to **overfitting**: performance on unseen data eventually gets worse. This was seen at epoch 4 on IMDb (p.138), around epoch 9 on Reuters, and after 120-140 epochs on housing (p.157).
5. With little training data, use a **small model** with one or two intermediate layers.
6. With many categories, intermediate layers that are **too small create information bottlenecks**. Squeezing Reuters through 4 units cost about 8 points of validation accuracy (p.149).
7. With little data, **K-fold validation** provides a reliable evaluation (p.153-157).

Taken together, bullets 5 and 6 bound the hidden-layer width from both sides: big enough to carry the information the output needs, small enough not to memorize a small dataset. Bullets 4 and 7 are the evaluation side of the same story. Chapter 5 (p.160) formalizes these intuitions as the tension between optimization and generalization. Binary classification uses binary_crossentropy, multiclass classification uses categorical_crossentropy, and scalar regression uses mean_squared_error. Preprocess raw data into tensors, and scale each feature independently. Networks eventually overfit as training continues, so tune training length on validation data. Small data calls for a small model (one or two intermediate layers). Many classes call for layers that are not too narrow. With little data, use K-fold validation for reliable evaluation.

title: Chapter 5 opener: Fundamentals of machine learning
text:
What chapter 5 covers: the optimization-generalization tension, evaluation methods, improving fit, and improving generalization Chapter 4 showed overfitting in practice. Chapter 5 turns that experience into a conceptual framework built on accurate evaluation and on balancing fitting the training data against generalizing to new data. This is the opening page of **chapter 5, "Fundamentals of machine learning"** (PDF pp.160-194). The *This chapter covers* box lists four themes:

- **The tension between generalization and optimization**, called *the fundamental issue in machine learning* (section 5.1, p.160).
- **Evaluation methods** for machine learning models (section 5.2, p.173: training/validation/test sets, common-sense baselines).
- **Best practices to improve model fitting** (section 5.3, p.177: tuning gradient-descent parameters, better architecture priors, more capacity).
- **Best practices to achieve better generalization** (section 5.4, p.182: dataset curation, feature engineering, early stopping, regularization).

The introductory paragraph links back to chapter 4. After the IMDb, Reuters and housing examples you should be comfortable with classification and regression, and you have *witnessed the central problem of machine learning: overfitting*. Chapter 5 will **formalize** that intuition into a solid conceptual framework, stressing **accurate model evaluation** and the **balance between training and generalization**.

Section **5.1, "Generalization: The goal of machine learning"**, begins at the bottom of the page. It recalls that all three chapter 4 examples split the data into training, validation and test sets. The sentence continues on p.161, which explains why: performance on unseen data diverges from training performance after a few epochs.

*How to use this page:* treat the four bullets as a map of the chapter (see the diagram) and keep the chapter 4 examples in mind as concrete cases of each idea. Chapter 5 formalizes chapter 4's practical intuition about overfitting. Its four themes are the optimization-generalization tension, evaluation methods, improving fit, and improving generalization. Generalization is the goal of machine learning (section 5.1).

title: Optimization vs. generalization; underfitting and overfitting
text:
Defining optimization and generalization, their tension, and the universal training-time pattern of underfitting, then robust fit, then overfitting shown in figure 5.1 Optimization fits the model to its training data. Generalization is how well it does on unseen data, and that is the real goal. You only control optimization, though, and pushing it too far causes overfitting. Every model shows the same pattern: validation loss first falls together with training loss (underfitting), reaches a minimum (robust fit), then rises while training loss keeps falling (overfitting). The page finishes the opening sentence of section 5.1. In all three chapter 4 examples the data was split into **training, validation and test sets**. The reason not to evaluate on training data became evident quickly: after a few epochs, performance on unseen data **diverged** from training performance, which *always improves as training progresses*. The models started to **overfit**, and *overfitting happens in every machine-learning problem*.

The second paragraph names **the fundamental issue in machine learning: the tension between optimization and generalization**.
- **Optimization** is adjusting a model to get the best possible performance *on the training data*. This is the "learning" in machine learning.
- **Generalization** is how well the trained model performs *on data it has never seen*.

The goal is generalization, but **you don't control it**. You can only fit the model to its training data, and if you do that *too well*, overfitting kicks in and generalization suffers. A short paragraph then poses the questions for the rest of the chapter: *what causes overfitting, and how can we achieve good generalization?*

**5.1.1 Underfitting and overfitting.** For every chapter 4 model, validation performance improved at first and then *inevitably peaked*. The book calls this pattern **universal**, regardless of model type or dataset, and draws it in **figure 5.1, "Canonical overfitting behavior"**. Loss is plotted against training time. The dotted training curve decreases monotonically. The dashed validation curve tracks it at first, bottoms out at the point labeled **Robust fit**, then rises in the region labeled **Overfitting**. The region to the left is **Underfitting**.

The last paragraph explains the left side. **Early in training, optimization and generalization are correlated**: lower training loss means lower test loss. Such a model is **underfit**, because the network has not yet modeled all relevant patterns in the training data. After enough iterations, generalization stops improving and **validation metrics stall and then degrade**. The model is starting to overfit, beginning to learn training-specific patterns (the sentence continues on p.162, which says these patterns are misleading or irrelevant for new data). Optimization fits training data. Generalization is performance on unseen data. Their tension is the fundamental issue in machine learning. You don't control generalization directly. Fitting the training data too well causes overfitting. Overfitting happens in every machine-learning problem, and the validation peak is universal. Figure 5.1: underfitting (both losses fall together), then robust fit (validation minimum), then overfitting (validation rises while training falls). Underfit means there is still progress to be made: not all relevant patterns in the training data have been modeled.

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Why overfitting happens: noisy training data
text:
The first of three sources of overfitting: noisy training data (invalid inputs and mislabeled samples). Overfitting is most likely when data is noisy, uncertain, or contains rare features. Real datasets like MNIST contain invalid inputs and mislabeled samples, and a model that bends itself to fit those outliers will generalize worse. The page finishes the definition of overfitting started on p.161: once a model has overfit, it begins to learn patterns that are **specific to the training data** but misleading or irrelevant for new data. The authors then name the three situations in which overfitting is particularly likely: the data is **noisy**, it involves **uncertainty**, or it contains **rare features**. Each gets its own subsection; this page covers the first.

**Noisy training data.** Real-world datasets commonly contain *invalid* inputs. The book shows twelve strange MNIST training images (figure 5.2): blobs, scribbles, a heart-like shape, a cursive-looking stroke. Nobody, the authors included, can say which digit they are, yet they sit in the official training set with a label attached.

Worse are *perfectly valid* inputs carrying the *wrong label* (figure 5.3): a clear 4 labeled 9, a 1 labeled 7, a 7 labeled 4, a 9 labeled 3, and a 3 labeled 5 (the figure even prints each image's index in the training set, e.g. 14582 for the 4-labeled-9).

The consequence: if a model "goes out of its way" to incorporate such outliers, its generalization degrades (previewing figure 5.4 on p.163). Concretely, if the network memorizes that the mislabeled 4 is a "9", then a genuine test 4 that looks very similar may also be classified as a 9. The model has carved out a small region of input space around the bad sample and assigned it the wrong class.

The takeaway is that the training set is not ground truth; a sufficiently flexible model will learn its errors along with its signal, and that is one mechanism behind the validation-loss rise in figure 5.1 (p.161). Overfitting means learning training-set-specific patterns that are misleading for new data. It is most likely with noisy data, uncertain/ambiguous data, or rare features. MNIST contains invalid inputs (figure 5.2) and mislabeled valid inputs (figure 5.3). Mislabeled valid inputs are worse than invalid ones because they contradict their neighbours. Fitting an outlier, such as the 4 labeled 9, can cause similar test inputs to be misclassified.

title: Outliers and ambiguous features
text:
Figure 5.4 (robust fit vs. overfitting with outliers) and the second source of overfitting: ambiguous features and inherent uncertainty. Even perfectly labeled data can be noisy when the task is inherently ambiguous or random. A model overfits such data by drawing confident, convoluted boundaries through regions where classes genuinely overlap; a robust model keeps a simple boundary and accepts uncertainty there. **Figure 5.4** completes the noisy-data discussion of p.162. It shows two classes of points (light and dark) with a few outliers: light points sitting inside the dark cloud and vice versa. On the left, a green dashed **robust fit** is a smooth curve that separates the bulk of the two classes and simply misclassifies the outliers. On the right, a red dashed **overfit** boundary snakes around and draws little loops to capture every outlier. The overfit boundary scores perfectly on training data but its loops are pockets of wrong predictions for future data.

**Ambiguous features.** The authors then point out that noise does not only come from *inaccuracies*. Even "perfectly clean and neatly labeled" data is noisy when the problem itself involves **uncertainty and ambiguity**: some regions of feature space are associated with several classes at once. Two examples:

- Classifying a banana image as *unripened*, *ripe* or *rotten*: the categories have no objective boundaries, so different human labelers may disagree on the same picture.
- Predicting rain from atmospheric pressure: the same measurements are followed sometimes by rain and sometimes by clear sky, with some probability. The randomness is in the world, not in the labels.

**Figure 5.5** draws this: a shaded "Area of uncertainty" where light and dark points are mixed. The robust fit (left, green dashed) runs a simple line through the middle of the zone; the overfit model (right, red dashed) carves loops around individual points inside it.

The closing paragraph says a model overfits probabilistic data by being **too confident** about ambiguous regions (the text cites figure 5.6, but figure 5.5 is the one that shows this). A more robust fit ignores individual data points and looks at the bigger picture. Figure 5.4: a robust fit accepts errors on outliers; an overfit boundary loops around them. Noise can come from the problem itself: ambiguous categories and random outcomes. Banana ripeness (subjective classes) and rain from pressure (randomness) are the book's examples. In ambiguous regions the right output is a probability, not a confident class. Overfitting probabilistic data shows up as overconfidence; robust models look at the bigger picture.

title: Robust fit
text: A model that captures the main structure of the data and does not distort itself to fit outliers or individual points in ambiguous regions. Drawing the border between two neighbourhoods along the main street, not around every house that is on the 'wrong' side. Typically a lower-complexity or regularized decision function; it accepts nonzero training error in exchange for lower variance. Figure 5.4's smooth green dashed boundary that misclassifies a few outlier points.
snippet: A model that captures the main structure of the data and does not distort itself to fit outliers or individual points in ambiguous regions.
section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Ambiguous features / inherent uncertainty
text: Inputs for which the correct class is genuinely uncertain, either because category boundaries are subjective or because the outcome is random given the input. Two experts look at the same banana and disagree; the same barometer reading is followed by rain on some days and sun on others. p(y | x) is spread over several classes; the irreducible error equals the expected conditional entropy (or Bayes error rate) in those regions. Banana ripeness classification; rain prediction from atmospheric pressure.
snippet: Inputs for which the correct class is genuinely uncertain, either because category boundaries are subjective or because the outcome is random given the input.
section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Overconfidence
text: Predicting probabilities more extreme than warranted by the data, especially in ambiguous regions. A forecaster who always says '100% rain' or '0% rain' when the honest answer is '60%'. Measured by calibration error; under cross-entropy, a confident wrong prediction incurs a large loss, which is why validation loss can rise even when validation accuracy changes little. Figure 5.5 right panel: loops assign each point in the uncertainty zone a definite class.
snippet: Predicting probabilities more extreme than warranted by the data, especially in ambiguous regions.

title: Rare features, spurious correlations, and the noise-channel experiment
text:
The third source of overfitting: rare or meaningless features that correlate with targets by chance, and the setup of an MNIST experiment that adds 784 noise or zero columns. When a feature value is rare, or its association with the target is a statistical fluke, a model will still use it, learning a spurious correlation that does not hold for new data. Adding pure white-noise features to MNIST, which carries no information, is enough to provoke this. This page introduces the third cause of overfitting named on p.162: **rare features and spurious correlations**.

It opens with a human analogy: if you had only ever met two orange tabby cats and both were antisocial, you might conclude that orange tabbies are antisocial. That's overfitting; exposure to more cats would show that color doesn't predict character.

Models do the same. In sentiment classification, if the word **"cherimoya"** (an Andean fruit; a footnote quotes Mark Twain calling it "the most delicious fruit known to men") appears in only one training text and that text is negative, a poorly regularized model may give the word a large negative weight and label every future cherimoya-mentioning text negative.

Rarity in the sense of a couple of occurrences isn't required. A word occurring in **100 samples**, positive 54% of the time and negative 46%, may show a difference that is a **complete statistical fluke**, yet the model will likely learn to use it. The authors call this "one of the most common sources of overfitting."

Then comes a **striking experiment**: take MNIST, flatten each image to 784 values, and build two new training sets of 1,568 columns, one by appending **784 white-noise columns** and one by appending **784 all-zero columns** (Listing 5.1). Neither addition changes the information content of the data; a human classifier wouldn't be affected at all. The page ends by announcing that the chapter 2 model will be trained on both sets (Listing 5.2, p.165), with the outcome shown in figure 5.6 (p.166). Rare or meaningless features let models learn spurious correlations, a top source of overfitting. A word seen once (cherimoya) can receive a huge weight in a poorly regularized model. Even 100 occurrences with a 54/46 split can be pure chance, and the model will still use it. Listing 5.1 builds two 1,568-feature MNIST datasets: pixels plus 784 noise columns, or plus 784 zero columns. Both have identical information content; any accuracy difference comes from fitting noise.

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Spurious correlation
text: An association between a feature and the target that appears in the training sample by chance but doesn't hold in general. Two grumpy orange cats don't make orange cats grumpy. With finite n, the empirical correlation of an irrelevant feature with the target fluctuates around zero with spread about 1/sqrt(n); a flexible model exploits these fluctuations to reduce training loss. 'cherimoya' appearing once in a negative review; a word 54% positive over 100 samples.
snippet: An association between a feature and the target that appears in the training sample by chance but doesn't hold in general.
section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Rare features
text: Feature values that occur in very few training samples. A word that appears in one review can be assigned any meaning the model likes. Their weights are constrained by very few gradient contributions and can grow large to fit those few samples. 'cherimoya' in a sentiment dataset.
snippet: Feature values that occur in very few training samples.

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: How big is a chance fluctuation over 100 samples? (not in the book)
text: Not printed in the book; quantifies the page's '100 samples … 54% … 46%' example. \mathrm{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.5\cdot 0.5}{100}} = 0.05 Shows that a 54/46 split is fully consistent with a neutral word. The observed 0.54 is only (0.54-0.50)/0.05 = 0.8 standard errors above 0.5; splits this lopsided or more occur by chance roughly 4 times in 10 for a neutral word. p True probability that a sample containing the word is positive (0.5 if the word is neutral). n Number of training samples containing the word (100). \hat p Observed fraction of positive samples (0.54 in the book's example). \mathrm{SE} Standard error: typical size of the random deviation of \hat p from p.
snippet: Not printed in the book; quantifies the page's '100 samples … 54% … 46%' example. — Shows that a 54/46 split is fully consistent with a neutral word.

title: Listing 5.1 Adding white noise channels or all-zeros channels to MNIST
text:
from keras.datasets import mnist
import numpy as np

(train_images, train_labels), _ = mnist.load_data()
train_images = train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))
train_images = train_images.astype("float32") / 255

train_images_with_noise_channels = np.concatenate(
    [train_images, np.random.random((len(train_images), 784))], axis=1
)

train_images_with_zeros_channels = np.concatenate(
    [train_images, np.zeros((len(train_images), 784))], axis=1
) Loads MNIST training data, flattens each 28 × 28 image into 784 values scaled to [0, 1], and creates two augmented copies with 1,568 columns: one with 784 uniform random columns appended, one with 784 zero columns appended. Flatten → normalize → horizontally concatenate either noise or zeros.

title: Training on noise vs. zero channels (Listings 5.2-5.3)
text:
Code for the controlled experiment set up on p.164: train an identical two-layer MNIST model on the noise-augmented and zero-augmented datasets, and start plotting their validation accuracies. To isolate the effect of spurious correlations, the same freshly initialized model (via a get_model() factory) is trained with identical hyperparameters on both datasets, recording the History objects so their validation accuracy curves can be compared. This page is entirely code, implementing the experiment announced at the end of p.164.

**Listing 5.2** defines `get_model()`, a factory that builds and compiles the same network each time: a `keras.Sequential` with `Dense(512, activation="relu")` followed by `Dense(10, activation="softmax")`, which is the chapter 2 MNIST model. It is compiled with the **Adam** optimizer, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` loss (labels are integers 0-9) and an `accuracy` metric. The listing then calls `get_model()` twice to obtain two **independent, freshly initialized** models. One is trained on `train_images_with_noise_channels`, the other on `train_images_with_zeros_channels`, both for **10 epochs**, **batch size 128**, with **`validation_split=0.2`**: Keras holds out the last 20% of the arrays (12,000 samples) as validation data and trains on the first 48,000. The returned `History` objects are stored as `history_noise` and `history_zeros`.

Because the input now has 1,568 features, the first Dense layer has 1568 × 512 + 512 = 803,328 parameters (twice the 401,920 of the plain 784-input model). In the zeros model, half of those weights receive no gradient.

**Listing 5.3** begins the comparison plot. It extracts the per-epoch validation accuracy lists `history_noise.history["val_accuracy"]` and `history_zeros.history["val_accuracy"]`, builds `epochs = range(1, 11)` for the x-axis, and calls `plt.plot` for the noise curve with a blue solid line style `"b-"` and the label "Validation accuracy with noise channels". A second `plt.plot(epochs, …` call starts at the bottom of the page and is completed on p.166, where the zeros curve, the title, axis labels and legend are added and the resulting figure 5.6 is discussed. get_model() returns a fresh, identically configured model, so the two runs differ only in their data. Model: Dense(512, relu) → Dense(10, softmax), Adam, sparse categorical crossentropy, accuracy. Both runs: 10 epochs, batch size 128, last 20% of the data held out for validation. history.history['val_accuracy'] provides the curves compared in figure 5.6. Listing 5.3 starts here and finishes on p.166.

title: Noise channels cost accuracy; feature selection
text:
Result of the noise-channel experiment (figure 5.6) and feature selection as a remedy for noisy features. Although both datasets contain the same information, the model trained with noise channels ends about one percentage point lower in validation accuracy, purely because of spurious correlations. When unsure whether features are informative, select features by a usefulness score such as mutual information with the labels. The page opens with the end of **Listing 5.3**: the second `plt.plot` call draws the zeros-channel validation accuracy as a red dashed line (`"r--"`), then the figure gets a title ("Effect of noise channels on validation accuracy"), axis labels ("Epochs", "Accuracy"), integer x-ticks (`plt.xticks(epochs)`) and a legend before `plt.show()`.

**The result (figure 5.6).** The zeros-channel model (red dashed) starts around 0.954 after epoch 1 and plateaus near 0.977. The noise-channel model (blue solid) starts much lower, around 0.911, climbs unevenly (dipping at epochs 4 and 9) and ends near 0.965. The book summarizes: despite the data holding the same information, the noise model ends **about one percentage point lower**, purely through spurious correlations, and **the more noise channels you add, the further accuracy would degrade**.

**Remedy: feature selection.** "Noisy features inevitably lead to overfitting." So when you are not sure whether your features are informative or distracting, it is common to do **feature selection** before training. Restricting IMDB to the 10,000 most common words (chapter 4) was a crude form of it. The typical method is to compute a **usefulness score** for each feature, a measure of how informative it is about the task, such as the **mutual information** between the feature and the labels, and keep only features above a threshold. Applied to this experiment, it would filter out the white-noise channels, which have (near-)zero mutual information with the digit labels.

This closes subsection 5.1.1; the next page starts 5.1.2 on why deep learning generalizes at all. Listing 5.3 finishes by plotting the zeros curve (red dashed) and decorating figure 5.6. With identical information, the noise-channel model ends about 1 point lower in validation accuracy. The gap is due purely to spurious correlations; more noise channels would widen it. Noisy features inevitably cause overfitting, so select features when unsure. Feature selection: score each feature (e.g. mutual information with labels) and keep those above a threshold.

title: Mutual information
text: A measure of how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another; named in the book as a usefulness score between a feature and the labels. How many yes/no questions about the label you save by looking at the feature. I(X;Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) ≥ 0, with equality iff X and Y are independent. Captures nonlinear dependence, unlike correlation. A pixel in the centre of MNIST images has positive MI with the digit; a white-noise column has MI ≈ 0.

title: Mutual information between a feature and the labels
text: Named in words only: 'the mutual information between the feature and the labels'. The formula is not printed in the book. I(X_j; Y) = \sum_{x,\,y} p(x, y)\,\log\frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)\,p(y)} = H(Y) - H(Y\mid X_j) Serves as the per-feature usefulness score for threshold-based feature selection. Zero if the feature is independent of the label (p(x,y) = p(x)p(y)); larger values mean the feature is more informative. X_j Feature j (e.g. one pixel or noise column, discretized). Y The label (digit class 0-9). p(x, y) Joint probability of feature value x and label y. p(x), p(y) Marginal probabilities. H(Y) Entropy (uncertainty) of the label. H(Y \mid X_j) Remaining uncertainty about the label after observing feature j.

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Deep nets can fit random labels
text:
Opening of 5.1.2: a model with enough capacity can fit anything, even MNIST with shuffled labels, which raises the question of why deep learning generalizes at all. Training loss can go down on data with no input-target relationship, because the model just memorizes. So the ability to fit data says nothing about generalization; the explanation for generalization must lie in the structure of real-world data rather than in the models themselves. Subsection **5.1.2, The nature of generalization in deep learning**, opens with a "remarkable fact": deep learning models can be trained to **fit anything**, as long as they have enough representational power.

The demonstration is **Listing 5.4**: load and flatten MNIST as before, shuffle the labels with `np.random.shuffle` so that they bear no relation to the images, and train the familiar `Dense(512, relu)` → `Dense(10, softmax)` model (compiled with **rmsprop** this time) for **100 epochs**, batch size 128, `validation_split=0.2`. The book reports that the **training loss goes down just fine**, even with this relatively small model, while the **validation loss does not improve at all**, because there is nothing to generalize.

You don't even need real images: white-noise inputs with random labels can also be fit, given enough parameters. The model then simply **memorizes** specific inputs, "much like a Python dictionary" that stores key → value pairs with no notion of similarity between keys.

This raises the section's central puzzle: **if models can memorize arbitrary mappings, why do they generalize at all?** Why wouldn't they learn an ad hoc lookup table, a "fancy `dict`", that is useless on new inputs? The authors' answer, developed from the next page on (the manifold hypothesis, p.168), is that generalization in deep learning "has rather little to do with deep learning models themselves and much to do with the **structure of information in the real world**."

The practical implication: low training loss is never evidence of learning by itself. Only performance on held-out data tells you whether the model has captured structure rather than memorized samples. With enough representational power, deep models can fit anything, including random labels. On shuffled MNIST labels, training loss falls while validation loss doesn't improve. Such a model is just memorizing, like a Python dict. So fitting ability can't explain generalization; the structure of real-world data does (developed from p.168). Pitfall: train_labels[:] is a NumPy view, not a copy.

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: The manifold hypothesis
text:
Why real data (MNIST digits) occupies a tiny, continuous, connected, low-dimensional subspace — a manifold — of its encoding space Of the 256^784 possible 28 × 28 uint8 arrays, valid handwritten digits fill only a minuscule, highly structured region that is continuous and connected by smooth paths; this region is a manifold, and the manifold hypothesis claims all natural data looks like this. The page opens the subsubsection **"The manifold hypothesis"**, the first step in explaining why deep learning models generalize even though, as p.167 showed, they are perfectly capable of memorizing random labels.

**The raw input space is astronomically large.** An unpreprocessed MNIST input is a $28\times 28$ array of integers in $[0,255]$, so there are $256^{784}$ possible inputs — far more than the number of atoms in the universe. Yet almost none of those arrays look like a handwritten digit: real digits occupy a tiny *subspace* of the parent space of all $28\times28$ `uint8` arrays.

**That subspace is highly structured, not random.** The authors name two properties:

1. It is *continuous*: perturb a valid digit slightly and it remains recognizable as the same digit.
2. It is *connected*: between any two digits A and B there is a sequence of intermediate images morphing A into B with consecutive images very close to each other. Near class boundaries there may be ambiguous shapes, but they still look digit-like. Figure 5.7 shows four such morphing sequences (3→6, 8→5, 2→6→0, 6→0), generated with code from chapter 17.

**Technical name: a manifold.** A manifold is a lower-dimensional subspace of a parent space that is *locally* similar to a linear (Euclidean) space. A smooth curve in the plane is a 1D manifold in 2D space, because at every point it can be approximated by its tangent line; a smooth surface in 3D is a 2D manifold.

**The manifold hypothesis** generalizes this: all natural data lies on a low-dimensional manifold within the high-dimensional space where it is encoded. The authors call this a strong statement about the structure of information in the universe, say that as far as we know it is accurate, and claim it is *the reason deep learning works*. The sentence continues onto p.169, which lists faces, tree morphology, voices and natural language as further examples and draws the consequences for interpolation. The raw MNIST input space has 256^784 ≈ 10^1888 points, but valid digits occupy a vanishingly small part of it. That part is structured: continuous (small changes keep the digit) and connected (smooth paths link any two digits, figure 5.7). A manifold is a lower-dimensional subspace that is locally Euclidean — a curve in a plane is 1D, a surface in 3D is 2D. The manifold hypothesis: all natural data lies on low-dimensional manifolds in its encoding space; the authors call it the reason deep learning works. Generalization is explained by the structure of the data, not by the model alone.

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Manifold hypothesis
text: The hypothesis that all natural data lies on a low-dimensional manifold within the high-dimensional space in which it is encoded. A photo has millions of numbers, but real photos only vary along a comparatively small number of meaningful directions; random pixel arrays are almost never photos. If data lives on a d-dimensional manifold M inside R^D with d ≪ D, a model only needs to be accurate on (a neighbourhood of) M, which makes learning from finitely many samples feasible. MNIST: D = 784 pixel coordinates, but valid digits form a continuous, connected region describable with far fewer degrees of freedom.
snippet: The hypothesis that all natural data lies on a low-dimensional manifold within the high-dimensional space in which it is encoded.
section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Manifold
text: A lower-dimensional subspace of a parent space that is locally similar to a linear (Euclidean) space. Earth's surface looks flat when you stand on it, even though globally it is a sphere: that local flatness is what 'locally Euclidean' means. At each point there is a tangent line/plane/space approximating the manifold; the dimension of that tangent space is the manifold's dimension. A smooth curve in the plane (1D in 2D); a smooth surface in 3D (2D in 3D).
snippet: A lower-dimensional subspace of a parent space that is locally similar to a linear Euclidean space.

Correctly classifying a newly written 7 that is a slight variation of training 7s.

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Interpolation as a source of generalization
text:
Consequences of the manifold hypothesis: models fit latent manifolds and generalize by interpolating on them; manifold vs linear interpolation; local vs extreme generalization Because data lies on latent manifolds, a model can make sense of unseen points by interpolating between nearby training points on the manifold — not by averaging in pixel space. This yields only local generalization; humans additionally achieve extreme generalization through reason. The page completes the statement of the manifold hypothesis (true for MNIST digits, human faces, tree morphology, the human voice and even natural language) and draws its two **implications**:

- Models only have to fit relatively simple, low-dimensional, highly structured subspaces of their potential input space — **latent manifolds**.
- Within such a manifold it is always possible to **interpolate** between two inputs: morph one into another along a continuous path whose points all stay on the manifold.

The authors then make the central claim: *the ability to interpolate between samples is the key to understanding generalization in deep learning.*

**Interpolation as a source of generalization.** If data points can be interpolated, you can make sense of never-seen points by relating them to nearby points on the manifold — understanding the *totality* of the space from only a *sample*, "filling in the blanks."

**Manifold vs linear interpolation (figure 5.8).** Interpolating on the latent manifold is not the same as linear interpolation in the parent (encoding) space. The figure shows a 2 and a 0: the intermediate point on the manifold is a valid digit (a 6, taken from a morphing row), whereas the pixel average of the 2 and the 0 is a blurry overlay that is not a digit.

**Interpolation is only the tip of the iceberg.** Deep learning generalizes by interpolating on a *learned approximation* of the data manifold, but this only handles inputs very close to what was seen before: **local generalization**. Humans handle extreme novelty constantly — every day is new, and one can spend a week each in NYC, Shanghai and Bangalore without lifetimes of rehearsal. This **extreme generalization** relies on other cognitive mechanisms — abstraction, symbolic world models, reasoning, logic, common sense, innate priors — collectively *reason*, as opposed to intuition and pattern recognition (sentence continues on p.170; the topic returns in chapter 19). Implication 1: models only need to fit low-dimensional, highly structured latent manifolds, not the whole input space. Implication 2: within a manifold you can always interpolate between two inputs along a path that stays on the manifold. Interpolation lets a model make sense of unseen points from a sample — the key to generalization in deep learning. Manifold interpolation is not pixel averaging: the average of two digits is usually not a digit (figure 5.8). Interpolation gives only local generalization; humans achieve extreme generalization through reason (abstraction, logic, common sense, priors).

section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning

title: Why deep learning works
text:
Deep learning models as smooth, high-dimensional curves fitted gradually by gradient descent; why an intermediate stage of training approximates the data manifold A deep learning model is a smooth, differentiable, high-dimensional curve fitted incrementally by gradient descent. It has enough parameters to memorize anything, but because the data lies on a structured manifold and fitting is gradual, there is an intermediate point in training where the model roughly follows the data manifold and can therefore generalize by interpolation. The page closes the discussion of extreme generalization — reason vs intuition and pattern recognition; the latter are largely interpolative, both are essential to intelligence, and chapter 19 returns to this — and opens the subsubsection **"Why deep learning works."**

**Paper-ball metaphor.** Recalling chapter 2 (p.63), a sheet of paper is a 2D manifold in 3D space; a deep learning model is a tool for *uncrumpling paper balls*, i.e. for **disentangling latent manifolds** (figure 5.9: crumpled ball → flat sheet).

**A model is a high-dimensional curve.** It is smooth and continuous — with extra structural constraints from architecture priors — because it must be differentiable. It is fitted to data via gradient descent, smoothly and incrementally. *By construction*, deep learning means taking a big, complex curve (a manifold) and incrementally adjusting its parameters until it fits training points.

**Why it doesn't just memorize.** The curve has enough parameters to fit anything; trained long enough, it will purely memorize the training data and not generalize. But the data is not isolated points sparsely scattered in the space — it forms a structured, low-dimensional manifold (the manifold hypothesis). Because fitting is gradual and smooth, there is an **intermediate point during training** where the model roughly approximates the natural manifold of the data (figure 5.10, next page). Moving along the model's curve at that point is close to moving along the true latent manifold, so the model can make sense of new inputs by interpolating between training inputs.

**Properties that suit deep learning to manifold learning** (beyond sufficient representational power). The first, on this page: deep learning models implement a **smooth, continuous mapping** from inputs to outputs — necessarily, because they must be differentiable for gradient descent — and this smoothness helps approximate latent manifolds, which have the same properties. The second property (architecture priors mirroring the structure of the data) is on p.171. Interpolative intuition and non-interpolative reason are both essential to intelligence. A deep learning model is a tool for uncrumpling paper balls — disentangling latent manifolds. A model is a smooth, continuous, very high-dimensional curve, fitted gradually by gradient descent; smoothness is required by differentiability. Trained long enough, the model memorizes; but because data lies on a manifold and fitting is gradual, an intermediate training state approximates the manifold and generalizes via interpolation. Smooth, continuous mappings are well suited to approximating smooth, continuous latent manifolds.

title: Robust fit as an intermediate state; training data is paramount
text:
Figure 5.10 (random → robust fit → overfit), architecture priors that mirror data structure, and why generalization depends primarily on data quality and dense sampling of the manifold A robust fit appears transiently during training between a random model and an overfit one. Deep learning suits manifold learning thanks to smoothness and architecture priors, but generalization is mostly a consequence of the data's structure: you need informative, low-noise features and a dense sampling of the input manifold, especially near decision boundaries. **Figure 5.10** (top of the page) visualizes the argument of p.170 on a 2D toy problem with light and dark points separated by a dashed decision boundary. Training panels: *before training* the model starts in a random state; at the *beginning of training* it gradually moves toward a better fit; with *further training* a robust fit is achieved — transitively, in the process of morphing from initial to final state; in the *final state* the model overfits, reaching perfect training loss with a convoluted boundary. Test-time panels show the robustly fit model handling new points well, while the overfit model's contorted boundary misclassifies them.

**Second property suiting deep learning to manifold learning**: models tend to be structured to mirror the "shape" of information in their training data via **architecture priors** — notably image models (chapters 8–12) and sequence models (chapter 13). More generally, deep networks organize learned representations **hierarchically and modularly**, echoing how natural data is organized.

**Training data is paramount.** Although deep learning is well suited to manifold learning, *the power to generalize is more a consequence of the natural structure of your data than of any property of your model*. You can only generalize if the data forms a manifold where points can be interpolated. More informative, less noisy features give a simpler, better-structured input space and better generalization; hence **data curation and feature engineering are essential**.

**Dense sampling.** Because deep learning is curve fitting, a model must be trained on a *dense sampling of its input space* — training data that densely covers the entire input data manifold (figure 5.11, next page), especially near **decision boundaries**. With dense enough sampling, new inputs can be understood by interpolating between past training inputs (sentence continues on p.172, which adds that this requires no common sense or abstract reasoning and that the best way to improve a model is more or better data). A robust fit is a transient intermediate state of training, between the random initial model and the final overfit model (figure 5.10). Deep learning suits manifold learning because of smooth mappings and architecture priors that mirror data structure, with hierarchical, modular representations. Generalization is more a consequence of the data's natural structure than of the model. Informative, low-noise features make the input space simpler; data curation and feature engineering are essential. Models need a dense sampling of the input manifold, especially near decision boundaries, to interpolate reliably.
