title: Dense sampling, more data, and regularization
text:
Figure 5.11 (sparse vs dense sampling of the latent space), the primacy of more/better data, regularization as the fallback, and the transition to model evaluation Deep learning models do nothing more than crude interpolation between training samples, so the best way to improve them is more or better data that covers the manifold densely; when that is impossible, limit what the model can memorize or constrain its smoothness (regularization). To know whether any of this helps, you need model evaluation. **Figure 5.11** shows an *original latent space* (a winding dotted curve) and two attempts to learn it. With **sparse sampling** (few points), the learned solid curve passes through the samples but cuts across the loops of the true curve — it doesn't match the latent space and leads to incorrect interpolation. With **dense sampling** (many points along the curve), the learned curve hugs the true one, and interpolation leads to generalization.

Completing the sentence from p.171: with dense sampling, new inputs can be understood by interpolating between past training inputs *without* common sense, abstract reasoning or external knowledge — all things ML models have no access to.

**Data first.** Hence the best way to improve a deep learning model is to train it on **more or better data** (but overly noisy or inaccurate data harms generalization). Denser coverage of the input manifold yields better generalization. You should never expect a model to do anything more than **crude interpolation** between training samples, so make interpolation as easy as possible. *The only thing you will find in a deep learning model is what you put into it*: the priors encoded in its architecture and the data it was trained on.

**Regularization as the next-best option.** When more data isn't available, **modulate the quantity of information the model can store** or **constrain the smoothness of the model curve**. A network that can only memorize a few patterns, or very regular ones, is forced by optimization to focus on the most prominent patterns, which are more likely to generalize. Fighting overfitting this way is called **regularization** (section 5.4.4).

**Next: evaluation.** Before tweaking a model to generalize better, you need a way to assess how it's doing — the subject of section 5.2, model evaluation. Sparse sampling makes the learned curve cut across the true latent space and interpolate incorrectly; dense sampling makes it follow the manifold (figure 5.11). Models can't use common sense, abstract reasoning or external knowledge — they rely on coverage. The best way to improve a deep learning model is more or better data; noisy or inaccurate data hurts. Expect nothing more than crude interpolation; a model contains only its architecture priors and its data. When data is limited, regularize: limit stored information or constrain smoothness so the model focuses on prominent patterns. You need model evaluation before you can tune for generalization.

title: Training, validation, and test sets
text:
Why evaluation needs three data splits: hyperparameter tuning is a form of learning that leaks validation information into the model, so a never-touched test set is required You train on training data, tune on validation data and measure generalization once on test data. Because every tuning decision based on validation performance leaks information about the validation set into the model, repeated tuning overfits the validation set; only a test set the model never influenced gives an honest generalization estimate. Section **5.2, Evaluating machine-learning models**, opens with a principle: *you can only control what you can observe*. Since the goal is generalization to new data, you need a reliable measure of generalization power. The section formalizes evaluation methods, most of which appeared in chapter 4.

**5.2.1 Training, validation, and test sets.** Evaluation always comes down to three splits. You **train** on the training data, **evaluate** on the validation data while developing, and once the model is ready you **test** it one final time on the test data — meant to be as similar as possible to production data — before deploying.

**Why not just two sets?** Because developing a model always involves tuning its configuration — the number or size of layers — i.e. its **hyperparameters**, as opposed to its **parameters** (the weights). Tuning uses validation performance as a feedback signal, and is therefore itself a form of *learning*: a search for a good configuration in some parameter space. So tuning on the validation set can quickly lead to **overfitting to the validation set**, even though the model never trains on it directly.

**Information leaks.** Each time you tune a hyperparameter based on validation performance, some information about the validation data leaks into the model. Once, for one parameter, very few bits leak and the validation set stays reliable. Repeated many times — run, evaluate, modify — the leak becomes significant, and the model ends up performing *artificially well* on the validation data because that's what you optimized it for.

**Hence the test set.** You care about completely new data, so final evaluation needs a never-before-seen dataset. The model must not have had access to *any* information about the test set, even indirectly; if anything was tuned on test performance, your generalization measure is flawed.

Finally, the page previews three classic evaluation recipes for when little data is available — **simple hold-out validation, K-fold validation, and iterated K-fold validation with shuffling** — plus common-sense baselines (continued on p.174). You can only control what you can observe: reliable measurement of generalization is essential. Train on the training set, tune on the validation set, test once on a test set that resembles production data. Hyperparameters (number/size of layers) differ from parameters (weights); tuning them is a form of learning. Every tuning decision based on validation results leaks information; repeated tuning overfits the validation set. The test set must remain completely unseen — no information, even indirectly. Hold-out, K-fold and iterated K-fold with shuffling are the classic recipes, useful especially with little data.

title: Simple hold-out validation and the start of K-fold validation
text:
The simple hold-out validation protocol (Figure 5.12, Listing 5.5), its weakness on small datasets, and the opening definition of K-fold validation Hold-out validation sets aside a fixed slice of the data for validation, tunes the model against it, then retrains the final model on all non-test data and evaluates once on the test set. It is simple but unreliable when data is scarce, because a small validation set gives scores that swing with the random split; K-fold validation is introduced as the remedy. The page finishes the sentence from p.173 announcing that the chapter will later discuss **common-sense baselines** (section 5.2.2, p.176), then presents the first concrete evaluation protocol.

**Simple hold-out validation.** You set apart part of the data as a test set and train on the rest. Because tuning the model on the test set would leak information about it into the model (the argument made on p.173), you *also* reserve a validation set. Figure 5.12 shows the split: of the "total available labeled data", the large left block is the **training set** ("train on this"), and a smaller right block is the **held-out validation set** ("evaluate on this").

**Listing 5.5** implements it with labels omitted: it shuffles `data`, takes the first `num_validation_samples = 10000` samples as `validation_data` and the rest as `training_data`, builds a model with `get_model()`, fits on the training data and computes `validation_score`. The `...` stands for the tuning loop: tune, retrain, re-evaluate, repeat. Once the hyperparameters are fixed, the callout notes it is common to **train the final model from scratch on all non-test data** (`np.concatenate([training_data, validation_data])`) and only then compute `test_score` on `test_data`.

**The flaw.** With little data, the validation and test sets may be too small to be statistically representative. The diagnostic is simple: if different random shuffles before splitting give very different performance measures, you have this problem. **K-fold validation** and **iterated K-fold validation** address it.

**K-fold validation** begins at the bottom: split the data into `K` equal partitions; for each partition `i`, train a model on the other `K - 1` partitions and evaluate it on partition `i`. The averaging of the K scores, Figure 5.13 and Listing 5.6 follow on p.175. Hold-out validation: test set reserved, then a fixed validation slice of the remaining data guides tuning. Never tune on the test set; reserve a validation set as well. After tuning, it is common to retrain from scratch on training + validation data and evaluate once on test. Its flaw: small validation/test sets give noisy, unrepresentative scores; diagnose by re-splitting with different shuffles. K-fold validation trains on K - 1 partitions and evaluates on the remaining one, rotating through all K.

title: K-fold cross-validation: averaging scores, Figure 5.13 and Listing 5.6
text:
Completing the description of K-fold validation: the final score is the average of the K fold scores; three-fold schematic; a schematic implementation K-fold validation trains K fresh models, each validated on a different partition, and reports the average of the K validation scores, which is far less sensitive to a particular split. It still does not replace a distinct validation process for calibration, and the final model is retrained on all non-test data before a single test evaluation. This page completes the K-fold procedure begun on p.174. After training K models (each on K - 1 partitions, evaluated on the remaining one), **the final score is the average of the K scores**. The method helps "when the performance of your model shows significant variance based on your train/test split". Like hold-out validation, it "doesn't exempt you from using a distinct validation set for model calibration": the K-fold score is still a validation signal you tune against, so a separate test set remains necessary for the final unbiased check.

**Figure 5.13** shows three-fold validation: the data is split into 3 partitions; in Fold 1 the first partition is the validation set and the other two are training data; in Fold 2 the middle partition validates; in Fold 3 the last. Each fold yields a validation score (#1, #2, #3), and the final score is their average.

**Listing 5.6** implements this schematically (labels omitted). With `k = 3`, it computes the partition size `len(data) // k`, shuffles, and loops over folds. For fold `f` it slices `data[n*f : n*(f+1)]` as validation data and concatenates the slices before and after it as training data, creates a brand-new untrained model with `get_model()`, fits it, evaluates on the fold's validation data and appends the score. The validation score is `np.average(validation_scores)`. Finally, as in Listing 5.5, a new model is trained on **all non-test data** (`model.fit(data, ...)`) and evaluated once on `test_data`.

Note (not in the book): the printed `np.concatenate(a, b)` call would need to be `np.concatenate([a, b])` to run, since NumPy's second positional argument is the axis. K-fold final score = average of the K fold scores. Use it when scores vary a lot with the split, i.e. small datasets. It is still a validation signal; keep a separate test set. Each fold trains a brand-new model; the final model is retrained on all non-test data. Listing 5.6's np.concatenate call needs a list of arrays to actually run.

num_validation_samples = len(data) // k
np.random.shuffle(data)

    model.fit(training_data, ...)
    validation_score = model.evaluate(validation_data, ...)
    validation_scores.append(validation_score)
validation_score = np.average(validation_scores)
model = get_model()
model.fit(data, ...)
test_score = model.evaluate(test_data, ...) title: Iterated K-fold, common-sense baselines, and evaluation pitfalls
text:
The third evaluation protocol (iterated K-fold with shuffling), the need to beat a trivial baseline, and the start of the checklist of evaluation pitfalls When data is scarce and precision matters, repeat K-fold P times with reshuffling and average (P x K models). Whatever protocol you use, a score only means something relative to a trivial baseline such as random guessing or always predicting the majority class; a model that cannot beat it is worthless. Finally, training and test sets must be representative of the data. **Iterated K-fold validation with shuffling** is the third protocol. It is for when you have relatively little data and need the most precise evaluation possible; the author reports it has been extremely helpful in Kaggle competitions. You run K-fold validation several times, reshuffling the data before each K-way split, and the final score is the average over all runs. With `P` iterations you train and evaluate `P * K` models, which can be very expensive.

**5.2.2 Beating a common-sense baseline.** Training a deep model is likened to launching a rocket in a parallel world: you cannot see the manifold-learning process happening in thousands of dimensions, and your only feedback is validation metrics, an "altitude meter". The crucial question is whether you have left the ground at all: is 15% accuracy any good? Before working on a dataset, pick a trivial baseline to beat; crossing it shows the model is genuinely using information in the input to make predictions that generalize. The baseline can be a random classifier or the simplest non-ML technique you can imagine. Examples: MNIST, validation accuracy above 0.1 (random over 10 classes); IMDb, above 0.5; Reuters, about 0.18-0.19 because of class imbalance; a binary problem with 90%/10% classes, 0.9, achieved by always predicting the majority class. A baseline is essential for problems nobody has solved before: if you cannot beat a trivial solution, your model is worthless, perhaps because the model is wrong or because the problem cannot be approached with ML at all.

**5.2.3 Things to keep in mind** opens a checklist. The first item, **data representativeness**, requires training and test sets both to be representative of the data; its digit-classification example (data sorted by class) continues on p.177. Iterated K-fold: repeat K-fold P times with reshuffling, average; costs P x K models. Always pick a trivial baseline before training; a score is only meaningful relative to it. Baselines: MNIST 0.1, IMDb 0.5, Reuters about 0.18-0.19, 90/10 binary 0.9. If you cannot beat the baseline, rethink the model or whether ML applies. Training and test sets must be representative of the data.

title: Evaluation pitfalls and the goal of improving model fit
text:
The remaining evaluation pitfalls (sorted data, the arrow of time, redundant samples), the first milestone of a project (a model that beats the baseline and can overfit), the three problems that block it, and the start of 5.3.1 on stuck training Splits must be representative, respect time order for forecasting, and be free of duplicates across sets. With reliable evaluation in place, the first goal is a model that generalizes somewhat and can overfit, because you can only find the boundary between underfitting and overfitting by crossing it. The page completes the checklist from section 5.2.3.

- **Data representativeness** (continued): if digit images are stored sorted by class and you take the first 80% for training and the last 20% for testing, training contains only classes 0-7 and test only 8-9. "A ridiculous mistake, but it's surprisingly common"; hence you should usually **randomly shuffle** before splitting.
- **The arrow of time**: when predicting the future from the past (weather, stock movements), do *not* shuffle, because that creates a **temporal leak**: the model is effectively trained on data from the future. All test data must be *posterior* to training data.
- **Redundancy in your data**: if some points appear twice (common in real data), shuffling and splitting puts copies in both training and validation sets, so you are testing on training data, "the worst thing you can do". Make the sets **disjoint**.

Reliable evaluation is how you monitor the central tension of ML: optimization versus generalization, underfitting versus overfitting.

**5.3 Improving model fit.** "To achieve the perfect fit, you must first overfit": since the boundary is unknown, you must cross it to find it. The initial goal is a model that shows some generalization power and can overfit; then you refine generalization by fighting overfitting. Three common problems arise: (1) training doesn't get started (training loss does not go down); (2) training works but the model doesn't meaningfully generalize (cannot beat the baseline); (3) training and validation losses both go down and the baseline is beaten, but the model cannot overfit, so it is still underfitting. Solving them achieves the first big milestone.

**5.3.1 Tuning key gradient descent parameters** begins: when training doesn't start or stalls early and the loss is stuck, this is *always* surmountable, because, as shown earlier, you can fit a model even to random data (the sentence continues on p.178). Shuffle before splitting so splits are representative, except for time series. For forecasting, the test set must be strictly later than the training set to avoid temporal leaks. Remove duplicates so training and validation sets are disjoint. First milestone: beat the baseline and be able to overfit; then fight overfitting. Three blockers: training doesn't start, no generalization beyond baseline, can't overfit. A stuck training loss is always fixable via gradient-descent settings.

title: Stuck training: tuning learning rate and batch size (Listings 5.7-5.8)
text:
Why a training loss that won't decrease always points to the gradient descent configuration, and a concrete MNIST demonstration with RMSprop at learning rate 1.0 versus 1e-2 Any model should be able to at least memorize its training data; if training stalls, the culprit is the optimizer, weight initialization, learning rate or batch size. Since these interact, tuning learning rate and batch size is usually enough. The chapter 2 MNIST model with RMSprop(learning_rate=1.0) gets stuck at 20-40% accuracy; lowering it to 1e-2 fixes it. Continuing from p.177: even if nothing about your problem makes sense, you should *still* be able to train something, if only by memorizing the training data. So a stuck loss is **always a problem with the configuration of the gradient descent process**: the choice of optimizer, the distribution of initial weight values, the learning rate, or the batch size. Because these are interdependent, it is usually sufficient to tune the **learning rate and the batch size** while keeping the rest constant.

The concrete example retrains the chapter 2 MNIST model with an inappropriately large learning rate of 1. **Listing 5.7** loads MNIST, flattens images to `(60000, 784)` and scales them to [0, 1], builds `Dense(512, relu)` -> `Dense(10, softmax)`, compiles with `RMSprop(learning_rate=1.0)`, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` and accuracy, and fits for 10 epochs with batch size 128 and `validation_split=0.2`. The model quickly reaches 20-40% training and validation accuracy and cannot get past it.

The fix is to lower the learning rate to the "more reasonable" `1e-2`. **Listing 5.8** rebuilds the same model and compiles it with `RMSprop(learning_rate=1e-2)`; the fit call and the result ("The model is now able to train") follow on p.179, along with general advice: raise or lower the learning rate, or increase the batch size.

Note (not in the book): Keras's default RMSprop learning rate is 1e-3, so 1.0 is 1,000 times the default and 1e-2 is 10 times it. Every model can at least memorize its training data; a stuck loss is an optimization configuration bug. Suspects: optimizer, weight initialization, learning rate, batch size. Usually tune only learning rate and batch size. RMSprop at learning rate 1.0 stalls the MNIST model at 20-40% accuracy. Lowering it to 1e-2 lets the model train.

RMSprop at 1.0 stalls at 20-40% accuracy on MNIST; at 1e-2 it trains.

title: Getting training started, architecture priors, and the push to overfit
text:
The end of Listing 5.8 and tips for stuck training (learning rate, batch size); 5.3.2 on models that train but don't generalize (uninformative data or wrong architecture priors); the opening of 5.3.3 on increasing capacity Stuck training is fixed by adjusting the learning rate in either direction or increasing the batch size. A model that trains but stays at random-classifier level on validation signals something fundamentally wrong: either the inputs lack the information needed, or the architecture makes the wrong assumptions, so use the right architecture priors. Once you have some generalization, the next step is to make the model overfit. The page opens with the **final lines of Listing 5.8** (the listing starts on p.178): `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=10, batch_size=128, validation_split=0.2)`, identical to Listing 5.7's fit call. With learning rate `1e-2` "the model is now able to train".

In a similar situation, try:
- **Lowering or increasing the learning rate.** Too high produces updates that "vastly overshoot a proper fit" (the previous example); too low makes training so slow it appears to stall.
- **Increasing the batch size.** More samples per batch give gradients that are more informative and less noisy (lower variance).

Eventually you will find a configuration that gets training started.

**5.3.2 Using better architecture priors.** The model fits, but validation metrics don't improve at all, staying at random-classifier level: it trains but doesn't generalize. This is "perhaps the worst machine learning situation": *something is fundamentally wrong with your approach*, and it may be hard to tell what. Two possibilities: (1) the input data simply lacks the information to predict the targets, as with MNIST trained on shuffled labels, where training went fine but validation accuracy stayed at 10%; (2) the model type is unsuited to the problem; chapter 13 will show a timeseries problem where a densely connected network can't beat a trivial baseline but a recurrent architecture generalizes well. You need a model that makes the right assumptions, the right **architecture priors**. Later chapters cover the best architectures for images, text, timeseries, etc.; always read up on best practices for your task, since you're probably not the first to attempt it.

**5.3.3 Increasing model capacity** begins: once you have a model that fits, with validation metrics going down and some generalization, you're almost there; next, get it to start overfitting. With learning rate 1e-2 the MNIST model trains; the learning rate alone caused the earlier stall. For stuck training, try lowering or raising the learning rate, or increasing the batch size. Trains but stays at baseline: the data may lack the information, or the architecture priors are wrong. Use architectures suited to the data modality and read up on best practices. Once the model generalizes somewhat, increase capacity until it overfits.

title: A model too small to overfit
text:
Diagnosing insufficient model capacity using a single-layer logistic regression on MNIST A one-layer softmax classifier (logistic regression) on raw MNIST pixels trains, but its validation loss flattens around 0.26 and never turns upward: it cannot overfit, which is the signature of too little capacity. Section 5.3.3 opens with a deliberately weak model. **Listing 5.9** builds `keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])`: a single dense layer that maps the 784 pixel values of each MNIST image directly to 10 class probabilities. The book calls it what it is, *a simple logistic regression* (strictly, multinomial or softmax logistic regression). It is compiled with `rmsprop`, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` and an accuracy metric, then trained for 20 epochs with batches of 128, holding out the last 20% of the training data as validation data via `validation_split=0.2`. The `History` object is stored in `history_small_model`.

A second snippet uses Matplotlib to plot `history_small_model.history["val_loss"]` against epochs 1 to 20, producing **Figure 5.14**, "Effect of insufficient model capacity on loss curves". The curve drops quickly from about 0.36 after the first epoch, then flattens: by about epoch 10 it is near 0.267 and it ends around 0.26.

The text interprets the shape. Validation metrics *stall or improve very slowly* instead of **peaking and reversing course**, which is what overfitting looks like. The loss "goes to 0.26 and just stays there." The sentence continues on p.181: you can fit, but you cannot clearly overfit, however long you train. The book then argues it should always be possible to overfit, and that the fix is more representational power: more layers, bigger layers, or better-suited layer types.

The lesson for practice: a curve that never turns upward is not good news. It means the model has too little capacity to memorize the training data, so it is also leaving generalization performance unused. Dense(10, softmax) on raw pixels is a logistic regression: 7,850 parameters and linear decision boundaries. Its validation loss falls to about 0.26 and plateaus. It never peaks and reverses. A curve that cannot overfit signals insufficient capacity, not good regularization. validation_split=0.2 plus the History object give you the curves you need for this diagnosis. The remedy, given on p.181, is more representational power.

title: Model capacity (representational power)
text: How much information a model can store, and how complex a function it can represent. In practice it is governed by the number of layers, their size (number of parameters), and the types of layers used. Think of capacity as memory size. A tiny model cannot memorize 48,000 training images, so it settles for a coarse rule that works on average. A Dense(10) layer on 784 inputs represents only affine maps followed by softmax, so the class boundaries are hyperplanes. Adding hidden layers with nonlinear activations lets the model represent piecewise-linear boundaries of far greater complexity. Listing 5.9 (7,850 parameters) plateaus at a validation loss of about 0.26. The 2×128-unit model on p.181 fits fast and starts overfitting after eight epochs.

title: It should always be possible to overfit
text:
Fixing insufficient capacity by adding two 128-unit hidden layers to the MNIST model If a model cannot overfit, it lacks representational power. Adding layers, enlarging them, or choosing better-suited layer types fixes this. A 2×128 ReLU MLP on MNIST fits quickly and starts overfitting after about eight epochs, which is the healthy curve shape. The page finishes the diagnosis begun on p.180: with the logistic regression, "you can't clearly overfit, even after many iterations over the training data," and the book warns you will meet such curves often.

Then comes the rule: **it should always be possible to overfit.** Like "the training loss doesn't go down," failure to overfit is a problem that can always be solved. If you cannot overfit, the issue is the **representational power** of your model. You need a bigger model with more **capacity**, which the book defines as being *able to store more information*. There are three ways to get it:

1. **add more layers**,
2. **use bigger layers** (more parameters per layer),
3. **use layer types better suited to the problem** (better architecture priors, connecting back to section 5.3.2).

The book then trains a bigger model: `Dense(128, relu)` → `Dense(128, relu)` → `Dense(10, softmax)`, with the same compile settings and the same `fit` call as Listing 5.9 (20 epochs, batch 128, `validation_split=0.2`), stored in `history_large_model`. The listing is unnumbered.

The result, **Figure 5.15** ("Validation loss for a model with appropriate capacity"), is described as looking "exactly like they should": the model fits fast and starts overfitting after about eight epochs. The plotted validation loss falls from about 0.18 to below 0.09 within a few epochs. That is already far below the logistic regression's 0.26 plateau. It then climbs back, noisily, to about 0.12-0.13 by epoch 20.

The contrast between Figures 5.14 and 5.15 is the point. A U-shaped validation curve is what you want at this stage, because it shows the model has enough capacity, and the next step is regularization and early stopping (section 5.4). The next page shows the opposite extreme, too much capacity. It should always be possible to overfit. If you can't, increase representational power. Three levers: more layers, bigger layers, better architecture priors. Capacity is defined as the ability to store more information. The 2×128 ReLU MLP (118,282 parameters) fits fast and overfits after about eight epochs. That is the healthy shape. Even when overfitting, it beats the logistic regression's validation loss by a wide margin.

title: Too much capacity, and the turn to generalization
text:
An oversized MNIST MLP (3×2,048 units) that overfits from the first epoch, and the transition to section 5.4 Overparameterization is normal in deep learning, but too much memorization capacity shows up as overfitting right away. Once a model generalizes somewhat and can overfit, the focus switches to maximizing generalization. The page first adds a caveat to the "make it bigger" advice of p.181. It is *standard* to work with models that are "way overparameterized for the problem at hand," yet there can be such a thing as ***too much* memorization capacity**. The symptom is specific: **the model starts overfitting right away**.

The demonstration is an MNIST MLP with **three intermediate layers of 2,048 ReLU units each** plus a 10-way softmax output. Compile settings are unchanged (rmsprop, sparse categorical crossentropy, accuracy), and training again runs 20 epochs with `validation_split=0.2`. One thing differs: `batch_size=32`. A margin callout explains that *when training larger models, you can reduce the batch size to limit memory consumption*. The history is stored in `history_very_large_model`.

**Figure 5.16** ("Effect of excessive model capacity on validation loss") shows the validation loss at its lowest, about 0.12, after the very first epoch. It then rises jaggedly, to about 0.15-0.16 around epochs 7-12 and to about 0.20 at epochs 14 and 20. There is no initial phase of improvement, unlike Figure 5.15. The curve is also noisier.

The page then opens **section 5.4, Improving generalization**: once a model "has shown to have some generalization power and to be able to overfit," you switch your focus to *maximizing generalization*. The following subsections cover dataset curation (p.183), feature engineering (p.183), early stopping (p.185) and regularization (p.185).

Together with pp.180-181, this page gives a complete picture. Too little capacity stalls (0.26 plateau). Appropriate capacity dips then rises (minimum about 0.09). Excessive capacity overfits immediately (best about 0.12, then worse). Too large a model shows itself by overfitting right away. Overparameterization is standard. Immediate overfitting is the warning sign. 3×2,048 units comes to about 10M parameters. Its best validation loss is about 0.12 at epoch 1, and it climbs to about 0.20. Reduce batch size to limit memory when models grow. Once the model can generalize somewhat and can overfit, switch to maximizing generalization (section 5.4).

title: Dataset curation and feature engineering
text:
Improving generalization through better data (curation) and better input representations (feature engineering) Generalization comes from the latent structure of the data, so the best investment is usually better data: enough of it, correctly labeled, clean, with useful features. Feature engineering applies hardcoded, human-designed transformations that make the model's job easier, as in the clock-reading example. **5.4.1 Dataset curation.** The book reminds us that generalization in deep learning *originates from the latent structure of your data*. If the data allows smooth interpolation between samples, a deep learning model can generalize. If the problem is too noisy or fundamentally discrete (the book's example is *list sorting*), deep learning won't help: "Deep learning is curve fitting, not magic."

So the dataset must be appropriate, and spending effort and money on data collection *almost always* returns more than spending the same on a better model. Four practices follow:

- **Enough data.** You need a *dense sampling* of the input-cross-output space. More data yields a better model, and some seemingly impossible problems become solvable with more data.
- **Minimize labeling errors.** Visualize inputs to find anomalies and proofread the labels.
- **Clean the data and handle missing values** (covered in chapter 6).
- **Feature selection** when you have many features of uncertain usefulness.

A particularly important lever is **feature engineering**, "a key ingredient for success" for most ML problems.

**5.4.2 Feature engineering** is defined as using your knowledge of the data *and* of the algorithm to apply **hardcoded (non-learned) transformations** to the data before it enters the model. Models can't be expected to learn from completely arbitrary data, so the data should be presented in a way that makes the model's job easier.

The running example (Figure 5.17, on p.184) is reading the time from an image of a clock. From **raw pixels** it is a hard problem that needs a convolutional network and substantial compute. If you understand how humans read clocks, though, a five-line script can trace the black pixels of the hands and output the **`(x, y)` coordinates of each hand's tip**. title: Better features, and why they still matter
text:
Completing the clock example with polar coordinates, the essence and history of feature engineering, and two reasons it still matters with deep learning Feature engineering makes a problem easier by expressing it more simply, making the latent manifold smoother and better organized. Deep learning automates most of it, but good features still save resources and, above all, data. **Figure 5.17** ("Feature engineering for reading the time on a clock") shows three levels of representation for two clock images:

| | Clock 1 | Clock 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Raw data: pixel grid | image | image |
| Better features: hand coordinates | {x1: 0.7, y1: 0.7}, {x2: 0.5, y2: 0.0} | {x1: 0.0, y2: 1.0}, {x2: -0.38, y2: 0.32} |
| Even better features: hand angles | theta1: 45, theta2: 0 | theta1: 90, theta2: 140 |

The text continues the example from p.183. Do a **coordinate change** to polar coordinates around the image center, so each hand becomes an angle `theta`. The problem is then so easy that **no machine learning is required**: rounding and a dictionary lookup recover the approximate time.

That, the book says, is the **essence of feature engineering**: "making a problem easier by expressing it in a simpler way. Make the latent manifold smoother, simpler, and better organized." It usually requires understanding the problem in depth.

**Historically**, feature engineering was the most important part of the ML workflow, because classical *shallow* algorithms lacked hypothesis spaces rich enough to learn useful features themselves. For MNIST, before convnets succeeded, solutions used hardcoded features such as the **number of loops** in a digit, the **height** of each digit, and **histograms of pixel values**.

Modern deep learning **removes the need for most feature engineering**, because networks extract useful features from raw data automatically. It is still not irrelevant, for two reasons:

1. **Elegance and resources.** Good features solve problems more elegantly and cheaply. Using a convnet to read a clock face would be "ridiculous."
2. **Less data.** Deep learning's ability to learn features depends on lots of training data. With only a few samples, the information value of the features becomes critical. Figure 5.17: pixels → hand coordinates → hand angles, each representation easier than the last. With angle features no ML is needed: rounding plus a lookup recovers the time. The essence of feature engineering: express the problem more simply and make the latent manifold smoother and better organized. Shallow ML depended on hand-crafted features; deep learning learns most features itself. Features still matter, for elegance and lower resource use, and for solving problems with far less data.

title: Early stopping and reducing network size
text:
Why overparameterized deep models are fine as long as you stop training early, what regularization means, and reducing network size as the first regularization technique You never fully fit a deep learning model. Stopping at the boundary between underfitting and overfitting is one of the most effective generalization tools. Regularization deliberately impedes a perfect fit to the training data. The simplest form is limiting model size, which forces compressed, predictive representations. **5.4.3 Using early stopping.** Deep learning models are always *vastly overparameterized*: they have far more degrees of freedom than needed to fit the latent manifold. That is not a problem because ***you never fully fit a deep learning model***. A full fit wouldn't generalize at all, so you always interrupt training long before the minimum training loss.

Finding the exact point of the **most generalizable fit**, the boundary between an underfit and an overfit curve, is called *one of the most effective things you can do to improve generalization*. The approach used in chapter 4 was to train longer than needed, read off the best epoch from the validation metrics, then **retrain a new model** for exactly that many epochs. That is standard but redundant and possibly expensive. Alternatives are to save the model at the end of each epoch and reuse the one closest to the best epoch, or, typically in Keras, to use an **`EarlyStopping` callback**. It interrupts training as soon as validation metrics stop improving and remembers the best model state. Callbacks are covered in chapter 7.

**5.4.4 Regularizing your model.** *Regularization techniques* are best practices that **actively impede the model's ability to fit the training data perfectly**, in order to improve validation performance. The name comes from making the model simpler, more "regular", smoother and more "generic": less specific to the training set and closer to the latent manifold. Regularization must always be guided by an accurate evaluation procedure: "You will only achieve generalization if you can measure it." The techniques will be applied to the chapter 4 movie-review classifier.

**Reducing the network's size.** A too-small model can't overfit, so the simplest mitigation for overfitting is to reduce the number of learnable parameters, which is set by the number of layers and units per layer. With limited memorization resources, the model must learn **compressed representations with predictive power** about the targets, which are exactly the representations we want. But it must not be *starved*: there is a compromise between *too much capacity* and *not enough capacity*. Deep models are always vastly overparameterized. That's fine because you never fully fit them. Stopping at the most generalizable fit is one of the most effective generalization tools. Use EarlyStopping (chapter 7) rather than train-then-retrain, to avoid redundant work. Regularization deliberately impedes a perfect training fit so the model is smoother and more generic. Always measure its effect. Reducing network size forces compressed, predictive representations, but don't starve the model.

title: Finding the right model size: the IMDb reference model
text:
Choosing model size empirically on the validation set, and the 16-16-1 IMDb model used as the baseline for the regularization experiments No formula gives you the right number of layers or units. You find it by experiment: start small and grow the model until validation loss stops improving much. The condensed chapter 4 IMDb model (listing 5.10) is the reference that the smaller model (listing 5.11, starting here) and later variants are compared against. This page continues the subsubsection **Reducing the network's size** (started on p.185). The authors first point out a hard fact: there is **no magical formula** for the right number of layers or the right size for each layer. You have to evaluate several architectures, and you do it **on the validation set, not on the test set**, because the test set must stay untouched for the final unbiased evaluation (see p.135 and p.173). They recommend a concrete search procedure: **start with relatively few layers and parameters, then increase layer size or add layers until validation loss shows diminishing returns.**

To make this concrete, they bring back the movie-review classifier from chapter 4 in condensed form as **Listing 5.10, "Original model"**. It loads IMDb with the 10,000 most frequent words, multi-hot encodes every review into a 10,000-dimensional 0/1 vector with `vectorize_sequences`, and builds a `keras.Sequential` model with two `Dense(16, activation="relu")` layers and a `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` output. It compiles the model with `rmsprop`, `binary_crossentropy` and accuracy, then trains it for 20 epochs with batch size 512, keeping 40% of the training data for validation (`validation_split=0.4`). The returned `History` object is kept as `history_original` so its validation loss curve can serve as the **reference** in the comparisons that follow.

The page ends with the start of **Listing 5.11, "Version of the model with lower capacity"**, where the first hidden layer has only **4 units** instead of 16. The listing continues on p.187, where the second hidden layer also has 4 units and the compile/fit settings are identical, so the only variable is capacity. Figure 5.18 on p.187 then compares the two validation-loss curves. No formula gives the right model size. Find it by experiment on the validation set, never the test set. Start with few layers and parameters, then grow until validation loss shows diminishing returns. Listing 5.10 is the reference model: 16-16-1 Dense layers on 10,000-dimensional multi-hot input, rmsprop, binary crossentropy, 20 epochs, batch 512, validation_split=0.4. Its history is stored as history_original so later variants can be compared against it. Listing 5.11 changes only the hidden width (16 to 4), isolating the effect of capacity.

title: Model capacity (model size)
text: How much information a model can store: its number of learnable parameters, set by the number of layers and units per layer. Capacity is the model's 'memory budget'. With a big budget it can memorize the training set. With a small one it has to compress, keeping only patterns that predict the target. For a Dense stack, parameters = sum over layers of (inputs x units + units). The reference IMDb model has 10000x16+16 + 16x16+16 + 16x1+1 = 160,305 parameters. Shrinking the hidden layers from 16 to 4 units (listing 5.11) cuts parameters from about 160K to about 40K.
snippet: How much information a model can store: its number of learnable parameters, set by the number of layers and units per layer.

title: Validation set for architecture search
text: Held-out data used to compare candidate models and hyperparameters, such as layer sizes. It is the practice exam you use to decide how to study. The test set is the real exam, which you take only once. Here the validation data is created by `validation_split=0.4`, which holds out the last 40% of the training arrays (10,000 of the 25,000 reviews) and reports `val_loss` and `val_accuracy` after every epoch. You compare the val_loss curves of the 16-unit and 4-unit models and keep the size that reaches the lowest val_loss.

title: Listing 5.10 Original model
text:
from keras.datasets import imdb

(train_data, train_labels), _ = imdb.load_data(num_words=10000)

def vectorize_sequences(sequences, dimension=10000):
    results = np.zeros((len(sequences), dimension))
    for i, sequence in enumerate(sequences):
        results[i, sequence] = 1.0
    return results

train_data = vectorize_sequences(train_data)

model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(16, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"),
    ]
)
model.compile(
    optimizer="rmsprop",
    loss="binary_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
history_original = model.fit(
    train_data,
    train_labels,
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=512,
    validation_split=0.4,
) Loads the IMDb training reviews, multi-hot encodes them into 10,000-dimensional vectors, builds and compiles the 16-16-1 binary classifier from chapter 4, and trains it for 20 epochs with 40% of the data held out for validation. It stores the training history as `history_original` for later comparison. Mini-batch gradient descent (RMSprop) on binary crossentropy, evaluating on a fixed held-out split after every epoch.

title: Smaller model vs. original: figure 5.18
text:
Completing the lower-capacity IMDb model (4-4-1), comparing its validation loss with the 16-16-1 reference, and starting the high-capacity (512-unit) variant Cutting the hidden layers from 16 to 4 units delays overfitting (it begins after about six epochs instead of four) and makes validation loss degrade more slowly afterwards. The page then sets up the opposite experiment with a model far larger than the problem warrants. The page completes **Listing 5.11**, the lower-capacity model, which began on p.186. Both hidden layers are `Dense(4, activation="relu")`, followed by `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")`. Compilation (`rmsprop`, `binary_crossentropy`, accuracy) and training (20 epochs, batch size 512, `validation_split=0.4`) are exactly as in the reference listing 5.10. The result is stored as `history_smaller_model`.

**Figure 5.18** plots the validation loss of both models over 20 epochs. The original model (red dashed line) drops quickly to a minimum of about 0.28 around epoch 4, then climbs steadily to about 0.56 by epoch 20. The smaller model (solid line) starts higher (about 0.49 at epoch 1) because it learns more slowly, reaches its minimum of roughly 0.27-0.28 a few epochs later, and then rises only gently, to about 0.38 at epoch 20. The authors summarize: **the smaller model starts overfitting later than the reference model (after six epochs rather than four), and its performance degrades more slowly once it starts overfitting.**

The authors then turn to the other extreme: "let's add to our benchmark a model that has much more capacity, far more than the problem warrants." **Listing 5.12, "Version of the model with higher capacity"**, begins at the bottom of the page with `layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")`. The rest (a second 512-unit layer and the same compile/fit, stored as `history_larger_model`) is on p.188, together with figure 5.19. Listing 5.11 is the reference with 4 units per hidden layer instead of 16. Everything else is identical. In figure 5.18 the smaller model starts overfitting after about six epochs instead of four. title: A much larger model overfits fast; Occam's razor
text:
The 512-512-1 high-capacity IMDb model against the reference (figure 5.19), the general capacity/overfitting relationship, and the start of 'Adding weight regularization' with Occam's razor A model with far too much capacity drives training loss to near zero almost at once but overfits after a single epoch, more severely and more noisily. More capacity means faster fitting and greater susceptibility to overfitting. This motivates preferring simpler models, which is Occam's razor, the idea behind weight regularization. The page finishes **Listing 5.12**: a second `Dense(512, activation="relu")` layer and the `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` output, compiled and trained exactly like the reference, with the result stored in `history_larger_model`. This model has roughly 5.4 million parameters, against 160K for the reference.

**Figure 5.19** compares its validation loss with the reference's. The book's reading: **the bigger model starts overfitting almost immediately, after just one epoch, and it overfits much more severely. Its validation loss is also noisier.** It gets training loss near zero very quickly. In the plot, the larger model's curve jumps around (for example, a spike to about 0.56 at epoch 3) and climbs to about 0.70 by epoch 20, well above the reference's about 0.56.

The authors then state the general principle: **the more capacity the model has, the more quickly it can model the training data (resulting in a low training loss), but the more susceptible it is to overfitting (resulting in a large difference between the training and validation loss).**

A new subsubsection, **Adding weight regularization**, begins. It invokes **Occam's razor**: given two explanations for something, the one most likely to be correct is the simplest, the one that makes fewer assumptions. The authors say this idea also applies to the models learned by neural networks. The argument continues on p.189: many weight configurations can explain the data, and simpler ones are less likely to overfit. The 512-512-1 model overfits after only one epoch, much more severely and with a noisier validation loss. It drives training loss near zero very quickly. General rule: more capacity means faster fitting (low training loss) and more susceptibility to overfitting (a large train/validation gap). Occam's razor: among explanations that fit, prefer the simplest. This motivates weight regularization.

title: Weight regularization: L1, L2 and weight decay
text:
Simple models as low-entropy weight distributions, L1 and L2 weight penalties added to the loss, weight decay, and adding L2 regularization to the IMDb model in Keras Many weight settings can explain the training data, and simpler ones overfit less. You can push a model toward simplicity by adding to the loss a cost for large weights: L1 (proportional to absolute values) or L2 (proportional to squares, also called weight decay). In Keras you do this by passing a regularizer such as l2(0.002) to a layer's kernel_regularizer argument. Continuing the Occam's razor argument from p.188: **given training data and an architecture, multiple sets of weight values (multiple *models*) could explain the data. Simpler models are less likely to overfit than complex ones.**

The authors define a ***simple model*** here as one where **the distribution of parameter values has less entropy**, or one with fewer parameters, as in the previous section. A common way to mitigate overfitting is therefore to constrain the model's complexity by **forcing its weights to take only small values**, which makes the distribution of weight values more *regular*. This is **weight regularization**, and it is implemented by **adding to the loss function a cost associated with having large weights**. The cost comes in two flavors:

- **L1 regularization**: the added cost is proportional to the *absolute value of the weight coefficients* (the *L1 norm* of the weights), i.e. $\lambda\sum_i |w_i|$.
- **L2 regularization**: the added cost is proportional to the *square of the value of the weight coefficients* (the *L2 norm* of the weights), i.e. $\lambda\sum_i w_i^2$. In neural networks L2 regularization is also called **weight decay**. The authors stress that it is *mathematically the same* as L2 regularization, despite the different name.

In Keras, weight regularization is added by passing **weight regularizer instances** to layers as keyword arguments. **Listing 5.13** rebuilds the 16-16-1 IMDb model with `kernel_regularizer=l2(0.002)` on both hidden Dense layers, imported via `from keras.regularizers import l2`. The output layer is left unregularized. The compile and fit settings are the same as the reference, and the history is stored as `history_l2_reg`. Its effect is shown in figure 5.20 on p.190. Many weight sets can explain the data. Simpler ones overfit less. A simple model has a lower-entropy, more regular weight distribution, or fewer parameters. Weight regularization adds a cost for large weights to the loss: L1 is proportional to |w|, L2 to w². L2 regularization is called weight decay in neural networks and is mathematically the same thing. In Keras: layers.Dense(16, kernel_regularizer=l2(0.002), activation="relu").

title: Weight regularization
text: Adding to the loss a cost associated with large weights, which forces the weights to stay small and regular. A tax on weight magnitude. The model may use large weights only where they buy a lot of reduction in data loss. $L_{total} = L_{data} + \lambda\sum_i |w_i|$ (L1) or $+\,\lambda\sum_i w_i^2$ (L2). kernel_regularizer=l2(0.002) on the two 16-unit layers.
snippet: Adding to the loss a cost associated with large weights, which forces the weights to stay small and regular.

title: L1 regularization
text: A penalty proportional to the sum of the absolute values of the weights (the L1 norm). A constant-size push toward zero for every weight, regardless of its size. Its gradient is $\lambda\,\mathrm{sign}(w)$. It tends to give sparse solutions with many exact zeros (added explanation). regularizers.l1(0.001) (p.190).
snippet: A penalty proportional to the sum of the absolute values of the weights the L1 norm.

title: L2 regularization / weight decay
text: A penalty proportional to the sum of the squared weights. In neural networks it is called weight decay. Big weights are expensive, small weights almost free. Each update shrinks every weight a little. The gradient is $2\lambda w$, so the SGD update multiplies $w$ by $(1-2\eta\lambda)$ before applying the data gradient. l2(0.002): each coefficient adds 0.002·w² to the loss (p.190).
snippet: A penalty proportional to the sum of the squared weights. In neural networks it is called weight decay.

title: Simple model (low-entropy weights)
text: A model whose parameter values have a less entropic, more regular distribution, or that simply has fewer parameters. Weights that are mostly small and similar, without a few extreme values doing idiosyncratic work. The book uses 'entropy' informally. Penalizing weight magnitude concentrates the distribution near zero. The same 16-16-1 network, with or without an L2 penalty.
snippet: A model whose parameter values have a less entropic, more regular distribution, or that simply has fewer parameters.

title: L1 penalty
text: The cost added is proportional to the absolute value of the weight coefficients (the L1 norm of the weights). \Omega_{L1}(W) = \lambda \sum_{i} |w_i| = \lambda\,\|W\|_1 Penalize large weights linearly. Every unit of weight magnitude costs λ, wherever it sits. w_i An individual weight coefficient of a layer's kernel \lambda Regularization strength (the proportionality constant, e.g. 0.001 in l1(0.001)) \|W\|_1 L1 norm: the sum of absolute values
snippet: The cost added is proportional to the absolute value of the weight coefficients the L1 norm of the weights. — Penalize large weights linearly.

title: L2 penalty (weight decay)
text: The cost added is proportional to the square of the value of the weight coefficients (the L2 norm of the weights). \Omega_{L2}(W) = \lambda \sum_{i} w_i^2 = \lambda\,\|W\|_2^2 Penalize large weights quadratically. Doubling a weight quadruples its cost, so a few large weights are discouraged in favour of many small ones. w_i An individual weight coefficient \lambda Regularization strength, 0.002 in listing 5.13 \|W\|_2^2 Squared L2 norm: the sum of squares
snippet: The cost added is proportional to the square of the value of the weight coefficients the L2 norm of the weights. — Penalize large weights quadratically.

title: Regularized loss and the weight-decay update
text: adding to the loss function of the model a cost associated with having large weights … L2 regularization is also called weight decay \begin{aligned} L_{\text{total}} &= L_{\text{data}}(W) + \lambda \sum_i w_i^2 \\ w &\leftarrow w - \eta\left(\frac{\partial L_{\text{data}}}{\partial w} + 2\lambda w\right) = (1 - 2\eta\lambda)\,w - \eta\,\frac{\partial L_{\text{data}}}{\partial w} \end{aligned} Show why L2 is called weight decay. Each SGD step multiplies the weight by a factor slightly below 1, so it decays, before the data gradient is applied. L_{\text{data}} The original loss (binary crossentropy here) \eta Learning rate \lambda L2 strength
snippet: adding to the loss function of the model a cost associated with having large weights … L2 regularization is also called weight decay — Show why L2 is called weight decay.

title: Effect of L2 regularization; other regularizers; when to prefer dropout
text:
What l2(0.002) adds to the loss, the train-only nature of the penalty, figure 5.20 (L2 against the reference), the L1 and L1+L2 regularizers, the limits of weight regularization for large models, and the start of the dropout subsubsection l2(0.002) adds 0.002·w² per kernel coefficient to the training loss only. With it, the 16-16-1 model becomes much more resistant to overfitting with the same number of parameters. Keras also offers l1 and l1_l2. Weight regularization mainly helps smaller models, and for large overparameterized ones dropout is preferred. The page explains the meaning of `l2(0.002)` from listing 5.13: **every coefficient in the layer's weight matrix adds `0.002 * weight_coefficient_value ** 2` to the total loss**. Because **this penalty is only added at training time**, the loss for this model will be much higher at training than at test time.

**Figure 5.20** compares the validation loss of the L2-regularized model with the original. The regularized model starts higher (about 0.49 at epoch 1) and reaches a minimum of about 0.355 around epoch 6. After that it stays nearly flat, around 0.38-0.41, through epoch 20, while the original climbs to about 0.56. In the authors' words, **the L2 model has become much more resistant to overfitting than the reference model, even though both models have the same number of parameters.** (Read from the plot, not stated in the text: its best validation loss is higher than the original's best of about 0.28.)

As alternatives to L2, **Listing 5.14** shows other Keras weight regularizers: `regularizers.l1(0.001)` for L1 regularization and `regularizers.l1_l2(...)` for **simultaneous L1 and L2 regularization**. The printed second line contains a typo (`l2 01)`). It should read `l2=0.001` or a similar value.

The authors add an important caveat: **weight regularization is more typically used for smaller deep learning models.** Large models tend to be so overparameterized that constraining weight values has little effect on capacity and generalization. In those cases a different technique is preferred: **dropout**.

The subsubsection **Adding dropout** begins: dropout, developed by **Geoff Hinton and his students at the University of Toronto**, is one of the most effective and most commonly used regularization techniques for neural networks (continued on p.191). l2(0.002) adds 0.002·w² for every kernel coefficient to the loss, at training time only. A regularized model's training loss is therefore much higher than its test-time loss. With L2, the IMDb model is much more resistant to overfitting, with the same number of parameters. Keras also provides regularizers.l1 and regularizers.l1_l2. The printed l1_l2 line has a typo. Weight regularization suits smaller models. For large overparameterized models, dropout is preferred.

title: How dropout works: masking and rescaling
text:
The mechanics of dropout: randomly zeroing output features during training, the dropout rate, test-time scaling versus training-time rescaling (inverted dropout), with NumPy snippets and figure 5.21 Dropout zeroes a random fraction (the dropout rate, usually 0.2-0.5) of a layer's output features at each training step. To keep the expected activation consistent between training and test, you either scale the outputs down at test time or, as is usual in practice, scale them up during training and leave test-time outputs unchanged. Dropout, applied to a layer, consists of **randomly *dropping out* (setting to zero) a number of output features of the layer during training**. The book's example: a layer that would return `[0.2, 0.5, 1.3, 0.8, 1.1]` for a sample might, after dropout, return `[0, 0.5, 1.3, 0, 1.1]`, with zeros at random positions. The ***dropout rate*** is the fraction of features zeroed out. It is **usually set between 0.2 and 0.5**. **At test time no units are dropped**. Instead, the layer's outputs are scaled down to compensate for the fact that more units are active than during training. (The book says 'by a factor equal to the dropout rate'. In general the multiplier is the keep probability, 1 − rate, which equals 0.5 in the page's example.)

The authors then show the computation in NumPy on a matrix `layer_output` of shape `(batch_size, features)`:

- **Training time**: `layer_output *= np.random.randint(low=0, high=2, size=layer_output.shape)`. This multiplies by a random 0/1 mask, dropping about 50% of the units.
- **Test time**: `layer_output *= 0.5`, scaling down because half the units were dropped during training.

This can equivalently be done **entirely at training time**, leaving the output unchanged at test time, **which is often how it is implemented in practice**: apply the mask, then `layer_output /= 0.5`. The callout notes that this scales *up* rather than down.

**Figure 5.21** illustrates this on a 4×4 activation matrix. 50% dropout zeroes eight cells (shaded), and the result is multiplied by 2 during training. At test time the activation matrix is unchanged. Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of a layer's output features at each training step. The dropout rate is the fraction zeroed, usually 0.2 to 0.5. No units are dropped at test time. Activations must be rescaled so training and test magnitudes match. Either scale down at test time (*= 0.5) or, more commonly, scale up during training (/= 0.5) and leave inference unchanged. In general the scale factor is the keep probability 1 − rate. It equals the rate only when the rate is 0.5.

title: Dropout
text: Randomly setting a fraction (the dropout rate) of a layer's output features to zero at each training step. At test time no units are dropped. Every training step trains a different random 'thinned' sub-network, so no unit can rely on specific partners. Mask $m \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1-p)$ element-wise. Train: $m\odot h/(1-p)$. Test: $h$ (inverted form). [0.2, 0.5, 1.3, 0.8, 1.1] becomes [0, 0.5, 1.3, 0, 1.1].
snippet: Randomly setting a fraction the dropout rate of a layer's output features to zero at each training step. At test time no units are dropped.

title: Dropout rate
text: The fraction of features zeroed out. The book gives a usual range of 0.2 to 0.5. How hard you shake the network during training. Keep probability = 1 − rate. The rescaling factor is 1/(1 − rate) in training, or (1 − rate) at test time. Rate 0.5: each feature is kept with probability 0.5, and kept features are doubled in training.
snippet: The fraction of features zeroed out. The book gives a usual range of 0.2 to 0.5.

title: Training vs. inference behaviour
text: Some layers compute differently during training and inference. Dropout is the first example in the book. Practice under hard conditions, then perform at full strength. In Keras, layers receive a `training` argument. Dropout is the identity when training=False. Figure 5.21: training applies the mask and ×2. At test time the matrix is unchanged.
snippet: Some layers compute differently during training and inference. Dropout is the first example in the book.

title: Dropout with test-time scaling (first scheme on the page)
text: layer_output *= np.random.randint(low=0, high=2, size=layer_output.shape)  …  layer_output *= 0.5 \begin{aligned} \text{train: } & y = m \odot h, \quad m_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1-p) \\ \text{test: } & y = (1-p)\, h \end{aligned} Make the test-time output equal the expected training-time output. $\mathbb{E}[m_{ij} h_{ij}] = (1-p)h_{ij}$, which is what the test-time formula produces. h The layer output matrix, shape (batch_size, features) m Random 0/1 mask of the same shape. randint(0, 2) gives keep probability 0.5 p Dropout rate (fraction dropped). p = 0.5 on this page \odot Element-wise multiplication
snippet: layeroutput = np.random.randintlow=0, high=2, size=layeroutput.shape … layeroutput = 0.5 — Make the test-time output equal the expected training-time output.

title: Inverted dropout (rescaling during training)
text:
layer_output *= np.random.randint(low=0, high=2, size=layer_output.shape)
layer_output /= 0.5 \begin{aligned} \text{train: } & y = \frac{m \odot h}{1-p} \\ \text{test: } & y = h \end{aligned} Keep inference unchanged, which is the common practical implementation. $\mathbb{E}[y] = h$ during training, so no correction is needed later. 1-p Keep probability. Dividing by it (0.5 here) scales the surviving values up
snippet: layeroutput = np.random.randintlow=0, high=2, size=layeroutput.shape layeroutput /= 0.5 — Keep inference unchanged, which is the common practical implementation.

title: Dropout mask at training time
text: layer_output *= np.random.randint(low=0, high=2, size=layer_output.shape) Multiplies the layer output in place by a random matrix of 0s and 1s of the same shape. Callout: 'At training time, drops out 50% of the units in the output.' Bernoulli(0.5) masking.
snippet: Multiplies the layer output in place by a random matrix of 0s and 1s of the same shape. Callout: 'At training time, drops out 50% of the units in the output.'

title: Scaling at test time
text: layer_output *= 0.5 At test time (callout: 'At test time'), multiplies all outputs by 0.5 to match the average magnitude seen during training with 50% dropout. Deterministic rescaling.
snippet: At test time callout: 'At test time', multiplies all outputs by 0.5 to match the average magnitude seen during training with 50% dropout.

title: Both operations at training time (inverted dropout)
text:
layer_output *= np.random.randint(low=0, high=2, size=layer_output.shape)
layer_output /= 0.5 During training (callout: 'At training time'), applies the random mask and then divides by 0.5, doubling the survivors. The callout notes: 'Note that we're scaling up rather scaling down in this case.' At test time the output is left unchanged. Inverted dropout.

title: Why dropout works, and adding it to the IMDB model
text:
The intuition behind dropout (Hinton's bank-teller story), the Keras Dropout layer, and Listing 5.15, which adds two Dropout(0.5) layers to the IMDB classifier Randomly zeroing a layer's outputs during training injects noise that breaks up accidental, insignificant co-adaptations ('conspiracies') the network would otherwise memorize. In Keras this is one line: a Dropout layer placed after the layer whose output you want to perturb, and on IMDB it beats both the reference model and L2 regularization. This page completes the discussion of **dropout** begun on p.191 and opens the chapter's final recap.

**Why should dropout work?** The authors admit the technique "may seem strange and arbitrary" and quote Geoffrey Hinton's account of its inspiration: bank tellers were rotated frequently, presumably because defrauding the bank would require *cooperation* between employees. Hinton realized that "randomly removing a different subset of neurons on each example would prevent conspiracies and thus reduce overfitting."

The book then states the core idea in technical terms: injecting **noise into a layer's output values** breaks up *happenstance patterns that aren't significant* — Hinton's "conspiracies" — which the model would otherwise memorize. A unit can no longer rely on a specific other unit being present, so fragile, sample-specific feature combinations stop paying off.

**In Keras**, dropout is a `Dropout` layer that acts on the output of the layer just before it. **Listing 5.15** rebuilds the IMDB model — `Dense(16, relu)` → `Dropout(0.5)` → `Dense(16, relu)` → `Dropout(0.5)` → `Dense(1, sigmoid)` — compiles it with `rmsprop` and `binary_crossentropy`, and trains for 20 epochs with batch size 512 and `validation_split=0.4`, storing the result in `history_dropout`.

The results (figure 5.22, printed on p.193) are described as "a clear improvement over the reference model," and dropout "seems to be working much better than L2 regularization since the lowest validation loss reached has improved."

The page then begins a **recap** of the most common ways to maximize generalization: getting more or better training data, and developing better features; the remaining items (reducing capacity, weight regularization for smaller models, adding dropout) continue on p.193. Dropout injects noise into a layer's outputs, breaking up insignificant 'conspiracies' between units that the model would otherwise memorize. Hinton's intuition came from banks rotating tellers so that fraud requiring cooperation becomes impossible. In Keras, `layers.Dropout(rate)` acts on the output of the preceding layer and is active only during training. Listing 5.15 inserts Dropout(0.5) after each Dense(16, relu) layer of the IMDB model; everything else is unchanged. On IMDB, dropout lowers the minimum validation loss more than L2 regularization does. The recap of generalization techniques starts with more/better data and better features.

title: Dropout
text: A regularization technique that, during training, randomly sets a fraction (the rate) of a layer's output features to zero for each example, with a fresh random mask every time. No unit can count on a specific partner being present, so units cannot form training-set-specific 'conspiracies'; each must carry useful information that holds up in many random company. Keras implements inverted dropout: in training, outputs are multiplied by a Bernoulli mask and scaled by 1/(1−rate) so expected values are unchanged; at inference the layer is the identity (see figure 5.21 on p.191). `layers.Dropout(0.5)` after each `Dense(16, relu)` layer in Listing 5.15.
snippet: A regularization technique that, during training, randomly sets a fraction the rate of a layer's output features to zero for each example, with a fresh random mask every time.

title: Conspiracies / co-adaptation
text: Hinton's term for happenstance patterns encoded jointly by several units that are not significant in the data but fit the training sample. Like tellers colluding: the fraud only works if everyone involved is present. Beyond the book, the literature calls this co-adaptation of feature detectors; noise in activations makes such joint dependencies unreliable. Two hidden units that together detect a rare word pair occurring only in a few training reviews.
snippet: Hinton's term for happenstance patterns encoded jointly by several units that are not significant in the data but fit the training sample.

title: Regularization
text: Any technique that makes a model more likely to generalize by discouraging it from fitting the training data too closely. Make memorization harder so the model has to learn the general shape of the data. Section 5.4.4 covers reducing size, weight regularization (L1/L2) and dropout. Adding Dropout(0.5) layers; adding kernel_regularizer=l2(0.002).
snippet: Any technique that makes a model more likely to generalize by discouraging it from fitting the training data too closely.

title: Noise as a regularizer
text: Injecting random perturbations into inputs or intermediate activations during training to prevent memorization of insignificant patterns. If the training signal keeps shifting slightly, only the robust regularities are worth learning. Dropout is multiplicative Bernoulli noise on activations; data augmentation (p.278) is structured noise on inputs. Random image flips and rotations in chapter 8.
snippet: Injecting random perturbations into inputs or intermediate activations during training to prevent memorization of insignificant patterns.

title: Inverted dropout as used by the Keras Dropout layer

With r = 0.5, surviving activations are doubled and half are zeroed on average; at test time the layer passes h through unchanged. h_i the i-th output of the preceding layer (e.g. one of the 16 relu units) m_i random mask bit: 1 (keep) with probability 1−r, 0 (drop) with probability r r dropout rate, the argument of Dropout(r); 0.5 in Listing 5.15 \tilde{h}_i output of the Dropout layer during training

    epochs=20,

title: Figure 5.22, end of the recap, and the chapter 5 summary
text:
The plot comparing validation loss with and without dropout on IMDB, the last three items of the list of generalization techniques, and the first half of the chapter summary (generalization, interpolation on the latent manifold, optimization vs. generalization, evaluation) Dropout slows and delays the rise of validation loss on IMDB; the toolbox against overfitting ends with reducing capacity, weight regularization for small models, and dropout. The chapter summary restates the key thesis: deep learning generalizes by interpolating along a learned latent manifold, and every best practice manages the tension between optimization and generalization. **Figure 5.22** plots validation loss over 20 epochs for the original IMDB model (dashed red) and the dropout-regularized model from Listing 5.15 (solid blue). Reading the plot: the original model starts lower (about 0.40), bottoms out around epoch 4 (about 0.275) and then climbs steeply to about 0.56 by epoch 20. The dropout model starts higher (about 0.53, because training is noisier), reaches its minimum a little later, around epoch 6 (about 0.27), and then rises much more slowly, ending near 0.51. This is the "clear improvement" the previous page described.

The **recap list** from p.192 finishes with three model-side techniques: **reducing the capacity of the model**, **adding weight regularization (for smaller models)**, and **adding dropout** — joining more/better data and better features.

Then the **chapter summary** begins:

- The purpose of an ML model is to **generalize** — perform accurately on never-before-seen inputs — and that's harder than it seems.
- A deep network generalizes by learning a parametric model that can **interpolate** between training samples; it can be said to have learned the **latent manifold** of the training data. Hence deep learning models only make sense of inputs very close to what they've seen.
- The fundamental problem is **the tension between optimization and generalization**: you must fit the training data to generalize, but fitting it better eventually hurts generalization. Every best practice manages this tension.
- Generalization comes from approximating the latent manifold and making sense of new inputs via interpolation.
- Accurate evaluation is essential; the methods range from simple hold-out validation to K-fold and iterated K-fold with shuffling. The bullet continues on p.194 with the advice to keep a completely separate test set. In figure 5.22, dropout starts worse, reaches its best validation loss later (≈epoch 6), and rises much more slowly afterward than the original model. The five common anti-overfitting techniques: more/better data, better features, reduced capacity, weight regularization (small models), dropout. Generalization — accuracy on never-before-seen inputs — is the purpose of a model. Deep networks generalize by interpolating along a learned latent manifold, so they handle only inputs close to their training data. The central problem is the tension between optimization and generalization; every best practice manages it. Evaluate carefully: hold-out, K-fold, or iterated K-fold with shuffling, plus a separate test set.

title: Latent manifold
text: The low-dimensional, structured subspace of input space on which real data lies. Of all possible 28×28 pixel grids, real digits occupy a thin, connected sheet; the network learns that sheet. A model that approximates the manifold can map new points by interpolating between nearby training points. Morphing smoothly from one handwritten 4 to another passes through valid-looking 4s.

title: Chapter 5 summary, concluded: separate test set and the two-phase workflow
text:
The last three summary points of chapter 5: keep a separate test set because of validation leakage; first get a model that generalizes somewhat and can overfit; then switch to regularization, with more/better data as the number-one lever Model development has two phases: first push optimization until you have a model with some generalization power that can overfit (tune learning rate and batch size, better architecture priors, more capacity, longer training), then fight overfitting (reduce capacity, dropout, weight regularization, early stopping). A completely separate test set guards the final evaluation against leakage from tuning on validation data. This short page finishes the chapter 5 summary that began on p.193.

1. **Keep a completely separate test set** for final evaluation (continuing the evaluation bullet from p.193). The reason: *information leaks from your validation data to your model may have occurred*. Every time you adjust a hyperparameter based on validation results, a little knowledge of the validation set flows into the model's configuration, so the validation score becomes optimistically biased.

2. **Phase one — get a model that can overfit.** When you start, your goal is a model that has *some generalization power* and *can overfit*. Ways to get there: tune the learning rate and batch size, use better architecture priors, increase model capacity, or simply train longer. (These are the topics of section 5.3, p.177–181.)

3. **Phase two — regularize.** Once the model starts overfitting, the goal switches to improving generalization through **model regularization**: reduce capacity, add dropout or weight regularization, and use early stopping. And "naturally, a larger or better dataset is always the number one way to help a model generalize." (These are section 5.4, p.182–193.)

Together these bullets turn chapter 5's theory — the tension between optimization and generalization — into a procedure: cross the overfitting boundary to find it, then pull back with regularization, measuring honestly at each step and touching the test set only at the end. Keep a completely separate test set: validation-based tuning leaks information. Phase one: reach a model with some generalization power that can overfit (learning rate, batch size, architecture priors, capacity, longer training). Phase two: regularize (reduce capacity, dropout, weight regularization, early stopping). More or better data is always the number one way to improve generalization.
