title: Chapter 6 opener: The universal workflow of machine learning
text:
Opening of chapter 6: what the chapter covers (framing a problem, developing a working model, deploying and maintaining it) and the premise that real projects start from a problem, not a dataset Up to now every example came with a ready-made labeled dataset. In practice you start from a problem — like the first two consulting projects listed here (photo search, spam/offensive content flagging) — and need a universal step-by-step blueprint to get from that problem to a deployed, maintained model. This is the opening page of **chapter 6, "The universal workflow of machine learning."**

**This chapter covers:**
- Framing a machine learning problem
- Developing a working model
- Deploying your model in production and maintaining it

The opening text points out that all previous examples assumed a labeled dataset already existed, so training could start immediately. In the real world, "you don't start from a dataset; you start from a problem."

To make this concrete, the authors ask you to imagine launching your own ML consulting shop. Projects start rolling in; the first two on this page are:
- a **personalized photo search engine** for a picture-sharing social network (type "wedding" and retrieve your wedding pictures with no manual tagging), and
- **flagging spam and offensive text** in the posts of a budding chat app.

The list continues on p.196 (music recommendation, credit card fraud, ad click-through rate, anomalous cookies on a production line, archaeological sites from satellite images), followed by the three-part structure of the workflow: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model.

**How to use this page:** treat the chapter map below as your roadmap; as you read each project, ask yourself what the input data, target, and success metric would be — that is exactly what section 6.1 teaches. Chapter 6 covers framing an ML problem, developing a working model, and deploying and maintaining it. You don't start from a dataset; you start from a problem. Real requests (photo search, spam/offensive content flagging) are phrased in business terms and arrive without data.

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: The three parts of the universal workflow, and starting 6.1 Defining the task
text:
The rest of the list of example ML projects, the three-part structure of the universal workflow (define the task, develop a model, deploy the model), and the opening questions of section 6.1 about understanding the context of a task Real projects don't come with a keras.datasets dataset; a universal blueprint — define the task, develop a model, deploy the model — consolidates chapters 4 and 5. It starts with deeply understanding the customer's context: why they need it, how the model will be used, what data exists, and which ML task maps to the business problem. The page completes the list of hypothetical consulting projects begun on p.195: a **music recommendation** system for an online radio, **credit card fraud** detection for an e-commerce site, predicting **display ad click-through rate** to choose which ad to serve to a given user at a given time, flagging **anomalous cookies** on a manufacturing conveyor belt, and using **satellite images** to locate as-yet unknown **archaeological sites**.

It would be convenient to import the right dataset from `keras.datasets` and start fitting, but in reality "you'll have to start from scratch."

The chapter therefore presents a **universal step-by-step blueprint** for any ML problem, consolidating chapters 4 and 5 and giving context for the rest of the book. It has three parts:

1. **Define the task** — understand the problem domain and the business logic behind the request; collect a dataset; understand what the data represents; choose how to measure success.
2. **Develop a model** — prepare the data for a model; select an evaluation protocol and a simple baseline to beat; train a first model that has generalization power and can overfit; then regularize and tune until you get the best possible generalization.
3. **Deploy the model** — present your work to stakeholders; ship the model to a web server, mobile app, web page or embedded device; monitor its performance in the wild; start collecting the data for the next model generation.

**Section 6.1, Defining the task**, opens with a series of questions: Why is the customer trying to solve this problem? What value will they get? How will the model be used and fit into their business processes? What data is available or could be collected? What kind of ML task maps to the business problem?

**Section 6.1.1, Framing the problem**, begins: framing usually involves many detailed discussions with stakeholders, and a list of key questions follows on p.197. Real projects are diverse (recommendation, fraud, CTR, visual anomaly detection, remote sensing) and don't come with a ready dataset. The universal workflow has three parts: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model. Developing a model reuses chapter 5: baseline, model that can overfit, then regularize and tune. Deployment includes stakeholder communication, shipping, monitoring, and collecting data for the next model generation. Defining the task starts with questions about why, value, usage, business processes, available data, and the matching ML task.

title: Framing the problem: inputs, task type, existing solutions, constraints
text:
The four framing questions of section 6.1.1 — what are the inputs and targets, what type of ML task is this, what do existing solutions look like, what constraints apply — with each of the chapter's seven example projects mapped to a task type Framing means pinning down inputs and targets (limited by data availability), the task type (which may not even call for ML, or not for deep learning), what already exists, and the constraints (privacy, latency, deployment target). The example projects show that the right framing is often non-obvious. Section 6.1.1 lists the questions to keep in mind during framing discussions with stakeholders.

**1. What will your input data be? What are you trying to predict?** You can only learn to predict something if training data exists — e.g., classifying movie-review sentiment requires reviews *and* sentiment annotations. **Data availability is usually the limiting factor**, and often you must collect and annotate a new dataset yourself (section 6.1.2).

**2. What type of ML task is it?** Binary or multiclass classification, scalar or vector regression, multiclass multilabel classification, image segmentation, ranking, or something else like clustering, generation or reinforcement learning. Sometimes ML isn't the best tool at all and plain statistical analysis is better. Applied to the projects:
- Photo search → **multiclass, multilabel classification**.
- Spam detection → **binary classification**; with "offensive" as its own class, **three-way classification**.
- Music recommendation → better handled **not by deep learning but by matrix factorization (collaborative filtering)**.
- Credit card fraud → **binary classification**.
- Click-through rate → **scalar regression**.
- Anomalous cookies → **binary classification**, with an **object detection** first stage to crop cookies out of raw images; "anomaly detection" techniques would *not* be a good fit.
- Archaeological sites → **image similarity ranking**: retrieve new images that look most like known sites.

**3. What do existing solutions look like?** Maybe a hand-crafted algorithm with nested `if` statements for spam or fraud, or a human removing bad cookies or crafting playlists. Understand what's in place and how it works.

**4. Are there particular constraints?** If the chat app is end-to-end encrypted, the spam model must live on the user's phone and be trained on an external dataset. If the cookie filter has tight latency requirements, it must run on an embedded device at the factory rather than a remote server. Understand the full context your work fits into. Framing asks four questions: inputs/targets, task type, existing solutions, constraints. You can only predict what you have annotated training data for; data availability is usually the limiting factor. The task type is a design decision, and sometimes ML — or deep learning — is not the right tool. Book's mappings: photo search multilabel; spam binary/3-way; music via matrix factorization; fraud binary; CTR scalar regression; cookies binary after object detection; archaeology similarity ranking. Existing rule-based or human processes must be understood — they are the baseline and a source of knowledge. Constraints like end-to-end encryption or latency can dictate on-device or embedded deployment and the training data source.

title: Hidden hypotheses, an ethics warning, and the start of data collection
text:
The two hypotheses implicit in framing an ML problem, the ethical dimension of task choice, and the cost of data collection Framing a problem as 'predict targets Y from inputs X' rests on two unproven hypotheses (Y is predictable from X, and your data is informative enough to learn the mapping); some tasks should not be attempted at all for ethical reasons; and once the task is fixed, collecting and labeling data is usually the most expensive part of the project. This page closes subsection 6.1.1 (*Framing the problem*) and opens 6.1.2 (*Collecting a dataset*).

After your research you should know your **inputs**, your **targets**, and the **broad task type**. The authors stress that this framing hides two **hypotheses**:

1. your targets *can* be predicted from your inputs, and
2. the data you have (or will collect) is *sufficiently informative* to learn that input-target relationship.

Until a working model exists, both are just hypotheses "waiting to be validated or invalidated." Having examples of X and Y does not mean X contains enough information to predict Y. The example is **stock prediction from recent price history**: you are unlikely to succeed, because price history carries little predictive information.

A sidebar, **Note on ethics**, looks at a project such as "building an AI that rates the trustworthiness of someone from a picture of their face." The authors reject it on two grounds. First, **validity**: there is no clear reason trustworthiness would show on a face. Second, **ethics**: the labels would just record the annotators' biases. A model trained on them would encode those biases in a black box that gives them "a thin veneer of legitimacy," because "the AI algorithm said" sounds more objective than "John Smith said," even though the model is only a learned approximation of John Smith. Such a model would be "laundering and operationalizing at scale" bad human judgment. The sidebar ends: *technology is never neutral; technical choices are also ethical choices.*

Section **6.1.2** then calls data collection "the most arduous, time-consuming, and costly part of most machine learning projects" and starts going through the example projects. The **photo search engine** needs a label set (10,000 common categories) and manual tagging of hundreds of thousands of past user uploads. The **chat spam detector** cannot train on user chats because they are end-to-end encrypted, so it needs a separate dataset (this continues on p.199). Framing a task implies two hypotheses: targets are predictable from inputs, and your data is informative enough to learn that mapping. These hypotheses are only validated by a working model; not every problem is solvable with ML (e.g., stock moves from past prices). Models trained on biased human labels reproduce those biases with a false aura of objectivity; some projects are invalid and harmful. Technical choices are ethical choices; be deliberate about the values your work supports. Data collection and annotation is usually the most arduous, time-consuming and costly part of an ML project.
snippet: This page closes subsection 6.1.1 Framing the problem and opens 6.1.2 Collecting a dataset. After your research you should know your inputs, your targets, and the broad task type.…
chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: The two framing hypotheses
text: When you frame an ML task you implicitly assume (1) targets can be predicted from inputs and (2) your available data is informative enough to learn that relationship. Before building, you are betting that the signal exists and that your data captures it. Hypothesis 1 is about the joint distribution p(X, Y): Y must depend on X. Hypothesis 2 is about the finite sample: its size, label noise and coverage must allow a learner to approximate that dependency. Stock moves from past prices: hypothesis 1 likely fails. A great idea trained on 50 mislabeled examples: hypothesis 2 fails.
snippet: When you frame an ML task you implicitly assume 1 targets can be predicted from inputs and 2 your available data is informative enough to learn that relationship.

text: The amount of information the inputs carry about the target; ML can only use what is present. A model can't read tomorrow's price in yesterday's chart if it isn't there. chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Label bias / bias laundering
text: When labels encode human prejudice, a model trained on them reproduces that prejudice while appearing objective. The model is a learned copy of the annotators; dressing their opinion up as 'AI' doesn't change what it is. Supervised learning fits the conditional distribution that generated the labels; if that process is biased, the optimum is biased. A face-based 'trustworthiness' rater trained on human ratings learns the raters' stereotypes.
snippet: When labels encode human prejudice, a model trained on them reproduces that prejudice while appearing objective.

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Data needs of each project, why data beats algorithms, and annotation choices
text:
Concrete data-collection plans for the example projects, the primacy of data over modeling, and how to source annotations Projects range from needing no new data (likes, click logs) to needing cameras, factory staff or archaeologists to collect and label data. Because generalization comes almost entirely from the training data, extra effort is usually best spent on more and better data, and the annotation process sets the quality of your targets and so of your model. The page finishes the list of data-collection plans begun on p.198.

- **Chat spam detection**: because chats are end-to-end encrypted, you need a separate dataset of *tens of thousands of unfiltered social media posts*, labeled by hand as **spam, offensive, or acceptable** (the three-way framing from p.197).
- **Music recommendation**: users' "likes" already serve as data, so *no new data needs to be collected*. The same holds for **click-through rate prediction**, with years of logged CTR for past ads.
- **Cookie flagging**: install cameras over the conveyor belts, collect *tens of thousands of images*, and have someone label them. The domain experts are factory workers, and others can be trained to do the job.
- **Satellite archaeology**: archaeologists must build a database of known sites, find satellite images of each in *different weather conditions*, and you will need *thousands of different sites*.

The authors then recall chapter 5: **generalization comes almost entirely from the training data**, meaning the number of data points, the reliability of the labels and the quality of the features. A good dataset is "an asset worthy of care and investment." With an extra 50 hours, you are probably better off collecting more data than chasing incremental modeling gains. They cite Google's 2009 paper **"The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data"** (a riff on Eugene Wigner's 1960 *The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences*) and note that deep learning has only *increased* the importance of data.

Supervised learning needs **annotations**, the targets to predict. Some can be **retrieved automatically** (likes, clicks), but often you must **annotate by hand**, which takes a lot of labor.

The subsection **Investing in data annotation infrastructure** begins: the annotation process determines target quality, and target quality determines model quality. The options are to annotate yourself, to use a **crowdsourcing platform such as Mechanical Turk**, or to hire a **specialized data-labeling company** (discussed on p.200). Data-collection cost varies widely: some projects reuse logs (likes, CTR), others need cameras, trained labelers or expert archaeologists. Generalization comes almost entirely from data: quantity, label reliability and feature quality. Extra time is usually best spent on collecting more data, not incremental model tweaks ('The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data', 2009). Supervised learning needs annotations; sometimes retrieved automatically, often made by hand at considerable labor. Annotation process -> target quality -> model quality; choose between self-annotation, crowdsourcing, or a labeling company deliberately.

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Choosing how to annotate, and the danger of nonrepresentative data
text:
Trade-offs in annotation sourcing and tooling; requirement that training data be representative of production data Choose an annotation strategy by weighing control, cost, noise and the expertise the labels require, and invest early in annotation software. Above all, training data must be representative of production data. A model with over 90% test accuracy can be wrong 8 times out of 10 in deployment if it was trained on the wrong kind of data. The page continues **Investing in data annotation infrastructure** from p.199. **Outsourcing** can save time and money but *takes away control*. **Mechanical Turk** is likely inexpensive and scales well, but annotations may be *quite noisy*.

To choose, the book asks you to consider three constraints:

- **Do labelers need to be subject matter experts?** Anyone can label cat vs. dog, dog breeds need specialized knowledge, and annotating **CT scans of bone fractures** "pretty much requires a medical degree."
- **If expertise is needed, can you train people?** If not, how will you reach the experts?
- **Do you yourself understand how experts annotate?** If not, the dataset is a **black box** and you cannot do manual feature engineering. This "isn't critical, but it can be limiting."

If you label **in-house**, decide what software will record annotations. You may have to build it, and *productive annotation software* is worth investing in early.

The next subsection, **Beware of nonrepresentative data**, states the main principle: models only make sense of inputs similar to what they have seen, so training data must be **representative of production data**. This should be "the foundation of all of your data collection work."

The example is a dish-recognition app trained on polished photos from a foodie social network. Test accuracy is **well over 90%**, but in production it is **wrong 8 times out of 10**. Users' casual phone photos look nothing like the training images. The authors call this "a cardinal sin—welcome to machine learning hell."

The remedy is to **collect data directly from the deployment environment**. An IMDB sentiment model should run on new IMDB reviews, not Yelp reviews or tweets. To score tweets, annotate real tweets from similar users. If that is impossible, *fully understand how training and production data differ and actively correct for it*. The page ends by introducing **concept drift**, which is defined on p.201. Outsourcing annotation saves time and money but takes away control; crowdsourcing is cheap and scalable but noisy. Choose an annotation strategy by asking whether labelers need expertise, whether it can be taught, and whether you understand the experts' logic. Invest early in productive annotation software if labeling in-house. Training data must be representative of production data; this is the foundation of all data collection work. A high test score on unrepresentative data says nothing about production: >90% test vs. 8/10 wrong in deployment. Collect data from the real deployment environment and user population, or understand and actively correct the differences.

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Concept drift, learning from the past, and sampling bias
text:
Two forms of nonrepresentative data: concept drift over time, and sampling bias from the collection process Training data can stop being representative over time (concept drift), and it can be unrepresentative from the start because the way you collect it is correlated with what you predict (sampling bias). In both cases the model only recognizes patterns it has seen and assumes the future resembles the past. The page finishes the discussion of **nonrepresentative data** from p.200 with two more cases.

**Concept drift** happens when "the properties of the production data change over time, causing model accuracy to gradually decay." It is especially common with user-generated data. The book's examples:

- a **music recommender trained in 2013** "may not be very effective today";
- the **IMDB dataset was collected in 2011**, so a model trained on it would probably do worse on 2020 reviews than on 2012 reviews, "as vocabulary, expressions, and movie genres evolve over time";
- drift is **particularly acute in adversarial contexts** such as **credit card fraud detection**, where "fraud patterns change practically every day."

Fast drift calls for **constant data collection, annotation, and model retraining**.

The authors then state a general limit: ML can only **memorize patterns present in the training data**, and "you can only recognize what you've seen before." Training on the past to predict the future assumes **the future will behave like the past**, which "often isn't the case."

The sidebar **The problem of sampling bias** calls it "a particularly insidious and common case of nonrepresentative data." It occurs when **the data collection process interacts with what you are trying to predict**, which biases the measurements. The historical example is the **1948 US presidential election**. On election night the *Chicago Tribune* printed **"DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN"** based on a **phone survey**, and Truman won. Phone users in 1948 were not a random, representative sample of voters. They were more likely to be richer, conservative and Dewey (Republican) voters. Phone surveys now account for sampling bias. The bias still exists in polling, but pollsters are aware of it and correct for it. The page shows the famous photo of Truman holding up the mistaken headline. Concept drift: production data properties change over time and accuracy gradually decays; it shows up in almost all real-world problems. Drift is fastest in adversarial settings like fraud detection and demands constant collection, annotation and retraining. ML only memorizes patterns present in training data; predicting the future assumes it behaves like the past. Sampling bias occurs when the data collection process interacts with the target, as in the 1948 phone survey that predicted Dewey. Sampling bias is insidious: the data look fine internally, and only awareness and active correction protect you.
snippet: The page finishes the discussion of nonrepresentative data from p.200 with two more cases. Concept drift happens when "the properties of the production data change over time,…

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Understanding your data and choosing a measure of success
text:
Exploratory checks before training (samples, histograms, maps, missing values, class balance, target leaking) and picking a success metric aligned with business goals Don't treat your dataset as a black box. Inspect it to see what makes it predictive and to catch problems such as missing values, class imbalance and target leaking. Then define success with a metric that matches your high-level goals, because that metric will guide every technical choice in the project. **6.1.3 Understanding your data** opens with "It's bad practice to treat a dataset as a black box." Before training, explore and visualize the data to learn **what makes it predictive** (which informs feature engineering) and to **screen for issues**:

- **Images or text**: look at a few samples and their labels directly.
- **Numerical features**: plot **histograms** to see value ranges and frequencies.
- **Location data**: plot it on a **map** and look for patterns.
- **Missing values**: note them for data preparation (covered next, p.204).
- **Classification**: **count instances per class**. If the classes are imbalanced, you must account for it.
- **Target leaking**: features that give information about the target but *may not be available in production*. The example is a model predicting whether someone *will be treated for cancer* from medical records that include "This person has been diagnosed with cancer." The target leaks into the inputs. The test to apply: *is every feature available in the same form in production?*

**6.1.4 Choosing a measure of success** begins with "To control something, you need to be able to observe it." You must define success (accuracy, precision and recall, customer retention rate). That metric **guides all technical choices** and should **align with higher-level goals** such as the customer's business success.

Metric guidance:

- **Balanced classification** (every class equally likely): **accuracy** and **ROC AUC** (area under the curve of the receiver operating characteristic).
- **Class-imbalanced, ranking, or multilabel** problems: **precision and recall**, or a metric built from **true/false positives/negatives**.
- Defining a **custom metric** is not unusual.

To see the range of metrics used in practice, the authors suggest browsing **Kaggle** competitions. Explore and visualize data before training: samples, histograms, maps, missing values, class counts. Target leaking: a feature that reveals the target but won't be available in production; always ask whether each feature exists in the same form at prediction time. Define success before building: the metric guides every technical choice and must align with business goals. Balanced classification: accuracy, ROC AUC. Imbalanced, ranking or multilabel: precision and recall or TP/FP/FN/TN-based metrics. Custom metrics are common; Kaggle competitions showcase the variety.

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Developing a model: preparing data by vectorization and normalization
text:
Start of the model-development phase; data preprocessing basics: vectorization and value normalization Model development is only one step of the workflow, and not the hardest. Its first task is preprocessing: turning raw data into floating-point tensors (vectorization) and scaling values to be small and homogeneous (normalization), because large or heterogeneous values can trigger large gradient updates that keep the network from converging. Section **6.2 Developing a model** starts once you know how to measure progress. The authors note that most tutorials and research projects treat model development as *the only step*. They assume problem definition and data collection are already done and that deployment and maintenance are someone else's job. In fact model development is only *one step*, and "not the most difficult one." The hardest parts are **framing problems and collecting, annotating, and cleaning data**, so "what comes next will be easy in comparison!"

**6.2.1 Preparing the data.** Deep learning models typically don't ingest raw data. Preprocessing makes data "more amenable to neural networks" through **vectorization, normalization, or handling missing values**. Many techniques are domain-specific (text, images) and are covered in later chapters. This section covers the basics common to all domains.

**Vectorization.** Inputs and targets must typically be **tensors of floating-point data** (sometimes integers or strings). Sound, images and text all have to be turned into tensors first, which is called **data vectorization**. The chapter 4 text examples started from lists of integers (word indices) and used **multi-hot encoding** to produce `float32` tensors. MNIST and house prices were already vectorized.

**Value normalization.** MNIST images were integers in **0-255** (grayscale), cast to `float32` and **divided by 255** to fall in **0-1**. House-price features had mixed ranges, some small floats and some large integers, so each feature was normalized **independently to mean 0 and standard deviation 1**.

In general it is unsafe to feed networks **relatively large values** (multi-digit integers, much larger than the initial weights) or **heterogeneous data** (one feature in 0-1, another in 100-200). Doing so "can trigger large gradient updates that will prevent the network from" converging. The sentence finishes on p.204, which lists the desired properties: small values and homogeneous ranges. Model development is only one step of the workflow, and not the hardest; framing and data work are harder. Preprocessing basics common to all domains: vectorization, normalization, handling missing values. Vectorization turns any data into (usually float) tensors, e.g., multi-hot encoding of word-index lists into float32. Normalization examples: MNIST cast to float32 and divided by 255; house-price features standardized to mean 0, std 1 independently. Large or heterogeneous input values can trigger large gradient updates that prevent convergence.

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Normalization, missing values, and the start of evaluation protocols
text:
Finishing data preparation (value normalization and missing-value handling) and opening the discussion of evaluation protocols. Neural networks learn more easily from small, homogeneous inputs, ideally standardized per feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1; missing values should be encoded in ways that do not distort the feature space, and the model must be trained on the same kinds of missingness it will see at test time. Every later modeling decision will be guided by validation metrics that estimate generalization. This page completes the **Value normalization** part of section 6.2.1 *Preparing the data*, covers **Handling missing values**, and begins **6.2.2 Choosing an evaluation protocol**.

**Value normalization.** Continuing from p.203 (feeding large or heterogeneous values can trigger large gradient updates that keep the network from converging), the authors list two properties input data should have: values should be *small* (typically mostly in the 0–1 range) and *homogeneous* (all features in roughly the same range). A stricter, common practice — helpful but not always required (the MNIST digit example skipped it) — is to normalize each feature independently to **mean 0** and **standard deviation 1**. With a 2D NumPy matrix of shape `(samples, features)` this takes two lines: `x -= x.mean(axis=0)` and `x /= x.std(axis=0)`.

**Missing values.** Using the house-price example, where the second feature was the median age of houses in a district, the authors ask what to do if that value is unavailable for some samples. Dropping the feature is possible but not required:

- For a **categorical** feature, add a new category meaning "the value is missing"; the model learns what this implies for the targets.
- For a **numerical** feature, do *not* plug in an arbitrary value like 0, which can create a discontinuity in the latent space of features and hurt generalization. Use the feature's mean or median instead, or train a model to predict the missing value from the other features.

A warning follows: if test data will contain missing categorical features but the training data had none, the network has never learned to ignore missing values. The fix is to synthesize training samples with missing entries by copying some samples and dropping the categorical features you expect to be missing at test time.

**6.2.2 Choosing an evaluation protocol** opens by recalling chapter 5: a model exists to generalize, and every modeling decision will be guided by *validation metrics* that seek to measure generalization performance (the sentence continues on p.205, where the three protocols are listed). Input values should be small (mostly 0–1) and homogeneous across features, otherwise large gradient updates can prevent convergence. Standardizing each feature independently to mean 0, std 1 is common and helpful but not always required. In NumPy: `x -= x.mean(axis=0); x /= x.std(axis=0)` for a (samples, features) matrix; compute the statistics on training data. Missing categorical value: add a 'missing' category. Missing numerical value: impute mean or median, or predict it; never an arbitrary 0. If missing values will appear at test time, synthesize them in training by copying samples and dropping those features. Every modeling decision is guided by validation metrics that estimate generalization; choosing the protocol is the next step.

chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Evaluation protocols and beating a baseline
text:
Picking a validation protocol, then building a first small model with statistical power by focusing on features, architecture priors and the training configuration, including choosing a loss function as a proxy for the success metric. The validation protocol exists to estimate the success metric on production data, so pick one of the three chapter-5 protocols (usually hold-out) and keep it representative and free of train/validation duplicates. Then aim for statistical power: a small model that beats a simple baseline, driven by feature engineering, the right architecture priors and a good-enough training configuration. Since success metrics such as ROC AUC often cannot be optimized directly, you train on a differentiable, mini-batch-computable proxy loss such as crossentropy. The page first finishes **6.2.2 Choosing an evaluation protocol**. Its goal is to *accurately estimate what your success metric (e.g. accuracy) will be on actual production data*, and the reliability of that estimate is critical. Chapter 5 gave three protocols:

- **Hold-out validation set**: when you have plenty of data.
- **K-fold cross-validation**: when you have too few samples for hold-out validation to be reliable.
- **Iterated K-fold validation**: for highly accurate evaluation when little data is available.

"Just pick one of these"; in most cases hold-out is good enough. Two cautions recur: keep validation sets **representative**, and avoid **redundant samples** shared between training and validation sets.

**6.2.3 Beating a baseline.** The first goal of modeling is **statistical power** (from chapter 5): a *small* model that beats a simple baseline. At this stage focus on three things:

1. **Feature engineering**: filter out uninformative features (feature selection) and use domain knowledge to build new, likely-useful ones.
2. **Architecture priors**: dense network, ConvNet, RNN, Transformer, or perhaps not deep learning at all.
3. **Training configuration**: loss function, batch size, learning rate.

The sidebar **Picking the right loss function** explains that you often cannot optimize the success metric directly. A loss must be computable from a mini-batch (ideally from a single data point) and differentiable so backpropagation can be used. ROC AUC meets neither requirement, so classification models are trained on a **proxy**, crossentropy, in the hope that lower crossentropy means higher ROC AUC. Table 6.1 (printed on p.206) maps common problem types to a last-layer activation, loss and metrics. A validation protocol's job is to estimate the success metric on production data accurately. Hold-out for plenty of data, K-fold for little data, iterated K-fold for highly accurate evaluation with little data; hold-out usually suffices. Keep validation sets representative and free of samples duplicated from training. First milestone: statistical power, a small model that beats a simple baseline. Focus on feature engineering, architecture priors and a good-enough training configuration. Losses must be mini-batch-computable and differentiable; when the metric is not (e.g. ROC AUC), optimize a proxy such as crossentropy.

title: Evaluation protocol
text: The procedure for estimating a model's success metric on production data from held-out portions of the available data: hold-out, K-fold or iterated K-fold. A measuring instrument for generalization; it must be both unbiased (representative, no leakage) and precise (enough validation samples). Hold-out trains once on a fixed split; K-fold averages K validation scores; iterated K-fold averages over P shuffles × K folds. With 404 house-price samples, K=4 folds instead of a ~100-sample hold-out (p.153).

title: K-fold cross-validation
text: Splitting data into K partitions, training K models each validated on a different partition, and averaging the K scores. Everyone gets a turn being the exam, so the score does not hinge on one lucky or unlucky split. Costs K trainings; reduces the variance of the validation estimate when data is scarce. Iterated K-fold repeats this with reshuffling. K = 4 on the house-price dataset.

text: The loss is the differentiable, mini-batch-computable quantity minimized during training; the metric is the measure of success you report. They often differ. The loss is the steering signal, the metric is the destination. Requirements for a loss: computable from a mini-batch (ideally a single sample) and differentiable. ROC AUC fails both; crossentropy is used as a proxy. Train with binary crossentropy, monitor ROC AUC.
snippet: The loss is the differentiable, mini-batch-computable quantity minimized during training; the metric is the measure of success you report. They often differ.
chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning

title: Crossentropy as a proxy
text: A per-sample, differentiable loss on predicted probabilities, used as a surrogate for classification metrics like ROC AUC. Rewards confident correct probabilities and heavily punishes confident mistakes, which tends to also improve ranking. Binary form: $-[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]$. The book only says that lower crossentropy can be hoped to bring higher ROC AUC; the correlation is not guaranteed. A model whose crossentropy falls from 0.69 to 0.30 will usually rank positives above negatives far more often.
snippet: A per-sample, differentiable loss on predicted probabilities, used as a surrogate for classification metrics like ROC AUC.

title: Table 6.1, prior art, and scaling up to overfit
text:
A lookup table of last-layer activations, losses and metrics per task type; using prior art; what it means when you cannot beat a baseline; and the second milestone, deliberately building a model that overfits. Standard task types have standard output configurations (Table 6.1), and most problems have existing templates. If no reasonable architecture beats a baseline, your hypotheses about the data may be false. Once you do have statistical power, find out how much capacity the problem needs by crossing the underfitting/overfitting border: add layers, widen them, train longer. **Table 6.1** (referenced by the loss-function sidebar on p.205) matches task types to output configurations:

| Task | Last-layer activation | Loss | Metrics |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary classification | Sigmoid | Binary crossentropy | Binary accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Multiclass, single-label | Softmax | Categorical crossentropy | Categorical accuracy, top-k categorical accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Multiclass, multi-label | Sigmoid | Binary crossentropy | Binary accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Regression | None | Mean squared error | Mean absolute error |

The authors then point out that most problems have **existing templates**: you are not the first to build a spam detector, music recommender or image classifier, so research **prior art** to find the feature engineering techniques and architectures most likely to work.

Statistical power is **not always achievable**. If several reasonable architectures fail to beat a simple baseline, the answer may simply not be in the input data. Every project rests on two hypotheses: (1) the outputs can be predicted from the inputs, and (2) the available data is informative enough to learn that relationship. If either is false, go back to the drawing board.

**6.2.4 Scaling up.** With statistical power in hand, ask whether the model is *powerful enough*. A logistic regression model has statistical power on MNIST but is not sufficient to solve it well. The universal tension is between **optimization and generalization**; the ideal model sits right at the border between underfitting and overfitting (undercapacity and overcapacity), and *to find that border you must first cross it*. So deliberately develop a model that overfits, which is easy: **add layers, make the layers bigger, train for more epochs.** (The next page adds: monitor training and validation loss and metrics until validation performance degrades.) Binary: sigmoid + binary crossentropy. Single-label multiclass: softmax + categorical crossentropy. Multi-label: sigmoid + binary crossentropy. Regression: no activation + MSE (monitor MAE). Research prior art; most problems already have templates for features and architectures. If several reasonable architectures cannot beat a baseline, question the two hypotheses: predictability and informativeness of the data. Statistical power is not sufficiency: logistic regression on MNIST has it but is not good enough. The ideal model sits at the underfitting/overfitting border; you find it by crossing it. Overfit deliberately: add layers, widen layers, train for more epochs.

title: Setting expectations and why you export an inference model
text:
Communicating model performance honestly to non-specialist stakeholders (failure modes, concrete false-negative and false-positive rates, threshold choices), and the reasons a trained Python model is usually exported and optimized before production. Half of a project's success is setting appropriate expectations: show failure modes, express performance as concrete error rates and counts tied to business goals rather than an abstract accuracy, and decide launch parameters such as the decision threshold together with stakeholders. On the engineering side, the production model is rarely the same Python object used in training: it may need to run outside Python, and since it only does inference it can be optimized for speed and memory. **6.3.1 Explaining your work to stakeholders and setting expectations.** Customer trust comes from consistently meeting or exceeding expectations, and the delivered system is only half of that; the other half is **setting appropriate expectations before launch**.

Non-specialists often expect an AI system to *understand* its task and apply human-like common sense. Counter this by showing the model's **failure modes**, e.g. misclassified samples, especially surprising ones. They may also expect **human-level performance**, especially where people did the job before. Most models, being imperfectly trained to approximate human-generated labels, do not come close. So communicate performance clearly: avoid statements like "The model has 98% accuracy" (people mentally round this up to 100%) and talk about **false-negative and false-positive rates** instead. The authors' example: *a fraud model with a 5% false-negative rate and a 2.5% false-positive rate; each day about 200 valid transactions would be flagged for manual review, about 14 fraudulent transactions would be missed, and about 266 would be caught.* Relate metrics to business goals.

Discuss **key launch parameters** with stakeholders, such as the probability threshold for flagging a transaction. Different thresholds give different false-negative/false-positive rates, and choosing among them requires deep understanding of the business context.

**6.3.2 Shipping an inference model.** A project does not end with a Colab notebook that saves a trained model; you rarely deploy the exact Python object used in training. First, you may need to **export beyond Python**: the production environment may not support Python (a mobile app, an embedded system), or the rest of the app is in JavaScript, C++ or another language, so serving through Python adds significant overhead. Second, a production model only computes predictions (**inference**), which leaves room for optimizations that make it faster and lighter in memory. The following pages survey deployment options, starting with REST APIs (p.209). Delivering the system is half of success; setting expectations before launch is the other half. Counter 'it understands' expectations by showing failure modes, especially surprising errors. Most models do not reach human-level performance; report false-negative and false-positive rates and concrete counts, not '98% accuracy'. Agree on launch parameters, such as the probability threshold, with stakeholders; they encode business trade-offs. You rarely ship the exact Python training object: export it when production is not Python, and optimize it since it only does inference.

title: Deploying a model as a REST API: export() to SavedModel and ONNX
text:
Serving a model behind a REST API using TensorFlow Serving or ONNX through Keras's export() method, and the conditions under which this setup is appropriate. The easiest way to productize a model is to serve it online via a REST API. Keras supports TensorFlow Serving and ONNX out of the box through model.export(); both lift the weights and the computation graph out of Python, much like the compilation mechanism of chapter 3, so the model can be served from other environments such as a C++ server. Use this setup when the client has reliable internet, latency requirements are loose (about 500 ms round trip), and the input data is not highly sensitive. **Deploying a model as a REST API** is perhaps the easiest way to turn a model into a product. Among the many libraries for this, Keras supports two popular ones out of the box: **TensorFlow Serving** and **ONNX** (Open Neural Network Exchange). Both work by **lifting all model weights and a computation graph out of the Python program**, so the model can be served from other environments, for example a C++ server. This is essentially the **compilation mechanism of chapter 3**: TensorFlow Serving is a library for serving `tf.function` computation graphs with a specific set of saved weights.

Both are reachable through the **`export()`** method available on every Keras model. For TensorFlow Serving:

```python
model.export("path/to/location", format="tf_saved_model")
reloaded_artifact = tf.saved_model.load("path/to/location")
predictions = reloaded_artifact.serve(input_data)
```

The first line exports a TensorFlow SavedModel artifact; the reload lines can run in a different process, environment or programming language. ONNX follows the same flow with `format="onnx"`, then `onnxruntime.InferenceSession(...)` and `ort_session.run(None, input_data)`.

Use REST API deployment when:

- the consuming application has **reliable internet access**. A mobile app served from a remote API will not work in airplane mode or with poor connectivity;
- there are **no strict latency requirements**: request, inference and answer typically take **around 500 ms** round trip;
- the input data is **not highly sensitive**, because it must be available decrypted on the server for the model to see it (still use SSL encryption for the HTTP request and answer).

The next page lists example projects that fit this setup and discusses self-hosting versus managed cloud services, then turns to on-device deployment. Serving via a REST API is perhaps the easiest way to turn a model into a product. title: Weight quantization, monitoring in the wild, and maintaining models
text:
The end of inference optimization (pruning tradeoff, int8 weight quantization with model.quantize), section 6.3.3 on monitoring deployed models (A/B tests, manual audits, user surveys), and the start of 6.3.4 on maintenance under concept drift. Deployment does not end a project. After shrinking the model (pruning, int8 quantization) and shipping it, you must measure its real impact with A/B tests, audits or surveys, and plan for its decay as concept drift erodes performance over days, weeks or years. The page opens by finishing the **weight pruning** bullet from p.211. Keeping only the most significant coefficients reduces the model's memory and compute footprint *at a small cost in performance metrics*, and the amount of pruning lets you control the **size/accuracy tradeoff**.

The second technique is **weight quantization**. Models are trained with `float32` weights, but the weights can be quantized to 8-bit signed integers (`int8`). The result is an inference-only model that is **four times smaller** (1 byte vs. 4 bytes per weight) and *remains near the accuracy of the original*. Keras has a built-in `quantize()` API, and `model.quantize("int8")` compresses each weight to a single byte.

**Section 6.3.3, Monitoring your model in the wild.** Suppose you have exported the model, integrated it, done a dry run on production data, and written unit tests and logging/status-monitoring code, so it is time to "press the big red button". Even then you must keep monitoring the model's behavior, its performance on new data, its interaction with the rest of the application, and its **impact on business metrics**:

- Did user engagement on the online radio go up after the new recommender? Did ad click-through rate rise? Use **randomized A/B testing**: route some cases through the new model and keep a control subset on the old process. With enough cases, the difference in outcomes is likely attributable to the model.
- Where possible, run a regular **manual audit**, reusing the annotation infrastructure: send a fraction of production data to be annotated and compare it with the model's predictions. The book says to definitely do this for the image search engine and the bad-cookie system.
- When audits are impossible, use alternatives such as **user surveys**, e.g., for the spam and offensive-content flagging system.

**Section 6.3.4, Maintaining your model**, begins: *no model lasts forever*. Because of **concept drift** (p.201), production data changes and performance and relevance slowly decay. The book estimates lifespans of *weeks* for the music recommender, *days* for credit card fraud detection, and *a couple of years at best* for the image search engine. Getting ready for the next model generation continues on p.213. The amount of pruning you apply controls the tradeoff between model size and accuracy. int8 quantization makes a model 4× smaller (1 byte vs. 4 per weight) with near-original accuracy; in Keras, call model.quantize("int8"). After launch, monitor behavior, performance on new data, integration with the app, and business metrics. Use randomized A/B tests with a control group to attribute outcome changes to the model. Audit production predictions by reusing the annotation pipeline; use user surveys when audits are impossible (e.g., encrypted chat). Concept drift means no model lasts forever: days for fraud, weeks for music recommendation, a couple of years for image search.
snippet: The page opens by finishing the weight pruning bullet from p.211. Keeping only the most significant coefficients reduces the model's memory and compute footprint at a small cost…

title: Preparing the next model generation and chapter 6 summary
text:
The last maintenance advice (watch production data, keep annotating, focus on hard samples), the authors' closing remarks on the big picture, and the chapter summary of the three-phase universal workflow. Prepare the replacement model as soon as the current one launches: watch for new features and label changes, and keep collecting data, especially hard examples. Model development is only one of three phases (define the task, develop a model, deploy) that make up every ML project. The page finishes section **6.3.4 Maintaining your model**. As soon as a model launches, you should start getting ready to train the **next generation** that will replace it:

- **Watch for changes in production data.** Are new features becoming available? Should the label set be expanded or edited?
- **Keep collecting and annotating data**, and keep improving the annotation pipeline. Pay special attention to **samples that seem difficult for the current model**, because they are the most likely to improve performance.

The authors then close the **universal workflow of machine learning**. It is a lot to keep in mind, and expertise takes time, but the reader now sees the *entire spectrum* of an ML project. Most of the book focuses on model development, which is only one part of the workflow: "Always keep in mind the big picture!"

The **chapter summary** restates the workflow in three phases:

1. **Define the problem**: understand the broader context (end goal, constraints); collect and annotate a dataset and understand it in depth; choose how to measure success and which metrics to monitor on validation data.
2. **Develop a model**: prepare the data; pick an evaluation protocol (hold-out or K-fold, and which portion to use for validation); achieve statistical power by beating a simple baseline; scale up to a model that can overfit; then regularize and tune hyperparameters using validation performance. The authors note that a lot of ML research focuses only on this last step.
3. **Deploy** once the model performs well on the test data: set appropriate expectations with stakeholders; optimize a final model for inference and ship it to the chosen environment (web server, mobile, browser, embedded device, etc.); monitor production performance and keep collecting data for the next generation.

The last step leads back to the first, so the workflow forms a loop. Start preparing the next model generation as soon as the current one launches. Watch production data for new features and needed changes to the label set. Keep collecting and annotating data, prioritizing samples the current model finds difficult. The universal workflow has three phases: define the task, develop a model, deploy it. Development order: prepare data, pick a protocol, beat a baseline, overfit, then regularize and tune. Deployment: set expectations, optimize and ship, then monitor and keep collecting data. Model development is only one part of the big picture.

Opening page of chapter 7: what the chapter covers (ways to build Keras models, built-in training loops with custom metrics/losses, callbacks, TensorBoard, custom training loops) and a recap of the reader's Keras experience so far. This is the opening page of **Chapter 7, "A deep dive on Keras"** (PDF pp. 214–254). The "This chapter covers" box lists five topics:

- **The different ways to create Keras models**: the `Sequential` class, the **Functional API**, and **model subclassing** (section 7.2, from p.216).
- **The built-in Keras training and evaluation loops**, including **custom metrics and custom losses** (section 7.3, from p.230).
- **Keras callbacks** to further customize how training proceeds (p.232–p.234).
- **TensorBoard** for monitoring training and evaluation metrics over time (p.236).
- **Writing your own training and evaluation loops from scratch** (section 7.4, from p.238).

The sentence continues on p.215, which mentions using the gradient APIs of TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch for a step-by-step training loop, and explains that later applications need much more than `Sequential` and the default `fit()`.

**How to use this page:** treat the bullet list as a roadmap. The chapter follows Keras's principle of *progressive disclosure of complexity* (p.215): each section adds flexibility on top of the previous one. You will get the most from it if you are comfortable with `fit()` and custom `Layer` subclasses. Chapter 7 covers three ways to build Keras models: Sequential, Functional API, and model subclassing. It shows how to customize built-in loops with custom metrics, losses and callbacks, and how to monitor them with TensorBoard. It ends with writing training and evaluation loops from scratch. title: A spectrum of workflows: progressive disclosure of complexity
text:
Why chapter 7 is needed, and the design philosophy behind Keras: progressive disclosure of complexity, a spectrum of workflows trading usability for flexibility, shared Layer/Model APIs that let workflows interoperate, and the analogy of Keras as the 'Python of deep learning'. Keras offers no single 'true' workflow but a spectrum, from scikit-learn-like fit() calls to NumPy-like full control. All of them are built on the same Layer and Model abstractions, so you can grow from beginner to expert without switching tools. The page finishes the chapter introduction. In chapter 3 the reader learned to use the gradient APIs of TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch to write a step-by-step training loop. The coming chapters (computer vision, timeseries forecasting, natural language processing, generative deep learning) will need *much more than a `Sequential` architecture and the default `fit()` loop*, so this chapter aims to "turn you into a Keras expert" with a complete overview of the key ways to work with the Keras APIs.

**Section 7.1, A spectrum of workflows**, sets out the design philosophy. Keras is guided by **progressive disclosure of complexity**: getting started should be easy, high-complexity use cases should be *possible*, and each step should require only incremental learning. However niche the goal, there should be a clear path to it that builds on what you learned from simpler workflows, so that you grow from beginner to expert *using the same tools, only in different ways*.

So there is **no single "true" way** to use Keras. There is a **spectrum of workflows**, with different ways to build models and to train them, each a tradeoff between **usability and flexibility**. At one end you use Keras *like scikit-learn*, calling `fit()` and letting the framework work. At the other you use it *like NumPy*, controlling every detail.

All the workflows rest on **shared APIs such as `Layer` and `Model`**, so components from any workflow can be used in any other, and *they can all talk to each other*. What you learn as a beginner stays relevant as an expert, and you can move gradually toward writing more logic from scratch without switching frameworks, whether going from student to researcher or from data scientist to deep learning engineer.

The authors compare this to **Python**. Some languages support only one paradigm, such as object-oriented or functional programming, while Python is *multiparadigm*, with usage patterns that work well together. That makes it suitable for system administration, data science, ML engineering, web development and learning to program. Likewise, Keras is "**the Python of deep learning**": a user-friendly deep learning language with workflows for different user profiles. Section 7.2 (p.216) then presents the three model-building APIs. Later application chapters need more than Sequential and the default fit(), which is why chapter 7 exists. Keras follows progressive disclosure of complexity: easy to start, anything possible, incremental learning at each step. There is no single true way to use Keras, but a spectrum of workflows trading usability for flexibility. You can use Keras like scikit-learn (just fit()) or like NumPy (full control). Shared Layer and Model APIs let components from any workflow interoperate. Keras is 'the Python of deep learning': multiparadigm and user-friendly.

title: Three ways to build Keras models; the Sequential class
text:
The three model-building APIs in Keras (Sequential, Functional, Model subclassing) arranged along a spectrum of complexity, and the first of them, the Sequential model. Keras offers three model-building APIs that trade usability for flexibility: Sequential (a list of layers), the Functional API (graphs of layers, the most commonly used), and Model subclassing (write everything yourself). Section 7.2.1 starts with the simplest, keras.Sequential. Section 7.2 opens by listing the **three APIs for building models in Keras**:

- **The Sequential model** – the most approachable API; "basically a Python list" of layers. Because it is a list, it can only express *simple stacks of layers*.
- **The Functional API** – focuses on *graph-like* architectures. It is a "nice mid-point between usability and flexibility" and is therefore **the most commonly used** model-building API.
- **Model subclassing** – a low-level option in which you write everything yourself. You get full control, but you lose access to many built-in Keras features and are more at risk of making mistakes.

**Figure 7.1** draws these on a single arrow labelled *progressive disclosure of complexity*: Sequential API + built-in layers (novice users, simple models) → Functional API + built-in layers (engineers with standard use cases) → Functional API + custom layers, custom metrics, custom losses, … (engineers with niche use cases requiring bespoke solutions) → Subclassing: write everything yourself from scratch (researchers). The point is that it is one continuum: you move right only as far as your problem requires.

Subsection **7.2.1** then starts with the Sequential model, "which you already know about". **Listing 7.1** builds a `keras.Sequential` from a Python list of two layers: `Dense(64, activation="relu")` followed by `Dense(10, activation="softmax")` — a small 10-class classifier. Notice no input shape is given, which becomes important on the next page (p.217): the model has no weights yet.

The page closes by noting that the same model can be built **incrementally** with the `add()` method, just as you would `append()` to a Python list (Listing 7.2 on p.217). Keras has three model-building APIs: Sequential, Functional, and Model subclassing. Sequential is basically a list of layers: easy, but limited to simple stacks. The Functional API handles graph-like models and is the most commonly used. Subclassing gives full control but loses built-in features and raises the risk of mistakes. Figure 7.1 orders these along progressive disclosure of complexity; custom components can still live in the Functional API. Listing 7.1 defines a 64-relu / 10-softmax Sequential model; add() builds the same thing incrementally.

title: Building a Sequential model incrementally; deferred weight creation; summary()
text:
Incremental construction with add(), why an unbuilt model has no weights, building it with build(input_shape=...), and inspecting it with summary(). Layer weights depend on input shape, so a Sequential model without a declared input shape has no weights until it is called on data or built with build(); once built, summary() shows each layer's output shape and parameter count. **Listing 7.2** builds the model of Listing 7.1 incrementally: start from an empty `keras.Sequential()` and call `model.add(...)` twice with the same two `Dense` layers.

The text then recalls a fact from chapter 3: **layers are built — i.e. create their weights — only when they are called for the first time**, because the *shape of the weights depends on the shape of the input*. A `Dense(64)` layer needs a kernel of shape `(input_dim, 64)`, and `input_dim` is unknown until data arrives. Consequently the Sequential model just defined has **no weights**: **Listing 7.3** shows `model.weights` returning `[]` (callout: "At that point, the model isn't built yet").

To create them you either call the model on data or call **`build()`** with an input shape. **Listing 7.4** runs `model.build(input_shape=(None, 3))`. The callout explains that the model now expects samples of shape `(3,)`, and that `None` means the batch size can be anything. `model.weights` now lists four variables: kernel `(3, 64)`, bias `(64,)`, kernel `(64, 10)`, bias `(10,)`.

Once built, **`summary()`** (Listing 7.5) displays the model's contents — handy for debugging. The table for model `"sequential_1"` shows `dense_2 (Dense)` with output `(None, 64)` and 256 parameters, and `dense_3 (Dense)` with output `(None, 10)` and 650 parameters: **906 total parameters (3.54 KB)**, all trainable. These numbers follow directly from the weight shapes: $3\cdot64+64=256$ and $64\cdot10+10=650$. add() builds a Sequential model incrementally, like list.append(). Layers create weights only when the input shape is known — at first call or via build(). An unbuilt model has model.weights == []. build(input_shape=(None, 3)): None is the batch axis, 3 features per sample. summary() works only on a built model and shows output shapes and parameter counts (256 + 650 = 906).

title: Naming models and layers; declaring the input shape with keras.Input
text:
Giving explicit names to models and layers via the name argument, and making a Sequential model build on the fly by declaring keras.Input(shape=...) first. Every Keras model and layer can be named; and if you add a keras.Input with the per-sample shape at the start of a Sequential model, it is built immediately, so you can call summary() after each add() to watch shapes evolve. The page continues the Sequential-model walkthrough with two practical tools.

**1. Naming.** The summary on p.217 showed an auto-generated name, `sequential_1`. In Keras you can name *everything* — every model, every layer — with the `name` argument. **Listing 7.6** creates `keras.Sequential(name="my_example_model")`, adds `Dense(64, activation="relu", name="my_first_layer")` and `Dense(10, activation="softmax", name="my_last_layer")`, builds it with `model.build((None, 3))` and prints a summary. The table is identical to Listing 7.5 (256 + 650 = 906 parameters, 3.54 KB) except that the model and layers now carry the chosen names.

**2. Declaring the input shape in advance.** When building incrementally, you'd like to print a summary after each `add()` — but a summary needs a built model. The fix is to tell the model its input shape up front with the **`Input` class**. **Listing 7.7** does `model.add(keras.Input(shape=(3,)))` before adding `Dense(64, activation="relu")`. The callout stresses that `shape` must be **the shape of each sample, not the shape of one batch** — so `(3,)`, not `(None, 3)` as in `build()`.

Because the input shape is known, each added layer is built immediately, and `summary()` works at any point. The output shown, for model `"sequential_2"`, lists just `dense_4 (Dense)` with output `(None, 64)` and 256 parameters (`Total params: 256 (1.00 KB)`). The next page (p.219) continues by adding the 10-unit layer and noting that this is a common debugging workflow for layers that transform shapes in complex ways, such as the convolutional layers of chapter 8. Every Keras model and layer can be given a name via name=. summary() requires a built model. Adding keras.Input(shape=...) first makes a Sequential model build as you add layers. Input's shape is per sample (3,), not per batch. Use summary() after each add() to track output shapes.

title: Symbolic tensors and the Model constructor
text:
Step-by-step explanation of Listing 7.8: what a symbolic tensor is, how layers called on symbolic tensors return new symbolic tensors, and how keras.Model is built from inputs and outputs. keras.Input returns a symbolic tensor — a data-free placeholder carrying shape and dtype that stands for future tensors. Calling layers on symbolic tensors produces new symbolic tensors with updated shapes, and keras.Model(inputs, outputs) captures the resulting graph of layers. This page walks through Listing 7.8 line by line.

**The input.** `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(3,), name="my_input")` produces an object that holds the **shape** and **dtype** of the data the model will process: `inputs.shape` is `(None, 3)` and `inputs.dtype` is `"float32"`. The callouts explain: the model will process batches where each sample has shape `(3,)`, the number of samples per batch is variable (the `None`), and the batches will have dtype float32.

The book calls this a **symbolic tensor**: it *doesn't contain any actual data*, but it *encodes the specifications* of the actual data tensors the model will see. It *stands for* future tensors of data.

**Calling a layer.** `features = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")(inputs)` creates a layer and calls it on the input. **All Keras layers can be called on real tensors or on symbolic tensors**; on a symbolic tensor they return **a new symbolic tensor with updated shape and dtype**, so `features.shape` is `(None, 64)`.

**Building the model.** After getting the final `outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)`, the model is created with `keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs, name="my_functional_model")`.

**The summary** of `"my_functional_model"` lists three rows: `my_input (InputLayer)` `(None, 3)` with **0** parameters, `dense_8 (Dense)` `(None, 64)` 256, and `dense_9 (Dense)` `(None, 10)` 650. Unlike the Sequential summaries on pp.217-219, the Functional summary shows the input as its own `InputLayer` row; the named input appears as `my_input`. keras.Input returns a symbolic tensor with shape (None, 3) and dtype float32. A symbolic tensor holds no data; it stands for future tensors. Layers called on symbolic tensors return new symbolic tensors with updated shape/dtype. keras.Model(inputs=..., outputs=...) defines the model by its endpoints. The Functional summary includes an InputLayer row with 0 parameters.

title: Multi-input, multi-output models: the ticket-routing example
text:
A Functional model with three inputs (ticket title, body, tags) and two outputs (priority score, department), built with Input, Concatenate and Dense layers. Most real models look like graphs, not lists. The Functional API expresses them directly: declare several Inputs, merge them with Concatenate, transform with a shared Dense layer, and branch into several output heads with different activations. The page opens with the totals of the `my_functional_model` summary from p.220: **906 total params (3.54 KB)**, all trainable.

**Multi-input, multi-output models.** Unlike that toy model, *most deep learning models don't look like lists — they look like graphs*: they may have multiple inputs or multiple outputs, and this is where the Functional API *really shines*.

The running example is a system that **ranks customer support tickets by priority and routes them to the appropriate department**. It has **three inputs**:

- the ticket **title** (text),
- the ticket **text body** (text),
- user-added **tags** (categorical, assumed multi-hot encoded).

The text inputs are encoded as arrays of 1s and 0s of size `vocabulary_size` (text encoding is covered in chapter 14). And **two outputs**:

- a **priority score**, a scalar between 0 and 1 (**sigmoid** output),
- the **department** that should handle the ticket (a **softmax** over the set of departments).

**Listing 7.9** builds it in a few lines. With `vocabulary_size = 10000`, `num_tags = 100`, `num_departments = 4`, it declares three named `keras.Input`s (`title` and `text_body` of shape `(10000,)`, `tags` of shape `(100,)`); combines them into a single tensor with `layers.Concatenate()([title, text_body, tags])`; applies an intermediate `Dense(64, activation="relu", name="dense_features")` to *recombine input features into richer representations*; and defines two output heads on those shared features: `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid", name="priority")` and `Dense(num_departments, activation="softmax", name="department")`. The listing continues on the next page (p.222), where the model object is created from these inputs and outputs. Most real models are graphs; the Functional API shines for multiple inputs and outputs. The ticket model has three inputs (title, body, tags) and two outputs (priority, department). Text and tags are multi-hot encoded; vocabulary_size = 10000, num_tags = 100. Concatenate merges inputs into one feature tensor; a shared Dense(64, relu) recombines them. priority uses a 1-unit sigmoid head; department a 4-unit softmax head. title: Training a multi-input, multi-output Functional model with lists
text:
Finishing the ticket-routing model of Listing 7.9 and training, evaluating and running it with fit(), evaluate() and predict() by passing lists of input and target arrays whose order matches the Model() constructor. A Functional model is created by naming its input and output tensors; once built, a multi-input, multi-output model is compiled and trained exactly like a Sequential model, except that losses, metrics, inputs and targets are given as lists aligned with the order of the model's inputs and outputs. The page opens with the last statement of **Listing 7.9**: `keras.Model(inputs=[title, text_body, tags], outputs=[priority, department])`. Everything before it (on p.221) defined three `keras.Input` objects (`title` and `text_body` of shape `(vocabulary_size,)` = 10,000, `tags` of shape `(num_tags,)` = 100), concatenated them, passed them through a 64-unit `Dense` layer, and attached two heads: a 1-unit sigmoid `priority` and a 4-way softmax `department`. Handing the start and end tensors to `keras.Model` turns this graph of layer calls into a model. The authors sum up: the Functional API is a "simple, LEGO-like, yet very flexible way to define arbitrary graphs of layers."

Under the heading **Training a multi-input, multi-output model**, the book explains that training works "in much the same way" as for a Sequential model: you call `fit()` with **lists** of input data and output data, and the lists must follow the same order as the `inputs` and `outputs` lists given to `Model()`.

**Listing 7.10** makes this concrete with random data for 1,280 samples: binary (0/1) matrices for the two text inputs and the tags, uniform random floats in [0, 1) for the priority target, and integer class ids in `[0, num_departments)` for the department target. `compile()` receives a list of two losses (`"mean_squared_error"` for the regression-like priority head, `"sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` for the integer-labelled department head) and a nested list of metrics (`[["mean_absolute_error"], ["accuracy"]]`), one inner list per output. `fit()` runs one epoch, `evaluate()` takes the same two lists, and `predict()` takes only the input list and returns one array per output, unpacked into `priority_preds, department_preds`.

The page closes by noting that relying on order becomes awkward with many inputs or outputs; instead you can use the **names** given to the `Input` objects and output layers and pass data as dictionaries, which Listing 7.11 shows on p.223. A Functional model is created with keras.Model(inputs=..., outputs=...) from symbolic tensors. Multi-input, multi-output models are trained with the same fit() call, using lists of arrays. Data lists, losses and metric lists must follow the order of inputs/outputs given to Model(). Each output gets its own loss and metrics; Keras optimizes their sum. predict() returns one array per output. Names on Inputs and output layers allow dict-based feeding instead of positional lists.

title: Listing 7.10 Training a model by providing lists of input and target arrays
text:
import numpy as np

num_samples = 1280

title_data = np.random.randint(0, 2, size=(num_samples, vocabulary_size))
text_body_data = np.random.randint(0, 2, size=(num_samples, vocabulary_size))
tags_data = np.random.randint(0, 2, size=(num_samples, num_tags))

priority_data = np.random.random(size=(num_samples, 1))
department_data = np.random.randint(0, num_departments, size=(num_samples, 1))

model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=["mean_squared_error", "sparse_categorical_crossentropy"],
    metrics=[["mean_absolute_error"], ["accuracy"]],
)
model.fit(
    [title_data, text_body_data, tags_data],
    [priority_data, department_data],
    epochs=1,
)
model.evaluate(
    [title_data, text_body_data, tags_data], [priority_data, department_data]
)
priority_preds, department_preds = model.predict(
    [title_data, text_body_data, tags_data]
) Generates dummy inputs and targets for 1,280 tickets, compiles the model with per-output losses and metrics, trains for one epoch, evaluates, and gets predictions for both heads. Mini-batch gradient descent with Adam on the sum of the two losses.

title: Training with dicts, and the Functional model as an inspectable graph
text:
Listing 7.11 trains the ticket model with name-keyed dictionaries; then the page introduces the key advantage of Functional models, access to layer connectivity, starting with plotting the model graph via keras.utils.plot_model(). Because inputs and output layers are named, losses, metrics, inputs and targets can be passed as dictionaries keyed by those names. More generally, a Functional model is an explicit graph data structure, which lets you inspect connectivity, visualize it, and reuse intermediate nodes in new models. **Listing 7.11** repeats Listing 7.10 (p.222) but replaces every positional list with a dictionary keyed by names that were assigned in Listing 7.9 (p.221). In `compile()`, `loss` is `{"priority": "mean_squared_error", "department": "sparse_categorical_crossentropy"}` and `metrics` is `{"priority": ["mean_absolute_error"], "department": ["accuracy"]}`. `fit()` and `evaluate()` receive an input dict `{"title": ..., "text_body": ..., "tags": ...}` and a target dict `{"priority": ..., "department": ...}`; `predict()` receives the input dict and the two predictions are still unpacked as `priority_preds, department_preds`. Input keys match the `name=` of each `keras.Input`; output keys match the `name=` of the output layers.

Under **The power of the Functional API: Access to layer connectivity**, the authors explain that a Functional model is an *explicit graph data structure*. You can therefore *inspect how layers are connected* and *reuse previous graph nodes* (layer outputs) in new models. This matches the mental model most researchers have of a deep network: a graph of layers. Two use cases follow: **model visualization** and **feature extraction**.

**Plotting layer connectivity** begins: you can plot the topology of the model with `keras.utils.plot_model(model, "ticket_classifier.png")`. **Figure 7.2** shows the result for the ticket classifier: three `InputLayer` boxes feed a `Concatenate` box, which feeds one `Dense` box, which branches into two `Dense` boxes (the priority and department heads). The default plot shows only layer types; the next page (p.224) adds names and shapes. Losses, metrics, inputs and targets can all be passed as dicts keyed by input/output names. Dict keys come from name= on keras.Input and on the output layers. A Functional model is an explicit graph data structure that can be inspected and partially reused. This enables model visualization and feature extraction. keras.utils.plot_model(model, file) draws the model topology (figure 7.2).
