title: Plotting shapes, and the start of feature extraction
text:
Adding shapes and layer names to plot_model output (figure 7.3), the meaning of None in shapes, and the start of feature extraction via model.layers, layer.input and layer.output (Listing 7.12). plot_model(show_shapes=True, show_layer_names=True) turns the topology plot into a debugging tool showing every layer's name and input/output shapes; and because a Functional model's connectivity is accessible, you can list its layers and query each layer's input and output tensors for reuse. The page continues the plotting discussion from p.223. Passing `show_shapes=True` and `show_layer_names=True` to `keras.utils.plot_model(model, "ticket_classifier_with_shape_info.png", ...)` adds each layer's name (rather than just its type) and its input and output shapes, which "can be helpful during debugging."

**Figure 7.3** shows the result: `title (InputLayer)` with output shape `(None, 10000)`, `text_body (InputLayer)` `(None, 10000)`, and `tags (InputLayer)` `(None, 100)` feed `concatenate (Concatenate)`, whose input shape is the list `[(None, 10000), (None, 10000), (None, 100)]` and whose output is `(None, 20100)`. Next comes `dense_10 (Dense)`, `(None, 20100) -> (None, 64)`, which branches into `priority (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 1)` and `department (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 4)`. Note that the shared Dense layer appears as `dense_10`, a name Keras generated automatically. That is odd at first sight, because Listing 7.9 (p.221) passes `name="dense_features"`. The authors do not explain the mismatch; the plot was most likely made from an earlier version of the code.

The authors explain that `None` in the shapes is the batch size: the model accepts batches of any size.

The new subsection **Feature extraction with a Functional model** states that access to connectivity also lets you inspect and reuse individual nodes (layer calls). `model.layers` gives the list of layers in the model, and for each layer you can query `layer.input` and `layer.output`. **Listing 7.12** starts here: `>>> model.layers` prints a list beginning with `<InputLayer name=title, built=True>`. The rest of the output, including `model.layers[3].input` and `.output`, is on p.225. show_shapes=True and show_layer_names=True make plot_model a debugging tool. Figure 7.3 confirms 10000+10000+100 = 20100 features, then 64, then heads of size 1 and 4. None in a shape is the batch size, so any batch size is allowed. model.layers lists all layers (including InputLayer); layer.input and layer.output give their symbolic tensors. These tensors can be reused to build new models (feature extraction).

title: Feature extraction: adding a difficulty head to the ticket model
text:
The rest of Listing 7.12 (querying model.layers, layer.input and layer.output), the definition of feature extraction, and Listing 7.13, which builds a new three-output model by attaching a difficulty classifier to the intermediate Dense layer's output. Because a Functional model's intermediate tensors are accessible, you can create new models that reuse them. To add a three-way 'difficulty' prediction you just take model.layers[4].output, put a new softmax Dense on it, and build keras.Model(inputs=[...], outputs=[priority, department, difficulty]); there is no need to recreate and retrain the model from scratch. The page first completes **Listing 7.12**. `model.layers` lists seven layers in graph order: the three `InputLayer`s (`title`, `text_body`, `tags`), `Concatenate` (`concatenate`), `Dense` (`dense_10`), and the two head `Dense` layers `priority` and `department`. `model.layers[3]` is the Concatenate layer. Its `.input` is a **list** of three `KerasTensor`s with shapes `(None, 10000)`, `(None, 10000)` and `(None, 100)` (named `title`, `text_body`, `tags`), and its `.output` is a single `KerasTensor` of shape `(None, 20100)`, dtype `float32`.

The authors then name the technique: **feature extraction**, creating models that reuse intermediate features from another model. Their example: you also want to predict how long a ticket will take to resolve, a difficulty rating that is a classification over three categories ("quick," "medium," "difficult"). You don't need to recreate and retrain a model from scratch, because you can start from the intermediate features of the previous model.

**Listing 7.13** does this in three statements. `features = model.layers[4].output` (the callout notes that `layers[4]` is the intermediate Dense layer) picks out the 64-dimensional shared representation. `difficulty = layers.Dense(3, activation="softmax", name="difficulty")(features)` adds a new head. `new_model = keras.Model(inputs=[title, text_body, tags], outputs=[priority, department, difficulty])` creates a three-output model from the original input tensors, the two existing heads, and the new one. The page ends with the `plot_model` call that produces figure 7.4 (`"updated_ticket_classifier.png"`, with shapes and layer names). The figure itself is on p.226. model.layers[3] is Concatenate; its input is a list of 3 tensors and its output is (None, 20100). Feature extraction = building models that reuse intermediate features of another model. Listing 7.13 adds a 3-class difficulty head on model.layers[4].output, the shared Dense layer. new_model reuses the original inputs and heads; no rebuilding from scratch. The reused layers share weights with the original model.

title: Figure 7.4 and the start of Model subclassing
text:
The plot of the extended three-head ticket model (figure 7.4), then the introduction of the third model-building pattern, subclassing keras.Model, with the beginning of Listing 7.14, which reimplements the ticket model as a CustomerTicketModel class. Subclassing Model works like subclassing Layer: create sublayers in __init__(), define the forward pass in call() reusing those layers, then instantiate and call the object on data to create its weights. Listing 7.14 rebuilds the ticket model this way. **Figure 7.4** plots `new_model` from Listing 7.13 (p.225). The top is the same as figure 7.3: `title`, `text_body` and `tags` InputLayers `(None, 10000)`, `(None, 10000)`, `(None, 100)` feed `concatenate` `(None, 20100)`, then `dense_10` `(None, 64)`. The shared Dense layer now fans out into **three** heads: `priority (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 1)`, `department (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 4)`, and the new `difficulty (Dense)` `(None, 64) -> (None, 3)`.

Section **7.2.3 Subclassing the Model class** introduces the last and most advanced pattern. It resembles the `Layer` subclassing from chapter 3:

- in `__init__()`, define the layers the model will use;
- in `call()`, define the forward pass, reusing the layers created earlier;
- instantiate the subclass and call it on data to create its weights.

Under **Rewriting our previous example as a subclassed model**, the authors reimplement the customer-support ticket model. **Listing 7.14** begins with `class CustomerTicketModel(keras.Model)`. The constructor takes `num_departments`, calls `super().__init__()` (callout: "Don't forget to call the super constructor!"), and defines four sublayers (callout: "Defines sublayers in the constructor"): `concat_layer = layers.Concatenate()`, `mixing_layer = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")`, `priority_scorer = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` and `department_classifier = layers.Dense(num_departments, activation="softmax")`. The method `call(self, inputs)` (callout: "Defines the forward pass in the call() method") starts with `title = inputs["title"]`. The rest of the forward pass continues on p.227.

Notice what is missing compared with the Functional version: no `keras.Input` objects and no input shapes. The model learns its input shapes only when first called on data. Figure 7.4: the shared (None, 64) Dense output now feeds three heads, including difficulty (None, 3). Model subclassing: layers in __init__(), forward pass in call(), weights created on first call. Always call super().__init__() in the constructor. CustomerTicketModel mirrors the Functional ticket model layer for layer. No Inputs or input shapes are declared in a subclassed model.

title: Finishing the subclassed ticket model; Layer vs Model; training it
text:
The rest of CustomerTicketModel.call(), instantiating the model and creating its weights by calling it on data, the difference between a Layer subclass and a Model subclass, and compiling and fitting the subclassed model with structures that match what call() expects and returns. A subclassed model creates its weights the first time it is called on data. It differs from a Layer mainly in being the top-level object you train and export: it has fit(), evaluate() and predict() (and can be saved). It is compiled and trained like any other model, but the structure of the losses, metrics, inputs and targets must match exactly what call() consumes and returns. The page completes **Listing 7.14**. After reading `title` (p.226), `call()` reads `text_body = inputs["text_body"]` and `tags = inputs["tags"]`. It then computes `features = self.concat_layer([title, text_body, tags])` and `features = self.mixing_layer(features)`, applies the two heads (`priority = self.priority_scorer(features)`, `department = self.department_classifier(features)`), and ends with `return priority, department`. This is exactly the computation of the Functional model of Listing 7.9, written as imperative code.

The model is instantiated with `model = CustomerTicketModel(num_departments=4)`. The authors note that it only creates its weights the first time you call it on some data, much like `Layer` subclasses. The example calls it on the dict `{"title": title_data, "text_body": text_body_data, "tags": tags_data}` and gets `priority, department`.

What distinguishes a `Layer` subclass from a `Model` subclass? A **layer** is a building block you use to create models; a **model** is the top-level object that you actually train, export for inference, and so on. In short, a `Model` has `fit()`, `evaluate()` and `predict()`; layers don't. Otherwise the two classes are "virtually identical," except that a model can also be saved to a file on disk, which is covered a few sections later.

Finally, the subclassed model is compiled and trained like a Sequential or Functional model: `loss=["mean_squared_error", "sparse_categorical_crossentropy"]`, `metrics=[["mean_absolute_error"], ["accuracy"]]`, and `fit()` with a dict of inputs and a list `[priority_data, department_data]` of targets for one epoch. The two callouts state the rule. The structure of loss and metrics must match exactly what `call()` returns (two elements, so lists of two). The input data must match what `call()` expects (a dict with keys `title`, `text_body`, `tags`), and the target data must match what it returns (a list of two elements). call() of CustomerTicketModel reproduces the Functional ticket model's computation and returns (priority, department). Subclassed models create their weights on the first call on data. Layer = building block; Model = top-level object with fit(), evaluate(), predict() and saving. Subclassed models are compiled and trained like any other model. Loss, metrics and targets must match call()'s output structure; inputs must match what call() expects.

title: Limits of subclassed models; mixing model-building styles
text:
What Model subclassing gains and loses compared with the Functional API, and how the three model-building styles interoperate A subclassed model is arbitrary Python code rather than an inspectable graph of layers: that buys unlimited flexibility (loops, recursion) at the cost of debugging burden, summary()/plot_model() connectivity, and feature extraction. None of this locks you in, because Sequential, Functional and subclassed components can be freely nested inside each other. The page opens by finishing the `CustomerTicketModel` example from p.226-227. After compiling and fitting the subclassed model, you call `model.evaluate()` with the same dict of three inputs (`title`, `text_body`, `tags`) and the list of two targets (`priority_data`, `department_data`), and `model.predict()` with just the input dict, which returns a pair of arrays that unpack into `priority_preds` and `department_preds`. The structures must match what `call()` consumes and returns.

The authors then step back. **Model subclassing is the most flexible workflow**: since the forward pass is ordinary Python, it can express models that are *not* directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of layers, for example a `call()` that applies layers in a `for` loop or calls them recursively.

The sidebar **"Beware: What subclassed models don't support"** lists the price:

- You own more of the model logic, so the *error surface* is larger and you will debug more: "you are developing a new Python object, not just snapping together LEGO bricks."
- A Functional model is an **explicit data structure**, a graph of layers you can view, inspect and modify. A subclassed model is **bytecode**: a class whose `call()` contains raw code.
- Because connectivity lives inside `call()`, Keras cannot see it. `summary()` will not show how layers connect, `plot_model()` cannot draw the topology, and you cannot reach intermediate nodes for **feature extraction**, "because there is simply no graph." After instantiation the forward pass is a **black box**.

Section **7.2.4** then makes the reassuring point that picking one pattern doesn't lock you out of the others. Sequential models, Functional models and subclassed models or layers all interoperate as parts of one *spectrum of workflows* (p.215). The first example is a subclassed component used inside a Functional model. **Listing 7.15** begins here with `class Classifier(keras.Model)` and its `__init__(self, num_classes=2)` calling `super().__init__()`. The rest of the listing, which chooses sigmoid or softmax and wires the class into a Functional graph, is on p.229. Subclassed models support evaluate() and predict() with the same input/target structure rules as fit(). Subclassing can express non-DAG models (loops, recursion) that the Functional API cannot. The cost is more of your own logic to debug, plus no connectivity in summary(), no plot_model() topology and no intermediate-node feature extraction. Functional model = inspectable data structure; subclassed model = opaque code in call(). Sequential, Functional and subclassed components interoperate. Listing 7.15 (continued on p.229) puts a subclassed model inside a Functional one.

title: Nesting subclassed and Functional models; choosing a workflow
text:
Two directions of interoperability (subclassed inside Functional, Functional inside subclassed) and the recommendation to prefer the Functional API Listing 7.15 completes a subclassed Classifier and drops it into a Functional model like any layer. Listing 7.16 does the reverse, using a Functional model as a component of a subclassed model. Given the choice, prefer the Functional API whenever the model is a DAG of layers, because it balances ease of use with flexibility and exposes layer connectivity. The page opens with the rest of **Listing 7.15** (started on p.228). The `Classifier(keras.Model)` constructor picks its output head from `num_classes`. With 2 classes it uses **1 unit with a sigmoid** (binary classification). Otherwise it uses **`num_classes` units with a softmax**. It stores the result as `self.dense = layers.Dense(num_units, activation=activation)`, and `call()` just returns `self.dense(inputs)`. The class is then used inside a **Functional** model: `keras.Input(shape=(3,))` → `layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")` → `Classifier(num_classes=10)` → `keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)`. The subclassed model is called on a symbolic tensor exactly as a built-in layer would be.

"Inversely, you can use a Functional model as part of a subclassed layer or model." **Listing 7.16** first builds a tiny Functional model, `binary_classifier`, that maps a `(64,)` input to one sigmoid unit. It then defines `MyModel(keras.Model)`, which creates `self.dense = layers.Dense(64, activation="relu")` and stores `self.classifier = binary_classifier` in `__init__`, and chains them in `call()`. `model = MyModel()` instantiates it. Weights are created on the first call.

Section **7.2.5, "Remember: Use the right tool for the job,"** wraps up the model-building spectrum from Sequential, the simplest, to subclassing, the most advanced. Each has pros and cons. In general **the Functional API offers a good trade-off between ease of use and flexibility** and gives **direct access to layer connectivity**, which helps with model plotting and feature extraction. The rule: *if you can* use the Functional API, meaning the model can be expressed as a directed acyclic graph of layers, the authors recommend it over subclassing. The discussion continues on p.230, where the book commits to Functional models with subclassed layers. A subclassed model can be called on symbolic tensors inside a Functional model (Listing 7.15). A Functional model can be assigned as an attribute and called inside a subclassed model's call() (Listing 7.16). Classifier picks 1 sigmoid unit for 2 classes and num_classes softmax units otherwise. Choose the API that fits the job. If the model is a DAG of layers, prefer the Functional API. The Functional API's advantage is direct access to layer connectivity, used for plotting and feature extraction.

title: Functional API as default; the standard training workflow
text:
The book's choice of Functional models with subclassed layers, and the compile/fit/evaluate/predict workflow as the simplest point on the training spectrum From here on the book uses Functional models, often containing subclassed layers, for the best of both worlds. Training follows the same progressive disclosure of complexity as model building, and its simplest form is Listing 7.17's compile() → fit() → evaluate() → predict() on MNIST. The page first closes section 7.2. **From now on, every example in the book uses the Functional API**, because every model the book builds is expressible as a graph of layers, while making frequent use of **subclassed layers**. Functional models with subclassed layers inside give "the best of both worlds": high development flexibility while keeping the Functional API's advantages, such as layer connectivity for plotting and feature extraction (p.229).

Section **7.3, "Using built-in training and evaluation loops,"** applies the principle of **progressive disclosure of complexity** to training. Model building ranged from Sequential to subclassing. Training likewise ranges from just calling `fit()` to writing a brand-new training algorithm from scratch (the later part of the chapter, 7.4).

As a reminder of the simplest end, **Listing 7.17** shows the standard workflow on MNIST:

- `get_mnist_model()` builds a Functional model: `Input(shape=(28*28,))` → `Dense(512, relu)` → `Dropout(0.5)` → `Dense(10, softmax)`. It is wrapped in a function "so as to reuse it later."
- The data is loaded with `mnist.load_data()`, flattened to 784-vectors and scaled to [0, 1] by dividing the `float32` values by 255. The first 10,000 training images are **reserved for validation**, leaving 50,000 for training. The 10,000 test images are kept separate.
- `compile()` specifies the **optimizer** (`"adam"`), the **loss** to minimize (`"sparse_categorical_crossentropy"`, for integer labels) and the **metrics** to monitor (`["accuracy"]`).
- `fit()` trains for 3 epochs, with `validation_data` used to monitor performance on unseen data.
- `evaluate()` computes loss and metrics on new data. `predict()` returns class probabilities for new data.

The next page (p.231) lists the first two ways to customize this workflow: custom metrics and callbacks. The book uses Functional models with subclassed layers from here on: flexibility plus Functional advantages. Training also follows progressive disclosure of complexity, from fit() to custom training algorithms. Listing 7.17 is the baseline: get_mnist_model(), a 50k/10k/10k data split, compile(adam, sparse CCE, accuracy), fit(3 epochs, validation_data), evaluate(), predict(). get_mnist_model() is a function so later sections can get a fresh model. predict() returns class probabilities; evaluate() returns loss and metrics.

title: Listing 7.17 Listing 7.17: The standard workflow: compile(), fit(), evaluate(), predict()
text:
from keras.datasets import mnist

def get_mnist_model():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))
    features = layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")(inputs)
    features = layers.Dropout(0.5)(features)
    outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
    model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
    return model

(images, labels), (test_images, test_labels) = mnist.load_data()
images = images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28)).astype("float32") / 255
test_images = test_images.reshape((10000, 28 * 28)).astype("float32") / 255
train_images, val_images = images[10000:], images[:10000]
train_labels, val_labels = labels[10000:], labels[:10000]

model = get_mnist_model()
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
model.fit(
    train_images,
    train_labels,
    epochs=3,
    validation_data=(val_images, val_labels),
)
test_metrics = model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)
predictions = model.predict(test_images) Defines a reusable Functional MNIST classifier, prepares the data with a validation split, then compiles, trains, evaluates and predicts. Mini-batch gradient descent with Adam minimizing crossentropy, with validation metrics computed at the end of each epoch.

title: Customizing fit(); writing a custom RMSE metric
text:
Two ways to customize the built-in workflow (custom metrics, callbacks), and how a custom metric is implemented as a stateful keras.metrics.Metric subclass A Keras metric is a Layer-like object holding state in Keras variables. Since that state is not learned by backpropagation, you write the update yourself in update_state(). The example RootMeanSquaredError accumulates the summed squared error and the sample count across batches. The page lists **two ways to customize** the simple workflow of Listing 7.17 (p.230):

- by providing your own **custom metrics**, and
- by passing ***callbacks*** to `fit()` to schedule actions at specific points during training (section 7.3.2, p.232).

**7.3.1 Writing your own metrics.** Metrics measure model performance, and in particular the gap between performance on the training data and on the test data. Common classification and regression metrics are built into `keras.metrics`, and most of the time you'll use those. For anything out of the ordinary you'll need your own, and "it's simple!"

A Keras metric subclasses **`keras.metrics.Metric`**. Like a layer, it has **internal state stored in Keras variables**. Unlike a layer's weights, those variables are **not updated via backpropagation**, so you write the update logic yourself in **`update_state()`**.

**Listing 7.18** implements **root mean squared error (RMSE)**:

- In `__init__`, two scalar state variables are created with `self.add_weight(..., initializer="zeros")`: `mse_sum` (accumulated squared error) and `total_samples` (accumulated sample count). The callout notes you have access to `add_weight()` just as for layers.
- `update_state(self, y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=None)` receives one batch of targets and predictions. To match the MNIST model, which takes **integer labels** and outputs **categorical (softmax) predictions**, it one-hot encodes `y_true` with `num_classes=ops.shape(y_pred)[1]`, sums the squared differences over the whole batch, and adds that sum and the batch size to the state with `assign_add`. `sample_weight` is ignored.

The listing continues on p.232 with `result()`, which returns the current metric value, and `reset_state()`, which clears the state between epochs or between training and evaluation. The built-in workflow can be customized with custom metrics and with callbacks passed to fit(). Metrics measure performance, especially the training vs. test gap. Built-in keras.metrics cover most needs. A custom metric subclasses keras.metrics.Metric. Its state lives in Keras variables created with add_weight(). Metric state isn't updated by backpropagation; you write update_state() yourself. RootMeanSquaredError accumulates Σ squared error (with one-hot targets) and the sample count across batches.

title: Listing 7.18 Listing 7.18 (first part): RootMeanSquaredError metric, constructor and update_state()
text:
from keras import ops

class RootMeanSquaredError(keras.metrics.Metric):
    def __init__(self, name="rmse", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(name=name, **kwargs)
        self.mse_sum = self.add_weight(name="mse_sum", initializer="zeros")
        self.total_samples = self.add_weight(
            name="total_samples", initializer="zeros"
        )

    def update_state(self, y_true, y_pred, sample_weight=None):
        y_true = ops.one_hot(y_true, num_classes=ops.shape(y_pred)[1])
        mse = ops.sum(ops.square(y_true - y_pred))
        self.mse_sum.assign_add(mse)
        num_samples = ops.shape(y_pred)[0]
        self.total_samples.assign_add(num_samples) Defines a stateful RMSE metric. Its state is two scalar accumulators, and update_state() adds one batch's summed squared error and sample count. result() and reset_state() follow on p.232. Accumulate sufficient statistics (Σ squared error, N) across batches. The final value √(Σ/N) is computed in result() on p.232.

title: Finishing the RMSE metric; introducing callbacks
text:
The result() and reset_state() methods of a custom metric, using it in compile(), and the motivation and definition of Keras callbacks A custom metric is completed by result(), which computes the value from the state, and reset_state(), which zeroes the state so one metric object can serve every epoch and both training and evaluation. It is then used exactly like a built-in metric. Callbacks turn fit() from an uncontrolled 'paper airplane' into a 'drone' that observes training and acts on it. The page completes the custom metric started in **Listing 7.18** (p.231):

- **`result()`** returns the current metric value from the accumulated state: `ops.sqrt(self.mse_sum / self.total_samples)`.
- **`reset_state()`** sets both variables back to `0.` with `assign`. You need it so you can reset the metric **without re-instantiating it**. That lets the *same* metric object be used across epochs of training, or for both training and evaluation.

**Custom metrics are used just like built-in ones.** The test drive rebuilds the model with `get_mnist_model()`, compiles it with `metrics=["accuracy", RootMeanSquaredError()]`, passing an *instance* next to the string name of a built-in, then trains for 3 epochs with validation data and evaluates on the test set, as in Listing 7.17. The `fit()` progress bar now shows the model's RMSE.

**7.3.2 Using callbacks.** Launching a long `fit()` run on a large dataset is compared to throwing a **paper airplane**: after the initial impulse you have no control over its trajectory or where it lands. A better vehicle is a **drone** that senses its environment, reports back to its operator and steers itself based on its current state. The Keras ***callbacks*** API turns `model.fit()` into such a self-introspecting, self-acting drone.

Definition: a ***callback*** is an object, a class instance implementing specific methods, that is **passed to the model in the call to `fit()`** and **called by the model at various points during** training. The sentence continues on p.233, which explains that callbacks can see the model's state and performance and can act on it: interrupt training, save the model, load other weights. result() computes the metric value from its state: √(mse_sum / total_samples). reset_state() zeroes the state so a single metric object can be reused across epochs and across training and evaluation. Custom metric instances go into compile(metrics=[...]) next to built-in names, and fit() then shows them. fit() alone is a 'paper airplane'. Callbacks make it a 'drone' that observes and acts during training. A callback is a class instance passed to fit() whose methods the model calls at various points during training.

title: What callbacks can do; EarlyStopping and ModelCheckpoint
text:
Capabilities and typical uses of callbacks, the built-in keras.callbacks, and the rationale for early stopping combined with model checkpointing Callbacks see the model's full state and performance during training and can act on it. The canonical pair is EarlyStopping, which stops once a monitored metric stops improving for a set number of epochs, and ModelCheckpoint, which saves the model continually or only when it is the best so far. Together they replace the wasteful 'train once to find the epoch count, then retrain' strategy. The page finishes the definition begun on p.232. A callback **has access to all available data about the model's state and performance** and **can take action**: interrupt training, save a model, load a different weight set, or otherwise alter the model's state.

Example uses:

- ***Model checkpointing***: saving the model's current state at different points during training.
- ***Early stopping***: interrupting training when validation loss stops improving, and saving the best model obtained.
- ***Dynamically adjusting parameters during training***, such as the optimizer's learning rate.
- ***Logging training and validation metrics, or visualizing learned representations as they update***. The familiar **`fit()` progress bar is itself a callback**.

The `keras.callbacks` module has many built-ins (the list is not exhaustive): `ModelCheckpoint`, `EarlyStopping`, `LearningRateScheduler`, `ReduceLROnPlateau` and `CSVLogger`. The authors review two of them.

**The EarlyStopping and ModelCheckpoint callbacks.** You can't predict at the start how many epochs you'll need to reach the optimal validation loss. The book's earlier examples trained long enough to start overfitting, used that run to find the best epoch count, then retrained from scratch for that many epochs. That strategy is **wasteful**. It's better to **stop as soon as validation loss stops improving**, which is what `EarlyStopping` does.

`EarlyStopping` **interrupts training once a monitored target metric has not improved for a fixed number of epochs**. This lets you stop as soon as overfitting begins, without retraining for fewer epochs. It is typically combined with **`ModelCheckpoint`**, which saves the model continually during training, or optionally **only the best model so far**, meaning the version with the best performance at the end of an epoch. The code (Listing 7.19, passing `callbacks=` to `fit()`) is on p.234. Callbacks can see everything about the model's state and performance, and can interrupt training, save, load weights or alter the model. Typical uses: checkpointing, early stopping, adjusting parameters such as the learning rate, and logging/visualization. The progress bar is a callback. Built-ins include ModelCheckpoint, EarlyStopping, LearningRateScheduler, ReduceLROnPlateau and CSVLogger. Training once to find the epoch count and then retraining is wasteful. EarlyStopping stops when the monitored metric hasn't improved for a fixed number of epochs. Pair EarlyStopping with ModelCheckpoint (save best only) to keep the best model.

title: EarlyStopping + ModelCheckpoint in fit(); writing your own callbacks
text:
Passing a list of built-in callbacks to fit(), saving/reloading models, and the start of the custom Callback API Callbacks are passed to fit() as a list; EarlyStopping halts training when a monitored quantity stops improving, and ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only=True keeps the best model on disk. When no built-in callback fits, you subclass keras.callbacks.Callback and override hook methods such as on_epoch_begin and on_epoch_end. The page opens with **Listing 7.19**, the concrete example promised at the end of p.233. A Python list `callbacks_list` holds two built-in callbacks:

- `keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="accuracy", patience=1)` interrupts training once the monitored accuracy has stopped improving for more than one epoch (the callout clarifies: that is, two epochs).
- `keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(filepath="checkpoint_path.keras", monitor="val_loss", save_best_only=True)` saves the model after every epoch, but because of `save_best_only=True` and `monitor="val_loss"` it only overwrites the file when validation loss has improved, so the file always holds the best model seen so far.

The model from `get_mnist_model()` is compiled with Adam, sparse categorical crossentropy, and `metrics=["accuracy"]` - the callouts stress that accuracy must be among the compiled metrics because a callback monitors it. `fit()` is then called with `epochs=10`, `callbacks=callbacks_list` and `validation_data=(val_images, val_labels)`; validation data is required because the checkpoint watches `val_loss`.

The text adds that you can always save a model manually with `model.save("my_checkpoint_path.keras")` and reload a saved model with `keras.models.load_model("checkpoint_path.keras")` - here reloading the file produced by the checkpoint.

title: Callback hooks, the logs dict, and the LossHistory callback
text:
The remaining Callback hook methods, what the logs argument contains, and a complete custom callback (Listing 7.20) that records and plots per-batch loss Keras calls batch-, epoch- and training-level hook methods on every callback, passing a logs dictionary of metrics (and an integer index for epoch/batch hooks). Listing 7.20 uses three of these hooks - on_train_begin, on_batch_end, on_epoch_end - to collect per-batch losses and save a plot each epoch. This page completes the list of hook methods begun on p.234. Besides `on_epoch_begin`/`on_epoch_end`, a `keras.callbacks.Callback` subclass can implement:

- `on_batch_begin(batch, logs)` - right before processing each batch
- `on_batch_end(batch, logs)` - right after processing each batch
- `on_train_begin(logs)` - at the start of training
- `on_train_end(logs)` - at the end of training

All hooks receive a `logs` argument, a **dictionary** with information about the previous batch, epoch or training run - training and validation metrics, and so on. The `on_epoch_*` and `on_batch_*` hooks additionally take the epoch or batch index (an integer) as their first argument.

**Listing 7.20** defines `LossHistory`, a callback that keeps a list of per-batch loss values and plots it at the end of each epoch:

1. `on_train_begin` creates an empty list `self.per_batch_losses`.
2. `on_batch_end` appends `logs.get("loss")` after every batch.
3. `on_epoch_end` clears the current matplotlib figure, plots loss against batch index with the label "Training loss for each batch", labels the axes (`Batch (epoch {epoch})`, `Loss`), adds a legend, saves the figure as `plot_at_epoch_{epoch}` at 300 dpi, and then **resets the list**, so each plot covers one epoch.

The page then begins a "test-drive": build the MNIST model with `get_mnist_model()`, compile it with Adam, sparse categorical crossentropy and accuracy, and start `model.fit(` - the arguments (including `callbacks=[LossHistory()]`) continue on p.236, where figure 7.5 shows the resulting plot. Hooks exist at three levels: train (on_train_begin/end), epoch (on_epoch_begin/end) and batch (on_batch_begin/end). All hooks receive a logs dict of metrics; epoch and batch hooks also receive an integer index first. LossHistory initialises state in on_train_begin, accumulates in on_batch_end, and plots/saves/resets in on_epoch_end. A custom callback is used by passing an instance in fit(callbacks=[...]).

title: Listing 7.20 Creating a custom callback by subclassing the Callback class
text:
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

class LossHistory(keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def on_train_begin(self, logs):
        self.per_batch_losses = []

    def on_batch_end(self, batch, logs):
        self.per_batch_losses.append(logs.get("loss"))

    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs):
        plt.clf()
        plt.plot(
            range(len(self.per_batch_losses)),
            self.per_batch_losses,
            label="Training loss for each batch",
        )
        plt.xlabel(f"Batch (epoch {epoch})")
        plt.ylabel("Loss")
        plt.legend()
        plt.savefig(f"plot_at_epoch_{epoch}", dpi=300)
        self.per_batch_losses = [] Records the loss reported after every batch and, at the end of each epoch, saves a plot of that epoch's per-batch losses to plot_at_epoch_<epoch>, then starts a fresh list. init list -> append per batch -> plot+save+reset per epoch.
snippet: Records the loss reported after every batch and, at the end of each epoch, saves a plot of that epoch's per-batch losses to plotatepoch<epoch, then starts a fresh list.

title: LossHistory output (fig. 7.5) and why TensorBoard (7.3.4)
text:
Finishing the LossHistory test-drive, its per-batch loss plot, and the motivation for TensorBoard: the idea-experiment-results loop of progress Passing callbacks=[LossHistory()] to fit() produces per-epoch plots of per-batch training loss (figure 7.5). Section 7.3.4 then argues that progress is an iterative loop - idea, experiment, results - and that, while Keras and GPUs speed up the first two arcs, TensorBoard is the tool for processing results. The page first finishes the test-drive started on p.235. The `model.fit(` call continues with `train_images`, `train_labels`, `epochs=10`, `callbacks=[LossHistory()]` and `validation_data=(val_images, val_labels)`. The authors say "We get plots that look like figure 7.5".

**Figure 7.5**, "The output of our custom history-plotting callback", is one of the saved plots: the x-axis is labelled `Batch (epoch 0)` and runs to about 1,600 batches, the y-axis is `Loss`, and the legend reads "Training loss for each batch". The loss starts near 2.3, falls steeply below 1.0 within the first ~100 batches, and then decreases slowly to roughly 0.3 by the end of the first epoch.

**Section 7.3.4, Monitoring and visualization with TensorBoard**, opens with a broader argument. Good research and good models need "rich, frequent feedback" about what's going on inside the model; that is the point of experiments. Progress is a **loop**: start with an idea, express it as an experiment that tries to validate or invalidate it, run the experiment, process the information it generates, and let that inspire the next idea. The more iterations you can run, the more refined and powerful your ideas become. **Figure 7.6**, "The loop of progress", shows Idea -> Experiment (via the deep learning framework, Keras) -> Results (via GPUs, TPUs) -> back to Idea (via the visualization framework, TensorBoard). Keras minimises the time from idea to experiment, and fast GPUs the time from experiment to result; for processing the results, "That's where TensorBoard comes in". What TensorBoard actually offers is described on p.237. Custom callbacks are used just like built-in ones: callbacks=[LossHistory()]. Figure 7.5: per-batch training loss in epoch 0 falls from ~2.3 to ~0.3 over ~1,600 batches. A starting crossentropy of ~2.3 is what a uniform 10-class guess gives (ln 10) - a useful sanity check (beyond the book). Progress is a loop - idea, experiment, results - and its speed determines how refined your ideas become. Keras speeds idea->experiment, GPUs/TPUs experiment->results, TensorBoard results->idea.

title: What TensorBoard does and how to launch it from fit()
text:
TensorBoard's capabilities, the keras.callbacks.TensorBoard callback, and starting a local TensorBoard server TensorBoard is a locally run, browser-based app for monitoring training. With Keras you enable it by adding keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir=...) to fit()'s callbacks; the callback writes logs to that directory, and running `tensorboard --logdir <dir>` serves the interface at a URL. TensorBoard is described as "a browser-based application that you can run locally" and "the best way to monitor everything that goes on inside your model during training". With it you can:

- visually monitor metrics during training,
- visualize your model architecture,
- visualize histograms of activations and gradients,
- explore embeddings in 3D.

The authors argue that monitoring more than the model's final loss gives a clearer picture of what the model does and doesn't do, and lets you make progress more quickly.

The easiest integration with `fit()` is the **`keras.callbacks.TensorBoard`** callback: in the simplest case you only specify where logs should be written. The code builds and compiles the MNIST model (Adam, sparse categorical crossentropy, accuracy), creates `tensorboard = keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir="/full_path_to_your_log_dir")`, and calls `fit()` for 10 epochs with validation data and `callbacks=[tensorboard]`.

Once training starts, logs are written to the target location. On a local machine you launch the server with `tensorboard --logdir /full_path_to_your_log_dir`; the `tensorboard` executable should already be present if TensorFlow was installed via `pip`, otherwise install it with `pip install tensorboard`. Then open the URL the command prints. For Colab, an embedded TensorBoard can run inside the notebook - the commands for that are on p.238. TensorBoard is a locally run, browser-based monitoring app. It shows training metrics, model architecture, activation/gradient histograms and 3D embeddings. Use keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir=...) in fit(callbacks=[...]) to write logs. View them with `tensorboard --logdir <dir>` (install with pip install tensorboard if needed) and open the printed URL. Monitoring more than the final loss helps you understand the model and iterate faster.

title: TensorBoard in Colab, figure 7.7, and why write your own loops
text:
Embedding TensorBoard in a notebook, the TensorBoard metrics dashboard, and the limits of fit() that motivate custom training loops In Colab, two IPython magics embed TensorBoard in the notebook, where you can watch live training and evaluation curves (figure 7.7). Section 7.4 then explains that fit(), even with custom metrics, losses and callbacks, is built for supervised learning; generative, self-supervised and reinforcement learning, or novel research tweaks, call for custom training logic. The page first gives the Colab commands announced on p.237:

```
%load_ext tensorboard
%tensorboard --logdir /full_path_to_your_log_dir
```

In the TensorBoard interface you can monitor **live graphs of training and evaluation metrics**, as in **figure 7.7**. The screenshot shows the Time Series tab with two runs, `train` and `validation`, an `epoch_accuracy` chart over steps 0-9 (both curves rising to about 0.98), a collapsed `epoch_learning_rate` card, and a settings panel with smoothing set to 0.6.

**Section 7.4, Writing your own training and evaluation loops**, begins. The `fit()` workflow balances ease of use and flexibility and is what you will use most of the time, but it isn't meant to support everything a researcher may want - even with custom metrics, losses and callbacks. The built-in `fit()` is focused on **supervised learning**: known *targets* (also called *labels* or *annotations*) are associated with the inputs, and the loss is computed from these targets and the model's predictions. Not all machine learning fits this mould. Setups without explicit targets include:

- **generative learning** (introduced in chapter 16),
- **self-supervised learning**, where targets are obtained from the inputs,
- **reinforcement learning**, driven by occasional "rewards" - "much like training a dog".

And even in ordinary supervised learning, a researcher may want "novel bells and whistles that require low-level flexibility". The next page recaps the three steps of a training loop and announces reimplementing `fit()` from scratch. In Colab: %load_ext tensorboard then %tensorboard --logdir <dir>. TensorBoard shows live training and evaluation curves (figure 7.7: train vs validation epoch_accuracy). fit() is what you'll use most of the time, but it is built around supervised learning. Generative, self-supervised and reinforcement learning - and novel research tweaks - may require custom training logic. Section 7.4 will teach you to write training loops from scratch.

section: 7.4 Writing your own training and evaluation loops

title: The three-step training loop; training vs. inference
text:
Recap of what a training loop does and two subtleties for writing one correctly: the training flag and trainable vs non-trainable weights A training loop repeats forward pass -> gradients -> weight update, which is what fit() does under the hood. To do it correctly you must call the model with training=True (so layers like Dropout behave in training mode) and differentiate with respect to model.trainable_weights rather than model.weights. Section 7.4 continues: whenever `fit()` is not enough, you write your own training logic. As in the low-level loops of chapters 2 and 3, a typical training loop does:

1. Run the **forward pass** (compute the model's output) to obtain a loss value for the current batch.
2. Retrieve the **gradients** of the loss with regard to the model's weights.
3. **Update** the weights so as to lower the loss on the current batch.

These steps repeat for as many batches as necessary - "essentially what `fit()` does under the hood". The section will reimplement `fit()` from scratch, building up to a fully featured custom loop in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.

**7.4.1 Training vs. inference.** So far, step 1 was `predictions = model(inputs)` and step 2 used a backend-specific API: `gradients = tape.gradient(loss, model.weights)` in TensorFlow, `loss.backward()` in PyTorch, `jax.value_and_grad()` in JAX. In general there are two subtleties:

- **The `training` flag.** Some layers, such as `Dropout`, behave differently in training and in inference. They expose a Boolean `training` argument in `call()`: `dropout(inputs, training=True)` drops some activation entries, `dropout(inputs, training=False)` does nothing. Functional and Sequential models also expose this argument, so the forward pass becomes `predictions = model(inputs, training=True)`.
- **Trainable weights.** Retrieve gradients for `model.trainable_weights`, not `model.weights`. Layers own two kinds of weights: *trainable weights*, updated by backpropagation to minimize the loss (e.g. a `Dense` layer's kernel and bias), and *non-trainable weights*, updated during the forward pass by the layers that own them - e.g. a counter of processed batches in a custom layer. The explanation continues on p.240 (BatchNormalization). A training loop = forward pass -> gradients -> weight update, repeated over batches; this is what fit() does. Gradient retrieval is backend-specific: tape.gradient (TF), loss.backward() (PyTorch), jax.value_and_grad (JAX). Pass training=True when calling the model in a training step so layers like Dropout behave correctly. Differentiate with respect to model.trainable_weights, not model.weights. Trainable weights are updated by backprop; non-trainable weights are updated by their layers in the forward pass.

section: 7.4 Writing your own training and evaluation loops

title: From pseudocode train_step() to a TensorFlow setup
text:
The generic shape of a supervised training step, and why the gradient-retrieval line has to be backend specific Every supervised training step is: forward pass with training=True, compute the loss, get gradients of the loss with respect to the trainable weights only, and let the optimizer apply them. Only the gradient retrieval differs between TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX. The page opens by finishing the discussion of **non-trainable weights** started on p.239. Such weights are updated during the forward pass rather than by backpropagation (the book's example: a counter incremented at each batch). Among the built-in Keras layers, only `BatchNormalization` (introduced in chapter 9) has them: it keeps running estimates of the **mean and standard deviation** of the data passing through it, so it can do an *online approximation of feature normalization*.

Section **7.4.2** then combines the two subtleties from section 7.4.1 into a pseudocode `train_step(inputs, targets)`:

1. `predictions = model(inputs, training=True)`: forward pass in training mode, so layers like `Dropout` behave as they do in training.
2. `loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)`: loss for the current batch.
3. `gradients = get_gradients_of(loss, wrt=model.trainable_weights)`: gradients only for the **trainable** weights.
4. `optimizer.apply(gradients, model.trainable_weights)`: the optimizer updates those weights.

The authors say outright that this is pseudocode, because `get_gradients_of()` **does not exist**. How you get gradients depends on the backend (JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch). The plan is to write a real `train_step()` for each framework using what chapter 3 taught. TensorFlow and PyTorch come first because they make this "relatively easy". JAX comes last because it is "quite a bit more complex" (its stateless design is explained on p.242).

The **TensorFlow** subsection says TF code looks almost exactly like the pseudocode. The only change is that the forward pass must run inside a `GradientTape` scope, and the `tape` then returns the gradients. The page ends with the setup: import TensorFlow, build the MNIST model with `get_mnist_model()`, and create a `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy` loss and an `Adam` optimizer. The `train_step` function itself is on p.241. A supervised training step is: forward pass (training=True) → loss → gradients with respect to trainable weights → optimizer.apply. Only the gradient-retrieval line is backend specific. Keras has no universal get_gradients_of(). BatchNormalization is the only built-in Keras layer with non-trainable weights; they track running mean and standard deviation. TensorFlow is closest to the pseudocode: the forward pass just goes inside a GradientTape scope. The TensorFlow example uses get_mnist_model(), SparseCategoricalCrossentropy and Adam.

title: The TensorFlow train_step and the PyTorch gradient model
text:
A working TensorFlow training step built on GradientTape, and the three PyTorch mechanisms (backward, .grad, zero_grad) a PyTorch training step relies on In TensorFlow, wrapping the forward pass and loss in a GradientTape turns the pseudocode into real code. In PyTorch, Keras models are torch.nn.Module instances, so gradients are produced by loss.backward(), read from weight.value.grad, and must be cleared with model.zero_grad() because backward() accumulates. The page starts with the **TensorFlow training step**, whose setup (model, `loss_fn`, `optimizer`) was on p.240. The function opens a `tf.GradientTape()` as `tape`. Inside the scope it runs the forward pass with `training=True` and computes the loss. Outside the scope it calls `tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_weights)` and hands the gradients to `optimizer.apply(gradients, model.trainable_weights)`. It returns the loss. Apart from the `with` block, it is the pseudocode from p.240 line for line, with the imaginary `get_gradients_of()` replaced by `tape.gradient`.

The authors run it once on a single batch: `batch_size = 32`, then the first 32 `train_images` and `train_labels`, then `loss = train_step(inputs, targets)`. "Easy enough!"

Next comes the **PyTorch training step function**. On the PyTorch backend, every Keras layer and model *inherits from* `torch.nn.Module` and exposes the native `Module` API. So the model, its trainable weights and the loss tensor are all "aware of each other". They interact through three methods: `loss.backward()`, `weight.value.grad` and `model.zero_grad()`.

The authors repeat chapter 3's mental model in three bullets:

- Each forward pass builds a **one-time computation graph** of what was just computed.
- Calling `.backward()` on a scalar node (such as the loss) runs the graph backward and fills a `tensor.grad` attribute on every tensor involved that has `requires_grad=True`. That includes the trainable parameters.
- To clear `.grad`, set `tensor.grad = None`. More conveniently, call `model.zero_grad()`, which reaches every variable the model tracks. This is **critical**, because `backward()` is **additive**: if you skip it, gradients pile up across steps and "training won't proceed."

The PyTorch code that chains these steps is on p.242. The TF train_step is the pseudocode with the forward pass and loss inside a GradientTape and tape.gradient in place of get_gradients_of(). A training step is an ordinary function. Calling it once on 32 samples does one update. On the PyTorch backend, Keras models are torch.nn.Module instances that use loss.backward(), weight.value.grad and model.zero_grad(). PyTorch builds a one-time graph per forward pass; backward() populates .grad on tensors with requires_grad=True. backward() is additive, so clear gradients every step or training won't proceed.

title: PyTorch autograd (define-by-run)
text: PyTorch's autodiff: a one-time graph is built during each forward pass, and backward() fills .grad on tensors that require gradients. Gradients appear on the parameters themselves as a side effect, rather than being returned by a function. `loss.backward()` → `w.grad` holds $\partial L/\partial w$. Gradients accumulate across calls until cleared. On p.101, `torch.square(x)` at x=3 followed by backward() gives `x.grad == 6`.
snippet: PyTorch's autodiff: a one-time graph is built during each forward pass, and backward fills .grad on tensors that require gradients.

title: Gradient accumulation (additivity of backward)
text: Successive backward() calls sum their gradients into .grad. Like a running total that keeps growing until you clear it. After two backward passes without clearing, .grad = g1 + g2. The book stresses calling model.zero_grad() at every step. If each step's true gradient is 0.2, without clearing .grad reads 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, ...

title: TensorFlow train_step
text:
def train_step(inputs, targets):
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        predictions = model(inputs, training=True)
        loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)
    gradients = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_weights)
    optimizer.apply(gradients, model.trainable_weights)
    return loss Runs one supervised gradient update on one batch with the TensorFlow backend and returns the batch loss. Reverse-mode autodiff with a tape, followed by an Adam update.
snippet: Runs one supervised gradient update on one batch with the TensorFlow backend and returns the batch loss.

title: JAX statelessness
text: JAX functions keep no persistent state; any state they use must be passed in, and any state they change must be returned. A JAX function is like a mathematical function: it cannot quietly change anything in the background. Enables jit compilation and automatic parallelization. For training, the weights and non-trainable variables are function arguments and return values. Chapter 3's JAX training step returned new W and b (p.113).
snippet: JAX functions keep no persistent state; any state they use must be passed in, and any state they change must be returned.

title: Model.stateless_call()
text: Keras's stateless forward pass: like call, but it takes trainable and non-trainable weights as inputs (and, per p.243, returns updated non-trainable weights). A version of the model with no variables of its own; you supply the weights each time. Roughly `outputs, non_trainable_variables = model.stateless_call(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, training=True)`. The return value is described on p.243. Used in compute_loss_and_updates() on p.243.

title: Gradients via metaprogramming (JAX)
text: Obtaining a gradient function by transforming a loss function, for example `jax.grad(loss_fn)`. Instead of recording a computation (TF) or attaching gradients to tensors (PyTorch), JAX hands you a new function that computes derivatives. `jax.value_and_grad(f)` returns a function that gives (f(x), ∇f(x)), differentiating with respect to the first argument. p.110: grad of a squaring function.

title: PyTorch train_step for a Keras model
text:
import torch

model = get_mnist_model()
loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()
optimizer = keras.optimizers.Adam()

def train_step(inputs, targets):
    predictions = model(inputs, training=True)
    loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)
    loss.backward()
    gradients = [weight.value.grad for weight in model.trainable_weights]
    with torch.no_grad():
        optimizer.apply(gradients, model.trainable_weights)
    model.zero_grad()
    return loss Runs one gradient update for a Keras model on the PyTorch backend and returns the loss. Define-by-run backprop followed by an Adam update.
snippet: Runs one gradient update for a Keras model on the PyTorch backend and returns the loss.

title: stateless_call, compute_loss_and_updates and has_aux
text:
Building a stateless JAX loss function with model.stateless_call() and turning it into a gradient function with jax.value_and_grad(..., has_aux=True) stateless_call() returns outputs plus updated non-trainable weights, so the JAX loss function compute_loss_and_updates() returns (loss, non_trainable_variables). Since jax.grad and value_and_grad require a scalar-only return, has_aux=True is used to mark the second output as auxiliary. The page finishes the description of **`stateless_call()`**. Besides taking trainable and non-trainable weights as inputs (p.242), it **returns the model's updated non-trainable weights** together with its outputs: `outputs, non_trainable_weights = model.stateless_call(trainable_weights, non_trainable_weights, inputs)`.

This is used to write the JAX loss function. Because it also computes updates for the non-trainable variables, the authors name it **`compute_loss_and_updates()`**. It takes `(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, targets)`, calls `model.stateless_call(..., training=True)`, computes `loss = loss_fn(targets, outputs)` and returns `loss, non_trainable_variables`. The callouts note that **gradients are computed for the entries in the first argument** (`trainable_variables`), and that the function returns the scalar loss plus the updated non-trainable weights.

Next, the function is passed to **`jax.value_and_grad`**, with a generic template: `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(fn)`, then `loss, gradients = grad_fn(...)`.

There is a "small problem": `jax.grad()` and `jax.value_and_grad()` require `fn` to **return a scalar value only**, but `compute_loss_and_updates()` returns the scalar loss *and* the new non-trainable weights. The fix, already covered in chapter 3 (p.112), is the **`has_aux`** argument: `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss_and_updates, has_aux=True)`. This tells JAX that the first output is the value to differentiate and the rest is auxiliary data to pass through. How to call the resulting `grad_fn` is shown at the top of p.244. stateless_call takes weights explicitly and returns outputs plus updated non-trainable weights. compute_loss_and_updates(trainable, non_trainable, inputs, targets) returns (loss, non_trainable). JAX differentiates with respect to the first argument, so the trainable variables go first. grad and value_and_grad need a scalar-only return; has_aux=True lets extra outputs pass through. grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss_and_updates, has_aux=True) is the JAX gradient function for the step.

title: Optimizer state, stateless_apply and assembling the JAX step
text:
Using grad_fn, why optimizers carry their own state, Keras's optimizer.stateless_apply(), and the start of the end-to-end JAX train_step that threads all state through its arguments Plain SGD needs no state, but Adam and other momentum-based optimizers keep auxiliary variables that change every step. In JAX those must be passed in and returned too, which optimizer.stateless_apply() does. The full JAX train_step therefore takes a state tuple of (trainable, non-trainable, optimizer variables) and computes gradients with grad_fn. The page first shows how to call the `grad_fn` built on p.243 with `has_aux=True`: `(loss, non_trainable_weights), gradients = grad_fn(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, targets)`. The value and the auxiliary output come back nested together, followed by the gradients.

"Okay, that was a lot of JAXiness." One piece is still missing: the JAX equivalent of **`optimizer.apply()`**. The authors recall chapter 2's hand-written TensorFlow update:

```
for g, w in zip(gradients, weights):
    w.assign(w - g * learning_rate)
```

with `learning_rate = 1e-3`. This **corresponds to `keras.optimizers.SGD`**. Every other Keras optimizer is more complex: it **tracks auxiliary variables that speed up training**, and most use some form of **momentum** (chapter 2). These variables change at every step. In JAX that means you need a **stateless function that takes them as arguments and returns their new values**.

Keras provides that as **`optimizer.stateless_apply()`** on every optimizer: `trainable_variables, optimizer_variables = optimizer.stateless_apply(optimizer_variables, grads, trainable_variables)`. It takes the optimizer state, the gradients and the current trainable values, and returns new trainable values and new optimizer state.

With that, the **end-to-end JAX training step** can be put together. Create `keras.optimizers.Adam()` and call `optimizer.build(model.trainable_variables)` so its variables exist. `train_step(state, inputs, targets)` takes the whole **state as a function argument**, unpacks it into `(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, optimizer_variables)`, and calls `grad_fn` to get the loss, the updated non-trainable variables and the gradients. The rest of the function (applying the update and returning the new state) is on p.245. With has_aux, unpack as (loss, non_trainable), grads = grad_fn(...). The chapter 2 update w ← w − g·lr is what keras.optimizers.SGD does. Other optimizers keep auxiliary variables (mostly momentum-related) that change each step, and in JAX these must be passed in and returned. optimizer.stateless_apply(optimizer_variables, grads, trainable_variables) returns new trainable and optimizer variables. The JAX train_step takes state = (trainable, non-trainable, optimizer variables) as an argument; build the optimizer first.

title: Finishing the JAX step; low-level use of metrics
text:
Completing the stateless JAX train_step (stateless_apply and returning the new state), building the initial state from Keras variables, and using Keras metrics by hand with update_state() and result() The JAX train_step ends by applying the update with optimizer.stateless_apply and returning the loss together with the full new state. The initial state is made from the .value of each model and optimizer variable. In a hand-written loop, Keras metrics are driven manually: update_state(y_true, y_pred) per batch, result() to read the value. The page opens with the rest of the **JAX `train_step`** from p.244. After `grad_fn` produces the loss, the new non-trainable variables and the gradients, `optimizer.stateless_apply(optimizer_variables, grads, trainable_variables)` **updates the trainable variables and optimizer variables**. The function then returns `loss, (trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, optimizer_variables)`: the **updated state alongside the loss**. The shape is new_state = f(state, batch).

To run it for a single step, the authors take the usual 32-sample batch and **build the initial state from the Keras variables' raw values**: `[v.value for v in model.trainable_variables]`, the same for `model.non_trainable_variables` and for `optimizer.variables`. They pack these into `state`, then call `loss, state = train_step(state, inputs, targets)` and rebind `state` to the returned value. Their verdict: "definitely a bit more work than TensorFlow and PyTorch, but the speed and scalability benefits of JAX more than make up for it."

**Section 7.4.3, Low-level usage of metrics.** A custom loop will usually still want Keras metrics, built-in or custom. The API is the one already covered (p.231): call **`update_state(y_true, y_pred)`** for each batch and **`result()`** to get the current value. The example creates `SparseCategoricalAccuracy`, passes integer targets `[0, 1, 2]` and one-hot-like predictions `[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]]`, updates the metric, and prints `result: ...` with two decimals. Every prediction's argmax matches its target, so the printed value would be 1.00 (the book does not print the output).

The page ends by noting that you may also need to track the **average of a scalar** such as the loss, which `keras.metrics.Mean` does. Its code is on p.246. The JAX train_step ends with optimizer.stateless_apply and returns loss, (trainable, non_trainable, optimizer) state. The initial state is built from [v.value for v in ...] over model and optimizer variables; each step rebinds state. JAX takes more code than TF or PyTorch, but the authors judge its speed and scalability worth it. In a custom loop, call metric.update_state(y_true, y_pred) per batch and metric.result() to read the value. keras.metrics.Mean tracks the running average of a scalar such as the loss.

title: Stateless metrics in JAX, and a middle ground: custom train_step() inside fit()
text:
Finishing low-level metric usage (Mean, reset_state, and the stateless metrics API for JAX), then introducing the idea of overriding Model.train_step() so that fit() runs a custom learning algorithm. Keras metrics are small stateful objects (update_state / result / reset_state); under JAX you use their stateless twins, which take and return the metric's variables explicitly. Rather than rewriting the whole training loop, you can override train_step() and keep everything else fit() provides. The page opens by completing section **7.4.3, Low-level usage of metrics**. A short code block shows `keras.metrics.Mean`, which keeps a running average of whatever scalars you feed it: updating it with the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and calling `result()` prints `Mean of values: 2.00`. The authors remind you to call `metric.reset_state()` whenever you want to start over, which typically happens at the start of each training epoch and at the start of evaluation.

They then turn to JAX. Because JAX functions that are traced and compiled must be **stateless**, methods that mutate an object in place, such as `update_state()` or reset, cannot be used inside them. Keras therefore offers a **stateless metrics API**, analogous to `model.stateless_call()` and `optimizer.stateless_apply()` from the JAX training step: you take the metric's state variables out (`metric.variables`), pass them to `metric.stateless_update_state(metric_variables, targets, predictions)` which **returns** updated variables, compute the value with `metric.stateless_result(metric_variables)`, and get fresh zeroed variables with `metric.stateless_reset_state()`. The example uses `SparseCategoricalAccuracy` with three perfectly predicted samples, so the printed result is 1.00.

Section **7.4.4, Using fit() with a custom training loop**, then begins. Writing the loop entirely by hand gives maximal flexibility but costs a lot of code and loses features of `fit()` such as callbacks, performance optimizations and built-in distributed training. The middle ground is to **override the `train_step()` method of `Model`**: `fit()` calls this method for every batch, so your own learning algorithm runs under the hood while you keep calling `fit()` as usual. The page ends with the first step of the recipe, creating a class that subclasses `keras.Model`; the recipe continues on p.247. keras.metrics.Mean computes a running average; use it to average losses across batches. Call reset_state() at the start of each epoch and of evaluation; metrics otherwise keep accumulating. Under JAX, use stateless_update_state(), stateless_result() and stateless_reset_state(), which take and return metric variables explicitly. The stateless metrics API parallels model.stateless_call() and optimizer.stateless_apply(). Fully custom loops cost you callbacks, performance optimizations and built-in distributed training. Overriding Model.train_step(), which fit() calls per batch, lets fit() run your own algorithm.

title: Overriding train_step(): the recipe and the TensorFlow version (Listing 7.21)
text:
The remaining steps for customizing fit() via train_step(), two important notes, and a complete TensorFlow implementation with a loss-tracking metric exposed through the metrics property. A custom train_step() contains the same forward pass / GradientTape / optimizer.apply logic as a hand-written step, and returns a dict of metric values. Listing metric objects in the model's metrics property lets fit() reset them automatically each epoch and at the start of evaluate(). This page completes the recipe begun on p.246 for **customizing what `fit()` does**. After subclassing `keras.Model`, you (2) **override `train_step()`**, whose body is nearly identical to the training step functions written in section 7.4.2, and (3) **return a dictionary** mapping metric names, including the loss, to their current values.

Two notes follow. First, the pattern does **not** prevent you from using the Functional API: it works whether you build Sequential, Functional or subclassed models, because you only subclass `Model` to swap one method. Second, you **don't need `@tf.function` or `@jax.jit`** on your `train_step()`, since the framework compiles it for you.

Under the heading *Customizing fit() with TensorFlow*, **Listing 7.21** defines a module-level `loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()` and `loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss")`, then a `CustomModel` whose `train_step(self, data)` unpacks `inputs, targets`, runs `self(inputs, training=True)` inside a `tf.GradientTape`, computes the loss, takes `tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights)`, applies them with `self.optimizer.apply(...)`, updates the loss tracker, and returns `{"loss": loss_tracker.result()}`. The callouts explain that `self(...)` is used instead of `model(...)` because the model is the class itself, and that listing `loss_tracker` in the **`metrics` property** makes the model call `reset_state()` on it at the start of each epoch and of each `evaluate()` call, so you don't reset by hand.

The final paragraph says that we can now instantiate, compile **with only an optimizer** (the loss is defined outside the model), and train with `fit()` as usual; the code for that is on p.248. Recipe: subclass keras.Model, override train_step(), return a dict of metric values including the loss. Works with Sequential, Functional and subclassed models. No @tf.function / @jax.jit needed; fit() compiles train_step for you. Inside train_step use self(inputs, training=True), because the model is the class itself. List metrics in the metrics property so fit() and evaluate() reset them automatically. With the loss defined outside the model, compile() only needs an optimizer.

title: Listing 7.21 Customizing fit(): TensorFlow version
text:
import keras
from keras import layers

loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()
loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss")

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def train_step(self, data):
        inputs, targets = data
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            predictions = self(inputs, training=True)
            loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)
        gradients = tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights)
        self.optimizer.apply(gradients, self.trainable_weights)

        loss_tracker.update_state(loss)
        return {"loss": loss_tracker.result()}

    @property
    def metrics(self):
        return [loss_tracker] Defines a Model subclass whose per-batch training logic is written by hand with TensorFlow's GradientTape, while still being driven by fit(). Per batch: forward pass -> loss -> gradients -> optimizer update -> metric update -> logs.
snippet: Defines a Model subclass whose per-batch training logic is written by hand with TensorFlow's GradientTape, while still being driven by fit.

title: Training the custom TensorFlow model, and the PyTorch train_step()
text:
A reusable get_custom_model() factory that builds a Functional MNIST classifier inside CustomModel and compiles it with only an optimizer; training it with fit(); and the PyTorch version of the overridden train_step(). The same Keras contract (train_step returns a logs dict, metrics property lists trackers) holds across backends; only the gradient mechanism changes. In PyTorch it is loss.backward(), reading each variable's .value.grad, and applying updates under torch.no_grad(). The page continues *Customizing fit() with TensorFlow* by packaging the model definition into a **reusable function, `get_custom_model()`**. It builds a Functional graph: `keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))`, a `Dense(512, activation="relu")` layer, `Dropout(0.5)`, and a `Dense(10, activation="softmax")` output. Instead of `keras.Model(inputs, outputs)` it calls **`CustomModel(inputs, outputs)`**, so the Functional network gets the custom `train_step()` from Listing 7.21. It compiles with `optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam()` only, because the loss is defined outside the model, and returns the model. Training is then a plain `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`.

Under *Customizing fit() with PyTorch*, the authors give the PyTorch `CustomModel`. The module-level `loss_fn` and `loss_tracker` are the same. In `train_step()` the forward pass (`self(inputs, training=True)`) and the loss are computed normally (callout: *runs the forward pass*). Then `loss.backward()` populates gradients, and the gradients are **retrieved** by listing the trainable weights and reading `v.value.grad` for each, since a Keras variable wraps a torch tensor in its `.value`. The weights are **updated** with `self.optimizer.apply(gradients, trainable_weights)` inside `with torch.no_grad():`, so the update itself is not tracked by autograd. The loss tracker is updated and `{"loss": loss_tracker.result()}` is returned; the `metrics` property again lists `loss_tracker`.

The page ends with the identical two lines `model = get_custom_model()` and `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`. When this runs with the PyTorch backend, `get_custom_model()` picks up the PyTorch `CustomModel` that was just defined. The JAX version follows on p.249. get_custom_model() wraps a Functional 784-512-10 network in CustomModel and compiles it with Adam only. Training is the usual model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3). PyTorch's train_step: forward, loss.backward(), gradients from v.value.grad, optimizer.apply inside torch.no_grad(). Metric handling (loss_tracker, metrics property, returned dict) is identical across backends. Only the gradient mechanism is backend-specific.

def get_custom_model():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))
    features = layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")(inputs)
    features = layers.Dropout(0.5)(features)
    outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
    model = CustomModel(inputs, outputs)
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam())
    return model Builds a Functional MNIST classifier, wraps it in CustomModel so it uses the overridden train_step, compiles it with Adam only, and returns it. Functional graph construction then compilation.

title: Customizing fit(): PyTorch version
text:
import keras
from keras import layers

loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()
loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss")

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def train_step(self, data):
        inputs, targets = data
        predictions = self(inputs, training=True)
        loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)

        loss.backward()
        trainable_weights = [v for v in self.trainable_weights]
        gradients = [v.value.grad for v in trainable_weights]

        with torch.no_grad():
            self.optimizer.apply(gradients, trainable_weights)

        loss_tracker.update_state(loss)
        return {"loss": loss_tracker.result()}

    @property
    def metrics(self):
        return [loss_tracker] Defines the PyTorch-backend CustomModel whose train_step uses PyTorch autograd for gradients while staying inside fit(). Forward -> loss -> backward -> collect grads -> optimizer.apply (no_grad) -> metric update -> logs.

title: Customizing fit() with JAX: compute_loss_and_updates() and a stateless train_step
text:
The JAX version of overriding train_step(): a compute_loss_and_updates() method built on self.stateless_call(), and a train_step(self, state, data) that unpacks the state tuple and uses jax.value_and_grad with has_aux=True. Under JAX, Keras calls train_step with an explicit state tuple (trainable, non-trainable, optimizer and metrics variables) and expects new state back. The loss function must be a pure method returning both the loss and updated non-trainable variables, so jax.value_and_grad(..., has_aux=True) can differentiate it. The last backend for *Customizing fit()* is **JAX**. As in the from-scratch JAX step of section 7.4.2, you first need a function that returns the loss, but now it is a **method** of `CustomModel`: `compute_loss_and_updates(self, trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, targets, training=False)`. It runs the forward pass with **`self.stateless_call(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, training=training)`**, which returns the predictions together with updated non-trainable variables, computes `loss_fn(targets, predictions)`, and returns **both** the loss and the non-trainable variables (callout).

The authors then point out a simplification: unlike the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions, this one does **not compute a moving average of the loss**; it returns the per-batch loss value, which is less useful. Including a stateless loss tracker would make the code very verbose, and metric management is the topic of the next section (7.4.5).

The page then begins the **JAX `train_step(self, state, data)`**. Note the extra `state` argument: under JAX, Keras passes all variables explicitly. The state is unpacked into `trainable_variables`, `non_trainable_variables`, `optimizer_variables` and `metrics_variables` (callout: metrics_variables are part of it, although we won't use them here), and `data` into `inputs, targets`. A gradient function is created with **`jax.value_and_grad(self.compute_loss_and_updates, has_aux=True)`**, and calling it as `(loss, non_trainable_variables), grads = grad_fn(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, inputs, ...` computes the loss, the gradients with respect to the first argument (the trainable variables), and the updated non-trainable variables. The call continues on p.250, where the optimizer update and the returned `(logs, state)` appear. The JAX custom train_step has signature train_step(self, state, data). state = (trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, optimizer_variables, metrics_variables). compute_loss_and_updates() uses self.stateless_call and returns (loss, non_trainable_variables). jax.value_and_grad(..., has_aux=True) yields ((loss, aux), grads). This example reports the per-batch loss, not a moving average, for simplicity.
