title: JAX CustomModel: compute_loss_and_updates()
text:
import keras
from keras import layers

loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def compute_loss_and_updates(
        self,
        trainable_variables,
        non_trainable_variables,
        inputs,
        targets,
        training=False,
    ):
        predictions, non_trainable_variables = self.stateless_call(
            trainable_variables,
            non_trainable_variables,
            inputs,
            training=training,
        )
        loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)
        return loss, non_trainable_variables Defines a pure loss method on CustomModel that runs a stateless forward pass and returns the loss plus updated non-trainable variables. The class continues with train_step in the next code block. Pure forward pass + loss.

title: Finishing the JAX train_step; 7.4.5 Handling metrics with compile()'s loss and metrics
text:
The second half of the JAX train_step (optimizer.stateless_apply, logs, repacking state), training it with fit(), and the start of section 7.4.5: using self.compute_loss and self.metrics to reuse the loss and metrics passed to compile() inside a custom train_step. A JAX train_step must return (logs, state), with trainable and optimizer variables updated by optimizer.stateless_apply. Once a model is compiled with a loss and metrics, a custom train_step can use self.compute_loss (compiled loss plus layer regularization losses) and self.metrics (compiled metrics plus a loss tracker) instead of module-level objects. The page opens with the end of the **JAX `train_step`** from p.249. The `grad_fn` call is completed with `targets` and `training=True` (callout: computes gradients and updates to non-trainable variables). Then **`self.optimizer.stateless_apply(optimizer_variables, grads, trainable_variables)`** returns new `trainable_variables` and `optimizer_variables` (callout: updates trainable variables and optimizer variables). The logs are simply `{"loss": loss}`, the per-batch value rather than a moving average (callout). The state is repacked as `(trainable_variables, non_trainable_variables, optimizer_variables, metrics_variables)` and **`return logs, state`** sends back metric logs and updated state variables. Training uses the familiar `model = get_custom_model()` and `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`.

Section **7.4.5, Handling metrics in a custom train_step()**, then asks: what about the `loss` and `metrics` you can pass to `compile()`? After calling `compile()` you get access to:

- **`self.compute_loss`**, which combines the loss function passed to `compile()` with **regularization losses** that certain layers may add;
- **`self.metrics`**, the list of metrics passed to `compile()`, which **also includes a metric that tracks the loss**.

Under *train_step() metrics handling with TensorFlow*, a new `CustomModel` begins: `train_step(self, data)` unpacks the batch and, inside a `tf.GradientTape`, runs `self(inputs, training=True)` and computes **`loss = self.compute_loss(y=targets, y_pred=predictions)`** (callout: computes the loss via self.compute_loss). The rest of this listing, which updates every metric in `self.metrics` and returns a dict of their results, is on p.251. optimizer.stateless_apply(optimizer_variables, grads, trainable_variables) returns new trainable and optimizer variables. The JAX train_step returns (logs, state); here logs hold the per-batch loss. After compile(), self.compute_loss = compiled loss + layer regularization losses. After compile(), self.metrics = compiled metrics + a loss-tracking metric. A custom step can thus be configured through compile() instead of global objects.

title: Updating all compiled metrics in train_step (TensorFlow), then the same change for PyTorch
text:
Finishing the TensorFlow train_step that loops over self.metrics (loss metric updated with the loss, others with targets and predictions) and returns a dict of all metric results; compiling with loss and SparseCategoricalAccuracy; and starting the PyTorch version, which uses the identical self.compute_loss change. Once compile() supplies a loss and metrics, a custom train_step can update every metric generically, distinguishing the loss tracker by name, and return {m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}. The change is backend-independent: the PyTorch step differs from p.248 only in using self.compute_loss and the metric loop. The page completes the **TensorFlow** `train_step` begun on p.250. After computing the loss with `self.compute_loss`, it takes `tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights)` and calls `self.optimizer.apply(gradients, self.trainable_weights)` exactly as in Listing 7.21. Then comes the new part: a loop **`for metric in self.metrics:`**. If `metric.name == "loss"` the metric is updated with the loss value (`metric.update_state(loss)`); otherwise it is updated with `metric.update_state(targets, predictions)` (callout: updates the model's metrics, including the one that tracks the loss). The step returns **`{m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}`**, a dict mapping metric names to their current value (callout).

To try it, `get_custom_model()` is redefined so that `compile()` now receives **`optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam()`, `loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()` and `metrics=[keras.metrics.SparseCategoricalAccuracy()]`**; the architecture (784 inputs, Dense 512 relu, Dropout 0.5, Dense 10 softmax) is unchanged, and training is again `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`. The progress bar should now show both `loss` and the accuracy metric.

Under *train_step() metrics handling with PyTorch*, the authors note that it is **exactly the same code change**. The PyTorch `CustomModel` computes predictions with `self(inputs, training=True)`, the loss with `self.compute_loss(y=targets, y_pred=predictions)`, calls `loss.backward()` and gathers `gradients = [v.value.grad for v in trainable_weights]`. The page breaks here; the weight update under `torch.no_grad()`, the metric loop and the return are on p.252, followed by the JAX version, which uses `compute_loss()` inside `compute_loss_and_updates()`. Loop over self.metrics: update the 'loss' metric with the loss, others with (targets, predictions). Return {m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics} so fit() sees every metric. get_custom_model() now compiles with optimizer, loss and metrics. The PyTorch version needs exactly the same change: self.compute_loss plus the metric loop. The JAX version follows on p.252.

title: get_custom_model() compiled with loss and metrics, and training
text:
def get_custom_model():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))
    features = layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")(inputs)
    features = layers.Dropout(0.5)(features)
    outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
    model = CustomModel(inputs, outputs)
    model.compile(
        optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(),
        loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(),
        metrics=[keras.metrics.SparseCategoricalAccuracy()],
    )
    return model

model = get_custom_model()
model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3) Redefines the model factory so that compile() supplies loss and metrics for self.compute_loss and self.metrics, then trains. Standard compile/fit with a custom step.

        loss.backward()
        trainable_weights = [v for v in self.trainable_weights]

title: PyTorch metrics in train_step(), then the JAX version begins
text:
Finishing the PyTorch train_step() that uses the compiled loss and metrics, running it with fit(), and starting the JAX variant with a compute_loss_and_updates() method that calls self.compute_loss(). Once a model is compiled, a custom train_step() can reuse the compiled loss (via self.compute_loss) and the compiled metrics (via self.metrics). In PyTorch, as in TensorFlow, this means looping over self.metrics, updating the loss tracker with the loss and every other metric with (targets, predictions), and returning a dict of results. JAX needs the same idea expressed statelessly, starting with a compute_loss_and_updates() method. The page opens with the last lines of the **PyTorch** version of a `train_step()` that handles compiled metrics (the first half, with `self.compute_loss(...)`, `loss.backward()` and gradient collection, is on p.251). After the gradients are gathered, the optimizer is applied inside `with torch.no_grad():` so the weight update itself is not tracked by autograd. Then the code loops over `self.metrics`: the metric named `"loss"` (the loss tracker that Keras adds automatically, p.250) is updated with the scalar `loss`, every other metric with `(targets, predictions)`. Finally it returns `{m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}`, the dict that `fit()` shows in the progress bar and passes to callbacks. As the authors said on p.251, this is *exactly the same code change* as in TensorFlow.

"Let's see how it runs": the page then repeats `get_custom_model()`, a small Functional model (784 inputs, `Dense(512, relu)`, `Dropout(0.5)`, `Dense(10, softmax)`) wrapped in `CustomModel` and compiled with `Adam`, `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy` and `SparseCategoricalAccuracy`, and trains it with `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`. Because the custom `train_step()` now reads loss and metrics from `compile()`, the progress bar will show both `loss` and `sparse_categorical_accuracy`.

The last part starts **train_step() metrics handling with JAX**. The first step is to use `compute_loss()` inside the `compute_loss_and_updates()` method so it "hits" the loss passed to `compile()`. The method takes the trainable and non-trainable variables as explicit arguments (plus `inputs`, `targets` and a `training` flag) and runs the model with `self.stateless_call(...)`, which returns predictions and updated non-trainable variables without mutating the model. The listing is cut off here and continues on p.253, where the method also returns the predictions as auxiliary output so the metrics can use them. The metric-aware train_step() ends by updating each metric in self.metrics and returning {m.name: m.result()}. The loss tracker is updated with the loss; other metrics with (targets, predictions). In PyTorch the optimizer step is done inside torch.no_grad(). get_custom_model() and fit() stay identical across backends; only train_step() changes. The JAX version starts by calling self.compute_loss() inside a pure compute_loss_and_updates() that uses self.stateless_call().

title: Building, compiling and training the custom model
text:
def get_custom_model():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))
    features = layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")(inputs)
    features = layers.Dropout(0.5)(features)
    outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
    model = CustomModel(inputs, outputs)
    model.compile(
        optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(),
        loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(),
        metrics=[keras.metrics.SparseCategoricalAccuracy()],
    )
    return model

model = get_custom_model()
model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3) Creates a 784-512-10 classifier with dropout as a CustomModel, compiles it, and trains it for 3 epochs with fit(), which calls the custom train_step() on each batch. Mini-batch training via fit() delegating each step to the overridden train_step().

title: Stateless metric management in a JAX train_step()
text:
Completing compute_loss_and_updates() with self.compute_loss(), and writing a JAX train_step() that updates the compiled metrics statelessly by slicing a flat list of metric variables. Under JAX, metric variables are part of the explicit training state. The train_step() walks through self.metrics, cuts each metric's own variables out of the flat metrics_variables list, updates them with stateless_update_state(), reads the value with stateless_result(), and collects the new variables to return as new state. The page first finishes the JAX `compute_loss_and_updates()` begun on p.252: `stateless_call()` is given `inputs` and `training=training`, then `loss = self.compute_loss(y=targets, y_pred=predictions)` uses the loss passed to `compile()`, and the method returns `loss, (predictions, non_trainable_variables)`. Compared with the p.249 version, the auxiliary output now also carries the **predictions**, because the metrics will need them.

"Next up: metric management. As usual, it's a tad more complicated due to JAX's statelessness requirements." The new `train_step(self, state, data)` unpacks a four-part state: trainable, non-trainable, optimizer and **metrics variables** (callout: *Metric variables are part of the state*). It builds `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(self.compute_loss_and_updates, has_aux=True)` and calls it with `training=True`, unpacking `(loss, (predictions, non_trainable_variables)), grads`. The optimizer update is done with `self.optimizer.stateless_apply(optimizer_variables, grads, trainable_variables)`, returning new trainable and optimizer variables.

Then comes the metric loop. `new_metrics_vars = []` and `logs = {}` are initialized. For each metric in `self.metrics` (*Iterates over metrics*), the code computes `num_prev` (how many variables have already been consumed) and `num_current = len(metric.variables)`, and slices `metrics_variables[num_prev : num_prev + num_current]` (*Grabs the variables of the current metrics*). The loss tracker is updated with `stateless_update_state(current_vars, loss)`; other metrics with `stateless_update_state(current_vars, targets, predictions)` (*Updates the metric's state*). `logs[metric.name] = metric.stateless_result(current_vars)` stores the value (*Stores the results in the logs dict*). The listing continues on p.254, where `current_vars` is appended to `new_metrics_vars` and the new state is returned. compute_loss_and_updates() returns (loss, (predictions, non_trainable_variables)) so metrics can reuse the predictions. In JAX, metric variables are the fourth component of the training state. Each metric's variables are a contiguous slice of metrics_variables, located by num_prev and len(metric.variables). stateless_update_state() returns new metric variables; stateless_result() computes the value for logs. The updated metric variables must be collected and returned in the new state (p.254).

title: JAX train_step() with stateless metric handling (first part)
text:
def train_step(self, state, data):
        (
            trainable_variables,
            non_trainable_variables,
            optimizer_variables,
            metrics_variables,
        ) = state
        inputs, targets = data

        grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(
            self.compute_loss_and_updates, has_aux=True
        )

        (loss, (predictions, non_trainable_variables)), grads = grad_fn(
            trainable_variables,
            non_trainable_variables,
            inputs,
            targets,
            training=True,
        )
        (
            trainable_variables,
            optimizer_variables,
        ) = self.optimizer.stateless_apply(
            optimizer_variables, grads, trainable_variables
        )

        new_metrics_vars = []
        logs = {}
        for metric in self.metrics:
            num_prev = len(new_metrics_vars)
            num_current = len(metric.variables)
            current_vars = metrics_variables[num_prev : num_prev + num_current]
            if metric.name == "loss":
                current_vars = metric.stateless_update_state(current_vars, loss)
            else:
                current_vars = metric.stateless_update_state(
                    current_vars, targets, predictions
                )
            logs[metric.name] = metric.stateless_result(current_vars) Performs one JAX training step: gradients, weight update, and stateless updating of all compiled metrics. The last lines of the loop and the return of the new state are on p.254. Gradient step followed by a pass over metrics with offset-based slicing of a flat variable list.
snippet: Performs one JAX training step: gradients, weight update, and stateless updating of all compiled metrics. The last lines of the loop and the return of the new state are on p.254.

title: Finishing the JAX train_step() and the chapter 7 summary
text:
Returning the updated metric variables as part of the JAX training state, and the six-point summary of chapter 7. The JAX train_step() closes by collecting each metric's updated variables into new_metrics_vars and returning (logs, state) with the new state tuple. The chapter summary recaps Keras's spectrum of workflows: three ways to build models, fit()/evaluate(), callbacks, overriding train_step(), and fully custom loops. The page opens with the final lines of the JAX `train_step()` from p.253. Inside the metric loop, `new_metrics_vars += current_vars` appends the metric's updated variables (this is also what makes `num_prev = len(new_metrics_vars)` the correct offset for the next metric). After the loop, the new `state` is assembled from `trainable_variables`, `non_trainable_variables`, `optimizer_variables` and `new_metrics_vars` (callout: *Returns the new metrics variables as part of the state*), and the method returns `logs, state`. Unlike the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions, which return only the logs dict, the JAX step must return the state because nothing was mutated in place.

The authors close the section: "That was a lot of information, but by now you know enough to use Keras to do almost anything!"

The **Summary** of chapter 7 then lists six points:

- Keras offers a **spectrum of workflows** based on *progressive disclosure of complexity*, and they all interoperate smoothly.
- Models can be built with the **`Sequential`** class, the **Functional API**, or by **subclassing `Model`**; most of the time you will use the Functional API.
- The simplest way to train and evaluate is the default **`fit()`** and **`evaluate()`**.
- **Callbacks** monitor models during `fit()` and automatically act on the model's state.
- You can fully control what `fit()` does by **overriding `train_step()`** with APIs of your backend (JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch).
- Beyond `fit()`, you can write **training loops entirely from scratch** in a backend-native way, useful for researchers implementing new training algorithms. The JAX train_step() returns (logs, state) with new_metrics_vars as the fourth state element. Keras workflows follow progressive disclosure of complexity and interoperate. Sequential, Functional, subclassing: the Functional API is the everyday choice. fit()/evaluate() are the simplest training path; callbacks add monitoring and automatic actions. Override train_step() for custom training logic within fit(); write a full loop for brand-new algorithms.

title: Chapter 8 opener: Image classification
text:
Opening of chapter 8: what the chapter covers and the historical context of ConvNets as deep learning's first big success in computer vision. Convolutional neural networks drove the initial rise of deep learning (2011-2015) through wins on image classification competitions; this chapter teaches ConvNets, data augmentation, feature extraction with pretrained ConvNets, and fine-tuning. This is the opening page of **chapter 8, Image classification**. The box *This chapter covers* lists four topics:

- Understanding convolutional neural networks (**ConvNets**)
- Using **data augmentation** to mitigate overfitting
- Using a **pretrained ConvNet for feature extraction**
- **Fine-tuning** a pretrained ConvNet

The introduction sets the historical scene. Computer vision was *the first big success story of deep learning* and drove its initial rise between 2011 and 2015. Convolutional neural networks began getting remarkably good results on image classification competitions: first **Dan Ciresan** won two niche competitions (the **ICDAR 2011** Chinese character recognition competition and the **IJCNN 2011** German traffic signs recognition competition), and then, more notably, in fall **2012** **Hinton's group** won the high-profile **ImageNet** large-scale visual recognition challenge. Many more promising results followed in other vision tasks.

The second paragraph begins a twist: these early successes *weren't quite enough to make deep learning mainstream at the time; it took a few years*. The sentence continues on p.256, which describes the skepticism of the computer vision community until 2016.

How to use this page: treat the bullet list as the chapter roadmap. Section 8.1 (p.256) introduces ConvNets with an MNIST example and explains convolution (p.258) and max pooling (p.263); 8.2 (p.265) trains a ConvNet from scratch on a small dataset and introduces data augmentation (p.276); 8.3 (p.280) covers feature extraction and fine-tuning with a pretrained model. Chapter 8 covers ConvNets, data augmentation, feature extraction with pretrained ConvNets, and fine-tuning. ConvNets were deep learning's first big success, with wins in 2011 (ICDAR, IJCNN) and the 2012 ImageNet challenge. Mainstream adoption lagged the early results by a few years.

title: Why ConvNets, and a first small ConvNet (Listing 8.1)
text:
The adoption history of deep learning in computer vision, the chapter's focus on small datasets, and Listing 8.1: a small Functional-API ConvNet for MNIST built from Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers. Deep learning overcame years of skepticism to dominate computer vision by 2016 and now powers everyday vision products. A ConvNet is a stack of Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers; even a basic one will greatly outperform the 97.8%-accurate dense MNIST model of chapter 2. The page completes the historical introduction begun on p.255. The computer vision community had invested for years in methods other than neural networks and was not ready to drop them for "a new kid on the block." In 2013 and 2014 deep learning still faced intense skepticism from many senior researchers; it only became **dominant in 2016**. One author recalls urging an ex-professor in February 2014 to pivot to deep learning ("It's the next big thing!" / "Well, maybe it's just a fad"); by 2016 that whole lab was doing deep learning.

Today, deep learning vision models are everywhere: Google Photos, Google image search, phone cameras, YouTube, OCR software, and research in autonomous driving, robotics, AI-assisted medical diagnosis, autonomous retail checkout and autonomous farming. The chapter introduces **convolutional neural networks (ConvNets or CNNs)**, used by most computer vision applications, and focuses on image classification with **small training datasets**, the most common case for anyone outside a large tech company.

**Section 8.1** starts practically: before the theory, a simple ConvNet will classify **MNIST** digits, the task solved in chapter 2 with a dense network at **97.8% test accuracy**. Even this basic ConvNet will "blow out of the water" that result. The model is a stack of `Conv2D` and `MaxPooling2D` layers built with the **Functional API**.

**Listing 8.1** defines an input of shape `(28, 28, 1)`, then `Conv2D(64, 3, relu)` -> `MaxPooling2D(2)` -> `Conv2D(128, 3, relu)` -> `MaxPooling2D(2)` -> `Conv2D(256, 3, relu)` -> `GlobalAveragePooling2D()` -> `Dense(10, softmax)`, wrapped in `keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)`. The resulting shapes and parameter counts are shown by `model.summary()` on p.257. Deep learning became dominant in computer vision only in 2016, after years of skepticism. ConvNets power most vision applications; the chapter focuses on small-data image classification. The dense MNIST baseline from chapter 2 reached 97.8% test accuracy; a basic ConvNet will beat it clearly. A basic ConvNet is a stack of Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers, here followed by GlobalAveragePooling2D and a Dense softmax. Listing 8.1 uses the Functional API with an input of shape (28, 28, 1).

title: Convolutional neural network (ConvNet)
text: A neural network built mainly from convolution and pooling layers, used by most computer vision applications. Small learned pattern detectors scan the image; pooling summarizes their responses at coarser scales. Takes (height, width, channels) inputs (p.257) and produces feature maps whose spatial size shrinks and channel count grows with depth. Listing 8.1.
snippet: A neural network built mainly from convolution and pooling layers, used by most computer vision applications.

title: Conv2D layer
text: A layer that applies learned filters of size kernel_size over local windows of its input. A small stencil slid over the image, computing a response at every position. filters sets the number of output channels; kernel_size=3 means 3x3 windows. Details from p.258. layers.Conv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")
snippet: A layer that applies learned filters of size kernelsize over local windows of its input.

title: MaxPooling2D layer
text: Downsampling layer that keeps the maximum value in each pool_size x pool_size window. Keeps the strongest response in each neighbourhood, halving height and width with pool_size=2. Explained in 8.1.2 (p.263). layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)
snippet: Downsampling layer that keeps the maximum value in each poolsize x poolsize window.

title: GlobalAveragePooling2D
text: Averages each channel over all spatial positions, turning (h, w, c) into a vector of length c. One summary number per feature detector: how strongly, on average, did it fire across the image? In Listing 8.1 it turns the last (3, 3, 256) feature map into a 256-vector for the Dense classifier (shapes on p.257). x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
snippet: Averages each channel over all spatial positions, turning h, w, c into a vector of length c.

title: Listing 8.1 Instantiating a small ConvNet
text:
import keras
from keras import layers

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=128, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=256, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs) Builds a small ConvNet for 28x28 grayscale digits with three convolution layers, two max-pooling layers, global average pooling and a 10-way softmax classifier. Alternating convolution and pooling to extract increasingly abstract, spatially coarser features, followed by global pooling and a linear softmax classifier.
snippet: Builds a small ConvNet for 28x28 grayscale digits with three convolution layers, two max-pooling layers, global average pooling and a 10-way softmax classifier.

title: ConvNet input shape and model.summary() of the first ConvNet
text:
The (height, width, channels) input convention, Listing 8.2's model summary with output shapes and parameter counts, and the channels-last versus channels-first sidebar. A ConvNet consumes rank-3 image tensors (height, width, channels), excluding the batch axis. As data passes through Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers, height and width shrink while the number of channels, set by each Conv2D's filters argument, grows. Keras defaults to channels-last; channels-first is a configurable convention. The page explains what the ConvNet of Listing 8.1 consumes and produces. A ConvNet takes input tensors of shape `(image_height, image_width, image_channels)`, *not including the batch dimension*; for MNIST this is `(28, 28, 1)`.

**Listing 8.2** calls `model.summary()` on the model, named `"functional"`:

| Layer | Output shape | Params |
|---|---|---|
| input_layer | (None, 28, 28, 1) | 0 |
| conv2d | (None, 26, 26, 64) | 640 |
| max_pooling2d | (None, 13, 13, 64) | 0 |
| conv2d_1 | (None, 11, 11, 128) | 73,856 |
| max_pooling2d_1 | (None, 5, 5, 128) | 0 |
| conv2d_2 | (None, 3, 3, 256) | 295,168 |
| global_average_pooling2d | (None, 256) | 0 |
| dense | (None, 10) | 2,570 |

Total params: **372,234** (1.42 MB), all trainable. `None` is the batch axis of unknown size.

The authors point out that the output of every `Conv2D` and `MaxPooling2D` layer is a 3D tensor `(height, width, channels)`; **width and height shrink** deeper in the model, and the **number of channels is set by the first argument of `Conv2D`** (64, 128, 256).

The sidebar **Image data formats in deep learning frameworks** notes that some libraries, notably much of the PyTorch ecosystem, put channels first: `(channels, height, width)`. This is purely a convention and is configurable in Keras, globally with `keras.config.set_image_data_format("channels_first")` or per layer with the `data_format` argument of conv and pooling layers. Generally, keep the default unless you specifically need `"channels_first"`.

Beyond the book: the parameter counts follow from $(k^2 C_{in} + 1) C_{out}$ for a $k\times k$ convolution (see the math section), and the shapes from the valid 3x3 convolution shrinking each side by 2 and the 2x2 pooling halving it with rounding down. A Keras ConvNet takes (height, width, channels) inputs, without the batch axis; MNIST is (28, 28, 1). Spatial size shrinks (28 -> 26 -> 13 -> 11 -> 5 -> 3) while channels grow (64 -> 128 -> 256). The model has 372,234 trainable parameters; pooling layers have none. Channel count is the first argument (filters) of Conv2D. channels_first vs channels_last is a convention; Keras defaults to channels_last and can be switched globally or per layer.
snippet: The page explains what the ConvNet of Listing 8.1 consumes and produces. A ConvNet takes input tensors of shape imageheight, imagewidth, imagechannels, not including the batch…

snippet: The rank-3 per-sample representation of an image used by Keras ConvNets; batches add a leading axis.

title: Conv2D parameter count
text: Number of trainable weights in a Conv2D layer: one k x k x C_in kernel plus one bias per output channel. Each filter looks at every input channel over a small window; the count does not depend on image size. (k^2 * C_in + 1) * C_out. For conv2d_1: (9*64+1)*128 = 73,856. First conv: (9*1+1)*64 = 640.

title: channels_last vs channels_first

P_{\text{conv}} = (k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}} + 1)\, C_{\text{out}} Reproduce and check the Param # column. Each filter has k*k*C_in weights; the count is independent of image size. k Kernel size (3 here). C_{\text{in}} Number of input channels. C_{\text{out}} Number of filters (output channels). +1 One bias per filter.

H_{\text{conv}} = H_{\text{in}} - k + 1, \qquad H_{\text{pool}} = \left\lfloor \frac{H_{\text{in}}}{2} \right\rfloor Predict the Output Shape column. A 3x3 window fits in H-2 positions per axis; 2x2 pooling keeps one value per 2x2 block. H_{\text{in}} Input height (width behaves the same). k Kernel size, 3. H_{\text{conv}}, H_{\text{pool}} Output height after convolution (stride 1, no padding) or after 2x2 pooling (stride 2).

title: Finishing, training and evaluating the first ConvNet
text:
How the small MNIST ConvNet turns its (3, 3, 256) feature map into a 10-way prediction, how it is trained and evaluated, and the opening of the explanation of convolution. A GlobalAveragePooling2D layer collapses the last spatial feature map into a 256-dimensional vector that a softmax Dense layer can classify; trained exactly like the chapter 2 dense network, the ConvNet reaches 99.1% test accuracy versus 97.8%, and the reason is that convolutions learn local rather than global patterns. The page finishes the first ConvNet example of chapter 8.

**From feature maps to a prediction.** After the third `Conv2D` layer the model holds a tensor of shape `(3, 3, 256)`: a 3 × 3 spatial grid with 256 channels. `Dense` classifiers expect 1D vectors, so the authors insert a `GlobalAveragePooling2D` layer, which averages each 3 × 3 channel map into a single number, producing a `(256,)` vector. A final `Dense(10, activation="softmax")` gives the 10-way class probabilities.

**Training (listing 8.3).** The MNIST arrays are reshaped from `(60000, 28, 28)` to `(60000, 28, 28, 1)` (adding an explicit channels axis, as required by `Conv2D`), cast to `float32` and divided by 255. The model is compiled with the `adam` optimizer, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` loss (integer labels + softmax output) and accuracy as metric, then trained for 5 epochs with batches of 64.

**Evaluation (listing 8.4).** `model.evaluate` on the 10,000 test images gives a test accuracy of **0.991**. The chapter 2 dense network reached 97.8%, so the error rate fell from 2.2% to 0.9%, about a 60% relative reduction.

**Why does it work?** The authors announce that the answer lies in what `Conv2D` and `MaxPooling2D` do, and open section 8.1.1, *The convolution operation*, with the key contrast: `Dense` layers learn **global** patterns over the whole input feature space (for MNIST, patterns involving all pixels), while convolution layers learn local patterns (the sentence continues on p.259). GlobalAveragePooling2D averages each channel's spatial map, turning (3, 3, 256) into a (256,) vector for the Dense classifier. The head is Dense(10, softmax) for 10-way classification. Conv2D input requires an explicit channel axis: MNIST becomes (60000, 28, 28, 1), scaled to [0, 1]. Integer labels + softmax output -> sparse_categorical_crossentropy. The basic ConvNet reaches 99.1% test accuracy vs 97.8% for the dense model: about 60% fewer errors. The key difference: Dense layers learn global patterns, convolution layers learn local ones.
snippet: The page finishes the first ConvNet example of chapter 8. From feature maps to a prediction. After the third Conv2D layer the model holds a tensor of shape 3, 3, 256: a 3 × 3…

title: Global average pooling
text: An operation that averages each channel of a (height, width, channels) feature map over all spatial positions, producing a vector of length channels. For each feature detector, ask 'on average, how much of this feature is in the image?' and forget where it was. Output $v_c = \frac{1}{HW}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\sum_{j=1}^{W} F_{i,j,c}$. It has no trainable parameters. For (3, 3, 256) it outputs (256,). A 3 × 3 map [[0,1,0],[2,4,2],[0,1,0]] averages to 10/9 ≈ 1.11.
snippet: An operation that averages each channel of a height, width, channels feature map over all spatial positions, producing a vector of length channels.

title: Feature map
text: The spatial grid of activations produced by one filter (channel) of a convolution layer. A heat map showing where in the image a particular pattern was detected. A conv output of shape (h, w, c) contains c feature maps of size h × w; in this model the last one is 3 × 3 with 256 channels. (26, 26, 64) after the first Conv2D means 64 maps of 26 × 26.
snippet: The spatial grid of activations produced by one filter channel of a convolution layer.

title: Sparse categorical crossentropy
text: Categorical crossentropy loss computed directly from integer class labels. Penalizes the model by the negative log of the probability it assigned to the correct digit. For label $y \in \{0..9\}$ and softmax output $p$, loss $= -\log p_y$. Identical to categorical crossentropy with one-hot targets. If the model assigns 0.9 to the true class, loss = -ln 0.9 ≈ 0.105; if 0.1, loss ≈ 2.30.
snippet: Categorical crossentropy loss computed directly from integer class labels.

title: Convolution layer vs Dense layer
text: Dense layers learn global patterns over the whole input; convolution layers learn local patterns in small windows. A Dense unit looks at the entire digit at once with a fixed template; a conv filter is a small magnifying glass slid over the image. Dense: every output connects to every input. Conv2D: each output connects to a k × k × c_in window, and weights are shared across positions. A 3 × 3 kernel in this model sees 9 pixels at a time.
snippet: Dense layers learn global patterns over the whole input; convolution layers learn local patterns in small windows.

title: Relative error reduction
text: The fraction by which the error rate shrinks: (e_old - e_new) / e_old. How many of the old mistakes did the new model eliminate? From 97.8% to 99.1% accuracy: (2.2 - 0.9) / 2.2 ≈ 0.59. On 10,000 test digits: ~220 errors vs ~90 errors.
snippet: The fraction by which the error rate shrinks: eold - enew / eold.

title: Global average pooling
text: This layer will take the average of each 3 × 3 feature map in the tensor of shape (3, 3, 256), resulting in an output vector of shape (256,). v_c = \frac{1}{3\cdot 3}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\sum_{j=1}^{3} F_{i,j,c}, \qquad c = 1,\dots,256 Turn a rank-3 feature tensor into a vector for the Dense classifier. Each component measures the average presence of one learned feature across the image. F The (3, 3, 256) output of the last Conv2D layer F_{i,j,c} Activation at row i, column j, channel c v_c Component c of the pooled 256-dimensional vector
snippet: This layer will take the average of each 3 × 3 feature map in the tensor of shape 3, 3, 256, resulting in an output vector of shape 256,. — Turn a rank-3 feature tensor into a…

title: Relative error reduction
text: we decreased the error rate by about 60% (relative) \frac{e_{\text{dense}} - e_{\text{conv}}}{e_{\text{dense}}} = \frac{(1-0.978) - (1-0.991)}{1-0.978} = \frac{0.022-0.009}{0.022} \approx 0.59 Quantify the improvement in a way that is meaningful near 100% accuracy. The ConvNet eliminates about 59% of the dense model's mistakes. e_{\text{dense}} Test error of the chapter 2 dense model (2.2%) e_{\text{conv}} Test error of the ConvNet (0.9%)
snippet: we decreased the error rate by about 60% relative — Quantify the improvement in a way that is meaningful near 100% accuracy.

title: Sparse categorical crossentropy
text: loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy" \mathcal{L}(y, p) = -\log p_{y}, \qquad p = \operatorname{softmax}(z) Training objective chosen on this page for integer labels with softmax output. Low when the model is confident and right, very high when confident and wrong. y Integer label of the digit, 0-9 z The 10 pre-activation outputs of the last Dense layer p_y Softmax probability assigned to the true class
snippet: loss="sparsecategoricalcrossentropy" — Training objective chosen on this page for integer labels with softmax output.

title: Listing 8.3 Training the ConvNet on MNIST images
text:
from keras.datasets import mnist

(train_images, train_labels), (test_images, test_labels) = mnist.load_data()
train_images = train_images.reshape((60000, 28, 28, 1))
train_images = train_images.astype("float32") / 255
test_images = test_images.reshape((10000, 28, 28, 1))
test_images = test_images.astype("float32") / 255
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=5, batch_size=64) Loads MNIST, reshapes images to include a single channel axis, scales pixel values to [0, 1], compiles the ConvNet from listing 8.1 and trains it for 5 epochs. Mini-batch gradient descent with Adam on crossentropy loss.
snippet: Loads MNIST, reshapes images to include a single channel axis, scales pixel values to 0, 1, compiles the ConvNet from listing 8.1 and trains it for 5 epochs.

title: Local patterns: translation invariance and spatial hierarchies
text:
Why learning local patterns in small windows gives ConvNets two key properties: translation-invariant patterns and spatial hierarchies of patterns. Convolution layers learn patterns in small 2D windows (3 × 3 in the MNIST model). Because the same pattern detector is applied everywhere, a pattern learned at one location is recognized at any location (data efficiency), and stacking layers composes small patterns into larger, more abstract ones, mirroring a visual world that is translation invariant and spatially hierarchical. Continuing the sentence begun on p.258, the authors state the fundamental difference between layer types: `Dense` layers learn **global** patterns (for an MNIST digit, patterns involving all pixels), whereas convolution layers learn **local** patterns, i.e. patterns found in small 2D windows of the input. In the MNIST ConvNet these windows were all 3 × 3. Figure 8.1 shows a handwritten digit with several small square windows highlighted; each extracted patch contains a simple local pattern such as a stroke fragment or edge.

This local character gives ConvNets two properties:

1. **The patterns they learn are translation invariant.** After learning a pattern in the lower-right corner of an image, a ConvNet can recognize it anywhere, e.g. in the upper-left corner. A densely connected model would have to learn the pattern anew at every new location. Hence ConvNets are **data efficient** on images, because *the visual world is fundamentally translation invariant*: they need fewer training samples to learn representations that generalize.
2. **They can learn spatial hierarchies of patterns.** A first convolution layer learns small local patterns such as edges; a second learns larger patterns made of first-layer features; and so on. This lets ConvNets efficiently learn increasingly complex and abstract visual concepts, because *the visual world is fundamentally spatially hierarchical*.

Figure 8.2 illustrates the hierarchy: a cat image at the bottom is decomposed into elementary lines and textures (a row of small boxes with curves and strokes), which combine into simple object parts (an eye, a nose, an ear), which in turn combine into the high-level concept "cat" at the top. Dense layers learn global patterns; convolution layers learn local patterns in small 2D windows (3 × 3 in the MNIST model). ConvNet patterns are translation invariant: learned once, recognized anywhere. Translation invariance makes ConvNets data efficient, because the visual world is translation invariant. Stacked conv layers learn spatial hierarchies: edges -> parts -> objects. Hierarchy lets ConvNets learn increasingly complex and abstract concepts because the visual world is spatially hierarchical.

title: Feature maps, filters and the two key conv parameters
text:
What convolutions operate on (rank-3 feature maps with height, width and depth), what output channels mean (filters and their response maps), and the two parameters that define a convolution. A convolution reads a (height, width, depth) feature map, extracts small patches, applies the same learned transformation to each, and writes a new feature map whose depth is the number of filters; each output channel is a 2D response map of one filter over the input. **Feature maps.** Convolutions operate on rank-3 tensors called *feature maps*, with two spatial axes (*height*, *width*) and a *depth* axis, also called the *channels* axis. An RGB image has depth 3 (red, green, blue); a grayscale MNIST digit has depth 1. A convolution extracts patches from its input feature map and applies **the same transformation to all patches**, producing an *output feature map*, which is again rank-3. Its depth is a free parameter of the layer, and its channels no longer stand for colors but for *filters*, each encoding some aspect of the input (at a high level, a filter could encode "presence of a face in the input").

**Response maps.** In the MNIST model the first conv layer maps `(28, 28, 1)` to `(26, 26, 64)`: it computes 64 filters. Each output channel is a 26 × 26 *response map* showing how strongly that filter's pattern is present at each location (figure 8.3: an MNIST zero, a single 3 × 3 filter, and the resulting response map highlighting part of the stroke). That is what *feature map* means: each depth index is a feature, and `output[:, :, n]` is the 2D spatial map of filter n's response.

**Two key parameters.**
- *Size of the patches* (typically 3 × 3 or 5 × 5; 3 × 3 in the example).
- *Depth of the output feature map*, i.e. the number of filters (the text says the example went from 32 to 64; note that listing 8.1 actually uses 64, 128 and 256).

In Keras these are the first arguments: `Conv2D(output_depth, (window_height, window_width))`.

**Sliding.** A convolution slides the 3 × 3 or 5 × 5 window over the 3D input, stopping at every possible location, and extracts a 3D patch of shape `(window_height, window_width, input_depth)`. Each patch is transformed into a 1D vector of shape `(output_depth,)`; the sentence finishes on p.261 (a tensor product with a learned kernel, reused across every patch). Convolutions operate on rank-3 feature maps: (height, width, depth/channels). Input depth = color channels (3 for RGB, 1 for MNIST); output depth = number of filters, a layer parameter. Each output channel is a response map: output[:, :, n] shows where filter n's pattern is present. Two key parameters: patch size (typically 3 × 3 or 5 × 5) and output depth: Conv2D(output_depth, (window_height, window_width)). A convolution slides the window over every location, extracting (window_height, window_width, input_depth) patches and mapping each to an (output_depth,) vector with the same transformation.

title: How convolution works: kernel, reassembly, figure 8.4
text:
The second half of the convolution mechanism: each patch is transformed by a tensor product with a shared learned kernel, and the resulting vectors are reassembled spatially into the output feature map; output size can differ from input size because of border effects and strides. One learned kernel, reused for every patch, maps each (3, 3, input_depth) patch to an (output_depth,) vector; placing those vectors back at their spatial positions gives a (height, width, output_depth) output in which every location summarizes the corresponding input location. This page finishes the sentence from p.260: each 3D patch is transformed into a 1D vector of shape `(output_depth,)` **via a tensor product with a learned weight matrix, the *convolution kernel***, and **the same kernel is reused across every patch**. The vectors, one per patch, are then **spatially reassembled** into a 3D output map of shape `(height, width, output_depth)`.

Because each vector is put back where its patch came from, every spatial location in the output corresponds to the same location in the input: for example, the lower-right corner of the output carries information about the lower-right corner of the input. With 3 × 3 windows, the book writes that `output[i, j, :]` comes from the patch `input[i-1:i+1, j-1:j+1, :]`, i.e. the 3 × 3 neighbourhood centred on (i, j) (as Python code the slice would need `i+2`; see the note below).

**Figure 8.4** shows the whole process top to bottom: an input feature map with width, height and input depth; several 3 × 3 input patches extracted from it (one highlighted in blue); each patch passes through a *dot product with kernel* to become a column vector of length *output depth* (the *transformed patches*); these columns are assembled into the *output feature map*, a block whose depth is the output depth (the blue column corresponds to the blue patch).

Finally, the output width and height may differ from the input's for two reasons:
- **border effects**, which can be countered by **padding** the input;
- the use of **strides**, defined shortly.

The next pages (p.262 onward) take a deeper look at both. Each patch is turned into an (output_depth,) vector by a tensor product with the learned convolution kernel. The same kernel is reused across every patch (weight sharing). The per-patch vectors are reassembled spatially into a (height, width, output_depth) output. Output locations correspond to input locations: output[i, j, :] comes from the 3 × 3 neighbourhood of (i, j). Output height/width can differ from the input because of border effects (countered by padding) and strides.

title: Border effects and padding
text:
Why an unpadded convolution shrinks the feature map (border effects), and how padding restores the input's spatial size. A 3 × 3 window can only be centred on interior tiles, so a 5 × 5 input gives a 3 × 3 output (and 28 × 28 gives 26 × 26); adding one row/column of padding on every side (two for a 5 × 5 window) lets a centred window fit around every input tile, keeping the output size equal to the input size. **Border effects.** Take a 5 × 5 feature map (25 tiles). A 3 × 3 window must fit entirely inside the input, so it can be centred on only 9 tiles, the interior 3 × 3 grid (figure 8.5: the 5 × 5 grid with the central 3 × 3 shaded, next to the nine possible 3 × 3 patch placements). The output feature map is therefore 3 × 3: it shrinks by exactly two tiles along each dimension. This is the border effect already visible in the MNIST ConvNet, where 28 × 28 inputs become 26 × 26 after the first convolution layer.

**Padding.** To obtain an output with the same spatial dimensions as the input, use *padding*: add an appropriate number of rows and columns on each side of the input so that a centred window fits around every input tile. For a 3 × 3 window, add one column on the left, one on the right, one row at the top and one at the bottom. For a 5 × 5 window, add two rows (two on each side). Figure 8.6 shows a 5 × 5 input surrounded by a ring of padding tiles (drawn with crosses), making a 7 × 7 grid from which 25 3 × 3 patches can be extracted, one centred on each original tile; several of these patches are drawn, with their crossed padding tiles visible, followed by "etc."

The next page shows how this is configured in Keras (`padding="valid"` or `"same"`) and introduces strides. Without padding, a 3 × 3 window can only be centred on interior tiles: 5 × 5 → 3 × 3, 28 × 28 → 26 × 26. The output shrinks by k − 1 tiles per dimension (two for 3 × 3): the border effect. Padding adds rows/columns on each side so a centred window fits around every input tile. Pad one per side for 3 × 3 windows, two per side for 5 × 5 windows, to keep output size equal to input size. Figure 8.6: a padded 5 × 5 input yields 25 3 × 3 patches.

title: Padding in Keras, strides, and the start of max pooling
text:
The Conv2D padding argument ("valid" vs "same"), strided convolutions as a second way output size changes, and the introduction of max pooling as the usual downsampling tool in classification models. padding="valid" (default) means no padding while "same" preserves width and height; the stride is the distance between successive windows (default 1), and stride 2 halves width and height. Classification ConvNets usually downsample with max pooling instead, which halved 26 × 26 to 13 × 13 in the MNIST model. **Padding in Keras.** `Conv2D` exposes padding through the `padding` argument with two values: `"valid"`, no padding (only valid window locations are used), and `"same"`, "pad in such a way as to have an output with the same width and height as the input." The default is `"valid"`, which is why the MNIST model's convolutions shrink their inputs by two tiles.

**Strides.** So far the window centres were assumed contiguous. The distance between two successive windows is a parameter called the **stride**, default 1. Convolutions with stride greater than 1 are *strided convolutions*. Figure 8.7 shows a 3 × 3 convolution with stride 2 on a 5 × 5 input without padding: only four patches are extracted, centred on the tiles labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 (the corners of the central 3 × 3 region), giving a 2 × 2 output. Stride 2 downsamples width and height by a factor of 2, in addition to any border effects. Strided convolutions are rarely used in classification models but are handy for some model types, as the next chapter shows.

**Max pooling instead.** Classification models typically downsample with the **max-pooling** operation, already used in the first ConvNet example.

**8.1.2 The max-pooling operation.** In the MNIST ConvNet the feature-map size is halved after each `MaxPooling2D` layer: 26 × 26 before the first one, 13 × 13 after. That is max pooling's role: to aggressively downsample feature maps, much like strided convolutions. How it works and why downsampling is needed follow on p.264. Conv2D padding: "valid" (no padding, the default) or "same" (output width and height equal the input's). Stride = distance between successive windows; default 1; stride > 1 gives strided convolutions. Figure 8.7: 3 × 3, stride 2 on 5 × 5 without padding extracts 4 patches (2 × 2 output). Stride 2 downsamples width and height by 2, in addition to border effects. Classification models usually downsample with max pooling, not strides; MaxPooling2D halved 26 × 26 to 13 × 13.

title: Max pooling vs. a ConvNet without pooling
text:
What max pooling does, how it differs from convolution, and a counter-example model (Listing 8.5) that omits max pooling Max pooling extracts small windows (usually 2 × 2, stride 2) and keeps the per-channel maximum, halving the spatial size. To show why this downsampling matters, the authors build a ConvNet with three stacked convolutions and no pooling, and start listing what goes wrong with it. This page continues section 8.1.2. The authors first define **max pooling**: windows are extracted from the input feature maps and the **maximum value of each channel** in each window is output. This is *conceptually similar to convolution*. Both work on local patches. The difference is that convolution transforms each patch with a **learned linear transformation** (the kernel), while max pooling applies a **hardcoded `max` operation** with no trainable weights. The two also differ in their usual settings. Max pooling typically uses **2 × 2 windows with stride 2**, which downsamples the feature maps by a factor of 2. Convolution typically uses **3 × 3 windows with no stride (stride 1)**.

The authors then ask why we downsample at all. Why not drop pooling and keep large feature maps throughout? To find out, **Listing 8.5** builds an "incorrectly structured" ConvNet. It has three `Conv2D` layers (64, 128 and 256 filters, kernel size 3, ReLU) applied to 28 × 28 × 1 MNIST inputs, followed by `GlobalAveragePooling2D` and a 10-way softmax `Dense` layer. The `summary()` output shows the spatial size shrinking only by the border effect, 28 → 26 → 24 → 22, while the channels grow to 256. The model has 372,234 parameters in total, almost all of them in the convolution layers.

The page ends by asking "What's wrong with this setup?" and starts the first of two answers. The model is not conducive to learning a **spatial hierarchy of features**, because the 3 × 3 windows of the third layer only contain information from 7 × 7 windows of the input. That sentence, and the second problem (a huge 22 × 22 final feature map that global average pooling then crushes), continue on p.265. Max pooling outputs, per channel, the maximum over each window. It is a hardcoded operation with no weights, unlike convolution's learned kernel. Usual settings: pooling uses 2 × 2 windows with stride 2 (halving resolution); convolution uses 3 × 3 windows with stride 1. Listing 8.5 removes pooling: spatial size only shrinks 28 → 26 → 24 → 22, while there are still 372,234 parameters. Without downsampling, three 3 × 3 conv layers see only a 7 × 7 patch of the input, so no meaningful spatial hierarchy forms. Conv parameter count = k·k·C_in·C_out + C_out, independent of image size.
snippet: This page continues section 8.1.2. The authors first define max pooling: windows are extracted from the input feature maps and the maximum value of each channel in each window is…

title: Max pooling
text: An operation that slides (usually non-overlapping) windows over a feature map and outputs, for each channel separately, the maximum value inside each window. It keeps the strongest response in each small neighbourhood: "was this feature present anywhere in this 2 × 2 tile, and how strongly?" With pool size 2 and stride 2, (H, W, C) → (⌊H/2⌋, ⌊W/2⌋, C). There are no trainable weights. During backprop the gradient flows only to the argmax position of each window. A 2 × 2 window [[1, 3], [0, 2]] in one channel becomes 3.
snippet: An operation that slides usually non-overlapping windows over a feature map and outputs, for each channel separately, the maximum value inside each window.

title: Convolution (contrast)
text: Transforms each local patch through a learned linear transformation (the kernel) shared across positions. A learned pattern detector applied everywhere in the image. Typically 3 × 3 windows, stride 1. With valid padding, each spatial dimension shrinks by k − 1 = 2. All input channels are mixed into each output channel. Conv2D(64, 3) on a 28 × 28 × 1 input gives 26 × 26 × 64.
snippet: Transforms each local patch through a learned linear transformation the kernel shared across positions.

title: Spatial hierarchy of features
text: The arrangement in which successive layers detect increasingly large and abstract patterns. Edges → strokes → loops → digits. It requires the receptive field of deep units to cover a large fraction of the input. Downsampling between conv layers makes receptive fields grow multiplicatively rather than additively. Without pooling, three 3 × 3 convs only reach 7 × 7 of a 28 × 28 image.
snippet: The arrangement in which successive layers detect increasingly large and abstract patterns.

title: Receptive field
text: The region of the input image that influences a given unit. How much of the picture a neuron can "see". For stride-1 k × k convs stacked L times: 1 + L(k − 1). A stride-2 pooling doubles the step of every later layer. Conv(3) → Conv(3) → Conv(3): 3, 5, 7.
snippet: The region of the input image that influences a given unit.

title: Global average pooling
text: Averages each channel over the entire spatial extent, turning (H, W, C) into (C,). One number per feature: its average presence over the whole image. There are no parameters. In Listing 8.5 it maps (22, 22, 256) to (256,). (None, 22, 22, 256) → (None, 256).
snippet: Averages each channel over the entire spatial extent, turning H, W, C into C,.

title: 2 × 2 max pooling with stride 2
text: extracting windows from the input feature maps and outputting the max value of each channel (2 × 2 windows, stride 2) y_{i,j,c} = \max_{a,b \in \{0,1\}} x_{2i+a,\;2j+b,\;c} It formalizes the verbal definition on the page. Each output records the strongest activation of a feature within a 2 × 2 tile. x Input feature map of shape (H, W, C) y Output feature map of shape (⌊H/2⌋, ⌊W/2⌋, C) i, j Output row and column c Channel index (the same in input and output) a, b Offsets inside the 2 × 2 window

title: Why downsample, why max pooling, and the start of 8.2
text:
The end of the max-pooling argument (both defects of the pooling-free model, why max beats average pooling and strides), then the introduction to training a ConvNet from scratch on a small cats-vs-dogs dataset Downsampling makes later layers see a larger fraction of the input and moves information from space into channels. Max pooling over dense, unstrided feature maps is the best way to do this for classification, because the maximal presence of a feature is more informative than its average. Section 8.2 then sets up a small-data problem: 2,000 training images of cats and dogs. The page finishes the critique of the pooling-free ConvNet from Listing 8.5 (p.264).

1. **No spatial hierarchy.** The third layer's features only see 7 × 7 windows of the input. They stay small relative to the 28 × 28 image, which "may not be enough to learn to classify digits". The last conv layer's features should contain information about the *totality* of the input.
2. **The final map is huge.** It is 22 × 22. Global averaging over 22 × 22 positions destroys much more information than averaging a 3 × 3 map, which is the size the pooled model reaches.

**In short:** downsampling reduces the size of feature maps, so information becomes *less spatially distributed and more contained in the channels*. It also induces **spatial-filter hierarchies**, because successive convolutions look at increasingly large windows relative to the original input.

Max pooling is not the only way to downsample. **Strided convolutions** and **average pooling** also work, but max pooling tends to work better. The reason given is that features encode the *spatial presence* of a pattern over the tiles of a feature map, and the **maximal presence** of a feature is more informative than its **average presence**. The recommended strategy is therefore to produce dense feature maps with unstrided convolutions and then take the max over small patches. Strided convolutions look at sparser windows, and averaging can dilute feature-presence information; both can make the model miss it.

**Section 8.2** then starts. Training an image classifier on very little data is a common professional situation, where "few" can mean anywhere from a few hundred to a few tens of thousands of images. The example is dogs vs. cats: 5,000 images from the Kaggle dataset (2,500 per class), split into **2,000 training, 1,000 validation and 2,000 test** images. The first strategy is to train a small ConvNet from scratch with no regularization as a baseline. It reaches **about 80%** accuracy (the sentence continues on p.266). Without pooling, the last conv features see only 7 × 7 pixels and the final map is a huge 22 × 22, so global averaging destroys information. Downsampling concentrates information in channels and makes later layers cover larger fractions of the input. Max pooling over dense, unstrided feature maps usually beats strided convolutions and average pooling, because the maximal presence of a feature is more informative than its average presence. Section 8.2 uses 5,000 cats-vs-dogs images: 2,000 train, 1,000 validation, 2,000 test. A naive from-scratch ConvNet reaches about 80%, and overfitting is the main obstacle.

title: Small-data strategies, feature reuse, and getting Dogs vs. Cats
text:
The chapter roadmap (from scratch → data augmentation → pretrained models), why deep learning works with small data (8.2.1), and where to get the Dogs vs. Cats dataset (8.2.2) 'Enough data' is relative to model size and task difficulty. ConvNets are data-efficient because they learn local, translation-invariant features, and deep models are highly reusable, so pretrained models can bootstrap strong results from little data. The Dogs vs. Cats data comes from a 2013 Kaggle competition and can be downloaded with kagglehub in Colab. The page finishes the roadmap started on p.265. Training a small ConvNet from scratch on 2,000 images reaches about 80% accuracy, and its main problem is **overfitting**. **Data augmentation** is introduced as a powerful computer-vision technique against overfitting, and it raises test accuracy to **about 84%**. Section 8.3 then adds **feature extraction with a pretrained model** and **fine-tuning a pretrained model**, reaching a final **98.5%**. These three strategies make up "your future toolbox" for small-dataset image classification.

**8.2.1 The relevance of deep learning for small-data problems.** Whether you have "enough samples" depends first on the size and depth of the model. A few tens of samples cannot train a ConvNet on a complex problem, but a few hundred can suffice if the model is small, well regularized and the task is simple. ConvNets learn **local, translation-invariant features**, which makes them **highly data efficient on perceptual problems**. Training one from scratch on a tiny dataset still yields reasonable results without custom feature engineering. Deep learning models are also **highly repurposable**. A model trained on a large dataset (e.g., image classification or speech-to-text) can be reused on a significantly different problem with minor changes. Many pretrained vision models are publicly available, and this **feature reuse** is "one of the greatest strengths of deep learning".

**8.2.2 Downloading the data.** Dogs vs. Cats is not packaged with Keras. Kaggle released it for a computer-vision competition in late 2013, "back when ConvNets weren't mainstream". It can be downloaded from `www.kaggle.com/c/dogs-vs-cats/data` (a free Kaggle account is required) or through the Kaggle API in Colab. A sidebar explains that the API is available through the **`kagglehub`** package, preinstalled on Colab, and that two preparation steps are needed before downloading. Those steps are listed on p.267. Chapter 8's toolbox for small-data image classification: from scratch (≈80%), plus augmentation (≈84%), then pretrained feature extraction and fine-tuning (98.5%). 'Enough data' depends on model size, regularization and task complexity. ConvNets are data efficient because they learn local, translation-invariant features. Feature reuse through pretrained models is one of deep learning's greatest strengths. Dogs vs. Cats comes from a 2013 Kaggle competition and is downloaded via the Kaggle website or the kagglehub API.

title: Building the small Dogs vs. Cats subset (Listing 8.6, part 1)
text:
Context of the 2013 competition, dataset size, the rationale for subsampling, the target directory structure, and the first half of the copying utility From the 25,000 labelled images, the authors build a deliberately small, balanced dataset: 1,000/500/1,000 images per class for train/validation/test, stored in a train|validation|test × cat|dog directory tree. A make_subset helper written with pathlib, os and shutil creates the directories and copies the files. **Historical context.** The 2013 Kaggle Dogs vs. Cats competition was, "unsurprisingly", won by entrants using ConvNets, and the best entries reached **up to 95% accuracy**. The authors promise to get fairly close to this in the next section, while training on **less than 10%** of the data the competitors had.

**Dataset facts and subsampling.** The full dataset has **25,000 images** (12,500 per class) and is 543 MB compressed. From it the authors build a new dataset with three subsets:

| subset | per class | total |
|---|---|---|
| train | 1,000 | 2,000 |
| validation | 500 | 1,000 |
| test | 1,000 | 2,000 |

Why subsample? Many image datasets in practice contain only a few thousand samples, and more data would make the problem easier, so "it's good practice to learn with a small dataset".

**Directory structure.** The data goes in `dogs_vs_cats_small/`, with `train/`, `validation/` and `test/` folders, each holding `cat/` and `dog/` subfolders. Callouts give the counts (1,000 / 1,000, 500 / 500, 1,000 / 1,000). One folder per class is the convention that lets Keras infer labels from folder names later (p.271).

**Listing 8.6 (first half).** The authors use `shutil` ("a Python library for running shell-like commands") together with `os` and `pathlib`. `original_dir` points to `train` (where the original data was uncompressed) and `new_base_dir` to `dogs_vs_cats_small`. The helper `make_subset(subset_name, start_index, end_index)` copies cat (respectively, dog) images with indices in `[start_index, end_index)` into `new_base_dir/{subset_name}/cat` (resp. `dog`). On this page it loops over the two categories, builds the target path with pathlib's `/` operator, and calls `os.makedirs(dir)`. The filename construction, copy loop and the three calls (`train` 0-1000, `validation` 1000-1500, `test` 1500-2500) are on p.269. The 2013 competition winners used ConvNets and reached up to 95%; the chapter gets close using less than 10% of the data. Full dataset: 25,000 images (12,500 per class), 543 MB compressed. Subset per class: 1,000 train / 500 validation / 1,000 test, stored under dogs_vs_cats_small/{split}/{cat,dog}. Learning with a small dataset is good practice because real datasets often only have a few thousand samples. make_subset uses pathlib, os.makedirs and shutil; Listing 8.6 continues on p.269.

text:
The end of Listing 8.6 (copying files into the subsets), the balanced binary setup, and the design of the small ConvNet for 180 × 180 RGB images (Listing 8.7 begins) make_subset copies the first 1,000, next 500 and next 1,000 images of each class into train, validation and test, which gives a balanced problem where accuracy is a valid metric. The model reuses the Conv2D/MaxPooling2D stack, made larger (two more stages) for bigger images. It goes from 180 × 180 to 7 × 7 spatially while depth grows from 32 to 512. It starts with a Rescaling layer and ends with a 1-unit sigmoid Dense layer. **End of Listing 8.6.** Inside `make_subset`, for each category, `fnames` lists `f"{category}.{i}.jpg"` for `i` in `range(start_index, end_index)`. Each file is then copied with `shutil.copyfile(src=original_dir / fname, dst=dir / fname)`. Three calls build the splits:

- `make_subset("train", 0, 1000)`: the first 1,000 images of each category
- `make_subset("validation", 1000, 1500)`: the next 500
- `make_subset("test", 1500, 2500)`: the next 1,000

That gives **2,000 training, 1,000 validation and 2,000 test** images, with equal class counts in every split. This is a **balanced binary classification problem**, so **accuracy** is an appropriate measure of success.

**8.2.3 Building your model.** The model reuses the structure of the first example: alternating `Conv2D` (ReLU) and `MaxPooling2D` layers. Because the images are bigger and the problem harder, it gets **two more `Conv2D`/`MaxPooling2D` stages**. These both **increase capacity** and **further reduce the feature-map size** so the maps aren't overly large at the final pooling layer, which is exactly the problem diagnosed on p.265. Starting from **180 × 180** inputs ("a somewhat arbitrary choice"), the feature maps are **7 × 7** just before `GlobalAveragePooling2D`. A **NOTE** stresses that depth increases (32 → 512) while spatial size decreases (180 × 180 → 7 × 7), "a pattern you'll see in almost all ConvNets".

For binary classification, the model ends with a **`Dense` layer of size 1 with `sigmoid`** activation, which encodes the probability of one class versus the other. It starts with a **`Rescaling`** layer that maps pixel values from [0, 255] to [0, 1].

**Listing 8.7** begins with `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(180, 180, 3))` (RGB images of 180 × 180) and `x = layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255)(inputs)`. The rest of the model is on p.270. Splits: train = images 0-999, validation = 1000-1499, test = 1500-2499 of each class, which gives 2,000 / 1,000 / 2,000. Balanced binary classification means accuracy is an appropriate metric (chance = 50%). The dogs-vs-cats ConvNet reuses the Conv2D + MaxPooling2D template with two extra stages, for capacity and smaller final maps (7 × 7). ConvNets almost always grow in depth (32 → 512) while shrinking spatially (180 → 7). Binary head: Dense(1, sigmoid). Input: Rescaling(1/255) for 180 × 180 × 3 RGB.

title: The dogs-vs-cats ConvNet and its summary
text:
The convolutional body of the dogs-vs-cats model (listing 8.7, continued) and the shape/parameter table printed by model.summary() Five Conv2D stages (32 to 512 filters) interleaved with four 2x2 max-pooling layers shrink a 180x180x3 image to a 7x7x512 feature map, which GlobalAveragePooling2D collapses to a 512-vector feeding a single sigmoid unit; the summary table makes every shape change and parameter count explicit. This page completes **listing 8.7**, the small ConvNet for dogs-vs-cats classification that was introduced on p.269. The previous page set up `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(180, 180, 3))` and a `Rescaling(1./255)` layer; here we see the rest of the stack: five `Conv2D` layers with 3x3 kernels and ReLU, whose filter counts double at each stage (32, 64, 128, 256, 512), separated by four `MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)` layers. After the last convolution a `GlobalAveragePooling2D` layer — the callout explains — turns the 3D activations of shape `(height, width, 512)` into a 1D vector of shape `(512,)` by averaging over the spatial dimensions. A `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` layer outputs the probability of one of the two classes, and `keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)` ties it together.

The authors then print `model.summary()` to show "how the dimensions of the feature maps change with every successive layer." The table reads as a story of shrinking space and growing depth:

- 180x180x3 → (conv) 178x178x32 → (pool) 89x89x32
- → 87x87x64 → 43x43x64
- → 41x41x128 → 20x20x128
- → 18x18x256 → 9x9x256
- → 7x7x512 → (global average pool) 512 → (dense) 1

Each 3x3 convolution without padding loses one pixel on every border (−2 per dimension); each pooling halves the size, rounding down (87 → 43, 41 → 20). The parameter column shows that almost all weights live in the convolution kernels, with the last `Conv2D` alone holding 1,180,160 of them, while pooling, rescaling and global averaging have none. The final `Dense` layer needs only 513 parameters, because global average pooling reduced the features to just 512 numbers — a much smaller head than flattening 7x7x512 = 25,088 values would require. This matches the NOTE on p.269: depth increases from 32 to 512 while feature-map size decreases from 180x180 to 7x7, a pattern found in almost all ConvNets. The model is five 3x3 Conv2D layers (32→512 filters) with four 2x2 max pools, global average pooling and a single sigmoid unit. Each valid 3x3 conv removes 2 pixels per dimension; each 2x2 pool halves (rounding down): 180 → … → 7. Conv params = 3·3·C_in·C_out + C_out; the last conv alone has 1,180,160 parameters. GlobalAveragePooling2D turns (7, 7, 512) into (512,) by averaging over space, keeping the classifier head at 513 parameters. Depth grows while spatial size shrinks — the standard ConvNet pattern.
snippet: This page completes listing 8.7, the small ConvNet for dogs-vs-cats classification that was introduced on p.269. The previous page set up inputs = keras.Inputshape=180, 180, 3 and…

title: Conv2D stage
text: A layer that slides learned 3x3 filters across the input feature map, producing one output channel per filter. Each filter is a small pattern detector; the output channel is a map of where that pattern appears. With kernel_size=3, no padding and stride 1, output height/width = input − 2. Parameters = 3·3·C_in·C_out + C_out. conv2d_6 maps (180,180,3) to (178,178,32) with 3·3·3·32+32 = 896 parameters.
snippet: A layer that slides learned 3x3 filters across the input feature map, producing one output channel per filter.
section: 8.2 Training a convnet from scratch on a small dataset

title: Max pooling (2x2)
text: Downsampling that keeps the maximum of each non-overlapping 2x2 window, halving height and width. Keep the strongest response in each neighbourhood and throw away exact position. MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2) uses stride 2 by default; output = floor(input/2), so odd sizes lose a row/column (87→43, 41→20). It has no parameters. max_pooling2d_3: (87,87,64) → (43,43,64).
snippet: Downsampling that keeps the maximum of each non-overlapping 2x2 window, halving height and width.
section: 8.2 Training a convnet from scratch on a small dataset

title: Global average pooling
text: A layer that averages each channel of a feature map over all spatial positions, turning (H, W, C) into (C,). For each of the 512 detectors, ask 'how strongly did you fire on average across the whole image?' y_c = (1/(H·W)) Σ_i Σ_j x_{i,j,c}; no trainable weights. Here (7,7,512) → (512,). A channel whose 49 values average to 0.8 contributes 0.8 to the 512-vector.
snippet: A layer that averages each channel of a feature map over all spatial positions, turning H, W, C into C,.

Depth 32→512, size 180x180→7x7 in this model. Elements per sample: 178·178·32 ≈ 1.01M after the first conv vs 7·7·512 = 25,088 after the last.

title: Compiling the model and starting the image pipeline
text:
Parameter totals of the dogs-vs-cats ConvNet, compiling it with adam and binary crossentropy, and turning JPEG files into batched tensors with image_dataset_from_directory A single-sigmoid-unit model is compiled with binary crossentropy, adam and accuracy; then the raw JPEGs on disk must be read, decoded, converted to floats, resized to 180x180 and batched — all of which Keras's image_dataset_from_directory does automatically by treating each subdirectory as a class. The page opens with the end of the `model.summary()` output from p.270: **1,569,089 total parameters (5.99 MB)**, all of them trainable, none non-trainable. (5.99 MB is simply 1,569,089 float32 values × 4 bytes.)

**Listing 8.8** compiles the model. As usual, the optimizer is `adam`; because the model ends in a single sigmoid unit, the loss is `binary_crossentropy`; accuracy is tracked as the metric (appropriate because the splits are balanced, p.269). The authors refer back to table 6.1 in chapter 6 as a cheat sheet for choosing a loss.

**Section 8.2.4, Data preprocessing**, recalls that models consume preprocessed floating-point tensors, whereas our data are JPEG files on a drive. Five steps are needed: (1) read the picture files, (2) decode the JPEG content to RGB grids of pixels, (3) convert them into floating-point tensors, (4) resize them to a shared size — 180x180 — and (5) pack them into batches (the text says batches of 32 images). Keras automates this with `image_dataset_from_directory`, which lists the subdirectories of a directory, assumes each contains the images of one class, indexes the files, and returns a `tf.data.Dataset` that reads, shuffles, decodes, resizes and batches them.

**Listing 8.9** begins at the bottom of the page with the import `from keras.utils import image_dataset_from_directory` and `batch_size = 64` — note that this differs from the 32 mentioned in the numbered list; the actual calls that build the train, validation and test datasets follow on p.272. Note that pixel scaling to [0, 1] is not part of this pipeline: it is handled inside the model by the `Rescaling` layer (p.269). The model has 1,569,089 parameters (about 6 MB in float32), all trainable. Single sigmoid output → binary_crossentropy; adam as the default optimizer; accuracy as metric. JPEGs must be read, decoded, converted to floats, resized to 180x180 and batched. image_dataset_from_directory does all of this and infers labels from subfolder names, returning a tf.data.Dataset. The text mentions batches of 32 but the code uses batch_size = 64.

title: Binary crossentropy
text: The loss −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)] for a binary target y and predicted probability p. Penalizes confident wrong predictions heavily; zero loss when p equals the true label. Negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli distribution parameterized by the sigmoid output. y=1, p=0.9 → loss 0.105; y=1, p=0.1 → loss 2.30.

Keeps exponential moving averages of gradients and squared gradients, bias-corrected, and scales updates by their ratio. optimizer="adam" uses Keras's default learning rate of 0.001.
