title: Building the datasets; introducing tf.data.Dataset
text:
Creating train/validation/test datasets with image_dataset_from_directory, and an introduction to the tf.data.Dataset class Three calls to image_dataset_from_directory produce batched 180x180 datasets for each split; these are tf.data.Dataset objects — backend-agnostic iterators that yield batches, can be passed straight to fit(), parallelize preprocessing and prefetch data, and expose a functional API, illustrated by building a Dataset from a NumPy array with from_tensor_slices(). The page first finishes **listing 8.9**. With `image_size = (180, 180)` and the `batch_size = 64` set on p.271, three calls to `image_dataset_from_directory` build `train_dataset`, `validation_dataset` and `test_dataset` from `new_base_dir / "train"`, `"validation"` and `"test"` (the directories created when the data were copied in section 8.2.2). Each resizes images to 180x180 and batches them.

A short subsection, **Understanding TensorFlow Dataset objects**, then explains what these objects are. TensorFlow's `tf.data` API builds efficient input pipelines; its core class is `tf.data.Dataset`. The authors make four points:

1. `Dataset` is **framework-independent**: it can be used with JAX or PyTorch too, and with a Keras model it works the same whatever the backend.
2. A `Dataset` is an **iterator** — usable in a `for` loop — that typically yields batches of inputs and labels, and can be passed directly to `fit()`.
3. It handles features that are cumbersome to write yourself: **parallel preprocessing** across CPU cores and **asynchronous prefetching** (preparing the next batch while the model processes the current one, so execution flows without interruption).
4. It exposes a **functional-style API** for transforming datasets.

**Listing 8.10** starts a toy example: 1,000 samples, each a vector of 16 random normal numbers, are turned into a dataset with `tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(random_numbers)`. The callout notes that `from_tensor_slices()` accepts a NumPy array or a tuple or dict of arrays. As the last sentence says, this dataset initially yields **single samples** — each of shape `(16,)` — slicing along the first axis. Iteration, batching and `map()` follow on p.273. Three image_dataset_from_directory calls create the train, validation and test datasets at 180x180 with batch_size 64. These are tf.data.Dataset objects — iterators of (inputs, labels) batches that fit() accepts directly. tf.data works with any Keras backend (TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch). Dataset provides parallel preprocessing and asynchronous prefetching. from_tensor_slices slices an array along its first axis; the toy dataset yields single (16,) samples.

title: Iterating, batching and mapping a Dataset
text:
Hands-on use of the tf.data.Dataset API on the toy dataset from listing 8.10: iteration, .batch(), .shuffle(), .prefetch() and .map() The toy dataset yields single (16,) samples; .batch(32) groups them into (32, 16) tensors; shuffle, prefetch and map are further transformations, and map(function, num_parallel_calls) — demonstrated by reshaping each sample to (4, 4) with 8 parallel calls — is the workhorse for per-element preprocessing. Continuing the toy example of p.272 (a `Dataset` built from a `(1000, 16)` NumPy array), the page shows the basic `Dataset` operations.

- **Listing 8.11** iterates over the dataset with `enumerate`, printing the shape of the first three elements and breaking: each element is a single sample of shape `(16,)`.
- **Listing 8.12** calls `dataset.batch(32)`; the new `batched_dataset` yields tensors of shape `(32, 16)` — 32 samples stacked along a new leading batch axis.

The authors then list other useful methods:

- `.shuffle(buffer_size)` shuffles elements within a buffer;
- `.prefetch(buffer_size)` prefetches a buffer of elements in GPU memory for better device utilization;
- `.map(callable)` applies an arbitrary transformation to each element (the callable receives a single element yielded by the dataset).

`.map(function, num_parallel_calls)` is singled out as one you will use often. **Listing 8.13** uses it to reshape every toy element from `(16,)` to `(4, 4)` via `lambda x: tf.reshape(x, (4, 4))`, running up to 8 calls in parallel; iterating shows three elements of shape `(4, 4)`.

These operations are lazy and chainable: each call returns a new dataset, leaving the original unchanged — which is why `dataset` can still be mapped in listing 8.13 after being batched in 8.12. Note that the order matters: mapping before batching applies the function to single samples, mapping after batching would apply it to whole batches. The next page (p.274) returns to the image datasets and fits the model. Iterating over the toy dataset yields single (16,) samples. batch(32) yields (32, 16) tensors — a new leading batch axis. shuffle(buffer_size) randomizes within a buffer; prefetch(buffer_size) prepares elements ahead for better device utilization. map(function, num_parallel_calls) applies a function to every element in parallel; e.g. reshape (16,) → (4, 4). Dataset methods return new datasets and can be chained.

title: Inspecting batches and fitting with ModelCheckpoint
text:
Checking the shapes yielded by the image Dataset, then training the ConvNet for 50 epochs with validation monitoring and a ModelCheckpoint callback that keeps the best model by validation loss The training Dataset yields (images, labels) batches of shape (batch, 180, 180, 3) and (batch,); fit() takes the training and validation Datasets directly, and ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True, monitor="val_loss") ensures the saved file always holds the epoch with the lowest validation loss, so overfitting later in training does not require retraining. The page closes the tf.data detour ("You're about to see more `map()` action over the next chapters") and begins **Fitting the model**.

First, the authors inspect one batch of `train_dataset` (**listing 8.14**): iterating with `for data_batch, labels_batch in train_dataset:` and breaking after one step prints `data batch shape: (32, 180, 180, 3)` and `labels batch shape: (32,)` — 180×180 RGB images and integer labels. The text says there are 32 samples per batch, the batch size; note, however, that listing 8.9 set `batch_size = 64`, so running the code as printed would show 64 (see the review flag).

Next, **listing 8.15** trains the model. `fit()` receives `train_dataset` directly (labels come from the dataset), runs for `epochs=50`, and uses `validation_data=validation_dataset` to compute validation metrics on a separate `Dataset` at the end of each epoch.

The key addition is a **`ModelCheckpoint` callback**, configured with `filepath="convnet_from_scratch.keras"`, `save_best_only=True` and `monitor="val_loss"`. It saves the model after an epoch only if `val_loss` is lower than at any previous time, overwriting the previous file. Consequently the saved file always contains the model state from the best-performing epoch on validation data. The payoff, as the authors put it: if the model starts overfitting, we don't need to retrain it for fewer epochs — we just reload the saved file. (Earlier in the book, the approach was to note the best epoch and retrain from scratch.)

The returned `history` object records per-epoch metrics; the page ends by announcing plots of training/validation loss and accuracy in **figure 8.9** (p.275), which will show clear overfitting. A batch from train_dataset is (batch, 180, 180, 3) images with (batch,) integer labels; the page prints 32, though listing 8.9 sets 64. fit() accepts Dataset objects directly for both training and validation_data. ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True, monitor="val_loss") saves only when validation loss reaches a new minimum. The saved file is the best epoch, so overfitting does not require retraining — just reload. history records per-epoch metrics for the plots in figure 8.9.

title: Plotting the training curves: clear overfitting
text:
Plotting training and validation accuracy and loss from the History object (listing 8.16) and interpreting figure 8.9 as a textbook case of overfitting Training accuracy climbs to nearly 100% and training loss falls toward zero, while validation accuracy peaks around 80% and validation loss stops improving early — the signature of overfitting on 2,000 images; the model will therefore be evaluated from the checkpoint saved before overfitting began. **Listing 8.16** pulls four lists from the `History` object returned by `fit()` — `accuracy`, `val_accuracy`, `loss`, `val_loss` — builds `epochs = range(1, len(accuracy) + 1)`, and draws two matplotlib figures: training accuracy (red dashed, `"r--"`) vs validation accuracy (blue solid, `"b"`), then, after `plt.figure()` opens a new figure, training vs validation loss in the same styles.

**Figure 8.9** shows the result over 50 epochs. Reading the plots (approximately): training accuracy rises from about 0.52 to essentially 1.0 by around epoch 35–40; validation accuracy rises with it at first, then levels off around 0.80–0.83. Training loss falls from ~0.69 (the loss of a 50/50 guess, ln 2) to nearly 0; validation loss falls to about 0.5 and then climbs and becomes erratic, with a spike of ~1.28 near epoch 37 and ~0.95 at epoch 50.

The authors' reading: these plots are **characteristic of overfitting**. Training accuracy increases linearly until it reaches nearly 100%, whereas validation accuracy peaks around 80%. The validation loss reaches its minimum after only 10 epochs and then stalls, whereas the training loss keeps decreasing linearly. (In the printed figure the validation-loss minimum looks closer to epoch 20 — see the review flag — but the conclusion is the same: the model memorizes the 2,000 training images while generalization stops improving.)

Finally, the authors announce the test evaluation: they will **reload the model from its saved file** — the `ModelCheckpoint` file from p.274, which holds the lowest-validation-loss epoch — so that it is evaluated as it was before it started overfitting. The test accuracy (78.6%) follows on p.276. history.history holds per-epoch accuracy, val_accuracy, loss and val_loss for plotting. Figure 8.9: training accuracy → ~100% and training loss → ~0, but validation accuracy peaks around 80%. The validation loss stops improving early (the text says after ~10 epochs) while training loss keeps falling — classic overfitting. Both losses start near ln 2 ≈ 0.69, the loss of a 50/50 guess. The test evaluation uses the reloaded checkpoint, i.e. the model before it overfit.

title: Test accuracy of the baseline and introducing data augmentation
text:
Evaluating the from-scratch convnet on the test set (78.6%) and motivating data augmentation as the vision-specific remedy for overfitting on 2,000 images The baseline convnet reaches about 78.6% test accuracy and is limited by overfitting because it has only 2,000 training images. Data augmentation fights this by applying random, believable transformations to training images so the model never sees exactly the same picture twice; in Keras it is expressed as a list of augmentation layers that can run either inside the model or in the tf.data pipeline. The page opens by finishing the baseline experiment. **Listing 8.17** reloads the model file `convnet_from_scratch.keras`, which the `ModelCheckpoint` callback wrote at the epoch with the best validation loss, and calls `evaluate()` on `test_dataset`. The result is a **test accuracy of 78.6%**. Because random weight initialization differs from run to run, the authors warn that your own figure may differ by about one percentage point.

Next the authors say what has been holding the model back. With only **2,000 training samples**, *overfitting* is the main concern. The reader has already met dropout and weight decay (L2 regularization). This page introduces a third technique that is "specific to computer vision and used almost universally": **data augmentation**.

Section **8.2.5** frames overfitting as a data-scarcity problem. Given infinite data, a model would see every aspect of the distribution and could not overfit. Augmentation imitates having more data: it applies **random transformations that produce believable-looking images** to existing samples, so that at training time the model *never sees the exact same picture twice*.

In Keras, augmentation is done with **data augmentation layers**, and the page lists two places to put them:

- **At the start of the model**, right before the `Rescaling` layer. Augmentation then runs on the GPU along with the rest of the model.
- **Inside the data pipeline**, applied to the `Dataset` with `map()`. Augmentation then runs on the CPU, usually in parallel across several cores.

The authors say the in-model option sometimes performs better, but the pipeline option is "usually the better option", and the chapter goes with it.

**Listing 8.18** defines the augmentation stage as a plain Python list, `data_augmentation_layers`, containing `RandomFlip("horizontal")`, `RandomRotation(0.1)` and `RandomZoom(0.2)`. The next page (p.277) explains what each argument means and shows the augmented images. The from-scratch baseline convnet reaches about 78.6% test accuracy, give or take about 1 point between runs. Always evaluate the checkpoint chosen on validation data, reloaded from disk, rather than the final overfit weights. With 2,000 images, overfitting is the main obstacle. Data augmentation applies random, believable, label-preserving transformations so the model never sees the same image twice. Keras augmentation layers can sit inside the model (GPU) or be mapped over the Dataset (CPU). The book prefers the pipeline. Listing 8.18 defines the augmentation as a list: horizontal flip, rotation 0.1, zoom 0.2.

title: Applying the augmentation layers in a tf.data pipeline
text:
Mapping the augmentation layers over the training Dataset with parallel CPU calls and prefetching; the meaning of RandomFlip, RandomRotation and RandomZoom arguments; Figure 8.10 A small function applies the augmentation layers one after another to each batch. It is mapped over `train_dataset` with 8 parallel calls and followed by `prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)`. The three layers flip 50% of images horizontally, rotate by up to ±10% of a full circle (±36°), and zoom by up to ±20%, producing the varied images in Figure 8.10. The page continues **Listing 8.18** from p.276. It defines `data_augmentation(images, targets)`, which loops over `data_augmentation_layers` and applies each layer in turn to the image batch, returning the targets unchanged (callout: *"Creates a function that applies them sequentially"*). The function is applied to the training set with `train_dataset.map(data_augmentation, num_parallel_calls=8)` (*"Maps this function into the dataset"*). The result is then prefetched with `prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)`, which the callout says *"enables prefetching of batches on GPU memory; important for best performance"*. Only `train_dataset` is mapped, so validation and test data stay unaugmented.

The authors note that these are only a few of the available augmentation layers and refer you to the Keras documentation for more. They then explain the arguments:

- `RandomFlip("horizontal")` flips a **random 50%** of the images horizontally.
- `RandomRotation(0.1)` rotates by a random value in **[–10%, +10%] of a full circle**, which is **[–36°, +36°]**.
- `RandomZoom(0.2)` zooms in or out by a random factor in **[–20%, +20%]**.

**Figure 8.10** ("Generating variations of a very good boy via random data augmentation") shows a 3×3 grid of a single German-shepherd-like dog photo after random augmentation. The panels differ in orientation (some are mirrored), tilt, and framing or zoom. In several of them, the regions exposed by rotation are filled with stretched or reflected pixels from the image edges. The figure illustrates the claim from p.276 that the model will "never see the exact same picture twice". The next page gives the code that displayed these images (Listing 8.19) and adds dropout to the model. Augmentation is applied by mapping a function over train_dataset that calls each augmentation layer in turn. num_parallel_calls=8 parallelizes augmentation on the CPU, and prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE) overlaps it with GPU training. RandomFlip("horizontal") mirrors 50% of images. RandomRotation(0.1) means ±36°. RandomZoom(0.2) means ±20%. Rotation factors are fractions of a full circle, not degrees. Figure 8.10 shows how one photo becomes many plausible training images. Only training data is augmented.

title: Visualizing augmented images and adding dropout to the convnet
text:
Listing 8.19 (plotting nine augmentations of one image), why augmentation alone does not fully stop overfitting, and Listing 8.20 (the same convnet with Dropout(0.25) before the classifier), trained for 100 epochs Augmentation ensures the model never sees the same input twice, but the inputs are still highly correlated because they all derive from 2,000 originals: augmentation remixes information rather than creating it. So the authors add a Dropout(0.25) layer right before the final Dense classifier and plan to train for 100 epochs, evaluating on unaugmented images. **Listing 8.19** produces Figure 8.10 (p.277). It takes a single batch from `train_dataset` with `take(1)`. The callout explains that `take(N)` samples only N batches, "equivalent to inserting a break in the loop after the Nth batch". It keeps the first image, `image_batch[0]`, and then calls `data_augmentation(image, None)` nine times, plotting each result in a 3×3 grid. Because the layers draw fresh random parameters on every call, "for each of the nine iterations, this is a different augmentation of the same image." Each result is converted to NumPy with `keras.ops.convert_to_numpy` and cast to `uint8` for `imshow`.

The authors then qualify what augmentation can do. A model trained this way "will never see the same input twice", but its inputs are **heavily intercorrelated** because they come from a small number of originals: *"you can't produce new information; you can only remix existing information."* Augmentation may therefore not be enough to fully stop overfitting, so a **`Dropout` layer** is added "right before the densely connected classifier."

**Listing 8.20** rebuilds the baseline architecture with the Functional API. It starts with `Rescaling(1/255)` on 180×180×3 inputs. Five `Conv2D` layers (32, 64, 128, 256, 512 filters, 3×3 kernels, ReLU) alternate with four `MaxPooling2D(2)` layers. Then come `GlobalAveragePooling2D`, the new **`Dropout(0.25)`**, and `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")`. The model is compiled with `binary_crossentropy`, `adam` and accuracy.

Finally, the authors plan to train with augmentation and dropout for **100 epochs**, twice the baseline's 50, because overfitting is expected much later. Evaluation uses **unaugmented** images: augmentation is "usually only performed at training time, as it is a regularization technique." The training call and the results follow on p.279. Listing 8.19 plots nine random augmentations of a single training image (Figure 8.10). Augmentation remixes existing information. Augmented inputs are heavily intercorrelated, so overfitting is reduced but not eliminated. A Dropout(0.25) layer is added right before the Dense sigmoid classifier. Everything else matches the baseline model. The model goes from (180,180,3) to (7,7,512), then 512 features, then 1 probability, with about 1.57 M parameters. Stronger regularization calls for longer training: 100 epochs instead of 50. Validation and test use unaugmented images.

title: Training the regularized convnet and its improved learning curves
text:
Listing 8.21 trains the dropout convnet on augmented_train_dataset for 100 epochs with checkpointing; Figure 8.11 shows overfitting delayed to epochs 60–70 and validation accuracy above 85%; Listing 8.22 evaluates the best checkpoint on the test set With augmentation and dropout, the gap between training and validation metrics opens much later: around epochs 60–70 instead of epoch 10. Validation accuracy peaks above 85%. The best model by validation loss is checkpointed and then reloaded for an honest test evaluation. **Listing 8.21** trains the regularized model from Listing 8.20. A `ModelCheckpoint` callback saves to `convnet_from_scratch_with_augmentation.keras` only when `val_loss` improves (`save_best_only=True`). `model.fit` runs on `augmented_train_dataset` for **100 epochs**, with the unaugmented `validation_dataset` for validation. The callout says: *"Since we expect the model to overfit slower, we train for more epochs."*

The results (**Figure 8.11**) are much better than the baseline's. The authors say overfitting now begins **around epochs 60–70, compared with epoch 10 for the original model**, and validation accuracy **peaks above 85%**, "a big improvement over our first try".

Reading the plot (approximate values):

- **Accuracy.** Training accuracy (dashed red) rises steadily from 0.5 to about 0.95 by epoch 100. Validation accuracy (solid blue) tracks it closely until roughly epoch 40, then levels off and fluctuates in the 0.78–0.87 band.
- **Loss.** Training loss falls almost linearly from about 0.7 to about 0.15. Validation loss falls with it to around 0.4–0.45 and then stops improving, while becoming very noisy. Spikes reach about 0.9 near epoch 42 and about 0.8 near epoch 98.

That noise is exactly why the checkpoint monitors `val_loss` and keeps only the best epoch rather than the last one.

The page ends with **Listing 8.22**, which mirrors Listing 8.17: it reloads the saved best model and evaluates it on `test_dataset`. The result, **83.9%**, appears on the next page (p.280). That is about 5 points above the baseline's 78.6% (p.276). The regularized model is trained for 100 epochs on augmented data, with clean validation data and best-val_loss checkpointing. Overfitting now begins around epochs 60–70 instead of about epoch 10. Validation accuracy peaks above 85%, up from about 80% for the baseline. Validation loss becomes very noisy late in training, so checkpointing the best epoch is essential. Listing 8.22 reloads the best checkpoint for the test evaluation, which gives 83.9% (p.280).

title: From-scratch ceiling, and introducing pretrained models and feature extraction
text:
The regularized from-scratch convnet reaches 83.9% test accuracy with a ceiling of about 90%; pretrained models as reusable generic visual features; Xception trained on ImageNet; the two ways to reuse a model (feature extraction, fine-tuning); the definition of feature extraction and the convolutional base Training from scratch on 2,000 images tops out at roughly 90% even with tuning. To go further you reuse a model pretrained on a large, general dataset such as ImageNet, whose hierarchy of features acts as a generic model of the visual world. Feature extraction runs new samples through the pretrained network's convolutional base and trains only a new classifier on the resulting features. The page first closes section 8.2. The augmented, dropout-regularized convnet reaches **83.9% test accuracy**, up from the 78.6% baseline (p.276). Colab users are told to download `convnet_from_scratch_with_augmentation.keras` because the next chapter reuses it. The authors estimate that tuning the architecture (filters per layer, number of layers) might reach **about 90%**, but that going higher from scratch is hard "because you have so little data". The way forward is a **pretrained model**.

**Section 8.3** defines a pretrained model as one previously trained on a large dataset, typically a large-scale image-classification task. If that dataset is large and general enough, the **spatial hierarchy of features** the model learned acts as "a generic model of the visual world". Its features can then help with problems whose classes are entirely different. The authors' example is an ImageNet model (mostly animals and everyday objects) repurposed to recognize furniture. This *portability of learned features* is presented as a key advantage of deep learning over older shallow methods, and as the reason it works well on small data.

For this problem the authors pick a large convnet trained on **ImageNet**, which has **1.4 million labeled images in 1,000 classes**. It includes many cat and dog species, so it should do well here. The architecture is **Xception**. The authors note the "cutesy" names (Xception, ResNet, EfficientNet) and defer Xception's architecture to the next chapter. They name the two ways to use a pretrained model, **feature extraction** and **fine-tuning**, and start with the first.

**Section 8.3.1** defines feature extraction: use the representations learned by a previously trained model to extract features from new samples, then run those features through a **new classifier trained from scratch**. The authors recall that image-classification convnets have two parts, a stack of convolution and pooling layers followed by a densely connected classifier. The first part is called the **convolutional base** or **backbone**, and the sentence continues on p.281. Augmentation plus dropout give 83.9% test accuracy, about 5 points above the baseline. From scratch on 2,000 images, accuracy likely tops out near 90% even with tuning. Pretrained models trained on large, general datasets provide reusable, generic visual features. The chapter uses Xception trained on ImageNet (1.4M images, 1,000 classes, including cats and dogs). There are two ways to reuse a model: feature extraction (frozen base, new classifier) and fine-tuning. A convnet's conv/pool part is called the convolutional base or backbone.

text: Reusing a model trained on a large source dataset as the starting point for a new task. An experienced photographer can learn to recognize furniture styles faster than a newborn, because they already understand edges, shapes and textures. The pretrained weights encode a spatial hierarchy of features. If the source data is large and general enough, those features approximate a generic model of the visual world. An ImageNet-trained Xception reused for dogs vs. cats, or for furniture recognition.

title: Why reuse only the convolutional base (Figure 8.12)
text:
Feature extraction as swapping the classifier on a frozen pretrained convolutional base; why the dense classifier is generally not reused (class-specific, no spatial information); how layer depth determines how generic features are For convnets, feature extraction means running new data through a previously trained convolutional base, kept frozen, and training a new, randomly initialized classifier on its output. The base is reused because its feature maps are generic presence maps of visual concepts that keep spatial information. The original classifier encodes only the original classes and discards location. Earlier layers are more generic than deeper ones, so for very different datasets you may reuse only the first few layers. The page finishes the definition begun on p.280. For convnets, **feature extraction** means taking the **convolutional base** of a previously trained network, running the new data through it, and training a new classifier on top of its output.

**Figure 8.12** shows this in three panels. On the left is the original network: input, trained convolutional base, trained classifier, prediction. In the middle, the trained classifier is **crossed out**. On the right, a **new classifier (randomly initialized)** sits on top of the **trained convolutional base (frozen)**. Arrows between the panels show that the same base is carried across.

The authors then answer **why only the base is reused**. Reusing the classifier "should be avoided" in general, for two reasons:

1. **Generality.** Convolutional feature maps are "presence maps of generic concepts over a picture", useful for any vision problem. Classifier representations are specific to the original class set and encode only the probability that each class is present in the whole picture.
2. **Spatial information.** Densely connected layers "get rid of the notion of space". Convolutional feature maps still describe where objects are, so for problems where location matters, dense features are "largely useless".

A final refinement: generality also **depends on depth within the base**. Early layers extract local, highly generic features (edges, colors, textures). Higher layers extract abstract concepts such as "cat ear" or "dog eye". So if your new dataset differs a lot from the original training data, you may be better off using only the first few layers of the model (the sentence finishes on p.282). The next page adds that, for dogs vs. cats, reusing ImageNet's dense layers could actually help, but the authors deliberately skip it to cover the general case. Convnet feature extraction means a frozen pretrained convolutional base plus a new, randomly initialized classifier (Figure 8.12). Reuse the base, not the classifier. Base features are generic presence maps, while classifier outputs are specific to the original classes. Dense layers discard spatial information. Convolutional feature maps keep object location. Feature generality decreases with depth: edges, colors and textures early, "cat ear" and "dog eye" later. For a very different dataset, reuse only the first few layers of the base.

title: Loading the Xception backbone with KerasHub

Choosing which part of a pretrained model to reuse, and instantiating the ImageNet-trained Xception convolutional base (backbone) plus its matching preprocessing via KerasHub. For dogs vs. cats the authors deliberately reuse only the convolutional base of an ImageNet-trained Xception model, loaded with `keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet")`; to use it correctly, input images must be rescaled exactly as during pretraining, which KerasHub's `ImageConverter` handles. - **Depth of reuse.** If a new dataset differs a lot from the original one, you might reuse only the first few layers (the most generic features) rather than the whole convolutional base.
- **Why not reuse the classifier here?** ImageNet already contains many dog and cat classes, so the original dense layers would probably help. The authors *choose not to* use them, in order to demonstrate the more general case where the new task's classes do not overlap the original ones. The plan: run cat and dog images through the pretrained **convolutional base**, then train a new dogs-versus-cats classifier on the resulting features.
- **KerasHub.** All pretrained models in the book come from KerasHub, a separate package (`pip install keras-hub`, preinstalled on Colab/Kaggle) containing Keras implementations of popular architectures (Xception, ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet, and larger generative models) together with downloadable pretrained weights.

- **The "41"** in the preset name is the model's depth: 41 trainable layers (conv and dense), by far the deepest model in the book so far.
- **Preprocessing must match.** Every pretrained ConvNet was trained on images rescaled and resized in a particular way (some expect pixels in `[0, 1]`, others in `[-1, 1]`). Feeding a different range would force the network to relearn its features. KerasHub's `ImageConverter` layer, also created with `from_preset()`, applies the correct rescaling for a given checkpoint (shown on the next page, Listing 8.24). When the new data differ strongly from the original data, consider reusing only the first few layers. ImageNet's dense head could help for dogs vs. cats, but the book reuses only the convolutional base to show the general case. KerasHub (a separate package) provides pretrained architectures + weights; `Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet")` loads Xception's convolutional base. 'Backbone' = convolutional base without the classification head; '41' = number of trainable conv/dense layers. Inputs must be preprocessed exactly as during pretraining; KerasHub's `ImageConverter.from_preset()` handles this.

title: Two feature-extraction strategies; extracting features
text:
Creating the Xception-matched image preprocessor, comparing the two ways of doing feature extraction, and implementing the fast one by precomputing backbone features as NumPy arrays. You can either (1) run the frozen convolutional base once over the data and train a small classifier on the stored features (fast, no data augmentation), or (2) stack new Dense layers on the base and train end to end (allows augmentation, far more expensive). Listing 8.25 implements option 1 with `conv_base.predict()`. **Listing 8.24** completes the setup from p.282 by creating the preprocessing that matches the checkpoint: `keras_hub.layers.ImageConverter.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", image_size=(180, 180))`. It rescales pixel values to the range Xception was pretrained on and resizes images to 180 x 180, the size used for the dogs-vs-cats data.

The authors then present **two ways to proceed**:

1. **Precompute features.** Run the convolutional base over the dataset once, save its output as NumPy arrays, and train a standalone densely connected classifier (as in chapters 4 and 5) on those arrays. This is fast and cheap because the expensive convolutional base runs only once per image. For the same reason it **cannot use data augmentation**: each image is seen by the base exactly once, so there are no new random variants.
2. **End-to-end.** Add `Dense` layers on top of `conv_base` and train the whole thing on the raw inputs. Augmentation works because every image passes through the base every time it is seen, but this is far more expensive.

Both will be covered; this page starts the first one, under the heading **"Fast feature extraction without data augmentation"**. **Listing 8.25** defines `get_features_and_labels(dataset)`, which loops over `(images, labels)` batches, applies `preprocessor`, calls `conv_base.predict(..., verbose=0)` to get features, collects features and labels in lists, and concatenates them with `np.concatenate`. It is called on the training, validation and test datasets, producing `train_features`/`train_labels`, `val_features`/`val_labels` and `test_features`/`test_labels`. The next page explains why labels are split off (`predict()` only accepts images) and gives the feature shape `(samples, 6, 6, 2048)`. Listing 8.24 pairs the backbone with `ImageConverter.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", image_size=(180, 180))`. Option 1 (cache features, train a standalone dense classifier) is fast and cheap but forbids data augmentation. Option 2 (Dense layers on top of `conv_base`, end to end) allows augmentation but is far more expensive. Listing 8.25 preprocesses each batch, calls `conv_base.predict(..., verbose=0)`, and concatenates features and labels for train, validation and test.

title: Training a dense classifier on Xception features
text:
Shape of the extracted Xception features and the small classifier (global average pooling, Dense 256, dropout, sigmoid output) trained on them, plus the start of the plotting code. The precomputed features have shape (2000, 6, 6, 2048); a tiny model that averages away the 6x6 spatial grid and applies two Dense layers with dropout can be trained on them in under a second per epoch on CPU. The page first explains a detail of Listing 8.25 (p.283): `predict()` expects **only images**, but the datasets yield `(images, labels)` batches, which is why the helper loop splits them and collects labels separately.

The extracted features have shape `(samples, 6, 6, 2048)`; concretely `train_features.shape` is `(2000, 6, 6, 2048)`: 2,000 training images, each represented by a 6 x 6 grid of 2,048-channel feature vectors from the Xception backbone.

**Listing 8.26** defines and trains the new densely connected classifier with the Functional API:

- `keras.Input(shape=(6, 6, 2048))`
- `GlobalAveragePooling2D()` — per the callout, it *averages the spatial dimensions to flatten the feature map*, producing a 2,048-vector per image.
- `Dense(256, activation="relu")`, then `Dropout(0.25)` for regularization.
- `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` for the dog/cat probability.
- Compiled with `binary_crossentropy` loss, `adam` optimizer and `accuracy` metric.
- A `ModelCheckpoint` callback saves the model with the lowest `val_loss` to `feature_extraction.keras`.
- `model.fit` runs 10 epochs on `train_features`/`train_labels`, validating on `val_features`/`val_labels`.

Training is very fast: only two `Dense` layers need to be processed, so an epoch takes **less than 1 second even on CPU**. The page then begins **Listing 8.27** to plot loss and accuracy curves (figure 8.13), extracting `acc` and `val_acc` from `history.history`; the remainder of the plotting code is on p.285. predict() takes only images, so the extraction loop keeps labels separately and aligned. Xception features for 180x180 inputs have shape (6, 6, 2048); the training set gives (2000, 6, 6, 2048). The head: GlobalAveragePooling2D -> Dense(256, relu) -> Dropout(0.25) -> Dense(1, sigmoid), trained with binary crossentropy and Adam. ModelCheckpoint saves the lowest-val_loss model to feature_extraction.keras. Training takes under 1 second per epoch on CPU because only two Dense layers are involved.

title: Global average pooling
text: A layer that averages each channel of a feature map over all spatial positions, turning (H, W, C) into (C,). For each detector channel, ask 'how strongly, on average, is this feature present anywhere in the image?' For input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{6\times6\times2048}$, output $z_c = \frac{1}{36}\sum_{i,j} X_{i,j,c}$. No trainable parameters. `layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(inputs)` in Listing 8.26; callout: 'Averages spatial dimensions to flatten the feature map'.

title: Dropout
text: Randomly setting a fraction of a layer's outputs to zero during training. Prevents the network from relying on any single feature. `Dropout(0.25)` zeroes 25% of the 256 activations each training step and scales the rest by 1/0.75; inactive at inference. Placed between Dense(256) and the sigmoid output.
snippet: Randomly setting a fraction of a layer's outputs to zero during training.

title: ModelCheckpoint callback
text: A Keras callback that saves the model during training. Keep a snapshot of the best version, not just the last one. With `save_best_only=True, monitor="val_loss"`, it overwrites `feature_extraction.keras` only when validation loss improves. `keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(filepath="feature_extraction.keras", save_best_only=True, monitor="val_loss")`.
snippet: A Keras callback that saves the model during training.

title: Precomputed (cached) feature extraction
text: Training a classifier on backbone outputs computed once in advance. Do the expensive reading once, then train on the notes. Training cost per epoch is just the head: here about 525k parameters on 2,000 samples. `model.fit(train_features, train_labels, epochs=10, ...)`.

title: Global average pooling
text: layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()  (callout: "Averages spatial dimensions to flatten the feature map") z_c = \frac{1}{H W}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\sum_{j=1}^{W} X_{i,j,c}, \qquad H=W=6,\; c=1,\dots,2048 Convert the spatial feature map to a fixed-length vector suitable for Dense layers. Each $z_c$ measures the average activation of one learned visual detector over the whole image. X_{i,j,c} Feature value at spatial position (i, j) and channel c of the 6x6x2048 Xception output. H, W Spatial height and width of the feature map (6 and 6). z_c Pooled value of channel c; the output vector z has 2,048 entries.

title: Classifier head and binary crossentropy
text: Dense(256, activation="relu") -> Dropout(0.25) -> Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"); loss="binary_crossentropy" \hat{y} = \sigma\big(w_2^{\top}\,\operatorname{dropout}(\operatorname{relu}(W_1 z + b_1)) + b_2\big),\quad \mathcal{L} = -\big[y\log\hat{y} + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})\big] Writes Listing 8.26's model and loss as formulas. The head learns a nonlinear decision on top of fixed Xception features. z 2,048-dim pooled feature vector. W_1, b_1 Weights (256 x 2048) and bias (256) of the hidden Dense layer. w_2, b_2 Weights (256) and bias (scalar) of the output layer. \sigma Sigmoid function, mapping a score to a probability in (0, 1). y True label (0 or 1, cat or dog). \hat{y} Predicted probability of the positive class.

title: Results of plain feature extraction
text:
Plotting training/validation curves for the classifier trained on cached Xception features (figure 8.13), interpreting them, and evaluating the best checkpoint on the test set. Plain feature extraction reaches slightly over 98% validation accuracy, far above the from-scratch ConvNet, partly because ImageNet already knows about cats and dogs; but without data augmentation the classifier overfits almost from the start, despite dropout. The page completes **Listing 8.27** (begun on p.284): it pulls `loss` and `val_loss` from `history.history`, builds `epochs = range(1, len(acc) + 1)`, and draws two matplotlib figures, training accuracy (red dashed `"r--"`) versus validation accuracy (blue `"b"`), and the same for loss.

**Figure 8.13** shows the result for plain feature extraction over 10 epochs. Training accuracy climbs quickly to about 100% and training loss falls almost to zero, while validation accuracy hovers around 97-98.5% and validation loss bounces between roughly 0.08 and 0.13 without a steady downward trend.

The authors draw two conclusions:

1. **Accuracy is excellent.** Validation accuracy is slightly over 98%, much better than the small model trained from scratch in section 8.2 (which peaked above 85% even with augmentation, p.279). But the comparison is *a bit unfair*: ImageNet contains many dog and cat instances, so the pretrained model already has exactly the knowledge needed. That will not always be true for pretrained features.
2. **Overfitting starts almost immediately**, despite dropout with a fairly large rate, because this technique does not use data augmentation, which is essential for preventing overfitting on small image datasets.

Finally, the code reloads the best checkpoint `feature_extraction.keras` (saved by ModelCheckpoint on lowest validation loss) with `keras.models.load_model`, evaluates it on `test_features`/`test_labels`, and prints the test accuracy with three decimals. The result (98.1%) is reported on p.286. Listing 8.27 plots training (red dashed) vs validation (blue) accuracy and loss: figure 8.13. Plain feature extraction reaches slightly over 98% validation accuracy, far above the from-scratch model. The comparison is a bit unfair because ImageNet already contains many cats and dogs. The head overfits almost from the start, despite dropout, because there is no data augmentation. The best checkpoint (lowest val_loss) is reloaded and evaluated on test features.

title: Freezing the convolutional base
text:
Test result of plain feature extraction (98.1%), then the second technique: freeze the Xception backbone and chain it with a new dense classifier to train end to end with data augmentation. To train a new randomly initialized head on top of a pretrained base end to end, you must first freeze the base (trainable=False), otherwise large gradient updates from the random head would destroy the pretrained representations. The page opens with the result of the fast approach: **98.1% test accuracy**, a very nice improvement over the model trained from scratch.

Under the heading **"Feature extraction together with data augmentation"**, the authors turn to the second technique from p.283: chain `conv_base` with a new dense classifier and train end to end on the inputs. It is much slower and more expensive, but allows data augmentation.

First, the convolutional base must be **frozen**: its weights are prevented from being updated during training. Otherwise the representations it learned would be modified; since the new `Dense` layers start randomly initialized, *very large weight updates would be propagated through the network, effectively destroying the representations previously learned*. In Keras you freeze a layer or model by setting its `trainable` attribute to `False`.

- **Listing 8.28** recreates the backbone with `Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", trainable=False)`.
- Setting `trainable = False` **empties the list of trainable weights**. **Listing 8.29** demonstrates it: with `trainable = True`, `len(conv_base.trainable_weights)` is **26**; after `trainable = False`, it is **0**.

Finally, a new model is built that chains everything: `keras.Input(shape=(180, 180, 3))` -> `preprocessor` -> frozen `conv_base` -> `GlobalAveragePooling2D` -> `Dense(256)` -> `Dropout(0.25)` -> `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")`. Unlike the fast approach, this model takes raw images, so augmented images can be fed to it on every epoch. The model construction and compilation finish on p.287, which also notes that only the four weight tensors of the two Dense layers will be trained. Plain feature extraction gives 98.1% test accuracy. End-to-end feature extraction with augmentation requires freezing the base first. Without freezing, large updates from the randomly initialized head would destroy the pretrained representations. Freeze with `trainable=False`; this empties `trainable_weights` (26 -> 0 for conv_base). The new model chains Input(180,180,3) -> preprocessor -> frozen conv_base -> GAP -> Dense(256) -> Dropout(0.25) -> Dense(1, sigmoid).

title: Training the frozen-base model with augmentation
text:
Compiling the end-to-end model with frozen Xception, the rule that trainability changes need a (re)compile, training 30 epochs on augmented data, GPU requirement, and test evaluation. With the backbone frozen, only the four weight tensors of the two new Dense layers are trained; thanks to augmentation the model can train longer (30 epochs) before overfitting, reaching 98.2% validation accuracy, but the approach is so expensive that it needs a GPU. The page completes the code started on p.286: `model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)` and `model.compile(loss="binary_crossentropy", optimizer="adam", metrics=["accuracy"])`.

**What gets trained.** Only the weights of the two added `Dense` layers are trained: **four weight tensors** in total, two per layer (the main weight matrix and the bias vector). Freezing only takes effect once the model is compiled; **if you change trainability after compilation, you must recompile**, or the change will be ignored.

**Training.** The model is trained on the augmented dataset `augmented_train_dataset` from section 8.2. Because augmentation delays overfitting much longer, it can run more epochs: **30** (vs 10 for the cached-feature head). A `ModelCheckpoint` saves the lowest-`val_loss` model to `feature_extraction_with_data_augmentation.keras`, with validation on `validation_dataset`.

**Cost.** A NOTE warns the technique is expensive enough that you should only attempt it with a GPU (such as Colab's free GPU); it is *intractable on CPU*. Without a GPU, the previous (cached-feature) technique is the way to go.

**Results.** The curves (figure 8.14, printed on p.288) show **98.2% validation accuracy**. **Listing 8.30** reloads the best checkpoint and calls `evaluate(test_dataset)`: note that the test set is now raw images, since preprocessing and backbone are inside the model. The resulting test accuracy (98.4%, p.288) is no better than the 98.1% of plain feature extraction, which the authors find a bit disappointing. With the frozen base, only four weight tensors are trained: kernel and bias of each of the two Dense layers. Trainability changes require compiling; if you change them after compiling, recompile. Augmentation delays overfitting, so the model trains for 30 epochs on augmented_train_dataset. This approach is intractable on CPU; use a GPU or fall back to cached features. Validation accuracy reaches 98.2%; Listing 8.30 evaluates the best checkpoint directly on test_dataset.

title: Feature extraction results; introducing fine-tuning
text:
The results of feature extraction with data augmentation (figure 8.14, 98.4% test accuracy), and the definition and five-step procedure of fine-tuning a pretrained convolutional base. Feature extraction with a frozen Xception base plus data augmentation reaches 98.4% test accuracy, no better than plain feature extraction. Fine-tuning goes one step further: after the new classifier has been trained on a frozen base, you unfreeze the base and train everything jointly so the reused representations are slightly adjusted to the new task. The page opens with **figure 8.14**, the training and validation metrics for *feature extraction with data augmentation*: the frozen Xception `conv_base` chained with a new dense classifier and trained end to end for 30 epochs on `augmented_train_dataset` (set up on pp.286-287). Validation accuracy sits around 98-99% from the first epoch, while training accuracy starts much lower (about 93%) and climbs to the same level; training loss falls steeply from about 0.17 while validation loss stays roughly flat near 0.05. The previous page reported a best validation accuracy of 98.2%.

The **test accuracy is 98.4%**, which the authors call "a bit disappointing" because it is not an improvement over plain feature extraction (pp.284-285). Their hypothesis: the data augmentation configuration may not match the distribution of the test data, so the extra variety it creates does not translate into better test performance.

Subsection **8.3.2** then introduces **fine-tuning**, a technique "complementary to feature extraction". Fine-tuning means *unfreezing* the base that was frozen for feature extraction and *jointly training* both the newly added classifier and the base. The name reflects that it only *slightly adjusts* the more abstract representations of the reused model to make them more relevant to the new problem.

The second paragraph gives the key ordering constraint. Just as the base had to be frozen to train a randomly initialized classifier (p.286), the base can only be fine-tuned **once the classifier on top has already been trained**. Otherwise the error signal propagated back through the network is too large and destroys the representations learned by the layers being fine-tuned. Hence the five-step recipe:

1. Add your custom network on top of an already trained base network.
2. Freeze the base network.
3. Train the part you added.
4. Unfreeze the base network.
5. Jointly train both these layers and the part you added.

Steps 1-3 were already done during feature extraction; the next page (p.289) continues with step 4. Feature extraction with augmentation reaches 98.4% test accuracy, no improvement over plain feature extraction. In figure 8.14, validation accuracy is ~98% from the first epoch because the frozen pretrained features are already excellent. Augmentation helps only if its transformations match the variation in the test data. Fine-tuning = unfreeze the base and jointly train it with the new head, slightly adjusting the reused representations. The head must be trained before the base is unfrozen; otherwise large error signals destroy the pretrained features. Recipe: add head, freeze base, train head, unfreeze base, train jointly.

Phase 2: base.trainable = True (or only top layers), recompile with a very small learning rate (1e-5 in Listing 8.31), and train all trainable weights together. title: Unfreezing the base, partial fine-tuning, low learning rate
text:
Carrying out step 4 of fine-tuning (unfreezing conv_base), the caveat about BatchNormalization layers, the partial fine-tuning alternative, and recompiling with a very low learning rate (Listing 8.31). To fine-tune, unfreeze the pretrained base (but not its BatchNormalization layers), optionally only its top layers, and recompile with a very small learning rate (1e-5) so that updates to the pretrained representations stay small. The page continues the fine-tuning recipe from p.288.

**BatchNormalization caveat.** You should *not* unfreeze batch normalization layers (`BatchNormalization`); the reason is explained in the next chapter (p.302: unfrozen BN layers keep updating their internal mean and variance, which interferes with the very small updates applied to the surrounding `Conv2D` layers).

**Step 4.** Steps 1-3 (add head, freeze base, train head) were already completed during feature extraction (pp.286-287), so now you unfreeze `conv_base`.

**Sidebar: Partial fine-tuning.** The authors unfreeze and fine-tune *all* of the Xception base here, but with large pretrained models you may unfreeze only the *top* layers and leave lower layers frozen, for two reasons:

- Earlier layers encode more-generic, reusable features; higher layers encode more-specialized ones. The specialized ones are the ones that need repurposing, and there are fast-decreasing returns in fine-tuning lower layers.
- The more parameters you train, the more you risk overfitting. The base has **15 million parameters**, risky to train on a small dataset (2,000 training images).

So a good strategy can be to fine-tune only the top three or four layers, e.g. set `conv_base.trainable = True` and then set `trainable = False` on every layer in `conv_base.layers[:-4]`.

**Very low learning rate.** Fine-tuning starts with a very low learning rate to limit the magnitude of the modifications made to the representations being fine-tuned; updates that are too large may harm them.

**Listing 8.31** recompiles the model with `binary_crossentropy`, `Adam(learning_rate=1e-5)` and accuracy, and defines a `ModelCheckpoint` callback saving the best model (by `val_loss`) to `fine_tuning.keras`. The `model.fit(...)` call that completes the listing is on p.290. Don't unfreeze BatchNormalization layers when fine-tuning. Steps 1-3 were feature extraction; step 4 is unfreezing conv_base. Partial fine-tuning (top 3-4 layers) is often wise: top layers are specialized, and fewer trainable parameters means less overfitting. The Xception base has 15 million parameters, a lot for a 2,000-image dataset. Fine-tune with a very low learning rate (Adam 1e-5) to keep changes to pretrained features small. Recompile after changing trainable flags, and checkpoint the best model by val_loss.

title: Fine-tuning results: 98.6% test accuracy
text:
Running the fine-tuning fit (end of Listing 8.31), evaluating the best checkpoint on the test set, figure 8.15, and putting the 98.6% result in context. Fine-tuning the Xception base with augmentation for 30 epochs at a 1e-5 learning rate gives a test accuracy of 98.6%, the best result of the chapter, achieved with about 10% of the data available in the original Kaggle competition, though helped by pretrained knowledge about cats and dogs. The page finishes **Listing 8.31**: `model.fit` on `augmented_train_dataset` for **30 epochs**, with `validation_dataset` and the `ModelCheckpoint` callbacks defined on p.289. Then the best checkpoint is reloaded with `keras.models.load_model("fine_tuning.keras")` and evaluated on `test_dataset`, printing the accuracy with three decimals.

**Figure 8.15** shows the training and validation metrics for fine-tuning. Both accuracy curves start at about 0.982, the level the feature-extraction model had already reached. Validation accuracy climbs slowly and steadily to about 0.987; training accuracy fluctuates between roughly 0.985 and 0.997. Validation loss decreases smoothly from about 0.052 to about 0.043; training loss is noisy, between about 0.015 and 0.035. The y-axis ranges are very narrow: these are small refinements of an already strong model.

The **test accuracy is 98.6%** (results may vary by about half a percentage point). In the original Kaggle dogs-vs-cats competition this would have been one of the top results, but the authors flag that the comparison is not fair: the pretrained features already contained prior knowledge about cats and dogs, which competitors in 2013 could not use.

On the positive side, the result uses only **about 10%** of the training data that was available in the competition: 2,000 vs 20,000 samples. The page ends by noting that you now have a solid toolbox for image classification, especially with small datasets: training from scratch with augmentation, feature extraction, and fine-tuning. title: Chapter 8 summary
text:
The five take-home points of chapter 8: ConvNets for vision, hierarchical patterns, overfitting and data augmentation on small datasets, feature extraction, and fine-tuning. ConvNets learn a hierarchy of modular visual patterns and work well even on small datasets; overfitting is the main risk there, fought with data augmentation, and pretrained ConvNets can be reused through feature extraction and, a bit further, fine-tuning. This is the **end-of-chapter summary** for chapter 8, five bullets:

1. **ConvNets excel at computer vision tasks**, and you can train one from scratch even on a very small dataset with decent results. In the chapter: a small ConvNet trained on 2,000 dog/cat images reached 78.6% test accuracy (p.276) and about 84% with augmentation (p.266).
2. **ConvNets learn a hierarchy of modular patterns and concepts** to represent the visual world: early layers learn local patterns such as edges, later layers combine them into larger, more abstract concepts (section 8.1, pp.256-264).
3. **On a small dataset, overfitting is the main issue**, and **data augmentation** is a powerful remedy for image data (section 8.2.5, p.276).
4. **Feature extraction** makes it easy to reuse an existing ConvNet on a new dataset, a valuable technique for small image datasets (section 8.3.1, pp.280-288): about 98% accuracy with a frozen Xception base.
5. **Fine-tuning** complements feature extraction by adapting some of the representations previously learned by an existing model to the new problem, which "pushes performance a bit further" (section 8.3.2, pp.288-290): 98.6%.

The wording "a bit further" is deliberate: in the chapter's experiments, fine-tuning added a few tenths of a percentage point on top of feature extraction, while switching from a model trained from scratch to a pretrained model added about 14 points. The page is otherwise blank; chapter 9 (ConvNet architecture patterns) begins on p.292. ConvNets can be trained from scratch on small datasets with decent results. They learn a hierarchy of modular visual patterns. Overfitting is the main problem on small datasets; data augmentation is the key image-specific remedy. Feature extraction reuses a pretrained ConvNet easily and gives the largest gains. Fine-tuning complements feature extraction and pushes performance a bit further.

title: Chapter 9 opener: ConvNet architecture patterns
text:
Opening page of chapter 9: what the chapter covers, and the definition of a model's architecture as the choices that define its hypothesis space. A model's architecture (which layers, how configured, how connected) defines its hypothesis space, and a good hypothesis space encodes prior knowledge about the problem. The chapter presents the modularity-hierarchy-reuse formula and the standard ConvNet best practices: residual connections, batch normalization and depthwise separable convolutions. This is the **opening page of chapter 9, "ConvNet architecture patterns."** The box *This chapter covers* lists three topics:

- **The modularity-hierarchy-reuse formula** for model architecture (section 9.1, p.293).
- **Standard best practices for building ConvNets**: **residual connections** (9.2, p.296), **batch normalization** (9.3, p.300) and **depthwise separable convolutions** (9.4, p.302), combined in a mini Xception-like model (9.5, p.304).
- **Ongoing design trends** for computer vision models, including Vision Transformers (9.6, p.306).

The first paragraph defines a model's **architecture** as the sum of the choices that went into creating it: which layers to use, how to configure them, and in what arrangement to connect them. These choices define the model's **hypothesis space**: the space of possible functions that gradient descent can search over, parameterized by the model's weights. Like feature engineering, a good hypothesis space encodes **prior knowledge** about the problem and its solution. For example, using convolution layers means you know in advance that the relevant patterns in your input images are translation-invariant (the sentence finishes on p.293).

**How to use this page:** read it as a map. If you used Xception in chapter 8 without knowing why it looks the way it does, this chapter explains its ingredients one by one. Chapter 9 covers the modularity-hierarchy-reuse formula, residual connections, batch normalization, depthwise separable convolutions, and current design trends. Architecture = which layers, how configured, how connected. Architecture defines the hypothesis space that gradient descent searches. A good architecture encodes prior knowledge, e.g. convolutions encode translation invariance.

title: Why architecture matters; the MHR formula
text:
Why model architecture often decides success or failure, why it is more art than science but has best practices, and the modularity-hierarchy-reuse (MHR) formula for building complex systems. A good architecture makes the problem easier for gradient descent by shrinking the search space or making good solutions easier to reach. The universal recipe for managing complexity, in buildings, bodies, organizations, codebases and deep learning models, is modularity, hierarchy and reuse. The page finishes the chapter's opening paragraph: using convolutions encodes the prior knowledge that relevant patterns in images are **translation-invariant**, and in general, to learn effectively from data **you need to make assumptions about what you're looking for**.

**Architecture is often the difference between success and failure.** Bad choices can leave a model stuck with suboptimal metrics, and *no amount of training data will save it*. A good architecture accelerates learning, uses the available data efficiently, and reduces the need for large datasets. Concretely, a good architecture either **reduces the size of the search space** or **makes it easier to converge to a good point** of it. Like feature engineering and data curation, it is about *making the problem simpler for gradient descent*, which is "a pretty stupid search process" that needs all the help it can get.

**More art than science.** Experienced engineers *intuitively* assemble high-performing models on the first try while beginners struggle to get a model to train; no one can clearly explain what works, and experts rely on pattern matching acquired through practice. But there are **best practices**, as in any engineering discipline. The chapter reviews three: **residual connections**, **batch normalization** and **separable convolution**, applied to the dogs-vs-cats problem.

**Section 9.1: Modularity, hierarchy, and reuse.** The universal recipe for making a complex system simpler: structure the "amorphous soup of complexity" into **modules**, organize the modules into a **hierarchy**, and **reuse** the same modules where appropriate (reuse = **abstraction**). This **MHR formula** (figure 9.1, p.294) underlies architecture in every domain: a cathedral, your body, the US Navy, the Keras codebase. Software engineers already know it as good code structure (modular, hierarchical, no reimplementation). And **deep learning itself is this recipe applied to continuous optimization via gradient descent**: the sentence continues on p.294, where the search space is structured into layers, organized in a hierarchy, with reuse such as convolution's reuse of the same weights at every location. To learn from data you must make assumptions; architecture is where you encode them. A bad architecture can't be rescued by more data; a good one reduces the need for data. Good architectures shrink the search space or make good points easier to reach. Gradient descent is a 'pretty stupid' search process that needs all the help it can get. Architecture is more art than science, but best practices exist: residual connections, batch normalization, separable convolutions. MHR: modularity, hierarchy, reuse (reuse = abstraction), the recipe behind complex systems and deep learning itself.

title: Modularity, hierarchy, and reuse in deep learning architectures
text:
How the modularity-hierarchy-reuse (MHR) formula shows up in deep learning: layers as modules, stacks as hierarchies, convolution as reuse, repeated blocks of layers, and pyramid-shaped feature hierarchies where filter counts grow while feature maps shrink. Deep learning applies the MHR recipe to gradient-descent search: layers are modules, deep stacks are hierarchies, and weight sharing (convolution) is reuse. Good ConvNets go one step further by repeating whole blocks of layers and arranging them into a pyramid in which depth (number of filters) grows as spatial size shrinks. The page opens with Figure 9.1 and then finishes the argument started on p.293: **deep learning is the modularity-hierarchy-reuse (MHR) recipe applied to continuous optimization**.

**Figure 9.1** pairs two historical engravings: a floor plan of the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence (left) and an anatomical plate of the human musculature from Vesalius (right). The caption says complex systems are hierarchical, organized into distinct modules, and reuse those modules many times: your 4 limbs are variants of one blueprint, and so are your 20 fingers (and toes).

**Deep learning as MHR.** You take gradient descent over a continuous function space and structure the search space into:

- **modules** - layers;
- a **deep hierarchy** - often just a stack, the simplest kind of hierarchy;
- **reuse** wherever possible - convolution is the prime example, because it reuses the same weights (the same "information") at every spatial location.

**Blocks.** Architecture design is "primarily about making clever use of modularity, hierarchy, and reuse." Popular ConvNets are organized not only into layers but into **repeated groups of layers**, called *blocks* or *modules*. Xception, used in chapter 8, is built from repeated `SeparableConv` - `SeparableConv` - `MaxPooling` blocks (Figure 9.2, next page).

**Feature hierarchies (pyramids).** Most ConvNets are pyramid-shaped. The first ConvNet of chapter 8 used 32, 64, then 128 filters: **the number of filters grows with depth while the feature maps shrink**. The Xception blocks follow the same pattern (Figure 9.2 goes from 299 x 299 x 3 down to 19 x 19 x 728).

These two observations become the first two items of the chapter's architecture checklist on p.304. Deep learning is the MHR recipe applied to gradient descent: layers are modules, stacks are hierarchies, convolution is reuse. Popular ConvNets are built from repeated blocks of layers, e.g. Xception's SeparableConv - SeparableConv - MaxPooling. ConvNets are pyramid-shaped: the number of filters grows with depth while feature maps shrink (32, 64, 128 in chapter 8). Figure 9.1 illustrates MHR in a cathedral plan and in human anatomy: repeated, nested variants of a few blueprints.

In deep learning: layers are the modules, the stack of layers (or blocks) is the hierarchy, and weight sharing plus repeated block designs provide reuse. Xception: one block design (SeparableConv - SeparableConv - MaxPooling) repeated at several widths.

Xception's SeparableConv - SeparableConv - MaxPooling block.

title: Xception's entry flow, deep vs. shallow, and the start of the ablation sidebar
text:
Figure 9.2 (the entry flow of Xception, showing repeated blocks and a feature pyramid from 299 x 299 x 3 to 19 x 19 x 728), why deeper hierarchies are better, the vanishing-gradient limit that motivates residual connections, and the opening of the sidebar on ablation studies. Xception's entry flow is a textbook case of MHR: a stem of two convolutions followed by three nearly identical blocks whose feature maps shrink while channels deepen. Depth encourages feature reuse and abstraction, so deep-and-narrow beats shallow-and-wide, but depth is limited by vanishing gradients, which residual connections address. **Figure 9.2** shows the *entry flow* of the Xception architecture. Reading top to bottom:

1. Input: 299 x 299 x 3 images.
2. A stem of two regular convolutions: `Conv 32, 3x3, stride=2x2` + ReLU (feature maps 149 x 149 x 32), then `Conv 64, 3x3` + ReLU.
3. Three blocks with the same structure, using 128, 256 and 728 filters: (ReLU) `SeparableConv N, 3x3` - ReLU - `SeparableConv N, 3x3` - `MaxPooling 3x3, stride=2x2`. In the first block the leading ReLU is absent, since the stem already ends with one.
4. Next to each block, a side branch with `Conv 1x1, stride=2x2` carries the block's input around the block; the two paths are added at a `+` node.
5. Output: 19 x 19 x 728 feature maps.

The shapes on the right (299 x 299 x 3, 149 x 149 x 32, 74 x 74 x 128, 37 x 37 x 256, 19 x 19 x 728) make the caption's point: **repeated layer blocks** and **gradually shrinking and deepening feature maps**.

**Main text.** Deeper hierarchies are intrinsically good because they encourage **feature reuse and therefore abstraction**. In general, **a deep stack of narrow layers performs better than a shallow stack of large layers**. But depth has a limit: **vanishing gradients**. This motivates the first essential architecture pattern, **residual connections** (section 9.2, p.296).

**Sidebar (begins): On the importance of ablation studies in deep learning research.** Deep learning architectures are often more *evolved* than designed: they result from repeatedly trying things and keeping what seemed to work. As in biological systems, if you take a complicated experimental setup... (the sentence continues on p.296: you can often remove modules with no loss of performance). Xception's entry flow is a stem plus three copies of one block (128, 256, 728 filters), going from 299 x 299 x 3 to 19 x 19 x 728. Each block has a 1x1 strided convolution shortcut added at '+': a residual connection, previewing section 9.2. Deeper hierarchies encourage feature reuse and abstraction; deep-and-narrow generally beats shallow-and-wide. Depth is limited by vanishing gradients, which motivates residual connections. Architectures are often evolved rather than designed, so their components should be tested by ablation.
snippet: Figure 9.2 shows the entry flow of the Xception architecture. Reading top to bottom: 1. Input: 299 x 299 x 3 images. 2. A stem of two regular convolutions: Conv 32, 3x3,…

title: Xception architecture
text: A ConvNet built from repeated blocks of depthwise separable convolutions with residual connections, organized into entry, middle and exit flows. One well-designed block, stamped out at several widths, with shortcuts around each block. The entry flow takes 299 x 299 x 3 inputs through a stem (Conv 32 stride 2, Conv 64) and three SeparableConv-SeparableConv-MaxPool blocks of 128, 256 and 728 filters, each with a 1x1 strided conv shortcut, reaching 19 x 19 x 728. Figure 9.2.
snippet: A ConvNet built from repeated blocks of depthwise separable convolutions with residual connections, organized into entry, middle and exit flows.

title: Feature hierarchy (pyramid structure)
text: Feature maps shrink spatially while the number of filters grows with depth. Trade resolution for richness of description as you go deeper. Xception's entry flow: 299x299x3 -> 149x149x32 -> 74x74x128 -> 37x37x256 -> 19x19x728. Figure 9.2's right-hand column of shrinking, deepening slabs.
snippet: Feature maps shrink spatially while the number of filters grows with depth.

title: Deep and narrow vs. shallow and wide
text: The empirical rule that a deep stack of narrow layers generally performs better than a shallow stack of large layers. Many small steps that build on each other beat a few giant leaps. Depth enables feature reuse: intermediate features are shared by many later features, which is a form of abstraction. Xception reaches 728 channels through many moderate-width layers rather than one huge layer.
snippet: The empirical rule that a deep stack of narrow layers generally performs better than a shallow stack of large layers.

title: Vanishing gradients
text: The problem that, in a very deep chain of functions, error information backpropagated to early layers is overwhelmed by noise or becomes negligible, so those layers stop learning. A message whispered along a long line of people arrives garbled (the book's game-of-telephone image on p.296). The gradient for early layers is a product of many per-layer derivatives; with many factors it tends to shrink (or become dominated by noise). A plain 50-layer ConvNet may train worse than a 20-layer one without residual connections.
snippet: The problem that, in a very deep chain of functions, error information backpropagated to early layers is overwhelmed by noise or becomes negligible, so those layers stop learning.

title: Residual connection
text: A shortcut that adds a block's input (possibly projected) to the block's output. A direct line that lets information and gradients bypass the block. In Figure 9.2 the shortcut uses a Conv 1x1 with stride 2x2 so its shape matches the downsampled, wider block output before the '+' merge. The three '+' nodes in Figure 9.2.
snippet: A shortcut that adds a block's input possibly projected to the block's output.

title: Ablation study
text: Systematically removing parts of a system to find where its performance comes from. Take pieces out one at a time and see what breaks. title: Ablation studies; residual connections and the game of telephone
text:
The end of the sidebar on ablation studies (unneeded complexity, peer-review incentives, causality, the X + Y + Z recipe) and the opening of section 9.2, which explains the vanishing-gradient problem as noise accumulating along a chain of functions, like the game of telephone. Because architectures evolve by trial and error and incentives reward complexity, you should test which parts actually matter by removing them (ablation studies). Separately, backpropagation through a deep chain y = f4(f3(f2(f1(x)))) is like the game of telephone: each function adds noise, and if the chain is too deep the gradient information reaching early layers is overwhelmed, so the model does not train: the vanishing-gradient problem. **Sidebar, continued: On the importance of ablation studies.** In a complicated experimental deep learning setup, chances are you can remove a few modules (or replace some trained features with random ones) with no loss of performance. Researchers' incentives make this worse: a system made more complex than necessary looks more interesting or novel and is more likely to pass peer review. Papers are often optimized for peer review in ways that hurt clarity and reliability; mathematics in them is rarely used to formalize concepts or derive unobvious results, and instead acts as a *signal of seriousness*, "like an expensive suit on a salesperson."

The goal of research should be to *generate reliable knowledge*, and *understanding causality* in your system is the most direct way to get there. A low-effort tool for that is the **ablation study**: systematically remove parts of the system (make it simpler) to see where performance actually comes from. If X + Y + Z works well, also try X, Y, Z, X + Y, X + Z and Y + Z. Always ask: could there be a simpler explanation? Is this complexity necessary? Why?

**9.2 Residual connections.** In the game of *telephone* (*Chinese whispers* in the UK, *téléphone arabe* in France), a message whispered from player to player ends up barely resembling the original, a metaphor for cumulative errors in sequential transmission over a noisy channel.

Backpropagation in a sequential model is similar. With a chain `y = f4(f3(f2(f1(x))))`, each function's parameters are adjusted from the error on the output of `f4` (the loss). To adjust `f1`, error information must percolate through `f2`, `f3` and `f4`, and each function adds some noise. If the chain is too deep, the noise overwhelms the gradient information, backpropagation stops working and the model won't train at all: the **vanishing gradients** problem. The fix, residual connections, follows on p.297. Complex experimental setups often contain removable parts; incentives in peer review encourage unnecessary complexity. Ablation studies (try X, Y, Z, X + Y, X + Z, Y + Z alongside X + Y + Z) reveal where performance really comes from. Always ask whether a simpler explanation exists and whether added complexity is necessary. Backpropagation through y = f4(f3(f2(f1(x)))) resembles the game of telephone: each function adds noise to the error signal. In too deep a chain, the noise overwhelms the gradient, the model won't train: the vanishing-gradient problem.

title: Vanishing gradients
text: In a very deep chain of functions, the error information backpropagated to early functions is overwhelmed by noise, so backpropagation stops working. The game of telephone: the message is lost after too many relays. The gradient of the loss with respect to early parameters is a product of many local derivatives; with depth, it can shrink toward zero or be dominated by noise. In y = f4(f3(f2(f1(x)))), updating f1 requires passing the error through f2, f3 and f4.

title: Backpropagation through a chain

To update f1, error from y must pass through f4, f3 and f2; every pass adds noise. x Model input. f_1, \dots, f_4 Successive layers (or blocks), each with its own parameters. y Model output, on which the loss is computed.
