title: Residual connections: the fix, Listing 9.1 and shape matching
text:
How residual connections solve the vanishing-gradient problem by adding a block's input back to its output, their pseudocode (Listing 9.1), their origin in ResNet (He et al., 2015), and how to handle blocks that change the shape of the tensor with a 1x1 Conv2D projection (start of Listing 9.2). Make each block nondestructive by adding its input back to its output: x = add([block(x), x]). The shortcut carries a noiseless copy of the information forward and a clean gradient path backward. When the block changes the number of filters or downsamples, project the residual with a 1x1 Conv2D (no activation, strides to match pooling) so the shapes agree. **The fix.** Force each function in the chain to be *nondestructive*: keep a noiseless version of the information in its input. The easiest implementation is the **residual connection**: add the input of a layer or block of layers back to its output (Figure 9.3). It acts as an *information shortcut* around destructive or noisy blocks (for example blocks with ReLU activations or dropout), so error gradient information from early layers can propagate noiselessly through a deep network. The technique was introduced in 2015 with the **ResNet** family (He et al., Microsoft; footnote: "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition," CVPR 2015).

**Figure 9.3** shows Input -> Block -> (+) -> Output, with a line labelled *Residual connection* going from the input around the block to the `+`.

**Listing 9.1 (pseudocode).**

```
x = ...
residual = x
x = block(x)
x = add([x, residual])
```

The callouts: `x` is some input tensor; `residual = x` saves a reference to the original input, called the *residual*; `block` can be destructive or noisy, "and that's fine"; adding the residual back means the final output always preserves full information about the original input.

**Shape matching.** Adding requires the block output and input to have the same shape. That fails if the block increases the number of filters or contains max pooling. Then use a **1 x 1 `Conv2D` with no activation** to linearly project the residual to the required shape. Use `padding="same"` in the block's convolutions to avoid downsampling due to padding, and use **strides** in the projection to match downsampling caused by max pooling.

**Listing 9.2** (target block changing the number of output filters) begins here with the imports and `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))`; the rest is on p.298. A residual connection adds a block's input back to its output, making the block nondestructive. It is an information shortcut that lets gradients propagate noiselessly through deep networks; introduced by ResNet (He et al., 2015). Pattern: residual = x; x = block(x); x = add([x, residual]). The block may be destructive or noisy; the residual preserves full information about the input. If the block changes filters or downsamples, project the residual with a 1x1 Conv2D with no activation (and strides to match pooling), and use padding='same' in the block.

title: Residual projections in code (Listings 9.2-9.3) and a residual_block function
text:
Keras code for residual connections around blocks that change the number of filters (end of Listing 9.2) or downsample with max pooling (Listing 9.3), and the beginning of a small ConvNet built from a reusable residual_block utility function. When a block changes the channel count, project the residual with Conv2D(filters, 1); when it also max-pools by 2, use Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2). Use padding='same' inside the block. Packaging this logic in a residual_block(x, filters, pooling) function lets you build a whole ConvNet from repeated residual blocks. **End of Listing 9.2 (target block changing the number of filters).** After `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))` (p.297): a `Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")` produces `x`, which is set aside as `residual`. The block is a single `Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")`: it increases the filters from 32 to 64 and uses same padding to avoid downsampling. Because the residual only had 32 filters, `layers.Conv2D(64, 1)(residual)` projects it to the correct shape, and `layers.add([x, residual])` merges them.

**Listing 9.3 (target block including a max pooling layer).** Same start, but the block is `Conv2D(64, 3, ..., padding="same")` followed by `MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")`. Both layers use same padding so that the only downsampling is the 2x pooling. The residual projection is `Conv2D(64, 1, strides=2)`: `strides=2` matches the downsampling of the pooling layer. Then the block output and residual have the same shape and are added.

**A simple residual ConvNet.** To make it concrete, the book builds a ConvNet from blocks of two convolution layers and an optional max pooling layer, each wrapped in a residual connection. It starts with `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(32, 32, 3))` and `Rescaling(1.0 / 255)`, then defines a utility function `residual_block(x, filters, pooling=False)`: save the residual, apply two `Conv2D(filters, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")` layers, and, if `pooling`, apply `MaxPooling2D(2, padding="same")` and project the residual with a strided `Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2)`. The `elif` branch, the add, the three block calls and the classifier head are on p.299. Channel change only: project the residual with Conv2D(filters, 1). Channel change plus 2x2 max pooling: project with Conv2D(filters, 1, strides=2). Use padding='same' in the block's convolution and pooling layers so only intentional downsampling occurs. A residual_block(x, filters, pooling) function packages the pattern for reuse across a ConvNet.

title: End of the residual-net summary; introducing batch normalization
text:
The tail of the residual model's summary, the wrap-up of residual connections, and the motivation for normalizing intermediate activations Residual connections let you stack arbitrarily deep networks without vanishing gradients. The next pattern, batch normalization, starts from the familiar idea of normalizing input data (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) and asks whether the same thing should be done to the activations inside the network. The page opens with the **second half of the `model.summary()` output** started on p.299, for the small residual ConvNet built from three calls to `residual_block` (filters 32, 64, 128). The rows shown here cover the end of the second block and the whole third block:

- `conv2d_11` is a **1x1 convolution** on the residual path (2,112 parameters) that projects the 32-channel output of `add_2` to 64 channels so it can be added to the main path; `add_3` sums it with `max_pooling2d_2`.
- `conv2d_12` and `conv2d_13` are the two 3x3 convolutions of the third block (128 filters), and `conv2d_14` is another 1x1 projection (64 to 128 channels, 8,320 parameters). Because the third block was built with `pooling=False`, the spatial size stays at 8x8 and `add_4` sums `conv2d_13` and `conv2d_14` directly.
- `GlobalAveragePooling2D` collapses the (8, 8, 128) tensor to a 128-vector, and a `Dense(1)` sigmoid classifier adds 129 parameters. The model totals **297,697 parameters (1.14 MB)**, all trainable.

The authors then close section 9.2: with residual connections, depth is no longer limited by **vanishing gradients**.

Section **9.3 Batch normalization** starts by defining *normalization* broadly, as any method that makes the samples a model sees more similar to one another, which helps learning and generalization. The most common form, used repeatedly earlier in the book, centers data on zero and scales it to unit standard deviation:

`normalized_data = (data - np.mean(data, axis=...)) / np.std(data, axis=...)`

The authors note this implicitly assumes a roughly Gaussian distribution that is being centered and scaled to unit variance. Their key point is that until now normalization happened **only before the data entered the model**. Even if the input to a `Dense` or `Conv2D` stack has zero mean and unit variance, nothing guarantees the outputs of those layers do. The page ends on the question that motivates the rest of the section: *could normalizing intermediate activations help?* The answer, the `BatchNormalization` layer, follows on p.301. The residual model totals 297,697 parameters; most sit in the 128-filter block's two 3x3 convolutions. Rows with a 1x1 Conv2D reading from an Add layer are residual projections that match channel counts. Residual connections remove depth as a practical limit imposed by vanishing gradients. Normalization = making samples more similar; the standard form subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation. Normalizing inputs does not keep activations normalized after Dense or Conv2D transformations, which motivates normalizing intermediate activations.

The axis argument determines which values share statistics, e.g. axis=0 for per-feature normalization of a (samples, features) matrix. title: Standard data normalization
text: normalized_data = (data - np.mean(data, axis=...)) / np.std(data, axis=...) \hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}, \qquad \mu = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i-\mu)^2} Make the data zero-mean and unit-variance so that features are on comparable scales. Each normalized value is a z-score: its signed distance from the mean in units of standard deviation. x A data value (an entry of `data`) \mu Mean of the data along the chosen axis (`np.mean(data, axis=...)`) \sigma Standard deviation along the same axis (`np.std`, which by default divides by N, not N-1) N Number of values the statistics are computed over \hat{x} Normalized value

title: The BatchNormalization layer: how it works, why (nobody knows), and use_bias=False
text:
What batch normalization does in training vs. inference, its uncertain theoretical justification, its practical effect on gradient flow, and how to insert it after a bias-free Conv2D BatchNormalization normalizes activations with the current batch's mean and variance during training and with exponential moving averages of those statistics at inference. Why it helps is not known with certainty; in practice it aids gradient propagation and enables deeper networks. Because it re-centers its input, the preceding layer can drop its bias (use_bias=False). The page answers the question posed on p.300 ("Could normalizing intermediate activations help?") with the **`BatchNormalization` layer**, introduced by Ioffe and Szegedy in 2015 (footnote 2: *Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift*, ICML 2015).

**How it works.** The layer adaptively normalizes data even as its mean and variance change during training. *During training*, it normalizes each batch with that batch's own mean and variance. *During inference*, when a large representative batch may not be available, it uses an **exponential moving average** of the batchwise means and variances seen during training.

**Why it works: unknown.** The original paper attributed the benefit to "reducing internal covariate shift", but the authors stress that *no one really knows for sure* why batch normalization helps. They turn this into a broader point: deep learning is "a set of ever-changing, empirically derived engineering best practices, woven together by unreliable narratives". The book often tells you *how* without a satisfying *why*, because the why is not known; reliable explanations are mentioned when they exist, and batch normalization is not such a case.

**What it does in practice.** It mainly seems to help **gradient propagation**, like residual connections, and so allows deeper networks. Some very deep networks can only be trained with multiple BatchNormalization layers, and Keras's packaged architectures (ResNet50, EfficientNet, Xception) use it liberally.

**How to use it.** It can follow any layer (`Dense`, `Conv2D`, ...). The code example uses `layers.Conv2D(32, 3, use_bias=False)` followed by `layers.BatchNormalization()`. A NOTE explains why: Dense and Conv2D compute `y = dot(x, kernel) + bias` / `y = conv(x, kernel) + bias`, where the bias makes the layer affine. Batch normalization re-centers the output on zero anyway, so the bias is redundant and can be dropped, which makes the layer slightly leaner.

Finally, the authors begin a recommendation that continues on p.302: put the previous layer's **activation after** the batch normalization layer (still debated). BatchNormalization (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015) normalizes with batch statistics in training and with exponential moving averages at inference. Why it helps is not known; 'reducing internal covariate shift' is a hypothesis, not an established mechanism. Deep learning is largely empirically derived engineering practice: the book gives the how even when the why is unknown. In practice it helps gradient propagation, like residual connections, enabling deeper networks; ResNet50, EfficientNet and Xception use it. It can follow any layer; the preceding layer can use use_bias=False because normalization cancels the bias. The recommended ordering puts the activation after batch normalization (continued on p.302).
snippet: The page answers the question posed on p.300 "Could normalizing intermediate activations help?" with the BatchNormalization layer, introduced by Ioffe and Szegedy in 2015 footnote…

title: Batch normalization
text: A layer that normalizes activations using the current batch's mean and variance during training and exponential moving averages of those statistics at inference. Re-standardize the data flowing through the network at each point where you place the layer, so later layers always see well-scaled inputs. Per channel: x_hat = (x - mu) / sqrt(var + eps); y = gamma * x_hat + beta (gamma, beta learned; beyond the book). mu/var are batch statistics in training, moving averages at inference. x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, use_bias=False)(x); x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
snippet: A layer that normalizes activations using the current batch's mean and variance during training and exponential moving averages of those statistics at inference.

title: Exponential moving average
text: A running average updated as avg <- m*avg + (1-m)*new_value, where older values decay geometrically. A memory of recent batch statistics that changes slowly and smoothly. BatchNormalization keeps moving_mean and moving_variance as non-trainable weights, updated in training and used at inference. Keras default momentum is 0.99 (beyond the book). With m = 0.99, a batch mean of 2.0 moves a running mean of 0.0 to 0.02.
snippet: A running average updated as avg <- mavg + 1-mnewvalue, where older values decay geometrically.

title: Internal covariate shift
text: The change in the distribution of a hidden layer's inputs as earlier layers' parameters update during training. Each layer is chasing a moving target because the layers before it keep changing. Ioffe and Szegedy proposed batch normalization as a way to reduce it; the authors note that it is not established that this is why batch normalization helps. The positive mean drift after a ReLU layer described on p.300.
snippet: The change in the distribution of a hidden layer's inputs as earlier layers' parameters update during training.

title: Bias vector and use_bias=False
text: The learned constant that makes Dense/Conv2D affine; it can be omitted when a normalization layer follows. title: Batch normalization in training and inference
text: Described in words: uses the mean and variance of the current batch during training, and an exponential moving average of the batchwise mean and variance at inference. \begin{aligned} \text{train:}\quad & \hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \epsilon}}, \quad \mu_{\text{run}} \leftarrow m\,\mu_{\text{run}} + (1-m)\,\mu_B,\quad \sigma^2_{\text{run}} \leftarrow m\,\sigma^2_{\text{run}} + (1-m)\,\sigma_B^2 \\ \text{inference:}\quad & \hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu_{\text{run}}}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_{\text{run}} + \epsilon}} \\ \text{both:}\quad & y = \gamma\,\hat{x} + \beta \end{aligned} Formalizes the book's verbal description of the two modes. In training, the output for one sample depends on the other samples in its batch; at inference it does not. \mu_B, \sigma_B^2 Mean and variance of the current batch, per channel \mu_{\text{run}}, \sigma^2_{\text{run}} Exponential moving averages of the batch statistics (non-trainable weights) m Momentum of the moving average (Keras default 0.99) \epsilon Small constant to avoid division by zero (Keras default 0.001) \gamma, \beta Learned per-channel scale and offset

title: Activation after batch norm, freezing BN when fine-tuning, and separable convolutions
text:
Recommended ordering Conv2D -> BatchNormalization -> ReLU, the fine-tuning quirk of BatchNormalization, and the introduction of depthwise separable convolutions Put the activation after batch normalization so the zero-centered output meets ReLU's zero pivot, though the ordering is not critical. Keep BatchNormalization layers frozen when fine-tuning. Then a new pattern: SeparableConv2D, which factors a convolution into independent per-channel spatial convolutions followed by a 1x1 pointwise convolution, under the assumption that spatial locations are highly correlated while channels are fairly independent. The page finishes the sentence started on p.301 ("So instead of doing"): rather than

`Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")` -> `BatchNormalization()`

the authors recommend

`Conv2D(32, 3, use_bias=False)` -> `BatchNormalization()` -> `Activation("relu")`,

with callouts noting the *lack of activation* in the Conv2D and that *the activation is placed after the BatchNormalization layer*. The intuition: batch normalization centers inputs on zero, and ReLU uses zero as its pivot for keeping or dropping values, so normalizing first "maximizes the utilization of the ReLU". The authors immediately soften this: the ordering is **not exactly critical**; conv-activation-BN will still train and won't necessarily do worse.

A **NOTE** on batch normalization's quirks: when **fine-tuning** a model containing `BatchNormalization` layers, leave them **frozen** (`trainable = False`). Otherwise they keep updating their internal mean and variance, which can interfere with the very small updates being applied to the surrounding `Conv2D` layers.

Section **9.4 Depthwise separable convolutions** then begins with a pitch: a drop-in replacement for `Conv2D` that makes the model **smaller** (fewer trainable parameters), **leaner** (fewer floating-point operations) and a few percentage points **better**. This is `SeparableConv2D`. It performs a spatial convolution on **each input channel independently**, then mixes channels with a **pointwise (1x1) convolution** (figure 9.4, on p.303). This separates learning spatial features from learning channel-wise features. Just as convolution assumes patterns are not tied to specific locations, separable convolution assumes that **spatial locations in intermediate activations are highly correlated, but different channels are highly independent**. The sentence explaining why that assumption is useful continues on p.303. Recommended block: Conv2D(use_bias=False) -> BatchNormalization() -> Activation('relu'). Reason: BN centers values on zero, ReLU's pivot, which maximizes the ReLU's utilization; but the ordering is not critical. Keep BatchNormalization layers frozen when fine-tuning, or their changing statistics will disrupt the small updates to nearby Conv2D layers. SeparableConv2D = per-channel spatial convolution + 1x1 pointwise convolution; smaller, leaner, often a bit better. Its prior: spatial locations are highly correlated, channels highly independent.

title: Figure 9.4, why separable convolutions work, and their parameter savings
text:
The structure of a depthwise separable convolution, its role as an accurate prior, its practical advantages, Xception, and a concrete parameter comparison with regular convolution A depthwise separable convolution splits the channels, convolves each one spatially with its own 3x3 filter, concatenates the results and mixes them with a 1x1 pointwise convolution. Because its assumption (channels are fairly independent) is accurate for learned image representations, it acts as a useful prior: far fewer parameters and computations, comparable representational power, faster convergence and less overfitting. For a 3x3, 64-to-64 layer: 36,864 vs. 4,672 parameters. **Figure 9.4** draws the depthwise separable convolution: the input's channels are **split**, each channel goes through its own **3x3 conv** (the callout: *depthwise convolution: independent spatial convs per channel*), the results are **concatenated**, and a **1x1 conv (pointwise conv)** mixes them into the output channels.

The text completes the sentence from p.302: because the assumption that spatial locations are highly correlated but channels highly independent is **generally true for representations learned by deep networks**, it serves as a **useful prior** that helps the model use its training data more efficiently. The general principle: *a model with stronger priors about the structure of its information is a better model, as long as the priors are accurate*.

Practical consequences: depthwise separable convolutions need **significantly fewer parameters** and **fewer computations** than regular convolutions, with **comparable representational power**. They give **smaller models that converge faster and are less prone to overfitting**, which matters most when **training small models from scratch on limited data**. At larger scale, they are the basis of **Xception**, a high-performing ConvNet packaged with Keras (footnote 3: Chollet, *Xception: Deep Learning with Depthwise Separable Convolutions*, CVPR 2017).

A sidebar, **"The co-evolution of hardware, software, and algorithms"**, starts with numbers. A regular 3x3 convolution with 64 input and 64 output channels has $3\times3\times64\times64 = 36{,}864$ trainable parameters, and its floating-point operation count is proportional to that. The equivalent separable convolution has $3\times3\times64 + 64\times64 = 4{,}672$, with proportionally fewer FLOPs, and the advantage grows with more filters or larger windows. The sidebar continues on p.304 with the twist: on GPUs, separable convolutions are not actually much faster, because cuDNN's regular convolutions are far more heavily optimized. Figure 9.4: split channels -> independent 3x3 convs -> concatenate -> 1x1 pointwise conv. Separable convolution's assumption is accurate for learned image representations, so it is a useful prior that improves data efficiency. Stronger priors make better models, as long as they are accurate. Fewer parameters and FLOPs, comparable power, faster convergence, less overfitting; especially valuable for small models trained from scratch on limited data. 3x3, 64->64: 36,864 vs. 4,672 parameters; the gap grows with more filters or larger windows. Xception, packaged with Keras, is built on separable convolutions.

title: Hardware lock-in and the start of the mini Xception-like model
text:
Why separable convolutions are not faster on GPUs, how the co-evolution of hardware, software and algorithms entrenches ConvNets trained by backpropagation, and the first two of the chapter's ConvNet design principles Although separable convolutions need far fewer parameters and FLOPs, on GPUs they run only about as fast as regular convolutions, because cuDNN's regular convolutions are micro-optimized and separable ones are not. They are still worth using for their lower overfitting risk and faster convergence. More broadly, the deep learning ecosystem has co-evolved around ConvNets trained with backpropagation, making alternative algorithms very costly to explore. Section 9.5 then begins recapping the design principles to combine into a mini Xception. The sidebar **"The co-evolution of hardware, software, and algorithms"** (begun on p.303) delivers its twist. Given 36,864 vs. 4,672 parameters, you would expect separable convolutions to be dramatically faster. That holds for **simple CUDA or C++** implementations, and you do see a meaningful speedup on **CPU** (parallelized C++). But on a **GPU** you are running a **cuDNN kernel**, code optimized down to individual machine instructions, a worthwhile investment since cuDNN convolutions perform many exaflops every day. The side effect is that alternative approaches, even ones with intrinsic advantages like separable convolutions, cannot compete on speed.

Despite repeated requests to NVIDIA, separable convolutions have not received comparable optimization, so they remain **only about as fast as regular convolutions** despite using quadratically fewer parameters and FLOPs. They are **still a good idea**: fewer parameters means less overfitting risk, and the assumption that channels are uncorrelated gives **faster convergence and more robust representations**.

What is a slight inconvenience here can be an **impassable wall** elsewhere. Because the hardware and software ecosystem is micro-optimized for **ConvNets trained by backpropagation**, deviating is very costly: early implementations of alternatives such as **gradient-free optimization** or **spiking neural networks** would be orders of magnitude slower than a ConvNet, however clever, and a hard sell to other researchers even if better.

The authors call modern deep learning the product of a **co-evolution**: NVIDIA GPUs and CUDA enabled the early success of backprop-trained ConvNets, NVIDIA then optimized for those algorithms, and the research community consolidated around them. A different path would need a **multiyear reengineering** of the ecosystem.

Section **9.5 Putting it together: A mini Xception-like model** opens with a recap of the principles learned so far (list continues on p.305):

- organize the model into repeated **blocks** of layers, usually several convolution layers and a max pooling layer;
- **increase the number of filters** as the spatial size of the feature maps decreases. Separable convolutions are faster on CPU but only about as fast as regular convolutions on GPU, because cuDNN's regular convolutions are micro-optimized. Use them anyway: less overfitting, faster convergence, more robust representations. The ecosystem is optimized for backprop-trained ConvNets, so alternative algorithms face an extremely high cost of entry. Modern deep learning is the product of co-evolution between hardware, software and algorithms. Principles: build repeated blocks of convolution + max pooling layers; increase filters as feature maps shrink.

title: Co-evolution of hardware, software and algorithms
text: The feedback loop in which GPUs/CUDA enabled backprop-trained ConvNets, which led NVIDIA to optimize for them, which consolidated research around them. The road gets paved where traffic already goes, and traffic goes where the road is paved. title: The mini Xception-like model: design principles in code
text:
The rest of the chapter's design checklist and the code of a small Xception-like ConvNet for dogs vs. cats that combines blocks, increasing filters, batch normalization, separable convolutions and residual connections The model rescales its 180x180 RGB input, applies one regular 5x5 Conv2D (separable convolution's channel-independence assumption fails for RGB), then five residual blocks with 32, 64, 128, 256 and 512 filters. Each block is BN -> ReLU -> SeparableConv2D twice, then max pooling, with a strided 1x1 Conv2D on the residual. Global average pooling replaces Flatten. The list of principles begun on p.304 (blocks of layers; more filters as feature maps shrink) continues with four more:

- **Deep and narrow is better than broad and shallow.**
- **Residual connections** around blocks help you train deeper networks.
- It can be beneficial to add **batch normalization** after your convolution layers.
- It can be beneficial to replace `Conv2D` with **`SeparableConv2D`**, which is more parameter efficient.

The authors combine them into one model, a smaller version of **Xception**, for the **dogs-versus-cats** task of chapter 8. Data loading and training are reused unchanged from section 8.2; only the model definition changes.

The code:

1. `keras.Input(shape=(180, 180, 3))` and `Rescaling(1.0 / 255)` (callout: *don't forget input rescaling!*).
2. A **regular** `Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=5, use_bias=False)`. Callout: separable convolution assumes *feature channels are largely independent*, which **does not hold for RGB images**, whose red, green and blue channels are highly correlated. So the first layer is a regular Conv2D and SeparableConv2D is used only afterward.
3. A loop over `size in [32, 64, 128, 256, 512]`, building blocks with **increasing feature depth**. Each block saves `residual = x`, then does `BatchNormalization -> Activation("relu") -> SeparableConv2D(size, 3, padding="same", use_bias=False)` twice, then `MaxPooling2D(3, strides=2, padding="same")`. The residual is projected with `Conv2D(size, 1, strides=2, padding="same", use_bias=False)` so its shape matches, and the two are combined with `layers.add`. Callout: *each block consists of two batch-normalized depthwise separable convolution layers and a max pooling layer, with a residual connection around the entire block*.
4. `GlobalAveragePooling2D()`. Callout: the original model used `Flatten` before the `Dense` layer.

The listing ends with `Dropout`, the sigmoid `Dense` output and `keras.Model` on p.306, where the authors report 721,857 parameters and 90.8% test accuracy. Full checklist: blocks; more filters as maps shrink; deep and narrow; residual connections; batch normalization after convolutions; SeparableConv2D for parameter efficiency. The mini Xception-like model reuses chapter 8's data and training setup; only the architecture changes. The first layer is a regular Conv2D because RGB channels are highly correlated. Each block: [BN, ReLU, SeparableConv2D] x2, MaxPooling2D(3, strides=2), plus a strided 1x1 residual projection. All convolutions use use_bias=False since their outputs are batch-normalized. GlobalAveragePooling2D replaces Flatten before the classifier.

title: When not to use separable convolution
text: Separable convolution assumes feature channels are largely independent. Red, green and blue at a pixel are strongly related (a bright pixel is bright in all three), so treating them separately wastes the most important cross-channel information. Hence the first layer is a regular Conv2D; once the network has produced learned feature channels, SeparableConv2D is used. Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=5) as the stem.

title: BN -> ReLU -> convolution ordering inside the block
text: Each separable convolution is preceded by BatchNormalization and ReLU, so the block starts with normalization of its input. Normalize, rectify, then convolve, repeated twice. Equivalent to the Conv -> BN -> ReLU rule of p.302 seen from a different starting point: every convolution output is batch-normalized before its activation. The stem conv's output is normalized by the first block's first BN. x = BN(x); x = relu(x); x = SeparableConv2D(...)(x)

title: Global average pooling instead of Flatten
text: Averaging each feature map over space to produce one value per channel. Ask 'how strongly is each feature present anywhere?' rather than keeping every position. (None, 6, 6, 512) -> (None, 512). Flatten would give 18,432 features and a much larger Dense layer. Dense(1) after GAP has 513 parameters vs. 18,433 after Flatten.

title: Mini Xception-like ConvNet for dogs vs. cats (first part)
text:
import keras
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(180, 180, 3))
x = layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255)(inputs)
x = layers.Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=5, use_bias=False)(x)
for size in [32, 64, 128, 256, 512]:
    residual = x
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.Activation("relu")(x)
    x = layers.SeparableConv2D(size, 3, padding="same", use_bias=False)(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.Activation("relu")(x)
    x = layers.SeparableConv2D(size, 3, padding="same", use_bias=False)(x)
    x = layers.MaxPooling2D(3, strides=2, padding="same")(x)
    residual = layers.Conv2D(
        size, 1, strides=2, padding="same", use_bias=False
    )(residual)
    x = layers.add([x, residual])
x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(x) Defines the input, rescaling, a regular 5x5 stem convolution, five residual blocks of batch-normalized separable convolutions with max pooling, and global average pooling. The listing continues on p.306 with `x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)`, `outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)` and `model = keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)`. Stem convolution, then five pre-normalized residual blocks of separable convolutions that each halve resolution and (from block 2) double channels, then global average pooling.

title: Every convolution in the code has usebias=False. Justify this for the SeparableConv2D…
text: Every convolution in the code has use_bias=False. Justify this for the SeparableConv2D layers and for the residual projection. The first SeparableConv2D of each block is followed directly by BatchNormalization, which subtracts the per-channel mean and cancels any constant bias. The second one and the residual projection feed the add; whatever constant they would contribute is cancelled by the next block's first BatchNormalization on the main path. On the shortcut chain it would only propagate as a constant offset through 1x1 convolutions and adds to global average pooling, where the Dense layer's own bias can absorb it. So the biases would be redundant.

title: Results of the mini Xception model; introducing Vision Transformers
text:
The payoff of section 9.5 (a smaller, better-performing Xception-like ConvNet on dogs vs. cats) and the opening of section 9.6 on Vision Transformers as an emerging alternative to ConvNets Combining the chapter's best practices (residual connections, batch normalization, depthwise separable convolutions, global average pooling) yields a model with less than half the parameters of the chapter 8 ConvNet (721,857 vs. 1,569,089) that reaches 90.8% test accuracy instead of 83.9%. Beyond convolution, Vision Transformers now compete with ConvNets, although ConvNets remain the best option in most cases. The page opens with the **last three lines of the mini Xception-like model** whose body starts on p.305: after `GlobalAveragePooling2D`, a `Dropout(0.5)` layer ("like in the original model", for regularization), a single-unit `Dense` layer with `sigmoid` activation that outputs the probability of one class, and `keras.Model(inputs=inputs, outputs=outputs)` to tie the graph together.

The authors then report the result. The new ConvNet has **721,857 trainable parameters**, far fewer than the **1,569,089** of the chapter 8 model, *yet it performs better*. **Figure 9.5** shows its training and validation accuracy and loss over 100 epochs: training accuracy climbs steadily toward ~0.97 while validation accuracy rises, more noisily, to the high 0.8s; training loss falls smoothly to ~0.1 while validation loss fluctuates strongly in the 0.4–0.8 range with occasional spikes above 1.0. On the test set, the model reaches **90.8% accuracy versus 83.9%** for the previous model, which shows that following architecture best practices has an "immediate, sizeable effect on model performance."

To go further, you should **systematically tune the architecture's hyperparameters** (chapter 18). That was not done here: the configuration comes purely from the best practices listed on p.305 plus "a small amount of intuition" for model size.

**Section 9.6, Beyond convolution: Vision Transformers**, begins. ConvNets have dominated computer vision since the mid-2010s but now compete with **Vision Transformers (ViTs)**. ViTs may replace ConvNets in the long term, but **for now ConvNets remain the best option in most cases**. Transformers themselves are covered in chapter 15; the short version, continued on p.307, is that the architecture was developed to process text and is fundamentally a sequence-processing architecture. The mini Xception model ends with Dropout(0.5) and a single sigmoid unit, wrapped with keras.Model. It has 721,857 trainable parameters versus 1,569,089 for the chapter 8 model, yet reaches 90.8% test accuracy versus 83.9%. Architecture best practices alone, without tuning, produce an immediate, sizeable improvement; systematic hyperparameter tuning (chapter 18) is the next step. Figure 9.5 shows steadily improving training metrics and noisier validation metrics that still improve substantially. Vision Transformers now compete with ConvNets in computer vision, but ConvNets remain the best option in most cases for now.

title: Parameter efficiency
text: How much performance a model gets per trainable parameter. Structure that matches the problem lets fewer weights do more work, like a well-organized team outperforming a larger disorganized one. The Xception-like model reaches 90.8% test accuracy with 721,857 parameters; the chapter 8 model reaches 83.9% with 1,569,089. Separable convolutions and global average pooling remove weights that do not help, and residual connections and batch normalization make the remaining capacity usable at depth. A 3×3 convolution 64→64 has 36,864 weights; its separable equivalent has 4,672 (p.303).
snippet: How much performance a model gets per trainable parameter.

title: Dropout
text: A regularization layer that randomly sets a fraction of its inputs to zero during training (here 50%). The classifier cannot rely on any single feature, so it learns redundant, more robust evidence. `layers.Dropout(0.5)` zeroes each input with probability 0.5 at training time and scales the survivors by 1/(1−0.5)=2 so expected activations are unchanged; at inference it is the identity. Of the 512 pooled features feeding the sigmoid unit, about 256 are dropped on each training step.
snippet: A regularization layer that randomly sets a fraction of its inputs to zero during training here 50%.

title: Sigmoid output for binary classification
text: A single Dense unit with sigmoid activation that outputs a probability in (0, 1) for the positive class. One number answers "how sure am I that this is a dog (or cat)?". `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` computes $\sigma(w\cdot h + b)$ on the pooled feature vector $h$; it is trained with binary crossentropy in the chapter 8 setup. An output of 0.93 means the model assigns 93% probability to class 1.
snippet: A single Dense unit with sigmoid activation that outputs a probability in 0, 1 for the positive class.

title: Hyperparameter tuning
text: Systematic search over architecture and training settings that are not learned by gradient descent. Once the overall design is sound, you adjust the knobs methodically instead of by feel. The book defers it to chapter 18. The mini Xception configuration was set from best practices plus intuition only. Search over the number of blocks, filters per block and dropout rate, scoring each on validation accuracy.
snippet: Systematic search over architecture and training settings that are not learned by gradient descent.

title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
text: A Transformer that processes an image as a sequence of patches; an alternative to ConvNets for computer vision. Instead of sliding local filters, it reads the image as a sequence of patches and lets every patch interact with every other. Introduced on this page and explained on p.307: split image into 1D sequence of patches, flatten each patch into a vector, process the vector sequence with a Transformer. Large-scale generative image models (chapter 17) are a context where you will probably meet ViTs (p.307).

title: How Vision Transformers work, when to use them, and chapter 9 summary
text:
The mechanism of Vision Transformers (images as sequences of patch vectors), their strengths and weaknesses relative to ConvNets, and the chapter 9 summary ViTs split an image into a 1D sequence of patches, flatten each patch into a vector and process the sequence with a Transformer, which lets them capture long-range relationships. They excel with massive datasets but are suboptimal on small ones because they lack the spatial prior of ConvNets and need to be very large, so for small-scale image classification ConvNets remain the best bet. The page finishes the sentence from p.306: the Transformer is **fundamentally a sequence-processing architecture**, and a very good one, which raises the question of whether it can be used for images.

**How ViTs work.** Since ViTs are Transformers, they process sequences: they **split an image into a 1D sequence of patches, turn each patch into a flat vector, and process the vector sequence**. The Transformer lets ViTs capture **long-range relationships between different parts of the image**, something ConvNets can sometimes struggle with.

**When to use them.** In the authors' experience, Transformers are a great choice for **massive datasets** because they are simply better at using large amounts of data. On **smaller datasets they tend to be suboptimal** for two reasons:
1. They **lack the spatial prior of ConvNets**. ConvNets' 2D patch-based architecture builds in more assumptions about the local structure of visual space, which makes them more data efficient.
2. ViTs need to be **really large** to shine, which makes them unwieldy for anything smaller than ImageNet.

The battle for image recognition is far from over, but ViTs have opened a new chapter. You will probably work with them in **large-scale generative image models** (chapter 17). For **small-scale image classification, ConvNets remain your best bet**.

This closes the chapter's ConvNet best practices; the next topic is **interpreting how a model arrives at its predictions** (chapter 10).

**Chapter summary:** architecture encodes key assumptions about the problem; the modularity-hierarchy-reuse formula underpins nearly all complex systems, including deep learning models; key vision patterns are residual connections, batch normalization and depthwise separable convolutions; and ViTs are an up-and-coming alternative to ConvNets for large-scale vision tasks. ViTs split an image into a 1D sequence of patches, flatten each patch into a vector and process the sequence with a Transformer. Transformers capture long-range relationships between image parts, which ConvNets can sometimes struggle with. ViTs are great with massive datasets but suboptimal on small ones: they lack ConvNets' spatial prior and need to be very large. For small-scale image classification ConvNets remain the best bet; ViTs appear mostly in large-scale (e.g. generative) models. Chapter 9 in four points: architecture encodes assumptions; modularity-hierarchy-reuse; residual connections, batch normalization and separable convolutions; ViTs as the emerging alternative.

title: Vision Transformer (ViT)
text: A Transformer that processes an image as a 1D sequence of flattened patch vectors. Treat each image tile like a word in a sentence and let the Transformer relate all of them to each other. Image → grid of patches → each patch flattened to a vector → sequence of vectors → Transformer. Captures long-range relationships directly. Beyond the book (original ViT paper): a 224×224×3 image cut into 16×16 patches gives 14×14 = 196 patches, each flattened to 16·16·3 = 768 numbers.
snippet: A Transformer that processes an image as a 1D sequence of flattened patch vectors.

title: Spatial prior / inductive bias
text: Assumptions built into an architecture about the structure of its input; for ConvNets, the local, translation-invariant structure of visual space. Knowing in advance where to look means you need fewer examples to learn. Convolution restricts each output to a local window and shares weights across positions, which shrinks the hypothesis space compared with a fully global model such as a Transformer. A ConvNet does not have to learn that an ear in the top-left corner and an ear in the bottom-right corner are the same pattern.
snippet: Assumptions built into an architecture about the structure of its input; for ConvNets, the local, translation-invariant structure of visual space.

title: Long-range relationships
text: Dependencies between parts of the input that are far apart. Recognizing that a tail on the right and a head on the left belong to the same animal. In a Transformer any two patches interact in one attention layer; in a ConvNet, distant regions interact only after the receptive field has grown through many layers. Two 3×3 convolutions see a 5×5 region; seeing across a 180-pixel image needs many layers or downsampling.
snippet: Dependencies between parts of the input that are far apart.

title: Data efficiency and scale
text: How well an architecture performs as a function of training data size. Strong priors win with small data; flexible models win with big data. ViTs need massive datasets and very large models to shine (unwieldy below ImageNet scale); ConvNets are more data efficient because of their spatial prior. Dogs vs. cats with a few thousand images: use a ConvNet. Training a large image generator on hundreds of millions of images: ViT-style models are common.
snippet: How well an architecture performs as a function of training data size.

title: Modularity-hierarchy-reuse
text: The design formula of building systems from reusable modules organized into a hierarchy. Like Lego: a few block types repeated and stacked into larger structures. In ConvNets: repeated conv blocks with increasing filters and decreasing spatial size, e.g. the five blocks of the mini Xception model (p.305). The `for size in [32, 64, 128, 256, 512]` loop on p.305 reuses the same block design at each level.
snippet: The design formula of building systems from reusable modules organized into a hierarchy.

title: Chapter 10 opener: Interpreting what ConvNets learn
text:
Why interpretability matters for computer vision models, and why ConvNets, unlike many deep learning models, are not 'black boxes' Interpretability, understanding why a classifier made a decision, is a fundamental problem in computer vision, particularly when deep learning complements human expertise as in medical imaging. ConvNets learn representations of visual concepts, which makes them highly amenable to visualization; the chapter teaches several such techniques. This is the opening page of **chapter 10, "Interpreting what ConvNets learn"** (PDF pp.308–331). The box **This chapter covers** lists three topics:

- interpreting how ConvNets **decompose an input image** (intermediate activations, section 10.1, p.309),
- **visualizing the filters** learned by ConvNets (section 10.2, p.315),
- visualizing the **areas of an image responsible for a classification decision** (class activation heatmaps, section 10.3, p.323).

The chapter outline also includes section 10.4, visualizing the latent space of a ConvNet (p.330).

The first paragraph frames the problem of **interpretability**: *why* did your classifier think an image contained a fridge when all you can see is a truck? This matters most when deep learning **complements human expertise**, as in **medical imaging**, where a prediction alone is not enough and practitioners need to see what drove it. The chapter introduces a range of techniques for visualizing what ConvNets learn and understanding their decisions.

The second paragraph addresses the common claim that deep learning models are **"black boxes"** whose representations are hard to extract and present in human-readable form. The authors grant that this is partly true for some models, but **definitely not for ConvNets**: their representations are highly amenable to visualization, largely because they are **representations of visual concepts**. The sentence beginning "Since 2013, a…" continues on p.309, which lists the techniques the chapter will cover.

Use this page as a map for the chapter. Sections 10.2 and 10.3 come in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX versions (pp.318–319, 326–327). Chapter 10 covers interpreting how ConvNets decompose an image, visualizing their filters, and visualizing the image regions responsible for a classification. Interpretability matters most where deep learning complements human experts, such as medical imaging. ConvNets are not black boxes: their representations are of visual concepts and are easy to visualize.
snippet: This is the opening page of chapter 10, "Interpreting what ConvNets learn" PDF pp.308–331. The box This chapter covers lists three topics: - interpreting how ConvNets decompose an…

title: Interpretation techniques for ConvNets; starting 10.1 on intermediate activations
text:
The menu of ConvNet visualization techniques in chapter 10 and the definition and set-up of intermediate activation visualization, starting by reloading the chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats ConvNet Several accessible techniques exist for interpreting ConvNets (intermediate activations, filter visualization, class activation heatmaps, semantically organized latent manifolds), each answering a different question. Visualizing intermediate activations means plotting the outputs of convolution and pooling layers for a given input, one 2D image per channel, which shows how the network decomposes the input into its learned filters. The page completes the sentence begun on p.308: since 2013 a wide array of techniques has been developed for visualizing and interpreting ConvNet representations. The authors won't survey them all, but cover "three of the most accessible and useful ones". The list that follows actually has **four** bullets:

1. **Visualizing intermediate ConvNet outputs (intermediate activations)**: how successive layers transform their input, and a first idea of what individual filters mean.
2. **Visualizing ConvNet filters**: precisely what visual pattern or concept each filter is receptive to.
3. **Visualizing heatmaps of class activation**: which parts of an image were identified as belonging to a given class, which lets you **localize objects**.
4. **Visualizing the semantically organized manifolds** ConvNets learn: detecting **outliers** and images the model sees as **semantically ambiguous**, so you can clean and improve your training dataset and refine your evaluation dataset.

Activation visualization uses the **small ConvNet trained from scratch on dogs vs. cats in chapter 8**; the next two methods use a **pretrained Xception model**.

**Section 10.1** defines the first technique: display the values returned by the model's **convolution and pooling layers** for a given input. A layer's output is often called its **activation** (the output of the activation function). This shows how an input is **decomposed into the different filters** the network has learned. Feature maps have three dimensions (width, height, depth/channels), and because **each channel encodes relatively independent features**, the proper way to visualize them is to **plot every channel independently as a 2D image**.

The code starts by loading the model saved in section 8.2 with `keras.models.load_model("convnet_from_scratch_with_augmentation.keras")` and printing `model.summary()`. The first rows of the table show the `InputLayer` and `Rescaling` with output `(None, 180, 180, 3)` and 0 parameters, then `conv2d_11` with output `(None, 178, 178, 32)` and **896** parameters. The table continues on p.310. Chapter 10 covers intermediate activations, filter visualization, class activation heatmaps and latent manifolds, each answering a different question (the text says 'three' but lists four). Activation visualization uses the chapter 8 small ConvNet; the next two methods use a pretrained Xception. A layer's output is its activation; conv/pool outputs are 3D feature maps of width, height and channels. Because channels encode relatively independent features, each channel is plotted as its own 2D image. The reloaded model starts with Input and Rescaling (180×180×3, 0 params) and a Conv2D giving 178×178×32 with 896 params.
snippet: The page completes the sentence begun on p.308: since 2013 a wide array of techniques has been developed for visualizing and interpreting ConvNet representations. The authors…

title: Intermediate activation visualization
text: Displaying the outputs of a model's convolution and pooling layers for a given input, channel by channel. An X-ray of the network's processing of one image: each layer's view of it. Build a multi-output model returning each Conv2D/MaxPooling2D output (p.311), run one image, plot each channel $A_{:,:,c}$ as a 2D image. The first Conv2D layer of the chapter 8 model gives 32 maps of 178×178 for a 180×180 image.
snippet: Displaying the outputs of a model's convolution and pooling layers for a given input, channel by channel.

title: Feature map
text: The 3D output tensor (width, height, depth/channels) of a convolution or pooling layer. A stack of detector maps, one per filter, each lighting up where its pattern occurs. For `conv2d_11`, the feature map has shape (178, 178, 32) per image, (None, 178, 178, 32) with the batch axis. Channel 7 of the first layer might respond to diagonal edges (see p.313).
snippet: The 3D output tensor width, height, depth/channels of a convolution or pooling layer.

title: Filter visualization
text: Showing the visual pattern each filter responds to most strongly. Ask the filter to draw its ideal input. Gradient ascent in input space to maximize a filter's activation (p.315). Early Xception filters produce edge and colour patterns; deeper ones produce textures.
snippet: Showing the visual pattern each filter responds to most strongly.

title: Class activation heatmap
text: A 2D grid of scores over an image indicating how important each location is for a given class. Where in the picture did the model see the cat? Implemented with Grad-CAM in section 10.3 (p.323). A heatmap for "cat" highlights the cat's face and body.
snippet: A 2D grid of scores over an image indicating how important each location is for a given class.

title: Semantically organized latent manifold
text: The structured space of a ConvNet's learned representations, where semantically similar images lie close together. A map where all dog photos form one neighbourhood and cats another. Covered in section 10.4 (p.330); used to find outliers and ambiguous images. An image labeled "dog" sitting deep in the cat cluster may be mislabeled.
snippet: The structured space of a ConvNet's learned representations, where semantically similar images lie close together.

Each conv layer without padding trims a 1-pixel border from each side; the depth becomes the number of filters (32). title: The chapter 8 ConvNet's summary and preprocessing a test image (listing 10.1)
text:
The remaining layers and parameter totals of the reloaded dogs-vs-cats ConvNet, and listing 10.1, which downloads a cat image and turns it into a (1, 180, 180, 3) batch tensor The model being inspected is a stack of five Conv2D layers (32→512 filters) interleaved with four MaxPooling2D layers, followed by global average pooling, dropout and a 1-unit Dense layer: 1,569,089 trainable parameters. To visualize its activations you need one input image the network has never seen, loaded at the training resolution and wrapped as a batch of one sample. The page continues the `model.summary()` table from p.309 for the ConvNet trained from scratch with data augmentation in chapter 8. After `conv2d_11` (178×178×32), the layers are:

| layer | output shape | params |
|---|---|---|
| max_pooling2d_6 | (None, 89, 89, 32) | 0 |
| conv2d_12 | (None, 87, 87, 64) | 18,496 |
| max_pooling2d_7 | (None, 43, 43, 64) | 0 |
| conv2d_13 | (None, 41, 41, 128) | 73,856 |
| max_pooling2d_8 | (None, 20, 20, 128) | 0 |
| conv2d_14 | (None, 18, 18, 256) | 295,168 |
| max_pooling2d_9 | (None, 9, 9, 256) | 0 |
| conv2d_15 | (None, 7, 7, 512) | 1,180,160 |
| global_average_pooling2d_3 | (None, 512) | 0 |
| dropout | (None, 512) | 0 |
| dense_3 | (None, 1) | 513 |

The totals are **Total params: 4,707,269 (17.96 MB)**, **Trainable params: 1,569,089 (5.99 MB)**, **Non-trainable params: 0** and **Optimizer params: 3,138,180 (11.97 MB)**. The trainable count is the 1,569,089 that p.306 compares against the mini Xception model.

Next you need an input image: **a picture of a cat that was not part of the training images**. **Listing 10.1** downloads `cat.jpg` with `keras.utils.get_file` and defines `get_img_array(img_path, target_size)`, which:
1. opens the file and resizes it with `keras.utils.load_img(..., target_size=target_size)`,
2. turns it into a float32 NumPy array of shape (180, 180, 3) with `keras.utils.img_to_array`,
3. adds a leading axis with `np.expand_dims(array, axis=0)` to make a "batch" of a single sample, of shape **(1, 180, 180, 3)**.

It is called with `target_size=(180, 180)` to produce `img_tensor`, the input used for all activation plots in section 10.1. The chapter 8 ConvNet alternates five Conv2D layers (32→512 filters) and four MaxPooling2D layers, shrinking 180×180 to 7×7 while depth grows to 512. Every Param # can be reproduced as 3·3·C_in·C_out + C_out; the total of 1,569,089 trainable parameters matches p.306. Total params (4,707,269) include 3,138,180 optimizer variables; there are no non-trainable params. Listing 10.1 downloads an unseen cat image, resizes it to 180×180, converts it to float32 and adds a batch axis: shape (1, 180, 180, 3). No manual pixel scaling is needed because the model contains its own Rescaling layer.

title: Keras model summary
text: A table of a model's layers with output shapes and parameter counts, plus totals. A blueprint of the network you are about to probe. Total params = trainable + non-trainable + optimizer params. Here 1,569,089 + 0 + 3,138,180 = 4,707,269. Sizes in MB assume 4 bytes per float32 value (1,569,089 × 4 B ≈ 5.99 MB). conv2d_15 outputs (None, 7, 7, 512): 512 channels of 7×7.
snippet: A table of a model's layers with output shapes and parameter counts, plus totals.

title: Max pooling
text: Downsampling by taking the maximum over windows, here 2×2 with stride 2. Keep the strongest response in each neighbourhood and halve the resolution. Output size $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$: 178→89, 87→43, 41→20, 18→9. No parameters. An 87×87 map becomes 43×43 (the odd last row/column is dropped).
snippet: Downsampling by taking the maximum over windows, here 2×2 with stride 2.

title: Batch axis
text: The leading dimension of a model input that indexes samples. Models always expect a pile of images, even if the pile has one image. `np.expand_dims(array, axis=0)` turns (180, 180, 3) into (1, 180, 180, 3), matching the model's (None, 180, 180, 3) input. Shape (180, 180, 3) → (1, 180, 180, 3).
snippet: The leading dimension of a model input that indexes samples.

Put the image into exactly the format the network was trained on. load_img(target_size) → img_to_array (float32) → expand_dims. Pixel rescaling is not done here because the model contains a Rescaling layer (p.309). cat.jpg → (1, 180, 180, 3) float32 tensor with values 0–255.

title: Spatial sizes through the conv/pool stack
text: (None, 178, 178, 32) → (None, 89, 89, 32) → (None, 87, 87, 64) → (None, 43, 43, 64) → (None, 41, 41, 128) → (None, 20, 20, 128) → (None, 18, 18, 256) → (None, 9, 9, 256) → (None, 7, 7, 512) \begin{aligned} \text{conv (valid, } 3\times3\text{)}: &\; n \mapsto n-2 \\ \text{max-pool (}2\times2\text{, stride 2)}: &\; n \mapsto \lfloor n/2 \rfloor \end{aligned} Explains every output shape in the printed summary. Resolution drops from 180 to 7 while depth grows from 3 to 512: the typical ConvNet trade of spatial detail for feature richness. n Height (= width) of the feature map entering the layer \lfloor\cdot\rfloor Floor (round down)

The last conv layer alone has 1,180,160 parameters, about 75% of the model: parameters concentrate where channel counts are largest. title: Displaying the test picture and building a multi-output activation model
text:
Listing 10.2 (showing the preprocessed cat image with matplotlib, figure 10.1) and listing 10.3 (a Functional API model that maps the original model's input to the outputs of all its Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers) Because a Keras Functional model keeps every layer's symbolic output, you can build a new model that reuses the trained layers and returns any intermediate outputs you choose. Collecting the outputs of all Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layers gives an activation model whose prediction for one image is the list of its feature maps. First the authors display the test image (**figure 10.1**, a white cat with blue eyes). **Listing 10.2** imports `matplotlib.pyplot`, turns the axes off, and calls `plt.imshow(img_tensor[0].astype("uint8"))`. Indexing `[0]` removes the batch axis added in listing 10.1, giving a (180, 180, 3) array, and casting to `uint8` makes matplotlib treat the 0–255 float values as ordinary 8-bit pixel intensities.

Next comes the core tool of section 10.1: **a Keras model that takes batches of images as input and outputs the activations of all convolution and pooling layers**. **Listing 10.3** loops over `model.layers`. For each layer that is an instance of `layers.Conv2D` or `layers.MaxPooling2D`, it appends `layer.output` (the layer's symbolic output tensor) to `layer_outputs` and saves `layer.name` in `layer_names` for later use as plot titles. Then

```
activation_model = keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs)
```

creates a new model that shares the trained layers and weights of the original one but returns all of these intermediate outputs, given the model input.

From the summary on pp.309–310, the selected layers are 5 Conv2D and 4 MaxPooling2D layers, so the activation model has **one input and nine outputs**, which p.312 confirms. It is the book's first practical multi-output model. Listing 10.2 shows the test cat (figure 10.1) using img_tensor[0].astype("uint8") to drop the batch axis and get displayable pixels. Listing 10.3 loops over model.layers and collects layer.output for every Conv2D and MaxPooling2D layer, saving names for plot titles. keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs) builds a multi-output model that shares the trained weights. For the chapter 8 ConvNet this gives one input and nine outputs (five conv, four pooling).

title: Computing and plotting one layer activation
text:
Running the multi-output activation model on the cat image and plotting a single channel of the first convolution layer's output The activation model built on the previous page has one input and nine outputs, so `predict` returns a list of nine arrays, one per Conv2D/MaxPooling2D layer. Indexing the first array, `(1, 178, 178, 32)`, and slicing one channel gives a 178 × 178 image that can be shown with `plt.matshow`. The page continues section 10.1. On the previous page (listing 10.3, p.311) the authors built `activation_model`, a Keras `Model` whose inputs are the original model's input and whose outputs are the outputs of every `Conv2D` and `MaxPooling2D` layer. Here they point out what makes that model special: it is the **first multi-output model actually used in practice** in the book (multi-output models were introduced in chapter 7). It has **one input and nine outputs**, one per layer activation.

**Listing 10.4** runs it on the preprocessed cat image: `activations = activation_model.predict(img_tensor)`. The callout explains that the result is a Python list of nine NumPy arrays, one array per layer activation.

The authors then take the first element, the activation of the first convolution layer, and print its shape: `(1, 178, 178, 32)`. That is a batch of one image, with a **178 × 178 feature map with 32 channels**. The 178 comes from applying a 3 × 3 convolution without padding to the 180 × 180 input (180 − 3 + 1 = 178), and the 32 is the number of filters in that `Conv2D` layer, as shown in the model summary on p.309.

**Listing 10.5** plots the sixth channel (index 5) with `plt.matshow(first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5], cmap="viridis")`. **Figure 10.2** shows the result: a dark-blue rendering of the cat in which only some edges light up in bright green/yellow. Most visibly, the right-hand edge of the right ear, a few strokes around the eyes and nose, and a short edge near the chin. On the next page (p.313) the authors interpret this channel as a diagonal edge detector and warn that your own channels may differ because learned filters are not deterministic.

The main point is that each channel of a convolution layer's output is a 2D map of where one learned pattern occurs in the image. That is why section 10.1 says such feature maps should be visualized one channel at a time (p.309). `activation_model` has one input and nine outputs, so `predict` returns a list of nine NumPy arrays. The first convolution layer's activation has shape (1, 178, 178, 32): batch, height, width, channels. 178 = 180 − 3 + 1, the border effect of an unpadded 3 × 3 convolution. `first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5]` extracts the sixth channel as a 178 × 178 2D map. `plt.matshow` with a colormap turns that map into an image; figure 10.2 shows a filter that highlights certain edges of the cat.

title: Intermediate activation
text: The output of a hidden layer (here a Conv2D or MaxPooling2D layer) for a particular input. It is a snapshot of how the network has re-described the image at that depth. For a convnet layer it is a tensor of shape `(batch, height, width, channels)`; for the first layer of this model `(1, 178, 178, 32)`. `activations[0]` holds the 32 feature maps of `conv2d_11` for the cat image.
snippet: The output of a hidden layer here a Conv2D or MaxPooling2D layer for a particular input.

title: Multi-output model
text: A functional Keras model built with a list of output tensors, which returns a list of arrays from `predict`. Instead of only reading the final answer, you put probes at several points in the network and read them all at once. `keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer_outputs)` where `layer_outputs` contains the symbolic outputs of nine existing layers; the new model shares the trained weights. `activation_model` has one input and nine outputs.
snippet: A functional Keras model built with a list of output tensors, which returns a list of arrays from predict.

title: Feature map (channel view)
text: A rank-3 tensor of spatial positions × channels; each channel is a 2D grid recording how strongly one filter responds at each location. Think of 32 transparent overlays on the image, each highlighting where a particular small pattern occurs. Channel $c$ of a Conv2D+ReLU output at position $(i,j)$ is $\operatorname{relu}(\sum_{u,v,d} K_c[u,v,d]\,x[i+u,j+v,d] + b_c)$. `first_layer_activation[0, :, :, 5]` is a 178 × 178 map shown in figure 10.2.
snippet: A rank-3 tensor of spatial positions × channels; each channel is a 2D grid recording how strongly one filter responds at each location.

title: Valid convolution border effect
text: Without padding, a k × k convolution with stride 1 can only be centered on positions where the window fits, so the output loses k − 1 rows and columns. A 3 × 3 stamp cannot be centered on the outermost ring of pixels. $H_{out} = H_{in} - k + 1$; $180 - 3 + 1 = 178$. 180 × 180 input → 178 × 178 after `conv2d_11`.
snippet: Without padding, a k × k convolution with stride 1 can only be centered on positions where the window fits, so the output loses k − 1 rows and columns.

title: Spatial size of the first convolution output
text: (1, 178, 178, 32) — a 178 × 178 feature map with 32 channels H_{out} = H_{in} - k + 1 = 180 - 3 + 1 = 178 Explain where the 178 in the printed shape comes from. Each output position corresponds to one valid placement of the 3 × 3 window. H_{in} Input height (and width): 180 pixels, from `target_size=(180, 180)` k Kernel size of the Conv2D layer: 3 H_{out} Output height (and width) with stride 1 and no padding
snippet: 1, 178, 178, 32 — a 178 × 178 feature map with 32 channels — Explain where the 178 in the printed shape comes from.

title: Plotting every channel of every activation
text:
Interpreting the sixth first-layer channel, then listing 10.6, which tiles all channels of all nine activations into one normalized grid per layer Channel 6 of the first layer looks like a diagonal edge detector, but learned filters vary from run to run. To see everything at once, listing 10.6 loops over the nine activations. For each one it standardizes every channel to the 0–255 display range, places the channels into a grid 16 channels wide with 1-pixel separators, and shows the grid with `imshow`. The page opens by interpreting figure 10.2 (p.312): the sixth channel of the first layer **appears to encode a diagonal edge detector**. The authors add a caveat: your own channels may look different, because **the specific filters learned by convolution layers aren't deterministic**. Random initialization and stochastic training produce a different set of filters, in a different order, each time.

They then move from one channel to all of them: "a complete visualization of all the activations in the network" (figure 10.3, p.314). Every channel of each of the nine layer activations is extracted and plotted, and for each layer the channels are stacked side by side in one big grid.

**Listing 10.6** does this:

- `images_per_row = 16` fixes the grid width at 16 channels.
- It iterates over `zip(layer_names, activations)`, so each grid gets its layer's name as a title.
- For each activation, of shape `(1, size, size, n_features)`, it reads `n_features` (channels) and `size` (spatial side), computes `n_cols = n_features // 16` and allocates an empty `display_grid` with a 1-pixel gap between tiles.
- For each channel it copies the 2D map. If the map is not all zero, it standardizes it (subtract mean, divide by std), then scales by 64 and shifts by 128. Finally it clips to [0, 255] and casts to `uint8`. The callout states that this normalizes channel values within [0, 255] and that **all-zero channels are kept at zero**.
- It writes the tile into its slot of the grid.
- It creates a figure sized proportionally to the grid (`scale = 1.0 / size`), sets the title to the layer name, turns off grid lines and axes, and shows the grid with `imshow(..., cmap="viridis")`.

The output is nine large images, one per layer, which together form figure 10.3. The authors' observations about them (edge detectors, rising abstraction, rising sparsity) follow on p.314. The sixth first-layer channel looks like a diagonal edge detector, but learned filters vary between runs. Listing 10.6 renders all channels of all nine activations, 16 tiles per row with 1-pixel separators. Each channel is standardized, mapped to mean 128 with 64 levels per std, clipped to [0, 255] and cast to uint8. All-zero channels are left at zero, so blank tiles in figure 10.3 really are inactive filters. Figure size scales with the grid so every layer's figure is about 16 inches wide.

title: Non-determinism of learned filters
text: Different training runs of the same architecture learn different specific filters, in different orders. There are many equally good sets of filters, and randomness decides which one you end up with. Sources include random initialization, random shuffling and augmentation, and non-deterministic GPU kernels. Permutation symmetry of units means channel indices carry no inherent meaning. In your run the diagonal-edge filter might be channel 17, and channel 5 might respond to a color.
snippet: Different training runs of the same architecture learn different specific filters, in different orders.

title: Per-channel normalization for display
text: Rescaling each channel independently so its values fill a common display range, here via standardization, ×64, +128 and clipping to [0, 255]. Each channel is given its own contrast setting so faint and strong channels are both visible. $x' = \operatorname{clip}(64\,(x-\mu)/\sigma + 128,\ 0,\ 255)$; values within ±2σ of the mean fill the range and outliers saturate. A channel with mean 0.4 and std 0.2: value 0.8 → 64·2 + 128 = 256 → clipped to 255.
snippet: Rescaling each channel independently so its values fill a common display range, here via standardization, ×64, +128 and clipping to 0, 255.

title: Intermediate activation
text: The output of a hidden Conv2D or MaxPooling2D layer for a given input. A snapshot of the image's re-description at each depth. Shape (1, size, size, n_features), as the listing's callout states. The last one, conv2d_15, is (1, 7, 7, 512): 32 grid rows of 16 tiny 7 × 7 tiles.

title: Per-channel display normalization
text: channel_image -= channel_image.mean(); channel_image /= channel_image.std(); channel_image *= 64; channel_image += 128; np.clip(channel_image, 0, 255).astype("uint8") x'_{ij} = \operatorname{clip}\!\left(64\,\frac{x_{ij}-\mu}{\sigma} + 128,\; 0,\; 255\right), \quad \mu = \tfrac{1}{S^2}\sum_{i,j}x_{ij},\; \sigma = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{S^2}\sum_{i,j}(x_{ij}-\mu)^2} Bring every channel into the same visible range regardless of its raw scale. The mean maps to mid-gray level 128; one standard deviation corresponds to 64 levels, so the range [μ − 2σ, μ + 2σ] spans [0, 256] and anything beyond saturates. x_{ij} Raw activation of the channel at row i, column j \mu, \sigma Mean and (population) standard deviation of the channel over all S × S positions S Spatial size of the activation (`size`) x'_{ij} Display value in [0, 255], cast to uint8

The grid is always 16 tiles wide; its height grows with the number of channels. S `size`, the side of each channel image n_{features} Number of channels in the layer n_{cols} Number of tile rows stacked vertically (despite the name)

title: Listing 10.6 Visualizing every channel in every intermediate activation
text:
images_per_row = 16
for layer_name, layer_activation in zip(layer_names, activations):
    n_features = layer_activation.shape[-1]
    size = layer_activation.shape[1]
    n_cols = n_features // images_per_row
    display_grid = np.zeros(
        ((size + 1) * n_cols - 1, images_per_row * (size + 1) - 1)
    )
    for col in range(n_cols):
        for row in range(images_per_row):
            channel_index = col * images_per_row + row
            channel_image = layer_activation[0, :, :, channel_index].copy()
            if channel_image.sum() != 0:
                channel_image -= channel_image.mean()
                channel_image /= channel_image.std()
                channel_image *= 64
                channel_image += 128
            channel_image = np.clip(channel_image, 0, 255).astype("uint8")
            display_grid[
                col * (size + 1) : (col + 1) * size + col,
                row * (size + 1) : (row + 1) * size + row,
            ] = channel_image
    scale = 1.0 / size
    plt.figure(
        figsize=(scale * display_grid.shape[1], scale * display_grid.shape[0])
    )
    plt.title(layer_name)
    plt.grid(False)
    plt.axis("off")
    plt.imshow(display_grid, aspect="auto", cmap="viridis") For each of the nine layer activations, builds one image that tiles all its channels (16 per row) after normalizing each channel to [0, 255], and displays it titled with the layer name. For each layer: allocate grid → for each channel: copy, normalize if non-zero, clip/cast, paste → display.

title: What the activation grids reveal
text:
Figure 10.3 (all channels of all nine layer activations for the cat image) and three observations: first-layer edge detectors, increasing abstraction with depth, and increasing sparsity with depth Early convnet activations are edge detectors that keep almost all of the image's information. Deeper activations become abstract ("cat ear", "cat eye"), carry less information about the image's appearance and more about its class, and become sparser, with more and more filters completely blank because their pattern is absent from the input. This page shows **figure 10.3**, the output of listing 10.6 (p.313): every channel of every intermediate activation for the test cat picture. In the printed figure the grids are arranged in pairs by depth, each convolution grid next to the grid of the pooling layer that follows it, with the deepest convolution grid alone at the bottom. Grids get taller as channel counts grow (32 → 512), and tiles get smaller as spatial size shrinks (178 → 7). In the upper grids the cat's outline is visible in many tiles. In the lower grids the tiles hold small, blob-like yellow spots, and a large share of tiles are flat dark purple.

The authors draw three conclusions:

1. **The first layer acts as a collection of various edge detectors.** At this stage the activations retain almost all of the information present in the initial picture, so you can still recognize the cat in nearly every channel.
2. **Higher activations are increasingly abstract and less visually interpretable.** They begin to encode higher-level concepts such as "cat ear" and "cat eye." Higher representations carry *less* information about the visual contents of the image and *more* information related to the image's class.
3. **Sparsity increases with depth.** In the first layer all filters are activated by the input image, but in the following layers more and more filters are blank. A blank filter means the pattern it encodes is not found in this input image.

On the following page (p.315) the authors generalize these observations: features become increasingly abstract with depth, and a deep network acts as an **information distillation pipeline** that filters out irrelevant detail and refines what matters for the target. Figure 10.3 shows all channels of all nine layer activations for the test cat picture. The first layer is a bank of edge detectors and retains almost all of the image's information. Higher layers are more abstract ("cat ear", "cat eye") and carry more class-related, less appearance-related information. Sparsity grows with depth: more and more filters are blank, meaning their pattern is absent from the image. Together these observations lead to the 'information distillation pipeline' view on the next page.

title: Hierarchy of features with depth
text: Convnet layers learn progressively more complex and abstract features: edges, then textures and parts, then class-related concepts. Letters make words, and words make sentences. Edges combine into ears and eyes, and those combine into 'cat'. Each layer applies local filters to the previous layer's feature maps, so receptive fields and feature complexity grow with depth. First layer: edge detectors; higher layers: 'cat ear', 'cat eye'.

title: Activation sparsity
text: The share of channels (or units) that are zero for a given input; it increases with depth in this convnet. Specialized detectors stay silent unless their specific pattern is present. Due to ReLU, a channel is exactly zero when its pre-activation is ≤ 0 everywhere. Listing 10.6 displays such channels as uniform blank tiles. Every first-layer filter responds to the cat image, while many tiles in the deepest grid of figure 10.3 are flat dark purple.
snippet: The share of channels or units that are zero for a given input; it increases with depth in this convnet.

title: Information distillation
text: Deeper representations hold less information about the specific input's appearance and more about the target (class). Like boiling down a stock, the volume shrinks and the essential flavor concentrates. Spatial resolution drops (178 → 7) and features become class-selective; appearance detail is discarded. The 7 × 7 × 512 activation no longer shows a recognizable cat, but it is what the classifier uses to decide 'cat'.
