title: Information distillation; visualizing filters
text:
The information-distillation view of deep representations, illustrated with drawing bicycles from memory, and the introduction of filter visualization by gradient ascent in input space on Xception Features become more abstract with depth, and a deep network acts as an information distillation pipeline that filters out irrelevant appearance and refines what is useful for the target, much as human memory keeps 'bicycle' but not what a bicycle looks like. Section 10.2 then visualizes what each filter responds to: starting from a blank image, it adjusts the input pixels by gradient ascent to maximize a chosen filter's activation. **End of section 10.1.** The authors turn the observations on p.314 into a general principle: an *important universal characteristic* of representations learned by deep neural networks is that **features become increasingly abstract with depth**. Higher-layer activations carry less and less information about the specific input and more and more about the **target**, here the class cat or dog. A deep network therefore acts as an **information distillation pipeline**. Raw data (RGB pictures) goes in and is repeatedly transformed so that irrelevant information, such as the specific visual appearance, is filtered out, while useful information, such as the class, is magnified and refined.

They compare this to human and animal perception. After seeing a scene for a few seconds, you remember *which* abstract objects were there (bicycle, tree) but not their specific appearance. Most people cannot draw a generic bicycle from memory even remotely correctly, despite having seen thousands. **Figure 10.4** shows two wobbly bicycle drawings made from memory (left) next to a correct schematic bicycle (right). The brain has learned to abstract its visual input into high-level concepts and discard visual detail, which is why remembering how things look is so hard.

**Section 10.2, Visualizing ConvNet filters.** A second easy way to inspect learned filters is to display the visual pattern each filter is meant to respond to. This uses **gradient ascent in input space**: gradient descent is applied to the *input image* so as to *maximize* the response of a specific filter, starting from a blank input. The resulting image is one the chosen filter responds to maximally.

The example uses the filters of the **Xception** model. The recipe is to build a loss that maximizes the value of a given filter in a given convolution layer, then use stochastic gradient descent to adjust the input image's values so as to maximize that activation. The authors call it the reader's second example of a low-level gradient descent loop, which the next page (p.316) says will be shown for TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX. Features become increasingly abstract with depth, which the authors call a universal characteristic of deep representations. A deep network is an information distillation pipeline: irrelevant appearance is filtered out and target-relevant information is refined. Human memory works similarly; we remember 'bicycle' but can't draw one correctly (figure 10.4). Filter visualization uses gradient ascent in input space: keep the weights fixed and optimize a blank image to maximize one filter's response. The example uses ImageNet-trained Xception and a hand-written gradient loop, the book's second after chapter 2.
snippet: End of section 10.1. The authors turn the observations on p.314 into a general principle: an important universal characteristic of representations learned by deep neural networks…

RGB cat picture → edges → parts → 'cat'.

title: Gradient ascent in input space
text: Optimizing the input image, with the network's weights fixed, so as to maximize some activation. Instead of teaching the network about the image, you ask the network to sculpt the image it 'likes' best. Compute $\nabla_x$ of a chosen activation (via autodiff) and step the input in that direction, starting from a blank image. Maximizing a filter in an early Xception layer yields an image of oriented colored edges (p.322).

title: Gradient descent (applied to inputs)
text: Iteratively moving a variable against the gradient of a loss, or along it to maximize. Walk uphill on the filter's response surface. Maximizing $f$ is minimizing $-f$; the update uses $\nabla_x f$. Each step slightly changes every pixel to increase the filter's mean activation.

title: Loading Xception and building a feature extractor
text:
Instantiating the ImageNet-pretrained Xception backbone and its preprocessor with KerasHub, listing its convolutional layers, and building a single-output feature-extractor model for layer block3_sepconv1 To visualize filters, you need a model that maps an input image to the activation of one chosen convolutional layer. Because the KerasHub Xception backbone is a functional model, you can look up any layer by name with `get_layer` and wrap `model.input` → `layer.output` in a new `keras.Model`, with no need to rewrite Xception. The page completes the sentence from p.315: filter visualization will be the reader's second example of a low-level gradient descent loop (the first was in chapter 2), and it will be shown for **TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX**.

**Listing 10.7** instantiates the ImageNet-trained Xception model with KerasHub, "exactly as we did in chapter 8". `keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet")` builds the feature-extractor network from pretrained weights. `keras_hub.layers.ImageConverter.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", image_size=(180, 180))` loads the matching preprocessing that scales input images. (In KerasHub a *backbone* is the network without its classification head, p.282.)

The convolutional layers of interest are the `Conv2D` and `SeparableConv2D` layers, and their names are needed to retrieve their outputs. **Listing 10.8** prints those names in depth order by looping over `model.layers` and filtering with `isinstance`. The `SeparableConv2D` layers have names like `block6_sepconv1` and `block7_sepconv2`, because **Xception is structured into blocks**, each containing several convolutional layers.

Next comes a second model, a **feature extractor**, that returns the output of one specific layer. Because the backbone is a **Functional API model, it is inspectable**: you can query a layer's `output` and reuse it in a new model, with no need to copy the entire Xception code. **Listing 10.9** picks `layer_name = "block3_sepconv1"` (any layer of the convolutional base could be used instead), fetches the layer object with `model.get_layer(name=layer_name)`, and builds `feature_extractor = keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer.output)`. Given an input image, this model returns the output of the target layer.

The next page (p.317) applies the feature extractor with the model-specific preprocessing and defines the loss to maximize. Filter visualization uses a hand-written gradient loop, the book's second after chapter 2, shown for TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX. Listing 10.7 loads the Xception backbone and its matching preprocessor via KerasHub presets. Listing 10.8 prints Conv2D/SeparableConv2D layer names; Xception names them by block (blockN_sepconvM). Listing 10.9 builds a feature extractor from `model.input` to `get_layer("block3_sepconv1").output`. This works because functional models are inspectable; no Xception code needs to be copied.

title: The filter-activation loss; predict vs. model(x)
text:
Calling the feature extractor on preprocessed input, defining compute_loss as the mean activation of one filter away from the borders, and a sidebar contrasting model.predict(x) with model(x) The quantity maximized by gradient ascent is a scalar: the mean activation of filter `filter_index` in the chosen layer, computed on the central region (2 border pixels dropped on each side) to avoid border artifacts. The model is called directly as `model(x)`, not with `predict()`, because `predict()` batches and converts outputs to NumPy and so cannot be backpropagated through. **Using the feature extractor.** You can simply call `feature_extractor` on input data, but you must first apply the model-specific preprocessing so that images are scaled to the same range as Xception's pretraining data. **Listing 10.10**: `activation = feature_extractor(preprocessor(img_tensor))`.

**The loss.** The authors define a function returning a scalar that quantifies how much an input image *activates* a given filter of the layer. This is the loss that will be maximized by gradient ascent:

```python
def compute_loss(image, filter_index):
    activation = feature_extractor(image)
    filter_activation = activation[:, 2:-2, 2:-2, filter_index]
    return ops.mean(filter_activation)
```

The callouts explain it: the function takes an image tensor and the integer index of the filter; it **avoids border artifacts** by involving only non-border pixels (it discards the first 2 pixels along the sides of the activation); and it returns the **mean** of the activation values for that filter. Using `keras.ops` keeps it backend-agnostic, so the same function works in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.

**Sidebar: `model.predict(x)` vs. `model(x)`.** The previous chapter used `predict(x)` for feature extraction, while here the model is called directly. Both mean "run the model on `x` and retrieve `y`", but they differ. `predict()` loops over the data in batches (configurable with `batch_size=64`, for example) and extracts the **NumPy** value of the outputs, schematically like a loop that calls the model on each batch, converts with `.numpy()` and concatenates. So `predict()` **scales to very large arrays**, while `model(x)` runs in memory and doesn't scale. However, **`predict()` is not differentiable**: TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX cannot backpropagate through it. The sidebar continues on p.318 with the rule: use `model(x)` when you need gradients of the model call, and `predict()` otherwise. Always preprocess inputs with the model's ImageConverter before calling a pretrained backbone. compute_loss = mean activation of one filter over interior positions, cropping 2 pixels per side to avoid border artifacts. That scalar is maximized by gradient ascent on the input image. predict() batches and returns NumPy, so it scales but is not differentiable. model(x) runs in memory and is differentiable, so it is the right call inside a low-level gradient loop.
snippet: Using the feature extractor. You can simply call featureextractor on input data, but you must first apply the model-specific preprocessing so that images are scaled to the same…

title: Filter-activation loss
text: The mean activation of one filter (channel) of a chosen layer, over the batch and non-border positions; the objective maximized by gradient ascent. A score for how strongly the image excites this one detector. `ops.mean(feature_extractor(image)[:, 2:-2, 2:-2, filter_index])`. `compute_loss(image, 0)` scores filter 0 of block3_sepconv1.
snippet: The mean activation of one filter channel of a chosen layer, over the batch and non-border positions; the objective maximized by gradient ascent.

title: Avoiding border artifacts
text: Excluding activations near the edges of a feature map from the loss. Edge positions see partly padded or incomplete inputs, so their values are less trustworthy. Slice `2:-2` on both spatial axes drops the first and last 2 positions. A 10 × 10 activation map becomes 6 × 6 before averaging.
snippet: Excluding activations near the edges of a feature map from the loss.

title: model.predict(x) vs model(x)
text: predict batches the data and returns NumPy values (scalable, non-differentiable); calling the model returns backend tensors in memory (differentiable, not scalable). predict is for answers, and the call is for gradients. predict ≈ loop over batches → model(batch).numpy() → np.concatenate. compute_loss calls `feature_extractor(image)` directly.
snippet: predict batches the data and returns NumPy values scalable, non-differentiable; calling the model returns backend tensors in memory differentiable, not scalable.

title: Model-specific preprocessing
text: Scaling input images exactly as during the model's pretraining. Speak to the model in the 'units' it learned in. `feature_extractor(preprocessor(img_tensor))` with the ImageConverter preset. Listing 10.10.
snippet: Scaling input images exactly as during the model's pretraining.

title: Gradient normalization and the TensorFlow gradient-ascent step
text:
Preparing the gradient-ascent step that turns an input image into the pattern a chosen Xception filter responds to most strongly: when to use model(x) versus predict(), the L2 gradient-normalization trick, and the start of the TensorFlow implementation with GradientTape and tape.watch(). To visualize a filter we maximize its mean activation with respect to the input pixels. That needs a differentiable forward pass (model(x), not predict()), a gradient whose size is kept constant by L2 normalization, and backend-level gradient machinery. In TensorFlow that machinery is a GradientTape that must be told explicitly to watch the image tensor. The page opens by finishing the sidebar from p.317 on **`model.predict(x)` versus `model(x)`**. Its conclusion is practical: use `model(x)` when you need gradients of the model call, and use `predict()` when you only need output values. In other words, always use `predict()` unless you are writing a low-level gradient loop, as the authors are doing here. (On p.317 the sidebar explained why: `predict()` runs batch by batch and returns NumPy values, so it scales to large arrays but cannot be differentiated through.)

Next comes a **non-obvious trick**: before using the gradient, divide it by its **L2 norm**, the square root of the sum of the squares of all its values. The update direction stays the same, but every update to the input image now has roughly the same magnitude, so gradient ascent is not thrown off by gradients that are very large or very small.

The authors then point out that anything involving gradients requires a **backend-level API**: `GradientTape` in TensorFlow, `.backward()` in PyTorch, `jax.grad()` in JAX. They present the step function once for each backend, starting with TensorFlow in **section 10.2.1**. In TensorFlow you open a `GradientTape` scope, compute the loss inside it, and retrieve the gradients; a `@tf.function` decorator compiles the step for speed.

A recap code block collects the shared setup. It loads the Xception backbone (`xception_41_imagenet`) from KerasHub, picks the layer `block3_sepconv1`, builds a `feature_extractor` model that outputs that layer's activations, and defines `compute_loss(image, filter_index)`. That function returns the **mean activation of one filter**, computed only over spatial positions at least 2 pixels from the border.

Finally, **Listing 10.11** begins: `import tensorflow as tf`, the `@tf.function`-decorated `gradient_ascent_step(image, filter_index, learning_rate)`, a `with tf.GradientTape() as tape:` block, and `tape.watch(image)`. The callout explains that the image must be watched explicitly because it is not a TensorFlow `Variable`, and only Variables are watched automatically. The rest of the listing (loss, gradient, normalization, update, return) is on p.319. Use model(x) when you need gradients; use predict() for everything else. Normalize the gradient by its L2 norm so each update has a consistent magnitude. Gradient computation is the only backend-specific part: GradientTape, .backward(), or jax.grad(). compute_loss is the mean activation of one filter of block3_sepconv1, with 2-pixel borders excluded. In TensorFlow, call tape.watch(image), because the image is not a Variable; @tf.function compiles the step for speed.

title: Gradient ascent in input space
text: Optimizing the input of a fixed, trained network (here, image pixels) to maximize some internal or output quantity, by repeatedly stepping in the direction of that quantity's gradient with respect to the input. Instead of asking 'which weights fit the data?', we ask 'which image would make this filter fire as strongly as possible?' The network is frozen; the image is what we train. Given a loss L(x) = mean activation of filter f, iterate x_{t+1} = x_t + eta * grad_x L(x_t) / ||grad_x L(x_t)||_2. The gradient is computed by backpropagating through the feature extractor down to the input tensor. Start from a gray-ish noisy 200x200 image (p.320) and, over about 30 steps, it turns into a texture of the stripes or dots that filter 2 of block3_sepconv1 detects.
snippet: Optimizing the input of a fixed, trained network here, image pixels to maximize some internal or output quantity, by repeatedly stepping in the direction of that quantity's…

title: L2 gradient normalization
text: Dividing a gradient tensor by its L2 norm so that it has unit length, keeping only its direction. The gradient says which way is uphill. Its length depends on how steep the slope is right now, which can vary enormously. Normalizing means 'always take a step of the same size uphill'. g_hat = g / sqrt(sum_i g_i^2). In practice a small epsilon is added to the denominator to avoid division by zero when the gradient vanishes. g = (3, 4) has norm 5, so g_hat = (0.6, 0.8). With learning rate 10 the pixels move by (6, 8), whatever the original gradient size was.
snippet: Dividing a gradient tensor by its L2 norm so that it has unit length, keeping only its direction.

title: GradientTape
text: TensorFlow's autodiff API: a context manager that records operations on watched tensors and can then return gradients of a result with respect to them. Think of it as a tape recorder for math. Press record, do the computation, then play the recording backwards to get derivatives. Trainable tf.Variables are watched automatically. Plain tensors (like the image here) must be registered with tape.watch(tensor). Gradients are retrieved with tape.gradient(target, sources). with tf.GradientTape() as tape: tape.watch(image); loss = compute_loss(image, 2); grads = tape.gradient(loss, image).
snippet: TensorFlow's autodiff API: a context manager that records operations on watched tensors and can then return gradients of a result with respect to them.

title: Feature extractor model
text: A Keras Model built with the functional API whose output is an intermediate layer's output of a pretrained network. It cuts the network at a chosen layer and exposes what that layer 'sees'. keras.Model(inputs=model.input, outputs=layer.output) reuses the pretrained layers and weights up to block3_sepconv1; it returns a tensor of shape (batch, height, width, channels) for that layer. feature_extractor(image)[:, :, :, 2] is the activation map of filter 2.
snippet: A Keras Model built with the functional API whose output is an intermediate layer's output of a pretrained network.

title: model(x) vs model.predict(x)
text: Two ways to run a Keras model: a direct differentiable call on tensors, and a batched, NumPy-returning, non-differentiable inference loop. model(x) is a calculator you can take derivatives through; predict() is a factory line that turns out finished NumPy results. predict() iterates in batches (batch_size argument) and converts outputs to NumPy, which leaves the autodiff graph. model(x) stays in backend tensors. Inside gradient_ascent_step: feature_extractor(image). For extracting features from 10,000 images: feature_extractor.predict(images, batch_size=64).
snippet: Two ways to run a Keras model: a direct differentiable call on tensors, and a batched, NumPy-returning, non-differentiable inference loop.

title: The gradient-ascent step in TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX
text:
The rest of the TensorFlow gradient-ascent step (Listing 10.11) and the equivalent PyTorch (Listing 10.12) and JAX (Listing 10.13) step functions, which differ only in how the gradient of the filter-activation loss with respect to the input image is obtained. All three step functions do the same four things: compute the loss, get d(loss)/d(image), normalize the gradient, and add learning_rate × gradient to the image. Only the gradient retrieval is backend-specific: tape.gradient in TensorFlow, loss.backward() plus image.grad in PyTorch, and a jax.grad-generated function in JAX. The page finishes **Listing 10.11** (TensorFlow) and presents the PyTorch and JAX versions of the same step function.

**TensorFlow (end of 10.11).** Still inside the `GradientTape` scope, `loss = compute_loss(image, filter_index)` computes a scalar that says how much the current image activates the filter. After the scope, `grads = tape.gradient(loss, image)` gets the gradient of the loss with respect to the image. `grads = ops.normalize(grads)` applies the "gradient normalization trick" from p.318. `image += learning_rate * grads` moves the image a little in the direction that activates the target filter more strongly. `return image` hands back the updated image so the step function can be run in a loop.

**PyTorch (10.2.2, Listing 10.12).** Gradients come from `loss.backward()` and `image.grad`. The first line, `image = image.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True)`, creates a copy of the image that gradients can be computed for. Then the loss is computed, `loss.backward()` backpropagates, `image.grad` is read, normalized, and the image is updated with the out-of-place `image = image + learning_rate * grads`. The authors note that there is **no need to reset the gradients**, because the image tensor is recreated at each iteration. Contrast this with the training loop on p.103, where `.grad` had to be reset to avoid accumulation.

**JAX (10.2.3, Listing 10.13).** `grad_fn = jax.grad(compute_loss)` turns the loss function into a function that returns the gradient of the loss with respect to its first argument, the image. The step function is decorated with `@jax.jit` for compilation and calls `grads = grad_fn(image, filter_index)`; normalization, update and return are identical to the TensorFlow version.

The three listings share `compute_loss`, `ops.normalize`, and the update rule $x \leftarrow x + \eta\,\hat g$. Only the line or lines that produce `grads` differ, which is exactly the point made on p.318. All three step functions compute loss, gradient, normalized gradient and update; only the gradient retrieval is backend-specific. TensorFlow: compute the loss inside GradientTape, then tape.gradient(loss, image). PyTorch: make a fresh leaf with clone().detach().requires_grad_(True), call loss.backward(), read image.grad. No reset is needed because the leaf is new each time. JAX: grad_fn = jax.grad(compute_loss) differentiates with respect to the first argument; @jax.jit compiles the step. The + in image += learning_rate * grads is what makes this gradient ascent.
snippet: The page finishes Listing 10.11 TensorFlow and presents the PyTorch and JAX versions of the same step function. TensorFlow end of 10.11. Still inside the GradientTape scope, loss…

title: Gradient ascent in input space
text: Updating the input image in the direction of the gradient of a filter's activation so as to increase that activation, with the network weights frozen. Each step nudges the pixels toward 'more of what this filter likes'. Update rule in all three listings: image <- image + learning_rate * normalize(d loss / d image). The plus sign makes it ascent. One call of gradient_ascent_step slightly increases the mean activation of filter filter_index of block3_sepconv1.
snippet: Updating the input image in the direction of the gradient of a filter's activation so as to increase that activation, with the network weights frozen.

title: GradientTape
text: TensorFlow context manager that records operations so tape.gradient(target, source) can compute gradients. Record the forward pass, then replay it backwards. Here tape.gradient(loss, image) is called after the with block closes; one tape supports one gradient call unless persistent=True. grads = tape.gradient(loss, image) returns a tensor shaped like image.
snippet: TensorFlow context manager that records operations so tape.gradienttarget, source can compute gradients.

title: PyTorch autograd (backward and .grad)
text: PyTorch's dynamic reverse-mode autodiff: operations on tensors with requires_grad=True are tracked, and loss.backward() writes gradients into the leaves' .grad attributes. Gradients are delivered by side effect onto the tensors, not returned as values. clone() copies the data; detach() cuts it from any previous graph, making a fresh leaf; requires_grad_(True) enables tracking in place. Because the leaf is new at each step, .grad starts at None. image = image.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True); loss.backward(); image.grad.
snippet: PyTorch's dynamic reverse-mode autodiff: operations on tensors with requiresgrad=True are tracked, and loss.backward writes gradients into the leaves' .grad attributes.

title: jax.grad function transformation
text: A JAX transformation that maps a scalar-valued function f to a function computing the gradient of f with respect to its first argument. Instead of asking for a gradient, you ask for a gradient-computing function and then call it. grad_fn = jax.grad(compute_loss); grad_fn(image, filter_index) returns d compute_loss / d image. It is combined with @jax.jit to compile the step. Listing 10.13's grad_fn = jax.grad(compute_loss).
snippet: A JAX transformation that maps a scalar-valued function f to a function computing the gradient of f with respect to its first argument.

title: Gradient normalization trick
text: Rescaling the gradient to unit L2 norm before the update so step sizes stay in a consistent range. Keep the direction, fix the stride. Implemented by grads = ops.normalize(grads) in all three listings. Beyond the book: Keras 3's ops.normalize(x, axis=-1, order=2) normalizes along the last axis by default, i.e. each pixel's 3-channel gradient vector is scaled to unit length. That is a per-pixel variant of the whole-tensor L2 normalization described on p.318. A pixel gradient (0.003, -0.004, 0) becomes (0.6, -0.8, 0).
snippet: Rescaling the gradient to unit L2 norm before the update so step sizes stay in a consistent range.

The positive sign means ascent: for a small enough eta, the filter's activation increases at each step. Beyond the book: ops.normalize with its default axis=-1 normalizes each pixel's channel vector, so in code the norm is taken per pixel rather than over the whole tensor. x The image tensor being optimized. f filter_index. \mathcal{L}(x, f) compute_loss(image, filter_index): mean activation of filter f, borders excluded (p.318). g grads, the gradient of the loss with respect to the image. \eta learning_rate.

title: Listing 10.12 Loss maximization via stochastic gradient ascent: PyTorch
text:
import torch

def gradient_ascent_step(image, filter_index, learning_rate):
    image = image.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True)
    loss = compute_loss(image, filter_index)
    loss.backward()
    grads = image.grad
    grads = ops.normalize(grads)
    image = image + learning_rate * grads
    return image The PyTorch version of the step: it makes a fresh gradient-tracking copy of the image, backpropagates the filter-activation loss to it, reads the gradient from image.grad, normalizes it and takes an ascent step. One normalized gradient-ascent step using dynamic autograd.
snippet: The PyTorch version of the step: it makes a fresh gradient-tracking copy of the image, backpropagates the filter-activation loss to it, reads the gradient from image.grad,…

title: Listing 10.13 Loss maximization via stochastic gradient ascent: JAX
text:
import jax

grad_fn = jax.grad(compute_loss)

@jax.jit
def gradient_ascent_step(image, filter_index, learning_rate):
    grads = grad_fn(image, filter_index)
    grads = ops.normalize(grads)
    image += learning_rate * grads
    return image The JAX version: it builds a gradient function from compute_loss once, then defines a JIT-compiled step that calls it, normalizes the result and takes an ascent step. One normalized gradient-ascent step via function transformation.
snippet: The JAX version: it builds a gradient function from computeloss once, then defines a JIT-compiled step that calls it, normalizes the result and takes an ascent step.

title: Which lines of the three listings are identical, and why can they be shared?

def deprocess_image(image):
    image -= ops.mean(image)
    image /= ops.std(image)
    image *= 64
    image += 128
    image = ops.clip(image, 0, 255)
    image = image[25:-25, 25:-25, :]

title: Figure 10.5 and stitching a grid of 64 filter patterns
text:
The first filter visualization (filter 2 of block3_sepconv1: horizontal, water- or fur-like lines), and Listing 10.16, which generates patterns for the first 64 filters of the layer and pastes them into an 8×8 grid image saved to disk. A single pattern shows what one filter detects. Sweeping the filter index and tiling the results shows the whole vocabulary of features a layer has learned, and repeating this for several layers shows how that vocabulary changes with depth (figure 10.6). **Figure 10.5** shows the result of the snippet on p.320: the pattern that "the second channel" of `block3_sepconv1` responds to most strongly. (The code used `filter_index=2`; with zero-based indexing that is the third channel, so the caption's wording is slightly loose.) The image is a dense, noisy texture of multicolored, roughly **horizontal wavy stripes**. The authors read it as filter 2 being responsive to **a horizontal lines pattern, somewhat water-like or fur-like**.

The authors call the next step "the fun part": visualizing every filter in the layer, and even every filter in every layer (figure 10.6, on the next page).

**Listing 10.16** has four parts:
1. **Generate**: for `filter_index in range(64)`, print progress, run `deprocess_image(generate_filter_pattern(filter_index))` and append the result to `all_images` (callout: "Generates and saves visualizations for the first 64 filters in the layer").
2. **Prepare a blank canvas**: `margin = 5`, `n = 8` (an 8×8 grid), `box_width = img_width - 25 * 2` and `box_height = img_height - 25 * 2` (150 each, the size after the crop in `deprocess_image`). Then `full_width = n * box_width + (n - 1) * margin` and likewise `full_height`, which gives $8\cdot150 + 7\cdot5 = 1235$. `stitched_filters = np.zeros((full_width, full_height, 3))` is the black canvas.
3. **Fill the picture**: a double loop over `i, j in range(n)` takes `all_images[i * n + j]` and assigns it to the slice that starts at `(box_width + margin) * i` along the first axis and `(box_height + margin) * j` along the second, spanning one box.
4. **Save**: `keras.utils.save_img(f"filters_for_layer_{layer_name}.png", stitched_filters)` writes the canvas to disk, named after the layer.

Changing `layer_name` (and rebuilding the feature extractor) and rerunning produces grids like those in figure 10.6 for `block2_sepconv1`, `block4_sepconv1` and `block8_sepconv1`. Filter 2 of block3_sepconv1 responds to a horizontal lines pattern that looks somewhat water- or fur-like (figure 10.5). Listing 10.16 visualizes the first 64 filters and tiles them in an 8×8 grid. Each tile is 150×150 (200 minus the 25-pixel crop on each side); with 5-pixel margins the canvas is 1235×1235×3. Filter k = i·8 + j goes to row i, column j. The grid is saved as filters_for_layer_{layer_name}.png; rerun with other layer names for figure 10.6.

title: What filter visualizations reveal: a hierarchy of filter banks
text:
Figure 10.6 compares filter patterns from block2_sepconv1, block4_sepconv1 and block8_sepconv1 of Xception, and the text interprets them: each layer learns a filter bank onto which its input can be decomposed, much like a Fourier basis, and the filters grow more complex with depth. Each ConvNet layer learns a bank of filters such that its inputs can be expressed as a combination of them, much as the Fourier transform expresses a signal as a combination of cosines. Going up the network, these filters move from directional edges and colors to textures, and then (p.323) to natural-image textures such as feathers, eyes and leaves. **Figure 10.6** shows ten filter patterns from each of three Xception layers, produced with the grid code of Listing 10.16 (p.321):
- **block 2** (`block2_sepconv1`): smooth, regular **stripes** at various orientations and frequencies (diagonal, horizontal, wavy). Some are almost uniform with faint color, others are clean colored gratings.
- **block 4** (`block4_sepconv1`): denser **textures** built from those stripes, such as lattices, diamond and scale-like patterns, grids of small blobs and herringbone shapes.
- **block 8** (`block8_sepconv1`): much more **intricate, organic patterns** with curved strokes, eye-like spots, leaf- or feather-like shapes and swirls.

The authors draw a general lesson. **Each layer learns a collection of filters such that its inputs can be expressed as a combination of the filters.** They compare this to the **Fourier transform**, which decomposes signals onto a bank of cosine functions. The filters in these banks **get increasingly complex and refined as you go higher in the model**:
- the first layers encode **simple directional edges and colors** (or colored edges);
- layers a bit higher, such as `block4_sepconv1`, encode **simple textures made from combinations of edges and colors**;
- (continued on p.323) higher layers produce filters that resemble **textures found in natural images: feathers, eyes, leaves**, and so on.

This matches what section 10.1 found by visualizing activations: representations become more abstract and specialized with depth. The filter patterns show it from the input side, as the stimulus each unit wants, rather than as the response to a given image. Each ConvNet layer learns a filter bank such that its inputs can be expressed as a combination of the filters. This is similar to the Fourier transform decomposing a signal onto a bank of cosines, but with learned, nonlinear, stacked filters. First layers encode simple directional edges and colors (figure 10.6, block 2). Layers such as block4_sepconv1 encode simple textures built from edges and colors. Higher layers (block 8) resemble natural-image textures such as feathers, eyes and leaves (p.323).

title: Hierarchy of learned features
text: The progression of what ConvNet filters detect with depth: edges and colors, then textures, then complex natural-image parts. Letters make syllables, syllables make words: each layer combines the previous layer's features into larger, more specific ones. A unit's receptive field and the nonlinear composition of lower-layer features both grow with depth, so higher-level units can represent larger and more structured patterns. block2: stripes; block4: lattices and scales; block8: feather-, eye- and leaf-like patterns (figure 10.6, p.323).

text: The collection of filters learned by one layer; its outputs describe the input as a vector of responses to each filter. A dictionary of local patterns that the layer uses to describe what it sees. For a conv layer with C output channels, the bank has C filters; the activation at each location is the vector of C responses. block3_sepconv1's first 64 filters, shown as a grid by Listing 10.16.

title: Fourier-transform analogy
text: The comparison between a layer expressing its input in terms of its filters and the Fourier transform expressing a signal as a combination of cosines. Both describe something complicated as 'how much of each simple ingredient it contains'. Fourier: $x(t) = \sum_k a_k \cos(\omega_k t + \phi_k)$, fixed basis. ConvNet: learned, data-dependent filters with nonlinearities, stacked so that each basis is built from the previous one. A square wave is mostly a fundamental cosine plus smaller odd harmonics; a local image patch is mostly a vertical-edge filter response plus smaller color responses.

title: Introducing class activation heatmaps and Grad-CAM
text:
The page ends the filter-visualization discussion (higher-layer filters look like feathers, eyes, leaves) and opens section 10.3: class activation map (CAM) visualization, the Grad-CAM method of Selvaraju et al., and Listing 10.17, which downloads and loads the elephant test image as a batched NumPy array. A class activation heatmap scores every location of an input image by how important it is for a chosen class. Grad-CAM computes it by taking a conv layer's output feature map and weighting each channel by the gradient of the class score with respect to that channel, which turns 'how strongly each channel fires where' into 'how strongly the class is activated where'. The page opens with the **last bullet** of the filter hierarchy from p.322: filters in higher layers begin to resemble **textures found in natural images: feathers, eyes, leaves**, and so on.

**Section 10.3** then introduces a final visualization technique for understanding **which parts of an image led a ConvNet to its classification decision**. It is useful for "debugging" the decision process, especially when the model makes a mistake (the field of **model interpretability**), and it can also **locate specific objects** in an image.

The general family is **class activation map (CAM) visualization**: producing heatmaps of class activation over input images. A **class activation heatmap** is a 2-D grid of scores for one output class, computed for every location of the input, that indicates how important each location is for that class. In a dogs-versus-cats ConvNet you could produce a "cat" heatmap (how cat-like each part of the image is) and a separate "dog" heatmap.

The authors use **Grad-CAM** (Selvaraju et al., footnote 1, arXiv 1610.02391). It takes the **output feature map of a convolution layer** for a given input and **weights every channel by the gradient of the class with respect to that channel**. Intuitively, a spatial map of "how intensely the input activates different channels" is weighted by "how important each channel is with regard to the class", which gives a spatial map of "how intensely the input image activates the class".

The demonstration uses the pretrained **Xception** model on a photo of **two African elephants** (possibly a mother and calf) in the savanna (figure 10.7, next page). **Listing 10.17** downloads the image with `keras.utils.get_file` (cached locally under `img_path`), loads it as a PIL image with `keras.utils.load_img`, and converts it to a NumPy array with a batch dimension using `np.expand_dims(img, axis=0)`. Despite the listing's title, no model-specific scaling is applied yet. The next page uses a KerasHub classification task, which includes its own preprocessing. Higher-layer filters resemble natural-image textures: feathers, eyes, leaves. Class activation heatmaps show which parts of an image led a ConvNet to its decision; they are used for debugging (interpretability) and localization. A CAM is a class-specific 2-D grid of importance scores over the input locations. Grad-CAM weights each channel of a conv layer's output by the gradient of the class with respect to that channel: activation intensity × channel importance = class activation intensity. Listing 10.17 downloads elephant.jpg, loads it as a PIL image and makes a (1, H, W, 3) NumPy batch.

title: Class activation map (CAM)
text: A 2-D grid of scores for a specific output class, one per location of the input image, indicating how important each location is for that class. A 'where is the evidence for class c?' overlay on the image. Computed on a conv layer's spatial grid (coarse), then upsampled and overlaid on the input for display. For a dogs-versus-cats ConvNet: a 'cat' heatmap and a 'dog' heatmap of the same photo.
snippet: A 2-D grid of scores for a specific output class, one per location of the input image, indicating how important each location is for that class.

title: Grad-CAM
text: Gradient-weighted class activation mapping: weighting each channel of a conv layer's output feature map by the gradient of the class score with respect to that channel, then aggregating into a heatmap. Where features fire × how much the class cares about those features = where the class is activated. alpha_k^c = (1/Z) sum_{i,j} d y^c / d A^k_{ij}; L^c = ReLU(sum_k alpha_k^c A^k). The book's code (p.325-328) uses the last conv layer block14_sepconv2_act of Xception. Heatmap for 'African elephant' on figure 10.7, expected to highlight the elephants.
snippet: Gradient-weighted class activation mapping: weighting each channel of a conv layer's output feature map by the gradient of the class score with respect to that channel, then…

title: Model interpretability
text: Understanding and explaining why a model makes the predictions it makes. Opening the black box enough to see what it is looking at. This chapter covers four tools: intermediate activations, filter visualizations, class activation heatmaps and latent-space visualization. Checking whether a misclassified image's heatmap focuses on the background instead of the object.
snippet: Understanding and explaining why a model makes the predictions it makes.

title: Hierarchy of learned features
text: Edges and colors in low layers, textures in middle layers, natural-image textures (feathers, eyes, leaves) in higher layers. Simple parts combine into complex parts. Completed on this page by the third bullet. block8_sepconv1 patterns in figure 10.6.
snippet: Edges and colors in low layers, textures in middle layers, natural-image textures feathers, eyes, leaves in higher layers.

title: Grad-CAM heatmap (formalizing the verbal description)
text: weighting every channel in that feature map by the gradient of the class with respect to the channel \alpha_k^{c} = \frac{1}{HW}\sum_{i=1}^{H}\sum_{j=1}^{W} \frac{\partial y^{c}}{\partial A^{k}_{ij}}, \qquad L^{c}_{ij} = \operatorname{ReLU}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \alpha_k^{c}\, A^{k}_{ij}\Big) To turn channel activations into a single class-specific spatial map. Large positive L^c_{ij} means location (i, j) strongly activates features that increase the class score. The book's code (p.325-328) computes the channel-wise mean instead of the sum, which only scales the map, and then clips negatives with np.maximum(heatmap, 0). A^k_{ij} Activation of channel k at location (i, j) of the chosen conv layer's output feature map (shape H×W×K). y^c Score for class c (the top predicted class in the book's code). \alpha_k^c Importance of channel k for class c: the spatially averaged gradient. L^c_{ij} Class activation heatmap value at (i, j). H, W, K Spatial size and number of channels of the feature map.
snippet: weighting every channel in that feature map by the gradient of the class with respect to the channel — To turn channel activations into a single class-specific spatial map.

title: Loading the full Xception classifier with the KerasHub task API
text:
Why Grad-CAM needs the complete Xception model (including its ImageNet classification head), and how the KerasHub ImageClassifier task bundles preprocessing, backbone and head so that a single predict() call returns a 1,000-way probability vector for the elephant test image. Grad-CAM explains a class decision, so it needs the network's class scores, not just its convolutional features. KerasHub's high-level task API (here keras_hub.models.ImageClassifier) wraps preprocessing, the feature-extraction backbone and the classification head into one object; with a softmax activation its output for one image is a (1, 1000) probability vector, which the decoding utility turns into readable ImageNet labels. The page continues the Grad-CAM setup begun on p.323.

**Figure 10.7** shows the test picture: two African elephants (an adult with raised trunk and tusks, and a calf) walking through tall grass. This is the image whose classification we want to explain.

**Why a different model is needed.** Up to now in the chapter, KerasHub was only used to build a *feature extractor* through the **backbone** class (the convolutional base, as on p.316). Grad-CAM, however, measures how important each location is *for a specific class*, so it needs the **entire Xception model, including the classification head**. The book reminds us that Xception was trained on ImageNet, about 1 million labeled images in 1,000 classes (p.280 gives 1.4 million; see review flag).

**The task API.** KerasHub offers high-level *tasks* for end-to-end workflows such as image classification, text classification and image generation. A task wraps three things in one class:

1. preprocessing,
2. a feature-extraction network (the backbone),
3. a task-specific head.

**The code.** `keras_hub.models.ImageClassifier.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", activation="softmax")` downloads the full classifier; the callout explains that `activation` configures the classifier's final activation, and softmax makes the outputs probabilities. `model.predict(img_array)` returns an array of shape `(1, 1000)`: one image in the batch, one entry per ImageNet class. `keras_hub.utils.decode_imagenet_predictions(preds)` maps the largest entries to human-readable labels: `African_elephant` 0.90331, `tusker` 0.05487, `Indian_elephant` 0.01637, ... (the listing continues on p.325 with `triceratops` and `Mexican_hairless`).

Note that `img_array` was not preprocessed by hand: the task's built-in preprocessor handles that inside `predict()`, a point the book makes explicitly on p.325. Grad-CAM explains a class decision, so it needs the full classifier with its head, not only the backbone. A KerasHub task bundles preprocessing, a backbone and a task-specific head; ImageClassifier.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", activation="softmax") gives a ready ImageNet classifier. predict() on one image returns shape (1, 1000): one probability per ImageNet class. decode_imagenet_predictions turns the vector into labels: African_elephant 0.90331, tusker 0.05487, Indian_elephant 0.01637, and so on. The task preprocesses raw input inside predict(), so img_array was passed in unprocessed.

title: Grad-CAM (gradient-weighted class activation map)
text: A class activation map technique that weights each channel of a convolutional feature map by the gradient of a chosen class score with respect to that channel, then averages the weighted channels into a 2D heatmap. It combines 'how strongly each location activates each channel' with 'how much each channel matters for the class', giving 'how strongly each location activates the class' (p.323). Requires a differentiable path from the conv feature map to the class score, which is why the full model with its classification head is needed. For the elephant image, the heatmap for the class African_elephant highlights the elephants (Figure 10.9, p.329).

title: KerasHub task API
text: High-level KerasHub classes for end-to-end workflows that wrap preprocessing, a feature-extraction network and a task-specific head into one model. A ready-to-use appliance: raw input in, final answer out, with the internal parts still reachable. Created with from_preset(); the image classifier exposes .preprocessor and .backbone and accepts raw images in predict(). keras_hub.models.ImageClassifier.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet", activation="softmax")

title: Backbone vs full pretrained classifier
text: A backbone is the pretrained feature extractor without the classification head; the full classifier adds the head that outputs scores for the original training classes (here the 1,000 ImageNet classes). The backbone sees patterns; the head names them. Xception's backbone outputs a spatial feature map; the head pools it and applies a 1,000-way dense layer with (optionally) softmax. Section 10.2 used the backbone; section 10.3 uses ImageClassifier.

title: Softmax final activation
text: The activation that converts a vector of scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to 1. Turns 'how much evidence for each class' into 'what share of belief each class gets'. Setting activation="softmax" on the ImageClassifier makes predict() return a probability distribution over 1,000 classes for each image. The top three probabilities on this page are 0.90331, 0.05487 and 0.01637.

African_elephant receives about 90% of the probability mass, tusker 5.5%, Indian_elephant 1.6%. z_c The head's raw score (logit) for class c. p_c The probability for class c, one of the 1,000 entries of preds[0].

title: Top-class prediction and splitting Xception for Grad-CAM
text:
Reading the classifier's top-five predictions for the elephant image, finding the top class index (386, African elephant), preprocessing the image explicitly with the task's preprocessor, and starting to cut the model into two submodels: input -> last convolutional activations (Listing 10.18) and last convolutional activations -> class predictions (Listing 10.19, continued on p.326). To get the gradient of the class score with respect to the last convolutional feature map, the model is split at layer block14_sepconv2_act into a feature-map model and a classifier model. Because these submodels bypass the task's built-in preprocessing, the image must first be passed through model.preprocessor. The page first finishes the prediction output from p.324: the last two decoded entries are `("triceratops", 0.00029)` and `("Mexican_hairless", 0.00018)`. The text then lists the **top five classes**: African elephant (90%), tusker (5%), Indian elephant (2%), and triceratops and Mexican hairless dog (each under 0.1%).

The network has recognized "an undetermined quantity of African elephants" (the classifier says *what* is in the picture, not how many). The maximally activated entry of the prediction vector is **index 386**, the African elephant class: `np.argmax(preds[0])` returns `386`.

The goal now is to see which parts of the image are the most "African elephant-like", so the Grad-CAM process is set up:

- **Preprocessing.** We did not preprocess the image before calling the task, because `ImageClassifier` preprocesses inputs inside `predict()`. For Grad-CAM we will call parts of the network directly, so we preprocess ourselves: `img_array = model.preprocessor(img_array)` (callout: KerasHub tasks have a preprocessor layer).
- **Listing 10.18.** A model that maps the input image to the activations of the last convolutional layer: the layer `"block14_sepconv2_act"` is fetched from `model.backbone` with `get_layer()`, and `keras.Model(model.inputs, last_conv_layer.output)` creates `last_conv_layer_model`.
- **Listing 10.19 (begins).** A second model maps those activations to the final class predictions. It starts with `classifier_input = last_conv_layer.output` and `x = classifier_input`; the rest (applying the `pooler` and `predictions` layers) is on p.326.

Splitting the network at the last conv layer turns its output into an explicit input of the classifier part, which is exactly the tensor we need gradients with respect to. The top five predictions are African elephant (90%), tusker (5%), Indian elephant (2%), triceratops and Mexican hairless dog (<0.1%). The top class is index 386 (African elephant), found with np.argmax(preds[0]). predict() preprocesses automatically; to use submodels directly, preprocess explicitly with model.preprocessor. Listing 10.18 builds last_conv_layer_model from model.inputs to the output of block14_sepconv2_act in the backbone. Listing 10.19 starts a second model whose input is that conv output, so the class score becomes a function of the feature map.

title: Listing 10.20 Computing the top class gradients with TensorFlow
text:
import tensorflow as tf
def get_top_class_gradients(img_array):
    last_conv_layer_output = last_conv_layer_model(img_array)
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        tape.watch(last_conv_layer_output)
        preds = classifier_model(last_conv_layer_output)
        top_pred_index = ops.argmax(preds[0])
        top_class_channel = preds[:, top_pred_index]
    grads = tape.gradient(top_class_channel, last_conv_layer_output)
    return grads, last_conv_layer_output
grads, last_conv_layer_output = get_top_class_gradients(img_array)
grads = ops.convert_to_numpy(grads)
last_conv_layer_output = ops.convert_to_numpy(last_conv_layer_output) Computes the last conv feature map for the image and the gradient of the top predicted class's output with respect to that feature map, then converts both to NumPy arrays. Forward to feature map -> taped forward through head -> select top class -> reverse-mode gradient.

title: Top-class gradients in PyTorch and JAX
text:
The rest of the PyTorch implementation of get_top_class_gradients (Listing 10.21: clone/detach/requires_grad_, backward(), .grad) and the JAX implementation (Listing 10.22: a separate loss function returning the top-class activation, turned into a gradient function with jax.grad). All three backends compute the same tensor, the gradient of the top predicted class's output with respect to the last conv feature map, but with different autodiff styles: PyTorch marks a leaf tensor as requiring gradients and calls backward(); JAX transforms a pure function returning a scalar into its gradient function. **Listing 10.21 continued (PyTorch).** After computing the last conv activations (p.326), the function replaces them with

`last_conv_layer_output.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True)`

which, per the callout, "creates a copy of last_conv_layer_output that we can get gradients for": a fresh **leaf tensor** cut off from the backbone's computation graph, with gradient tracking enabled. Then the classifier runs on it, the top class index is found with `ops.argmax(preds[0])`, the activation channel of that class is selected with `preds[:, top_pred_index]`, and `top_class_channel.backward()` backpropagates. The gradient is read from `last_conv_layer_output.grad`. As in TensorFlow, the function is called on `img_array` and both outputs are converted with `ops.convert_to_numpy`.

**10.3.3 JAX version (Listing 10.22).** JAX needs a **separate loss computation function**. `loss_fn(last_conv_layer_output)` runs `classifier_model`, finds the top class and returns `top_class_channel[0]`, the scalar activation value of the top-class channel, which serves as the "loss" to differentiate. `grad_fn = jax.grad(loss_fn)` creates a gradient function. Inside `get_top_class_gradients`, the feature map is computed and `grads = grad_fn(last_conv_layer_output)`; as the callout says, retrieving the gradient "is just a matter of calling the gradient function!" The same NumPy conversion follows.

In all three backends the result is the pair `(grads, last_conv_layer_output)`, two NumPy arrays of the same shape, ready for the pooling and channel weighting of section 10.3.4 (p.328).

Note: the prose says the loss function "takes the final layer's output"; in the code it takes the last *convolutional* layer's output (see review flag). PyTorch: make the feature map a leaf with clone().detach().requires_grad_(True), run the classifier, call backward() on the top-class output, read .grad. JAX: write loss_fn(feature_map) returning the scalar top-class activation, build grad_fn = jax.grad(loss_fn), call it on the feature map. All three backends produce the same grads tensor with the shape of the feature map. ops.convert_to_numpy makes the rest of Grad-CAM backend-independent. The book's 'final layer's output' in 10.3.3 should be read as the last convolutional layer's output.

title: Three autodiff styles
text: Automatic differentiation as exposed by TensorFlow (GradientTape records operations), PyTorch (tensors with requires_grad build a graph; backward() fills .grad) and JAX (jax.grad transforms a function). Recorder, self-tracking tensors, and function transformer: three interfaces to the same chain rule. PyTorch requires a leaf tensor with requires_grad=True; JAX requires a pure function with scalar output whose first argument is the differentiation variable. Listings 10.20 (TF), 10.21 (PyTorch), 10.22 (JAX).

title: Pooling gradients into channel weights and building the heatmap
text:
Turning the gradient tensor and the last conv feature map into a class activation heatmap: average the gradients per channel to get channel importances, multiply each feature-map channel by its importance, average over channels, then clip negatives, normalize to [0, 1] and display the result (Figure 10.8). Grad-CAM's heatmap is a weighted combination of feature-map channels, where each channel's weight is the spatial mean of the class gradient for that channel. Keeping only positive values and normalizing gives a coarse map (here 10 x 10) of where the image supports the class African elephant. Section **10.3.4** turns the gradients into a picture.

**Listing 10.23, gradient pooling and channel importance weighting.**

- `pooled_grads = np.mean(grads, axis=(0, 1, 2))` averages the gradient over the batch axis and the two spatial axes. The result is a vector with one entry per channel: "the mean intensity of the gradient for a given channel", which "quantifies the importance of each channel with regard to the top predicted class" (callout).
- `last_conv_layer_output = last_conv_layer_output[0].copy()` drops the batch axis and makes a copy so the original array is not modified.
- The `for` loop multiplies each channel `[:, :, i]` by `pooled_grads[i]`: "each channel in the output of the last convolutional layer" is scaled "by how important this channel is".
- `heatmap = np.mean(last_conv_layer_output, axis=-1)`: "the channel-wise mean of the resulting feature map is our heatmap of class activation".

**Listing 10.24, heatmap post-processing.** For visualization the heatmap is normalized between 0 and 1: `np.maximum(heatmap, 0)` sets negative values to zero, `heatmap /= np.max(heatmap)` scales the maximum to 1, and `plt.matshow(heatmap)` displays it.

**Figure 10.8** shows the standalone heatmap: a coarse 10 x 10 grid (one cell per spatial position of the last conv layer) with a bright blob in the upper-middle part and dark values elsewhere, especially at the bottom. On its own it is hard to interpret; p.329 superimposes it on the elephant photo.

In formula form, the heatmap is $\max\big(0, \tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k \alpha_k A^k\big)$ normalized to a maximum of 1, with $\alpha_k$ the spatially averaged gradient of channel $k$. pooled_grads = mean of grads over batch and spatial axes: one importance weight per channel. Each channel of the last conv output is multiplied by its weight; the channel-wise mean is the heatmap. np.maximum(heatmap, 0) keeps positive evidence; dividing by the max normalizes to [0, 1]. Figure 10.8 is a coarse 10 x 10 map with a bright region in the upper middle, matching the last conv layer's grid. This step is pure NumPy and identical for all backends.

title: Superimposing the Grad-CAM heatmap on the original picture
text:
Producing Figure 10.9: reloading the original elephant photo, converting the [0, 1] heatmap to 0-255 integers, colorizing it with the jet colormap, and resizing the colored heatmap to the photo's size so it can be blended with the image (Listing 10.25, finished on p.330). A 10 x 10 heatmap is meaningless until it is mapped back onto the image. Turning heatmap values into colors with a lookup table (jet) and upsampling the colored map to the original resolution lets you see that the evidence for 'African elephant' sits on the elephants, especially around the calf. The last step of Grad-CAM is to **superimpose the original image on the heatmap** (Figure 10.9).

**Figure 10.9** shows the elephant photo of Figure 10.7 with a rainbow-colored jet overlay. The colored region is concentrated on the elephant calf and extends toward the adult's head and front, while the sky and the foreground grass are only faintly tinted. Because the heatmap has only 10 x 10 cells, the overlay is a smooth, blurry blob rather than a precise outline.

**Listing 10.25 (first part)**:

1. `import matplotlib.cm as cm` for colormaps.
2. **Loads the original image** again with `keras.utils.load_img(img_path)` and converts it to an array with `img_to_array`. The full-resolution photo is used, not the preprocessed `img_array`.
3. **Rescales the heatmap to 0-255**: `heatmap = np.uint8(255 * heatmap)`, so its values can serve as indices.
4. **Uses the "jet" colormap to recolorize the heatmap**: `jet = cm.get_cmap("jet")`, `jet_colors = jet(np.arange(256))[:, :3]` builds a 256 x 3 RGB lookup table (dropping the alpha channel), and `jet_heatmap = jet_colors[heatmap]` replaces each heatmap value with its color.
5. **Creates an image that contains the recolorized heatmap**: `array_to_img` turns the array into a PIL image, `.resize((img.shape[1], img.shape[0]))` upsamples it to the photo's width and height, and `img_to_array` converts it back to an array.

The listing ends on p.330, where the colored heatmap is blended with the photo (`jet_heatmap * 0.4 + img`) and saved as `elephant_cam.jpg`. The heatmap is superimposed on the original (reloaded) image to make it interpretable (Figure 10.9). np.uint8(255 * heatmap) turns the [0, 1] map into indices for a 256-color jet lookup table. The colorized 10 x 10 map is resized to the photo's (width, height) before blending. Figure 10.9 shows the African elephant evidence concentrated on the elephants, especially the calf. The blend (0.4 x heatmap + image) and saving are on p.330.

title: Grad-CAM (class activation heatmap)
text: A technique that produces a heatmap over an input image showing how important each location is for a given class, computed by weighting a conv layer's feature maps by the gradient of the class score. Ask the network 'which parts of this picture made you say African elephant?' and paint the answer over the photo. Channel weights are the spatially averaged gradients of the class score with respect to the last conv layer's feature maps. The heatmap is the channel-weighted mean of the maps, clipped at zero and normalized (pp.325-328). Listing 10.25 colorizes it and blends it with the image. On the elephant photo, the ears of the calf light up strongly.

title: Latent space
text: The space in which a model embeds its inputs. In the book's words, a manifold where spatially close points represent semantically similar inputs and where classes become separable. An internal map the network draws of its inputs, organized by meaning rather than by pixels. For a layer k, the latent point of input x is z = f_k(…f_1(x)), a vector in R^D. The set of such points over the data distribution forms the layer's latent manifold. In the penultimate layer of an ImageNet classifier, all elephant photos form a region near each other and away from car photos.
snippet: The space in which a model embeds its inputs. In the book's words, a manifold where spatially close points represent semantically similar inputs and where classes become separable.

title: Latent manifold
text: A lower-dimensional curved surface inside a high-dimensional space on which a model's representations (and the data) lie. A crumpled sheet of paper is a 2D surface sitting in 3D space; flattening it reveals its simple shape. The book describes it as 'a manifold (or curve)' here and defines it on p.331 as a lower-dimensional curve inside a higher-dimensional space. Earth's surface is 2D even though Earth is 3D, which is why world maps exist (p.331).

Beyond the book: linear (PCA) or nonlinear neighbor-preserving (t-SNE, UMAP) methods are typical. The page only states the goal. 10,000 test images × 2048 features → 10,000 × 2 coordinates to scatter-plot, colored by class.

title: Manifolds, map projections, and the chapter 10 summary
text:
Why projecting a high-dimensional latent manifold to 2D is feasible (low intrinsic dimensionality) but always lossy (the world-map analogy), followed by the chapter summary on filters, filter visualizations, response maps, and Grad-CAM. Latent points may be 2048-dimensional, but the manifold they lie on has a much lower intrinsic dimension, so a 2D projection is possible, as Earth's 2D surface can be mapped onto a plane. Like every map projection, it will distort and destroy some information. The chapter's techniques together make ConvNets highly interpretable. The page finishes section 10.4, which began on p.330 with the problem of projecting latent points that have hundreds or thousands of dimensions onto a 2D surface.

**Why it is feasible.** The points might be, say, **2048-dimensional**, but the curve they trace has a much lower **intrinsic dimensionality**. That is what the word *manifold* means here: a lower-dimensional curve inside a higher-dimensional space. Planet Earth is 3D, but its surface is 2D, which is why it can be projected onto a plane, and that is what world maps do.

**Why it is never perfect.** World maps show both the feasibility and the cost of such projections. All projections distort reality. The authors' example is the **Mercator** projection, which in their words distorts distances, making areas near the equator look smaller than they are and stretching areas near the poles toward infinity. This happens even though Earth's surface really is 2D, while deep learning latent manifolds may have a much higher intrinsic dimension than that. Conclusion: *there's no projection that won't destroy at least some information.* The section stops here, without code or a worked example of a projection.

**Chapter summary.**

- ConvNets process images by applying learned filters. Early-layer filters detect edges and basic textures; later ones detect increasingly abstract concepts.
- You can visualize both the pattern a filter detects (gradient ascent, section 10.2) and a filter's response map across an image (intermediate activations, section 10.1).
- Grad-CAM shows which area(s) of an image were responsible for a classifier's decision (section 10.3).
- Together these techniques make ConvNets highly interpretable.

The next page (p.332) opens chapter 11, Image segmentation. Latent points can be 2048-dimensional while the manifold they lie on has a much lower intrinsic dimension. A manifold is a lower-dimensional curve inside a higher-dimensional space, like Earth's 2D surface in 3D. That low intrinsic dimension makes 2D projections feasible, as world maps show. Every projection distorts: Mercator stretches the poles toward infinity, and latent manifolds may be much higher-dimensional than 2D. No projection avoids destroying some information, so read latent-space plots with care. Chapter summary: filters go from edges and textures to abstract concepts; you can visualize filter patterns and response maps; Grad-CAM localizes decisions; together they make ConvNets highly interpretable.

title: Intrinsic dimensionality
text: The number of independent degrees of freedom of the manifold that data points lie on, as opposed to the number of coordinates (ambient dimension) used to write them down. A road through 3D terrain is still a 1D object: you can only move forward or back along it. A manifold of intrinsic dimension k embedded in R^D (k ≪ D) is locally homeomorphic to R^k. Earth's surface: ambient dimension 3, intrinsic dimension 2.
snippet: The number of independent degrees of freedom of the manifold that data points lie on, as opposed to the number of coordinates ambient dimension used to write them down.
section: 10.4 Visualizing the latent space of a ConvNet

title: Manifold (as defined here)
text: A lower-dimensional curve inside a higher-dimensional space. The surface of a balloon is 2D even though the balloon floats in 3D. p.168 gives the fuller definition: a subspace locally similar to Euclidean space. The manifold hypothesis says natural data lies on such low-dimensional manifolds. MNIST digits form a manifold within the space of 28 × 28 uint8 arrays (p.168).
snippet: A lower-dimensional curve inside a higher-dimensional space.
section: 10.4 Visualizing the latent space of a ConvNet

title: Projection distortion
text: The unavoidable loss or warping of geometric information (distances, areas, neighborhoods) when a manifold is mapped onto fewer dimensions. Peeling an orange and pressing the peel flat always tears or stretches it. Beyond the book: by Gauss's Theorema Egregium, a sphere cannot be mapped to the plane while preserving distances. Projection methods choose which properties to keep. Mercator makes polar regions such as Greenland look huge and stretches the poles toward infinity.
snippet: The unavoidable loss or warping of geometric information distances, areas, neighborhoods when a manifold is mapped onto fewer dimensions.

title: Hierarchy of ConvNet filters
text: Earlier layers learn filters for edges and basic textures; later layers learn increasingly abstract concepts. Letters, then words, then sentences. Each layer's filters operate on combinations of the previous layer's features and over growing receptive fields, so complexity increases with depth. Figure 10.6 (p.322): block2 filters show edges and colors, block4 filters show textures, block8 filters show more complex patterns.
snippet: Earlier layers learn filters for edges and basic textures; later layers learn increasingly abstract concepts.

title: Chapter 11 opener: Image segmentation
text:

title: Classification, segmentation, and detection
text:
Definitions and real-world examples of the three essential computer vision tasks, illustrated by figure 11.1 on a single photo of two cyclists. The three tasks differ in what they output. Classification assigns one or more labels to the whole image (single-label or multilabel). Segmentation partitions the image into areas, each usually a category, at pixel-level precision. Object detection draws labeled bounding boxes around objects of interest. The page lists the **three essential computer vision tasks** announced on p.332.

1. **Image classification**: assign one or more labels to an image. It is either *single-label* (categories mutually exclusive) or *multilabel* (tag every category the image belongs to). Example: a keyword search in the Google Photos app queries a very large multilabel classifier with **over 20,000 classes, trained on millions of images**.
2. **Image segmentation**: "segment" or "partition" the image into areas, each usually representing a category. Example: Zoom or Google Meet custom backgrounds use a segmentation model to separate you from what is behind you, **with pixel-level precision**.
3. **Object detection**: draw rectangles, called **bounding boxes**, around objects of interest and associate each with a class. Example: a self-driving car monitoring cars, pedestrians, and signs in its cameras' view.

**Figure 11.1** applies all of these to one photo of two people cycling in a park:

- *Single-label multi-class classification*: radio buttons Biking (chosen), Running, Swimming. Exactly one answer.
- *Multi-label classification*: checkboxes, with Bike, Person, and Tree ticked and Boat, Car, House not ticked. Any number of answers.
- *Image segmentation*: the two riders are filled in one color (labeled "person") and the bicycles in another ("bike"). Every pixel of those objects is assigned a class.
- *Object detection*: labeled rectangles for each person, each bike, and two street lamps.

Read together, the panels show increasing spatial detail. Classification says *what* is in the image, detection adds roughly *where* each object is, and segmentation gives the *exact shape* of each region. The next page (p.334) mentions more niche tasks (similarity scoring, keypoints, pose, depth...) and says almost every vision application reduces to one of these three. Image classification assigns one or more labels to a whole image, either single-label (exclusive) or multilabel (all that apply). Google Photos search is a multilabel classifier with over 20,000 classes trained on millions of images. Image segmentation partitions an image into areas, usually one category each, with pixel-level precision (for example, video-call backgrounds). Object detection draws labeled bounding boxes around objects of interest (for example, self-driving cars). Figure 11.1 shows the same photo under all four output formats, with spatial detail increasing from labels to boxes to masks.

title: Other vision tasks and the three types of segmentation
text:
Niche vision tasks beyond the main three, the plan for chapters 11-12, a definition of image segmentation as per-pixel classification, and the semantic, instance, and panoptic variants illustrated in figure 11.2. Almost all vision applications reduce to classification, segmentation, or detection. Segmentation assigns a class to every pixel. Semantic segmentation labels category only, instance segmentation separates individual objects, and panoptic segmentation assigns both a semantic and an instance label to every pixel, which makes it the most informative. The page first widens the view. Besides classification, segmentation, and detection, deep learning for vision includes more **niche tasks**: *image similarity scoring* (how visually similar two images are), *keypoint detection* (pinpointing attributes such as facial features), *pose estimation*, *3D mesh estimation*, *depth estimation*, and others. Still, the main three are "the foundation that every machine learning engineer should be familiar with," and almost all vision applications **boil down to one of these three**.

The plan: classification was covered in chapter 8. This chapter covers segmentation, which is "very useful and very versatile" and can be approached straightforwardly with what you already know. Chapter 12 covers object detection in detail.

**11.1.1 Types of image segmentation.** Segmentation with deep learning means using a model to **assign a class to each pixel**, dividing the image into zones such as background/foreground or road/car/sidewalk. Applications include image and video editing, autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging. There are three flavors:

- **Semantic segmentation**: each pixel is independently classified into a semantic category. Two cats are both just "cat".
- **Instance segmentation**: parses out individual object instances, separating "cat 1" from "cat 2".
- **Panoptic segmentation**: combines both, giving each pixel a semantic label ("cat") and an instance label ("cat 2"). It is the **most informative** of the three.

**Figure 11.2** shows a basket of cats. On the left (semantic), all cats are one "cat" region against "background". On the right (instance), each cat gets its own color and label, cat 1 to cat 4. The next page starts section 11.2, which trains a **semantic** segmentation model on the Oxford-IIIT Pets dataset. Niche vision tasks include similarity scoring, keypoint detection, pose estimation, 3D mesh estimation, and depth estimation. Classification, segmentation, and detection are the foundation; almost all vision applications boil down to one of them. Segmentation assigns a class to each pixel, splitting the image into zones. Semantic segmentation labels category only; two cats are both 'cat'. Instance segmentation separates individual objects: cat 1 vs cat 2. Panoptic segmentation gives each pixel both labels and is the most informative. Chapter 11 does segmentation (semantic first); chapter 12 does detection.

text:
Start of the from-scratch semantic segmentation example: the task (separate the main subject from its background), the Oxford-IIIT Pets dataset and its three-valued segmentation masks, downloading and extracting it, and building sorted lists of image and mask paths. A segmentation mask is the segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the same size as the input, with one channel, where each integer is the class of the corresponding pixel. Here the values are 1 (foreground), 2 (background), and 3 (contour). Inputs and masks share filenames, so sorting both path lists pairs them up. A transition sentence proposes training a **small segmentation model from scratch** to get familiar with segmentation.

**Section 11.2** focuses on **semantic segmentation**. It uses cats and dogs again (as in chapter 8), but this time the goal is to **tell apart the main subject and its background** pixel by pixel instead of classifying the whole picture.

**11.2.1 Downloading a segmentation dataset.** The dataset is **Oxford-IIIT Pets**: 7,390 pictures of various breeds of cats and dogs, each with a segmentation mask. The book defines a **segmentation mask** as the segmentation equivalent of a label: an image the **same size as the input**, with a **single color channel**, where each integer value is the class of the corresponding input pixel. Here the values are:

- `1`: foreground
- `2`: background
- `3`: contour

The first code block uses `wget` to download `images.tar.gz` and `annotations.tar.gz`, and `tar -xf` to extract them. The leading `!` runs shell commands from a notebook cell.

Images are JPGs in `images/` (for example, `images/Abyssinian_1.jpg`). Each mask is a PNG with the **same name** in `annotations/trimaps/` (for example, `annotations/trimaps/Abyssinian_1.png`).

Because both lists are sorted by the shared filename stem, element *i* of one corresponds to element *i* of the other.

1. **The input image.** A three-line snippet imports `matplotlib.pyplot` and three helpers from `keras.utils` (`load_img`, `img_to_array`, `array_to_img`), turns the axes off, and displays `load_img(input_img_paths[9])`. The result is figure 11.3: an Abyssinian cat lying on a carpet next to a blue bag.

2. **The target mask.** A small helper, `display_target`, takes a mask array, casts it to `uint8`, subtracts 1 and multiplies by 127. The callout explains why: the original labels are 1, 2 and 3; subtracting 1 makes them 0–2 and multiplying by 127 spreads them to 0, 127 and 254 so they can be told apart visually (black, gray, near-white). The function then shows channel 0 of the array (`normalized_array[:, :, 0]`). The mask itself is loaded with `load_img(target_paths[9], color_mode="grayscale")` and converted with `img_to_array`; the second callout explains that `grayscale` makes Keras treat the PNG as having a **single color channel**, matching the definition of a mask given on p.335 (one integer class per pixel). The resulting picture is figure 11.4, which appears on the next page (p.337).

The take-home is methodological: a mask is a label image whose raw values are class ids, not intensities, so you must remap them before eyeballing them, and you should always verify that inputs and targets correspond before training. On p.337 the authors move on to loading all images and masks into NumPy arrays. Always visually inspect a sample image and its label before training. Load masks with color_mode="grayscale" so they have one channel. Mask values are class ids (1, 2, 3); remap them with (x - 1) * 127 to see them. Displayed: foreground 0, background 127, contour 254. Display uses channel 0 because imshow expects a 2-D array for single-channel data.
