title: Loading arrays, splitting, and the encoder-decoder model
text:
Filling the input/target arrays, holding out 1,000 validation samples, and defining a segmentation ConvNet of strided Conv2D layers followed by Conv2DTranspose layers All images go into a float32 array of shape (num_imgs, 200, 200, 3) and all masks into a uint8 array of shape (num_imgs, 200, 200, 1); the last 1,000 become validation data. The model rescales pixels to [0, 1], compresses them with six Conv2D layers (three with stride 2) and expands them back with six Conv2DTranspose layers (three with stride 2), all with padding="same". The page finishes the data preparation and starts the model.

**Loading.** The first block allocates `input_imgs = np.zeros((num_imgs,) + img_size + (3,), dtype="float32")` and `targets = np.zeros((num_imgs,) + img_size + (1,), dtype="uint8")`, i.e. shapes `(num_imgs, 200, 200, 3)` and `(num_imgs, 200, 200, 1)`, then loops over all indices calling the two helpers from p.337. The callout stresses that images and masks are stored in the same order, that inputs have three RGB channels and that targets have one channel holding integer labels.

**Splitting.** "As always", the arrays are split: `num_val_samples = 1000` are reserved for validation; `[:-num_val_samples]` takes everything except the last 1,000 for training and `[-num_val_samples:]` takes the last 1,000. Because the paths were shuffled on p.337, this tail is a random sample.

**Model (section 11.2.2).** `get_model(img_size, num_classes)` builds a Functional model:

- `keras.Input(shape=img_size + (3,))` and `Rescaling(1.0 / 255)`. The callout says not to forget to rescale input images to the [0–1] range;
- an **encoder** of six `Conv2D` layers with 64, 64, 128, 128, 256 and 256 filters, 3 × 3 kernels and ReLU, where every other layer has `strides=2`: 200 → 100 → 50 → 25;
- a **decoder** of six `Conv2DTranspose` layers with 256, 256, 128, 128, 64 and 64 filters, where every other layer has `strides=2`: 25 → 50 → 100 → 200.

A callout explains that `padding="same"` is used everywhere *to avoid the influence of border padding on feature map size*. Without it, each 3 × 3 convolution would trim two pixels and the decoder would not land exactly on 200 × 200. The final softmax layer and `keras.Model(...)` call are on p.339, where the authors also explain why strides replace max pooling and what `Conv2DTranspose` does. Inputs: float32 (N, 200, 200, 3); targets: uint8 (N, 200, 200, 1) with labels 0–2. The last 1,000 shuffled samples form the validation set. Rescaling(1/255) inside the model normalizes pixels. Encoder: Conv2D with stride 2 every other layer, 200 → 25; decoder: Conv2DTranspose with stride 2 every other layer, 25 → 200. padding="same" everywhere makes feature-map sizes depend only on strides.

title: Encoder-decoder segmentation ConvNet
text: A ConvNet that first downsamples an image into compact feature maps and then upsamples them back to the input resolution to produce per-pixel outputs. An hourglass: squeeze the image into a small, information-rich summary, then paint the answer back at full size. Encoder: Conv2D 64/64/128/128/256/256 with strides 2 on layers 1, 3, 5 → (25, 25, 256). Decoder: Conv2DTranspose 256/256/128/128/64/64 with strides 2 on layers 2, 4, 6 → (200, 200, 64), then a softmax Conv2D (p.339). A 200 × 200 cat photo becomes a 25 × 25 × 256 code, then a 200 × 200 × 3 map of class probabilities.
snippet: A ConvNet that first downsamples an image into compact feature maps and then upsamples them back to the input resolution to produce per-pixel outputs.

title: get_model: rescaling, Conv2D encoder, Conv2DTranspose decoder (continues on p.339)
text:
import keras
from keras.layers import Rescaling, Conv2D, Conv2DTranspose

def get_model(img_size, num_classes):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=img_size + (3,))
    x = Rescaling(1.0 / 255)(inputs)

    x = Conv2D(64, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(128, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(128, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2D(256, 3, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu")(x)
    x = Conv2D(256, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)

    x = Conv2DTranspose(256, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(256, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(128, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(128, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, activation="relu", padding="same")(x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, strides=2, activation="relu", padding="same")(x) Defines the first part of the segmentation model: input, rescaling, a six-layer strided Conv2D encoder down to (25, 25, 256), and a six-layer Conv2DTranspose decoder back up to (200, 200, 64). The output softmax layer, the return statement and the call get_model(img_size=img_size, num_classes=3) are on p.339. Downsample ×8 with learned strided convolutions, then upsample ×8 with learned transposed convolutions.

title: Strides instead of pooling; Conv2DTranspose upsampling
text:
Why the encoder downsamples with strided convolutions rather than max pooling, and how Conv2DTranspose layers upsample the (25, 25, 256) bottleneck back to (200, 200, 3) Segmentation needs location information, which 2 × 2 max pooling throws away, so the encoder downsamples with strides. A Conv2DTranspose layer is a convolution that learns to upsample and inverts the shape change of a matching strided Conv2D. The model ends with a per-pixel 3-way softmax. The listing ends with `outputs = Conv2D(num_classes, 3, activation="softmax", padding="same")(x)` and `return keras.Model(inputs, outputs)`, followed by `model = get_model(img_size=img_size, num_classes=3)`. The callout: *we end the model with a per-pixel three-way softmax to classify each output pixel into one of our three categories*.

The authors then explain the architecture.

- **First half = encoder.** It resembles a classification ConvNet: `Conv2D` layers with gradually increasing filter counts. Downsampling three times by a factor of two gives activations of shape **(25, 25, 256)**. Each spatial location in these maps carries information about a large chunk of the original image, which the authors describe as *a kind of compression*.
- **Strides, not max pooling.** In chapter 8, downsampling was done with `MaxPooling2D`. Here, every other convolution has a stride instead (see section 8.1.1). The reason is that segmentation must output per-pixel masks, so the *spatial location* of information matters. 2 × 2 max pooling returns one scalar per window *with zero knowledge of which of the four locations it came from*. It works well for classification but hurts segmentation, whereas strided convolutions downsample while *retaining location information*. The authors note that the book uses strides instead of pooling in any model that cares about feature location, such as the generative models of chapter 17.
- **Second half = decoder of `Conv2DTranspose` layers.** The output must be `(200, 200, num_classes)` = `(200, 200, 3)`, so the network needs *a kind of inverse* of the downsampling, something that **upsamples**. `Conv2DTranspose` is *a kind of convolution layer that learns to upsample*. Example: `(100, 100, 64)` → `Conv2D(128, 3, strides=2, padding="same")` → `(50, 50, 128)` → `Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, strides=2, padding="same")` → `(100, 100, 64)`, the original shape again. The sentence explaining how the (25, 25, 256) maps are brought back to full size continues on p.340. The model ends in Conv2D(3, softmax): a 3-way classifier at every pixel. The encoder compresses 200 × 200 × 3 images into 25 × 25 × 256 feature maps. Max pooling discards where in a window a feature was; strided convolutions keep that information, so segmentation uses strides. Conv2DTranspose is a learnable upsampling layer that inverts a strided Conv2D's shape change. Use strides instead of pooling whenever feature location matters (segmentation, generative models).

title: Transposed convolution (Conv2DTranspose)
text: A convolution-like layer that learns to upsample feature maps, inverting the spatial shape change of a strided convolution. Instead of sliding a window to summarize many inputs into one output, each input pixel 'stamps' a learned 3 × 3 pattern onto a larger output canvas. With strides=2 and padding="same", output spatial size = 2 × input. Weights: kernel of shape (3, 3, out_channels, in_channels) plus bias. (50, 50, 128) → Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, strides=2, padding="same") → (100, 100, 64).

title: Strided convolution
text: A convolution whose windows are spaced by a stride > 1, downsampling the feature map. A learned, position-aware way to shrink an image. Output = Σ position-specific weights × inputs; stride 2 with padding "same" halves the size. Conv2D(128, 3, strides=2, padding="same"): (100, 100, 64) → (50, 50, 128).

If you run this output through the layer Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, strides=2, padding="same"), you get back an output of shape (100, 100, 64), the same as the original. \begin{aligned} (100,100,64) &\xrightarrow{\text{Conv2D}(128,\,3,\,s=2)} (50,50,128) \\ (50,50,128) &\xrightarrow{\text{Conv2DTranspose}(64,\,3,\,s=2)} (100,100,64) \end{aligned} Shows that Conv2DTranspose undoes the shape change of a strided Conv2D. title: Intersection over Union; compiling and fitting
text:
The IoU metric for segmentation, its Keras implementation for the foreground class, and the compile/fit setup with a best-only checkpoint Segmentation quality is measured by IoU = area of overlap / area of union between predicted and true masks. Keras's IoU metric is configured for 3 classes, the foreground class 0, sparse integer targets and dense softmax predictions. The model is compiled with Adam and sparse categorical cross-entropy and trained for 50 epochs, saving the best model. The page first completes the sentence from p.339: after compressing inputs to `(25, 25, 256)`, the model *simply applies the corresponding sequence of `Conv2DTranspose` layers followed by a final `Conv2D` layer* to produce outputs of shape `(200, 200, 3)`.

**Intersection over Union (IoU).** To evaluate the model, the authors introduce IoU, a measure of the match between ground-truth and predicted masks. It can be computed separately for each class or averaged over several classes. The recipe has three steps:

1. compute the **intersection**, the area where prediction and ground truth overlap;
2. compute the **union**, the total area covered by both masks, which is *the target object and any extra bits your model might have included by mistake*;
3. divide intersection by union. The result lies between 0 (complete miss) and 1 (perfect match).

**Keras metric.** Rather than coding it by hand, they use `keras.metrics.IoU(num_classes=3, target_class_ids=(0,), name="foreground_iou", sparse_y_true=True, sparse_y_pred=False)`. The callouts explain that `num_classes` is the total number of classes, `target_class_ids=(0,)` selects the class to compute IoU for (0 = foreground), and the targets are sparse integer class IDs *but our model's predictions are a dense softmax!*

**Training.** The model is compiled with `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` (integer masks vs per-pixel softmax) and `metrics=[foreground_iou]`. A `ModelCheckpoint("oxford_segmentation.keras", save_best_only=True)` callback keeps the best model. `model.fit(train_input_imgs, train_targets, epochs=50, callbacks=callbacks, ...)` starts training, and its remaining arguments (`batch_size=64` and the validation data) are on p.341. IoU = intersection / union of predicted and true masks, from 0 (miss) to 1 (perfect). It can be computed per class or averaged; here only foreground (class 0) is tracked. keras.metrics.IoU needs num_classes, target_class_ids and the sparse flags matching targets (integers) and predictions (softmax). Integer masks + per-pixel softmax → sparse_categorical_crossentropy. ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True) keeps the best validation-loss model.

Finishing training (batch size 64, validation data), plotting training vs validation loss (figure 11.5), and reloading the best checkpoint to predict on a validation image Training loss keeps falling for all 50 epochs while validation loss bottoms out and then climbs, a clear sign of overfitting from about the middle of training. The page opens with the last lines of `model.fit(...)`: `batch_size=64` and `validation_data=(val_input_imgs, val_targets)`. After that the training loss keeps decreasing steadily, to under 0.1 by epoch 50 (with a small bump near epoch 46). The validation loss flattens around 0.36–0.40 for epochs 10–20 and then rises, noisily, to about 0.85 by epoch 50, with dips near epochs 39 and 46.

title: Predicting a mask with the from-scratch model; introducing SAM
text:
Running inference with the trained Oxford-IIIT Pets segmentation model, visualizing its per-pixel class prediction, and the transition to the pretrained Segment Anything Model (SAM). A segmentation model outputs a per-pixel probability distribution over classes; taking the argmax over the last axis turns it into a displayable mask. Having trained such a model from scratch, the chapter now turns to a much stronger option: the large pretrained Segment Anything Model. The page opens with the end of the from-scratch segmentation example. The best checkpoint (`oxford_segmentation.keras`, reloaded on p.341) is run on a single validation image: `np.expand_dims(test_image, 0)` adds a batch axis so the model receives a batch of one, `model.predict` returns an array of shape `(1, 200, 200, 3)`, and `[0]` pulls the single prediction back out. A small utility, `display_mask`, converts the per-pixel softmax probabilities into a class map with `np.argmax(pred, axis=-1)`, scales the class indices 0/1/2 by 127 (to 0/127/254, the same trick used when visualizing the ground-truth masks on p.336), and shows it with `plt.imshow`.

**Figure 11.6** shows the result: on the left, a white dog in front of a dark background; on the right, the predicted mask, with the dog (foreground, class 0) in dark purple, the background (class 1) in teal and the contour (class 2) as a yellow outline. The authors note a few small artifacts — for example, a spurious purple blob in the background on the right — which they attribute to geometric shapes in the foreground and background, but conclude that the model works nicely.

Section **11.3** then begins. Just as a pretrained ConvNet boosted accuracy on a small image-classification dataset in chapter 8, a pretrained model can help with segmentation. The authors introduce the **Segment Anything Model (SAM)**, developed by Meta AI and released in April 2023, trained on 11 million images and their masks covering over 1 billion object instances (footnote: Kirillov et al., "Segment Anything," ICCV 2023, arXiv:2304.02643). The paragraph continues on p.343, which explains that this scale of data gives SAM built-in knowledge of virtually any object and that it is not restricted to a fixed set of classes. To predict on one image, add a batch axis with `np.expand_dims(x, 0)` and take `[0]` of the result. The model outputs (200, 200, 3) per-pixel probabilities; `np.argmax(pred, axis=-1)` turns them into a (200, 200) class map. In Figure 11.6, purple = pet, teal = background, yellow = contour; the small stray blobs are the artifacts the authors mention. The from-scratch model works nicely, but pretrained models help segmentation just as they help classification (chapter 8). SAM (Meta AI, April 2023) was trained on 11 million images and over 1 billion object masks.

title: Segmentation mask
text: An image the same height and width as the input, where each pixel holds the class index of the corresponding input pixel (p.335). A paint-by-numbers version of the photo: every pixel is tagged with a label. For the pets model the target mask has shape (200, 200) with values in {0, 1, 2} after the -1 shift (p.337); the model predicts (200, 200, 3) probabilities, reduced to a mask by argmax. title: Loading SAM with KerasHub and the SA-1B data engine
text:
What makes SAM different (class-agnostic, promptable, no fine-tuning), loading it as a KerasHub ImageSegmenter task (`sam_huge_sa1b`, 641M parameters), and how the SA-1B dataset was built together with the model. SAM segments any object you indicate with a prompt, without a fixed class list or fine-tuning. Its capability comes mainly from the scale of SA-1B, a dataset built in a feedback loop with the model itself. The page finishes the SAM introduction from p.342: training on 11 million images and over 1 billion masks gives the model **built-in knowledge of virtually any object in natural images**. Its main innovation is that it is **not limited to a predefined set of object classes**: you segment a new object just by giving an example of what you are looking for (a prompt), and you **don't need to fine-tune** the model.

**11.3.1 Downloading the Segment Anything Model.** As with the `ImageClassifier` task from the previous chapter (p.324), KerasHub provides a task, `ImageSegmenter`, that wraps a pretrained segmentation model into a high-level model with standard inputs and outputs. The preset is `sam_huge_sa1b`: `sam` is the model, `huge` refers to its parameter count, and `sa1b` is the SA-1B dataset released with it (1 billion annotated masks). Two lines load it: `import keras_hub` and `ImageSegmenter.from_preset("sam_huge_sa1b")`. `model.count_params()` returns **641,090,864**. At 641 million parameters this is the largest model used so far in the book; the trend toward larger models and more data is discussed in chapter 16.

**11.3.2 How Segment Anything works.** Much of SAM's capability comes from the scale of its pretraining data. Meta built SA-1B **together with the model**: a partially trained SAM helped label data, which then trained a better model, in a kind of feedback loop. The goal was *fully segmented* images where every object gets its own mask (Figure 11.7, on p.344). Images have about 100 masks on average, some over 500. The data was collected through increasingly automated stages, starting with human experts segmenting a small set by hand; this continues on p.344. SAM's main innovation: no predefined class set; you indicate the object with a prompt and need no fine-tuning. `keras_hub.models.ImageSegmenter.from_preset("sam_huge_sa1b")` loads it; the name encodes model, size and dataset. SAM has 641,090,864 parameters, the largest model in the book so far (more on scaling in chapter 16). SAM's power comes largely from SA-1B, built in a feedback loop with the model itself. SA-1B images are fully segmented: about 100 masks per image on average, some over 500.

title: SA-1B example, (image, prompt, mask) training, and SAM's components
text:
How SAM is trained and structured: the semiautomated data stage, a densely segmented SA-1B example image, training on (image, prompt, mask) triples with point or box prompts, and the image encoder / prompt encoder / mask decoder design. SAM learns a mapping from (image, prompt) to the mask of the indicated object, supervised by ground-truth masks. Architecturally, an image encoder produces a compact image embedding, a prompt encoder embeds the prompt, and a mask decoder combines them into several candidate masks. The page finishes the SA-1B story from p.343: a small manually segmented set trained an **initial model**, which then drove a **semiautomated stage** where images were first segmented by SAM and then improved by human correction and further annotation. **Figure 11.7** shows an SA-1B example: a street scene with a tram, buildings, trees, a sign board and people, in which nearly every object and part (windows, wheels, panels, foliage, sky) is covered by its own colored mask, which illustrates what a "fully segmented" image means.

SAM is trained on **(image, prompt, mask) triples**. The image and the prompt are the inputs; the prompt can be:

- a **point inside** the object to mask, or
- a **box around** the object to mask.

The model must predict an accurate mask for the indicated object, which is compared with the ground-truth `mask` label, just as targets were compared with predictions in the from-scratch model.

The model has three components. An **image encoder**, which the authors compare to the Xception model of earlier chapters, maps the input image to a much smaller **image embedding**. A **prompt encoder** maps a prompt (point or box) to an embedded vector. A **mask decoder** takes both embeddings and outputs **a few possible predicted masks**. The internals of the prompt encoder and mask decoder are left for later, since they use techniques covered in later chapters. The predicted masks are compared with the ground truth as before (Figure 11.8, on p.345, where each candidate mask comes with a score).

Note (not in the book): in the original SAM paper the image encoder is a Vision Transformer rather than a ConvNet like Xception; the comparison is about its role. SA-1B grew through a semiautomated stage: SAM segments first, humans correct and add annotations. Figure 11.7 shows a fully segmented SA-1B image with a separate mask for almost every object and part. Training examples are (image, prompt, mask) triples; prompts are a point inside or a box around the object. SAM = image encoder (compact image embedding) + prompt encoder (prompt embedding) + mask decoder (a few candidate masks). Predicted masks are compared with the ground truth, as in ordinary supervised segmentation.
snippet: The page finishes the SA-1B story from p.343: a small manually segmented set trained an initial model, which then drove a semiautomated stage where images were first segmented by…

title: Promptable segmentation

Training data: (image, prompt, mask) triples; inputs are image and prompt, label is the mask. A point on the tram in Figure 11.7 should return the tram's mask.

Outputs several candidate masks, each with a score (Figure 11.8, p.345). A point on a fruit could give the fruit, a group of fruits, or the whole bowl as candidates.

title: SAM architecture overview, sampling training prompts, loading a test image
text:
Figure 11.8's high-level view of SAM, how (image, prompt, mask) training triples are generated from SA-1B, and loading the fruit-bowl test image with Keras utilities. All SAM components are trained jointly on triples sampled from SA-1B: pick a random mask, then make a point prompt (a random pixel inside it) or a box prompt (its bounding box). In practice, you start by loading an image into a NumPy array. **Figure 11.8** gives SAM's high-level architecture. An input image (a stylized landscape with a sun, mountains and water) goes into an **image encoder**; prompts, drawn as a red box, a purple star (a point) and a small blue box, go into a **prompt encoder**. Both feed a larger **mask decoder**, which outputs **three candidate masks, each with a score**; in the drawing, each candidate highlights a different region (for example the sun or the mountains), which illustrates that one prompt can have several plausible answers.

All components are **trained simultaneously** on batches of new (image, prompt, mask) triples built from SA-1B. The recipe is simple:

1. For an input image, choose a **random mask**.
2. Randomly choose a **box** or a **point** prompt.
3. Point prompt: a **random pixel inside** the mask. Box prompt: a **box around all points** of the mask (its bounding box).

Repeating this indefinitely samples many triples from each image, so SA-1B's ~100 masks per image (p.343) yield a huge supply of training examples.

**11.3.3 Preparing a test image.** To make this concrete, the authors load a picture of a bowl of fruits (Figure 11.9, p.346). `keras.utils.get_file` downloads `fruits.jpg` and returns the local path; `keras.utils.load_img` opens it as a PIL image; `keras.utils.img_to_array` turns it into a NumPy array (float32, shape height × width × 3); and `plt.imshow(image_array.astype("uint8"))` displays it with axes turned off. The next page resizes it to SAM's expected 1024 × 1024 input without distorting the aspect ratio. Figure 11.8: image → image encoder, prompt → prompt encoder, both → mask decoder → three masks, each with a score. All SAM components are trained jointly on (image, prompt, mask) triples sampled from SA-1B. Point prompt = random pixel inside the mask; box prompt = box around all mask pixels. Sampling can be repeated indefinitely, giving many triples per image. The test image is loaded with `get_file` → `load_img` → `img_to_array`, and cast to uint8 for display.
snippet: Figure 11.8 gives SAM's high-level architecture. An input image a stylized landscape with a sun, mountains and water goes into an image encoder; prompts, drawn as a red box, a…

title: Sampling prompts from masks
text: Generating training prompts from ground-truth masks: a random pixel inside the mask (point) or the box around the mask (box). Pretend to be a user who clicks somewhere on the object or draws a box around it. For a mask $M$: point $= (x, y)$ drawn uniformly from $\{(x, y): M_{yx}=1\}$; box $= (\min x, \min y, \max x, \max y)$ over the same set. For a mask of an apple, any pixel on the apple is a valid point prompt; its bounding rectangle is the box prompt.
snippet: Generating training prompts from ground-truth masks: a random pixel inside the mask point or the box around the mask box.

title: Mask decoder with scored candidates
text: The component that combines image and prompt embeddings and outputs a few candidate masks, each with a score (Figure 11.8). Several guesses, each with a confidence. Figure 11.8 shows three outputs labelled '…, score'. For the fruit image, candidates might be one fruit, a cluster of fruits, or the whole bowl.
snippet: The component that combines image and prompt embeddings and outputs a few candidate masks, each with a score Figure 11.8.

title: Joint (end-to-end) training
text: Training all components of a model together from a single objective. The encoders learn whatever features help the decoder predict good masks. Gradients from the mask loss flow back through the decoder into both encoders. Image encoder, prompt encoder and mask decoder are updated on each batch of triples.
snippet: Training all components of a model together from a single objective.

title: Point and box prompts derived from a mask
text: To create a point prompt, choose a random pixel inside the mask label. To create a box prompt, draw a box around all points inside the mask label. \begin{aligned} S &= \{(x,y) : M_{y,x} = 1\} \\ \text{point} &\sim \operatorname{Uniform}(S) \\ \text{box} &= \big(\min_{S} x,\ \min_{S} y,\ \max_{S} x,\ \max_{S} y\big) \end{aligned} Formalizes the prompt-generation recipe described in words on the page. A point is any location on the object; a box is the tightest rectangle containing it. M The chosen binary ground-truth mask (1 inside the object). S The set of pixel coordinates inside the mask. (x, y) Column and row coordinates of a pixel.
snippet: To create a point prompt, choose a random pixel inside the mask label. To create a box prompt, draw a box around all points inside the mask label. — Formalizes the…

title: Resizing the test image for SAM and planning display utilities
text:
Preparing the fruit test image for SAM's fixed 1024 × 1024 input by resizing the longest side to 1,024 and padding the rest (`ops.image.resize` with `pad_to_aspect_ratio=True`), and listing the plotting helpers needed later. Resizing straight to a square would distort a non-square image; instead, scale it so the longest side is 1,024 pixels and fill the remaining area with a constant (0), which keeps the aspect ratio. **Figure 11.9** shows the test image: two bananas lying on a white marble surface beside a wooden bowl holding a yellow mango and three red-and-yellow peaches (the point prompt on p.348 is described as "landing on a peach", and p.351 boxes "the mango"). The image is wider than it is tall.

SAM expects **1024 × 1024** inputs. Forcing an arbitrary image to that size would **distort its aspect ratio**, and this image isn't square. The better approach is to **resize so the longest side becomes 1,024 pixels**, then **pad** the remaining pixels with a filler value such as 0. Keras does both in one call with the `pad_to_aspect_ratio` argument of `keras.ops.image.resize()`:

```python
image_size = (1024, 1024)
def resize_and_pad(x):
    return ops.image.resize(x, image_size, pad_to_aspect_ratio=True)
image = resize_and_pad(image_array)
```

The result `image` is a 1024 × 1024 × 3 tensor in which the fruit photo keeps its proportions and the leftover rows are filled with black (0). Beyond the book: in Keras the padding is split evenly between the two sides (top and bottom for a landscape image).

The page then lists **four display utilities** needed for working with the model: show images, show segmentation masks overlaid on an image, highlight specific points, and show boxes overlaid on an image. Each takes a Matplotlib axis object `ax`, so all of them can draw on the **same figure**; for example, image, mask and prompt point stacked together. The code for the utilities is at the top of p.347. SAM expects 1024 × 1024 inputs. Don't stretch non-square images: resize so the longest side is 1,024 and pad the rest with 0. `ops.image.resize(x, (1024, 1024), pad_to_aspect_ratio=True)` does this in one call. Prompt coordinates live in the resized, padded image space. Four helpers (image, mask, points, box) all draw on a shared Matplotlib axis `ax` so they can be layered.

title: Display utilities and the first point prompt
text:
The four Matplotlib helpers (`show_image`, `show_mask`, `show_points`, `show_box`), the two prompt types (point and box), labeled points (1 = foreground, 0 = background), and defining and plotting a single foreground point at (580, 450). To use SAM you must prompt it with points or boxes. A point prompt is a pair of coordinates plus a label: 1 marks a pixel of the object you want, 0 a pixel to exclude, and several labeled points can resolve ambiguity. The page opens with the code for the four display utilities announced on p.346, each taking a Matplotlib `ax`:

- `show_image` converts the backend tensor to NumPy, casts to `uint8` and draws it.
- `show_mask` builds an **RGBA overlay**: the color `[30/255, 144/255, 255/255, 0.6]` (a blue at 60% opacity) is multiplied by the mask (reshaped to `(h, w, 1)`), so mask pixels become translucent blue and pixels outside the mask become fully transparent (all zeros, including alpha).
- `show_points` draws each point as a large green star with a white edge.
- `show_box` flattens a box `[x0, y0, x1, y1]`, computes width and height, and adds an unfilled red rectangle.

**11.3.4 Prompting the model with a target point.** SAM needs a prompt, either:

- a **point prompt**: select a point and let the model segment the object the point belongs to; or
- a **box prompt**: draw an approximate box around an object (it doesn't need to be precise) and let the model segment the object in it.

Starting with points: each point carries a **label**, **1 for foreground** (the object you want) and **0 for background** (everything around it). In ambiguous cases you can pass **several labeled points** to refine what should be included (1s) and excluded (0s).

The test uses a single foreground point: `input_point = np.array([[580, 450]])` (x = 580, y = 450 in the 1024 × 1024 image) and `input_label = np.array([1])`. The image and the point are plotted together on the current axes (`plt.gca()`), producing Figure 11.10 on p.348, where the point lands on a peach. Four helpers draw on a shared `ax`: image, RGBA mask overlay, star-shaped points, red boxes. `show_mask` broadcasts (h, w, 1) × (1, 1, 4) into a 60%-opaque blue overlay with transparent background. SAM needs a prompt: a point (segment the object it belongs to) or an approximate box. Point labels: 1 = foreground (include), 0 = background (exclude); several points resolve ambiguity. The test prompt is `np.array([[580, 450]])` with label `[1]`, given as (x, y) in the 1024 × 1024 image.

Inside the mask: 60%-opaque blue; outside: (0, 0, 0, 0), fully transparent. M_{ij} Mask value at pixel (i, j), 1 inside the object and 0 outside. \mathbf{c} RGBA color: R ≈ 0.118, G ≈ 0.565, B = 1.0 (a blue), alpha = 0.6. O_{ij} RGBA overlay value at pixel (i, j).

title: Display utilities for images, masks, points and boxes
text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from keras import ops
def show_image(image, ax):
    ax.imshow(ops.convert_to_numpy(image).astype("uint8"))
def show_mask(mask, ax):
    color = np.array([30 / 255, 144 / 255, 255 / 255, 0.6])
    h, w, _ = mask.shape
    mask_image = mask.reshape(h, w, 1) * color.reshape(1, 1, -1)
    ax.imshow(mask_image)
def show_points(points, ax):
    x, y = points[:, 0], points[:, 1]
    ax.scatter(x, y, c="green", marker="*", s=375, ec="white", lw=1.25)
def show_box(box, ax):
    box = box.reshape(-1)
    x0, y0 = box[0], box[1]
    w, h = box[2] - box[0], box[3] - box[1]
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0, y0), w, h, ec="red", fc="none", lw=2)) Defines the four plotting helpers announced on p.346; each draws onto a given Matplotlib Axes `ax` so they can be layered in one figure. Each helper converts its data into a Matplotlib primitive: imshow (image or RGBA overlay), scatter (points), Rectangle patch (box).
snippet: Defines the four plotting helpers announced on p.346; each draws onto a given Matplotlib Axes ax so they can be layered in one figure.

title: Prompting SAM with a point and reading its mask outputs
text:
Running Segment Anything (SAM) with a single foreground point prompt, inspecting the shape of the returned masks, and converting one mask into a full-resolution boolean array for display. A SAM call takes a batch of images plus a batch of labeled points and returns four 256 × 256 candidate masks (with predicted IoU scores); a small helper picks one mask, upsamples it to the 1024 × 1024 padded image frame and thresholds it at 0 to get a boolean mask. The page opens with **Figure 11.10**, the 1024 × 1024 padded test image (black bars top and bottom from `resize_and_pad`, p.346) with a green star marking the prompt point `(580, 450)` defined on p.347. The point lands on a peach in the fruit bowl.

The authors then call the pretrained model with `model.predict(...)`, passing a dictionary with three entries: `"images"`, `"points"` and `"labels"`. Each array is wrapped with `ops.expand_dims(..., axis=0)` so that it carries a leading **batch axis** of size 1: SAM, like every Keras model, processes batches, even when the batch holds a single image and a single prompt.

The returned value `outputs` is a dictionary. Its `"masks"` entry holds **four 256 × 256 candidate masks** for the object indicated by the prompt; the book says they are ranked by decreasing match quality, and that the model's own quality estimate for each mask is in the `"iou_pred"` field. The shape check `outputs["masks"].shape` prints `(1, 4, 256, 256)`: batch of 1, 4 candidates, 256 × 256 pixels each.

Finally, the page defines a helper `get_mask(sam_outputs, index=0)` that

1. picks the first (only) batch element and the requested candidate,
2. adds a trailing channel axis so the mask looks like an image `(256, 256, 1)`,
3. resizes it with `resize_and_pad` to the same `1024 × 1024` frame as the image, and
4. converts it to NumPy and thresholds it with `> 0.0`, producing a boolean mask.

The page ends by calling `mask = get_mask(outputs, index=0)`; the resulting overlay (Figure 11.11, "Segmented peach") is shown on the next page (p.349). SAM point prompts are passed as a dict with images, points and labels, each with a leading batch axis. The output "masks" has shape (1, 4, 256, 256): four low-resolution candidate masks per prompt. "iou_pred" holds the model's predicted IoU for each candidate, a quality estimate you can use to choose among them. get_mask selects a candidate, adds a channel axis, resizes it to the padded 1024 × 1024 frame and thresholds at 0. Masks must be mapped into the same coordinate frame as the image (same resize_and_pad) to overlay correctly.

title: Segment Anything Model (SAM)
text: A pretrained promptable segmentation model from Meta AI: given an image and a prompt (point or box), it returns masks for the indicated object. Instead of being trained for a fixed list of classes, SAM answers the question 'what object is at this spot?' for any image. Image encoder produces an image embedding once; a lightweight prompt encoder embeds points/boxes; a mask decoder combines both to output several mask logits plus predicted IoU scores (p.344-345). Point (580, 450) with label 1 → a mask covering the peach (Figure 11.11).
snippet: A pretrained promptable segmentation model from Meta AI: given an image and a prompt point or box, it returns masks for the indicated object.

title: Point prompt
text: A set of (x, y) pixel coordinates with labels (1 = foreground, 0 = background) that indicates which object SAM should segment. Like clicking on an object in an image editor's 'magic select' tool. Passed as `points` with shape (batch, num_points, 2) and `labels` with shape (batch, num_points). Here (1, 1, 2) and (1, 1). `input_point = [[580, 450]]`, `input_label = [1]` (p.347), batched with `expand_dims(axis=0)` on this page.
snippet: A set of x, y pixel coordinates with labels 1 = foreground, 0 = background that indicates which object SAM should segment.

title: Intersection over Union (IoU)
text: Overlap between two masks divided by the area covered by either; ranges from 0 to 1. How much of 'what you drew' and 'what was there' coincide, relative to everything either of them covers. SAM's `iou_pred` is a learned regression of this quantity between each candidate mask and the true mask; at inference there is no ground truth, so it is a self-assessment. Predicted mask of 900 px, true mask of 1000 px, overlap 850 px → IoU = 850 / (900+1000-850) = 850/1050 ≈ 0.81.
snippet: Overlap between two masks divided by the area covered by either; ranges from 0 to 1.

title: Thresholding mask logits
text: Turning real-valued per-pixel scores into a boolean mask by comparing them to a threshold, here 0.0. Positive score = 'this pixel belongs to the object', negative = 'it does not'. If the values are logits z, then sigmoid(z) > 0.5 is equivalent to z > 0, so `> 0.0` is the natural decision boundary. Pixel values [-3.1, 0.4, 2.7] → [False, True, True].
snippet: Turning real-valued per-pixel scores into a boolean mask by comparing them to a threshold, here 0.0.

title: Batch axis
text: The leading dimension of a model input that indexes independent samples. Models are built to process stacks of examples, so a single example must be wrapped in a stack of one. `ops.expand_dims(image, axis=0)` turns (1024, 1024, 3) into (1, 1024, 1024, 3); the output masks keep it as the first axis of (1, 4, 256, 256), which is why `get_mask` indexes `[0]`. points (1, 2) → (1, 1, 2); labels (1,) → (1, 1).
snippet: The leading dimension of a model input that indexes independent samples.

title: Intersection over Union (what iou_pred estimates)
text: The quality scores of the masks are available under the "iou_pred" field (IoU itself defined in words on p.340: intersection area divided by union area) \operatorname{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|} = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B| - |A \cap B|} Measures how well a mask matches the target object; SAM's iou_pred head predicts this number for each of its four candidates. 1 means a perfect match, 0 a complete miss (p.340). A Set of pixels in the predicted mask B Set of pixels in the ground-truth mask of the intended object |\cdot| Number of pixels in a set
snippet: The quality scores of the masks are available under the "ioupred" field IoU itself defined in words on p.340: intersection area divided by union area — Measures how well a mask…

title: Why the threshold is 0.0
text: return ops.convert_to_numpy(mask) > 0.0 \hat m_{ij} = \mathbb{1}\left[z_{ij} > 0\right] \iff \sigma(z_{ij}) > 0.5, \quad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} Converts continuous logits into a binary mask. A pixel is in the mask when the model's implied probability of membership exceeds 50%. z_{ij} Mask value (logit) at pixel row i, column j after resizing \hat m_{ij} Boolean mask value at that pixel \sigma Sigmoid function
snippet: return ops.converttonumpymask  0.0 — Converts continuous logits into a binary mask.

text: Why would a promptable segmentation model return several candidate masks rather than one? A single point is ambiguous: it can belong to nested objects or parts. Returning several masks with quality scores lets the user or a program pick the intended one.

title: Overlaying the peach mask and prompting a banana
text:
Displaying SAM's first candidate mask on the image (Figure 11.11), then repeating the whole point-prompt pipeline with a new point (300, 550) on a banana. Once `get_mask` and the display utilities exist, segmenting any object is a three-step routine: choose a labeled point, call `model.predict`, extract and overlay a mask. Only the point coordinates change between objects. The page completes the peach example begun on p.348. A short code block creates a 10 × 10-inch figure, draws the image, overlays the boolean `mask` returned by `get_mask(outputs, index=0)`, and marks the prompt point. **Figure 11.11, "Segmented peach"**, shows the result: a semi-transparent blue region covering exactly the red fruit under the green star at (580, 450), with the neighbouring apple, the yellow fruit the book later calls a mango (p.351) and the bowl left uncovered. The authors' verdict: "Pretty good!"

The text then moves to a second object, a banana. The new prompt point is `(300, 550)`, which lands on the **second banana from the left**. The listing repeats every step from scratch:

- `input_point = np.array([[300, 550]])` and `input_label = np.array([1])` (one foreground point),
- the same `model.predict` call with the `images`, `points` and `labels` dict, each with a batch axis,
- `mask = get_mask(outputs, index=0)` to extract the first candidate,
- the same four plotting lines as the peach example.

The output of this listing, Figure 11.12 ("Segmented banana"), appears at the top of the next page (p.350). The repetition makes the key point implicitly: nothing about the model or the post-processing is object-specific. Changing two numbers, the x and y of the prompt, retargets the segmentation. Coordinates are in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame, with x measured to the right and y measured downward, which is why (300, 550) falls in the lower-left area of the image where the bananas lie. Figure 11.11 shows SAM cleanly separating the peach from touching fruit using a single click. The visualization layers image, mask and point on the same Matplotlib axis. Retargeting SAM to a different object only requires a new (x, y) point; the rest of the code is unchanged. Coordinates are (x, y) in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame with y increasing downward. The banana prompt is set up to illustrate ambiguity, explored on the next page.

title: The segmented banana and SAM's alternative masks
text:
Figure 11.12 shows the first candidate for the banana prompt; the text then plots the three remaining candidate masks (Figure 11.13) to show how they help with ambiguous prompts. A single point is ambiguous; SAM's extra candidates represent alternative interpretations of the prompt (here: one banana vs. both bananas), and you can inspect them by indexing masks 1-3. The page opens with **Figure 11.12, "Segmented banana"**: the first candidate (index 0) for the prompt point (300, 550) covers the second banana from the left only, cleanly separated from the first banana even though their stems touch.

The text then asks about "the other mask candidates" and says they "can come in handy for ambiguous prompts". A listing plots the remaining three:

- `plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(20, 60))` creates one row of three axes;
- `masks = outputs["masks"][0][1:]` slices off the batch axis and keeps candidates 1, 2 and 3 (shape (3, 256, 256));
- in the loop, each axis gets the image, the prompt point and `get_mask(outputs, index=i + 1)` overlaid, titled `Mask 1`, `Mask 2`, `Mask 3`, with axes hidden.

**Figure 11.13** shows the result. In *Mask 1* the blue region again covers only the second banana. In *Mask 2* and *Mask 3* the region covers **both bananas**; the next page (p.351) states this explicitly: "an alternative segmentation found by the model includes both bananas."

The lesson: a click on one banana could legitimately mean "this banana" or "the bunch of bananas". SAM does not have to guess; it returns several plausible masks at different granularities, and it is up to the user (or to the `iou_pred` scores introduced on p.348) to pick the intended one. Figure 11.12: candidate 0 for the point (300, 550) covers only the second banana. outputs["masks"][0][1:] selects the three alternative candidates. Figure 11.13: Mask 1 covers one banana; Masks 2 and 3 cover both. Alternative masks are SAM's answer to prompt ambiguity. Matplotlib subplots plus axis-based helpers make side-by-side comparisons easy.

title: Box prompts: drawing a box around the mango
text:
Closing remark on the banana alternatives, then introduction of box prompts: a box given by its top-left and bottom-right corners, visualised around the mango (Figure 11.14), and the start of the SAM call that uses it. Instead of points, SAM can be prompted with an approximate bounding box given as two corner coordinates [[x0, y0], [x1, y1]]; the box tells the model the spatial extent of the object to segment. The page first wraps up the banana experiment: "an alternative segmentation found by the model includes both bananas" (Masks 2 and 3 in Figure 11.13, p.350).

**Section 11.3.5** then introduces the second prompt type listed on p.347. Besides one or more target points, SAM accepts **boxes approximating the location** of the object to segment. A box is passed by the coordinates of its **top-left** and **bottom-right** corners. The example box surrounds the mango (the yellow fruit at the top of the bowl):

```
input_box = [[520, 180],   # top-left corner (x0, y0)
             [770, 420]]   # bottom-right corner (x1, y1)
```

The box is therefore 250 px wide (770 − 520) and 240 px tall (420 − 180) in the padded 1024 × 1024 frame. The listing draws it with `show_box` (p.347), which flattens the array to `[x0, y0, x1, y1]`, computes width and height, and adds a red, unfilled `plt.Rectangle`. **Figure 11.14, "Box prompt around the mango"**, shows the red rectangle around the mango; it also clips slightly into the apples below, illustrating that the box "does not need to be particularly precise" (p.347).

The page ends with "Let's prompt SAM with it (see figure 11.15)" and the first two lines of the `model.predict(` call; the dictionary contents (`"images"` and `"boxes"`), the mask extraction, and Figure 11.15 are on p.352. An alternative banana mask covers both bananas, confirming the prompt's ambiguity. SAM also accepts box prompts given by top-left and bottom-right corners. The mango box is [[520, 180], [770, 420]], i.e. 250 × 240 px. show_box converts corners to corner + width/height for Matplotlib. The box-prompt call starts here and continues on p.352.

title: Segmenting the mango from a box, and chapter 11 summary
text:
Finishing the box-prompted SAM call, showing the segmented mango (Figure 11.15), noting SAM's value for dataset annotation, and summarising chapter 11. A box prompt is passed under the "boxes" key with shape (1, 1, 2, 2) and yields a clean mask of the mango; SAM can therefore accelerate the creation of segmentation datasets. The chapter's lessons: segmentation means pixel-level masks; you can build a Conv2D/Conv2DTranspose model yourself or use a pretrained promptable model like SAM. The page finishes the listing begun on p.351. The input dictionary now has only two keys: `"images"` (the padded image with a batch axis) and `"boxes"`, built with `ops.expand_dims(input_box, axis=(0, 1))`. Expanding along two axes turns the (2, 2) corner array into shape **(1, 1, 2, 2)**: batch of 1, one box per image, two corners, (x, y). No points or labels are supplied. The first candidate is extracted with `get_mask(outputs, 0)` and drawn together with the image and the red box.

**Figure 11.15, "Segmented mango"**, shows the result: the blue mask covers the mango and stops at its outline, even though the box also includes parts of the apples and the bowl. The box only indicated roughly where and how big the object is; SAM found the object's exact pixels.

The authors then make a practical observation: **SAM can be a powerful tool to quickly create large datasets of images annotated with segmentation masks.** This echoes how SA-1B itself was built in a model-in-the-loop process (p.343-344).

The chapter **Summary** has three bullets:

1. Image segmentation is one of the main categories of computer vision tasks; it computes segmentation masks describing image contents at the pixel level (11.1, p.332-334).
2. To build your own segmentation model, stack strided `Conv2D` layers that compress the image into a smaller feature map, then corresponding `Conv2DTranspose` layers that expand it back into a mask of the same size as the input (11.2, p.338-341).
3. You can also use a pretrained model: Segment Anything, available in KerasHub, which the book says supports image, text, point and box prompting (11.3). Only point and box prompts were actually covered in the chapter (see review flag). Box prompts use the "boxes" key with shape (1, 1, 2, 2); no points or labels needed. Figure 11.15: SAM masks only the mango, not the whole box. SAM can quickly produce large mask-annotated datasets. Segmentation = pixel-level masks; build it with Conv2D down / Conv2DTranspose up, or use pretrained SAM. The summary's mention of text prompting is not covered in the chapter.

title: Chapter 12 opener: Object detection
text:
Opening page of chapter 12: what the chapter covers, a definition of object detection as drawing bounding boxes around objects of interest, and three common applications (counting, tracking, cropping). Object detection tells you not just which objects are in an image but where they are, by predicting bounding boxes; the chapter explains two-stage vs. single-stage detectors, trains a simple single-stage (YOLO) detector from scratch, and uses a pretrained detector (RetinaNet). This is the opening page of **chapter 12, Object detection**. The "This chapter covers" box lists four topics:

- understanding the object detection problem,
- two-stage and single-stage object detectors,
- training a simple single-stage detector from scratch,
- using a pretrained object detector.

The opening paragraph defines the task: object detection is "all about drawing boxes (called *bounding boxes*) around objects of interest in a picture" (see Figure 12.1, printed on p.354). Detection tells you **which** objects are present and **where** they are. Three common applications follow:

- **Counting**: how many instances of an object are in an image;
- **Tracking**: following how objects move in a scene by running detection on every frame of a movie;
- **Cropping**: locating the region containing an object of interest so that a higher-resolution patch can be sent to a classifier or an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model.

How to use this page: treat it as a map. title: Why detection, and the two families of detectors
text:
Justifying object detection as a cheaper alternative to segmentation, and introducing the split between two-stage (R-CNN) and single-stage (RetinaNet, YOLO) detectors Segmentation contains strictly more information than detection, but it costs more to run and much more to label; when you do not need pixel-level information, a detector is the right tool. Detectors come in two broad families: two-stage R-CNN models that first propose regions and then classify them, and single-stage models such as RetinaNet and YOLO. The page opens with **figure 12.1**, a photograph of two riders on horses on which a detector has drawn labelled boxes: two `person` boxes, two `horse` boxes, and two small `tie` boxes. The boxes overlap freely — each rider's box sits inside a horse's box — which already shows that detection outputs a *set* of independent rectangles, each with one class, rather than a partition of the image.

The authors then anticipate an objection. If you have an instance segmentation mask, you can compute the smallest box that contains it, so why not always segment? They agree that **segmentation is a strict superset of detection**: it returns everything a detector returns, plus much more. But that extra information has two prices:

- **Compute**: a good detector typically runs much faster than a segmentation model.
- **Labeling**: training a segmenter requires pixel-precise masks, which take far longer to produce than bounding boxes.

Hence the rule of thumb: if you do not need pixel-level information — for instance, if you only want to **count** objects — use an object detection model.

Section **12.1** then splits detection architectures into two families:

1. **Two-stage detectors**, which first extract *region proposals* — the Region-based Convolutional Neural Networks (**R-CNN**) family;
2. **Single-stage detectors**, such as **RetinaNet** or the **You Only Look Once (YOLO)** family.

Subsection **12.1.1** begins describing R-CNN: it is a two-stage model whose first stage takes an image and produces *a few thousand partially overlapping bounding boxes* around object-like areas. The sentence continues on p.355, where these boxes are named region proposals and the second, classifying stage is described. Detection outputs labelled bounding boxes; boxes can overlap (figure 12.1). Segmentation is a strict superset of detection — a box can be computed from an instance mask, but not the reverse. Detection is preferred when pixel-level detail is unnecessary because it is faster to run and much cheaper to label. Detectors split into two-stage (R-CNN: proposals then classification) and single-stage (RetinaNet, YOLO). R-CNN's first stage produces a few thousand partially overlapping candidate boxes.

title: How R-CNN works, and why it is expensive
text:
The two stages of an R-CNN (region proposals, then ConvNet classification and box refinement), the move from Selective Search to a Region Proposal Network, and the authors' view that two-stage detectors are rarely the right practical choice An R-CNN first proposes thousands of object-like regions with a not-very-smart first stage, then a ConvNet classifies every proposal, discards low-scoring ones and refines the survivors. This works well but is too expensive for real-time or embedded use; the authors argue you should either segment (with a big GPU) or use a single-stage detector (when resource-constrained). This page finishes the description of the **two-stage R-CNN detector** started on p.354.

**Stage 1 — region proposals.** The first stage outputs a few thousand partially overlapping boxes around areas that look object-like, called *region proposals*. It "isn't very smart": at this point we don't know whether a proposal contains an object, or which.

**Stage 2 — classification.** A ConvNet, like the classifiers of chapter 9, looks at each proposal and classifies it into a fixed set of classes. **Figure 12.2** draws this: an input image, a stage-1 box with three coloured proposals over the picture, and a stage-2 CNN whose outputs are *Dog*, *Cat* and *Car*. Proposals with a low score for every class are discarded, leaving a much smaller set of boxes, each with a high score for one class. Finally, the boxes are refined to **eliminate duplicates** and become as precise as possible.

**History of stage 1.** Early R-CNNs used **Selective Search**, a *heuristic model* relying on a notion of spatial consistency. The authors define *heuristic* as "a bundle of hard-coded rules someone made up", opposed to learned models (rules derived automatically) and theory-derived models. In later versions such as **Faster R-CNN**, proposal generation became a deep learning model, the **Region Proposal Network**.

**Cost and the authors' verdict.** R-CNN works well but is computationally expensive, mainly because it classifies thousands of patches per image, which rules out most real-time and embedded uses. The authors' take: you rarely need it. With a beefy server GPU you are better off running a segmentation model such as **Segment Anything** (chapter 11); when resource-constrained, use a **single-stage detector** — which leads into 12.1.2. R-CNN stage 1 proposes thousands of object-like regions without knowing what they contain. Stage 2 classifies each proposal with a ConvNet, discards low-scoring ones, then removes duplicates and refines boxes. Early R-CNNs used the heuristic Selective Search; Faster R-CNN replaced it with a learned Region Proposal Network. A heuristic is 'a bundle of hard-coded rules someone made up', as opposed to learned or theory-derived models. Classifying thousands of patches per image makes R-CNN too costly for real-time and embedded use. Authors' advice: segment with a big GPU, use a single-stage detector when resource-constrained.

title: Single-stage detectors, YOLO, and the COCO download
text:
Introducing single-stage detectors (RetinaNet, SSD, YOLO), deciding to rebuild the original 2015 YOLO, and starting to download the COCO 2017 dataset Since around 2015, single-stage detectors predict box coordinates and labels jointly with one model; they are much faster than two-stage detectors at a minor potential cost in accuracy, and YOLO is the most popular. The chapter rebuilds the simplest version, the original 2015 YOLO, trained on the bounding boxes of COCO 2017. **12.1.2 Single-stage detectors.** Around 2015, researchers started using a *single* deep learning model to jointly predict bounding-box coordinates and their labels — a **single-stage detector**. The main families are **RetinaNet**, **Single Shot MultiBox Detectors (SSD)** and **You Only Look Once (YOLO)** — named after the meme, on purpose. Single-stage detectors, especially recent YOLO versions, are significantly faster and more efficient than two-stage ones, with only a *minor potential tradeoff in accuracy*. YOLO is arguably the most popular detector today, particularly for real-time use; a new version usually appears every year, each tending to come from a different organization.

**12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch.** The authors warn that building a detector is an undertaking — not because the theory is hard, but because of the amount of code needed to manipulate bounding boxes and predicted outputs. To keep it simple they recreate the **very first YOLO model (2015)**; there are 12 YOLO versions at the time of writing, but the original is simpler.

**12.2.1 Downloading the COCO dataset.** The training data is **COCO** (*Common Objects in Context*), one of the best-known detection datasets: real-world photos from many sources with human annotations — object labels, bounding boxes and full segmentation masks. The chapter ignores the masks and uses only boxes. The 2017 version is about **18 GB**, the largest dataset in the book, so downloading it is "a good chance to take a breather".

**Listing 12.1** begins: it imports `keras` and `keras_hub` and calls `keras.utils.get_file("coco", "http://images.cocodataset.org/zips/train2017.zip", extract=True, ...` to download and unzip the training images. The call is closed, and the annotations archive downloaded, at the top of p.357. Single-stage detectors (RetinaNet, SSD, YOLO) predict boxes and labels jointly with one model; they emerged around 2015. They are significantly faster than two-stage detectors with a minor potential accuracy cost; YOLO is the most popular for real-time use. The chapter rebuilds the original 2015 YOLO because it is simpler than the 12 later versions. Detection code is mostly box bookkeeping rather than complex theory. COCO 2017 (18 GB) provides labels, boxes and masks; only boxes and labels are used. Listing 12.1 downloads and extracts the training images with `keras.utils.get_file`; the annotations follow on p.357.

title: Parsing COCO annotations and normalizing boxes
text:
Downloading the COCO annotations JSON, joining boxes to images by image ID, and rescaling pixel boxes to a unit square COCO stores images and box annotations separately, linked by image IDs. Listing 12.2 builds one record per image containing its file path, its list of boxes and its list of labels, converting each `x, y, width, height` pixel box into coordinates on a [0, 1] square so later code can ignore image sizes. The page opens with the end of **listing 12.1**: after closing the image download, a second `keras.utils.get_file` call fetches `annotations_trainval2017.zip` (with `extract=True`) into `annotations_path`.

The authors then explain the "input massaging" needed. The first download is just an **unlabeled directory of images**; the second contains **all image metadata as a JSON file**. COCO assigns each image an ID and pairs each bounding box with one of these IDs, so the boxes must be **collated** with their images.

Each COCO box is given as **`x, y, width, height` in pixels, measured from the top-left corner**. While loading, the authors rescale boxes to points in a **`[0, 1]` unit square**, so later code can manipulate boxes without checking each image's size.

**Listing 12.2** does this:

1. Loads `instances_train2017.json`.
2. Builds `images`, a dict from image ID to image record (the callout says "Sorts image metadata by ID"; it is really an ID-indexed lookup table).
3. Defines `scale_box(box, width, height)`: multiplies all four values by `1 / max(width, height)` and shifts `x` (for portrait images) or `y` (for landscape images) by half of the size difference — exactly the coordinates the box would have if the image were **centred inside a square** of side max(width, height), then scaled to [0, 1].
4. Loops over every annotation, creating `{"boxes": [], "labels": []}` for a new `image_id`, appending the scaled box and the `category_id` label, and storing the image's file path under `images_path + "/train2017/"`.
5. Converts the dict to a list, `metadata`, one entry per image that has annotations.

The page ends with "Let's take a look at the data we just loaded", leading to listing 12.3 on p.358. COCO images and annotations come as separate downloads linked by image IDs. COCO boxes are `x, y, width, height` pixels from the top-left corner. `scale_box` normalizes boxes to a [0, 1] square using one factor, 1/max(W, H), and centres the shorter side — equivalent to padding the image to a square. `metadata` is a list of per-image records with `boxes`, `labels` (COCO category IDs) and `path`. Normalized boxes let later code ignore each image's original size.

text: Scaling box coordinates by 1/max(W, H) and offsetting the shorter axis by half the size difference. Place the image in the middle of a square canvas, then measure boxes as fractions of the canvas. Equivalent to letterbox padding the image to a max(W,H) square and normalizing by its side. Landscape 640 × 480: vertical offset (640 − 480)/640/2 = 0.125.
snippet: Scaling box coordinates by 1/maxW, H and offsetting the shorter axis by half the size difference.

title: The scale_box transformation
text: scale = 1.0 / max(width, height); x, y, w, h = [v * scale for v in box]; x += (height - width) * scale / 2 if height > width else 0; y += (width - height) * scale / 2 if width > height else 0 \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{1}{\max(W, H)} \\ x' &= s\,x + \mathbb{1}[H > W]\,\frac{(H - W)\,s}{2} \\ y' &= s\,y + \mathbb{1}[W > H]\,\frac{(W - H)\,s}{2} \\ w' &= s\,w, \quad h' = s\,h \end{aligned} Put all boxes on a common [0, 1] square regardless of image size, without distorting aspect ratio. The offset $(H-W)s/2$ (or $(W-H)s/2$) is the width of the padding band on one side if the image is centred in a square of side $\max(W,H)$. W, H Image width and height in pixels (`image["width"]`, `image["height"]`). x, y, w, h COCO box: top-left corner and size in pixels (`annotation["bbox"]`). s Single scale factor, 1 / max(W, H). \mathbb{1}[\cdot] Indicator: 1 if the condition holds, else 0. x', y', w', h' Normalized box on the unit square.

title: Listing 12.2 Parsing the COCO data
text:
import json

with open(f"{annotations_path}/annotations/instances_train2017.json", "r") as f:
    annotations = json.load(f)

images = {image["id"]: image for image in annotations["images"]}

def scale_box(box, width, height):
    scale = 1.0 / max(width, height)
    x, y, w, h = [v * scale for v in box]
    x += (height - width) * scale / 2 if height > width else 0
    y += (width - height) * scale / 2 if width > height else 0
    return [x, y, w, h]

metadata = {}
for annotation in annotations["annotations"]:
    id = annotation["image_id"]
    if id not in metadata:
        metadata[id] = {"boxes": [], "labels": []}
    image = images[id]
    box = scale_box(annotation["bbox"], image["width"], image["height"])
    metadata[id]["boxes"].append(box)
    metadata[id]["labels"].append(annotation["category_id"])
    metadata[id]["path"] = images_path + "/train2017/" + image["file_name"]
metadata = list(metadata.values()) Loads the COCO training annotations, indexes images by ID, converts every box to normalized unit-square coordinates, and groups boxes and labels per image into a list of records. Hash join of annotations onto images by ID, with a per-row geometric transformation and grouping.
snippet: Loads the COCO training annotations, indexes images by ID, converts every box to normalized unit-square coordinates, and groups boxes and labels per image into a list of records.

section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Filtering COCO and the design of a single-stage YOLO model
text:
Shrinking and shuffling the COCO metadata, then laying out the YOLO design: a grid of predictions (one box, one confidence score and one class label per cell) computed on top of a pretrained ResNet backbone at 448 x 448 input resolution After reducing COCO to images with at most four boxes and shuffling it, the authors describe YOLO as a single-stage detector that splits the image into a grid and, at every cell, predicts a bounding box with a confidence score and a class label, using a pretrained ConvNet backbone (ResNet, chosen because its strided convolutions preserve spatial information better than pooling). The page finishes the data-loading part of section 12.2 and opens subsection 12.2.2.

**Trimming the dataset.** The full COCO training data is about 18 GB. To keep the example runnable on modest hardware, the authors keep only images with **four or fewer bounding boxes**, which, they say, both makes the learning problem easier and roughly halves the data. They then call `random.shuffle(metadata)` because the metadata is grouped by object type; feeding batches in that order would expose the model to long runs of a single kind of image, which is bad for stochastic gradient descent.

**YOLO as a single-stage detector.** Unlike the two-stage R-CNN family (p.354), which first proposes candidate regions and then classifies them, YOLO proposes boxes and labels **in one go**.

**The output format.** The model divides the image into a **grid** and predicts, at each grid location, a **bounding box** and a **class label**. The original paper by Redmon et al. predicted several boxes per cell; the book simplifies to **one box per cell**. Because objects are not spread evenly over the grid, each box comes with a **confidence score**, which should be high where an object is detected and zero where there is none. Most cells contain no object, so most confidences should be near zero.

**The backbone.** Like many vision models, YOLO computes high-level features with a **ConvNet backbone** (chapter 8). The paper's authors designed and ImageNet-pretrained their own; the book instead loads a pretrained **ResNet** through KerasHub rather than the Xception used so far. ResNet's structure is similar but it downsamples with **strides instead of pooling**, and as chapter 11 noted, strided convolutions are preferable when the spatial location of features matters, which is exactly the case in detection.

Finally, images will be resized to **448 x 448**; the authors stress that input size is important for object detection. The loading code itself (listing 12.5) appears on the next page (p.361). The dataset is reduced to images with at most four boxes (easier problem, about half the data) and shuffled because it is grouped by object type. YOLO is single-stage: boxes and labels are predicted in one pass, with no region-proposal step. The image is divided into a grid; each cell predicts one bounding box, a confidence score and a class label (the paper used several boxes per cell). Confidence should be high where an object is present and near zero elsewhere, which is the case for most cells. A pretrained ResNet backbone from KerasHub is used instead of Xception, because its strided downsampling preserves spatial location better than pooling. Input resolution matters for detection; images are resized to 448 x 448.
snippet: The page finishes the data-loading part of section 12.2 and opens subsection 12.2.2. Trimming the dataset. The full COCO training data is about 18 GB. To keep the example runnable…
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Single-stage object detector
text: A detector that predicts bounding boxes and class labels directly in one network pass, without a separate region-proposal step. Instead of first circling candidate objects and then asking 'what is this?', the network looks once and fills in a table of boxes and labels for the whole image. The network maps an image to a fixed-size tensor (here per grid cell: box coordinates, confidence, class scores). Training is a combined regression and classification problem; inference is a single forward pass plus thresholding. YOLO (this chapter) and RetinaNet (p.370) are single-stage detectors.
snippet: A detector that predicts bounding boxes and class labels directly in one network pass, without a separate region-proposal step.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
text: A single-stage detector that divides the image into a grid and predicts, at each grid cell, bounding box(es) with confidence scores and a class probability map. Each grid cell is a tiny detector responsible for objects whose center lands in it. In the book's simplified version: one box (x, y, w, h) plus one confidence per cell and a softmax over 91 labels per cell, computed by dense layers on top of a ResNet-50 backbone. With a 6 x 6 grid (p.362), the model always outputs 36 candidate boxes per image.
snippet: A single-stage detector that divides the image into a grid and predicts, at each grid cell, bounding boxes with confidence scores and a class probability map.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Box confidence score
text: A scalar predicted with each box, trained to be high when an object is present at that grid location and zero otherwise. A 'there is really something here' flag that lets the model ignore boxes in empty cells. Thresholding confidences converts the fixed number of predicted boxes into a variable number of detections. Later in the chapter its target is related to the IoU between predicted and true boxes (p.366, p.374). In the training targets (p.364) a cell containing a box center has confidence 1.0; every other cell has 0.
snippet: A scalar predicted with each box, trained to be high when an object is present at that grid location and zero otherwise.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: ConvNet backbone
text: A (usually pretrained) convolutional network used as a feature extractor, onto which task-specific layers are attached. A general-purpose visual 'eye' that you reuse and fit with a different 'brain' for each task. Here, KerasHub's `resnet_50_imagenet` backbone maps a 448 x 448 x 3 image to a 14 x 14 x 2048 feature map (p.362). Chapter 8 reused pretrained convolutional bases for classification; here the same idea serves detection.
snippet: A usually pretrained convolutional network used as a feature extractor, onto which task-specific layers are attached.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Strided convolution (vs. pooling)
text: A convolution applied with a step larger than 1, which downsamples feature maps while learning how to do so. Pooling keeps 'the strongest signal' in a window and forgets where it was; a strided conv can learn a summary that still encodes position. Stride s reduces each spatial dimension by roughly a factor s. Unlike max pooling, its output is a learned linear combination of the whole window, so positional information can be retained. Listing 12.6 (p.362) itself adds a `Conv2D(512, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))` that downsamples 14 x 14 to 6 x 6.
snippet: A convolution applied with a step larger than 1, which downsamples feature maps while learning how to do so.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Shuffling training data
text: Randomly permuting the training samples so that each batch is representative of the whole dataset. Like shuffling a deck before dealing: you do not want all the hearts in one hand. Mini-batch SGD's gradient estimate is unbiased only if batches are random samples; ordered data yields correlated, biased updates. `random.shuffle(metadata)` permutes the list in place.

title: Figure 12.4, loading ResNet-50, and the shape of the YOLO head
text:
The original YOLO output scheme (grid, boxes + confidence, class probability map, final detections), loading a pretrained ResNet-50 backbone and image converter from KerasHub at 448 x 448, and the recipe for the prediction head YOLO overlays an S x S grid on the image and produces two maps, boxes with confidences and a per-cell class probability map, which combine into final detections. The book loads `resnet_50_imagenet` with a matching 448 x 448 preprocessor and will attach a head of two dense layers whose output, per grid cell, is split into 5 box numbers (x, y, w, h, confidence) and 91 class scores. **Figure 12.4**, reproduced from the first YOLO paper, shows the method in four panels. On the left an **S x S grid** is overlaid on the input photo (a person walking a dog on a beach). From this the model produces two things in parallel: at the top, many candidate **bounding boxes with confidence** (thick outlines for confident boxes around the person and the dog, thin ones elsewhere); at the bottom, a **class probability map** in which each grid cell is colored by its most likely class (blue cells over the person, red cells over the dog). Combining them gives the **final detections** on the right: one blue box for the person and one red box for the dog.

**Listing 12.5** sets `image_size = 448` and loads two KerasHub objects from the same preset, `"resnet_50_imagenet"`: a `Backbone` (the convolutional feature extractor, without a classification head) and an `ImageConverter`, the matching preprocessing layer that resizes images to `(448, 448)` and rescales pixel values the way the backbone expects.

The text then gives the **head recipe** from the YOLO paper: take the backbone's output, pass it through **two densely connected layers with an activation in the middle**, and **split** the output. For each grid location, the **first five numbers** are the bounding-box prediction, four for the box and one for the box confidence, and **the rest** form the class probability map: a classification prediction over all **91 labels** for each grid location. "Let's write this out" leads to listing 12.6 on the next page (p.362), which also inserts a strided convolution before the dense layers and uses a 6 x 6 grid. Figure 12.4: grid on input, boxes with confidence and a class probability map computed in parallel, merged into final detections. Listing 12.5 loads the `resnet_50_imagenet` backbone and its matching `ImageConverter`, resized to 448 x 448. The head recipe: backbone output, two dense layers with an activation between them, then split. Per grid cell, 5 numbers describe the box (4 coordinates + confidence) and 91 numbers give the class prediction. Backbone and preprocessing should come from the same preset so the pixel scaling matches pretraining.

title: Listing 12.6: attaching the YOLO prediction head
text:
Building the full YOLO model with the Functional API: ResNet-50 backbone, strided Conv2D, Flatten, Dense(2048, relu), Dropout, Dense(6*6*96), Reshape to a 6 x 6 x 96 grid, and a split into box and softmax class outputs; reading the model summary Listing 12.6 turns the backbone into a detector whose two named outputs are a `(6, 6, 5)` box tensor and a `(6, 6, 91)` softmax class tensor. The model summary shows how the spatial size shrinks from 448 x 448 to 14 x 14 (backbone) to 6 x 6 (strided conv) and where the parameters live: most are in the first dense layer. **Listing 12.6** builds the YOLO model with the Functional API. It fixes `grid_size = 6` and `num_labels = 91`, then:

1. `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(448, 448, 3))` and `x = backbone(inputs)` give ResNet-50 feature maps of shape `(None, 14, 14, 2048)`.
2. `layers.Conv2D(512, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))` shrinks them to `(None, 6, 6, 512)` and `Flatten` turns them into a vector of 18,432 values (callout: *makes our backbone outputs smaller and then flattens the output features*).
3. Two dense layers (callout: *passes our flattened feature maps through two densely connected layers*): `Dense(2048, activation="relu", kernel_initializer="glorot_normal")`, `Dropout(0.5)`, then `Dense(grid_size * grid_size * (num_labels + 5))`, that is 6 x 6 x 96 = 3,456 linear outputs.
4. `Reshape((6, 6, 96))` restores the grid (callout: *reshapes outputs to a 6 x 6 grid*).
5. The last axis is split (callout: *split box and class predictions*): `box_predictions = x[..., :5]` stays linear, while `class_predictions` applies a softmax to `x[..., 5:]`.
6. The model returns a dictionary `{"box": ..., "class": ...}`.

The **model summary** (`functional_3`) confirms the shapes and parameter counts: the backbone has 23,580,512 parameters, the strided conv 9,437,696, the first dense layer 37,750,784 (the largest single layer), and the output dense layer 7,081,344. The `GetItem` rows come from the slicing operations; `get_item_7` has shape `(None, 6, 6, 91)`. The table continues on the next page with the 5-channel box slice, the softmax activation and the totals (77,850,336 parameters, p.363). The model is backbone -> strided Conv2D -> Flatten -> Dense(2048, relu) -> Dropout(0.5) -> Dense(3456) -> Reshape(6, 6, 96) -> split. The box output `(6, 6, 5)` is linear; the class output `(6, 6, 91)` uses a softmax. Outputs are returned as a dict with keys `"box"` and `"class"`, enabling one loss per output. The strided conv turns 14 x 14 x 2048 features into 6 x 6 x 512 = 18,432 values per image. Most parameters are in the head, especially the 37.75 M-parameter first dense layer.
