title: YOLO detection head
text: The layers added on top of the backbone that convert its feature maps into per-grid-cell box and class predictions. A translator from 'what visual features are where' into 'which objects are where'. Conv2D(512, 3, stride 2) -> Flatten -> Dense(2048, relu) -> Dropout(0.5) -> Dense(3456) -> Reshape(6, 6, 96) -> split into 5 box values and a softmax over 91 classes. Listing 12.6.

section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Strided convolution
text: A convolution whose window moves by more than one position, downsampling the feature map. It reduces 14 x 14 to 6 x 6 so the flattened vector is small enough for a dense layer. With 'valid' padding (the Conv2D default), output size = floor((14 - 3) / 2) + 1 = 6. Parameters: 3 x 3 x 2048 x 512 + 512 = 9,437,696. `layers.Conv2D(512, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))`.
snippet: A convolution whose window moves by more than one position, downsampling the feature map.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Multi-output Functional model
text: A Keras model whose outputs are given as a dict (or list) of several tensors, each of which can have its own loss. One network, two answers: where and what. `keras.Model(inputs, {"box": box_predictions, "class": class_predictions})`; losses and targets can be passed as dicts keyed by the same names. `outputs = {"box": box_predictions, "class": class_predictions}`.
snippet: A Keras model whose outputs are given as a dict or list of several tensors, each of which can have its own loss.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Softmax over class scores
text: Turns a vector of scores into a probability distribution. Each grid cell votes a probability for each of the 91 labels; the votes sum to 1. Applied along the last axis of `x[..., 5:]`, giving `(None, 6, 6, 91)` with $\sum_k p_k = 1$ for every cell. `layers.Activation("softmax")(x[..., 5:])`.
snippet: Turns a vector of scores into a probability distribution.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Dropout
text: Randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training to reduce overfitting. Prevents the huge first dense layer from relying on fragile co-adaptations. `Dropout(0.5)` after the 2,048-unit dense layer; it has no parameters. `dropout_3 (Dropout)` in the summary, 0 parameters.
snippet: Randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training to reduce overfitting.
section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Output size of the strided convolution
text: conv2d_3 (Conv2D) (None, 6, 6, 512) after res_net_backbone_12 (None, 14, 14, 2048) H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor \frac{H_{\text{in}} - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1 = \left\lfloor \frac{14 - 3}{2} \right\rfloor + 1 = 6 Explains why the grid is 6 x 6 and why `grid_size = 6` matches the conv output. The strided conv sets the spatial resolution of the flattened features; the grid of predictions is then created by the Reshape, not inherited directly. H_{\text{in}} Input height (and width): 14. k Kernel size: 3. s Stride: 2.

title: Listing 12.6 Attaching a YOLO prediction head
text:
from keras import layers

grid_size = 6
num_labels = 91

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(image_size, image_size, 3))
x = backbone(inputs)
x = layers.Conv2D(512, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))(x)
x = keras.layers.Flatten()(x)
x = layers.Dense(2048, activation="relu", kernel_initializer="glorot_normal")(x)
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
x = layers.Dense(grid_size * grid_size * (num_labels + 5))(x)
x = layers.Reshape((grid_size, grid_size, num_labels + 5))(x)
box_predictions = x[..., :5]
class_predictions = layers.Activation("softmax")(x[..., 5:])
outputs = {"box": box_predictions, "class": class_predictions}
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs) Builds a two-output Keras Functional model: a 448 x 448 RGB image goes through the ResNet-50 backbone and a fully connected head, producing per-cell box predictions `(6, 6, 5)` and per-cell class probabilities `(6, 6, 91)`. Backbone feature extraction, spatial downsampling, global fully connected mixing, reshape into a grid, channel split.

section: 12.2 Training a YOLO model from scratch

title: Why the head is shaped this way, and encoding boxes relative to the grid
text:
Interpreting the model summary totals and the design of the head (strided downsampling, dense layers, reshape, softmax, no locality constraint); then the YOLO box encoding (x, y relative to the responsible cell, w, h relative to the image) and the `to_grid` / `from_grid` utilities The head downsamples 401,408 backbone floats to 18,432, mixes them with dense layers so every grid cell sees the whole image, and reshapes the result to a 6 x 6 grid. To train it, each ground-truth box is assigned to the grid cell containing its center, and its center is re-expressed as an offset in [0, 1] within that cell while width and height stay relative to the whole image. The page first finishes the **model summary** from p.362: `get_item_6` is the box slice `(None, 6, 6, 5)` and `activation_33` is the softmax over the class slice `(None, 6, 6, 91)`. In total the model has **77,850,336 parameters (296.98 MB)**, of which 77,797,088 are trainable and 53,248 are non-trainable.

The authors then explain the head. The backbone outputs `(batch_size, 14, 14, 2048)`, i.e. **401,408 floats per image**, too many for dense layers, so a **strided conv** reduces them to `(batch_size, 6, 6, 512)`, **18,432 floats**. The flattened map goes through a `Dense` with `relu` and a final `Dense` with exactly the number of predictions needed: 5 for box and confidence plus 91 class scores per grid location. The output is reshaped to **6 x 6**, split, and a **softmax** is applied to the class part as usual; the box outputs "will need more special consideration" later. Because the whole feature map is flattened, **every grid detector can use the entire image's features**: there is no locality constraint, by design, since large objects do not stay inside one cell.

**Section 12.2.3** aligns the data with the prediction grid. **Each grid detector is responsible for the boxes whose center falls inside its cell.** The model outputs five floats per cell, `(x, y, w, h, confidence)`: `x` and `y` are the object's **center relative to the bounds of the grid cell** (0 to 1), while `w` and `h` are the object's **size relative to the image**. The `w` and `h` in the data are already correct, but `x` and `y` must be translated to and from the grid, using two utilities. `to_grid(box)` computes the center in grid units, `cx, cy = (x + w/2) * grid_size, (y + h/2) * grid_size`, takes the integer cell indices `ix, iy`, and returns `((ix, iy), (cx - ix, cy - iy, w, h))`. `from_grid(loc, box)` starts here and, on p.364, converts back to a top-left box in image coordinates. The model has 77,850,336 parameters (296.98 MB), nearly all trainable: the backbone is fine-tuned. A strided conv cuts the backbone's 401,408 floats per image to 18,432 before the dense layers. The dense head gives every grid cell access to the whole image; this lack of locality is intentional for large objects. Each box is the responsibility of the grid cell containing its center. Box encoding: x, y = center offset within the cell (0 to 1); w, h = size relative to the image. `to_grid` and `from_grid` convert between image and grid coordinates and are exact inverses.

title: YOLO box encoding

title: Listing 12.7: building the YOLO class and box targets
text:
Finishing `from_grid` and converting every COCO annotation into two grid-shaped target arrays: a class probability map marking every cell a box overlaps, and a box array holding (x, y, w, h, 1.0) in the cell containing each box's center Training targets must have the same structure as the model's outputs. `class_array` (N, 6, 6) holds an integer label per cell, set for every cell a box intersects; `box_array` (N, 6, 6, 5) holds the grid-encoded box and a confidence of 1 in the responsible cell and zeros everywhere else, and the class at the center cell is forced to match the box. The page opens with the last three lines of **`from_grid`**: `x = (xi + x) / grid_size - w / 2`, `y = (yi + y) / grid_size - h / 2`, `return (x, y, w, h)`. It adds the cell index to the in-cell offset, divides by the grid size to get the center in image units, and subtracts half the width/height to recover the top-left corner, undoing `to_grid` (p.363).

Next the training data is reworked to fit the grid. Two arrays, each as long as the dataset, are created:

- a **class probability map**, in which **all grid cells that intersect a bounding box** get that box's label (overlapping boxes are ignored for simplicity);
- a **box array**, in which each box is translated to the grid and written into the **correct grid cell** (the one holding its center). The **confidence is always 1** for a real box and **0 everywhere else**.

**Listing 12.7** implements this. `class_array = np.zeros((len(metadata), grid_size, grid_size))` and `box_array = np.zeros((len(metadata), grid_size, grid_size, 5))`. The first loop computes, for each box, `left, right = floor(x * S), ceil((x + w) * S)` and the analogous row bounds, and fills `class_array[index, bottom:top, left:right] = label`. The second loop calls `to_grid(box)` (callout: *transforms the box to the grid coordinate system*), sets `box_array[index, yi, xi] = [*grid_box, 1.0]`, and re-sets `class_array[index, yi, xi] = label` (callout: *makes sure the class label for the box's center location matches the box*), so that an overlapping box drawn later in the first loop cannot leave the wrong label at another box's center.

Finally the authors announce a visualization of these targets (figure 12.5, p.365), drawing the class map over the first image together with each box's confidence and label. `from_grid` inverts `to_grid`: (cell index + offset) / S - size / 2. `class_array` (N, 6, 6) labels every cell a box intersects; 0 means no object. `box_array` (N, 6, 6, 5) stores (dx, dy, w, h, 1.0) only in each box's center cell; all else is zero confidence. Overlaps are not handled: later boxes overwrite earlier ones, and two centers in one cell lose a box. The second loop re-asserts the label at each center cell so box and class agree.

title: Listing 12.7 Creating the YOLO targets
text:
import numpy as np
import math

class_array = np.zeros((len(metadata), grid_size, grid_size))
box_array = np.zeros((len(metadata), grid_size, grid_size, 5))

for index, sample in enumerate(metadata):
    boxes, labels = sample["boxes"], sample["labels"]
    for box, label in zip(boxes, labels):
        (x, y, w, h) = box
        left, right = math.floor(x * grid_size), math.ceil((x + w) * grid_size)
        bottom, top = math.floor(y * grid_size), math.ceil((y + h) * grid_size)
        class_array[index, bottom:top, left:right] = label

for index, sample in enumerate(metadata):
    boxes, labels = sample["boxes"], sample["labels"]
    for box, label in zip(boxes, labels):
        (xi, yi), (grid_box) = to_grid(box)
        box_array[index, yi, xi] = [*grid_box, 1.0]
        class_array[index, yi, xi] = label Builds the class-map targets `(N, 6, 6)` and box targets `(N, 6, 6, 5)` for all N images in `metadata`. Two passes: (1) rasterize each box's extent onto the grid for the class map; (2) place each box's encoded coordinates and confidence at its center cell and fix the center label.

title: Listing 12.8: drawing the YOLO grid, class map and boxes (figure 12.5)
text:
A reusable `draw_prediction` function that overlays the 6 x 6 grid with class-colored cells and draws every box whose confidence is at or above a cutoff, applied to the first training target `draw_prediction` works on grid-shaped data, so it can display both targets (now) and model predictions (later). It colors each grid cell by its class label, converts each cell's box back to image coordinates with `from_grid`, and draws it with its class name and confidence, filtering by `cutoff`. Applied to the first target, it shows a single 'giraffe 1.00' box over a block of giraffe-labeled cells. **Listing 12.8** defines `draw_prediction(image, boxes, classes, cutoff=None)`, a visualization for grid-shaped YOLO data:

1. It creates a figure (`dpi=300`) and draws the image with `draw_image`, which places it in the unit square with (0, 0) at the top left, padding non-square images (p.359).
2. **Grid and class map** (callout: *draws the YOLO output grid and class probability map*): for each row `yi` and column `xi` of `classes`, it picks `label_to_color(label)` if the label is non-zero and `"none"` otherwise, computes the cell's rectangle `(xi/6, yi/6, 1/6, 1/6)`, and adds a `Rectangle` with a black edge and the class color at `alpha=0.5`. Every cell gets a black outline, so the full 6 x 6 grid is visible.
3. **Boxes** (callout: *draws all boxes at each grid location above our cutoff*): for each cell it splits the 5-vector into `box[:4]` and `confidence = box[4]`; if no cutoff is given or `confidence >= cutoff`, it converts the box to image coordinates with `from_grid((xi, yi), box)`, takes the label from `classes[yi, xi]`, and calls `draw_box` with the caption `f"{name} {max(confidence, 0):.2f}"`, where `name` comes from `keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name`.

The call `draw_prediction(metadata[0]["path"], box_array[0], class_array[0], cutoff=1.0)` draws the targets of the first (shuffled) image. With `cutoff=1.0`, only the real boxes (confidence 1) are drawn.

**Figure 12.5** shows the result: a landscape photo of a giraffe beside a tree, with white padding rows at top and bottom, a 6 x 6 grid, a tinted block of cells covering the giraffe's extent, and one box labeled **"giraffe 1.00"**. `draw_prediction` paints the 6 x 6 grid with class colors and draws decoded boxes whose confidence passes a cutoff. Cell geometry is `(xi, yi, 1, 1) / grid_size` in unit-square coordinates. Boxes are decoded with `from_grid` and labeled from the class map at their cell. With targets, `cutoff=1.0` draws only real boxes; figure 12.5 shows one 'giraffe 1.00' box. Figure 12.5 visualizes targets, not predictions; the same function will be reused for predictions.

title: Building the tf.data pipeline and starting on the YOLO loss
text:
Streaming COCO images and YOLO grid targets with tf.data (Listing 12.9), then introducing the two-part YOLO loss: crossentropy for class maps and a custom sum-squared box loss The images are too large in decoded form to hold in memory, so Listing 12.9 builds a lazy tf.data pipeline that reads, decodes, preprocesses, zips with the precomputed box/class targets, batches by 16, prefetches and splits off validation batches. Training then needs one more ingredient: a loss per output, where the class output uses sparse categorical crossentropy and the box output needs a custom sum-squared error restricted to cells that contain objects, with a special treatment for the confidence value. The page finishes data preparation and opens **section 12.2.4, Training the YOLO model**.

**Listing 12.9** builds the training data with `tf.data`. A small function `load_image(path)` reads a JPEG file from disk, decodes it into a 3-channel image tensor and passes it through the `preprocessor` (the KerasHub image converter set up earlier, which resizes to 448 x 448 and rescales). A dataset of file paths is created from `metadata` and mapped through `load_image` with 8 parallel calls. The targets prepared in Listing 12.7 (`box_array` and `class_array`) are wrapped into a second dataset whose elements are dicts `{"box": ..., "class": ...}`, matching the names of the model's two outputs. The two datasets are zipped into `(image, labels)` pairs, batched by 16 and prefetched two batches ahead. Finally the first 500 batches become `val_dataset` and the rest `train_dataset`.

A **NOTE** explains why streaming matters here: decoded image tensors are much larger than compressed JPEGs, so loading the whole dataset at once would overwhelm system memory. `tf.data` loads images batch by batch and frees them afterward; `prefetch(2)` keeps two batches ready so training does not stall while new images are loaded and resized.

Section 12.2.4 then names the last missing ingredient before `fit()`: **the loss function**. The model has two outputs, predicted boxes and predicted grid labels. As in chapter 7, each output can have its own loss and Keras sums them. The class output simply uses `sparse_categorical_crossentropy`. The box output needs care. The basic YOLO loss is a **sum-squared error** between target and predicted box parameters, computed **only for grid cells that contain an actual box**. The tricky part is the **confidence** value: the YOLO authors wanted it to reflect not just whether an object is present but how good the predicted box is. The sentence continues on p.367, where IoU becomes the confidence target. Listing 12.9 streams images: read -> decode -> preprocess (8 in parallel), zipped with dict targets matching the output names. batch(16).prefetch(2) keeps memory small and the accelerator busy. take(500)/skip(500) after batching splits 500 batches for validation. Decoded images are far bigger than JPEGs, which is why streaming is required. Total loss = box loss + sparse categorical crossentropy on the class map; Keras sums per-output losses. The basic box loss is sum-squared error only in cells that contain a labeled box. The confidence output should reflect box quality, which requires a custom loss (continued on p.367).

title: IoU as the confidence target and YOLO's loss-scaling tricks
text:
Using IoU between predicted and true box as the target for the confidence output, implementing IoU with keras.ops (Listing 12.10), and the three loss-scaling tricks from the YOLO paper The confidence target is 0 in empty cells and the IoU between the current predicted box and the actual box in occupied cells, so confidence rises as localization improves. Listing 12.10 computes IoU for tensors of (cx, cy, w, h) boxes; the loss then weights box placement by 5, halves the confidence loss in empty cells, and compares square roots of widths and heights. The page completes the sentence from p.366: the confidence output should reflect *how good the predicted box is*. To get a **smooth estimate** of box quality the YOLO authors use **Intersection over Union (IoU)**, the metric from chapter 11 (p.340). The rule: if a grid cell is empty, the target confidence is **0**; if it contains an object, the target is the **IoU between the current box prediction and the actual box**. As the model localizes better, IoU rises and so do the learned confidences.

Because the target depends on the prediction, a **custom loss** is needed. The first building block is **Listing 12.10**, written with backend-agnostic `keras.ops`:

- `unpack(box)` splits the last axis of a box tensor into `cx, cy, w, h` (the `...` keeps any leading batch/grid axes).
- `intersection(box1, box2)` converts centers and sizes to edges, takes the larger left/bottom edge and the smaller right/top edge, and multiplies the clamped width and height of the overlap (zero if the boxes don't overlap).
- `intersection_over_union` computes each box's area (clamping negative widths/heights to 0), the union as $a_1 + a_2 - \text{intersection}$, and returns intersection/union via `divide_no_nan` so an empty union gives 0 instead of NaN.

The page then lists **loss scaling tricks** from Redmon et al.:

1. **Scale the box placement loss up by 5**, making localization a bigger part of training.
2. **Scale the confidence loss in empty cells down by 2**, since most cells are empty and their zero-confidence terms would otherwise overwhelm the loss.
3. **Take the square root of width and height** before computing the error, so large boxes don't dominate small ones. The book uses a **sign-preserving** `sqrt` because an untrained model may predict negative widths and heights.

"Let's write this out" leads to Listing 12.11 on p.368. Confidence target: 0 for empty cells, IoU(pred, true) for occupied cells. IoU = intersection / (a1 + a2 - intersection), computed from inner edges with clamping. Listing 12.10 is vectorized with keras.ops and uses divide_no_nan for safety. Box placement loss is scaled up by 5. Empty-cell confidence loss is scaled down by 2 because empty cells are the vast majority. Widths and heights are compared after a sign-preserving square root so small boxes matter.

title: Intersection over Union (IoU)
text: Ratio of the area where two regions overlap to the area they cover together. How much of the combined footprint of two boxes is shared; identical boxes score 1, disjoint boxes 0. IoU = |A ∩ B| / (|A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|). For axis-aligned boxes the intersection is a rectangle whose edges are the inner edges of the two boxes. Boxes (0.5, 0.5, 0.4, 0.4) and (0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.4): intersection 0.3 x 0.4 = 0.12, union 0.16 + 0.16 - 0.12 = 0.20, IoU = 0.6.

title: Listing 12.10 Computing IoU for two boxes
text:
from keras import ops

def unpack(box):
    return box[..., 0], box[..., 1], box[..., 2], box[..., 3]

def intersection(box1, box2):
    cx1, cy1, w1, h1 = unpack(box1)
    cx2, cy2, w2, h2 = unpack(box2)
    left = ops.maximum(cx1 - w1 / 2, cx2 - w2 / 2)
    bottom = ops.maximum(cy1 - h1 / 2, cy2 - h2 / 2)
    right = ops.minimum(cx1 + w1 / 2, cx2 + w2 / 2)
    top = ops.minimum(cy1 + h1 / 2, cy2 + h2 / 2)
    return ops.maximum(0.0, right - left) * ops.maximum(0.0, top - bottom)

def intersection_over_union(box1, box2):
    cx1, cy1, w1, h1 = unpack(box1)
    cx2, cy2, w2, h2 = unpack(box2)
    intersection_area = intersection(box1, box2)
    a1 = ops.maximum(w1, 0.0) * ops.maximum(h1, 0.0)
    a2 = ops.maximum(w2, 0.0) * ops.maximum(h2, 0.0)
    union_area = a1 + a2 - intersection_area
    return ops.divide_no_nan(intersection_area, union_area) Computes, element-wise over any leading axes, the IoU between two tensors of boxes given as (cx, cy, w, h, ...) on the last axis. Center/size -> edges -> clamped overlap -> areas -> inclusion-exclusion -> safe division.
snippet: Computes, element-wise over any leading axes, the IoU between two tensors of boxes given as cx, cy, w, h, ... on the last axis.

title: The YOLO box loss in code, and training the model
text:
Implementing the YOLO bounding-box loss with signed square root, IoU-based confidence targets and scaling factors (Listing 12.11), then compiling and fitting the model (Listing 12.12) box_loss splits targets and predictions into center, size and confidence; masks placement errors to occupied cells and weights them by 5; uses IoU as the confidence target in occupied cells and 0 in empty ones, down-weighting empty cells by 0.5; and returns one summed loss per image. The model is compiled with Adam(2e-4) and this loss plus sparse crossentropy, and trained for 4 epochs: over an hour on a free Colab GPU and still undertrained. **Listing 12.11** writes the YOLO bounding-box loss.

- `signed_sqrt(x) = sign(x) * sqrt(|x| + epsilon)`: a square root that preserves sign and avoids sqrt(0) issues.
- `box_loss(true, pred)` slices both tensors along the last axis into `xy` (channels 0-1), `wh` (2-3) and `conf` (4, kept as a length-1 axis) (callout: *Unpacks values*).
- `no_object = conf_true == 0.0` marks empty grid cells (callout: *If confidence_true is 0.0, there is no object in this grid cell*).
- Placement errors: squared center error, and squared error between signed square roots of widths/heights (callout: *Computes box placement errors*).
- Confidence: IoU between `true` and `pred` is the target where there is an object, 0 elsewhere; the error is squared (callout: *Computes confidence error*).
- The three error tensors are concatenated with the **scaling hacks**: placement errors x5 and zeroed in empty cells; confidence errors x0.5 in empty cells and x1 in occupied cells.
- `ops.sum(error, axis=(1, 2, 3))` sums over the 6 x 6 grid and the 5 error channels, returning **one loss value per sample**.

The text then notes that metrics are skipped purely to keep the example short; in a real setting you'd want several, such as accuracy at different confidence cutoffs.

**Listing 12.12** compiles the model with `Adam(2e-4)` and `loss={"box": box_loss, "class": "sparse_categorical_crossentropy"}`, then fits on `train_dataset` with `val_dataset` for **4 epochs**.

Training takes **over an hour on the free Colab GPU**, and the model is **still undertrained**: validation loss is still falling. The next step is visualizing a prediction (figure 12.6) with a **low confidence cutoff**, because the model is not yet a good detector. box_loss slices targets/predictions into centers, sizes and confidence and masks by conf_true == 0. Placement errors are x5 and only in occupied cells; empty-cell confidence errors are x0.5. The confidence target is IoU(true, pred) in occupied cells and 0 elsewhere. Widths/heights are compared via signed square roots. The loss returns one value per image; Keras reduces over the batch. Training: Adam(2e-4), loss dict, 4 epochs, over an hour on free Colab, still undertrained.

title: Listing 12.11 Defining the YOLO bounding box loss
text:
def signed_sqrt(x):
    return ops.sign(x) * ops.sqrt(ops.absolute(x) + keras.config.epsilon())

def box_loss(true, pred):
    xy_true, wh_true, conf_true = true[..., :2], true[..., 2:4], true[..., 4:]
    xy_pred, wh_pred, conf_pred = pred[..., :2], pred[..., 2:4], pred[..., 4:]
    no_object = conf_true == 0.0
    xy_error = ops.square(xy_true - xy_pred)
    wh_error = ops.square(signed_sqrt(wh_true) - signed_sqrt(wh_pred))
    iou = intersection_over_union(true, pred)
    conf_target = ops.where(no_object, 0.0, ops.expand_dims(iou, -1))
    conf_error = ops.square(conf_target - conf_pred)
    error = ops.concatenate(
        (
            ops.where(no_object, 0.0, xy_error * 5.0),
            ops.where(no_object, 0.0, wh_error * 5.0),
            ops.where(no_object, conf_error * 0.5, conf_error),
        ),
        axis=-1,
    )
    return ops.sum(error, axis=(1, 2, 3)) Computes the YOLO box loss for a batch: masked and scaled squared errors of centers, square-rooted sizes and IoU-targeted confidences, summed into one value per image. Split -> mask -> per-component squared error -> IoU-based target -> weighted select -> concatenate -> sum.
snippet: Computes the YOLO box loss for a batch: masked and scaled squared errors of centers, square-rooted sizes and IoU-targeted confidences, summed into one value per image.

title: Visualizing the trained YOLO model's predictions
text:
Running the trained YOLO model on one validation image, converting its outputs (boxes and per-cell argmax labels) and drawing predictions above a confidence cutoff (Listing 12.13, figure 12.6) After 4 epochs the model already places a plausible box around the giraffe and labels the right grid cells, but with only 0.16 confidence. A cutoff of 0.1 shows that one box; cutoff=None shows every box the model predicts (figure 12.7 on the next page). **Listing 12.13** (captioned, somewhat confusingly, "Training the YOLO model") inspects the trained model on one image:

1. `val_dataset.rebatch(1)` re-splits the validation batches of 16 into batches of 1, and `next(iter(...))` takes the first: an image tensor `x` of shape (1, 448, 448, 3) and its targets `y` (callout: *Rebatches our dataset to get a single sample instead of 16*).
2. `model.predict(x)` returns a dict; `preds["box"][0]` is the (6, 6, 5) box grid of that image.
3. `np.argmax(preds["class"][0], axis=-1)` turns the (6, 6, 91) softmax into a (6, 6) map of the most likely label per cell (callout: *Uses argmax to find the most likely label at each grid location*).
4. `path = metadata[0]["path"]`: because the validation set is the first 500 batches in metadata order, the first validation sample is `metadata[0]`. The original file is reloaded so the image can be viewed at full size (callout).
5. `draw_prediction(path, boxes, classes, cutoff=0.1)` shades grid cells by predicted class and draws only boxes with confidence at least 0.1.

A block of cells around the giraffe is shaded in one class color, and a single box labeled **"giraffe 0.16"** frames the animal reasonably well. The text concludes that the model is *starting to understand box locations and class labels, though it is still not very accurate*.

To see everything the model outputs, the page calls `draw_prediction(path, boxes, classes, cutoff=None)`, which draws **every** predicted box, even those with zero confidence; the result is figure 12.7 on p.370. rebatch(1) + next(iter(...)) pulls a single validation image. Boxes come out as a (6, 6, 5) grid; labels come from argmax over 91 classes per cell. draw_prediction shows boxes with confidence >= cutoff; None shows all. After 4 epochs the model boxes the giraffe correctly but with confidence only 0.16. The model is starting to learn locations and labels but is not yet accurate.

title: Feature pyramid networks: how RetinaNet handles small and large objects
text:
The scale problem of detecting from the final ConvNet features only, and RetinaNet's solution: a feature pyramid network (FPN) that upsamples deep features and sums them with same-size earlier features through lateral connections Final ConvNet features are semantically rich but coarse, so they miss small objects; early features are fine-grained but semantically weak. An FPN upsamples the deep features step by step and adds, through lateral connections, the same-size maps from the backbone, producing feature maps that are both semantically meaningful and high-resolution at several scales. The page completes the sentence from p.370: the biggest conceptual difference between the book's YOLO model and **RetinaNet** is that RetinaNet **uses its ConvNet differently to handle small and large objects simultaneously**.

**The problem.** The YOLO model used only the **final outputs** of the ConvNet (a 14 x 14 x 2048 ResNet map for a 448 x 448 image, p.363). Each of these features corresponds to a large area of the input, so they are **not very effective at finding small objects**.

**A naive fix and why it fails.** One could use the outputs of **earlier layers**, which are high-resolution and map to small, localized areas. But early features are **not very semantically interesting**: they respond to simple patterns such as edges and curves; only later layers build latent representations of whole objects.

**The FPN solution.** RetinaNet uses a **feature pyramid network**. The final backbone features are **upsampled with progressive `Conv2DTranspose` layers**, as in the segmentation model of chapter 11, and, critically, **lateral connections** **sum** each upsampled map with the backbone feature map **of the same size**. This combines semantically rich, low-resolution deep features with high-resolution, small-scale early features.

**Figure 12.8** sketches this: on the left an image and a stack of shrinking backbone feature maps (bottom-up, arrows upward); on the right a stack of growing maps (top-down, arrows downward); horizontal arrows link same-level maps (lateral connections); and each right-hand level emits its own output arrow, meaning predictions are made at several scales.

FPNs **substantially boost performance** for objects of both small and large pixel footprint, and **recent YOLO versions use the same setup**.

The page then turns to practice: try the pretrained RetinaNet, also trained on **COCO**, on an **out-of-distribution** image, Seurat's pointillist painting *A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte*, starting by downloading it and converting it to a NumPy array (code on p.372). The book's YOLO detects only from final ConvNet features, which cover large input areas and miss small objects. Early-layer features are high-resolution but only capture edges and curves. An FPN upsamples deep features with Conv2DTranspose and sums them with same-size backbone maps via lateral connections. The result: semantically meaningful feature maps at several scales, each used for prediction. FPNs substantially help with both small and large objects; recent YOLOs use them too. The pretrained, COCO-trained RetinaNet will be tested on an out-of-distribution pointillist painting.
snippet: The page completes the sentence from p.370: the biggest conceptual difference between the book's YOLO model and RetinaNet is that RetinaNet uses its ConvNet differently to handle…

title: Feature pyramid network (FPN)
text: An architecture that turns a backbone's multi-resolution features into a pyramid of semantically strong maps by top-down upsampling and lateral summation with same-size backbone maps. Pass the big-picture understanding from the top of the network back down to the detailed layers, so every resolution knows what it's looking at. Bottom-up: backbone stages with decreasing resolution. Top-down: upsample (Conv2DTranspose in the book's description) and add the lateral backbone map of equal size. Each level feeds a detection head. With a 448 x 448 input and a ResNet (beyond the book's figures): backbone maps at 56 x 56, 28 x 28 and 14 x 14 produce pyramid levels at those same resolutions.
snippet: An architecture that turns a backbone's multi-resolution features into a pyramid of semantically strong maps by top-down upsampling and lateral summation with same-size backbone…

title: Lateral connection
text: A connection that sums an upsampled top-down feature map with the backbone feature map of the same size. A side door letting fine detail from the way up join the semantic information on the way down. Requires matching spatial size (and, beyond the book, matching channels via a 1 x 1 conv). Upsampled 14 x 14 -> 28 x 28 map + backbone 28 x 28 map.
snippet: A connection that sums an upsampled top-down feature map with the backbone feature map of the same size.

title: Resolution vs. semantics trade-off
text: In a ConvNet, early layers have high spatial resolution but low-level features; later layers have rich semantics but low resolution. Close-up eyes see detail but not meaning; far-away eyes see meaning but not detail. Downsampling grows receptive fields and abstraction while shrinking feature maps (p.265). Edges and curves in early layers vs. object representations in later layers.
snippet: In a ConvNet, early layers have high spatial resolution but low-level features; later layers have rich semantics but low resolution.

title: RetinaNet
text: A single-stage detector that uses an FPN over its ConvNet backbone; used pretrained on COCO in section 12.3. YOLO-like detection, but looking at several zoom levels at once. Predictions are made from each pyramid level. Tested on A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.

title: Running a pretrained RetinaNet with KerasHub
text:
Downloading an out-of-distribution test image (Seurat's pointillist painting), instantiating a COCO-pretrained RetinaNet through the KerasHub ObjectDetector task API with a chosen bounding-box format, inspecting the structure of its predictions, and starting the drawing loop of Listing 12.15. A pretrained single-stage detector can be loaded and run in three lines with `keras_hub.models.ObjectDetector.from_preset(...)`; asking for boxes in the same `rel_xywh` format used for the YOLO model lets you reuse the chapter's drawing utilities, and the model returns a fixed-size set of 100 candidate detections (boxes, confidences, labels) plus a count of how many are valid. The page puts the pretrained **RetinaNet** detector to work on a deliberately unusual test image: Georges Seurat's pointillist painting *A Sunday on La Grande Jatte* (1884), chosen on p.371 because it is out-of-distribution for a model trained on COCO photographs.

1. **Getting the image.** A Wikimedia URL for a 1280-pixel-wide version of the painting is downloaded with `keras.utils.get_file`, loaded with `keras.utils.load_img`, and wrapped in a list before `np.array(...)`, which adds a **batch axis** so the array has shape `(1, height, width, 3)`.
2. **Listing 12.14 — creating the detector.** As with the segmentation model in the previous chapter, the high-level KerasHub **task API** is used: `keras_hub.models.ObjectDetector.from_preset("retinanet_resnet50_fpn_v2_coco", bounding_box_format="rel_xywh")`. The task object bundles preprocessing, so `detector.predict(image)` works directly on raw pixels.
3. **Bounding-box format.** Most Keras models and layers that handle boxes accept a `bounding_box_format`. Choosing `"rel_xywh"` makes RetinaNet output boxes in the same convention as the YOLO model, so the existing drawing functions can be reused. `rel` means coordinates are **relative to the image size**, in $[0, 1]$.
4. **The outputs.** `predictions` is a dict of four arrays: `boxes` of shape `(1, 100, 4)`, `confidence` `(1, 100)`, `labels` `(1, 100)`, and `num_detections` `(1,)`. The structure resembles the YOLO model's outputs (box, confidence, class). The model returns at most **100 detections per image**; the first box printed is `[0.53, 0.00, 0.81, 0.29]`.
5. **Listing 12.15 begins.** A Matplotlib figure is created at 300 dpi, the painting is drawn with `draw_image`, `num_detections` is read from the predictions, and a loop over `range(num_detections)` starts; its body (drawing each labeled box) and the resulting figure 12.9 are on p.373.

The overall lesson: with a hub preset, a state-of-the-art detector is three lines of code, and the main things you must get right are the box format and how to read the padded output. A pretrained detector is three lines with KerasHub: from_preset, then predict on a batched image; preprocessing is included. Always set bounding_box_format to the convention your downstream code expects; rel_xywh means fractions of image width/height in [0, 1]. RetinaNet returns a padded set of 100 detections (boxes, confidence, labels) plus num_detections; only the first num_detections entries are real. The output structure mirrors the YOLO model's box/confidence/class outputs. The test image is a pointillist painting, chosen to probe out-of-distribution generalization.

title: RetinaNet
text: A single-stage object detector that uses a ConvNet backbone (here ResNet-50) with a feature pyramid network to predict boxes and classes at multiple scales in one pass. Like YOLO, it looks at the whole image once; unlike the chapter's YOLO, it makes predictions from several feature-map resolutions so both small and large objects are found. Preset `retinanet_resnet50_fpn_v2_coco`: ResNet-50 backbone, FPN neck, trained on COCO. Beyond the book: the original RetinaNet paper (Lin et al., 2017) also introduced the focal loss to deal with the huge imbalance between background and object anchors; the book does not discuss it on this page. Run on Seurat's painting, it finds people, umbrellas and dogs (figure 12.9, p.373).
snippet: A single-stage object detector that uses a ConvNet backbone here ResNet-50 with a feature pyramid network to predict boxes and classes at multiple scales in one pass.

title: Bounding-box format
text: The convention used to encode a rectangle with four numbers, e.g. corners (xyxy), top-left plus size (xywh), centre plus size, in pixels or relative to the image. The same box can be written many ways, like a date in different calendars; all code that touches boxes must agree on one. Keras models and layers that support boxes take `bounding_box_format`; `"rel_xywh"` means $(x, y, w, h)$ with each coordinate divided by the image width or height. A box with top-left (320, 0), size 256×215 in a 1280×860 image is `rel_xywh` ≈ (0.25, 0.0, 0.2, 0.25).
snippet: The convention used to encode a rectangle with four numbers, e.g. corners xyxy, top-left plus size xywh, centre plus size, in pixels or relative to the image.

title: KerasHub task API (ObjectDetector)
text: High-level KerasHub model classes that package a pretrained backbone, a task head and preprocessing, created with `from_preset`. A ready-to-use appliance instead of a kit of parts. `keras_hub.models.ObjectDetector.from_preset(name, bounding_box_format=...)` returns a Keras model whose `predict` accepts raw images and returns a dict of post-processed detections. `detector.predict(image)` on a `(1, H, W, 3)` uint8 array.
snippet: High-level KerasHub model classes that package a pretrained backbone, a task head and preprocessing, created with frompreset.

title: Padded detection outputs and num_detections
text: Returning a fixed maximum number of detections per image (here 100) plus a count of how many are valid. A form with 100 lines where only the first few are filled in; `num_detections` tells you where to stop reading. Shapes: boxes (batch, 100, 4), confidence (batch, 100), labels (batch, 100), num_detections (batch,). Beyond the book: the fixed-size list typically results from non-max suppression with a cap of 100 outputs. If `num_detections[0]` is 12, only `boxes[0][:12]` are real.
snippet: Returning a fixed maximum number of detections per image here 100 plus a count of how many are valid.

title: Relative box coordinates
text: "rel_xywh" ... rel stands for relative to the image size (e.g., from [0, 1]) (x_{rel},\, y_{rel},\, w_{rel},\, h_{rel}) = \left(\frac{x}{W},\ \frac{y}{H},\ \frac{w}{W},\ \frac{h}{H}\right) \in [0,1]^4 Make box coordinates independent of image resolution, matching the unit-square canvas of draw_image. A relative width of 0.5 means the box spans half the image width, whatever its pixel size. x, y pixel coordinates of the box's top-left corner (as used by the chapter's draw_box) w, h box width and height in pixels W, H image width and height in pixels

title: RetinaNet on a pointillist painting; end of the vision chapters
text:
The loop body of Listing 12.15 that draws each RetinaNet detection, figure 12.9 with the detections on Seurat's painting, why single-stage detectors generalize to such out-of-distribution inputs better than two-stage R-CNNs, and the close of the book's computer-vision section. The COCO-trained RetinaNet correctly finds people, umbrellas and dogs in a pointillist painting it never saw in training; the authors attribute this robustness to single-stage detectors using features from the whole image, while two-stage detectors must classify small patches in isolation, which look very different from photographs at the pixel level. The page opens with the **end of Listing 12.15** (started on p.372). Inside the loop over the `num_detections` valid detections, each iteration reads the box `predictions["boxes"][0][i]` and label `predictions["labels"][0][i]`, converts the integer COCO id into a readable name with `keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name`, and calls `draw_box(ax, box, label_name, label_to_color(label))`; `plt.show()` displays the result.

Each class has its own colour from `label_to_color`.

The authors draw a lesson: RetinaNet **generalizes to a pointillist painting with ease** despite never being trained on that style. They see this as an advantage of **single-stage** detectors. Paintings and photographs differ greatly **at the pixel level** but share **similar high-level structure**. A **two-stage** R-CNN must classify small patches of the image **in isolation**, which is especially hard when those patches look unlike the training data, whereas a single-stage detector can draw on **features from the entire input**, making it more robust to novel inputs.

The final paragraph closes the **computer-vision section** of the book: the reader has trained image classifiers, segmenters and object detectors from scratch and built intuition for ConvNets, 'the first major success of the deep learning era'. title: Chapter 12 summary: object detection
text:
The end-of-chapter summary of chapter 12: what object detection is, two-stage R-CNNs vs. single-stage detectors, YOLO's two outputs (boxes with IoU-trained confidences, and a class probability map), and RetinaNet's feature pyramid network. Object detection locates objects with bounding boxes, a cheaper relative of segmentation; detectors are either two-stage (propose then classify) or single-stage (both at once, faster); YOLO pairs each box with a confidence trained toward IoU plus a class map, and RetinaNet adds a feature pyramid network to handle objects of different sizes. This is the **summary of chapter 12**, four bullet points:

- **What detection is.** Object detection identifies and locates objects in an image with **bounding boxes**. The authors call it 'basically a weaker version of image segmentation' — a box is a coarse stand-in for a pixel mask — 'but one that can be run much more efficiently'.
- **Two families.** *Region-based ConvNets (R-CNNs)* are **two-stage**: they first propose regions of interest, then classify each with a ConvNet. *Single-stage detectors* such as **RetinaNet and YOLO** do both in one step; they are generally **faster and more efficient**, which suits real-time applications such as self-driving cars.
- **YOLO's outputs.** YOLO computes two outputs at once during training: candidate **bounding boxes**, each paired with a **confidence score trained to target the Intersection over Union (IoU)** between the predicted and ground-truth box, and a **class probability map** that classifies image regions as belonging to different objects.
- **RetinaNet and FPNs.** RetinaNet builds on this with a **feature pyramid network**, combining features from multiple ConvNet layers into feature maps at different scales, so it detects objects of different sizes more accurately.

Together these bullets trace the chapter's path: the task (12.1), a from-scratch YOLO (12.2), and a pretrained RetinaNet (12.3). Object detection = boxes + labels; a coarser but much cheaper relative of segmentation. R-CNNs are two-stage (propose, then classify); YOLO and RetinaNet are single-stage and generally faster. YOLO outputs boxes with confidences trained toward IoU, plus a class probability map. RetinaNet's feature pyramid network fuses features from several layers to detect objects of different sizes.
snippet: This is the summary of chapter 12, four bullet points: - What detection is. Object detection identifies and locates objects in an image with bounding boxes. The authors call it…

title: Object detection
text: Identifying and locating objects in an image with labeled bounding boxes. Drawing a labeled rectangle around each thing of interest. Outputs a variable-length set of (box, class, score) triples per image. Figure 12.9's persons, umbrellas and dogs (p.373).

title: Intersection over Union (IoU)
text: Overlap area of two regions divided by the area of their union. How much two boxes agree, from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (identical). Used in YOLO as the regression target for the box confidence score. Two 2×2 boxes offset by 1 unit horizontally: intersection 2, union 6, IoU = 1/3.

title: Feature pyramid network (FPN)
text: A neck architecture combining features from several ConvNet depths into multi-scale feature maps. Give every resolution level the 'understanding' of the deepest layers. Top-down pathway with upsampling plus lateral additions of backbone feature maps of matching size (p.371). RetinaNet preset retinanet_resnet50_fpn_v2_coco.

title: Chapter 13 opener: Timeseries forecasting
text:
Opening of chapter 13: what the chapter covers (machine learning for timeseries, recurrent neural networks, a temperature-forecasting example), a short introduction to forecasting, and the start of section 13.1 defining a timeseries. Timeseries are data where temporal order is everything; the chapter focuses on forecasting — using the recent past to predict the near future — and introduces recurrent neural networks through a temperature-forecasting example. This is the **opening page of chapter 13, Timeseries forecasting**. The 'This chapter covers' box lists three topics:

- an overview of **machine learning for timeseries**;
- understanding **recurrent neural networks (RNNs)**;
- applying RNNs to a **temperature forecasting example**.

The introduction says the chapter tackles timeseries, 'where temporal order is everything', and focuses on the most common and valuable timeseries task, **forecasting**: using the recent past to predict the near future, e.g. to anticipate energy demand, manage inventory or forecast the weather.

**Section 13.1, Different kinds of timeseries tasks**, begins by defining a *timeseries* as any data obtained via **measurements at regular intervals** — the daily price of a stock, a city's hourly electricity consumption, a store's weekly sales. Timeseries appear in natural phenomena (seismic activity, fish populations in a river, the weather at a location) and in human activity (website visitors, a country's GDP, credit card transactions). The final sentence, 'Unlike the types of data you’ve encountered so far,' continues on p.376, where the authors explain that working with timeseries means understanding a system's *dynamics*.

How to use this page: treat it as a roadmap. The chapter builds the Jena weather dataset (p.376–382), sets a commonsense baseline (p.383), tries dense and 1D-convolutional models (p.384–387), and then develops RNNs, recurrent dropout, stacking and bidirectional RNNs (p.388–402). Chapter 13 covers ML for timeseries, RNNs and a temperature-forecasting example. A timeseries is data measured at regular intervals; temporal order is everything. The chapter focuses on forecasting: predicting the near future from the recent past.

title: Kinds of timeseries tasks and the Jena temperature-forecasting problem
text:
What makes timeseries different (system dynamics), forecasting and three other timeseries tasks (anomaly detection, classification, event detection), and the definition of the chapter's running problem: predicting temperature 24 hours ahead from the Jena Climate dataset. Working with timeseries means understanding a system's dynamics; forecasting is the most common task, alongside anomaly detection, classification and event detection; the chapter will predict temperature 24 hours ahead from hourly multivariate sensor data recorded in Jena, a challenging problem used to show why dense and convolutional networks fall short and RNNs shine. The page completes the definition from p.375: unlike earlier data types, working with timeseries involves understanding the **dynamics** of a system — its **periodic cycles**, how it **trends** over time, its **regular regime**, and its **sudden spikes**.

**Forecasting** — predicting what happens next — is 'by far' the most common timeseries task: electricity consumption hours ahead to anticipate demand, revenue months ahead to plan a budget, weather days ahead to plan a schedule. It is the chapter's focus, but the authors list three other tasks:

- **Anomaly detection**: spotting anything unusual in a continuous stream (an attacker on a corporate network, odd readings on a manufacturing line). It is typically **unsupervised**, because you often do not know what kind of anomaly to expect and so cannot train on labeled anomaly examples.
- **Classification**: assigning one or more categorical labels to a timeseries, e.g. deciding from a visitor's activity whether they are a **bot or a human**.
- **Event detection**: identifying a specific, expected event in a stream — notably **hotword detection** ('OK, Google', 'Hey, Alexa') in audio.

The chapter will teach **recurrent neural networks (RNNs)** for forecasting.

**Section 13.2** defines the running problem: **predict the temperature 24 hours in the future**, given a timeseries of **hourly** measurements (atmospheric pressure, humidity and more) from rooftop sensors over the recent past — 'a fairly challenging problem'. The task will show what makes timeseries fundamentally different, that **dense and convolutional networks are not well equipped** for it, and that **RNNs really shine** on it.

The data is the **Jena Climate dataset** from the weather station of the Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry in Jena, Germany (footnote: Adam Erickson and Olaf Kolle). **14 quantities** (temperature, pressure, humidity, wind direction, …) were recorded **every 10 minutes** for years; the data goes back to 2003, but the downloaded subset covers **2009–2016**. The download commands follow on p.377. Timeseries work is about a system's dynamics: cycles, trends, regular regime, spikes. Forecasting is the most common task; others are anomaly detection (usually unsupervised), classification and event detection (e.g. hotwords). The chapter's single problem: predict temperature 24 hours ahead from hourly multivariate sensor data. The Jena dataset has 14 quantities every 10 minutes; the subset used covers 2009–2016. The task is designed to show the limits of dense and convolutional networks and the strength of RNNs.

title: Downloading and inspecting the Jena weather data
text:
Downloading the Jena Climate CSV, reading it into lines and a header (Listing 13.1), the 15 column names and the 420,551 records, and the start of Listing 13.2, which parses the data into NumPy arrays. The raw dataset is a CSV with a 'Date Time' column plus 14 weather quantities, one row per 10-minute timestep, 420,551 rows; it will be parsed into a temperature array (the target) and an array of features, discarding the timestamp. The page starts with two notebook shell commands: `!wget` fetches `jena_climate_2009_2016.csv.zip` from the Keras datasets S3 bucket and `!unzip` extracts the CSV.

**Listing 13.1** inspects the data with plain Python: open `jena_climate_2009_2016.csv`, read the whole file into a string, split it into lines on `"\n"`, split the first line on commas to get the **header**, keep the remaining lines as data, and print the header and the number of lines.

The output is **420,551 lines** — each line is one **timestep**: a date plus **14 weather-related values** — and a header with 15 names: `"Date Time"`, `"p (mbar)"` (pressure), `"T (degC)"` (temperature), `"Tpot (K)"` (potential temperature), `"Tdew (degC)"` (dew point), `"rh (%)"` (relative humidity), `"VPmax (mbar)"`, `"VPact (mbar)"`, `"VPdef (mbar)"` (saturation, actual and deficit vapour pressure), `"sh (g/kg)"` (specific humidity), `"H2OC (mmol/mol)"` (water vapour concentration), `"rho (g/m**3)"` (air density), `"wv (m/s)"` and `"max. wv (m/s)"` (wind speed and maximum wind speed), and `"wd (deg)"` (wind direction). (The expansions of the abbreviations are ours; the page shows only the names.)

Next, all 420,551 lines are to be converted into **NumPy arrays**: one for the **temperature in degrees Celsius** (the target), and one for 'the rest of the data' — the features used to predict future temperatures. The **"Date Time" column is discarded**. **Listing 13.2** begins here with `import numpy as np` and `temperature = np.zeros((len(lines),))`; the allocation of `raw_data` and the parsing loop are on p.378 (where, note, `raw_data` keeps all 14 values, temperature included). The Jena CSV has a Date Time column plus 14 weather quantities; 420,551 data rows, one per 10 minutes over 8 years. Listing 13.1 reads it with plain Python: split lines, split the header, drop it from the data. The date is discarded; temperature (°C, index 1 after dropping the date) becomes the target array. Listing 13.2 starts by preallocating temperature with np.zeros((len(lines),)); the rest is on p.378. The code keeps temperature among the features as well, which is legitimate because the target lies 24 hours in the future.

title: Parsing the Jena data and plotting the temperature
text:
Finishing the CSV-to-NumPy parsing of the Jena climate dataset and taking a first look at the temperature timeseries at two timescales (full eight years and first 10 days). Each of the 420,551 CSV lines becomes one row of a (420551, 14) float array plus one entry of a temperature vector; plotting that vector reveals a strong yearly cycle, and zooming to 1,440 points (10 days at 144 points per day) sets up the look at daily cycles. This page completes **Listing 13.2** (begun on p.377) and adds two quick exploratory plots.

**Parsing.** After `temperature = np.zeros((len(lines),))` on p.377, the code allocates `raw_data = np.zeros((len(lines), len(header) - 1))`, a 420,551 x 14 array: one row per timestep and one column per weather quantity, the `-1` removing the "Date Time" column. The loop then walks over every line, splits it on commas, drops the first field (the date string) with `[1:]`, and converts the remaining 14 fields to floats. Column 1 of those values, which is `T (degC)` in the header of p.377, is stored in `temperature[i]`; the full list of 14 values, temperature included, is stored in row `i` of `raw_data`, as the two callouts say.

**Full-range plot.** Listing 13.3 imports `pyplot` and plots `temperature` against its index. Figure 13.1 shows values from roughly -20 to about 35 degrees Celsius with eight clear yearly humps: the data covers eight years (2009 to 2016, p.376). The x axis is the timestep index, not a date.

**First 10 days.** Because one record is taken every 10 minutes, a day contains $24 \times 6 = 144$ records, so 10 days are $1{,}440$ records. Listing 13.4 plots `temperature[:1440]`; that plot (Figure 13.2) is on p.379, where the book discusses daily periodicity.

Note: the text calls the figures "Figure 10.1" and "Figure 10.2", while the captions say Figure 13.1 and 13.2. The numbers seem to be left over from the previous edition. Listing 13.2 produces raw_data of shape (420551, 14) (all non-date columns, including temperature) and temperature of shape (420551,). values[1] after dropping the date is T (degC), the forecasting target. Figure 13.1 shows a clear yearly cycle repeated eight times, from about -20 to 35 degC. Sampling every 10 minutes gives 6 records per hour, 144 per day and 1,440 per 10 days. Always plot a timeseries at several timescales before modeling it. The text's 'Figure 10.1/10.2' refers to Figures 13.1/13.2.

title: Daily periodicity and a chronological data split
text:
Reading the 10-day temperature plot, the general importance of multi-timescale periodicity, why day-scale forecasting is hard, and splitting the data chronologically into 50% train, 25% validation, 25% test. Timeseries show cycles at several timescales; the yearly cycle makes long-horizon averages easy to predict, but day-scale temperature is chaotic. Because the task is to predict the future from the past, the validation and test sets must come after the training data in time. **Figure 13.2** is the output of Listing 13.4 (p.378): the first 1,440 ten-minute records, i.e. the first 10 days of January 2009. The temperature stays between about -22 and 0 degC. The book points out the **daily periodicity**, which is clearest in the last four days (the regular peaks and troughs after timestep ~900, about 144 steps apart), and concludes that the period must come from a fairly cold winter month. Before that, the curve shows a multi-day warm spell and a sharp cold drop, which are weather events rather than daily cycles.

A **NOTE** generalizes: periodicity over several timescales is very common in timeseries. Weather, mall parking, website traffic, grocery sales and fitness-tracker steps all show daily and yearly cycles, and human-generated data often also has weekly cycles. Look for these patterns when exploring data.

The book then frames the challenge. Predicting next month's *average* temperature from a few months of data would be easy because of the reliable yearly cycle, but at the scale of days the series looks much more chaotic. The question for the rest of the chapter is whether it is predictable at a daily scale.

Finally, the **split**: in all experiments, the first 50% of the timeline is training data, the next 25% validation and the last 25% test. Validation and test data must be **more recent** than training data, because the goal is to predict the future from the past, and the evaluation should reflect that ordering. The book adds that some problems become considerably simpler if the time axis is reversed. **Listing 13.5** computes the sizes with `int(0.5 * len(raw_data))` and `int(0.25 * len(raw_data))`, giving the test set the remainder; the print statements and their output (210,225 / 105,112 / 105,114) are on p.380. Figure 13.2 (first 10 days, a cold January) shows daily cycles most clearly in the last four days, on top of large irregular weather swings. Timeseries commonly have daily and yearly cycles; human-generated data often adds weekly cycles. Look for them during exploration. Month-scale average temperature is easy to predict from the yearly cycle; 24-hour-ahead temperature is much harder. The chapter uses a chronological 50% / 25% / 25% train/validation/test split, with evaluation data always more recent than training data. Listing 13.5 gives the test set the remainder so the three sizes add up exactly to len(raw_data).

title: Normalizing the data and planning the dataset
text:
The split sizes, the exact forecasting problem (five days of hourly data to predict the temperature 24 hours later), per-feature normalization with training-set statistics, and the plan to generate overlapping windows on the fly with timeseries_dataset_from_array(). Each of the 14 feature series is standardized with the mean and standard deviation of the first 210,225 timesteps only. Training samples are overlapping windows of the series, so they are generated lazily from raw_data and temperature instead of being materialized. The page opens with the end of **Listing 13.5**: printing the split sizes gives `num_train_samples: 210225`, `num_val_samples: 105112` and `num_test_samples: 105114`.

**Section 13.2.1** states the exact problem: *given data covering the previous five days and sampled once per hour, can we predict the temperature in 24 hours?*

Preprocessing is simple because the data is already numerical, so no vectorization is needed. But the 14 series have very different scales. Atmospheric pressure, in mbar, is around 1,000, while H2OC, in millimoles per mole, is around 3. Each series is therefore **normalized independently** so that all of them take small values on a similar scale. Since the first 210,225 timesteps are the training data, the **mean and standard deviation are computed only on that fraction**. **Listing 13.6** does this in place: `mean = raw_data[:num_train_samples].mean(axis=0)`, subtract it, then compute `std` on the same slice and divide by it. `axis=0` gives one statistic per column (feature). Note that only `raw_data` is normalized; the `temperature` target array stays in degrees Celsius, so errors later on (MAE) are measured in degrees.

Next, the book plans a `Dataset` that yields batches of five-day windows with a target temperature 24 hours in the future. Samples are **highly redundant**: sample `N` and sample `N + 1` share most of their timesteps. Allocating every sample explicitly would waste memory, so samples are generated **on the fly**, and only `raw_data` and `temperature` are kept in memory. You could write a Python generator for this, but Keras has a built-in utility, `timeseries_dataset_from_array()`, that can be used for any timeseries forecasting task.

The sidebar **"Understanding timeseries_dataset_from_array()"** begins: you provide an array of timeseries data (the `data` argument) and the function returns windows extracted from it, called "sequences". The worked example is on p.381. The split sizes are 210,225 / 105,112 / 105,114 timesteps. Problem: from five days of hourly data, predict the temperature 24 hours later. Each of the 14 features is standardized independently, with the mean and std computed only on the training timesteps. Listing 13.6 normalizes raw_data in place; the temperature target array stays in degC. Overlapping windows are generated on the fly with keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array instead of being stored.

title: How timeseries_dataset_from_array builds windows and targets
text:
A toy example of keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array with integers 0-9, how to align a targets array by offsetting it, and the parameter values for the Jena datasets: sampling_rate = 6, sequence_length = 120 and delay = sampling_rate * (sequence_length + 24 - 1). The utility slides a window of sequence_length steps along data and pairs the window starting at data[N] with targets[N]. To forecast k steps after the start, pass targets as the same series shifted by k. For Jena, keeping one point per hour over 120 hours and shifting targets by 858 raw steps gives the temperature 24 hours after the window ends. The sidebar on `timeseries_dataset_from_array()` (begun on p.380) gives a concrete example. With `data = [0 1 2 3 4 5 6]` and `sequence_length=3`, the generated samples are `[0 1 2]`, `[1 2 3]`, `[2 3 4]`, `[3 4 5]`, `[4 5 6]`: every window of three consecutive steps, sliding by one.

You can also pass a **targets** array. Its **first entry must be the desired target for the first sequence**. For forecasting, simply pass the same series as `data`, **offset** by some amount. To predict the next step after a 3-step window, use `targets = [3 4 5 6 ...]`.

The code builds `int_sequence = np.arange(10)` (sorted integers 0-9), then calls `keras.utils.timeseries_dataset_from_array` with `data=int_sequence[:-3]` (sequences are sampled from `[0 1 2 3 4 5 6]`), `targets=int_sequence[3:]` (the target for the sequence starting at `data[N]` is `data[N + 3]`), `sequence_length=3` and `batch_size=2`. Iterating over the batches and printing each row gives

```
[0, 1, 2] 3
[1, 2, 3] 4
[2, 3, 4] 5
[3, 4, 5] 6
[4, 5, 6] 7
```

The book will use the utility to build three datasets (training, validation, test) with these parameters:

- `sampling_rate = 6`: keep one data point out of six, i.e. one per hour.
- `sequence_length = 120`: look back five days (120 hours).
- `delay = sampling_rate * (sequence_length + 24 - 1)`: the target is the temperature 24 hours after the end of the sequence.

Numerically, delay = 6 x 143 = 858 raw (10-minute) steps. A window starting at raw index $i$ ends at $i + 6 \times 119 = i + 714$, and its target is at $i + 858$, exactly 144 steps (24 hours) later. The `start_index`/`end_index` settings that confine each dataset to its split follow on p.382. timeseries_dataset_from_array slides a window of sequence_length steps (stride 1) along data; sequence N starts at data[N]. targets[N] is the label for sequence N; for forecasting, pass the same series shifted by the offset. Toy example: data = 0..6, targets = 3..9, length 3 gives [0,1,2] paired with 3, up to [4,5,6] with 7. Jena parameters: sampling_rate = 6 (hourly), sequence_length = 120 (five days), delay = 6 x (120 + 24 - 1) = 858 rows. The '- 1' makes the target exactly 24 hours after the last input hour.

title: Inspecting the dataset and the commonsense baseline
text:
Checking batch shapes (Listing 13.8), the purpose of commonsense baselines, the 'tomorrow equals today' baseline for 24-hour temperature forecasting, the MAE metric, and the start of the evaluation loop (Listing 13.9). Before training any model, establish a trivial, non-learning baseline that a model must beat to be useful. Since temperature is continuous and has a daily period, predicting that the temperature in 24 hours equals the current temperature is a strong baseline, evaluated with mean absolute error. The sentence from p.382 ends: because samples are shuffled, consecutive sequences in a batch (such as `samples[0]` and `samples[1]`) are not necessarily close in time.

**Listing 13.8** takes one batch from `train_dataset` and prints `samples shape: (256, 120, 14)` and `targets shape: (256,)`. That is 256 windows of 120 hourly steps with 14 features, plus 256 target temperatures.

**13.2.2 A commonsense, non-machine-learning baseline.** Before trying black-box deep learning models, try a simple commonsense approach. It is a **sanity check** and sets a **baseline you must beat** to show that more advanced models are useful. Such baselines help especially on new problems without a known solution. The classic example is an **imbalanced classification** task: with 90% class A and 10% class B, always predicting "A" gives 90% accuracy, so any learning-based model must beat 90%. Elementary baselines can be surprisingly hard to beat.

For the temperature series, two assumptions are safe: it is **continuous** (tomorrow's temperatures are likely close to today's) and **periodic with a daily period**. The commonsense prediction is therefore: *the temperature 24 hours from now equals the temperature right now*. It is evaluated with the **mean absolute error (MAE)**, `np.mean(np.abs(preds - targets))`, i.e. $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i |\hat{y}_i - y_i|$, in degrees Celsius.

**Listing 13.9** begins `evaluate_naive_method(dataset)`. It initializes a running sum of absolute errors (`total_abs_err = 0.0`) and a counter (`samples_seen = 0`), then loops over the dataset's `(samples, targets)` batches. The rest of the listing, on p.384, takes the last timestep's temperature feature of each sample, un-normalizes it with `std[1]` and `mean[1]`, accumulates the errors and returns their average. The results (2.44 degC validation, 2.62 degC test) are on p.384. Batches are (256, 120, 14) inputs and (256,) targets, and rows are not temporally ordered. Always establish a commonsense, non-learning baseline first: it is a sanity check and the bar to beat. On imbalanced classification, the majority-class rule's accuracy (for example 90%) is the bar. Jena baseline: the temperature 24 hours from now equals the temperature now, justified by continuity and the daily period. Evaluation metric: MAE = np.mean(np.abs(preds - targets)), in degC. Listing 13.9 accumulates absolute errors and sample counts over batches; it continues on p.384.

title: Commonsense (non-learning) baseline
text: A trivial, hand-specified prediction rule used as a reference score and sanity check before training models. If your expensive model can't beat a coin flip or 'same as yesterday', something is wrong. Classification: always predict the majority class (accuracy = its frequency). Forecasting: predict the value one period earlier; here, the current temperature for 24 hours later. 90% class A: always predicting A gives 90% accuracy.

title: Imbalanced classification
text: Classification where class frequencies differ greatly. Rare-event detection: most of the time nothing happens. The majority-class predictor reaches an accuracy equal to the majority class's frequency, without learning anything. 90% A / 10% B gives a 90% accuracy baseline.

title: Baseline MAE result and a first densely connected forecaster
text:
Finishing the commonsense-baseline evaluation (MAE 2.44 val / 2.62 test) and starting a small Flatten + Dense regression model trained with MSE and monitored with MAE The naive 'temperature in 24 hours equals temperature now' heuristic is off by about 2.5 °C on average; before trying expensive recurrent models, you should check whether a small, cheap densely connected network can beat that number. The page opens with the end of **Listing 13.9**, the evaluation loop for the commonsense baseline that began on p.383. For each batch, the prediction is the last temperature value in the input window, `samples[:, -1, 1]` (temperature is feature column 1, `-1` is the last timestep). Because the features were normalized earlier, the code un-normalizes it with `* std[1] + mean[1]` to get degrees Celsius. Absolute errors are summed over all samples and divided by the number of samples seen, giving the mean absolute error (MAE). The function is run on the validation and test datasets.

The result: a **validation MAE of 2.44 °C** and a **test MAE of 2.62 °C**. If you always assume the temperature 24 hours from now equals the current temperature, you are off by about two and a half degrees on average. The authors call this "not too bad" but not good enough for a forecasting service, and challenge the reader to beat it with deep learning.

**Section 13.2.3** then gives a methodological rule: just as you set a commonsense baseline before using ML, you should try *simple, cheap* ML models (such as small densely connected networks) before *complicated, computationally expensive* ones such as RNNs. That is how you make sure that any extra complexity is **legitimate and delivers real benefits**.

The page then describes **Listing 13.10**: a fully connected model that first **flattens** the `(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1])` input, i.e. `(120, 14)`, and passes it through two `Dense` layers, a hidden `Dense(16, activation="relu")` and an output `Dense(1)` with **no activation**, which is standard for regression. The loss is **mean squared error**, not MAE, because MSE is smooth around zero, which helps gradient descent. MAE is still tracked as a metric in `compile()`. The listing starts building a `callbacks` list containing a `ModelCheckpoint("jena_dense.keras", save_best_only=True)` callback that saves the best-performing model. The listing continues on p.385 with `compile()`, `fit()` and the test evaluation. The persistence baseline scores 2.44 °C validation MAE and 2.62 °C test MAE: the numbers to beat. `samples[:, -1, 1] * std[1] + mean[1]` is the last temperature of each window, converted back to °C. Try cheap ML models (small dense nets) before expensive ones (RNNs) so that added complexity has to justify itself. Listing 13.10: Flatten (120×14 → 1680) → Dense(16, relu) → Dense(1) with no activation for regression. Train with MSE (smooth near zero), monitor MAE (interpretable, comparable to the baseline). ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only=True keeps the best epoch's model in jena_dense.keras.

title: Commonsense (persistence) baseline
text: A non-learning forecast that predicts the temperature 24 hours ahead equals the most recent observed temperature. Weather is continuous and roughly periodic with a 24-hour cycle, so 'same time tomorrow ≈ now' is a reasonable guess. Implemented as `samples[:, -1, 1] * std[1] + mean[1]`; scored with MAE: 2.44 °C (val), 2.62 °C (test). If it is 12 °C now, the baseline predicts 12 °C for this time tomorrow.
snippet: A non-learning forecast that predicts the temperature 24 hours ahead equals the most recent observed temperature.

title: Mean absolute error
text: Average absolute difference between predictions and targets. 'On average, how many degrees am I off?' Computed incrementally here: sum of |preds − targets| over all batches divided by the number of samples seen. Errors of 1, −3, 2 °C give MAE = (1+3+2)/3 = 2 °C.
snippet: Average absolute difference between predictions and targets.

title: Mean squared error
text: Average squared difference between predictions and targets. Penalizes large errors much more than small ones, and its slope shrinks to zero as the error shrinks. Gradient w.r.t. a prediction is 2(ŷ − y)/N, which is continuous; MAE's gradient sign(ŷ − y)/N is discontinuous at 0. Errors 1, −3, 2 give MSE = (1+9+4)/3 ≈ 4.67 °C².
snippet: Average squared difference between predictions and targets.

title: Dense layer on flattened sequences
text: A fully connected layer applied to the flattened (timesteps × features) window. Each hidden unit computes one weighted sum over all 1,680 numbers of the window, ignoring that they are ordered in time. Dense(16) on 1,680 inputs has 1680·16 + 16 = 26,896 parameters; Dense(1) adds 17. Shape flow: (None, 120, 14) → Flatten → (None, 1680) → (None, 16) → (None, 1).
snippet: A fully connected layer applied to the flattened timesteps × features window.

title: ModelCheckpoint callback
text: A Keras callback that saves the model to disk during training. Keep a snapshot of the best epoch so overfitting in later epochs doesn't cost you. With `save_best_only=True` it overwrites `jena_dense.keras` only when the monitored quantity (by default `val_loss`) improves. If val loss is lowest at epoch 4, the file holds the epoch-4 weights after 10 epochs.
snippet: A Keras callback that saves the model to disk during training.

The persistence forecast: whatever the thermometer read last is the forecast. z_{i,-1,1} Normalized value of feature 1 (temperature) at the last timestep of sample i \sigma_1 Standard deviation of temperature over the training data (std[1]) \mu_1 Mean of temperature over the training data (mean[1]) \hat{T}_i Baseline prediction in °C for sample i

title: MSE loss versus MAE metric
text: We use mean squared error (MSE) as the loss, rather than MAE, because unlike MAE, it’s smooth around zero \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i(\hat y_i - y_i)^2,\qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}}{\partial \hat y_i} = \frac{2}{N}(\hat y_i - y_i),\qquad \frac{\partial\,\text{MAE}}{\partial \hat y_i} = \frac{1}{N}\operatorname{sign}(\hat y_i - y_i) Shows formally what 'smooth around zero' means. The MSE gradient fades as the error shrinks, giving gentle final steps; the MAE gradient keeps a constant magnitude and flips sign at zero error. \hat y_i Model prediction y_i Target temperature N Batch size

from keras import layers

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1]))
x = layers.Flatten()(inputs)
x = layers.Dense(16, activation="relu")(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(1)(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)

callbacks = [
    keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint("jena_dense.keras", save_best_only=True) Builds a Functional-API regression model Flatten → Dense(16, relu) → Dense(1) and begins a callbacks list with a ModelCheckpoint. title: Training the dense model and plotting its MAE curves
text:
Compiling, training, reloading and test-evaluating the densely connected Jena model, and plotting training versus validation MAE (Figure 13.3) The dense model is trained for 10 epochs with Adam and MSE loss while MAE is tracked. The best checkpoint is reloaded for testing, and Figure 13.3 shows training MAE falling to about 2.0 °C while validation MAE stays around 2.55–2.73 °C, never below the 2.44 °C baseline. The page finishes **Listing 13.10**. The `callbacks` list opened on p.384 is closed. The model is compiled with `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="mse"` and `metrics=["mae"]`, then trained with `model.fit(train_dataset, epochs=10, validation_data=val_dataset, callbacks=callbacks)`. The `ModelCheckpoint` callback saves the epoch with the best validation loss to `jena_dense.keras`. After training, the code **reloads that best model** with `keras.models.load_model` and prints the test MAE: `model.evaluate(test_dataset)` returns `[loss, mae]`, so index `[1]` is the MAE.

**Listing 13.11** plots the results with matplotlib. It reads `history.history["mae"]` and `history.history["val_mae"]`, builds an x-axis `range(1, len(loss) + 1)`, and plots training MAE as a red dashed line and validation MAE as a solid blue line. The variables are named `loss`/`val_loss` even though they hold MAE values.

**Figure 13.3** shows the result. Training MAE drops steeply from about 2.93 °C after epoch 1 to about 2.3 at epoch 2, then keeps declining to about 1.96 °C by epoch 10. Validation MAE starts around 2.57 °C, reaches its minimum of roughly 2.55 °C at epoch 3, and then drifts upward to about 2.7 °C. In other words, the model starts overfitting after only a few epochs. Even at its best it stays above the commonsense baseline's 2.44 °C validation MAE (p.384). The authors discuss this on the next page (p.386): the baseline is hard to beat, and gradient descent doesn't find the simple solution even though it exists in the hypothesis space. The dense model is compiled with Adam, MSE loss and an MAE metric, and trained for 10 epochs. The best checkpoint (by validation loss) is reloaded before the single test evaluation; evaluate()[1] is MAE. Listing 13.11 plots MAE (not loss) for training and validation. Even at its best, the dense model's validation MAE is above the 2.44 °C commonsense baseline.
