title: Why the dense model fails, and introducing 1D convnets
text:
The hypothesis-space explanation for why gradient descent misses the simple baseline solution, the importance of architecture priors, and the first lines of a Conv1D model with a 24-hour window A good simple solution existing in the hypothesis space doesn't mean gradient descent will find it. You must encode what to look for through feature engineering and architecture priors. A 1D convnet, built on the translation-invariance prior, is the next attempt. The page first interprets the dense model's results from Figure 13.3. Some validation losses come close to the no-learning baseline, **but not reliably**. This shows why the baseline was worth having: it is not easy to beat, because your common sense contains valuable information the model has no access to.

The authors then ask why the model doesn't simply *find* the commonsense solution and improve on it. The **hypothesis space** is the set of all two-layer networks with the defined configuration. The commonsense heuristic (copy the last temperature) is just one model among millions in that space, a *needle in a haystack*. A good solution that technically exists isn't necessarily reachable via **gradient descent**. They call this a significant limitation of machine learning in general: unless the learning algorithm is hardcoded to look for a specific kind of simple model, it can fail to find a simple solution to a simple problem. Hence the importance of **feature engineering** and **relevant architecture priors**: you must tell the model precisely what to look for.

**Section 13.2.4** applies this idea. The sequences have daily cycles, so a **temporal ConvNet** could reuse the same representations across different days, just as a 2D ConvNet reuses representations across image locations. Besides `Conv2D` and `SeparableConv2D`, Keras offers `Conv1D`, `SeparableConv1D` and `Conv3D`. A footnote adds that there is no `SeparableConv3D`, not for theoretical reasons but because it hasn't been implemented. `Conv1D` slides 1D windows over sequences and `Conv3D` slides cubic windows over volumes. 1D ConvNets suit sequence data that satisfies the **translation invariance assumption**: a window's content should have the same properties wherever the window is placed.

The model uses an initial window of **24** (one daily cycle of hourly data) and shrinks the window as `MaxPooling1D` downsamples the sequence. The page shows the first three lines: `Input(shape=(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1]))`, `Conv1D(8, 24, activation="relu")` and `MaxPooling1D(2)`. The rest of the model and its training follow on p.387. The dense model only sometimes gets close to the baseline: commonsense baselines are hard to beat. A good solution existing in the hypothesis space doesn't mean gradient descent will find it. Feature engineering and architecture priors tell the model what to look for. Conv1D, SeparableConv1D and Conv3D generalize 2D convolution to sequences and volumes; there is no SeparableConv3D only because it isn't implemented. 1D convnets assume translation invariance along time. The convnet starts with a 24-hour window (Conv1D(8, 24)) and shrinks kernels as MaxPooling1D halves the sequence.

title: Hypothesis space
text: The set of all models that the chosen architecture can represent. The haystack in which training searches for the needle. For Listing 13.10 it is all functions $x \mapsto W_2\,\mathrm{relu}(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2$ with $W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{16\times1680}$. Persistence is in the space but occupies a minuscule region of weight space.
snippet: The set of all models that the chosen architecture can represent.

title: Architecture prior
text: Structural assumptions in a model that shape what it can learn easily. Telling the search where to look. Examples: weight sharing over positions (convolution), local receptive fields, recurrence over ordered steps. Choosing a 24-step kernel to match the daily cycle.
snippet: Structural assumptions in a model that shape what it can learn easily.

title: 1D convolution (Conv1D)
text: A layer that slides learned 1D filters along the time axis of a sequence. The same pattern detector is applied at every time position. Input (batch, T, C) with kernel size k and F filters gives output (batch, T−k+1, F) with valid padding; parameters k·C·F + F. Conv1D(8, 24) on (120, 14) → (97, 8), with 24·14·8 + 8 = 2,696 parameters.
snippet: A layer that slides learned 1D filters along the time axis of a sequence.

title: Translation invariance assumption
text: A window's content follows the same properties regardless of its location in the sequence. A pattern means the same thing wherever it appears. Justifies weight sharing across positions; combined with global pooling it discards absolute position. A falling-pressure pattern 1 hour ago is far more predictive than the same pattern 4 days ago, which violates the assumption.
snippet: A window's content follows the same properties regardless of its location in the sequence.

title: MaxPooling1D
text: Downsampling of a sequence by taking the maximum over windows. Halves time resolution, keeping the strongest activations. MaxPooling1D(2) maps (97, 8) → (48, 8) (floor of 97/2). After one pooling each step represents 2 hours, so a 12-step kernel covers 24 hours.
snippet: Downsampling of a sequence by taking the maximum over windows.

title: Output length and parameters of the first Conv1D layer
text: x = layers.Conv1D(8, 24, activation="relu")(inputs) T_{\text{out}} = T_{\text{in}} - k + 1 = 120 - 24 + 1 = 97,\qquad P = k\,C_{\text{in}}\,F + F = 24\cdot 14\cdot 8 + 8 = 2696 Lets you trace shapes through the model being built. Each of the 97 outputs per filter summarizes one 24-hour window across all 14 features. T_{\text{in}} Input timesteps (sequence_length = 120) k Kernel (window) size, 24 C_{\text{in}} Input features, raw_data.shape[-1] = 14 F Number of filters, 8 P Trainable parameters (weights + biases)
snippet: x = layers.Conv1D8, 24, activation="relu"inputs — Lets you trace shapes through the model being built.

title: 1D convolution operation
text: Conv1D layer relies on 1D windows that slide across input sequences y_{t,f} = \operatorname{relu}\Big(b_f + \sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\sum_{c=1}^{C} W_{j,c,f}\, x_{t+j,\,c}\Big) Formalizes 'windows that slide across input sequences' and the weight sharing across t. The same W is used for every t; this is the translation-invariance prior. x_{t+j,c} Input feature c at timestep t+j W_{j,c,f} Kernel weight for offset j, input channel c, filter f b_f Bias of filter f y_{t,f} Output of filter f at position t
snippet: Conv1D layer relies on 1D windows that slide across input sequences — Formalizes 'windows that slide across input sequences' and the weight sharing across t.

title: The 1D convnet's training and its disappointing results
text:
Completing and training the Conv1D forecaster, Figure 13.4's MAE curves, and the start of the diagnosis of why it does worse than the dense model The 1D convnet (Conv1D/MaxPooling1D stack with GlobalAveragePooling1D and a Dense(1) head) does even worse than the dense model: validation MAE around 2.9–3.1 °C, far from the 2.44 °C baseline. The first reason given is that weather data doesn't really satisfy the translation invariance assumption. The page finishes the convnet begun on p.386. After the first `Conv1D(8, 24)` and `MaxPooling1D(2)`, the model adds `Conv1D(8, 12, activation="relu")`, a second `MaxPooling1D(2)` and `Conv1D(8, 6, activation="relu")`. The kernel size halves with each pooling, so each conv still spans roughly 24 hours. A `GlobalAveragePooling1D()` then averages each of the 8 feature maps over time, and `Dense(1)` produces the temperature. Training mirrors the dense model exactly: a `ModelCheckpoint("jena_conv.keras", save_best_only=True)`, `compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])`, 10 epochs with validation, reload of the best checkpoint and a printed test MAE.

**Figure 13.4** plots training and validation MAE. Training MAE falls from about 3.67 °C at epoch 1 to about 2.38 °C at epoch 10. Validation MAE is flat and noisy, between roughly 3.05 and 3.24 °C. This is far worse than both the dense model (≈ 2.55 °C at best, Figure 13.3) and the commonsense baseline (2.44 °C).

The text says this model performs *even worse than the densely connected one*, reaching only *about 2.9 degrees* of validation MAE, and asks what went wrong. It gives two reasons. The first starts on this page: **weather data doesn't quite respect the translation invariance assumption**. There are daily cycles, but morning data follows different properties than evening or night data (the sentence continues on p.388, which also gives the second reason: order matters, and pooling destroys order information). The convnet stacks Conv1D(8, 24/12/6) with MaxPooling1D(2), then GlobalAveragePooling1D and Dense(1), about 3.9k parameters. Training is identical to the dense model (Adam, MSE, MAE metric, 10 epochs, best checkpoint). Result: validation MAE ≈ 2.9–3.1 °C, worse than both the dense model and the 2.44 °C baseline. Reason 1: weather data isn't translation invariant except at the daily timescale; morning and night differ. A prior helps only when it matches the data; a mismatched prior can be worse than none.
snippet: The page finishes the convnet begun on p.386. After the first Conv1D8, 24 and MaxPooling1D2, the model adds Conv1D8, 12, activation="relu", a second MaxPooling1D2 and Conv1D8, 6,…

title: GlobalAveragePooling1D
text: Averages each feature channel over the entire time axis, producing one value per channel. 'How strongly did each detector fire on average over the window?', with no record of *when*. (batch, 13, 8) → (batch, 8); no parameters. A spike in filter 3 at the last step and the same spike at the first step give the same pooled value.
snippet: Averages each feature channel over the entire time axis, producing one value per channel.

title: Stacked Conv1D with shrinking kernels
text: Conv1D layers with kernel sizes 24, 12, 6 interleaved with MaxPooling1D(2). Each level looks at about one day of (progressively coarser) data. Shapes (120,14)→(97,8)→(48,8)→(37,8)→(18,8)→(13,8); parameters 2,696 + 776 + 392. Conv1D(8, 12) after one pooling: 12 steps × 2 h ≈ 24 h.
snippet: Conv1D layers with kernel sizes 24, 12, 6 interleaved with MaxPooling1D2.

title: Violated translation invariance
text: The condition in which a pattern's meaning depends on where (or when) it appears. Morning, evening and night behave differently. Convolution's weight sharing assumes stationarity of local statistics across positions; weather is stationary only under 24-hour shifts. A 2 °C drop between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. is normal; between 9 a.m. and 10 a.m. it signals a change in weather.
snippet: The condition in which a pattern's meaning depends on where or when it appears.

title: Diverging train/validation curves
text: Training error improving while validation error stagnates or worsens. The model learns training-period specifics. Figure 13.4: train MAE 3.67 → 2.38, val MAE ~3.05–3.24 with no trend. Epoch 10: train ≈ 2.38, val ≈ 3.08.
snippet: Training error improving while validation error stagnates or worsens.

title: Why order matters, and a first LSTM that beats the baseline
text:
Finishing the diagnosis of the convnet's failure (limited translation invariance; destroyed order information), introducing recurrent neural networks, and a simple LSTM(16) model that reaches 2.39 °C validation MAE Flattening removes time and pooling destroys order, but in this data order and causality matter a lot. Recurrent networks are designed to treat data as a sequence, and a minimal LSTM model beats the commonsense baseline, though only slightly. The page completes the explanation of why the 1D convnet underperformed (p.387). **First**, weather data is only translation invariant at a very specific timescale: morning data behaves differently from evening or night data. **Second**, *order matters, a lot*. The recent past is far more informative about the next day's temperature than data from five days ago, and a 1D ConvNet can't exploit this. Its max pooling and global average pooling layers largely destroy order information.

**Section 13.3, Recurrent neural networks**, opens with a summary of what went wrong in both previous attempts. The dense approach flattened the timeseries, which **removed the notion of time**. The convolutional approach treated every segment of the data the same way and applied pooling, which **destroyed order information**. Machine learning can still help here, but the data should be treated as what it is: a **sequence, where causality and order matter**. Recurrent neural networks are a family of architectures designed for this. Among them, the **Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)** layer has long been popular. The authors try it first and promise to explain how it works shortly.

**Listing 13.12** is minimal: `Input(shape=(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1]))` → `layers.LSTM(16)` → `layers.Dense(1)`, trained with the same routine as before (checkpoint to `jena_lstm.keras`, Adam, MSE loss, MAE metric, 10 epochs, reload best and evaluate). The final print line is missing its `f` prefix (see review flag).

The results, shown in Figure 13.5 (next page), are *much better*: validation MAE as low as **2.39 °C** and test MAE **2.55 °C**. The LSTM model **finally beats the commonsense baseline** (2.44 / 2.62), *albeit just by a bit, for now*, which demonstrates the value of machine learning on this task. Convnet failure reasons: weather is translation invariant only at the daily timescale, and pooling destroys the order information that matters. Flattening removed the notion of time; pooling destroyed order. The data should be treated as a sequence with causality and order. RNNs, and the LSTM in particular, are designed for this. Listing 13.12: LSTM(16) → Dense(1), same training routine; its final print lacks the f prefix. LSTM: val MAE 2.39 °C, test 2.55 °C, the first model to beat the baseline (by about 2–3%).

title: LSTM results and the idea of memory in RNNs
text:
Figure 13.5 (LSTM training/validation MAE) and the conceptual introduction of recurrent networks: feedforward networks have no memory, while RNNs iterate over a sequence and maintain a state Dense networks and ConvNets are feedforward. They process each input independently, so a sequence must be shown all at once as a single data point. An RNN instead loops over the sequence elements while keeping a state that summarizes what it has seen, a highly simplified version of how people read. **Figure 13.5** shows training and validation MAE of the LSTM model from Listing 13.12. Epoch 1 is omitted because its training MAE of **7.75** would distort the scale. From epoch 2 to 10, training MAE falls steadily from about 2.89 to about 2.27 °C. Validation MAE drops from about 2.58 to a minimum of about **2.40 °C around epochs 4–5**, consistent with the 2.39 reported on p.388 and below the 2.44 °C baseline. It then creeps back up to about 2.47 °C by epoch 10. The curves cross around epoch 5–6, after which the model overfits.

The authors then ask why the LSTM did *markedly better* than the dense model and the ConvNet, and how it can be refined. To answer that, they take a closer look at recurrent networks.

**Section 13.3.1** starts from a property of every network seen so far, dense and convolutional: they have **no memory**. Each input is processed independently, with no state kept between inputs. To process a sequence with such a network, you have to show it the whole sequence at once as a single data point, which is what the dense model did by flattening five days of data into one big vector. These are called **feedforward networks**.

By contrast, when you read a sentence you process it word by word (really, *eye saccade by eye saccade*) while remembering what came before, which gives you a fluid representation of its meaning. Biological intelligence processes information **incrementally**, maintaining an internal model built from past information and updated as new information arrives. A **recurrent neural network (RNN)** adopts the same principle in an *extremely simplified* form. It iterates through the sequence elements while maintaining a **state** that contains information about what it has seen so far. In effect, an RNN is a network with an internal **loop** (Figure 13.6, next page). Figure 13.5: LSTM validation MAE bottoms out around 2.40 °C (epochs 4–5), below the 2.44 baseline, then rises: overfitting. Epoch 1 is omitted from the plot because its training MAE (7.75) would distort the scale. Dense networks and ConvNets are feedforward: no memory, each input processed independently, so a sequence must be one data point. Humans read incrementally while maintaining an internal model; RNNs copy this in an extremely simplified way. An RNN iterates over sequence elements, maintains a state and is effectively a network with an internal loop.

title: Recurrent neural network

title: The RNN as a loop with state: pseudocode to NumPy
text:
Making the loop-and-state idea of a recurrent neural network concrete through two pseudocode listings and the start of a NumPy implementation An RNN still treats one whole sequence as one data point, but it processes it internally in a loop: at each timestep it combines the current input with its state (the previous output) through output_t = activation(dot(W, input_t) + dot(U, state_t) + b), and the state starts as an all-zero vector. This page continues section 13.3.1 by pinning down what an RNN actually computes.

First, a clarification about **state and data points**: the RNN's state is reset between two independent sequences (for example two samples in a batch), so one sequence is still *one data point*, one input to the network. What has changed relative to feedforward networks (p.389) is only that this data point is no longer processed in one step: the network **internally loops over the sequence elements**. Figure 13.6 shows this as a box labeled "RNN" with an input arrow, an output arrow and a *recurrent connection* that feeds the output back into the box.

To make "loop" and "state" precise, the authors implement the forward pass of a **toy RNN**. Its input is a sequence of vectors encoded as a rank-2 tensor of shape `(timesteps, input_features)`. At each timestep `t` the network takes its current state and the input at `t` (shape `(input_features,)`), combines them into the output at `t`, and then sets the state for the next step to this output. Because there is no previous output at the first step, the state starts as an all-zero vector, the **initial state**.

Three listings build up the algorithm:

- **Listing 13.13** is pure pseudocode: `state_t = 0`, then for each `input_t`, `output_t = f(input_t, state_t)` and `state_t = output_t`.
- **Listing 13.14** fleshes out `f` using two matrices `W` and `U` and a bias vector `b`: `output_t = activation(dot(W, input_t) + dot(U, state_t) + b)`. The authors note this is similar to a densely connected layer, just with a second term for the state.
- **Listing 13.15** begins a naive NumPy implementation; on this page only `import numpy as np`, `timesteps = 100` and `input_features = 32` appear. The rest (output size 64, random weights, the loop with `np.tanh`) is on p.391.

Taken together: an RNN is a loop that reuses what it computed at the previous iteration, which is exactly the summary given at the top of p.391. The RNN state is reset between independent sequences, so a sequence remains one data point; the novelty is the internal loop over its elements. Input to the toy RNN: a rank-2 tensor (timesteps, input_features); each step sees one vector of shape (input_features,). Each step combines the current input and the current state into an output, which becomes the next state; the initial state is all zeros. The simple RNN step is activation(dot(W, input_t) + dot(U, state_t) + b), a Dense layer with an extra recurrent term. The same W, U, b are used at every timestep.

title: Recurrent neural network (RNN)
text: A network that processes a sequence element by element while maintaining a state; at each step it combines the current input with its state to produce an output, and that output feeds into the next step. Like reading a sentence word by word while keeping a running mental summary, which you update with each new word. Given inputs x_1..x_T, a simple RNN computes s_t = activation(W x_t + U s_{t-1} + b) with s_0 = 0. The same parameters (W, U, b) are applied at every step. For the Jena data, each sample is 120 hourly vectors of 14 features; an RNN reads them in order, updating its state after each hour.
snippet: A network that processes a sequence element by element while maintaining a state; at each step it combines the current input with its state to produce an output, and that output…

title: RNN state and initial state
text: The vector carried from one timestep to the next. In the simple RNN of this page, the state at step t+1 is the output at step t; before the first step it is an all-zero vector called the initial state. A scratchpad that the network rewrites after each input. Its size equals the number of output features. It is reset to the initial state for every new independent sequence. With output_features = 64 (p.391), the state is a vector of 64 numbers, starting as np.zeros((64,)).
snippet: The vector carried from one timestep to the next. In the simple RNN of this page, the state at step t+1 is the output at step t; before the first step it is an all-zero vector…

title: Simple RNN step function
text: The step output_t = activation(dot(W, input_t) + dot(U, state_t) + b), with two weight matrices and one bias vector. A Dense layer that, besides the current input, also receives its own previous output. Equivalent to a Dense layer applied to the concatenation [input_t, state_t]. Weights are shared over time. With 32 input features and 64 outputs: W is 64x32, U is 64x64, b has 64 entries.
snippet: The step outputt = activationdotW, inputt + dotU, statet + b, with two weight matrices and one bias vector.

title: Feedforward network (contrast)
text: A network with no memory that processes each input in a single pass, like the dense and convolutional models seen before. A function with no scratchpad: the same input always yields the same output, regardless of what came before. To handle a sequence it must receive the whole sequence at once, e.g. flattened into one vector. The densely connected Jena model flattened 5 days of data into one vector (p.389).
snippet: A network with no memory that processes each input in a single pass, like the dense and convolutional models seen before.

title: Generic RNN recurrence (Listing 13.13)
text: state_t = 0; for input_t in input_sequence: output_t = f(input_t, state_t); state_t = output_t \begin{aligned} s_0 &= 0 \\ o_t &= f(x_t, s_{t-1}) \\ s_t &= o_t \end{aligned} Defines the control flow common to all RNNs. o_T depends on the whole sequence through the chain of states: o_T = f(x_T, f(x_{T-1}, ... f(x_1, 0))). x_t input vector at timestep t (input_t), shape (input_features,) s_{t-1} state before step t (state_t in the code) o_t output at timestep t (output_t) f the step function, same at every timestep
snippet: statet = 0; for inputt in inputsequence: outputt = finputt, statet; statet = outputt — Defines the control flow common to all RNNs.

title: Simple RNN step function (Listing 13.14)
text: output_t = activation(dot(W, input_t) + dot(U, state_t) + b) o_t = \operatorname{activation}\left(W x_t + U s_t + b\right), \qquad s_{t+1} = o_t Makes f concrete and shows its kinship with a Dense layer. W decides how the new input moves the output; U decides how the past (state) carries over. W input weight matrix, shape (output_features, input_features) U recurrent weight matrix, shape (output_features, output_features) b bias vector, shape (output_features,) x_t input at step t s_t current state (state_t in the code), equal to the previous output o_t output at step t
snippet: outputt = activationdotW, inputt + dotU, statet + b — Makes f concrete and shows its kinship with a Dense layer.

title: Listing 13.13 Pseudocode RNN
text:
state_t = 0
for input_t in input_sequence:
    output_t = f(input_t, state_t)
    state_t = output_t Expresses the RNN as a loop: start with zero state, compute each output from input and state, and carry the output forward as the new state. Left fold of f over the sequence with initial value 0.
snippet: Expresses the RNN as a loop: start with zero state, compute each output from input and state, and carry the output forward as the new state.

title: Listing 13.14 More detailed pseudocode for the RNN
text:
state_t = 0
for input_t in input_sequence:
    output_t = activation(dot(W, input_t) + dot(U, state_t) + b)
    state_t = output_t Replaces the abstract f with the simple RNN transformation: two matrix products, a bias and an activation. Simple (Elman-style) recurrence with shared weights.

title: Finishing the NumPy RNN; the step function unrolled
text:
The complete NumPy forward pass of a simple RNN, the summary 'an RNN is a for loop that reuses previous results', and figure 13.7 showing the RNN unrolled over time A simple RNN is nothing more than a for loop that, at every timestep, computes tanh(W·input_t + U·state_t + b), stores the output and feeds it back as the next state; an RNN is characterized by its step function. The page completes **Listing 13.15**, the naive NumPy forward pass of a simple RNN begun on p.390 (where `timesteps = 100` and `input_features = 32` were set).

- `output_features = 64` sets the dimensionality of the output (and therefore of the state).
- `inputs` is random noise of shape `(timesteps, input_features)`, "for the sake of the example".
- `state_t = np.zeros((output_features,))` is the initial state, an all-zero vector.
- `W` `(64, 32)`, `U` `(64, 64)` and `b` `(64,)` are random weight matrices.
- The loop takes each `input_t` (a vector of shape `(input_features,)`), computes `output_t = np.tanh(np.dot(W, input_t) + np.dot(U, state_t) + b)`, appends it to `successive_outputs`, and sets `state_t = output_t`. The callout notes `tanh` adds nonlinearity and that any other activation could be used.
- Finally the outputs are combined into `final_output_sequence`, which the callout describes as a rank-2 tensor of shape `(timesteps, output_features)` (see the review note: as printed, `np.concatenate` actually yields a flat vector).

The authors then summarize: **an RNN is a `for` loop that reuses quantities computed during the previous iteration of the loop, nothing more.** Many RNNs fit this definition; this one is among the simplest. RNNs are characterized by their **step function**, here `output_t = tanh(matmul(input_t, W) + matmul(state_t, U) + b)`.

**Figure 13.7** draws the RNN *unrolled over time*: three copies of the same cell for steps t-1, t, t+1. Each receives `input t` from below and `State t` from the left (the previous output), computes `output_t = activation(Wo • input_t + Uo • state_t + bo)`, emits `output t` upward and passes it right as the next state. The unrolled picture makes explicit that the copies share the same weights. The NOTE at the top of p.392 adds that each output at `t` contains information about inputs 0..t, so often only the last output is needed. The NumPy RNN uses W (64, 32), U (64, 64), b (64,), a zero initial state of shape (64,), and loops over 100 inputs of shape (32,). Each step: output_t = tanh(W·input_t + U·state_t + b); store it; set state_t = output_t. An RNN is a for loop that reuses quantities computed in the previous iteration, nothing more. RNN variants are characterized by their step function. Figure 13.7 unrolls the loop into a chain of identical cells connected by the state. As printed, np.concatenate flattens the outputs; np.stack gives the intended (timesteps, output_features) tensor.

title: Recurrent neural network (RNN)
text: In the book's summary: a for loop that reuses quantities computed during the previous iteration of the loop. One cell applied again and again along the sequence, each time handing its result to its next application. output_t = step(input_t, state_t); state_{t+1} = output_t; repeat for t = 1..timesteps. title: Step function
text: The per-timestep computation that characterizes an RNN; for the simple RNN, tanh(W·input_t + U·state_t + b). The 'body' of the loop. Different RNN families (SimpleRNN, LSTM, GRU) differ only in their step function and the number of state tensors carried. Figure 13.7 writes it inside the middle cell: output_t = activation(Wo • input_t + Uo • state_t + bo).

title: Simple RNN
text: The RNN whose step is a single dense-like transform of input and previous output followed by an activation (tanh here). A Dense layer that also listens to its own last answer. Parameters: W (output_features x input_features), U (output_features x output_features), b (output_features). With 32 inputs and 64 outputs: 2048 + 4096 + 64 = 6208 parameters. Listing 13.15 on this page.

title: Unrolling an RNN over time

The unrolled graph is a deep feedforward network with shared weights; backpropagation through it is called backpropagation through time (not named on this page). Three cells for t-1, t, t+1, with State t and State t+1 arrows between them.

title: tanh activation
text: The hyperbolic tangent, squashing values into (-1, 1); used here to add nonlinearity. A smooth S-curve centered at 0. tanh(z) = (e^z - e^{-z}) / (e^z + e^{-z}); bounded outputs keep the recurrently fed-back state from growing without limit. tanh(0) = 0, tanh(1) = 0.762, tanh(3) = 0.995.

Each output depends on the current input and, through the state, on all previous inputs. x_t input_t, shape (32,) s_t state_t, shape (64,), starts as zeros W shape (64, 32) U shape (64, 64) b shape (64,) o_t output_t, shape (64,)

title: From NumPy to Keras: the SimpleRNN layer and return_sequences
text:
The Keras SimpleRNN layer as the batched version of the NumPy RNN; variable-length inputs via timesteps=None; the two output modes controlled by return_sequences SimpleRNN implements the loop of p.391 on batches of shape (batch_size, timesteps, input_features). Setting timesteps to None allows arbitrary sequence lengths, and return_sequences chooses between returning every timestep's output (rank 3) or only the last one (rank 2, the default). The page opens with a **NOTE** closing section 13.3.1: in the NumPy example the final output is a rank-2 tensor of shape `(timesteps, output_features)` in which the output at each timestep `t` carries information about input timesteps `0` to `t`, the entire past. Hence often you need only the **last output**, which already contains information about the whole sequence.

**Section 13.3.2** maps the NumPy loop to the Keras **`SimpleRNN`** layer. The one minor difference: like all Keras layers, `SimpleRNN` processes **batches** of sequences, taking inputs of shape `(batch_size, timesteps, input_features)` rather than `(timesteps, input_features)`. In `keras.Input(shape=...)` the `timesteps` entry may be `None`, letting the network process sequences of **arbitrary length**. **Listing 13.16** shows this with `num_features = 14` and `layers.SimpleRNN(16)`.

The authors add that variable length is useful when your sequences actually vary; if they all have the same length, they recommend a complete input shape, because `model.summary()` can then display output lengths and some **performance optimizations** become possible (sidebar "On RNN runtime performance" in section 13.3.4, on p.398).

Finally, all Keras recurrent layers (`SimpleRNN`, `LSTM`, `GRU`) have **two output modes**, selected by the constructor argument **`return_sequences`**:

- full sequence of outputs: rank-3 tensor `(batch_size, timesteps, output_features)`;
- only the last output: rank-2 tensor `(batch_size, output_features)`.

**Listing 13.17** builds an input of shape `(120, 14)` and applies `SimpleRNN(16, return_sequences=False)`; printing the output shape gives `(None, 16)`. The callout notes that `return_sequences=False` is the **default**. The full-sequence variant follows on p.393. Each output of an RNN carries information about all previous inputs, so the last output often suffices. Keras recurrent layers take (batch_size, timesteps, input_features). timesteps=None in keras.Input allows arbitrary-length sequences; use a full shape when lengths are fixed. return_sequences=True gives (batch_size, timesteps, units); False (default) gives (batch_size, units). SimpleRNN(16) on (120, 14) input outputs (None, 16).

title: Full sequences, stacking, and why SimpleRNN gives way to LSTM
text:
return_sequences=True and stacking recurrent layers; the vanishing-gradient weakness of SimpleRNN; introduction of LSTM as a conveyor belt that carries information across timesteps To stack RNN layers, every intermediate layer must return its full output sequence. SimpleRNN is rarely used in practice because the vanishing-gradient problem makes long-term dependencies impossible to learn; LSTM (and GRU) fix this by adding a way to carry information intact across many timesteps. The page completes the tour of the `SimpleRNN` API and then motivates the LSTM.

**Listing 13.18** repeats the setup of Listing 13.17 (14 features, 120 steps) but sets `return_sequences=True`; the output shape is now `(None, 120, 16)`, one 16-dimensional output per timestep.

**Stacking.** Stacking several recurrent layers can increase a network's representational power, but then *all intermediate layers must return the full sequence of outputs*. **Listing 13.19** stacks three `SimpleRNN(16)` layers: the first two with `return_sequences=True`, the last with the default, so the model ends with a rank-2 output.

**Why SimpleRNN is rarely used.** It is generally too simplistic. In theory it can retain at time `t` information about inputs seen many timesteps earlier; in practice such **long-term dependencies prove impossible to learn**. The cause is the **vanishing gradients problem**, similar to what happens in very deep feedforward networks, which eventually become untrainable as layers are added. The theory was studied by Hochreiter, Schmidhuber and Bengio in the early 1990s (footnote 3 cites Bengio, Simard and Frasconi, 1994).

**LSTM and GRU.** Keras offers two other recurrent layers designed to address these issues: `LSTM` and `GRU`. The Long Short-Term Memory algorithm was developed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997 (footnote 4), the culmination of their research on vanishing gradients. The LSTM is a variant of `SimpleRNN` that **adds a way to carry information across many timesteps**. The authors' image: a **conveyor belt** running parallel to the sequence; information can jump on at any point, ride to a later timestep, and jump off *intact* when needed. LSTM thus saves information for later and prevents older signals from gradually vanishing. The sentence continues on p.394, where the authors compare this to residual connections and begin building the LSTM cell from the SimpleRNN cell. return_sequences=True gives (None, 120, 16) for SimpleRNN(16) on (120, 14) input. In a stack of recurrent layers, every intermediate layer must return full sequences. SimpleRNN is rarely used: long-term dependencies are impossible to learn in practice due to vanishing gradients. LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) and GRU were designed to address this. LSTM adds a carry track, a conveyor belt that transports information across timesteps intact.

Several readers reading the same text one after another, each reading the previous reader's notes rather than the raw text. snippet: Makes a recurrent layer output its value at every timestep.

title: Vanishing gradients problem
text: The effect by which gradients shrink as they are propagated through many layers or timesteps, making deep networks and long-term dependencies untrainable. A whisper passed along a long line of people: each passes on a bit less, until nothing arrives. Backpropagation multiplies per-step derivatives; if their magnitude is below 1, the product decays exponentially with the number of steps. Beyond the book: a per-step factor of 0.5 over 20 steps gives 0.5^20 ≈ 1e-6.
snippet: The effect by which gradients shrink as they are propagated through many layers or timesteps, making deep networks and long-term dependencies untrainable.

title: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)
text: A variant of SimpleRNN that adds a carry track to transport information across many timesteps; developed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997). A conveyor belt parallel to the sequence: information hops on, rides along, hops off intact. Adds a carry state C_t that modulates the output and is updated through gating (detailed on pp.394-395). layers.LSTM(16) as a drop-in replacement for layers.SimpleRNN(16).
snippet: A variant of SimpleRNN that adds a carry track to transport information across many timesteps; developed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997.

title: Building the LSTM: from SimpleRNN cell to a carry track
text:
First steps in deriving the LSTM cell: the SimpleRNN cell with output-indexed weights Wo, Uo, bo (figure 13.8), then an added carry dataflow C_t that modulates the output and the next state (figure 13.9) An LSTM starts as a SimpleRNN cell and adds a carry track C_t running parallel to the sequence; the carry enters the output computation through a dense transformation (a Vo · c_t term) and influences the state sent to the next timestep, so it modulates the next output and next state. The page continues the LSTM introduction begun on p.393. The conveyor-belt idea, information riding a separate track and jumping off intact, **should remind you of residual connections** from chapter 9: "it's pretty much the same idea."

To understand the process in detail, the authors start from the **`SimpleRNN` cell** (figure 13.8, which is the same drawing as figure 13.7). Because many weight matrices will appear, they index the cell's `W` and `U` with the letter **`o` for output**: `Wo`, `Uo` (and bias `bo`). The cell computes `output_t = activation(Wo • input_t + Uo • state_t + bo)`.

Next they add **an additional data flow that carries information across timesteps**, whose values are called `Ct`, **C for carry**. Its effect on the cell is twofold:

1. it is **combined with the input connection and the recurrent connection** via a dense transformation (a dot product with a weight matrix, a bias add and an activation), and
2. it **affects the state sent to the next timestep** via an activation function and a multiplication operation.

Conceptually, the carry dataflow **modulates the next output and the next state**. Figure 13.9 shows it as a horizontal *carry track* running above the cells (`c t-1`, `c t`, `c t+1`); each cell receives `c t`, and its formula gains a term: `output_t = activation(Wo • input_t + Uo • state_t + Vo • c_t + bo)`. "Simple so far," say the authors; the subtlety, how the *next* carry value is computed with three SimpleRNN-like transformations indexed `i`, `f` and `k`, comes on p.395. The LSTM carry is the time-axis analogue of a residual connection. The derivation starts from the SimpleRNN cell with weights renamed Wo, Uo, bo. A carry dataflow C_t runs parallel to the sequence. The carry enters the output's dense transformation (Vo · c_t) and affects the next state through an activation and a multiplication. Conceptually, the carry modulates the next output and the next state.

title: The LSTM carry update: i_t, f_t, k_t
text:
How an LSTM computes the next carry value from three SimpleRNN-like transformations, completing the anatomy of the LSTM cell (figure 13.10) The next carry is computed as c_{t+1} = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t, where i_t, f_t and k_t are three transformations of the same form as a SimpleRNN cell, each with its own weights; together with the carry-aware output, this is the whole LSTM. Picking up from figure 13.9 (p.394), the authors turn to "the subtlety": **how the next value of the carry is computed.** It involves **three distinct transformations**, each with the form of a SimpleRNN cell:

`y = activation(dot(state_t, U) + dot(input_t, W) + b)`

Each has its own weight matrices, indexed with the letters **`i`, `f` and `k`**. **Listing 13.20** collects what we have so far ("it may seem a bit arbitrary, but bear with us"):

- `output_t = activation(dot(state_t, Uo) + dot(input_t, Wo) + dot(C_t, Vo) + bo)`
- `i_t = activation(dot(state_t, Ui) + dot(input_t, Wi) + bi)`
- `f_t = activation(dot(state_t, Uf) + dot(input_t, Wf) + bf)`
- `k_t = activation(dot(state_t, Uk) + dot(input_t, Wk) + bk)`

The new carry is obtained by combining the three (**Listing 13.21**):

`c_t+1 = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t`

Adding this gives **figure 13.10, the anatomy of an LSTM**: the unrolled cells of figure 13.9 plus, between consecutive cells, a **"Compute new carry"** block that takes `c t`, the state and the input and puts `c t+1` on the carry track. "And that's it. Not so complicated—merely a tad complex."

The last sentence opens a more philosophical discussion that continues on p.396: one can interpret the operations, e.g. multiplying `c_t` by `f_t` as a way to deliberately forget irrelevant information while `i_t` and `k_t` add information about the present. On p.396 the authors caution that such interpretations do not mean much, because what the operations do is determined by the learned weights; the cell's structure defines a hypothesis space, not a design.

Note (not in the book): in standard LSTM terminology `i_t` is the input gate, `f_t` the forget gate and `k_t` the candidate value; the gates use a sigmoid so their values lie in (0, 1). The carry update uses three SimpleRNN-form transformations with their own weights: i, f, k. Listing 13.20: output_t reads the carry via Vo; i_t, f_t, k_t read state and input. Listing 13.21: c_t+1 = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t (elementwise). Figure 13.10 adds a 'Compute new carry' block between cells: that is the whole LSTM. Interpretations of the gates (e.g. f_t as forgetting) are only interpretations; the weights determine behavior (p.396).

title: Interpreting the LSTM cell, and a roadmap for getting the most out of RNNs
text:
The end of the LSTM walkthrough (why the gate interpretations are not to be taken literally; a cell architecture is a constraint on the hypothesis space), the start of section 13.3.3 with its list of advanced RNN techniques (recurrent dropout, stacking, bidirectional layers), and the opening of 13.3.4 on recurrent dropout One can tell stories about what the forget, input and candidate transformations of an LSTM do, but what a cell actually does is determined by its learned weights; the cell's equations only define the hypothesis space. What matters practically is the LSTM's purpose: letting past information be reinjected later, fighting vanishing gradients. The chapter then turns to three techniques for improving recurrent models. **Closing the LSTM walkthrough.** The page finishes the 'philosophical' reading of the LSTM pseudocode from p.395. Multiplying the carry `c_t` by `f_t` can be read as a way to *deliberately forget* irrelevant information in the carry dataflow, while `i_t` and `k_t` 'provide information about the present', writing new information onto the carry track. The authors then undercut these stories: what the operations *actually* do is determined by the weights that parameterize them, and those weights are learned end to end, starting over with each training round, so you cannot credit any single operation with a specific purpose. The specification of a cell determines the **hypothesis space**, the space searched during training, but not the cell's behavior; the same cell with different weights can do very different things. A cell's combination of operations is therefore best seen as a set of **constraints on the search**, not as a *design* in the engineering sense.

The authors go further: choosing such constraints (how to implement RNN cells) is arguably better left to optimization algorithms such as genetic algorithms or reinforcement learning than to human engineers, and 'in the future, that's how we'll build our models'. The practical summary: you do not need to understand the specific LSTM architecture. Just remember its purpose: **allow past information to be reinjected at a later time, thus fighting the vanishing gradients problem**.

**13.3.3 Getting the most out of recurrent neural networks.** A recap (what RNNs are, what an LSTM is and why it beats a naive RNN on long sequences, how to use Keras RNN layers) is followed by the plan for the rest of the section:

- **Recurrent dropout**, a dropout variant for fighting overfitting in recurrent layers;
- **Stacking recurrent layers**, more representational power at a higher computational cost;
- **Bidirectional recurrent layers**, presenting the same information in different ways to increase accuracy and mitigate forgetting.

All three will be used to refine the temperature forecasting RNN.

**13.3.4 Using recurrent dropout to fight overfitting** begins by returning to the LSTM-based model of p.388, the first model to beat the commonsense baseline; its training and validation curves (discussed on p.397) show it overfitting quickly. Reading f_t as 'forget' and i_t, k_t as 'present information' is a convenient story, not a guarantee; trained weights determine what each operation does. A cell architecture defines a hypothesis space: a set of constraints on the search, not an engineering design. The authors suggest choosing such constraints may be better left to optimization algorithms (genetic algorithms, reinforcement learning). What to remember about LSTM: it lets past information be reinjected later, fighting vanishing gradients. Three refinements follow: recurrent dropout (overfitting), stacking (capacity, at a compute cost), bidirectional layers (accuracy, less forgetting). The starting point is the LSTM of p.388, the first model to beat the commonsense baseline.

title: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)
text: A recurrent layer that adds a carry track c_t to the SimpleRNN cell; the carry is updated as c_t+1 = i_t * k_t + c_t * f_t and modulates the output. A conveyor belt running alongside the sequence: information can be placed on it, kept, or removed, and picked up again many steps later. Four affine transformations of (input_t, state_t), each with its own weights (Wo/Uo, Wi/Ui, Wf/Uf, Wk/Uk), followed by activations; elementwise products combine them into the new carry (p.395). On the Jena task, LSTM was the first model to beat the commonsense baseline (p.388).
snippet: A recurrent layer that adds a carry track ct to the SimpleRNN cell; the carry is updated as ct+1 = it  kt + ct  ft and modulates the output.

title: Hypothesis space (architecture as constraint)
text: The set of functions a model architecture can represent; training searches it for good weights. The architecture draws the map's boundaries; training picks the location within them. The page states that an RNN cell's specification determines the hypothesis space but not what the cell does, which is up to the weights; the combination of operations is a set of constraints on the search. Two LSTMs with identical equations but different trained weights can implement very different input-output behaviors.
snippet: The set of functions a model architecture can represent; training searches it for good weights.

title: Vanishing gradients
text: Gradients shrinking toward zero as they are backpropagated through many layers or timesteps. A whisper passed down a long line of people fades out before reaching the end. In a SimpleRNN, the gradient with respect to an early state is a product of many Jacobians of the recurrent transformation; when their norms are below 1 the product decays exponentially in the number of steps. A dependency 100 timesteps back would require the gradient to traverse 100 recurrent steps.
snippet: Gradients shrinking toward zero as they are backpropagated through many layers or timesteps.

title: Recurrent dropout
text: A dropout variant for recurrent layers, listed on this page as the first technique to fight overfitting in RNNs. Hide the same parts of the memory at every step of a sequence so the network cannot rely on any single memory unit. Detailed on p.397: a temporally constant dropout mask applied to the inner recurrent activations, exposed in Keras via the recurrent_dropout argument. layers.LSTM(32, recurrent_dropout=0.25) in Listing 13.22 (p.397).
snippet: A dropout variant for recurrent layers, listed on this page as the first technique to fight overfitting in RNNs.

First term: new information written onto the carry. Second term: the old carry, scaled elementwise. title: Recurrent dropout: Yarin Gal's time-constant masks and Listing 13.22
text:
Why the first LSTM model overfits, why naive dropout fails in recurrent networks, the correct scheme (the same dropout mask at every timestep, applied both to inputs and to inner recurrent activations), Keras's dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments, and the first half of Listing 13.22 Dropout in an RNN must use a temporally constant mask, both on the layer's inputs and on its recurrent activations (recurrent dropout); a mask that changes every timestep disrupts the error signal propagated through time. Keras exposes this through the dropout and recurrent_dropout arguments, and with that regularization the LSTM can be made twice as wide and trained five times longer. **The problem.** Finishing the sentence from p.396: the training and validation curves of the first LSTM model (Listing 13.12, `LSTM(16)`, p.388) show that it overfits quickly despite having very few units; the training and validation losses diverge considerably after a few epochs. The classic remedy is **dropout**, which randomly zeros out input units of a layer to break happenstance correlations in the training data. But applying dropout correctly in recurrent networks 'isn't a trivial question'.

**The answer (Yarin Gal).** It has long been known that applying dropout *before* a recurrent layer hinders learning rather than regularizing. In 2015, as part of his PhD thesis on Bayesian deep learning (footnote 5), Yarin Gal determined the proper way:

1. Apply **the same dropout mask** (the same pattern of dropped units) at every timestep, instead of a mask that varies randomly from timestep to timestep.
2. To regularize the representations formed by the recurrent gates of layers like `GRU` and `LSTM`, also apply a temporally constant mask to the **inner recurrent activations** of the layer: a *recurrent dropout mask*.

A constant mask lets the network properly propagate its learning error through time; a temporally random mask would disrupt this error signal.

**In Keras.** Gal did his research with Keras and helped build the mechanism into its recurrent layers. Every Keras recurrent layer has two arguments: `dropout` (rate for the layer's input units) and `recurrent_dropout` (rate for the recurrent units).

**The experiment.** Dropout means less reliance on small network size for regularization, so the `LSTM` gets **twice as many units** (32 instead of 16); without dropout this network would overfit right away. Dropout-regularized networks take longer to converge, so training runs for **five times as many epochs** (50 instead of 10). Listing 13.22 builds `LSTM(32, recurrent_dropout=0.25)`, followed by `Dropout(0.5)` to regularize the `Dense(1)` output layer, and a `ModelCheckpoint` callback saving the best model to `jena_lstm_dropout.keras`. Compilation and training continue on p.398. The first LSTM model overfits quickly even with only 16 units: training and validation losses diverge after a few epochs. Dropout applied before a recurrent layer hinders learning. Gal's rule: use the same dropout mask at every timestep, and a temporally constant mask on the inner recurrent activations (recurrent dropout). A temporally random mask disrupts the error signal propagated through time. Keras recurrent layers implement this via dropout (input units) and recurrent_dropout (recurrent units). Listing 13.22: LSTM(32, recurrent_dropout=0.25), then Dropout(0.5), then Dense(1); twice the units and five times the epochs of the first LSTM.

title: Recurrent dropout
text: Dropout applied with a temporally constant mask to the inner recurrent activations of a recurrent layer; exposed as recurrent_dropout in Keras. For a whole sequence, the same memory units are switched off at every step, so the network cannot rely on any one of them, yet the signal passed through time stays consistent. One Bernoulli mask m_h is sampled per sequence (and per training step) and applied elementwise to h_{t-1} before it enters the cell's recurrent transformations at all timesteps. layers.LSTM(32, recurrent_dropout=0.25)
snippet: Dropout applied with a temporally constant mask to the inner recurrent activations of a recurrent layer; exposed as recurrentdropout in Keras.

title: Dropout
text: Randomly zeroing out a fraction of a layer's units during training to break happenstance correlations in the training data. No unit can count on any particular partner being present, so units must be individually useful. In Keras, the Dropout layer applies to the output of the previous layer; layers.Dropout(0.5) here drops half of the 32 LSTM outputs before the Dense layer. x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
snippet: Randomly zeroing out a fraction of a layer's units during training to break happenstance correlations in the training data.

title: Temporally constant dropout mask
text: A dropout mask sampled once and reused at every timestep of a sequence. Like covering the same keys of a piano for an entire song rather than different keys for each note. Applies to both the inputs (Keras dropout argument) and the recurrent state (recurrent_dropout argument). With 6 units and mask [1,0,1,1,0,1], units 2 and 5 are zero at t=1, 2, ..., 120.
snippet: A dropout mask sampled once and reused at every timestep of a sequence.

title: Overfitting
text: The model fits training data specifics so that validation performance stops improving while training performance keeps improving. Memorizing the answers to practice questions instead of learning the subject. Seen here as training and validation losses diverging after a few epochs for the LSTM(16) model. The first LSTM reached val MAE 2.39 but its curves diverge early (p.388, p.397).

title: Recurrent layer with time-constant input and recurrent dropout masks
text: Described in words: 'the same dropout mask ... should be applied at every timestep' and 'a temporally constant dropout mask should be applied to the inner recurrent activations of the layer' h_t = \phi\big(W\,(m_x \odot x_t) + U\,(m_h \odot h_{t-1}) + b\big),\qquad m_x \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1-p_x),\ m_h \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(1-p_h)\ \text{sampled once per sequence} Formalizes Gal's prescription described in prose on the page. Note that the masks carry no t subscript: that is the whole point. Contrast with the harmful scheme, where m_x and m_h would be m_{x,t} and m_{h,t}, resampled at every step. x_t Input vector at timestep t (14 weather features in the Jena task). h_{t-1} Recurrent state from the previous timestep. m_x Input dropout mask (Keras dropout argument, rate p_x), the same for all t. m_h Recurrent dropout mask (Keras recurrent_dropout argument, rate p_h), the same for all t. W, U, b Input weights, recurrent weights and bias (as in the SimpleRNN form on p.395). \phi Activation function.

title: Results of the dropout-regularized LSTM (Figure 13.11) and RNN runtime performance on CPU vs GPU
text:
The end of Listing 13.22 (compile with Adam/MSE/MAE, fit for 50 epochs), the results (validation MAE 2.27, test MAE 2.45, no overfitting in the first 20 epochs), Figure 13.11, and the start of the sidebar on RNN runtime performance: small RNNs are faster on CPU; Keras LSTM/GRU use cuDNN kernels on GPU by default, which are fast but inflexible Recurrent dropout works: the 32-unit LSTM no longer overfits early and improves on the commonsense baseline by about 7% (validation) and 6.5% (test). Separately, RNN speed depends on hardware: tiny RNNs are dominated by a sequential loop of small matrix products and run faster on CPU, while larger ones benefit from the GPU's cuDNN kernels, provided you stay within what those kernels support. **End of Listing 13.22.** The model is compiled with `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="mse"` and `metrics=["mae"]`, exactly as in the earlier models, and trained with `model.fit(train_dataset, epochs=50, validation_data=val_dataset, callbacks=callbacks)`: 50 epochs, five times the 10 used for the first LSTM, because dropout-regularized networks converge more slowly.

**Results (Figure 13.11).** 'Success! We're no longer overfitting during the first 20 epochs.' The model reaches a **validation MAE as low as 2.27 degrees**, a 7% improvement over the no-learning baseline (2.44 on p.384), and a **test MAE of 2.45 degrees**, a 6.5% improvement over the baseline (2.62). For comparison, the unregularized `LSTM(16)` reached 2.39 / 2.55 (p.388). In the figure, the training MAE (red dashed) declines steadily from about 3.0 to about 2.52 over 50 epochs, while the validation MAE (blue) is roughly flat around 2.27-2.32. There is no upturn in validation error, which is the overfitting signature seen before. The caption says 'loss', but the plotted quantities are MAE.

**Sidebar: On RNN runtime performance.** Recurrent models with very few parameters, like this chapter's, tend to be **significantly faster on a multicore CPU than on GPU**: they involve only small matrix multiplications, and the chain of multiplications cannot be parallelized well because of the `for` loop over timesteps. Larger RNNs, however, can greatly benefit from a GPU. On GPU with default keyword arguments, Keras `LSTM` and `GRU` layers use a **cuDNN kernel**, a highly optimized, low-level, NVIDIA-provided implementation. cuDNN kernels are a mixed blessing: fast but inflexible. If you do anything the default kernel does not support, you suffer a dramatic slowdown (the sentence continues on p.399, which names recurrent dropout as one such unsupported feature). Listing 13.22 trains with Adam, MSE loss, MAE metric, for 50 epochs (five times the first LSTM). Result: validation MAE 2.27 (7% better than the baseline) and test MAE 2.45 (6.5% better); no overfitting in the first 20 epochs. In Figure 13.11 the validation MAE stays flat around 2.3 while training MAE keeps falling; training MAE is higher because dropout is active only in training. Small RNNs are often faster on a multicore CPU: small matrix products plus a sequential for loop. Keras LSTM/GRU on GPU use cuDNN kernels with default arguments: fast but inflexible; unsupported options cause a dramatic slowdown.

title: cuDNN fallback and RNN unrolling; 13.3.5 Stacking recurrent layers and the GRU
text:
End of the RNN runtime sidebar (recurrent dropout disables the cuDNN kernel, a 2-5x slowdown on GPU; unrolling as a speed-up for short, fixed-length sequences) and the start of section 13.3.5: increase capacity once overfitting is under control, stack recurrent layers with return_sequences=True, and switch to GRU layers Using non-default options like recurrent dropout pushes Keras off the cuDNN fast path; unrolling the RNN loop can recover speed at the cost of memory, but only for short sequences of known length. With overfitting fixed by dropout, the next step in the universal workflow is to add capacity, classically by stacking recurrent layers, each intermediate one returning its full sequence. **Sidebar, continued: cuDNN and unrolling.** The 'dramatic slowdown' from p.398 'more or less forces you [to] stick to what NVIDIA happens to provide'. Example: **recurrent dropout is not supported by the LSTM and GRU cuDNN kernels**, so adding it forces a fallback to the regular TensorFlow implementation, **generally two to five times slower on GPU**, even though the computational cost is the same. One way to speed up an RNN that can't use cuDNN is **unrolling**: removing the `for` loop and in-lining its body N times. For an RNN, this can help TensorFlow optimize the computation graph, but it considerably increases memory consumption, so it is only viable for relatively small sequences (around 100 steps or fewer), and only when the number of timesteps is known in advance (an `Input()` shape with no `None` entries). Example: `layers.LSTM(32, recurrent_dropout=0.2, unroll=True)` on `keras.Input(shape=(sequence_length, num_features))`.

**13.3.5 Stacking recurrent layers.** The model is no longer overfitting but seems to have hit a performance bottleneck, so it is time to increase capacity. Recall the universal workflow: increase capacity until overfitting becomes the primary obstacle (assuming basic mitigation such as dropout is in place); 'as long as you aren't overfitting too badly, you're likely under capacity'.

Capacity is typically increased by adding units or adding layers. **Recurrent layer stacking** is a classic way to build more powerful RNNs; not long ago Google Translate was powered by a stack of **seven large LSTM layers**. To stack recurrent layers in Keras, all intermediate layers must return their **full sequence of outputs (a rank-3 tensor)** rather than only the last timestep, via `return_sequences=True`.

The next example uses a stack of two dropout-regularized recurrent layers, and for a change uses **GRU** layers. The Gated Recurrent Unit is very similar to an LSTM, a 'slightly simpler, streamlined version'. It was introduced in 2014 by Cho et al. (footnote 6), just as recurrent networks were regaining interest in a then-tiny research community. The listing (13.23) is on p.400. Recurrent dropout is not supported by the LSTM/GRU cuDNN kernels; the fallback is generally 2-5x slower on GPU at the same computational cost. Unrolling (unroll=True) in-lines the RNN loop N times, which can speed it up but costs considerable memory; use it only for short sequences (about 100 steps or fewer) of known length. Once a model no longer overfits but plateaus, increase capacity; if you're not overfitting too badly, you're likely under capacity. Capacity comes from more units or more layers; stacking recurrent layers is the classic RNN approach (e.g. seven large LSTM layers in Google Translate). Intermediate recurrent layers must use return_sequences=True to output rank-3 sequences. The GRU, introduced by Cho et al. in 2014, is a slightly simpler, streamlined LSTM.

title: Listing 13.23: a dropout-regularized stacked GRU and its results (Figure 13.12)
text:
The full code for two stacked GRU layers (32 units each, recurrent_dropout=0.5, the first with return_sequences=True) plus Dropout(0.5) and Dense(1), trained 50 epochs; result: test MAE 2.39, an 8.8% improvement over the baseline; signs of diminishing returns from capacity Stacking a second recurrent layer improves the test MAE from 2.45 to 2.39 (8.8% better than the commonsense baseline), but only slightly; adding capacity now gives diminishing returns. **Listing 13.23.** The input has shape `(sequence_length, raw_data.shape[-1])`, i.e. (120, 14). It goes through `layers.GRU(32, recurrent_dropout=0.5, return_sequences=True)`, which outputs one 32-dimensional vector per timestep, then a second `layers.GRU(32, recurrent_dropout=0.5)`, which returns only its last output, then `layers.Dropout(0.5)` and `layers.Dense(1)`. A `ModelCheckpoint` saves the best model to `jena_stacked_gru_dropout.keras`. The model is compiled with Adam, MSE loss and MAE metric, trained for 50 epochs with validation, then the best checkpoint is reloaded and evaluated on the test set (`print(f"Test MAE: ...")`). Compared with Listing 13.22, the changes are: GRU instead of LSTM, two recurrent layers instead of one, and a higher recurrent dropout rate (0.5 instead of 0.25).

**Results.** Figure 13.12 shows the results: a **test MAE of 2.39 degrees**, an **8.8% improvement over the baseline** (2.62 on p.384), compared with 2.45 for the single dropout-regularized LSTM (p.398). 'The added layer does improve the results a bit, though not dramatically.' The authors conclude you 'may be seeing **diminishing returns** from increasing network capacity at this point'.

**Reading the figure.** Training MAE (red dashed) falls steadily from about 2.9 to about 2.27 over 50 epochs. Validation MAE (blue) is lowest, about 2.25, around epochs 10-16, then rises steadily after about epoch 20, reaching about 2.43 at epoch 50. It crosses above the training curve around epoch 32. So the larger model does overfit after roughly 20 epochs. The text does not point this out; the checkpoint callback ensures the evaluated model is the one from the best epoch. (As with Figure 13.11, the caption says 'loss' but the curves are MAE.) Listing 13.23 stacks GRU(32, recurrent_dropout=0.5, return_sequences=True) and GRU(32, recurrent_dropout=0.5), then Dropout(0.5) and Dense(1). Test MAE 2.39 degrees: 8.8% better than the baseline, versus 6.5% for the single LSTM; a small gain. The authors read this as diminishing returns from increasing capacity. Figure 13.12 also shows the validation MAE rising after about epoch 20: the larger model overfits again; checkpointing preserves the best epoch. Only intermediate recurrent layers need return_sequences=True.

title: Bidirectional RNNs: order dependence and the reversed-sequence experiment
text:
Introduction of bidirectional RNNs; RNNs' order dependence; the experiment of feeding reversed (antichronological) sequences to the LSTM, which underperforms the commonsense baseline on weather data; why reversed order works as well as forward order on text; why different-yet-useful representations are worth exploiting RNNs are order-sensitive, so running one forward and one backward over the same sequence yields two different representations. On weather forecasting, the reversed direction is much worse because the recent past is most predictive and the LSTM remembers recent inputs best. On text, either order works, so the two directions give different but equally useful views, which is what a bidirectional RNN exploits. **13.3.6 Using bidirectional RNNs.** The last technique of the section. A **bidirectional RNN** is a common RNN variant that can outperform a regular RNN on certain tasks; it is frequently used in natural language processing, 'the Swiss Army knife of deep learning for natural language processing'.

**Order dependence.** RNNs process timesteps in order, so shuffling or reversing them can completely change the representations extracted. That is why RNNs do well where order matters, as in temperature forecasting. A bidirectional RNN *exploits* this order sensitivity: it uses two regular RNNs (e.g. `GRU` or `LSTM`), one processing the sequence chronologically and the other antichronologically, and merges their representations, so it can catch patterns a unidirectional RNN may overlook.

**Was chronological order arbitrary?** So far all RNNs here processed sequences oldest-first, a decision 'we made no attempt to question'. To test it, reverse the input sequences along the time axis (`samples[:, ::-1, :]`). Training the same LSTM model as in the first experiment on reversed data, you would find it **strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline**. So chronological processing matters here, and it makes sense: an LSTM is typically better at remembering the recent past than the distant past, and recent weather data is more predictive than older data (which is also why the commonsense baseline is fairly strong). Reading in reverse puts the most useful data furthest from the output.

**Text is different.** For many other problems, including natural language, a word's importance does not depend strongly on its position in the sentence. On text, reversed processing works just as well as chronological: 'you can read text backwards just fine'. Word order matters, but *which order* you use is not crucial.

**Different but useful.** An RNN trained on reversed sequences learns different representations, as you would have different mental models if time ran backward and you were born on your last day. In machine learning, representations that are *different* yet *useful* are always worth exploiting, and the more they differ, the better (continued on p.402, which links this to ensembling). A bidirectional RNN runs two regular RNNs over the same sequence, chronologically and antichronologically, and merges their representations. RNNs are order dependent; this is why they suit forecasting and why two directions give two different views. On the Jena task, an LSTM fed reversed sequences strongly underperforms even the commonsense baseline. Reason: the LSTM remembers the recent past best, and recent weather data is the most predictive. On text, reversed processing works as well as forward: order matters, but which order you use isn't crucial. Different yet useful representations are always worth exploiting; this underlies bidirectional RNNs and ensembling.

title: Bidirectional RNNs: the Bidirectional layer and why it fails on temperature forecasting
text:
How a bidirectional RNN combines a chronological and an antichronological recurrent layer, how to build one in Keras with `layers.Bidirectional`, and why it underperforms a plain LSTM on the Jena temperature task but is a strong choice for text. A bidirectional RNN runs two separate copies of a recurrent layer, one over the sequence in order and one over the reversed sequence, and merges their outputs. That gives it two different views of the data, but on the temperature task the reversed half contributes almost nothing useful while doubling capacity, so the model overfits sooner and does worse than a plain LSTM. The page continues the argument from p.401. An RNN trained on reversed sequences learns *different* representations from one trained on the original order, and in machine learning, representations that are "different yet useful" are worth exploiting: the more they differ, the better, because they show the data from a new angle. The authors say this is the intuition behind **ensembling**, which comes back in chapter 18.

A **bidirectional RNN** applies this idea inside a single layer. Figure 13.13 shows the input sequence `a, b, c, d, e` fed to one RNN in its original order and to a second RNN as `e, d, c, b, a`. The two RNNs' outputs are then **merged**, by adding or concatenating them. The goal is a richer representation that catches patterns the chronological RNN alone might miss.

In Keras you build one with the `Bidirectional` layer. Its first argument is a recurrent layer *instance*. `Bidirectional` creates a second, separate instance of that layer, with its own weights, and uses one copy on the chronological sequence and the other on the reversed sequence. **Listing 13.24** tries this on the temperature task. It wraps an `LSTM(16)` in `Bidirectional`, adds a `Dense(1)` regression head, compiles with Adam, MSE loss and an MAE metric, and trains for 10 epochs.

The result is negative: the bidirectional model **does worse than the plain `LSTM`**. The authors give two reasons:

1. All of its useful predictive power has to come from the chronological half. The antichronological half is known (from p.401) to perform very badly on this task, because the recent past matters much more than the distant past.
2. The extra half **doubles the network's capacity**, so the model **starts overfitting much earlier**.

The page ends by saying where bidirectional RNNs do fit: **text**, and any data where order matters but *which* order you read in does not. Around 2016, bidirectional LSTMs were state of the art on many NLP tasks, until the Transformer took over (chapter 15). A bidirectional RNN = two independent RNNs (one forward, one on the reversed sequence) whose outputs are merged by add or concatenate. In Keras: `layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(16))`. The wrapper creates a second, separately weighted copy of the layer. The motivation is ensembling: different but useful representations improve performance. On Jena temperature forecasting it does worse than a plain LSTM: the backward half is weak, and the doubled capacity overfits earlier. Use it for text and other data where order matters but direction doesn't. Bidirectional LSTMs were state of the art in NLP around 2016, before the Transformer.
snippet: The page continues the argument from p.401. An RNN trained on reversed sequences learns different representations from one trained on the original order, and in machine learning,…

title: Bidirectional RNN
text: A recurrent layer made of two independent RNNs, one processing the input in chronological order and one in reversed order, whose outputs are merged by addition or concatenation. Two people read the same document, one from the start and one from the end, and then compare notes. Each notices things the other misses. Given $x_1,\dots,x_T$, the forward RNN produces $\overrightarrow{h}_T$ and the backward RNN, run on $x_T,\dots,x_1$, produces $\overleftarrow{h}_1$. In Keras the default output is their concatenation. The two directions have separate weights. `layers.Bidirectional(layers.LSTM(16))` turns `(batch, 120, 14)` inputs into `(batch, 32)` outputs.
snippet: A recurrent layer made of two independent RNNs, one processing the input in chronological order and one in reversed order, whose outputs are merged by addition or concatenation.

title: Ensembling
text: Combining several models (or views of the data) whose representations differ, so the combination captures aspects any single one misses. A panel of experts with different backgrounds usually decides better than any one of them, provided each is competent. The gains come from errors that are not perfectly correlated. Covered in chapter 18. Averaging the predictions of a chronological LSTM and a model trained on different features.
snippet: Combining several models or views of the data whose representations differ, so the combination captures aspects any single one misses.

title: Overfitting (from extra capacity)
text: When a model fits training data so closely that validation performance stops improving and gets worse. More parameters give the model more room to memorise noise. Doubling the parameter count with an antichronological copy adds capacity without adding useful signal, so validation loss bottoms out earlier. Listing 13.24 trains for 10 epochs. The bidirectional model starts overfitting earlier than the unidirectional `LSTM(16)` of p.388.
snippet: When a model fits training data so closely that validation performance stops improving and gets worse.

title: Order sensitivity vs. direction invariance
text: Data where order matters but the reading direction does not (text) suits bidirectional models. Data where recency dominates (weather) does not. You can understand a sentence read backward. You can't forecast tomorrow well by focusing on last week's weather first. An LSTM's memory is biased toward the most recently processed steps. A backward reader of a timeseries therefore remembers best the oldest, least predictive readings. Text classification (p.431) versus temperature forecasting (this page).
snippet: Data where order matters but the reading direction does not text suits bidirectional models. Data where recency dominates weather does not.

(1) All the predictive power has to come from the chronological half, because the antichronological half performs very badly on this task (the recent past matters more than the distant past). (2) The antichronological half doubles the network's capacity, so it starts overfitting much earlier.

title: Why are bidirectional RNNs a good fit for text but not for the Jena timeseries?
text: Why are bidirectional RNNs a good fit for text but not for the Jena timeseries? In text, order matters but reading direction doesn't: backward reading gives an equally useful, different view, and words often depend on later context. In the weather series, the most recent readings are by far the most predictive, so the backward reader, whose memory favours the oldest steps, adds little useful information.

title: Going even further: tuning ideas, realistic limits, and why not to forecast markets
text:
Further directions for improving the Jena temperature forecaster, a realistic ceiling on what this dataset allows, and a sidebar warning against using these techniques to predict financial markets. There are many knobs left to turn (units, dropout, learning rate, optimizer, regression head, input windowing, feature engineering), but deep learning is empirical and you must iterate. With single-location data, about a 10% improvement over the no-learning baseline is likely the ceiling. Markets are a different kind of problem: the past doesn't predict the future, and public data gives no information advantage. Section 13.4 wraps up the temperature-forecasting experiments with a list of things you could still try:

- **Recurrent layer sizes and dropout** in the stacked setup. The current values are "largely arbitrary and thus probably suboptimal."
- **The optimizer**: change Adam's learning rate or try another optimizer.
- **The regressor**: put a stack of `Dense` layers on top of the recurrent layer instead of a single `Dense` layer.
- **The input**: longer or shorter sequences, a different sampling rate, or feature engineering.

The authors then stress that deep learning is **"more an art than a science"**. Guidelines can suggest what is likely to work, but every dataset is unique, no theory tells you in advance the optimal solution, and **you must iterate**, evaluating strategies empirically.

Next comes a realistic expectation: in the authors' experience, **improving on the no-learning baseline by about 10%** is likely the best you can do with this dataset. The chapter's best model, the stacked GRU at 2.39 °C test MAE versus the baseline's 2.62 °C, reached 8.8% (p.400), so it is already close to that ceiling. The reason is informational, not architectural. Near-future weather is very predictable from a **wide grid of locations**, but not from **a single station**, because local weather depends on what is happening in surrounding areas right now.

The **"Markets and machine learning"** sidebar warns against applying these techniques to stock prices or exchange rates. Markets have very different statistical characteristics from natural phenomena: **past performance is not a good predictor of future returns** ("looking in the rear-view mirror is a bad way to drive"). ML suits datasets where the past *does* predict the future, such as weather, electricity consumption or store foot traffic. Trading is fundamentally **information arbitrage**, gaining an edge from data or insights others lack, so well-known techniques on public data give no advantage and are "effectively a dead end." Next things to try: units and dropout, learning rate and optimizer, a Dense-stack regressor, and better inputs (window length, sampling rate, feature engineering). Deep learning is empirical: no theory gives the optimal setup, so iterate against a validation set. About 10% over the no-learning baseline is likely the ceiling for this single-station dataset. The chapter's best is 8.8%. The limit is informational: weather depends on surrounding locations, which one station can't see. ML forecasting fits data where the past predicts the future (weather, electricity, foot traffic), not markets. Trading is information arbitrage, so public data plus well-known ML gives no edge.
