title: Chapter 13 summary: baselines, simple models first, RNNs, recurrent dropout, stacking
text:
The five take-home lessons of the timeseries-forecasting chapter. Establish a commonsense baseline, try cheap models before expensive ones, use RNNs (LSTM or GRU) when order matters, regularise them with time-constant dropout via `recurrent_dropout`, and stack recurrent layers only when the problem is complex enough to justify the cost. This one-page chapter summary lists five lessons from chapter 13:

1. **Baselines first.** When approaching a new problem, set a commonsense baseline for your metric. Without one you can't tell whether you're making real progress. In this chapter the baseline, "the temperature in 24 hours equals the temperature now", scored 2.44 °C validation and 2.62 °C test MAE (p.383) and proved hard to beat. *(The page says this was "first learned in chapter 6"; see the review flag. Baselines were introduced in chapter 5, p.176.)*
2. **Simple models before expensive ones**, to justify the extra expense. Sometimes the simple model is the best option. The chapter tried a small dense network (p.384) before any RNN.
3. **Recurrent networks when ordering matters**, especially for timeseries. They "easily outperform" models that flatten the temporal data first. The two essential Keras RNN layers are `LSTM` and `GRU`.
4. **Dropout in RNNs** must use a **time-constant dropout mask** on the inputs and a **time-constant recurrent dropout mask** on the recurrent activations (Gal's method, p.397). Keras builds this in, so you just set the `dropout` and `recurrent_dropout` arguments of a recurrent layer. (The page names only `recurrent_dropout`; the input-mask counterpart is the layer's `dropout` argument, used in the chapter's listings.)
5. **Stacked RNNs** give more representational power but cost much more, so they aren't always worth it. They pay off on complex problems such as machine translation, less so on smaller, simpler ones. In this chapter stacking improved the test MAE only from 2.45 to 2.39 °C (p.398, p.400).

The chapter's last technique, **bidirectional RNNs** (p.401-p.402), has no bullet. Its lesson, that bidirectionality helps on text but hurt on this forecasting task, is worth adding to your own notes. Always establish a commonsense baseline first. Try simple models before expensive ones. The simple one may win. RNNs (LSTM, GRU) fit ordered data and beat models that flatten time away. Regularise RNNs with time-constant dropout masks via the layer's `dropout` and `recurrent_dropout` arguments. Stack RNN layers only when the problem's complexity justifies the cost. Bidirectional RNNs, covered on p.401-p.402, aren't in the summary. Remember they hurt on this forecasting task.

title: Chapter 14 opener: Text classification
text:
Opening page of chapter 14: what the chapter covers, its role as the foundation for the three text chapters, and the first lines of a short history of NLP. Chapter 14 introduces NLP, shows how to turn text into numbers, and builds simple text classifiers in several ways, preparing for the Transformer in chapter 15. The history section begins by contrasting designed machine languages (rules first) with natural languages (usage first). This is the **opening page of chapter 14, "Text classification."** The "This chapter covers" box lists three topics:

- An introduction to the field of **natural language processing (NLP)**
- **Preprocessing text input into numeric input**
- **Building simple text classification models**

The introductory paragraph says this chapter lays the foundation for working with text that the *next two chapters* build on (chapter 15, "Language models and the Transformer", and chapter 16, "Text generation"). By the end, you will be able to build a simple text classifier in several different ways, which sets up more complex models such as the Transformer in chapter 15.

Section **14.1, "A brief history of natural language processing,"** then begins. In computer science, human languages such as English or Mandarin are called "natural" to distinguish them from languages designed for machines, such as LISP, Assembly and XML. Every machine language was *designed*: an engineer first wrote down formal rules for which statements are valid and what they mean, and people used the language only once the rules were complete. The sentence "With human language," breaks off at the page end and continues on p.406: *"it's the reverse: usage comes first, and rules arise later."*

**How to use this page:** read it as a roadmap. The chapter outline runs from history (p.405), to text preparation and tokenization (p.408-p.418), to sets versus sequences and the IMDb dataset (p.419-p.421), to set models such as bag-of-words and bigrams (p.422-p.428), and finally to sequence models (RNNs and word embeddings, p.429-p.444). Chapter 14 covers an introduction to NLP, turning text into numbers, and simple text classifiers. It's the foundation for chapters 15 (language models and the Transformer) and 16 (text generation). Machine languages are designed rules-first. Natural languages evolved usage-first, which is why they're messy.

title: A brief history of NLP: from hand-written rules to machine learning
text:
Why natural language is messy, what NLP is, and how the field moved from hand-crafted symbolic rules (the 1954 Georgetown-IBM demo, the funding collapse) to data-driven machine learning in the late 1980s. Natural language evolved through use, and its rules were formalised afterward and are often broken, so it is ambiguous and constantly changing. Early NLP tried to write down 'the rule set of English' and failed to generalise beyond handpicked examples. Once computers and data grew, engineers began searching for rules automatically from corpora, which is machine learning. The page completes the contrast begun on p.405. With human language **usage comes first and rules arise later**. Natural language was shaped by an evolutionary process, like biological organisms, which is what makes it "natural." Its grammar was formalised after the fact and is often ignored or broken. So while machine-readable language is structured and rigorous, natural language is **messy: ambiguous, chaotic, sprawling, and constantly in flux**.

Computer scientists have long wanted systems that can read or produce language, because text underpins most communication and culture, stores centuries of knowledge, and makes up most of the internet. Using computers to interpret and manipulate language is **natural language processing (NLP)**. It was proposed as a field right after World War II, when some saw understanding language as **"code cracking"**.

Early researchers naively thought you could write down **"the rule set of English"** the way one writes down LISP's. In the early 1950s, **IBM and Georgetown** demonstrated Russian-to-English translation using **six hardcoded grammar rules** and a **lookup table of a couple of hundred words and suffixes**, which correctly translated **60 handpicked sentences**. The demo succeeded at raising excitement and funding, and its authors claimed translation would be solved within five years. Funding flowed for nearly a decade, but generalisation proved "maddeningly difficult": word meanings change with context and every grammar rule needs countless exceptions. An influential US report a decade later criticised the lack of progress, and funding dried up.

Even so, **handcrafted rules remained dominant into the 1990s**, simply because there was no viable alternative. In the late 1980s, faster computers and more data opened a new direction. An engineer facing "big piles of ad hoc rules" naturally asks whether a **corpus** could automate finding them, by **searching a rule space** instead of inventing rules by hand. That is machine learning. The first ML approaches to NLP, in the late 1980s, were based on **decision trees**. The sentence continues on p.407. Natural language evolved usage-first. Its rules came later and are often broken, so it is messy. NLP means using computers to interpret and manipulate language. It began after WWII with a code-cracking view. The 1950s Georgetown-IBM demo (6 rules, about 200 lexicon entries, 60 handpicked sentences) produced hype that collapsed when generalisation failed. Handcrafted rules lasted into the 1990s for lack of alternatives. From the late 1980s, compute and data enabled searching for rules with a corpus, i.e. machine learning, starting with decision trees.
snippet: The page completes the contrast begun on p.405. With human language usage comes first and rules arise later. Natural language was shaped by an evolutionary process, like…

section: 14.1 A brief history of natural language processing

title: From statistical NLP to LSTMs and Transformers
text:
The rest of the NLP history: decision trees, then statistical models and learned parametric models; NLP as pattern recognition on words, with example tasks; the 2010s LSTM era and its limits; and the Transformer's scalability, which led to today's large language models. Modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words. It finds statistical regularities rather than human-like understanding, and that turns out to be enough for many tasks. LSTMs pushed accuracy up in the 2010s but struggled with long-range dependencies and slow training. The Transformer fixed the scalability problem: it keeps improving as model and data grow, and its training parallelises well. The page continues the history from p.406. The first ML approaches to NLP, based on decision trees, aimed to **automate the development of the if/then/else rules** of hardcoded systems. Then **statistical approaches** gained ground, **starting with logistic regression**. Over time **learned parametric models took over**, and some came to see linguistics baked directly into a model as a **hindrance**. Frederick Jelinek, an early speech-recognition researcher, joked: *"Every time I fire a linguist, the performance of the speech recognizer goes up."* (The book dates this to the 1990s; see the review flag.)

Just as **computer vision is pattern recognition applied to pixels**, **modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words**. Three example applications:

- Spam probability of an email → **text classification**
- Most likely Russian translation of an English sentence → **translation**
- The next word of an incomplete sentence → **language modeling**

The models in this book **won't possess a human-like understanding of language**. They look for **statistical regularities**, which turns out to be enough for many real-world tasks.

In the last decade, researchers found how "shockingly effective" it can be to learn answers to **narrow statistical questions about text**. In the **2010s, LSTMs** were applied to text, greatly increasing parameter counts and compute. They generalised far better than earlier approaches but hit limits: they **struggled with dependencies across long text** (many sentences and paragraphs), and they were **slow and unwieldy to train** compared with vision models.

At the end of the 2010s, Google researchers found the **Transformer**, which solved many of these scalability issues. **If model size and training data grew together, Transformers kept getting more accurate**, and their training **could be parallelised effectively, even for long sequences**: doubling the machines roughly halves the wait. Together with faster GPUs and CPUs, this produced an explosion of investment. Chat systems such as **ChatGPT** captured public attention. Their training text is a significant portion of the internet's written language, and training one model can cost **tens of millions of dollars**. The page ends warning that some hype should be cut down to size: "these are pattern" (continued on p.408: "recognition machines"). NLP went from decision trees to logistic regression to learned parametric models, with hand-built linguistics increasingly seen as a hindrance. Modern NLP is pattern recognition applied to words. Example tasks: text classification, translation, language modeling. These models learn statistical regularities, not human-like understanding. 2010s LSTMs were more accurate but struggled with long-range dependencies and were slow to train. The Transformer scaled: it improved as model and data grew and trained in parallel. That made ChatGPT-scale models possible, at tens of millions of dollars per model.

title: From NLP history to preparing text: tokens and regex splitting
text:
Why text has to be turned into numbers, the choice between character- and word-level representations, and splitting text into tokens with a regular expression Neural networks consume tensors of numbers, but text is a string of symbols with no single natural numeric form. Every text pipeline therefore starts with a splitting step that cuts text into small units called tokens; regular expressions are a flexible tool for doing this, starting with the simplest pattern "." that splits a string into characters. The page opens with the end of section 14.1's historical survey. The authors finish a thought begun on p.407 about modern large language models: despite our tendency to see intelligence in "things that talk," these models **copy and synthesize training data** in a way that is wholly distinct from, and much less efficient than, human intelligence. Yet they concede that the emergence of complex behaviour from a training setup as simple as "guess the missing word" is one of the most shocking empirical results of the last decade of machine learning. They then preview the next three chapters: skipping the hand-coded linguistic features that dominated until the 1990s, they will cover everything from logistic-regression text classifiers to LSTMs for translation, and examine closely why the Transformer is so scalable and generalizes so well on text.

**Section 14.2, Preparing text data**, starts with the example sentence `The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.` The obstacle is that this input is **not numeric**, while every technique from previous chapters needs tensors of numbers. Images have a fairly natural numeric form (pixel intensities), but text can be encoded numerically in several ways.

Two intuitive options are offered:

- a **character-level** representation, borrowing from text file encodings such as ASCII: chop the input into characters and give each a unique index;
- a **word-level** representation: break sentences apart on spaces and punctuation and map each word to a unique number.

Both are reasonable, and both share a step present in all text preprocessing: **splitting** the text into small units called **tokens**. Regular expressions are introduced as a powerful splitting tool because they can flexibly match patterns of characters. The most basic regex, `"."`, matches any single character, so `re.findall(r".", text)` returns the list of characters. The page ends just before the function is applied to the example sentence (shown on p.409). Modern language models are powerful pattern recognizers, not human-like minds, but their emergence from "guess the missing word" training was a genuine surprise. Chapters 14-15 skip hand-coded linguistic features and go from logistic regression on text to LSTMs and the Transformer. Text is not numeric and has no single natural numeric form, unlike images. Character-level and word-level representations are both reasonable starting points. All text preprocessing includes splitting text into tokens; regular expressions are a flexible way to do it. re.findall(r".", text) splits a string into individual characters.
snippet: The page opens with the end of section 14.1's historical survey. The authors finish a thought begun on p.407 about modern large language models: despite our tendency to see…

title: Tokenization (splitting)
text: The preprocessing step that splits a text string into a sequence of small units called tokens. Like cutting a sentence into Lego bricks: the model can only build from bricks, so first decide how big the bricks are and cut the text into them. A function from a string to a list of strings, e.g. via re.findall with a pattern. The token granularity (character, word, subword) sets vocabulary size, sequence length and how much meaning each unit carries. Character-level: "The quick" -> ["T","h","e"," ","q","u","i","c","k"]. Word-level: ["The","quick"].
snippet: The preprocessing step that splits a text string into a sequence of small units called tokens.

title: Token
text: A small individual unit of text produced by the splitting step. The atom of text that a model sees. Tokens are later mapped to integer indices through a vocabulary (p.409) and then to vectors (one-hot, multi-hot or embeddings). In split_chars, each character of "The quick brown fox..." (including spaces) is a token.
snippet: A small individual unit of text produced by the splitting step.

title: Regular expression
text: A pattern language that flexibly matches sequences of characters in text; the book uses it to split strings into tokens. A search template: "." means "any one character", so finding all matches of it lists every character. re.findall(pattern, text) returns all non-overlapping matches. The book imports the third-party regex package as re; it is largely a superset of Python's built-in re module. re.findall(r".", "dog.") -> ["d","o","g","."]
snippet: A pattern language that flexibly matches sequences of characters in text; the book uses it to split strings into tokens.

title: Character-level vs. word-level representation
text: Two ways to make text numeric: give each character a unique index (as ASCII does), or split on spaces and punctuation and give each word a unique index. Characters are a small alphabet that produces long sequences; words are a big dictionary that produces short sequences. Character vocabularies are small (dozens to thousands) and have no unknown words, but sequences are long and each unit carries little meaning. Word vocabularies are large (tens of thousands or more) and give out-of-vocabulary words, but each unit carries more meaning. The example sentence has 45 characters but 10 word-and-punctuation tokens.
snippet: Two ways to make text numeric: give each character a unique index as ASCII does, or split on spaces and punctuation and give each word a unique index.

title: Word splitting with regex, indexing, and the idea of a vocabulary
text:
Character and word splitting with regular expressions, then mapping tokens to integer indices through a vocabulary instead of raw ASCII codes After splitting text into tokens (characters or words-plus-punctuation), we index them: each token is mapped to a unique integer. ASCII/Unicode code points scale poorly, so NLP builds a vocabulary, a mapping from the tokens that actually occur in the training data to indices, which works equally well for characters and words. The page continues the hands-on introduction to text preprocessing. First it shows the result of the character splitter from p.408: `split_chars("The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog.")[:12]` gives `["T", "h", "e", " ", "q", "u", "i", "c", "k", " ", "b", "r"]`. Every character, spaces included, is a token.

Next the authors switch to **word-level splitting** by combining two patterns with the regex alternation `|`: `[\w]+` grabs a run of word characters, and `[.,!?;]` matches a single punctuation mark from that set. `split_words` returns `re.findall(r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]", text)`; on the test sentence "The quick brown fox jumped over the dog." it yields `["The", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumped", "over", "the", "dog", "."]`. The final period is a separate token, and the capital "T" is kept.

Splitting produces string tokens, but models need numbers. The most common approach is **indexing**: map each token to a unique integer. The authors call this flexible and reversible, and note that how indices are later mapped into a latent space the model ingests (for example, embeddings) is a separate decision.

For characters one could index with ASCII codes, `ord('A')` -> 65 and `ord('z')` -> 122, but this scales poorly across languages, since Unicode defines over a million characters. The more robust technique is a **vocabulary**: a mapping built from the tokens that actually occur in our training data to indices. It works for word tokens as easily as for character tokens. The page ends by starting to build such a vocabulary as a Python dictionary, `"[UNK]": 0, "the": 1, "quick": 2, "brown": 3, "fox": 4, "jumped": 5, ...`, which continues on p.410. Character splitting keeps every character, spaces included, as a token. The regex [\w]+|[.,!?;] splits text into words and single punctuation marks, dropping whitespace. Indexing, which maps each token to a unique integer, is the most common way to make tokens numeric; it is flexible and reversible. How indices become vectors (the latent space) is a separate, later choice. ASCII/Unicode codes scale poorly; a vocabulary built from training data works for both characters and words. The hand-built vocabulary reserves index 0 for [UNK].
snippet: The page continues the hands-on introduction to text preprocessing. First it shows the result of the character splitter from p.408: splitchars"The quick brown fox jumped over the…

title: Word-level tokenization with regex
text: Splitting text into word and punctuation tokens with a regex such as [\w]+|[.,!?;]. Grab each run of letters as a word; grab each punctuation mark on its own; skip the spaces. re.findall scans left to right and returns every non-overlapping match. Each match is either a maximal run of \w characters or one character from [.,!?;]. Characters matching neither (spaces, apostrophes, hyphens, quotes) are discarded. split_words("The quick brown fox jumped over the dog.") -> ["The", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumped", "over", "the", "dog", "."]
snippet: Splitting text into word and punctuation tokens with a regex such as w+|.,!?;.

title: Indexing
text: Mapping each token to a unique integer index. Give every distinct token a ticket number. A function from tokens to integers in 0..V-1, applied element-wise to a token sequence. The integers have no numeric meaning; they are identifiers later turned into vectors (one-hot or embedding rows). With the vocabulary on pp.409-410, "quick" -> 2, "fox" -> 4.
snippet: Mapping each token to a unique integer index.

title: Vocabulary
text: A mapping from specific tokens occurring in the training data to integer indices. A dictionary of only the words (or characters) you have actually seen, each with a number. Usually built by counting tokens in the training set, keeping the most frequent ones, and reserving indices for special tokens such as [UNK] (and, in Keras, a padding index). Its size V determines one-hot dimension and embedding-table rows. {"[UNK]": 0, "the": 1, "quick": 2, "brown": 3, "fox": 4, "jumped": 5, ...}
snippet: A mapping from specific tokens occurring in the training data to integer indices.

title: Regex character classes and alternation
text: [...] matches one listed character, \w matches a word character, + repeats one or more times, | chooses between alternatives. Small building blocks combine into a tokenizer rule. [\w]+|[.,!?;] matches either a maximal run of word characters or one punctuation mark. Alternatives are tried left to right at each position. re.findall(r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]", "Hi, you!") -> ["Hi", ",", "you", "!"]
snippet: ... matches one listed character, w matches a word character, + repeats one or more times, | chooses between alternatives.

title: Indexing with [UNK], and why text needs standardization
text:
Completing the vocabulary lookup with an unknown-token fallback, then introducing text standardization (lowercasing, punctuation and accent removal, stemming/lemmatization) A vocabulary lookup with a default of [UNK] = 0 lets us index any input, even unseen words. Superficial encoding differences (case, punctuation, accents, word forms) make near-identical sentences look completely different after indexing, so we standardize text before splitting; lowercasing and removing punctuation is the simplest widespread scheme. The page completes the hand-built vocabulary from p.409 with `"over": 6, "dog": 7, ".": 8`, splits the full sentence with `split_words`, and indexes each word with `vocabulary.get(word, 0)`. The output is `[0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 0, 7, 8]`.

The authors explain the special token **`[UNK]`** ("unknown"): it lets us index all input, even terms that only appear in test data. In the example, "lazy" is not in the vocabulary and maps to index 0. *Note (not in the book):* the **first** 0 has the same cause. `split_words` keeps "The" capitalized, while the vocabulary only has lowercase "the", so "The" is also unknown. That illustrates the next topic.

**Standardization.** The two sentences "sunset came. i was staring at the Mexico sky. Isnt nature splendid??" and "Sunset came; I stared at the México sky. Isn't nature splendid?" are almost identical, yet they would get very different indices: "i" vs. "I", "Mexico" vs. "México", "isnt" vs. "isn't", "staring" vs. "stared". A model does not know these equivalences a priori. Standardizing text is described as **a basic form of feature engineering** that erases encoding differences you don't want the model to deal with, and the authors note that search engines need the same thing.

The simplest widespread scheme is to **lowercase and remove punctuation**, which gives "sunset came i was staring at the mexico sky isnt nature splendid" and "sunset came i stared at the méxico sky isnt nature splendid". Removing accent marks would bring them even closer. Standardization used to be one of the most critical areas for improving performance: for decades NLP used regexes to map words to a common root ("tired" -> "tire", "trophies" -> "trophy"), called **stemming** or **lemmatization**. The sentence continues on p.411, which says that this kind of heavy standardization now tends to do more harm than good for large models. vocabulary.get(word, 0) indexes tokens, sending unknown ones to [UNK] = 0. [UNK] lets us index any input, including terms seen only in test data, at the cost of losing their identity. In the example both "lazy" and the capitalized "The" become 0. Near-identical sentences can get very different indices because of case, accents, punctuation and word forms. Standardization is a basic form of feature engineering; lowercasing and removing punctuation is the simplest common scheme. Stemming/lemmatization ("tired" -> "tire") used to be critical but is a reversal point the text picks up on p.411.
snippet: The page completes the hand-built vocabulary from p.409 with "over": 6, "dog": 7, ".": 8, splits the full sentence with splitwords, and indexes each word with vocabulary.getword,…

title: Unknown token [UNK] / out-of-vocabulary handling
text: A reserved vocabulary entry to which every token not in the vocabulary is mapped. A catch-all bin for words the tokenizer has never seen. Implemented as the default in vocabulary.get(token, unk_id). Index 0 here. All OOV tokens become indistinguishable. "lazy" -> 0 and "The" -> 0 in [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 0, 7, 8].
snippet: A reserved vocabulary entry to which every token not in the vocabulary is mapped.

title: The three-stage text pipeline and a character-level tokenizer
text:
Why modern models use only light standardization; the standardization -> splitting -> indexing pipeline (figure 14.1); and Listing 14.1, a CharTokenizer class Heavy standardization such as stemming now tends to hurt large models, because tense and plurality carry meaning, so standardization is kept as light as possible. Text preprocessing has three stages, standardization, splitting and indexing, which together are called tokenization; an object performing them is a tokenizer. Listing 14.1 implements a character-level tokenizer as a class with one method per stage. The page finishes the sentence from p.410 about stemming and lemmatization: **as models have grown more expressive, this type of standardization tends to do more harm than good**. The tense and plurality of a word are necessary signals to its meaning. For today's larger models, standardization is as light as possible, for example just converting all inputs to a standard character encoding before further processing.

The authors then summarize the **three distinct stages** of text preprocessing, shown in **figure 14.1**:

1. **Standardization**: normalize input with basic text-to-text transformations;
2. **Splitting**: split the text into sequences of *tokens*;
3. **Indexing**: map the tokens to indices using a *vocabulary*.

Figure 14.1 runs "The cat sat on the mat." through the pipeline: standardized text "the cat sat on the mat", then tokens "the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat", then token indices 3, 26, 65, 9, 3, 133. The repeated "the" gets the same index 3 both times.

People often call the entire process **tokenization**, and an object that maps text to a sequence of token indices a **tokenizer**.

**Section 14.2.1** starts building tokenizers. The first is character-level and maps each character to an integer, using only one standardization step: lowercasing. **Listing 14.1** defines `CharTokenizer`: the constructor stores a vocabulary dict and looks up `unk_id = vocabulary["[UNK]"]`; `standardize` returns `inputs.lower()`; `split` returns `re.findall(r".", inputs)`; `index` maps each token with `self.vocabulary.get(t, self.unk_id)`; and `__call__` chains standardize and split (the final indexing and return lines are on p.412). The vocabulary itself is computed from data in Listing 14.2 on p.412. Stemming-style standardization tends to do more harm than good for expressive modern models; tense and plurality carry meaning. For large models, standardization is as light as possible, e.g. a standard character encoding. Text preprocessing has three stages: standardization, splitting, indexing (figure 14.1). The whole process is often called tokenization; the object doing it is a tokenizer. Listing 14.1's CharTokenizer has one method per stage: lower(), findall("."), and a vocabulary lookup with unk_id. The vocabulary is passed in; computing it from data comes in Listing 14.2.

title: Listing 14.2 Computing a character-level vocabulary
text:
import collections

def compute_char_vocabulary(inputs, max_size):
    char_counts = collections.Counter()
    for x in inputs:
        x = x.lower()
        tokens = re.findall(r".", x)
        char_counts.update(tokens)
    vocabulary = ["[UNK]"]
    most_common = char_counts.most_common(max_size - len(vocabulary))
    for token, count in most_common:
        vocabulary.append(token)
    return dict((token, i) for i, token in enumerate(vocabulary)) Counts characters over an iterable of strings and returns a dict from the top max_size - 1 characters (plus [UNK]) to indices ordered by frequency. Frequency counting followed by top-k selection.
snippet: Counts characters over an iterable of strings and returns a dict from the top maxsize - 1 characters plus UNK to indices ordered by frequency.

Finishing WordTokenizer, computing a word vocabulary (Listing 14.4), downloading Moby Dick, and inspecting the resulting character vocabulary and the character-level length of the novel's first line Swapping the word regex into the vocabulary function gives compute_word_vocabulary. On real text, the full Moby Dick, the character tokenizer needs only 64 vocabulary entries, even with a cap of 100, ordered by frequency from space and "e" down to rare symbols like "<" and ">". But it encodes the 63-character opening sentence as 63 tokens, one per character, which sets up the comparison with the word tokenizer on p.414. The page first completes **Listing 14.3**: `WordTokenizer.__call__` ends with `indices = self.index(tokens)` and `return indices`, exactly like CharTokenizer.

It lowercases, counts, puts `[UNK]` first, keeps the `max_size - 1` most common words and returns a token -> index dict.

The authors then try both tokenizers on **real-world input: the full text of *Moby Dick* by Herman Melville**. They import `keras`, download the Project Gutenberg file with `keras.utils.get_file(origin="https://www.gutenberg.org/files/2701/old/moby10b.txt")`, read it as a list of lines (`list(open(filename, "r"))`), compute a character vocabulary with `max_size=100`, and build `char_tokenizer = CharTokenizer(vocabulary)`.

Inspecting the results:

- **Vocabulary length: 64**. The whole novel, lowercased, contains only 63 distinct characters (excluding newlines), so the cap of 100 is never reached.
- **Vocabulary start**: `["[UNK]", " ", "e", "t", "a", "o", "n", "i", "s", "h"]`. After `[UNK]`, the entries are in descending frequency: space first, then the familiar English letter-frequency order e, t, a, o, n, i, s, h.
- **Vocabulary end**: `["@", "$", "%", "#", "=", "~", "&", "+", "<", ">"]`. These are the rarest symbols, likely mostly from the Gutenberg license text and markup.
- **Line length: 63** for "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely.", one index per character.

The page ends with "Now what about the word-level tokenizer?", answered on p.414. WordTokenizer ends exactly like CharTokenizer: index tokens and return them. The character vocabulary for the whole book has only 64 entries, under the cap of 100. Vocabulary order reflects frequency: space, e, t, a, o, n, i, s, h at the top; rare symbols at the bottom. The 63-character opening line becomes 63 character tokens: small vocabulary, long sequences.

title: Listing 14.4 Computing a word-level vocabulary
text:
def compute_word_vocabulary(inputs, max_size):
    word_counts = collections.Counter()
    for x in inputs:
        x = x.lower()
        tokens = re.findall(r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]", x)

    vocabulary = ["[UNK]"]
    most_common = word_counts.most_common(max_size - len(vocabulary))
    for token, count in most_common:
        vocabulary.append(token)
    return dict((token, i) for i, token in enumerate(vocabulary)) Counts word and punctuation tokens over the inputs and returns a frequency-ordered vocabulary of at most max_size entries, [UNK] at index 0. Count, then top-k.

title: Word-level tokenizer on Moby Dick, and the case for subwords
text:
Comparing character- and word-level tokenization on Moby Dick, then motivating subword tokenization as a compression problem Character tokenizers have tiny vocabularies but produce very long sequences; word tokenizers produce short sequences but need huge vocabularies or lose information to "[UNK]". Subword tokenization tries to get both: short sequences from a small vocabulary, which the authors frame as finding an ideal compression of the input. The page finishes the Moby Dick experiment begun on p.413. After the character-level tokenizer, the authors build a **word-level vocabulary** capped at 2,000 terms with `compute_word_vocabulary(moby_dick, max_size=2_000)` and wrap it in a `WordTokenizer`. The printed statistics show:

- **Vocabulary length: 2000.** The cap is reached; the book has far more distinct words than that.
- **Vocabulary start:** `"[UNK]"`, `","`, `"the"`, `"."`, `"of"`. Index 0 is reserved for unknown tokens, and the rest are sorted by frequency, so punctuation and function words come first.
- **Vocabulary end:** `"tambourine"`, `"subtle"`, `"perseus"`, `"elevated"`, `"repose"`. These are rare words that only just made the cut.
- **Line length: 13** tokens for the opening sentence *"Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely."* The character tokenizer needed 63 (p.413).

The authors then name the trade-off. Characters cover the whole book with **64** vocabulary terms but produce long sequences. Words fill a 2,000-term vocabulary at once (indexing every word would take about **17,000** terms) but produce much shorter outputs. At modern scale, with datasets of *trillions* of words, a full word vocabulary would have hundreds of millions of entries. Capping it hard sends much of the text to `"[UNK]"` and throws information away. Those problems are why **subword tokenization** became popular as a middle ground.

Section **14.2.2** states the goal: keep the `WordTokenizer`'s concise output and the `CharTokenizer`'s ability to encode almost any input with a small vocabulary. The authors frame this as **compression**. Shorter token sequences compress the length of each example, and a smaller vocabulary reduces the bytes needed per token. A tokenizer that does both gives the model *short, information-rich sequences*. The next page (p.415) builds on this idea with byte-pair encoding, a 1990s compression algorithm. The word-level vocabulary for Moby Dick reaches its 2,000-term cap; full coverage would need about 17,000 terms. Frequency ordering puts "[UNK]" at 0, then ',', 'the', '.', 'of'; the tail holds rare words like 'tambourine' and 'repose'. The test sentence costs 13 word tokens versus 63 character tokens, the 'compression' that word tokenization offers. At web scale, word vocabularies become unworkably large, and capping them sends information to "[UNK]". Subword tokenization aims for the WordTokenizer's concise output with the CharTokenizer's small, full-coverage vocabulary. The authors frame tokenizer design as compression: short sequences and a small vocabulary give short, information-rich inputs.

title: Tokenization
text: Turning text into a sequence of integer IDs through standardization, splitting into tokens, and indexing against a vocabulary. Choosing the 'alphabet' the model reads in: letters, whole words, or something in between. In the book's tokenizers, __call__ runs standardize (lowercase), split (a regex) and index (vocabulary.get(t, unk_id)). The word tokenizer maps the opening line of Moby Dick to 13 IDs; the char tokenizer maps it to 63.

title: Word-level tokenization
text: Splitting text into words (and here, the punctuation marks . , ! ? ;) and giving each distinct word its own ID. Each token is a unit a human reader recognizes, so sequences are short and easy to interpret. Split regex r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]"; vocabulary = "[UNK]" plus the max_size-1 most frequent tokens. With max_size=2,000 the least frequent kept words are 'tambourine', 'subtle', 'perseus', 'elevated', 'repose'; rarer words become "[UNK]".

title: Subword tokenization
text: Tokenization with units between characters and words: frequent words stay whole, rare words are split into frequent pieces. Common words get their own tokens; rare words are built from smaller pieces, so nothing becomes "[UNK]". Learned from data, for example by byte-pair encoding, which starts from characters and repeatedly merges frequent adjacent pairs (p.415). From p.418: the SubWordTokenizer encodes the test line in 16 tokens (vs. 13 words, 63 chars) and handles every word in Moby Dick.

title: Tokenization as compression
text: Viewing a tokenizer as a code that should represent text with few tokens, each drawn from a small vocabulary. Like packing a suitcase: fewer items (short sequences), each item cheap to label (small vocabulary). Sequence length L shrinks as tokens get longer; the per-token cost grows with vocabulary size V (about log2 V bits, or V embedding rows). A good tokenizer keeps both low. chars: L=63, V=64; words: L=13, V=2,000 (lossy because of "[UNK]"); subwords aim for small L with moderate V and no loss.

title: Byte-pair encoding: initializing the word counts
text:
Byte-pair encoding as a tokenizer, and Listing 14.5, which builds the starting state (character-split word counts) Byte-pair encoding, a 1990s lossless compression algorithm, works as a tokenizer: start from a vocabulary of characters and repeatedly merge common adjacent pairs into longer symbols. The first step is to count every word in the corpus and store each one as its characters separated by spaces. Building on the compression framing of p.414, the authors introduce **byte-pair encoding (BPE)**. It is a lossless compression algorithm from the 1990s (Philip Gage, 1994, footnote 1) that turned out to be one of the most effective tricks in the last decade of NLP when reused for tokenization. The book notes that ChatGPT and many other models still use it.

The core idea: **start with a basic vocabulary of characters and progressively "merge" common pairings into longer and longer character sequences.** The authors use a toy corpus of three lines: "the quick brown fox", "the slow brown fox" and "the quick brown foxhound".

Like the `WordTokenizer`, BPE starts by **counting words**. Each word is stored as its characters **joined by spaces**, so that the next step can treat adjacent pairs of symbols easily. **Listing 14.5**, `count_and_split_words`, lowercases each line, splits it into words and punctuation with the same regex as `WordTokenizer`, splits each word into characters with `re.findall(r".", word)`, joins them with `" "` and increments a `Counter`. It returns a plain `dict`.

On the toy data the result is:

```
{"t h e": 3, "q u i c k": 2, "b r o w n": 3,
 "f o x": 2, "s l o w": 1, "f o x h o u n d": 1}
```

Each key is a word written as a sequence of current *symbols* (at this point single characters), and each value is how often that word occurs. Merges will never cross word boundaries, because each word is a separate key. Counting by word means a pair inside "brown" is counted with weight 3 in a single step. The merge loop itself follows on p.416. Byte-pair encoding is a 1990s lossless compression algorithm reused for tokenization; the book says ChatGPT and many other models still use it. BPE starts from a character vocabulary and repeatedly merges common adjacent pairs into longer symbols. Listing 14.5 builds the starting state: a dict mapping each word, written as space-separated characters, to its corpus frequency. On the toy corpus this gives {'t h e': 3, 'q u i c k': 2, 'b r o w n': 3, 'f o x': 2, 's l o w': 1, 'f o x h o u n d': 1}. Counting per distinct word weights pair statistics by frequency and stops merges from crossing word boundaries.
snippet: Building on the compression framing of p.414, the authors introduce byte-pair encoding BPE. It is a lossless compression algorithm from the 1990s Philip Gage, 1994, footnote 1…

title: Byte-pair encoding (BPE)
text: A subword tokenization algorithm that starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent symbol pair into a new symbol, adding it to the vocabulary. Let the corpus decide which letter combinations are common enough to become their own tokens. State: dict of word -> frequency, where each word is a space-separated list of symbols. Loop: count all adjacent pairs weighted by word frequency, take the most frequent, replace it everywhere, record the merge rule. In the toy data, the first merge will be ("o", "w"), which occurs 4 times (brown ×3, slow ×1); see p.416.

title: Byte-pair merging step by step (Listing 14.6)
text:
Counting adjacent symbol pairs and merging the most frequent one, repeated ten times on the toy corpus BPE repeatedly counts all adjacent symbol pairs (weighted by word frequency), picks the most frequent, and merges it everywhere into a new symbol. Merged symbols can merge again, so common words end up as single tokens while rare words stay partly split. Starting from the character-split word counts of p.415, the authors apply **byte-pair merging**. In each step they consider **all pairs of adjacent symbols in all words**, weighting each by its word's frequency, and **merge only the most common one**. Initially that is `("o", "w")`: it occurs in "brown" (3 occurrences) and "slow" (1 occurrence), so it gets weight 4. It becomes the new symbol `"ow"`, and every `"o w"` is replaced. Counting and merging then continue, and `"ow"` now behaves as one unit that could, for example, merge with `"l"` into `"low"`. Repeating this builds **larger and larger subwords**.

**Listing 14.6** implements it with two helpers:

- `count_pairs(counts)` splits each word into its symbols and adds `freq` for every adjacent pair `zip(symbols[:-1], symbols[1:])`.
- `merge_pair(counts, first, second)` compiles the regex `(?<!\S)first second(?!\S)`, which matches the pair only when it is bounded by spaces or string ends (a whole-symbol match, "Matches an unmerged pair"). It rewrites every key, replacing the match with `first+second` ("Replaces all occurrences with a merged version").

A loop runs 10 iterations: count pairs, take `max(pairs, key=pairs.get)`, merge, print the keys. The printed trace shows `ow` → `th` → `the` → `br` → `brow` → `brown` → `fo` → `fox` → `qu` → `qui`. After ten merges, **"the", "brown" and "fox" are single symbols**. "quick" is part-way (`"qui c k"`), while the rare words "slow" (`"s l ow"`) and "foxhound" (`"fox h o u n d"`) are only partly merged. The authors' conclusion: **common words are merged entirely, less common words only partially**. That is what lets a subword vocabulary encode frequent words compactly while still spelling out rare ones. Each BPE step counts all adjacent symbol pairs across all words, weighted by word frequency, and merges only the most frequent one. The first toy merge is ("o","w") with count 4 (brown ×3 + slow ×1). merge_pair uses regex lookarounds so only whole symbols are merged, and it rewrites every word at once. Merged symbols can merge again, building up longer subwords: ow → brow → brown. After ten merges, common words (the, brown, fox) are single symbols; rare ones (slow, foxhound) are only partially merged.

title: Byte-pair encoding (BPE)
text: Greedy, iterative merging of the most frequent adjacent symbol pair into a new symbol, starting from characters. Repeatedly glue together the two pieces that appear side by side most often. Each iteration: pairs = Σ_words freq(word)·[adjacent pairs]; best = argmax; rewrite all words; add best to the vocabulary and record the merge rank. Toy merges in order: ow, th, the, br, brow, brown, fo, fox, qu, qui.
snippet: Greedy, iterative merging of the most frequent adjacent symbol pair into a new symbol, starting from characters.

title: Merge rule
text: A learned instruction 'replace adjacent symbols A B with AB', together with the order (rank) in which it was learned. One entry in the tokenizer's shorthand legend. Here produced by max(pairs, key=pairs.get) and applied via merge_pair; p.417 stores them in a ranked dictionary. Rule 1: o w → ow; rule 2: t h → th; rule 3: th e → the.
snippet: A learned instruction 'replace adjacent symbols A B with AB', together with the order rank in which it was learned.

title: Subword tokenization

title: Regex lookarounds for whole-symbol matching
text: (?<!\S) asserts that the preceding character isn't a non-space (so it is a space or the string start); (?!\S) asserts the same for the following character. Only match "o w" where both o and w are complete symbols, not the tail of "fo" or the head of "wn". Zero-width assertions, so the bounding spaces aren't consumed and remain as separators after substitution. In "fo x h o u n d", pattern for (o,u) matches "o u" but pattern for (o,x) does not match "fo x".
snippet: ?<!S asserts that the preceding character isn't a non-space so it is a space or the string start; ?!S asserts the same for the following character.

title: Frequency-weighted pair count
text: Implemented in code as: for pair in zip(symbols[:-1], symbols[1:]): pairs[pair] += freq \operatorname{count}(a,b) = \sum_{w \in \text{words}} \operatorname{freq}(w)\cdot \#\{i : s_i(w)=a,\ s_{i+1}(w)=b\} The score that decides which pair BPE merges next. Merging (a,b) reduces the total number of symbols in the encoded corpus by exactly count(a,b). w a distinct word (key of counts) \operatorname{freq}(w) number of times w appears in the corpus s_i(w) the i-th symbol of w's current segmentation (a,b) an adjacent symbol pair

title: Learning a BPE vocabulary and the SubWordTokenizer (Listing 14.7)
text:
Turning the merge loop into a full vocabulary-learning function with ranked merge rules, and a tokenizer that applies those rules to new text A BPE vocabulary starts with every character in the corpus and grows by one merged symbol per merge until it reaches the target size. The merges are stored with their rank. To tokenize new text, each word is split into characters and the learned merges are applied in rank order (earliest learned first) until no learned merge applies. The authors extend the merge loop of p.416 into a **full function for computing a BPE vocabulary**. The vocabulary **starts with all characters found in the input text**, and **merged symbols (larger and larger subwords) are added until it reaches the desired length**. A **separate dictionary of merge rules** is also kept, **including the rank order in which they were applied**. These ranked rules are what the tokenizer uses on new text.

**Listing 14.7** has two parts:

1. `compute_sub_word_vocabulary(dataset, vocab_size)` calls `count_and_split_words`, then sums **character frequencies** weighted by word counts (`char_counts[char] += counts[word]`) and sorts them with `most_common()`. This is why the vocabulary on p.418 begins `"[UNK]", "e", "t", "a", ...`. It then builds `vocab = ["[UNK]", ...]`.
2. A `SubWordTokenizer` class with the same interface as the earlier tokenizers. Its key method, **`bpe_merge(word)`**, loops: find all adjacent symbol pairs with `re.findall(r"(?<!\S)\S+ \S+(?!\S)", word, overlapped=True)`; stop if there are none; pick `best = min(pairs, key=lambda pair: self.merges.get(pair, 1e9))`, the pair with the **lowest rank** ("we apply merge rules in 'rank' order; more frequent pairs are merged first"); stop if `best` isn't a known merge; otherwise merge it with the same lookaround regex as `merge_pair`. `split` finds words, joins their characters with spaces, applies `bpe_merge` and collects the resulting symbols. `index` and `__call__` are the same as in the other tokenizers.

**Caution:** the printed listing is **typographically corrupted**. A large block after `vocab = ["[` (the rest of the training function, the class header and `__init__`, the start of `bpe_merge`) is missing, and so are the splitting regex and the character-joining line in `split`. These notes explain the surviving lines and give a clearly labeled reconstruction. The page ends by introducing a test on the full text of Moby Dick (p.418). The BPE vocabulary starts with [UNK] plus all characters (ordered by frequency) and grows by one merged symbol per merge until vocab_size. Training also returns a merges dict that maps each pair string to its rank. bpe_merge repeatedly merges the present pair with the lowest rank and stops when no pair has a learned rule. Finding pairs needs overlapping matches (regex module, overlapped=True). SubWordTokenizer has the same standardize/split/index/__call__ interface as the earlier tokenizers. The printed Listing 14.7 is corrupted; a large middle section and part of split are missing.

title: Byte-pair encoding (BPE)
text: A subword algorithm with a training phase (learn ranked merges from a corpus) and an encoding phase (apply them to new words in rank order). Training writes the recipe; encoding follows it step by step. Training: vocabulary = [UNK] + characters, then greedy merges until vocab_size. Encoding: split a word into characters, repeatedly merge the present pair with the lowest rank, stop when no pair has a rank. With the toy merges of p.416, 'brownie' → 'brown i e'.
snippet: A subword algorithm with a training phase learn ranked merges from a corpus and an encoding phase apply them to new words in rank order.

title: Ranked merge rules
text: A dictionary mapping a pair string such as "o w" to its rank (the order in which it was learned). A prioritized list: try the most important shortcuts first. bpe_merge picks min(pairs, key=lambda pair: self.merges.get(pair, 1e9)); unknown pairs get rank 1e9, effectively infinity. Toy ranks: 'o w'→0, 't h'→1, 'th e'→2, 'b r'→3, ...
snippet: A dictionary mapping a pair string such as "o w" to its rank the order in which it was learned.

Standard findall resumes after the end of each match, so adjacent pairs that share a symbol would be skipped. The book imports `regex as re` on p.408; the stdlib re module has no overlapped argument. title: Subword tokenizer on Moby Dick: results and trade-offs
text:
Training the BPE SubWordTokenizer on Moby Dick, comparing it with the word and character tokenizers, its training cost, and the move to Keras's built-in tokenization With a 2,000-term vocabulary, the BPE tokenizer encodes the test sentence in 16 tokens (13 for words, 63 for characters) and can tokenize every word in Moby Dick without [UNK]. Learning it is slower (about a minute), but that one-time cost is negligible next to model training. The authors train the BPE tokenizer on Moby Dick with `compute_sub_word_vocabulary(moby_dick, 2_000)`, which returns both a `vocabulary` and the ranked `merges`, and wrap them in a `SubWordTokenizer`. The same diagnostics as before give:

- **Vocabulary length: 2000.**
- **Vocabulary start:** `"[UNK]", "e", "t", "a", "o", "n", "i", "s", "h", "r"`: the unknown token followed by single characters in frequency order. There is no space, since spaces never occur inside words.
- **Vocabulary end:** `"bright", "pilot", "sco", "ben", "dem", "gale", "ilo"`: the last merges learned, a mix of whole words and word fragments.
- **Line length: 16** for "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely."

16 tokens is slightly more than the `WordTokenizer`'s 13, far fewer than the character tokenizer's 63. But unlike the word tokenizer, it **can tokenize every word in Moby Dick without `"[UNK]"`**. Every character is in the vocabulary, so the worst case is spelling a word out character by character. The result is a **short *average* token length with a small vocabulary that still handles rare words**, the advantage of subword tokenizers.

The downside is speed. Learning merge rules takes about **a minute** on the authors' hardware, much slower than counting words. That rarely matters, because a vocabulary is learned once per model and costs little compared with training the model.

With three tokenization approaches covered, the authors move on to training models. They add that you will **rarely need to build a tokenizer yourself**: Keras and most frameworks include tokenization utilities, and the rest of the chapter uses Keras's built-in functionality.

A sidebar, **"Which tokenization technique should I use?"**, begins here. For a *pretrained* model the question is trivial, because you must keep that model's exact tokenization (continued on p.419). BPE with 2,000 terms encodes the test sentence in 16 tokens, against 13 for words and 63 for characters. It tokenizes every word in Moby Dick without [UNK]; the worst case is one token per character. The vocabulary is [UNK], then characters by frequency, then merged subwords in the order learned. Learning merges is slower (about a minute) but done once per model, so it is negligible next to training. In practice you use built-in tokenizers; the rest of the chapter uses Keras's. With a pretrained model you must keep its exact tokenization.

title: Choosing a tokenizer; sets vs. sequences
text:
Practical advice on choosing a tokenizer, then the central modeling question of how to represent word order (sets vs. sequences) For a pretrained model you must keep its tokenizer. From scratch, the compression of word or subword tokenizers is usually worth having, and subword dominates modern language models, though characters or words can suit specific needs. Representing individual tokens is easy, since they are categorical. How to represent their order is the question that separates bag-of-words (set) models, RNNs and Transformers. The sidebar **"Which tokenization technique should I use?"** concludes here. With a pretrained model you must preserve its tokenization, or you **throw away the useful representations of input tokens stored in its weights**. If you build a model **from scratch**, you can tailor the tokenizer to the problem. In general, though, the **compression of word and subword tokenizers is too important to pass up**: the shorter the inputs on average, the better a model can **track long-range dependencies**, which improves performance. That is why **subword tokenization is the dominant choice for modern language models**. It handles rare or misspelled words without making common inputs longer. There is still **no one-size-fits-all** approach. **Spelling correction** might benefit from character-level tokenization, and **word-level** tokenization is simple and **interpretable**, since each input is a word a human would read, which makes ranking tokens by importance to a prediction easy. The book uses all three types in its text chapters.

**Section 14.3, Sets vs. sequences**, turns to modeling. Representing *individual tokens* is uncontroversial: they are **categorical features**, encoded as dimensions in a feature space or as category (token) vectors. The hard question is **how to encode token order**. Unlike timeseries steps, words have **no natural, canonical order**. Languages order words very differently (English vs. Japanese), the same idea can be expressed with words reshuffled, and even a fully shuffled short sentence is sometimes understandable, though often ambiguous. Order matters, but its link to meaning is not simple.

How to represent order is **the pivotal question from which NLP architectures spring**:

1. **Discard order**: treat text as an unordered set, giving **bag-of-words** models (14.4).
2. **Strict order**: process words one at a time like timeseries steps, using the **recurrent models** of the previous chapter.
3. **Hybrid**: the **Transformer** is technically order-agnostic but **injects word-position information**, so it can look at different parts of a sentence at once (unlike RNNs) while staying order-aware.

RNNs and Transformers take word order into account, so both are called **sequence models**. With a pretrained model, keep its exact tokenizer, or its learned token representations are wasted. From scratch, the compression of word/subword tokenizers usually wins, since shorter inputs help track long-range dependencies. Subword tokenization dominates modern language models: it handles rare and misspelled words without making common inputs longer. Characters can suit spelling correction; words are simple and interpretable. Tokens are categorical features (one-hot or token vectors); the hard question is how to represent their order. Bag-of-words discards order, RNNs process it step by step, and Transformers inject position info; RNNs and Transformers are sequence models.
snippet: The sidebar "Which tokenization technique should I use?" concludes here. With a pretrained model you must preserve its tokenization, or you throw away the useful representations…

Spelling correction → characters; bag-of-words sentiment with interpretable weights → words; large language model → subwords.

title: Bag-of-words vs. sequences, and downloading raw IMDb
text:
Why both set (bag-of-words) and sequence models still matter, and how to download and inspect the raw IMDb review dataset Early NLP mostly used order-discarding bag-of-words models, while sequence models came back around 2015 with RNNs; both are still useful. The chapter will compare them on the raw IMDb sentiment dataset, which is downloaded with `keras.utils.get_file` and laid out as train/test folders with `pos/`, `neg/` and an unlabeled `unsup/` directory. The page finishes the introduction to **section 14.3, Sets vs. sequences**, and starts the practical work.

**Historical context.** Most early machine-learning work on natural language used **bag-of-words** models, which treat a text as an unordered set of tokens and so throw away word order. Interest in **sequence models**, which do use order, only took off around **2015, with the rebirth of RNNs**. The authors say both approaches are still relevant today, and the coming sections show how each works and when to choose which.

**The benchmark.** Both approaches will be tested on the **IMDb movie-review sentiment-classification** dataset. In chapters 4 and 5 you used a *prevectorized* version, where reviews were already lists of integer word indices (p.130). Now you start from the **raw text files**, as you would on a new real-world text-classification problem.

**Listing 14.8** imports `os`, `pathlib`, `shutil` and `random` (used on the next page to copy files into a validation split), then calls `keras.utils.get_file` with the Stanford URL of `aclImdb_v1.tar.gz`, `fname="imdb"` and `extract=True`. The function downloads, caches and extracts the archive under `~/.keras/datasets/`. Appending `"aclImdb"` to the returned path gives `imdb_extract_dir`.

The page then lists the directories two levels deep using `glob("*/*")`:

- `train/pos`, `train/neg`, `train/unsup`
- `test/pos`, `test/neg`

Reviews with a **low** IMDb user rating are in `neg/`, and those with a **high** rating are in `pos/`. The `unsup/` (unsupervised) directory holds reviews that the dataset's creator **deliberately left unlabeled**, so each could be positive or negative. They are ignored for now, but section 14.5.4 uses them for pretraining word embeddings (p.438).

The page ends with a general methodological point: **look at your data before you start modeling**. Seeing what the inputs really are gives you intuition for what the model is actually doing. The next page (p.421) prints one review to do exactly this. Bag-of-words (set) models discard order and dominated early NLP; sequence models rose from 2015 with RNNs. Both are still relevant. Chapter 14 compares both families on raw IMDb text instead of the prevectorized chapter 4 version. `keras.utils.get_file(..., extract=True)` downloads, caches and unpacks the archive under ~/.keras/datasets. Labels are encoded by folder: pos/ = high rating, neg/ = low rating. train/unsup/ holds unlabeled reviews. Always inspect raw samples before modeling.

title: Bag-of-words (set) model
text: A text model whose input representation records which tokens occur in a document but not their order. Cut every word out of a review, throw the pieces in a bag and shake it. You can still tell that 'terrible', 'boring' and 'waste' are in there. A document becomes a vocabulary-sized vector (multi-hot, counts or TF-IDF), which is fed to a dense classifier. The representation is permutation-invariant. 'not good, quite bad' and 'not bad, quite good' map to the same unigram bag.
snippet: A text model whose input representation records which tokens occur in a document but not their order.

title: Sequence model
text: A model that processes tokens in order and can use word order, for example an RNN or a Transformer. Reading a sentence left to right instead of glancing at a word cloud. The input is an integer tensor of shape (batch, sequence_length), usually embedded into (batch, sequence_length, embedding_dim) and processed by recurrent or attention layers. An LSTM reading 'not good' can learn that 'not' flips the meaning of the word after it.
snippet: A model that processes tokens in order and can use word order, for example an RNN or a Transformer.

title: IMDb sentiment dataset (raw aclImdb)
text: Movie reviews labeled positive or negative by user rating, distributed as one text file per review in train/test × pos/neg folders, plus an unlabeled train/unsup folder. A labeled pile of opinions, sorted into two boxes according to whether the reviewer liked the movie. The archive aclImdb_v1.tar.gz from ai.stanford.edu. The labeled reviews are 25,000 for training and 25,000 for testing, each half positive and half negative (p.130). The unsup/ folder has another 25,000 unlabeled reviews (p.438). train/pos/ holds files of reviews with high ratings; test/neg/ holds held-out low-rated reviews.
snippet: Movie reviews labeled positive or negative by user rating, distributed as one text file per review in train/test × pos/neg folders, plus an unlabeled train/unsup folder.

title: Previewing a review and splitting off a validation set
text:
Inspecting one raw IMDb review and building train/validation/test directories on disk A raw review is informal, noisy text with HTML line breaks. Before tokenizing, the authors copy the test set unchanged and shuffle each training class with a fixed seed, sending 20% of the files to a new validation directory. The result can then be loaded with `text_dataset_from_directory`, the text counterpart of chapter 8's `image_dataset_from_directory`. **Listing 14.9** reads and prints one positive training review, `train/pos/4077_10.txt`. The text is typical of user-written data: lowercase 'i', misspellings ('hole castle part', 'there own'), run-on sentences, and leftover **HTML line-break tags** (`
`) before the final 'Enjoy'. This is what the tokenizers of section 14.2 will have to handle. Before tokenizing, the authors **copy the data into a new layout** with two changes: 1. The **unsupervised reviews are ignored** (only `neg` and `pos` are copied). 2. A separate **validation set** is created to monitor accuracy during training, by moving **20% of the training files** into a new directory. **Listing 14.10** defines three local paths, `imdb_train`, `imdb_test` and `imdb_val`. It copies the whole test folder unchanged with `shutil.copytree` (the callout says 'Moves the test data unaltered'). Then, for each category in `("neg", "pos")`, it: - lists the training files of that class, - shuffles them with `random.Random(1337)`, a seeded generator so the split is reproducible, - computes `num_val_samples = int(len(src_files) * 0.2)`, - copies the first `num_val_samples` files into `imdb_val//` and the rest into `imdb_train//`. Because the split is done **per class**, the validation set keeps the 50/50 class balance. Each class has 12,500 training reviews, so 2,500 per class go to validation. That gives 20,000 training and 5,000 validation reviews, as p.422 confirms. Finally, the authors remind you of chapter 8's `image_dataset_from_directory`, which built a labeled `Dataset` from a folder structure. **`text_dataset_from_directory`** does the same for text files, and the next page creates the three `Dataset` objects (Listing 14.11). Raw reviews are informal and contain HTML `
` tags, so preprocessing has to cope with that. The test split is copied unchanged; validation is carved out of the training data. 20% of each class (2,500 files) goes to validation, leaving 20,000 training and 5,000 validation reviews in total. A seeded `random.Random(1337)` makes the split reproducible. unsup/ is excluded by looping only over neg and pos. `text_dataset_from_directory` is the text version of `image_dataset_from_directory`.

title: Validation set
text: A held-out portion of the training data used to monitor performance during training and to guide modeling decisions. Practice exams you take while studying, kept separate from the final exam (the test set). Here, 20% of each class's training files (2,500 negative and 2,500 positive) are copied to imdb_val/. Training uses the remaining 20,000. int(12500 * 0.2) = 2500 files per class go to validation.

title: Per-class (stratified) split
text: Splitting each class separately with the same fraction, so every split keeps the original class proportions. Take 20% from the positive pile and 20% from the negative pile, rather than 20% from a mixed pile. Listing 14.10 loops over ("neg", "pos") and applies the same 0.2 fraction inside each loop. 2,500 neg and 2,500 pos in validation, 10,000 of each in training.

title: Seeded shuffling for reproducibility
text: Using a random generator with a fixed seed so that the shuffle, and therefore the split, is the same every run. Shuffling a deck the same way every time, so everyone gets the same hands. `random.Random(1337)` creates an independent generator seeded with 1337. Its `shuffle` permutes the file list in place, without affecting the global `random` state. Running Listing 14.10 twice on the same os.listdir order puts the same files in imdb_val.

title: Loading IMDb Datasets and the idea of set models
text:
Creating tf.data Datasets from the IMDb directories, and turning a review into an unordered bag of tokens encoded as a multi-hot vector Three Datasets (20,000 train, 5,000 validation, 25,000 test reviews) are built with `text_dataset_from_directory`. The simplest way to deal with token order is to discard it: tokenize, convert the token IDs to a set, and multi-hot encode that set into a vocabulary-length vector, which a model can then weight word by word. **Listing 14.11** imports `text_dataset_from_directory` from `keras.utils` and creates `train_ds`, `val_ds` and `test_ds` from the three directories prepared on p.421, each with `batch_size=32`. Each Dataset yields batches of raw review strings with integer labels inferred from the `neg`/`pos` folders. The text notes the sizes: originally 25,000 training and 25,000 test examples, and after the validation split, **20,000 for training and 5,000 for validation**.

**Section 14.4, Set models**, starts with the simplest answer to the ordering question: **discard order**. Reviews are still tokenized normally into a sequence of token IDs, but immediately afterwards each example is converted to a **set**, an unordered 'bag' of tokens that are either present or absent.

The model built on top of this **assigns a weight to every individual word**. The presence of `"terrible"` probably (though not always) indicates a bad review, and `"riveting"` might indicate a good one. Such a model is called a **bag-of-words model**.

A worked toy example follows:

- Sentence: `"this movie made me cry"`
- Vocabulary: `{"[UNK]": 0, "movie": 1, "film": 2, "made": 3, "laugh": 4, "cry": 5}`
- Tokenized: `[0, 1, 3, 0, 5]`. 'this' and 'me' are out of vocabulary, so they map to `[UNK]` = 0.
- As a set: `{0, 1, 3, 5}`. The duplicate 0 and the order are gone.
- **Multi-hot** vector of vocabulary length 6: `[1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]`.

The page ends just before the explanation, continued on p.423, that the 0 in position 5 means 'laugh' is absent and the final 1 means 'cry' is present. That vector can be fed directly to a model. text_dataset_from_directory gives batched (string, label) Datasets: 20,000 train, 5,000 val, 25,000 test. Set models tokenize normally, then discard order (and repetition) by converting each example to a set. A bag-of-words model learns one weight per vocabulary word. Multi-hot encoding turns a set into a fixed vector of vocabulary length. In the toy example, unknown words 'this' and 'me' both become [UNK] = 0.
snippet: Listing 14.11 imports textdatasetfromdirectory from keras.utils and creates trainds, valds and testds from the three directories prepared on p.421, each with batchsize=32. Each…

title: Bag-of-words (set) model
text: A text classifier that discards token order, represents each text as the set of tokens it contains, and learns a weight for each vocabulary word. Each word votes for 'positive' or 'negative' with a learned strength. Only the words present get to vote. Input: multi-hot $x\in\{0,1\}^V$. Model: dense layers on top, at minimum $\sigma(w^\top x + b)$. 'terrible' gets a negative weight and 'riveting' a positive one.
snippet: A text classifier that discards token order, represents each text as the set of tokens it contains, and learns a weight for each vocabulary word.

title: Multi-hot encoding
text: Encoding a set of token IDs as a vocabulary-length binary vector with 1 at each present ID. A checklist of every word in the vocabulary, with a tick next to each word that appears in the review. $x_i = 1$ if $i\in S$, else 0. The length is the vocabulary size $V$, and the vector is sparse for realistic $V$. {0,1,3,5} with V = 6 becomes [1,1,0,1,0,1].
snippet: Encoding a set of token IDs as a vocabulary-length binary vector with 1 at each present ID.

title: Out-of-vocabulary ([UNK]) token
text: A reserved vocabulary entry that all unknown words map to. A 'miscellaneous' bin for words the tokenizer has never learned. Index 0 in the page's toy vocabulary. 'this' and 'me' both map to it. [0, 1, 3, 0, 5]: positions 1 and 4 of the sentence are unknown.
snippet: A reserved vocabulary entry that all unknown words map to.

title: text_dataset_from_directory
text: A Keras utility that creates a batched tf.data.Dataset of (text, label) pairs from a directory with one subfolder per class. Point it at a filing cabinet and it reads every document and labels it by its folder. Labels are inferred from subfolder names in alphanumeric order (neg=0, pos=1). Here batch_size=32, and the elements are string tensors of shape (32,) with int32 labels of shape (32,). train_ds = text_dataset_from_directory(train_dir, batch_size=32)
snippet: A Keras utility that creates a batched tf.data.Dataset of text, label pairs from a directory with one subfolder per class.

title: Multi-hot encoding of a token set
text: {0, 1, 3, 5} → [1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1] x_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i \in S \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \qquad i = 0,\dots,V-1 Map a variable-size set to a fixed-length vector. Each coordinate answers 'does word i appear in this review?' S Set of token IDs present in the review ({0,1,3,5} here). V Vocabulary size (6 in the toy example, 20,000 on p.423). x_i Entry i of the multi-hot vector.
snippet: {0, 1, 3, 5} → 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1 — Map a variable-size set to a fixed-length vector.

title: A bag-of-words model as a sum of per-word weights
text: "a very simple model that assigns a weight to every individual word in a review" (prose; no formula printed) \hat{y} = \sigma\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^{V-1} w_i x_i + b\right) = \sigma\!\left(\sum_{i\in S} w_i + b\right) Formalizes 'assigns a weight to every individual word'. Only the words present contribute, and each contributes its own weight regardless of position. w_i Learned weight of vocabulary word i (for example, negative for 'terrible'). b Bias. \sigma Sigmoid, which maps the score to the probability of a positive review. \hat{y} Predicted probability that the review is positive.
snippet: "a very simple model that assigns a weight to every individual word in a review" prose; no formula printed — Formalizes 'assigns a weight to every individual word'.

title: Bag-of-words encoding of IMDb with TextVectorization
text:
Using Keras's TextVectorization layer with adapt() and multi-hot output to turn IMDb reviews into 20,000-dimensional bag-of-words vectors Instead of extending the hand-written WordTokenizer, you can use Keras's TextVectorization layer. It splits on whitespace, learns a 20,000-word vocabulary with adapt() on the label-free training texts, and outputs multi-hot vectors. Mapping it over all three Datasets gives batches of shape (32, 20000), ready for a linear model. The page first completes the toy example from p.422. In `[1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1]`, the 0 in the **fifth position** means `"laugh"` is absent, and the 1 in the **sixth position** means `"cry"` is present (positions counted from 1). This simple encoding can be used directly to train a model.

**Section 14.4.1, Training a bag-of-words model.** You could extend the `WordTokenizer` written earlier in the chapter, but it is easier to use Keras's built-in **`TextVectorization`** layer. It handles word and character tokenization and has extra features, including **multi-hot encoding** of its output.

Like many Keras preprocessing layers, `TextVectorization` has an **`adapt()`** method that learns layer state from data. Here that state is a **vocabulary**, built on the fly by iterating over a dataset. The authors choose **20,000 words**, which they call a good starting place for text classification.

**Listing 14.12**:

- creates `TextVectorization(max_tokens=20_000, split="whitespace", output_mode="multi_hot")` (callout: 'Learns a word-level vocabulary');
- strips labels with `train_ds.map(lambda x, y: x)` and calls `adapt` on the resulting text-only Dataset;
- maps `lambda x, y: (text_vectorization(x), y)` over the train, validation and test Datasets with `num_parallel_calls=8`, producing `bag_of_words_train_ds`, `bag_of_words_val_ds` and `bag_of_words_test_ds`.

A quick inspection of one batch, `next(bag_of_words_train_ds.as_numpy_iterator())`, shows `x.shape == (32, 20000)`: 32 reviews, each a 20,000-dimensional presence/absence vector. The printed `y.shape` is `(32, 1)`. (Note: with the default integer labels of Listing 14.11 you may see `(32,)` instead; see the review flag.) The next page builds a linear model with 20,001 parameters on these inputs (p.424). In the toy vector, 'fifth position' = 'laugh' (absent) and 'sixth position' = 'cry' (present). TextVectorization does word or character tokenization and multi-hot output in one layer. adapt() learns the vocabulary (20,000 words) from training texts with the labels stripped. The same fitted layer is mapped over the train, val and test Datasets with num_parallel_calls=8. Each batch is (32, 20000): one presence vector per review.

text: A Keras preprocessing layer that standardizes, splits and indexes text and can output integer sequences or encodings such as multi-hot. A configurable 'text-to-numbers' machine whose dictionary you fill by showing it your training data. Key arguments on this page: max_tokens=20_000, split="whitespace", output_mode="multi_hot". The output for a batch of N strings has shape (N, max_tokens). text_vectorization(["great movie"]) gives a 1×20000 vector with ones at the IDs of 'great' and 'movie'.

title: Logistic regression (linear classifier)
text: A model that computes $\sigma(w^\top x + b)$, one Dense unit with a sigmoid, and outputs the probability of the positive class. Add up the votes of the words present, then squash the total into a probability. Here $x\in\{0,1\}^{20000}$, $w\in\mathbb{R}^{20000}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$. It is trained with binary crossentropy, so it is exactly logistic regression on bag-of-words features. If 'superb' has a large positive weight and 'boring' a large negative weight, a review containing both is decided by their weights plus everything else present.

title: Listing 14.13 Building a bag-of-words regression model
text:
def build_linear_classifier(max_tokens, name):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(max_tokens,))
    outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(inputs)
    model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name=name)
    model.compile(
        optimizer="adam",
        loss="binary_crossentropy",
        metrics=["accuracy"],
    )
    return model

model = build_linear_classifier(max_tokens, "bag_of_words_classifier") Defines a function that builds and compiles a one-layer sigmoid classifier for vocabulary-length inputs, and instantiates it for the 20,000-token bag-of-words data. Logistic regression trained by Adam on binary crossentropy.
