title: Training the bag-of-words model and plotting accuracy
text:
Finishing the fit call with EarlyStopping, noting training speed, and plotting training vs. validation accuracy (figure 14.2) The 20,001-parameter model trains in well under a minute, and tokenization and encoding cost more than the parameter updates. In figure 14.2, training accuracy keeps rising toward about 0.97 while validation accuracy levels off around 0.89 instead of falling. The authors conclude that the model is so simple it cannot really overfit. The page opens with the **rest of Listing 14.14**. `model.fit` receives `bag_of_words_train_ds`, `validation_data=bag_of_words_val_ds`, `epochs=10` and `callbacks=[early_stopping]`. The callback (defined on p.424) monitors `val_loss` with `patience=2` and restores the best weights.

The model **trains in much less than a minute**, which is unsurprising for 20,001 parameters. The authors point out that **tokenization and encoding of the input are actually more expensive than updating the model parameters**. Turning text into 20,000-dimensional multi-hot vectors happens on the CPU for every batch of every epoch, while the parameter update is one small matrix–vector product.

A standard matplotlib snippet then plots `history.history["accuracy"]` (red dashed) and `history.history["val_accuracy"]` (blue solid) against `epochs = range(1, len(accuracy) + 1)`, with a title and legend.

**Figure 14.2** (captioned 'Training and validation metrics for our bag of words model') shows **9 epochs**. Since `epochs=10`, early stopping ended the run one epoch early. Reading the plot approximately:

- **training accuracy** rises steadily from about 0.84 at epoch 1 to about 0.975 at epoch 9;
- **validation accuracy** starts around 0.88, reaches about 0.89 by epoch 3, and stays nearly flat (peaking near 0.893 around epoch 7).

The authors interpret this as validation performance that **levels off rather than significantly declining**: the model is so simple it cannot really overfit. The growing gap between the curves shows that the model fits the training set ever better, but the extra fit does not hurt validation accuracy much. title: Test accuracy of the bag-of-words model, and efficient text preprocessing
text:
Evaluating the bag-of-words (unigram) linear classifier on the IMDb test set, justifying word-level tokenization, and a sidebar on keeping CPU text preprocessing from starving the GPU A 20,001-parameter linear model over multi-hot word vectors reaches about 88% test accuracy on IMDb sentiment. Because text must be tokenized on the CPU, the preprocessing pipeline only needs to be "fast enough" to keep the accelerator busy, which is what tf.data's parallel map achieves, on any Keras backend. The page finishes subsection 14.4.1. **Listing 14.15** evaluates the bag-of-words model trained on p.424-425 with `model.evaluate(bag_of_words_test_ds)`; the printed test accuracy is **0.88388**. The authors stress that this 88% accuracy comes from a training job light enough to run efficiently on a single CPU: the model is one `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` layer over a 20,000-dimensional multi-hot vector (20,001 parameters, p.424).

They then justify **word tokenization**. A "bag" of characters would say almost nothing about a review's content, because nearly every review uses nearly every character. Subword tokenization with a big enough vocabulary would also work, but there is little need for it here: the model is tiny, and a word vocabulary is quick to learn and makes each weight correspond to an actual English word. That makes the model easy to interpret.

The sidebar **"Preprocessing text efficiently"** makes five points:

1. Preprocessing speed matters because accelerators are expensive, and you don't want a GPU sitting idle waiting for input.
2. Text preprocessing must run on the CPU, because GPUs only handle numeric input. You *can* precompute token IDs, since tokenization doesn't depend on model weights, but tokenizing on the fly allows faster experimentation and is unavoidable at inference time on unseen inputs.
3. The goal is to be **"fast enough"**: if the GPU always has a fresh batch waiting, the GPU is the bottleneck and faster tokenization gains nothing.
4. `tf.data` is built to keep the CPU from bottlenecking the accelerator. In this chapter, `keras.utils.text_dataset_from_directory()` produces a `tf.data.Dataset`, and `map()` applies the `TextVectorization` layer, running in parallel over several CPU cores.
5. The code is still multi-backend. The chapter's outputs were generated with JAX, and Keras converts the `tf.data` tensors to whatever format the backend needs. The bag-of-words linear classifier reaches 0.88388 (about 88%) test accuracy on IMDb, cheap enough to train on one CPU. Word tokenization suits this model: character bags are uninformative, subwords are unnecessary, and word weights are interpretable. Text tokenization must run on the CPU before the accelerator's train step. Precomputing token IDs is possible but limits experimentation and is impossible for unseen inference inputs. Preprocessing only needs to be fast enough to keep the GPU busy; tf.data's parallel map usually achieves this. tf.data works with every Keras backend; the chapter's outputs were produced with JAX.

title: Bag-of-words model
text: A text model that discards word order and represents a document by which vocabulary terms it contains (here multi-hot), then learns one weight per term. Each word gets a vote for positive or negative; the review's score is the sum of the votes of the words present. Input $\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{20000}$ from TextVectorization(output_mode="multi_hot"); output $\sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}+b)$ trained with binary crossentropy. A review containing "riveting" and "masterpiece" adds their (positive) weights to the logit.

title: Choice of tokenization
text: Splitting text into units (characters, words or subwords) that are mapped to integer IDs. The tokenizer decides what the model's features are; for a set model, the units must carry meaning on their own. Character bags are almost the same for every document. Word vocabularies are learned by counting, are fast to build and are interpretable. Subword (BPE) vocabularies handle rare words but take longer to learn (p.418). The character set of almost any review is {a..z, space, punctuation}: useless as features.
snippet: Splitting text into units characters, words or subwords that are mapped to integer IDs.

title: Input-pipeline bottleneck
text: The situation where the CPU-side preparation of batches is slower than the accelerator's training step, so the accelerator waits. A fast chef (GPU) stuck waiting for a slow vegetable chopper (CPU). Pipelined step time is about $\max(t_{cpu}, t_{gpu})$. Preprocessing only needs to satisfy $t_{cpu} \le t_{gpu}$ ("fast enough"). On p.441 the CBOW model is bottlenecked on preprocessing, so caching makes later epochs more than three times faster.

title: From unigrams to bigrams: adding local word order
text:
Motivating n-grams and building a multi-hot encoding over a joint unigram + bigram vocabulary with TextVectorization(ngrams=2) Discarding all word order loses meaning carried by multi-word expressions ("United States", "not bad"). A cheap fix that keeps the set-based model is to treat pairs of consecutive tokens (bigrams) as extra vocabulary terms. TextVectorization does this out of the box with ngrams=2 and a larger 30,000-term vocabulary. Section 14.4.2 starts by admitting the main weakness of the bag-of-words model: **discarding all word order is very reductive**. Some concepts span several words. "United States" means something quite different from "united" and "states" taken separately, and a movie that is "not bad" should get a different sentiment score from one that is "bad".

The fix keeps the simple set-based model but injects **local** word order through **bigrams**, pairs of consecutive tokens. For "this movie made me cry" the **unigrams** are `{"this", "movie", "made", "me", "cry"}` and the bigrams are `{"this movie", "movie made", "made me", "me cry"}`. The model just trained is therefore a *unigram model*, and an **n-gram** is an ordered sequence of n tokens.

To add bigrams, bigram frequencies are counted while building the vocabulary. You can either build a vocabulary of bigrams only, or let unigrams and bigrams **compete for the same vocabulary slots** by frequency. In that case "United States" would enter the vocabulary before "ventriloquism" if it occurs more often.

The authors could extend their `WordTokenizer` but don't need to: **`TextVectorization` supports this out of the box**. **Listing 14.16** raises `max_tokens` to **30,000** to make room for bigrams, keeps `split="whitespace"` and `output_mode="multi_hot"`, adds **`ngrams=2`** (the callout says this "considers all unigrams and bigrams"), re-runs `adapt()` on the unlabeled training texts, and maps the layer over the train, validation and test datasets with `num_parallel_calls=8`, producing `bigram_train_ds`, `bigram_val_ds` and `bigram_test_ds`. The page ends by announcing an inspection of a preprocessed batch, shown on p.428. Discarding all word order loses multi-word meaning such as "United States" and "not bad". Bigrams (pairs of consecutive tokens) add local order while keeping the simple set model. The bag-of-words model is a unigram model; an n-gram is an ordered sequence of n tokens. Unigrams and bigrams can share one vocabulary and compete for slots by frequency. Listing 14.16 only changes max_tokens to 30,000, adds ngrams=2 and re-adapts the vocabulary.

title: Training and evaluating the bigram model, and the limits of n-grams
text:
Inspecting the bigram multi-hot encoding, training the unchanged linear classifier on it (30,001 parameters), reaching 90% test accuracy, and why n-grams beyond trigrams become intractable With a shared unigram + bigram vocabulary of 30,000 terms, the same linear classifier improves from about 88% to 90% test accuracy at almost no extra cost. Going much beyond bigrams or trigrams fails: the space of word n-grams grows exponentially, so coverage needs immense vocabularies and the model starts memorizing snippets instead of generalizing. The page continues from listing 14.16 (p.427). Pulling one batch from `bigram_train_ds` gives `x.shape == (32, 30000)`: each of 32 reviews is now a 30,000-dimensional multi-hot vector. Slicing the learned vocabulary, `text_vectorization.get_vocabulary()[100:108]` returns `["in a", "most", "him", "dont", "it was", "one of", "for the", "made"]`. Unigrams and bigrams sit side by side, ranked by frequency, which confirms that they compete for the same vocabulary slots. ("dont" also shows the default standardization stripping the apostrophe.)

Because only the encoding changed, the model needs no changes. **Listing 14.17** calls `build_linear_classifier(max_tokens, "bigram_classifier")` with `max_tokens = 30_000` and fits it for up to 10 epochs with the same `early_stopping` callback. The model has **30,001 parameters** instead of 20,001 but trains in about the same time.

**Listing 14.18** evaluates on `bigram_test_ds`: **0.90116**. That is 90% test accuracy, "a noticeable improvement" over the bag-of-words model's 0.88388 (p.426). The error rate drops from about 11.6% to 9.9%.

The last paragraph sets the limits. **Trigrams** (triplets of words) could help further, but beyond trigrams the problem quickly becomes **intractable**. The space of possible English 4-grams is immense and grows exponentially with n. Decent coverage would need an immense vocabulary, and the model would lose its ability to generalize, *memorizing entire snippets of sentences with weights attached*. Robustly modelling longer-range order needs more advanced techniques, which is the transition to the sequence models of section 14.5. The bigram encoding produces batches of shape (32, 30000), with unigrams and bigrams interleaved in a frequency-ranked vocabulary. The linear classifier is reused unchanged and has 30,001 parameters; training time is about the same. Test accuracy rises from 0.88388 to 0.90116 (90%). Trigrams might help a bit more, but beyond that the n-gram space explodes and models memorize instead of generalizing. Longer-range word order needs sequence models (section 14.5).

title: n-gram features and their limits
text: Using sequences of n consecutive tokens as vocabulary terms in a set model. Short phrases help, but long phrases are so varied that almost every one is new. Possible n-grams grow as $V^n$. Fixed-size vocabularies cover a shrinking fraction, and weights on rare n-grams memorize training snippets. "in a", "it was", "one of" are frequent bigrams; a 4-gram like "one of the worst" is far rarer.
snippet: Using sequences of n consecutive tokens as vocabulary terms in a set model.

title: Overfitting via memorization
text: Fitting training-specific details that don't generalize to new data. Learning "this exact sentence fragment means positive" instead of a general pattern. Rare high-order n-gram features let a linear model assign a weight to the label of a few training reviews. A 4-gram seen once in a positive review gets a positive weight that has nothing to do with sentiment.
snippet: Fitting training-specific details that don't generalize to new data.

title: Sequence models: why, which architectures, and padding/truncation
text:
Moving from hand-engineered n-gram features to models that learn from the raw token sequence, and preparing fixed-length integer sequences with [PAD] padding and truncation to 600 tokens Instead of manually engineering order features (n-grams), expose the model to the full token sequence and let it learn positional dependencies. Sequence models (RNNs, 1D ConvNets, Transformers) need rectangular batches, so variable-length reviews are padded with a special [PAD] token or truncated; for IMDb, truncating at 600 words keeps 95% of reviews whole. Section 14.5 begins by drawing the lesson of the last two models: **sequence information matters**. The bigram model improved on the bag-of-words model with features carrying some local word order. But those features were **manually engineered** and only scale to the order of a few neighbouring words (p.428). In the usual deep learning spirit, the better approach is to **expose the model to the raw word sequence** and let it **learn positional dependencies** between tokens itself.

Models that take the full token sequence are **sequence models**. Three architecture choices are listed: an **RNN**, as for timeseries in the previous chapter; a **1D ConvNet**, like the image models but convolving over one sequence dimension; and a **Transformer**, the subject of the next chapter.

All of them need inputs preprocessed into **ordered integer sequences of token IDs**, with one extra wrinkle: batched GPU computation requires **rectangular** inputs, but reviews vary from a few sentences to several paragraphs. The fix is to **truncate** long sequences and **pad** short ones with a special `"[PAD]"` token, analogous to `"[UNK]"`. With a target length of 8, "the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog" is truncated to its first eight tokens (dropping "dog"), and "the slow brown badger" gets four `[PAD]`s. Padding speeds up batch computation, but care is needed so that **padding tokens don't affect predictions**.

For IMDb the authors **truncate at 600 words**: the average review has 233 words and only 5% are longer than 600. The vectorization layer (named `Vectorization` in the text; it is `TextVectorization`) can pad or truncate and reserves index 0 of its vocabulary for padding. The code follows on p.430. Set models showed that word order matters, but n-gram features are hand-engineered and only capture a few words of local order. Sequence models ingest the full token sequence and learn positional dependencies; options are RNNs, 1D ConvNets and Transformers. Batches must be rectangular, so variable-length sequences are padded with [PAD] or truncated. Padding speeds up batched computation, but pad tokens must not influence predictions. IMDb reviews are truncated at 600 words (average 233; only 5% longer); index 0 is reserved for padding.
snippet: Section 14.5 begins by drawing the lesson of the last two models: sequence information matters. The bigram model improved on the bag-of-words model with features carrying some…

title: Sequence model
text: A model that ingests the complete, ordered token sequence and learns positional dependencies between tokens. Reading the review in order instead of checking which words appear. Input: integer tensor (batch, length) -> token vectors -> RNN / 1D conv / attention layers -> classifier. The LSTM classifier of 14.5.1 (p.430).
snippet: A model that ingests the complete, ordered token sequence and learns positional dependencies between tokens.

title: Padded integer sequences for IMDb, and starting the LSTM model
text:
Listing 14.19 turns reviews into padded/truncated integer sequences of length 600, the resulting (32, 600) batch is inspected, and section 14.5.1 starts by motivating one-hot encoding of token IDs as input to an LSTM TextVectorization with output_mode="int" and output_sequence_length=600 produces rectangular batches of token IDs, padded at the end with 0s. Before an LSTM can use them, the integer IDs must become float vectors; the simplest option is one-hot encoding each token. **Listing 14.19** implements the plan from p.429. With `max_length = 600` and `max_tokens = 30_000`, a new `TextVectorization` layer splits on whitespace (callout: "Learns a word-level vocabulary"), uses `output_mode="int"` ("Outputs a integer sequence of token IDs") and `output_sequence_length=max_length` ("Pads and truncates to 600 tokens"). It is adapted on `train_ds_no_labels`, then mapped over the train, validation and test datasets with `num_parallel_calls=8`, producing `sequence_train_ds`, `sequence_val_ds` and `sequence_test_ds`. Unlike listings 14.12 and 14.16, there is no multi-hot output and no `ngrams` argument: the order of tokens is kept.

Inspecting one batch (drawn from `sequence_test_ds`) gives `x.shape == (32, 600)`. Each row starts with token IDs (e.g. `11, 29, 7, ...`, `1825, 3, 25819, ...`) and ends with `0, 0, 0`. The batch has shape `(batch_size, sequence_length)`, and almost all samples end with a run of 0s for padding, as expected since the average review is 233 words (p.429). *Note (not in the book):* the `1` in the last row is the `[UNK]` index, an out-of-vocabulary word.

Section **14.5.1** starts with an LSTM, which the previous chapter showed works efficiently on sequence data. Token IDs are integers, though, and must first be mapped to floating-point data that neural layers can use. The most straightforward approach is **one-hot encoding**, analogous to the multi-hot encoding of a whole review: each token becomes a long vector of 0s with a single 1 at the token's vocabulary index. The page ends by announcing a layer that does this (listing 14.20, p.431). Listing 14.19 uses output_mode="int" and output_sequence_length=600 to produce ordered, fixed-length token-ID sequences. Batches have shape (batch_size, sequence_length) = (32, 600); most rows end with 0s for padding. Integer IDs are categorical and must be converted to float vectors before neural layers can use them. One-hot encoding, a single 1 at the token's index, is the most straightforward conversion; it is the per-token analogue of multi-hot.

title: A one-hot encoding layer and a bidirectional LSTM classifier
text:
Implementing one-hot encoding as a custom Keras layer with backend-agnostic keras.ops (eye + take + reshape), and building a Bidirectional LSTM sequence classifier on top of it One-hot encoding is a row lookup into an identity matrix: flatten the token IDs, gather the matching rows of eye(depth), and reshape back, turning a (32, 600) batch into (32, 600, 30000). Feeding this into a Bidirectional(LSTM(64)) lets information flow both forward and backward along the review, which suits classification. **Listing 14.20** builds a custom layer, `OneHotEncoding(keras.Layer)`, using only backend-agnostic `keras.ops`. The constructor stores `depth` (the vocabulary size). `call` does four steps, each marked by a callout:

1. **Flattens the inputs**: `ops.reshape(ops.cast(inputs, "int"), [-1])` casts token IDs to integers and flattens the batch into a 1-D vector of IDs.
2. **Builds an identity matrix with all possible one-hot vectors**: `ops.eye(self.depth)`. Row *i* of the identity matrix is exactly the one-hot vector of token *i*.
3. **Uses the token IDs to gather the correct vector for each token**: `ops.take(one_hot_vectors, flat_inputs, axis=0)`.
4. **Unflattens the output**: `ops.reshape(outputs, ops.shape(inputs) + (self.depth,))` restores the batch and sequence axes and adds a feature axis.

The layer is instantiated as `OneHotEncoding(max_tokens)`. Applied to a batch from `sequence_train_ds` it gives shape **(32, 600, 30000)**.

The authors put this layer directly into the model and use a **bidirectional LSTM** so information propagates both forward and backward along the sequence. They note that text *generation* (later in the book) needs **unidirectional** models, where a token's state depends only on earlier tokens, but for classification a bidirectional LSTM is a good fit.

**Listing 14.21** builds the model with the Functional API: `Input(shape=(max_length,), dtype="int32")` -> `one_hot_encoding` -> `Bidirectional(LSTM(64))` -> `Dropout(0.5)` -> `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")`. It is named `"lstm_with_one_hot"` and compiled with Adam, binary crossentropy and accuracy, the same training setup as the set models. The page ends by turning to the model summary and its parameter count (p.432: about 15.4 million parameters). One-hot encoding can be implemented as gathering rows of an identity matrix: flatten -> ops.take(ops.eye(depth)) -> reshape. Written with keras.ops, the custom layer works on any Keras backend and has no weights. The one-hot output for a batch is (32, 600, 30000), which is huge. A bidirectional LSTM reads the sequence both ways and suits classification; generation needs unidirectional models. Listing 14.21: Input(600, int32) -> OneHot -> Bidirectional(LSTM(64)) -> Dropout(0.5) -> Dense(1, sigmoid), compiled like the set models.
snippet: Listing 14.20 builds a custom layer, OneHotEncodingkeras.Layer, using only backend-agnostic keras.ops. The constructor stores depth the vocabulary size. call does four steps, each…

title: One-hot encoding as an identity-matrix lookup

The identity matrix is a catalog of all possible one-hot vectors; you look up the row for each token. ops.take(ops.eye(V), ids, axis=0) gathers rows; reshape restores (batch, length, V). With V = 4, ID 2 -> row 2 of eye(4) = [0, 0, 1, 0].

The output tensor has shape (B, T, V) with exactly one 1 per (b, t). title: Training and evaluating the one-hot bidirectional LSTM
text:
The parameter count of the one-hot-encoded bidirectional LSTM (about 15.4 million), its training (Listing 14.22) and evaluation (Listing 14.23), and why it is slow and less accurate than the set-based models Feeding one-hot token vectors of size 30,000 into a bidirectional LSTM makes the model huge (15,393,409 parameters) and each review an 18-million-number matrix, so training is slow, and the model reaches only about 84-85% test accuracy, worse than the bag-of-words (88%) and bigram (90%) models. The page opens with the output of `model.summary()` for the model `lstm_with_one_hot` built in Listing 14.21 (p.431). The layers and shapes are:

| Layer | Output shape | Params |
|---|---|---|
| `input_layer_2` (InputLayer) | (None, 600) | 0 |
| `one_hot_encoding` (OneHotEncoding) | (None, 600, 30000) | 0 |
| `bidirectional` (Bidirectional) | (None, 128) | 15,393,280 |
| `dropout` (Dropout) | (None, 128) | 0 |
| `dense_2` (Dense) | (None, 1) | 129 |

In total there are **15,393,409 parameters (58.72 MB)**, all trainable. The authors point out that this is a big step up from the unigram and bigram models (20,001 and 30,001 parameters, p.428). At about 15 million parameters it is one of the larger models in the book so far, even though it has only a single LSTM layer.

**Listing 14.22** trains it with `model.fit` on `sequence_train_ds`, validating on `sequence_val_ds`, for up to 10 epochs with the `early_stopping` callback. **Listing 14.23** evaluates it on `sequence_test_ds` and gets a test accuracy of **0.84811**.

The closing paragraph gives the verdict. The model works, but it trains very slowly, because every review is encoded as a `(600, 30000)` matrix: **18,000,000 floating-point numbers per review**, almost all of them zeros. On top of being slow, it reaches only about 84% test accuracy, clearly worse than the fast set-based models (88% for bag-of-words, p.426; 90% for bigrams, p.428). The next page draws the lesson: one-hot encoding words was the simplest option but a poor one, and **word embeddings** are the better way (p.433). The one-hot BiLSTM has 15,393,409 parameters, almost all of them in the LSTM input kernels: 2 × 4 × (64·30000 + 64² + 64). Each review becomes a (600, 30000) matrix, 18 million floats, which makes training very slow. Listing 14.22 reuses the training setup of the set models (10 epochs, early stopping); Listing 14.23 gives 0.84811 test accuracy. The sequence model is worse than both bag-of-words (0.884) and bigrams (0.901). The problem is the input representation, which leads to word embeddings on the next page.

title: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)
text: A recurrent layer with a cell state and three gates plus a candidate update, which processes a sequence step by step and can carry information across many timesteps. A conveyor belt (the cell state) runs along the sequence, and gates decide what to write onto it, what to erase, and what to read out at each step. Each of the four internal transforms has an input kernel $(d, h)$, a recurrent kernel $(h, h)$ and a bias $(h)$, so the parameter count is $4(dh + h^2 + h)$. Here $d = 30{,}000$, which makes the input kernels dominate. LSTM(64) on 30,000-dimensional inputs: 7,696,640 parameters.

title: Why one-hot vectors fail and what word embeddings are
text:
The hidden assumption of one-hot encoding (all words are independent and orthogonal), the requirement that geometric distance reflect semantic distance, and the contrast between sparse hardcoded one-hot vectors and dense, learned, low-dimensional word embeddings (figure 14.3) One-hot encoding is a feature-engineering choice that wrongly assumes every word is unrelated to every other. Word embeddings instead map words into a dense, low-dimensional, learned geometric space in which distances reflect meaning. The page draws the lesson from p.432: one-hot encoding words, the simplest option available, **wasn't a great idea**, and there is a better way, **word embeddings**.

**Section 14.5.2** explains why. One-hot encoding is a **feature-engineering decision**, and it injects an assumption about the feature space: that all tokens are **independent of each other**. Geometrically, one-hot vectors are all **orthogonal**. For words this is clearly wrong, because words form a structured space and share information. "Movie" and "film" are interchangeable in most sentences, so their vectors should be the same or nearly so, not orthogonal.

More abstractly, the **geometric relationship between word vectors should reflect the semantic relationship between the words**. Synonyms should get similar vectors, and in general the geometric distance (for example **cosine distance** or **L2 distance**) should relate to "semantic distance": unrelated words far apart, related words close together. **Word embeddings** are vector representations that do exactly this, mapping human language into a structured geometric space.

One-hot vectors are **binary, sparse and very high-dimensional** (as many dimensions as there are words in the vocabulary, 30,000 here). Embeddings are **low-dimensional floating-point (dense) vectors**, commonly 256-, 512- or 1,024-dimensional even for very large vocabularies. So embeddings pack more information into far fewer dimensions.

**Figure 14.3** shows this visually. On the left, four tall one-hot vectors, each almost entirely black (zeros) with a single white cell: *sparse, high-dimensional, hardcoded*. On the right, four short vectors with varied gray levels: *dense, lower-dimensional, learned from data*. The caption adds that hashing gives representations just as sparse and hardcoded as one-hot encoding. One-hot encoding is a feature-engineering choice that assumes all words are independent (orthogonal). For language that assumption is wrong: "movie" and "film" should have nearly identical vectors. In a good embedding space, geometric distance (cosine, L2) reflects semantic distance. One-hot vectors are binary, sparse, vocabulary-sized and hardcoded; embeddings are dense, low-dimensional (256-1,024) and learned. Embeddings pack more information into far fewer dimensions.
snippet: The page draws the lesson from p.432: one-hot encoding words, the simplest option available, wasn't a great idea, and there is a better way, word embeddings. Section 14.5.2…

title: Structured embedding spaces and the Keras Embedding layer
text:
Embedding spaces are structured and learned: meaningful directions (figure 14.4, pet→wild and canine→feline; gender and plural vectors). There is no universal embedding, so embeddings are learned per task, and the Embedding layer works as an integer-to-vector dictionary with shapes (batch_size, sequence_length) → (batch_size, sequence_length, embedding_size) Good embedding spaces have meaningful geometry: nearby points are similar words, and consistent directions encode relations. Because the best geometry depends on the task, you usually learn an embedding jointly with each new task by training the weights of a Keras Embedding layer, which is just a learned lookup table from token indices to dense vectors. The page first expands on the idea of embeddings from p.433. Embeddings are not only dense but also **structured**, and their **structure is learned from data**. Similar words end up close together, and moreover **specific directions in the space are meaningful**.

**Figure 14.4** is a toy 2D example with four words: Wolf and Tiger near the top (y ≈ 0.8), Dog and Cat lower down (y ≈ 0.4), with the canines (Dog, Wolf) on the left (x ≈ 0.4) and the felines (Cat, Tiger) on the right (x ≈ 0.75). The **same vector** takes cat → tiger and dog → wolf (a "from pet to wild animal" vector). **Another vector** takes dog → cat and wolf → tiger (a "from canine to feline" vector).

In real embedding spaces, typical meaningful transformations are **"gender" and "plural" vectors**: king + female → queen, king + plural → kings. Real spaces typically have **thousands** of such interpretable, potentially useful directions.

**Section 14.5.3** asks whether there is an ideal embedding space that maps human language perfectly for every task. Possibly, but nobody has computed one. There is also no single human language: languages are **not isomorphic**, since each reflects a specific culture and context. More pragmatically, the best space **depends on the task**. The ideal space for English movie-review sentiment differs from the one for English legal-document classification, because different semantic relationships matter.

So it is reasonable to **learn a new embedding space for each task**. Backpropagation makes this easy, and Keras even easier, since it just means learning the weights of the **`Embedding` layer**. That layer is best understood as a **dictionary** mapping integer indices (words) to dense vectors: integers in, a lookup, vectors out (figure 14.5, p.435). It takes a rank-2 integer tensor of shape `(batch_size, sequence_length)` and returns a float tensor of shape `(batch_size, sequence_length, embedding_size)`. Embedding spaces are structured: similar words are close and directions encode relations. In figure 14.4 one vector maps pet → wild (cat → tiger, dog → wolf) and another canine → feline (dog → cat, wolf → tiger). Real spaces have gender and plural vectors (king → queen, king → kings) and thousands of other meaningful directions. No universal embedding exists; the best geometry depends on language and task, so embeddings are often learned per task. The Keras Embedding layer is a learned dictionary: (batch_size, sequence_length) ints → (batch_size, sequence_length, embedding_size) floats.

title: Listing 14.24 Building an LSTM sequence model with an Embedding layer
text:
hidden_dim = 64
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(max_length,), dtype="int32")

    input_dim=max_tokens,
    output_dim=hidden_dim,
    mask_zero=True,
)(inputs)
x = keras.layers.Bidirectional(keras.layers.LSTM(hidden_dim))(x)
x = keras.layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
outputs = keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name="lstm_with_embedding")
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="binary_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
) It builds and compiles a binary sentiment classifier: token ids, a learned 64-dimensional embedding (with padding masked), a bidirectional LSTM, dropout and a sigmoid output. Embedding lookup, masked bidirectional recurrence, dropout, then logistic regression on the 128-dimensional summary.

title: mask_zero: masking padding tokens, and the embedding model's summary
text:
Why padded sequences need masking, how mask_zero=True in the Embedding layer marks token id 0 ([PAD]) so the LSTM outputs the last non-masked representation, the optional explicit mask argument, and the model summary of lstm_with_embedding (Embedding 1,920,000; NotEqual mask layer; Bidirectional 66,048; Dense 129) Padding tokens added to reach length 600 should not influence the prediction. mask_zero=True makes the Embedding layer emit a mask (token id ≠ 0) that the LSTM uses to ignore padded steps, so the final representation corresponds to the last real token. The page explains the third argument of the Embedding layer in Listing 14.24: **`mask_zero=True`**. It tells Keras which inputs are `"[PAD]"` tokens so they can be **masked** later in the model.

When sequences are preprocessed to a fixed length, a lot of padding may be added, so a sequence can look like `["the", "movie", "was", "awful", "[PAD]", "[PAD]", "[PAD]", "[PAD]"]`. Without masking, these pads are embedded and fed into the LSTM, so its final representation may be the result of processing the `[PAD]` vector over and over. What we actually want is the representation at **"awful"**, the last non-padding token. Equivalently, we want to mask all `[PAD]` tokens so they do not affect the prediction.

`mask_zero=True` is a **shorthand** for this. Keras marks every position whose input was **0**, the assumed id of `[PAD]`. The mask is used internally by the `LSTM`: instead of outputting the last representation of the whole sequence, it outputs the **last non-masked representation**. This masking is **implicit** and easy to use. For explicit or custom masking, `LSTM` takes an optional **`mask`** call argument.

The page ends with `model.summary()` for `lstm_with_embedding`:

| Layer | Output | Params |
|---|---|---|
| input_layer_3 | (None, 600) | 0 |
| embedding | (None, 600, 64) | 1,920,000 |
| not_equal (NotEqual) | (None, 600) | 0 |
| bidirectional_1 | (None, 128) | 66,048 |
| dropout_1 | (None, 128) | 0 |
| dense_3 | (None, 1) | 129 |

The extra `not_equal` layer is the mask computation (input ≠ 0), and the Bidirectional layer is connected to both the embedding and the mask. The totals, 1,986,177 parameters (7.58 MB), appear at the top of p.437. Padding to a fixed length adds many [PAD] tokens that would otherwise pass through the LSTM. mask_zero=True marks positions with id 0 ([PAD]) and passes the mask to the LSTM. The masked LSTM outputs the last non-masked representation, e.g. at "awful". For custom masking, pass a mask argument when calling the LSTM. The summary shows Embedding 1,920,000 + BiLSTM 66,048 + Dense 129 parameters, plus a weightless NotEqual mask node.
snippet: The page explains the third argument of the Embedding layer in Listing 14.24: maskzero=True. It tells Keras which inputs are "PAD" tokens so they can be masked later in the model.…

title: Training the embedding LSTM: smaller and faster, but still 84%
text:
The embedding LSTM's totals (1,986,177 parameters), Listing 14.25 (training and evaluation, test accuracy 0.84436), why accuracy did not improve (not enough data to learn a good embedding; overfitting, with train accuracy above 99%), the motivation for pretraining, and the start of the sidebar on text augmentation Replacing one-hot inputs with a learned Embedding layer makes the model roughly 10× smaller and faster, but accuracy stays at about 84%, because 20,000 reviews are too few to learn good embeddings before the model overfits. The fix is to pretrain the embedding separately on more, unlabeled data. The top of the page finishes the model summary from p.436: **Total params 1,986,177 (7.58 MB)**, all trainable. The authors note that the parameter count fell from **15 million to 2 million** compared with the one-hot LSTM.

**Listing 14.25** trains the model exactly as before (`sequence_train_ds`, validation on `sequence_val_ds`, `epochs=10`, `callbacks=[early_stopping]`) and evaluates it on `sequence_test_ds`. Test accuracy: **0.8443599939346313**.

The embedding cut both **training time and model size by an order of magnitude**, so a learned embedding is clearly far more efficient than one-hot encoding. **However, accuracy did not change.** It stayed stubbornly around **84%**, far from the bag-of-words (88%) and bigram (90%) models.

Does that mean structured embeddings aren't useful, or aren't useful for classification? **Quite the contrary**: a well-trained embedding can dramatically raise a model's performance ceiling. The problem here is the **training setup**. The **20,000 training reviews** are not enough to learn a good word embedding. By the end of training, **train accuracy exceeds 99%**: the model has started to **overfit and memorize** before it has learned an optimal set of embeddings.

The remedy is **pretraining**: train the embedding **separately, on more data**, without needing positive/negative labels, instead of jointly with the classifier.

A sidebar, **"Augmenting text data"**, begins. Since augmentation was so important for vision, can it be done for text? Yes, but it is **not nearly as effective**. Basic techniques make small edits to the input text to improve robustness, for example random deletion of words (continued on p.438, which also covers swapping words, the risk of changing meaning, synonym replacement and generative augmentation). The embedding LSTM has 1,986,177 parameters versus about 15.4M for the one-hot version. Listing 14.25 gives 0.84436 test accuracy, the same as before (about 84%). Embeddings fixed efficiency (size and training time), not accuracy. Diagnosis: 20,000 reviews are too few to learn good embeddings; train accuracy exceeds 99%, so the model overfits first. Remedy: pretrain embeddings separately on more, unlabeled data. Text augmentation exists but is much less effective than image augmentation.
snippet: The top of the page finishes the model summary from p.436: Total params 1,986,177 7.58 MB, all trainable. The authors note that the parameter count fell from 15 million to 2…

title: Why text augmentation is hard, and the idea of pretraining a word embedding
text:
The end of the "Augmenting text data" sidebar (deleting/swapping words, its pitfalls, generative augmentation) and the start of section 14.5.4: pretraining as the dominant NLP approach, using the IMDb unsup/ reviews, and introducing the Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) model Text augmentation is brittle because language is order-dependent and small edits can change meaning, so it is usually better to find more text. A better way to use extra unlabeled text is pretraining: an unsupervised task (here CBOW, predicting a word from its neighbors) trains the Embedding layer's parameters before the model is specialized to the labeled classification task. The page opens with the end of the sidebar **"Augmenting text data"**, begun on p.437. Basic augmentation edits text to make a model more robust: randomly delete words or swap their positions, so "The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain" becomes "The rain Spain falls plain on the mainly." Training on such edited inputs can make a model robust to typos and grammar mistakes. But the example also shows the **big pitfall**: it is easy to change the meaning of an example by accident. A cat photo is still a cat after cropping, rotating or recoloring. Language, by contrast, is **order-dependent and highly sensitive to tiny changes**, and swapping two words can reverse a sentence's meaning. Replacing words with synonyms from a table is also brittle, because a word can have several meanings and the wrong one may be picked. For these reasons text augmentation is not widespread, and the authors advise that **it is usually better to seek more text examples**. They add that generative models (coming chapters) offer a new kind of augmentation: generating new, coherent inputs that plausibly resemble the data, useful where data is sparse.

**Section 14.5.4** then introduces **pretraining**, which has been the dominant approach to text modeling during the last decade of NLP progress. Sequence models with millions or billions of parameters are very data-hungry, and labeled examples are usually the bottleneck. The idea is to design an **unsupervised task** that trains parameters without labels, on text from a similar domain or on arbitrary text in the target languages. This "primes" the model with general patterns of language before it is specialized to the final task.

Word embeddings were one of the first big successes of pretraining. The authors recall the `unsup/` directory of IMDb that was ignored earlier: it holds another 25,000 reviews, the same size as the training data. They will combine all of this text and pretrain the parameters of an `Embedding` layer with an unsupervised task. The setup is the **Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)** model (Mikolov et al., 2013, footnote 2): slide a window over the text and guess the missing middle word from its neighbors (the sentence continues on p.439). Basic text augmentation deletes or swaps words to build robustness to typos and grammar mistakes. Its big pitfall is changing meaning by accident, because language is order-dependent; synonym tables are brittle too. The authors recommend seeking more text rather than investing in text augmentation; generative models may offer a new kind of augmentation. Pretraining on an unsupervised task is the dominant NLP approach because large sequence models are data-hungry and labels are scarce. Section 14.5.4 pretrains the Embedding layer on all IMDb text, including the 25,000 unlabeled unsup/ reviews, using CBOW (Mikolov et al. 2013).
snippet: The page opens with the end of the sidebar "Augmenting text data", begun on p.437. Basic augmentation edits text to make a model more robust: randomly delete words or swap their…

title: Text data augmentation
text: Making modified copies of training texts, for example by randomly deleting or swapping words, replacing words with synonyms, or generating new examples with a generative model. It shows the model the kind of noise it will meet in practice, such as typos and slightly wrong grammar. It assumes the label is invariant under the edit. For text this assumption often fails, because meaning depends on word order and word sense. "The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain" -> "The rain Spain falls plain on the mainly."
snippet: Making modified copies of training texts, for example by randomly deleting or swapping words, replacing words with synonyms, or generating new examples with a generative model.

title: Pretraining
text: Training model parameters on an unsupervised task over large amounts of unlabeled text, before specializing the model to the final task. The model first reads a lot of text to learn how language works in general, and only then learns the specific job. The targets come from the text itself (a hidden word), so every window of text is a training example. The learned weights initialize the task model. Pretraining an Embedding layer with CBOW on the 25,000 unsup/ reviews plus the labeled reviews.
snippet: Training model parameters on an unsupervised task over large amounts of unlabeled text, before specializing the model to the final task.

title: Word embedding
text: A learned dense vector for each token in the vocabulary, stored as the weight matrix of an Embedding layer. Words used in similar ways end up close to each other in the vector space. An Embedding layer of shape (vocab_size, 64) maps token IDs to rows; its weights can be trained jointly with a task or pretrained separately. In the book's run, the LSTM with a jointly trained embedding reached about 84% test accuracy (p.437).
snippet: A learned dense vector for each token in the vocabulary, stored as the weight matrix of an Embedding layer.

title: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)
text: An unsupervised setup that slides a window over text and predicts each window's middle word from the surrounding words. Like a fill-in-the-blank exercise: "sail, wave, mast" suggest "boat" (p.439). Context embeddings are averaged (order is ignored, hence "bag") and a softmax over the vocabulary predicts the target word. The embedding matrix is what we keep. With nine-token windows (p.439), the eight outer words predict the middle one.
snippet: An unsupervised setup that slides a window over text and predicts each window's middle word from the surrounding words.

title: Unsupervised (self-supervised) pretraining task
text: A training objective built from unlabeled data, where the target is part of the input itself. Hide something in the text and ask the model to recover it. Examples: CBOW (middle word from neighbors), masked language modeling (p.479), next-token prediction (chapter 15). Each position of each IMDb review yields one (context, target) pair.
snippet: A training objective built from unlabeled data, where the target is part of the input itself.

title: The CBOW idea and preparing IMDb text for it
text:
How CBOW guesses a missing word from its neighbors (figure 14.6), the goal of learning a 64-dimensional vector per vocabulary word, Listing 14.26 (a TextVectorization layer without padding) and the start of Listing 14.27 (nine-token windows with context_size = 4) CBOW slides a window over text and predicts the middle word from the unordered bag of surrounding words with a shallow network. To prime the LSTM's embedding, the authors reuse the existing vocabulary, tokenize reviews without truncation or padding, and cut them into windows of nine tokens: eight context words and one middle label. The page finishes the description of the **Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)** model begun on p.438: slide a window over the text in a dataset and repeatedly try to **guess a missing word from the words directly to its left and right**. If the bag of surrounding words contains "sail," "wave," and "mast," the middle word might be "boat" or "ocean." **Figure 14.6** shows the model as a shallow network: the context words "the," "quick" (left) and "fox," "jumped" (right) are combined in a "sum" box that predicts the target word "brown."

For the IMDb problem the goal is to **prime the word embedding of the LSTM** trained just before. The authors reuse the `TextVectorization` vocabulary computed earlier, so all they need to learn is **a good 64-dimensional vector for each word in this vocabulary**.

**Listing 14.26** creates a new `TextVectorization` layer, `tokenize_no_padding`, with the same vocabulary (`text_vectorization.get_vocabulary()`), `split="whitespace"` and `output_mode="int"`, and without the fixed sequence length the classifier used. It therefore **does not truncate or pad** its output: each review becomes a token-ID sequence of its natural length, ready for a sliding context window.

The preprocessing slides a window over the training data to make **"bags" of nine consecutive tokens**: the **middle word is the label** and the **other eight words are an unordered context** used to predict it. As before, `tf.data` does the preprocessing, which, the authors note, **does not limit the backend** used for the actual model training.

**Listing 14.27** begins at the bottom of the page with `import tensorflow as tf` and `context_size = 4`, the number of words to the left or right of the label. The rest of the listing, the windowing function, the label split and the dataset pipeline over the full `train` directory including `unsup/`, is on p.440. CBOW guesses a missing word from its left and right neighbors; the context is an unordered bag. Figure 14.6 shows a shallow network: context words -> sum -> target word. The goal is a good 64-dimensional vector for each word of the existing IMDb vocabulary, to prime the LSTM's embedding. Listing 14.26 reuses the vocabulary in a TextVectorization layer that neither pads nor truncates. Windows have nine tokens: eight context words (context_size = 4 per side) and a middle-word label. tf.data does the preprocessing without restricting the Keras backend; Listing 14.27 continues on p.440.
snippet: The page finishes the description of the Continuous Bag of Words CBOW model begun on p.438: slide a window over the text in a dataset and repeatedly try to guess a missing word…

title: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)
text: A shallow model that predicts a word from the unordered set of its neighboring words. Fill in the blank: "sail, wave, mast" suggests "boat" or "ocean." Embed each context token, combine the embeddings (figure 14.6: sum; Listing 14.28: average), and predict the target over the vocabulary. "the quick ___ fox jumped" -> "brown" (figure 14.6).

title: Context window

title: Building CBOW windows with tf.data and the start of the CBOW model
text:
The body of Listing 14.27 (window_data, split_label, and a tf.data pipeline over the full IMDb train directory including unsup/), and the start of Listing 14.28: an Embedding layer plus GlobalAveragePooling1D for the CBOW model Each unpadded review is turned into all of its nine-token windows with a vectorized gather, each window is split into an eight-token context bag and the middle token as label, and the CBOW model embeds the bag and averages the embeddings to predict the middle word. The page holds most of **Listing 14.27**. `window_size = 9` is the total window size. **`window_data(token_ids)`** computes the number of complete windows, `tf.maximum(tf.size(token_ids) - context_size * 2, 0)`, then builds an index matrix by broadcasting: `tf.range(window_size)[None, :] + tf.range(num_windows)[:, None]` has shape `(num_windows, 9)`, row *i* being `i, i+1, ..., i+8`. `tf.gather` uses it to collect the tokens of every window at once, and `Dataset.from_tensor_slices` emits the windows one by one. **`split_label(window)`** takes the four tokens to the left (`window[:context_size]`) and four to the right (`window[context_size + 1 :]`), concatenates them into the `bag`, and uses `window[4]`, the middle token, as the `label`.

The pipeline loads text with `keras.utils.text_dataset_from_directory(imdb_extract_dir / "train", batch_size=None)`. That is the original IMDb training directory, so it **uses all training data, including the `unsup/` directory**. It then **drops the label** (`lambda x, y: x`), **tokenizes** with `tokenize_no_padding`, **creates context windows** with `interleave(window_data, cycle_length=8, ...)` (which mixes windows from eight reviews at a time), and **splits the middle word into a label** with `split_label`. Every step uses `num_parallel_calls=8`.

After preprocessing, each example is **eight integer token IDs as context paired with a single token ID label**.

The model is **exceedingly simple**: an `Embedding` layer embeds all context tokens, and `GlobalAveragePooling1D` computes **the average embedding of the bag**, which is used to predict the middle token. "That's it!" By repeatedly refining the embedding space to be good at predicting a word from nearby word embeddings, we learn a rich embedding of the tokens used in movie reviews.

**Listing 14.28** begins with `hidden_dim = 64`, `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(2 * context_size,))` (8 tokens), `cbow_embedding = layers.Embedding(max_tokens, hidden_dim)`, then `x = cbow_embedding(inputs)` and `x = layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D()(x)`. The output layer, compilation and summary are on p.441. The embedding layer is kept in its own variable, `cbow_embedding`, so its weights can be reused later. window_data extracts all max(n - 8, 0) overlapping nine-token windows of a review in one vectorized gather. split_label turns each window into an 8-token bag and the middle token as label. The pipeline reads the original train directory, so the unsup/ reviews are included; class labels are dropped. Each training example is eight token IDs paired with one token ID. The CBOW model embeds the 8 tokens in 64 dimensions and averages them with GlobalAveragePooling1D; the listing continues on p.441. The Embedding layer is kept as cbow_embedding so its weights can be transferred later.
snippet: The page holds most of Listing 14.27. windowsize = 9 is the total window size. windowdatatokenids computes the number of complete windows, tf.maximumtf.sizetokenids - contextsize …

title: Sliding context windows via gather
text: All windows of length 9 in a sequence, extracted at once by gathering with an index matrix. Write down the start positions 0..n-9, add 0..8 to each, and read off those tokens. idx = range(9)[None,:] + range(n-8)[:,None] (broadcast to (n-8, 9)); windows = gather(tokens, idx). n = 11 tokens -> idx rows [0..8], [1..9], [2..10]: 3 windows.
snippet: All windows of length 9 in a sequence, extracted at once by gathering with an index matrix.

title: CBOW model
text: Embedding -> average over the context -> prediction of the middle word. The average of the neighbors' vectors should point to the missing word. Input (None, 8) -> Embedding(max_tokens, 64) -> (None, 8, 64) -> GlobalAveragePooling1D -> (None, 64) -> Dense(max_tokens) (p.441). Listing 14.28.

title: GlobalAveragePooling1D
text: Averages a sequence of vectors over the time axis. Collapses eight word vectors into their mean. (batch, steps, features) -> (batch, features); permutation-invariant over steps. (None, 8, 64) -> (None, 64).
snippet: Averages a sequence of vectors over the time axis.

An assembly line: read a review, strip its label, tokenize it, cut it into windows, split each window. map applies a function per element; interleave maps each element to a dataset and mixes elements from cycle_length of them; num_parallel_calls runs transformations in parallel. dataset.interleave(window_data, cycle_length=8, num_parallel_calls=8).

Permuting the bag leaves h unchanged. E Embedding matrix of shape (max_tokens, 64) \text{bag}_k k-th context token ID h Average context vector fed to the output layer

title: Listing 14.27 Preprocessing our IMDb data for pretraining a CBOW model (continued)
text:
window_size = 9
def window_data(token_ids):
    num_windows = tf.maximum(tf.size(token_ids) - context_size * 2, 0)
    windows = tf.range(window_size)[None, :]
    windows = windows + tf.range(num_windows)[:, None]
    windowed_tokens = tf.gather(token_ids, windows)
    return tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(windowed_tokens)
def split_label(window):
    left = window[:context_size]
    right = window[context_size + 1 :]
    bag = tf.concat((left, right), axis=0)
    label = window[4]
    return bag, label
dataset = keras.utils.text_dataset_from_directory(
    imdb_extract_dir / "train", batch_size=None
)
dataset = dataset.map(lambda x, y: x, num_parallel_calls=8)
dataset = dataset.map(tokenize_no_padding, num_parallel_calls=8)
dataset = dataset.interleave(window_data, cycle_length=8, num_parallel_calls=8)
dataset = dataset.map(split_label, num_parallel_calls=8) Continues Listing 14.27 from p.439 (where import tensorflow as tf and context_size = 4 appear). It defines the windowing and label-splitting functions and builds a tf.data pipeline that turns every review in the IMDb train directory (pos/, neg/ and unsup/) into (8-token bag, middle-token label) pairs. For each review: tokenize -> all overlapping 9-token windows -> (context, middle) pairs.

Even ignoring that, left = window[:3] takes positions 0-2 and right = window[4:] takes positions 4-8, so the bag skips position 3 and includes position 4, which is exactly the label window[4]: the model would be asked to predict a token it is given as input.

title: Finishing, compiling and training the CBOW model
text:
The output layer, compilation and summary of the CBOW model (3.87 million parameters), Listing 14.29 training with batch(1024).cache() for 4 epochs, why caching helps when preprocessing is the bottleneck, and the ~12% middle-word accuracy over a 30,000-word vocabulary The CBOW model ends with a 30,000-way Dense output and is trained as a word classifier. Because the model is tiny, a large batch is affordable and the CPU preprocessing is the bottleneck, so the batched windows are cached in memory, which makes later epochs more than three times faster. Guessing the exact middle word 12% of the time from eight neighbors is reasonable given 30,000 choices. The page completes **Listing 14.28**. The averaged context vector goes into `layers.Dense(max_tokens, activation="sigmoid")`, one output per vocabulary word, and the model is wrapped as `cbow_model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)`. It is compiled with `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` (the label is an integer token ID) and `metrics=["sparse_categorical_accuracy"]`.

`cbow_model.summary()` shows:

| Layer | Output shape | Params |
|---|---|---|
| InputLayer | (None, 8) | 0 |
| Embedding | (None, 8, 64) | 1,920,000 |
| GlobalAveragePooling1D | (None, 64) | 0 |
| Dense | (None, 30000) | 1,950,000 |

The total is **3,870,000 parameters (14.76 MB)**, all trainable. The vocabulary size `max_tokens` is therefore 30,000, and the embedding table is $30{,}000 \times 64$.

Because the model is so simple, a **large batch size** can be used to speed up training without memory worries. The authors also call **`cache()`** on the batched dataset, so the whole preprocessed dataset is stored in memory instead of being recomputed every epoch. For this very simple model, training is **bottlenecked on preprocessing**: tokenizing text and computing sliding windows on the CPU is slower than updating parameters on the GPU. In such cases, saving preprocessed outputs in memory or on disk is usually a good idea; later epochs run **more than three times faster** than the first thanks to the cache.

**Listing 14.29**: `dataset = dataset.batch(1024).cache()` and `cbow_model.fit(dataset, epochs=4)`.

At the end of training the model guesses the middle word **about 12% of the time** from the eight neighbors alone. That may sound low, but with **30,000 words to choose from** each time it is a reasonable score. The next step is to use this embedding to improve the LSTM (p.442). The CBOW model ends with Dense(max_tokens) over 30,000 words and is compiled with Adam and sparse categorical cross-entropy. Its 3,870,000 parameters split into 1,920,000 (Embedding) and 1,950,000 (Dense). A small model allows a large batch size (1024). When CPU preprocessing is the bottleneck, cache the preprocessed data; later epochs become more than 3x faster. Four epochs give about 12% middle-word accuracy, reasonable for 30,000 choices. The learned embedding is next used to prime the LSTM.

title: CBOW as a 30,000-way classifier
text: The CBOW model treats each vocabulary word as a class and predicts the middle word's class from the averaged context embedding. A multiple-choice question with 30,000 options for every window. (None, 64) -> Dense(30,000) -> per-word scores; trained with sparse categorical cross-entropy on integer labels. 12% accuracy after 4 epochs.
snippet: The CBOW model treats each vocabulary word as a class and predicts the middle word's class from the averaged context embedding.

title: Sparse categorical cross-entropy
text: Cross-entropy loss for single-label multiclass classification where the label is an integer index rather than a one-hot vector. Penalizes the model by how little probability it gave the correct word. loss = -log p(label); the "sparse" version avoids building 30,000-long one-hot targets. If the model gives the true word probability 0.12, the loss is -ln 0.12 = 2.12.
snippet: Cross-entropy loss for single-label multiclass classification where the label is an integer index rather than a one-hot vector.

title: Caching preprocessed data
text: Storing the output of a deterministic input pipeline after the first epoch so later epochs reuse it. Cook the meal once and reheat it, instead of cooking from scratch every day. tf.data.Dataset.cache() (memory) or cache(path) (disk), placed after the expensive, deterministic steps. dataset.batch(1024).cache()
snippet: Storing the output of a deterministic input pipeline after the first epoch so later epochs reuse it.

title: Preprocessing-bound training
text: A training run where the CPU input pipeline, not the accelerator, limits speed. A fast chef waiting for slow ingredient deliveries. Tokenization and windowing run on the CPU; the CBOW step on the GPU is cheap, so the GPU idles without caching. This CBOW model.

title: Priming the LSTM with the pretrained CBOW embedding
text:
Rebuilding the bidirectional LSTM classifier, copying the CBOW-pretrained embedding matrix into its Embedding layer with assign(), then training and evaluating it (test accuracy 0.89139) Transfer learning at its simplest: the 30,000 x 64 embedding matrix learned by the CBOW word-prediction task (p.438-441) is copied into the LSTM's Embedding layer as a better initializer, and the whole model is then trained on the labeled IMDb reviews as usual. Test accuracy rises from about 84% (p.437) to about 89%. Section 14.5.5 cashes in the word embedding pretrained with CBOW on p.438-441.

**Listing 14.30** rebuilds the LSTM classifier *exactly as before* (compare Listing 14.24, p.435): an integer input of length `max_length`, an `Embedding(input_dim=max_tokens, output_dim=hidden_dim, mask_zero=True)`, a `Bidirectional(LSTM(hidden_dim))`, `Dropout(0.5)` and a `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")` output. The one change in style is that the Embedding layer is created and stored in a variable, `lstm_embedding`, before being called on the inputs, so that we can reach its weights later. The model is named `"lstm_with_cbow"`.

**Listing 14.31** is a single line: `lstm_embedding.embeddings.assign(cbow_embedding.embeddings)`. It overwrites the randomly initialized embedding matrix of the LSTM with the matrix learned by CBOW. The authors describe this as "a new and better initializer for the roughly 2 million embedding parameters" ($30{,}000 \times 64 = 1{,}920{,}000$). This works because both layers use the same vocabulary (the CBOW tokenizer reused the IMDb `TextVectorization` vocabulary, p.439) and the same dimension (64).

**Listing 14.32** compiles (`adam`, `binary_crossentropy`, `accuracy`) and fits for up to 10 epochs with the `early_stopping` callback, exactly as for the earlier LSTMs. The embedding is **not frozen**: it keeps being trained (fine-tuned) together with the LSTM.

**Listing 14.33** evaluates on the test set: **`test_acc = 0.89139`**. For comparison, the one-hot LSTM reached 0.84811 (p.432) and the randomly initialized Embedding LSTM 0.84436 (p.437). The next page (p.443) puts this in context: slightly better than the unigram bag-of-words model (0.88388, p.426) and slightly worse than the bigram model (0.90116, p.428). The LSTM is rebuilt unchanged, keeping a handle (lstm_embedding) on its Embedding layer. One line, embeddings.assign(...), transfers 1.92 million pretrained parameters. The pretrained embedding is an initializer; it is fine-tuned with the rest of the model. Test accuracy rises from about 84% to 0.89139 with no architectural change. Weight transfer requires identical vocabularies and embedding sizes.

text: Reusing parameters learned on one task (CBOW word prediction) as the starting point for another task (sentiment classification). Instead of learning the meaning of 30,000 words from 20,000 labeled reviews, the model starts with word vectors that already know which words behave alike. The CBOW Embedding matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{30000 \times 64}$ is copied into the LSTM's Embedding variable before `fit()`. All weights, including $E$, are then updated by the classification loss. Listing 14.31: `lstm_embedding.embeddings.assign(cbow_embedding.embeddings)`.

title: Pretraining
text: Training on an unsupervised task with plentiful data before the supervised task. Learn general language patterns first, specialize later. CBOW predicts the middle token of a 9-token window from the 8 surrounding ones; its embedding is the pretrained artifact. CBOW on all IMDb text, then the LSTM classifier on labeled reviews.

title: Embedding layer weights
text: The `embeddings` variable of a Keras Embedding layer: a (input_dim, output_dim) matrix whose row i is the vector for token i. A lookup table that can be read, written or copied like any other variable. Here shape (30000, 64). `Variable.assign(value)` replaces its contents in place; shapes must match exactly. `lstm_embedding.embeddings.shape == (30000, 64)`.

Nearly all of the LSTM model's parameters are in the embedding. The bidirectional LSTM adds $2\times 4\times(64\cdot 64 + 64\cdot 64 + 64) = 66{,}048$ and the output Dense 129 (AI calculation, not printed on this page). V vocabulary size, max_tokens = 30,000 d embedding dimension, hidden_dim = 64 E the embedding matrix

title: Interpreting the pretrained LSTM result; chapter summary begins
text:
Why the pretrained LSTM only matches the set-based models (it is still data-constrained), why Transformers trained on lots of ordered text will do better, the cost-effectiveness of set models, and the first half of the chapter summary (tokenization, its three steps and three types, set vs. sequence models) Sequence models are expressive enough to beat bag-of-words models but need far more ordered training data than 20,000 reviews; until that data (or pretraining on large text corpora) is available, cheap set-based models like the bigram model are hard to beat per unit of compute. The page first interprets the result of p.442. With pretrained embedding weights, the LSTM's test accuracy (0.89139) is **roughly the same as the set-based models**: slightly better than the unigram bag-of-words model (0.88388, p.426) and slightly worse than the bigram model (0.90116, p.428).

Is learning on the full ordered sequence a bad idea, then? No. The authors argue the LSTM is ***still data-constrained***: it is expressive enough that with enough movie reviews it would easily outperform set-based approaches, but it needs much more training on ***ordered data*** before reaching its performance ceiling. That problem is solvable with enough compute. The next chapter introduces the **Transformer**, which is slightly better at learning dependencies across long token sequences, but, more importantly, is typically trained on large amounts of English text *including word order*, so it learns roughly a statistical form of the grammatical patterns of language. Those word-order patterns are exactly what the small LSTM lacks the data to learn.

Still, simple set-based regression approaches like the bigram model give a lot of **"bang for your buck"**: they are lightning-fast and tiny compared to billion-parameter LLMs. When compute is limited and some accuracy can be sacrificed, set models are often the most cost-effective approach.

The **chapter summary** begins:

- Every text modeling problem starts with **tokenization**: turning text into integers.
- Tokenization has three steps: **standardization** (normalize), **splitting** (into tokens), **indexing** (assign integer IDs).
- Three main types: **character**, **word**, and **subword**; with an expressive model and enough data, subword is usually best.
- NLP models differ mainly in how they treat token order: **set models** (presence/absence of tokens, or of bigrams/trigrams; very fast) versus **sequence models** (ordered tokens; need lots of data).

The summary continues on p.444 with embeddings and pretraining. The pretrained LSTM (0.891) lands between unigram (0.884) and bigram (0.901). The LSTM is still data-constrained: it needs much more ordered data to reach its ceiling. Transformers help mainly because they are trained on large amounts of ordered text. Set models give the best accuracy per unit of compute; use them when resources are tight. Tokenization = standardization + splitting + indexing; subword is usually best with enough data and capacity. Set models ignore order (except n-grams); sequence models use it but are data hungry.
snippet: The page first interprets the result of p.442. With pretrained embedding weights, the LSTM's test accuracy 0.89139 is roughly the same as the set-based models: slightly better…

title: Data-constrained model
text: A model whose accuracy is limited by the amount of training data rather than by its capacity. A powerful learner with too few examples memorizes instead of generalizing. Symptoms: high train accuracy with a large train-validation gap (the LSTM hit 99% train accuracy, p.437) and gains from extra (even unlabeled) data via pretraining. Pretrained-embedding LSTM: 0.891 vs bigram 0.901.

title: Chapter 14 summary (cont.): embeddings and pretraining
text:
The final two takeaways of Chapter 14: learned embeddings as an efficient input representation, and pretraining as the remedy for the data hunger of sequence models. An Embedding layer maps token IDs into a learned, dense latent space trained by ordinary gradient descent; and because sequence models need far more data than labeled sets usually provide, an unsupervised pretraining task on unlabeled text can learn parameters that are then transferred to the downstream task. This page is the tail of the **Chapter 14 summary**, which starts on p.443 with bullets on tokenization (standardization, splitting, indexing), the three kinds of tokenization (character, word, subword) and the distinction between set models and sequence models. Two bullets remain here.

1. **Embeddings.** An *embedding* is "an efficient way to transform token IDs into a learned latent space." Instead of turning each token ID into a sparse one-hot vector of vocabulary length (as the first LSTM did in section 14.5.1), an `Embedding` layer looks up a short dense vector for each ID. The lookup table is just a weight matrix, so it is "trained normally with gradient descent" alongside the rest of the model. In the chapter this cut training time and model size by about an order of magnitude (p.437), though accuracy stayed around 84% because the model overfit before learning good embeddings.

2. **Pretraining.** *Pretraining* is "critical for sequence models as a way to get around the data-hungry nature of these models." An *unsupervised* task, one whose targets come from the text itself, lets the model learn from large amounts of **unlabeled** text, and "the learned parameters can then be transferred to a downstream task." The chapter demonstrated this with a CBOW model trained on the IMDb reviews including the 25,000 unlabeled `unsup/` reviews (p.438-440), whose embedding then initialized the LSTM classifier's roughly 2 million embedding parameters (p.442). That lifted the LSTM to roughly the level of the set-based models (p.443).

The rest of the page is blank: the chapter ends here, and Chapter 15 (*Language models and the Transformer*) opens on p.445. The pretraining idea is scaled up there: instead of pretraining just an embedding with CBOW, whole Transformer models are pretrained with language-modeling objectives and then fine-tuned. An Embedding layer is a trainable lookup table from token IDs to dense vectors, far more efficient than one-hot inputs. Embedding weights are ordinary parameters trained by gradient descent and backpropagation. Sequence models are data-hungry; with only about 20,000 labeled reviews the LSTM overfit before learning good embeddings. Pretraining on an unsupervised task over unlabeled text, then transferring the parameters, works around the shortage of labeled data. This pretrain-then-transfer recipe is the template that Chapter 15's Transformers scale up.
snippet: This page is the tail of the Chapter 14 summary, which starts on p.443 with bullets on tokenization standardization, splitting, indexing, the three kinds of tokenization…

title: Embedding (learned token embedding)
text: A trainable lookup table that maps each integer token ID to a dense vector in a learned latent space. Each word gets a short list of coordinates. Training moves words that act similarly for the task closer together, so the downstream layers start from meaningful positions instead of arbitrary IDs. A weight matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$. Input of shape `(batch, seq_len)` of ints becomes `(batch, seq_len, d)` floats via row lookup. Gradients flow only to the rows used in the batch. Equivalent to one-hot multiplied by $E$, without materializing the one-hot vectors. With a 20,000-token vocabulary and 256-dimensional vectors (an illustrative size), the embedding has 5.12 million parameters, and each review token becomes one 256-float vector instead of a 20,000-float one-hot vector.
snippet: A trainable lookup table that maps each integer token ID to a dense vector in a learned latent space.

title: Pretraining
text: Learning model parameters on an unsupervised task over large amounts of unlabeled data, then transferring those parameters to a downstream task. Learn the language first and the task second. Reading lots of unlabeled reviews teaches which words are used alike, so the classifier no longer has to learn that from 20,000 labeled examples. Stage 1: optimize a self-derived objective (CBOW middle-word prediction on p.440; next-token prediction in Chapter 15; masked-token prediction for BERT on p.479). Stage 2: initialize the downstream model's matching layers with the learned weights, then train, or fine-tune, on labeled data. Chapter 14: a CBOW embedding trained on train + `unsup/` reviews initializes the LSTM's embedding, raising LSTM accuracy to about the level of the unigram and bigram models (p.443).
snippet: Learning model parameters on an unsupervised task over large amounts of unlabeled data, then transferring those parameters to a downstream task.

title: Transfer of learned parameters
text: Reusing parameters learned on one task as the starting point for another. Like starting a new job with relevant experience instead of from scratch. In Keras, copying weights between layers of matching shapes, e.g. `layer.set_weights(other_layer.get_weights())`, as the book does with the CBOW and LSTM embeddings (p.442). The roughly 2 million CBOW embedding parameters act as a 'new and better initializer' for the LSTM (p.442).
snippet: Reusing parameters learned on one task as the starting point for another.

title: Chapter 15 opener: Language models and the Transformer
text:
Opening of Chapter 15: generating text, English-to-Spanish translation, and the Transformer; the start of section 15.1 contrasts text classification with text generation. Chapter 14 only had to map text to one number (or N numbers); Chapter 15 tackles problems where the output is itself text, which leads to language models, sequence-to-sequence translation and the Transformer. This is the **opening page of Chapter 15, *Language models and the Transformer***. The "This chapter covers" box lists three goals:

- **How to generate text with a deep learning model.** Section 15.1 builds a character-level Shakespeare language model (p.446-452).
- **Training a model to translate from English to Spanish.** Section 15.2 frames translation as sequence-to-sequence learning, first with RNNs (p.452-460).
- **The Transformer, a powerful architecture for text modeling problems.** Section 15.3 covers dot-product attention, encoder and decoder blocks, and positional embeddings (p.461-477). Section 15.4 then fine-tunes a pretrained Transformer encoder on IMDb (p.478-484), and section 15.5 asks what makes the Transformer effective (p.485).

The introductory paragraph says the chapter builds on Chapter 14's preprocessing basics to tackle "more involved language problems such as machine translation," and to build intuition for the Transformer, which "powers products like ChatGPT."

Section **15.1 The language model** begins at the bottom of the page. Chapter 14 converted text to numbers to classify reviews, but classification is "a uniquely simple problem": the output is a single float for binary classification, or at worst N numbers for N-way classification. The next page (p.446) shows why generating text is harder. The space of possible output sequences is astronomically large, so the practical approach is a model that predicts one token at a time, $p(\text{token} \mid \text{past tokens})$.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a roadmap. The pretraining idea from the end of Chapter 14 (p.444) reappears here at scale, since language modeling is the unsupervised task that Transformers are pretrained on. Chapter 15 covers text generation, English-to-Spanish translation, and the Transformer. Text classification is simple on the output side: one number, or N numbers. Generating text requires a new framing, the language model, introduced in section 15.1.
snippet: This is the opening page of Chapter 15, Language models and the Transformer. The "This chapter covers" box lists three goals: - How to generate text with a deep learning model.…

title: Language model
text: A model that predicts a probability distribution over the next token given the tokens seen so far, p(token | past tokens). Defined on p.446. Autocomplete: guess the next word, append it, and guess again. Outputs a softmax over the vocabulary at each position. Repeated sampling generates sequences of any length while the output layer stays the size of the vocabulary. The chapter's first model predicts the next character of Shakespeare text (section 15.1.1).
snippet: A model that predicts a probability distribution over the next token given the tokens seen so far, ptoken | past tokens. Defined on p.446.
