title: From classifying text to generating it: the language model
text:
Why generating text cannot be treated as one giant classification problem, and how a language model, p(token | past tokens), makes generation tractable; the first listing downloads the Shakespeare dataset. Output text can be represented as an integer token sequence, but there are far too many possible sequences to classify directly (20,000^4 = 160 quadrillion for four words). A language model instead predicts one token at a time, a distribution over only the vocabulary, and generates long text by repeating that prediction. The page opens by moving beyond classification: for tasks such as question answering or translation we want a model that **generates text output**. Chapter 14 built tools for text "on the *way in*" (tokenizers, embeddings); now we need tools for the "*way out*."

The representation does not change: text stays an **integer sequence**. Tokenizing maps tokens to ints; **detokenizing** reverses it, mapping ints back to string tokens and joining them. So the task becomes predicting an integer sequence of tokens.

The naive approach, a classifier with one class per possible output sequence, is shown to be **intractable**. With a 20,000-word vocabulary there are $20{,}000^4$, or **160 quadrillion**, possible 4-word sequences, and there are fewer atoms in the universe than possible 20-word sequences. No model could have an output for each.

The practical solution is to predict **one token at a time**. A **language model** learns the distribution $p(\text{token} \mid \text{past tokens})$: given all tokens so far, it outputs a probability distribution over every possible next token. With a 20,000-word vocabulary that is just 20,000 outputs, and by *repeatedly* predicting the next token the model can generate arbitrarily long text.

To make this concrete, the authors will build a small **character-level** model that predicts the next character and produces Shakespeare-like text. Section **15.1.1** starts with **Listing 15.1**, which downloads an abbreviated collection of Shakespeare's plays and sonnets with `keras.utils.get_file` and reads it into the string `shakespeare`. The listing is complete on this page; the data is inspected and chunked on p.447. Generation keeps the integer-sequence representation of text; detokenizing maps IDs back to text. Classifying whole output sequences is intractable: 20,000^4 = 160 quadrillion 4-word sequences. A language model learns p(token | past tokens), a V-way distribution, and generates by repeated next-token prediction. The first example is a character-level Shakespeare model; Listing 15.1 downloads the corpus into one string.
snippet: The page opens by moving beyond classification: for tasks such as question answering or translation we want a model that generates text output. Chapter 14 built tools for text "on…

title: Language model
text: A model that learns p(token | past tokens): given all tokens observed up to a point, it outputs a probability distribution over all possible next tokens. A very good autocomplete. Predict the next word, append it, and predict again. Output layer: softmax over a vocabulary of size V. Training target at each position is the next token (cross-entropy). Generation: sample or take the argmax of the distribution, append it to the input, and repeat. The chain rule makes the product of conditionals equal to the joint probability of the sequence. Given 'To be or not to b', a character-level language model should put high probability on 'e'.
snippet: A model that learns ptoken | past tokens: given all tokens observed up to a point, it outputs a probability distribution over all possible next tokens.

title: Detokenization
text: Mapping a sequence of integer token IDs back to string tokens and joining them into text. Running the tokenizer backwards. Requires the inverse vocabulary (ID to token). For character tokens, join with the empty string; for word tokens, join with spaces; subword tokenizers have their own merge rules. [20, 8, 5] with the vocabulary {20:'t', 8:'h', 5:'e'} detokenizes to 'the'.
snippet: Mapping a sequence of integer token IDs back to string tokens and joining them into text.

title: Combinatorial explosion of output sequences
text: The number of possible length-L sequences over a vocabulary of size V is V^L, which grows exponentially with L. Each additional word multiplies the number of possibilities by 20,000. 20,000^4 = 1.6e17; 20,000^20 is about 1.05e86. A softmax over that many classes is impossible to store or compute. Even 2-word outputs would need 400 million classes.
snippet: The number of possible length-L sequences over a vocabulary of size V is V^L, which grows exponentially with L.

title: Number of possible 4-word sequences
text: 20,000 ^ 4, or 160 quadrillion possible 4-word sequences 20{,}000^{4} = 1.6\times10^{17} \;(160 \text{ quadrillion}) Shows that a direct classifier over output sequences would need an absurd number of output classes. Even very short outputs have an astronomically large output space. 20{,}000 Vocabulary size V (number of distinct words). 4 Sequence length L in tokens.
snippet: 20,000 ^ 4, or 160 quadrillion possible 4-word sequences — Shows that a direct classifier over output sequences would need an absurd number of output classes.

title: The language model distribution
text: p(token|past tokens) p(\text{token}_t \mid \text{token}_1, \ldots, \text{token}_{t-1}) Defines what a language model learns, a single-token prediction with only V outputs. Applying it repeatedly, sampling a token, appending it and conditioning on the longer context, generates sequences of any length. \text{token}_t The next token to predict, one of V vocabulary entries. \text{token}_1,\ldots,\text{token}_{t-1} All tokens observed so far (the 'past tokens').
snippet: ptoken|past tokens — Defines what a language model learns, a single-token prediction with only V outputs.

title: Chain-rule factorization (why next-token prediction suffices)
text: Not printed in the book; implied by 'by repeatedly predicting the next token'. p(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_L) = \prod_{i=1}^{L} p(t_i \mid t_1, \ldots, t_{i-1}) Shows that a model of the conditional (V outputs) fully determines the distribution over whole sequences (V^L outcomes). Nothing is lost by predicting one token at a time; the factorization is exact. t_i Token at position i. L Sequence length.
snippet: Not printed in the book; implied by 'by repeatedly predicting the next token'. — Shows that a model of the conditional V outputs fully determines the distribution over whole…

title: Preparing Shakespeare for next-character prediction
text:
Inspecting the Shakespeare corpus and turning the raw string into (features, labels) pairs of 100-character chunks, where the labels are the input shifted by one character. A language model's training data comes from the text itself: cut the corpus into fixed-length chunks, and use as target for each chunk the same text offset by one character, so the label at every position is the next character. The page continues section 15.1.1 by looking at the data loaded in Listing 15.1 (p.446). Printing `shakespeare[:250]` shows a play script: speaker names such as `First Citizen:` and `All:`, each followed by its lines ("Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.", "Speak, speak.", "...Caius Marcius is chief enemy to the people.").

To build a *language model*, the text has to be "massaged":

- **Chunking.** The data is split into **equal-length chunks** that can be batched, "much as we did for weather measurements in the timeseries chapters." Because the tokenizer will be character-level, chunking can be done **directly on the string**: a 100-character string maps to a 100-integer sequence.
- **Features and labels.** Each input is split into a feature sequence and a label sequence, where the label sequence is "simply the input sequence offset by a single character."

**Listing 15.2** implements this. `sequence_length = 100` (the callout: "We only train on sequences of 100 characters at a time"). The generator `split_input` yields consecutive, non-overlapping slices `input[i : i + sequence_length]` with step `sequence_length`. Features are the chunks of `shakespeare[:-1]` (all but the last character), and labels are the chunks of `shakespeare[1:]` (all but the first). Since both are cut at the same offsets, label chunk *k* is feature chunk *k* moved one character to the right in the original text. `tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((features, labels))` pairs them up.

The sample shows the result: `x[:50]` is `b"First Citizen:\nBefore we proceed any further, hear"` and `y[:50]` is `b"irst Citizen:\nBefore we proceed any further, hear "`. At every position the label is the **next character**. The strings are still raw bytes; turning them into integers with a character-level `TextVectorization` layer comes next (p.448). The corpus is a play script; speaker tags, newlines and punctuation are all characters to predict. Text is cut into non-overlapping 100-character chunks; with character tokens this gives 100-token sequences. Labels are the input shifted by one character: features from shakespeare[:-1], labels from shakespeare[1:]. Each chunk provides a next-character target at every one of its positions. The pairs are still raw byte strings; tokenization to integers follows on p.448.
snippet: The page continues section 15.1.1 by looking at the data loaded in Listing 15.1 p.446. Printing shakespeare:250 shows a play script: speaker names such as First Citizen: and All:,…

title: Shifted-by-one targets (next-token labels)
text: The training target sequence for a causal language model is the input sequence offset by one token, so the label at each position is the following token. Slide the text one step to the left and use it as the answer key. features = text[:-1], labels = text[1:], both chunked at the same offsets. Loss is per-position cross-entropy over the vocabulary, and each chunk of length L contributes L prediction targets. Text 'hear me': feature 'hear m', label 'ear me'. Position 0 sees 'h' and must predict 'e'.
snippet: The training target sequence for a causal language model is the input sequence offset by one token, so the label at each position is the following token.

title: Language model
text: A model of p(token | past tokens); here at the character level. Predict the next character from all previous characters in the chunk. Trained with the shifted-label datasets built on this page. After 'First Citize' the model should predict 'n'.

title: Character-level tokenization

The model at position t sees x_0..x_t and is trained to output y_t = c_{100k+t+1}. c_j The j-th character of the corpus string shakespeare. k Index of the chunk (0, 1, 2, ...). t Position within the chunk, from 0 to sequence_length - 1 = 99. x_t, y_t Feature and label characters at position t of chunk k.

title: Listing 15.2 Splitting text into chunks for language model training
text:
import tensorflow as tf

sequence_length = 100

def split_input(input, sequence_length):
    for i in range(0, len(input), sequence_length):
        yield input[i : i + sequence_length]

features = list(split_input(shakespeare[:-1], sequence_length))
labels = list(split_input(shakespeare[1:], sequence_length))
dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((features, labels)) Cuts the corpus into consecutive 100-character chunks twice, once for inputs and once for inputs shifted by one character, and wraps the aligned pairs in a tf.data.Dataset. Non-overlapping windowing with an offset-by-one target copy.
snippet: Cuts the corpus into consecutive 100-character chunks twice, once for inputs and once for inputs shifted by one character, and wraps the aligned pairs in a tf.data.Dataset.

title: Character-level vocabulary and choosing a GRU language model
text:
Tokenizing the Shakespeare chunks into integers with a character-level TextVectorization layer (vocabulary of 67), building the batched training dataset, and motivating an Embedding + single-GRU architecture for next-character prediction. Setting split='character' and standardize=None in TextVectorization gives a 67-entry vocabulary that preserves case and punctuation. Mapping features and labels through it, then shuffling, batching (64) and caching, produces the training data. An RNN is the natural model because its recurrent state carries information about past characters, exactly what p(char | past chars) needs. The (features, labels) pairs from p.447 are still byte strings. To turn them into integer sequences the authors reuse **`TextVectorization`** from Chapter 14 with two changes: `split="character"` instead of the default `"whitespace"`, so the vocabulary is learned over characters, and **no standardization** (`standardize=None`), so case and punctuation pass through unchanged. `output_sequence_length=sequence_length` fixes every output at 100 integers (**Listing 15.3**). `tokenizer.adapt(...)` learns the vocabulary from the feature strings only (`dataset.map(lambda text, labels: text)`).

The resulting `vocabulary_size` is **67**: "We need only 67 characters to handle the full source text." (Beyond the book: two of those entries are TextVectorization's reserved padding `""` and `[UNK]` tokens.)

The tokenizer is then mapped over both features and labels (`num_parallel_calls=8` for parallelism), and the dataset is **shuffled** with a 10,000-element buffer, **batched** in 64s and **cached** "so we don't need to recompute it every epoch." With that, the data is ready.

The page then motivates the model. We want **the probability of a character given all past characters**. Of the models seen so far, an **RNN** fits most naturally: its recurrent state carries information about past characters while it predicts the label at the current character. An **`Embedding`** (as in Chapter 14) maps each input character to a unique **256-dimensional** vector. To keep the model small and easy to train there will be just **one recurrent layer**. Any recurrent layer would work, but a **`GRU`** is chosen because it is fast and has a simpler internal state than an `LSTM`. The model itself is built in Listing 15.4 on p.449. TextVectorization with split='character' and standardize=None gives a case- and punctuation-preserving character tokenizer. The vocabulary has 67 entries, so the output softmax is tiny. Features and labels are both tokenized; the data is shuffled, batched in 64s and cached (cache after shuffle freezes the order). An RNN fits p(char | past chars) naturally because its state carries only past information. The model will use a 256-d Embedding and a single GRU, chosen for speed and its simpler state.
snippet: The features, labels pairs from p.447 are still byte strings. To turn them into integer sequences the authors reuse TextVectorization from Chapter 14 with two changes:…

title: Character-level TextVectorization
text: Using Keras's TextVectorization layer with split='character' to map each character to an integer ID from a vocabulary learned with adapt(). Build a dictionary of every distinct symbol in the text and number them. adapt() scans the data and sorts tokens by frequency; index 0 is padding and index 1 is [UNK]. output_sequence_length pads or truncates outputs to a fixed length. 'All:' becomes four IDs, one each for 'A', 'l', 'l', ':'.
snippet: Using Keras's TextVectorization layer with split='character' to map each character to an integer ID from a vocabulary learned with adapt.

title: RNN as a causal sequence model
text: A recurrent network processes a sequence step by step, carrying a state that summarizes past inputs. Reading left to right while keeping notes of what you have read so far. h_t = f(x_t, h_{t-1}); with return_sequences=True, h_t is emitted at every step and a Dense softmax maps it to p(next char). At step 3 of 'First', the state has seen 'Firs' and predicts 't'.
snippet: A recurrent network processes a sequence step by step, carrying a state that summarizes past inputs.

title: GRU (gated recurrent unit)
text: A gated recurrent layer with a single hidden state; the book calls it fast and simpler than an LSTM. An LSTM with the cell state and hidden state merged into one. Update gate z, reset gate r and a candidate state. Parameter count (Keras, reset_after=True) is 3(d_in·u + u² + 2u). GRU(1024) on 256-d inputs: 3(256·1024 + 1024² + 2·1024) = 3,938,304 parameters (p.449).
snippet: A gated recurrent layer with a single hidden state; the book calls it fast and simpler than an LSTM.

title: Character embedding
text: An Embedding layer giving each of the 67 character IDs its own 256-dimensional trainable vector. Each character gets coordinates that training arranges usefully, e.g. vowels near each other. A weight matrix of shape (67, 256) = 17,152 parameters (p.449). ID for 'e' maps to row 'e' of the matrix.
snippet: An Embedding layer giving each of the 67 character IDs its own 256-dimensional trainable vector.

title: Listing 15.3 Learning a character-level vocabulary with the TextVectorization layer
text:
from keras import layers

tokenizer = layers.TextVectorization(
    standardize=None,
    split="character",
    output_sequence_length=sequence_length,
)
tokenizer.adapt(dataset.map(lambda text, labels: text)) Creates a character-level tokenizer that keeps case and punctuation and outputs fixed-length (100) integer sequences, then learns its vocabulary from the feature strings. Frequency-based vocabulary construction over characters.
snippet: Creates a character-level tokenizer that keeps case and punctuation and outputs fixed-length 100 integer sequences, then learns its vocabulary from the feature strings.

title: A miniature GRU character language model
text:
Listing 15.4 (Embedding 256 -> GRU 1024 with return_sequences -> Dropout -> per-step softmax over 67 characters), its 4,024,131-parameter summary, and why language modeling is many simultaneous classification problems (6,400 labels per batch) A character language model is just a sequence classifier that makes one softmax prediction per time step: at each of the 100 positions it outputs a probability distribution over the 67-token vocabulary for the next character, trained with sparse categorical cross-entropy averaged over positions and batch. **Listing 15.4** defines the miniature language model. With `embedding_dim = 256` and `hidden_dim = 1024`:

1. `layers.Input(shape=(sequence_length,), dtype="int", name="token_ids")`: 100 character IDs.
2. `Embedding(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)`: each of the 67 tokens becomes a 256-d vector.
3. `GRU(hidden_dim, return_sequences=True)`: a 1,024-unit GRU that returns its output at **every** step, not just the last.
4. `Dropout(0.1)`.
5. `Dense(vocabulary_size, activation="softmax")`: applied at each step, it "outputs a probability distribution over all potential tokens in our vocabulary" (callout).

`model.summary()` shows output shapes (None, 100) -> (None, 100, 256) -> (None, 100, 1024) -> (None, 100, 67) and parameter counts **17,152** (Embedding), **3,938,304** (GRU) and **68,675** (Dense), for a total of **4,024,131 parameters (15.35 MB)**, all trainable. Almost 98% of the parameters are in the GRU.

The model outputs a softmax probability for every character and is compiled with a cross-entropy loss. The authors stress that it is **still a classification problem**; it just makes one classification prediction per token of the sequence. A batch of 64 samples of 100 characters means **6,400 individual labels**. Keras's reported loss and accuracy are averaged first across each sequence, then across the batch.

**Listing 15.5** begins: `model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", ...)`. It continues on p.450 with `sparse_categorical_accuracy` and `model.fit(training_data, epochs=20)`, after which the model predicts the next character about 70% of the time. The language model is Embedding(67, 256) -> GRU(1024, return_sequences=True) -> Dropout(0.1) -> Dense(67, softmax). 4,024,131 parameters, 98% in the GRU. It makes a 67-way classification at each of 100 positions: 6,400 labels per batch of 64. Loss and accuracy are averaged over the sequence, then over the batch. return_sequences=True is what turns a sequence classifier into a per-token predictor.

title: From a trained language model to an autoregressive generator
text:
Rebuilding the character-level GRU language model so it can be called one token at a time with an explicit recurrent state, in preparation for autoregressive text generation. A model trained to predict the next character over fixed 100-character windows can generate whole sequences if it is called in a loop, feeding each prediction back in. To do this efficiently, the authors build a second model with the same weights that takes one token plus the GRU state as input and returns the next-token distribution plus the new state. The page opens with the last lines of **Listing 15.5**: the language model is compiled with a `sparse_categorical_accuracy` metric and trained with `model.fit(training_data, epochs=20)`. After 20 epochs it predicts the next character about **70%** of the time.

Section **15.1.2 Generating Shakespeare** then asks how to turn this next-character predictor into something that writes a whole passage. The answer is to call the model **in a loop**: the character predicted at one step becomes the input at the next step. The authors name this an **autoregressive** model.

The training model is awkward for this. It was built for a fixed input length of 100 tokens, and the `GRU` managed its state internally inside a single layer call. For generation we want to:

- feed **one token** at a time,
- get the GRU's state **back as an output**, and
- pass that state in again on the next call, because it holds everything the model has encoded about the characters seen so far.

**Listing 15.6** builds such a `generation_model`. It has two inputs: `token_ids` with shape `(1,)` and `state` with shape `(hidden_dim,)`. It has two outputs: the softmax distribution over the vocabulary and the new state. The `GRU` is created with `return_state=True` and called with `initial_state=input_state`. The computation is the same as in the trained model, so all the learned parameters can be copied over with `generation_model.set_weights(model.get_weights())`.

The page ends by saying the next steps are to build lookup tables between characters and integer IDs, and to choose a **prompt**: a snippet of text fed to the model before it starts predicting new tokens. That code is on p.451. After 20 epochs the character-level GRU predicts the next character about 70% of the time. Autoregressive generation means calling the model in a loop, feeding each predicted token back in as input. The training model used fixed 100-token sequences and implicit state; generation needs one token per call and an explicit state. `return_state=True` and `initial_state=` expose the GRU's state as a model output and input. Because weight shapes do not depend on sequence length, `set_weights(model.get_weights())` turns the trained model into a generator with no retraining. A prompt is the text fed in before generation begins.

title: Autoregressive generation
text: Producing a sequence by repeatedly predicting the next token and feeding each prediction back to the model as the next input. Like writing one word at a time while rereading what you have written so far: each choice depends on all your earlier choices. Given a model of $p(x_t\mid x_{<t})$, pick $x_t$ (by argmax or by sampling), append it to the context, and repeat. In an RNN the context is summarized by the hidden state, so each step only needs the new token and the previous state. The prompt "KING RICHARD III:\n" primes the GRU. The model then picks one character, feeds it back, and repeats this 250 times (p.451).
snippet: Producing a sequence by repeatedly predicting the next token and feeding each prediction back to the model as the next input.

title: Language model
text: A model that learns the probability distribution of the next token given the past tokens, p(token | past tokens). A very well-read autocomplete. Here it is a character-level model: Embedding(67, 256) -> GRU(1024) -> Dense(67, softmax), trained with sparse categorical crossentropy on the next character at each of 100 positions. About 70% next-character accuracy after 20 epochs on Shakespeare.
snippet: A model that learns the probability distribution of the next token given the past tokens, ptoken | past tokens.

title: Explicit recurrent state
text: Exposing the hidden state of a recurrent layer as a model output and accepting it as an input, so state can be carried across separate model calls. Instead of the model keeping its memory to itself and wiping it after each call, you take the memory out and hand it back next time. In Keras, `layers.GRU(units, return_state=True)` returns `(output, state)`. Calling the layer with `initial_state=...` sets the starting state instead of zeros. For a GRU the output of the last step equals the final state $h_T$. `x, output_state = layers.GRU(hidden_dim, return_state=True)(x, initial_state=input_state)` in Listing 15.6.
snippet: Exposing the hidden state of a recurrent layer as a model output and accepting it as an input, so state can be carried across separate model calls.

title: Reusing trained weights in a differently shaped model
text: Building an inference model with the same layer configuration as a training model and copying the trained parameters into it with `set_weights(get_weights())`. Same engine, different chassis: the parameters do not care how long the input sequence is. `get_weights()` returns a flat list of NumPy arrays in layer order. `set_weights` requires the same number of arrays with matching shapes. Sequence length and the extra state input do not change any weight shape. Dropout has no weights, so leaving it out does not break the list. Both models hold embedding (67x256), GRU kernel (256x3072), recurrent kernel (1024x3072), bias (2x3072), Dense kernel (1024x67) and bias (67).

Each factor is exactly what the language model outputs at one timestep. Generating means choosing $x_t$ from factor $t$ and moving to factor $t+1$. x_t the token (here a character ID) at position t T sequence length p(x_t \mid x_{<t}) the next-token distribution produced by the softmax output of the model

title: Priming the GRU with a prompt and generating greedily
text:
Character/ID lookup tables, the prompt, priming the recurrent state (Listing 15.7) and the greedy token-by-token generation loop (Listing 15.8). Generation happens in two phases. First the prompt is fed through the one-step model character by character, building the exact state the model would have reached on that text. Then, starting from that state and the last prediction, the most likely next character is repeatedly chosen, fed back in, and the new state kept. The page begins with the setup promised at the end of p.450. `tokenizer.get_vocabulary()` returns the 67 vocabulary entries, and zipping them with `range(vocabulary_size)` builds two dictionaries: `char_to_id` (character to integer) and `id_to_char` (integer to character). The prompt is the triple-quoted string `"""\nKING RICHARD III:\n"""`, a speaker heading in the style of the play scripts in the training text.

**Priming.** Before generating, the GRU's internal state must be primed with the prompt. The prompt is fed to the model one token at a time, which computes exactly the RNN state the model would have reached if it had read this prompt during training. After the last prompt character, the state summarizes the whole prompt, and the final output prediction is kept so the first character of the response can be chosen from it. **Listing 15.7** converts the prompt to IDs, starts with a zero state `keras.ops.zeros(shape=(1, hidden_dim))`, and for each ID calls `generation_model.predict((inputs, state), verbose=0)`, overwriting `predictions` and `state` each time.

**Generating.** **Listing 15.8** loops `max_length = 250` times. At each step it:

1. takes the most likely next character, `int(np.argmax(predictions, axis=-1)[0])` (greedy selection);
2. appends it to `generated_ids`;
3. feeds it back as the next input along with the current state, obtaining new `predictions` and a new `state`.

This way the model writes a whole sequence one token at a time.

The page ends by announcing detokenization: map every generated token ID back to its string and join them. That code and the resulting Shakespeare-like sample are on p.452. `char_to_id` and `id_to_char`, built from `tokenizer.get_vocabulary()`, translate between characters and IDs. The prompt "\nKING RICHARD III:\n" is fed one character at a time to prime the GRU state, starting from zeros. Priming reproduces exactly the state the model would have after reading that text during training. The prediction after the last prompt character supplies the first generated character. Listing 15.8 runs greedy decoding for 250 steps: argmax, append, feed back, keep the new state. Detokenizing joins `id_to_char` lookups of the generated IDs into a string (p.452).

title: Priming the state with a prompt
text: Running the prompt tokens through a recurrent model one at a time, carrying the state, so the model's state encodes the prompt before generation. Reading the first line of a script aloud before improvising the next one. $h_0 = 0$; for each prompt token $x_i$: $(\hat y_i, h_i) = f(x_i, h_{i-1})$. Keep $h_n$ and $\hat y_n$. Feeding '\n', 'K', 'I', 'N', 'G', ' ', 'R', ... ':' , '\n' of the prompt into `generation_model`.
snippet: Running the prompt tokens through a recurrent model one at a time, carrying the state, so the model's state encodes the prompt before generation.

title: Greedy decoding
text: At each generation step, select the token with the highest predicted probability. Always take the locally best move. $x_{t+1} = \arg\max_k \hat y_t[k]$, implemented as `int(np.argmax(predictions, axis=-1)[0])`. If the model gives 'S' a probability of 0.31 and every other character less, 'S' is chosen (as in 'Stay, men!' on p.452).
snippet: At each generation step, select the token with the highest predicted probability.

title: Vocabulary lookup tables
text: Dictionaries mapping each vocabulary string to its integer index and back. A two-way phrasebook between characters and numbers. `get_vocabulary()` returns the list in index order. Index 0 is the padding token `""` and index 1 is `"[UNK]"` for a TextVectorization layer, so `dict(zip(tokens, range(vocabulary_size)))` lines up exactly with the tokenizer's integer IDs. `char_to_id['K']` gives the ID used for 'K'; `id_to_char[that_id]` gives 'K' back.
snippet: Dictionaries mapping each vocabulary string to its integer index and back.

title: Tokenization and detokenization
text: Mapping text to integer token IDs, and the reverse mapping from IDs to text. Encode and decode. Character level: one character per ID; detokenization is `"".join(id_to_char[i] for i in ids)`. [ids of 'S','t','a','y'] -> "Stay".
snippet: Mapping text to integer token IDs, and the reverse mapping from IDs to text.

A deterministic map from state to next character. \hat{y}_t[k] predicted probability of character k x_{t+1} the chosen next character ID h_t current GRU state

token_ids = range(vocabulary_size)

state = keras.ops.zeros(shape=(1, hidden_dim))
for token_id in input_ids:
    inputs = keras.ops.expand_dims([token_id], axis=0)
    predictions, state = generation_model.predict((inputs, state), verbose=0) Converts the prompt to IDs and feeds them to the one-step generation model character by character, updating the state each time. Sequential RNN unrolling with an explicit state.

import numpy as np

generated_ids = []
max_length = 250
for i in range(max_length):
    next_char = int(np.argmax(predictions, axis=-1)[0])
    generated_ids.append(next_char)
    inputs = keras.ops.expand_dims([next_char], axis=0)

title: Generated Shakespeare, causality, and the start of seq2seq
text:
Detokenizing and inspecting the generated text, why the language-model setup only works with a forward-only (causal) model, why inference needs its own loop, and an introduction to sequence-to-sequence learning. A model trained only to guess the next character can generate open-ended, Shakespeare-like text, but only if it cannot see future tokens during training. Unlike other models in the book, it needs an inference-time loop that feeds predictions back in. Section 15.2 extends this idea to translation: generating a target sequence conditioned on a source sequence. The page finishes the Shakespeare example. Two lines of code turn `generated_ids` back into a string by looking up each ID in `id_to_char` and joining the characters, then print `prompt + output`. The output shows speaker headings (`KING RICHARD III:`, `FRIAR LAURENCE:`, `BUCKINGHAM:`) followed by lines such as "Stay, men! hear me speak." and "Thou bear them both. Here comes the king;". The text has the format, archaic vocabulary and rhythm of a play, but little coherent meaning.

The authors note this is "not terrible for two minutes of training on a minimal dataset." The point is the **power of the language-model setup**: a model trained on the narrow task of guessing one character is used for a much broader one, generating open-ended text.

They then explain why the setup works at all. An RNN passes information **only forward** in the sequence. If you replace the `GRU` with `Bidirectional(GRU(...))`, training accuracy jumps above **99%** immediately, but generation stops working. During training the model sees the whole sequence, so letting the next token influence the current prediction makes the task trivially easy, and the model never learns to predict from the past alone.

This *language modeling* setup is fundamental in the text domain and unusual compared with earlier models in the book. You cannot just call `model.predict()`. There is a whole loop with nontrivial logic that exists only at inference time. The RNN's state loop runs in both training and inference, but **at no point during training are predicted labels fed back as inputs**.

Section **15.2 Sequence-to-sequence learning** begins: the language-model idea is extended to **machine translation**, part of a class of problems called **sequence-to-sequence** (seq2seq). The model takes a source text as a fixed input sequence and generates the translated sequence. Question answering is another classic seq2seq problem. Detokenizing is a dictionary lookup per ID plus `"".join`. Two minutes of training yields text with correct play formatting and archaic style but little meaning. Narrow training (next character) supports broad use (open-ended generation): the power of the language-model setup. The setup requires causality: a Bidirectional GRU sees the label, reaches over 99% training accuracy, and fails at generation. Language models need an inference-only loop; predictions are never fed back during training. Seq2seq extends the idea to generating a target sequence from a fixed source sequence, as in translation and question answering.

title: Causality in language-model training
text: The requirement that the prediction at position t uses only tokens at positions up to t, never future tokens. You cannot use tomorrow's newspaper to predict tomorrow's news. With labels $y_t = x_{t+1}$, any path from $x_{t+1}$ to the output at $t$ leaks the label. A forward RNN has no such path; a bidirectional RNN does. `Bidirectional(GRU(...))` reaches over 99% training accuracy and generation stops working (p.452).

Inference: priming plus a token-by-token loop with explicit state (pp.450-451). Listings 15.6 to 15.8 exist only for inference.

title: The encoder-decoder template for seq2seq
text:
How sequence-to-sequence models are trained (encoder plus a decoder trained as a language model on the target) and how they generate at inference (start from a [start] seed token and loop until [end]), illustrated by figure 15.1. A seq2seq model is an encoder that summarizes the source plus a decoder that is a conditional language model over the target. In training the decoder sees the true target shifted right by one step. At inference it generates one token at a time from "[start]", feeding its predictions back in until it emits "[end]". This page gives the **general template** for sequence-to-sequence models, illustrated in **figure 15.1**.

**During training:**

- An **encoder** turns the source sequence (for example, `how, is, the, weather, today`) into an intermediate representation.
- A **decoder** is trained with the **language-modeling setup** from section 15.1. It predicts the next target token by looking at all previous target tokens *and* the encoder's representation of the source. In the figure, the decoder input is `[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy` and its training target is `qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]`: the same sequence shifted one step into the future.

**During inference** the target sequence is unknown; it has to be predicted from scratch. It is generated one token at a time, "just as we did with our Shakespeare generator":

1. Get the encoded source sequence from the encoder.
2. The decoder looks at the encoded source and an initial **seed token** such as `"[start]"` and predicts the first real token (in the figure, `qué`).
3. The predicted sequence so far is fed back into the decoder, in a loop, until it generates a **stop token** such as `"[end]"`.

The figure caption summarizes this: the decoder looks at the target sequence so far and predicts the target offset by one step, and during inference each generated token is fed back into the decoder (the curved arrow). The page ends with: "Let's build a sequence-to-sequence translation model."

Compared with the Shakespeare model, the decoder has a second source of information (the encoded source), and generation can stop on its own because the model learned to produce `[end]`. Seq2seq = encoder (source to representation) + decoder (a conditional language model over the target). In training, the decoder input is [start] + target and its labels are target + [end]: offset by one step. The decoder conditions on all previous target tokens and the encoded source. Inference: encode the source, seed the decoder with [start], feed predictions back until [end]. This is the Shakespeare generation loop with an extra conditioning input and a learned stop token.
snippet: This page gives the general template for sequence-to-sequence models, illustrated in figure 15.1. During training: - An encoder turns the source sequence for example, how, is,…

title: Encoder-decoder architecture
text: A seq2seq model made of an encoder that represents the source sequence and a decoder that generates the target sequence conditioned on that representation. A translator first reads and understands the sentence (encoder), then writes the translation word by word (decoder). Encoder: $z = \mathrm{Enc}(x_1..x_n)$. Decoder: $p(y_t\mid y_{<t}, z)$, trained with the shifted target and run autoregressively at inference. Figure 15.1: 'how is the weather today' becomes 'qué tiempo hace hoy'.

title: Sequence-to-sequence learning

snippet: Learning to map a source sequence to a target sequence; the decoder learns the next target token given past target tokens and the source.

title: [start] and [end] tokens
text: Special tokens added to target sequences: [start] seeds generation and [end] signals that generation should stop. Quotation marks around the answer. Decoder input = [start] + target; decoder label = target + [end]. At inference, begin with [start] and stop when [end] is the argmax (or at a maximum length). '[start] qué tiempo hace hoy' as input, 'qué tiempo hace hoy [end]' as labels.

title: Training on the shifted true target
text: Feeding the decoder the true previous target tokens during training rather than its own predictions. Training wheels: the correct prefix is always provided. All target positions are computed in parallel from the true prefix. Beyond the book: this is called teacher forcing. Figure 15.1's training panel feeds '[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy' regardless of what the decoder would have predicted.

title: Seq2seq decoder objective
text: Described in words: the decoder predicts the next token in the target sequence by looking at all previous target tokens and the encoder's representation of the source sequence. p(y_1,\dots,y_m \mid x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{t=1}^{m} p\big(y_t \mid y_0,\dots,y_{t-1},\ \operatorname{Enc}(x_1,\dots,x_n)\big),\quad y_0=\texttt{[start]},\ y_m=\texttt{[end]} It states what the decoder learns and what inference generates step by step. A language model over the target that also always sees the encoded source. x_1..x_n source tokens (how, is, the, weather, today) y_1..y_m target tokens (qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]) y_0 the seed token [start] \operatorname{Enc} the encoder, producing the intermediate representation

Downloading spa-eng.zip, parsing tab-separated English/Spanish sentence pairs, wrapping each Spanish target in [start] ... [end] tokens, and making a shuffled 70/15/15 train/validation/test split A translation dataset is a list of (source, target) sentence pairs. The target is wrapped in explicit start and end markers so a decoder can later be seeded with [start] and know to stop at [end]; the pairs are shuffled and split before any tokenizer is fitted. Section 15.2.1 starts the translation example with an **English-to-Spanish** dataset.

1. **Download**: `keras.utils.get_file` fetches `spa-eng.zip` from `storage.googleapis.com`, extracts it (`extract=True`), and `text_path` points to `spa-eng/spa.txt` inside the extracted folder.
2. **Parse**: the file holds one example per line: *English sentence, a tab, the Spanish sentence*. The code reads the file, splits on `"\n"` and drops the last (empty) element with `[:-1]`. Each line is split on `"\t"`; the Spanish side is rewritten as `"[start] " + spanish + " [end]"` and the pair is appended to `text_pairs`.
3. **Inspect**: a random pair looks like `("Who is in this room?", "[start] ¿Quién está en esta habitación? [end]")`.
4. **Split**: after `random.shuffle(text_pairs)`, `val_samples = int(0.15 * len(text_pairs))`, `train_samples = len(text_pairs) - 2 * val_samples`; the list is sliced into `train_pairs` (~70%), `val_pairs` (15%) and `test_pairs` (the remaining ~15%).

The page ends by announcing **two separate `TextVectorization` layers**, one per language, with customized string preprocessing (detailed on p.455).

Why the markers? Following Figure 15.1 (p.453), the decoder is seeded with `"[start]"` at inference time and generation stops when it emits `"[end]"`. Only the target (Spanish) needs them, because only the target is generated; the English source is simply encoded. The dataset is a tab-separated file of English/Spanish sentence pairs. Each Spanish target is wrapped as '[start] ... [end]' for the decoder. Pairs are shuffled, then split 15% validation, 15% test, ~70% training. Two separate TextVectorization layers will tokenize English and Spanish.

title: Custom standardization and tokenizers for translation
text:
Why the Spanish tokenizer needs a custom standardization (keep [ and ], strip ¿), Listing 15.9 building English and Spanish TextVectorization layers (15,000-token vocabularies, length 20 and 21) and adapting them on the training pairs, and the planned (inputs, target, sample_weights) dataset format Each language gets its own tokenizer. The Spanish one uses a custom standardization that lowercases and removes punctuation except the brackets of [start]/[end], and also removes ¿; its output length is 21 so it can be split into a 20-token decoder input and a 20-token target shifted by one. The page continues the list of reasons the tokenizers must be customized (introduced at the bottom of p.454):

- **Keep the brackets.** By default `TextVectorization` strips `[` and `]`, which would turn `"[start]"` into `"start"` and make it indistinguishable from the ordinary word *start*.
- **Punctuation differs by language.** If punctuation is stripped for Spanish, the inverted question mark **¿** must be stripped too, since it isn't in Python's `string.punctuation`.

For a non-toy translator one would keep punctuation as separate tokens so the model can generate correctly punctuated sentences; here, for simplicity, all punctuation is removed.

**Listing 15.9**:

- `strip_chars = string.punctuation + "¿"`, then `[` and `]` are removed from it.
- `custom_standardization` lowercases with `tf.strings.lower` and deletes every character in `strip_chars` with `tf.strings.regex_replace(lowercase, f"[{re.escape(strip_chars)}]", "")`.
- `vocab_size = 15000`, `sequence_length = 20`.
- `english_tokenizer`: `TextVectorization(max_tokens=vocab_size, output_mode="int", output_sequence_length=sequence_length)` with the default standardization.
- `spanish_tokenizer`: the same but with `output_sequence_length=sequence_length + 1` and `standardize=custom_standardization`.
- Both are `adapt`ed on the **training** texts only (`train_english_texts`, `train_spanish_texts`).

Separate 15,000-token vocabularies; English length 20, Spanish 21 for the offset. Adapt tokenizers on training data only. The dataset yields (inputs dict, shifted target, sample_weights masking padding).

title: Building the tf.data pipeline for translation (Listing 15.10) and starting seq2seq RNNs
text:
Turning English/Spanish sentence pairs into batched (features, labels, sample_weights) tuples for a sequence-to-sequence model, and introducing RNN-based seq2seq learning Each training example gives the model the full tokenized English sentence plus the Spanish sentence minus its last token, and asks it to predict the Spanish sentence shifted one step ahead; a boolean `labels != 0` mask is used as sample weights so padding positions are ignored by the loss and metrics. The page finishes the description of the translation data pipeline that began on p.455. The pipeline returns a tuple `(inputs, target, sample_weights)`. The **sample weights** tell Keras which label positions count when computing the loss and metrics. Translations differ in length, so many label sequences end in padding zeros, and the authors "only care about predictions for non-zero labels that represent actual translated text."

This is the same **off-by-one** label setup as the Shakespeare generation model, with one addition: a fixed encoder input (the English sentence), which the model will handle separately.

**Listing 15.10** does the work:
- `format_dataset(eng, spa)` tokenizes a batch of English strings (to length 20) and Spanish strings (to length 21, see p.455). The features are a dict, `{"english": eng, "spanish": spa[:, :-1]}`. The labels are `spa[:, 1:]`, and the sample weights are the boolean mask `labels != 0`.
- `make_dataset(pairs)` unzips the list of `(english, spanish)` pairs into two lists, builds a `tf.data.Dataset` from them, batches by `batch_size = 64`, maps `format_dataset` over the batches with 4 parallel calls, then shuffles (buffer 2048) and caches.
- `train_ds` and `val_ds` are built from `train_pairs` and `val_pairs`.

Pulling one batch shows four tensors that are all `(64, 20)`: the English tokens, the shifted Spanish decoder input, the Spanish targets, and the sample-weight mask.

With the data ready, **section 15.2.2** starts on RNNs for sequence-to-sequence learning. Before building the twin encoder/decoder from figure 15.1 (p.453), the authors look at a simpler option first: the "easiest, naive way" to turn one sequence into another with an RNN. That sentence continues on p.457, where the idea turns out to be a model that predicts one output token at every input time step, and where its flaw is explained. Each example is `({"english": eng, "spanish": spa[:, :-1]}, spa[:, 1:], spa[:, 1:] != 0)`. The Spanish tokenizer outputs 21 tokens so that the shifted input and label are both 20 tokens long. Sample weights `labels != 0` remove padding from the loss and from weighted metrics. Batching before mapping lets tokenization run vectorized over 64 strings; shuffling and caching come last. All four tensors in a batch have shape `(64, 20)`. Section 15.2.2 starts from the naive single-RNN approach before introducing the encoder-decoder.
snippet: The page finishes the description of the translation data pipeline that began on p.455. The pipeline returns a tuple inputs, target, sampleweights. The sample weights tell Keras…

title: Sample weights as a padding mask
text: A per-token weight tensor, here `labels != 0`, that multiplies each position's loss and metric contribution, so padded positions contribute nothing. It works like grading an exam where only the questions actually asked are marked, and the blank lines after the last question are ignored. `labels != 0` yields a boolean `(64, 20)` tensor that Keras casts to float. The loss for each token is multiplied by its weight before reduction. Weighted metrics such as accuracy compute $\sum w_i c_i / \sum w_i$, where $c_i$ is 1 for a correct prediction. Labels `[12, 87, 3, 0, 0]` give weights `[1, 1, 1, 0, 0]`. Only the first three predictions are scored.
snippet: A per-token weight tensor, here labels != 0, that multiplies each position's loss and metric contribution, so padded positions contribute nothing.

title: Off-by-one decoder inputs (teacher forcing)
text: During training, the decoder receives the ground-truth target sequence shifted right (`spa[:, :-1]`) and must predict the sequence shifted left (`spa[:, 1:]`). At every position the model is told the correct previous words and asked only for the next one, so all positions can be trained in parallel from a single sequence. With a 21-token Spanish sequence $s_0\dots s_{20}$, the decoder input is $s_0\dots s_{19}$ and the target is $s_1\dots s_{20}$. Position $t$ learns $p(s_{t+1}\mid s_{\le t}, x)$. `[start] tú lo sabes [end]` becomes input `[start] tú lo sabes` and target `tú lo sabes [end]`.
snippet: During training, the decoder receives the ground-truth target sequence shifted right spa:, :-1 and must predict the sequence shifted left spa:, 1:.

title: tf.data input pipeline
text: A `tf.data.Dataset` chain (`from_tensor_slices` → `batch` → `map` → `shuffle` → `cache`) that produces model-ready batches. It is an assembly line: raw string pairs go in, and batches of integer tensors with labels and masks come out. Batching before mapping lets the `TextVectorization` layers tokenize 64 strings at once. `num_parallel_calls=4` runs the map on four threads, and `cache()` keeps the processed batches in memory after the first pass. `next(iter(train_ds))` yields `(inputs_dict, targets, sample_weights)`.
snippet: A tf.data.Dataset chain fromtensorslices → batch → map → shuffle → cache that produces model-ready batches.

title: Sequence-to-sequence learning
text: Mapping a source sequence to a target sequence of possibly different length, such as an English sentence to a Spanish one. It amounts to reading one sentence and writing another. The model is usually an encoder that represents the source and a decoder that generates the target autoregressively, conditioned on that representation. English "You know that." maps to Spanish "tú lo sabes".
snippet: Mapping a source sequence to a target sequence of possibly different length, such as an English sentence to a Spanish one.

title: Off-by-one slicing of the Spanish sequence
text: features = {"english": eng, "spanish": spa[:, :-1]}; labels = spa[:, 1:] \begin{aligned} \text{decoder input}_t &= s_t, \quad t = 0,\dots,19 \\ \text{label}_t &= s_{t+1}, \quad t = 0,\dots,19 \end{aligned} Aligns each decoder input position with the token that follows it, so one forward pass trains 20 next-token predictions at once. Position t's label is position t+1's input. s_t The t-th integer token of the 21-token tokenized Spanish sentence (s_0 is usually the `[start]` token) t Position index in the 20-step decoder sequence
snippet: features = {"english": eng, "spanish": spa:, :-1}; labels = spa:, 1: — Aligns each decoder input position with the token that follows it, so one forward pass trains 20 next-token…

title: Masked (sample-weighted) token loss and accuracy
text: sample_weights = labels != 0 \text{acc} = \frac{\sum_{b,t} w_{b,t}\,[\hat y_{b,t} = y_{b,t}]}{\sum_{b,t} w_{b,t}}, \qquad w_{b,t} = [\,y_{b,t} \neq 0\,], \qquad \mathcal{L} \propto \sum_{b,t} w_{b,t}\,\bigl(-\log p_{b,t}(y_{b,t})\bigr) Only real tokens affect training and the reported accuracy. Weighted accuracy is the fraction of real (non-padding) target tokens predicted correctly. This is the "65% accuracy" reported on p.459. y_{b,t} True label token at batch row b, position t \hat y_{b,t} Predicted token (argmax of the softmax output) w_{b,t} Sample weight: 1 for a real token, 0 for padding p_{b,t}(y) Model probability assigned to token y at that position
snippet: sampleweights = labels != 0 — Only real tokens affect training and the reported accuracy.

title: Listing 15.10 Tokenizing and preparing the translation data
text:
batch_size = 64

def format_dataset(eng, spa):
    eng = english_tokenizer(eng)
    spa = spanish_tokenizer(spa)
    features = {"english": eng, "spanish": spa[:, :-1]}
    labels = spa[:, 1:]
    sample_weights = labels != 0
    return features, labels, sample_weights

def make_dataset(pairs):
    eng_texts, spa_texts = zip(*pairs)
    eng_texts = list(eng_texts)
    spa_texts = list(spa_texts)
    dataset = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((eng_texts, spa_texts))
    dataset = dataset.batch(batch_size)
    dataset = dataset.map(format_dataset, num_parallel_calls=4)
    return dataset.shuffle(2048).cache()

train_ds = make_dataset(train_pairs)
val_ds = make_dataset(val_pairs) Builds training and validation `tf.data` pipelines that turn raw English/Spanish string pairs into batches of `({"english": (64,20), "spanish": (64,20)}, labels (64,20), sample_weights (64,20))`. Transpose pairs → slice into dataset → batch → tokenize and shift → mask → shuffle → cache.
snippet: Builds training and validation tf.data pipelines that turn raw English/Spanish string pairs into batches of {"english": 64,20, "spanish": 64,20}, labels 64,20, sampleweights 64,20.

title: Why a single RNN can't translate, and the RNN encoder-decoder (figure 15.2)
text:
The naive per-timestep RNN translator, its causal limitation, and the standard encoder-decoder RNN in which the encoder's final state initializes the decoder A single RNN that emits one target token per source time step can only use source tokens 0...N when producing target token N, which fails when word order differs between languages. The fix is to let an encoder RNN read the whole source sentence first and pass its final state to a decoder RNN, which then works as a language model conditioned on that state. The page first shows the **naive** way to use an RNN for sequence-to-sequence mapping: keep the RNN output at every time step and predict an output token from each one. In Keras this is an `Input(shape=(sequence_length,))` of int tokens, an `Embedding(vocab_size, 128)`, an `LSTM(32, return_sequences=True)` and a `Dense(vocab_size, activation="softmax")` applied at each step.

The authors call out a **critical issue**. Because RNNs process the sequence step by step, the model sees only source tokens `0...N` when predicting target token `N`. Take "I will bring the bag to you." The Spanish is "Te traeré la bolsa," and its first word, "Te", corresponds to "you", the *last* word of the English. There is no way to emit the first word of the translation without having seen the end of the source.

A human translator reads the whole source sentence first, which matters most for languages with very different word order. Standard **sequence-to-sequence models** do the same (figure 15.2):
- An **encoder RNN** turns the entire source sequence into a single representation, either its last output or its final internal state vectors.
- That representation becomes the **initial state of a decoder RNN** used in the language-model setup, replacing the zero initial state of the Shakespeare generator.
- The decoder learns to predict the next Spanish word given the current one. *All* information about the English sentence reaches it through that initial state.

Figure 15.2 shows the English input "how, is, the, weather, today" going into the encoder. The decoder receives "[start], qué, tiempo, hace, hoy" and outputs "qué, tiempo, hace, hoy, [end]".

The implementation will use **GRU** layers. The authors start with the encoder and note that, since no tokens are predicted on the encoder side, passing information from the end of the source back to its beginning is not cheating. In fact it is desirable. The argument continues on p.458, which uses a `Bidirectional` layer. A naive RNN that emits one target token per source step only sees source tokens 0...N when producing target token N. Reordering between languages ("Te" ↔ "you") makes that fatal. Seq2seq RNNs encode the entire source first, then decode. The encoder's final output or state becomes the decoder's initial state, replacing zeros. The decoder is a language model over Spanish; English information enters only via the initial state. The encoder may use future source context (no cheating); the decoder may not.
snippet: The page first shows the naive way to use an RNN for sequence-to-sequence mapping: keep the RNN output at every time step and predict an output token from each one. In Keras this…

title: Encoder-decoder (seq2seq) RNN
text: Two RNNs: the encoder reads the whole source sequence into a state vector, and the decoder starts from that state and generates the target as a language model. Read the whole sentence, keep its gist in mind, then write the translation word by word. $h_0^{dec} = \text{enc}(x_{0:T})$. The decoder is trained with shifted targets (teacher forcing) and run autoregressively at inference. Figure 15.2: "how is the weather today" becomes a state vector, which the decoder turns into "qué tiempo hace hoy [end]".
snippet: Two RNNs: the encoder reads the whole source sequence into a state vector, and the decoder starts from that state and generates the target as a language model.

title: Fixed-size state bottleneck
text: In an RNN encoder-decoder, all information about the source must pass through one fixed-size vector. It is like summarizing a paragraph in one fixed-length note before translating it: long or complex inputs get compressed lossily. The capacity of $c \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ ($d = 1024$ on p.458) does not grow with the sentence length. A 5-word sentence and a 50-word sentence are both squeezed into 1,024 numbers.
snippet: In an RNN encoder-decoder, all information about the source must pass through one fixed-size vector.

title: Causal decoder versus bidirectional encoder
text: The decoder must not see future target tokens, while the encoder may freely use the whole source. The answer sheet (target) must stay hidden, but the question (source) can be read as many times as you like. Encoder: any function of $x_{0:T}$. Decoder output at t: a function of $y_{0:t}$ and the encoder output only. On p.458 the authors warn that a Bidirectional decoder 'would break training by making the loss function trivially easy'.
snippet: The decoder must not see future target tokens, while the encoder may freely use the whole source.

title: Recurrent neural network
text: A layer that processes a sequence one step at a time, maintaining a state vector. It reads left to right while keeping a running memory. $h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$. The output at step t depends only on $x_{0:t}$ and $h_0$. `layers.LSTM(32, return_sequences=True)` produces one output per step.
snippet: A layer that processes a sequence one step at a time, maintaining a state vector.

title: The naive RNN translator is causal
text: the model will only look at tokens 0...N in the source sequence to predict token N in the target sequence \hat y_N = g\bigl(h_N\bigr), \qquad h_N = f\bigl(h_{N-1}, \operatorname{emb}(x_N)\bigr) \;\Rightarrow\; \hat y_N \text{ depends only on } x_0, \dots, x_N Formalizes the 'critical issue' with the naive approach. Target position 0 depends only on source position 0. x_N Source token at position N h_N LSTM output/state at step N \hat y_N Predicted target token at position N f, g The LSTM update and the Dense+softmax output layer
snippet: the model will only look at tokens 0...N in the source sequence to predict token N in the target sequence — Formalizes the 'critical issue' with the naive approach.

title: Encoder-decoder conditioning through the initial state
text: We can use this representation as the initial state of a decoder RNN in the language model setup instead of an initial state of zeros \begin{aligned} c &= \operatorname{Encoder}(x_0,\dots,x_T) \\ s_0 &= c \\ s_t &= \operatorname{GRU}\bigl(s_{t-1}, \operatorname{emb}(y_t)\bigr) \\ p(y_{t+1}\mid y_{\le t}, x) &= \operatorname{softmax}(W s_t + b) \end{aligned} Shows that all information about x enters the decoder through s_0. The decoder is a language model whose starting memory is the meaning of the English sentence. c The encoder's single representation of the source: its final output or final internal state s_t Decoder state after reading target token y_t y_t Target (Spanish) token at position t; y_0 = [start] W, b Weights of the Dense softmax layer over the Spanish vocabulary
snippet: We can use this representation as the initial state of a decoder RNN in the language model setup instead of an initial state of zeros — Shows that all information about x enters…

title: Bidirectional GRU encoder and GRU decoder (Listings 15.11-15.12)
text:
Implementing the RNN encoder-decoder in Keras: a Bidirectional GRU encoder summarizing the English sentence, and a causal GRU decoder initialized with that summary and topped with a softmax over the Spanish vocabulary The encoder embeds English tokens (256-d, padding masked) and runs a Bidirectional GRU(1024) whose two final outputs are summed into one 1,024-d vector. The decoder embeds Spanish tokens, runs a GRU(1024, return_sequences=True) with `initial_state=encoder_output`, applies dropout and a Dense softmax over 15,000 tokens. The decoder must stay unidirectional, because a Bidirectional decoder would see the answers. The page completes the argument begun on p.457. The encoder predicts no tokens, so it is free to pass information from the end of the source to the beginning, and that is desirable, because "we want a rich representation of the source sequence". A **`Bidirectional`** layer provides this.

**Listing 15.11 (encoder).** `embed_dim = 256` and `hidden_dim = 1024`. The source is `keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int32", name="english")`, a variable-length sequence of token ids. An `Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim, mask_zero=True)` maps ids to 256-d vectors and marks padding. A `GRU(hidden_dim)` without `return_sequences` is wrapped in `Bidirectional(..., merge_mode="sum")`, so the forward and backward final outputs are added into a single 1,024-d `encoder_output`.

**Listing 15.12 (decoder).** A second input named `"spanish"`, its own `Embedding` with `mask_zero=True`, and a `GRU(hidden_dim, return_sequences=True)` called with `initial_state=encoder_output`. That one argument is the whole connection between English and Spanish. Next come `Dropout(0.5)` and `Dense(vocab_size, activation="softmax")`, which "predicts the next word of the translation, given the current word". The model is `keras.Model([source, target], target_predictions)`. The authors stress that the decoder must predict the next tokens only from what came before, so a `Bidirectional` decoder "would break training by making the loss function trivially easy".

The start of `seq2seq_rnn.summary()` shows the model named `"functional_1"`, the two `InputLayer`s with shape `(None, None)`, `embedding_1` with output `(None, None, 256)` and 3,840,000 parameters (15,000 × 256), and a `not_equal (NotEqual)` layer. That layer is the padding mask computed from the English input and passed on to the encoder. The rest of the table is on p.459. The encoder is an Embedding(15000, 256, mask_zero) followed by Bidirectional(GRU(1024), merge_mode="sum"), giving one 1,024-d vector. The decoder is an Embedding followed by GRU(1024, return_sequences=True, initial_state=encoder_output), Dropout(0.5) and Dense(15000, softmax). `initial_state=encoder_output` is the only bridge from English to Spanish. `sum` merging keeps dimensions compatible with the decoder state. The decoder must be causal; a Bidirectional decoder makes the loss trivially easy. Input names match the dataset dict keys; `mask_zero=True` adds the `not_equal` mask seen in the summary.

title: Bidirectional RNN
text: Two RNNs over the same sequence, one forward and one reversed, whose outputs are merged (`concat`, `sum`, `mul`, `ave`). Read the sentence left to right and right to left, then combine both impressions. Without `return_sequences`, the merged output is $\overrightarrow{h}_T \oplus \overleftarrow{h}_0$. With `merge_mode="sum"` the dimension stays at `hidden_dim`. Parameters double: 7,876,608 = 2 × 3,938,304 (p.459). `layers.Bidirectional(layers.GRU(1024), merge_mode="sum")` → `(None, 1024)`.
snippet: Two RNNs over the same sequence, one forward and one reversed, whose outputs are merged concat, sum, mul, ave.

title: Embedding layer with mask_zero
text: A trainable lookup table from token ids to dense vectors. With `mask_zero=True`, it also emits a boolean mask marking id 0 as padding. A dictionary from word ids to learned coordinates, plus a sticky note saying 'ignore these slots'. Weights are `(vocab_size, embed_dim)` = 15,000 × 256 = 3,840,000. The mask `inputs != 0` propagates to downstream mask-aware layers such as the GRU. Ids `[12, 7, 0, 0]` give mask `[True, True, False, False]`.
snippet: A trainable lookup table from token ids to dense vectors. With maskzero=True, it also emits a boolean mask marking id 0 as padding.

title: Conditioning via `initial_state`
text: Passing the encoder's output as the decoder GRU's starting hidden state: `rnn_layer(x, initial_state=encoder_output)`. The decoder wakes up already remembering the English sentence. The initial state must match the GRU's state size, `hidden_dim = 1024`. A Bidirectional encoder with `concat` would yield 2,048 and fail, which is why `sum` is used. `encoder_output` of shape `(None, 1024)` is used as `initial_state`.
snippet: Passing the encoder's output as the decoder GRU's starting hidden state: rnnlayerx, initialstate=encoderoutput.

title: GRU layer
text: Gated Recurrent Unit, an RNN with update and reset gates and a single hidden state. A lighter LSTM: it decides at each step how much old memory to keep and how much new content to write. Keras parameter count (reset_after=True): $3\,[u(d+u) + 2u]$. With $d=256$, $u=1024$ this is 3,938,304, matching `gru_2` on p.459. `layers.GRU(1024, return_sequences=True)`.
snippet: Gated Recurrent Unit, an RNN with update and reset gates and a single hidden state.

title: Bidirectional encoder output with merge_mode="sum"
text: rnn_layer = layers.Bidirectional(rnn_layer, merge_mode="sum"); encoder_output = rnn_layer(x) c = \overrightarrow{\mathrm{GRU}}(e_1,\dots,e_T) + \overleftarrow{\mathrm{GRU}}(e_T,\dots,e_1) \in \mathbb{R}^{1024} Produce one source vector that is the right size to initialize a 1,024-unit decoder GRU. Each component of c mixes a left-to-right and a right-to-left summary. e_t 256-d embedding of English token t (padding masked) \overrightarrow{\mathrm{GRU}} Forward GRU; returns its final output after reading the last real token \overleftarrow{\mathrm{GRU}} Backward GRU (separate weights); returns its output after reading back to the first token c encoder_output, shape (batch, 1024)
snippet: rnnlayer = layers.Bidirectionalrnnlayer, mergemode="sum"; encoderoutput = rnnlayerx — Produce one source vector that is the right size to initialize a 1,024-unit decoder GRU.

text: embedding_1 (Embedding) │ (None, None, 256) │ 3,840,000 \#\text{params} = \text{vocab\_size} \times \text{embed\_dim} = 15{,}000 \times 256 = 3{,}840{,}000 Explains the first non-zero row of the summary. The decoder's Spanish embedding (`embedding_2`, p.459) has the same count. vocab_size 15,000 tokens (p.455) embed_dim 256

title: Decoder recurrence and readout
text: x = rnn_layer(x, initial_state=encoder_output); x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x); target_predictions = layers.Dense(vocab_size, activation="softmax")(x) \begin{aligned} s_0 &= c \\ s_t &= \mathrm{GRU}\bigl(s_{t-1}, E_{es}[y_t]\bigr) \\ p_t &= \operatorname{softmax}\bigl(W\,\mathrm{dropout}(s_t) + b\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^{15000} \end{aligned} The formal content of Listing 15.12. p_t estimates $p(y_{t+1} \mid y_{\le t}, x)$. s_t Decoder GRU state/output at step t (1,024-d) E_{es}[y_t] 256-d Spanish embedding of input token y_t W, b Dense weights (1024 × 15000) and biases (15000) p_t Distribution over the next Spanish token y_{t+1}
snippet: x = rnnlayerx, initialstate=encoderoutput; x = layers.Dropout0.5x; targetpredictions = layers.Densevocabsize, activation="softmax"x — The formal content of Listing 15.12.

title: Listing 15.11 Building a sequence-to-sequence encoder
text:
embed_dim = 256
hidden_dim = 1024

source = keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int32", name="english")
x = layers.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim, mask_zero=True)(source)
rnn_layer = layers.GRU(hidden_dim)
rnn_layer = layers.Bidirectional(rnn_layer, merge_mode="sum")
encoder_output = rnn_layer(x) Encodes a variable-length sequence of English token ids into one 1,024-dimensional vector. Embed → masked bidirectional GRU → sum of the two final outputs.
snippet: Encodes a variable-length sequence of English token ids into one 1,024-dimensional vector.

title: Listing 15.12 Building a sequence-to-sequence decoder
text:
target = keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int32", name="spanish")
x = layers.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim, mask_zero=True)(target)
rnn_layer = layers.GRU(hidden_dim, return_sequences=True)
x = rnn_layer(x, initial_state=encoder_output)
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
target_predictions = layers.Dense(vocab_size, activation="softmax")(x)
seq2seq_rnn = keras.Model([source, target], target_predictions) Builds a causal GRU decoder conditioned on the encoder output and assembles the full two-input seq2seq model. Embed target → GRU with initial state = encoder output → dropout → per-step softmax.
snippet: Builds a causal GRU decoder conditioned on the encoder output and assembles the full two-input seq2seq model.

The decoder's target at position t is its input at position t+1. A backward RNN carries information from later positions to earlier ones, so position t would 'see' its own label and the model could copy it rather than learn to translate.

title: Model summary totals, training the seq2seq RNN, and why next-token accuracy misleads
text:
The remaining layers and the 34.9M-parameter total of the RNN translator, compiling and fitting it with sparse categorical crossentropy and weighted accuracy, the meaning and limits of the 65% next-token accuracy, BLEU, and the plan for autoregressive inference The RNN translator (about 35M parameters, 44% of them in the output Dense layer) reaches about 65% next-token validation accuracy. That metric is crude because it assumes all previous target tokens are correct (teacher forcing), whereas real translation generates from scratch. Proper MT evaluation uses metrics like BLEU against reference translations. Inference feeds `[start]` plus the encoded source to the decoder and re-injects each predicted token until `[end]` or the maximum length. The top of the page finishes `seq2seq_rnn.summary()`:
- `embedding_2` (Spanish Embedding): `(None, None, 256)`, **3,840,000** params.
- `bidirectional`: `(None, 1024)`, **7,876,608** params, connected to `embedding_1` and the `not_equal` mask.
- `gru_2` (decoder GRU): `(None, None, 1024)`, **3,938,304** params, connected to `embedding_2` and `bidirectional` (as initial state).
- `dropout_1`: 0 params.
- `dense_1`: `(None, None, 15000)`, **15,375,000** params.
- **Total 34,869,912 params (133.02 MB)**, all trainable.

Training is then a single `compile` + `fit`: `optimizer="adam"`, `loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"` (integer labels against a softmax over 15,000 tokens), and `weighted_metrics=["accuracy"]`, so the accuracy respects the padding sample weights from p.456. The model is trained for 15 epochs on `train_ds`, validated on `val_ds`.

The authors call accuracy "a crude way to monitor validation set performance". The model reaches **65%**: on average it correctly predicts the next Spanish word 65% of the time. Next-token accuracy is a poor MT metric, though, because it *assumes the correct target tokens 0 to N are already known* when predicting token N + 1. At inference you generate from scratch, and earlier generated tokens may be wrong. Real MT systems need carefully designed metrics, such as **BLEU**, which measures similarity between the machine output and a set of high-quality reference translations and tolerates slightly misaligned sequences.

Finally, the authors describe inference. Pick test sentences, start the decoder with the seed token `"[start]"` and the encoded English sentence, get a next-token prediction, and re-inject it into the decoder repeatedly, one new token per iteration, until `"[end]"` appears or the maximum sentence length is reached. The code is Listing 15.13 on p.460. The RNN translator has 34,869,912 parameters (133.02 MB); the output Dense layer alone has 15,375,000. Training: Adam + sparse categorical crossentropy + `weighted_metrics=["accuracy"]`, 15 epochs. About 65% next-token validation accuracy is a crude, teacher-forced measure. Next-token accuracy assumes correct prefixes; real inference builds on the model's own guesses. Real MT evaluation uses metrics like BLEU that compare against reference translations and tolerate misalignment. Inference: seed with `[start]` and the encoded source, re-inject predictions until `[end]` or the maximum length.
snippet: The top of the page finishes seq2seqrnn.summary: - embedding2 Spanish Embedding: None, None, 256, 3,840,000 params. - bidirectional: None, 1024, 7,876,608 params, connected to…

title: Next-token (teacher-forced) accuracy
text: The share of non-padding target positions where the model's top prediction equals the true next token, given the true previous tokens. It is like a quiz where you're always shown the correct previous words and asked only for the next one. Computed by Keras `accuracy` with sample weights. The model gets 65% on validation. Predicting `sabes` after the true prefix `[start] tú lo` counts as correct even if, in free generation, the model would have produced `[start] yo` and gone astray.
snippet: The share of non-padding target positions where the model's top prediction equals the true next token, given the true previous tokens.

title: Train/inference mismatch (exposure bias)
text: During training the decoder sees ground-truth prefixes. At inference it sees its own, possibly wrong, outputs. It is like practicing a speech with a prompter who corrects every slip, then delivering it alone. Training conditions on $y^{*}_{\le t}$ while inference conditions on $\hat y_{\le t}$. Errors can compound along the sequence. On p.460, "The prisoner was set free yesterday" becomes "el plan fue ayer a un atasco": once a wrong word appears, the rest follows it.
snippet: During training the decoder sees ground-truth prefixes. At inference it sees its own, possibly wrong, outputs.

title: BLEU score
text: A machine-translation metric that measures n-gram overlap between a candidate translation and one or more reference translations. It counts how many word chunks of the output also appear in good human translations. Beyond the book: the geometric mean of clipped n-gram precisions (n = 1..4) times a brevity penalty for outputs shorter than the references. Candidate "te lo diré mañana" against reference "mañana te lo diré" shares all unigrams and the bigrams "te lo" and "lo diré", despite the shift.
snippet: A machine-translation metric that measures n-gram overlap between a candidate translation and one or more reference translations.

title: Sparse categorical crossentropy
text: Negative log-probability of the true class, with integer labels. It punishes the model for putting low probability on the correct next word. $-\log p_{b,t}(y_{b,t})$ per position, weighted by the padding mask. If the model gives the correct token probability 0.25, the loss is −ln 0.25 ≈ 1.386.
snippet: Negative log-probability of the true class, with integer labels.
