title: Transformer versus RNN efficiency
text: The Transformer passes information across a sequence by attention alone, without recurrence. Everyone reads the whole sentence at once instead of passing notes down a line. No sequential loop at training time; attention over all positions is computed in a single batched matrix operation, so each epoch runs about three times faster than the GRU here. 67% accuracy with about 14.4M parameters versus 65% with 34.9M for the GRU.
snippet: The Transformer passes information across a sequence by attention alone, without recurrence.

title: Recurrent computation as a bottleneck
text: RNN layers such as GRU process timesteps sequentially, passing a state from one to the next. A relay race: no runner can start before receiving the baton. Each timestep depends on the previous state, so the L steps cannot be parallelized across time during training. The GRU translator of p.458 with hidden_dim = 1024.
snippet: RNN layers such as GRU process timesteps sequentially, passing a state from one to the next.

title: Listing 15.18 Building a Transformer model with positional embeddings

hidden_dim = 256
intermediate_dim = 2056
num_heads = 8

source = keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int32", name="english")
x = PositionalEmbedding(sequence_length, vocab_size, hidden_dim)(source)
encoder_output = TransformerEncoder(hidden_dim, intermediate_dim, num_heads)(
    source=x,
    source_mask=source != 0,
)

target = keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int32", name="spanish")
x = PositionalEmbedding(sequence_length, vocab_size, hidden_dim)(target)
x = TransformerDecoder(hidden_dim, intermediate_dim, num_heads)(
    target=x,
    source=encoder_output,
    source_mask=source != 0,
)
x = layers.Dropout(0.5)(x)
target_predictions = layers.Dense(vocab_size, activation="softmax")(x)
transformer = keras.Model([source, target], target_predictions) Builds the encoder-decoder translator of listing 15.16 again, replacing both Embedding layers with PositionalEmbedding so the model sees word order in both the English source and the Spanish target. title: Generating translations with the Transformer
text:
Greedy, token-by-token decoding of Spanish translations from the trained sequence-to-sequence Transformer (Listing 15.19) and a look at its sample outputs. Although the Transformer is trained in parallel on whole target sequences, at inference time it must still generate one token at a time: feed the source sentence plus the Spanish prefix so far, read the prediction at the current position, append the argmax token, and repeat until `[end]`. With positional embeddings restored, the Transformer of Listing 15.18 reached about 67% next-word accuracy (p.476). This page puts it to work. The authors note that the generation code is essentially the one used for the RNN in Listing 15.13 (p.460).

**Listing 15.19** builds a reverse lookup `spa_index_lookup` from token index to Spanish word, then defines `generate_translation()`. The English sentence is tokenized once. The Spanish output starts as the string `"[start]"`. For up to `sequence_length` (20) steps, the code re-tokenizes the whole partial Spanish sentence, drops its last position with `[:, :-1]`, runs the full model on `[english, spanish_prefix]`, and takes the **argmax** of the softmax distribution at position `i`. That is the model's guess for the token that follows the `i`-th input token. The word is appended to the string, and the loop stops early once `[end]` is produced. The driver code picks five random English test sentences and prints each with its translation.

Two details are not spelled out on the page. First, the slice: the Spanish tokenizer pads to `sequence_length + 1` = 21 tokens (p.455), but the Transformer's `PositionalEmbedding` only has `sequence_length` = 20 position slots (p.475), so the decoder input must be trimmed to 20. Second, the causal mask in the decoder guarantees that position `i` only sees tokens `0..i`, so the zero padding to its right does not affect the prediction.

The **sample output** shows mostly fluent and correct translations ("te veré en la biblioteca mañana", "sabes montar en bici", "ya ha vuelto"). The first one contains a clear error: "cantantes" (singers) is inserted, and "son asombrosa" has number/gender agreement mistakes. Another loses "dirty" ("su trabajo" instead of "su trabajo sucio"). The next page calls the result "a better toy model" than the GRU, judged subjectively (p.478). Listing 15.19 decodes greedily: re-run the model on the source plus the current Spanish prefix, take the argmax at position i, append, stop at [end]. The only code change from the RNN version is `[:, :-1]`, which trims the 21-token Spanish tokenization to the 20 positions the learned positional embedding supports. The causal mask makes it safe to read row i of a padded, fixed-length decoder input. Transformers train in parallel but still generate sequentially; this naive loop recomputes everything at every step. The sample translations are mostly good but include a hallucinated word and agreement errors, so the model is still a toy.

title: Autoregressive (greedy) decoding
text: Generating a sequence one token at a time. Each new token is chosen from the model's predicted distribution conditioned on the source and all previously generated tokens; greedy decoding always takes the most probable token. Like writing a sentence word by word, rereading what you have written so far before choosing the next word. At step $i$ the decoder input is `[start] y_1 ... y_i` padded to length 20; the model outputs a (1, 20, vocab_size) tensor; row `i` is $p(\cdot \mid y_{\le i}, x)$ and `np.argmax` picks $y_{i+1}$. Step 0: input `[start]` → model predicts `te`. Step 1: `[start] te` → `veré`. ... until `[end]`.
snippet: Generating a sequence one token at a time. Each new token is chosen from the model's predicted distribution conditioned on the source and all previously generated tokens; greedy…

title: Causal mask during generation
text: The decoder's self-attention mask that prevents position $i$ from attending to positions $> i$. Each position wears blinders that hide everything to its right. Because of the mask, the output at position `i` depends only on target tokens `0..i` (plus the full encoder output). The zero padding after the current prefix therefore cannot change `next_token_predictions[0, i, :]`. With prefix `[start] te` (positions 0,1) and 18 pad tokens, the prediction read at `i = 1` sees only `[start]` and `te`.
snippet: The decoder's self-attention mask that prevents position i from attending to positions  i.

title: Fixed-size learned positional embedding
text: A learned `Embedding(sequence_length, dim)` table indexed by token position, added to token embeddings (Listing 15.17, p.475). A lookup table with one learned vector per seat number, so it has a fixed number of seats. Because the table has only `sequence_length` = 20 rows, inputs longer than 20 positions would index out of range. This is why the 21-token Spanish tokenization is trimmed with `[:, :-1]` before calling the Transformer. `spanish_tokenizer(["[start] te"])` has shape (1, 21); after slicing, (1, 20), positions 0..19.
snippet: A learned Embeddingsequencelength, dim table indexed by token position, added to token embeddings Listing 15.17, p.475.

title: Greedy next-token choice
text: sampled_token_index = np.argmax(next_token_predictions[0, i, :]) y_{i+1} = \arg\max_{v \in \mathcal{V}} \; p_\theta\left(v \mid y_0, y_1, \dots, y_i;\; x\right), \qquad y_0 = \texttt{[start]} Formalizes the decoding rule implemented in Listing 15.19. Greedy decoding commits to the locally most likely word at each step. It does not search for the most likely complete sentence. x the tokenized English source sentence (`tokenized_input_sentence`) y_0, \dots, y_i the Spanish tokens generated so far, starting with `[start]` \mathcal{V} the Spanish vocabulary (`spa_vocab`) p_\theta the softmax output of the trained Transformer at position i, i.e. `next_token_predictions[0, i, :]` y_{i+1} the next token appended to `decoded_sentence`
snippet: sampledtokenindex = np.argmaxnexttokenpredictions0, i, : — Formalizes the decoding rule implemented in Listing 15.19.

title: Listing 15.19 Generating translations with a Transformer
text:
import numpy as np
spa_vocab = spanish_tokenizer.get_vocabulary()
spa_index_lookup = dict(zip(range(len(spa_vocab)), spa_vocab))
def generate_translation(input_sentence):
    tokenized_input_sentence = english_tokenizer([input_sentence])
    decoded_sentence = "[start]"
    for i in range(sequence_length):
        tokenized_target_sentence = spanish_tokenizer([decoded_sentence])
        tokenized_target_sentence = tokenized_target_sentence[:, :-1]
        inputs = [tokenized_input_sentence, tokenized_target_sentence]
        next_token_predictions = transformer.predict(inputs, verbose=0)
        sampled_token_index = np.argmax(next_token_predictions[0, i, :])
        sampled_token = spa_index_lookup[sampled_token_index]
        decoded_sentence += " " + sampled_token
        if sampled_token == "[end]":
            break
    return decoded_sentence
test_eng_texts = [pair[0] for pair in test_pairs]
for _ in range(5):
    input_sentence = random.choice(test_eng_texts)
    print("-")
    print(input_sentence)
    print(generate_translation(input_sentence)) Defines a greedy decoding function for the trained English-to-Spanish Transformer and prints translations for five random test sentences. Greedy autoregressive decoding: encode source; prefix ← [start]; repeat {predict distribution for position i; append argmax; stop on [end]}.

title: Wrapping up the Transformer; why pretrain
text:
A reflective close to section 15.3 (the Transformer is effective but empirically discovered and not provably optimal), then the opening of section 15.4: Transformers scale well with data, which led to large pretrained models such as BERT. The Transformer's details are the outcome of empirical trial and error, not a derivation of the optimal design. Its two practical advantages, parallel training and continued improvement with more data, explain the shift toward large pretrained models that are then adapted to specific tasks. The page first closes section 15.3. Judging by the sample translations on p.477, the authors find the Transformer **subjectively** much better than the GRU-based translator, though "still a toy model, but ... a better toy model."

They then raise a fair objection: the Transformer has many design details that a reader is asked to take on faith. Is this configuration optimal? **No.** Researchers have since modified attention, normalization and positional embeddings. For very long sequences, newer models replace attention with something less costly altogether, and the authors expect that something may eventually displace the Transformer. Machine learning is an **empirical** field. Attention began as an add-on to RNNs, and the Transformer emerged from years of "guessing and checking." The authors promise an explanation of *why* it works at the end of the chapter (section 15.5).

**Section 15.4** begins with why Transformers were scaled up after "Attention is all you need":
- **Faster training** than RNNs, since there are no sequential loops, which suits GPUs and TPUs (p.476 measured about 3x faster epochs).
- **Data hunger.** In this chapter the RNN translator's validation performance plateaued after about 5 epochs, while the Transformer was still improving after 30.

Scaling data, layers and parameters gave strong results. The field shifted toward **large pretrained models** that can cost millions to train but perform noticeably better across many text problems. The chapter's last code example will revisit IMDb classification with a pretrained Transformer.

**Section 15.4.1** introduces **BERT** (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers; Devlin et al., footnote 2), one of the first popular pretrained Transformers. The description continues on p.479. The Transformer translator is better than the GRU but remains a toy model; the comparison is partly subjective. The Transformer's design is empirical and not optimal; attention, normalization and positional embeddings keep evolving. Two properties drove scaling: no training-time loops (accelerator-friendly) and data hunger (keeps improving with more data). Scaling led to large pretrained models that are expensive to train once but help across many text tasks. BERT, a pretrained Transformer encoder, is the starting point of section 15.4.1.
snippet: The page first closes section 15.3. Judging by the sample translations on p.477, the authors find the Transformer subjectively much better than the GRU-based translator, though…

title: BERT, masked language modeling, RoBERTa
text:
How BERT was pretrained (a bidirectional Transformer encoder trained with masked language modeling on unlabeled text), why that produced contextual word representations, and the introduction of RoBERTa and of the three things needed to reuse a pretrained model. BERT is the encoder half of a Transformer, pretrained by hiding about 15% of tokens and predicting them from both sides. The objective needs no labels, so it scales to huge text corpora and yields context-dependent token representations that can be fine-tuned for many tasks. RoBERTa applies the same idea with ten times more data. **BERT** was released a year after "Attention Is All You Need." Its structure is exactly the **encoder** of the translation Transformer built in this chapter. It is **bidirectional**: every position attends to positions both before and after it. That makes it good at computing rich representations of input text, but it is not a model for generating text in a loop.

BERT came in sizes from about 100M to 300M parameters, far more than the roughly 14M-parameter translation Transformer, so it needed a lot of training data. The authors therefore used **masked language modeling (MLM)**: replace about 15% of the tokens in a text with a special `[MASK]` token and train the model to recover the originals. A classic (**causal**) language model predicts `p(token|past tokens)`; a masked LM predicts `p(token|surrounding tokens)`. The setup is **unsupervised**: any text can be masked automatically, with no labels, so the authors could use a lot of text, mostly from Wikipedia.

Pretrained word embeddings (chapter 14) were already common, but they give each word a single vector. A pretrained Transformer instead computes a word's representation **in the context** of the surrounding words, at a scale and quality new at the time. Fine-tuned, BERT achieved state-of-the-art results on several NLP benchmarks, starting the shift toward very large pretrained models adapted with only a small amount of fine-tuning.

**Section 15.4.2** uses **RoBERTa** (Robustly Optimized BERT, Liu et al. 2019) instead. It slightly simplifies BERT's architecture, but its main change is more data: **160 GB** of web text vs. BERT's **16 GB**, mainly Wikipedia. Training cost an estimated few hundred thousand dollars, and the model performs noticeably better at an equal parameter count. To use a pretrained model you need several things. The first, a **matching tokenizer**, is introduced at the bottom of the page: text must be tokenized exactly as during pretraining (continued on p.480, which also lists the matching architecture and the pretrained weights). BERT is exactly a Transformer encoder: bidirectional, good for representations, not for generating text in a loop. Masked language modeling hides about 15% of tokens and predicts them from both sides: p(token | surrounding tokens), vs. a causal LM's p(token | past tokens). MLM is unsupervised, so huge unlabeled corpora (mostly Wikipedia for BERT) can be used. Pretrained Transformers give contextual embeddings, a major step beyond static word embeddings. RoBERTa is a lightly simplified BERT trained on 10x more data (160 GB vs. 16 GB), and performs noticeably better. Reusing a pretrained model requires a matching tokenizer (plus matching architecture and weights, p.480).

title: Masked language modeling
text: A self-supervised pretraining objective: randomly replace about 15% of tokens with `[MASK]` and train the model to predict the original tokens from the rest of the sequence. A cloze test: fill in the blanks in a paragraph using clues from both sides. Loss is cross-entropy over the vocabulary, computed only at masked positions; the encoder sees the full corrupted sequence with bidirectional attention. Input: "the [MASK] sat on the mat" → target at position 1: "cat".
snippet: A self-supervised pretraining objective: randomly replace about 15% of tokens with MASK and train the model to predict the original tokens from the rest of the sequence.

title: Causal language model
text: A model of the probability of each token given the preceding tokens, $p(\text{token} \mid \text{past tokens})$. Reading left to right and guessing the next word. Implemented with causal masking in a Transformer decoder or with an RNN; supports generation by sampling. Given "the cat sat on the", predict "mat".
snippet: A model of the probability of each token given the preceding tokens, ptext{token} mid text{past tokens}.

title: Contextual word embedding
text: A token representation that depends on the surrounding words, produced by running the whole sequence through a pretrained Transformer. A word's meaning shifts with its neighbors; the vector shifts too. Output of the final encoder layer at the token's position, shape (768,) per token for RoBERTa base (p.484). "bank" in "river bank" vs. "bank account" gets two different vectors.
snippet: A token representation that depends on the surrounding words, produced by running the whole sequence through a pretrained Transformer.

title: BERT / RoBERTa
text: Pretrained Transformer encoders. BERT (Devlin et al. 2018) introduced MLM pretraining; RoBERTa (Liu et al. 2019) trained a slightly simplified variant on 10x more data. Same engine, more fuel: RoBERTa is better mainly because it read ten times more text. Encoder-only, bidirectional self-attention; base size has 12 layers and a 768-dimensional hidden state (pp.481, 484). BERT pretraining: 16 GB of text; RoBERTa: 160 GB.
snippet: Pretrained Transformer encoders. BERT Devlin et al. 2018 introduced MLM pretraining; RoBERTa Liu et al. 2019 trained a slightly simplified variant on 10x more data.

title: Tokenizer-model matching
text: The requirement that inputs to a pretrained model be tokenized exactly as during pretraining. A codebook: send messages in a different code and the receiver reads nonsense. Token id $k$ selects row $k$ of the learned embedding matrix; any change in vocabulary or splitting breaks the correspondence. RoBERTa maps "The" to id 133 (p.480); a chapter 14 vectorizer would assign it some other id.

title: Causal vs. masked language modeling objectives
text: p(token|past tokens) ... p(token|surrounding tokens) \begin{aligned} \text{causal LM:}\quad & p(x_t \mid x_1, \dots, x_{t-1}) \\ \text{masked LM:}\quad & p(x_i \mid x_{\setminus M}),\; i \in M \end{aligned} Formalizes the book's contrast between the two pretraining setups. The causal model can be sampled left to right to generate text; the masked model sees two-sided context, which gives better representations but no direct generation procedure. x_t the token at position t x_1, \dots, x_{t-1} the past tokens (left context only) M the set of masked positions (about 15% of the sequence) x_{\setminus M} the surrounding, unmasked tokens on both sides

Lower loss means the model reconstructs hidden words better from context, which forces it to encode syntax and meaning. \tilde{x} the corrupted input sequence, with masked positions replaced by `[MASK]` x_i the original token at masked position i (the target) n sequence length \theta model parameters

title: Loading RoBERTa with KerasHub
text:
The three ingredients needed to reuse a pretrained Transformer (tokenizer, architecture, weights) and loading all three for RoBERTa with KerasHub's from_preset() A pretrained model is only useful if you reproduce exactly the tokenizer, the architecture and the weights it was trained with. KerasHub bundles all three behind `from_preset("roberta_base_en")`, giving a subword `Tokenizer` with a ~50,000-term vocabulary and a task-agnostic `Backbone`. The page finishes the list, started on p.479, of what you need in order to use a pretrained model:

1. **A matching tokenizer.** Text must be split into tokens and mapped to the *same integer indices* as during pretraining. If the words of the IMDb reviews mapped to different indices, the learned representation of each token (its row in the embedding matrix) would be attached to the wrong token and would be useless.
2. **A matching model architecture.** You have to recreate *exactly* the computation the model did during pretraining, so that the weights mean the same thing.
3. **The pretrained weights.** For RoBERTa these came from about a day of training on 1,024 GPUs over billions of words, which is not something you would redo.

The authors note that rewriting the tokenizer and architecture would not be hard, because RoBERTa's internals almost exactly match the `TransformerEncoder` built earlier in the chapter. Still, matching an implementation exactly takes time, so, as in earlier chapters, they use **KerasHub**. **Listing 15.20** loads a `Tokenizer` and a `Backbone` with `from_preset("roberta_base_en")`, which fetches the weights, configuration and tokenizer assets for RoBERTa *base*, the smallest checkpoint released with the RoBERTa paper.

The RoBERTa tokenizer is almost the same as the `SubWordTokenizer` from chapter 14, with tweaks to handle Unicode from any language. The page argues that subword tokenization is a must at this scale: character tokens would make sequences far too long (expensive training), and word tokens would need a huge vocabulary and an unworkably large `Embedding` layer. With subwords, any word can be encoded with a vocabulary of only about 50,000 terms. A demo shows `tokenizer("The quick brown fox")` returning `[133, 2119, 6219, 23602]`.

The page ends by asking what the `Backbone` is. In chapter 8 a backbone was a vision network that maps images to a latent space without a prediction head. The KerasHub definition continues on p.481. Reusing a pretrained model requires three matched pieces: tokenizer, architecture and weights. A mismatched tokenizer is a silent failure: the embedding rows no longer correspond to the right tokens. KerasHub's `from_preset("roberta_base_en")` loads a consistent tokenizer and backbone in two lines. Subword tokenization balances sequence length against vocabulary and embedding size, and about 50,000 tokens cover any word. A backbone is a pretrained model without a task head; a head is attached for each downstream task.
snippet: The page finishes the list, started on p.479, of what you need in order to use a pretrained model: 1. A matching tokenizer. Text must be split into tokens and mapped to the same…

title: Transfer learning with a pretrained Transformer
text: Reusing a model pretrained on a large generic corpus as the starting point for a specific task, by loading its tokenizer, architecture and weights and then fine-tuning. Someone else has already taught the model how English works. You only have to teach it what a positive movie review looks like. It requires an exact match of the tokenizer (token to id mapping), the architecture (the function the weights parameterize) and the weights. KerasHub's `from_preset` provides all three. Load `roberta_base_en`, attach a classification head, fine-tune on 20,000 IMDb reviews (pp.481-484).
snippet: Reusing a model pretrained on a large generic corpus as the starting point for a specific task, by loading its tokenizer, architecture and weights and then fine-tuning.

title: Subword tokenization at scale
text: Splitting text into units between characters and words, learned from data, so that common words are single tokens and rare words are a few pieces. It is a compromise: short sequences like word tokenization and complete coverage like character tokenization. RoBERTa uses byte-level BPE with about 50,000 tokens. Sequence length drives attention cost and vocabulary size drives embedding size, and subwords keep both manageable. `tokenizer("The quick brown fox")` gives `[133, 2119, 6219, 23602]`: four common words, four tokens.
snippet: Splitting text into units between characters and words, learned from data, so that common words are single tokens and rare words are a few pieces.

title: Backbone
text: A pretrained network that maps inputs to a latent representation and has no task-specific head. It is the body of a screwdriver, and different heads fit onto it (p.481). RoBERTa's backbone takes token ids (and a padding mask) and outputs a (batch_size, sequence_length, 768) tensor (p.481). `keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("roberta_base_en")`.
snippet: A pretrained network that maps inputs to a latent representation and has no task-specific head.

title: KerasHub preset / from_preset()
text: A named bundle of configuration, weights and tokenizer assets, loaded by the `from_preset()` class constructor. It is like ordering a complete kit by its catalog number instead of buying the parts separately. `Tokenizer.from_preset(name)` and `Backbone.from_preset(name)` read the same preset, so the vocabulary and the embedding rows correspond. `"roberta_base_en"`: RoBERTa, base size, English.

title: Backbone
text: In KerasHub, any pretrained model that is not yet specialized for a task: it maps inputs to latent features and has no loss or output head. It is the handle of a screwdriver; you click on whichever head the job needs. The RoBERTa backbone takes `token_ids` and `padding_mask`, both (batch, seq_len), and returns (batch, seq_len, 768). The same RoBERTa backbone can serve sentence classification, span identification or POS tagging.
snippet: In KerasHub, any pretrained model that is not yet specialized for a task: it maps inputs to latent features and has no loss or output head.

title: Classification head
text: Task-specific layers attached on top of a backbone to produce class predictions. It is the Phillips or flat head in the screwdriver analogy. It usually pools the per-token features (for example, takes the first token) and applies Dense layers with a softmax or sigmoid output. A 2-class head for IMDb positive/negative reviews.
snippet: Task-specific layers attached on top of a backbone to produce class predictions.

title: Stacked Transformer encoder
text: A deep network made of identical encoder blocks (self-attention plus feedforward, with residuals and layer norm) applied one after another. Each layer refines every token's representation by looking at all the other tokens again. RoBERTa-base: 12 layers, hidden size 768, feedforward size 3,072, 12 heads; 7,087,872 parameters per layer. transformer_layer_0 to transformer_layer_11 in the summary.
snippet: A deep network made of identical encoder blocks self-attention plus feedforward, with residuals and layer norm applied one after another.

title: Where a Transformer's parameters live
text: The breakdown of model size between embedding tables and the encoder stack. The vocabulary lookup table is a big one-off cost; each extra layer adds a fixed amount. Embeddings scale with (vocab + max_positions) × d; each layer scales with roughly 12d² (4d² for attention, 8d² for an FFN with 4d inner width). $12 \times 768^2 = 7{,}077{,}888$, close to the printed 7,087,872; the difference is biases and layer norms.
snippet: The breakdown of model size between embedding tables and the encoder stack.

About 31% of RoBERTa-base is lookup tables. V Vocabulary size (50,265 for RoBERTa's BPE; about 50,000 in the book's wording) L_{\max} Maximum number of positions (512) d Hidden size (768)

title: Packing IMDb reviews for RoBERTa
text:
Converting raw IMDb review strings into the exact input format RoBERTa saw during pretraining, `<s> tokens </s> <pad>...`, using KerasHub's `StartEndPacker` inside a `tf.data` map, and inspecting a resulting batch. A pretrained model works best when inputs mimic its pretraining format. Listing 15.21 tokenizes each batch of reviews, adds start/end tokens, truncates or pads to 512 tokens, and returns `token_ids` plus a boolean `padding_mask`, the two inputs the RoBERTa backbone expects. The page opens with the example promised at the end of p.482. RoBERTa saw every pretraining sequence as `<s>`, the tokens, `</s>`, then `<pad>` tokens up to a fixed length. Two toy sequences of length 8 show this: "the quick brown fox jumped ." fills the length exactly, and "the panda slept ." is padded with two `<pad>` tokens.

The authors stress matching pretraining's token ordering as closely as possible; the model then trains faster and more accurately. KerasHub's **`StartEndPacker`** layer does this: it appends start, end and padding tokens and trims long sequences to a given length.

**Listing 15.21** defines `preprocess(text, label)`. It creates a `StartEndPacker` with `sequence_length=512` and the tokenizer's own start, end and pad token ids, and asks it to also return a padding mask. It applies `packer(tokenizer(text))` and returns a dict `{"token_ids": ..., "padding_mask": ...}` plus the unchanged label. The dict keys match the backbone's two named inputs (p.481). The function is mapped over the train, validation and test datasets.

**One preprocessed batch** has `token_ids` of shape **(16, 512)** (int32) and `padding_mask` of shape (16, 512) (bool), with labels of shape (16,). Every row begins with **0** (`<s>`). Rows ending in `1, 1, 1` are short reviews padded with `<pad>` = 1, and their mask ends in `False`. Rows ending in `..., 2` are long reviews truncated to 512 tokens and closed by `</s>` = 2, with an all-`True` mask. The page ends with the inputs ready for fine-tuning (p.484). RoBERTa expects `<s>` tokens `</s>` followed by `<pad>`s; matching this makes fine-tuning faster and more accurate. `StartEndPacker` adds start/end tokens, truncates or pads to 512, and can return a padding mask, using the tokenizer's own special ids. `preprocess` returns a dict whose keys match the backbone's inputs: `token_ids` and `padding_mask`. A batch has `token_ids` and `padding_mask` of shape (16, 512) and labels of shape (16,). In the printout, 0 = `<s>`, 2 = `</s>`, 1 = `<pad>`; all-True mask rows are truncated long reviews.

title: Sequence packing with special tokens
text: Formatting each tokenized text as `<s>` + tokens + `</s>`, then padding to a fixed length, exactly as during pretraining. Putting a letter in the envelope the post office's machines are built for. For RoBERTa: start id 0, pad id 1, end id 2 (visible in the printed batch). Length fixed at 512. ["<s>", "the", "panda", "slept", ".", "</s>", "<pad>", "<pad>"]

title: Padding mask
text: A boolean tensor, the same shape as `token_ids`, that is True for real tokens and False for padding. A sticky note marking which seats are empty so nobody tries to talk to them. The backbone uses it so attention ignores `<pad>` positions as keys. Without it, real tokens would mix in information from hundreds of pad embeddings in short reviews. Row 1 of the printed batch: `[True, True, True, ..., False, False, False]`, a short review.
snippet: A boolean tensor, the same shape as tokenids, that is True for real tokens and False for padding.

title: Truncation to the maximum sequence length
text: Cutting token sequences longer than `sequence_length` so they fit the model's fixed number of positions. Reading only the first two pages of a long review. `sequence_length=512` matches RoBERTa base's maximum number of learned positions. Long reviews keep their first ~510 tokens, and `</s>` is still placed at the end. Printed row 2 ends `..., 101, 24, 2`: a truncated review, all-True mask.
snippet: Cutting token sequences longer than sequencelength so they fit the model's fixed number of positions.

[
    ["<s>", "the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumped", ".", "</s>"],
    ["<s>", "the", "panda", "slept", ".", "</s>", "<pad>", "<pad>"],
] Shows two token sequences of length 8 packed as RoBERTa expects: start token, content, end token, then padding. Prepend start, append end, right-pad to fixed length.

title: Listing 15.21 Preprocessing IMDb movie reviews with RoBERTa's tokenizer
text:
def preprocess(text, label):
    packer = keras_hub.layers.StartEndPacker(
        sequence_length=512,
        start_value=tokenizer.start_token_id,
        end_value=tokenizer.end_token_id,
        pad_value=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
        return_padding_mask=True,
    )
    token_ids, padding_mask = packer(tokenizer(text))
    return {"token_ids": token_ids, "padding_mask": padding_mask}, label
preprocessed_train_ds = train_ds.map(preprocess)
preprocessed_val_ds = val_ds.map(preprocess)
preprocessed_test_ds = test_ds.map(preprocess) Defines a `tf.data` mapping function that tokenizes a batch of reviews with RoBERTa's tokenizer, packs them to 512 tokens with start/end/pad tokens, and returns the backbone's input dict plus the label; applies it to the three datasets. Tokenize → pack (start + truncated tokens + end + pads) → mask = not pad.

title: Fine-tuning RoBERTa on IMDb, and the opening of 'What makes the Transformer effective?'
text:
Adding a classification head on top of the pretrained RoBERTa backbone (first-token pooling, dropout, a 768-unit ReLU layer, a sigmoid output), fine-tuning it with Adam at 5e-5 for one epoch to reach about 93.7% test accuracy on IMDb, then starting section 15.5 with the story of Word2Vec A pretrained Transformer encoder becomes a strong sentiment classifier with only a tiny head and a single epoch of low-learning-rate fine-tuning: it beats the 90% ceiling of chapter 14's bigram model. The page then turns to why Transformers work so well, starting from Word2Vec's idea of turning word co-occurrence into vector proximity. The page finishes section 15.4.4 and starts section 15.5.

**Listing 15.22** turns the pretrained RoBERTa **backbone** (loaded on p.480) into a binary classifier. It reuses the backbone's own input tensors (`backbone.input`), runs them through the backbone to get one 768-dimensional hidden vector per token, and keeps only the vector of the **first token** (`x[:, 0, :]`, the callout: "Uses the hidden representation of the first token"). On top it stacks `Dropout(0.1)` → `Dense(768, relu)` → `Dropout(0.1)` → `Dense(1, sigmoid)`, and wraps everything in a functional `keras.Model`.

**Listing 15.23** compiles the model with **Adam at a learning rate of 5e-5**, `binary_crossentropy` loss and accuracy, and calls `fit()` on the preprocessed training set with the validation set. No `epochs` argument is passed, so Keras trains for its default of **one epoch**. Every weight, including the roughly 125 million of the backbone (figure not in the book), is updated: this is full fine-tuning.

Evaluating on the test set returns `[0.168127179145813, 0.9366399645805359]`: a loss of about 0.168 and **93.7% accuracy**. The authors stress that this comes after **a single epoch** and beats the **90% ceiling** of chapter 14 (the bigram model, p.428). The model is far more expensive to run than that bigram classifier, but the benefit is clear, and this is only the *base* RoBERTa; the larger (~300M-parameter) model reaches **over 95%**.

**Section 15.5, "What makes the Transformer effective?"** opens with history. In 2013 Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google built **Word2Vec**, a pretrained embedding similar to the chapter 14 CBOW model. Its objective turned **correlation relationships between words into distance relationships**: each word gets a vector, and vectors are optimized so that frequently co-occurring words have a dot-product (cosine proximity) near 1. The sentence, and the "word arithmetic" discovery, continue on p.486. A pretrained encoder becomes a classifier by pooling one vector (the first token's) and adding a small dropout-regularized MLP with a sigmoid output. Fine-tuning uses a small learning rate (5e-5) and updates the whole network; one epoch was enough here. Fine-tuned RoBERTa base reaches 93.66% test accuracy on IMDb, beating chapter 14's 90% bigram ceiling; RoBERTa large would exceed 95%. The accuracy gain comes with a large increase in inference cost compared with simple n-gram models. Section 15.5 starts from Word2Vec: an embedding objective that turns word co-occurrence into vector (cosine) proximity.

title: Fine-tuning a pretrained Transformer
text: Taking a model pretrained on a large unlabeled corpus, attaching a small task-specific head, and continuing training on labeled task data with a small learning rate. The backbone already 'reads' English well. Fine-tuning teaches it what to look for in this task, without starting from scratch. In Listing 15.23 all weights are trainable (the backbone is not frozen), and the learning rate is 5e-5, about 20 times smaller than Adam's default of 1e-3, so the pretrained weights move only slightly. One epoch is enough to reach 93.7% on IMDb. RoBERTa base + Dropout/Dense/Dropout/Dense head, trained for one epoch on 20,000 IMDb reviews → 93.66% test accuracy.
snippet: Taking a model pretrained on a large unlabeled corpus, attaching a small task-specific head, and continuing training on labeled task data with a small learning rate.

title: First-token pooling
text: Using the encoder's output vector at position 0 (RoBERTa's `<s>` start token, BERT's `[CLS]`) as a fixed-size representation of the whole sequence. Because attention is bidirectional, the first token can attend to every other token in every layer, so its final vector can gather information about the whole review. The backbone outputs a tensor of shape `(batch, sequence_length, 768)`; `x[:, 0, :]` slices out shape `(batch, 768)`. The start token sits at position 0 because the `StartEndPacker` (p.483) prepends it to every sequence. For a 512-token review, 512 × 768 numbers come out of the backbone; only the first 768 are passed to the classifier.
snippet: Using the encoder's output vector at position 0 RoBERTa's <s start token, BERT's CLS as a fixed-size representation of the whole sequence.

title: Transfer learning for text
text: Reusing knowledge learned on one task or dataset (pretraining on web text) to improve performance on another (IMDb sentiment). Like hiring an experienced reader and teaching them a narrow skill, instead of teaching someone to read from scratch. The pretrained token embeddings and attention weights act as a very good initialization, in the same spirit as reusing the CBOW embedding to prime the LSTM in chapter 14 (p.442), but for the entire network instead of one layer. Chapter 14 LSTM: about 84% (p.437). Bigram: 90% (p.428). Fine-tuned RoBERTa base: 93.7%. RoBERTa large: over 95%.
snippet: Reusing knowledge learned on one task or dataset pretraining on web text to improve performance on another IMDb sentiment.

title: Word2Vec
text: A pretrained word embedding from Mikolov et al. (Google, 2013) whose training objective turns word co-occurrence into vector proximity. Words that keep showing up together are pulled together in space; words that rarely do are pushed apart. One vector per vocabulary word; the dot-product (cosine proximity) of frequently co-occurring words is optimized toward 1, of rarely co-occurring words toward 0 (p.486). 'coffee' and 'cup' co-occur often, so their vectors end up with high cosine similarity.

title: From Word2Vec's word arithmetic to attention as embedding refinement
text:
Why Transformers work: the Word2Vec analogy, the 'gender vector' (V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) = V(queen)), and attention as a mechanism that turns token co-occurrence into embedding proximity, giving semantically continuous and interpolative spaces Large Transformers and the humble Word2Vec rest on the same principle: tokens that occur together end up close in a vector space. Attention is what connects the Transformer's next-word loss to that principle. It builds each new embedding space by recombining the previous one, weighting tokens by their dot-product closeness, and so produces spaces that are semantically continuous and interpolative. The page continues the Word2Vec story begun on p.485. In 2013 Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google trained an embedding in which the dot-product (cosine proximity) of vectors for frequently co-occurring words was pushed **toward 1**, and for rarely co-occurring words **toward 0**.

The resulting space did more than capture similarity. It showed an emergent **"word arithmetic"**: one vector, a **gender vector**, could be added to many male nouns to land near their female equivalents, as in `V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) = V(queen)`. Nobody trained the model for this. There seemed to be dozens of such **magic vectors**: a plural vector, a wild-animal-to-pet vector, and so on.

About ten years later, large pretrained Transformers produce fluent text and seem knowledgeable about almost anything, which Word2Vec never could. Yet the authors argue they share Word2Vec's core: both **embed tokens in a vector space**; both learn that space on the principle that **tokens appearing together end up close**; both compare tokens with **cosine distance**; and the authors put both at roughly **1,000-10,000 dimensions** (a figure that does not hold for Word2Vec; see the review flag).

The obvious objection: a Transformer is trained to predict missing words, not to group tokens. The answer is **attention**, "by far, the most critical component". Attention learns a new token embedding space by **linearly recombining** embeddings from a prior space, weighting tokens that are already close (higher dot-product) more heavily. Over time this pulls close tokens closer, so **correlation relationships become proximity relationships**. A Transformer is a **series of incrementally refined embedding spaces**, each built from the previous one.

Attention gives two properties. The learned spaces are **semantically continuous**: a small move in the space changes meaning only a little (Word2Vec had this too). They are also **semantically interpolative**: the midpoint between two points represents an "intermediate meaning". That sentence continues on p.487. Word2Vec turned word co-occurrence into dot-product/cosine proximity, and analogy 'word arithmetic' (the gender vector) emerged without being trained for. The authors argue that large Transformers share Word2Vec's core: token embeddings, the co-occurrence-to-proximity principle, and cosine comparison. Attention connects the language-modeling loss to that principle: it recombines token vectors weighted by dot-product closeness, pulling close tokens closer. A Transformer is a stack of incrementally refined embedding spaces, each built from the previous one. Attention-built spaces are semantically continuous (small moves mean small changes in meaning) and semantically interpolative (midpoints mean in-between things). Treat the page's '1,000-10,000 dimensions' figure with caution: Word2Vec typically uses 300 dimensions and RoBERTa base uses 768.
snippet: The page continues the Word2Vec story begun on p.485. In 2013 Tomas Mikolov and colleagues at Google trained an embedding in which the dot-product cosine proximity of vectors for…

title: Word / token embedding space
text: A mapping from each token to a dense vector, learned so that geometric relationships reflect semantic or co-occurrence relationships. A map of meaning where related words are neighbours and consistent relations are consistent directions. Word2Vec learns one static vector per word with a shallow model. A Transformer starts from a static embedding table and then produces a new, context-dependent embedding at every layer. Vectors for 'movie' and 'film' should be nearly identical (p.433).
snippet: A mapping from each token to a dense vector, learned so that geometric relationships reflect semantic or co-occurrence relationships.

title: Word arithmetic / magic vectors
text: The emergent property that semantic relations are approximately constant vector offsets, so analogies can be solved by vector addition and subtraction. The step from 'man' to 'woman' is the same arrow as the step from 'king' to 'queen'. Solve a:b :: c:? by computing $V(b)-V(a)+V(c)$ and returning the nearest word by cosine, excluding a, b and c. V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) ≈ V(queen) (gender vector); a plural vector maps cat to cats.
snippet: The emergent property that semantic relations are approximately constant vector offsets, so analogies can be solved by vector addition and subtraction.

title: Attention as embedding refinement
text: The authors' interpretation of attention: it learns a new embedding space by linearly recombining the previous space's token vectors, weighted toward tokens that are already close (higher dot-product). Every token takes a similarity-weighted average of the crowd around it, so similar tokens drift together. $\mathbf{y}_i = \sum_j \operatorname{softmax}_j(\mathbf{q}_i\cdot\mathbf{k}_j/\sqrt{d})\,\mathbf{v}_j$. The output is a convex combination of value vectors. Stacked blocks give a sequence of refined spaces. In 'the bank of the river', the vector for 'bank' gets mixed with 'river', moving it toward the geographic sense.
snippet: The authors' interpretation of attention: it learns a new embedding space by linearly recombining the previous space's token vectors, weighted toward tokens that are already close…

title: Semantic continuity
text: Moving a small distance in the embedding space changes the human-facing meaning only slightly. There are no sudden jumps in meaning; nearby points mean nearby things. Roughly, meaning is a Lipschitz-like function of position near the data manifold. Nudging the vector for 'warm' slightly toward 'hot' produces something like 'very warm', not an unrelated word.
snippet: Moving a small distance in the embedding space changes the human-facing meaning only slightly.

title: Semantic interpolation
text: The point between two embeddings represents an intermediate meaning between the two tokens. Halfway between 'cat' and 'tiger' sits something like 'wild cat'. $\mathbf{z}(t)=(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$. The authors attribute the property to the fact that each attention layer builds its space by interpolating vectors of the previous one (p.487). Averaging the vectors for 'king' and 'queen' gives a point near 'monarch' or 'royal'.
snippet: The point between two embeddings represents an intermediate meaning between the two tokens.

title: Cosine similarity / cosine distance
text: The cosine of the angle between two vectors, $\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|}$. Cosine distance is 1 minus that value. It measures whether two vectors point the same way, ignoring their length. For unit-normalized vectors it equals the dot-product. The page treats 'dot-product' and 'cosine proximity' as interchangeable, which is exact only after normalization. a=(1,0), b=(1,1): cos = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707.
snippet: The cosine of the angle between two vectors, frac{mathbf{a}cdotmathbf{b}}{|mathbf{a}||mathbf{b}|}. Cosine distance is 1 minus that value.

title: The gender vector analogy
text: V(king) - V(man) + V(woman) = V(queen) V(\text{king}) - V(\text{man}) + V(\text{woman}) \approx V(\text{queen}) Demonstrates that semantic relations are encoded as directions in the learned space. Remove the 'male' component of king, add the 'female' component, and you land near queen. The book writes '='. In practice it means 'the nearest vocabulary vector is'. V(w) The learned embedding vector of word w V(\text{woman}) - V(\text{man}) The 'gender vector', an offset approximately shared by many male/female pairs
snippet: Vking - Vman + Vwoman = Vqueen — Demonstrates that semantic relations are encoded as directions in the learned space.

title: Cosine proximity used by both models
text: the dot-product (cosine proximity) … The distance function used to compare tokens is cosine distance in both cases. \cos(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\,\|\mathbf{b}\|},\qquad d_{\cos}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) = 1-\cos(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) Measures how aligned two embeddings are. title: Hebbian learning, vector programs, and the Transformer as an interpolative database
text:
Why attention-built spaces are interpolative; the Hebbian 'fire together, wire together' parallel; how Word2Vec differs from Transformers (a toy vs. a deep, billion-parameter model); 'vector programs'; and the Transformer as a continuous, interpolative database that can generalize or hallucinate Transformers and Word2Vec both turn correlations into vector proximities, much like Hebbian learning in the brain. A Transformer's depth and autoregressive objective let it store arbitrarily complex 'vector programs' rather than simple linear offsets. Because its 'database' is a continuous space you can move and interpolate within, you can retrieve more than was put in, which yields both generalization and hallucination. The page completes the second property from p.486. Attention-built spaces are **interpolative** *because each new embedding space is built by interpolating between vectors from the previous space*.

The authors then compare this to the brain. Its key learning principle is **Hebbian learning**, "neurons that fire together, wire together". Correlations between firing events become **proximity relationships** in the neural network, just as Word2Vec and the Transformer turn correlations into vector proximity. "Both are maps of a space of information."

**Differences from Word2Vec.** Word2Vec was not designed for generative sampling, and it is a **toy model**. It relates to today's LMs as logistic regression on MNIST pixels relates to state-of-the-art vision models: same principles, little representation power. It was a **shallow, single-layer** model. Transformers have **dozens of stacked attention and feedforward layers** and **billions of parameters**.

**Vector programs.** Like Word2Vec, the Transformer learns useful semantic functions as a by-product of organizing tokens. With more representation power and a refined **autoregressive** objective, it is no longer limited to *linear* maps like the gender or plural vectors. Word2Vec could do `plural(cat) → cats` or `male_to_female(king) → queen`. A large Transformer can do `write_this_in_style_of_shakespeare("...your poem...") → "...new poem..."`, and a single model holds **millions of such programs**.

**Transformer as database.** A Transformer stores information you retrieve via input tokens, with two differences from a database. First, it is **continuous and interpolative**: data is stored as a vector space, "a curve", that you can move along and interpolate on. So you can retrieve more than you stored, though not all of it accurate. Interpolation gives **generalization** but also **hallucinations**. Second, a Transformer doesn't just contain data. The sentence about RoBERTa's training documents continues on p.488, where the point turns out to be that it is also a database of programs. Attention-built spaces are interpolative because each layer's space is made by interpolating vectors of the previous layer. Brains (Hebbian learning), Word2Vec and Transformers all turn correlations into proximity, yielding 'maps of a space of information'. Word2Vec is a shallow toy; Transformers have dozens of attention/feedforward layers and billions of parameters, and far more representation power. Transformers learn nonlinear 'vector programs' (e.g. rewrite in Shakespeare's style), not just linear offsets like the gender vector; one model holds millions of them. A Transformer is like a continuous, interpolative database: you can retrieve more than you stored, which gives generalization but also hallucination. A Transformer stores programs as well as data (completed on p.488).
snippet: The page completes the second property from p.486. Attention-built spaces are interpolative because each new embedding space is built by interpolating between vectors from the…

title: Hebbian learning
text: The neuroscience principle that connections between neurons that fire together are strengthened: 'neurons that fire together, wire together'. Things that happen together get linked. Classic form $\Delta w_{ij}=\eta\,x_i x_j$. It is a local, unsupervised rule, unlike backpropagation. Repeatedly seeing lightning and then hearing thunder strengthens the association between the two.
snippet: The neuroscience principle that connections between neurons that fire together are strengthened: 'neurons that fire together, wire together'.

title: Vector program
text: A complex, highly nonlinear function stored in a Transformer that maps the latent embedding space onto itself; the deep-model generalization of Word2Vec's magic vectors. A learned skill (translate, summarize, restyle) that the right input tokens can invoke. Implemented implicitly by stacks of attention and feedforward layers, and selected by context (the prompt). write_this_in_style_of_shakespeare("...your poem...") → "...new poem..."
snippet: A complex, highly nonlinear function stored in a Transformer that maps the latent embedding space onto itself; the deep-model generalization of Word2Vec's magic vectors.

title: Transformer as a continuous, interpolative database
text: The view that a Transformer stores data and programs as a continuous vector space retrieved via input tokens, rather than as discrete entries. A smooth map instead of a filing cabinet: you can ask for places between the labeled points. Continuity lets you move to nearby related points; interpolation lets you blend points. Outputs are not restricted to stored items. Asking about a fictional book can produce a plausible but invented summary that blends real ones.
snippet: The view that a Transformer stores data and programs as a continuous vector space retrieved via input tokens, rather than as discrete entries.

title: Hallucination
text: Generated output that is fluent and plausible but inaccurate or meaningless. Confidently filling in the gap between two things you know with something that sounds right. On the authors' account, it results from interpolating in a continuous space where the in-between point does not correspond to a true fact. An LM inventing a citation that blends real author names with a real-sounding title.
snippet: Generated output that is fluent and plausible but inaccurate or meaningless.

title: Representation power
text: How complex the functions a model can express are. A single-layer model can draw straight lines; a deep model can draw almost any shape. It grows with depth, width and parameter count. Word2Vec has one shallow layer; modern Transformers have dozens of blocks and billions of parameters. Logistic regression on MNIST pixels vs. a modern ConvNet or vision Transformer.
snippet: How complex the functions a model can express are.

title: Word2Vec 'programs' as constant offsets

The book gives only the function-style notation. Every Word2Vec 'program' is the same kind of operation, a translation. A Transformer program is instead a deep nonlinear map $f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{1:n})$ that depends on the whole context. \mathbf{x} Embedding of the input word (e.g. cat, king) \mathbf{p} The plural vector \mathbf{g} The gender vector, e.g. V(woman) - V(man)

title: Transformers as databases of programs, and the chapter 15 summary (language models, attention)
text:
The end of 15.5 (Transformers store vector programs; they are fundamentally interpolative and cannot synthesize something fundamentally new) and the first part of the chapter summary: causal, masked and sequence-to-sequence language models; encoder/decoder; attention A Transformer trained on internet text stores facts, but perhaps primarily nonlinear 'vector programs' that map its latent space onto itself. However magical the outputs seem, such models are fundamentally interpolative. The chapter summary then restates the key tools: language models as learned distributions over tokens, seq2seq encoder-decoder models, and dot-product attention. The page finishes the sentence from p.487. A model like RoBERTa, trained on internet text, contains a lot of data ("facts, places, people, dates, things, and relationships"), but it is "also—perhaps primarily—a **database of programs**." These are not Python-style programs, sequences of symbolic statements executed step by step. They are **highly nonlinear functions that map the latent embedding space unto itself**, like Word2Vec's magic vectors but far more complex.

Looking ahead, chapter 16 will push Transformers to **billions of parameters** trained on **trillions of words**. The outputs can feel like an intelligent operator pulling the strings. The authors insist these models are **fundamentally interpolative**: thanks to attention, they learn an interpolative embedding space for much of all written English. Wandering that space gives interesting, unexpected generalizations, but it "cannot synthesize something fundamentally new with anything close to genuine, human-level intelligence."

**Chapter summary (part 1).**
- A **language model** learns `p(token|past tokens)`. Its key use is generating text in a loop, feeding each output token back as the next input.
- A **masked language model** learns `p(tokens|surrounding tokens)` and helps classify text and individual tokens.
- A **sequence-to-sequence language model** predicts the next target token from past target tokens *and* a separate, fixed source sequence (translation, question answering). It usually has an **encoder** that represents the source and a **decoder** that predicts the next target token from that representation and the past tokens.
- **Attention** lets a model pull information from anywhere in a sequence based on the current token's context. It avoids RNNs' long-range-dependency problems, and it scores pairs by **dot-product**, so vectors close in embedding space are summed together.

The Transformer bullet continues on p.489. A Transformer stores facts but, the authors argue, perhaps primarily vector programs: nonlinear maps of latent space onto itself. However magical their output, LLMs are fundamentally interpolative; they can generalize unexpectedly but cannot synthesize something fundamentally new. Causal LM: p(token|past tokens), used to generate text in a loop. Masked LM: p(tokens|surrounding tokens), used for classification. A seq2seq LM conditions on a fixed source sequence via an encoder; a decoder predicts the next target token. Attention scores are dot-products, so close vectors are summed together; this sidesteps RNNs' long-range-dependency problems.
snippet: The page finishes the sentence from p.487. A model like RoBERTa, trained on internet text, contains a lot of data "facts, places, people, dates, things, and relationships", but it…

title: Vector program
text: A highly nonlinear function, learned by a Transformer, that maps the latent embedding space onto itself. A skill encoded as a continuous transformation rather than a list of instructions. Realized by stacked attention and feedforward blocks that preserve the (sequence, hidden) shape and compose. Restyling a poem as Shakespeare (p.487).
snippet: A highly nonlinear function, learned by a Transformer, that maps the latent embedding space onto itself.

title: Language model
text: A model that learns p(token|past tokens). An autocomplete that has learned the statistics of text. Trained with cross-entropy on next-token prediction; generates by sampling in a loop. The Shakespeare character model of 15.1.
snippet: A model that learns ptoken|past tokens.

title: Masked language model
text: A model that learns p(tokens|surrounding tokens) by predicting masked tokens from context on both sides. A fill-in-the-blank exercise. BERT/RoBERTa pretraining, with about 15% of tokens replaced by [MASK] (p.479). RoBERTa fine-tuned on IMDb.

title: Sequence-to-sequence model (encoder-decoder)
text: A language model that predicts the next target token from past target tokens and a separate, fixed source sequence, usually split into an encoder and a decoder. Read the whole question, then answer word by word while looking back at it. The encoder maps source to representation; the decoder computes p(y_t | y_{<t}, encoder representation). The chapter's English-to-Spanish translator.
snippet: A language model that predicts the next target token from past target tokens and a separate, fixed source sequence, usually split into an encoder and a decoder.

title: Attention
text: A mechanism that lets a model pull information from anywhere in a sequence, selectively, based on the context of the current token. Each token asks 'who here is relevant to me?' and takes a weighted blend of the answers. Dot-product scores, softmax, weighted sum of values. A pronoun attending strongly to the noun it refers to.
snippet: A mechanism that lets a model pull information from anywhere in a sequence, selectively, based on the context of the current token.

A high dot-product gives a high weight, so close vectors dominate the sum. \mathbf{q} Query vector of the current token \mathbf{k}_j,\mathbf{v}_j Key and value vectors of token j

title: Chapter 15 summary: the Transformer
text:
Final summary bullet of chapter 15: the Transformer as an attention-only sequence architecture, its stacked attention/feedforward blocks, scalability, parallel training without sequence loops, bidirectional encoders and causal decoders The Transformer passes information across a sequence only through attention, stacks alternating attention and two-layer feedforward blocks, keeps improving with more parameters and data, trains in parallel because it has no sequence-length loop, and comes in two flavours: bidirectional encoders for representations and causal decoders for next-word prediction. This page contains the **last bullet of the chapter 15 summary**; the earlier bullets (language models, masked language models, sequence-to-sequence models, attention) are on p.488.

The bullet defines the **Transformer** as a sequence modeling architecture that uses **attention as the only mechanism to pass information across a sequence**. No recurrence and no convolution move information between positions; every other operation (feedforward layers, normalization) acts on each position independently. Five sub-points follow:

1. **Structure**: the Transformer stacks blocks of **alternating attention and two-layer feedforward networks** (the encoder block of p.468 and the decoder block of p.470).
2. **Scaling**: it can grow to **many parameters and lots of training data while still improving accuracy** on language modeling, which is what made the pretrained models of section 15.4 (BERT, RoBERTa) and chapter 16 (GPT) possible.
3. **Parallelism**: unlike RNNs, it involves **no sequence-length loops at training time**, so all positions are processed at once and training is much easier to parallelize across many machines.
4. **Encoders** use **bidirectional attention** to build a rich representation of a sequence; every token can look at tokens before and after it (as in RoBERTa, p.479).
5. **Decoders** use **causal attention** to predict the next word in a language-model setup; each token can only look at earlier tokens.

The page then ends; chapter 16 (p.490) puts the decoder to work in a GPT-style text generator. In a Transformer, attention is the only way information moves between positions. The architecture is a stack of blocks alternating attention and a two-layer feedforward network. It keeps improving as parameters and data grow, which enabled large-scale pretraining. No sequence-length loop at training time makes it far easier to parallelize than an RNN. Encoders use bidirectional attention for representations; decoders use causal attention for next-word prediction.

title: Transformer
text: A sequence architecture in which attention is the only mechanism that moves information between positions, organized as stacked blocks of attention and per-position feedforward networks. Instead of reading a sentence word by word and keeping a running memory, every word looks at the other words at the same time and decides which ones matter. Each block: (masked or unmasked) multi-head attention → residual + layer normalization → Dense–Dense feedforward → residual + layer normalization. Positional embeddings (p.475) supply order information, because attention by itself is order-agnostic. RoBERTa base (encoder, fine-tuned on p.485); the mini-GPT of chapter 16 (decoder-only).
snippet: A sequence architecture in which attention is the only mechanism that moves information between positions, organized as stacked blocks of attention and per-position feedforward…

title: Causal (masked) attention
text: Attention in which each position can attend only to itself and earlier positions. When predicting the next word you are not allowed to peek at it. Implemented by adding $-\infty$ (or a large negative number) to attention scores above the diagonal before the softmax, so their weights become 0. In 'the cat sat', the representation of 'cat' can use 'the' and 'cat' but not 'sat'.
snippet: Attention in which each position can attend only to itself and earlier positions.

title: Bidirectional attention
text: Unmasked self-attention in which every position may attend to every other position. Each word gets to read the whole sentence, before and after it, before deciding what it means. Used in Transformer encoders; combined with masked language modeling in BERT/RoBERTa pretraining (p.479). RoBERTa's first-token vector summarizes the whole review because it attends to all tokens (p.485).
snippet: Unmasked self-attention in which every position may attend to every other position.

A Transformer processes all positions with matrix products in one pass, so the work can be spread across many cores and machines.

title: Chapter 16 opener: Text generation
text:
Opening of chapter 16: generative modeling history, training a mini-GPT, building a chatbot from a pretrained Transformer, and a multimodal image-describing model; the introduction recalls the 2014 prediction that AI would help create much of our cultural content Chapter 16 moves from classifying and translating text to generating it with large decoder-only Transformers, and frames generative AI as something that, within a decade, went from implausible to a common creative tool. This is the **opening page of chapter 16, *Text generation***. The "This chapter covers" box lists four goals:

- **A brief history of generative modeling**: section 16.1 (p.492) traces sequence generation from early models to GPT.
- **Training a miniature GPT model from scratch**: section 16.2 (p.494) pretrains a decoder-only Transformer on part of the C4 corpus, then explores generative decoding and sampling strategies (pp.502-507).
- **Using a pretrained Transformer model to build a chatbot**: section 16.3 (p.508) generates text with the Gemma model, then covers instruction fine-tuning and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).
- **Building a multimodal model that can describe images in natural language**: part of section 16.4 (Multimodal LLMs, p.522), alongside RLHF, retrieval-augmented generation and "reasoning" models. Section 16.5 (p.528) asks where LLMs are heading.

The introduction opens with a first-person recollection (François Chollet's voice): in **2014**, his claim that most of the cultural content we consume would soon be created with substantial help from AI met with "utter disbelief", even among long-time ML practitioners. A decade later that disbelief has largely receded. Generative tools are built into word processors, image editors and development environments, and prestigious awards have gone to AI-assisted art and literature, "to considerable controversy and debate". **Footnote 1** gives the examples: Jason Allen won a digital-art award in 2022 with an image made in Midjourney, and in 2024 Rie Kudan won one of Japan's most prestigious literary awards for a novel written with substantial help from generative software. The sentence continues on p.491, where the authors argue for AI as *augmented* rather than artificial intelligence. Chapter 16 covers generative-model history, pretraining a mini-GPT, building a chatbot from a pretrained LLM, and a multimodal image-describing model. The authors frame generative AI as having gone from 'utter disbelief' in 2014 to a common tool by the mid-2020s. AI-assisted art and literature are already winning major awards, with considerable controversy.

title: Augmented intelligence: latent-space sampling as an artist's brush
text:
The authors' view of generative AI in creative work: AI should augment rather than replace artists; models learn statistical latent spaces of images, music and stories and sample from them; meaning comes from human interpretation; Figure 16.1 shows a Midjourney image Much of art is pattern recognition and technical skill, which have statistical structure that deep learning can learn. Sampling from a learned latent space is a mathematical operation, not creation in itself, but in an artist's hands it becomes a new brush that separates art from craft. The page continues the chapter introduction from p.490: it no longer feels like science fiction to imagine a world where **AI and artistic endeavors are intertwined**.

The authors then state their position. In any practical sense, AI is **nowhere close to rivaling human screenwriters, painters, or composers**, and replacing humans "need not, and should not, be the point". Especially in creative fields, people will use AI to augment their abilities: **"more augmented intelligence than artificial intelligence."**

The next paragraph explains why AI can help at all. Much of artistic creation is **pattern recognition and technical skill**. Perception, language and artwork all have **statistical structure**, which deep learning excels at learning. Models can learn the **statistical latent spaces** of images, music and stories and then **sample** from them, producing new works with characteristics similar to their training data. The authors insist that this sampling is not artistic creation in itself but **"a mere mathematical operation"**: only human interpretation gives meaning to the output. Steered by a skilled artist, though, algorithmic generation can become meaningful and beautiful. Latent-space sampling becomes **a brush** that expands what we can imagine, and it can make creation more accessible by removing the need for technical skill and practice, "**factoring art apart from craft**."

**Figure 16.1** illustrates the point: an image generated with Midjourney from the prompt "A hand-drawn, sci-fi landscape of residents living in a building shaped like a red letter K." The result is a detailed red K-shaped tower with balconies and small figures in a snowy landscape: the human supplied the idea in words, the model supplied the craft. The authors see AI as augmenting creators, 'more augmented intelligence than artificial intelligence', not replacing them. Art involves much pattern recognition and technical skill, which have statistical structure that deep learning can learn. Generative models learn latent spaces of images, music and stories and sample from them, producing works similar to their training data. Sampling is a mathematical operation; meaning comes from human interpretation and steering. Latent-space sampling can act as a new brush, 'factoring art apart from craft'.

title: Augmenting creativity, and the early history of sequence generation
text:
Why generative models are framed as tools that augment human creators and rote work, followed by the opening of the history of sequence generation (LSTM 1997, Eck 2002, Magenta 2016, Graves 2013). Generative models free people from mechanical work so they can steer and explore a space of possibilities, like Xenakis's composer-as-pilot. Sequence generation with recurrent networks has a long history (LSTM in 1997, LSTM music in 2002, RNN handwriting in 2013) that predates its 2016 move into the mainstream. The page finishes the chapter's introduction and opens section 16.1.

**Augmenting creators.** Following on from p.491's claim that AI should *augment* rather than replace artists, the authors quote the composer **Iannis Xenakis** (1963). He describes a composer who, "freed from tedious calculations", can explore a new musical form by changing the input data. The composer becomes "a sort of pilot" steering "a cosmic vessel sailing in the space of sound." In deep learning terms the input data is the set of parameters and prompts, and the space of sound is the latent space the model has learned.

**Beyond art.** Generative AI also applies to everyday professional work where the pattern recognition is even more obvious: summarizing documents, transcribing speech, fixing typos, flagging common code mistakes. The authors say these rote tasks "play directly to the strengths of deep learning", and they add that deploying AI at work has real societal implications.

**Roadmap.** Chapters 16 (text) and 17 (images) will show how to *curate latent spaces and pull new content from them*. Chapter 16 starts by scaling up the chapter 15 language model into **large language models (LLMs)**, the technology behind assistants like ChatGPT.

**16.1 History.** Sequence generation was a niche topic until generative recurrent networks went mainstream around **2016**, but its roots go back to the **LSTM (1997)**. In **2002 Douglas Eck** applied LSTM to music. He later founded **Magenta** at Google Brain in 2016 ("good ideas take 15 years to get started"). **Alex Graves** pushed recurrent networks to new kinds of sequence data, and his **2013** work used recurrent *mixture density networks* to generate handwriting from timeseries of pen positions. A comment hidden in his LaTeX source read: "Generating sequential data is the closest computers get to dreaming." The author says this idea of dreaming machines inspired the creation of Keras. The authors frame generative AI as augmentation: the human steers through a space of possibilities, as in Xenakis's composer-as-pilot. Rote, pattern-heavy tasks like summarization, transcription, typo editing and code review suit deep learning well, and deploying AI for them has societal implications. Chapters 16-17 are about curating latent spaces and sampling new content from them, for text and then images. LLMs are scaled-up versions of the chapter 15 next-token language model. Sequence generation has a long history: LSTM 1997, Eck's LSTM music 2002, Graves's handwriting 2013, mainstream and Magenta 2016.

title: Mixture density network
text: A network whose output layer gives the parameters of a mixture distribution over continuous targets. It outputs $(\pi_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k, \rho_k)$ for each component and is trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood. Graves added a Bernoulli output for pen-up events. Sampling from a mixture of 20 bivariate Gaussians gives the next pen offset.

title: GPT: generative pretraining and scaling from GPT-1 to GPT-3
text:
The 2018 GPT paper's recipe (next-token pretraining, a Transformer, lots of book text), OpenAI's scaling from GPT-1 to GPT-3, and the shift from fine-tuning to prompting. GPT added no new modeling technique. It showed that a general recipe, a Transformer pretrained to predict the next token on lots of text, could beat specialized methods, and that scaling this recipe up made its generated text much better, to the point where prompting could replace fine-tuning. In **2018**, a year after "Attention Is All You Need", OpenAI published **"Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training"** (Radford et al.). It combined three ingredients:

- **unsupervised pretraining of a language model**, i.e. training it to "guess the next token", as the chapter 15 Shakespeare generator did;
- **the Transformer architecture**;
- **a lot of text**: thousands of self-published books.

Fine-tuned on downstream tasks, this pretrained model reached **state-of-the-art results on many text classification tasks**, from sentence similarity to multiple-choice question answering. The model was named **GPT, Generative Pretrained Transformer**.

The authors stress that GPT brought **no modeling or training advances**. What was interesting was that such a *general* setup beat more involved, task-specific techniques: no complex text normalization, no per-benchmark architecture or data, "just a lot of pretraining data and compute." OpenAI then **scaled** the idea, changing the architecture only slightly:

| Model | Year | Parameters | Training tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-1 | 2018 | 117 million | 1 billion |
| GPT-2 | 2019 | 1.5 billion | > 10 billion |
| GPT-3 | 2020 | 175 billion | ~0.5 trillion |

Because each of these is a language model, each can generate text, and the quality of the generated text **shot up with each jump in scale**. For **GPT-1**, generation was a by-product. The model was evaluated by fine-tuning with an extra dense layer, as was done with RoBERTa in chapter 15. With **GPT-2**, the authors found that you could **prompt** the model with a few examples of a task and get good output **without any fine-tuning**. The page ends by introducing such a prompt for translating "cheese" into French, which is printed on p.494. GPT (2018) = next-token pretraining + Transformer + lots of text. It added nothing new architecturally. Its lesson was that a general setup plus data and compute beats task-specific engineering. GPT-1 to GPT-3 grew from 117M to 175B parameters and from about 1B to about 0.5T tokens, with the architecture almost unchanged. Generated text improved substantially with each jump in scale. Use moved from fine-tuning (GPT-1, with a dense head) to prompting with examples and no fine-tuning (GPT-2 onward, per the book).
