title: Few-shot and zero-shot prompting, GPT-3's limits, and the C4 pretraining data
text:
Prompting pretrained LLMs with examples (few-shot) or plain instructions (GPT-3), the persistent failure modes of LLMs, the step from GPT-3 to ChatGPT, and choosing a pretraining corpus (BooksCorpus vs C4) for the mini-GPT. Large pretrained language models can do new tasks from a prompt alone, with a few examples or even just an instruction, but they still hallucinate, are brittle to prompt wording and fail outside their training distribution. To understand them, the chapter trains a small GPT on a slice of C4. The page first shows the prompt promised at the end of p.493:

```
Translate English to French:
sea otter => loutre de mer
peppermint => menthe poivrée
plush giraffe => peluche girafe
cheese =>
```

This is **few-shot learning**: teaching a model a new problem with only a handful of supervised examples, "too few for standard gradient descent." No weights change. The model infers the pattern from the prompt and continues it, ideally with "fromage".

With **GPT-3**, examples were often unnecessary. A bare description of the task plus the input (`Translate English to French:` / `cheese =>`) was frequently enough.

The authors then point out that GPT-3 had **fundamental issues that are still unsolved**:

1. **Hallucination**: output can go from accurate to completely false with no warning sign.
2. **Prompt sensitivity**: small rewordings can cause large jumps up or down in performance.
3. **No adaptation to novel problems**: models fail on problems that were not well represented in their training data.

Even so, GPT-3's output was good enough to become the basis for **ChatGPT**, the first widely used consumer-facing generative model, which set off a wave of investment in LLMs.

**Section 16.2** begins the hands-on part: building a **mini-GPT** to see how such a model works, what it can do and where it fails. Pretraining needs a lot of text. GPT-1 used **BooksCorpus**, a set of free self-published books added without the authors' explicit permission and since taken down. The chapter instead uses Google's **C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, 2020)**. At **750 GB** it is far too large for a book example, so **less than 1%** of it is used. Listing 16.1 starts with `import keras` and `import pathlib`, and the download call follows on p.495. Few-shot learning means putting a handful of examples in the prompt, too few to train on, but enough for a large pretrained model to infer the task. GPT-3 could often do tasks from a plain instruction (zero-shot). Unsolved LLM problems: hallucination, sensitivity to prompt wording, and failure on problems not well covered by training data. GPT-3 was good enough to become the basis for ChatGPT, which set off the LLM boom. The mini-GPT is pretrained on less than 1% of C4 (750 GB). BooksCorpus, used by GPT-1, was taken down over consent issues.

title: Getting the mini-C4 data, compute expectations, and choosing SentencePiece
text:
Downloading and inspecting the mini-C4 pretraining shards, the compute cost of running chapter 16, and the decision to tokenize with SentencePiece and a premade 32,000-term vocabulary. Pretraining starts with a lot of raw text (50 shards of about 75 MB, one web document per line) and a fast subword tokenizer to turn it into integers. This is the most compute-intensive chapter of the book. **Listing 16.1 (continued).** `keras.utils.get_file(fname="mini-c4", origin="https://hf.co/datasets/mattdangerw/mini-c4/resolve/main/mini-c4.zip", extract=True)` downloads a zip of the C4 subset from Hugging Face, caches it and extracts it. The code then builds `extract_dir = pathlib.Path(extract_dir) / "mini-c4"`, the folder that holds the shard files.

**Sidebar: Running the code in this chapter.** Generative LMs are big, and this is the **most compute-intensive chapter in the book**. On the free **Colab T4** GPU the mini-GPT takes **about 6 hours** to train, and you must **restart the runtime** partway through to free GPU memory before loading a larger pretrained model. On an **A100** the whole chapter runs in **a little over an hour**. You can read the expensive `fit()` calls and **reduce the number of training steps** for quick experiments. Future hardware may make all of this trivial.

**The data.** There are **50 shards**, each with **about 75 MB** of raw text, about 3.75 GB in total. **Each line is one crawled document**, with its newlines escaped as the two characters `\n`. Printing the first 100 characters of the first line of `shard0.txt` (after turning the escapes back into real newlines) shows a web page: *"Beginners BBQ Class Taking Place in Missoula! Do you want to get better at making delicious BBQ? You"*.

The authors say its technique is the same byte-pair encoding built by hand in chapter 14, but it is faster and adds a `detokenize()` function that maps integers back to strings and joins them. A **premade 32,000-term vocabulary**, stored in SentencePiece's own format, is used. Listing 16.2 on p.496 loads it. Listing 16.1 downloads and extracts mini-C4 with keras.utils.get_file and points extract_dir at the shard folder. This is the book's most compute-intensive chapter: about 6 h on a free T4, a little over 1 h on an A100. Restart the runtime before loading the big pretrained model. The data is 50 shards of about 75 MB, one web document per line with newlines escaped. Fast tokenization matters at this scale. title: A SentencePiece tokenizer and per-file preprocessing for mini-GPT pretraining
text:
Loading a premade 32,000-term SentencePiece vocabulary through KerasHub, tokenizing and detokenizing text, marking document boundaries with <|endoftext|>, and a read_file() function that restores newlines, tokenizes each document and appends the boundary token, ready to be interleaved across file shards Pretraining data is prepared GPT-style: every document in every shard is tokenized with a fast subword tokenizer and followed by a special <|endoftext|> token, and the documents are later concatenated into one long token stream without trying to align samples with document boundaries. The page sets up tokenization and the first half of the data pipeline for pretraining the mini-GPT.

**Listing 16.2.** As in chapter 15, KerasHub provides LLM utilities; here it wraps the **SentencePiece** library as a Keras layer. `keras.utils.get_file()` downloads a premade vocabulary file (`vocabulary.proto`, the 32,000-term vocabulary introduced on p.495), and `keras_hub.tokenizers.SentencePieceTokenizer(vocabulary_file)` builds the tokenizer.

The tokenizer maps text to ints **bidirectionally**: `tokenize("The quick brown fox.")` returns `array([450, 4996, 17354, 1701, 29916, 29889], dtype=int32)`, and `detokenize()` of the same ids gives back `"The quick brown fox."`. Four words and a period become six subword tokens, so one word is split into two pieces.

The tokenizer will be used to tokenize the corpus, and **`tf.data`** to window it into sequences of length **256**. Following the GPT developers, the authors make **no attempt to keep document boundaries out of the middle of a sample**. Instead each document is followed by a special **`<|endoftext|>`** token. `tf.data` is again used so training works with any backend.

Each **file shard is loaded separately** and the outputs are **interleaved** into a single dataset. This keeps loading fast, avoids worrying about text lining up across sample boundaries (each sample is independent), and lets each CPU core read and tokenize a different file at the same time.

**Listing 16.3** fixes `batch_size = 128` and `sequence_length = 256`, looks up the id of `<|endoftext|>` with `tokenizer.token_to_id()` as a one-element NumPy array `suffix`, and defines `read_file(filename)`: a `TextLineDataset` yields one document per line; `regex_replace` turns the escaped `\n` sequences back into real newlines (callout "Restores newlines"); `ds.map(tokenizer, num_parallel_calls=8)` tokenizes ("Tokenizes data"); and `tf.concat([x, suffix], -1)` appends the boundary token ("Adds the <|endoftext|> token"). Interleaving, windowing and batching follow on p.497. KerasHub's SentencePieceTokenizer wraps a fast C++ subword tokenizer with a premade 32,000-term vocabulary. Tokenization is reversible: tokenize() maps text to ids, detokenize() maps ids back to text. GPT-style pretraining packs documents into one stream, separated by <|endoftext|>, and ignores document boundaries when cutting samples. read_file() restores escaped newlines, tokenizes each document in parallel, and appends the end-of-text id. Shards are loaded separately and interleaved so several CPU cores can read and tokenize files at once.
snippet: The page sets up tokenization and the first half of the data pipeline for pretraining the mini-GPT. Listing 16.2. As in chapter 15, KerasHub provides LLM utilities; here it wraps…

title: Subword tokenization with SentencePiece
text: Splitting text into frequent subword units drawn from a fixed vocabulary (here 32,000 entries) and mapping each to an integer id. Common words get one token; rare words are built from a few pieces, so any text can be represented without an unknown-word token. SentencePiece implements byte-pair encoding (and unigram LM) in C++; KerasHub wraps it as a layer with `tokenize()`, `detokenize()` and `token_to_id()`. 'The quick brown fox.' → [450, 4996, 17354, 1701, 29916, 29889].
snippet: Splitting text into frequent subword units drawn from a fixed vocabulary here 32,000 entries and mapping each to an integer id.

title: End-of-text token and sequence packing
text: Concatenating documents into one token stream separated by a special <|endoftext|> token and cutting the stream into fixed-length samples regardless of document boundaries. Like gluing all books end to end with a 'THE END' marker and cutting the scroll into equal pages. `read_file()` appends `suffix` (the id of <|endoftext|>) to each tokenized line with `tf.concat([x, suffix], -1)`; `rebatch()` on p.497 then cuts the stream. A sample might be '...best BBQ in town. <|endoftext|> Welcome to our garden shop...'.

title: Parallel input pipelines with tf.data
text: Building the training input as a chain of tf.data transformations that run on CPU threads in parallel with training. Several workers each read and prepare a different file while the GPU trains on the previous batch. `map(…, num_parallel_calls=8)` parallelizes per-element work; `interleave(…, num_parallel_calls=32)` parallelizes across files; `prefetch()` overlaps input and training (p.497). 50 shard files, read 32 at a time by `interleave` (p.497).
snippet: Building the training input as a chain of tf.data transformations that run on CPU threads in parallel with training.

sequence_length = 256

title: Finishing the pretraining pipeline; GPT as a decoder-only Transformer
text:
Interleaving shard datasets, windowing the token stream into 257-token chunks with rebatch(), splitting inputs and labels offset by one, batching and prefetching; counting 29,373 batches (about a billion tokens) and holding out 500 for validation; then the GPT design choice of dropping the encoder and keeping only a causal decoder The token streams of all shards are merged, cut into equal chunks of sequence_length + 1 tokens, and turned into (input, next-token label) pairs, giving just under a billion training tokens. The model that will learn from them is decoder-only: one sequence, one set of parameters, information flowing only left to right. **Finishing Listing 16.3.** The shard filenames (`extract_dir.glob("*.txt")`) become a dataset with `from_tensor_slices`. `interleave(read_file, cycle_length=32, num_parallel_calls=32)` runs `read_file()` on 32 shards at once and merges their tokenized documents ("Combines our file shards into a single dataset"). `rebatch(sequence_length + 1, drop_remainder=True)` treats the stream of variable-length token vectors as one long sequence and cuts it into equal chunks of 257 tokens ("Windows tokens into even samples of 256 tokens"). `map(lambda x: (x[:-1], x[1:]))` turns each chunk into a 256-token input and the same tokens **shifted by one** as labels ("Splits labels, offset by one"). Finally `batch(batch_size)` groups 128 samples and `prefetch(8)`, as first done in chapter 8, keeps batches ready for the GPU.

**Size.** There are **29,373 batches**. You could count them with `ds.reduce(0, lambda c, _: c + 1)`, but merely tokenizing this much data takes a few minutes on a fast CPU. At 128 samples × 256 tokens, that is **just under a billion tokens** ($29{,}373 \times 128 \times 256 \approx 9.6 \times 10^8$). The first **500 batches** become a quick validation set (`take`), the rest the training set (`skip`), and both are `repeat()`ed.

**16.2.1 Building the model.** The original GPT simplifies the sequence-to-sequence Transformer of chapter 15: it **drops the encoder entirely and keeps only the decoder**, so information can only travel **left to right**. This was a bet. A decoder-only model can still handle sequence-to-sequence problems like question answering, but the question and answer must be **combined into a single sequence**. Question tokens are then handled exactly like answer tokens: **all tokens share the same latent space and the same parameters**. The other consequence is that information flow is **no longer bidirectional, even for the input**: in "Where is the capital of France?" (continued on p.498), "Where" cannot attend to later words. interleave() merges 32 shards at a time; rebatch(257) cuts the token stream into equal chunks; map() splits inputs and next-token labels; batch(128) and prefetch(8) finish the pipeline. Chunks have sequence_length + 1 tokens so that inputs and labels each have 256. 29,373 batches × 128 × 256 ≈ 0.96 billion tokens; 500 batches are held out for validation with take/skip. GPT drops the encoder and uses only a causal decoder; inputs and outputs are combined into one sequence sharing all parameters. The price is that information flows only left to right, even across the prompt.

title: Input/label shift for language modeling
text: Building training pairs from a chunk of $T+1$ tokens by using the first $T$ as inputs and the last $T$ as labels, so the label at position $t$ is the token at $t+1$. Every position in the chunk becomes a 'guess the next word' exercise. `ds.map(lambda x: (x[:-1], x[1:]))` on 257-token chunks gives 256 inputs and 256 labels; with causal attention all 256 predictions are trained in one forward pass. Chunk [The, cat, sat, on] → inputs [The, cat, sat], labels [cat, sat, on].
snippet: Building training pairs from a chunk of T+1 tokens by using the first T as inputs and the last T as labels, so the label at position t is the token at t+1.

title: Decoder-only Transformer (GPT)
text: A Transformer with no encoder: a stack of causal self-attention + feedforward blocks over a single token sequence. One model that only ever reads left to right and continues text. Sequence-to-sequence tasks are expressed as a single sequence (prompt followed by response); all tokens share embeddings and parameters; no cross-attention. The mini-GPT built in section 16.2.
snippet: A Transformer with no encoder: a stack of causal self-attention + feedforward blocks over a single token sequence.

title: Windowing a token stream with rebatch()
text: Using `Dataset.rebatch(n, drop_remainder=True)` on a dataset of variable-length 1-D token tensors to re-slice their concatenation into chunks of exactly `n` tokens. Pour all documents into one long tape, then cut equal-length pieces. rebatch treats axis 0 of each element as a batch axis, so documents of lengths 120, 300, 90 … are re-split into elements of exactly 257 tokens; the incomplete final chunk is dropped. Documents of 100 and 200 tokens → one 257-token chunk (100 + first 157) and a 43-token remainder carried into the next chunk.
snippet: Using Dataset.rebatchn, dropremainder=True on a dataset of variable-length 1-D token tensors to re-slice their concatenation into chunks of exactly n tokens.

title: A decoder-only Transformer block for mini-GPT
text:
Consequences of the decoder-only (GPT) design and the Keras implementation of a Transformer decoder block without cross-attention (Listing 16.4) A GPT model is just a stack of Transformer decoder blocks with causal self-attention and no cross-attention; everything, including a question and its answer, is one left-to-right sequence. Listing 16.4 builds that block by stripping cross-attention from chapter 15's decoder and adding dropout inside each block, because the model will stack many of them. The page finishes the argument, begun on p.497, about what it means for GPT to drop the encoder and keep only a decoder. Because information can only flow left to right, in a prompt like "Where is the capital of France?" the representation of "Where" **cannot attend** to the later words "capital" and "France". That limits expressivity compared with a bidirectional encoder, but it makes pretraining enormously simpler: no curated input/output pairs are needed, every piece of text is just one sequence, and the model can be trained on any text found on the internet at massive scale.

The authors then build the repeated unit of their mini-GPT. They take the `TransformerDecoder` from chapter 15, **remove the cross-attention layer** (there is no encoder sequence to attend to any more), and make one change: **dropout after the attention block and after the feedforward block**. In chapter 15 a single Transformer layer was used, so a single dropout at the end of the model was enough; a GPT stacks many layers, so per-layer dropout is needed to prevent overfitting.

**Listing 16.4** defines the layer. The constructor creates a `MultiHeadAttention` with `key_dim = hidden_dim // num_heads` and attention dropout of 0.1, a `LayerNormalization` for the attention sublayer, two `Dense` layers (ReLU expansion to `intermediate_dim`, then projection back to `hidden_dim`), a second `LayerNormalization`, and one `Dropout(0.1)`. The `call` method runs causal self-attention (`query=x, key=x, value=x, use_causal_mask=True`), dropout, a residual add and LayerNorm; then the feedforward pair, dropout, residual add and LayerNorm. Input and output shapes are identical, so blocks can be stacked.

The page closes by announcing that the `PositionalEmbedding` layer from chapter 15 will be reused (learned position embeddings added to token embeddings), and starts describing a memory-saving trick: the biggest weights in a Transformer are the input token embedding and the output dense prediction layer, a point continued on p.499 as weight tying. Decoder-only means strictly left-to-right information flow: early tokens of a prompt cannot see later ones, even inside the 'input' part. The trade-off is deliberate: less expressivity, but any raw text becomes training data at internet scale. Listing 16.4 = chapter 15 decoder minus cross-attention, plus Dropout(0.1) after each sublayer (and attention dropout 0.1). use_causal_mask=True is what enforces the left-to-right constraint inside MultiHeadAttention. Each block preserves the (batch, seq_len, hidden_dim) shape, so blocks can be stacked; the mini-GPT stacks eight. The token embedding and output projection are the largest weights; p.499 ties them to save memory.
snippet: The page finishes the argument, begun on p.497, about what it means for GPT to drop the encoder and keep only a decoder. Because information can only flow left to right, in a…

title: Decoder-only Transformer (GPT architecture)
text: A Transformer consisting only of stacked decoder blocks with causal self-attention and no encoder or cross-attention; it models text as a single sequence and is trained to predict the next token. Like reading a book once, front to back, without ever being allowed to peek ahead: every word is understood only in light of what came before it. Each block maps (batch, seq_len, hidden_dim) to the same shape. Causal masking makes the output at position i depend only on inputs at positions <= i, so a single forward pass yields next-token predictions for every position simultaneously. To answer a question, the question and answer are concatenated into one token sequence; the model reads the question and then continues it with the answer.
snippet: A Transformer consisting only of stacked decoder blocks with causal self-attention and no encoder or cross-attention; it models text as a single sequence and is trained to predict…

title: Causal attention mask
text: A lower-triangular mask that stops each position from attending to positions after it. Each token gets a window that only looks backward. In Keras, MultiHeadAttention(..., use_causal_mask=True) builds a boolean mask M with M[i, j] = 1 iff j <= i, and masked scores are excluded from the softmax (set to a very large negative value before it), so the attention weights to future tokens are zero. In 'Where is the capital of France ?', the row for 'Where' allows only 'Where'; the row for '?' allows all six tokens.
snippet: A lower-triangular mask that stops each position from attending to positions after it.

title: Cross-attention
text: Attention whose queries come from one sequence (the decoder) and whose keys and values come from another (the encoder output). The translator looking back at the source sentence while writing the translation. In the chapter 15 decoder, a second MultiHeadAttention took query = target states and key = value = encoder output. In English-to-Spanish translation, each Spanish token attended to English source tokens via cross-attention.
snippet: Attention whose queries come from one sequence the decoder and whose keys and values come from another the encoder output.

title: Dropout (per-block residual dropout)
text: Randomly zeroing a fraction (here 10%) of a layer's output during training, rescaling the rest by 1/(1-rate). Forces each block not to rely on any single activation, so features are more robust. In Listing 16.4, Dropout(0.1) is applied to the attention output and to the feedforward output before each residual add; MultiHeadAttention also has dropout=0.1 applied to the attention weights. During training, about 10 of every 100 entries of the attention output are zeroed and the others multiplied by 1/0.9.
snippet: Randomly zeroing a fraction here 10% of a layer's output during training, rescaling the rest by 1/1-rate.

title: Residual connection with post-LayerNorm
text: Adding a sublayer's input back to its output, then normalizing: x = LayerNorm(x + F(x)). Each sublayer only has to learn a correction to the representation, not rebuild it. Listing 16.4 stores residual before each sublayer and applies LayerNormalization after the add (the 'post-LN' ordering of the original Transformer and of chapter 15). residual = x; x = attention(x); x = dropout(x); x = x + residual; x = layernorm(x).
snippet: Adding a sublayer's input back to its output, then normalizing: x = LayerNormx + Fx.

title: Weight tying (preview)
text: Using the transpose of the input token-embedding matrix as the output projection to vocabulary logits. Embedding maps token to vector; the output layer maps vector back to token, so they can share the same dictionary. Embedding E has shape (vocab_size, hidden_dim); logits = h E^T. Introduced on this page as a GPU-memory trick and detailed on p.499. With vocab 32,000 and hidden 512, each matrix has about 16.4M parameters; tying saves one of them.
snippet: Using the transpose of the input token-embedding matrix as the output projection to vocabulary logits.

title: What one decoder block computes (from Listing 16.4)
text: Not printed as a formula; written out from the call() method of Listing 16.4 \begin{aligned} h &= \operatorname{LN}_1\big(x + \operatorname{Dropout}(\operatorname{MHA}(x, x, x;\ M))\big) \\ y &= \operatorname{LN}_2\big(h + \operatorname{Dropout}(W_2\,\operatorname{relu}(W_1 h + b_1) + b_2)\big) \end{aligned} Makes the code's data flow explicit and shows that input and output shapes match, so blocks can be stacked. The first line mixes information across (earlier) positions; the second updates each position independently. x Input to the block, shape (batch, seq_len, hidden_dim) M Causal mask, M_{ij}=1 iff j <= i (use_causal_mask=True) \operatorname{MHA} MultiHeadAttention with num_heads heads of size key_dim = hidden_dim // num_heads W_1, b_1 feed_forward_1: Dense(intermediate_dim, relu) W_2, b_2 feed_forward_2: Dense(hidden_dim) \operatorname{LN}_1, \operatorname{LN}_2 self_attention_layernorm and feed_forward_layernorm y Output, same shape as x

title: Listing 16.4 A Transformer decoder block without cross-attention
text:
from keras import layers

class TransformerDecoder(keras.Layer):
    def __init__(self, hidden_dim, intermediate_dim, num_heads):
        super().__init__()
        key_dim = hidden_dim // num_heads
        self.self_attention = layers.MultiHeadAttention(
            num_heads, key_dim, dropout=0.1
        )
        self.self_attention_layernorm = layers.LayerNormalization()
        self.feed_forward_1 = layers.Dense(intermediate_dim, activation="relu")
        self.feed_forward_2 = layers.Dense(hidden_dim)
        self.feed_forward_layernorm = layers.LayerNormalization()
        self.dropout = layers.Dropout(0.1)

    def call(self, inputs):
        residual = x = inputs
        x = self.self_attention(query=x, key=x, value=x, use_causal_mask=True)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = x + residual
        x = self.self_attention_layernorm(x)
        residual = x
        x = self.feed_forward_1(x)
        x = self.feed_forward_2(x)
        x = self.dropout(x)
        x = x + residual
        x = self.feed_forward_layernorm(x)
        return x Defines a Keras layer implementing one GPT-style decoder block: causal multi-head self-attention followed by a two-layer feedforward network, each wrapped with dropout, a residual connection and LayerNormalization. Post-LN Transformer block: x = LN(x + Drop(CausalMHA(x))); x = LN(x + Drop(FFN(x))).

text: Why are the token embedding and the output prediction layer the biggest weights in a Transformer like this one? Both scale with the vocabulary size: the embedding has shape (vocab_size, hidden_dim) and the output projection (hidden_dim, vocab_size). For a large vocabulary these dwarf the per-block matrices, which scale only with hidden_dim and intermediate_dim.

title: Weight tying and the start of the mini-GPT model
text:
Tying the token-embedding and output-projection weights via a 'reverse' mode of PositionalEmbedding (Listing 16.5), and the first lines of the mini-GPT model with mixed precision (Listing 16.6) The output projection to vocabulary logits can reuse the transpose of the token-embedding matrix, a 'reverse embedding' from hidden space to token space. This saves the largest block of weights and is a good idea in practice; the layer gets a reverse=True switch. The model is then configured with mixed precision, the 32,000-token vocabulary, hidden_dim 512 and intermediate_dim 2056. Continuing from p.498, the page explains why the input token embedding and the output prediction layer are the biggest weights in a Transformer: both live in vocabulary space. The embedding has shape `(vocab_size, hidden_dim)` (one vector per possible token) and the output projection has shape `(hidden_dim, vocab_size)` (one logit per possible token).

These two matrices can be **tied**. Final predictions are computed by multiplying the hidden states by the **transpose of the token-embedding matrix**. The authors describe the output projection as a **"reverse embedding"**: an embedding maps token space to hidden space, the projection maps hidden space back to token space, and using the same weights for both turns out to be a good idea. Implementing it only requires adding a `reverse` argument to `PositionalEmbedding.call`.

**Listing 16.5** shows the layer. It owns two `Embedding` tables: `token_embeddings` (`input_dim` x `output_dim`) and `position_embeddings` (`sequence_length` x `output_dim`). In reverse mode it returns `ops.matmul(inputs, ops.transpose(token_embeddings))`, where `token_embeddings` is the raw weight matrix. In forward mode it builds the position indices `0, 1, ..., L-1` with `ops.cumsum(ops.ones_like(inputs), axis=-1) - 1`, embeds tokens and positions, and adds them.

The authors then announce the model: **eight decoder layers** stacked into a "mini" GPT. They turn on **mixed precision**, which lets Keras run some computations much faster at the cost of some numerical fidelity; the full explanation is deferred to chapter 18. **Listing 16.6** begins with `keras.config.set_dtype_policy("mixed_float16")`, `vocab_size = tokenizer.vocabulary_size()` (32,000 for the SentencePiece vocabulary of p.495), `hidden_dim = 512` and `intermediate_dim = 2056`; the listing continues on p.500 with `num_heads = 8`, `num_layers = 8` and the functional model, which uses the same `embedding` object at the input and, with `reverse=True`, at the output. The token embedding (vocab_size, hidden_dim) and the output projection (hidden_dim, vocab_size) are the largest weights; here 16.4M parameters each. Weight tying computes logits as hidden states times the transposed embedding matrix: a 'reverse embedding'. Listing 16.5 implements tying with a reverse flag on PositionalEmbedding; one layer object, one weight matrix, used at both ends of the model. Positions are computed as cumsum(ones_like(inputs)) - 1, giving 0..L-1 for any batch. Mixed precision (set_dtype_policy("mixed_float16")) speeds training at some cost in numerical fidelity; explained in chapter 18. The mini-GPT uses vocab 32,000, hidden_dim 512, intermediate_dim 2056 and (p.500) 8 heads and 8 layers.
snippet: Continuing from p.498, the page explains why the input token embedding and the output prediction layer are the biggest weights in a Transformer: both live in vocabulary space. The…

title: Weight tying
text: Using the transpose of the input token-embedding matrix as the output projection from hidden states to vocabulary logits. The same 'dictionary' is read in both directions: token to vector on the way in, vector to token on the way out. logits = H @ E^T where E is the (vocab_size, hidden_dim) embedding table. In Listing 16.5 this is ops.matmul(inputs, ops.transpose(self.token_embeddings.embeddings)). If token 'Paris' has embedding e, the model predicts 'Paris' with high probability when its final hidden state h has a large dot product with e.
snippet: Using the transpose of the input token-embedding matrix as the output projection from hidden states to vocabulary logits.

title: Learned positional embedding
text: A trainable vector for each position index 0..sequence_length-1, added to the token embedding. A stamp saying 'I am the 5th token' added to each token's meaning vector. positions = cumsum(ones_like(inputs), axis=-1) - 1 gives [0, 1, ..., L-1] for every sequence in the batch; position_embeddings is an Embedding(sequence_length, output_dim). For inputs of shape (128, 256), positions has shape (128, 256) with each row equal to 0..255.
snippet: A trainable vector for each position index 0..sequencelength-1, added to the token embedding.

title: Token embedding
text: A lookup table mapping each token id to a dense vector. A dictionary from integers to learned vectors (p.435). layers.Embedding(input_dim, output_dim) stores a weight matrix accessible as .embeddings with shape (input_dim, output_dim). Embedding(32000, 512): 16,384,000 parameters.
snippet: A lookup table mapping each token id to a dense vector.

title: Mixed precision
text: Running most computations in a lower-precision float type (float16) while keeping variables in float32. Doing rough arithmetic fast where exactness does not matter, while keeping the master copy of the weights precise. keras.config.set_dtype_policy("mixed_float16") sets every subsequently created layer's compute dtype to float16 and variable dtype to float32. A Dense layer under this policy casts its float32 kernel to float16 for the matmul.
snippet: Running most computations in a lower-precision float type float16 while keeping variables in float32.

title: Tied output projection (reverse embedding)
text: "we will multiply our hidden states by the transpose of our token embedding matrix"; code: ops.matmul(inputs, ops.transpose(token_embeddings)) \text{logits} = H\,E^{\top},\qquad H \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d},\ E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d},\ \text{logits} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times V} Produce next-token logits without a separate output weight matrix. $\text{logits}_{t,j} = h_t \cdot e_j$: the score of token $j$ at position $t$ is how aligned the hidden state is with that token's embedding. H Hidden states from the last decoder block (per sequence), one row per position E Token embedding matrix, shape (vocab_size, hidden_dim) L Sequence length (256 in this chapter) d hidden_dim = 512 V vocab_size = 32,000
snippet: "we will multiply our hidden states by the transpose of our token embedding matrix"; code: ops.matmulinputs, ops.transposetokenembeddings — Produce next-token logits without a…

title: Position indices and the combined embedding

title: Assembling mini-GPT and a learning-rate warmup
text:
The end of Listing 16.6 (functional mini-GPT with eight decoder blocks and a tied output), its 41M-parameter size, and the start of pretraining: why Transformers need learning-rate warmup and a WarmupSchedule implementation (Listing 16.7) The mini-GPT is a PositionalEmbedding, a LayerNormalization, eight TransformerDecoder blocks and the same embedding used in reverse to output logits, about 41 million parameters. Deep Transformer stacks are finicky to train and prone to exploding gradients, so the learning rate is ramped linearly from 0 to a peak of 2e-4 over the first 1,000 steps. The page opens with the rest of **Listing 16.6** (begun on p.499). It sets `num_heads = 8` and `num_layers = 8`, declares `inputs = keras.Input(shape=(None,), dtype="int32")`, creates one `PositionalEmbedding(sequence_length, vocab_size, hidden_dim)`, embeds the inputs, applies a `LayerNormalization`, loops eight times over `TransformerDecoder(hidden_dim, intermediate_dim, num_heads)`, and produces `outputs = embedding(x, reverse=True)`, the tied "reverse embedding" logits. The result, `mini_gpt`, has **41 million parameters**: large for this book, but small next to today's LLMs, which range from a couple of billion to trillions of parameters.

Section **16.2.2 Pretraining the model** begins. Training a large Transformer is "famously finicky": it is sensitive to parameter initialization and to the choice of optimizer. With many stacked layers it is easy to get **exploding gradients**, where parameters update too quickly and the loss does not converge. A trick that works well is **warmup**: ease linearly into the full learning rate over a number of steps so that early updates are small. Keras makes this easy with a `LearningRateSchedule`.

**Listing 16.7** defines `WarmupSchedule` with a peak rate `2e-4` and `warmup_steps = 1_000.0`. Its `__call__(step)` casts the step to float and returns `rate * min(step / warmup_steps, 1.0)`: a linear ramp from 0 to 2e-4 over 1,000 steps, then constant. A short snippet evaluates the schedule at steps 0, 100, ..., 4,900 and plots learning rate against train step with matplotlib, which yields figure 16.2 on p.501. mini-GPT = PositionalEmbedding -> LayerNorm -> 8 x TransformerDecoder -> same embedding with reverse=True. It has 41 million parameters, tiny next to modern LLMs (billions to trillions). Deep Transformers are sensitive to initialization and optimizer choice and can suffer exploding gradients. Linear warmup keeps early updates small: lr = 2e-4 * min(step / 1000, 1). Custom schedules subclass keras.optimizers.schedules.LearningRateSchedule and implement __call__(step). Plot a schedule before a long training run to verify it.

title: Warmup curve and launching mini-GPT pretraining
text:
Figure 16.2 (the plotted warmup learning-rate schedule) and Listing 16.8, which compiles mini-GPT with Adam on the warmup schedule and a from-logits sparse cross-entropy loss and runs one pass over about a billion tokens split into eight 'epochs' The warmup schedule ramps the learning rate linearly from 0 to 2e-4 over the first 1,000 steps and then holds it constant. Mini-GPT is then trained for a single pass over its ~1 billion training tokens, chopped into eight pseudo-epochs so that validation loss and accuracy can be checked periodically. This is the most expensive training run in the book. The page opens with **Figure 16.2**, the plot produced by the snippet at the bottom of p.500: the learning rate rises in a straight line from 0 at step 0 to **0.0002** at step **1,000**, then stays flat (the plot is drawn up to step ~4,900). The caption states the purpose: warmup makes updates to the parameters smaller at the beginning of training and can help with stability.

The authors then describe the training plan. The model will see **one pass over the ~1 billion tokens** of the C4 subset, but that pass is **split across eight epochs** purely so that validation loss and accuracy are reported periodically. They put the run in perspective: mini-GPT has about **3× fewer parameters than GPT-1** and uses **100× fewer training steps**; it is two orders of magnitude cheaper than the smallest GPT, yet this `fit()` call is still **the most computationally expensive training run in the whole book** (readers are told to start it and take a break).

**Listing 16.8** sets `num_epochs = 8`, `steps_per_epoch = num_train_batches // num_epochs` and `validation_steps = num_val_batches` (a callout suggests lowering these if you do not want to wait). It compiles `mini_gpt` with `keras.optimizers.Adam(schedule)` (the `WarmupSchedule` instance as the learning rate), `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True)` as loss (the model outputs raw logits; explained in the sidebar on p.502) and an accuracy metric, then calls `fit()` on the infinitely repeating `train_ds`, with `val_ds` as validation data. With 28,873 training batches of 128 × 256 tokens (p.497), each epoch is 3,609 steps and the whole run about 28,872 steps, so warmup occupies only the first ~3.5% of training. Figure 16.2 confirms the warmup schedule: linear from 0 to 2e-4 over 1,000 steps, then constant. The model is trained for a single pass over ~1 billion tokens, split into eight pseudo-epochs of 3,609 steps only to get periodic validation reports. With infinite (repeated) datasets, steps_per_epoch and validation_steps define what an epoch is. Adam accepts a LearningRateSchedule object as its learning rate. SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True) is used because mini-GPT outputs raw logits, not probabilities. Despite being ~100x cheaper than the smallest GPT, this is the most expensive training run in the book.

title: Learning-rate warmup
text: A schedule that starts the learning rate near zero and increases it (here linearly) to its target value over a fixed number of steps. Do not sprint before you know where you are: early gradients from a random network are unreliable and can be huge, so take small steps until training settles. Figure 16.2 plots lr(t) = 2e-4 * min(t / 1000, 1). For Adam, warmup also compensates for second-moment estimates that are noisy in the first steps, which can make the effective per-parameter step unexpectedly large. At step 250 the learning rate is 5e-5; at step 1,000 and beyond it is 2e-4.
snippet: A schedule that starts the learning rate near zero and increases it here linearly to its target value over a fixed number of steps.

title: steps_per_epoch / validation_steps
text: fit() arguments that fix how many batches make up one epoch of training and of validation. When the dataset is an endless stream, you have to tell Keras where to draw the line between 'epochs'. Required when train_ds and val_ds are infinite (created with .repeat(), p.497). Here steps_per_epoch = 28,873 // 8 = 3,609 and validation_steps = 500. 8 epochs x 3,609 steps = 28,872 training steps, about one pass over the 28,873 training batches.
snippet: fit arguments that fix how many batches make up one epoch of training and of validation.

title: Logits and from_logits=True
text: Unnormalized scores output by the model; passing from_logits=True tells the loss to apply the softmax itself. The model hands over raw scores and the loss function turns them into probabilities internally. SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True) computes -z_y + log(sum_j exp z_j) with a numerically stable log-sum-exp, which avoids taking the log of a softmax output that has underflowed to zero. Logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] correspond to probabilities [0.66, 0.24, 0.10].
snippet: Unnormalized scores output by the model; passing fromlogits=True tells the loss to apply the softmax itself.

title: Next-token pretraining
text: Training a model to predict each next token of real text, using the sequence shifted by one position as the target. Fill in the next word billions of times and the model absorbs grammar, facts and style. Targets are x[1:] for inputs x[:-1] (p.496), so a batch of 128 sequences of 256 tokens yields 32,768 next-token classification problems, each over a 32,000-token vocabulary, averaged by the sparse cross-entropy loss. For the input 'the cat sat', the targets are 'cat sat on'.

title: Logits, training results, and greedy decoding
text:
A sidebar defining logits and from_logits=True, the result of pretraining (about 36% next-token accuracy, undertrained), and the start of 16.2.3 with Listing 16.9, a simple greedy autoregressive generation loop Mini-GPT outputs logits (unnormalized log probabilities); softmax turns them into probabilities, and Keras lets you put that softmax in the loss instead of the model. After one pass over the data the model guesses the next token about 36% of the time and is clearly undertrained. Text is generated by repeatedly feeding the sequence in, taking the most likely next token at the last position, appending it and repeating. A sidebar, **"What is a logit?"**, explains the new loss argument seen in Listing 16.8 (p.501), `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True)`. The output projection at the end of mini-GPT has **no softmax**; its outputs can be thought of as **unnormalized log probabilities**, one per vocabulary token. Exponentiating them and normalizing them to sum to 1, which is all `softmax` does, yields probabilities. An unnormalized log probability is called a **logit**, and logits are easier to work with when generating text (as the next section shows). Keras lets you choose where the softmax lives: either as the model's last activation (model outputs probabilities) or inside the loss (model outputs logits, and you pass `from_logits=True`).

Back in the main text, the trained model predicts the next token correctly **about 36% of the time** on the validation set, which the authors call a crude heuristic. The model is **undertrained**: validation loss keeps decreasing every epoch, unsurprising with 100x fewer training steps than GPT-1; more training would help but costs time and money.

Section **16.2.3 Generative decoding** reuses the approach of chapter 15 (Shakespeare and Spanish translation): feed a prompt, read the model's distribution over the vocabulary for the next token at every position, **select the most likely token at the last position, append it and repeat**, producing a sequence one token at a time. **Listing 16.9** implements this as `generate(prompt, max_length=64)`: tokenize the prompt into a Python list, then for `max_length - prompt_length` iterations call `mini_gpt` on the whole current sequence, take the logits at position `[0, -1]`, append `np.argmax(...)` as an int, and finally detokenize all tokens, prompt included. A logit is an unnormalized log probability; softmax (exponentiate, normalize) turns logits into probabilities. Keras lets you put softmax in the model or in the loss; with logits outputs use SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True). Mini-GPT reaches about 36% next-token validation accuracy, a crude measure, and is still undertrained. Generative decoding repeatedly feeds the sequence back and appends the predicted token at the last position. title: Logits
text: Unnormalized log probabilities output by a model before softmax. Raw scores: higher means more likely, but they do not sum to anything in particular. z_i = log p_i + C. softmax(z) = exp(z) / sum(exp(z)) recovers p. Adding a constant to all logits does not change the probabilities. Logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] give probabilities [0.659, 0.242, 0.099].

title: Softmax
text: Function mapping a score vector to a probability distribution by exponentiating and normalizing. Make everything positive, then divide by the total. softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j); monotonic, so it preserves the ranking of the scores. softmax([0, 0]) = [0.5, 0.5]; softmax([10, 0]) is about [0.99995, 0.00005].

title: Greedy decoding
text: Generating text by always appending the single most likely next token. Always take the locally best step without looking ahead. next = argmax_i z_i at the last position; deterministic: the same prompt always gives the same output. Listing 16.9 uses np.argmax(prediction).

title: Autoregressive language model
text: A model that outputs a distribution over the next token given the previous ones and can generate text by feeding its outputs back in. A very sophisticated autocomplete. Trained with a causal mask so position t only sees tokens up to t; at inference the last position's output is the next-token distribution. Prompt 'A piece of advice' -> model predicts ',' -> appended -> repeat.

title: From logits to probabilities (softmax)
text: If you exponentiate each output value and normalize all values to sum to 1 (this is all the softmax function does), you will get a probability value. p_i = \operatorname{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j}}, \qquad z_i = \log p_i + \log \sum_{j=1}^{V} e^{z_j} Formalizes the sidebar's definition of a logit. Differences between logits are what matter: z_i - z_j = log(p_i / p_j). z_i Logit (model output) for vocabulary token i p_i Probability of token i being the next token V Vocabulary size (32,000 for mini-GPT)

title: Listing 16.9 A simple generation function for the mini-GPT model

title: Greedy output, slowness, and compiled generation
text:
Running Listing 16.9 on the prompt 'A piece of advice' (repetitive output, minutes of runtime), why direct model calls are slow (no compilation), and Listing 16.10, which uses predict() on a fixed-length zero-padded sequence to avoid recompilation Calling the model directly runs the forward pass eagerly and unoptimized, so greedy generation takes minutes. predict() compiles the computation, but compilation is tied to an input shape; padding the sequence to a constant max_length and reading the prediction at position i - 1 keeps the shape fixed so the compiled function is reused at every step. The page first runs `generate()` from Listing 16.9 on the prompt **"A piece of advice"**. The output is fluent but quickly gets stuck: "...you can get a sense of what you are doing. You can get a sense of what you are doing, and you can get a sense of what" (the repetition is analyzed on p.504-505).

Two problems are noted, and this page addresses the first: speed. Generation **takes minutes**, which is puzzling because training processed about **200,000 tokens per second** on the authors' reference hardware. The main reason, at least on the **JAX and TensorFlow backends**, is that the computation is **uncompiled**. Every time you run `fit()` or `predict()`, Keras compiles the per-batch computation: the `keras.ops` are lifted out of Python and heavily optimized by the backend, slow for the first batch but massively faster afterwards. A direct call such as `mini_gpt(...)` instead runs the forward pass live and unoptimized at each step.

The easy fix is `predict()`, with one gotcha: TensorFlow and JAX compile a function **for a specific input shape**, which lets the backend optimize for the hardware knowing exactly how many processor instructions each tensor operation needs. Listing 16.9 feeds a sequence that **grows by one token per step**, which would trigger a recompilation on every `predict()` call. The solution is to **pad the input to a fixed length**.

**Listing 16.10**, `compiled_generate(prompt, max_length=64)`, pads the token list with zeros up to `max_length`, loops `i` from `prompt_length` to `max_length - 1`, calls `mini_gpt.predict(np.array([tokens]), verbose=0)` on the constant-shape `(1, 64)` input, reads the logits at position `i - 1` (the prediction for token `i`), and writes the argmax into `tokens[i]`. The page ends by announcing a timing test (result on p.504: under half a second). Greedy decoding with mini-GPT gives fluent but repetitive text ('get a sense of what you are doing'). Calling the model directly in a loop runs eagerly and unoptimized; on JAX/TensorFlow that makes generation take minutes. fit() and predict() compile the computation, which is slow once and fast afterwards. Compiled functions are specialized to input shapes; a growing sequence would force recompilation at every step. Listing 16.10 pads to a fixed length and reads the prediction at i - 1; the causal mask makes the padding harmless.

Write the recipe once, have a chef optimize the whole kitchen workflow, then cook many times quickly. Keras compiles train/predict step functions (jax.jit, tf.function/XLA). Compiled programs are specialized to input shapes and dtypes; new shapes trigger retracing. mini_gpt(x) in a loop runs eagerly; mini_gpt.predict(x) compiles once per input shape.

title: Listing 16.10 A compiled generation function for the mini-GPT model
text:
def compiled_generate(prompt, max_length=64):
    tokens = list(ops.convert_to_numpy(tokenizer(prompt)))
    prompt_length = len(tokens)
    tokens = tokens + [0] * (max_length - prompt_length)
    for i in range(prompt_length, max_length):
        prediction = mini_gpt.predict(np.array([tokens]), verbose=0)
        prediction = prediction[0, i - 1]
        tokens[i] = np.argmax(prediction).item()
    return tokenizer.detokenize(tokens) Greedy generation that keeps the model input at a constant shape (1, max_length) so that predict() compiles once and is reused for every generated token. Fixed-shape autoregressive greedy decoding: for i = prompt_length..max_length-1: logits = f(tokens); tokens[i] = argmax(logits[i-1]).

title: Compiled speed, KV caching, and the repetition problem
text:
Timing the compiled generation loop, why key/value caching is the next big speedup for causal Transformers, and the start of the discussion on sampling strategies. Padding to a fixed shape and using predict() brings generation from minutes to under half a second, but the loop still recomputes the whole sequence each step; caching each attention layer's keys and values gives a causal Transformer an RNN-like state so each step processes a single token. Separately, greedy decoding makes the model repeat itself. The page opens by finishing the speed experiment begun on p.503. Using Python's `timeit`, the authors call `compiled_generate(prompt)` (listing 16.10, which pads the token list to a fixed `max_length` of 64 and calls `mini_gpt.predict()`) ten times and average: about **0.487 seconds per generation**. Compared with the uncompiled loop of listing 16.9, which took *minutes*, this is a dramatic improvement that comes purely from letting the backend (JAX or TensorFlow) compile the forward pass once for a fixed input shape.

A sidebar titled **Cached generation** then points out the remaining waste. At every step the model is run on the *entire* sequence, yet only the prediction at one position is kept, even though the sequence changes by just one token between steps. The authors connect this to chapter 15's RNN generation, where the recurrent state carried all needed information about the past so each step processed only one token. They argue that a causal Transformer has an equivalent state: attention is the *only* place where information flows between positions (feedforward blocks act per position), and inside attention, past tokens contribute only through their `key` and `value` vectors. Because past input is fixed and the causal mask forbids looking ahead, those vectors never change. Caching them at every layer therefore lets the model process a single new token per step. The implementation is "clunky" (intermediate arrays must be saved and reused in every attention layer), but the payoff is large: inputs shrink from the full output length to one token, and for generations thousands of tokens long the authors say this can amount to a thousandfold speedup. Every efficient generative sampler uses key/value caching.

Finally, section **16.2.4 Sampling strategies** begins with a second problem: the model repeats itself, looping on the phrase "get a sense of what you are doing" (visible in the p.503 output). The explanation and the fix (sampling instead of greedy search) follow on p.505. Compiling a shape-stable generation loop with predict() cut generation from minutes to ≈0.49 s per call. Even compiled, the loop recomputes the entire sequence at every step and keeps only one position's prediction. Attention is the only cross-position operation in a Transformer; everything else is per token. Because of the causal mask, past keys and values never change, so caching them at every layer gives the Transformer an RNN-like state. With a KV cache each step processes one token; for thousands of tokens this can mean roughly a thousandfold speedup, and every efficient sampler uses it. Greedy decoding makes the mini-GPT loop on phrases like "get a sense of what you are doing", motivating sampling strategies.

title: Key/value caching
text: Storing the key and value vectors of all previously processed positions at every attention layer of a causal Transformer, so that each generation step only computes the new token's query, key and value. The past is fixed and the causal mask means it never looks at the future, so what each layer 'knows' about past tokens never changes; save it instead of recomputing it. At layer l and step t: q_t, k_t, v_t = x_t W_Q, x_t W_K, x_t W_V; K ← [K; k_t], V ← [V; v_t]; output = softmax(q_t K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. Cache size per sequence ≈ 2 × layers × t × d_model numbers. Generating token 1,001 after a 1,000-token context: without a cache the model runs on 1,001 positions; with a cache it runs on 1 position and attends to 1,000 cached keys/values.

title: Greedy search and pluggable sampling functions
text:
Why the mini-GPT repeats itself under greedy decoding, and refactoring compiled_generate() to accept a sampling strategy function. Repetition is a natural consequence of next-token training plus always choosing the argmax (greedy search). The model actually outputs a full distribution over 32,000 tokens; by making the token-choice rule a parameter (sample_fn), we can explore that distribution, starting with greedy search as one such function and then random categorical sampling. The page continues 16.2.4 by diagnosing the repetition seen on p.503-504. The authors argue it is **not a bug but a consequence of the training objective**: the model predicts the most likely next token across roughly a billion words on many topics, and when there is no obvious continuation, guessing common words or repeated word patterns is an effective strategy that the model learns almost immediately. Stopped very early, it would emit "the" over and over, the most common English word.

The generation loop so far has always taken the most likely token, yet the model's output at each step is a **probability distribution over all 32,000 vocabulary tokens**. Taking the argmax each step is called **greedy search**: the simplest use of the predictions but not the only one. Adding randomness lets us explore the learned distribution more broadly and avoid getting stuck in loops of high-probability sequences.

To experiment, the authors refactor `compiled_generate()` to take a `sample_fn`, a function mapping the model's prediction vector (at the last real position) to the next token. They call this the **sampling strategy**. The loop is otherwise identical to listing 16.10: tokenize, pad to `max_length=64`, call `mini_gpt.predict()` on the fixed-shape input, read `prediction[0, i - 1]`, and now set `tokens[i]` from `sample_fn(prediction)`, converted to NumPy and to a Python int.

Greedy search becomes a one-liner, `ops.argmax(preds)`, passed as `compiled_generate(prompt, greedy_search)`. Finally the authors note that the Transformer's outputs define a **categorical distribution** per time step, which we could sample directly instead of taking the maximum: `keras.random.categorical()` applies a softmax to the predictions (logits) and draws a random sample. The code and its output follow on p.506. The mini-GPT repeats itself because next-token training favours common words and patterns, and greedy decoding always picks them. An early-stopped model would print "the" endlessly, the most frequent English word. The model's output is a distribution over 32,000 tokens; greedy search keeps only its argmax. compiled_generate() now takes a sample_fn: the sampling strategy is a swappable function. greedy_search is just ops.argmax(preds). keras.random.categorical() softmaxes logits and samples, giving random sampling.

title: Greedy search vs categorical sampling

Greedy uses only the mode of the distribution; sampling uses all of it. z logit vector at the last real position, prediction[0, i-1] V vocabulary size, 32,000 p_i probability of token i x_t the token chosen for position t (tokens[i] in the code)

title: compiled_generate() with a pluggable sampling function
text:
def compiled_generate(prompt, sample_fn, max_length=64):
    tokens = list(ops.convert_to_numpy(tokenizer(prompt)))
    prompt_length = len(tokens)
    tokens = tokens + [0] * (max_length - prompt_length)
    for i in range(prompt_length, max_length):
        prediction = mini_gpt.predict(np.array([tokens]), verbose=0)
        prediction = prediction[0, i - 1]
        next_token = ops.convert_to_numpy(sample_fn(prediction))
        tokens[i] = np.array(next_token).item()
    return tokenizer.detokenize(tokens) Generates text from a prompt up to 64 tokens, using a caller-supplied function to choose each next token from the model's logits. Autoregressive decoding with fixed-shape padded inputs and a pluggable token-selection rule.

title: Random sampling and temperature
text:
Sampling the next token from the full categorical distribution, controlling exploration with a temperature parameter, and introducing top-K sampling. Pure random sampling removes the repetition loops but explores too much. Dividing logits by a temperature before softmax sharpens (T < 1) or flattens (T > 1) the distribution: T = 2.0 gives non-English gibberish, T = 0.2 approaches greedy repetition, T = 0.8 gives fluent but meandering text. Top-K sampling is another way to shape the distribution. The page implements **random sampling**. `random_sample(preds, temperature=1.0)` divides the logits by `temperature` and calls `keras.random.categorical(preds[None, :], num_samples=1)[0]`, which applies softmax and draws one token. With the default temperature of 1.0 and the prompt "A piece of advice", the output ("...just read my knees and stick with getables and a hello to me. However, the bar napkin doesn't last as long...") is diverse and no longer loops, but, in the authors' words, the sampling now **explores too much**: the text jumps around without continuity.

The authors then explain the `temperature` parameter: it sharpens or widens the distribution so sampling explores less or more. A **low temperature** makes all logits larger before softmax, making the most likely output even more likely; a **high temperature** makes logits smaller, spreading the distribution out. They run three experiments with `functools.partial` to bind the temperature:

- **T = 2.0**: output is no longer English; a stream of seemingly random tokens, fragments, code-like words and foreign scripts ("tran writes using ignore unnecessary pivot ... AnyкаTextView cardinal spiritual heavenToen").
- **T = 0.8**: fluent, mostly grammatical English about writing a blog, with some repetition ("I am writing this blog" appears twice) but no tight loop.
- **T = 0.2**: behaviour resembling greedy search, repeating "I think it's a good idea to have a good understanding of the...".

The conclusion: high temperature leads to random tokens, low temperature to greedy-like repetition. Finally, the page introduces **top-K sampling**, restricting sampling to the K most likely tokens, and points to figure 16.3 (next page), which shows top-K as a middle ground between greedy and random sampling. random_sample divides logits by temperature and samples with keras.random.categorical. At T = 1, random sampling ends the loops but the text loses continuity. Low T sharpens the distribution (toward greedy); high T flattens it (toward uniform). T = 2.0 gave non-English gibberish, T = 0.8 fluent text, T = 0.2 greedy-like repetition. functools.partial binds the temperature so the function fits the sample_fn interface. Top-K sampling restricts sampling to the K most likely tokens, a middle ground shown in figure 16.3.

title: Temperature-scaled softmax
text: preds = preds / temperature, followed by keras.random.categorical(...), which applies softmax p_i(T) = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V} \exp(z_j / T)}, \qquad \frac{p_i(T)}{p_j(T)} = \exp\!\left(\frac{z_i - z_j}{T}\right) Formalizes 'sharpen or widen our probability distribution'. An undertrained model's tail is also poorly calibrated.

title: Top-K sampling: figure and code
text:
Figure 16.3 comparing greedy, top-K and random sampling on one next-token distribution at three temperatures; a top_k sampling function built from keras.ops.top_k and keras.random.categorical; mini-GPT outputs with K = 5 and K = 20; how top-K differs from temperature Top-K sampling keeps only the K most likely tokens and samples among them, a middle ground between greedy search (K = 1) and sampling from the full distribution. Temperature reshapes probabilities but never rules any token out; top-K sets everything outside the K candidates to zero probability. **Figure 16.3** shows one next-token distribution over six candidate words, *that, to, is, and, on, for*, drawn at three temperatures (0.5, 1.0, 2.0). At temperature 1.0, *that* has probability about 0.57, *to* about 0.21, *is* about 0.13 and the rest under 0.05. Lowering the temperature to 0.5 sharpens it (*that* about 0.83); raising it to 2.0 flattens it (*that* about 0.36, the tail around 0.08-0.10). Under the axis, three brackets mark which tokens each strategy can pick: **Greedy** only *that*, **Top-K (k=3)** *that, to, is*, **Random** all of them. Top-K is a middle ground between greedy and random (as stated at the end of p.506).

The code uses `keras.ops.top_k` to find the top K elements of an array. `top_k(preds, k=5, temperature=1.0)` divides the logits by the temperature, takes the K largest values and their vocabulary indices (`sorted=False`), samples one position among those K with `keras.random.categorical` (which applies softmax to the given logits), and maps that position back to a vocabulary id with `ops.take_along_axis`.

Two runs are shown with `compiled_generate(prompt, partial(top_k, k=5))` and `k=20`. With **K = 5** the text reads like a coherent first-person forum post ("I'm not going to be able to do anything for a few months..."); with **K = 20** it is more varied and less grounded ("advice and guidance from the Audi Bank in 2015... a great year for you in 2017").

The page ends by contrasting the two controls: a low temperature makes likely tokens more likely but **does not rule any token out**; top-K sampling (continued on p.508) zeros out everything outside the K candidates. Figure 16.3: greedy picks only the top token, top-K samples among the K best, random samples from everything; temperature reshapes the bars. Temperature scaling corresponds to raising probabilities to the power 1/T and renormalizing. top_k() = scale logits by 1/T, ops.top_k, keras.random.categorical over the shortlist, then take_along_axis back to token ids. K = 5 gives more coherent text, K = 20 more diverse but less coherent text. Low temperature never rules a token out; top-K zeros out everything outside the candidates, and the two can be combined.

title: A top-K sampling function
text:
def top_k(preds, k=5, temperature=1.0):
    preds = preds / temperature
    top_preds, top_indices = ops.top_k(preds, k=k, sorted=False)
    choice = keras.random.categorical(top_preds[None, :], num_samples=1)[0]
    return ops.take_along_axis(top_indices, choice, axis=-1) Given a vector of next-token logits, returns a token id sampled from the K most likely tokens after temperature scaling. Scale by 1/T -> select top K -> softmax over K -> sample -> gather the token id.

title: Combining top-K and temperature; from mini-GPT to pretrained LLMs
text:
End of 16.2.4 (top-K combined with temperature, beam search, and an assessment of mini-GPT against GPT-1 and modern LLMs) and the opening of 16.3: why the industry relies on a few pretrained models, the cost and energy footprint of pretraining (Llama 2), and the choice of Gemma 3 Top-K and temperature can be combined (top 5 at T = 0.5 gives the most plausible mini-GPT text), but mini-GPT's output has little practical use, just as GPT-1's generations were a curiosity. The training recipe is the same one used for today's LLMs; only scale is missing (at least 100x parameters and 1,000x steps). Because pretraining is so costly in money and energy, the chapter switches to a pretrained billion-parameter model, Gemma 3. The page completes p.507's contrast: top-K sampling **zeros out** the probability of anything outside the K candidates, whereas temperature only reshapes. The two can be combined, for example **top 5 with temperature 0.5**: `compiled_generate(prompt, partial(top_k, k=5, temperature=0.5))` yields clean, advice-like English ("The first thing you need to do is to get the job done..."), though it starts repeating a sentence frame. Sampling strategies are an important control and there are many others, e.g. **beam search**, which heuristically explores several chains of predicted tokens by keeping a fixed number of **beams** at each timestep.

The authors then assess the result: with top-K the text is closer to plausible English but has **little apparent utility**. This matches **GPT-1**, whose generations were a curiosity; its state-of-the-art results came from **fine-tuning classifiers**. Mini-GPT is far less trained than GPT-1. Reaching today's generative LLMs would need **at least 100x more parameters and 1,000x more training steps**, and would bring the same leaps in quality OpenAI saw. The recipe used here is **the exact blueprint** everyone uses to train LLMs; the missing pieces are a very large compute budget and multi-machine training tricks (chapter 18). So the chapter switches to a pretrained model.

**16.3 Using a pretrained LLM** opens: rather than pretraining, use a **billion-parameter pretrained model**. Because pretraining is so expensive, the industry relies on models from a short list of companies, for **cost and environmental** reasons: generative-model training is now a large share of big tech companies' data-center power use. Meta reported that **Llama 2** (2023), smaller than GPT-3, needed an estimated **1.3 million kWh** to train, the daily electricity use of about **45,000 American households**; if every organization pretrained its own LLM, the energy would be a noticeable share of global consumption. The chapter will use Google's **Gemma 3** (2025), in its smallest variant (continued on p.509). Top-K removes tokens outside the candidates; temperature reshapes; combining top-5 with T = 0.5 gives mini-GPT's most fluent text. Beam search keeps a fixed number of candidate chains at each timestep. Fluent text is not useful text: GPT-1's generations were a curiosity and its successes came from fine-tuning classifiers. Reaching modern LLMs needs at least 100x parameters and 1,000x steps, plus large compute and distributed training, but the same recipe. Pretraining is costly in money and energy (Llama 2: about 1.3 million kWh), so most practitioners use pretrained models such as Gemma 3.

The smallest Gemma 3 model (about 1 billion parameters, ~2 trillion training tokens), accessing its weights on Kaggle (terms of use, API key, kagglehub.login), instantiating it with keras_hub.models.CausalLM.from_preset (Listing 16.11), and the CausalLM task API Gemma 3 1B is about 25x larger than mini-GPT and was trained on about 2,000x more tokens. Completing the sentence from p.508, the authors use the smallest Gemma 3 variant, which has **almost exactly 1 billion parameters**. This "small" model was trained on roughly **2 trillion tokens**, 2,000 times more than mini-GPT's ~1 billion.

title: Gemma's model summary and first generations with generate()
text:
Reading the summary of the pretrained Gemma 3 1B CausalLM, and generating text from it with the built-in, compilable generate() method using greedy sampling The KerasHub Gemma CausalLM bundles a 262,144-token tokenizer with a ~1-billion-parameter backbone (hidden size 1152) whose token embedding is reused as the output projection. Its built-in generate() method, compiled with a sampler such as "greedy", produces text far more coherent than the mini-GPT, but a pure pretrained model just continues text like a web document and is not yet useful. The page opens with the rest of `gemma_lm.summary()` (begun on p.509). The **preprocessor** contains a `gemma3_tokenizer` (`Gemma3Tokenizer`) with a **vocabulary of 262,144** tokens. The model, `"gemma3_causal_lm"`, has two `InputLayer`s, `padding_mask` and `token_ids`, both shaped `(None, None)` (batch size and sequence length are both variable). They feed a `gemma3_backbone` (`Gemma3Backbone`) with **999,885,952** parameters that outputs `(None, None, 1152)`: one 1152-dimensional vector per token. A `token_embedding` layer (`ReversibleEmbedding`) then maps those vectors to `(None, None, 262144)`, i.e. one logit per vocabulary entry for every position. It lists **301,989,888** parameters, but the total is still 999,885,952 (3.72 GB). All parameters are trainable and none are non-trainable.

The arithmetic explains the apparent double count: $262{,}144 \times 1152 = 301{,}989{,}888$, the size of the embedding matrix. That matrix lives inside the backbone and is *reused* ("reversed") as the output projection, the same weight-tying trick the mini-GPT used (p.498). So it is counted only once in the total. And $999{,}885{,}952 \times 4$ bytes $\approx 3.72$ GiB, because the model was loaded with `dtype="float32"` (p.509).

The authors then skip writing a decoding loop like Listing 16.9/16.10 (p.502–503) and use the `generate()` method that comes with the `CausalLM` class. It can be **compiled with different sampling strategies** (section 16.2). With `gemma_lm.compile(sampler="greedy")` and `max_length=40`, the prompt "A piece of advice" continues as a quote from "a former student of mine" with a stray `<blockquote>` HTML tag. "How can I make brownies?" turns into a forum-style post (`[User 0001]`, "I'm trying to make brownies for my son's birthday party…").

Two observations close the page. The output is **much more coherent** than the mini-GPT's, hard to tell apart from the C4 training data. But it is **still not that useful**: vaguely plausible text whose purpose is unclear. The model answers no question; it imitates web documents. p.511 explains why. Gemma 3 1B: 262,144-token vocabulary, 1152-dim hidden states, 999,885,952 parameters (3.72 GB in float32). The token_embedding (262,144 × 1152 = 301,989,888 params) is shared between input and output, so it is not double-counted. CausalLM.compile(sampler=...) chooses the decoding strategy; generate(prompt, max_length=...) runs the whole loop. Pretrained Gemma is far more coherent than mini-GPT, but it continues text like a web document rather than helping.

title: Greedy search (greedy decoding)
text: A decoding strategy that picks the single most probable next token at each generation step. Always take the locally best step; deterministic, so the same prompt gives the same output. $x_{t} = \arg\max_{v} p_\theta(v \mid x_{<t})$ repeated until `max_length`. Selected here with `sampler="greedy"`. Both generations on this page are greedy and would be identical on every run.
snippet: A decoding strategy that picks the single most probable next token at each generation step.

title: Tied (reversible) token embedding
text: Using the same matrix both to embed input token IDs into vectors and, transposed, to project the final hidden states back to vocabulary logits. The vector that represents a word on the way in is also the 'template' the output is compared with when deciding whether to predict that word. Embedding matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$ with $V=262{,}144$, $d=1152$. Input: $h_0 = E[\text{ids}]$; output logits: $z = h_L E^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{V}$. KerasHub's `ReversibleEmbedding` layer implements both directions. The summary lists token_embedding at 301,989,888 parameters, yet the total (999,885,952) equals the backbone alone, because the matrix is shared.
snippet: Using the same matrix both to embed input token IDs into vectors and, transposed, to project the final hidden states back to vocabulary logits.

title: Prompting a pretrained LLM, and hallucination
text:
Why a pretrained LLM behaves like an internet autocomplete, how prompt design steers it toward useful continuations, the limits of prompting, and hallucination Gemma's unhelpful outputs are a consequence of the next-token pretraining objective, not a bug. You can steer the model by writing a prompt for which the desired output is the most likely continuation, but this control is hand-wavy and unpredictable. Because a most-likely next token always exists, the model will confidently produce unfounded text: hallucination. The page explains the disappointing outputs on p.510. As with the mini-GPT (p.505), they are **not a bug but a consequence of the pretraining objective**. Gemma was trained to "guess the next word", so it is "effectively a **fancy autocomplete for the internet**": it keeps producing the most probable continuation, as if the prompt were a snippet from a random web document.

The first remedy is a **longer, more specific prompt** that makes the desired output type obvious. Prompting with the start of a recipe ("The following brownie recipe is easy to make in just a few steps.\n\nYou can start by", `max_length=40`) gives a useful continuation: "melting the butter and sugar in a saucepan over medium heat. Then add the eggs and vanilla extract". The authors stress that the model does not interpret the prompt in a human, conversational way. We have just built a prompt for which a real recipe is a *more likely continuation* than a forum post asking for help.

Prompting can go further: **role instructions** ("You are a large language model that gives short, helpful answers to people's questions.") or a list of **harmful topics** to avoid. If this sounds "hand-wavy and hard to control", the authors agree. Visiting different parts of a model's distribution through prompting is often useful, but predicting how a model will respond to a prompt is very difficult.

Finally, **hallucinations**: "a model will always say something—there is always a most-likely next token to a given sequence." Asked about "the 542nd president of the United States", Gemma states that he "was James A. Garfield". There have been fewer than 50 presidents, and Garfield was the 20th. It is easy to find places in the distribution with no grounding in fact. p.512 calls this "utter nonsense" and turns to instruction fine-tuning. A pretrained LLM is 'a fancy autocomplete for the internet': it continues prompts like web documents. Prompting steers it by making the desired output the most likely continuation; this is statistics, not comprehension. Role prompts and lists of banned topics can help, but their effects are hard to predict. Hallucination follows from the objective: there is always a most-likely next token, so the model always answers, even nonsense questions.
