title: Instruction fine-tuning: idea and the Dolly-15k dataset
text:
Using fine-tuning on instruction/response pairs to make a pretrained LLM a useful conversation partner, and starting to load the Databricks Dolly-15k dataset with prompt/response templates Hallucination and uncontrollable output have no silver bullet, but fine-tuning on examples of the desired outputs helps a lot. Instruction fine-tuning joins each user instruction and model response into one marked-up sequence and trains on it with the same next-token loss as pretraining. This nudges the already learned representation toward the desired tone and content. The page finishes the hallucination example. The answer 'James A. Garfield' to the 542nd-president question is "utter nonsense, but the model could not find a more likely way to complete this prompt." **Hallucinations and uncontrollable output are fundamental problems** with language models, and no silver bullet has been found. One approach that "helps immensely" is to **fine-tune further on examples of the outputs you want**. For a chatbot that follows instructions this is called **instruction fine-tuning**, and the authors set out to apply it to Gemma.

**Section 16.3.2.** Instruction fine-tuning feeds the model **input/output pairs**, a user instruction followed by a model response, **joined into a single sequence** that becomes new training data. Special markers such as `"[instruction]"` and `"[response]"` are added so the model can tell where each part ends. The exact markup matters little as long as it is consistent.

The joined sequence is trained with the **same "guess the next word" loss** used in pretraining. Training on examples with the desired responses "bends" the model's output in the desired direction. No new latent space for language is learned (that took trillions of pretraining tokens); the learned representation is only **nudged** to control tone and content.

The dataset is Databricks' public **Dolly** collection: about **15,000 instructions with handwritten responses** written by Databricks employees. **Listing 16.12** starts by importing `json` and defining two templates. `PROMPT_TEMPLATE` produces `[instruction]\n{instruction}[end]\n[response]\n` and `RESPONSE_TEMPLATE` produces `{response}[end]`. It downloads `databricks-dolly-15k.jsonl` from Hugging Face with `keras.utils.get_file`, creates `data = {"prompts": [], "responses": []}`, and begins looping over the file's lines. The loop body, which parses each JSON line, skips examples that have context and fills the lists, is on p.513.

Note: `PROMPT_TEMPLATE` is printed with four opening quotes, which would add a literal `"` at the start of every prompt (see review flag). Hallucination and uncontrollable output are fundamental; fine-tuning on desired outputs helps a lot but is not a silver bullet. Instruction fine-tuning serializes instruction + response into one sequence with consistent markers. It reuses the next-token loss and only nudges the pretrained representation toward the desired tone and content. The book uses Databricks' ~15k handwritten instruction/response pairs (Dolly-15k), loaded in Listing 16.12. As printed, PROMPT_TEMPLATE has four opening quotes, which would add a stray quote character; three are intended.

title: Finishing the Dolly dataset, tf.data split, and the CausalLM preprocessor
text:
Turning Dolly-15k instruction/response records into a batched tf.data pipeline and inspecting what Gemma's preprocessor produces from a batch. Each Dolly record becomes a templated prompt string and a templated response string; these are batched into a tf.data.Dataset, and the CausalLM's preprocessor layer turns a batch into fixed-length token IDs, next-token labels and a sample-weight mask. The page completes **Listing 16.12**, which reads the Databricks Dolly-15k file line by line. Each line is parsed with `json.loads`; if the record has a non-empty `"context"` field it is skipped with `continue`, otherwise the instruction is wrapped with `PROMPT_TEMPLATE` and appended to `data["prompts"]`, and the response is wrapped with `RESPONSE_TEMPLATE` and appended to `data["responses"]`. The authors explain that some examples carry additional context (textual information related to the instruction) and that, to keep things simple, those are discarded.

Printing the first element shows the format: the prompt is `[instruction]`, a newline, `Which is a species of fish? Tope or Rope[end]`, a newline, `[response]`; the response is `Tope[end]`. The authors point out that this template gives every example a **predictable structure**. Gemma is not a sequence-to-sequence (encoder-decoder) model like the English-to-Spanish translator of chapter 15, yet it can be used in a sequence-to-sequence way: train on such prompts and, at inference, only generate the output after the `"[response]"` marker.

Next, the dict of two string lists becomes a `tf.data.Dataset` via `from_tensor_slices`, shuffled with a 2,000-element buffer and batched in pairs (`batch(2)`). The first 100 batches (200 examples) become `val_ds`, the rest `train_ds`.

Finally, the authors open up the `CausalLM` task object: it wraps a **`preprocessor`** layer (text in, tensors out) and a **`backbone`** model (the numerics of the forward pass). Preprocessing runs automatically inside `fit()` and `predict()`, but here it is called by hand on one batch with `sequence_length = 512`. It returns a triple `x, y, sample_weight`; `x["token_ids"]` has shape `(2, 512)`, and the listing continues on p.514 with the shapes of `padding_mask`, `y` and `sample_weight`. Dolly records with a non-empty `context` are skipped to keep the format to instruction → response. The template gives each example a predictable structure: `[instruction]\n…[end]\n[response]\n` then `…[end]`. A decoder-only LLM can act as a seq2seq model by generating only after the `[response]` marker. `batch(2)` then `take(100)`/`skip(100)` yields 200 validation examples and the rest for training. A KerasHub CausalLM = `preprocessor` (text → tensors) + `backbone` (forward-pass numerics). In training mode the preprocessor returns `(x, y, sample_weight)`; with sequence_length 512 and batch 2, token IDs are (2, 512).

text: A high-level Keras model for end-to-end causal language modeling composed of a preprocessor layer and a backbone model. The preprocessor is the clerk who turns text into numbers; the backbone is the engine that computes. `gemma_lm.preprocessor(batch)` → `(x, y, sample_weight)` with `x = {token_ids, padding_mask}`; `gemma_lm.backbone` maps token IDs to hidden states. `preprocessor.sequence_length = 512` → `x["token_ids"].shape == (2, 512)`.

title: Sequence-to-sequence via a decoder-only model
text:
Using a single causal decoder on concatenated source + separator + target so that it learns to generate the target given the source. Instead of separate reader and writer networks, one network reads the question and keeps writing the answer. Causal self-attention over the prompt replaces encoder + cross-attention; generation begins after the `[response]` marker. Feed `[instruction]
How can I make brownies?[end]
[response]
` and let the model continue (p.518).

title: Padding masks, response-only loss, and the memory wall that motivates LoRA
text:
What the preprocessor's outputs mean (padding mask, next-token labels, sample weights) and why full fine-tuning of a 1B-parameter model does not fit in 16 GB of GPU memory. Instruction fine-tuning uses ordinary next-token labels but weights the loss so only response tokens count; however, training all ~1B parameters with Adam needs ~15 GB just for weights and optimizer state, so we must reduce what is trainable. The page first completes the preprocessor inspection begun on p.513: `padding_mask`, `y` and `sample_weight` all have shape `(2, 512)`, matching `token_ids`. The authors explain the roles: the preprocessor **pads every input to a fixed length** and computes a **padding mask** marking which positions are just padded zeros. The **`sample_weight`** tensor makes the loss count **only response tokens**: the user prompt is fixed, so its loss does not matter, and the zero padding should certainly not be scored.

Printing the first five token IDs and labels of the first example shows `[2, 77074, 22768, 236842, 107]` and `[77074, 22768, 236842, 107, 24249]`: each label is simply the **next token**, the regular language-model setup (ID 2 is the start-of-sequence token).

Section **16.3.3 Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)** then raises a problem: calling `fit()` now on a Colab GPU with 16 GB would immediately run **out of memory**, even though loading and generating worked. The 1-billion-parameter model takes about **3.7 GB**. Adam needs **three extra floats per parameter**: the gradient, a velocity value and a momentum value. That gives about **15 GB for weights plus optimizer state**, leaving nothing for the few gigabytes of forward-pass activations, so training would crash on the first step. For LLMs, fitting the model in accelerator memory matters more than raw throughput.

The authors recall that **freezing** parts of a model during fine-tuning (seen earlier in the book) also **saves memory**, because frozen parameters need no optimizer variables. Research on which Transformer parameters to leave trainable found that the **attention mechanism** matters most, but attention layers alone still hold hundreds of millions of parameters. "Can we do even better?" sets up LoRA on p.515. The preprocessor pads to a fixed length and returns a padding mask, next-token labels and sample weights, all (2, 512). sample_weight restricts the loss to response tokens; prompt and padding get weight 0. Labels are inputs shifted by one: the same objective as pretraining. Full fine-tuning of a 1B float32 model with Adam needs ~15 GB for weights + gradients + two moment buffers, too much for a 16 GB GPU with activations. Frozen parameters need no optimizer state, so freezing saves memory. Attention weights matter most during fine-tuning, but they are still hundreds of millions of parameters, which motivates LoRA.

title: LoRA: freezing the kernel and learning a low-rank update
text:
How Low-Rank Adaptation replaces the update to a frozen weight matrix with the product of two thin trainable matrices, and how to enable it in KerasHub. Freeze the pretrained kernel W and learn its update as alpha @ beta with a small inner rank; for a 2048×2048 kernel and rank 8 this cuts trainable parameters from 4,194,304 to 32,768, which is enough expressive power for fine-tuning. In 2021, Microsoft researchers proposed **LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models)** to solve exactly the memory problem described on p.514. To explain it, the authors start from a minimal `Linear` layer: one `kernel` weight of shape `(input_dim, output_dim)` and `call` returning `ops.matmul(inputs, self.kernel)`.

LoRA **freezes the kernel** and adds a **low-rank decomposition** of the kernel projection: two new matrices, `alpha` with shape `(input_dim, rank)` and `beta` with shape `(rank, output_dim)`, which project down to and back up from a small inner `rank`. The `LoraLinear` layer creates the kernel with `trainable=False`, computes `frozen = inputs @ kernel` and `update = (inputs @ alpha) @ beta`, and returns their sum.

The savings are dramatic. A **2048 × 2048** kernel has **4,194,304** frozen parameters; with **rank 8**, the decomposition has only **32,768** (2 × 2048 × 8), 128 times fewer. The update is less expressive than the full kernel: at the narrow middle the whole update must pass through just **eight floats**. But fine-tuning does not need the expressive power pretraining needed (figure 16.4, on p.516).

The authors then state that the LoRA paper suggests freezing the entire Transformer and adding LoRA weights only to the **query and key** projections of attention (the paper itself recommends query and *value*; see the review flag). KerasHub has this built in: **Listing 16.13** enables it with one line, `gemma_lm.backbone.enable_lora(rank=8)`. A footnote cites J. Edward Hu et al., arXiv:2106.09685. LoRA freezes the pretrained kernel and learns an additive update alpha @ beta through a small inner rank. Forward pass: inputs @ kernel + (inputs @ alpha) @ beta. 2048×2048 kernel: 4,194,304 frozen parameters vs 32,768 trainable at rank 8 (128× fewer). Low rank limits expressive power, but fine-tuning needs much less than pretraining. KerasHub enables LoRA on a backbone with `enable_lora(rank=8)` (listing 16.13). The book says query and key projections; the LoRA paper recommends query and value.
snippet: In 2021, Microsoft researchers proposed LoRA Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models to solve exactly the memory problem described on p.514. To explain it, the authors start…

title: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
text: A fine-tuning method that freezes pretrained weight matrices and learns an additive update factored as the product of two thin matrices. Instead of repainting the whole wall, you add a thin stripe; most fine-tuning changes can be described with very few directions. $y = xW + (x\,\alpha)\,\beta$, $W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times d_{out}}$ frozen, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times r}$, $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{out}}$ trainable. 2048×2048 kernel, rank 8: 32,768 trainable vs 4,194,304 frozen.
snippet: A fine-tuning method that freezes pretrained weight matrices and learns an additive update factored as the product of two thin matrices.

title: Low-rank matrix
text: A matrix whose rank (number of independent rows/columns) is much smaller than its dimensions; it factors as a product of thin matrices. A big table that can be rebuilt from a few column patterns and a few row weightings. $\operatorname{rank}(\alpha\beta) \le r$ for $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times r}, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times n}$. $m=n=2048$, $r=8$: 32,768 vs 4,194,304.
snippet: A matrix whose rank number of independent rows/columns is much smaller than its dimensions; it factors as a product of thin matrices.

title: Freezing parameters
text: Marking weights non-trainable so they are not updated. Lock the knobs you do not want to touch. `add_weight(..., trainable=False)` for the LoRA kernel. `self.kernel = self.add_weight(shape=(input_dim, output_dim), trainable=False)`.
snippet: Marking weights non-trainable so they are not updated.

title: LoRA forward pass
text: frozen = ops.matmul(inputs, self.kernel); update = ops.matmul(ops.matmul(inputs, self.alpha), self.beta); return frozen + update y = xW + (x\,\alpha)\,\beta = x\,(W + \alpha\beta) Learn a weight update without training W. The output is the pretrained projection plus a correction confined to an r-dimensional subspace. x input, shape (…, input_dim) W frozen kernel, (input_dim, output_dim) \alpha trainable down-projection, (input_dim, rank) \beta trainable up-projection, (rank, output_dim) y output, (…, output_dim)
snippet: frozen = ops.matmulinputs, self.kernel; update = ops.matmulops.matmulinputs, self.alpha, self.beta; return frozen + update — Learn a weight update without training W.

title: Parameter count: full kernel versus low-rank update
text: If our kernel is shape 2048 × 2048, that is 4,194,304 frozen parameters. But if we keep the rank low, say, 8, we will have only 32,768 parameters \underbrace{d_{in}\,d_{out}}_{\text{full}} = 2048^2 = 4{,}194{,}304 \qquad \underbrace{r\,(d_{in}+d_{out})}_{\text{LoRA}} = 8\cdot(2048+2048) = 32{,}768 Quantify the savings. Ratio 4,194,304 / 32,768 = 128; it grows as d/(2r) for square kernels. d_{in}, d_{out} kernel input and output dimensions r LoRA rank
snippet: If our kernel is shape 2048 × 2048, that is 4,194,304 frozen parameters. But if we keep the rank low, say, 8, we will have only 32,768 parameters — Quantify the savings.

title: LoRA's low-rank decomposition and per-layer LoRA control
text:
Figure 16.4 (frozen kernel plus trainable alpha/beta low-rank matrices), a sidebar showing how to enable LoRA layer by layer on Gemma's attention projections, and the start of the post-LoRA model summary. LoRA keeps the huge pretrained (hidden_size, hidden_size) kernel frozen and learns only two thin matrices of shapes (hidden_size, rank) and (rank, hidden_size); in KerasHub this can be switched on for the whole backbone at once or, with more control, on individual Dense projections inside each decoder block. The page opens with **Figure 16.4**, which visualizes the LoRA layer sketched as `LoraLinear` on p.515. On the left, a large blue square labelled *Pretrained weights (hidden_size, hidden_size)* sits between *Inputs* and *Outputs*: this is the frozen kernel. Next to it, two green trapezoids form a narrow-waisted path: *Alpha (hidden_size, rank)* squeezes the input down to `rank` dimensions, and *Beta (rank, hidden_size)* expands it back. The caption makes the key point: the low-rank decomposition contains **far fewer parameters** than the kernel itself (with the numbers of p.515: 2048 × 2048 = 4,194,304 frozen weights versus 2 × 2048 × 8 = 32,768 trainable ones).

A sidebar, **Customizing LoRA training**, then explains that `enable_lora()` is not just a backbone-level convenience (listing 16.13, `gemma_lm.backbone.enable_lora(rank=8)`); it is also a method of individual `Dense` layers. The sidebar's code first freezes the whole backbone (`gemma_lm.backbone.trainable = False`), then loops over `gemma_lm.backbone.num_layers` decoder blocks, fetches each with `get_layer(f"decoder_block_{i}")`, and for both `attention.key_dense` and `attention.query_dense` sets `trainable = True` and calls `enable_lora(rank=8)`. The authors present this as an equivalent, more verbose version of the one-liner, and note that this style lets you put more trainable parameters earlier or later in the network, or add LoRA to the **value** projection too.

Finally, the main text calls `gemma_lm.summary()` again. On this page we only see the head of the output: the preprocessor `gemma3_causal_lm_preprocessor` with its `gemma3_tokenizer` (vocab size 262,144), and the start of the `gemma3_causal_lm` model table. The rest, including the crucial trainable-parameter count (1,304,576, about 5 MB), is on p.517.

*Note (not in the book):* to my knowledge KerasHub's default LoRA targets are the query and value projections, which is also the configuration recommended by the LoRA paper; see the review flag. Figure 16.4: a frozen (hidden_size, hidden_size) kernel in parallel with trainable alpha (hidden_size, rank) and beta (rank, hidden_size); their outputs are added. LoRA's trainable parameter count is 2·hidden_size·rank per square projection, e.g. 32,768 vs 4,194,304 for hidden_size 2048, rank 8. `enable_lora(rank=...)` is a per-layer Keras method; `backbone.enable_lora` is a convenience that applies it to default attention projections. Per-layer control (freeze all, then unfreeze + enable LoRA on chosen projections) lets you vary depth, rank and which of query/key/value get adapted. Check `summary()` to confirm the trainable count before training; the numbers are on p.517.
snippet: The page opens with Figure 16.4, which visualizes the LoRA layer sketched as LoraLinear on p.515. On the left, a large blue square labelled Pretrained weights hiddensize,…

title: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
text: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that freezes a pretrained weight matrix and learns an additive update expressed as the product of two thin matrices, alpha (hidden_size × rank) and beta (rank × hidden_size). Instead of repainting a whole mural, you add a thin transparent overlay that can only express a few broad strokes; fine-tuning needs only those few strokes. Output = x·W0 + (x·A)·B. Only A and B receive gradients, so optimizer memory scales with r·(d_in + d_out) rather than d_in·d_out per adapted layer. hidden_size = 2048, rank = 8: 4,194,304 frozen kernel parameters vs 32,768 LoRA parameters (p.515).
snippet: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that freezes a pretrained weight matrix and learns an additive update expressed as the product of two thin matrices, alpha hiddensize ×…

title: Low-rank matrix product
text: A matrix that can be written as the product of a (d × r) and an (r × d) matrix with r much smaller than d; its rank is at most r. All information must squeeze through r numbers at the narrow middle point, like the waist of the two trapezoids in Figure 16.4. rank(AB) ≤ min(rank(A), rank(B)) ≤ r. Storage is 2dr instead of d². For d = 1152 (Gemma3-1B) and r = 8: 2 × 1152 × 8 = 18,432 numbers instead of 1,327,104 for a square matrix.
snippet: A matrix that can be written as the product of a d × r and an r × d matrix with r much smaller than d; its rank is at most r.

title: Freezing layers (trainable = False)
text: Marking a layer or model as non-trainable so its weights receive no updates and need no optimizer state. Locking parts of the machine so only selected knobs can turn. In Keras, setting `trainable` on a model propagates to all its sublayers; setting it back to True on a specific sublayer re-enables only that sublayer. `gemma_lm.backbone.trainable = False` followed by `layer.attention.key_dense.trainable = True`.
snippet: Marking a layer or model as non-trainable so its weights receive no updates and need no optimizer state.

title: Query/key/value projections
text: The dense projections in a Transformer attention layer that map each token representation to query, key and value vectors. Queries ask, keys advertise, values carry the content; LoRA adjusts how the model asks and advertises. In KerasHub's Gemma decoder blocks they are accessible as `layer.attention.query_dense`, `key_dense` and `value_dense`. For Gemma3-1B, the query projection maps 1152 → 4 heads × 256 and the key/value projections map 1152 → 1 head × 256 (grouped-query attention); not shown on the page.
snippet: The dense projections in a Transformer attention layer that map each token representation to query, key and value vectors.

title: LoRA's memory savings and fine-tuning Gemma
text:
The post-LoRA model summary (1,304,576 trainable out of 1,001,190,528 parameters), Figure 16.5 on where training memory goes, and listing 16.14, which instruction-tunes Gemma for one epoch and reaches 55% next-token accuracy. After enabling LoRA, only about 5 MB of Gemma's 3.7 GB of weights are trainable, so gradients and optimizer state shrink from gigabytes to megabytes and the 1B-parameter model can be fine-tuned with an ordinary `compile()`/`fit()` call. The page completes the `gemma_lm.summary()` output started on p.516. The model has two inputs (`padding_mask` and `token_ids`, both `(None, None)`), the `gemma3_backbone` producing `(None, None, 1152)` hidden states with 1,001,190,… parameters (truncated in the table), and a `token_embedding` layer of type `ReversibleEmbedding` with output `(None, None, 262144)` and 301,989,888 parameters, which projects hidden states back to vocabulary logits. The totals are what matter: **Total params: 1,001,190,528 (3.73 GB)**, **Trainable params: 1,304,576 (4.98 MB)**, **Non-trainable params: 999,885,952 (3.72 GB)**.

The authors stress that the weights still occupy 3.7 GB, but the trainable part is only 5 MB, which they call 'a thousandfold decrease'. Because gradients and optimizer variables are needed only for trainable parameters, optimizer state drops 'from many gigabytes to just megabytes'. **Figure 16.5** illustrates this with a bar of memory blocks, `Total memory = parameters + gradients + optimizer state + forward pass`: in the *Normal* row, gradients and especially optimizer state take up most of the bar; in the *LoRA* row, parameters are unchanged, but gradients and optimizer state nearly vanish, leaving much of the bar free.

With memory under control, **listing 16.14** fine-tunes the model: `compile()` with `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True)`, `Adam(5e-5)`, and `weighted_metrics=[SparseCategoricalAccuracy()]`, then `fit(train_ds, validation_data=val_ds, epochs=1)`. After training, the model guesses the next word of the response correctly 55% of the time, versus 35% for the mini-GPT trained from scratch earlier in the chapter, which the authors attribute to a larger model and more extensive pretraining. After LoRA: 1,001,190,528 total parameters (3.73 GB), only 1,304,576 trainable (4.98 MB). LoRA reduces gradient and optimizer memory, not parameter or activation memory (Figure 16.5). Listing 16.14 uses next-token crossentropy from logits, `Adam(5e-5)`, sample-weighted accuracy and one epoch. `weighted_metrics` makes the metric respect the response-only sample weights. Fine-tuned Gemma reaches 55% next-token accuracy on responses vs 35% for the from-scratch mini-GPT.

title: Testing the instruction-tuned Gemma: better answers, same hallucinations
text:
Qualitative evaluation of the LoRA instruction-fine-tuned Gemma 1B: it now answers questions, but still hallucinates. After one epoch of LoRA instruction tuning, Gemma responds to instructions in the trained format and stops with [end], instead of continuing the prompt; yet it still confidently invents an answer to an impossible question, which instruction tuning can only partly mitigate (e.g., by training refusals). Having fine-tuned Gemma 1B with LoRA on the Dolly instructions (listing 16.14, p.517), the authors check whether it now follows directions. They call `gemma_lm.generate()` with prompts written in the **exact training template**, `"[instruction]\n…[end]\n[response]\n"`, and `max_length=512`.

Asked *How can I make brownies?*, the model replies with a recipe-like answer: mix flour, sugar, butter, milk and chocolate chips, bake in a 9x13 pan for 30 minutes at 350°F, optionally add vanilla, and it ends with `[end]`. Asked *What is a proper noun?*, it gives a reasonable definition with examples ("The White House", "The Eiffel Tower"), again terminated by `[end]`. The authors' verdict: **"Much better."** The model now **responds to questions instead of simply carrying on the thought of the prompt text**, which was the problem with the base model on p.510-511.

*Note (not in the book):* the answers are fluent but not flawless: the recipe lists "1/2 cup of chocolate chips" twice and omits eggs, a small reminder that fluency is not correctness.

Then the key test: **Have we solved the hallucination problem?** Asked *Who is the 542nd president of the United States?*, the model answers confidently, "The 542nd president of the United States was James A. Garfield." The answer: **"Not at all."** Instruction tuning can still make **some inroads**: a common technique is to train on many instruction/response pairs whose desired response is a refusal such as `"I don't know"` or `"As a language model, I cannot help you with that"`, teaching the model to avoid answering topics where it would often give poor-quality results. Prompts at inference use the exact training template `[instruction]\n…[end]\n[response]\n`. After LoRA instruction tuning, Gemma answers questions and ends with `[end]` instead of continuing the prompt. Hallucination is not solved: the model still names a '542nd president'. Training on refusal responses ('I don't know') can reduce hallucinations on specific topics. Fine-tuning shapes format and behaviour more than factual knowledge.

title: Going further with LLMs: from supervised fine-tuning to RLHF
text:
Why supervised fine-tuning is limited, and how RLHF uses human preference rankings to train a reward model that then supervises the LLM through reinforcement learning. Handwritten responses are slow, expensive and capped at human performance; what we really want to optimize is human preference. RLHF starts from supervised fine-tuning, trains a reward model on human rankings of responses, and then improves the LLM by letting it learn from rewards on its own generated outputs. Section **16.4 Going further with LLMs** opens by noting that we have trained a GPT model from scratch and fine-tuned a language model into a chatbot, but this only scratches the surface. The section will cover a non-exhaustive list of extensions to the basic "autocomplete the internet" setup.

**16.4.1 RLHF.** The instruction tuning just performed is called **supervised fine-tuning** (SFT): supervised because we curate, by hand, the prompts and responses we want. Manual data has two problems: it is a **bottleneck** (slow and expensive), and it is limited by the **human performance ceiling**. To exceed human performance in a chatbot, we cannot rely on manually written outputs.

The real objective is our **preference** for some responses over others. With enough people this is perfectly well defined, but translating "our preferences" into a loss we can compute gradients of is tricky. **Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF)** addresses this.

The recipe: (1) start with SFT on handwritten prompts and responses as a baseline. (2) Build a **reward model** as a proxy for human preference: gather many prompts and candidate responses (handwritten, generated by the model, or by other chatbots), and have human evaluators **rank** the responses for each prompt from most to least helpful. This is slow and expensive but faster than writing all the desired responses. (3) Train the reward model on this ranked dataset: it takes a **prompt-response pair** and outputs **a single float**, higher meaning better; it is usually **another, smaller Transformer** that reads the whole sequence instead of predicting the next token. (4) Use the reward model to tune the LLM with **reinforcement learning**, which the authors define broadly as any setup where a model learns by making predictions (**actions**) and receiving feedback on them (**rewards**). In short, the model's own predictions become its training data. The concrete loop follows on p.520. Instruction tuning on curated examples is called supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Manual examples are a bottleneck and cap performance at human level. The true objective is human preference, which is hard to express as a differentiable loss. RLHF: SFT baseline → human rankings of responses → reward model (prompt+response → float, usually a smaller Transformer) → RL tuning. Reinforcement learning = learning from rewards on one's own actions; the model's predictions become its training data.

title: The simplest RLHF loop, and loading an instruction-tuned Gemma
text:
Pseudocode for a minimal RLHF algorithm (generate, score, filter, fine-tune), its limitations and iterative nature, and loading the 4B instruction-tuned Gemma 3 checkpoint. In RLHF for LLMs the action is generating a response and the reward is a regression model's score; the simplest algorithm keeps high-reward responses and fine-tunes on them, while practical algorithms use all responses. Companies release such preference-tuned 'instruct' models, like gemma3_instruct_4b. The page makes the RL vocabulary of p.519 concrete. For an LLM, the **action** is simply generating a response to a prompt with `generate()`, and the **reward** is applying a separate **regression model** (the reward model) to that output string.

**Listing 16.15** gives the simplest possible RLHF algorithm in pseudocode: for each batch of prompts, generate responses (*takes an action*), score them with `reward_model.predict` (*receives a reward*), keep those with `score > cutoff`, and call `model.fit(good_responses)` (*updates the model parameters; the reward model is not updated*). In effect, the "good" outputs become new data for more supervised fine-tuning, as in section 16.3.

The authors note that in practice you usually **don't discard bad responses**: specialized gradient update algorithms use **all responses and rewards**, since a bad response is a good signal of what not to do. OpenAI described RLHF in a 2022 paper (footnote 5, Ouyang et al.) and used this setup to go from GPT-3's pretrained parameters to the first ChatGPT (see review flag on the history). The setup is also **iterative**: the improved model generates better responses, humans rank them, and a better reward model is trained.

Under the heading *Using a chatbot trained with RLHF* (printed with the odd number "4.1.1."), the authors propose trying a model trained with such iterative preference tuning. Because chatbots are the "killer app" of large Transformers, companies that release pretrained models like Gemma also release **instruction-tuned** versions built for chat. **Listing 16.16** loads `"gemma3_instruct_4b"` with `CausalLM.from_preset` and `dtype="bfloat16"`: a **4-billion-parameter** model, four times the size of the previous one and the largest used in the book. The dtype choice is explained on p.521. For LLMs, action = generating a response; reward = a separate regression model's score. Simplest RLHF: generate, score, keep responses above a cutoff, fine-tune on them; the reward model stays fixed. Practical RLHF uses all responses with specialized gradient algorithms, since bad responses carry signal. RLHF is iterative: better model → new rankings → better reward model. Model providers release instruction-tuned checkpoints; Listing 16.16 loads gemma3_instruct_4b in bfloat16 (4B params, largest in the book).

title: bfloat16 for big models and a first chat with instruction-tuned Gemma
text:
Why the 4B instruction-tuned Gemma is loaded in bfloat16, the chat prompt template it expects, and a first question-answer exchange with it For billion-parameter models, bytes per parameter decide whether the model fits in memory; for inference-only use, 2-byte bfloat16 halves memory versus float32. An instruction-tuned checkpoint must be prompted with the same turn markers it was tuned with, and the result is a model that answers questions far more helpfully than a raw pretrained one. **Sidebar: choosing a dtype for large models.** The first Gemma model (p.509) was loaded with `dtype="float32"`; the 4-billion-parameter instruction-tuned Gemma in Listing 16.16 (p.520) uses `dtype="bfloat16"`. The sidebar explains why. For models with more than a billion parameters, the **number of bytes per floating-point number** becomes a key consideration. When **training**, 32 bits (4 bytes) per parameter is often a good idea, because float32 can represent very small values and helps keep **gradients stable**. Here the model is only used for **inference**, so `bfloat16` (2 bytes per parameter) is enough: there are no gradients to worry about, and the lower precision saves "many gigabytes" of memory. For a 4B model that is roughly 16 GB versus 8 GB of weights. Chapter 18 (pp.582-583) treats floating-point precision in detail.

**A chat template.** Like the model fine-tuned in section 16.3.2, this instruction-tuned checkpoint expects a specific input format. The exact wording does not matter in principle; what matters is that **the prompt template matches what was used to tune the model**. Gemma's template wraps the user's text between `<start_of_turn>user` and `<end_of_turn>`, then opens a `<start_of_turn>model` turn so the model's continuation is its reply.

**A first question.** Asked "Why can't you assign values in Jax tensors? Be brief!", the model returns a short, on-topic answer ending with `<end_of_turn>`, its learned signal that the reply is complete.

**Where the ability comes from.** The authors say this model was pretrained on 14 trillion tokens (see the review flag: the Gemma 3 report gives that figure for the 27B model) and then extensively fine-tuned using three things: **supervised fine-tuning** as in section 16.3.2, **RLHF** as in section 16.4.1, and other techniques such as using an **even larger model as a "teacher"**. The improvement in question answering is easy to see. The page ends by setting up a retry of the hallucination-prone question from earlier pages (the "542nd president" prompt, answered on p.522). Weight memory is params x bytes per param: 4B params take about 16 GB in float32 and about 8 GB in bfloat16. Use float32 (or mixed precision) for training stability; 16-bit formats are fine for inference only. bfloat16 keeps float32's range but has far less precision. Prompt an instruction-tuned model with exactly the chat template it was tuned with. The tuned model's helpfulness comes from post-training (SFT, RLHF, teacher models) on top of large-scale pretraining, not from a new architecture.

title: bfloat16 precision
text: A 16-bit floating-point format with 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 7 mantissa bits; 2 bytes per value. It is float32 with the last 16 bits of the mantissa chopped off: same range of magnitudes, coarser steps between neighbouring values. The relative spacing between representable numbers (machine epsilon) is 2^-7, about 0.0078, versus 2^-23, about 1.2e-7, for float32. Its maximum is about 3.4e38, like float32, unlike float16's 65,504. Gemma 4B: 4e9 x 2 bytes is about 8 GB in bfloat16, versus 16 GB in float32.

title: Whack-a-mole hallucinations and the idea of soft image tokens
text:
How an instruction-tuned Gemma avoids one hallucination but invents another, and how a Transformer LLM can accept images by turning them into a sequence of 'soft tokens' Instruction tuning and RLHF can teach a model to refuse a trick question, but hallucination is suppressed case by case rather than cured. Separately, because a Transformer is a general sequence learner, images can be fed to an LLM by encoding them into 256 vectors of the model's hidden size (2560 for the 4B Gemma) and splicing these 'soft tokens' into the text-embedding sequence. **The trick question, revisited.** The page opens by sending the instruction-tuned 4-billion-parameter Gemma (loaded on p.520 with the chat `PROMPT_TEMPLATE` from p.521) the question that tripped up earlier models: *"Who is the 542nd president of the United States?"* The base model on p.511 and the model fine-tuned in section 16.3.2 (p.518) both confidently answered "James A. Garfield". This model instead says it is a trick question, that the United States "has only had 46 presidents", and adds a friendly remark.

The authors stress two points. First, the improvement is **not a new modeling technique**: it comes from extensive training on trick questions with responses like this one (the supervised and RLHF tuning described on p.521). Second, the same answer shows why fixing hallucinations is like **whack-a-mole**: while refusing to invent a president, the model invents *today's date* ("November 2, 2023"). A language model has no clock; that date is just a plausible continuation.

**16.4.2 Multimodal LLMs.** A chatbot that can also take audio and images would be far more useful. Conceptually this is simple, because the Transformer is not a text-specific model but a model for *learning patterns in sequence data*. If you can turn another data type into a sequence of vectors, you can feed it to a Transformer and train.

The Gemma model already does this. It ships with a separate **420-million-parameter image encoder** that cuts an image into **256 patches** and encodes each as a vector of the same size as Gemma's hidden dimension, **2560**. An image therefore becomes a `(256, 2560)` sequence that can be **spliced into the text sequence right after the token embedding layer**. Each `(1, 2560)` vector is a **soft token**. Ordinary **hard tokens** can take only one of a fixed set of vectors, the rows of the embedding matrix. Soft tokens can be *any* vector the vision encoder produces. The page ends by downloading a test image (`learned-python.png`) with `keras.utils.get_file`. The image is displayed on p.523 (figure 16.7), and the splicing is drawn in figure 16.6. The instruction-tuned Gemma refuses the 542nd-president premise because of training data, not a new modeling technique. Hallucination suppression is whack-a-mole: the same answer invents today's date. A Transformer learns patterns in sequence data, not specifically text, so other modalities only need to be turned into sequences of vectors. Gemma's ~420M-parameter image encoder turns an image into 256 vectors of size 2560, a (256, 2560) sequence spliced in after the token embedding layer. Hard tokens are fixed embedding-matrix rows chosen by ID; soft tokens are arbitrary vectors produced by the encoder.

title: Hallucination
text: Generation of fluent but false or unsupported statements by a language model. The model's job is to write what plausibly comes next, and a plausible date or name is easy to write even when no true one exists. Sampling from p(token | past tokens) learned from data. The objective rewards likelihood, not truth. Fine-tuning shifts probability mass for prompt patterns it covers. Uncovered patterns, such as 'what is today's date', still yield confident inventions. The instruct Gemma refuses the 542nd-president premise but states 'As of today, November 2, 2023', a date it cannot know.
snippet: Generation of fluent but false or unsupported statements by a language model.

title: Multimodal LLM
text: A language model that processes inputs from more than one modality, here images together with text, in a single Transformer sequence. Translate the image into 'words' the Transformer understands, namely vectors of the right size, and then let it read them like any other tokens. A separate encoder maps the image to $(256, d_{model})$ vectors, which are concatenated with text token embeddings and processed by the unchanged decoder stack. Gemma 3 4B: 420M-parameter image encoder, 256 soft tokens of dimension 2560 per image.
snippet: A language model that processes inputs from more than one modality, here images together with text, in a single Transformer sequence.

title: Soft token (vs. hard token)
text: A vector inserted directly into a Transformer's input sequence (e.g. by a vision encoder), as opposed to a hard token, which is a row of the embedding matrix selected by an integer ID. Hard tokens are words from a fixed dictionary; soft tokens are free-form vectors that can say things no dictionary entry can. Hard: $e = E[t]$ with $E \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}$, $t \in \{0,\dots,|V|-1\}$, so there are only $|V|$ possible vectors. Soft: $s = f_{\text{enc}}(\text{patch}) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, any continuous value. Each image yields 256 soft tokens of shape (1, 2560).
snippet: A vector inserted directly into a Transformer's input sequence e.g. by a vision encoder, as opposed to a hard token, which is a row of the embedding matrix selected by an integer…

title: Transformer as a general sequence model
text: The book's characterization here: not a text-specific model but a highly effective learner of patterns in sequence data. It operates on lists of vectors; where the vectors come from is irrelevant to it. Self-attention and feedforward sublayers map $\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} \to \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with no reference to vocabulary. Splicing a (256, 2560) image sequence into a text sequence.
snippet: The book's characterization here: not a text-specific model but a highly effective learner of patterns in sequence data.

title: Hard tokens, soft tokens, and the spliced input sequence
text: Each image will be embedded as a (256, 2560) sequence. ... this image representation can simply be spliced into our text sequence after the token embedding layer. ... each (1, 2560) vector is sometimes called a "soft token" \begin{aligned} h_j &= E[t_j] \in \mathbb{R}^{2560} \quad (\text{hard token}) \\ S &= f_{\text{enc}}(\text{image}) \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 2560} \quad (\text{soft tokens}) \\ X &= [\,h_1;\dots;h_k;\ S;\ h_{k+1};\dots;h_n\,] \in \mathbb{R}^{(n+256) \times 2560} \end{aligned} Formalizes the page's description of how images enter the LLM after the token embedding layer. The decoder sees one matrix with n + 256 rows. Each hard row is one of |V| fixed vectors. Each soft row can be any point in R^2560. t_j integer ID of the j-th text token E token embedding matrix of shape (vocabulary size, 2560) h_j embedding vector of the j-th text (hard) token f_{\text{enc}} the separate ~420M-parameter image encoder S the image's 256 soft tokens, one 2560-dim row each k position in the text where the image is inserted n number of text tokens X the combined sequence fed to the decoder blocks

title: Figure 16.6: splicing hard and soft tokens; the test image
text: Displaying the test image and the diagram of how image soft tokens and text hard tokens are merged before the Transformer Figure 16.6 shows the mechanism from p.522. Text tokens (including `` placeholders) pass through the text-embedding matrix and become green 'hard' tokens. Image patches pass through the image encoder and become orange 'soft' tokens. The two are interleaved into one sequence for a stack of decoder blocks. Figure 16.7 is the test image used next. This page is mostly visual and finishes the image-loading code from p.522. **Code.** The downloaded file at `image_path` is read with `keras.utils.load_img`, which returns a PIL image, and converted to a NumPy array with `np.array`, giving a `(height, width, 3)` uint8 array. It is then shown with matplotlib, with the axes hidden. The array `image` is what is passed to Gemma on p.524 (`"images": [image]`). **Figure 16.6, "Handling image input by splicing text tokens and soft image tokens together."** On the left, the text prompt `What is ?` passes through a grid labelled **Text embedding** (the embedding matrix). Each token becomes a green **"hard" token**. title: Asking Gemma about an image; how multimodal LLMs are trained
text:
Running the multimodal Gemma on the test image and the training recipe for vision-language models A `<start_of_image>` marker in the prompt expands to 256 placeholder positions, which are filled with the image encoder's soft tokens. Training such a model is ordinary next-token pretraining and fine-tuning on mixed image-text sequences, with the loss zeroed at image positions. **Querying the image.** Using the test image loaded on p.523 (Figure 16.7, a snake in glasses reading in an armchair), the authors first set two preprocessor options. `max_images_per_prompt = 1` and `sequence_length = 512` **limit the maximum input size of the model**: at most one image and 512 total tokens per prompt. Each prompt ends with the special token `<start_of_image>`. It is formatted with the chat `PROMPT_TEMPLATE` from p.521 and passed to `generate()` as a dict, `{"prompts": ..., "images": [image]}`.

Asked "What is going on in this image? Be concise!", Gemma answers that a snake wearing glasses is sitting in a leather armchair surrounded by a large bookshelf, reading a book, and calls the image "whimsical, slightly surreal". Asked "What is the snake wearing?", it says a pair of red-framed glasses "perched on its head". The model has clearly grounded its text in the picture.

**What `<start_of_image>` does.** Inside the model the token is expanded into **256 placeholder values** in the input sequence. These are then **replaced by the 256 soft tokens** that the image encoder produced (p.522: a `(256, 2560)` array matching Gemma's hidden size).

**How such a model is trained.** It is very similar to ordinary LLM pretraining and fine-tuning:
1. Usually **pretrain the image encoder separately** first, as the book first did with image models in chapter 8.
2. Then run the same **"guess the next word" pretraining** on sequences that **mix image and text content**.
3. The Transformer is **not trained to output image soft tokens**: the **loss is zeroed at the image token positions**.

**Why it works.** It is "quite an expected result": a Transformer is a powerful general sequence model. Recast the image as sequence data and train a lot, and the model keeps its original ability to read and write text while also learning to embed images into its latent space. <start_of_image> expands to 256 placeholder positions that are filled with the image encoder's soft tokens. The preprocessor's max_images_per_prompt and sequence_length cap the model's input size; each image costs 256 positions. Multimodal training = pretrained image encoder + ordinary next-token training on mixed image-text sequences. The loss is zeroed at image token positions; the model reads images but is not trained to output them. A Transformer is a general sequence model, so recasting images as sequences makes multimodality an 'expected' result.

title: Multimodal LLM
text: A language model that accepts (and possibly produces) data of several modalities, such as text and images, by representing all of them as one sequence of vectors. Translate the picture into 'words' (vectors) the Transformer can read, then let it read everything together. An image encoder maps the image to N soft tokens of the LLM's hidden size (N=256, d=2560 for Gemma 4B). These are spliced into the token-embedding sequence at the placeholder positions. 'What is the snake wearing?' gives 'a pair of glasses! They are red-framed...'

title: Soft token
text: An input vector placed in the Transformer's sequence that comes from an encoder, not from the token embedding table. A 'word' with no spelling, just a meaning vector. Hard tokens are restricted to the rows of the embedding matrix; soft tokens can be any vector in R^2560. <start_of_image> becomes 256 placeholders, which become 256 soft tokens.

title: Loss masking
text: Excluding some sequence positions from the training loss by giving them zero weight. You only grade the answers you want the model to learn to write. The per-token cross-entropy is multiplied by a 0/1 mask and averaged over the unmasked positions. Mask = 0 for the 256 image positions; 1 for the text tokens that follow.

title: Foundation models, and why plain LLMs make poor search engines
text:
The definition and hallmarks of foundation models, and the motivation for retrieval-augmented generation Foundation models are models of any modality that are trained on broad data with self-supervised (reconstruction) objectives and then adapted to many downstream tasks. Starting from such a model now usually beats training from scratch. Used as a search engine, though, an LLM hallucinates and has a knowledge cutoff. RAG fixes this by using the LLM as a conversational interface over information retrieved by traditional search. **Foundation models (sidebar-style subsection).** Now that LLMs handle images, audio and maybe structured data, the name "large language model" can mislead: they *do* model language, but not only language. The next chapter introduces **diffusion models**, which are structurally very different but have the same feel: they are trained on massive "internet-scale" data with a **self-supervised loss**.

The umbrella term is **foundation models**: *any model trained on broad data (generally using self-supervision at scale) that can be fine-tuned to a wide range of downstream tasks*. One way to think about it: a foundation model learns to **reconstruct** internet data **given a partial representation of it**. Next-token prediction reconstructs the rest of a text from its prefix; masked modelling and denoising are other variants. LLMs are the first and best-known such models but not the only ones. The two **hallmarks** are (1) a **self-supervised, reconstruction-style objective** and (2) **not being specialized** to any single task.

The authors call this an important and striking recent shift in machine learning. Instead of training from scratch on your own dataset, you will often do better by taking a foundation model's **rich representation** of your input and **specializing** it for your task. The downside is having to run models with **billions of parameters**, so it is not a fit for every real-world application.

**16.4.3 Retrieval Augmented Generation.** Putting extra information into the prompt is not just for images; it is a general way to extend an LLM. Consider LLMs as search engines. Two **fatal flaws** appear:
- They **make things up**: false "facts" interpolated from, but not present in, the training data, ranging from misleading to dangerous.
- They have a **knowledge cutoff**, at best the pretraining date. Training is too expensive to do continuously, so their knowledge just stops.

Nobody wants a search engine stuck six months in the past. But if an LLM is seen as **"conversational software"** that can process any sequence in its prompt, we can use it as the **interface to information retrieved by traditional search**. That is **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**, detailed on p.526. A foundation model is trained on broad data with self-supervision at scale and then adapted to many downstream tasks. Its hallmarks are a reconstruction-style self-supervised objective and not being specialized to one task. LLMs are only one kind of foundation model; diffusion models (chapter 17) are another. Starting from a foundation model often beats training from scratch, at the cost of running billion-parameter models. Used naively as a search engine, an LLM hallucinates and has a knowledge cutoff. RAG uses the LLM as a conversational interface over information retrieved by traditional search.
snippet: Foundation models sidebar-style subsection. Now that LLMs handle images, audio and maybe structured data, the name "large language model" can mislead: they do model language, but…

title: Foundation model
text: Any model trained on broad data, generally with self-supervision at scale, that can be fine-tuned to a wide range of downstream tasks. A general-purpose 'base layer' of knowledge about some kind of data, on which many specific applications are built. The objective is a reconstruction loss from partial input (next-token, masked-token, denoising). It is adapted by fine-tuning, parameter-efficient tuning (LoRA), instruction tuning or prompting. Gemma (text + images), BERT (text encoder), diffusion models (images).
snippet: Any model trained on broad data, generally with self-supervision at scale, that can be fine-tuned to a wide range of downstream tasks.

title: Self-supervised learning (reconstruction objective)
text: Training where the targets come from the input data itself, typically by reconstructing data from a partial view. Hide part of the data and make the model guess it; the data grades itself. Examples: maximize p(x_t | x_<t) (causal LM), p(x_masked | x_visible) (MLM), or predict the clean image or the added noise from a noisy image (diffusion). Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens.
snippet: Training where the targets come from the input data itself, typically by reconstructing data from a partial view.

title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
text: Using an LLM as the interface to information retrieved by a separate search or retrieval system, by inserting that information into the prompt. An open-book exam instead of a closed-book one. Retrieve the top-k relevant passages for the query, build a prompt with the question and context, and generate an answer conditioned on the context. Detailed on p.526 with a sleep-advice prompt.
snippet: Using an LLM as the interface to information retrieved by a separate search or retrieval system, by inserting that information into the prompt.

title: Hallucination
text: LLM output presenting false 'facts' that are not in the training data but are interpolated from it. Confident filling-in of gaps with something plausible-sounding. It results from sampling high-probability continuations without any mechanism to verify facts. Naming a '542nd US president' (pp.511, 518).

title: How RAG works, and the start of 'reasoning' models
text:
The RAG pipeline with vector databases and its benefits, and why LLMs struggled with math until chain-of-thought prompting RAG retrieves relevant text (often by nearest-neighbour search over embedding vectors in a vector database) and pastes it into the prompt. This works around the knowledge cutoff, gives access to private data and reduces hallucinations. Separately, LLMs long failed at math and logic, until it was found that prompting them to 'show their work' (chain-of-thought) greatly improves accuracy because the model can attend to its own intermediate steps. **How RAG works.** RAG starts from the user's question and runs **some form of query** to pull in extra text context, from a database, a search engine or "anything that can give further information". That information is **added straight into the prompt**, for example:

> Use the following pieces of context to answer the question. Question: What are some good ways to improve sleep? Context: {text from a medical journal on improving sleep} Answer:

**Vector databases.** A common retrieval method. Use an LLM, or any model, to **embed each source document as a vector**. Store the document text in the database with its **embedding as the key**. At query time, **embed the user's query** with the same model, and the database **finds the key vectors closest to the query vector** and returns their text. The authors note that this resembles attention itself: the terms **query, key and value** actually came from database systems.

**Benefits of surfacing information:**
- an obvious way around the model's **cutoff date**;
- access to **private data**: a company can use a publicly trained LLM as an interface to privately stored information;
- **factual grounding**: there is no silver bullet against hallucinations, but an LLM is much less likely to make up facts when given correct context in the prompt.

**16.4.4 "Reasoning" models.** For years LLMs were **abysmal at math problems and logic puzzles**. They might answer a problem that appeared in training perfectly, but substituting a few names or numbers revealed that the model had no grasp of what it was solving. For many NLP problems, more data meant better benchmark scores, but **grade-school math defied progress**.

Then Google researchers noticed that prompting a model with a few examples of **"showing your work"**, writing out intermediate steps as on a homework assignment, made the model do the same, and it then reached correct answers far more often **by attending to its own output**. They called it **"chain-of-thought" prompting**. (The book dates this to 2023; the paper appeared in 2022, see the review flag.) The sentence about another research group continues on p.527. RAG = retrieve relevant text for the question, then put it straight into the prompt. Vector databases store document text keyed by embeddings and return the documents nearest to the embedded query. Query, key and value in attention are borrowed from database terminology; retrieval is a hard top-k version of attention's soft lookup. RAG works around cutoff dates, enables private data and helps ground facts, but does not eliminate hallucinations. LLMs long failed at math because they matched memorized patterns; changing names or numbers exposed this. Chain-of-thought prompting (showing your work) improves accuracy because the model attends to its own intermediate steps.
snippet: How RAG works. RAG starts from the user's question and runs some form of query to pull in extra text context, from a database, a search engine or "anything that can give further…

title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

title: Vector database
text: A database that stores document text with an embedding vector as its key and returns the documents whose keys are closest to a query vector. A library shelved by meaning: you walk to where your question 'lives' and take the nearby books. Index: k_i = embed(doc_i). Query: q = embed(question); return the top-k documents ranked by similarity (cosine or dot product), typically using approximate nearest-neighbour search. A query 'trouble falling asleep' retrieves an article titled 'Improving sleep onset'.
snippet: A database that stores document text with an embedding vector as its key and returns the documents whose keys are closest to a query vector.

title: Query/key/value (link to attention)
text: Database terminology adopted by attention: a query is compared with keys to decide which values to return. Attention is a 'soft' database lookup; a vector database is a 'hard' one. Attention: softmax(q·K^T / sqrt(d)) V gives a weighted average of values. A vector DB returns the top-k values by similarity, unblended. The book's remark that 'query', 'key' and 'value' came from database systems.
snippet: Database terminology adopted by attention: a query is compared with keys to decide which values to return.

title: Chain-of-thought prompting
text: Prompting an LLM, with worked examples or an instruction, to write out intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. Showing your work on homework helps you get the right answer. Generated steps become context that later tokens attend to, which adds computation and working memory per problem. Examples of step-by-step solutions in the prompt, or 'Let's think step by step' (p.527).

title: Chain-of-thought fine-tuning and a Gemma word-problem experiment
text:
Zero-shot chain-of-thought, the o1/r1 'reasoning' models, the RLHF-like recipe for chain-of-thought fine-tuning, and sampling several step-by-step answers from Gemma Simply asking a model to think step by step improves its answers. Reasoning models go further by training on their own correct step-by-step outputs, an RLHF-like loop: supervised examples, then generate, check the final answer, and tune on what worked. Sampling the instruction-tuned Gemma randomly on one word problem shows why such checking is needed: different samples reason differently, and one of them reaches a wrong answer. **Zero-shot chain-of-thought.** Completing the sentence from p.526: another research group noticed that **you didn't even need examples**. Prompting a model with **"Let's think step by step"** was enough to get better output.

**Reasoning models.** Since then there has been heavy interest in **training** LLMs directly to get better at chain-of-thought reasoning. **OpenAI's o1** and **DeepSeek's r1** made headlines with big gains in math and coding by training models to **"think out loud"** on difficult questions.

**The recipe is very similar to RLHF:**
1. Train on a few **supervised examples** of showing your work and reaching a correct answer.
2. **Prompt** the model with new math questions and **check whether the final answer is correct**.
3. **Use these generated outputs to further tune** the model's weights.

The difference from RLHF is that the reward is not a learned preference model; it is a simple **correctness check** on the final answer.

**Trying it with Gemma.** The authors write a word problem: *"Judy wrote a 2-page letter to 3 friends twice a week for 3 months. How many letters did she write? Be brief, and add "ANSWER:" before your final answer."* The `ANSWER:` marker makes the final answer easy to extract by string parsing (used on p.528). They then call `gemma_lm.compile(sampler="random")`, which **turns on random sampling to get a diverse range of outputs**: each call samples a different chain of thought.

**Response 1.** 3 friends x 2 letters/week = 6 letters/week; x 4 weeks/month = 24 letters/month; x 3 months = 72 letters; then **"Total letters: 72 letters x 2 = 144 letters"**, giving `ANSWER: 144`. The last step multiplies by the number of **pages**, a distractor, so 144 is wrong under the book's intended reading (72).

**Response 2** starts the same way (6 letters/week) and is completed on p.528, where it reaches 72. The two samples illustrate the point of the recipe: random sampling produces both correct and incorrect chains, and an automatic answer check can separate them. 'Let's think step by step' (zero-shot CoT) improves output without any examples. Reasoning models (o1, r1) are trained to think out loud; their training is very similar to RLHF. Recipe: supervised examples of showing work, then generate answers to new problems, check the final answers, and tune on the outputs. An 'ANSWER:' marker makes final answers machine-checkable. sampler="random" yields diverse reasoning paths, which here lead to both a wrong answer (144) and a right one (72).

The policy is the LLM, actions are generated sequences, and the reward is a binary output from a program (string match on 'ANSWER:', unit tests). title: Model size flattens, data grows: Figure 16.8
text:
Recent LLM scaling trends: parameter counts levelling off while pretraining dataset sizes keep rising; continued investment in scale Once it became clear that GPT-3-era models were too big for their compute (a smaller model trained on more data does better), parameter counts trended flatter while training data grew by orders of magnitude. Scaling compute still improves next-token prediction with no plateau in sight, so companies keep investing billions. **Finishing the compute argument (from p.528).** With a fixed pretraining budget you must split floating-point operations between **model size** and **amount of data**. Research showed GPT-3 (175B parameters) was too large for its budget: a smaller model trained on more data would give **better model performance**. "So recently, **model sizes have trended flatter while data sizes have trended up**."

**Scaling is not over.** The authors stress that this does *not* mean scaling will stop. More computing power **does** generally lead to better LLM performance, and there is **no sign yet of an asymptote** where next-token prediction performance levels off. Companies keep investing **billions of dollars** in scaling LLMs to see what new capabilities emerge.

**Figure 16.8** shows major LLMs released from 2018 to 2025. Both panels have log-scale y-axes.
- **Top, parameters (billions):** GPT-1 (~0.1B, 2018), BERT and RoBERTa (~0.3B), GPT-2 (~1.5B, 2019), Turing-NLG (~17B, 2020), GPT-3 (~175B, 2020), Gopher (~280B, late 2021), BLOOM (~176B, 2022), Llama (~65B) and Llama 2 (~70B, 2023), Gemma (~7B, 2024), Gemma 2 (~27B, 2024), Llama 3 (~405B, 2024). After GPT-3, the points no longer climb steadily: many important models are *smaller*.
- **Bottom, pretraining tokens (billions):** a near-straight line on the log scale, from a few billion tokens (GPT-1) to about 300B (GPT-3, Gopher), about 1.4T (Llama), 2T (Llama 2), about 6T (Gemma) and about 13-15T (Gemma 2, Llama 3), roughly 1,000x growth in five years.

The caption notes that many recent **proprietary** LLMs (GPT-4, Gemini) are not included because their details have not been disclosed. The figure's BERT/RoBERTa token values look anomalously low (see review flags). Since GPT-3, model sizes have trended flatter while pretraining data has grown by orders of magnitude. A smaller model trained on more data can beat a larger, undertrained one at the same compute. More compute still improves next-token prediction, with no visible asymptote, so investment in scale continues. In Figure 16.8, parameters jump about 1,000x from 2018 to 2020 and then scatter (about 7B-405B), while tokens rise steadily to about 15T. Proprietary frontier models (GPT-4, Gemini) are absent from the figure because their details are undisclosed.

title: Why scaling alone won't carry LLMs, and the chapter 16 summary (part 1)
text:
The practical and data limits on simply making LLMs bigger, the role of reinforcement learning as a source of fresh training signal, and the first half of the chapter summary (LLM ingredients, sampling strategies, scale) Parameter counts have stopped growing monotonically because deployment cost matters and because high-quality human text is running out; reinforcement learning in self-contained environments is one way to keep generating training signal. The deeper problem is that LLMs learn far less efficiently than humans, yet they already enable fluent natural-language interfaces built on a simple recipe: Transformer + next-token prediction + lots of unlabeled text, plus a sampling strategy at generation time. The page finishes section 16.5. Building on figure 16.8 (p.529), the authors observe that **tokens used for pretraining have climbed steadily, while parameter counts have varied a lot since GPT-3**. Two reasons: GPT-3 is now known to have been *undertrained* for its size (p.528), and, practically, a smaller model that runs on cheaper hardware is often worth a small loss in quality, because a great model that is too expensive to serve is of limited use.

A second brake on naive scaling is **data scarcity**: companies are struggling to find more high-quality, public, human-written text, and models increasingly train on text produced by other LLMs ("eating their own tail"), which raises new concerns. This is one reason **reinforcement learning** is attracting attention: a difficult, self-contained *environment* that keeps generating new problems lets a model keep training on its own outputs instead of on scraped web text (compare the reasoning-model loop on p.527–528).

The authors then step back: none of these fixes is a silver bullet. The core problem is that **LLMs are wildly inefficient learners** compared to humans — their abilities come from reading orders of magnitude more text than any person ever will — so research into learning from limited data will continue alongside scaling. Still, fluent natural-language interfaces alone will reshape computing, and the chapter has shown the basic recipe behind them.

The **Summary** begins: an LLM combines (1) the Transformer, (2) a language-modeling task (predict the next token from past tokens) and (3) a large amount of unlabeled text. An LLM learns a probability distribution over the next token; a **sampling strategy** turns this into long text — *greedy search* (always the most likely token), *random sampling* (sample the full categorical distribution) and *top-K sampling* (sample only among the K most likely tokens). LLMs use billions of parameters and trillions of words of training text. The summary continues on p.531. Since GPT-3, data sizes have grown steadily but parameter counts vary: GPT-3 was undertrained, and smaller models are cheaper to deploy. High-quality human-written text is running out; training on LLM output raises new problems. RL in self-contained environments lets models keep training on their own (checked) outputs. LLMs are far less sample-efficient than humans; research on learning from limited data will continue. LLM = Transformer + next-token prediction + lots of unlabeled text, at the scale of billions of parameters and trillions of words. Greedy, random and top-K sampling turn the same next-token distribution into very different text.
snippet: The page finishes section 16.5. Building on figure 16.8 p.529, the authors observe that tokens used for pretraining have climbed steadily, while parameter counts have varied a lot…

title: Compute-optimal scaling (model size vs. data)
text: For a fixed training compute budget, there is a best split between model parameters and training tokens; GPT-3 put too much into parameters. A big brain that has read too little underperforms a smaller brain that has read much more, for the same total effort. Training flops grow roughly with parameters × tokens. Empirical studies (beyond the book: Hoffmann et al., 2022, 'Chinchilla') found compute-optimal models use roughly 20 tokens per parameter, far more than GPT-3's ~1.7. Training a smaller model on more tokens can beat a 175B-parameter model with the same compute.
snippet: For a fixed training compute budget, there is a best split between model parameters and training tokens; GPT-3 put too much into parameters.

title: Deployment cost trade-off
text: Choosing a smaller model than the best-performing one so it runs on cheaper hardware. A model you cannot afford to serve to users is of little practical use. Beyond the book: inference memory and latency scale with parameter count; a smaller model trained on more tokens can be cheaper to serve at similar quality. The book uses a 1-billion-parameter Gemma 3 model because it fits on a free Colab GPU (p.509).
snippet: Choosing a smaller model than the best-performing one so it runs on cheaper hardware.

title: Pretraining data scarcity
text: The supply of high-quality, public, human-written text is limited, constraining further scaling of dataset size. You can buy more GPUs, but not more books that humans have already written. Training on LLM-generated text ('eating their own tail') risks reinforcing errors and losing diversity. A web crawl increasingly contains AI-written pages, which then end up in the next model's training set.
snippet: The supply of high-quality, public, human-written text is limited, constraining further scaling of dataset size.

title: Reinforcement learning from a self-contained environment
text: Training a model by letting it attempt problems produced by an environment and learning from feedback on its own outputs. Like a student doing endless practice problems with an answer key, instead of reading more textbooks. For LLMs the environment can generate verifiable tasks (math, code); correct trajectories are rewarded or kept for fine-tuning (p.527–528). Sampling several chain-of-thought solutions to a math problem, checking the final answers, and fine-tuning on the correct ones.
snippet: Training a model by letting it attempt problems produced by an environment and learning from feedback on its own outputs.

title: Sampling strategy
text: The rule that turns the model's next-token distribution into an actual token during generation. The model proposes odds; the sampling strategy decides how adventurous to be when betting. Greedy: argmax. Random: sample the softmax (possibly temperature-scaled). Top-K: zero out all but the K largest probabilities, renormalize, sample. Greedy decoding of the mini-GPT got stuck repeating phrases; top-K produced more plausible English (p.505–508).
snippet: The rule that turns the model's next-token distribution into an actual token during generation.

title: Large language model (LLM)
text: A Transformer trained to predict the next token on a large amount of unlabeled text, with billions of parameters. An extremely well-read autocomplete. Learns $P(x_t\mid x_{<t})$ with cross-entropy loss; generation repeatedly samples from this distribution. The mini-GPT (p.494) and Gemma 3 (p.509).
snippet: A Transformer trained to predict the next token on a large amount of unlabeled text, with billions of parameters.

title: The three sampling strategies in the summary (formalized)
text: Greedy search takes the most likely predicted token at each generation step. Random sampling directly samples the predicted categorical distribution over all tokens. Top-K sampling restricts the categorical distribution to the top set of K candidates. \begin{aligned} p_i &= \frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}} \\ \text{greedy: } x_t &= \arg\max_i p_i \\ \text{random: } x_t &\sim \operatorname{Categorical}(p) \\ \text{top-}K\text{: } x_t &\sim \operatorname{Categorical}(\tilde p),\quad \tilde p_i = \frac{p_i\,\mathbb{1}[i\in \mathcal{K}]}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{K}} p_j} \end{aligned} Make precise the verbal definitions in the summary bullet. Greedy is the limit of random sampling as T → 0; top-K with K = 1 also equals greedy, and with K = vocabulary size equals random sampling. z_i logit for vocabulary token i output by the model at the current step T temperature (T = 1 is the plain softmax; p.506) p_i predicted probability of token i \mathcal{K} the set of the K tokens with the largest probabilities \tilde p the renormalized distribution restricted to the top K x_t the token chosen at step t
snippet: Greedy search takes the most likely predicted token at each generation step. Random sampling directly samples the predicted categorical distribution over all tokens. Top-K…

title: What are the three key ingredients of an LLM according to the chapter summary?
text: What are the three key ingredients of an LLM according to the chapter summary? The Transformer architecture, a language-modeling task (predicting the next token from past tokens), and a large amount of unlabeled text data.
snippet: The Transformer architecture, a language-modeling task predicting the next token from past tokens, and a large amount of unlabeled text data.

title: Can you explain, in your own words, what the authors mean by 'LLMs are wildly inefficient…
text: Can you explain, in your own words, what the authors mean by 'LLMs are wildly inefficient at learning compared to humans,' and why that suggests scaling alone isn't the full answer? LLMs need orders of magnitude more text than a human ever reads to reach their abilities; if data is running out and humans learn from far less, better learning algorithms (not only more data and compute) are needed.
