title: Chapter 16 summary (part 2): reliability, fine-tuning, memory, LoRA, modalities
text:
The second half of the chapter 16 summary: hallucination, instruction fine-tuning (supervised and RL-based), accelerator memory as the bottleneck, LoRA, multimodal LLMs and foundation models Pretrained LLMs are unreliable and hallucinate; instruction fine-tuning (from simple instruction/response training to RL) turns them into chat assistants; memory is the main practical constraint, which LoRA addresses by training only a low-rank update to attention projections; and the same sequence-prediction recipe extends to other modalities, giving rise to the broader notion of foundation models. This page completes the chapter 16 summary started on p.530 and then ends the chapter.

- **LLM output is unreliable**: every LLM will sometimes hallucinate factually incorrect information (p.494, p.512).
- **Instruction fine-tuning** adapts an LLM to follow instructions in a chat dialog. The simplest form trains directly on instruction/response pairs with the ordinary next-token loss (*supervised fine-tuning*, p.512, p.519); more advanced forms use **reinforcement learning** (RLHF, p.519; RL for reasoning, p.527–528).
- **Accelerator memory** is the most common resource bottleneck: weights, gradients and optimizer state must all fit on the GPU/TPU (p.514).
- **LoRA** reduces memory by freezing most Transformer parameters and only training a *low-rank decomposition* added to the attention projection weights (p.515–516). With rank 8 on a 2048×2048 kernel, 32,768 trainable parameters replace 4,194,304.
- **Multimodality**: LLMs can take in or produce images, audio and other data if you can frame those inputs/outputs as sequences in a sequence-prediction problem (p.522–524).
- **Foundation model** is the general term for models of any modality trained with self-supervision on broad data and usable for many downstream tasks (p.525).

The rest of the page is blank; chapter 17 (image generation) begins on p.532 and picks up the foundation-model theme with diffusion models. All LLMs hallucinate occasionally; outputs need verification where correctness matters. Instruction fine-tuning ranges from supervised training on instruction/response pairs to reinforcement learning. Accelerator memory is the usual bottleneck: weights, gradients and optimizer state must fit on the device. LoRA freezes the base model and trains a small low-rank update to attention projections, slashing memory. Other modalities can be handled by framing them as sequence prediction. Foundation models: self-supervised, broad-data models of any modality, adaptable to many tasks.
snippet: This page completes the chapter 16 summary started on p.530 and then ends the chapter. - LLM output is unreliable: every LLM will sometimes hallucinate factually incorrect…

title: Hallucination
text: Confident, fluent generation of incorrect information by an LLM. The model is an expert at sounding right, not at being right. Next-token likelihood training rewards plausible continuations; nothing in the objective checks facts. Gemma producing a nonsensical completion on p.512 because it couldn't find a more likely continuation.
snippet: Confident, fluent generation of incorrect information by an LLM.

title: Instruction fine-tuning
text: Additional training that makes a pretrained LLM follow user instructions in a dialog. Teaching an autocomplete engine to behave like an assistant by showing it examples of good answers. Simplest form: next-token loss on concatenated instruction/response sequences (supervised). Advanced: reinforcement learning (e.g., RLHF). Fine-tuning Gemma on instruction/response pairs from the Databricks dataset (p.512).
snippet: Additional training that makes a pretrained LLM follow user instructions in a dialog.

title: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
text: Fine-tuning by freezing pretrained weights and training a low-rank additive update. Instead of repainting the whole wall, add a thin transparent overlay that only needs a few brush strokes. Output $= xW + (xA)B$ with $W$ frozen, $A\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times r}$, $B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{out}}$, $r\ll d$. Rank 8 on a 2048×2048 kernel: 32,768 trainable parameters instead of 4,194,304 (p.515).
snippet: Fine-tuning by freezing pretrained weights and training a low-rank additive update.

title: Accelerator memory bottleneck
text: The limit imposed by GPU/TPU memory on which models can be trained or served. It doesn't matter how fast the oven is if the dish doesn't fit inside. Training memory ≈ weights + gradients + optimizer state + activations; with Adam, the first three are several times the weight memory. 1B-parameter Gemma: ~3.7 GB of weights, ~15 GB with Adam state, on a 16 GB GPU (p.514).
snippet: The limit imposed by GPU/TPU memory on which models can be trained or served.

title: Multimodal LLM
text: An LLM that reads or generates data from modalities other than text. Anything you can turn into a sequence of tokens, a Transformer can learn to predict. Non-text inputs are encoded into token-like embeddings and interleaved with text tokens. A model that takes an image plus a question and outputs a textual answer (p.522–524).
snippet: An LLM that reads or generates data from modalities other than text.

title: Foundation model
text: A model of any modality trained with self-supervision on broad data and adaptable to many downstream tasks. A general-purpose base that many specific applications are built on. Hallmarks: self-supervised reconstruction objective, internet-scale data, no single target task (p.525). Gemma (text) and text-to-image diffusion models (chapter 17).
snippet: A model of any modality trained with self-supervision on broad data and adaptable to many downstream tasks.

title: LoRA parameter count (behind the LoRA summary bullet)
text: frozen = ops.matmul(inputs, self.kernel); update = ops.matmul(ops.matmul(inputs, self.alpha), self.beta); return frozen + update (p.515) \begin{aligned} y &= xW + (xA)B \\ \#\text{frozen} &= d_{in}\,d_{out}, \qquad \#\text{trainable} = r\,(d_{in}+d_{out}) \end{aligned} Quantifies how LoRA 'reduces memory usage' as stated in the summary. The update $AB$ is a $d_{in}\times d_{out}$ matrix of rank at most r, so it can only change W in r independent directions. x input to the projection layer W frozen pretrained kernel (`kernel`), shape (d_in, d_out) A trainable `alpha`, shape (d_in, r) B trainable `beta`, shape (r, d_out) r the LoRA rank (8 in the book)
snippet: frozen = ops.matmulinputs, self.kernel; update = ops.matmulops.matmulinputs, self.alpha, self.beta; return frozen + update p.515 — Quantifies how LoRA 'reduces memory usage' as…

title: What is the simplest form of instruction fine-tuning according to the summary?
text: What is the simplest form of instruction fine-tuning according to the summary? Training directly on instruction and response pairs
snippet: Training directly on instruction and response pairs

title: Why is accelerator memory, rather than raw compute, usually the bottleneck when…
text: Why is accelerator memory, rather than raw compute, usually the bottleneck when fine-tuning an LLM? Training must hold weights, gradients, optimizer state (Adam adds several values per parameter) and activations on the device; for a 1B model this already reaches ~15 GB before activations, so the model may simply not fit.
snippet: Training must hold weights, gradients, optimizer state Adam adds several values per parameter and activations on the device; for a 1B model this already reaches ~15 GB before…

title: A projection kernel has shape 4096 × 4096. How many trainable parameters does a rank-16…
text: A projection kernel has shape 4096 × 4096. How many trainable parameters does a rank-16 LoRA update have, and what fraction of the kernel's parameters is that? 16 × (4096 + 4096) = 131,072 trainable parameters; the kernel has 16,777,216, so about 0.78%.
snippet: 16 × 4096 + 4096 = 131,072 trainable parameters; the kernel has 16,777,216, so about 0.78%.

title: Why does freezing parameters save memory during training, beyond simply not updating them?
text: Why does freezing parameters save memory during training, beyond simply not updating them? Frozen parameters need no stored gradients and no optimizer state (e.g., Adam's moment estimates), which for Adam is several times the size of the weights themselves.
snippet: Frozen parameters need no stored gradients and no optimizer state e.g., Adam's moment estimates, which for Adam is several times the size of the weights themselves.

title: Which statement best matches the book's definition of a foundation model?
text: Which statement best matches the book's definition of a foundation model? A model of any modality trained with self-supervision for a wide range of downstream tasks
snippet: A model of any modality trained with self-supervision for a wide range of downstream tasks

title: What must you figure out to make an LLM work with a new modality such as audio?
text: What must you figure out to make an LLM work with a new modality such as audio? How to frame the audio input or output as a sequence (of tokens or embeddings) so the problem becomes sequence prediction.
snippet: How to frame the audio input or output as a sequence of tokens or embeddings so the problem becomes sequence prediction.

title: Without looking back, can you explain to a friend why LLMs hallucinate and name two…
text: Without looking back, can you explain to a friend why LLMs hallucinate and name two techniques from chapter 16 that make LLM outputs more useful or controllable? They optimize for likely text, not true text. Techniques: instruction fine-tuning (supervised or RLHF), retrieval augmented generation, reasoning via chain of thought.
snippet: They optimize for likely text, not true text. Techniques: instruction fine-tuning supervised or RLHF, retrieval augmented generation, reasoning via chain of thought.

title: Chapter 17 opener: Image generation
text:
Introduction to chapter 17: generating images by learning latent visual spaces and sampling from them, using VAEs, diffusion models and pretrained text-to-image models Image generation means learning a latent space of images and sampling from it to produce new pictures interpolated from real ones; the chapter covers two main techniques, variational autoencoders and diffusion models, then pretrained text-to-image models and their latent spaces. This is the opening page of **chapter 17, Image generation**. The 'This chapter covers' box lists four topics: **variational autoencoders**, **diffusion models**, **using a pretrained text-to-image model**, and **exploring the latent image spaces learned by text-to-image models**.

The opening paragraph calls image generation the most popular and successful application of creative AI today, and defines it compactly: *learning latent visual spaces and sampling from them* to create new pictures *interpolated from real ones* — imaginary people, places, cats and dogs.

Section **17.1, Deep learning for image generation**, then begins: this section and the next review high-level concepts and implementation details of the two main techniques, VAEs and diffusion models. The authors add (the sentence finishes on p.533) that these techniques are not specific to images — the same ideas could be used for sound or music — but images have produced the most interesting results so far.

How to use this page: treat it as the map for the chapter. VAEs are covered in 17.1.2–17.1.3 (p.534–541), diffusion models in 17.2 (p.542–554), and text-to-image models in 17.3 (p.555 onward). Chapter 17 covers VAEs, diffusion models, a pretrained text-to-image model, and exploring its latent space. Image generation = learn a latent visual space, sample from it, decode to new images. The two main techniques implemented are VAEs and diffusion models.
snippet: This is the opening page of chapter 17, Image generation. The 'This chapter covers' box lists four topics: variational autoencoders, diffusion models, using a pretrained…

title: Image generation
text: Creating new images by learning a latent visual space and sampling from it. Learn a 'map' of possible pictures, then visit new spots on the map. A generator/decoder maps latent vectors to pixel grids; training makes points in latent space decode to realistic images. Imaginary faces or landscapes interpolated from real photos.
snippet: Creating new images by learning a latent visual space and sampling from it.

title: Latent space
text: A learned, typically lower-dimensional vector space of representations. Coordinates that describe images by their meaningful features rather than their pixels. Points are vectors; generation decodes sampled vectors into images (p.533). Moving between two points smoothly morphs one image into another (explored in 17.3.1).
snippet: A learned, typically lower-dimensional vector space of representations.

title: What four topics does chapter 17 cover?
text: What four topics does chapter 17 cover? Variational autoencoders, diffusion models, using a pretrained text-to-image model, and exploring the latent image spaces learned by text-to-image models.
snippet: Variational autoencoders, diffusion models, using a pretrained text-to-image model, and exploring the latent image spaces learned by text-to-image models.

title: How does the opening paragraph describe image generation?
text: How does the opening paragraph describe image generation? Learning latent visual spaces and sampling from them to create new pictures
snippet: Learning latent visual spaces and sampling from them to create new pictures

title: Which two main image-generation techniques are reviewed and implemented in sections 17.1…
text: Which two main image-generation techniques are reviewed and implemented in sections 17.1 and 17.2? Variational autoencoders (VAEs) and diffusion models.
snippet: Variational autoencoders VAEs and diffusion models.

title: What does it mean that generated pictures are 'interpolated from real ones'?
text: What does it mean that generated pictures are 'interpolated from real ones'? New images correspond to latent points lying between the representations of training images, so they combine learned visual features in new ways rather than copying any one training image.
snippet: New images correspond to latent points lying between the representations of training images, so they combine learned visual features in new ways rather than copying any one…

title: Before reading on, can you explain why a 'latent space' might be easier to sample…
text: Before reading on, can you explain why a 'latent space' might be easier to sample meaningful images from than raw pixel space? Random pixel grids almost never look like real images; a learned latent space is organized so that (ideally) any point decodes to a plausible image.
snippet: Random pixel grids almost never look like real images; a learned latent space is organized so that ideally any point decodes to a plausible image.

title: Sampling from latent spaces of images; text-to-image generation
text:
The latent-space view of image generation: a decoder/generator maps latent points to images, and text conditioning maps prompts into that latent space Learn a low-dimensional latent vector space in which every point decodes to a realistic image; sampling points and decoding them yields new images (the in-betweens of training images). Text-conditioning maps natural-language prompts into the latent space, giving text-to-image models that can combine concepts never seen together. The page finishes the sentence from p.532: the same techniques could be used to learn latent spaces of sound or music, but images have given the most interesting results, so the chapter focuses on them.

**17.1.1 Sampling from latent spaces of images.** The key idea is to develop a **low-dimensional latent space** of representations — a vector space, like everything in deep learning — where *any* point maps to a 'valid' image, one that looks real. The module that performs this mapping, from a latent point to a grid of pixels, is called a **generator** or **decoder**. Once the space is learned, you sample points and decode them to get images never seen before: **the in-betweens of the training images**. Figure 17.1 shows this: a point in the latent image space, read as a vector, is fed to the decoder/generator, which outputs an image (a coral reef).

**Text-conditioning** goes further by mapping a space of natural-language prompts into the latent space (figure 17.2), enabling **language-guided image generation**. Models in this category are called **text-to-image models**. In figure 17.2 the prompt "Horse riding bike on the moon" goes through a *text encoder* into a *latent text/image space*, and an *image decoder* turns the resulting point into the picture.

Because such models interpolate across many training images, they can produce **infinite combinations of visual concepts**, including ones no one has explicitly produced before — a horse riding a bike on the moon. The authors call image generation a powerful brush for creative people. Its limitations (incoherent details, no real understanding of physics) are discussed at the top of p.534. Image generation learns a low-dimensional latent vector space where every point should decode to a realistic image. The module mapping latent points to images is the generator or decoder. Sampling and decoding latent points yields new images: the in-betweens of the training images. Text-conditioning maps prompts into the latent space, giving text-to-image models. Latent interpolation lets models combine concepts never seen together, like a horse riding a bike on the moon.
snippet: The page finishes the sentence from p.532: the same techniques could be used to learn latent spaces of sound or music, but images have given the most interesting results, so the…

title: Latent space
text: A low-dimensional vector space of learned representations where (ideally) every point decodes to a valid image. A compact map of 'all plausible pictures' where nearby points look alike. Points $z\in\mathbb{R}^k$; a decoder $g(z)$ produces images; structure (continuity, meaningful directions) depends on how it is trained. Sampling a random point and decoding it gives a coral reef image in figure 17.1.
snippet: A low-dimensional vector space of learned representations where ideally every point decodes to a valid image.

title: Generator / decoder
text: The module that maps a latent point to an image. A renderer that turns a short description (a vector) into a full picture. Typically a neural network with upsampling or transposed convolutions; in diffusion models, generation is an iterative denoising process instead. 'Decoder / generator' box in figure 17.1; 'Image decoder' in figure 17.2.
snippet: The module that maps a latent point to an image.

title: Text-to-image model
text: A model that maps a natural-language prompt into a latent space and decodes it to a matching image. Describe a picture in words; the model paints it. Text encoder → conditioning of latent space/sampling → image decoder (figure 17.2). "Horse riding bike on the moon".
snippet: A model that maps a natural-language prompt into a latent space and decodes it to a matching image.

title: Latent-space interpolation
text: Generating outputs from points between (or combining) the latent representations of training examples. Mixing paints from the training palette to get colors that weren't in any single tube. E.g., $z_\lambda = (1-\lambda) z_a + \lambda z_b$, decoded for $\lambda\in[0,1]$ (AI illustration). Combining 'horse', 'bike riding' and 'moon surface' concepts.
snippet: Generating outputs from points between or combining the latent representations of training examples.

title: Text prompt shown in figure 17.2
text:
"Horse
riding bike
on the
moon" Not executable code: it is the example text prompt, typeset in a monospaced font inside figure 17.2, that is fed to the text encoder of a text-to-image model. Prompt → text encoder → point in latent text/image space → image decoder → image.
snippet: Not executable code: it is the example text prompt, typeset in a monospaced font inside figure 17.2, that is fed to the text encoder of a text-to-image model.

title: What is the module that maps a latent point to an image called?
text: What is the module that maps a latent point to an image called? Generator or decoder
snippet: Generator or decoder

title: What property must the latent space have so that sampling it produces useful images?
text: What property must the latent space have so that sampling it produces useful images? Any point in it must map to a valid image, one that looks like the real thing.
snippet: Any point in it must map to a valid image, one that looks like the real thing.

title: Why does the book call generated images 'the in-betweens of the training images'?
text: Why does the book call generated images 'the in-betweens of the training images'? Training images correspond to points in latent space; new samples fall between these points, so the decoded images blend learned features rather than reproduce any training image.
snippet: Training images correspond to points in latent space; new samples fall between these points, so the decoded images blend learned features rather than reproduce any training image.

title: In figure 17.2, what component turns the prompt into a point in the shared latent space?
text: In figure 17.2, what component turns the prompt into a point in the shared latent space? Text encoder
snippet: Text encoder

title: What is language-guided image generation, and what are models that do it called?
text: What is language-guided image generation, and what are models that do it called? Generating pictures that correspond to a text description, by mapping prompts into the latent space; such models are text-to-image models.
snippet: Generating pictures that correspond to a text description, by mapping prompts into the latent space; such models are text-to-image models.

title: How can a model generate 'a horse riding a bike on the moon' if no such image was in its…
text: How can a model generate 'a horse riding a bike on the moon' if no such image was in its training data? It learned representations of horses, bike riding and the moon in a shared latent space; interpolating/combining these places a point that decodes to a novel combination.
snippet: It learned representations of horses, bike riding and the moon in a shared latent space; interpolating/combining these places a point that decodes to a novel combination.

Then add what changes in figure 17.2. 17.1: latent image space → point (a vector) → decoder/generator → generated image. 17.2 adds a text prompt and text encoder in front, and the space becomes a latent text/image space with an image decoder.

title: Limits of generated images, model families, and introducing VAEs
text:
Why generated images can be incoherent, the three main families of image generators (diffusion, VAEs, GANs), the chapter's scope, and the introduction of variational autoencoders as autoencoders combined with Bayesian inference Learned latent spaces don't encode a physical model of the world, so generated images can contain incoherent details. Of the main generator families, the book covers VAEs and diffusion models and skips GANs. VAEs are autoencoders — networks that encode an input to a low-dimensional latent space and decode it back — enriched with ideas from Bayesian inference; they're no match for diffusion in fidelity but remain valuable for interpretability, latent control and reconstruction. The page opens with **limitations** of image generation: like all deep learning models, the latent space doesn't encode a consistent model of the physical world, so you can see **hands with extra fingers, incoherent lighting or garbled objects**. Coherence is an active research area. Despite seeing tens of thousands of images of people riding bikes, the model in figure 17.2 doesn't understand riding (pedaling, steering, balance), so the horse is unlikely to pedal believably with its hind legs.

There are several strategies for learning latent image spaces. The most common model families are **diffusion models**, **variational autoencoders (VAEs)** and **generative adversarial networks (GANs)**. Earlier editions covered GANs, but they have fallen out of fashion and been all but replaced by diffusion models, so this edition covers **VAEs and diffusion models** and skips GANs. The models built in the chapter perform **unconditioned image generation** (sampling without text conditioning); you will also use a pretrained text-to-image model and explore its latent space.

**17.1.2 Variational autoencoders.** VAEs were discovered simultaneously by Kingma and Welling (December 2013) and Rezende, Mohamed and Wierstra (January 2014). They suit **image editing via concept vectors**. They are a kind of **autoencoder** — a network that encodes an input to a low-dimensional latent space and decodes it back — mixed with **Bayesian inference**.

VAEs are over a decade old but still used in research. They will never be the first choice for high-fidelity generation, where diffusion excels, but they remain important when **interpretability, control over the latent space and reconstruction** matter, and they are your first contact with autoencoders. A **classical image autoencoder** maps an image to a latent vector via an **encoder**, then decodes it back to an output with the same dimensions as the original (continued on p.535 with figure 17.3). Generated images can be incoherent because latent spaces don't encode a physical world model. Main image-generation families: diffusion models, VAEs, GANs; the book covers the first two. The chapter's own models do unconditioned generation; text-to-image is explored with a pretrained model. An autoencoder encodes an input into a low-dimensional latent space and decodes it back. VAEs combine autoencoders with Bayesian inference and remain useful for interpretable, controllable latent spaces.
snippet: The page opens with limitations of image generation: like all deep learning models, the latent space doesn't encode a consistent model of the physical world, so you can see hands…

title: Autoencoder
text: A network that encodes an input to a low-dimensional latent space and decodes it back, trained to reconstruct its input. Summarize a picture in a few numbers, then redraw it from the summary. Encoder $f: x \mapsto z$, decoder $g: z\mapsto x'$, loss $\ell(x, g(f(x)))$; no labels needed. MNIST digit → small code → reconstructed digit (figure 17.3, p.535).
snippet: A network that encodes an input to a low-dimensional latent space and decodes it back, trained to reconstruct its input.

title: Variational autoencoder (VAE)
text: An autoencoder that mixes deep learning with Bayesian inference, encoding inputs as distributions in latent space. Instead of a single address for each image, the encoder gives a fuzzy neighborhood, forcing nearby points to decode sensibly. Encoder outputs mean and log-variance; a latent sample is decoded; trained with reconstruction + KL loss (p.535–536). Kingma & Welling 2013; Rezende et al. 2014.
snippet: An autoencoder that mixes deep learning with Bayesian inference, encoding inputs as distributions in latent space.

title: Generative adversarial network (GAN)

title: Autoencoders vs. VAEs: encoding images as distributions
text:
How a classical autoencoder is trained (figure 17.3), why its latent space is poorly structured, and how a VAE instead encodes each image as a mean and variance, samples a latent point and decodes it A classical autoencoder learns to reconstruct its input through a constrained code, but its latent space is not useful for generation. A VAE encodes an image into the parameters of a distribution (z_mean, z_log_variance), samples z = z_mean + scale · epsilon, and decodes z; this randomness forces every latent point near an encoding to decode to something valid, giving a continuous, structured latent space. The page completes the description of a **classical autoencoder** (begun on p.534): an encoder maps an image to a latent code and a decoder maps it back to an image of the same size (**figure 17.3**: a handwritten '2' → encoder → small compressed representation → decoder → reconstructed '2'). It is trained with the **same images as inputs and targets**, so it learns to reconstruct its inputs. Constraints on the **code** (the encoder's output) shape what it learns; most commonly the code is **low-dimensional and sparse**, making the encoder a compressor.

In practice, classical autoencoders don't give useful or nicely structured latent spaces and aren't even good compressors, so they have largely fallen out of fashion. **VAEs** add 'a little bit of statistical magic' that forces continuous, highly structured latent spaces, making them powerful for image generation.

Instead of a fixed code, a VAE turns the image into **the parameters of a statistical distribution: a mean and a variance**. This assumes the image was produced by a random process whose randomness should be accounted for in encoding and decoding. The VAE samples one element of the distribution and decodes it back to the input (figure 17.4, p.536). This **stochasticity improves robustness** and forces the latent space to be meaningful **everywhere**: every sampled point decodes to a valid output.

Technically:
1. An encoder maps `input_img` to `z_mean` and `z_log_variance`.
2. A point is sampled: `z = z_mean + exp(z_log_variance) * epsilon`, with `epsilon` random. (Note: the correct scale is $\exp(0.5\cdot$`z_log_variance`$)$, the standard deviation, as the book's own Listing 17.2 on p.538 uses.)
3. A decoder maps `z` back to the image.

Because `epsilon` is random, every point near the encoding of `input_img` must decode to something similar to it — the sentence continues on p.536, where this is shown to make the latent space continuous. An autoencoder is trained to reconstruct its inputs; constraints on the code (low-dimensional, sparse) make it learn compact representations. Classical autoencoders give poorly structured latent spaces and have fallen out of fashion. A VAE encodes each image as a distribution (mean and log-variance), samples a point and decodes it. Random sampling forces every point near an encoding to decode to something similar, making the latent space continuous. Correct sampling: z = z_mean + exp(0.5 * z_log_variance) * epsilon with standard normal epsilon (as in Listing 17.2); the printed step 2 omits the 0.5.
snippet: The page completes the description of a classical autoencoder begun on p.534: an encoder maps an image to a latent code and a decoder maps it back to an image of the same size…

title: Autoencoder
text: A network trained to reconstruct its input through an encoder–decoder pair with a constrained latent code. Compress, then decompress, and learn the compression from data. Targets = inputs; constraints (low dimension, sparsity) stop it from learning the identity. Figure 17.3: '2' → compressed representation → reconstructed '2'.

title: Variational autoencoder (VAE)
text: An autoencoder that encodes inputs as Gaussian distributions (mean, log-variance), samples latent points and decodes them. Each image owns a fuzzy region of latent space, not a point. Encode → $\mu, \log\sigma^2$; sample $z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon$; decode; train with reconstruction + KL losses. VAE trained on MNIST digits in 17.1.3.
snippet: An autoencoder that encodes inputs as Gaussian distributions mean, log-variance, samples latent points and decodes them.

title: Reparameterization (sampling) step
text: Sampling a latent point as $z=\mu+\sigma\odot\epsilon$ with independent noise $\epsilon$. Roll a standard die, then shift and stretch the result using learned numbers. Makes sampling differentiable with respect to $\mu$ and $\sigma$; requires $\sigma=\exp(0.5\log\sigma^2)$ when the encoder outputs log-variance. Listing 17.2 (p.538): `z_mean + ops.exp(0.5 * z_log_var) * epsilon`.
snippet: Sampling a latent point as z=mu+sigmaodotepsilon with independent noise epsilon.

title: Low-dimensional, sparse code
text: The most common constraint on a classical autoencoder's code: few dimensions, mostly zeros. Describe each image with only a handful of active features. Achieved with a narrow bottleneck and, e.g., an L1 penalty on activations (AI detail). The small black-and-white column in figure 17.3.

text: z = z_mean + exp(z_log_variance) * epsilon z = \mu + \exp\!\left(\log \sigma^2\right) \odot \epsilon Draw a random latent point around the input's encoding. As printed, the noise is scaled by the variance $\sigma^2$, not the standard deviation $\sigma$. That is inconsistent with the book's own code on p.538 (see m2). z sampled latent point fed to the decoder \mu z_mean, the encoder's mean vector \log\sigma^2 z_log_variance, the encoder's log-variance vector \epsilon random noise tensor \odot element-wise multiplication

Then $\mathbb{E}[z]=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}[z]=\sigma^2$, matching the meaning of z_mean and z_log_variance. \sigma standard deviation, $\sqrt{\sigma^2} = e^{\frac12\log\sigma^2}$ \epsilon standard normal noise (keras.random.normal in the listing) \mathcal{N}(0,I) standard multivariate normal distribution

title: How a VAE encodes, samples, decodes and is trained
text:
The VAE pipeline of figure 17.4 (encoder to distribution parameters, random sampling, decoder) and its two training losses A VAE encodes each image as a probability distribution (a mean and a log-variance) rather than a single point, samples a latent point from that distribution and decodes it. Training with a reconstruction loss plus a KL-divergence regularization loss produces a continuous, well-structured latent space in which every direction is a meaningful axis of variation. The page opens with **figure 17.4**, which shows the VAE pipeline: an input image (an MNIST "2") goes into an **encoder**, which outputs two vectors, `z_mean` and `z_log_variance`. Together they define a **probability distribution over the latent space** (drawn as a bell-shaped bump). A point is **randomly sampled** from that distribution and passed to a **decoder**, which produces the reconstructed image.

The text continues the argument from p.535: because the decoder must turn *any* point sampled near the mean back into something similar to `input_img`, the latent space is forced to be **continuously meaningful**. Two close latent points decode to highly similar images. Continuity plus **low dimensionality** forces every direction in the latent space to encode a meaningful **axis of variation** of the data. The result is a structured latent space that suits manipulation with **concept vectors**.

A VAE is trained with **two losses**:

- a **reconstruction loss**, which makes decoded samples match the original inputs;
- a **regularization loss**, which encourages "well-rounded" latent distributions and reduces overfitting to the training data.

A four-line schematic shows the process: the encoder produces `z_mean, z_log_variance`; a latent point is drawn as `z = z_mean + exp(z_log_variance) * epsilon` with a small random `epsilon`; the decoder maps `z` to `reconstructed_img`; and `Model(input_img, reconstructed_img)` ties it together as an autoencoder. (Note: the real code on p.538 scales `epsilon` by `exp(0.5 * z_log_var)`, the standard deviation. The schematic's `exp(z_log_variance)` is the variance; see the review flag.)

For the regularization loss the authors name the **Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence**. It nudges the encoder's output distribution toward a well-rounded **normal distribution centered on 0**, which gives the encoder a sensible assumption about the structure of the latent space. The page ends by announcing the practical implementation in section 17.1.3. A VAE encoder outputs `z_mean` and `z_log_variance`, the parameters of a Gaussian over the latent space. A latent point is sampled as mean + std * epsilon and decoded; the randomness forces nearby points to decode to similar images. Continuity plus low dimensionality makes latent directions meaningful axes of variation, which makes concept-vector editing possible. Training uses a reconstruction loss plus a KL-divergence regularization loss toward a normal distribution centered on 0. The schematic's `exp(z_log_variance)` should be read as exp(0.5 * log variance), as implemented on p.538.

title: Variational autoencoder (VAE)
text: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs the parameters of a probability distribution (mean and log-variance) over the latent space. A latent point is sampled from that distribution and decoded, and training uses a reconstruction loss plus a KL regularization loss. Instead of pinning each image to one dot on a map, the VAE gives each image a small fuzzy region, and the decoder must recognize the image from anywhere in that region. Encoder: $x\mapsto(\mu,\log\sigma^2)$. Sampling: $z=\mu+\sigma\odot\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$. Decoder: $z\mapsto\hat x$. Loss: reconstruction$(x,\hat x)$ + $D_{KL}(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,I))$. An MNIST VAE with a 2-D latent space (p.537) whose plane can be scanned to show all digit shapes (p.542).
snippet: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs the parameters of a probability distribution mean and log-variance over the latent space. A latent point is sampled from that distribution and…

title: Latent space
text: A low-dimensional vector space of representations in which each point can be decoded to an image. A map where nearby locations correspond to similar-looking images. For the VAE on p.537 it is $\mathbb R^2$; continuity means the decoder is a smooth function of $z$. Moving along one axis might gradually turn a 1 into a 7.
snippet: A low-dimensional vector space of representations in which each point can be decoded to an image.

title: Kullback-Leibler divergence
text: A measure of how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution; used here as the VAE regularization loss toward a normal distribution centered on 0. It is a cost for wandering away from the origin or for having a spread that is too narrow or too wide. For diagonal Gaussians vs $\mathcal N(0,1)$ per dimension: $-\tfrac12(1+\log\sigma^2-\mu^2-\sigma^2)$ (implemented on p.541). $\mu=0,\sigma=1$ gives KL 0; $\mu=2,\sigma=1$ gives KL 2.
snippet: A measure of how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution; used here as the VAE regularization loss toward a normal distribution centered on 0.

title: Sampling with a random epsilon (reparameterization)
text: Drawing a latent point as mean plus scale times a standard normal noise `epsilon`, so the randomness is an input and gradients can flow to the mean and variance. Roll the dice first (epsilon), then shift and stretch the result using the network's outputs. $z=\mu+\exp(\tfrac12\log\sigma^2)\,\varepsilon$; $\partial z/\partial\mu=1$, $\partial z/\partial\log\sigma^2=\tfrac12\sigma\varepsilon$. Line 2 of the schematic on this page; Listing 17.2 on p.538.
snippet: Drawing a latent point as mean plus scale times a standard normal noise epsilon, so the randomness is an input and gradients can flow to the mean and variance.

title: Sampling a latent point from the encoder's distribution
text: z = z_mean + exp(z_log_variance) * epsilon z = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon,\qquad \sigma = \exp\!\big(\tfrac12 \log \sigma^2\big),\qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I) Draw a random point from $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ in a way that is differentiable with respect to $\mu$ and $\sigma$. The schematic as printed writes `exp(z_log_variance)`, which equals $\sigma^2$ (the variance). The correct scale is $\sigma=\exp(0.5\log\sigma^2)$, as used in Listing 17.2 on p.538. The LaTeX above gives the correct form. \mu `z_mean`, the encoder's mean vector \log\sigma^2 `z_log_variance`, the encoder's log-variance vector \sigma standard deviation per latent dimension \varepsilon a small random vector drawn from a standard normal z the sampled latent point fed to the decoder \odot elementwise multiplication

title: Implementing a VAE: overview and the encoder network
text:
The three components of the MNIST VAE and the strided-convolution encoder that maps a 28x28 image to z_mean and z_log_var in a 2-D latent space The VAE is built from an encoder, a sampling layer and a decoder. The encoder is a small ConvNet that downsamples with strides (not max pooling), because the model must keep information about where things are, and it ends in two parallel Dense heads that output the 2-D mean and log-variance. Section **17.1.3** starts the implementation of a VAE that can generate **MNIST digits**. The model has three parts:

1. an **encoder network** that turns a real image into a mean and a variance in the latent space;
2. a **sampling layer** that takes that mean and variance and samples a random latent point;
3. a **decoder network** that turns latent points back into images.

**Listing 17.1** defines the encoder. It is a simple ConvNet that maps the input image `x` to two vectors, `z_mean` and `z_log_var`. The authors point out one design detail: it **downsamples with strides instead of max pooling**, as in the image segmentation example of chapter 11. Strides are generally preferable to max pooling whenever a model cares about **information location**, that is, *where* things are in the image. A VAE does, because its encoding must be good enough to reconstruct a valid image.

The listing sets `latent_dim = 2`, so the latent space is a **2-D plane** (callout). That is small, but it means the learned space can be plotted directly later (p.542). The input is `keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))`. Two `Conv2D` layers with `strides=2, padding="same"` take it to 14x14x32 and then 7x7x64. `Flatten` gives 3,136 values and `Dense(16, relu)` compresses them. Two **parallel** `Dense(latent_dim)` heads, named `"z_mean"` and `"z_log_var"`, have no activation, so their outputs can be any real number. `keras.Model(image_inputs, [z_mean, z_log_var], name="encoder")` packages this as a **two-output** functional model (callout: "The input image ends up being encoded into these two parameters").

The page ends with the start of `encoder.summary()`, which continues on p.538 (69,076 parameters in total). The VAE consists of an encoder, a sampling layer and a decoder. The encoder is a ConvNet with stride-2 convolutions (28 to 14 to 7), Flatten, Dense(16) and two linear Dense(2) heads. Strides are used instead of max pooling because a reconstructing model must keep information about where things are. latent_dim = 2 makes the latent space a plane that can be visualized. The encoder is a functional model with two outputs: [z_mean, z_log_var].

title: Variational autoencoder (VAE)
text: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs distribution parameters and whose latent point is sampled before decoding. Encode to a fuzzy region, not a point. Implemented here as encoder (Listing 17.1) + Sampler (17.2) + decoder (17.3). MNIST VAE with a 2-D latent space.
snippet: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs distribution parameters and whose latent point is sampled before decoding.

title: Strided convolution for downsampling
text: A Conv2D layer with strides > 1, used to reduce spatial resolution in place of max pooling. A learned, location-aware way to shrink an image, unlike pooling, which simply keeps the strongest response. Conv2D(32, 3, strides=2, padding='same') maps 28x28 to 14x14; parameters = 3*3*1*32 + 32 = 320. Both Conv2D layers of the VAE encoder.
snippet: A Conv2D layer with strides  1, used to reduce spatial resolution in place of max pooling.

title: Functional API with multiple outputs
text: Building a keras.Model from an input tensor and a list of output tensors. One trunk, two heads. keras.Model(image_inputs, [z_mean, z_log_var]) returns a list of two tensors when called. `z_mean, z_log_var = encoder(x)`
snippet: Building a keras.Model from an input tensor and a list of output tensors.

title: Listing 17.1 VAE encoder network
text:
import keras
from keras import layers
latent_dim = 2
image_inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation="relu", strides=2, padding="same")(
    image_inputs
)
x = layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation="relu", strides=2, padding="same")(x)
x = layers.Flatten()(x)
x = layers.Dense(16, activation="relu")(x)
z_mean = layers.Dense(latent_dim, name="z_mean")(x)
z_log_var = layers.Dense(latent_dim, name="z_log_var")(x)
encoder = keras.Model(image_inputs, [z_mean, z_log_var], name="encoder") Builds a functional Keras model that maps a 28x28x1 image to two 2-D vectors, `z_mean` and `z_log_var`. Two stride-2 convolutions downsample 28 -> 14 -> 7, then flatten, compress to 16 features and project to the distribution parameters.
snippet: Builds a functional Keras model that maps a 28x28x1 image to two 2-D vectors, zmean and zlogvar.

title: Encoder summary and the latent-space Sampler layer
text:
Verifying the encoder via its summary (69,076 parameters) and implementing the sampling step as a custom Keras layer with a seed generator The Sampler layer turns z_mean and z_log_var into a random latent point z = z_mean + exp(0.5 * z_log_var) * epsilon, with epsilon drawn from a standard normal via keras.random and a SeedGenerator stored on the layer. The top of the page completes the **encoder summary** from p.537. The input is (None, 28, 28, 1). `conv2d` gives (None, 14, 14, 32) with 320 parameters, `conv2d_1` gives (None, 7, 7, 64) with 18,496, `flatten` gives (None, 3136), `dense` gives (None, 16) with 50,192, and the two heads `z_mean` and `z_log_var` give (None, 2) with 34 parameters each. Both heads are connected to `dense[0][0]`, which confirms the branching. Total: **69,076 trainable parameters** (269.83 KB).

Next the authors use `z_mean` and `z_log_var`, "the parameters of the statistical distribution assumed to have produced `input_img`", to generate a latent point `z`. **Listing 17.2** defines a custom layer `Sampler(keras.Layer)`:

- In `__init__`, it creates a `keras.random.SeedGenerator()`. The callout explains that a seed generator is needed to use `keras.random` functions inside `call()`. It also sets `self.built = True`, because the layer has no weights to create.
- In `call(self, z_mean, z_log_var)`, it reads the batch size and latent size from `ops.shape(z_mean)`, draws a batch of **random normal vectors** `epsilon` with shape `(batch_size, z_size)`, and returns `z_mean + ops.exp(0.5 * z_log_var) * epsilon`. The callout calls this the **VAE sampling formula**.

Because $\exp(0.5\log\sigma^2)=\sigma$, this is exactly $z=\mu+\sigma\varepsilon$, a sample from $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$. The randomness comes only from `epsilon`, so gradients flow through `z_mean` and `z_log_var` (the reparameterization trick, a term the book does not use).

The page closes by introducing the **decoder** (Listing 17.3, p.539). It reshapes `z` to image-like dimensions and uses convolution layers to output an image the same size as `input_img`. The encoder has 69,076 parameters, most of them in the Flatten-to-Dense(16) connection. The Sampler is a weightless custom keras.Layer that uses a SeedGenerator for keras.random calls. It returns z = z_mean + exp(0.5 * z_log_var) * epsilon, a sample from N(mean, variance). Moving the randomness into epsilon keeps the layer differentiable with respect to z_mean and z_log_var. Using keras.ops and keras.random keeps the layer backend-agnostic.

title: Sampling with a random epsilon (reparameterization)
text: Drawing z as mean plus standard deviation times standard-normal noise so that sampling is differentiable with respect to the mean and variance. Draw the randomness separately, then shift and scale it with the network's outputs. $z=\mu+e^{\frac12\log\sigma^2}\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$; $\partial z/\partial\mu=1$ and $\partial z/\partial(\log\sigma^2)=\tfrac12\sigma\varepsilon$. `return z_mean + ops.exp(0.5 * z_log_var) * epsilon`
snippet: Drawing z as mean plus standard deviation times standard-normal noise so that sampling is differentiable with respect to the mean and variance.

A counter that a layer keeps so each call gets new dice rolls. Stored as layer state; passed as `seed=self.seed_generator` to keras.random.normal. Needed especially with JAX, where random state must be explicit. `keras.random.normal((batch_size, z_size), seed=self.seed_generator)`

title: VAE sampling formula (Listing 17.2)
text: return z_mean + ops.exp(0.5 * z_log_var) * epsilon z = \mu + \exp\!\big(0.5\,\log\sigma^2\big)\odot\varepsilon = \mu + \sigma\odot\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0, I_{d}) Produce a random latent point from $\mathcal N(\mu,\operatorname{diag}\sigma^2)$. $\exp(0.5\log\sigma^2)=(\sigma^2)^{0.5}=\sigma$. Since $\varepsilon$ has mean 0 and variance 1, $z$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. \mu z_mean, shape (batch_size, z_size) \log\sigma^2 z_log_var, same shape \varepsilon epsilon from keras.random.normal d z_size = latent_dim = 2 \sigma standard deviation per dimension

title: The VAE decoder network
text:
A decoder that mirrors the encoder: Dense to 7*7*64, Reshape, two stride-2 Conv2DTranspose layers and a sigmoid Conv2D producing a 28x28x1 image The decoder reverses each encoder stage. A Dense layer recreates the 3,136 coefficients of the encoder's Flatten output, Reshape restores the 7x7x64 feature map, transposed convolutions upsample 7 to 14 to 28, and a final 1-filter sigmoid convolution gives pixel values in [0, 1]. **Listing 17.3** defines the **decoder**, which maps latent points back to images. Its structure mirrors the encoder of Listing 17.1:

- `latent_inputs = keras.Input(shape=(latent_dim,))`: the input "where we'll feed `z`", shape (None, 2).
- `layers.Dense(7 * 7 * 64, activation="relu")` produces **the same number of coefficients we had at the level of the Flatten layer in the encoder**: 3,136.
- `layers.Reshape((7, 7, 64))` turns that vector back into a 7x7x64 feature map. Together, the Dense and Reshape layers **revert the Flatten layer** of the encoder.
- Two `Conv2DTranspose` layers with `strides=2, padding="same"` (64 then 32 filters, ReLU) **revert the Conv2D layers** of the encoder. They upsample 7x7 to 14x14 to 28x28.
- `layers.Conv2D(1, 3, activation="sigmoid", padding="same")` collapses to one channel. **The output ends up with shape (28, 28, 1)**, with values in (0, 1) like the normalized MNIST pixels.
- `keras.Model(latent_inputs, decoder_outputs, name="decoder")` packages it.

The **summary** confirms this: `dense_1` (None, 3136) with 9,408 parameters, `reshape` (None, 7, 7, 64), `conv2d_transpose` (None, 14, 14, 64) with 36,928, `conv2d_transpose_1` (None, 28, 28, 32) with 18,464, and `conv2d_2` (None, 28, 28, 1) with 289. Total: **65,089 parameters** (254.25 KB), about the same size as the 69,076-parameter encoder. The layers are numbered `_1`, `_2` because they were created after the encoder's layers in the same session. There is no "Connected to" column this time, because the decoder is a simple linear stack with no branches. The decoder maps (None, 2) to (None, 28, 28, 1) and has 65,089 parameters. Dense(7*7*64) + Reshape reverts the encoder's Flatten layer. Two stride-2 Conv2DTranspose layers revert the encoder's two stride-2 Conv2D layers: 7 to 14 to 28. A final sigmoid Conv2D(1) gives pixel values in (0, 1), matching normalized MNIST and binary crossentropy. After training, the decoder alone is the image generator.
snippet: Listing 17.3 defines the decoder, which maps latent points back to images. Its structure mirrors the encoder of Listing 17.1: - latentinputs = keras.Inputshape=latentdim,: the…

title: Transposed convolution (Conv2DTranspose)
text: A learnable upsampling layer that, with strides=2, doubles spatial resolution; it is the transpose of the linear map computed by a strided convolution. Each input pixel 'stamps' a learned kernel onto a larger output grid, and overlapping stamps are summed. With padding='same' and stride s, output size = input size * s. Parameters = k*k*C_in*C_out + C_out, e.g. 3*3*64*64 + 64 = 36,928. (7, 7, 64) -> (14, 14, 64) -> (28, 28, 32).
snippet: A learnable upsampling layer that, with strides=2, doubles spatial resolution; it is the transpose of the linear map computed by a strided convolution.

title: Decoder / generator
text: The network that maps latent points to images. The 'painter' that turns 2 numbers into a picture of a digit. Here a 65,089-parameter ConvNet from R^2 to [0,1]^{28x28x1}. decoder.predict(np.array([[0.0, 0.0]]))
snippet: The network that maps latent points to images.

title: Sigmoid output for pixel intensities
text: Activation that squashes values into (0, 1). Each pixel is like a probability of being 'ink'. sigmoid(t) = 1/(1+e^{-t}); paired with binary crossentropy on pixels in [0, 1]. Final Conv2D(1, 3, activation='sigmoid').
snippet: Activation that squashes values into 0, 1.

title: Listing 17.3 VAE decoder network, mapping latent space points to images
text:
latent_inputs = keras.Input(shape=(latent_dim,))
x = layers.Dense(7 * 7 * 64, activation="relu")(latent_inputs)
x = layers.Reshape((7, 7, 64))(x)
x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, activation="relu", strides=2, padding="same")(
    x
)
x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(32, 3, activation="relu", strides=2, padding="same")(
    x
)
decoder_outputs = layers.Conv2D(1, 3, activation="sigmoid", padding="same")(x)
decoder = keras.Model(latent_inputs, decoder_outputs, name="decoder") Builds a functional model that maps a 2-D latent vector to a 28x28x1 image with values in (0, 1). Linear expansion -> reshape -> two learned 2x upsamplings -> per-pixel sigmoid.

title: A VAE model with a custom compute_loss() method
text:
Customizing training for a self-supervised model by overriding compute_loss() instead of train_step(), and the first half of the VAE model class Because a VAE is not ordinary supervised learning, its loss must be computed from the input and the latent parameters. Rather than writing a backend-specific train_step(), you can override compute_loss(x, y, y_pred, sample_weight, training), which the built-in train_step() calls, and keep the code backend-agnostic. The VAE model itself is the book's **first example of a model that isn't doing supervised learning**. An autoencoder is **self-supervised**, because it uses its inputs as targets. When you depart from classic supervised learning, the usual approach is to subclass `Model` and write a custom `train_step()` (chapter 7). The drawback is that `train_step()` has to be **backend specific**: `GradientTape` with TensorFlow, `loss.backward()` with PyTorch, and so on.

A simpler option is to override **`compute_loss()`** and keep the default `train_step()`. `compute_loss()` is "the key bit of differentiable logic called by the built-in `train_step()`". Because it never touches gradients directly, it is easy to keep **backend agnostic**.

Its signature is `compute_loss(x, y, y_pred, sample_weight=None, training=True)`:

- `x`: the model's input;
- `y`: the target, which is `None` here because the dataset has only inputs;
- `y_pred`: the output of `call()`, which for the VAE is the latent parameters, not an image.

A supervised model would compute the loss from `y` and `y_pred`. The VAE instead uses `x` and a `reconstruction` derived from `y_pred`. The method must **return a scalar** loss to minimize, and it can also **update metric state**, which the VAE does.

**Listing 17.4** starts the `VAE(keras.Model)` class. The constructor stores `encoder`, `decoder` and a new `Sampler()`, and creates two `keras.metrics.Mean` trackers, `"reconstruction_loss"` and `"kl_loss"`, to **track the loss averages over each epoch** (callout). `call(self, inputs)` returns only `self.encoder(inputs)`, that is `[z_mean, z_log_var]`. The page ends with the `compute_loss` signature; its body is on p.541. The authors stress that the class works with all backends with no code changes. An autoencoder is self-supervised: its inputs are its targets. Overriding train_step() works but is backend specific; overriding compute_loss() is simpler and backend agnostic. compute_loss(x, y, y_pred, sample_weight=None, training=True) must return a scalar and may update metrics. In the VAE, call() returns [z_mean, z_log_var], so y_pred holds latent parameters and y is None. Two keras.metrics.Mean trackers report reconstruction and KL loss averages per epoch.

Change what the model is graded on, not how the grading is turned into weight updates. Signature: compute_loss(x, y, y_pred, sample_weight=None, training=True) -> scalar. Called inside the backend-specific default train_step(), which handles gradients. The VAE computes reconstruction + KL from x and y_pred = [z_mean, z_log_var].

title: The VAE loss (reconstruction + KL) and training on MNIST
text:
Body of compute_loss(): sampling, decoding, summed per-pixel binary crossentropy, closed-form KL divergence, metric updates; then compiling without a loss and fitting without targets compute_loss() finishes the forward pass (sample z, decode) and returns reconstruction loss plus the mean KL divergence to a standard normal. Because the loss lives in the model, compile() takes no loss argument and fit() takes no targets. The page completes `compute_loss()` from **Listing 17.4**. Callouts mark that argument `x` is the model's input and that `y_pred` is the output of `call()`.

1. `z_mean, z_log_var = y_pred` unpacks the encoder's outputs.
2. `reconstruction = self.decoder(self.sampler(z_mean, z_log_var))` samples a latent point and decodes it ("This is our reconstructed image").
3. **Reconstruction loss**: `keras.losses.binary_crossentropy(x, reconstruction)` gives a per-pixel crossentropy of shape (batch, 28, 28), averaged over the last (channel) axis. It is **summed over the spatial dimensions (axes 1 and 2)** and **averaged over the batch dimension**.
4. **KL loss**: `-0.5 * (1 + z_log_var - ops.square(z_mean) - ops.exp(z_log_var))`, the closed-form KL divergence from $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ to $\mathcal N(0,1)$ for each latent dimension. It is added as `ops.mean(kl_loss)` ("Adds the regularization term (Kullback-Leibler divergence)").
5. The two `Mean` trackers are updated and `total_loss` is returned.

Next, **Listing 17.5** trains the model. Because `compute_loss()` handles the loss, `compile()` gets **no loss argument** (only `optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam()`), and `fit()` gets **no targets**. The text says you only pass `x_train`, but the code passes `mnist_digits`: the authors **concatenate the MNIST training and test images** (70,000 in total) because a generative model does not need a held-out test set here. Images get a channel axis with `np.expand_dims(..., -1)` and are scaled to [0, 1] with `astype("float32") / 255`. Training runs for **30 epochs with batch size 128**.

Once trained, the **decoder** network can turn arbitrary latent vectors into images. This is used on the next page to plot a grid of decoded points. compute_loss() samples z, decodes it and computes reconstruction + KL loss. Reconstruction: binary crossentropy summed over the 28x28 pixels and averaged over the batch. KL: -0.5 * (1 + log_var - mean^2 - exp(log_var)), zero only when mean = 0 and variance = 1; here averaged over batch and latent dims. compile() receives only an optimizer, and fit() receives only images: the model supplies its own loss. All 70,000 MNIST images (train + test) are used, normalized to [0, 1] with a channel axis, for 30 epochs at batch size 128.
snippet: The page completes computeloss from Listing 17.4. Callouts mark that argument x is the model's input and that ypred is the output of call. 1. zmean, zlogvar = ypred unpacks the…

title: Kullback-Leibler divergence (closed form for Gaussians)
text: The VAE regularization loss: how far each encoder Gaussian is from the standard normal prior. It penalizes means far from 0 and standard deviations far from 1 in either direction. Per dimension: $-\tfrac12(1+\log\sigma^2-\mu^2-\sigma^2)\ge 0$, zero iff $\mu=0,\sigma=1$. $\mu=1$, $\log\sigma^2=0$: KL = 0.5.
snippet: The VAE regularization loss: how far each encoder Gaussian is from the standard normal prior.

title: Binary crossentropy as reconstruction loss
text: Per-pixel crossentropy between the target intensity in [0, 1] and the predicted intensity. Each pixel is treated as a probability of ink; the loss is low when the prediction matches. $-[x\log\hat x+(1-x)\log(1-\hat x)]$, summed over 28x28 pixels, averaged over the batch. x = 1, prediction 0.9: 0.105; prediction 0.5: 0.693.
snippet: Per-pixel crossentropy between the target intensity in 0, 1 and the predicted intensity.

title: Overriding Model.compute_loss()

title: Reconstruction loss
text: reconstruction_loss = ops.mean(ops.sum(keras.losses.binary_crossentropy(x, reconstruction), axis=(1, 2))) \mathcal L_{\text{rec}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{i=1}^{28}\sum_{j=1}^{28} -\Big[x_{nij}\log \hat x_{nij} + (1-x_{nij})\log(1-\hat x_{nij})\Big] Make decoded samples match the inputs. Summing over 784 pixels (instead of averaging) makes this term large, so it carries much more weight than the KL term. N batch size (128) x_{nij} input pixel (row i, column j) of image n, in [0, 1] \hat x_{nij} decoded pixel from the sigmoid output
snippet: reconstructionloss = ops.meanops.sumkeras.losses.binarycrossentropyx, reconstruction, axis=1, 2 — Make decoded samples match the inputs.

title: KL divergence to a standard normal (per latent dimension)
text: kl_loss = -0.5 * (1 + z_log_var - ops.square(z_mean) - ops.exp(z_log_var)) D_{KL}\big(\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,1)\big) = -\tfrac12\big(1 + \log\sigma^2 - \mu^2 - \sigma^2\big),\qquad \sigma^2 = e^{\log\sigma^2} Regularize the encoder's distributions toward the prior N(0, 1). It is zero only at $\mu=0,\sigma^2=1$. $\mu^2/2$ penalizes off-center codes; $\tfrac12(\sigma^2-1-\log\sigma^2)$ penalizes variances that are too small or too large. \mu z_mean for one latent dimension \log\sigma^2 z_log_var for that dimension \sigma^2 ops.exp(z_log_var), the variance
snippet: klloss = -0.5  1 + zlogvar - ops.squarezmean - ops.expzlogvar — Regularize the encoder's distributions toward the prior N0, 1.

title: Total loss
text: total_loss = reconstruction_loss + ops.mean(kl_loss) \mathcal L = \mathcal L_{\text{rec}} + \frac{1}{N d}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{d} D_{KL}^{(n,k)} The single scalar returned by compute_loss and minimized by Adam. Beyond the book: the standard negative ELBO sums KL over latent dimensions; averaging divides it by d = 2, a slightly weaker regularization. With the reconstruction term summed over 784 pixels, reconstruction dominates. d latent_dim = 2 D_{KL}^{(n,k)} KL for sample n, dimension k
snippet: totalloss = reconstructionloss + ops.meanklloss — The single scalar returned by computeloss and minimized by Adam.

title: Listing 17.4 compute_loss() body (Listing 17.4, continued)
text:
original = x
        z_mean, z_log_var = y_pred
        reconstruction = self.decoder(self.sampler(z_mean, z_log_var))
        reconstruction_loss = ops.mean(
            ops.sum(
                keras.losses.binary_crossentropy(x, reconstruction), axis=(1, 2)
            )
        )
        kl_loss = -0.5 * (
            1 + z_log_var - ops.square(z_mean) - ops.exp(z_log_var)
        )
        total_loss = reconstruction_loss + ops.mean(kl_loss)
        self.reconstruction_loss_tracker.update_state(reconstruction_loss)
        self.kl_loss_tracker.update_state(kl_loss)
        return total_loss Finishes the VAE forward pass and computes reconstruction plus KL loss, updates the trackers and returns the scalar loss. Sample -> decode -> BCE (sum pixels, mean batch) + mean KL.

title: Decoding a grid of the VAE's 2D latent space; introducing diffusion models
text:
Visualizing what a trained VAE decoder has learned by sampling a regular 30 × 30 grid of 2D latent points, then opening section 17.2 on diffusion models via the idea of denoising autoencoders. Because the VAE's latent space is continuous and structured, decoding a regular grid of latent points produces a smooth map in which digits morph into each other. The page then pivots to diffusion models, starting from the oldest strength of autoencoders: removing a small amount of noise (denoising) and super-resolution. The page opens with **Listing 17.6**, which visualizes the 2-dimensional latent space of the VAE trained on MNIST in the previous pages. It builds a 30 × 30 grid of latent points, with each coordinate spaced linearly between -1 and 1 (`np.linspace(-1, 1, n)`; the y-axis is reversed so that larger `z[1]` values appear at the top). For each grid point it builds a `(1, 2)` latent vector, runs it through `vae.decoder.predict()`, reshapes the output to 28 × 28, and pastes it into the matching tile of a big `840 × 840` canvas (`figure`). The canvas is then shown with Matplotlib in grayscale. The result is Figure 17.5, printed on the next page.

The authors interpret the figure: the decoded digits form a **completely continuous distribution** of classes, and one digit **morphs into another** as you move along a path in latent space. Directions in the space carry meaning (a direction for 'four-ness', one for 'one-ness', and so on). This is the structured, continuous latent space the VAE's sampling and regularization loss were designed to produce (p.536).

After one transition sentence that calls diffusion models 'the architecture behind nearly all commercial image generation services today', **section 17.2 Diffusion models** begins. It starts from **denoising**: you feed an autoencoder a slightly noisy input (for example a low-quality JPEG) and get back a cleaned-up version. The authors call this 'the one task that autoencoders excel at.' In the late 2010s this led to **image super-resolution** models, which turn low-resolution, possibly noisy images into high-quality, high-resolution ones (Figure 17.6, next page). Such models now ship in every major smartphone camera app. The next pages turn this single denoising step into the repeated, loop-based denoising that defines diffusion models. Listing 17.6 decodes a 30 × 30 grid of 2D latent points over [-1, 1]² into a single 840 × 840 mosaic (Figure 17.5). The mosaic shows a continuous distribution of digit classes: walking through latent space morphs one digit into another, and directions carry meaning such as 'four-ness'. `plt.axis("off")` hides the tick setup in the listing; decoding one point per predict call is slow, so batch the 900 points in practice. Section 17.2 starts from denoising, the one task the authors say autoencoders excel at; super-resolution is its most widely shipped application. Diffusion models, the basis of nearly all commercial image generators, build on this denoising idea.

title: Latent space
text: A low-dimensional vector space of learned representations in which each point can be decoded into a data sample (here, a 28 × 28 digit). A map whose coordinates are 'idea knobs' rather than pixels. Turning the knobs smoothly changes the decoded image smoothly. In this VAE the latent space is ℝ². Listing 17.6 samples it on a regular 30 × 30 grid over [-1, 1]² and decodes each point with the trained decoder. z = [0.0, 0.0] might decode to a blend between several digit classes; moving along z[1] might go from 0 to 7 through 6, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9 as in Figure 17.5.

title: Variational autoencoder (VAE)
text: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs the parameters of a distribution (z_mean, z_log_var) from which a latent point is sampled, trained with a reconstruction loss plus a KL regularization loss. The randomness forces the decoder to work for every point in a neighbourhood, not just exact codes, which fills the space with valid images. This page uses only the trained `vae.decoder` sub-model, which maps a (batch, 2) tensor to (batch, 28, 28, 1) pixel probabilities. `vae.decoder.predict(np.array([[0.5, -0.3]]))` returns one 28 × 28 image.

text: A model trained to map a corrupted input (noise, compression artifacts, low resolution) to its clean version. It has seen so many clean images that it knows which details belong and which are corruption. Trained on (corrupted x, clean x) pairs with a reconstruction loss. In this section it becomes the building block of diffusion models, and on p.546 it predicts the noise rather than the clean image. Cleaning up a low-quality JPEG; super-resolving a phone photo.

title: Figures 17.5 and 17.6: the decoded latent grid and image super-resolution
text:
The output of Listing 17.6 (a 30 × 30 mosaic of digits decoded from the VAE's latent plane) and an example of image super-resolution, followed by the warning that super-resolution models guess rather than recover lost detail. Figure 17.5 shows the continuity of the VAE latent space; Figure 17.6 shows denoising/super-resolution at work. The text stresses that such models are hallucinating a plausible clean image, not retrieving hidden information. This page is mostly figures.

**Figure 17.5, 'Grid of digits decoded from the latent space'**, is the 840 × 840 mosaic produced by Listing 17.6 (p.542): 900 white-on-black digits decoded from a 30 × 30 grid of points over [-1, 1]² in the VAE's 2D latent space. Reading from the top, broad bands of 7s give way to 9s and 4s, then 8s, 5s, 3s and 2s, with 6s and finally 0s filling the lower part and the right side. At every boundary the digits blend: a 3 gradually turns into a 5 or an 8, a 2 into a 6, a 6 into a 0. This is the 'completely continuous distribution' described on p.542.

**Figure 17.6, 'Image super-resolution'**, shows a photo of bananas and a fruit bowl twice. On the left is a 'Low-resolution image with artifacts' (blurry, blocky, with compression halos); an arrow points to the right, a 'Crisp high-resolution image'. It illustrates the super-resolution models introduced at the start of section 17.2.

The text then gives the key caveat. These models are **not magically recovering lost details hidden in the input**, as in the 'enhance' scene from *Blade Runner* (1982). They make **educated guesses** about what the image should look like: they are **hallucinating** a cleaned-up, higher-resolution version (the sentence finishes on p.544). This guessing is the key to the next step: if a model can plausibly invent missing detail, repeated application can invent an entire image. Figure 17.5 is the output of Listing 17.6: digits decoded from a 30 × 30 grid over the VAE's 2D latent plane, blending continuously from class to class. Figure 17.6 shows super-resolution turning a low-resolution, artifact-laden photo into a crisp one. Super-resolution does not recover hidden detail; it makes educated guesses, i.e. it hallucinates a plausible clean image. That guessing ability is what diffusion models exploit to generate images from pure noise.

title: From denoising to reverse diffusion; the Oxford Flowers dataset
text:
Why super-resolution hallucinates detail, the key insight that repeated denoising can turn pure noise into an image (reverse diffusion), and the dataset used to build a diffusion model in Keras. If an autoencoder can remove a little noise, applying it repeatedly in a loop can remove a lot, all the way from pure noise to a sharp new image. A diffusion model is a denoising autoencoder in a loop. The page finishes the super-resolution caveat from p.543: these models produce a hallucinated, cleaned-up, higher-resolution version of their input. The authors' example: with some AI-enhanced cameras, a photo of something vaguely moon-like (even a printout of a severely blurred moon) becomes a crisp picture of lunar craters, because the camera's super-resolution model is **overfitted to moon photography**. The detail was never in the printout. Their advice: unlike Rick Deckard (Blade Runner), don't use this technique for forensics.

Next comes the central idea. Early successes in denoising raised a question: if an autoencoder removes a small amount of noise, can you **repeat it in a loop** to remove a large amount, and ultimately denoise an image made of **pure noise**? The answer is yes. Doing so hallucinates brand-new images out of nothing (Figure 17.7: a coral-reef scene emerges from static as **diffusion time** goes from 1 to 0.75, 0.5, 0.25 and 0). This is the key insight behind **diffusion models**. The authors note that they should more accurately be called **reverse diffusion** models, since 'diffusion' is the process of gradually adding noise until the image disperses into nothing; the generator runs that process backward.

In one sentence: a diffusion model is **a denoising autoencoder in a loop**, turning pure noise into sharp imagery. The authors adapt Michelangelo: every square of white noise has an image inside it, and the diffusion model's task is to discover it.

Section **17.2.1** then introduces the dataset for the Keras implementation: the **Oxford Flowers** dataset (102 Category Flower Dataset from Oxford's Visual Geometry Group), with **8,189 images** of flowers from **102 species**. The download code follows on p.545. Super-resolution models hallucinate detail; a model overfitted to moon photos can add craters to a blurred printout, so don't use it for forensics. Key insight: repeating a small denoising step in a loop can turn pure noise into a brand-new image. A diffusion model is a denoising autoencoder in a loop; 'reverse diffusion' would be the more accurate name, since diffusion means adding noise. Figure 17.7 shows diffusion time running from 1 (pure noise) to 0 (clean image). The Keras implementation uses the Oxford Flowers dataset: 8,189 images from 102 species.

title: Diffusion model
text: A generative model that creates images by applying a learned denoiser repeatedly, starting from pure noise; in the book's words, 'a denoising autoencoder in a loop'. Sculpting: start with a block of noise and chip away a little at each step until an image remains. One network is trained to remove noise at any noise level. Generation iterates it from diffusion time 1 (pure noise) to 0 (clean image). Figure 17.7: a coral reef emerges from static over diffusion times 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, 0.
snippet: A generative model that creates images by applying a learned denoiser repeatedly, starting from pure noise; in the book's words, 'a denoising autoencoder in a loop'.

title: Forward vs reverse diffusion
text: Forward diffusion gradually adds noise to an image until it disperses into nothing; reverse diffusion gradually removes noise to produce an image. Forward: a drop of ink spreading in water. Reverse: the spread-out ink gathering back into a drop, which needs a learned model to know where each bit belongs. Forward diffusion is a fixed, unlearned noising procedure used to create training pairs; reverse diffusion is performed by the trained denoiser at generation time. Reading Figure 17.7 left-to-right is reverse diffusion; right-to-left would be forward diffusion.
snippet: Forward diffusion gradually adds noise to an image until it disperses into nothing; reverse diffusion gradually removes noise to produce an image.

title: Hallucination (in generative models)
text: Producing plausible detail not present in the input, based on the model's learned statistics. Confidently filling in the gaps with what usually goes there. The less information an input carries, the more the output is determined by the model's prior; pure noise is the limit case where the output is essentially all prior, i.e. generation. A camera adding moon craters to a blurred printout.

title: Loading Oxford Flowers as 128 × 128 batches; the denoiser's job
text:
Downloading and extracting the Oxford Flowers archive, turning the JPEGs into a batched dataset of undistorted 128 × 128 crops, viewing one example, and starting the description of the denoising model reused at every diffusion step. The data pipeline produces fixed-size, aspect-preserving, unlabeled image batches of exactly 32. The denoiser is a single model reused at every step of the loop, and it is told how much noise to remove. The first code block downloads the Oxford Flowers archive (`102flowers.tgz` from the VGG site) with `keras.utils.get_file(..., extract=True)`. `fpath` is then the local path to the **extracted directory**, and the images are in its `jpg` subdirectory.

The second block builds an iterable dataset with `keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory()`. Images must be a fixed size, but distorting their aspect ratio would hurt the quality of generated images, so `crop_to_aspect_ratio=True` extracts the **largest undistorted crop** of the right aspect ratio and resizes it to **128 × 128**. `labels=None` because only images are needed (callout: 'We won't need the labels, just the images.'). The dataset is then `rebatch`ed to `batch_size = 32` with `drop_remainder=True`, so every batch has exactly 32 images and the last, irregular batch is dropped.

The third block takes the first image of the first batch and displays it (Figure 17.8: a pink lotus-like flower, with 0-120 pixel ticks on both axes). It is cast with `astype("uint8")` because the pipeline yields float32 values in [0, 255].

Section **17.2.2 A U-Net denoising autoencoder** begins: the **same denoising model is reused at every iteration** of the diffusion process, erasing a little noise each time. To make the model's job easier, it is told how much noise it is supposed to extract from the input image. The sentence finishes on p.546, where this extra input is named `noise_rates`. get_file(..., extract=True) downloads and unpacks the archive; images are in fpath/jpg. image_dataset_from_directory with labels=None, image_size=(128, 128) and crop_to_aspect_ratio=True yields undistorted square crops. rebatch(32, drop_remainder=True) makes every batch exactly 32 images; with 8,189 images, 29 are dropped per epoch. Pixels are float32 in [0, 255]; cast to uint8 for display. One denoising model is reused at every diffusion step and is told how much noise to remove.
