title: The U-Net denoiser: noise-rate input, noise-mask output, three stages
text:
What the denoising model takes in (noisy image plus noise rate) and outputs (a predicted noise mask), the U-Net architecture of Figure 17.9 with its downsampling, middle and upsampling stages and concatenative skip connections, and the start of the residual_block helper. The denoiser is a U-Net that receives the noisy image and its noise rate, and outputs the noise to subtract. Its encoder-decoder shape with skip connections lets it reason globally at 16 × 16 while keeping pixel-level detail at 128 × 128. The sentence from p.545 finishes: the denoiser is told how much noise it should extract, through the **`noise_rates` input**. Rather than outputting a denoised image, the model outputs a **predicted noise mask**, which can be **subtracted from the input** to denoise it.

The denoiser is a **U-Net**, a kind of ConvNet originally developed for image segmentation. Figure 17.9 shows it: a noise rate and a 128 × 128 image enter a **Concat** node; three blocks form the **downsampling stage**, which reaches a **16 × 16 feature map**; a **middle stage** keeps that size; three blocks form the **upsampling stage**, which returns to a **128 × 128 image**. Long arrows link each downsampling block to its mirror upsampling block through **Concat** nodes.

The text spells out the stages: (1) downsampling with several blocks of convolution layers, from 128 × 128 to 16 × 16; (2) a middle stage at constant size; (3) upsampling back to 128 × 128. Each upsampling block is the inverse of a downsampling block (a 1:1 mapping). **Concatenative residual connections** run from each downsampling block to its corresponding upsampling block and help avoid loss of image detail across the successive downsampling and upsampling operations.

The model is assembled with the **Functional API**. The page shows the start of the helper `residual_block(x, width)`: if the input's channel count (`x.shape[3]`) already equals `width`, the residual is `x` itself; otherwise a **1 × 1 `Conv2D`** projects it to `width` channels. Then `BatchNormalization(center=False, scale=False)` normalizes `x` without a learned shift or scale. The block continues on p.547 with two 3 × 3 convolutions and the residual addition. The denoiser takes two inputs: the noisy image and noise_rates (how much noise to extract). It outputs a predicted noise mask, which is removed from the input to denoise it. The denoiser is a U-Net: downsampling from 128 × 128 to 16 × 16, a constant-size middle stage, and upsampling back to 128 × 128. Concatenative skip connections from each down block to its mirror up block preserve image detail. residual_block uses an identity shortcut when channel counts match and a 1 × 1 Conv2D projection otherwise, then non-affine batch normalization.

title: U-Net
text: An encoder-decoder ConvNet that downsamples, processes at low resolution, and upsamples back, with skip connections between matching resolutions. Zoom out to understand the scene, zoom back in to draw it, while keeping your close-up notes from the way down. Here: 128 × 128 → 16 × 16 (three average-pooling steps), middle residual blocks, three bilinear upsampling steps back to 128 × 128, with Concatenate skips; output is a 3-channel noise mask. Figure 17.9; get_model() on p.547.
snippet: An encoder-decoder ConvNet that downsamples, processes at low resolution, and upsamples back, with skip connections between matching resolutions.

title: Concatenative skip connection
text: Passing a feature map from an earlier layer directly to a later one and concatenating it along the channel axis. A side road that carries fine detail past the low-resolution bottleneck. In get_model(), every downsampling residual block's output is saved in `skips` and later concatenated with the upsampled features at the same resolution: Concatenate()([x, skips.pop()]). At 128 × 128, a 64-channel upsampled map concatenated with a 32-channel skip gives 96 channels.
snippet: Passing a feature map from an earlier layer directly to a later one and concatenating it along the channel axis.

title: Predicting the noise mask
text: Training the denoiser to output the noise present in its input rather than the clean image. Instead of repainting the whole picture, point out the specks to remove. Output shape equals the image shape (128, 128, 3); the denoised estimate is obtained by removing the predicted noise from the input (scaled by the schedule rates in the actual training code). At low noise the ideal output is close to a small-magnitude mask; at very high noise the noisy input is mostly noise, and the mask is mostly the input.
snippet: Training the denoiser to output the noise present in its input rather than the clean image.

title: Residual connection (in residual_block)
text: Adding a block's input (possibly projected) to its output. The block only has to learn a correction to its input. If the input has `width` channels, the residual is x; otherwise it is projected with a 1 × 1 Conv2D so the shapes match for the later `x + residual` (p.547). First block: input has 33 channels (32 image features + 1 noise-rate channel), width 32, so a 1 × 1 projection is used.
snippet: Adding a block's input possibly projected to its output.

title: Batch normalization without affine parameters
text: Normalizing activations to zero mean and unit variance per channel, here without the learned shift (beta) and scale (gamma). Standardize the inputs before the block's convolutions process them. `BatchNormalization(center=False, scale=False)`: center=False drops beta, scale=False drops gamma. The following Conv2D has its own weights and bias, so it can rescale and shift anyway. A channel with batch mean 5 and std 2 maps a value 9 to (9 − 5)/2 = 2 (ignoring epsilon).
snippet: Normalizing activations to zero mean and unit variance per channel, here without the learned shift beta and scale gamma.

title: Denoising by subtracting the predicted noise mask
text: we make our model output a predicted noise mask, which we can subtract from the input to denoise it \hat{x}_{\text{denoised}} = x_{\text{noisy}} - \hat{\varepsilon}, \qquad \hat{\varepsilon} = f_\theta\!\left(x_{\text{noisy}},\, r_{\text{noise}}\right) Defines the model's output and how it is used to remove noise. The model separates its input into 'noise' (its output) and 'signal' (what is left). x_{\text{noisy}} The noisy input image, shape (128, 128, 3). r_{\text{noise}} The noise rate given to the model as the noise_rates input, shape (1, 1, 1) per image. f_\theta The U-Net denoiser with weights θ. \hat{\varepsilon} The predicted noise mask, same shape as the image. \hat{x}_{\text{denoised}} The denoised estimate.

title: get_model(): the full U-Net denoiser; diffusion time introduced
text:
The end of residual_block and the complete get_model() function that builds the two-input U-Net (noisy images + noise rates → predicted noise masks), how the widths argument shapes it, and the start of section 17.2.3 defining diffusion time. get_model() conditions the U-Net on the noise rate by broadcasting it to a full-resolution channel, runs downsampling, middle and upsampling stages built from residual blocks with concatenated skips, and ends with a zero-initialized 1 × 1 convolution so that the untrained model predicts 'no noise'. Diffusion time indexes progress through the denoising loop. The code continues `residual_block` from p.546: a **3 × 3 `Conv2D` with `swish` activation**, a second **3 × 3 `Conv2D` without activation**, then **`x = x + residual`**.

`get_model(image_size, widths, block_depth)` builds the denoiser:

- Two inputs: `noisy_images` of shape `(image_size, image_size, 3)` and `noise_rates` of shape `(1, 1, 1)`.
- The image goes through a 1 × 1 `Conv2D(widths[0])`. The noise rate is stretched to full resolution with `UpSampling2D(image_size, interpolation="nearest")` and **concatenated** as an extra channel.
- **Downsampling stage**: for each width except the last, `block_depth` residual blocks (each output pushed onto `skips`), then `AveragePooling2D(pool_size=2)`.
- **Middle stage**: `block_depth` residual blocks at `widths[-1]`.
- **Upsampling stage**: for each width in reverse, `UpSampling2D(size=2, interpolation="bilinear")`, then `block_depth` times: concatenate with `skips.pop()` and apply a residual block.
- Output: `Conv2D(3, 1, kernel_initializer="zeros")` produces `pred_noise_masks`. The callout explains that zero init makes the model predict only zeros at first, i.e. the default assumption before training is 'no noise'.

The model is instantiated with something like `get_model(image_size=128, widths=[32, 64, 96, 128], block_depth=2)`. `widths` lists the `Conv2D` sizes per stage: layers get bigger as resolution shrinks (32 to 128) and smaller as it grows back (128 to 32).

**Section 17.2.3** begins: the diffusion process is a series of denoising steps from a pure-noise image to a pure-signal image. The index of the current step is the **diffusion time** (Figure 17.7). The book uses a continuous value between 1 and 0 (the sentence finishes on p.548). residual_block = BatchNorm (non-affine) → 3 × 3 conv (swish) → 3 × 3 conv (linear) → add shortcut. The noise rate is tiled to a 128 × 128 channel with nearest-neighbour upsampling and concatenated with the image features. Down levels store skips; up levels pop them in reverse order (LIFO) and concatenate before each residual block. The last layer is a zero-initialized 1 × 1 conv, so the untrained model predicts 'no noise'. widths=[32, 64, 96, 128], block_depth=2 gives three resolution levels (128, 64, 32) plus a 16 × 16 middle stage with 128 channels. Diffusion time indexes the denoising loop, running continuously from 1 (pure noise) to 0 (pure signal).

For widths=[32, 64, 96, 128], block_depth=2: 6 residual blocks down, 2 in the middle, 6 up, 6 skip tensors, output (None, 128, 128, 3). get_model(image_size=128, widths=[32, 64, 96, 128], block_depth=2).

title: Noise-rate conditioning by concatenation
text: Feeding the scalar noise rate into a convolutional network by tiling it into a full-resolution channel and concatenating it with the image features. Write the damage level on every pixel so every convolution can see it. UpSampling2D(128, interpolation="nearest") turns (None, 1, 1, 1) into (None, 128, 128, 1); Concatenate with the (None, 128, 128, 32) image features gives 33 channels. noise rate 0.7 → a 128 × 128 channel filled with 0.7.

title: Zero-initialized output layer
text: Initializing the final layer's kernel to zeros so that the untrained model outputs zeros. Start from 'I see no noise' and learn corrections, rather than starting with random large noise predictions. Conv2D(3, 1, kernel_initializer="zeros"); the bias defaults to zeros too, so the initial output is exactly 0. Gradients still flow because the layer's input activations are non-zero. Before training, model.predict on any input returns an all-zero (128, 128, 3) mask.

title: Diffusion time
text: The index of the current step in the diffusion loop, a continuous value from 1 (pure noise) to 0 (pure signal). A progress bar for denoising that runs backward from 1 to 0. title: Swish activation
text: swish(x) = x · sigmoid(x), a smooth, non-monotonic alternative to ReLU. Like ReLU for large positive inputs, but smooth around zero and slightly negative for small negative inputs. Used in the first 3 × 3 convolution of each residual block; the second convolution is linear so the residual sum is not clipped. swish(1) ≈ 0.731, swish(−1) ≈ −0.269.

Three poolings give the 16 × 16 bottleneck of Figure 17.9. Every concatenation changes the channel count away from `width`, so the following residual block projects its shortcut. title: End of residual_block and get_model(): building the U-Net denoiser
text:
x = layers.Conv2D(width, 3, padding="same", activation="swish")(x)
    x = layers.Conv2D(width, 3, padding="same")(x)
    x = x + residual
    return x
def get_model(image_size, widths, block_depth):
    noisy_images = keras.Input(shape=(image_size, image_size, 3))
    noise_rates = keras.Input(shape=(1, 1, 1))
    x = layers.Conv2D(widths[0], 1)(noisy_images)
    n = layers.UpSampling2D(image_size, interpolation="nearest")(noise_rates)
    x = layers.Concatenate()([x, n])
    skips = []
    for width in widths[:-1]:
        for _ in range(block_depth):
            x = residual_block(x, width)
            skips.append(x)
        x = layers.AveragePooling2D(pool_size=2)(x)
    for _ in range(block_depth):
        x = residual_block(x, widths[-1])
    for width in reversed(widths[:-1]):
        x = layers.UpSampling2D(size=2, interpolation="bilinear")(x)
        for _ in range(block_depth):
            x = layers.Concatenate()([x, skips.pop()])
            x = residual_block(x, width)
    pred_noise_masks = layers.Conv2D(3, 1, kernel_initializer="zeros")(x)
    return keras.Model([noisy_images, noise_rates], pred_noise_masks) Completes residual_block (two 3 × 3 convolutions and the residual addition) and defines get_model(), which builds a two-input Functional model mapping (noisy images, noise rates) to predicted noise masks through a U-Net with residual blocks and concatenated skip connections. Embed image (1 × 1 conv) ⊕ tiled noise rate → [residual blocks + save skip] × depth, avg-pool, for each level → middle residual blocks → for each level in reverse: bilinear ×2 upsample, [concat skip + residual block] × depth → 1 × 1 zero-init conv.

title: The cosine diffusion schedule
text:
How a continuous diffusion time in [0, 1] is mapped to a noise rate and a signal rate with a cosine schedule (Listing 17.7). Each diffusion time is turned into an angle that moves linearly between arccos(0.95) and arccos(0.02); the signal rate is the cosine of that angle and the noise rate its sine, so noise_rate^2 + signal_rate^2 = 1 always holds. This page finishes the definition of **diffusion time** and introduces the **diffusion schedule**.

- The diffusion time is a continuous number between 1 and 0 (the sentence starts on p.547). In the book's wording, **1** marks the start of the (generation) process, where the image is maximally noisy and carries minimal signal, and **0** marks the end, where the image is almost all signal.
- The **diffusion schedule** is the relationship between the current diffusion time and how much noise and signal the image contains. The authors pick a **cosine schedule**, which moves smoothly between a high signal rate (0.95) and a low one (0.02).

**Listing 17.7** implements it as `diffusion_schedule(diffusion_times, min_signal_rate=0.02, max_signal_rate=0.95)`:

1. `start_angle = arccos(0.95)` (about 0.318 rad, 18.2 degrees) and `end_angle = arccos(0.02)` (about 1.551 rad, 88.9 degrees), both cast to `float32`.
2. The diffusion times are mapped linearly to angles: `diffusion_angles = start_angle + diffusion_times * (end_angle - start_angle)`.
3. `signal_rates = cos(angle)`, `noise_rates = sin(angle)`; the function returns `(noise_rates, signal_rates)` in that order.

So diffusion time 0 gives signal rate 0.95 (noise rate about 0.31) and diffusion time 1 gives signal rate 0.02 (noise rate about 0.9998). Because the two rates are the cosine and sine of the same angle, they always satisfy `noise_rates ** 2 + signal_rates ** 2 == 1`, which **Figure 17.10** shows as a quarter circle: signal rate on the vertical axis, noise rate on the horizontal axis.

The returned rates will "guide the denoising process": during training they set how much noise is mixed into each clean image (p.551), and during generation they tell the model how noisy the current image is and how to re-noise the next step (pp.551-552). Note that the two paragraphs describe the direction of the process differently (see the review flag): read "beginning" in the second paragraph as diffusion time 0. Diffusion time is a continuous index in [0, 1]: 1 = noisiest, 0 = almost clean. The diffusion schedule maps diffusion time to a (noise rate, signal rate) pair. Listing 17.7 interpolates an angle linearly between arccos(0.95) and arccos(0.02), then takes cos (signal) and sin (noise). Because the rates are cos and sin of the same angle, noise_rates**2 + signal_rates**2 == 1 (Figure 17.10). The function returns (noise_rates, signal_rates) in that order and works element-wise on whole tensors. The two paragraphs on this page describe the direction of the process differently; the code makes t=0 the low-noise end.

title: Diffusion time
text: A continuous value in [0, 1] indexing the noise level of an image in the diffusion process; 1 is the noisiest, 0 the cleanest. Think of it as a dial: turn it to 1 and the image is drowned in noise; turn it to 0 and the image is nearly clean. Generation turns the dial slowly from 1 down to 0. In this implementation, t is fed to diffusion_schedule() to get the rates. Training samples t ~ Uniform(0, 1) per image (p.551); generation uses t = 1, 1 - 1/T, 1 - 2/T, ... for T steps (p.551). With 20 generation steps the diffusion times visited are 1.00, 0.95, 0.90, ..., 0.05.

title: Diffusion schedule (cosine)
text: The mapping from diffusion time to (noise rate, signal rate). The book uses a cosine schedule: the rates are the sine and cosine of an angle that grows linearly with diffusion time. Picture a point moving along a quarter circle from near the top (mostly signal) to near the right edge (mostly noise). Its height is the signal rate and its horizontal position is the noise rate. angle(t) = arccos(0.95) + t (arccos(0.02) - arccos(0.95)); signal = cos(angle); noise = sin(angle). Endpoints: t=0 -> (noise 0.312, signal 0.95); t=1 -> (noise 0.9998, signal 0.02). t = 0.5 gives angle about 0.934 rad, so signal rate about 0.594 and noise rate about 0.804.

title: Listing 17.7 The diffusion schedule
text:
def diffusion_schedule(
    diffusion_times,
    min_signal_rate=0.02,
    max_signal_rate=0.95,
):
    start_angle = ops.cast(ops.arccos(max_signal_rate), "float32")
    end_angle = ops.cast(ops.arccos(min_signal_rate), "float32")
    diffusion_angles = start_angle + diffusion_times * (end_angle - start_angle)
    signal_rates = ops.cos(diffusion_angles)
    noise_rates = ops.sin(diffusion_angles)
    return noise_rates, signal_rates Maps a tensor of diffusion times in [0, 1] to two tensors of the same shape: the noise rates and the signal rates, following a cosine schedule between signal rate 0.95 (t=0) and 0.02 (t=1). 1) Convert extreme signal rates to angles with arccos. 2) Interpolate the angle linearly with t. 3) Take cos and sin.

title: Plotting the schedule; starting the DiffusionModel
text:
Visualizing the cosine diffusion schedule (Figure 17.11) and listing the ingredients of the DiffusionModel training class: the denoiser, an MAE loss on noise masks, and an image normalization layer. Plotted against diffusion time, the noise rate rises from about 0.31 to 1 while the signal rate falls from 0.95 to 0.02. The training class will predict the noise that was added, scored with mean absolute error, on images normalized to match the zero-mean, unit-variance noise. The page opens by **plotting the diffusion schedule** from Listing 17.7 (p.548). The snippet builds 100 diffusion times with `ops.arange(0.0, 1.0, 0.01)`, calls `diffusion_schedule()`, converts the three tensors to NumPy and plots noise rate and signal rate against diffusion time. A callout notes that the three `ops.convert_to_numpy()` lines are only needed with the **PyTorch** backend, where turning a tensor into NumPy is not automatic.

**Figure 17.11** shows the result. The noise rate (blue) climbs from about 0.31 at t = 0 to about 1.0 at t = 1, and the signal rate (orange) falls from 0.95 to about 0.02. The curves cross near t of about 0.38, where both equal about 0.707. Both are smooth trigonometric curves: the signal rate drops slowly at first and steeply near the end, and the noise rate flattens out as it approaches 1.

Section **17.2.4 The training process** then begins. The training logic will live in a `DiffusionModel` class, which holds the U-Net denoising autoencoder (pp.545-547) as an attribute and needs two more things:

- **A loss function**: mean absolute error between the real noise mask and the predicted one, `mean(abs(real_noise_mask - predicted_noise_mask))`. In other words, the network is trained to **predict the noise** that was added, not the clean image directly.
- **An image normalization layer**: the added noise has zero mean and unit variance, so the images should be normalized the same way, so that the value ranges of noise and images match.

The class itself is built on pp.550-552. Figure 17.11: noise rate rises from about 0.31 to 1, signal rate falls from 0.95 to 0.02; they cross near t = 0.38. ops.convert_to_numpy is only needed before plotting when using the PyTorch backend. Training lives in a DiffusionModel class that wraps the U-Net denoiser. The model is trained to predict the added noise mask, with mean absolute error as the loss. Images are normalized to zero mean and unit variance to match the scale of the Gaussian noise.

text: Training the denoiser to output the noise mask that was added to a clean image, scored against the real mask. Instead of asking 'what did the picture look like?', ask 'what is the static you see?'. Subtract the static and you get the picture back. Loss = mean(|epsilon - epsilon_hat|) with epsilon ~ N(0, I) and epsilon_hat = denoiser(x_t, n(t)). For a 128 x 128 x 3 image, the loss averages 49,152 absolute differences.

title: DiffusionModel constructor and denoise()
text:
The DiffusionModel constructor, the denoise() method that reconstructs clean images from predicted noise, and the plan for the training forward pass in call(). DiffusionModel wraps the U-Net, a seed generator, an MAE loss and a Normalization layer. denoise() asks the U-Net for the noise mask and inverts noisy = signal * image + noise * mask to recover the image. Training is done by putting the forward pass in call() and the loss in a custom compute_loss(), which keeps the model backend-agnostic. This page writes the first parts of the `DiffusionModel` class announced on p.549.

**Constructor.** `DiffusionModel(keras.Model)` takes `image_size`, `widths`, `block_depth` (forwarded to `get_model()`, p.547) and `**kwargs` (forwarded to `keras.Model`). It stores:

- `self.image_size`;
- `self.denoising_model`: the U-Net;
- `self.seed_generator = keras.random.SeedGenerator()`: a stateful source of randomness for sampling noise and diffusion times;
- `self.loss = keras.losses.MeanAbsoluteError()`: the loss (callout: "Our loss function");
- `self.normalizer = keras.layers.Normalization()`: used to normalize input images (callout).

**denoise().** Given noisy images and their noise and signal rates, it calls the denoiser with `[noisy_images, noise_rates]` to get `pred_noise_masks`, then reconstructs the clean image as `(noisy_images - noise_rates * pred_noise_masks) / signal_rates`. This is the noising equation `noisy = signal * image + noise * mask` solved for `image`. It returns both the predicted images and the predicted noise masks.

**Training logic.** As with the VAE, the authors implement a custom `compute_loss()` to stay **backend-agnostic**. You could write a custom `train_step()` instead, but that requires backend-specific code for gradient computation and weight updates. Because `compute_loss()` receives the output of `call()`, the denoising forward pass goes in `call()`, which takes a batch of clean images and:

1. normalizes them,
2. samples random diffusion times (to train on the full spectrum),
3. computes the matching noise and signal rates with the schedule,
4. adds random noise to the clean images based on those rates,
5. denoises the images.

The code for `call()` and `compute_loss()` follows on p.551. DiffusionModel holds the U-Net, a SeedGenerator, a MeanAbsoluteError loss and a Normalization layer. denoise() predicts the noise mask and reconstructs the image as (noisy - noise_rate * pred_noise) / signal_rate. Overriding compute_loss() and putting the forward pass in call() keeps training backend-agnostic. call() will normalize images, sample random diffusion times, compute rates, add noise and denoise. Random diffusion times train one network for all noise levels.

        self.loss = keras.losses.MeanAbsoluteError()
        self.normalizer = keras.layers.Normalization() Defines the DiffusionModel subclass of keras.Model and creates its components: the U-Net denoiser, a seed generator, the MAE loss and a Normalization layer. Composition: the diffusion training logic wraps a plain functional U-Net.

title: Training forward pass, loss, and start of generate()
text:
The call() method that builds noisy training images and denoises them, the compute_loss() override that scores noise prediction with MAE, and the opening of the generate() method. call() normalizes a batch, samples Gaussian noise masks and one uniform diffusion time per image, mixes them with the schedule's rates, and denoises; it returns predicted images, predicted noise masks and the real noise masks so that compute_loss() can compare the last two. Generation starts from pure Gaussian noise and walks the diffusion time down from 1 in steps of 1/diffusion_steps. The page completes the training logic of `DiffusionModel` and starts the generation logic.

**call() returns three things**: the predicted denoised images, the predicted noise masks and the actual noise masks it applied. The last two are what `compute_loss()` uses to score the model on the **noise mask prediction task**.

**call(images)** step by step (callouts in parentheses):

1. `images = self.normalizer(images)`: standardize the batch.
2. `noise_masks = keras.random.normal((batch_size, image_size, image_size, 3), seed=self.seed_generator)` ("Samples random noise masks").
3. `diffusion_times = keras.random.uniform((batch_size, 1, 1, 1), 0.0, 1.0, ...)` ("Samples random diffusion times"), one per image, shaped to broadcast over pixels.
4. `noise_rates, signal_rates = diffusion_schedule(diffusion_times)`.
5. `noisy_images = signal_rates * images + noise_rates * noise_masks` ("Adds noise to the images").
6. `pred_images, pred_noise_masks = self.denoise(noisy_images, noise_rates, signal_rates)` ("Denoises them").
7. Returns `pred_images, pred_noise_masks, noise_masks`.

**compute_loss(self, x, y, y_pred, sample_weight=None, training=True)** unpacks `y_pred`, discards the predicted images and returns `self.loss(noise_masks, pred_noise_masks)`, the MAE between real and predicted noise.

**17.2.5 The generation process.** Generation starts from pure random noise and repeatedly applies `denoise()` until the images are high-signal, low-noise. `generate(num_images, diffusion_steps)` samples standard Gaussian `noisy_images` of shape `(num_images, image_size, image_size, 3)` ("Starts from pure noise"), sets `step_size = 1.0 / diffusion_steps` and loops. At iteration `step`, the diffusion time is `1 - step * step_size` for every image (shape `(num_images, 1, 1, 1)`), and the matching rates come from `diffusion_schedule()` ("Computes appropriate noise rates and signal rates"). The loop body continues on p.552.

Note: `call()` uses `batch_size`, which is not an attribute or argument; it is the global `batch_size = 32` defined with the dataset on p.545. This works because the dataset was rebatched with `drop_remainder=True`, so every batch has exactly 32 images. call() normalizes, samples noise masks and per-image diffusion times, mixes them via the schedule, and denoises. call() returns (pred_images, pred_noise_masks, noise_masks) so compute_loss() can access the real noise. compute_loss() returns MAE(noise_masks, pred_noise_masks). generate() starts from N(0, 1) noise and uses diffusion times 1, 1 - 1/T, ..., 1/T. call() relies on the global batch_size = 32; the dataset's drop_remainder=True makes that safe.

text: Generating images by starting from Gaussian noise and repeatedly denoising while decreasing the diffusion time from 1 toward 0. Sculpting: each pass removes a bit more noise until an image emerges (the Michelangelo analogy on p.544). noisy_images ~ N(0, I); for step in range(T): t = 1 - step / T; (n, s) = schedule(t); denoise; re-noise at t - 1/T (p.552). diffusion_steps = 20: t = 1.00, 0.95, ..., 0.05.

Each pixel is a weighted mix of its true value and a random Gaussian value. x_0 normalized clean images (images after self.normalizer) \varepsilon noise_masks, standard Gaussian, same shape as the images t diffusion_times, one per image s(t), n(t) signal_rates and noise_rates from diffusion_schedule x_t noisy_images

The last step uses t = 1/T and re-noises to t = 0 (p.552). T diffusion_steps k step, the loop index t_k diffusion time at step k (same for all images)

title: call() and compute_loss(): the training logic
text:
def call(self, images):
        images = self.normalizer(images)
        noise_masks = keras.random.normal(
            (batch_size, self.image_size, self.image_size, 3),
            seed=self.seed_generator,
        )
        diffusion_times = keras.random.uniform(
            (batch_size, 1, 1, 1),
            minval=0.0,
            maxval=1.0,
            seed=self.seed_generator,
        )
        noise_rates, signal_rates = diffusion_schedule(diffusion_times)
        noisy_images = signal_rates * images + noise_rates * noise_masks
        pred_images, pred_noise_masks = self.denoise(
            noisy_images, noise_rates, signal_rates
        )
        return pred_images, pred_noise_masks, noise_masks

    def compute_loss(self, x, y, y_pred, sample_weight=None, training=True):
        _, pred_noise_masks, noise_masks = y_pred
        return self.loss(noise_masks, pred_noise_masks) call() turns a batch of clean images into noisy images at random noise levels and predicts their noise; compute_loss() returns the MAE between the real and predicted noise masks. Normalize -> sample eps and t -> schedule -> mix -> predict eps -> MAE.
snippet: call turns a batch of clean images into noisy images at random noise levels and predicts their noise; computeloss returns the MAE between the real and predicted noise masks.

title: Finishing generate(); a visualization callback
text:
The body of the generation loop (denoise, then re-noise to the next diffusion time), denormalization of generated images, and a Keras callback that shows a 3 x 6 grid of generated images at the end of each epoch. At each step generate() predicts the clean image and the noise, then rebuilds a noisy image for the next, lower diffusion time by mixing those predictions with the next step's signal and noise rates. After the last step, the predicted images are denormalized and clipped to [0, 255]. Since there is no proper metric for image quality, a custom callback calls generate() after every epoch so you can judge progress by eye. **End of generate().** Inside the loop started on p.551, each iteration:

1. calls `self.denoise(noisy_images, noise_rates, signal_rates)` to get `pred_images` and `pred_noises` ("Calls denoising model");
2. computes `next_diffusion_times = diffusion_times - step_size` and the matching `next_noise_rates, next_signal_rates` with `diffusion_schedule()`;
3. builds the input of the next iteration as `next_signal_rates * pred_images + next_noise_rates * pred_noises` ("Prepares noisy images for the next iteration").

So the image is not denoised in place. Instead, the model's current guess of the clean image is re-mixed with its current guess of the noise at a slightly lower noise level. After the loop, the method returns the **last predicted clean images**, denormalized with `self.normalizer.mean + pred_images * self.normalizer.variance**0.5` and clipped with `ops.clip(images, 0.0, 255.0)` ("Denormalizes images so their values fit between 0 and 255").

**17.2.6 Visualizing results with a custom callback.** There is no proper metric for the quality of generated images, so you should look at samples during training to see whether the model is improving. `VisualizationCallback(keras.callbacks.Callback)` stores `diffusion_steps=20`, `num_rows=3`, `num_cols=6`. In `on_epoch_end()` it calls `self.model.generate(num_images=18, diffusion_steps=20)`, creates a 12 x 6 inch figure, and fills a 3 x 6 grid of subplots: image `i = row * num_cols + col` is converted to NumPy, cast to `uint8` and shown without axes. Finally it calls `plt.tight_layout()`, `plt.show()` and `plt.close()`.

The callback is passed to `fit()` on pp.553-554. Each generation step denoises, then re-noises the predicted image with the predicted noise at the next diffusion time. The output is the last pred_images, denormalized with the adapted mean and standard deviation and clipped to [0, 255]. There is no proper metric for generated-image quality, so samples are inspected visually. VisualizationCallback generates 18 images with 20 steps after each epoch and shows them in a 3 x 6 grid. Callbacks can call any method of self.model, including custom ones like generate().

title: Reverse diffusion step (re-noising update)
text: One generation step: estimate the clean image and the noise at the current diffusion time, then recombine them with the rates of the next, lower diffusion time. Make your best guess of the final picture, then deliberately blur it back with a bit less static than before, and repeat. Each round the guess is made from a cleaner input. x_{t-dt} = s(t - dt) x_hat_0 + n(t - dt) eps_hat, where (x_hat_0, eps_hat) = denoise(x_t, n(t), s(t)). Beyond the book: this is the deterministic DDIM update (eta = 0). With 20 steps the noise rate used for re-noising goes 0.997, 0.990, ..., 0.37, 0.312 (at t = 0).

Normalized value 1.0 with mean 110, std 70 -> pixel 180.

title: VisualizationCallback
text:
class VisualizationCallback(keras.callbacks.Callback):
    def __init__(self, diffusion_steps=20, num_rows=3, num_cols=6):
        self.diffusion_steps = diffusion_steps
        self.num_rows = num_rows
        self.num_cols = num_cols

    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch=None, logs=None):
        generated_images = self.model.generate(
            num_images=self.num_rows * self.num_cols,
            diffusion_steps=self.diffusion_steps,
        )

        plt.figure(figsize=(self.num_cols * 2.0, self.num_rows * 2.0))
        for row in range(self.num_rows):
            for col in range(self.num_cols):
                i = row * self.num_cols + col
                plt.subplot(self.num_rows, self.num_cols, i + 1)
                img = ops.convert_to_numpy(generated_images[i]).astype("uint8")
                plt.imshow(img)
                plt.axis("off")
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()
        plt.close() A Keras callback that, after every training epoch, generates 18 images with 20 diffusion steps and displays them in a 3 x 6 grid. At epoch end: generate -> lay out in a grid -> show.

title: Instantiating, compiling and fitting the diffusion model
text:
Creating the DiffusionModel, adapting its normalizer, compiling with AdamW plus an InverseTimeDecay learning-rate schedule and exponential moving average (EMA) of weights, and starting fit() for 100 epochs. The model is built with widths [32, 64, 96, 128] and block depth 2; the normalizer must be adapted to the dataset. Training uses AdamW with a learning rate that decays as 1e-3 / (1 + 0.1 * step / 1000) and keeps an EMA of the weights, written into the model every 100 batches, to stabilize training on a noisy loss landscape. Section **17.2.7 It's go time!** trains the diffusion model on the Oxford Flowers dataset.

**Instantiation.** `model = DiffusionModel(image_size, widths=[32, 64, 96, 128], block_depth=2)` (image_size = 128 from p.545), followed by `model.normalizer.adapt(dataset)`. The callout insists: it "computes the mean and variance necessary to perform normalization, don't forget it!". Those statistics are used to normalize inputs in `call()` (p.551) and to denormalize outputs in `generate()` (p.552).

**Optimizer.** `AdamW` with two options that stabilize training and improve image quality:

- **Learning-rate decay** via `InverseTimeDecay(initial_learning_rate=1e-3, decay_steps=1000, decay_rate=0.1)`, which gradually lowers the learning rate. In Keras this computes $\text{lr} = 10^{-3}/(1 + 0.1\cdot\text{step}/1000)$: about 9.1e-4 after 1,000 steps and 5e-4 after 10,000.
- **Exponential moving average of model weights**, also called Polyak averaging (`use_ema=True`): the optimizer keeps a running average of the weights during training, and every 100 batches (`ema_overwrite_frequency=100`) overwrites the model's weights with it. This stabilizes the model's representations when the loss landscape is noisy, which is the case here since every batch uses fresh random noise and diffusion times.

`model.compile()` receives only the optimizer: the loss is computed by the custom `compute_loss()` (p.551).

**Fitting.** `model.fit(dataset, epochs=100, ...)` begins here; the callbacks list continues on p.554: `VisualizationCallback()` (p.552) plots generated samples after each epoch and `ModelCheckpoint` saves the weights. Instantiate DiffusionModel(image_size, widths=[32, 64, 96, 128], block_depth=2) and always call model.normalizer.adapt(dataset). AdamW with InverseTimeDecay: lr = 1e-3 / (1 + 0.1 * step / 1000), halving after 10,000 steps. use_ema=True keeps an exponential moving average of the weights; ema_overwrite_frequency=100 copies it into the model every 100 batches. compile() takes no loss because compute_loss() defines it. fit() runs 100 epochs with VisualizationCallback and ModelCheckpoint (p.554).

title: Learning-rate schedule (InverseTimeDecay)
text: A rule that changes the learning rate as training progresses; InverseTimeDecay divides the initial rate by a factor growing linearly with the step count. Take big strides at first, then shorter steps as you approach the goal. lr(step) = 1e-3 / (1 + 0.1 * step / 1000). Step 0: 1e-3; step 10,000: 5e-4; step 25,500: about 2.8e-4.
snippet: A rule that changes the learning rate as training progresses; InverseTimeDecay divides the initial rate by a factor growing linearly with the step count.

title: Exponential moving average of weights (Polyak averaging)
text: Maintaining a running exponential average of the model's weights during training and periodically using it as the model's weights. Smooth out the zig-zag of noisy training by averaging where the weights have recently been. ema <- m * ema + (1 - m) * w after each step (Keras default m = 0.99); with ema_overwrite_frequency=100, model weights are set to ema every 100 iterations. With m = 0.99, the average effectively covers about the last 100 steps.
snippet: Maintaining a running exponential average of the model's weights during training and periodically using it as the model's weights.

title: AdamW
text: The Adam optimizer with decoupled weight decay. Adam's adaptive steps plus a gentle pull of all weights toward zero. w <- w - lr * (Adam update + weight_decay * w); the decay term is not passed through Adam's adaptive scaling. keras.optimizers.AdamW(learning_rate=schedule, use_ema=True, ema_overwrite_frequency=100).
snippet: The Adam optimizer with decoupled weight decay.

title: Normalization layer adaptation
text: Computing the dataset mean and variance for a Normalization layer with adapt(). Measure the data before standardizing it. model.normalizer.adapt(dataset) iterates over the image batches and stores per-channel mean and variance. The callout: 'don't forget it!'.

title: InverseTimeDecay learning rate
text: InverseTimeDecay(initial_learning_rate=1e-3, decay_steps=1000, decay_rate=0.1) \eta(k) = \frac{\eta_0}{1 + r\,\dfrac{k}{K}} = \frac{10^{-3}}{1 + 0.1\,\dfrac{k}{1000}} Gradually reduce the learning rate during training. The rate halves after K/r = 10,000 steps and keeps decreasing slowly (proportional to 1/k for large k). \eta(k) learning rate at optimizer step k \eta_0 initial_learning_rate = 1e-3 r decay_rate = 0.1 K decay_steps = 1000 k optimizer iteration (batch) count

title: Training the diffusion model and first generated flowers
text:
Finishing the fit() call for the Oxford Flowers diffusion model, practical Colab advice, the results after 100 epochs, and the transition to text conditioning. The diffusion model is trained for 100 epochs with a visualization callback and a weight checkpoint. After about 90 minutes on a free T4 GPU it produces plausible flower images (figure 17.12). The next step is to condition generation on text. The page opens with the end of the `model.fit(...)` call started on p.553. The full call is `model.fit(dataset, epochs=100, callbacks=[...])`. Two callbacks run at the end of every epoch:

- `VisualizationCallback()` (defined on p.552) calls the model's `generate()` method to produce a 3×6 grid of flower images using 20 diffusion steps, then plots them. This lets you watch sample quality improve as training goes on.
- `keras.callbacks.ModelCheckpoint(filepath="diffusion_model.weights.h5", save_weights_only=True, save_best_only=True)` saves only the weights (not the full model) to an `.h5` file, and only when the monitored metric improves.

The authors then give a practical Colab tip. Because the training logs contain one image grid per epoch, a 100-epoch run can exceed a notebook cell's output limit and trigger "Buffered data was truncated after reaching the output size limit." The workaround is to run `model.fit(..., epochs=20)` five times in five cells. Keras models keep their weights and optimizer state between `fit()` calls, so this is equivalent to one `fit(..., epochs=100)` call.

After 100 epochs (about 90 minutes on a T4, the free Colab GPU), the model generates flowers like those in figure 17.12. They have vivid petal colors and textures, and the composition (a flower filling a frame with a green or dark background) looks right, although the shapes are still impressionistic. Training longer gives more realistic results.

The page closes the diffusion section and introduces the next idea: **text conditioning**. Giving the denoiser a representation of a text caption, in addition to the noisy image, gives a *text-to-image* model whose outputs match a prompt. Section 17.3 (p.555) develops this with Stable Diffusion. The diffusion model is trained with model.fit(dataset, epochs=100) plus two callbacks: one plots generated samples each epoch, one checkpoints the weights. Keras fit() is resumable: five fit(epochs=20) calls equal one fit(epochs=100) call, which avoids Colab's per-cell output limit. 100 epochs take about 90 minutes on a free T4 and give plausible but impressionistic flowers (figure 17.12); longer training helps. Adding text conditioning to the denoiser turns an unconditional diffusion model into a text-to-image model.

title: Diffusion model
text: A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process: a denoiser is trained to remove noise at every noise level, and images are generated by starting from pure noise and denoising step by step. Like a sculptor revealing a statue in a block of stone (p.544): every patch of noise contains an image, and the model chips away noise until the image appears. Training samples a diffusion time, mixes clean images with Gaussian noise according to the diffusion schedule (signal rate and noise rate), and trains the U-Net to predict the noise (mean absolute error loss in this chapter). Generation runs the denoiser for a fixed number of steps (20 in the callback), each time re-noising the current estimate to a slightly lower noise level. Figure 17.12: 18 flower images produced from Gaussian noise after 100 training epochs.

title: Text-to-image diffusion and Stable Diffusion in KerasHub
text:
How a diffusion model becomes a text-to-image model by conditioning the denoiser on embeddings from a pretrained text encoder, and loading the pretrained Stable Diffusion 3 model from KerasHub. Train the same denoising diffusion process on (prompt, image) pairs and feed the denoiser text embeddings alongside the noisy images. At inference you can denoise pure noise toward an image that matches a new prompt. Instead of training such a model, the book loads Stable Diffusion 3 Medium with `keras_hub.models.TextToImage.from_preset`. Section 17.3 extends the diffusion model of section 17.2 to **text-to-image generation**. The recipe has two parts:

1. A **pretrained text encoder**, such as a Transformer encoder like RoBERTa from chapter 15, maps a text prompt to vectors in a continuous embedding space.
2. A diffusion model is trained on **`(prompt, image)` pairs**, where each prompt is a short description of its image.

Images are handled as before: the model learns to map noisy input to a denoised output that progressively approaches the image. The key change is that the embedded prompt is also passed to the denoiser, so it takes two inputs, `noisy_images` and `text_embeddings`. This makes the job easier than for the flower denoiser. Instead of removing noise with no other information, the model gets a textual description of the final image to guide denoising.

After training, you can start from pure noise, supply a **never-before-seen prompt**, and denoise into an image for that prompt, because the model maps noise to images *conditioned on* a text representation.

The authors do not train such a model, because doing it well is expensive and slow. Instead they use **Stable Diffusion**, a pretrained model in KerasHub made by Stability AI, a company that builds open image and video generation models. Figure 17.13 shows an output: an astronaut riding a blue origami elephant on a New York street. **Listing 17.8** begins with `import keras_hub`, sets `height, width = 512, 512`, and calls `keras_hub.models.TextToImage.from_preset("stable_diffusion_3_medium", image_shape=(height, width, 3), ...)`. The call continues on p.556 with `dtype="float16"`, then defines the prompt and calls `task.generate(prompt)`. A text-to-image diffusion model is the same diffusion process with a denoiser that also receives text embeddings from a pretrained text encoder. It is trained on (prompt, image) pairs; at inference, noise plus a new prompt is denoised into a matching image. The text provides guidance that makes denoising easier than in the unconditional flower model. Training such a model well is expensive, so the book uses the pretrained Stable Diffusion 3 (medium) from KerasHub via TextToImage.from_preset.

title: Text-conditioned diffusion
text: A diffusion model whose denoiser receives text embeddings of a prompt in addition to the noisy image, so that generation is steered toward images matching the prompt. Restoring a badly damaged photo is much easier if someone tells you what it shows. Training data: (prompt, image) pairs. The denoiser predicts noise from (noisy image, noise level, text embedding). Inference: start from Gaussian noise, fix the prompt embedding, run the denoising loop. Figure 17.13: the prompt about an astronaut on an origami elephant produces a matching image.
snippet: A diffusion model whose denoiser receives text embeddings of a prompt in addition to the noisy image, so that generation is steered toward images matching the prompt.

title: Pretrained text encoder

A translator that turns words into coordinates the image model can understand. The prompt is tokenized and passed through the encoder. Its token-level outputs (a sequence) and/or a pooled vector are given to the denoiser. SD3 passes both (pp.558–559). RoBERTa from chapter 15; in SD3, CLIP and T5 encoders (beyond the book).

title: Generating with Stable Diffusion and negative prompts
text:
Completing Listing 17.8 with float16, generating an image from a prompt with TextToImage.generate(), steering away from concepts with a negative prompt, and the visual artifacts of diffusion output. KerasHub's TextToImage task wraps tokenization and the diffusion loop in one generate() call. Passing a dict with 'prompts' and 'negative_prompts' steers generation toward the positive prompt and away from the negative one; here it removes the color blue. Diffusion outputs still contain artifacts, such as duplicated tusks, because the model lacks real understanding of anatomy and physics. The page finishes **Listing 17.8**. The `from_preset` call gets one more argument, `dtype="float16"`. The callout calls this a trick to keep memory usage down, with details in chapter 18: storing weights and activations in 16-bit floats halves memory compared with float32. Then a prompt is defined, `"A NASA astraunaut riding an origami elephant in New York City"` (with a typo in the original), and `task.generate(prompt)` produces the image in figure 17.13.

Like the `CausalLM` task from chapter 16, `TextToImage` is a **high-level task class**. Its `generate()` call handles tokenization and the entire diffusion process.

Stable Diffusion also accepts a **negative prompt**, which steers the diffusion process *away* from certain text. The authors say there is nothing magic about it. You could train on triplets `(image, positive_prompt, negative_prompt)`, where the positive prompt describes the image and the negative prompt is words that do not describe it. Feeding both embeddings to the denoiser teaches it to steer toward images matching the positive prompt and away from those matching the negative one. The example passes a dictionary to `generate()`:

```python
task.generate({"prompts": prompt, "negative_prompts": "blue color"})
```

Figure 17.14 shows the result: the astronaut now rides a dark gray elephant through a warm, yellow-orange street, with no blue in sight.

A sidebar, **'Visual artifacts in the Stable Diffusion output'**, points out flaws such as the second elephant's duplicated tusks. Some artifacts are unavoidable with diffusion models: correctly drawing a human in a space suit on a paper elephant requires an understanding of anatomy and physics that the model lacks. The sidebar continues on p.557. dtype="float16" halves the memory needed to load and run Stable Diffusion 3 (details in chapter 18). TextToImage.generate() wraps tokenization and the entire diffusion process, like CausalLM.generate() for text. Passing {"prompts": ..., "negative_prompts": ...} steers generation away from the negative text; 'blue color' removed blue from the scene. The book explains negative prompts through training on triplets; in Stable Diffusion they work through classifier-free guidance at inference time. Diffusion outputs contain artifacts such as duplicated tusks because the model has no real understanding of anatomy or physics.

title: Negative prompt
text: A second text input that steers the diffusion process away from images matching it. Telling an illustrator 'not blue' as well as what to draw. Book's framing: a denoiser trained on (image, positive_prompt, negative_prompt) triplets learns to move toward the positive and away from the negative. Actual SD mechanism (beyond the book): classifier-free guidance with the negative prompt's prediction in place of the unconditional one. task.generate({"prompts": prompt, "negative_prompts": "blue color"}) removes blue from the astronaut-elephant scene (figure 17.14).
snippet: A second text input that steers the diffusion process away from images matching it.

title: Classifier-free guidance
text: A sampling technique that extrapolates from an unconditional (or negative-prompt) noise prediction toward the conditional one by a guidance scale s. Compute 'what the model would do with the prompt' and 'what it would do without it', then exaggerate the difference. noise = noise_neg + s * (noise_pos - noise_neg). s = 1 is ordinary conditional sampling; larger s gives stronger prompt adherence at some cost in diversity. guidance_scale=7.0 in Listing 17.9 (p.558).
snippet: A sampling technique that extrapolates from an unconditional or negative-prompt noise prediction toward the conditional one by a guidance scale s.

Each number takes half the bytes, so the model needs about half the memory. dtype="float16" in from_preset sets the variable and compute dtype. About 3 billion parameters take roughly 6 GB in float16 versus 12 GB in float32 (estimate, not from the book). title: Explain how a negative prompt can influence every step of the diffusion process rather…
text: Explain how a negative prompt can influence every step of the diffusion process rather than acting as a post-processing filter. At each denoising step the denoiser's noise prediction depends on the text embeddings. The negative prompt's embedding defines a direction to move away from (via the guidance combination), so the trajectory from noise to image is steered at every step. title: Model size, diffusion steps, and the text latent space
text:
Why the medium SD3 model produces artifacts, controlling the number of diffusion steps with num_steps (figure 17.15), and the idea of walking the continuous text-embedding manifold to morph between images. Stable Diffusion 3 Medium (about 3 billion parameters) is the smallest SD3, and larger models give fewer artifacts. More diffusion steps refine noise into a more coherent image. Because the text encoder learns a smooth, continuous manifold of prompts, you can interpolate between two prompts' embeddings and generate images that morph from one to the other. The page starts by finishing the **visual-artifacts sidebar** from p.556. The model always tries its best to interpolate an output from its training data, but it has no real understanding of the objects it draws. One factor is easy to fix: the book uses **Stable Diffusion 3 'medium'**, the smallest model Stability AI released, at about **3 billion parameters**. A larger model of about **9 billion parameters** would produce substantially better images with fewer artifacts. It is not used only to keep the example accessible, since 9 billion parameters need a lot of RAM.

Next, as with `generate()` for text models in chapter 16, extra arguments control the generation process. The authors vary the **number of diffusion steps** to show denoising in action:

```python
display([task.generate(prompt, num_steps=x) for x in [5, 10, 15, 20, 25]])
```

A small `display()` helper uses `np.concatenate(images, axis=1)` to place the images side by side and turns the result into a PIL image. In **figure 17.15**, the 5-step image is a blurry, barely recognizable scene. At 10 steps an origami elephant and astronaut appear. By 15–25 steps the image is crisp and coherent. Each call also starts from different random noise, so the elephant's color and pose change across the strip.

**Section 17.3.1** then begins exploring the latent space of the text-to-image model. The authors argue that text diffusion models may be the best demonstration of the *interpolative nature* of deep networks. The text encoder learns a **smooth, low-dimensional manifold** of prompts. It is continuous, so you can walk from one prompt's representation to another and every intermediate point has semantic meaning. Combined with diffusion, this lets you **morph between two images** by describing each end state with a text prompt. Pages 558–560 implement this. SD3 Medium (about 3B parameters) is the smallest SD3; a larger model (about 9B per the book) gives fewer artifacts but needs much more memory. generate() accepts num_steps; few steps give blurry images, and quality saturates around 20–25 steps (figure 17.15). The display() helper concatenates (H, W, 3) images along axis 1 into one strip. The text encoder learns a smooth, continuous manifold of prompts, so walking between two prompt embeddings gives meaningful intermediate images, a morph.

title: Breaking down generate(): text encoding, denoising, rescaling
text:
Listing 17.9 decomposes Stable Diffusion's high-level generate() into three functions (get_text_embeddings, denoise_with_text_embeddings, scale_output), and the shapes of the four text-embedding tensors. To manipulate text embeddings, for example to interpolate between prompts, we need access to the intermediate stages of generation: (1) tokenize and encode the prompt (plus an empty negative prompt) into embeddings, (2) denoise pure latent noise step by step using those embeddings, (3) map the decoded output from [-1, 1] to [0, 255]. The embeddings consist of four tensors with shapes (1, 154, 4096), (1, 154, 4096), (1, 2048), (1, 2048). To walk the text latent space (announced on p.557), the authors first break `generate()` into parts in **Listing 17.9**:

1. **`get_text_embeddings(prompt)`**: `task.preprocessor.generate_preprocess` tokenizes the prompt and an empty string `""` for the negative prompt. The callout says we don't care about negative prompts here, but the model expects them. `task.backbone.encode_text_step(token_ids, negative_token_ids)` turns both into embeddings.
2. **`denoise_with_text_embeddings(embeddings, num_steps=28, guidance_scale=7.0)`**: creates pure Gaussian noise `latents = random.normal((1, height // 8, width // 8, 16))`, which for 512×512 is a 64×64×16 latent. It then calls `task.backbone.denoise_step(latents, embeddings, step, num_steps, guidance_scale)` once per step, and finally `task.backbone.decode_step(latents)[0]` maps the latent to an image (first item of the batch).
3. **`scale_output(x)`**: converts to NumPy, maps $[-1, 1]$ to $[0, 1]$ with `(x + 1) / 2`, clips, multiplies by 255, rounds and casts to `uint8`.

The last three lines chain these steps for the astronaut prompt.

The text then summarizes the three steps: tokenize and embed the prompts; progressively denoise pure noise using the embeddings, the same as the flower model; and map outputs from `[-1, 1]` back to `[0, 255]` for display.

The embeddings are not one tensor but **four**:

```
[(1, 154, 4096), (1, 154, 4096), (1, 2048), (1, 2048)]
```

The page ends by starting to explain why. Rather than passing only the final embedded text vector, the Stable Diffusion authors pass both the final output vector and the last representation of the entire token sequence (continued on p.559). generate() = (1) tokenize and encode prompt plus empty negative prompt, (2) iteratively denoise random latents with guidance, (3) decode and rescale to [0, 255]. Latent noise has shape (1, height // 8, width // 8, 16): SD3 denoises in a compressed latent space and decodes at the end. denoise_step needs the step index and total num_steps (position on the schedule) and the guidance_scale (7.0). scale_output maps [-1, 1] to uint8 via round(255 · clip((x + 1)/2, 0, 1)). The text embeddings are four tensors: positive/negative token sequences (1, 154, 4096) and positive/negative pooled vectors (1, 2048).

title: The four text embeddings and slerp interpolation
text:
What the four text-embedding tensors of Stable Diffusion 3 are, and Listing 17.10: a spherical linear interpolation (slerp) function and a helper that interpolates the positive-prompt embeddings between two prompts. SD3 passes the denoiser both a per-token sequence and a pooled vector for both the positive and negative prompt, giving four tensors. To walk between two prompts, the book interpolates the positive sequence and vector with slerp, which moves along a great circle of a sphere rather than a straight chord. This keeps intermediate points at roughly the same magnitude as real embeddings, on the 'surface' of the learned manifold. The page finishes the explanation begun on p.558. Stable Diffusion passes the denoiser both the final output vector and the last representation of the **entire token sequence** learned by the text encoder, which gives it more information. Doing this for both prompts gives **four tensors**:

- the positive prompt's encoder sequence, `(1, 154, 4096)`
- the negative prompt's encoder sequence, `(1, 154, 4096)`
- the positive prompt's encoder vector, `(1, 2048)`
- the negative prompt's encoder vector, `(1, 2048)`

With `generate()` decomposed, we can walk the latent space between two prompts. **Listing 17.10** defines two functions:

- **`slerp(t, v1, v2)`** casts both tensors to float32 and computes their flattened norms and the cosine of the angle between them (`dot`). It takes `theta_0 = arccos(dot)` and returns $\frac{\sin((1-t)\theta_0)}{\sin\theta_0} v_1 + \frac{\sin(t\theta_0)}{\sin\theta_0} v_2$.
- **`interpolate_text_embeddings(e1, e2, start=0, stop=1, num=10)`** loops over `np.linspace(start, stop, num)`. For each `t` it builds a 4-tuple: slerp of the positive sequences (`e1[0]`, `e2[0]`), `e1[1]` unchanged, slerp of the positive vectors (`e1[2]`, `e2[2]`), `e1[3]` unchanged. The callout says the second and fourth embeddings are for the unused negative prompt.

The authors explain that **slerp** stands for *spherical linear interpolation*, a function used in computer graphics for decades to interpolate points on a sphere. They say the math details are not important, but the motivation is. If the text manifold is imagined as a sphere and two prompts as random points on it, directly linearly interpolating between them would... (continued on p.560: land inside the sphere, off the surface where embeddings have meaning). SD3's text conditioning consists of four tensors: positive and negative encoder sequences (1, 154, 4096) and positive and negative encoder vectors (1, 2048). Listing 17.10's slerp computes θ0 = arccos(cosine similarity) and returns sin((1−t)θ0)/sin θ0 · v1 + sin(tθ0)/sin θ0 · v2. interpolate_text_embeddings slerps only indices 0 and 2 (positive prompt) and keeps the negative embeddings fixed. Slerp stays on the sphere; linear interpolation cuts through the interior, giving shrunken embeddings unlike any the model was trained on. np.linspace(start, stop, num) controls which slice of the path is explored (p.560 uses 0.5 to 0.6).
snippet: The page finishes the explanation begun on p.558. Stable Diffusion passes the denoiser both the final output vector and the last representation of the entire token sequence…

title: Spherical linear interpolation (slerp)
text: Interpolation between two vectors along the great-circle arc connecting them, parameterized by t ∈ [0, 1]. Walking along the surface of a globe from one city to another, instead of tunnelling straight through the Earth. θ = arccos(v1·v2 / (|v1||v2|)); slerp(t) = sin((1−t)θ)/sin θ · v1 + sin(tθ)/sin θ · v2. At t = 0 it gives v1, at t = 1 it gives v2. Listing 17.10: slerp(t, e1[0], e2[0]) and slerp(t, e1[2], e2[2]).

In the code: dot = ops.sum(v1 * v2 / (v1_norm * v2_norm)), with norms computed over the flattened tensors. Orthogonal vectors have cosine 0 → θ0 = π/2.

At t = 0, s0 = 1 and s1 = 0 → v1; at t = 1, s0 = 0 and s1 = 1 → v2. For unit vectors, the result is a unit vector making angle tθ0 with v1. t Interpolation parameter in [0, 1] (from np.linspace(start, stop, num)). \theta_0 Angle between v1 and v2 (m1). s_0, s_1 The weights sin((1−t)θ0)/sin θ0 and sin(tθ0)/sin θ0 applied to v1 and v2.

title: Listing 17.10 A function to interpolate text embeddings
text:
from keras import ops
def slerp(t, v1, v2):
    v1, v2 = ops.cast(v1, "float32"), ops.cast(v2, "float32")
    v1_norm = ops.linalg.norm(ops.ravel(v1))
    v2_norm = ops.linalg.norm(ops.ravel(v2))
    dot = ops.sum(v1 * v2 / (v1_norm * v2_norm))
    theta_0 = ops.arccos(dot)
    sin_theta_0 = ops.sin(theta_0)
    theta_t = theta_0 * t
    sin_theta_t = ops.sin(theta_t)
    s0 = ops.sin(theta_0 - theta_t) / sin_theta_0
    s1 = sin_theta_t / sin_theta_0
    return s0 * v1 + s1 * v2
def interpolate_text_embeddings(e1, e2, start=0, stop=1, num=10):
    embeddings = []
    for t in np.linspace(start, stop, num):
        embeddings.append(
            (
                slerp(t, e1[0], e2[0]),
                e1[1],
                slerp(t, e1[2], e2[2]),
                e1[3],
            )
        )
    return embeddings slerp() spherically interpolates two tensors of any shape (treated as flattened vectors). interpolate_text_embeddings() produces `num` embedding 4-tuples for t evenly spaced between start and stop, interpolating the positive sequence and positive vector between prompts 1 and 2 and keeping prompt 1's negative embeddings. For each t in linspace(start, stop, num): positive_seq(t) = slerp(t, seq1, seq2); positive_vec(t) = slerp(t, vec1, vec2); negatives fixed.

title: Spherical interpolation and morphing between two prompts
text:
Why slerp (spherical linear interpolation) is used to walk between text embeddings, and using it to morph a dog into a tentacled creature with Stable Diffusion Straight-line interpolation between two embedding points cuts through the inside of the roughly sphere-shaped embedding manifold, where points have abnormally small norm and carry little meaning for the denoiser; interpolating along the sphere keeps intermediate points on the manifold. Walking that path between the embeddings of two prompts, and denoising at each step, produces a gradual visual morph from one image to the other. The page finishes the motivation for **slerp** begun on p.559. Picture the text-embedding manifold as a sphere and the embeddings of two prompts as two points on its surface. A straight line between them (the green chord in **figure 17.16**) passes *inside* the sphere: its intermediate points are no longer on the surface. The book's point is that we want to stay on the smooth manifold learned by the text encoder, because that is where embedding points mean something to the denoising model. Slerp moves along the arc of the sphere instead (the orange points), so every intermediate point keeps the same rough magnitude as the endpoints.

The authors then add an honest caveat: the real manifold is not a sphere. It is, however, a smooth surface of vectors that all have roughly the same magnitude, so it is *sphere-like*, and interpolating as if on a sphere approximates it better than interpolating along a line.

With the interpolation defined, the page runs the experiment. Two prompts are embedded with `get_text_embeddings`: *"A friendly dog looking up in a field of flowers"* and *"A horrifying, tentacled creature hovering over a field of flowers"*. Then `interpolate_text_embeddings(e1, e2, start=0.5, stop=0.6, num=9)` produces nine interpolated embedding tuples with $t$ evenly spaced from 0.5 to 0.6. Each one is passed through `denoise_with_text_embeddings`, which runs the full diffusion process conditioned on that embedding, and the result is rescaled for display with `scale_output`. The authors restrict $t$ to $[0.5, 0.6]$ to zoom in on the stretch where the morph becomes visually obvious. **Figure 17.17** shows the result: a dog in a flower field gradually turns into a purple tentacled creature while the flower field stays put. (The figure prints six images, although `num=9` would produce nine.)

The main lesson is that the text encoder has learned a continuous space. Points between two prompts are themselves meaningful conditioning signals, and the diffusion model turns them into coherent in-between images. Linear interpolation between two embeddings cuts inside the sphere-like manifold and produces lower-norm, off-distribution points; slerp follows the surface. The text manifold is not a true sphere, but its points have roughly constant magnitude, so slerp is the better approximation. Each interpolated embedding is fed to a full diffusion run; the resulting sequence of images morphs smoothly from one prompt to the other. Sampling densely in t = 0.5 to 0.6 focuses on the region where the visible concept switch happens. The smooth morph is visual evidence that the text encoder and denoiser together learned a continuous, interpolative latent space.

title: Spherical linear interpolation (slerp)
text: An interpolation between two vectors that moves along the great-circle arc joining them, rotating by a fraction t of the angle between them, instead of along the straight chord. Instead of tunnelling through the Earth from Paris to Tokyo, you fly along the surface. Every waypoint is still 'on the ground'. With $\theta_0 = \arccos(\hat v_1\cdot\hat v_2)$, slerp$(t) = \frac{\sin((1-t)\theta_0)}{\sin\theta_0} v_1 + \frac{\sin(t\theta_0)}{\sin\theta_0} v_2$. For unit vectors the result always has unit norm. Listing 17.10 (p.559) implements exactly this with keras.ops. Between (1,0) and (0,1), slerp at t=0.5 gives (0.707, 0.707), with norm 1. Lerp gives (0.5, 0.5), with norm 0.707.
snippet: An interpolation between two vectors that moves along the great-circle arc joining them, rotating by a fraction t of the angle between them, instead of along the straight chord.

title: Latent-space interpolation
text: Generating outputs from points along a path between two latent (or embedding) points to see how a model's output changes continuously between them. Choose endpoints $z_1, z_2$, a path $z(t)$ (lerp or slerp) and a decoder $G$. Render $G(z(t_k))$ for a grid of $t_k$. Here $z$ is the text-embedding tuple and $G$ is the whole diffusion sampling process. Figure 17.17: dog in flowers turning into a tentacled creature in flowers.

title: Slerp formula (implemented in Listing 17.10)

title: Interpolation machines, and the chapter 17 summary
text:
The authors' closing interpretation of the prompt-morphing experiment, and the five-point summary of chapter 17 The smooth dog-to-creature morph is not magic: deep networks are interpolation machines that map complex real-world distributions onto low-dimensional manifolds, and image generators exploit this by sampling and interpolating in learned latent spaces (VAEs, diffusion models, GANs). The page opens with the authors' reflection on the morphing experiment of the previous page. Watching a dog turn smoothly into a tentacled creature may feel like magic, but *interpolation is fundamental to the way deep neural networks learn*. The authors note that this is the **last substantive model in the book** and call it a fitting visual metaphor to end on. Their thesis: **deep neural networks are interpolation machines**. They map complex, real-world probability distributions to low-dimensional manifolds, and this holds even when the input is as complex as human language and the output as complex as natural images.

The **chapter summary** then recaps chapter 17 in five bullets:

1. Deep-learning image generation works by learning **latent spaces** that capture statistical information about an image dataset. Sampling and decoding points from such a space produces never-before-seen images. The three main tools are **VAEs, diffusion models, and GANs** (GANs were only mentioned in this edition, p.534).
2. **VAEs** learn highly structured, continuous latent representations. That makes them good for latent-space image editing (face swapping, turning a frown into a smile) and latent-space animations that walk along a cross-section of the space.
3. **Diffusion models** give very realistic outputs and are the dominant method today. They generate by *repeatedly denoising* an image starting from pure noise, and they are easy to condition on text captions to make text-to-image models.
4. **Stable Diffusion 3** is a state-of-the-art pretrained text-to-image model you can use yourself.
5. The visual latent space of text-to-image diffusion models is **fundamentally interpolative**. You can see this by interpolating between the text embeddings fed to the diffusion process and getting a smooth interpolation between output images.

The page therefore closes both chapter 17 and the book's run of model-building chapters. Chapter 18 (next page) turns to engineering best practices. The authors' closing thesis: deep neural networks are interpolation machines mapping complex distributions to low-dimensional manifolds. Image generators learn latent spaces and create new images by sampling and decoding; the main families are VAEs, diffusion models and GANs. VAEs give structured, continuous latent spaces ideal for editing and animation; diffusion models give the most realistic images and dominate today. Diffusion models generate by repeated denoising from pure noise and are easily conditioned on text. Smooth image morphs from interpolated text embeddings demonstrate that the text-to-image latent space is interpolative.

title: Deep networks as interpolation machines
text: The view that deep networks generalize by learning smooth mappings onto low-dimensional manifolds and then interpolating between the training examples on those manifolds. Like connecting the dots with a smooth curve: the network can produce sensible outputs between dots it has seen, but has no special knowledge far away from them. A differentiable model fitted by gradient descent is a smooth, high-dimensional curve. When data lie on a structured manifold, the fitted curve fills in that manifold, so nearby inputs map to nearby, valid outputs. Morphing a dog into a tentacled creature by walking between two prompts' text embeddings (p.560).
snippet: The view that deep networks generalize by learning smooth mappings onto low-dimensional manifolds and then interpolating between the training examples on those manifolds.

title: Variational autoencoder (VAE)
text: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs a distribution over latent codes, regularized so the latent space is continuous and structured. It makes the codes of similar images overlap smoothly, so the space has no holes and every point decodes to something plausible. The encoder predicts a mean and log-variance, a code is sampled with the reparameterization trick, and the loss combines reconstruction error and a KL term toward a standard normal (section 17.1.2). Turning a frowning face into a smiling one by moving its latent code.
snippet: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs a distribution over latent codes, regularized so the latent space is continuous and structured.

title: Diffusion model
text: A generative model that creates images by repeatedly denoising, starting from pure noise. Sculpting: start with a block of random noise and remove a little at a time until an image emerges. A denoising network (a U-Net in section 17.2.2) is trained on images corrupted at random noise levels according to a diffusion schedule. Sampling runs it over many steps from noise to image. Adding a text-embedding input makes it text-conditioned. Stable Diffusion 3 (section 17.3); the Oxford Flowers model (section 17.2).
snippet: A generative model that creates images by repeatedly denoising, starting from pure noise.

title: Chapter 18 opener: Best practices for the real world
text:
Opening of chapter 18: moving from small-scale, introductory models to state-of-the-art results and large-scale training You can now build every major type of model, but so far only at small scale and without squeezing out the best performance. Chapter 18 covers the techniques that close that gap: hyperparameter tuning, model ensembling, multi-GPU/TPU training, mixed precision and quantization. This is the opening page of **chapter 18, "Best practices for the real world."** The *This chapter covers* box lists five topics: **hyperparameter tuning**, **model ensembling**, **training Keras models on multiple GPUs or on TPU**, **mixed-precision training**, and **quantization**.

The introduction first takes stock. You can now train image classification and segmentation models, classification or regression models on vector data, timeseries forecasting models, text classification models, sequence-to-sequence models, and generative models for text and images. In the authors' words, "you've got all the bases covered."

Then comes the caveat. Every model so far was trained **at small scale**, on small datasets with a single GPU, and generally did **not reach the best achievable performance** on its dataset. The book is introductory, so to reach state-of-the-art results on brand-new problems there is "still a bit of a chasm" to cross. The chapter (continuing on p.563) is about bridging it.

**How to use this page:** treat the five bullets as a roadmap. The first two (tuning, ensembling) are about getting the most accuracy out of a model and make up section 18.1, starting on p.563. The last three are about compute: scaling training across devices (18.2, p.572) and using lower-precision numbers to speed up training and inference (18.3, p.580). Chapter 18 covers hyperparameter tuning, model ensembling, multi-GPU/TPU training, mixed precision and quantization. The book's models so far were small-scale and not fully optimized; this chapter addresses both performance and scale.

chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

title: Why and how to optimize hyperparameters automatically
text:
Hyperparameters vs parameters, why hand-tuning is not enough, and the generic loop of automatic hyperparameter optimization Architecture-level choices (number of layers, units, activation, batch norm, dropout rate) are hyperparameters, distinct from the weights learned by backpropagation. Rather than tweaking them by hand, you should search the space of configurations automatically and systematically: propose a configuration, build and train it, score it on validation data, propose the next one, repeat, and finally evaluate on the test set. The page finishes the chapter introduction: the chapter will help you go from machine learning student to a "fully fledged machine learning engineer". It first reviews techniques for systematically improving model performance (**hyperparameter tuning** and **model ensembling**), then techniques for speeding up and scaling up training (**multi-GPU and TPU training, mixed precision, quantization**).

**Section 18.1** sets the goal: blindly trying architecture configurations is fine if something that "works okay" is enough, but this section aims for models that "work great and win machine learning competitions".

**Section 18.1.1, Hyperparameter optimization.** Building a model involves many seemingly arbitrary decisions: how many layers, how many units or filters per layer, `relu` or another activation, whether to use `BatchNormalization` after a layer, how much dropout. These architecture-level choices are **hyperparameters**, as opposed to the **parameters** of a model, which are trained via backpropagation.

Experienced engineers develop an intuition for these choices, but there are no formal rules, and initial choices are almost always suboptimal, even with good intuition. Tweaking by hand and retraining repeatedly is what practitioners spend most of their time on, but the authors argue that "it shouldn't be your job as a human to fiddle with hyperparameters all day—that is better left to a machine." You should therefore explore the space of possible decisions **automatically, systematically and in a principled way**, searching the architecture space for the best-performing configurations empirically. That is the research field of **automatic hyperparameter optimization**.

The page ends with the typical process:
1. Choose a set of hyperparameters (automatically).
2. Build the corresponding model.
3. Fit it to the training data and measure performance on the **validation** data.
4. Choose the next set of hyperparameters to try (automatically).
5. Repeat.
6. Eventually, measure performance on the **test** data. Hyperparameters are architecture-level choices (layers, units, activations, BatchNormalization, dropout) not learned by backpropagation. Initial choices are almost always suboptimal; hand-tuning is slow and should be automated. Automatic hyperparameter optimization searches the configuration space empirically and systematically. The loop: choose → build → train and validate → choose next → repeat → finally test. Validation data drives the search; test data is used only at the end.
