title: Adversarial examples and brittleness
text:
Sensitivity of deep learning models to how their input is presented, illustrated by adversarial examples in vision By gradient ascent in input space, an image can be changed imperceptibly so that a classifier changes its prediction (a panda becomes a 'gibbon'); this shows how brittle models are and how different their input-to-output mapping is from human perception. LLMs show an analogous sensitivity to small prompt changes. The page opens by finishing the point from p.590: patching failing prompts one by one does not address the general issue, and "even already patched prompts will still fail if you make small changes to them!"

Section **19.1.2** then introduces a closely related problem: deep learning models are extremely sensitive to *how* their input is presented. For image models the classic demonstration is the **adversarial example**: an input designed to trick the network into misclassifying it. The authors connect this to chapter 10: gradient ascent in input space can generate inputs that maximize the activation of a ConvNet filter, which is how filters were visualized (p.317).

The same idea, applied to the *class prediction* instead of a filter, gives adversarial examples. Starting from a picture of a panda, you add a small "gibbon gradient" (the gradient of the gibbon class score with respect to the input pixels) and the network now classifies the image as a gibbon. **Figure 19.3** shows this: the original panda image (predicted "Panda"), a noise-like "Gibbon class gradient" image, and the resulting "Adversarial example" that looks identical to the panda for a person but is predicted "Gibbon!". The small f(x) curves above the images stand for the model's output.

The authors draw two conclusions: these models are brittle, and their input-to-output mapping differs deeply from human perception.

The last paragraph starts the parallel for LLMs: they are extremely sensitive to minor prompt details, and innocuous changes such as changing place and people's names (continued on p.592) can significantly degrade performance. Patched prompts still fail with small changes: patching does not address the general issue. Deep learning models are highly sensitive to how inputs are presented; adversarial examples are the image-model case. Adversarial examples are made by gradient ascent in input space, the same technique used for filter visualization in chapter 10, but aimed at a class score. Figure 19.3: a panda plus a small 'gibbon class gradient' looks unchanged to people but is classified as a gibbon, showing brittleness and a mapping very different from human perception. LLMs have the analogous problem with prompts: harmless changes such as names can degrade performance.
snippet: The page opens by finishing the point from p.590: patching failing prompts one by one does not address the general issue, and "even already patched prompts will still fail if you…

title: Adversarial example
text: An input crafted, usually by a small perturbation, so that a model misclassifies it while a human sees no meaningful change. A tiny nudge in exactly the direction the model is most sensitive to. Typically built by gradient ascent on a target class score (or descent on the true-class score) with respect to the input, under a bound on the perturbation size. Figure 19.3: panda + small gibbon class gradient -> classified as gibbon.
snippet: An input crafted, usually by a small perturbation, so that a model misclassifies it while a human sees no meaningful change.

title: Gradient ascent in input space
text: Modifying the input (not the weights) along the gradient of a chosen quantity in order to increase it. Ask the model 'which way should each pixel move to make you more confident of X?', then move them. With weights fixed, compute $\nabla_x g(x)$ for a target $g$ (a filter activation or class logit) and update $x \leftarrow x + \eta\, \nabla_x g(x)$. Starting from noise to visualize a filter (p.317), or starting from a panda to create a fake gibbon (this page).
snippet: Modifying the input not the weights along the gradient of a chosen quantity in order to increase it.

title: Brittleness / sensitivity to input presentation
text: The tendency of deep learning models to change their output under small changes in how an input is presented, even when the meaning is unchanged. The model's decision boundary passes very close to most natural inputs in some directions. Models fit a curve to the training data; off the data manifold, or along directions the training data never constrained, the function can vary sharply. Adversarial images; LLM performance dropping when names or variable names change.
snippet: The tendency of deep learning models to change their output under small changes in how an input is presented, even when the meaning is unchanged.

title: Building an adversarial example by gradient ascent

The gradient points in the direction of input space where the gibbon score rises fastest. Because images have very many pixels, a tiny change per pixel in that direction can produce a large change in the score. x The original image (the panda), as a tensor of pixel values s_{\text{gibbon}}(x) The model's score (logit or log-probability) for the class 'gibbon' given input x \nabla_x s_{\text{gibbon}}(x) The 'gibbon class gradient': how each pixel should change to increase the gibbon score (middle image of Figure 19.3) \epsilon A small step size that keeps the change imperceptible x_{\text{adv}} The adversarial example (right image of Figure 19.3)

title: Prompt sensitivity and prompt engineering
text:
LLM oversensitivity to phrasing, the Alice in Wonderland riddle, and prompt engineering as a search through latent space Because an LLM is a big interpolative curve, a prompt acts like an address in a database of memorized knowledge and programs; small rewordings land at nearby but different addresses, which is why performance changes with phrasing and why prompt engineering (trial-and-error search over prompts) is needed. The page continues 19.1.2. Innocuous changes such as different names in a text or different variable names in code can significantly degrade LLM performance. The example is the **Alice in Wonderland riddle** (footnote 1 cites Nezhurina et al., arXiv 2406.02061): "Alice has N brothers and she also has M sisters. How many sisters does Alice's brother have?" The answer is $M+1$: Alice's sisters plus Alice. With values common online (N = 3, M = 2) LLMs usually answer correctly; change M and N and incorrect answers follow quickly.

This oversensitivity gave rise to **prompt engineering**: formulating prompts to maximize performance, for example adding "Please think step by step" to reasoning prompts. The authors call the term an optimistic framing ("Your models are better than you know!"); the negative framing is that for any prompt that works, small changes may tank performance. They ask: to what extent does an LLM understand something if simple rewordings break it?

The explanation: an LLM is a big parametric curve, a medium for storing knowledge and programs in which you can interpolate between any two objects. A prompt **addresses a location** in this database. "How do you sort a list in Python? Answer like a pirate" retrieves a piece of knowledge (sorting) and a style-transfer program (pirate speech) and applies one to the other.

Because the stored content is interpolative, you can **move around in latent space**: "Explain Python list sorting, but answer like a buccaneer" lands nearby and gives a similar but not identical answer, and there are thousands of such variants. Nothing guarantees your first prompt is the best one; the model fetches whatever program the prompt points to rather than understanding what you meant.

So prompt engineering is a trial-and-error **search through latent space** for the best lookup query, like trying keywords in a Google search. If LLMs understood requests, no search would be needed, since the information about the task does not change with wording (continued on p.593). Changing names, variable names or numbers can significantly degrade LLM performance even when the logic is unchanged. The Alice riddle has answer M + 1; LLMs get common instances right and changed instances wrong. Prompt engineering exists because of oversensitivity to phrasing; the authors see the term as an optimistic framing of a weakness. In the book's model, a prompt is an address in an interpolable database of knowledge and programs; similar prompts land at similar but different locations. Prompt engineering is trial-and-error search through latent space; a model that truly understood requests would not need it.

title: Programs that don't generalize
text:
Why deep learning models fail to learn exact discrete algorithms such as multi-digit addition, and the start of the warning against anthropomorphizing models Even when you address the right program, programs learned by deep learning work for some inputs and fail for others, because a model is a static chain of continuous geometric transformations; that suits perception but not step-by-step discrete logic like carrying in addition. Most programs cannot be expressed, or learned, as deep learning models. The page closes the prompt-engineering argument: the information about your task doesn't change whether you say "rewrite" or "rephrase" or add "Think step by step." Never assume the LLM "gets it" the first time; your prompt is "but an address in an infinite ocean of programs," all memorized as a by-product of learning to complete token sequences.

**19.1.3** adds a third limitation. Even if you know exactly how to address a well-known program in latent space, the programs memorized by deep learning models **often don't generalize well**: they work for some input values and fail for others, especially programs with discrete logic.

The example is **multi-digit addition** written as character sequences ("4 3 5 7 + 8 9 3 6"). A Transformer trained on hundreds of thousands of such pairs reaches very high but not 100% accuracy: it never encodes the exact school algorithm and instead guesses by interpolating between training points. State-of-the-art LLMs that are not hardcoded to run such expressions in Python reach only about 70% accuracy, and accuracy depends on *which* digits are involved, with more common digits giving better results.

The reason: a deep learning model is "a static chain of simple, continuous geometric transformations" from one vector space to another. That suits perceptual pattern recognition but fits step-by-step discrete logic (place value, carrying) very poorly. It can only map a data manifold X to a manifold Y when a learnable continuous transform exists. A model can be seen as a kind of program, but *most programs can't be expressed as deep learning models*: for most tasks there is no network of reasonable size, or one exists but is not *learnable* (too complex a transform, or no suitable data).

Section **19.1.4** begins: human understanding of images, sounds and language is grounded in sensorimotor experience, which models don't have (continued on p.594). A prompt is 'an address in an infinite ocean of programs'; never assume the model gets your intent the first time. Even a correctly addressed program often fails to generalize: it works for some inputs and not others, especially for discrete logic. Transformers trained on digit addition reach very high but not 100% accuracy; LLMs without Python execution reach about 70%, better on common digits. Deep learning models are static chains of continuous geometric transformations: good for perception, poor for step-by-step logic like carrying. Most programs can't be expressed as deep learning models of reasonable size, and those that can may not be learnable from available data. Human understanding is grounded in sensorimotor experience, which models lack (start of 19.1.4).

title: A dim image in a mirror
text:
Why models' learned mappings are only a rough sketch of human concepts, the risk of projecting understanding onto them, and the opening question of section 19.2 (is scale all we need?) Models learn a geometric transform that matches human concepts on the training examples only; it is a dim reflection of concepts that humans built from embodied experience. Our theory of mind tempts us to believe language models understand what they say, but they were trained on a narrower task, mapping training inputs to targets point by point, and break on anything that deviates. Continuing 19.1.4: models have no access to human sensorimotor experience, so they can't understand their inputs in a human-relatable way. Training on many examples gives them a geometric transform that maps data to human concepts *on a specific set of examples*, but this is "a simplistic sketch of the original model in our minds," which was built from our experience as embodied agents: "a dim image in a mirror." Models will take any shortcut available to fit their training data.

**Figure 19.4** shows the chain: the *real world* is experienced by humans (*embodied human experience*), which produces *abstract concepts in the human mind*; these are exemplified in *labeled data*, which trains a *machine learning model* f(x). The return arrows show what is checked: the model *matches the training data* (check mark), *doesn't match the human mental model it came from* (not-equal sign), and *may not always transfer well to the real world* (question mark).

The main risk with contemporary AI is misreading what models do and overestimating them. Humans have a **theory of mind**: we project intentions, beliefs and knowledge onto things around us. A smiley face drawn on a rock makes it "happy" in our minds. With language models, this leads us to believe the model understands its word sequences as we do, and we're surprised when small departures from training patterns produce absurd answers.

Practitioners should never believe that networks understand their tasks, at least not in a way that makes sense to us. They were trained on a narrower task than the one we intended: mapping training inputs to training targets, point by point. Anything that deviates from the training data can break them in absurd ways.

Section **19.2, Scale isn't all you need**, opens: could we keep scaling models to overcome these limitations? This was the prevailing narrative, especially in early 2023 at peak LLM hype, when GPT-4 had just (continued on p.595) been released as essentially a scaled-up GPT-3. Models learn a mapping from data to human concepts only on the training examples: a dim image in a mirror of concepts built from embodied experience. Models take any shortcut available to fit their training data. Figure 19.4: the model matches the training data, doesn't match the human mental model, and may not transfer to the real world. Our theory of mind leads us to believe language models understand what they say; this causes overestimation and surprise at absurd failures. Networks are trained on a narrower task (mapping training inputs to targets point by point) than the one we intend. Section 19.2 opens by asking whether scale is all we need, the dominant narrative in early 2023.

title: Why scaling hasn't fixed the limits
text:
The argument that scaling laws measure memorization and that scaling cannot fix the fundamental problems of deep learning; start of the comparison between deep learning and biological intelligence Scaling laws show predictable gains on benchmarks that are effectively memorization tests; they say nothing about adaptation to novelty, oversensitivity to phrasing or learning generalizable programs, which are inherent to curve fitting. Since models are still parametric curves fitted by gradient descent with Transformers, these problems remain despite four to five orders of magnitude of scaling. The page continues the 'scale is all you need' story: in early 2023 GPT-4 had just been released, "essentially a scaled-up version of GPT-3: more parameters, more training data." Its much better performance suggested you could keep going to a GPT-5 that would be more of the same and from which AGI would spontaneously emerge.

Proponents cite **scaling laws**: empirical relationships between model size (and dataset size) and performance on specific tasks, suggesting that bigger models reliably and predictably perform better. The author's objection: the benchmarks used to measure "performance" are effectively **memorization tests**, like university exams. LLMs do well on them by memorizing answers, so cramming more questions and answers into bigger models naturally improves scores.

Scaling has not produced progress on the issues of section 19.1 (inability to adapt to novelty, oversensitivity to phrasing, inability to infer generalizable programs for reasoning problems) because they are **inherent to curve fitting**, the paradigm of deep learning. The author says he started pointing these out in 2017 and they persist with models four or five orders of magnitude larger, because *the models we're using are still the same*: parametric curves fitted via gradient descent, using the Transformer, for over seven years.

Scaling by adding layers and data won't solve three fundamental problems:
1. Models are limited to **interpolative programs memorized at training time** and can't synthesize new programs at inference time for substantially novel situations.
2. Even in known situations, these programs **generalize poorly**, causing oversensitivity to phrasing and confounder features.
3. Models are **limited in what they can represent**: most programs can't be expressed as a continuous geometric morphing of a data manifold, especially algorithmic reasoning.

Section **19.2.1, Automatons vs. intelligent agents**, begins: deep learning's geometric morphing from input to output differs fundamentally from how humans think and learn, not only because humans learn from embodied experience rather than explicit examples, but because the brain is "an entirely different beast compared to a differentiable parametric function." In early 2023, GPT-4's gains from scaling up GPT-3 fed the belief that more scaling would lead to AGI. Scaling laws are real empirical relationships, but the book argues the benchmarks they use are memorization tests. Scaling hasn't solved novelty, phrasing sensitivity or generalizable programs, because these are inherent to curve fitting, and the models are still parametric curves fitted by gradient descent with Transformers. Three fundamental problems remain: only memorized interpolative programs; poor generalization with confounder sensitivity; limited representational power for algorithmic tasks. 19.2.1 begins the contrast between a differentiable parametric function and the human brain: automatons vs. intelligent agents.

title: Brains as evolved behavioral programs
text:
The evolutionary origin of brains as machines that store and execute hardcoded behavioral programs, illustrated by the C. elegans connectome. Brains first appeared as a way to store and execute 'if this, then that' behavioral programs written in DNA and decoded as neural wiring; this let evolution search over behavior space, but such brains are automatons, not yet intelligent agents. The page steps back from the scaling debate on p.595 and asks a basic question: **what is intelligence for, and why did it arise?** The author says this can only be answered by informed speculation, and starts from the organ that produces intelligence, the brain.

Brains are described as an **evolutionary adaptation**: a mechanism built up over hundreds of millions of years by random trial and error filtered by natural selection, which greatly expanded organisms' ability to adapt to their environments. Their original job, more than half a billion years ago, was to **store and execute behavioral programs**. A behavioral program is a set of reactive rules ("If this happens, then do that") that connects sensory inputs to motor outputs. In early brains these programs were *hardcoded* as patterns of neural connectivity, and the author says insect-level nervous systems still work this way, naming flies, ants and *C. elegans*.

The key point is about **search**. The "source code" of these programs was DNA, which development decodes into wiring. Because DNA can encode an almost unlimited variety of wiring patterns, evolution could now **search over behavior space** in a largely unbounded way, which the author calls a major evolutionary shift.

**Figure 19.5** shows the connectome of the worm *C. elegans* as a dense graph of sensory neurons (blue), interneurons (orange), motor neurons (yellow-green) and muscles (purple), with a few large interneuron hubs (AVAL, AVAR, AVBL, AVBR, PVCL…). The caption calls it "a behavioral automaton 'programmed' by natural evolution."

The page prepares the contrast drawn on p.597: a system that only executes a fixed program, however complex, is an **automaton**. It is "intelligent" only in the sense that a thermostat or a trained deep network is. Brains began as an evolutionary adaptation for storing and executing behavioral programs: 'If this happens, then do that' rules linking senses to motor controls. In early brains, these programs were hardcoded as neural connectivity, with DNA as the source code; the author says insect-level nervous systems still work this way. Because DNA is decoded into wiring, evolution could search over behavior space in a largely unbounded way. Figure 19.5's C. elegans connectome is a behavioral automaton 'programmed' by natural evolution. Being produced by a powerful search process does not make a system intelligent. This sets up the automaton vs. intelligent-agent distinction on p.597.

title: Behavioral program
text: A set of instructions that makes an organism reactive to its environment ('If this happens, then do that'), linking sensory inputs to motor controls. A lookup table or rulebook from situations to actions, written by evolution instead of a programmer. In early brains it is implemented as fixed neural connectivity specified by DNA. Its domain is the set of situations evolution 'tested' it on; outside that domain, nothing guarantees appropriate behavior. A worm reverses direction when its nose touches an obstacle; a moth flies toward a light source.
snippet: A set of instructions that makes an organism reactive to its environment 'If this happens, then do that', linking sensory inputs to motor controls.

title: Evolution as search over behavior space
text: Natural selection, acting on DNA that is decoded into neural wiring, explores the space of possible behaviors by random variation and selective retention. Evolution is a blind programmer who keeps typing random edits and keeps whichever version of the program survives. The DNA-to-connectivity mapping makes the search space very large and expressive: neural wiring is a general computing substrate, so many behaviors are reachable through small genomic changes. This is why the author calls it 'a largely unbounded' search and a 'major evolutionary shift'. Ant colonies' foraging rules, or a fly's escape reflex, refined over millions of generations.
snippet: Natural selection, acting on DNA that is decoded into neural wiring, explores the space of possible behaviors by random variation and selective retention.

title: Automaton
text: A system that executes a fixed program crafted for specific situations, without the ability to adapt on the fly to novel ones. A very sophisticated vending machine: it can be elaborate, but it only does what it was set up to do. Formally, a fixed mapping from inputs (and possibly internal state) to outputs that does not change at use time. On this page, early brains are the example; on p.597 the class also includes a thermostat, a list-sorting program and a trained deep network. The C. elegans nervous system in Figure 19.5.
snippet: A system that executes a fixed program crafted for specific situations, without the ability to adapt on the fly to novel ones.

title: Automatons vs. extreme generalization
text:
The distinction between automatons (static programs that fail outside their programmed context) and intelligent agents (which adapt on the fly), and the definition of extreme generalization. Early brains, thermostats, sorting programs and trained deep networks are all automatons that execute fixed programs. Intelligence is the ability to handle novel situations using abstraction and reasoning, which the author calls extreme generalization. The page finishes the brain-evolution story and opens **19.2.2 Local generalization vs. extreme generalization**.

**Evolution as programmer.** Evolution wrote the code and brains executed it. Neural connectivity is a very general computing substrate, so the sensorimotor repertoire of brain-equipped species could expand dramatically: eyes, ears, mandibles, 4 legs, 24 legs. Given a brain, evolution will find behavioral programs that use them, and brains can handle any modality or combination of modalities.

**But automatons are not intelligent.** These early brains merely executed programs hardcoded in DNA. They were 'intelligent' only in the sense that a thermostat, a list-sorting program, or **a trained deep neural network** is. That leads to the question of what separates automatons from intelligent agents.

**Automation vs. intelligence.** The author says AI has long conflated the two. An **automaton** is static, built for specific things in a specific context ('If this, then that'). An **intelligent agent** adapts on the fly to novel, unexpected situations. Faced with something it was not 'programmed' for, an automaton fails, whether the program was written by humans, by evolution, or implicitly by fitting a model to a training set.

**Extreme generalization.** Humans use fluid intelligence to find a way forward. The test for real understanding is a **brand-new problem**, the same test that separates a student who memorized past exams from one who understands. Humans go beyond stimulus-response mapping: they build on-the-fly abstract models of their situation, themselves and others, use them to anticipate futures and plan, and learn new skills with little practice. This use of **abstraction and reasoning** for unprepared-for situations is what the author calls **extreme generalization**: adapting to never-before-seen situations using little or no new data.

**The other end.** A rigid automaton such as a Python `dict` or a hardcoded if-then-else Q&A program has *no* generalization. Deep nets do 'slightly better', and the sentence continues on p.598. Evolution was the programmer and brains the computers; neural connectivity is a general substrate that can handle any modality. Early brains, thermostats, sorting programs and trained deep networks are all automatons: they execute fixed programs. An automaton fails outside its programmed context, whether the program was hand-written, evolved, or obtained by fitting a model to data. Intelligence is the ability to adapt on the fly to novel situations; the test is a brand-new problem. Extreme generalization means adapting to never-before-experienced situations with little or no new data, using abstraction and reasoning. A Python dict has no generalization; deep nets do 'slightly better' (local generalization).

title: Automaton
text: A static system crafted to accomplish specific things in a specific context ('If this, then that') that fails when exposed to something outside what it was programmed to do. A rulebook that works perfectly until the situation isn't in the rulebook. The program can come from human coding, evolution, or the implicit programming of fitting a model to training data; in each case the input-to-output mapping is fixed at use time. A thermostat, a list-sorting program, a fly's nervous system, a trained image classifier.
snippet: A static system crafted to accomplish specific things in a specific context 'If this, then that' that fails when exposed to something outside what it was programmed to do.

title: Intelligence vs. automation
text: Automation executes fixed programs for anticipated contexts. Intelligence is the ability to adapt on the fly to novel, unexpected situations. A memorizing student versus an understanding student, distinguished only by giving them a brand-new problem. The difference is measured by performance on situations outside those the system's program was built or trained for, and by how little new data the system needs to adapt. A chess engine (automation of chess skill) versus a person who learns a new board game from a single explanation.
snippet: Automation executes fixed programs for anticipated contexts. Intelligence is the ability to adapt on the fly to novel, unexpected situations.

title: Extreme generalization
text: The ability to adapt to novel, never-before-experienced situations using little data or even no new data, through abstraction and reasoning. Facing something you've never seen and still working out what to do, because you can build a model of it from concepts you already have. It requires on-the-fly construction of abstract models of the situation (and of self and others), simulation of possible futures, and long-term planning, rather than a fixed stimulus-to-response mapping. Deriving rocket-launch parameters from physics in one or a few trials (p.598), or learning to avoid cars without ever being hit (p.599).
snippet: The ability to adapt to novel, never-before-experienced situations using little data or even no new data, through abstraction and reasoning.

title: Fluid intelligence
text: The capacity to reason through and solve novel problems, as opposed to applying stored knowledge. Problem-solving ability, as opposed to what you already know. Beyond the book: the term comes from psychology (Cattell's fluid vs. crystallized intelligence). The author uses it informally for the human ability to 'find a way forward' in unfamiliar situations. Solving a puzzle type you have never seen before.
snippet: The capacity to reason through and solve novel problems, as opposed to applying stored knowledge.

title: Local generalization and its limits
text:
Why deep nets achieve only local generalization (to known unknowns, via interpolation on a learned manifold), illustrated by Figure 19.6 and the rocket and city-navigation examples. Deep networks generalize only to inputs close to their training data, because they interpolate on a learned manifold. They therefore need dense sampling of the input space, while humans use abstract models to solve new problems in one or a few trials. The page completes p.597's sentence: deep nets 'can successfully process inputs that deviate a bit from what they're familiar with, which is precisely what makes them useful.' The chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats model classified unseen pet photos, as long as they were **close enough** to the training data.

The author names this **local generalization** (Figure 19.6): a deep net's input-to-output mapping 'quickly stops making sense as inputs start deviating from what the net saw at training time.' Deep nets generalize only to **known unknowns**, factors of variation that were anticipated during development and well represented in the training data, such as camera angle or lighting. The cause is that deep nets **generalize via interpolation on a manifold** (chapter 5): every factor of variation must be captured by the learned manifold. This is why **data augmentation** helps: it fills in factors of variation the data would otherwise lack. Unlike humans, the models cannot improvise when little or no data is available.

**Figure 19.6** shows a 'situations space' with three known situations (dots). A lower-intelligence system turns them into a small **operational area** (small discs around each dot), which is a *lower information conversion ratio*. A higher-intelligence system turns the same three situations into a much larger area, a *higher information conversion ratio*. This anticipates the efficiency-based definition of intelligence on p.604.

Two examples follow. **Rocket to the moon:** a deep net trained by supervised or reinforcement learning would need tens of thousands to millions of launch trials, a **dense sampling** of the input space. Humans use abstraction to build physical models (rocket science) and derive an exact solution in one or a few trials. **City navigation:** a deep net controlling a body would have to 'die many thousands of times' to infer that cars are dangerous, and would have to relearn most of it in a new city. Humans, as p.599 finishes, learn safe behavior without dying once. Deep nets handle inputs that deviate a bit from the training data, which is what makes them useful, but only locally. Local generalization: the learned mapping quickly stops making sense as inputs move away from what was seen in training. Deep nets generalize only to known unknowns, factors of variation anticipated and well represented in training data. The cause is interpolation on a learned manifold (chapter 5); this is also why data augmentation helps. Figure 19.6: from the same known situations, a more intelligent system gets a larger operational area (higher information conversion ratio). Deep nets need dense sampling (millions of rocket launches, thousands of deaths in traffic); humans use abstract models to succeed in one or a few trials.

title: Local generalization
text: Generalization that holds only for inputs close to the training data; the learned mapping quickly stops making sense as inputs deviate from what the model saw during training. Knowing a city only by the streets you've walked: you can find your way between familiar places, but not in a neighborhood you've never visited. Arises because deep nets generalize via interpolation on a learned approximation of the data manifold. Any factor of variation must be represented in the training data (known unknowns) for the manifold to capture it. The chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats convnet classifies new photos similar to its training set but cannot be trusted on, for example, cartoon drawings of pets.
snippet: Generalization that holds only for inputs close to the training data; the learned mapping quickly stops making sense as inputs deviate from what the model saw during training.

title: Known unknowns
text: Factors of variation that were anticipated during model development and are extensively featured in the training data. You don't know which exact photo will arrive, but you know it may come from different angles or lighting, and you included those in training. Deep nets can generalize across known unknowns because those directions of variation are covered by the training manifold. Unknown unknowns (unanticipated variation) are not covered and are not handled. Camera angle and lighting for pet photos, explicitly covered by data or augmentation.
snippet: Factors of variation that were anticipated during model development and are extensively featured in the training data.

title: Data augmentation
text: Expanding the training set with label-preserving random transformations of existing samples. Showing the model the same cat flipped, rotated and zoomed, so it learns that these changes don't matter. On this page, augmentation helps because it extends the learned manifold along factors of variation (known unknowns) the raw data underrepresents, making interpolation possible there. RandomFlip, RandomRotation and RandomZoom layers in the chapter 8 dogs-vs-cats model.
snippet: Expanding the training set with label-preserving random transformations of existing samples.

title: Information conversion ratio
text: How efficiently a system converts the information it has (known situations, experience, priors) into an operational area, the set of situations it can handle. Two students read the same three worked examples; the one who can then solve far more new problems has the higher ratio. Introduced visually in Figure 19.6 and defined on p.604 as an efficiency ratio between relevant available information and future operating area. A physicist deriving a launch trajectory from equations (high ratio) vs. a deep net needing millions of trials (low ratio).
snippet: How efficiently a system converts the information it has known situations, experience, priors into an operational area, the set of situations it can handle.

title: Why intelligence evolved
text:
The evolutionary explanation for intelligence: as environments became dynamic and unpredictable, hardcoded behavior became insufficient, and brains shifted to optimizing for adaptability itself. Then the start of 19.2.4, the history of biological intelligence as a climb up the spectrum of generalization. Intelligence evolved because complex, dynamic environments made it impossible to hardcode behavior in DNA. It is the ability to efficiently use the information at your disposal to produce successful behavior in an uncertain, ever-changing future, made possible by modular, reusable abstractions. The page closes 19.2.2 (humans learn safe behaviors 'without having to die even once', thanks to abstract modeling of novel situations) and turns to **why** intelligence arose.

**19.2.3 The purpose of intelligence.** The automaton/agent distinction leads back to brain evolution. Brains started as a medium for evolution to build behavioral automatons, so why did they become intelligent? Like every major evolutionary milestone, because **natural selection pressure** favored it.

The argument has three steps:
1. Brains exist to **generate behavior**. If the situations an organism faced were *static and known in advance*, evolution could find the right behaviors by trial and error and hardcode them in DNA, and the automaton stage would already be **optimal**.
2. As organisms, and with them their environments, grew more complex, situations became **dynamic and unpredictable**. Every day of your life is unlike any day you or your ancestors have lived. Evolution cannot find and hardcode the behavior sequence you've executed since waking. It has to be **generated on the fly**.
3. So the brain, as a behavior-generation engine, adapted: it **optimized for adaptability and generality themselves**, not for fitness to a fixed set of situations. This likely happened several times independently, producing highly intelligent animals in distant branches (apes, octopuses, ravens).

**Definition.** Intelligence is an answer to complex, dynamic ecosystems: *the ability to efficiently use the information at your disposal to produce successful behavior in the face of an uncertain, ever-changing future.* What 'Descartes calls "understanding"' is the key: mining past experience for **modular, reusable abstractions** that can be quickly repurposed for novel situations, which is extreme generalization.

**19.2.4 Climbing the spectrum of generalization.** As a 'crude caricature', the history of biological intelligence is a slow climb up the **spectrum of generalization**: from automaton-like brains capable only of local generalization, to organisms with broader generalization in more variable environments, to certain hominin species in the last few million years trending toward extreme generalization (continued on p.600). Humans learn safe behaviors without dying even once, thanks to abstract modeling of novel situations. Intelligence arose, like every evolutionary milestone, because natural selection pressures favored it. In a static, known world, hardcoded automaton brains would be optimal; complexity made situations dynamic and unique, so behavior had to be generated on the fly. Brains then optimized for adaptability and generality themselves, probably several times (apes, octopuses, ravens). Intelligence is the ability to efficiently use available information to produce successful behavior in an uncertain, ever-changing future. 'Understanding' means mining experience for modular, reusable abstractions that can be repurposed, which is the key to extreme generalization. Biological evolution is (as a crude caricature) a climb up the spectrum of generalization, from local to extreme.

title: Intelligence (author's definition)
text: The ability to efficiently use the information at your disposal to produce successful behavior in the face of an uncertain, ever-changing future. Not how much you can do, but how far you can get from what you know when the world surprises you. Emphasizes efficiency (output relative to information used), applies to novel situations, and relies on modular, reusable abstractions mined from experience. Quantified on p.604 as a conversion ratio between information and future operating area. A person who has never been to a given city but navigates it safely using general knowledge about traffic, maps and signs.
snippet: The ability to efficiently use the information at your disposal to produce successful behavior in the face of an uncertain, ever-changing future.

title: Abstraction (modular, reusable)
text: A compact unit of knowledge mined from past experience that can be quickly repurposed to handle novel situations. A Lego brick of understanding: extracted once, reused in many constructions. Modularity means abstractions can be combined independently. Reusability means they apply across many situations. Together they make extreme generalization possible, because a new situation can be modeled by recombining existing abstractions. The concept 'cars are dangerous' transfers to every city, unlike a map-specific avoidance policy.
snippet: A compact unit of knowledge mined from past experience that can be quickly repurposed to handle novel situations.

title: Spectrum of generalization
text: A scale ordering systems by how broadly they generalize: from automaton-like local generalization, through broader generalization, to extreme generalization. title: Selection for adaptability
text: The evolutionary shift in which brains were optimized for adaptability and generality themselves, rather than for fitness to a fixed set of situations. Instead of evolving the right answer for each situation, evolve the ability to come up with answers. Driven by increasing environmental complexity: when situations are dynamic and unique, hardcoded behavior cannot keep up, so selection favors on-the-fly behavior generation. Independent evolution of high intelligence in apes, octopuses and ravens.

title: AI's climb up the spectrum of generalization
text:
Mapping the history of AI onto the spectrum of generalization (automatons, local, broad, extreme), defining broad generalization, and arguing that deep learning is cognitive automation rather than intelligence; opening of 19.3 How to build intelligence. AI has moved from pure automatons to local generalization and may be approaching broad generalization, but deep learning remains cognitive automation. Its models map X to Y through a smooth transform learned from dense data, which breaks under disruption, while human cognition achieves extreme generalization. The 19.2.4 sentence ends: certain hominins reached extreme generalization, **'precipitating the start of the Anthropocene'** and changing the history of life on Earth.

**AI's history follows the same climb.** Early AI systems were **pure automatons**: ELIZA (1960s chatbot) and SHRDLU (a 1970 system that manipulated simple objects from natural-language commands; footnote 2: Winograd). The 1990s–2000s brought **machine learning with local generalization**, able to handle some uncertainty and novelty. The 2010s brought **deep learning**, which expanded local generalization by allowing much larger datasets and more expressive models.

**Next step: broad generalization**, defined as dealing with **unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks**, including situations the system wasn't trained for and its creators couldn't anticipate. Examples: a self-driving car that safely handles anything, or a domestic robot passing the **'Woz test'** of entering a random kitchen and making coffee (footnote 3). Combining deep learning with **painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world** is making visible progress.

**A category error.** Deep learning remains **cognitive automation**. Calling it 'intelligence' is a category error. The field would be better named **'artificial cognition'**, with **cognitive automation** and **artificial intelligence** as two nearly independent subfields. AI proper is a 'greenfield' where almost everything remains to be discovered.

**Credit where due.** Cognitive automation is very useful, and learning to automate tasks from data alone is more practical and versatile than explicit programming, a game changer for nearly every industry. But models still only **map space X to space Y via a smooth geometric transform learned from a dense sampling of X-to-Y data points**, and **any disruption** in X or Y invalidates the mapping. Humans achieve extreme generalization and long-term planning.

**19.3 How to build intelligence** opens: there is much more to intelligence than latent manifold interpolation, so what are the core missing pieces? Reaching extreme generalization let hominins start the Anthropocene. AI's history mirrors evolution: pure automatons (ELIZA, SHRDLU), then ML with local generalization, then deep learning with expanded local generalization. Broad generalization means handling unknown unknowns within a single broad domain; examples are a fully robust self-driving car and a robot passing the Woz coffee test. Deep learning is cognitive automation; calling it 'intelligence' is a category error. The author proposes 'artificial cognition' split into cognitive automation and AI. Deep models map X to Y via a smooth geometric transform learned from dense X-to-Y samples; any disruption in X or Y invalidates the mapping. Section 19.3 asks what core pieces are missing to build real intelligence.

title: The kaleidoscope hypothesis
text:
Why intelligence is possible at all: the world's apparent novelty is built from recombinations of a small number of reusable 'atoms of meaning', so past experience can be mapped onto new situations by analogy. Nothing is ever truly without precedent. Everything in the world's apparent complexity resembles something else, because it is made of a relatively small set of atoms of meaning recombined in endless ways, like a kaleidoscope's few beads producing endless patterns. Intelligence exploits this structure. **19.3.1 The kaleidoscope hypothesis** starts by restating intelligence as using past experience **and innate prior knowledge** to face novel, unexpected situations. It then states a limit: if the future were **truly novel**, sharing no common ground with anything seen before, no one could react to it, however intelligent.

**Intelligence works because nothing is truly without precedent.** We make sense of new things by **analogy** to past experience and by describing them with abstract concepts we've collected. A 17th-century person seeing a jet might call it a large, loud metal bird that doesn't flap its wings; a car is a 'horseless carriage'. Teachers explain electricity as water in a pipe and spacetime as a rubber sheet distorted by heavy objects.

Beyond such **explicit analogies**, we make small **implicit analogies** constantly, 'every second, with every thought'. We navigate a new supermarket by relating it to stores we know, read new people through people we've met, and see elephants, ships and fish in clouds.

The analogies are **not only in our minds**: physical reality is full of **isomorphisms**. Electromagnetism is analogous to gravity, animals are structurally similar through shared origins, and silica crystals resemble ice crystals.

**The hypothesis:** our experience seems to have incredible complexity and endless novelty, yet everything in it is similar to everything else. The number of **unique atoms of meaning** needed to describe the universe is relatively small, and everything around us is a **recombination** of these atoms: 'a few seeds, endless variation', like a kaleidoscope in which a few glass beads, reflected by mirrors, produce rich, seemingly endless patterns (**Figure 19.7**). On p.602 these atoms, once extracted, are called **abstractions**. Intelligence uses past experience and innate priors to face novel situations, but a truly novel situation (no common ground) would defeat any intelligence. Nothing is ever truly without precedent: we make sense of the new by analogy and with abstract concepts we've collected. We make implicit analogies constantly (new supermarkets, new people, cloud shapes). Physical reality is full of isomorphisms: electromagnetism and gravity, animal anatomies, silica and ice crystals. Kaleidoscope hypothesis: a relatively small number of unique atoms of meaning, recombined, describes everything; a few seeds, endless variation (Figure 19.7).

title: Abstraction acquisition, recombination, and the shortcut rule
text:
The two components of intelligence (abstraction acquisition and on-the-fly recombination), why efficiency defines intelligence, the two failings of classic deep learning, and the shortcut rule of optimizing a single metric Intelligence is the efficient extraction of reusable abstractions from experience plus their efficient recombination on the fly to model new situations. Classic deep learning does the first part inefficiently and lacks the second part entirely, and because systems are shaped by the metric they optimize, choosing the right target is the first step toward real AI. **19.3.2** turns the kaleidoscope hypothesis of p.601 into a definition. Intelligence is the ability to *mine your experience* for "atoms of meaning" that can be reused across many different situations, the "core beads of the kaleidoscope." Once extracted they are called **abstractions**. When you face a new situation, you make sense of it by *recombining abstractions on the fly* into a brand new "model" fitted to that situation.

The process has two parts:
- **Abstraction acquisition**: efficiently extracting compact, reusable abstractions (structures, principles, invariants) from a stream of experience or data.
- **On-the-fly recombination**: efficiently selecting and recombining them in novel ways to model new problems, even ones far from past experience.

The key word is **efficiency**. How intelligent you are depends on how efficiently you acquire good abstractions from *limited* experience and how efficiently you recombine them. Needing hundreds of thousands of hours of practice for a skill, or enumerating every chess move to find the best one, are signs of low intelligence.

This gives the two main problems of classic deep learning:
1. **No on-the-fly recombination.** Models acquire abstractions at training time with gradient descent but by design cannot recombine them at test time. They are a "static abstract database, limited purely to retrieval," missing "the most important half."
2. **Inefficiency.** Gradient descent needs many orders of magnitude more data than humans to distill good abstractions.

**19.3.3** asks how to get past these limits. Biological intelligence answered a question asked by nature, so to build true AI we must first ask the right question: AI systems' capabilities reflect the objectives they were optimized for. The **shortcut rule**: optimize one success metric and you reach it at the expense of everything the metric doesn't cover, taking every available shortcut. The example begins here: the 2009 Netflix Prize ($1 million for the best recommendation score) produced a winning system that Netflix never used because it was too complex and compute intensive (continued on p.603). Intelligence = abstraction acquisition + on-the-fly recombination, both done efficiently. Efficiency is the defining criterion: little experience and little search for a lot of new capability. Classic deep learning lacks on-the-fly recombination entirely and acquires abstractions very inefficiently. AI capabilities reflect the objectives they're optimized for, so choosing the target comes first. The shortcut rule: optimizing one metric sacrifices everything the metric ignores, as with the undeployed Netflix Prize winner.

title: Abstraction
text: A compact, reusable unit of meaning (a structure, principle or invariant) extracted from experience that applies across many situations. One of the kaleidoscope's beads: a small piece that shows up again and again in different arrangements. In deep learning, abstractions are stored as learned features and parametric curves fitted by gradient descent (p.609); in program synthesis they would be reusable functions. 'Containment' (something inside something else) applies to a cup holding water, a box holding toys, and a set holding elements.
snippet: A compact, reusable unit of meaning a structure, principle or invariant extracted from experience that applies across many situations.

title: Abstraction acquisition
text: Efficiently extracting compact, reusable abstractions from a stream of experience or data by identifying underlying structures, principles or invariants. Building a toolbox from what you've experienced. Classic deep learning does this at training time with gradient descent, but needs orders of magnitude more data than humans. A child who sees a few dogs extracts the concept 'dog' and recognizes a new breed; a classifier may need thousands of labeled images.
snippet: Efficiently extracting compact, reusable abstractions from a stream of experience or data by identifying underlying structures, principles or invariants.

title: On-the-fly recombination
text: Efficiently selecting and recombining abstractions in novel ways to model new problems and situations, even ones far removed from past experience. Using the toolbox to build a new tool for the job in front of you, at the moment you need it. Requires input-dependent computation at inference time; a frozen network running one forward pass doesn't do it. Test-time training and test-time search (p.606) are attempts to add it. Figuring out how to use an unfamiliar vending machine by combining what you know about buttons, payment and dispensers.
snippet: Efficiently selecting and recombining abstractions in novel ways to model new problems and situations, even ones far removed from past experience.

title: Efficiency as the measure of intelligence
text: Intelligence is determined by how efficiently abstractions are acquired from limited experience and recombined to deal with uncertainty and novelty. Not 'can you do it?' but 'how little did you need to be able to do it?' Formalized on p.604 as a conversion ratio between the information available and the set of novel situations handled. Enumerating every chess move can find the best move but signals low intelligence.
snippet: Intelligence is determined by how efficiently abstractions are acquired from limited experience and recombined to deal with uncertainty and novelty.

title: Shortcut rule
text: If you optimize for one success metric, you achieve it at the expense of everything in the system the metric doesn't cover, taking every available shortcut. You get exactly what you measure, and nothing else. Applies to optimizers (a loss function ignores everything outside it) and to engineering teams and research fields (benchmarks shape what gets built). The Netflix Prize winner was too complex and compute intensive to deploy.
snippet: If you optimize for one success metric, you achieve it at the expense of everything in the system the metric doesn't cover, taking every available shortcut.

title: Chess, Deep Blue, and why fixed tasks remove the need for intelligence
text:
The shortcut rule applied to Kaggle, to the history of AI (Newell's chess goal and Deep Blue), and to task-specific benchmarks in general As long as AI's success metric is skill at a specific task, the field will find unintelligent shortcuts: fixing the task allows skill to be 'bought' with data or hardcoded knowledge, which removes the need to handle novelty, and therefore the need for intelligence. Collecting task-specific skills doesn't add up to general intelligence. The Netflix sentence ends: the winners had **optimized for prediction accuracy alone** at the expense of inference cost, maintainability and explainability. The same holds for most Kaggle competitions: winning models rarely, if ever, go into production.

The shortcut rule has shaped AI for decades. In the 1970s, **Allen Newell**, worried that his field wasn't progressing toward a theory of cognition, proposed **chess** as AI's grand goal, reasoning that chess in humans seems to require perception, reasoning, memory and study, so a chess machine would need them too. In **1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat Kasparov**, and researchers found that a chess champion AI had taught them little about human intelligence: its search algorithm wasn't a model of the brain and didn't generalize beyond similar board games. Building a chess-only AI was easier than building a mind, so that's the shortcut taken.

More generally, *the driving success metric of AI has been to solve specific tasks*: chess, Go, MNIST, ImageNet, high school math tests, the bar exam. The field's history is a series of "successes" where *we figured out how to solve these tasks without featuring any intelligence*.

Why? Human-like intelligence isn't skill at any particular task but the **ability to adapt to novelty**, efficiently acquiring new skills for never-before-seen tasks. Fixing the task makes it possible to describe what needs to be done arbitrarily precisely, through hardcoded knowledge or huge amounts of data. Engineers can then **"buy" skill** by adding data or hardcoded rules without increasing generalization power (Figure 19.8, p.604). With near-infinite data, even nearest-neighbor search plays video games at superhuman level; with enough if-then-else rules a system can work too, until a small rule change, which a human would adapt to instantly, forces it to be rebuilt.

By fixing the task, you remove the need to handle uncertainty and novelty, and therefore the need for intelligence. Since an unintelligent solution to a specific task is always easier to find, that's the shortcut taken "100% of the time." General intelligence can produce task skills, but **there is no path from a collection of task-specific skills to general intelligence**. title: A new target: generalization power and the efficiency ratio
text:
Figure 19.8 (skill vs. task-relevant information for systems of different generalization power), the proposal to target generalization power itself, intelligence defined as an efficiency ratio, and the introduction of ARC-AGI Skill at a fixed task can be raised by adding information, so it can't measure intelligence. Instead, fix the information (priors plus experience) a system gets and measure how well it handles tasks sufficiently different from anything it saw, tasks its creators couldn't anticipate. Intelligence is the ratio between that information and the resulting range of handled novel situations. **Figure 19.8** plots *task-specific skill* (vertical axis) against *task-relevant information, priors + experience* (horizontal axis) for systems with different **generalization power** (= 1, 2, 3, and a steep curve labeled = N). Each system's skill rises as it gets more information. A green dashed line marks *fixed priors + experience*: at that fixed amount of information, systems with more generalization power reach more skill. The caption draws the other conclusion: a **low-generalization system can achieve arbitrary skill at a fixed task given unlimited task-specific information**. So skill alone can't tell you which curve a system is on.

**19.3.4** proposes the remedy. To make AI able to deal with the variability of the real world, stop seeking *task-specific skill* and target **generalization power itself**. The field needs new metrics of progress that point in the right direction and give actionable feedback. As long as the goal is "create a model that solves task X," the shortcut rule applies and you get a model that does X, period.

The author's definition: intelligence is an **efficiency ratio**, the conversion ratio between the *amount of relevant information* you have about the world (past experience or innate prior knowledge) and your *future operating area*, the set of novel situations in which you'll produce appropriate behavior (your *skill set*). A more intelligent agent handles a broader set of future situations with less experience.

To measure it: **fix the information** available to the system (experience and priors), then measure performance on reference tasks **sufficiently different** from what it has seen. Maximizing this ratio should lead toward intelligence. To avoid cheating, test only on tasks the system wasn't programmed or trained for, tasks its *creators could not have anticipated*.

In 2018-2019, the author developed the **Abstraction & Reasoning Corpus for Artificial General Intelligence (ARC-AGI)** (footnote: Chollet, "On the Measure of Intelligence," 2019) to capture this definition (continued on p.605). Figure 19.8: given unlimited task-specific information, even a low-generalization system reaches arbitrary skill, so skill can't measure intelligence. The new target is generalization power itself, not task-specific skill. Intelligence is an efficiency ratio between information (priors + experience) and the range of novel situations handled. Measure it by fixing priors and experience and testing on sufficiently different tasks the creators couldn't anticipate. ARC-AGI (2018-2019) was built to implement this definition.

title: How ARC-AGI works, and the ARC Prize
text:
The format of ARC-AGI tasks (Figure 19.9), what sets it apart from IQ tests (only unseen tasks, controlled priors through Core Knowledge), and the founding of the ARC Prize Foundation ARC-AGI is an IQ-test-like benchmark of grid puzzles, each defined by a few input-output examples, that measures generalization by testing only on never-seen tasks and controls prior knowledge by assuming only Core Knowledge priors. The ARC Prize competition (2024 onward) adds financial incentives to solve it. ARC-AGI is meant to be approachable by both machines and humans and looks like human IQ tests such as **Raven's progressive matrices**. At test time you see a series of **tasks**. Each is explained by three or four **examples**, pairs of an input grid and its output grid (Figure 19.9). You then get a new input grid and have **three tries** to produce the correct output grid.

**Figure 19.9** shows a task: three demonstration pairs (input -> output) and a test input followed by a question mark. In each input, a short light-blue diagonal sits on a black grid with a red wall along one edge; in each output, the diagonal continues as a green line that appears to reflect off the red wall. You must infer the rule from the examples and apply it to the new input.

Two things are unique compared with IQ tests:
1. **Only unseen tasks.** ARC measures generalization by testing only on tasks you've never seen, so it's *a game you can't practice for*, at least in theory. Each task has its own logic that must be understood on the fly; memorizing strategies from past tasks doesn't help.
2. **Controlled prior knowledge.** You never face a problem from scratch. ARC-AGI assumes all test takers start from the same knowledge priors, **Core Knowledge priors**, which represent the knowledge systems humans are born with. Unlike IQ tests, ARC never involves acquired knowledge such as English sentences.

**19.3.5 ARC Prize.** In 2024, to accelerate progress toward AI capable of the fluid abstraction and reasoning ARC-AGI measures, the author and Mike Knoop founded the nonprofit **ARC Prize Foundation**. It runs a yearly competition with a large prize pool (over $1 million in 2024) to incentivize researchers to build AI that can solve ARC-AGI and so display genuine fluid intelligence. An ARC-AGI task gives three or four input-output grid examples, then a new input with three tries to produce the output. ARC tests only on never-seen tasks, so it can't be practiced for by memorization. It controls priors: only Core Knowledge, never acquired knowledge like language. The ARC Prize Foundation (2024, Chollet and Mike Knoop) runs a yearly competition with over $1 million in prizes in 2024.

title: ARC-AGI resists scaling; the test-time adaptation era begins
text:
Why base LLM scaling made little progress on ARC-AGI, the ARC Prize 2024 results, test-time adaptation (test-time training and search), and OpenAI's o3 results on ARC-AGI A roughly 50,000x scale-up of base LLMs moved ARC-AGI scores only from 0% to about 10%, showing that scale alone doesn't give fluid intelligence. In 2024 the field shifted to test-time adaptation, where a system reasons or learns during the test itself; every top ARC Prize 2024 entry used it, and OpenAI's o3 reached 76-88% at very high compute cost. ARC-AGI has been **remarkably resistant to the deep learning scaling paradigm**. Most benchmarks saturated quickly in the LLM era because they can be hacked via memorization; ARC-AGI is designed to resist that. From 2019 to 2025, base LLMs scaled up roughly **50,000x** (say, GPT-2 in 2019 to GPT-4.5 in 2025), yet their score on the 2019 ARC-AGI went only from **0% to around 10%**, while a human reader would easily score **above 95%**.

A 50,000x scale-up without meaningful progress is a warning sign that new ideas are needed. Bigger models and more data didn't unlock the fluid intelligence ARC-AGI requires; ARC-AGI showed that **on-the-fly recombination** is necessary for reasoning.

**19.3.6 The test-time adaptation era.** In 2024 the narrative shifted, partly catalyzed by ARC Prize, from "Scale is all you need" (the dogma of 2023) to "Actually, we need on-the-fly recombination." The competition results (December 2024) showed that leading solutions didn't come from scaling existing architectures; they all used **test-time adaptation (TTA)**, either test-time search or test-time training.

TTA means the AI system performs active reasoning or learning *during the test itself*, using the specific problem's information, the component missing from classic deep learning. Two ways:
- **Test-time training**: the model adjusts some parameters with gradient descent on the examples given in the test task.
- **Search methods**: the system searches through many possible reasoning steps or solutions at test time, in natural language (**chain-of-thought synthesis**) or among symbolic, verifiable programs (**program synthesis**).

TTA makes systems more flexible with novelty than static models, and **every top entry in ARC Prize 2024** used it.

In late December 2024, OpenAI previewed **o3**, a test-time reasoning model, and used ARC-AGI to show its capabilities: **76% at about $200 per task** and **88% at over $20,000 per task**, surpassing the nominal human baseline. For the first time an AI model showed signs of genuine fluid intelligence. This started a wave of interest and investment in similar techniques, the **test-time adaptation era**, and ARC-AGI was one of the only benchmarks that clearly signaled the paradigm shift. A ~50,000x scale-up of base LLMs moved ARC-AGI-1 from 0% to ~10%; humans score above 95%. ARC-AGI resists memorization, so it didn't saturate like other benchmarks. Test-time adaptation (test-time training or test-time search) means reasoning or learning during the test itself. Every top ARC Prize 2024 entry used TTA. o3 scored 76% (~$200/task) and 88% (>$20,000/task) in December 2024, starting the test-time adaptation era.

title: Was o3 human-level? Efficiency, and the need for ARC-AGI-2
text:
Why o3's ARC-AGI results don't mean AGI is solved: brute-forcing with huge compute isn't intelligence, o3 still failed some easy tasks (Figure 19.10), and ARC-AGI-1 was a near-binary test that needed a harder, less brute-forcible successor o3's results were a landmark but came at tens of thousands of dollars per puzzle, and since intelligence is about efficiency, brute-forcing a solution space is a shortcut, not intelligence. o3 also failed tasks humans find easy. ARC-AGI-1 essentially separated 'no fluid intelligence' from 'some,' so a new version was needed to measure degrees of fluid reasoning up to human level. **19.3.7 ARC-AGI 2** opens with a question: does o3's result mean AGI is solved? Was o3 as intelligent as a human? *Not quite.*

**First, cost.** o3's performance came at tens of thousands of dollars of compute per ARC-AGI puzzle. Intelligence isn't just capability; it's fundamentally about **efficiency**. Brute-forcing the solution space with enormous compute is a shortcut that makes all kinds of tasks possible without intelligence. In principle, ARC-AGI could even be solved by walking down the tree of every possible solution program and testing each one on the demonstration pairs until one works. The o3 results felt more like cracking a code with a supercomputer than nimble, human-like fluid reasoning. The point of intelligence is to achieve results with the least resources possible.

**Second, failures on easy tasks.** o3 was still stumped by many tasks humans found very easy, such as the one in **Figure 19.10** (which o3 couldn't solve even at its highest compute setting, over $20,000 per task). So o3 wasn't quite human-level yet.

The 2019 ARC-AGI was intended to be easy: it was essentially a **binary test of fluid intelligence**. Systems with no fluid intelligence, like all base LLMs, scored near zero; anything with some genuine fluid intelligence immediately scored very high, like any human or o3. There wasn't much room in between. The benchmark needed to evolve with the capabilities it measured: a new version that was **less brute-forcible** and that could **better differentiate** systems with varying levels of fluid reasoning, up to human level. The ARC team had been working on one since 2022 (continued on p.608: ARC-AGI-2, released in March 2025).

**Figure 19.10** shows three demonstration pairs and a test input. Each input has gray diagonal shapes on black and a small row of colored cells in the top-left corner; the outputs color the gray shapes in bands that appear to follow the colors of that key. o3's ARC-AGI results were a landmark but cost tens of thousands of dollars per puzzle. Intelligence is about efficiency; brute-forcing a solution space with compute is a shortcut. o3 still failed tasks humans find very easy (Figure 19.10), so it wasn't human-level. ARC-AGI-1 was nearly a binary test of fluid intelligence, with little room between near-zero and very high. A new version needed to be less brute-forcible and graded up to human level; work on it began in 2022.

title: ARC-AGI-2 and the call for new ingredients
text:
Why ARC-AGI-2 was introduced (March 2025), how it differs from ARC-AGI-1, how current systems fared on it, and the opening of section 19.4 on what is still missing ARC-AGI-2 keeps ARC's format but uses tasks that need longer reasoning chains and resist brute-force search, so that efficiency matters. Even o3 drops to low double digits under reasonable compute budgets and base LLMs score about 0%, which shows that something beyond current test-time adaptation is needed. Section 19.4 then starts describing those missing ingredients: search and symbols. The page finishes section **19.3.7 ARC-AGI 2**. In **March 2025** the ARC Prize Foundation released **ARC-AGI-2**. It uses *exactly the same format* as ARC-AGI-1 (a few demonstration input/output grid pairs, then a new input grid to solve) but has much better task content. The new tasks need **longer, more complex reasoning chains** and are built to **resist exhaustive search**. The goal is a benchmark where **computational efficiency** becomes decisive, which pushes systems toward intelligent strategies instead of "exploring billions of possibilities." Most ARC-AGI-1 tasks could be solved by a human almost instantly. Every ARC-AGI-2 task needs some deliberate thought: in the authors' experiments human test takers took **5 minutes per task on average**.

**Figure 19.11** shows the difference. On the left is a typical ARC-AGI-1 task: a red line segment on black becomes a light-blue diamond centered on it, a rule you see at a glance. On the right is a typical ARC-AGI-2 task: a light-blue grid with several framed colored squares and a row of color swatches. Solving it means working out how the colors and positions interact, which takes several steps.

The first results were "sobering". **o3**, which had beaten the human baseline on ARC-AGI-1 at huge cost (p.607), fell back into the **low double digits** when held to reasonable compute budgets. **Base LLMs scored about 0%**, which fits the book's claim that base LLMs have no fluid intelligence. The author concludes that efficient, human-like fluid intelligence is still far from solved and that "we're going to need something beyond current TTA techniques."

**Section 19.4, The missing ingredients: Search and symbols**, then begins. It asks what it would take to fully solve ARC-AGI, especially version 2. Those ingredients are developed over the following pages (p.609-618). ARC-AGI-2 (March 2025) keeps the ARC format but uses tasks that need multi-step reasoning and resist exhaustive search. Its design makes computational efficiency decisive: brute force should not be enough. Humans need about 5 minutes per ARC-AGI-2 task on average; ARC-AGI-1 tasks were mostly instant. o3 drops to the low double digits under reasonable budgets, and base LLMs score about 0%. The author concludes that something beyond current TTA is needed. Section 19.4 names it: search and symbols.

title: Two poles of abstraction: value-centric analogy
text:
Two ways of comparing things (similarity vs. exact structural match) and the first of them, value-centric analogy, illustrated with beetles and linked to clustering and deep learning Abstractions come from comparing instances. Comparing by a continuous similarity (distance) function leads to value-centric analogies: clustering instances on a latent manifold and merging each cluster into an abstract prototype. This is what machine learning, including deep learning, does, and it is what enables local generalization. The page first restates the thesis of 19.3: intelligence = **abstraction acquisition** + **abstraction recombination**, and the two are tightly coupled because *the kind* of abstraction you work with determines how, and how well, you can recombine it. Deep learning models work only with abstractions stored as **parametric curves fitted by gradient descent**. The author asks whether there could be a better way.

**19.4.1 The two poles of abstraction.** Acquiring abstractions starts with *comparing things to one another*, and there are two distinct ways to compare. They give two kinds of abstraction and two modes of thinking, each suited to different problems, and together they "form the basis for all of our thoughts":

1. **Similarity comparison** leads to **value-centric analogies**.
2. **Exact structural match** leads to **program-centric (structure-centric) analogies**.

In both cases you start from *instances*, merge related instances, and get an *abstraction* that captures what they share. What differs is how you decide two instances are related and how you merge them.

**Value-centric analogy.** Picture beetles of several species in your backyard. Some look more alike than others. This implicit similarity is a smooth, continuous **distance function** that defines a **latent manifold** where the instances live. After enough beetles you cluster similar ones and merge each cluster into a **prototype** (Figure 19.12, on p.610). Prototypes are abstract: they don't look like any particular beetle, but they encode properties common to the cluster. A new beetle is compared only to the handful of prototypes. The nearest prototype is its *category*, which lets you predict things (does it bite? will it eat your apples?).

This is essentially unsupervised learning such as **K-means**. More broadly, *all of modern machine learning* learns latent manifolds of instances encoded through prototypes; the ConvNet filters visualized in chapter 10 were visual prototypes. Value-centric analogy is what lets deep learning models **generalize locally**. It also drives much of human cognition: it underlies pattern recognition, perception and intuition (continued on p.610). The type of abstraction you use determines how well you can recombine it; deep learning only uses parametric curves fitted by gradient descent. There are two ways to compare instances: similarity (value-centric analogy) and exact structural match (program-centric analogy). Value-centric abstraction clusters instances on a latent manifold and merges clusters into abstract prototypes; new instances are categorized by their nearest prototype. This is what K-means does, and more broadly all modern machine learning; ConvNet filters are visual prototypes. Value-centric analogy enables local generalization and underlies human pattern recognition, perception and intuition.
