title: From beetle prototypes to program-centric analogy
text:
Figure 19.12 (value-centric abstraction), the end of the value-centric discussion, and the introduction of program-centric analogy as exact structural matching (subgraph isomorphism) Value-centric analogy is fast, approximate and intuitive. Program-centric analogy is slow, exact and deliberate: it relates things by whether parts of them have exactly the same structure (e.g., shared subgraphs in programs' operator graphs), and it underlies reasoning, planning and rigor. **Figure 19.12** shows value-centric analogy in three panels: *Instances in the wild* (various beetles), *Similarity clustering* (the beetles grouped into two dashed circles of look-alikes), and *Abstract prototypes* (two dark silhouettes, one per cluster, matching no particular beetle).

The sentence from p.609 ends: value-centric abstraction underlies *pattern recognition, perception, and intuition*. If you can do a task **without thinking about it**, you rely heavily on value-centric analogies. Subconsciously sorting movie characters into "types" is value-centric abstraction.

**Program-centric analogy.** Cognition is more than this immediate, approximate, intuitive categorization. A second mechanism for generating abstractions is **slower, exact, deliberate**: program-centric (or structure-centric) analogy.

The example comes from software engineering. You notice that several functions or classes have a lot in common and ask whether a more abstract function could do the job and be reused, or whether an abstract base class could be shared through inheritance. You are *not* comparing them by *how similar* they look, the way you'd compare faces with an implicit distance function. You are asking whether **parts** of them have **exactly the same structure**. This is a search for a **subgraph isomorphism** (Figure 19.13, p.611): programs can be represented as **graphs of operators**, and you look for subgraphs (program subsets) shared exactly across programs.

This kind of analogy-making, exact structural match within discrete structures, is not limited to computer science or mathematics. People use it constantly without noticing. It underlies **reasoning**, **planning**, and the general idea of **rigor** (as opposed to intuition). Whenever you think about objects connected by a **discrete network of relationships** rather than a continuous similarity function, you are using program-centric analogies. Figure 19.12: instances, similarity clustering, abstract prototypes, the value-centric pipeline. Tasks you do 'without thinking' rely on value-centric analogies: pattern recognition, perception, intuition. Program-centric analogy is slower, exact and deliberate: it relates things by exactly shared structure. Refactoring code into a shared function or base class is program-centric analogy, formally a subgraph isomorphism on graphs of operators. Program-centric analogies underlie reasoning, planning and rigor, wherever objects are linked by discrete relationships.

title: Shared abstractions and the two poles compared
text:
Figure 19.13 (program-centric analogy as isolating isomorphic substructures, shown on graphs and on code), Table 19.1 comparing value-centric and program-centric abstraction, and the claim that all cognition combines both Program-centric analogy finds a substructure that two instances share exactly, such as the 'skip None, sum, count, divide' loop in two code fragments, and isolates it as a reusable abstraction (compute_mean). The two poles differ systematically (distance vs. exact match, geometry vs. topology, averaging vs. isolating substructures, intuition vs. reasoning, fuzzy vs. exact, data-hungry vs. experience-efficient), yet every real task mixes both. **Figure 19.13** shows program-centric analogy twice. On the left are two abstract node-link graphs labeled *Instance*. Each contains a highlighted five-node cycle (thick edges), surrounded by other nodes connected differently. The cycle is pulled out below as the *Shared abstraction*. On the right is the same idea in code: two Python fragments (*Instance*) that use different variable names, and other code around them, but contain an exactly isomorphic block (dashed boxes): initialize a sum and a count to 0, loop over a list, skip `None` entries, accumulate the sum and increment the count, divide. That block is isolated as the *Shared abstraction* `compute_mean(ls)`. The caption: program-centric analogy **identifies and isolates isomorphic substructures across different instances**.

**19.4.2 Cognition as a combination of both kinds of abstraction.** **Table 19.1** compares the two poles:

| Value-centric | Program-centric |
|---|---|
| Relates things by distance | Relates things by exact structural match |
| Continuous, grounded in geometry | Discrete, grounded in topology |
| Produces abstractions by "averaging" instances into "prototypes" | Produces abstractions by isolating isomorphic substructures across instances |
| Underlies perception and intuition | Underlies reasoning and planning |
| Immediate, fuzzy, approximative | Slow, exact, rigorous |
| Requires a lot of experience to produce reliable results | Experience efficient: can operate on as few as two instances |

The author then argues that **everything we do and think combines both**, and it is hard to find a task that uses only one. A "pure perception" task such as recognizing objects in a scene involves implicit reasoning about relationships between objects. A "pure reasoning" task such as proving a theorem involves intuition: a mathematician starts with a fuzzy sense of direction, and the discrete reasoning steps are guided by high-level intuition. (On p.612 the section concludes that the poles are complementary and that their interleaving enables extreme generalization.) Program-centric analogy identifies and isolates isomorphic substructures across instances (Figure 19.13). compute_mean is a shared abstraction extracted from two differently named code fragments; what differed became a parameter. Table 19.1: distance vs. exact match, geometry vs. topology, prototypes vs. isolated substructures, intuition vs. reasoning, fuzzy vs. rigorous, data-hungry vs. experience-efficient. Program-centric abstraction can work from as few as two instances. All cognition combines both poles: perception uses implicit reasoning, and reasoning is guided by intuition.

title: Why deep learning is only half the answer
text:
Deep learning covers value-centric abstraction but not program-centric abstraction. The poles form a spectrum, but sorting vs. MNIST shows each kind of problem has a natural fit, so AI needs a unified framework with both. The interleaving of both poles enables extreme generalization. Deep learning encodes value-centric abstraction well but can barely generate program-centric abstraction, so it misses 'arguably the most important half.' Each pole can emulate the other to some extent, but sorting is far easier as a program and digit recognition is far easier as a fitted model. The way forward is a framework that unifies both. Section 19.4.2 ends: the two poles are **complementary**, and **their interleaving enables extreme generalization**. No mind is complete without both.

**19.4.3 Why deep learning isn't a complete answer to abstraction generation.** Deep learning is very good at **value-centric** abstraction but has "basically no ability" to generate **program-centric** abstraction. Human-like intelligence tightly interleaves both, so we're missing half of what's needed, "arguably the most important half."

**Caveat: a spectrum, not a dichotomy.** You can partly do reasoning by **embedding discrete programs in continuous manifolds**, just as a polynomial with enough coefficients can pass through any set of discrete points. In the other direction, **discrete programs can emulate continuous distance functions**: linear algebra on a computer works in continuous spaces through discrete programs operating on 1s and 0s.

**But each kind of problem has a natural fit.**
- *Sorting with deep learning:* training a model to sort five numbers is possible with the right architecture but "an exercise in frustration". It needs massive data, still makes occasional mistakes on new numbers, and must be **completely retrained** (on more data) to sort 10 numbers. A Python sorting algorithm takes a few lines and, once checked on a couple of examples, works **every time on lists of any size**. That is strong generalization from a few demonstrations.
- *MNIST with discrete programs:* writing a pure-Python digit classifier without machine learning means hand-coding features such as the number of closed loops or the center of mass. After **thousands of lines** you might reach **90% test accuracy**. Fitting a parametric model is simpler, makes use of the abundant data, and gives more robust results. Rule of thumb: **with lots of data and a problem where the manifold hypothesis applies, use deep learning.**

So it's unlikely that reasoning will be reduced to manifold interpolation, or perception to discrete reasoning. **The way forward is a unified framework that includes *both* types of abstraction generation.** The two poles are complementary; their interleaving enables extreme generalization. Deep learning is strong at value-centric abstraction and has basically no ability to generate program-centric abstraction, 'arguably the most important half'. The poles form a spectrum (polynomials through points; discrete code doing linear algebra), but problems have natural fits. Sorting: a few lines of code generalize to any list, while a network needs massive data, errs and must be retrained for new lengths. Perception (MNIST): fitted models beat thousands of lines of hand-written rules. Use deep learning when data is abundant and the manifold hypothesis holds. The way forward is a unified framework incorporating both types of abstraction generation.

title: Program synthesis: the missing piece
text:
Program synthesis as discrete search over programs that satisfy an input/output specification, compared with machine learning (Table 19.2), and presented as the way to give AI program-centric abstraction Program synthesis automatically generates programs by searching a large space of candidate programs built from a vocabulary of building blocks (possibly by genetic search) until one matches the specification, often a few input/output pairs. Like machine learning it learns a mapping from examples, but it generates source code by discrete search instead of tuning parameters by gradient descent, and it is data-efficient. The author calls it the missing piece of the puzzle. **19.4.4 An alternative approach to AI: Program synthesis.** Until 2024, every AI system capable of genuine **discrete reasoning** was **hardcoded by human programmers**: software built on search algorithms, graph manipulation and formal logic. In the **test-time adaptation (TTA) era** this is starting to change. A particularly promising branch of TTA is **program synthesis**, still very niche but, the author expects, set to take off over the next few decades.

Program synthesis **automatically generates simple programs** by using a **search algorithm**, possibly **genetic search** as in *genetic programming*, to explore a large space of possible programs. The search stops when it finds a program that matches the **specification**, often given as **input/output pairs**. This closely resembles machine learning: from training data given as input/output pairs, we find a program mapping inputs to outputs that generalizes to new inputs. The difference: machine learning **learns parameter values in a hardcoded program** (a neural network), while program synthesis **generates source code through a discrete search process**.

**Figure 19.14** shows the loop. A *program specification* (`[3, 5, 1, 2, 7] -> [1, 2, 3, 5, 7]` and `[8, 5, 2, 9, 1, 13] -> [1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 13]`, i.e. sorting) and a *vocabulary of building blocks* (`+ = if == for - else * += -= *=`) feed a *search process*. The search assembles *candidate programs*, each tested against the specification. In the drawing seven fail (red X) and one passes (green check). The search continues until a valid program is found.

**Table 19.2, Machine learning vs. program synthesis:**

| Machine learning | Program synthesis |
|---|---|
| Model: differentiable parametric function | Model: graph of operators from a programming language |
| Engine: gradient descent | Engine: discrete search (such as genetic search) |
| Requires a lot of data to produce reliable results | Data efficient: can work with a couple of training examples |

Program synthesis is how program-centric abstraction will be added to AI systems: "the missing piece of the puzzle." (p.614 continues with how it will be blended with deep learning.) Until 2024, AI's discrete reasoning was hardcoded by humans; TTA-era program synthesis lets systems generate it. Program synthesis searches a large program space (e.g., by genetic search) until a program matches a specification, often input/output pairs. Like ML it learns from examples, but it generates source code by discrete search instead of fitting parameters by gradient descent. Table 19.2: differentiable parametric function vs. graph of operators; gradient descent vs. discrete search; data-hungry vs. data-efficient. Program synthesis is how program-centric abstraction will be added to AI: the missing piece of the puzzle.

title: Blending deep learning and program synthesis: hybrid systems
text:
Why program synthesis complements rather than replaces deep learning, and the first of two ways to combine them: hybrid systems mixing learned continuous modules with discrete algorithmic modules (AlphaGo, Waymo, and a generalized, primitive-rich RNN). The strongest AI systems today are already hybrids of hand-coded discrete programs and learned continuous models; the authors foresee such hybrids being learned end to end by machines, with networks free to use a large set of programming primitives (if, while, variables, storage, data structures) rather than only a single hardcoded for loop. Section 19.4.5 opens by insisting that **program synthesis is a complement, not a replacement**, for deep learning: it is "the hemisphere that has been so far missing from our artificial brains." The authors foresee two ways the two will be combined: (1) building systems that **integrate deep learning modules with discrete algorithmic modules**, and (2) **using deep learning to make program search itself more efficient**. This page covers the first avenue; the second begins on p.615.

The argument starts from the observation that many of today's most powerful AI systems are **already hybrids**. In DeepMind's **AlphaGo**, most of the displayed intelligence is hand-designed (notably **Monte Carlo Tree Search**), while learning from data is confined to specialized submodules, the **value network** and **policy network**. The **Waymo** self-driving car maintains a literal **3D model of the world** full of hand-coded assumptions, continuously updated by deep learning perception modules (which, the book notes, are powered by Keras). In both cases the combination of human-written discrete programs and learned continuous models yields performance neither approach could reach alone, neither an end-to-end deep net nor ML-free software.

The limitation today is that the discrete parts are **painstakingly hardcoded by engineers**. The authors predict that in future such hybrids may be **fully learned**. To make this concrete they use the **RNN** as a stepping stone: an RNN is a geometric transformation *repeatedly applied inside a `for` loop*, and that loop is a human-imposed, built-in assumption. RNNs remain limited because every step is a differentiable geometric map and information flows between steps only through points in a continuous space (state vectors). Now imagine generalizing this: instead of one hardcoded `for` loop and continuous memory, give the network a **large set of programming primitives** (`if` branches, `while` statements, variable creation, disk storage for long-term memory, sorting operators, lists, graphs, hash tables, …) that it can freely manipulate. The space of programs it could represent would be far broader, as the sentence continuing on p.615 says. Program synthesis complements deep learning; the authors expect both to be used together. Two integration avenues: hybrid systems with both module types, and deep learning guiding program search. AlphaGo (MCTS + policy/value networks) and Waymo (3D world model + Keras-powered perception) are existing hybrids whose discrete parts are hand-coded. An RNN is a geometric transformation inside a hardcoded for loop: one programming primitive added to a network, still limited by continuous, differentiable steps. The authors imagine networks free to use many primitives (if, while, variables, storage, sort, lists, graphs, hash tables), which would greatly expand the programs they can represent.

title: Hybrid algorithmic-geometric models and the cost of program search
text:
Finishing the hybrid-systems avenue (learned programs mixing geometric and algorithmic modules, figure 19.15) and starting the second avenue: program synthesis is crippled by combinatorial explosion and must become more like how humans write code. Future models will be learned programs blending formal algorithmic modules (reasoning, abstraction) with geometric modules (intuition, pattern recognition), built by a mix of discrete search and gradient descent; but naive program search explodes combinatorially, so it must be guided the way a programmer's experience narrows the options. The page completes the sentence begun on p.614: a neural network free to use many programming primitives could represent a space of programs **far broader** than current deep learning models, some with **superior generalization**. But such programs **won't be differentiable end to end**: only specific modules will be, so they will have to be produced by a **combination of discrete program search and gradient descent**.

The authors then describe the shift they expect. Today we have, on one side, **hardcoded algorithmic intelligence** (handcrafted software) and, on the other, **learned geometric intelligence** (deep learning). In the future we will have a **blend**: formal algorithmic modules providing reasoning and abstraction, and geometric modules providing informal intuition and pattern recognition (**figure 19.15**: a modular task-level program, learned on the fly, made of geometric and algorithmic subroutines, that receives data and feedback from a task and sends back actions). The whole system would be learned with little or no human involvement, which would dramatically expand the problems machine learning can solve. AlphaGo, and even RNNs, are "prehistoric ancestors" of such hybrids.

The second avenue, **using deep learning to guide program search**, starts here. Program synthesis today is **tremendously inefficient**: caricaturing, it tries every program in a search space until one fits the specification. As the specification grows more complex or the vocabulary of primitives expands, the search hits **combinatorial explosion**: the number of candidate programs grows very fast, "much faster than merely exponentially." Consequently program synthesis only produces **very short programs**; "You're not going to be generating a new OS for your computer anytime soon."

The way forward is to make synthesis resemble human programming. A programmer opening an editor doesn't consider every possible program; they consider a **handful of approaches**, using their understanding of the problem and past experience to cut the search space drastically. P.616 explains how deep learning could supply that kind of intuition. Primitive-rich learned programs could represent far more than current deep nets and generalize better, but they aren't differentiable end to end. They will be built by combining discrete program search (structure) and gradient descent (differentiable modules). Target: a blend of formal algorithmic modules (reasoning, abstraction) and geometric modules (intuition, pattern recognition), learned with little human involvement (figure 19.15). Program synthesis today is crippled by combinatorial explosion and can only produce very short programs. The fix is to make synthesis work like a human programmer: consider only a few promising approaches, guided by understanding and experience.

title: Learned intuition over program space; modular recombination
text:
How deep learning could guide program search by learning the shape of program space, and why future AI needs reuse of robust, modular program components across tasks, something current LLMs lack (recombination / function composition). Although programs are discrete, the space of useful programs may behave like a continuous manifold, so a network trained on many synthesis episodes could learn intuition about which path to take through it; and richer models will require reusing robust, modular components across tasks, which LLMs' brittle, non-composable memorized functions can't provide. The page first finishes the argument for **deep-learning-guided program search**. A program is a discrete object that performs non-interpolative data manipulation, but evidence suggests that *the space of all useful programs* may look like a **continuous manifold**. If so, a deep learning model trained on **millions of successful program-generation episodes** could develop **intuition about the path through program space** from a specification to its program, just as a software engineer immediately senses the overall architecture of a script and the intermediate functions and classes to use as stepping stones. Human reasoning is heavily guided by **value-centric abstraction** (pattern recognition and intuition), and program synthesis should be too. The author expects **guiding program search via learned heuristics** to attract growing research interest over the next 10 to 20 years.

**Section 19.4.6** then argues that as models become more complex and use richer algorithmic primitives, they will need **higher reuse between tasks** rather than training from scratch: many datasets don't contain enough information to build a complex model from scratch (you don't relearn English for each new book), and training from scratch is inefficient given the large overlap between tasks.

Foundation models move us toward systems with vast acquired knowledge and skills, but **LLMs lack recombination**: they are good at fetching and reapplying memorized functions, but not at recombining them on the fly into new programs. Citing **Dziri et al. (2023), "Faith and Fate"** (footnote 5), the book states they are "entirely incapable of performing function composition," and that the functions they learn aren't abstract or modular enough to recombine anyway (recall their poor large-integer addition, p.593). Solving **compositional generalization** will require reusing robust **program components**, like functions and classes in programming languages, evolved specifically for modular reuse and recombined on the fly to synthesize new programs (continued on p.617). Individual programs are discrete, but the space of useful programs may look like a continuous manifold that deep learning can learn to navigate. A network trained on millions of synthesis episodes could give search programmer-like intuition; the author expects this to be a major research theme for 10-20 years. Richer models will require reuse across tasks: single datasets carry too little information and tasks overlap heavily. LLMs store and reapply many functions but, per the book (citing Dziri et al. 2023), can't compose them on the fly, and their functions are too brittle to compose well. Compositional generalization needs robust, modular program components, like functions and classes, recombined on the fly.

title: A global library of reusable subroutines; the long-term vision begins
text:
How reusable components accumulated across all AI instances could make AI constantly self-improving, the software-library analogy, figure 19.16's perpetual meta-learner, and the start of 19.4.7's long-term vision. A meta-learning system would build task-specific programs by fetching subroutines (geometric or algorithmic) from a global library and push newly abstracted, reusable subroutines back into it, so every problem need only be solved once, much as engineers package solutions as shared libraries. Completing the sentence from p.616, our AIs will recombine robust components on the fly to synthesize **new programs adapted to the current task**. Crucially, libraries of these reusable components will be built from the **cumulative experience of all instances** of our AIs and then be **accessible by all in perpetuity**: any problem would only need to be solved once, making the systems **constantly self-improving**.

The analogy is **software development**. Once an engineer solves a problem (e.g., HTTP queries in Python), they package it as an abstract, reusable library available to everyone; later engineers search for, download and use it. Likewise, future **meta-learning systems** will assemble new programs by sifting through a **global library of high-level reusable blocks**. When the system finds itself developing similar subroutines for several tasks, it creates an *abstract*, reusable version and stores it in the library. Subroutines can be **geometric** (deep learning modules with pretrained representations) or **algorithmic** (closer to the libraries software engineers use today).

**Figure 19.16** shows the architecture: a **perpetual meta-learner** capable of quickly growing a task-level model across many tasks; it **fetches relevant subroutines** from the **global library of abstract subroutines** and **pushes reusable subroutines** back; it makes **design choices** for a **modular task-level program** learned on the fly (built from geometric and algorithmic subroutines), and receives **data and feedback** from it; that program interacts with the current task (Task #002456, with earlier tasks #002453-#002455 stacked behind) via data/feedback and actions. The caption says this achieves **extreme generalization**.

Section **19.4.7, The long-term vision**, begins with its first point: models will be **more like programs**, with capabilities far beyond the continuous geometric transformations of input data we use today, and closer to the abstract mental models humans maintain (continued on p.618). Reusable components built from all AIs' cumulative experience would make each problem need solving only once. The model for this is the software library ecosystem: package once, reuse everywhere. A meta-learner abstracts recurring subroutines and stores them in a global library; subroutines may be geometric or algorithmic. Figure 19.16: fetch subroutines → design a task-level program → interact with the task → push reusable subroutines back. The long-term vision starts: models will be more like programs, closer to human abstract mental models.

title: The long-term vision for AI
text:
The authors' five-point vision of future AI: program-like models, a blend of algorithmic and geometric modules, models grown from a global library of subroutines, discrete search guided by deep-learning intuition, and human-like extreme generalization; plus a rejection of singularitarian fears. Future AI will consist of program-like models grown automatically by a deep-learning-guided program search over a global, ever-growing library of reusable algorithmic and geometric subroutines, achieving human-like extreme generalization from little data; such a system could be called AGI, but robot-apocalypse fantasies are misguided. The page finishes the long-term vision begun on p.617. Point 1 concludes: program-like models will be closer to the **abstract mental models** humans maintain about their surroundings and themselves, and will generalize more strongly thanks to their **rich algorithmic nature**.

Point 2: models will blend **algorithmic modules** (formal reasoning, search, abstraction) with **geometric modules** (informal intuition, pattern recognition), achieving a blend of **value-centric and program-centric abstraction**. AlphaGo and self-driving cars, which required much manual engineering and human design decisions, are early examples of a symbolic-geometric blend.

Point 3: models will be **grown automatically** rather than hardcoded, from modular parts in a **global library of reusable subroutines**, a library evolved by learning high-performing models on thousands of previous tasks and datasets. Frequent problem-solving patterns identified by the **meta-learning system** become reusable subroutines, like functions and classes in software engineering.

Point 4: the process that searches combinations of subroutines to grow new models will be **discrete search (program synthesis)**, heavily guided by **program-space intuition** provided by deep learning.

Point 5: the library and model-growing system will achieve a form of **human-like extreme generalization**: given a new task, it will assemble a working model using **very little data**, thanks to program-like primitives that generalize well and experience with similar tasks, just as humans quickly learn a complex new video game when they've played many others, because their models of past experience are **abstract and program-like**, not mere stimulus-action mappings.

Finally, such a **perpetually learning model-growing system** could be interpreted as **artificial general intelligence (AGI)**. But the authors dismiss any **singularitarian robot apocalypse** as pure fantasy stemming from profound misunderstandings of intelligence and technology, a critique they leave outside the book. Future models will be program-like and generalize better thanks to their algorithmic nature. They will blend algorithmic and geometric modules, i.e., program-centric and value-centric abstraction. They will be grown automatically from a global library of subroutines evolved over thousands of tasks. Growing them will use discrete program synthesis guided by deep-learning intuition. The goal is human-like extreme generalization from little data; the authors call the result a form of AGI but reject singularity fantasies.

title: AI, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI
text:
A recap of how AI, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI nest inside each other, and why deep learning stands out Deep learning is one branch of machine learning, which is itself one subfield of AI; generative AI is a subset of deep learning. Deep learning is defined by chains of differentiable geometric transformations (layers) whose weights are learned by gradient descent, and it is a breakout success especially in machine perception. This page opens the review of key concepts (section 20.1) by restating the hierarchy introduced in chapter 1 (p.26, figure 1.1).

- **Artificial intelligence** is the broadest field: *all attempts to automate human cognitive processes*, from something as basic as a spreadsheet to a walking, talking humanoid robot. Note that this definition includes systems with no learning at all.
- **Machine learning** is the subfield of AI that develops programs, called **models**, *purely from exposure to training data*; turning data into a program is called **learning**. ML took off in the 1990s and became the dominant form of AI in the 2000s.
- **Deep learning** is one of many ML branches. Its models are **long chains of geometric transformations** organized into **layers** (stacks, or more generally graphs, of layers). Layers are parameterized by **weights**; the model's *knowledge* lives in those weights; learning means finding weight values that **minimize a loss function**. Because the whole chain is **differentiable**, this minimization can be done efficiently with **gradient descent**.
- **Generative AI** is a subset of deep learning: very large models (billions of parameters) that generate text, images, video, or sound. They are trained **self-supervised**, by reconstructing artificially missing or corrupted parts of their input (denoising an image, predicting the next word). This teaches them "maps" of their input space (**embedding manifolds**) from which new inputs can be sampled. Products like ChatGPT and Midjourney brought AI into its "consumer" era.

The page then begins section 20.1.2: although deep learning is only one ML approach, it is "a breakout success," achieving breakthroughs on tasks long considered very hard for computers, especially **machine perception** (extracting information from images, video, and sound), given enough (often human-labeled) training data. The sentence continues on p.621. AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning ⊃ generative AI; the terms are not interchangeable. A deep learning model is a chain (or graph) of layers; its knowledge lives in the weights. Learning = finding weights that minimize a loss; differentiability of the whole chain makes gradient descent efficient. Generative models are huge deep learning models trained self-supervised to reconstruct corrupted or missing input, learning samplable embedding manifolds. Deep learning's standout success is in machine perception, conditioned on enough (often human-labeled) data.

title: Artificial intelligence
text: All attempts to automate human cognitive processes. Anything that takes over a mental task people used to do, from adding up a column of numbers to holding a conversation. Includes symbolic AI (hand-written rules, search, logic) as well as learning-based approaches. A spreadsheet (very basic) or a humanoid robot that walks and talks (very advanced), as on this page.

title: Machine learning
text: The subfield of AI that automatically develops programs (models) purely from exposure to training data. Instead of writing the rules, you show examples and let an algorithm find the rules. A learning algorithm searches a hypothesis space for the model that best fits training data, guided by a feedback signal. Tagging vacation pictures by learning from pictures humans already tagged (p.28).
snippet: The subfield of AI that automatically develops programs models purely from exposure to training data.

title: Deep learning
text: The branch of ML whose models are long chains (or graphs) of differentiable geometric transformations, called layers, with weights learned by gradient descent to minimize a loss. A long assembly line of simple shape-changing steps whose settings are tuned automatically. $f(x) = f_n(\dots f_2(f_1(x; \theta_1); \theta_2) \dots; \theta_n)$, trained by minimizing $\mathcal{L}(f(x), y)$ over $\theta$ via gradients computed by backpropagation. The two-Dense-layer MNIST classifier of chapter 2.
snippet: The branch of ML whose models are long chains or graphs of differentiable geometric transformations, called layers, with weights learned by gradient descent to minimize a loss.

title: Differentiability of the model
text: Every transformation in the chain has a derivative with respect to its input and weights. Small changes in the weights produce small, predictable changes in the loss, so you can tell which direction improves it. Lets the chain rule (backpropagation) compute $\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}$ for all weights in one backward pass. relu, matrix multiplication, and softmax are (almost everywhere) differentiable; a hard argmax is not.
snippet: Every transformation in the chain has a derivative with respect to its input and weights.

title: Generative AI
text: A subset of deep learning: very large models that generate text, images, video, or sound. Models that learn what typical data looks like so well that they can produce new examples. Trained self-supervised (next-token prediction, denoising); they learn embedding manifolds of the input space that can be sampled. A language model predicting the next word; a diffusion model denoising images.
snippet: A subset of deep learning: very large models that generate text, images, video, or sound.

title: Self-supervised learning
text: Training where the targets are derived from the input itself by hiding or corrupting part of it. Fill-in-the-blank exercises the model sets for itself, so no human labeling is needed. E.g. target $x_{t+1}$ from input $x_{1..t}$; or target $x$ from input $x + \epsilon$. Predicting the next word in a sentence; denoising images.
snippet: Training where the targets are derived from the input itself by hiding or corrupting part of it.

title: The third AI summer; deep learning as geometry
text:
Why deep learning is a lasting revolution despite the hype, and the core mental model: everything is a vector, layers are simple geometric transformations, the model is their composition Deep learning has delivered real, sustained economic value (unlike earlier AI summers), even if short-term expectations are inflated. Conceptually it is surprisingly simple: large parametric models trained by gradient descent on many examples, mapping a vectorized input space to a target space through a chain of simple geometric transformations whose weights are iteratively updated. The page finishes the argument of 20.1.2. Given enough labeled data, deep learning can extract from perceptual data almost anything a human could, which is why people say it has "solved perception", although only for a fairly narrow definition of perception.

Its technical success has brought about the **third and largest AI summer**, a period of intense interest, investment, and hype. Whether and how it ends is debated, but unlike earlier summers, deep learning has produced **enormous business value** and consumer success: human-level speech recognition, chatbot assistants, photorealistic image generation, human-level machine translation. The authors compare it to the internet: overhyped for a few years, but a lasting revolution. They are optimistic because even with **no further technological progress**, deploying existing algorithms to every applicable problem would transform most industries. Progress is fast because of exponential investment in resources and headcount; still, short-term expectations are overoptimistic, and full deployment will likely take **multiple decades**.

Section **20.1.3 How to think about deep learning** starts with its most surprising property: **simplicity**. Fifteen years ago nobody expected that simple parametric models trained with gradient descent would achieve such results in perception and NLP; it turns out that all you need is *sufficiently large parametric models trained with gradient descent on sufficiently many examples*. Feynman's line about the universe applies: "It's not complicated, it's just a lot of it."

Then the geometric view: **everything is a vector**, a point in a geometric space. Inputs and targets are first **vectorized** into an input vector space and a target vector space. Each **layer** applies one simple geometric transformation; the chain of layers forms one complex transformation that tries to map the input space to the target space, one point at a time. The transformation is parameterized by the layers' weights, which are **iteratively updated** based on how well the model currently performs. The key characteristic of this transformation (differentiability) is stated on p.622. 'Solved perception' holds only for a narrow notion of perception. This is the third and largest AI summer, but unlike previous ones it rests on proven business and consumer value. Even without new research, deploying existing deep learning everywhere it applies would transform most industries, over decades. Deep learning is simple at its core: large parametric models + gradient descent + many examples. Everything is a vector; layers are simple geometric transformations; the model is their chain, mapping input space to target space with iteratively updated weights.
snippet: The page finishes the argument of 20.1.2. Given enough labeled data, deep learning can extract from perceptual data almost anything a human could, which is why people say it has…

title: Uncrumpling manifolds; key enabling technologies
text:
Differentiability as the key constraint, the paper-ball metaphor, meaning as geometry, why 'neural network' is a misleading name, and the first enabling factors of the deep learning revolution Deep learning learns smooth, differentiable transformations that 'uncrumple' high-dimensional data manifolds, relying on the idea that meaning lies in pairwise relationships captured by distances. The revolution came not from one invention but from an accumulation of factors: incremental algorithmic innovations (backpropagation, Transformers) and abundant data from the consumer internet, followed by hardware and software (p.623). The first paragraph completes p.621's sentence: the key characteristic of the model's geometric transformation is that it must be **differentiable**, so its parameters can be learned by gradient descent. Intuitively, the morphing from inputs to outputs must be **smooth and continuous**, a significant constraint.

The **paper-ball metaphor** (from chapter 2, p.62-63) returns: the crumpled paper ball is the *manifold* of the input data; each movement of the hands is one layer's simple transformation; the whole uncrumpling sequence is the model. "Deep learning models are mathematical machines for uncrumpling complicated manifolds of high-dimensional data." The magic is turning meaning into vectors, then learning complex transformations between spaces, which only requires spaces of high enough dimensionality to capture the relationships in the data.

This rests on **two core ideas**: *meaning is derived from the pairwise relationship between things* (words in a language, pixels in an image), and *these relationships can be captured by a distance function*. Whether the brain represents meaning geometrically is a separate question; vector spaces are just computationally efficient, and other structures such as **graphs** are conceivable. Neural networks originally came from using graphs to encode meaning (hence the name, and the old field name **connectionism**), but today the name is "extremely misleading": they are neither neural nor networks and have hardly anything to do with the brain. Better names: *layered/hierarchical representations learning*, *deep differentiable models*, or *chained geometric transforms*.

Section **20.1.4 Key enabling technologies** argues that the revolution was an accumulation of factors, "slowly at first, and then suddenly": (1) **incremental algorithmic innovations**, slowly over two decades starting with backpropagation, then faster after 2012, including the **Transformer** (2017); (2) **large amounts of image, video, and text data**, needed to realize that large models on large data are all we need, a by-product of the consumer internet and (on p.623) Moore's law for storage. The list continues with hardware and software on p.623. The model's transformation must be differentiable, i.e., smooth and continuous: a significant constraint. Deep learning models are machines for uncrumpling complicated high-dimensional data manifolds, one simple layer at a time. Geometric meaning rests on two ideas: meaning comes from pairwise relationships, and relationships are captured by distances. 'Neural network' is a historical, misleading name; 'chained geometric transforms' is closer to the truth. The revolution came from accumulated factors: algorithmic innovations (backpropagation to Transformers) and abundant data, plus hardware and software (p.623).
snippet: The first paragraph completes p.621's sentence: the key characteristic of the model's geometric transformation is that it must be differentiable, so its parameters can be learned…

title: Differentiability of the model
text: Every transformation in the chain has a derivative with respect to its inputs and weights. The geometric morphing must be smooth and continuous: no tears or jumps. Required for gradient descent; implies nearby inputs map to nearby outputs (local continuity). relu(Wx+b) is continuous; a step function or argmax inside the model would block gradients.
snippet: Every transformation in the chain has a derivative with respect to its inputs and weights.

title: Data manifold / uncrumpling
text: A continuous lower-dimensional surface on which the data lies inside a high-dimensional space. A crumpled paper ball: the sheet is 2D but sits folded in 3D. Layers progressively transform the space so that the manifold becomes flat and classes separable. Two crumpled sheets of different colors (two classes) separated by uncrumpling (p.62-63).
snippet: A continuous lower-dimensional surface on which the data lies inside a high-dimensional space.

title: Meaning as pairwise relationships captured by distance
text: The assumption that meaning derives from relationships between things, and that these can be represented by distances in a vector space. You know what 'puppy' means partly because it is close to 'dog' and far from 'spreadsheet'. Embeddings place items so that a distance or similarity function encodes relationships. Word embeddings where semantically related words are near each other.
snippet: The assumption that meaning derives from relationships between things, and that these can be represented by distances in a vector space.

title: Why 'neural network' is a misleading name
text: The name is historical, from connectionism's graphs; modern models are neither neural nor networks. They are chains of differentiable geometric transforms, not brain simulations. Suggested alternatives: layered/hierarchical representations learning, deep differentiable models, chained geometric transforms. A Dense layer is a matrix multiply, a bias add, and a relu.
snippet: The name is historical, from connectionism's graphs; modern models are neither neural nor networks.

title: Enabling factors of the deep learning revolution
text: Algorithmic innovations, large datasets, cheap parallel hardware, and a software stack, accumulating over time. 'Slowly at first, and then suddenly.' Backpropagation to Transformers; internet-scale data; NVIDIA GPUs; CUDA, TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch, Keras (the last two factors are on p.623). LLMs need Transformers + internet text + GPU clusters + autodiff frameworks together.

title: Hardware, software, and the universal ML workflow
text:
The last two enabling factors (GPUs and the software stack), the vision of deep learning as an everyday developer tool, and the first four steps of the universal machine learning workflow Cheap parallel hardware and a layered software stack (CUDA, autodiff frameworks, Keras) completed the enabling conditions; the future is deep learning in every developer's toolbox. But the hard part of ML is usually not model building: it is defining the problem, choosing a success metric, setting up leak-free validation, and preparing the data, the first steps of chapter 6's workflow. The page completes the list of **key enabling technologies** begun on p.622. The data bullet ends: large datasets are also a by-product of **Moore's law applied to storage media**, and today's state-of-the-art language models are trained on a large fraction of the entire internet. Two more factors follow:

- **Fast, highly parallel, cheap hardware**, especially NVIDIA GPUs, first gaming GPUs and then chips designed for deep learning; NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang bet the company on deep learning early, which paid off.
- **A complex software stack** that makes that compute usable: the **CUDA** language, frameworks with **automatic differentiation** (TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch), and **Keras**, which makes deep learning accessible to most people.

The authors then look ahead: deep learning will not stay a specialist tool; it will be in **every developer's toolbox**, like web technology. Just as every business needs a website, every product will need to make sense of user-generated data. That requires radically easy tools, and Keras was the first major step.

Section **20.1.5 The universal machine learning workflow** warns that the hard part is often everything before designing and training models (and, in production, after). Understanding the domain well enough to decide *what to predict, from what data, and how to measure success* is a prerequisite that Keras and TensorFlow cannot help with. The recap of chapter 6's workflow begins:

1. **Define the problem**: what data is available, what are you predicting, do you need more data or human labeling?
2. **Identify a way to reliably measure success**: accuracy for simple tasks, often domain-specific metrics.
3. **Prepare the validation process**: define training, validation, and test sets; validation and test labels must not leak into training (for temporal prediction, validation/test data must come *after* the training data).
4. **Vectorize the data** and preprocess it (normalization, etc.) for a neural network.

The remaining steps (baseline, overfit-then-regularize, deploy) are on p.624. Enabling factors 3 and 4: cheap parallel hardware (NVIDIA GPUs) and a software stack (CUDA, autodiff frameworks, Keras). The authors expect deep learning to become a standard tool for every developer; Keras is a step toward that. The hardest part of ML is usually framing: what to predict, from what data, and how to measure success. Workflow steps 1-4: define the problem, choose a reliable metric, set up leak-free validation (chronological for temporal data), vectorize and normalize the data.
snippet: The page completes the list of key enabling technologies begun on p.622. The data bullet ends: large datasets are also a by-product of Moore's law applied to storage media, and…

title: GPU acceleration
text: Running tensor operations on massively parallel processors such as NVIDIA GPUs. Thousands of simple arithmetic units working at once on the many independent multiply-adds of a matrix product. Accessed via CUDA and frameworks; first gaming GPUs, then deep-learning-specific chips. Training a convnet in minutes on a GPU vs hours on a CPU.
snippet: Running tensor operations on massively parallel processors such as NVIDIA GPUs.

title: Automatic differentiation
text: Framework machinery that computes gradients of a computation automatically. You write the forward pass; the framework derives the backward pass. Reverse-mode autodiff (backpropagation) in TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch. tf.GradientTape, jax.grad, or loss.backward() in PyTorch (chapter 3).

title: Universal machine learning workflow
text: Chapter 6's step-by-step process: define the problem, choose a success metric, set up validation, vectorize data, beat a baseline, overfit then regularize/tune, deploy and monitor. A checklist that keeps you from building the wrong model or fooling yourself about its quality. Steps 1-4 are on this page; the rest on p.624. A churn-prediction project: define churn, pick a metric matched to business cost, split by time, normalize features.

Validation and test labels must not leak into training; for temporal data, validation and test come after training data in time. Train on 2020-2022 data, validate on 2023, test on 2024.

title: Workflow wrap-up; key network architectures
text:
The last three steps of the universal workflow (baseline, overfit-then-regularize, deploy and monitor), and an overview of the architecture families with Table 20.1 mapping data modalities to architectures After setup, beat a common-sense baseline, then deliberately overfit and regularize based on validation data only (keeping the test set as a guard against validation overfitting), then deploy and monitor. Architectures encode assumptions about data structure (a hypothesis space); success depends on matching those assumptions to the data, and architectures combine like LEGO bricks. The workflow recap from p.623 concludes with three steps:

5. **Develop a first model that beats a trivial common-sense baseline**, demonstrating that ML can work on your problem, which is not always the case.
6. **Gradually refine the architecture** by tuning hyperparameters and adding regularization, making changes based on **validation data only** (not test or training data). First get the model to **overfit** (finding a capacity greater than needed), and only then add regularization or downsize. Beware of **validation-set overfitting**: hyperparameters can become overspecialized to the validation set; avoiding this is why a separate **test set** exists.
7. **Deploy the final model** (web API, JavaScript or C++ application, embedded device...), **keep monitoring** it on real-world data, and use the findings to refine the next iteration.

Section **20.1.6 Key network architectures** lists the families you should know: **densely connected networks, convolutional networks, recurrent networks, Diffusion Models, and Transformers**. Each targets specific data modalities because an architecture **encodes assumptions about the data's structure**, a **hypothesis space** in which the search for a good model proceeds; whether it works depends entirely on the match between data structure and these assumptions. Architectures combine like **LEGO bricks** into larger multimodal models.

**Table 20.1** maps modalities to models: vector data → densely connected network; timeseries → RNN or Transformer; images → ConvNet; text → Transformer (all four for class probability or regression outputs); text/images → text: Transformer; text/images → images: VAE or Diffusion Model.

The review of each family begins with **densely connected networks**: a stack of `Dense` layers for vector data, where each sample is a vector of numerical or categorical attributes (continued on p.625). Beat a common-sense baseline first; it may turn out that ML cannot solve the problem. Overfit deliberately, then regularize or downsize, making decisions on validation data only. Repeated tuning overfits the validation set; the separate test set guards against it. Deploy, monitor on real-world data, and iterate. Architectures encode assumptions (a hypothesis space); match them to the data's structure, and combine them like LEGO bricks (Table 20.1).
snippet: The workflow recap from p.623 concludes with three steps: 5. Develop a first model that beats a trivial common-sense baseline, demonstrating that ML can work on your problem,…

title: Common-sense baseline
text: The score of a trivial, non-learned predictor that a model must beat. If you cannot beat guessing intelligently, learning is not helping. E.g. majority class accuracy; predicting the mean; 'tomorrow = today' for forecasts. On a dataset with 70% negatives, any classifier under 70% accuracy is worse than always predicting negative.
snippet: The score of a trivial, non-learned predictor that a model must beat.

title: Overfit first, then regularize
text: Increase capacity until the model overfits, then add regularization or downsize to maximize validation performance. Find the edge of the cliff before stepping back to the best viewpoint. Overfitting shows as diverging training and validation loss; regularization (dropout, weight decay, smaller models) narrows the gap. Adding layers until validation loss starts rising after a few epochs, then adding dropout.
snippet: Increase capacity until the model overfits, then add regularization or downsize to maximize validation performance.

title: Validation-set overfitting
text: Hyperparameters becoming overspecialized to the validation set through repeated tuning. If you keep re-taking the same practice exam and adjusting, you learn that exam, not the subject. Each tuning decision leaks information about validation data into the model; the held-out test set provides an unbiased check. Trying 500 hyperparameter configurations and picking the top validation score.
snippet: Hyperparameters becoming overspecialized to the validation set through repeated tuning.

title: Architecture as a hypothesis space
text: An architecture encodes assumptions about data structure, restricting the space of functions searched during training. Choosing the right-shaped key ring before trying keys. Convolution: locality and translation invariance; recurrence: sequential order; attention: pairwise interactions; Dense: no structural assumption. A ConvNet on images vs a Dense network on flattened pixels: the ConvNet is far more data efficient.

title: Dense networks: last-layer and loss recipes
text:
What densely connected networks assume, where they are used, and the Keras templates for binary, single-label multiclass, and multilabel classification Dense layers assume no structure among input features (every input connects to every unit), so they suit attribute vectors and serve as the classification/regression head of most networks. The task type determines the last layer and loss: 1 sigmoid unit + binary_crossentropy for binary; N softmax units + categorical_crossentropy (or the sparse version for integer labels) for single-label multiclass; N sigmoid units + binary_crossentropy with k-hot targets for multilabel. Continuing from p.624, densely connected networks **assume no specific structure in the input features**: they are called *densely connected* because each unit of a `Dense` layer is connected to all units of the previous layer, so the layer can model relationships between **any two input features**, unlike a 2D convolution, which only looks at **local** relationships.

They are most commonly used for **categorical/attribute data** (the book cites "the Boston Housing Price dataset used in chapter 4"; chapter 4 actually uses the California Housing dataset, see review flag), and as the **final classification or regression stage** of most networks: chapter 8's ConvNets and chapter 13's recurrent networks typically end with one or two `Dense` layers.

Then three recipes, each written with the Functional API, two hidden `Dense(32, activation="relu")` layers, and the `rmsprop` optimizer:

- **Binary classification**: last layer `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")`, loss `binary_crossentropy`, targets 0 or 1.
- **Single-label categorical classification** (exactly one class per sample): `Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax")`; loss `categorical_crossentropy` for one-hot targets or `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` for integer targets.
- **Multilabel categorical classification** (several classes per sample): `Dense(num_classes, activation="sigmoid")`, loss `binary_crossentropy`, **k-hot encoded** targets. The code for this case starts here and finishes on p.626, where the regression recipe (no activation, `mse` loss) also appears.

The logic: sigmoid gives an independent probability per output; softmax gives a distribution where classes compete; the loss must match the output's probabilistic meaning and the target format. Dense layers assume no structure among input features; they model relationships between any pair of features. Dense networks handle attribute vectors and form the classification/regression head of most networks. Binary: Dense(1, sigmoid) + binary_crossentropy, 0/1 targets. Single-label multiclass: Dense(N, softmax) + categorical_crossentropy (one-hot) or sparse_categorical_crossentropy (integers). Multilabel: Dense(N, sigmoid) + binary_crossentropy, k-hot targets.
snippet: Continuing from p.624, densely connected networks assume no specific structure in the input features: they are called densely connected because each unit of a Dense layer is…

title: Densely connected (Dense) layer
text: A layer where every input feeds into every unit: $\operatorname{act}(Wx+b)$. Each unit looks at all the features at once, with no notion of neighborhood. Parameters: $\text{inputs} \times \text{units} + \text{units}$. No structural prior; models relationships between any two features. Dense(32, activation="relu") applied to num_input_features attributes.
snippet: A layer where every input feeds into every unit: operatorname{act}Wx+b.

title: Matching last-layer activation and loss to the task
text: The task type determines the size and activation of the last layer and the loss. The output must have the right probabilistic shape, and the loss must score that shape correctly. Binary: 1 sigmoid + binary_crossentropy; single-label: N softmax + (sparse_)categorical_crossentropy; multilabel: N sigmoid + binary_crossentropy; regression: N linear + mse (p.626). Reuters (46 topics, one per article) → Dense(46, softmax).
snippet: The task type determines the size and activation of the last layer and the loss.

title: Softmax output
text: Converts N scores into N probabilities summing to 1. Classes compete for a fixed budget of probability. $\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i = e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$. Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax").
snippet: Converts N scores into N probabilities summing to 1.

title: Crossentropy losses
text: Losses measuring the negative log-probability the model assigns to the correct target(s). Confident wrong predictions are punished heavily; confident right ones cost almost nothing. binary_crossentropy for sigmoid outputs (binary or multilabel); categorical_crossentropy for one-hot targets; sparse_categorical_crossentropy for integer targets. $p=0.9$ on the true class gives loss $\approx 0.105$; $p=0.1$ gives $\approx 2.303$.
snippet: Losses measuring the negative log-probability the model assigns to the correct targets.

title: Multilabel classification
text: Each sample may belong to several classes; targets are k-hot vectors. N independent yes/no questions answered at once. N sigmoid outputs, binary_crossentropy averaged over classes. A photo tagged 'beach', 'dog', 'sunset'.
snippet: Each sample may belong to several classes; targets are k-hot vectors.

title: Sigmoid output and binary crossentropy
text: Dense(1, activation="sigmoid") ... loss="binary_crossentropy" p = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}(y, p) = -\big[\,y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)\,\big] Formalizes what the binary classification recipe computes. The book names the activation and loss; the formulas are added here. Minimizing BCE is maximum-likelihood estimation of a Bernoulli model of $y$ given $x$. z The pre-activation output of the single last unit (a logit). p Predicted probability that the sample belongs to the positive class. y Target, 0 or 1 (the page: 'Your targets should be either 0 or 1').
snippet: Dense1, activation="sigmoid" ... loss="binarycrossentropy" — Formalizes what the binary classification recipe computes. The book names the activation and loss; the formulas are…

title: Softmax output and categorical crossentropy
text: Dense(num_classes, activation="softmax") ... loss="categorical_crossentropy" p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{z_j}}, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{CCE}}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{p}) = -\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i \log p_i = -\log p_{c} Shows why the two crossentropy variants on the page compute the same quantity and differ only in target format. Maximum likelihood for a categorical distribution over exactly one true class. z_i Score (logit) of class $i$ from the last Dense layer. N num_classes, the number of classes. \mathbf{y} One-hot target vector. c Index of the true class. sparse_categorical_crossentropy takes $c$ directly as an integer target.

title: Multilabel: per-class sigmoid with averaged binary crossentropy
text: Dense(num_classes, activation="sigmoid") ... binary_crossentropy ... k-hot encoded \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{p}) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big[\,y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\,\big], \quad p_i = \sigma(z_i) Explains the multilabel recipe: N independent binary problems. The $p_i$ need not sum to 1; several can be close to 1 simultaneously. y_i Entry $i$ of the k-hot target: 1 if class $i$ applies, else 0. p_i Independent predicted probability that class $i$ applies. N num_classes.

title: Regression templates and ConvNets in review
text:
The end of the densely connected network recap (multilabel classification, regression) and the start of the ConvNet recap: what convolution does, why it is data efficient, and a typical SeparableConv2D image classifier. The last layer and the loss are dictated by the task: regression ends with a Dense layer with no activation trained with MSE. ConvNets apply the same local transformation at every location, which makes them translation invariant and data efficient, and they alternate convolutions with pooling before collapsing to a vector for a Dense head. This page is part of section 20.1.6, a compact review of the network architectures used throughout the book. It finishes the **densely connected networks** recap from p.625 and starts the **ConvNets** recap.

**End of the multilabel template.** The first code block is the tail of the multilabel classification example started on p.625: a hidden `Dense(32, relu)` layer, then an output `Dense(num_classes, activation="sigmoid")`, compiled with `binary_crossentropy`. Each output unit is an independent yes/no probability, which is what k-hot targets need.

**Regression.** To predict a vector of continuous values, end with a `Dense` layer whose number of units equals the number of values to predict (often one, like a house price) and **no activation**, so the output can take any real value. Several regression losses exist; the most common is `mean_squared_error` (`"mse"`). The template is a two-hidden-layer MLP (`Dense(32, relu)` twice) compiled with `rmsprop`.

**ConvNets.** Convolution layers look at **spatially local patterns** by applying the *same* transformation to every patch of the input. The result is **translation invariant** (a pattern learned in one place is recognized anywhere), which makes convolution **data efficient and modular**. The idea works in any number of dimensions: `Conv1D` for sequences, `Conv2D` for images, `Conv3D` for volumes. **Depthwise separable convolutions** (`SeparableConv2D`) are a leaner, more efficient drop-in alternative.

A ConvNet stacks convolution and **max-pooling** layers. Pooling downsamples the feature maps, which keeps their size reasonable as the number of channels grows and lets later convolutions "see" a larger part of the input. At the end, a `Flatten` or **global pooling** layer turns the feature maps into a vector, and `Dense` layers do the classification or regression. The page closes with the first half of a typical image classifier built from `SeparableConv2D` layers (32, 64, pool, 64, 128 filters), which continues on p.627. Regression: end with Dense(num_values) and no activation; MSE is the default loss. Multilabel classification: Dense(num_classes, sigmoid) with binary_crossentropy and k-hot targets. Convolutions share one local transformation across all positions, giving translation invariance and data efficiency. Use Conv1D/Conv2D/Conv3D according to the number of spatial axes; SeparableConv2D is a leaner alternative to Conv2D. ConvNets alternate convolution and max pooling, then Flatten or global pooling, then Dense layers.
snippet: This page is part of section 20.1.6, a compact review of the network architectures used throughout the book. It finishes the densely connected networks recap from p.625 and starts…

title: Regression output layer
text: A final Dense layer with one unit per predicted value and no activation, usually trained with mean squared error. You want a number line, not a probability: the last layer must be free to output any real value. outputs = Dense(num_values)(x); loss='mse'. The absence of activation means the output is an affine function of the last hidden representation. Predicting a house price: Dense(1) output, MSE loss, MAE monitored as a readable metric.
snippet: A final Dense layer with one unit per predicted value and no activation, usually trained with mean squared error.

title: Mean squared error
text: The average of the squared differences between predictions and targets; the most common regression loss. Large errors count disproportionately: being off by 10 costs 100 times more than being off by 1. $\mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (\hat y_i - y_i)^2$. In Keras: loss='mse' or 'mean_squared_error'. Predictions [2, 5] for targets [3, 5] give MSE = ((2-3)^2 + 0)/2 = 0.5.
snippet: The average of the squared differences between predictions and targets; the most common regression loss.

title: Convolution layer
text: A layer that applies the same small learned filter to every local patch of its input, producing a feature map. A stencil you slide over the picture: wherever the stencil matches, the output lights up. Conv2D(filters, kernel_size) learns a kernel of shape (k, k, C_in, filters); weights are shared across positions. Conv1D and Conv3D do the same over 1 or 3 spatial axes. A 3×3 edge detector learned once detects edges anywhere in a 180×180 image.
snippet: A layer that applies the same small learned filter to every local patch of its input, producing a feature map.

title: Translation invariance
text: The property that a learned pattern is recognized wherever it appears in the input. A face is a face whether it is in the top-left or bottom-right of the photo. Arises from weight sharing in convolutions (equivariance) combined with pooling (invariance to small shifts) and global pooling (invariance to position). A Dense network trained on MNIST would have to relearn a stroke at every position; a ConvNet learns it once.
snippet: The property that a learned pattern is recognized wherever it appears in the input.

title: Depthwise separable convolution
text: A convolution factored into a per-channel spatial convolution followed by a 1×1 pointwise convolution that mixes channels. First look for spatial shapes in each channel separately, then decide how to combine channels. Parameters: k·k·C_in + C_in·C_out (+ biases), versus k·k·C_in·C_out for Conv2D. Assumes spatial correlations and cross-channel correlations can be learned separately. 3×3, 64→128 channels: Conv2D needs 73,728 weights, SeparableConv2D needs 576 + 8,192 = 8,768.
snippet: A convolution factored into a per-channel spatial convolution followed by a 1×1 pointwise convolution that mixes channels.

title: Max pooling and global pooling
text: Downsampling operations: max pooling keeps the maximum in each small window; global pooling reduces each whole channel to one number. Ask 'was this feature present somewhere in this region?' rather than 'exactly where?' MaxPooling2D(2) halves height and width. GlobalAveragePooling2D maps (h, w, c) to (c,). A (176, 176, 64) feature map becomes (88, 88, 64) after MaxPooling2D(2).
snippet: Downsampling operations: max pooling keeps the maximum in each small window; global pooling reduces each whole channel to one number.

title: ConvNet head, deep-ConvNet tips, and Transformers in review
text:
Completing the image-classifier template, the role of batch normalization and residual connections in deep ConvNets, and a recap of the Transformer: attention, positional encoding, encoder/decoder roles, and the start of a KerasHub seq2seq template. A ConvNet ends with global pooling and a Dense softmax head; very deep ones need batch normalization and residual connections for gradient flow. A Transformer uses attention to make each vector in a set context-aware, adds positional encoding for order, and comes as an encoder (for understanding one sequence) plus a decoder (for generating a target sequence). The page opens by finishing the **image-classification ConvNet** from p.626: one more `MaxPooling2D(2)`, two more `SeparableConv2D` layers (64 and 128 filters), then `GlobalAveragePooling2D` collapses the feature maps into a 128-dimensional vector. A `Dense(32, relu)` layer and a `Dense(num_classes, softmax)` output form the head, and the model is compiled with `rmsprop` and `categorical_crossentropy` (one-hot targets).

For **very deep ConvNets**, the authors recommend adding **batch normalization** layers and **residual connections**: two architecture patterns from chapter 9 that help gradient information flow smoothly through many layers.

The **Transformers** recap follows. A Transformer takes a *set* of vectors (such as word vectors) and uses **neural attention** to turn each one into a representation aware of the **context** provided by the others. Attention by itself ignores order, so for ordered sequences you add **positional encoding**; the resulting models take both global context and word order into account and handle long text paragraphs much better than RNNs or 1D ConvNets.

Transformers can do any set- or sequence-processing task, including text classification, but they shine at **sequence-to-sequence learning** such as translation. A seq2seq Transformer has two parts:

- a **`TransformerEncoder`** that turns the input sequence into a context-aware, order-aware sequence of vectors;
- a **`TransformerDecoder`** that reads the encoder output plus the target sequence so far, and predicts the next element of the target.

If you only process one sequence (or set), you only need the encoder. The page ends with the first half of a seq2seq template built from **KerasHub** layers: `TokenAndPositionEmbedding` embeds the integer source tokens and their positions, and a `TransformerEncoder(intermediate_dim=256, num_heads=8)` produces `encoder_outputs`. The decoder half is on p.628. The image classifier ends with GlobalAveragePooling2D, a Dense hidden layer and a softmax output trained with categorical crossentropy. Very deep ConvNets need batch normalization and residual connections for smooth gradient flow. Attention makes each vector context-aware; positional encoding adds word order. Seq2seq Transformers pair a TransformerEncoder (understand the source) with a TransformerDecoder (predict the next target token). Single-sequence tasks only need the encoder. KerasHub provides TokenAndPositionEmbedding, TransformerEncoder and TransformerDecoder as ready-made layers.
snippet: The page opens by finishing the image-classification ConvNet from p.626: one more MaxPooling2D2, two more SeparableConv2D layers 64 and 128 filters, then GlobalAveragePooling2D…

title: Batch normalization
text: A layer that normalizes intermediate activations with batch statistics during training (moving averages at inference), then applies a learned scale and offset. Keeps the signal flowing between layers at a sensible scale, so later layers are not fed wildly drifting inputs. $\hat x = (x - \mu_B)/\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \epsilon}$, output $\gamma \hat x + \beta$. Conv2D → BatchNormalization → relu, as in the chapter 9 Xception-like model.
snippet: A layer that normalizes intermediate activations with batch statistics during training moving averages at inference, then applies a learned scale and offset.

title: Residual connection
text: Adding the input of a block to its output, y = x + f(x). An express lane that lets information and gradients skip over blocks. Requires matching shapes; otherwise project the residual with a 1×1 convolution (p.297). ResNet, Xception, and each sublayer of TransformerEncoder use residuals.
snippet: Adding the input of a block to its output, y = x + fx.

title: Neural attention
text: A mechanism that recomputes each vector in a set as a relevance-weighted combination of the vectors in the set (or another set). Each word asks 'which other words help me understand myself here?' and mixes in their information accordingly. Scores from query·key dot products, softmax-normalized, used to average value vectors; multi-head attention runs several such operations in parallel. In 'the river bank', attention lets 'bank' pull in information from 'river'.
snippet: A mechanism that recomputes each vector in a set as a relevance-weighted combination of the vectors in the set or another set.

title: Positional encoding
text: Adding information about each token's position to its representation so an order-agnostic model can use word order. Stamping each word with its seat number before the shuffle-proof attention step. KerasHub's TokenAndPositionEmbedding sums a token embedding and a learned position embedding of size embed_dim. 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' get different representations only because of positions.
snippet: Adding information about each token's position to its representation so an order-agnostic model can use word order.

title: Transformer encoder and decoder
text: An architecture of attention blocks: the encoder makes a source sequence context- and order-aware; the decoder predicts the next target element using the target so far and the encoder output. A reader that understands the source sentence and a writer that drafts the translation word by word, glancing back at the reader's notes. Encoder block: self-attention + FFN; decoder block: causal self-attention + cross-attention + FFN; all with residuals and layer norm. Encoder-only for classification, encoder-decoder for translation, decoder-only for text generation.
