title: Transformer templates and RNNs in review
text:
The decoder half of the KerasHub seq2seq Transformer, an encoder-only Transformer classifier, and a recap of recurrent neural networks: when to use them, which layer to pick, how to stack them, and a single-LSTM template. A seq2seq Transformer joins the encoder and decoder into a two-input model that predicts the next target token; an encoder alone plus pooling makes a sequence classifier. RNNs process sequences step by step with a state and are preferable to 1D ConvNets when patterns depend on position in time; use LSTM or GRU and return full sequences from all but the last stacked layer. The page first completes the **sequence-to-sequence Transformer** from p.627. The decoder side takes `decoder_inputs`, the **target sequence so far** (integer ids of length `dst_seq_length`), embeds tokens and positions with `TokenAndPositionEmbedding`, and runs a `TransformerDecoder(intermediate_dim=256, num_heads=8)` called on `(x, encoder_outputs)`, so the target positions can attend to the encoded source. A `Dense(vocab_size, softmax)` gives, at each position, a probability distribution over the vocabulary: **predictions for the target sequence one step in the future**. The model has two inputs, `[encoder_inputs, decoder_inputs]`, and is compiled with `adamw` and `categorical_crossentropy`.

Next comes a **lone `TransformerEncoder`** for binary classification of integer sequences: token+position embedding, one encoder block, `GlobalMaxPooling1D` to collapse the sequence into one vector, then `Dense(1, sigmoid)` with `binary_crossentropy`.

The **recurrent neural networks** recap follows. RNNs process a sequence **one timestep at a time while maintaining a state** (a vector or set of vectors). The authors recommend them over 1D ConvNets when the patterns of interest are **not invariant to temporal translation**, for example timeseries where the recent past matters more than the distant past. Keras offers `SimpleRNN`, `GRU` and `LSTM`; in practice use **GRU or LSTM**. LSTM is more powerful but more expensive; GRU is a simpler, cheaper alternative. To **stack** RNN layers, every layer except the last must return its full output sequence (`return_sequences=True`); the last layer usually returns only its final output, which summarizes the whole sequence.

The page ends with a single `LSTM(32)` model for classification of vector sequences, compiled with `rmsprop` and `binary_crossentropy`. Note that its output layer is `Dense(num_classes, sigmoid)`, the multilabel head; for strictly binary classification the p.625 rule is a single sigmoid unit. The seq2seq Transformer has two inputs (source, target so far) and outputs next-token probabilities at every target position. An encoder-only Transformer + GlobalMaxPooling1D + Dense(1, sigmoid) is a complete text classifier. RNNs keep a state across timesteps and suit sequences where position in time (recency) matters. Use LSTM (more powerful) or GRU (cheaper); avoid SimpleRNN in practice. When stacking RNNs, all but the last layer need return_sequences=True.

title: Stacked RNNs and the limitations of deep learning
text:
The last architecture template (a stacked LSTM), then a recap of chapter 19's diagnosis of deep learning's limits: poor adaptation to novelty, sensitivity to phrasing and perturbations, inability to learn generalizable algorithms, the danger of anthropomorphizing, and the insufficiency of scaling. Deep learning can map almost anything to anything given enough data and a continuous mapping, but the models behave like interpolative databases of patterns: they generalize locally, break on novelty and superficial variations, and approximate rather than implement algorithms. Scaling alone does not fix this. The page opens with the last architecture template of 20.1.6: a **stacked RNN**. Three `LSTM(32)` layers are chained; the first two use `return_sequences=True` so the next LSTM receives a full sequence, and the last returns only its final output, which feeds a `Dense(num_classes, sigmoid)` head compiled with `binary_crossentropy`.

Section **20.2 Limitations of deep learning** then recaps chapter 19. Building models is like **playing with LEGO bricks**: layers can be plugged together to map essentially anything to anything, *provided* you have appropriate training data and the mapping is a **continuous geometric transformation of reasonable complexity**.

The catch is that such a mapping is often **not learnable in a way that generalizes**. Deep learning models work like **vast, interpolative databases of patterns**, and their pattern-matching strength is also their core weakness:

- **They struggle to adapt to novelty.** Parameters are fixed after training, so they can only retrieve or replicate patterns similar to their training data. On inputs far outside that distribution, however simple the task, performance drops sharply, which is why even large models fail on novel tasks or simple variations of familiar problems, such as **ARC-AGI** tasks.
- **They are very sensitive to phrasing and other distractors**: minor rewordings (prompt sensitivity in LLMs) or imperceptible perturbations (**adversarial examples** in vision) change their outputs, showing a lack of robust, human-like understanding.
- **They often can't learn generalizable algorithms.** Their continuous, geometric nature makes them ill-suited to exact, discrete, step-by-step procedures; they approximate such procedures by interpolation.

The authors warn against **anthropomorphizing** models: their performance rests on **pointwise statistical patterns**, not human-like experiential grounding, so it is brittle under deviations from the training data. Finally, the narrative that **scaling up model size and data** would yield general intelligence has proven insufficient; the sentence continues on p.630. In a stacked RNN, every layer but the last uses return_sequences=True. Deep learning can map anything to anything only given appropriate data and a continuous, reasonably simple mapping. Models act as interpolative databases of patterns: strong on the familiar, brittle on the novel. Three limitations: poor adaptation to novelty, sensitivity to phrasing/perturbations, no generalizable algorithms. Don't anthropomorphize models; scaling alone has not removed these limits.

title: Interpolative (local) generalization
text: Generalization obtained by interpolating between known training patterns, reliable only near the training distribution. A very large lookup table with smooth blending between entries. Models learn a smooth mapping on the data manifold; accuracy decays as inputs move away from densely sampled regions. A model trained on addition of up-to-10-digit numbers fails on 20-digit ones.

title: Adversarial example
text: An input with a small, often imperceptible perturbation that causes a model to make a wrong prediction. A few invisible brushstrokes that make a classifier see a gibbon in a picture of a panda. Found by gradient ascent on the loss with respect to the input, constrained to a small perturbation budget. Adding noise of magnitude 1/255 per pixel to flip an ImageNet prediction.

title: Beyond scaling: test-time adaptation and what lies ahead
text:
Why scaling did not overcome deep learning's limits, the 2024 shift to test-time adaptation (o3 on ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2 still unsolved), and the authors' forecast: combining value-centric and program-centric abstraction via hybrid models, deep-learning-guided program search, and modular recombination with lifelong learning. Scaling base models improves memorization-style benchmarks but leaves the core limitation (static, interpolative curve fitting) untouched. Test-time adaptation helps but at enormous cost. Human-like fluid intelligence will need systems that blend deep learning's intuition with discrete program-centric abstraction. The page completes the argument begun on p.629. Scaling up models and data improves performance on **benchmarks that amount to memorization tests**, but it does not touch the fundamental limitations of deep learning, which stem from the paradigm of **fitting static, interpolative curves to data**. Five years of exponential scaling of base LLMs have not overcome these constraints, because the underlying approach is unchanged.

By **2024**, this realization drove a shift to **test-time adaptation (TTA)**: models perform **search or fine-tuning during inference** to adapt to each new problem. TTA brought major breakthroughs, for example **OpenAI's o3 surpassing the human baseline on ARC-AGI-1** in late 2024, but at an **extreme computational cost**. Efficient, human-like adaptation remains open, and the **ARC-AGI-2** benchmark was still unsolved when the book was written. Further conceptual advances are needed beyond scaling or brute-force search.

Section **20.3 What might lie ahead** states the goal: solving human-like **fluid intelligence** (and ARC-AGI-2) requires going beyond current approaches. Deep learning excels at **value-centric abstraction** (pattern recognition, intuition) but lacks **program-centric abstraction** (discrete reasoning, planning, causal understanding). Humans integrate both, and future AI must too. The authors list likely developments:

- **Hybrid models** combining learned algorithmic modules (reasoning, symbol manipulation) with deep learning modules (perception, intuition), possibly learning to use control flow, variables, recursion and data structures dynamically.
- **Deep-learning-guided program search**: program synthesis offers program-centric abstraction but is bottlenecked by inefficient discrete search; deep learning can supply **learned intuition** to navigate huge combinatorial program spaces, as experienced developers do.
- **Modular recombination and lifelong learning**: instead of monolithic models trained from scratch, systems would draw on **large libraries of reusable modules**, both geometric and algorithmic, fetch the relevant ones for a new problem and recombine them; useful new components would be added back to the library (continued on p.631). Scaling improves memorization-style benchmarks but not the core limitation of static, interpolative curve fitting. Test-time adaptation (search or fine-tuning at inference) brought breakthroughs such as o3 on ARC-AGI-1, but at extreme cost. Deep learning provides value-centric abstraction; fluid intelligence also needs program-centric abstraction. The authors foresee hybrid models, deep-learning-guided program search, and modular recombination with lifelong learning.

title: Test-time adaptation (TTA)
text: Methods in which a model performs search or fine-tuning during inference to adapt to the specific problem in front of it. Instead of answering from memory, the model works on the problem: tries things, checks them, or briefly studies the examples it was given. Two families: test-time training (gradient updates on the task's demonstration examples) and test-time search (sampling and evaluating many reasoning chains or programs). Fine-tuning a small LoRA adapter on the three demonstration pairs of an ARC task before predicting its test output.
snippet: Methods in which a model performs search or fine-tuning during inference to adapt to the specific problem in front of it.

title: Value-centric abstraction
text: Abstraction based on comparing things through a continuous distance or similarity. Knowing that two faces look alike without being able to state a rule. Implemented by embeddings and continuous mappings; generalizes by interpolation. Word embeddings place 'cat' near 'dog'.
snippet: Abstraction based on comparing things through a continuous distance or similarity.

title: Program-centric abstraction
text: Abstraction based on comparing discrete structures exactly, underlying reasoning, planning and causal understanding. Recognizing that two different-looking sorting codes implement the same algorithm. Operates on graphs and programs; generalizes by applying the same discrete structure to new inputs. A proof or a plan that works for any instance of a problem.
snippet: Abstraction based on comparing discrete structures exactly, underlying reasoning, planning and causal understanding.

title: Program synthesis
text: Automatically discovering executable code that meets a specification, typically input-output examples. Machine learning where the learned object is source code rather than weights. Discrete search over a space of programs (enumerative, genetic, or neurally guided), stopping when a program satisfies the specification. Find f such that f([3,1,2]) = [1,2,3] and f([5,4]) = [4,5]: the sort function.
snippet: Automatically discovering executable code that meets a specification, typically input-output examples.

title: Fluid intelligence

In the book's framing, efficiency of abstraction acquisition and recombination in the face of novelty. Solving a never-seen puzzle from three examples.

title: Closing the outlook; Kaggle and arXiv
text:
The end of the authors' vision (a growing library of reusable components and on-the-fly adaptation), then practical advice for continuing to learn: practicing on Kaggle competitions and following research on arXiv. Human-like fluid intelligence will require blending continuous pattern recognition with discrete symbolic programs and on-the-fly adaptation. For the reader, the field moves so fast that the book is a starting point: keep practicing on real problems (Kaggle) and follow open research (arXiv). The page first finishes the **modular recombination and lifelong learning** bullet from p.630: whenever the system develops a reusable component while solving a problem, it is **added to the library** and becomes available for every future task. The section's conclusion follows: building AI that mirrors **human-like fluid intelligence** will require **blending continuous pattern recognition with discrete, symbolic programs** and fully embracing **on-the-fly adaptation**.

Section **20.4 Staying up to date in a fast-moving field** gives parting advice. Modern deep learning is only a few years old, despite a long, slow prehistory going back decades. Since **2013**, financial resources and research headcount have grown exponentially, and the field moves at a frenetic pace. What you learned in this book won't stay relevant forever and is not all you will need. Fortunately, many free online resources exist.

**20.4.1 Practice on Kaggle.** Machine learning competitions on Kaggle (https://kaggle.com) are an effective way to gain real-world experience. The authors repeat the book's philosophy: the only real way to learn is through **practice and actual coding**, and Kaggle is its natural continuation. Competitions are constantly renewed, many involve deep learning, and they are set by companies seeking solutions to hard problems, with sizable prizes. Taking part in a few, perhaps in a team, builds practical familiarity with **hyperparameter tuning, avoiding validation-set overfitting, and model ensembling**.

**20.4.2 arXiv.** Deep learning research takes place **in the open**: papers are freely available as soon as they're finalized, and much software is open source. **arXiv** (https://arxiv.org, pronounced "archive", the X being the Greek *chi*) is an **open-access preprint server** for physics, mathematics and computer science, and the de facto way to follow the cutting edge. Most researchers upload papers shortly after completion, which lets them **plant a flag** on a finding without waiting months for conference acceptance, a necessity given the pace and competition. The paragraph continues on p.632. Fluid intelligence will need continuous pattern recognition, discrete symbolic programs and on-the-fly adaptation. Deep learning moves fast; the book is a foundation, not the end of learning. Kaggle competitions build practical skill in hyperparameter tuning, avoiding validation-set overfitting, and ensembling. arXiv is the open-access preprint server where most deep learning research appears first.

title: Validation-set overfitting
text: Overfitting to the validation data caused by repeatedly selecting models or hyperparameters based on it. If you keep adjusting until the practice exam score is perfect, you may have learned the practice exam, not the subject. Each selection decision leaks a bit of information about the validation set into the model; with many decisions, validation performance becomes optimistically biased. Climbing a Kaggle public leaderboard by tuning on it, then dropping on the private leaderboard.

title: arXiv's downside, the Keras ecosystem, and final words
text:
The benefits and drawbacks of open preprint publishing, resources in the Keras ecosystem (documentation, guides, examples, source code, KerasHub, the authors on X), and the book's closing message. Open research lets the field move fast but makes it hard to separate signal from noise; tools such as Google Scholar help. The Keras documentation, guides and examples are the main reference for practice. Learning in AI is lifelong because most fundamental questions remain unanswered. The page finishes the arXiv discussion from p.631. Posting papers immediately **lets the field move extremely fast**: new findings are instantly available for everyone to see and build on. The **downside** is volume and lack of review: so many papers appear every day that you can't even skim them all, and because they **aren't peer-reviewed**, it is hard to tell which are both important and high quality. Finding the signal in the noise is hard and getting harder. One tool that helps is **Google Scholar** (https://scholar.google.com), which lets you follow publications by your favorite authors.

**20.4.3 Explore the Keras ecosystem.** With **over 2.5 million users as of early 2025**, Keras has a large ecosystem of tutorials, guides and open source projects:

- The main reference is the online documentation at **https://keras.io**, with extensive developer guides at https://keras.io/guides and dozens of high-quality code examples at https://keras.io/examples.
- The Keras source code is at https://github.com/keras-team/keras, and **Keras Hub** (the library behind `keras_hub.layers` used in the Transformer templates on p.627–628) is at https://github.com/keras-team/keras-hub.
- You can follow François (@fchollet) and Matt (@mattdangerw) on X.

**20.5 Final words.** This is the end of *Deep Learning with Python*. The authors hope you learned something about machine learning, deep learning, Keras, and perhaps cognition in general. Learning is a **lifelong journey**, especially in AI, where there are far more unknowns than certainties. Keep **learning, questioning and researching**, and never stop: despite the progress so far, **most of the fundamental questions in AI remain unanswered**, and many haven't even been properly asked yet. Open publishing on arXiv speeds up the field but leaves quality filtering to the reader. Google Scholar helps you track publications by authors you follow. keras.io (docs, guides, examples) is the main reference for working with Keras; Keras and Keras Hub source code are on GitHub. Learning in AI is lifelong: most fundamental questions remain unanswered.

title: Quick-reference tables (inside back cover)
text:
Two cheat-sheet tables: loss, last-layer activation and metrics by task (chapter 6), and model architecture by data type (chapter 20). For each common task, the table gives the matching last-layer activation, loss and metrics; for each input/output data type, the second table gives the model family to use. This back-matter page holds two quick-reference tables reproduced from the book.

**Loss, last-layer activation, and metrics to use for different tasks (chapter 6)**

| Task | Last-layer activation | Loss function | Metrics |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary classification | Sigmoid | Binary crossentropy | Binary accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Multiclass, single-label classification | Softmax | Categorical crossentropy | Categorical accuracy, Top-k categorical accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Multiclass, multi-label classification | Sigmoid | Binary crossentropy | Binary accuracy, ROC AUC |
| Regression | None | Mean squared error | Mean absolute error |

**Model architecture for different data types (chapter 20)**

| Input | Output | Model |
|---|---|---|
| Vector data | Class probability, regression value | Densely connected network |
| Timeseries | Class probability, regression value | RNN, Transformer |
| Images | Class probability, regression value | ConvNet |
| Text | Class probability, regression value | Transformer |
| Text, images | Text | Transformer |
| Text, images | Images | VAE, diffusion model |

The first table matches the output layer to the loss: sigmoid outputs pair with binary crossentropy (one independent probability per label), softmax outputs pair with categorical crossentropy (one distribution over mutually exclusive classes), and regression uses a linear output with MSE. The second table is the architecture summary from chapter 20's "Key network architectures" (PDF 624–629). Binary and multi-label classification: sigmoid + binary crossentropy. Single-label multiclass: softmax + categorical crossentropy. Regression: no activation + MSE, monitored with MAE. Architecture follows data type: dense for vectors, ConvNets for images, Transformers for text, VAEs/diffusion for generating images.

title: Last-layer activation and loss pairing
text: The output activation and the loss must match the task: sigmoid + binary crossentropy, softmax + categorical crossentropy, no activation + MSE. The output layer has to produce the kind of quantity the loss expects: a probability per label, a probability distribution over classes, or an unbounded number. Multi-label classification uses sigmoid, not softmax, because the labels are not mutually exclusive. Tagging a photo with any number of {cat, outdoor, night}: 3 sigmoid units + binary crossentropy.

title: Why is softmax wrong for a multi-label problem?
text: Why is softmax wrong for a multi-label problem? Softmax makes the outputs sum to 1, so labels compete; in multi-label problems several labels can be true at once.

title: Back cover
text:
The book's back cover: description, 'What's Inside', reader quotes and author bios. The back cover presents the third edition as a complete rewrite covering deep learning from the basics to generative AI (Transformers, a GPT-like LLM, diffusion models), with examples in Keras, PyTorch, JAX and TensorFlow. The **back cover** of *Deep Learning with Python, Third Edition* (Chollet and Watson).

The blurb says deep learning has changed the world twice in less than a decade: first when Python libraries such as Keras, TensorFlow and PyTorch moved neural networks from lab experiments to production systems, and again through large language models and other generative AI tools. The third edition is described as a **complete rewrite** with new chapters on Transformers, building your own GPT-like LLM, and generating images with diffusion models.

**What's Inside:** hands-on, code-first learning; coverage from basics to generative AI; intuitive math explanations; examples in **Keras, PyTorch, JAX and TensorFlow**. The audience is readers with intermediate Python skills; no previous machine learning or linear algebra experience is required.

Author bios: François Chollet is co-founder of Ndea and creator of Keras; Matthew Watson is a software engineer at Google working on Gemini and a core maintainer of Keras. Endorsement quotes come from Anthony Goldbloom (founder of Kaggle), Santiago Valdarrama (ml.school), Aran Komatsuzaki (EleutherAI) and Salvatore Sanfilippo (creator of Redis). Print book owners get the digital formats free at manning.com/freebook. The third edition is a complete rewrite that adds Transformers, a GPT-like LLM and diffusion models. Code examples cover Keras with the PyTorch, JAX and TensorFlow backends. Only intermediate Python is assumed.
